synopsis: Air carrier crew reported moderate turbulence on approach resulting in an un-stabilized approach condition and missed approached. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: the last portion of the flight into redacted experienced moderate turbulence. during the instrument landing system approach to runway xx, at approximately 3, 000 feet msl, the aircraft encountered severe turbulence, with altitude deviations of approximately ±2, 000 feet. moderate snowfall was present, and conditions were imc.the aircraft continuously annunciated 'sink rate.' a go-around was initiated due to unstable approach conditions. the flight subsequently returned to redacted 'divert' and landed safely.there were no injuries to crew or passengers, and no aircraft damage was reported.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: HS 125 Series First Officer reported while circling to land from an ILS approach they received a low altitude alert from Tower.
text: we were coming into redacted from redacted. we arrived on the redacted with the belief initially that we would be landing on runway xx. we briefed the approach for runway xx in the descent to the airport. the captain got the atis and said that we would be going to instrument landing system runway xy and that we would be asking for the circle. the knowledge of the runway and approach came in later than i would have wanted on the descent which we were already past redacted. we set up the minimums for the circle and was given direct redacted for the approach which we followed. we were then told to cross redacted at 3000 and intercept the localizer which we complied. our last instruction from air traffic control was maintain 2400 and cleared instrument landing system runway xy. started our descent to 2400 and we switched and the let air traffic control know instrument landing system xy and that we would like the circle to runway xz and we had the field in sight. tower cleared us for the circle and to land runway xz. what i believe happened next is that i asked the captain to set the minimums to 1560 for the circle which he did, i selected vertical speed and started down to the circling minimums. i am not sure where we started down on the approach but when we did get to 1560 air traffic control told us they got a low altitude alert, check altimeter setting. we read back altimeter setting and confirmed we had the right setting. captain noticed that we were a mile past redacted the final approach fix and we were at circling minimums and while being four miles from the airport so we were lower than we needed to be at that distance which i had realized after the callout for the altitude alert. we looked to make sure there were no obstacles that we needed to avoid which there were none visually or on the map and we circled and landed without incident at redacted.i believe getting the atis sooner would have given time to plan, brief and not rush the decision making process and also give both parties an opportunity to express any concerns and solidify expectations during the approach and give a chance to answer and clarify any questions. i feel that i should have verbally asked to be told when we were crossing the final approach fix and to make sure that i knew what the final approach fix was. also doing a better job of checking the approach on the pfd would have given better situational awareness. i also think the pilot monitoring could say when the next altitude is and verbalize when you can start down. monitor the progress and let the pilot flying know when its appropriate to descend especially when the approach has been rushed.i think i let myself get tunnel vision and be overly concerned on making sure to honor the circling minimums that i forgot to make sure that i was at the proper spot on the approach to start the descent to get to circling minimums. better planning, checking the flight management system, having the approach plate up or watching the map on the pfd could have solved this error.verbalizing, confirming intentions, next steps as well as actions being taken could have been better verbalized and communicated between both parties.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: A C210 pilot reported when they landed at a non-towered airport which was NOTAMed closed they lost control of the aircraft resulting in a runway excursion.
text: i landed on redacted runway xx to discover it covered in a layer of glaze ice with braking action nil.halfway down the runway at perhaps 35 knots i contemplated pushing the throttle forward to take off again but remembered many accident reports in which such an action led to fatalities so decided to stay on the ground.with 1000 feet left i pulled the mixture to kill the engine and the prop stopped.as the end of the runway approached i was still going 15 knots and steered toward the right side of the runway for what looked like an area clear of large snow banks and lights. the aircraft skidded sideways slightly but then went straight and into a low snow bank at about 8 to 10 knots.there was no damage to the aircraft.i checked the airport info on my ipad and saw then that the airport was notam'd closed.with the help of friends i pulled the airplane back out of the snow bank, turned it around at the end of the runway by hand, and departed to return to my nearby home field, which seemed the safest option given the fact that the entire airport surface including all ramps and taxiways was ice-covered with little to no braking action. my helpers and i were only able to stand and walk with microspikes on our boots. the takeoff and flight back were unremarkable.i now have a flight plan on my ipad that includes all local fields that i frequent and will use it to get a briefing so that current aerodrome notams are available on my ipad prior to takeoff. in retrospect my frequent visits to local airfields bred an attitude of complacency that led to this unfortunate event. fortunately the only injury was to my pride.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: An instructor pilot reported engine malfunction on initial climb and return to the airport.
text: the first indication of a problem, i was 8 miles away from redacted, and my low-voltage light illuminated. i took little to no credit in it being a real issue because it would come in and out during previous flights. i was told this was a common issue with that type of sensor but it was not an actual low voltage scenario. i checked the voltage, that along with other things gave me no other indications of an actual low-voltage scenario. i then did 4 landing's to hit the ppl requirements for my student. on the downwind of the last landing the panel light, out of nowhere doubled the level of illumination. this put me in an on edge mindset but ended up not factoring into the mechanical issues moving forward. we did our final full stop taxi back and took off on xx and departed straight out to the south, at about 4, 000 feet and 4 ish miles south of the airport. the engine cut out for what felt like 2-3 seconds. i immediately took control of the aircraft from my student and immediately started a turn back for the airport. before the 180-degree turn was complete the engine was back to normal as it seemed. i quickly advised air traffic control for a few reasons, one was that i knew from my weather briefing that redacted.x would not be unavailable in the area of this airport, two was that i was not on flight following nor did i file a visual flight rules flight plan. with the terrain in the area, it being night time, and no one knew i was out there i was worried that if the problem got worse which i was expecting it to i would either not have the time to get my distress out, or the line of sight, and with my already on edge brain and the sudden and significant loss of power that understandably put me in emergency mode a lot quicker than it needed to be. i had plenty of time and altitude looking back and i should have given myself more time to fully take a breath and evaluate the situation once i was heading back in the direction of the airport. i then advised an airliner above me and he transferred the message to air traffic control for me. i made minimal power adjustments because i was on edge that any big or sudden changes in power could kill the engine completely. i made the landing with no further issues. i ran the plane up on the ramp to get a better understanding of what happened in a safe and controlled environment and detected a 1, 000 rpm drop on my left magneto. i shut the plane down and called it a day. the reason for the sudden and abrupt power loss followed by an engine returning to what seemed normal was caused by two main factors in not only in my own, but also the mechanics opinion on the situation. the first was corrosion in the magneto wiring, and the second was fouled spark plugs from the fact that i was full rich mixture per the poh, and was for about the next 30 minutes doing full stop taxi backs on full rich the entire time.

text: i was flying for the company i work for, doing a survey/map of one of our locations. the site was closed and there was no one around. i flew from about xa15pm to xa45pm on day 0. i didn't realize until i was packing up that i didn't file for laanc authorization. filed it immediately and also filed this report.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported conducting a UAS flight in controlled airspace without LAANC authorization.
text: i am a newly licensed remote pilot (part 107) and recently purchased my first non-recreational uas. years ago with my recreational uas, i familiarized myself with airspace maps using dji's software. at that time, the airspace above my private residence did not display any issues on the mapping software for flight. after my most recent purchase, during pre-flight check for the initial test flight, i briefly checked the faa's airspace map to reaffirm my prior understanding. it appeared that my private residence was not in restricted airspace, but rather just outside the nearby class d airspace. the dji software i was using this time had just undergone a software update. it did not display to me any indication of being in a no-fly zone, which my previous recreational drone would do. i then conducted several test flights at maximum 80 ft agl above and around my private residence before landing safely.later the same day, while researching no-fly zones for a separate commercial operation i was planning at another location, i noticed a discrepancy in my earlier understanding. after cross-checking a few different airspace resources, i realized i apparently misread the first map. the class d boundary was not where i understood it to be, and my residence is actually just inside the border.as soon as i recognized the error, i contacted the faa to request guidance on the appropriate steps to take. my intent was to be transparent, take responsibility, and ensure proper compliance moving forward.in review of these events, i believe the primary contributing factor, besides my newness to non-recreational flight, was that my familiarity with the older boundaries/classifications led to an incorrect assumption that they remained the same. secondly, a lack of knowledge as to what new mapping resources are available to professional uas pilots. third, i should've cross-checked the maps i relied on sooner.as corrective action, i have researched laanc service providers such as aloft and autopylot to learn proper authorization procedures for controlled airspace. i have strengthened my understanding of my responsibilities and due diligence ahead of time as a remote pilot, and my commitment is to operate safely, responsibly, and in full compliance with faa regulations going forward.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported taking evasive action to avoid a ground collision with another aircraft that failed to hold short of taxiway 'T' used to exit Runway 28L at SFO.
text: after landing 28r at sfo and cleared to cross 28l at t intersection i noticed aircraft y taxiing on b. that aircraft had landed 28l, exited at taxiway e, and was instructed on ground control on b to hold short of t intersection. we were crossing 28l and entering onto b taxiway at the t intersection as instructed. i saw aircraft y and noticed they were taxiing fairly fast so as to be able to hold short of the taxiway t. after crossing the 28l hold short line, but certainly our aircraft was not clear of the runway 28l, i turned off our landing and turn off lights so as to not 'blind' other taxiing aircraft. at this point i noticed aircraft y was not going to stop at the t intersection and was on a collision course with us. i used aggressive braking to stop the airplane and illuminated all landing, turn off, and taxi lights. our airplane (tail section) was certainly not clear of 28l. aircraft y then made a sudden turn left to get around our airplane. aircraft y used taxiway t between b and a taxiway. i cannot at all understand how the pilots of aircraft y did not see us and give way as instructed. in my opinion this was careless and reckless operation of the airplane. it was as if aircraft y was in a hurry to get to their gate. but i have no idea. the sfo air traffic control ground controller was also not happy with aircraft y by the fact they did not hold short of t intersection.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported having a ground conflict with a shuttle bus that drove onto the taxiway. The Captain stopped and the bus drove under the wing.
text: during taxiout we were given a runway change to depart via runway xxl (instead of the expected runway xyr). ground gave us instructions to taxi via taxiway 1 and taxiway 2. as we were taxiing west on taxiway 1, a shuttle bus that is transporting passengers between terminal xx and terminal xy entered the taxiway by the construction area of terminal xz. we were moving and had our taxi light on. the shuttle buses did not yield and entered the taxiway driving the opposite direction and drove under our wing. we stopped when we saw the bus entering and not yielding. the bus had zero concern and appeared to be more concerned with getting to its destination than yielding to aircraft. it's a high likelihood one of these shuttles will contact an aircraft with this behavior.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a missed approach during final due to aircraft on the landing runway. Flight returned for an uneventful landing.
text: arriving into redacted the aircraft in front of us missed their turn off and we were given a go around at roughly 30p feet. when my first officer briefed the go around i added to it 'if it is a last minute (below 50 foot) go around i will stay off the radio. if it's a higher altitude please let me finish my radio call before beginning the go around process.' when redacted called the go around and while i was on the radio my first officer pressed the go around button and began making call outs for go around, flaps 15, check thrust. none of the i heard though i know them so i did them after i got off the radio. i forgot we did not have auto throttles engaged and checked the thrust but did not set it to the green carrot. we had climbed a few hundred feet and i noticed the gear hadn't been called yet while checking thrust so i called positive rate. my first officer then continued with that call out and asked for a heading. around the time the flight director vertical command bars dropped off. i initiated the level change set clean maneuvering to get them back, this was roughly at 1100 feet. we proceeded to accelerate, given another heading and off to departure. it was at this point we realized our climb was less than desired and bumped the thrust up. seeing them set roughly 8 n1 below the carrot before we advanced them to the carrots. the rest of the missed and return to land was uneventful.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported they stopped taxiing to avoid a collision with another taxiing aircraft.
text: we had taxi clearance to taxi [taxiway] 1 hold short of [taxiway] 2. as our gate was now open. as we taxied down 1 we approached taxi 3 i as always looked left then right as i continued on 1. all clear. as we were taxiing through the [taxiway] 3 intersection a rj (regional jet) was right on top of us from the left. it was snowing and you could barely see the taxi line. i stop in the intersection of 1 and 3. very surprised to see the rj come up on us so fast. the rj stopped short of the intersection. i then continued but the rj did not turn off his taxi light. so i stopped again. i attempted to contact ground to see what they were doing. i left my taxi light on because i was in the middle on the taxiway intersection. before ground could get back to us the rj continued to taxi on 3 crossing in front of us. missing us by less then five feet in front of our radome. i turned all of our landing lights. to make sure they see us. i thought the rj was going to hit us. i told redacted ground what had happened, he apologized. we taxed safely to the gate. the rj looked like his taxi speed was about 20 knots.

text: during push-back on xx at xa00 for flight abcd, after confirming the outer safety zone (osz) zone was clear, we got the go-ahead to proceed. halfway through, i saw the captain's side wing drift too far out of the osz and get dangerously close to a food truck that had been told multiple times to leave the chevron area, i signaled the pusher to stop, but with glycol all over the ground and freezing temperatures, the surface was incredibly slick. the plane didn't fully stop, slid a bit, and made contact with both a static wick and the food truck, slightly bending the static wick.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: A321 flight crew reported while reviewing the MEL's for the fuel quantity indicator; they did not perform the procedure as required per the MEL.
text: upon arriving at aircraft x and after completing my pre flight walk around, i was made aware of the aircraft having an an minimum equipment list for the left tank fuel quantity inop or questionable" (minimum equipment list 28-xx) with an associated minimum equipment list of 28-xy. the captain was reading the minimum equipment list procedure aloud and i asked him if we needed to "dip the tanks" and he replied no and i initially agreed that we had a single source failure being the flight deck fuel quantity indicator and that all we would require per the minimum equipment list was a fuel slip from looking up the mels and i did not read the original write ups. we waited for about 30 minutes for this fuel slip and a fueling supervisor came out to confirm what we needed. this caused me to look at the aircraft log book again and i noticed that the actual original write up for was "refuel panel quantity indication". the entry stated "required minimum equipment list 28-xy for left wing tank quantity indication on fue panel inop". when i looked up that minimum equipment list however i noticed that 28-xy was possibly incorrectly applied and that was for a flight deck fuel quantity inoperative implying that the refuel panel indication was working. this caused a massive amount of confusion between the ca and myself. i believe the correct minimum equipment list should have been 28-xz based on the actual original write up. this difference in mels calls for different procedures and upon reviewing this event several days later i realized that we failed to properly follow procedure indicated by ball note 2 of minimum equipment list 28-xx that states "when the refuel/defuel panel indication for the affected tank is also inoperative- as evidenced by the concurrent application of minimum equipment list 28-xy - fueler will determine fuel quantity in the affected tank using manual magnetic indicators (mmis)". to my knowledge we never did this and we thought it was not required. we pushed back from the gate and received 2 ecam's related to the number 2 engine that required the aircraft to return to the gate and go out of service and we wound up not flying this aircraft.cause: frustration, confusion, and an erroneous minimum equipment list all played a factor in this situation. when one reads minimum equipment list 28-xy it implies that the flight deck fuel gauge is inoperative and the original write up (for the other minimum equipment list of 28-xx) on further review didn't state whether or not it was the refuel/defuel panel gauge or the flight deck gauge. based off of this information to my knowledge as a crew we believed that we only had a flight deck gauge inoperative and we could dispatch with just the required fuel slip. i also feel that the specific procedure of measuring using mmi's required for minimum equipment list 28-xy should have been a bold item and not in a note in between procedures."

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported receiving a GPWS warning while making the turn to join the BGR Runway 23 final approach course.  The flight crew adjusted their descent and landed safely.
text: on our approach into bgr doing the visual to runway 33 we encountered a gpws warning, the winds were calm with clear skies and vis greater than 10sm with the airport insight. we were 2, 500ft 2nm away from the fix cuvot on the instrument landing system for 33 on a heading of 040 to join final . we were at 180kts with flaps 8, when cleared for the visual approach the captain disconnected the autopilot ato handfly the approach. when making the turn to join final we were around 2, 400ft and got one 'terrain terrain pull up' warning and stopped our decent and leveled off. after doing so the warning never went off again and we continued for a stable and safe landing on runway 33.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Flight instructor reported during climb after takeoff the air speed dropped and the flight returned and landed safely.
text: after takeoff runway xxr during climbout airspeed dropped from 72 to 56. stall horn did not go off. student pilot (sp) reduced angle of attack immediately and leveled out. with power set at 92% airspeed still indicated 55-65. sp turned pitot on. flight instructor (ip) took controls and sp notified air traffic control our intent to return for landing. air traffic control cleared us to land runway xy. airspeed indicated 80-90 while on base leg. on final with full flaps and power lever idle airspeed indicated an increase to 102 then the stall horn sounded. ip reduced angle of attack and increased power to prevent stall. after landing while taxing at approximately 10kts ground speed airspeed indicated 40 then slowly fell to 0 by the time we parked.

synopsis: SR20 pilot and passenger reported that during taxi for takeoff; the pilot had a taxiway excursion resulting in damage to the propeller and two taxiway lights.
text: on day 0, i went flying with my friend in a cirrus sr-20 aircraft which was based at redacted in location y. my friend was qualified to conduct the flight in every way (flight review, landings, instrument flight rules recency, medical certification, flight school rules). the idea was for him to fly some practice approaches in imc and for us to work our way over to location x and eat dinner at the restaurant on the field at redacted. since i have been retired from commercial flying for months, my status on the flight was that of an xx-year-old passenger. although i have no current faa medical certification, no current flight review, no recent instrument flight rules experience, and no recent landings, i'm still very much interested in flying. i have many type ratings, an airline transport pilot rating as well as a flight instructor rating in single and multiengine airplanes. since my initial solo flight in year x, i have logged thousands of hours in many different aircraft, including civil and military jet aircraft. it's unlikely that i will ever pass up a chance to fly somewhere for dinner with a friend! after dinner at the fabulous little restaurant at redacted, we taxied out in the dark to fly back to redacted. in retrospect, the left main gear went off of the taxiway and damaged two taxiway lights as well as one tip of the three-bladed propeller. at the time, we did not know that there had been any damage to the prop or the lights. all of the before takeoff checks were completed normally. the takeoff and flight back to redacted were uneventful. upon exiting the plane in redacted, we noticed the prop damage. my friend made the appropriate notifications and will keep up with the paperwork associated with the situation which is apparently neither an accident nor a reportable incident. my take-away is that, even as a passenger, i need to be vigilant at all times when i'm in any airplane.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Small transport pilot reported experiencing mountain waves and moderate turbulence during cruise. ATC cleared the flight to a lower altitude and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.
text: in cruise at fl430, was in light chop (turbulence) westbound, shortly before reaching tabll waypoint. then experienced sharp vertical accelerations and rolls (up to 10 degrees), possible mountain wave but this was unlike previous waves i have felt, motions were sharp and irregular. 'felt' turbulence was moderate. the autopilot could not hold altitude and was deviating +/- 200 feet from assigned fl430. then the autopilot disconnected. i called salt lake air traffic control and told them i could not hold altitude, was in a wave or other tubulence, and the autopilot had disconnected. the controller asked if i wanted a block altitude fl410 to fl450, i replied yes, and was subsequently given the clearance. i hand-flew for about 5-6 minutes, and then the autopilot re-engaged as the accelerations-turbulence subsided. the controller offered to ask other aircraft about their flight conditions, looking for a smoother altitude, which i gratefully accepted. they came back and offered fl400, we descended, air was smoother, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.i am in contact with garmin to download and review the autopilot data, to see if there is anything to learn. i am grateful for the controller's excellent assistance.
