synopsis: Beechcraft 1900 pilot reported missing approach due to lateral deviation prior to landing. Pilot missed approach and diverted.
text: normal flight until final approach. there was a rolling fog on the airport surface with shifting levels of visibility (1600 rvr to 2200 rvr) at 750' agl and below. clear visibility above the fog on the approach. i intercepted the glide slope and started down on final. for some reason i expected to see the approach light system sooner than the approach minimums (which in hindsight was an incorrect expectation). i transitioned from looking at my instruments to starting to look up and out to see if i could find the runway visual cues a little too early. that led to me starting to drift a little left then right as i corrected the plane based on the instruments and then looked outside again.approaching the last 200' of the glideslope descent, i got a little too far right of the instrument landing system centerline, likely 3/4 scale deflection and just as i was about to called missed approach the tower told me to go missed as well. in a subsequent call with the tower they told me i had triggered a warning in their system that i might be drifting too far right. i executed a missed approach/go around and ultimately ended up diverting to redacted to land since the visibility was getting worse at redacted.the critique i gave myself after the flight is that i should have waited until i was about to reach my decision altitude before looking outside for visual references. i would have maintained the instrument landing system lateral path with greater precision. allowing myself to start looking outside too early introduced some small but oscillating corrections that led to decreasing safety margins for a moment about 100' above the decision altitude of a challenging instrument landing system approach.also, the clear visibility on 95% of the approach with the last 5% in fog was a unique approach challenge i haven't had much opportunity to experience prior. usually it's the been the reverse for me where i'm descending through low visibility/clouds and breaking out into greater visibility before reaching my decision altitude.

text: while administering a check ride for an applicant going for a cfii-instrument instructor rating (asel), we encountered a runway excursion on runway xx at redacted. visual flight rules weather conditions were experienced throughout the entire flight. winds at redacted and redacted were at 33010g18kts. upon departing redacted for vor xy approach with a procedure turn, circle to land at redacted runway xx, i decided that the applicant teach me how to fly the approach and circle to xx. at that time i had the cfii instrument applicant to transfer the controls over to me. as we leveled off at the circling mda, the applicant was walking me through the circle to land xx. upon turning final, as i was into the flare, as the main wheels touched down the plane veered to the right like someone was pushing down on the right brake. i tried to keep it from veering to the right by stepping on the left rudder but it veered about 45 degrees to the right off the runway and into the grass. we were able to taxi over to the main terminal ramp to make sure the applicant and myself were ok and that the plane was not damaged. no damage to the aircraft or injuries to both myself or the applicant. i immediately called my inspector (managing specialist) and the flight school to notify them of the situation. i told my inspector that if i got the plane inspected by a certified a&p - ia that the applicant would like to finish his check. he agreed and a mechanic from the flight school said if a mechanic signs it off with a logbook sticker checking that the aircraft is not damaged and airworthy we could continue and finish the practical test. i did have a a&p sign it off and finished the check. no damage to aircraft and no damage to the airport property.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported witnessing an NMAC of two aircraft in landing phase.
text: i am a cfi-i out of the flight school located at redacted airport. i was not in the aircraft at the time of the near miss, but i witnessed it on the ground at the airfield. two aircraft were coming in for landing (aircraft x on runway xx, aircraft y for runway xy), aircraft x was making position reports coming in to land on left traffic runway xx, while aircraft y was making zero radio calls, directly coming in on a final runway xy. aircraft y came in first and landed, while aircraft x came in second on the crossing runway. they landed and appeared to get about 30-40ft within one another. after landing, aircraft y came on frequency and said 'sorry wrong frequency' and then proceeded to depart the airfield after taxiing back to runway xy. after reviewing track logs of aircraft y, it appears they do this quite often at almost every airfield they do land at.to prevent the situation, the pilot of aircraft y should receive corrective action and fly with a cfi to relearn how to enter controlled/uncontrolled airfields, along with traffic pattern operations and radio communication/phraseology. additionally, if the pilot doesn't hear anyone on frequency, they probably should double check their radios before they enter an airfield.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Corporate flight crew expressed concern about the design of the PBI RNAV (GPS) X Runway 28R approach; alleging the offset makes it difficult for departing aircraft flight crews to spot inbound aircraft.
text: our aircraft, aircraft x, was holding short of runway 28r at intersection l7 at pbi. the tower controller (frequency 119.1) cleared us for takeoff on runway 28r and advised of another approaching aircraft on a five-mile final to runway 32. my co-captain read back the takeoff clearance and finished final checklist items, and i looked to my three o'clock position to ensure the final approach was clear. i did not see any other aircraft, so i released the brakes. as i turned my head back to the left (forward), i then saw landing lights from about the one o'clock position. i immediately stopped the aircraft and called out the traffic, which my co-captain noticed simultaneously and called stop stop stop."in the air traffic control audio obtained, the controller seemed to be attempting to cancel our takeoff clearance in this moment, but the message was garbled. shortly after, the pilot of the jet on short final exclaimed that he was cleared to land but was going around. the controller did acknowledge the situation was a mistake on his end. we held position just past the hold short line but not yet on the runway, and awaited further instructions.our takeoff clearance was canceled, and we were told to line up and wait on 28r, which we did. we were cleared for takeoff shortly thereafter, and the rest of the flight was uneventful.after discussion, my co-captain and i agreed that the rnav (gps) x runway 28r approach that was in use that day was a major contributing factor. in addition, i posit that the design of the cockpit and possible expectation bias were also contributory.the rnav (gps) x runway 28r approach at pbi is offset 30 degrees from the final approach course to avoid overflight of the tfr over mar-a-lago. this places approaching aircraft in an area of the sky that controllers and pilots may not be used to looking at when clearing final approach prior to takeoff, and in our case, the aircraft windscreen structure temporarily obscured the jet from view.additionally, due to the geometry of the approach, the fix that we are expected to fly by to align with the runway (freby) is 0.9 nautical miles from the runway threshold. maneuvering this close in to the runway and low to the ground (approximately 356 feet above the tdze if my math is correct, based off the 3.1 degree descent angle prescribed by the approach plate is dangerous, and does not meet the stable approach criteria recommended by the organization, ac 120-108a, ac 91-79b, and the "stabilized approach and landing" fact sheet produced by the faasteam of being stabilized by 500 feet agl when in vmc.as far as human factors, i think expectation bias played a part here. as a pilot, i am used to not having another airplane on short final when cleared for takeoff at a towered airport, and, while helpful and prudent, being alerted to the airplane approaching runway 32 may have also influenced my bias when scanning the sky before crossing the hold short line because, surely, the controller would have also mentioned the airplane on short final to our runway, right? as a controller, one may get into a rhythm and temporarily let their guard down, especially if sops have changed recently. having a "trust but verify" mentality and making a conscious effort to recognize when one is feeling too comfortable may have prevented any of us having been put in this situation."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A SR22 pilot reported engine malfunction and diversion to a nearby airport.
text: i departed redacted direct to redacted with 3 souls on board. ceilings and visibility were unlimited and winds aloft were out of the northwest. we climbed direct to 11, 500 feet and had been in the cruise phase for about 5 minutes and the engine started vibrating. i was flying per the manufacturer's recommendation at 30.5' hg and 17 gph fuel flow which is lop and about 78% power. i enriched the mixture and pulled power back and the engine continued to run very rough. i shut off the auxiliary fuel pump and the engine smoothed out some but still vibrating. after reviewing cht's and egt's it was evident that cylinder #5 was dead and at that point i decided to not try and increase power from the engine by changing mixture or throttle. the nearest airport was redacted which was 10 miles south. i disabled autopilot and turned towards the airport. i listened to awos and called on the ctaf frequency to alert any pilots in the vicinity that we were descending for an urgent landing. i circled down over the airport slowly, not wanting to overspeed the engine by rapid descent and positioned for a landing on runway xx. i made a smooth landing and was able to taxi off of the runway and to the ramp before shutting the engine down. as i taxied in with the engine at 700 rpm, i could hear a steel on steel clanking in the engine. a large amount of oil drained out of the cowling within 10 minutes of shutdown. all passengers were safe and the aircraft undamaged other than mechanical problems in the engine.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: PA28 pilot reported loss of electrical system during cruise. Flight continued to destination and landed without incident.
text: i was conducting a short 35 minute visual flight rules flight from redacted to redacted using redacted tracon for traffic advisories and class b entry clearance. approximately 10 minutes prior to landing my airplane lost it's complete electrical system. i was no longer able to communicate with the tracon and would be unable to contact redacted control tower. i immediately descended to remain below the class b airspace and proceeded to redacted visual flight rules at about 3, 500 feet altitude. i entered the left hand pattern for runway xxl and made a full square pattern about 2000 feet above pattern altitude. i then performed the emergency landing gear extension procedure. next i descended to the actual pattern altitude of 1400 feet and was hoping to see steady green light signals from the control tower indicating i was cleared to land. i never did see the light signals but there appeared to be no preceding traffic for runway xxl so i continued descending and landed without incident. after landing i cleared the runway and followed an administration vehicle to a safe parking area. i phoned the control tower and they mentioned the last 2 lost communication aircraft that had come in to the airport in the last few weeks were also unable to see their light signals and suspected the equipment was too dim to see in bright sunlight. they mentioned no loss of separation had occurred between myself and any other aircraft and that no follow up would be necessary.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A military pilot conducting a PAR Approach reported after descending to minimum descent altitude as instructed by ATC they received a Low Altitude Alert from ATC.
text: instrument training flight conducting practice gca's (ground controlled approaches) at nip enroute to final destination. both instructor and student are fairly confident controller said 'descend to minimum descent altitude.' student initiated steady slow descent as we were still probably 8 nm from the field. the controller continued to offer course guidance and then stated 'low altitude alert, check altitude immediately.' we climbed, and later heard, what we thought for a second time, 'descend to minimum descent altitude.' at that point, we thought maybe we misheard the controller the first time, or that we climbed too high to comply with previous instructions.having heard that warning before years ago, it was usually when doing an asr and using the dive and drive method to get to mda. what was different this time was that we were a bit further from the field than past approaches at other locations. this time, i never got clarification whether we climbed too high in compliance with controller instructions leading him to state the instruction to descend a second time, or if we indeed descended too early and misheard. in the future, i will use a non-standard technique of crosschecking dme before accepting descent instructions on a gca. if more than 5 dme or so, i will crosscheck another approach's faf before beginning descent.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported damage to the bottom of the engine cowl and IDG occurred during taxi in an area of plowed berms of snow that had not been adequately cleared.
text: the aircraft was parked at the south ramp next to the fbo, where large piles of snow had accumulated and subsequently turned into ice. we both carefully reviewed the notams and agreed upon the taxi instructions provided by air traffic control prior to taxi. the only two notams (see attached release) that applied to our taxi route were:**new** phl day 0-day 1phl taxiway all ficon (field conditions) patchy compacted sn 4ft bermsphl runway 35 taxiway direction sign at taxiway d lgt u/s (unserviceable)during taxi, we observed several taxiways with residual snow and ice on the surface, as well as berms of snow and ice along taxiway edges. we maintained the taxiway centerline at all times and the taxi appeared uneventful. on taxiway sierra, the crew received an alert for elec idg 1 (integrated drive generator) low pressure. the first officer immediately advised ground control of the situation and requested permission to stop the aircraft. air traffic control approved the aircraft to stop and we ran the procedures. with the procedures complete, we advised operations, mx (maintenance) control, and advised ground our intent to return to the south ramp. we entered the south ramp from taxiway delta, thus avoiding (unbeknownst to us) the protruding frozen snow at the intersection of alpha and delta. after the aircraft was parked, maintenance personnel conducted an external inspection of the #1 engine and discovered damage to the bottom rear of the inlet cowl and idg. we immediately notified ground control of the damage and requested an inspection of the taxiways used during the taxi operation to check for debris and/or oil contamination. airport operations sent a vehicle which repeatedly drove the taxi route and was unable to find anything. after sunrise provided better visibility conditions, airport operations was able to locate the event site. the inspection revealed snow and ice protruding significantly onto the taxiway surface, extending well beyond the taxiway edge referenced in the notams.suggestions: the northeast (ga) side of the airfield did not receive the same level of snow removal service as the commercial terminal side. while notams were active for compacted snow and 4-foot berms, the actual snow and ice intrusion extended well beyond these parameters and protruded significantly into the taxiway surface area.notams definitions for compacted sn and berms were not followed by airport operations in their air traffic control reporting. airport operations admitted to the protrusion or frozen snow and swept it clear. interestingly, before it was found, the comment was made that the notam for berms covered protrusions, which it does not. there are very specific reporting requirements when the usable width of taxiways is reduced, which does include intersections. to prevent this happening in the future, we should either bias towards parking our aircraft where other heavy jet operators park. if unable to do that, the taxi route should be verified by airport personnel prior to taxi, at least to a point used by mainline aircraft.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a bank angle aural caution after missed approach. Crew corrected bank angle and returned for landing.
text: on day 0 on flight abcd redacted - redacted we accomplished a go around followed by a bank angle aural caution. the first officer (first officer) was pf and captain was pm. the weather was degrading at redacted but as we approached it seemed to be good enough for the first officer to continue the approach and land (on oe). at touchdown we began to drift off centerline so i called a go around and we went around. during the go around we were given a turn to 120 and a climb to 4000ft. the first officer still hand flying at this time banked too hard in the direction of the turn giving us the aural 'bank angle' so i corrected with aileron and gave him back the controls and setup the autopilot to be turned on. after we completed all of our checklists, and all other pertinent communications. we came back in to land again, now me as pf. we landed with no issue. the cause of the go around was due to the gusty wind conditions, contaminated runway surface, and a new first officer still getting the feel for crosswind landings. after the go around the bank angle was due to the fcp and subsequent fd (flight director) not yet giving accurate information to the pf. after the fcp and fd were set back up autopilot was engaged and we continued normally. the biggest threat in this was weather and oe. suggestions: stay ahead of the airplane, manage your time and workload effectively to avoid any uas (undesired aircraft state). after recovering from a uas understand how it occurred and how to move forward from it.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: ERJ-145 First Officer reported spurious EGPWS terrain pull up warning. Crew performed escape maneuver and continued approach.
text: while being vectored level at 6, 000 ft by redacted approach, we received a spurious egpws (enhanced ground proximity warning system) commanding 'terrain, terrain, pull up'. i disconnected the autopilot and performed an escape, as it was nighttime. we were in terrain mode and had no indication on the mfd (multi-function flight display) of conflicting terrain. additionally, air traffic control informed us that we were well above the mva for the area. there was no terrain caution prior to the warning. the warning cleared after approximately 1-2 seconds, and we returned to our assigned altitude and continued to a landing.cause: spurious egpws warning.suggestions: be sure to comply with egpws required escapes, even if the alert seems false.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: RV-8 pilot reported a collision during final approach with an object they believed to be a UAS. Upon landing; damage was found on the aircraft.
text: during normal visual flight rules flight operations on day 0, while operating an experimental amateur-built rv-8, i experienced what is believed to have been an in-flight contact with an unknown airborne object. no traffic advisory or visual contact with a uas or other aircraft was observed prior to or immediately following the event.the aircraft remained fully controllable, with no abnormal flight characteristics, vibrations, or system anomalies noted. a normal landing was conducted without incident.during post-flight inspection, localized impact damage was discovered on the aircraft consistent with contact from a small, lightweight airborne object. the damage appears cosmetic in nature, however, the aircraft was removed from service for further inspection.based on the size, nature, and location of the damage, contact with a small plastic unmanned aircraft system (uas/drone) is considered possible, though no definitive identification could be made.no emergency was declared, and no air traffic control notification was made at the time, as there was no immediate hazard or loss of control. this report is submitted voluntarily for aviation safety awareness and data collection purposes.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported a near miss with another aircraft during the initial climb from a non-towered airport. The pilot maneuvered to avoid the other aircraft and passed below the conflicting traffic.
text: i was taking of from an off airport location to the northeast of fd88. during my initial climb out i checked for traffic visually and turned oncourse southwest of fd88. my course took me within 1 mile of the approach end of 28 at fd88. at some point during the flight i was notified that the was an aircraft high and to the left that was turning final for runway 28. i did not see the aircraft dur the the aircraft overhead breaker panel obstructing my view. i took evasive action by lowering my altitude as low as i safely could and changing my heading to attempt to get a visual on the aircraft. the aircraft passed over at approximately 300+ feet and from what i can tell conducted a go-around.looking back on this situation, i believe there are 2 main factors that that lead to me being in this situation. the first factor was my visibility being blocked by the overhead breaker panel. i was not able to see any traffic high and to the left of me. the second factor was my decision to fly so close the to the runway end of fd88. in the future these types of situations can be avoided by giving a wider berth to fly in communities and insuring i continuously clear the high left blind spot.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a near ground collision with aircraft taxiing. Flight crew reported incident to ATC then proceeded with taxi clearance.
text: subject: near collisionlocation: ord taxiway a14date: day 0time: xa:42incident description: near miss collision with aircraft y.(ground 126.9) taxi clearance was: 'aircraft x a14, a, tt, hld shrt g.'clearance was acknowledged and we proceeded at near idle thrust to turn left into a14.then revised taxi instructions: 'give way to aircraft z on a' which was aircraft z coming from our left. bringing the aircraft to a stop to give way. well short of taxiway a.for unknown reasons aircraft z remained stationary holding short of a14.at this time we were still holding short of a but not of b as our clearance was to give way to traffic on a.then to our surprise aircraft y came from our right side southbound on taxiway b, at which time i commented to the ground controller that this aircraft was approaching our position at considerable speed. at this time it was not sure he would clear our position without a collision, he cleared our radome by approximately 1.0 meter or 3 feet.the controller commented on aircraft y's action: 'he was not supposed to be doing that'we were stationary during this whole time.aircraft a was following the first, which i communicated to the ground controller. ground controlmade him stop, and communicated to us that he was now holding short and clear of our position.we were then cleared to proceed on our taxi clearance with the mentioning that all tra'c was now giving way to us.we continued our taxi without further incidents.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: COS TRACON Controller reported failure to exchange conflict traffic to flight crew resulted in a NMAC event.
text: aircraft x was conducting jump operations over the air force academy and descending back down to aff. aircraft y was on a vector to pass east and north of aff and told to maintain visual flight rules at or above 095. i had a rnav approach that needed turned onto final in the same time frame. i saw aircraft x in the descent eastbound on a track to pass tightly behind aircraft y and told aircraft x about the aircraft y traffic 2 miles to the east northbound. aircraft x always had target resolution and when closest, was 1, 100 feet above aircraft y, aircraft x continued a eastbound circle around aircraft y always maintain target resolution. i failed to however, tell aircraft y about aircraft x descending in his vicinity, which led to the pilot in command of aircraft y calling 5 days later to make an inquiry about a near mid air situation.recommendation: i should have called traffic to aircraft y.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A Citation Latitude pilot reported flap failure on climbout resulting in a return to departure airport.
text: flight control issues on departure climb from redacted-redacted. i was right seat sic co-captain. on initial climb fairly early ca complained pitch trim didn't feel right. asked me if pitch trim was 'normal. it's normally down and it was in this case. no cas messages. it was bothering him enough that the conversation persisted. said it didn't feel right. he was correct. ap (auto pilot) failed or he disconnected. probably 10, 000 ft at this point. rudders began to pulsate about this time. decision to slow and get delay/return vectors quickly turns into return divert and advised air traffic control. workload is high on pm with short return time and perception on ground is best place to be before this deteriorates further. flaps 1 fairly early trying to test handling. slower is better per ca. flaps fail at selection to 1, quick reset per ca i agree. fixes it for now. flaps 2, flaps fail again. qrh started and flaps reset. i read ahead anticipating another failure. at flaps full they fail a 3rd time, i am able to reset and we conduct a normal landing. clearing runway select flaps up and flaps stop at 1. we also received five amber cas indications momentarily. i caught the first two flaps fail and primary trim stab fail. in each case when flaps are reset, handle position matches indicator except on ground where no reset is attempted but flaps are selected to up on after landing, flow. taxi clear and have fire department check condition of aircraft, nothing abnormal detected. we proceed to company x make appropriate reports and calls the company, short discussion with airport operations and fire department. secure aircraft at flaps 1.suggestions: none. given complexity of multiple closely spaced failures we believe we addressed issues prudently.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported rejected takeoff after temporary loss of control due to auto throttle failure.
text: after receiving the take off clearance from redacted tower, i advanced the thrust levers to about 40% and verified the engines were stable. i pressed the toga button and the engines spooled up but the auto throttle disengaged. the number one thrust lever advanced to about 41-42% while the number two did not move. immediately the airplane started to move to the right, and i quickly closed both thrust levers and regained the control of the aircraft returning to the center line and stopped the airplane. we called the tower and stated the problem, we taxied off the runway and we continued to the gate.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier pilot on approach reported abnormal engine readings and performance led them to shut down the engine and continue to land after troubleshooting.
text: while on arrival into redacted operating flight abcd on aircraft x, on the base leg for runway xxl at approximately 3, 000 feet msl, the aircraft experienced a sudden jolt followed by noticeable airframe vibration as the the power was coming out from idle. almost simultaneously, a burning odor was detected through the cockpit air vents.i immediately reviewed the upper ecam and observed engine #2 exhibiting surging indications on the epr (engine pressure ratio) gauge and the noise made by the engine and with a rapidly increasing egt. there were no associated ecam and no fire warnings. i reduced thrust to that engine to idle power and went mct (maximum continuous thrust) on the good engine. we advised air traffic control and broke off the approach and took vectors so we could finish the checklist. based on the abnormal engine parameters, surging condition, extremely high egt and presence of a burning odor, i elected to shut down engine #2 by accomplishing the applicable qrh procedures for egt overlimits. aircraft weight was verified to be below maximum landing weight.dispatch was notified via acars, and the flight attendants were advised and issued a briefing. a single-engine approach and landing were conducted without further incident. after landing, the aircraft was stopped on the runway to allow fire rescue personnel to inspect engine #2. no evidence of external fire was observed. we then proceeded to taxied to the gate normally. a detailed logbook entry was made to document the event for maintenance troubleshooting.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB ERJ 170 Captain reported engine failure and diversion to nearby airport.
text: we departed redacted, and we were climbing up to our cruising altitude of fl330. climbing through fl290, we felt the plane shudder, and we saw the low pressure vibrations on the number 2 engine went amber. following this, n1 dropped to about 18%. after this, we got an eng 2 fail eicas, and a fail indication on the engine 2 n1 indicator. my first officer called out identify cancel, and i responded with engine 2 fail. my first officer then called for the eng 2 fail qrh. during this time, the engine tried to auto relight, but it was unsuccessful. we began running the qrh, and advised air traffic control . we were over redacted, so i made the decision to divert there. my flight attendants called me, asking what was going on. i told them that we had an engine issue we were working through, and i would call them back. following the qrh, we made the decision to not restart the engine due to the vibrations prior to the failure. upon reaching the appropriate section of the qrh, i emergency called the flight attendants and gave them a briefing. i followed this by making a quick pa advising the passengers of an engine issue, that we'd be diverting to redacted, and that we'd be landing shortly. i briefed the approach, and we ran the engine out descent checklist. we were vectored onto the approach and ran the engine out landing checklist. we landed without incident and taxied to the gate.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported concern with distance between taxi way lines in the alleyway at ORD airport.
text: thank you for all the work you put forth..yes, i have read the ops alert. in 25yrs of flying this is the closest i've ever seen two wingtips on purpose. i recognize bulletin assures clearance for 'simultaneous large aircraft operations' in the fox-alley. situation: pushed back from gate xx and disconnected from tug in the fox alley) on east line in aircraft x abeam gate xy. an airliner taxied inbound in aircraft y (fences on wingtips) on the west line. i checked and if i am to believe googlemaps measurements, the distance between centerline of east and west is 130'. wingspan of aircraft x gives us allegedly @ 13' of clearance wingtip-to-wingtip. frankly, i don't buy the googlemaps measurements. the first officer with experience operating in close proximity to other jets, believed that we had less than 4' between wingtips. before i do this again, i will either have a wing walker in the fox alley (dangerous imo (in my opinion)) or refuse to taxi out until i know the exact clearances. i'm curious what turned up for the exact measurements between the wingtips of aircraft x and aircraft y? follow up question: what is the minimum wingtip clearance that ord is willing to accept during taxi-operations? 8 feet? 4 feet? 2 feet? 10 inches?

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: EC-130 maintenance technicians reported an engine component was incorrectly installed.
text: i was conducting a maintenance task of a reassembling a main rotor head on a ec130. this was my first time conducting this type of maintenance on this model aircraft. i had the maintenance manual open and following the maintenance steps to assemble the main rotor head. however, an oversight of the caution in the aircraft maintenance manual occurred resulting in incorrect installation of the frequency adapter. maintenance procedures have been reviewed to prevent recurrence. suggestions: review and reinforce proper use of maintenance manuals, with emphasis on warning and cautions prior to task execution.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Aircraft was under tow from the gate to hangar pad when a ground vehicle did not yield to the aircraft under tow resulting in the tow team braking to avoid a collision. No damage or injury occurred.
text: was towing aircraft from gate to hanger pad 1 a fuel company truck came through at high speed did not stop did not yield we had to hit our brakes to avoid collision.when the fuel company is done either loading or unloading or arrival they continually drive reckless going through the hangar pad area.cause: contract carrier the fuel company continues to drive at high speed when we are towing aircraft from hangar to gate or from gate to hangar, ignoring our air horns and our wing walkers.the employee in question was driving so erratically that he dropped his chalks and didn't even know it, which caused us to hit our brakes to avoid running over them picture to follow.suggestions: city x and ramp management need to provide another road for fuel trucks to go around us rather than through hangar. it is only a matter of time before employee runs into a aircraft engine or even worse, killing one of our wing walkers because they're not paying attention.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: King Air 300 pilot reported the right engine rolled back after takeoff resulting in momentary loss of aircraft control.
text: i was to ferry our king air 300 from redacted to redacted. a visual flight rules flight conducted at night. on departure just as i got airborne and reached for the landing gear handle, the right engine rolled back (as it does in many king airs when you release the throttle) and the aircraft began to roll to the right since i was slow and draggy as the landing gear was coming up. the engine did not fail, the power lever retarded to almost the idle position. i leveled the wings of the aircraft and pushed the throttle up to full power and accelerated to continue the climb. my flight path drifted off to the right side of the runway and i overflew the taxiway and a couple hangars as i corrected the flight path. i believe there were some people in the vicinity of the hangars as i saw some cars and movement when i taxied out. i am submitting this report because i don't know if the altitude / flight path startled them or not during my correction. after the aircraft was back on the climb schedule and any other problems were ruled out, i began a climbing left turn and proceeded on the flight. there was at no time any danger to any persons or property but i want to be sure this is not seen as intentional or lead to any punitive actions for handling a aircraft induced flight path deviation from the norm. i fly into and out of both redacted and redacted very frequently and do not desire any spotlight shed on my actions. the problem with the aircraft is not engine related, only the loose power lever that does not tighten appropriately with the friction lock. the aircraft is in inspection now and the friction locks will be addressed.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Cirrus SR20 pilot reported a main gear flat tire during landing roll out. Pilot notified ATC and aircraft was subsequently towed.
text: night landing. tower closed. landing fine but when slowing noticed hard to get to turn back to right. assumed flat tire and shut down on runway. tire was indeed flat and would not air up. not a hard landing tried to call redacted from radio but could not reach on ground. called air traffic control on phone and they were awesome. said they would monitor ctaf and could advise incoming traffic. asked them about notam to close runway and they started that process. they asked me to call back when clear. redacted turns class g at xa:00 from class d. redacted sent some help as i did not want to damage wheel towing or moving with flat and possible rubbing wheel. cirrus has 24 hour tech support and worked with me and airport personnel to get a dolly under the main wheel so it can be towed. excellent support by cirrus, redacted air traffic control, and redacted airport. as smooth a it could have gone. my takeaway was as i was concerned about an incoming aircraft not seeing plane on runway even though i had lights on. reaching air traffic control on phone was right move and i think every pilot should keep an air traffic control number in their cell phone.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported possible loss of separation during climb with corresponding TA alert. Flight continued climb.
text: on taxi-out for departure from runway 09 at eyw, air traffic control advised us to make a left turn heading 360 on departure. we were then cleared for takeoff from runway 09. as pf, after passing 400' agl, i requested heading select (360) and proceeded to start a left turn to heading 360 flying with the autopilot off. while making the turn and scanning outside the aircraft, i immediately saw a group of targets that i initially suspected might be very large birds. at some point during this turn eyw tower informed us of traffic on a left base into navy key west and directed us to contact departure. my initial instinct upon seeing what i now recognized as opposite direction air traffic (a flight of 4 military aircraft) was to continue my climbing left turn in an effort to see and avoid what i felt was a potential traffic conflict. at about the same time i recognized a tcas traffic alert and noted a target -300' (or 300 feet below us). i believe this occurred while we were at approximately 700' agl due to the fact that we received an audible traffic alert (which is inhibited below 600' agl). with the traffic visually acquired and verified on tcas, i rolled out on our assigned heading and continued our climb satisfied that we were no longer in a potential conflict. during this time the captain acting as pm, checked in with navy key west departure and queried them about the traffic and procedures for deconfliction since we were not given any information prior to beginning our takeoff roll. air traffic control simply stated that the two airports are extremely close to one another and that the military aircraft were maintaining visual separation with us. our flight continued on without further incident.i truly feel that if we were at a higher altitude, we would have received a tcas resolution advisory (resolution advisory) due to this traffic. according to our manual, resolution advisory's are inhibited below 1100' agl. since this all occurred at approximately 700', i believe we were too low for the aircraft to command a resolution advisory and instead simply announced an audible 'traffic, traffic' alert. cause: i believe the eyw tower's failure to alert us to the traffic inbound to navy eyw contributed to a possible loss of safe separation between our aircraft and the military aircraft. at a minimum it should be required to alert aircraft departing from runway 09 at eyw to traffic inbound to navy key west so that crews can factor it into their decision making process. it would be better for air traffic control to just delay instrument flight rules departures until visual flight rules traffic inbound to navy eyw is completely clear of the departure corridor. simply relying on military aircraft maintaining visual separation without our knowledge is not an appropriate solution to this kind of situation. this event occurred exactly a day prior to the anniversary of a tragedy in the industry that in my opinion it had striking similarities. a one-minute departure delay to allow the military aircraft to clear the departure corridor and land would have been appropriate to mitigate this potential threat.it would also be helpful to include a note in our company pages about the potential for this kind of traffic encounter, so that crews can include it in their threat forward briefing prior to departure. had we known about the inbound traffic, we could have made the decision to delay our takeoff in an effort to mitigate this threat.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: PA-28 pilot reported flying an unstable approach and executed a go around that resulted in a prop strike that was noticed after landing.
text: this was a solo flight operation to redacted and back. after contacting the tower at redacted, was cleared for a straight in approach rwy xx. during the approach, had to make power changes to maintain altitude and airspeed as there was no visual aid like papi available for the rwy. engine parameters were in the green during the approach. airspeed was kept at +5kts to adjust for the gusting winds.the aircraft was setup in the landing configuration and the before landing checklist was complete. over the threshold, the aircraft became unstable and by the time the go around was initiated, the aircraft had touched down and bounced.the go around checklist was complete and requested air traffic control for another lap in the pattern. engine parameters were in the green. there were no changes noted in the sound of the engine nor any vibrations. normal traffic pattern procedures were followed and the aircraft was again setup in the landing configuration with the checklists completed, a safe landing was made on rwy xx.taxi was requested back to the active, during taxi there was momentary drop in the oil pressure however, it went back to the normal range shortly. at the hold short for rwy xx, the line up checklist was completed and the engine parameters were in the green - oil pressure, rpm, fuel flow and egt.a normal takeoff was performed from rwy xx and returned back into redacted. climb checklists, cruise checklists were performed during the appropriate phases. the engine parameters were in the green. a go around was made at redacted xyl once before making the final landing on xyl.after the parking checklist, during postflight inspection the aircraft was tied down, the landing gears, nose gears - tires and struts were checked. the hook on the tail was checked for tail strike. however, visual inspection looked normal and no abnormalities were noted at that time.the prop strike was discovered later by the ground crew after flight.what could have been done better/corrective actions?* earlier go around could have been executed for unstable approach. power adjustments could have been minimised.* stop at redacted for inspection of the bounced landing and call maintenance if abnormalities were discovered at that point in time.* check engine and prop during the post-flight inspection at redacted.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS crew reported they flew in controlled airspace without authorization. They flew 12 hours before their approved LAANC time.
text: on day 0 while preparing for my operations i inadvertently submitted a laanc request with the incorrect local time. specifically i entered the start time as pm instead of am due to a combination of factors. i was using aloft and there format for time is 12 hr instead of 24 hr for what i believe can be seen as a trap for human error. other contributing factors are time pressure to finish the mission due to a tight schedule and insufficient allocated time, and lead to heightened stress and reduced attention to detail .this stress impaired my double checking process turning what would have been a caught mistake into a pilot error.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a fuel filter bypass indication during cruise. Flight crew referenced checklist and elected to divert.
text: departed redacted for redacted. in cruise the left fuel filter bypass light illuminated. we ran the checklist, contacted dispatch and maintenance control. not any troubleshooting or suggestions from maintenance control. checklist directs divert is opposite side fuel filter illuminates (it did not illuminate). the region was under a major winter storm. visibility 1/4 mile with heavy snow, low ceilings, and very strong winds gusting close to 50. this storm area comprised a large portion of our route to redacted. with concern for contaminated fuel we determined the safest course of action was to divert to redacted. this was done in coordination with dispatch. emergency was not declared but air traffic control was advised of the reason for the precautionary divert.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Strake seal was repaired using RTV instead of a new seal.
text: i responded to a gate call on aircraft x for rtv bleeding on #2 engine strake. checked maintenance records and saw that the strake seal had been previously written up on a logbook deferral sheet and signed off in accordance with company repair document 71-xx-xx-x. upon inspection found that the strake seal had not been replaced and therefore the company repair document had not been complied with and the repair had been overflown by 14 days.cause: it would seem that the technician who initially signed off the repair may have misunderstood the company repair document and assumed that rtv was an adequate substitute to a new seal.suggestions: fix company repair document 71-xx-xx-x to make it more clear what is expected.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported the UAS flew above 400 feet uncommanded. Reportedly; this was due to an internal component malfunction.
text: i am writing to voluntarily disclose a series of high-altitude excursions involving two separate units of the holy stone hs790 drone. on multiple occasions, the aircraft exceeded the 400ft agl limit, reaching altitudes as high as 1, 300 feet. these excursions were uncommanded, uncontrolled, and occurred despite active pilot efforts to maintain the legal ceiling.evidence from flight logs suggests a systemic firmware calculation error. while the flight controller was set to a maximum altitude of '396' (intended to be 396 feet), the aircraft physically ascended to approximately 1, 300 feet. the conversion bug: 396 meters is approximately 1, 299.2 feet. this indicates the firmware erroneously applied metric units to a numerical limit intended for imperial units.i have been in contact with a holy stone representative regarding these safety hazards. in official correspondence, the manufacturer stated: 'our preliminary assessment is that there may have been an internal component malfunction that caused the altitude limitation to fail.'

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: While in cruise flight; a Boeing 767 flight crew reported engine fluctuations; and surges with the right engine; resulting in an inflight engine shutdown. A diversion was accomplished followed by a successful single engine approach and landing.
text: at cruise flight approximately fl370 right engine started fluctuations and surges that led to engine parameter exceedences. this was quickly followed by a very noticeable burning small.it was decided to secure the engine which was accomplished using qrh checklist. procedure for in-flight contingencies (non-weather) along with oceanic engine inoperative driftdown was then accomplished.priority handling was requested with air traffic control. decision was made to divert to redacted or redacted.we descended to fl270 and after input from the company we decided redacted was our best option due to runway condition and landing winds.we accomplished appropriate checklists, reviewed the qrh checklist a second time along with reviewing the aom, fom and systems manual for divert guidance.we discussed what to expect at redacted and reviewed possible contingencies to include missed approach, go-around and wind shear during approach.after all briefings were completed, an uneventful instrument landing system and landing redacted rwy xx was accomplished by the captain.cfr (crash fire rescue) was at the ready and escorted us to parking. once parked, the left engine was shutdown and we were cleared by the fire chief - the situation was terminated.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757-200 flight crew reported a Cabin Altitude warning during initial descent. Flight crew referenced QRH; advised ATC; and landed uneventfully.
text: upon initial descent from fl210 into redacted, cabin altitude warning displayed on the eicas with aural warning. in response, crew accomplished cabin altitude qrh. left pack was initially off in accordance with fom procedure and turned back to auto as a part of the qrh and fom. with both packs in auto and aircraft in descent the cabin altitude still did not remain under 10, 000 ft and master warning reoccurred at least twice as cabin altitude fluctuated and could not remain below 10, 000 ft. the captain decided to request priority handling and crew requested further descent to 10, 000 ft. only at and below 10, 000 ft did cabin altitude remain below 10, 000.crew proceeded to redacted entered holding, coordinated with the company, canceled the priority handling once situation stabilized at lower altitude, and landed uneventfully at redacted.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: CRJ550 flight crew reported an upset occurred when they encountered wake turbulence on descent into ORD. Control was regained and the flight landed safely.
text: flight from redacted to ord on day 0. i was pf for this leg. we were cleared to descend and cross fytte at 11000ft and 300kts. around approximately 13000ft we encountered momentary wake turbulence from the aircraft in front of us. the aircraft rolled abruptly to the right then back to the left, with the total encounter being about five seconds. the pm checked in with the flight attendant and reported no injuries to herself or any passengers, as well as no damage in the cabin. while the pilot monitoring was checking in with the cabin i reported to air traffic control that we had encountered moderate to possible severe wake turbulence. we informed them that there were no injuries or damage to the aircraft. the flight continued without further incident. upon arrival at the gate, we talked to dispatch and maintenance. upon discussion with both the first officer and maintenance we both agreed that what we experienced was more in line with moderate turbulence.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: CRJ550 First Officer reported fuel imbalance and low fuel caution during climb. Crew notified ATC and returned to departure airport.
text: a fuel imbalance was noticed and we stopped to call maintenance to help diagnose and fix the imbalance issue. on the phone, cpt a stated the fuel quantities in each tank multiple times. maintenance assured us that the aircraft was normal and the condition of the fuel tanks were safe for flight. once we took off the wings were balanced but the imbalance condition quickly returned resulting in a low fuel caution message for the left tank. we requested priority handling and returned to redacted with no further issues.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B767-300 pilot reported abnormal nose landing gear extension related to absence of a deferred air driven hydraulic pump. Nose gear ultimately extended; and a normal landing ensued.
text: while on approach to redacted's runway xxl we began early configuration due to minimum equipment list 29-xx-xx air driven pump (adp). we began our initial flap extension about 25 miles from the airport and gear extension approximately 5 miles from redacted intersection. we took a time hack when we selected the gear down. after approximately two minutes, the left and right main gear was showing green, however, the nose gear was not illuminated. this condition persisted until we reached 1000 feet above airport in which time we decided to execute a missed approach. as earlier briefed, we elected to leave the gear in the down position and only clean up to flaps five. the rationale behind this decision was the fact we had a problem with the nose wheel coming down as well as the delayed retraction of flaps and gear associated with the minimum equipment list. the concern was possibly exacerbating the gear situation with the possibility of other gear not extending in the second attempt. it had been 10 minutes since we selected the landing gear lever to down with no nose gear indication thus far and with our fuel level in the back of our mind and the additional drag, we elected to run the qrh procedure for gear disagree. after running the checklist manually deploying the gear we heard and felt the nose gear release and fallen into place. we then received a green nose indication in advised air traffic control we would like to start the approach for the airport and as a precautionary, we decided to request priority handling to have equipment standing by. just in case the nose wheel was not locked and collapsed upon landing. one of our jump seaters who was an redacted first officer moved to the first observer seat and backed us up with the checklist as well as per our request, contacted maintenance and dispatch updating the company of our situation. the approaching landing was uneventful, and we proceeded to parking.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B767-300 crew member reported overheat of hydraulic pump indication during climb; and when on approach experienced abnormal landing gear operation. Gear finally deployed normally and a safe landing followed.
text: c dem hyd ovht eicas on climb out. qrh checklist turned c hyd dem pump off. on approach when gear down, flaps 20 was called, the flaps moved very slowly and the gear disagree eicas appeared. the nose gear did not come down and the gear doors did not close. missed approach was executed to troubleshoot. we decided to return c hyd dem pump to auto. the nose gear immediately fell and the gear doors closed. we selected flaps 25 and returned the c hyd dem pump to off. returned and landed uneventfully. according to the qrh, the gear and flaps should have functioned with the c hyd dem pump off.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: A300F First Officer reported a Main Cargo Mid 2 Loop Fault and Smoke Warning ECAM messages during cruise. The flight diverted to an alternate airport with no hot spots detected after landing.
text: while at cruise, fl360, a ecam chime and message appeared and disappeared quickly. i happened to be looking at the ecam when it happened and registered the words main cargo loop. it happened again, too quickly to read fully. the third time it happened, it stayed on the ecam and we were able to confirm the main cargo mid 2 loop fault. i ran the checklist for it out of the qrh, page 22-15, without incident. less than 10 minutes later, the master caution light and bell came on, with the ecam displaying the smoke warning and associated items. it went away without any input from us, but then came right back. the captain and i immediately donned our o2 masks and established comms, then accomplished the ecam items. the warning began to intermittently come back and go away within seconds of each other, so we made the decision to divert. i had just looked at the nearest airfield page, so i knew redacted was the closest major airport with crash fire rescue (cfr) capabilities. as a crew we agreed that redacted made the most sense, so i requested priority handling with redacted center and got a descent and direct turn to redacted coordinated with them. the ca flew a high speed descent while i messaged dispatch our divert intent and got all required information for landing at redacted. we flew a visual approach in a 15/20 flap configuration to xxl without incident, stopping straight ahead abeam taxiway 1. cfr used their thermal imaging instrument to ensure no hot spots were detected, which none were. after they gave us the all clear we taxied to the gateway and shut down.we never smelled any smoke, nor had any other indications of it in the flight deck. the ecam smoke warning went away after we initiated the descent. dispatch did a good job of letting redacted tower know of our situation before we got there, and all air traffic control agencies were quick and professional at getting us on the ground quickly.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B757-200 Captain reported the aircraft rolled forward a few feet after engine start when the parking brake was inadvertently released. Ground personnel alerted the flight crew and the aircraft was safely stopped.
text: after right engine start and during left engine start the mechanic verbalized brake brake brake on the interphone i pushed both brake pedals to the floor and verified that the aircraft was not moving and reset the parking brake. i apologized profusely to the mechanic for the movement of the a/c (aircraft) he indicated that there was no injuries or damage. i estimate that the a/c rolled forward a few feet before the aircraft was stopped from rolling. the first officer and i discussed the preflight check he noted that he visually saw the parking brake handle up in the set position and i recalled seeing the park brake light on the discreet light as being illuminated. i do not recall looking specifically for the park brake eicas message prior to the clearing of the various annunciations after the flight control check and before the first engine was started. looking back at what may have caused the brakes to be inadvertently released i can only surmise that due to the extreme cold temperatures outside from the preflight that i may have lost some of the feel of my foot position on the pedals as i was completing the flight control check and inadvertently caused the brakes to be released prior to the right engine starting. going forward i will do a secondary verification of the condition of the parking brake after the flight control check as well as incorporate looking specifically at the light and handle position prior to moving the fuel control switch from off to on.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Air traffic controller reported an aircraft flying through their airspace not participating in ATC services resulting in an airspace violation and the aircraft having a NMAC with another aircraft that was IFR on the airway.
text: aircraft x was instrument flight rules on vxxx eastbound, and i had just climbed them to 7, 000 to meet my flow to the next sector. aircraft y departed redacted visual flight rules and i noticed the track quickly because of their speed and rate of climb. the weather was either marginal visual flight rules or instrument flight rules, and an aircraft with that performance will usually depart redacted with either flight following or an instrument flight rules clearance. so the fast moving track caught my eye. the pilot was on a 1200 code. after a few seconds, i noticed they were still climbing, and i called the traffic to aircraft x, they responded that they were looking. aircraft y appeared to then increase their climb rate dramatically. i called a traffic alert to aircraft x and it was almost after i finished the call that they merged at what appeared to be the same altitude. aircraft x then responded that the aircraft missed them by about 50 feet and said that they would agree it was a near midair collision. the pilot of aircraft y went through the class c airspace without talking to air traffic control.recommendation: this scenario was created by pilot error. i was able to talk to the pilot and give them a brasher warning and they ended up calling the om desk.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air traffic controller reported departing aircraft on a RNO SID turning early resulting in flight towards terrain.  The Controller issued a low altitude alert and vector away from terrain.
text: i was conducting ojti on lcl, aircraft x was departing instrument flight rules on the fmg1 departure, climbing out of 049 they started an early left turn blow the mva to fmg vortac 1/2 mile south, they should not have started a turn until 3 dme south. we advised the pilot they were not flying the procedure correctly and they responded they are on the fmg1, i told them to fly southbound, they did not comply promptly, i then issued a low altitude alert. there was traffic inbound from the southeast that was becoming a factor rapidly, because they were still in a left turn, a turn to the south would have put them in unsafe proximity. i then cleared aircraft x direct fmg and to maintain 100 which was a vector below the mva of 084 they were entering.we have had a major problem with pilots flying the fmg1 departure incorrectly. there are plans to change it to an rnav sid in the future, i recommend expediting this process asap.

synopsis: DA40 Flight Instructor reported oil leak from the engine while entering the pattern for a training flight leading to a full stop landing.
text: when entering pattern at redacted noticed oil streaking down pilot side of canopy. decided to make a full stop landing and found oil leaking down pilot side (left) of aircraft from inside the engine cowling. oil streaking from front of cowling all the way back to tail. found oil underneath on nose wheel struct and inside of engine cowling coating the inner shell. no abnormalities or annunciations noted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A300 Captain reported a fire detection loop ECAM warning. Flight diverted to a nearby airport and landed safely.
text: during cruise at fl360, we experienced a mid 2 main deck loop a fault indication accompanied by an associated ecam warning. the main deck cargo loop checklist was accomplished, and it was determined that a cargo detection loop fault was present. loop a was selected off in accordance with the checklist. shortly thereafter, an ecam cargo smoke warning activated, along with the corresponding smoke warning light for the mid 2 compartment and loop b.this was a short and momentary warning. however it reoccurred a few moments later and a decision was made to divert to the nearest suitable airport. oxygen masks were donned, and priority handling was requested with air traffic control. a clearance for a 180 degree turn and descent towards redacted was received and initiated.the cargo smoke warning cycled on and off a few times, but shortly after the decent was started the warning extinguished and did not reoccur for the remainder of the flight. at no time were smoke, fumes, or unusual odors observed in the cockpit.after landing, the aircraft was stopped on the runway, and crash fire rescue personnel conducted an external inspection, including a thermal scan, to check for smoke or hot spots. once it was confirmed that no fire or smoke was present, we taxied to parking without further incident.i would like to commend the first officer for his outstanding performance during this event. he executed all required checklists and managed the fmc diversion setup in a meticulous and efficient manner. his professionalism and the high quality of training he had received was clearly evident and contributed significantly to the successful handling of this situation.

anomaly: Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: Corporate First Officer reported the MHR Taxiway A centerline and edge line paint are faint and almost unusable at night and in low visibility conditions.
text: while taxiing in low visibility at night, the aircraft was cleared from the fbo to runway 22l via taxiway a". the aircraft aligned with the "non movement" area taxiway markings instead of the taxiway centerline along taxiway "a" in front of the fbo. the error was caught when the blue taxiway edge lights came in to view as the aircraft approached the intersection of taxiway "b" and taxiway "a."the taxiway centerline and taxiway edge paint lines are very faint and almost unusable at night and in low visibility conditions across taxiway "a" and for that matter, on the entire airfield. this constitutes a safety hazard for aircraft operating at night, especially in low visibility conditions. there is little contrast between taxiway markings and the underlying tarmac."

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Vehicle
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported uncommanded aircraft movement after push back was completed resulting in contacting tug. Plane was towed back to gate.
text: push back out of gate xx in redacted. we ended up just shy of center line. we began rolling forward, which i believed to be the push crew making a minor correction to place us on center line. while rolling forward, the push crew called for us to set brakes." i immediately responded with, "confirm set brakes, we are still moving." i did not receive a reply. i asked a second time to verify to set brakes, were moving. no reply. there was a lateral shimmy from down below near the nose gear. i gradually applied brake pressure not to damage the tow bar if we were still under tow. i asked what was going on and was told to standby. the tug and one ramp personnel appeared in my left side window with the steering lock out pin as if indicating a normal wave off. at this point i still had not received any comms from the call to set brakes and to standby. i noticed the windshield of the tug had been shattered. with hand motions, i gestured for the push crew to come back and reconnect on comms. after hearing them connect, i asked what had happened. i was told to "standby." we initiated radio contact with the ramp to have maintenance come inspect the aircraft. the push crew reconnected comms and i also asked for them to have maintenance brought out to inspect. maintenance came and informed us that the aircraft had made contact with the tug, shattering the windshield and damaging the left nose gear door. we then shut down and were towed into the gate. visual inspection showed damage to the area of the nose gear door lock via a crack and other damage to the door. cause: break down in communication with the push back crew.suggestions: more aggressive training to ramp push back crews. the importance of clear concise communications at the right time."

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Vehicle
synopsis: Ground personnel reported the supertug towing the aircraft lost control during the tow. Tug struck and damaged the aircraft.
text: while towing an a320 from the hangar to [gate] xx i felt the supertug or plane kind of slide in one direction and in an effort to gain control my driver wound up jackknifing. this occurred on taxiway 1 between taxi lanes 2 and 3. the supertug swung around hit and went through the belly of the plane and wound up on the opposite side. during the impact i hit my head on something (possibly the radio). once we were stopped we checked on each other i tried to call the ground tower but the radios were not working at that moment. i tried to call the ground tower on my cell phone but was unable to connect and i then call the supervisor. before the supervisor showed up an operations officer showed up and questioned my driver and shortly after said the pavement was dry and conditions were clear. that clearly was not the case because for a stretch of the taxiway (not sure how much) there was a slippery substance that seemed to me like deicing fluid and temperatures were below freezing that made that section were slick.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Challenger 350 Captain reported a stall warning during landing flare. Flight crew continued the landing.
text: first officer was landing at redacted, there was about a 25-28 kt direct crosswind. in the flare i would guess approximately 10 feet we received the audible stall warning alert. before a reaction to the stall and a go around preformed the main tires were already touching down. the landing was continued. cause: possible gust from the crosswind. suggestions: it's possible that the combination of shorter runway and stronger crosswind could have led to letting the airspeed bleed off quicker in the flare.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: EMB-505 Captain reported smoke fumes during climb. Flight crew notified Tower and returned to the departure airport.
text: aircraft departing xxr had a strong odor of smoke fumes during climb out. both crew members agreed they could smell it. immediately notified tower of the return and continued climb to 3000 feet. reduction of power seemed to have reduced the fume smell significantly, entered a downwind and received landing clearance to land on xxr. landed cleared the runway and set the brake with engines on and fire trucks near by with the exterior of the plane appearing normal. talked with passenger and he appeared to be fine and we then taxied to back to the ramp uneventfully. spoke with fire rescue after parking and they were fine with us leaving the aircraft there.suggestions: given the location of the incident and reduction of appeared smell crew didn't don oxygen masks/goggles for the fumes. hindsight we should have complied with the procedure and then landed the plane in case the situation degraded.request priority handling prior to give tower a proper indication of distress.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL
synopsis: B737 MAX 8 flight crew reported an anti-ice master caution light during take off resulted in return to departure airport.
text: on takeoff, after 80 kts. master caution light with anti-ice illuminated. the overhead indication was cowl anti-ice and cowl valve. we continued the takeoff and climb, cleaned up and leveled off to complete qrh. we completed the anti-ice qrh first, then valve items. after conferring with maintenance and dispatch, we concluded that we could not continue the flight. we also concluded that we could not land overweight, so we elected to hold and burn off fuel to reduce our weight to land below max landing weight.cause: aircraft and a write up concerning the eng anti-ice on the previous flight. left engine anti-ice was deferred. there was some misunderstanding and the minimum equipment list was not clear, what would be our new normal indications of operating this flight. i had quite a bit of experience in the ng version of the b737, so there is some pause when one of the new max indications illuminate. the question is asked, what does this mean, and how does it relate to us?" we went through the checklist a couple of times, asking "did we miss anything?""

synopsis: B747-400 First Officer reported severe turbulence encounter during cruise. Crew recovered speed and altitude and notified ATC.
text: approximately 90nm south of redacted fix at fl360, aircraft encountered severe clear air turbulence which was not forecast, pirep'd, or identified on aircraft weather radar. turbulence caused an immediate airspeed increase of approximately 40 kts., vmo/mmo exceedance, altitude deviation of +600 to +800 feet, and automatic autopilot disconnect. turbulence encounter lasted approximately 30 seconds. aircraft was recovered to assigned altitude and airspeed with autopilot reengaged after another 30 seconds. air traffic control was then notified of the turbulence and altitude deviation. severe turbulence encounter and airspeed exceedance documented in aircraft logbook.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a hard landing during gusty wind conditions.
text: i was flying the leg to redacted from redacted. flight was normal. we knew redacted would be windy, but it was reported 20-30 degrees off runway heading at 22 gusting 30kts. i had a fairly normal approach with some speed variation due to gusts, but the approach was stable. upon flare and touchdown i believe i lost a gust leading to a hard landing according to maintenance. captain and both fas (flight attendants) said the landing was pretty firm but not anything they thought was incredibly hard, but we talked to maintenance and they advised it was a hard landing. captain and i debriefed it at the gate and discussed what next steps were when it came to reporting.i believe the hard landing was caused by a gust loss during the flare to touchdown and relative inexperience with gusty conditions in the aircraft.suggestions: during high gust landings, the flare and touchdown should be briefed in a way that ensures both pilots are aware of what will happen if a gust is lost.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an uncommanded push back from ground personnel and possible damage to the aircraft.
text: tug driver started pushback without captains clearance. tug driver never asked for 'brakes released' or 'cleared to push'. tug driver began push and forced tow bar into aircraft nose gear. bent tow bar connector 90 degrees and possibly damaged nose gear tires and strut. captain called maintenance and chief pilot. tug driver fled the scene soon thereafter.cause: tug driver did not communicate with crew.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: Ground personnel reported tractor towing aircraft was sliding due to taxiway conditions.
text: the weather in redacted has been snow and ice this past weekend making towing aircraft unsafe. while towing aircraft x there was sliding under the tires of the tractor used to tow the aircraft. just this past weekend there was aircraft damage because of ice and a tug sliding.i realized i was sliding with the aircraft under tow because i wasn't gaining speed or able to steer for a brief period.cause: the event occured due to request for the aircraft to be moved despite warnings that it is extremely unsafe. suggestions: when management is told that something is unsafe by someone they take it more seriously because this could have ended in serious injury or worse.

synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor and student reported a NMAC during departure climb resulted in taking evasive action.
text: on initial climb on departure leg from 20r at 0l7, our aircraft made appropriate radio calls following a go around. we were planning to follow behind the other aircraft. we announced our crosswind turn and saw the other aircraft head on to us. they made no radio calls or other position reports although they were earlier in the day. we took evasive action while the other aircraft did nothing. after which we had ahrs issues and decided to return home.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Citation X flight crew reported a false over speed and resulting climb during cruise and approach. Flight crew continued to destination.
