for this leg. because we were on single-pack operations and that this was a first flight of the day, we elected to depart bleeds closed as per recommended by the procedure. departure out of redacted was uneventful, at around 5000 feet, the captain and i accomplished the recommended bleed swap procedure that would reduce stress on the operating pack, and this went without incident and we continued our climb up to our assigned altitude of fl240. during our climbout, we revisited the potential issue of an overweight landing, and the captain and i calculated the required fuel that needs to be onboard to avoid an overweight landing. to help burn off fuel and reach this number, we inquired with air traffic control to give us approx. 10 minutes of delay vectors. shortly after our first delay vector, a caution cas message appeared indicating 'l pack hi temp', which disappeared about a second later. the captain and i were about to discuss our model to look into this issue and transferred controls to me. looking over at the cabin altitude, i saw it rising above 8000 feet. i alerted this to the captain, and it was around this point that we got a 'cabin alt' caution message. seeing that there was no sign of the cabin altitude decreasing and that this was a clear anomaly, we agreed that a descent was probably going to be needed. a short while later (30 sec-1 min), we received a 'cabin alt' warning message. the captain and i immediately donned our oxygen masks she initiated an urgent descent. we both initially had trouble re-establishing communications with each other through the masks (likely in part due to the shock of the situation) but managed to get back on the same page. i began to run our qrc for an urgent descent, item by item. the first officer announcement for 'urgent descent' was hindered by some troubleshooting getting my mask's microphone to transmit properly. due to the intensity of the situation, i cannot definitively recall whether i made the initial pa required by the qrc, or if i did, if it was done so properly. one of the steps in the qrc was to select pass oxy to 'select/on', during this step in the heat of the moment, i saw the switch already in the 'on' position and the masks deployed on the eicas page (which was induced due to the cabin altitude reaching a maximum of 15, 000 feet'. upon reaching a safe altitude, controls of the airplane stayed with her, i checked in with our flight attendant, to assess the condition of her and the cabin. upon hearing that the condition was good, the captain and i reviewed to ensure that we complied with all required qrh and qrc procedures, and at the conclusion of so, we elected to continue on to redacted. we flew at 10, 000 feet at 310 knots and were in consistent contact with air traffic control. we flew at 310 knots because the lack of air conditioning meant the cabin was beginning to get uncomfortably warm, and we wanted to get on the ground quickly. once stabilized in our new cruise, we input new fuel planning numbers to ensure that we would be landing above minimum fuel, and we still would be landing with enough for atleast 3 go-arounds. we continued to check in with our flight attendant and made proper pa announcements. i took over controls of the airplane while the captain monitored the situation and properly notified dispatch, maintenance, and air traffic control. we executed a visual approach for runway xxr at redacted, cancelling our priority status in the process due to the situation being under control and not life threatening, landed, and taxied to the gate. due to the peculiarity of the situation, i was under the belief that maintenance, who was at gate when we arrived, were going to take the airplane as soon as we disembarked. this, combined with the stress of the situation, meant that i unknowingly did not do a post flight walkaround.cause: the cause of this event can be attributed to a l pack failure when we were operating on single pack operations. the sudden ensuing cabin depressurization and urgent descent could have contributed to some qrc or standard procedures (such as a post flight walkaround) being done incompletely.suggestions: a major suggestion would be to not dispatch aircraft for single pack operations.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain and Flight Attendant reported a smoke in the cabin incident during climb. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: upon departure, at approximately 1, 000-3, 000 feet msl, the flight attendants contacted the flight deck via call light reporting visible thick smoke in the cabin. the flight attendants reported the smoke was located in the forward cabin and extended into the mid-cabin area by comfort plus. no flight deck indications, warnings, or abnormal system messages were present at that time.the crew immediately requested priority handling with air traffic control and requested to return to the departure airport. the crew accomplished the checklist for smoke or fumes removal procedure, followed by the associated qrh procedure. after completion of the procedures and subsequent communication with the flight attendants, the crew was advised that the smoke/haze had dissipated. no heat or additional abnormal indications were observed on the flight deck. a faint odor was noted in the cockpit, described as similar to burnt plastic, however, the source could not be identified.an uneventful approach and landing were completed. airport rescue and firefighting (arff) conducted an external inspection after landing, no evidence of fire, heat, or residual smoke was found. arff stated that a smoke odor was present in the cabin though. the aircraft was turned over to maintenance for further inspection. the aircraft had been de-iced approximately 5-10 minutes prior to departure. post-de-ice procedures per the special procedures manual were followed, including a 3:00-minute wait prior to restoring pack operation. no determination was made by the crew regarding the source of the reported smoke/fumes.cause is unknown. pack contamination suspected from de-icing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Embraer ERJ 145 First Officer reported a loss off pressurization control during initial climb out. A level off was initiated followed by a successful approach and landing at the departure airport.
text: while operating aircraft x to redacted out of redacted, we experience a complete loss of pressurization in the cabin. during all preflight, setup and before takeoff checks, pressurization indications were normal and no abnormalities were observed. upon the initial climb out, the climb check was completely and pressurization indications were normal with an increase in delta p and cabin altitude staying steady. climbing through 9000 ft, cabin altitude started climbing rapidly with delta p dropping to zero. a level off was initiated from the ca and the qrh was referenced. the issue was reported to air traffic control and crew communication was established. following the qrh, pressurization was reverted to manual mode where indications initially stabilized. cabin altitude momentarily climbed above approximately 10000 ft causing the cabin altitude alerter to go off. crew oxygen masks were donned for the rest of the flight. passenger oxygen masks never deployed. manual pressurization did not work. the entirety of the qrh was completed. due to pressurization being completely lost both in auto and manual mode, the crew decided to return back to redacted. a descent lower was immediately initiated with the cruise, descent, approach and landing checklists completed before arriving back into redacted with no incident.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a terrain warning during approach to CHO airport. Crew executed a missed approach and returned for uneventful second approach.
text: gpws 'terrain' warning occurred during an approach to runway 03 at cho. turning right base to runway 03, about 11 miles from the runway. a few moments earlier, we were given the visual approach to runway 03. captain (pm) accepted the visual, first officer (first officer) (pf) proceeded to maneuver for the approach. descended to 2600 ft msl to position to intercept final approach course for instrument landing system 03 faf sipme. upon hearing the terrain warning, we discontinued the approach and climbed to 4000 ft, informed tower. tower instructed us to fly runway heading at 4000 ft and contact approach control. vectored for complete instrument landing system. uneventful reattempt.cause: causal factors extended back to briefing, general tiredness, and a lack of assertiveness on my part. the first officer briefed the approach completely, and definitely briefed the company pages restriction on night visuals. i noted the same when the in range message came back. between then and actually beginning the approach, that element dropped off. it was a very clear night, approach gave the visual, we accepted. the first officer then started a descent to 2600 ft, which is typical in a normal visual to match the altitude for the fix you are about to intercept. then he extended the approach a bit, in order to be more stabilized on final. all seemed prudent, but something was off, and i should have been more assertive. it is my responsibility to command the aircraft, and direct adherence to policy. this is my biggest takeaway, and i expect to be hyper vigilant on night visuals in future.suggestions: while all responsibility was ours, air traffic control vectors for visual at night could come with a caution. the set up for an extended downwind it typical, and muscle memory tends to take over in such cases.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: DA40 Flight Instructor and student reported experiencing engine sputter on departure; resulting in the Flight Instructor taking control of the aircraft and returning to the departure airport where they landed safely.
text: we took to the centerline and took off from xxr. on our climb around 1200' i felt the engine struggle and sputter then return to regular operation after a second. i saw the red on our rpm. we exchanged controls and my instructor leveled off and immediately contacted tower to land xy/xz. after a couple seconds we received clearance for xz. my instructor started a decent and made left base for xz. we landed without further incident. i suspect the prop governor momentarily stopped working or 'didn't latch'.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: CRJ-200 Flight Attendant reported positioning cart incorrectly in cart holder during cabin depressurization. Cart was stable; no injuries.
text: attempted to secure cart during automatic mask drop/depressurization. end result secured with brake against bulkhead. no injuries from cart. cart stable.cause: depressurization in cabin.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Corporate pilot reported experiencing a severe shimmy in the nose wheel on landing; resulting in the aircraft being disabled on the runway with a flat tire.  The aircraft was towed to an FBO for maintenance.
text: this was a routine flight to pick up passengers from redacted. we performed a circling approach and joined the pattern for runway xx. upon landing, there was a severe shimmy in the nose wheel that got progressively worse as we slowed down. when we came to a rest, the nose was noticeably tilted forward, and i could see that the tire was flat when looking in the gear mirror. i was unable to exit the runway as the aircraft would not move. i called the fbo on unicom, and they were able to tow the aircraft off the runway. the aircraft was stuck on the runway for no longer than 5 minutes and did not disrupt any traffic at redacted. the aircraft was subsequently taken to a maintenance shop on the field, where the tire and tube were replaced, and we continued on with the planned flight without any further issues.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: RV-12 pilot reported entering the runway; causing a missed approach with aircraft on final approach. Pilot continued the takeoff and departed area.
text: about to depart a non-towered airport, i entered the active runway while an aircraft was on final approach approximately 1.5-2 nm out. the closure rate was higher than anticipated, causing the landing aircraft to initiate a go-around. i continued the takeoff and departed the area. the other aircraft remained in the pattern. there was no collision risk or loss of control. lesson learned: avoid entering the runway with landing traffic inside a wider spacing margin, especially when feeling pressure from other traffic wanting to depart.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: GA Flight Instructor with student reported an NMAC while in the pattern of a non-towered airport. Instructor took evasive action and continued to a landing.
text: training flight with my student in aircraft x. doing pattern work, making proper radio calls and position reports. i was aware of another local aircraft that was flying all over the traffic pattern area erratically, but who was not actually flying the traffic pattern. he crossed midfield below tpa (traffic pattern altitude) while i was midfield on the downwind. i got visual as well and confirmed on ads-b. we began our descent and i asked if he had us in sight. he said he did not. i told him where we were in relation to him and that we were beginning our base turn about 1 mile ahead of him, same altitude. i had to quickly take evasive actions as he began to descend into us, and he finally corrected his location after i queried him for his intentions. we corrected course, turned final, and executed a full stop landing. he then circled around after stating he was intent on landing, entered the upwind for the same runway (17), and crossed midfield at 400 feet agl to reenter the downwind leg. he would have run right into me while flying a non-standard traffic pattern and exercising poor communication if i had not taken evasive actions and alerted him to the danger he put us in.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A small aircraft Flight Instructor reported a NMAC while in the pattern with a student. Flight Instructor assumed control of aircraft and departed the area.
text: loss of situational awareness that resulted in a traffic conflict within approximately 400 feet of another aircraft. the flight departed visual flight rules from redacted en route to redacted. while climbing through 3, 500 feet for 4, 500 feet, a simulated diversion was initiated when i stated i was 'sick, ' and the student elected to divert to pwg. upon arrival, he initially entered the traffic pattern for runway 17 despite the airport operating runway 35. after correction, he maneuvered to the opposite side of the airport. i anticipated a standard 45-degree entry to the left downwind for runway 35. however, he instead initiated a descending teardrop entry, which resulted in a close proximity conflict with another aircraft established on the left crosswind for runway 35. i immediately assumed control upon visually acquiring the conflicting traffic and exited the area to the southwest practice area.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Sling 4 Flight Instructor reported experiencing a noise from the propeller on departure roll; resulting in a rejected takeoff .
text: had to abort a takeoff from redacted xxr, at approximately xa:45. upon entering the runway engine and propellor were performing well, right before take off we heard a noise which we believed to be the propellor and decided against rotation and aborted takeoff.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation pilots reported a near miss with another aircraft while in the traffic pattern during a training flight.
text: i was acting as safety pilot for currency of a fellow instrument pilot. at this time we were both visual flight rules. we were inbound from redacted returning to fnl. i activated the final leg of the rnav approach to runway 15 for situational awareness. we contacted tower and were given straight in 15 report 5 miles. the other pilot and i decided he could log an additional approach with me giving vectors to final. he went back under the hood and we started the practice approach. we notified tower of 5 miles and were cleared to land #3 runway 15. we started down the glide path and the controller called out 'traffic to follow is crossing the numbers', then came back on instantly and asked that we make a left 360. i took control of the aircraft as the other pilot was in foggels. i replied left 360.i started the turn and 180 degrees into the turn he asked us to 'fly extended downwind for jet on approach' i established the course and looked at my ipad to try to find the jet on the approach. i noticed through adsb that there was an aircraft almost on top of us with altitude fluctuating between 0 and 100 feet above, a little behind and to the right, about our 5 o clock. i didn't want to fly into the approach course of the jet and a turn to the right seemed like a bad choice as the other aircraft was closing in. i put the aircraft into a descent to gain separation from the conflicting aircraft. once the jet passed on our left i turned base to create more space. we were then cleared back in to land.it appears that we were turned out of a short final approach to not hinder the jet traffic that was inbound

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A small aircraft Flight Instructor reported they told their student to descend to an altitude less than 500 feet above the ground.
text: en route back to apa, i confused tpa (traffic pattern altitude) with bjc (6300 vs 6900) and instructed the student to level off at 6500 en route back from redacted once we were clear of the bravo. as we approached apa the terrain began to rise and i noticed we got lower to the ground, and verified with my agl which dipped below 500 momentarily. immediately upon noticing this i instructed the student to climb to 6900 (apa tpa) and the remainder of the flight was executed with no issues.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: PA28 Flight Instructor on short final to a non-towered airport reported a NMAC with another aircraft on short final flying 100 feet below them.
text: this event occurred during a training flight with my student. i am a cfii and my student is currently working on an instrument rating. we were completing an approach rnav runway xx into an untowered field, redacted. we received approach clearance from air traffic control, switched comms to ctaf, and made a 3.0 nm final call on ctaf. we did not hear any other traffic on ctaf nor did we see traffic displayed on our mfd (multi-function flight display). i was the pilot flying. i wanted to fly an approach so my student could observe and practice teaching me how to make corrections during my approach. my student has been progressing well through the instrument rating and i wanted to give him a different learning experience by having him practice being an instructor and walking me through how to fly an approach. during final, approximately 1.5-2.0nm from the threshold we receive a traffic alert. i look at the mfd and the traffic was showing 100 feet below us. at first, i thought it was our on shadow as i was making a lot of pitch corrections to show my student how much the advisory glidepath deviates and becomes more sensitive the closer we get to the runway.i asked my student if he saw any traffic. my student said he could not. nor could i. i took a few seconds to make a decision, but i decided to be safer and go-around and not assume it was our shadow. once we initiated the go-around and were climbing on the upwind, we hear a cessna make a ctaf call that they were clear of runway xx. we continued the go-around, joined a left traffic pattern (making crosswind, downwind, and base calls on ctaf) and landed without incident. on our downwind, we heard the cessna say they were taking off and making left traffic. during our left base call, the cessna made an incorrect call that they were also on base before correcting themselves and saying they were on left crosswind. contributing to the problem was a lack of the cessna making ctaf calls during their pattern work and the fact they were a high-wing and we were a low-wing aircraft. i carry a sentry with me but on instrument approaches, i leave my foreflight view on the approach plate. in the future, i will make sure to use the map function in order to see traffic the entire flight including during short final. i will also never hesitate again to initiate a go-around when in doubt.

anomaly: Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A C172 pilot reported they lost control of the aircraft while taxiing after landing resulting in a runway excursion.
text: i landed on runway xx in windy conditions 9-19kts from 36. i had been made to perform 3 left 360's in a very extended downwind. i floated the landing a bit in gusts. i braked to stop at [taxiway] 1 ramp, while turning a gust hit and forced the plane left despite holding ailerons into the wind. i was unable to complete the turn onto 1. i contacted tower and was told to shut down. on shutting down the plane, my model does not have emergency brakes, the nose wheel rolled 3' into the grass on the west corner exactly of 1 and xx as i exited the plane to meet the airport person dispatched to what was now an excursion. there were no injuries or damage, fbo staff were able to simply hand push the plane back onto the runway. i should have added power once pushed left, and simply taxied down to the next taxiway rather than try to complete the turn. i had completed flights in redacted under windy gusty conditions and was headed back to my own tie down at redacted. i stopped flying when conditions at redacted became to windy and they were still landing on xy with gusts at 36.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Flight instructor reported an NMAC with a UAS while in the traffic pattern. No evasive action was taken.
text: first saw drone about midfield while we were in left downwind for runway xx at redacted at pattern altitude (1000' agl). the drone was same altitude and coming towards us, it then turned to pass us on a parallel flight path opposite our direction ~300-500 feet off our right. on the next lap in the pattern we saw the drone again roughly ~200 feet above pattern altitude (~1200' agl) and roughly ~800-1000 feet off our right (south). we stayed in the pattern at redacted for another half hour but didn't see the drone again after that. from what i know of 14 cfr 107 this was against regulation and could have been prevented by either a notam (there were none for redacted regarding drones) or by the drone remaining under 400' as required by 14 cfr 107.51.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Ground Excursion Runway; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: General aviation pilot and Government large UAS pilot reported a ground conflict at a non-towered airport. GA pilot was on landing rollout when they were warned on CTAF of a large UAS departing the opposite end of the runway. Pilot exited the runway into gravel area to avoid the UAS. The UAS pilot reported using an incorrect frequency to make position reports.
text: on the morning of day 0, i (ppl / instrument rated) pilot certificate was forced to take immediate evasive (see & avoid) action to avoid a head on collision from an approaching aircraft while landing at redacted in my personal aircraft (a c172n). background - i filed a flight plan, received notams & wx, flew from my home airport (redacted) and was on center (ctr) flight following with redacted ctr (with an assigned transponder code) until making visual contact with redacted at which point (after verifying that the active tfr existed only above 9, 000' msl, and after verifying the ctrl tower was closed) squawked visual flight rules 1200, maintained visual flight rules and switched to advisory ctaf frequency for redacted. on my arrival segment, i made several location reports ( 'white skyhawk' 6 nm northwest of the field, inbound landing runway xx, left traffic, full stop, long landing, redacted traffic' with my intentions to enter a 1.5 sm left base for runway xx. then another position report as i entered left base 'long landing', another call on final, and even another position report on very short final advising that i would be 'landing long' runway xx (as runway xx is over xx, 000 ft long). shortly after touchdown, i continued my rollout toward txwy 1 as i attempted to navigate my way to the fbo / part of the ramp on the north side of the field. a few thousand feet short of intersection xx a voice came on ctaf and warned 'aircraft x' you have an aircraft on runway xy (same, but opposite direction runway) coming right at you. only then did i see the nose of what appeared to be a large uas coming down the runway, and i immediately exited (see & avoid) the runway onto the north dirt / gravel / grass area to avoid an imminent collision. i thanked the voice on the radio only to learn at that moment that it was my former flight instructor (not acting as an instructor that day) and friend, person a who just happened to be on a handheld radio and saw the un-announced uas barreling down runway xy directly at me. person a can confirm (as hopefully the recorded ctaf tapes will show) that i made all required / appropriate traffic position reports and intention calls. as i exited the runway, the drone 'rotated' and passed over me by what i estimate to be 150 to 200' agl. the uas never made any taxiing, takeoff, or other position reports on ctaf of any kind, until much later (more on that in a minute). after re-verifying that the runway xx was clear, and making yet another ctaf call announcing my intentions, i was able to taxi out of the brush / dirt / gravel area, back onto runway xx. i continued my rollout and exited runway xx @ txwy 1, announced on ctaf and crossed runway xz/xa, then continued my taxiing over to the hangars. as i exited txwy 1 @ 2, i finally heard a radio call from 'aircraft y' (i did not catch the full call sign, but i later learned this was the call sign for uas drones being operated by the government ) advising that it was 'headed into the tfr'. this confirms this aircraft radio(s) were working / functional. again, no taxi, rwy, rollout, or takeoff calls were ever heard from aircraft y on ctaf until i was already in the non-movement area by the ramp. i have all the track / flight data from my flight, as my flight deck is equipped with a garmin 345 adsb in/out transponder. i was on flight following earlier with an assigned squawk code. my efb (foreflight) connects directly to my transponder and displays traffic digitally on my screen. (none was displayed on runway xy or otherwise on the field). this uas was operating from a public use field, without transmitting any ads-b out signal (or i would have seen it) with civil and corporate traffic operating there simultaneously. i am familiar with redacted as it is the field where i executed all of my instrument training with person a. i find it highly objectionable and unconscionable that any operator would: 1. be permitted to operate at a shared use / public civil field (while the tower was closed) without first making appropriate position ctaf reports, and 2. be permitted to operate at a shared use / public civil field without broadcasting any outbound ads-b signal. if the government is going to operate on a shared use field, they should be held to the same expectations as all other operators / pilots / crew. they can turn their transponder off after they get into the restricted airspace from which they operate. there is no reason they should be flying 'black' on a public field. zero. had my former flight instructor not been watching / vigilant, this could have easily been a fatal accident, and unfortunately, i'm the only person that was at risk against an uas being operated by a pilot sitting in an office somewhere. that afternoon at approximately xf:30pm local time, after the incident, i tracked down the number for the government and reported the incident to government supervisor person b who assured me he would file a report internally. he was not authorized to give me the pilot (operators) name or info. he verbally advised me that the pilot made his radio calls 'on the ground frequency', not on ctaf. this doesn't explain why he didn't 'see' me, as i was continuously broadcasting my ads-b out data (which my flight instructor could see, because that's how he was tracking my inbound flight). imagine if it was instead of a single pilot small cessna, a corporate g650 or other 135 or 121 aircraft with passengers operating into redacted. would they have been able to avoid a collision? this could have been deadly. something needs to change with the governments standard operating procedures @ redacted. immediately. respectfully submitted.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A C182 pilot reported a NMAC with a flight of two military aircraft overtaking them at the same altitude.
text: flying in c182 cruising at 5500 feet msl and on flight following with redacted approach, flying near a lake. i was using foreflight efb with an ads-b in receiver, and noticed two traffic targets on display few miles behind me, doing 275 kts. ground speed. at the time i was doing 120 kts. ground speed. i noted they were at my same altitude and heading and were on a collision course towards the rear of my aircraft. redacted approach gave me a traffic alert and had me immediately turn right 90 degrees so traffic behind would not hit me, observed traffic as one v22 marine osprey. military aircraft was not talking to air traffic control controller and controller was unable to contact them. controller mentions they do a lot of training in the area and not communicating with air traffic control. after they had passed me i continued to my destination with no other issue.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A Center controller reported when an unmanned balloon was launched into their airspace they were not provided position or altitude reports of the balloon resulting in potential NMACs with enroute aircraft.
text: i was at least 10 aircraft over capacity due to tmu (traffic management unit) re-routing 6-10 aircraft into my airspace to avoid another busy airspace. i had intermittent to continuous light turbulence and altitudes with sigmets for severe turbulence fl340-fl430. conditions were imc all altitudes. while giving 3-4 clearances into and 3-4 clearances out of redacted with no d side. my supervisor told me a weather balloon was just released around redacted airport and was climbing east bound. at this time i had approximately 12-15 aircraft headed that direction who were imc and all needed updates. i asked my supervisor at least 15 times to give me updates on altitude and position of balloon climbing into a dozen imc aircraft's face. i had to take my attention away from my over capacity over complex over worked sector to beg for updates of this balloon from my supervisor that was just sitting at supervisor desk.numerous aircraft asked for vectors around it for avoidance due to being imc and not knowing what or where the balloon was at. i also had to inform sector x due to my supervisor and their supervisor not telling each other about it so that caused me to go offline and update them 4-5 times. i ask my supervisor does x know about this and he said did you send them a tag. it was in their airspace and on the boundary of mine. i told him he needs to tell them and coordinate with them as well. i don't know if he ever did. when me the controller is this busy and over worked is begging for updates of a unknown balloon to avoid a mid-air collision from over a dozen aircraft from a supervisor that doesn't give a crap or doesn't understand the severity of the situation is completely unacceptable. i also got to the point of asking for updates when it was going to pop and was told oh yea maybe 10-15 minutes over redacted. i had 2 aircraft what we're going to be there at that time and was told by my supervisor if he got distracted to ask him for updates, the whole time he was at the supervisor desk talking to another supervisor.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Tower Controller reported failure to ensure aircraft initiated climb prior to entering higher MVA resulted in a CFTT event.
text: aircraft x was the preceding departure. aircraft y was the second departure and was maintaining visual separation with aircraft x. aircraft y was faster then aircraft x and was closing the distance. i told aircraft y to maintain slowest practical speed. i told aircraft x to maintain best forward speed. i stopped aircraft y at 020 to keep 1, 000 feet vertical and coordinated with departure. remembering the mva was 021 i climbed aircraft y to 030 and switched both to departure. aircraft y may have leveled briefly at 020 in a 021 mva while on the sid.recommendation: pay closer attention to company specific performance.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported ground service vehicles did not yield to their aircraft during taxi.
text: after landing during taxi-in we were cleared to the southport via j-ss-b-sp, i was heads down typing in an elb entry report into the fmc after verifying the taxi instructions with the captain. i looked down for a second as we turned south on ss and as i did a white pickup truck drove right by the nose of the aircraft. the captain said something and i popped back to outside the cockpit to see a second silver jeep also drive right by the nose of the aircraft so close that he had to swerve out of the service road to miss us. i reported the incident and description to ground control, checked for cabin injuries and continued in my pm duties.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a severe turbulence encounter on descent. ATC and maintenance were notified.
text: while descending on the redacted star into redacted we encountered severe turbulence between 16, 000 and 13, 000 feet. aircraft speed and roll were uncontrollable. no injuries or observed damage. air traffic control advised and maintenance write up accomplished. no sigmets were present for severe turbulence but eddy dissipation rate (edr) was showing a few severe reports on the arrival.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported having to bring the airplane to an immediate stop due to vehicles not yielding to the aircraft on service road.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported a near collision with aircraft departing in opposite direction on landing roll out. Crew debriefed and continued trip.
text: during the landing rollout on runway xx, an opposite direction single engine general aviation aircraft departed on runway xy. the first officer was pm and was communicating on ctaf with several aircraft on and in the vicinity of the field, but there was never any communication from the aircraft that departed opposite direction. winds were 190 at 6 kts. all other traffic was landing and departing in the direction of the prevailing winds. prior to our arrival, an aircraft departed runway xz. a med evac was holding short of runway xx during our approach and landing. an inbound baron several miles behind us was also landing xx. we were in constant communication with all of these aircraft. i landed on the 1000 foot markers, opened the single operable thrust reverser, and began braking. during the rollout, the opposite direction aircraft came into view on the runway and i braked aggressively. the departing aircraft rotated and immediately made a turn toward the east to avoid us and departed the area. the departing aircraft did not have lights on and it was getting close to sunset which contributed to us being unable to see the aircraft until the rollout. we were unable to identify the aircraft despite requesting assistance from other aircraft on ctaf, airport personnel, air traffic control, and electronic means such as flightaware. we do not know if the aircraft departed from the airport or if they were transient and performed a touch and go.as a note, we did not receive a tcas traffic advisory, but 'traffic proximity - tcas traffic advisory' was the closest option to select.cause: no communication from departing aircraft. no lighting on departing aircraft. time of day (nearing sunset).suggestions: make radio communication on ctaf a requirement at all public use airports.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew on final approach to JAN reported a NMAC with traffic departing MBO airport.
text: we were cleared for a visual approach to rwy 16l at jan and backing ourselves up with an instrument landing system 16l. we were approaching on a five mile base and began our turn to final and began to descend. an unknown aircraft took off heading south from mbo and began climbing to pattern altitude. a tcas alert activated showing an amber symbol below us. tower made a traffic advisory call. we did not have traffic in sight. tcas symbology indicated the contact was directly below us. when tcas indicated a vertical separation of 400 feet i ordered a go around. the pf initiated a go around and vertical separation rapidly increased. tower then advised we were not in conflict and asked if we wanted to resume the approach. i declined to resume, continued the go around, and requested vectors back to final. approach then vectored us to a downwind and cleared us for a visual approach to rwy 16l. we then landed without incident.cause: loss of vertical separation with traffic at mbo. suggestion: add an entry to company operations pages that mbo traffic pattern altitude is very close to a 3 degree glideslope to rwy 16l at jan

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported becoming unstable on the approach to CMH airport below 500 feet. Crew initiated a missed approach and returned for landing.
text: i, first officer (first officer) was pilot flying. approaching cmh captain and i requested instrument landing system 10l and we briefed the potential of getting a short final from approach. prior to departing payjj we already got cleared down to 3000 and i am at 210 kts. air traffic control turned us onto base inside of mesre and captain advise to active vectors and i agreed. i also began to put out flaps 1 and further slow down. we then got cleared for the visual for 10l. worried that we are close to the localizer and may overshot it, i went direct to ccrew so that flight management system will capture the final approach course, and captain reminded me that we are above glideslope and needed to come down as we were still at 3000. initially i selected 2300 for altitude at ccrew and activated flch to catch up with the glideslope, then i realized that this was a visual approach and i can go down to field altitude+1000 so both captain and i agreed to select 1800 ft. the problem was that things were happening very quickly and i didn't realize i was still in flch. as i put out more flaps and drop the gear, descent rate began to skyrocket. realizing that i may about to exceed 2000 fpm below 2000 ft agl rule i immediately clicked off the autopilot and manually leveled off at 2000 ft as captain verbalized 'descent rate'. this is when the controller issued us a low altitude alert and advise us to check our altimeter setting. right after the alert was issued we intercepted the glideslope. after this the approach proceeded mostly normally, we established on the localizer and glideslope and was configured at 1000 ft and stable at 500, but perhaps i was still a bit shaken by the event i accidentally got high around 200 ft agl and had to initiate a go-around. the go-around proceeded normally and we landed without further incident.

synopsis: Air taxi pilot reported on departure ATC issued a low altitude alert resulting in the pilot increasing their climb rate.
text: on departure out of redacted on the the redacted departure on the afternoon of day 0, redacted departure gave me a low altitude alert advising me to climb, i responded that i was climbing and increased my climb rate in response to the controllers concern.before departure i loaded the redacted departure into the flight management system, briefed the departure, and made sure to go over all altitudes and fixes along the route as i hadn't flown the departure previously. i then verified the fixes and altitudes in the flight management system and then the depicted route on the mfd (multi-function flight display). i double checked and verified all this to what i thought was correct to make sure the flight director and autopilot would follow the correct route being that i was flying single pilot and task saturation would be high. upon taking the runway i selected heading mode and armed nav mode on the flight director/autopilot control panel. on initial climb after retracting the landing gear and climbing straight ahead on a heading of 306 the flight management system sequenced and the flight director changed to the previously armed nav mode to intercept the redacted [vor] radial to redacted. thinking back, it did seem a bit early being that the turn is supposed to be made at redacted dme 1.8 but i was task saturated during initial climb flying the aircraft, cleaning things up, and getting handed off to departure. i believe the flight management system sequencing early for some reason caused the low altitude alert for some reason. i'm not sure how this could be corrected as i verified what i thought to be all correct fixes and altitudes.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A B777 pilot reported a cargo door open warning during cruise. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: just after level off @ fl330, approximately 40min into flight, the door fwd cargo eicas caution illuminated. at captain's direction and as pm, i immediately accessed the electronic-checklist, on the lower control display panel (cdu), while pulling up the door synoptic on my multi-function flight display (mfd). door synoptic indicated the fwd cargo door open, with no indication of depressurization or airframe vibration (ever). captain transferred aircraft control to me, then requested priority handling to redacted [artcc] and asked for/cleared for a descent to 8000 feet (per checklist) and a turn back toward redacted, initially given direct, w/ subsequent routing provided later. captain called the relief pilot (newly settled in the crew rest bunk) to return forward. captain contacted dispatch and maintenance control to inform them of our situation and pending return. he then briefed crew and passengers to inform all of the plan. we agreed to dump fuel given the gusty crosswinds at redacted. i suspended the door fwd cargo electronic-checklist since we could not complete until level @ 8, 000.' per captain, i began the fuel jettison checklist. we subsequently dumped down to landing weight, completing fuel dump about 75 miles north of redacted, then completed the remaining items in door fwd cargo checklist & the descent checklist. step 1 of descent checklist, recall & notes, did not indicate any additional concerns/considerations from the eicas or the non-normal checklist notes. while cruising at 8000 feet door fwd cargo eicas caution went away, as did the open indication on the door synoptic. the remainder of arrival/approach was uneventful. when queried by redacted [tower] controller, we told them we'd like to clear the runway and return to the gate xx, w/ no assistance required. note, auto speed brake did not deploy initially upon touchdown/in ground mode. i watched it for ~2 extra seconds. as i was preparing to verbalize 'speed brake, ' the handle finally tracked aft to the proper position. autobrakes appeared to work normally. we did not have any trouble w/ deceleration or stopping the aircraft. upon clearing the runway xxr and crossing runway xxl, i accomplished after landing flow, verified completion w/ electronic-checklist then pulled up the status page, curious to see if additional messages appeared on landing in light of the delayed auto speed brake deployment. status page indicated the following messages: 1) auto speedbrake, 2) gear indication sys, & 3) passenger address. upon completion of parking checklist & debrief, we discussed whether to continue or not and agreed fatigue is an issue and would get worse w/ an uncertain timeline. all agreed to not continue. operations rep, chief pilot (crew scheduling through chief pilot) and maintenance personnel were extremely responsive after we opened the aircraft door. overall, the event was relatively straight-forward and we brought it to a successful conclusion w/ effective communication and crm, along w/ great support from all parties.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B787 flight crew reported temporary loss of control due to turbulence.
text: approaching the redacted fix in cruise at fl370, we received a pirep from airbus at fl350 of severe turbulence in the area. we were approximately 10 min from that area. captain called the purser to let her know that there would be an area of possible turbulence and to inform the rest of the crew members. we turned the seatbelt sign on. as we approached the area, the airspeed started to increase, indicating a mountain wave. the thrust levers were restarted to idle and the speed brake were deployed to arrest the increasing airspeed. with both action accomplished, the speed continued to increase into the 'barber pole'. the speed was approximately 10 kts above the barber pole for about 5 to 7 seconds. we had a climb of 500 feet from fl370 to fl375. as the altitude leveled, at fl375, it began to descent at fl367. shortly afterwards, the aircraft stabilized at fl370. we requested lower altitude to redacted air traffic control and we were given a block altitude of fl370 to fl330. we leveled at fl350.we made a pa for flight attendants to 'check in' and the purser called to say that no passengers or flight attendants were injured. we sent a pirep and informed dispatch of the event. we later called maintenance control to inform them of the event as well as submitting a maintenance write up. we proceeded to redacted without further incident. we called the chief pilot on arrival to redacted to verbally report the incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported excessive engine vibration and return to departure airport.
text: during the climb out of redacted enroute to redacted, the crew noticed the #1 engine vibe was at 4.3. the captain (pf) passed the controls and radios to the first officer (first officer) and went to the 'engine high vibration' checklist in the fm (flight manual). the level off at cruise altitude of fl380 coincided with the checklist step of 'retarding thrust' to try and bring the vibe within limits. as the thrust reduced below 95%, the vibe started to decrease. at cruise altitude (.76m) the vibe maintained between 1.7-2.3 (82-88% n1). all other engine indications were normal. after completion of the 'engine high vibration' checklist, the captain (pm) coordinated a call with dispatch and maintenance control. after discussions with this team and with the first officer, the captain made the decision to return to redacted and treat the engine as if it could not produce full thrust. the captain (pm) took the radios back, requested priority handling and coordinated a return to redacted. he then spoke with the fas (flight attendants) and then the passengers to inform them of our return to redacted due to a mechanical issue. the crew ran the 'one engine inoperative landing' checklist to set up for an approach/landing with a reduced thrust engine (flaps 15). air traffic control asked what runway was preferred and we coordinated for runway xxr due to its location on the west side of the field. at a good breaking point in the 'one engine inoperative' checklist the crew briefed the approach/landing plan. when everyone was comfortable and passing 12000' the captain took the controls back and the first officer resumed pm duties. air traffic control vectored the aircraft to a 15 nm final for the visual approach xxr (with instrument landing system backup). emergency equipment was not requested, but was standing by on the field. the captain completed an uneventful flaps 15 landing and then taxied to the gate. after shutdown, maintenance inspected the #1 engine and noted several fan blades that had broken off and damaged the abradable shroud. the crew (pilots and fas) were all moved to another aircraft and successfully completed the flight to redacted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported Master Caution light and slower flap retraction during take-off. Flight crew turned on hydraulic engine pumps and continued the flight.
text: during takeoff from redacted, shortly after raising the gear we got a master caution light. i punched the master caution light to extinguish the light until we were able to look at it once we were safely airborne. the gear and flaps both came up normally, although i did notice it took a little longer for the flaps to go from 1 to up and leading edge lights out. once we were safely away from the ground and above the terrain i hit the master caution recall and say the hyd annunciator illuminated on the first officer's (first officer's) panel. i looked up to the overhead panel and saw that both the left and right engine hydraulic switches were in the off position with the resulting low pressure lights illuminated. i turned them both on and the annunciator extinguished as did both low pressure lights. we continued to redacted with no further issues. how the switches ended up in the off position i'm at a loss to explain. during the before push checklist, i remember looking at the switches and seeing the two low pressure lights illuminated (as usual with both engines off) and normal hydraulic pressure readings. now i have to wonder if i just saw the two normal low pressure lights and the two electrical pump switches on and just saw what i normally see and missed the two engine pump switches being in the off position. but these switches being in the wrong position should have been caught twice during the two master recall checks in the after start and before takeoff checklists yet they weren't and i don't know why. nothing ever illuminated in front of me on my recall panel or my master caution light during both checks. we wondered if maybe we had a master caution recall panel issue that might need to be written up, so when we landed in redacted, while parked waiting on marshallers i turned off each engine hydraulic switch one at a time and then back on and the master caution and recall worked properly both times. my first officer and i debriefed the issue and how it might have happened. we still don't know how the switches ended up in the off position. he didn't recall turning them off at any time. he did say he turned on the electric pumps during his ground ops set up due to gusty winds. as for the lack of a master recall alerts, i mentioned that i have seen numerous times where my first officer's have pushed the recall panel and then immediately subconsciously immediately hit the master caution light extinguishing an annunciator that was lit. i happened to catch them because the annunciator was on my recall panel (example flt cntrl when the yaw damper kicked off) and i was able to fix the issue. since the hyd light is on the first officer panel, i would not have seen it and been able to intervene if this is indeed what happened. since the system worked properly on the ground in redacted, this is the only plausible explanation i can come up with.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier ERJ 175 flight crew reported after parking and setting the parking brake; the aircraft rolled backwards.
text: after landing at redacted, we taxied to the assigned gate and came to a complete stop. the captain set the parking brake, shut down engine 1 (2 was already shut off) and called for the shutdown checklist. i began the shutdown checklist, which starts with verifying the parking brake is set. both the captain and i visually confirmed the parking brake light was illuminated, indicating the brake was set. the captain called for the shutdown checklist as normal. while completing the checklist, i looked up and noticed the gate agent standing behind his controls and noticed the jet bridge begin to move. shortly after, the gate agent exited his position and began waving his arms to get our attention. the captain and i looked at him momentarily, and he then made a hand signal indicating the parking brake. at that time, we realized the parking brake release pin was loose and the parking brake had disengaged. no aircraft movement occurred that resulted in damage, and no injuries to passengers, crew, or ground personnel were reported. the situation was identified promptly and addressed. cause: the parking brake release pin being loose.suggestions: after discussing the event, we confirmed we followed aom procedures and checklist triggers stating, after the aircraft is parked at the gate with the parking brake set." the brake indication light was illuminated at the time and the aircraft should have been getting chocked while we completed the short checklist. moving forward, we will continue to stay heads up (not looking down at the checklist) until we receive the chocks in hand signal before continuing with the shutdown checklist."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported difficulty turning into a parking bay at MIA airport due to limited wingtip clearance and the need to execute a sharp turn. Reporter stated ramp lighting is inadequate and the ramp striping lines should be redone.
text: our flight landed and was scheduled to park at n2b. the parking angle has a large angle relative to the building and taxiway. the turn into the bay is maybe 160deg. there is little structural lighting and the lead in line is invisible in the dark. additionally, the angle is such that the first officer (first officer) couldn't see the lineup. we switched prior to entering the ramp to my taxiing from the left seat. the only guidance was from the follow me truck. that has its own issues because of the vehicle lightning is so bright that the flashing strobes makes it hard to see. marshallers were of little help and gave conflicting signals.i feel it is an understatement to say that was the most sketchy parking i have ever attempted with an aircraft. wing clearance on the right side is tight and impossible to judge in a sharp turn in the opposite direction from the wing. doing this in the dark you are totally dependent on the ramp for clearance of the wingtip with the other aircraft. this is an incident waiting for a time to happen. this should be a tow in only gate. i do not feel comfortable ever taxiing into that gate in the future with anything larger than a cessna 172! cause: design of the ramp is a major issue. the angles are due to aircraft length causing them to stick out. the area also is restricted on lighting as it is under the final visual segment of 26r and no large area lighting exist. ramp lines have no reflectivity and do not stand out due to buildup of dirt and other materials on the lines. suggestions: this spot should be a tow in only gate. the entire ramp striping needs to be redone with highly reflective paint. highly reflective wing clearance lines would also be beneficial for all spots. consider a solution with embedded led lighting for the line. new technology could support led lighting for the line using led strips embedded in the line with minimal challenges. the strip and power could be dropped into the concrete by cutting strips in the concrete and no need to dig it up like you need to with conventional airport lighting cans. this isn't a certified area. an alternative is to use glowing roadway paint that has been developed. this would keep the light pollution issue for runway operations to a minimum but provide a better lineup marking.

student was taxiing back for another take off i sent him a text message reminding him that he needs to do a go around if he bounces while landing. he responded, 'yeah, sorry about that'. the second take off was normal. pattern and landing were normal, during the 'flare' student over rotated and ballooned and preformed a successful go around. on the third landing attempt the student again has a normal approach but over rotated on the flare and ballooned again and executed a successful go around. on this go around the tower requested the student to fly right traffic, the three previous were left traffic. due to buildings and my position i was not able to see the entire pattern he was flying. at this point i contacted the tower via cell phone to inform them that i was his instructor and was monitoring the radio and to offer any help they felt would be appropriate. i also expressed my concern that he had two previous go around that i felt he may be becoming stressed with the situation.i observed him on the base leg and noted that he was low by about 100-200 feet and appeared fast. the student called the tower on the base leg and informed them he was going around. at this point instead of turning to align with the runway he continued flying straight head on the base leg. this put him in conflict with another aircraft on a extended left base. i was still on the phone with the tower (ground controller) at this point, the controller began berating me for teaching my student to fly like this and that he was now going head on with another aircraft. i explained that at no point have i ever instructed this student or any other student to do what he was doing and that he needed some assistance.tower was able to de-conflict the traffic and turned the student out bound from the airport. they turned him back to the airport with about a 3 mile final. the approach was normal until short final. at that time it sounded like the student was carrying extra power and was not at idle just prior to flare or touch down. just after the plane touched down i noted the right main landing gear lift off the runway 1 foot or less. when cleared to land tower advised winds were 120 @ 6 (runway xx with a magnetic heading of 076). i did not observe the student put in any crosswind correction.when the right main made contact with the runway the second time the plane began departing the right side of the runway into the runway safety area. the student was able to regain control of the aircraft without damaging any runway structures or the aircraft. the student taxied the plane to the hanger and shut the aircraft down. we immediately debriefed what had occurred.during the debrief we identified that the first attempt should have resulted in an immediate go around on the first bounce. he stated that he intended to do that but the plane began settling down before he was able to add power and execute the go around. we discussed always being ready for the go around and that if at any point something is not right to execute, and not 'wait and see' what happens. for the second and third landings we identified that everything was normal until the transition from the descent to landing (the flare). both times he was overly aggressive with the nose up pitch correction and the plane ballooned. several factors would cause this, excessive air speed on touch down and the plane being lighter than he was use to with not having me in the aircraft were identified as the primary causes in this situation.for the last landing we discussed that he had a slight crosswind and did not appear to put in any crosswind correction, he stated that he did not remember adding any when he touched down and that when the right main came up he did not know what to do and 'just froze'. we discussed proper crosswind techniques as well as not resigning yourself to the situation, it is imperative you keep flying the airplane until the engine is shut down and the plane is secured.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC during cruise. Pilot reported taking evasive action and continued flight.
text: on a clear night, both 1st and 2nd party were returning north after doing various (presumably) training work to the south. the 1st party, aircraft x, a high wing trainer, was returning to tix. the 2nd party, aircraft y, a low wing trainer, was returning to coi.the weather was clear and a million, a great night for visual flight rules or instrument flight rules training.1st party was cruising at 3000 feet, flying direct to lilaz for return to tix. 2nd party had been roughly paralleling 1st party at 4500 feet, a bit to our west, en route to coi.the site of the near-midair was west of cof airport/vor. the 2nd party initiated a turn and descent towards coi. being abeam and above our (1st party) wing, we were unable to spot them visually, however our graphical adsb-in display had allowed us to keep tabs on them as we cruised. accordingly, the adsb data broadcast from 2nd party -- including the descent and velocity data -- enabled us to realize that the 2nd party was forming a high risk conflict to us. their intended descent cut directly across our course, and the angle of descent had them right at our altitude exactly as they crossed our course.therefore, we initiated evasive action perhaps a minute before the would-be collision. while we were turning roughly 270 out of our 360, they crossed our would-have-been course at our altitude a bit over a mile ahead of where we began our turn.we cannot be sure, but if we had been unaware of the traffic, which we were only aware of thanks to adsb-in, there was a distressingly high probability of invisible collision (neither party seeing the other). we were doing roughly 100 kts at the time, so we would have been roughly a mile and a half further along our course (compared to 'a bit over a mile' ahead of our turn). optimistically, it would have been perhaps 3000 feet total separation, pessimistically zero feet. we can't know for sure without a detailed dynamics analysis of the mutual adsb data.we are deeply thankful we had adsb-in to save our bacon.as stated, they were above our high wing so we couldn't see them, and we were probably below their low wing so they probably couldn't see us. we had good position and anti-collision lights, and most probably they did as well, but this was probably irrelevant. we only were able to avoid the situation, take evasive action, because of adsb-in. if we did not have adsb-in we would have been a critical event, or worse.based on the fact that the 2nd party chose a descent path that generated such a high risk of conflict, most probably the 2nd party had neither visual contact (on account of us being under their low wing) nor adsb-in data. (that, or they were ignoring their adsb-in data.) only the fact that we had adsb-in prevented a (very high risk of) midair, in my opinion. see-and-avoid failed, essentially, due to the low-wing-above-high-wing phenomenon. as far as i can figure, see-and-avoid could only have been made to work if clearing turns were required before all changes in course or altitude, which is of course a non-starter in the real world.the only way this would-be midair was prevented was adsb-in. we had it, they apparently did not.as far as i can tell, there is no immediate corrective action, other than encouraging further adoption of adsb-in by any means practical in all aircraft flying in busy airspace (such as where we were). adsb-in clearly proved its merit in my eye, and should be embraced further. (not 'required', since edge cases exist everywhere, but in the typical case, adsb-in is clearly beneficial.)night-vs-day was not a factor, i believe. if anything, i find it easier to spot traffic at night, and as stated, all the lights on the planet could not have enabled us to have seen each other thru our wings, only clearing turns could have achieved that.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: ATC TRACON controller reported chronic frequency issues resulting in the inability to maintain positive control and a safe air traffic control environment.
text: i am submitting this report to formally document an ongoing and significant safety concern regarding frequency 119.3 at hcf.for an extended period of time, this frequency has presented persistent and unresolved operational issues that rise to the level of an extreme safety hazard. controllers working this position routinely experience severe frequency congestion, blocked transmissions, and unreliable communication that directly degrade our ability to maintain positive control and ensure safe separation.these problems are not isolated or intermittent. they are chronic, well known among controllers, and have repeatedly created situations where aircraft are unable to establish or maintain timely two-way communications. this has resulted in increased workload, delayed clearances, missed instructions, and an elevated risk of operational errors particularly during periods of high traffic volume or complexity.despite long-standing awareness of the issue, there has been no effective mitigation or permanent corrective action implemented. controllers are left to manage an unsafe communications environment using workarounds that are neither standardized nor sustainable. this places unnecessary stress on both controllers and flight crews and undermines the safety margins expected in air traffic control operations.i believe this issue warrants immediate technical evaluation and corrective action, including a review of frequency assignment, coverage, interference sources, and overall system design. continued operation under current conditions represents an unacceptable risk to safety.this report is submitted in the interest of protecting the national airspace system, supporting controller performance, and preventing a serious incident before one occurs.recommendation: real attention. i understand it has challenges but maybe it's time to consider moving it.

text: a fuel imbalance was noted during climb out due to imbalance alert. the fuel imbalance seemed to be rapidly increasing and the rapidly decreasing fuel on the #1 side created a feeling of time compression. as first officer and pf, i took the radios and continued as pilot flying so that the captain could focus on looking at the flight manual. at about 26, 000 feet to captain requested priority handling and requested a return to redacted with a suspected fuel leak. we were in engine icing conditions and turbulence from 10k to the time the captain decided to declare and return. i think the weather played into the decision to return earlier than we might have otherwise. leveling off didn't seem like a great option given the weather and neither did continuing to climb away from redacted.at this point, i was busy answering air traffic control's queries, manning the radios, flying the airplane, and setting up to land back in redacted while the captain ran checklists. initially a fuel leak was suspected prompting the captain to return us to redacted. but after having a flight attendant look and observe no leaking fuel, and seeing the fuel flow and quantity looking closer to normal after starting the descent, a fuel leak seemed less likely to me.upon starting the return to redacted the captain began to run the fuel leak engine checklist. when he asked if i was ready to shutdown an engine, i asked him to ensure there weren't more appropriate checklists to run as i remember a recommendation about this similar situation some time ago. at that point, we ran the fuel imbalance checklist as it now seemed more appropriate. with the throttles at idle the condition that confirms a fuel leak ('a change in fuel imbalance of 500lbs/30mins or less') was no longer satisfied. further leading us to suspect an indication issue or crossfeed problem.we had an uneventful landing. crash fire rescue confirmed we did not have fuel leaking after we landed.maintenance control since replaced 6 fuel probes in the left tank. of note the next crew had a write up about fuel indication issues in the #1 tank.

text: during a training flight into dca while conducting the mount vernon visual to runway 1, the student was flying the aircraft under my supervision. during the visual approach segment, the autothrottle was not responding as expected and remained at or near idle thrust, requiring manual thrust intervention.as the approach continued, the student became overly fixated on managing climb and descent cues and did not adequately monitor airspeed and altitude as required for the procedure. with decreasing airspeed and an increasing rate of descent, i took control of the aircraft to correct the flight path.upon taking control, i manually increased thrust and adjusted the descent rate to stabilize the approach. at that moment, air traffic control advised of a low altitude alert.from the flight deck perspective, the aircraft remained under control at all times. after the correction, the approach stabilized, and we continued the visual approach without further issue, landing normally at dca.no additional anomalies occurred during the remainder of the flight.cause: automation error and complacencysuggestions: be a bit more aware and react sooner

synopsis: Diamond DA40 Student Pilot reported a duel ECU (Engine Control Unit) indication on climb. Student Pilot returned to the departure airport.
text: this was a student solo that had an engine failure at takeoff. i began my ground roll and added full power, after rotation i saw 'engine control unit (ecu) a & ecu b fail' appear on the primary flight display (pfd). at that moment i was at full throttle (100%) but the load wouldn't surpass 64% and i couldn't climb pass 400 agl. as i pulled my flaps up to try and gain altitude and speed, there was no change in load or altitude. realizing this i made the call to traffic that i had an engine failure and was returning to land back on the opposite end of the runway.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: GA Flight Instructor reported abandoning a takeoff due to opposite direction landing aircraft on same runway. Landing aircraft conducted missed approach.
text: we were the only ones in the pattern at n51 - no one else was in the area other than the traffic of smq. winds were 240@3 so we chose runway22. by our third takeoff, we were already back taxiing runway22 and lined up to takeoff with power in already when we head a call from aircraft y saying they are left downwind for runway4. again there was no one in the pattern besides us and no other calls other than ours besides aircraft y left downwind call for runway4 - they made no previous calls to enter the pattern or anything. that's when i, as cfi, took over controls and radios and attempted to contact them at least 10 times while they were in the downwind and no response. aircraft y continued to fly the downwind for runway4 turning base and final as at this point it had been already 20 radio calls attempted to call aircraft y - not a single acknowledgement from them. they kept coming down all the way to short final and continued coming in for landing as i had continued attempting to call aircraft y. at this point, i began to start flashing my taxi and landing lights to try to get their acknowledgement and told my student to get ready to get out and go into the grass as we kept flashing our lights and calling on the radios. mind you, aircraft y only radio calls was their downwind - no base or final radio calls. it wasn't until aircraft y was roughly 100-200' above runway4 when they finally saw us at the end of runway22 when they made the call to go around and final got on the radios saying they are going around. i attempted to call them once more at which then they claim they heard us and never heard us before - even if they hadn't heard us and had something wrong with their radios, they still should be been able to see us on runway22 ready to depart the second they entered left downwind runway4.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Robinson R22 Flight Instructor reported a near miss event during the landing phase. Instructor expedited off the runway while conflict aircraft conducted a missed approach.
text: runway incursion/near miss at approximately xa:38. helicopter flight instructor was demonstrating to a student a stuck pedal scenario and was performing the landing to runway xx. instructor gave radio calls stating that 'aircraft x' was going to be landing on the runway. on final approach, runway was clear and there was one aircraft (aircraft y) in the right downwind for runway xx. we crossed the runway threshold and proceeded with our landing when we heard a base-to-final call from aircraft y. after the landing was completed the instructor brought the aircraft to a hover when we heard 'there's still a helicopter on the runway, ' from an aircraft in the 1 taxiway intersection runup area. the instructor turned the aircraft toward 2 taxiway to get off the runway and we saw aircraft y on the runway and half a taxi length distance apart (approximately 150 feet apart). both aircraft could have collided had the instructor not expedited to get off the runway. once safe on 2 taxiway the instructor asked the plane if they had seen the helicopter on the runway, which they responded with, 'no we did not see the helicopter.' instructor hovered toward parking area and discontinued flight.i believe improper traffic pattern spacing and expectation bias at redacted airport that training helicopters only use the taxiways for operations led to the near miss incident. a proper visual traffic scan of the runway environment prior to landing could have prompted the second landing aircraft to conduct a go-around maneuver.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: Zodiac CH60 pilot reported a loss of fuel system pressure during cruise. Pilot advised ATC; diverted and reported a safe and normal landing.
text: departed redacted in my experimental home-built airplane with approximately 26 gallons of fuel on board. climbed to 5, 500 msl and proceeded on route south, then southeast. all systems normal. twenty-nine minutes into my flight, flying straight and level, fuel system lost pressure and engine began to cavitate. i turned on my spare fuel pump, reduced throttle, and engine began to run smoothly. with airport directly in front of me and within easy glide range, i made a call on the ctaf frequency for redacted, reporting in the blind. reported my location, altitude, and loss of fuel pressure, and intentions to circle and land at the airport directly below me. a local pilot on frequency acknowledged my call and offered to call air traffic control on 121.5 for me. i agreed, set my controls for glide speed and landing configuration, then tuned my radio to 121.5 and hailed air traffic control. the controller confirmed my situation and location, asked me to tune to a new frequency. after changing frequency, i communicated my intentions to make a normal landing with power at idle at redacted, requesting priority handling. once on the ground i received a call from faa controller confirming i had safely landed with no injuries or damage. i reported a safe, normal landing. i determined that my newly installed fuel filters were possibly defective or contaminated. drained all fuel, replaced fuel filters, and strained the fuel while refilling the wing tanks. was able to depart without issue the following morning and began my return trip to my home. stayed over at redacted for two days to troubleshoot fuel system. arrived at my home airport redacted safely. i have a repairman's certificate for the subject aircraft and will do a thorough evaluation of the fuel delivery system now that i am back at my home airport.
