synopsis: B737 flight crew reported loss of anti skid and auto brake system on landing. Crew braked manually and taxied to ramp uneventfully.
text: planned landing at redacted via instrument landing system runway xx with flaps 40 and max autobrakes. arrival, approach, flare no significant events. captain flew on speed and touched down in zone per briefed short field procedures. after touchdown, we did not feel the expected deceleration or the nose drop from auto brakes max. captain deployed reversers, our approach target was 145 kts, approximately 120 kts during landing roll i noticed both autobrakes disarmed and antiskid inop lights illuminated. captain brought the airplane to a complete stop using manual braking and full reversers with approximately 600 feet remaining before the emas. we vacated the runway and taxied to parking without incident. after parking we completed an appropriate elb (electronic logbook) write up for inspection of brakes/tires and antiskid system, which resulted in a fault being discovered in the adiru-l system.

synopsis: Cessna 402 pilot reported engine power fluctuation during takeoff roll and rejected takeoff.
text: normal start up and run up. taxied to xxr. a corporate jet took off of xyl and was airborne before reaching xxr. i was then cleared to take off of xxr. i advanced the throttles and started the takeoff roll. all indications were normal. shortly before rotation speed i heard and felt one of the engines start to surge/ fluctuate. i noticed on the rpm gauge the right needle dropped to around 2400 and was fluctuating. i glanced at my airspeed and where i was at on the runway. i was just below rotation speed of 90 and crossing xyl. i knew i had plenty of runway remaining to stop so i elected to quickly abort and apply moderate braking. i was able to taxi off on taxi way xx. i taxied back to the gate with no other issue.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported a loss of both generators during cruise. Crew restored all systems and diverted.
text: first leg redacted-redacted started with the gate power disconnecting suddenly and we had an apu on minimum equipment list for a previous fume event. we waited for about 40 minutes for them to repair the cable to the jetway power unit. got underway late but that leg went fine.second leg redacted-redacted we were cruising at fl270 and lost both generators simultaneously. startle effect for a few seconds as the cockpit went dark and we heard all the systems shutting down and the relays powering off. first officer (first officer) was flying pilot and called 'my aircraft' and just as designed that got things moving. we realized he had no instruments so we switched roles. no autopilot so i hand flew while he began running ecam. no seat power so i had to interrupt him to help get my seat into position without losing focus on flying. airplane was slow to respond but we quickly realized she was flying fine on alternate law and manual throttles with two good engines. aircraft was in the emergency electrical configuration. we requested priority handling and discussed diversion alternates while first officer did a such a great job with the ecam that we soon had both generators up and running. he then was able to restore all the other computers that had failed. rat was deployed and we could hear and feel it running.with all systems restored we got the autopilot and auto throttle back on and decided on redacted for our diversion. talked to air traffic control, cabin crew, and passengers and let everyone know our plan. used flaps 3 for landing to keep speed up in case we lost the gens again - didn't want to lose the rat also. uneventful landing. crash crews were alerted and on standby but i didn't have them come out to runway as we were pretty normalized at that time. in the future i will have them come out.takeaway was never get too relaxed. things can change in an instant. first officer was awesome and his experience was invaluable. he had two previous priority incidents in his career and it showed. i guess i've been lucky with none until now.good communication and crm helped with the whole process. once we got over the initial shock things settled down and our training kicked in. being over many airports with pretty good weather also helped. we fly that route over water a lot and i'm sure it would have been a little more nerve racking over the dark ocean. inop apus are commonplace but i will now think more about how it can affect the situation if you don't have it. talking with maintenance they said it probably would have started and been available for electrical power if we couldn't restore the gens. definitely good intel as we hadn't really considered that since it had stickers plastered all over the buttons.cause: stay ready for the unexpected!

text: after push back from gate xx, the crew was cleared to taxi. the ca turned on the taxi light on the nose wheel, and the crew cleared the aircraft left and right to make a hard left turn to depart the gate area after the push left the aircraft straight back and still pointed at the gate. when the aircraft was rolling forward, and approximately 20° into the 90° left turn, a van proceeded to cut the aircraft off in our turn and barreled in front of us requiring the captain to apply brakes and stop the taxi in order to avoid a collision with the van. the van never looked at the aircraft, and did not slow down. the aircraft had to have the nose/wing cross over the vehicle drive lanes in order to make the left turn, and traffic was required to stop. after the van came within close distance of a possible collision, and the ca had the aircraft stopped. as the crew began our taxi again after the van had crossed from left to right the aircraft was once again moving when a different van entered close proximity from our right side. this van swerved off the road and into gate xx area in order to stay clear of the aircraft.ramp drivers not paying attention to aircraft moving in their vicinity and not giving way to aircraft as required. require van drivers to drive at a safe speed, and to give way to aircraft that are taxiing nearby them with their taxi lights engaged.

synopsis: A B787 flight crew pre-flighting the aircraft reported the crew oxygen masks were over serviced and began leaking in the flight deck.
text: this was my first flight after operating experience. during the pre-flight phase i was focused on my assigned duties, including cockpit flows, flight management system programming, and obtaining the atis. i observed the captain conducting the flight deck oxygen mask test and heard a prolonged, loud hissing sound. i initially suspected a stuck switch or regulator issue. i had the system page displayed and monitored the oxygen pressure, which was approximately 1870 psi and decreasing rapidly (1820, 1780, then about 1720).the captain stated that we needed to call maintenance. two mechanics came onboard. the captain disconnected his mask and the mechanic replaced it. at that time i had not yet performed my oxygen mask test. a mechanic then asked if my side was normal. then i conducted my test and it was normal. shortly afterward, while passengers were onboard and we were preparing for route verification, my oxygen mask began leaking with the same loud hissing sound suddenly.the captain instructed me that the mask be pulled and disconnected. i did not disconnect it myself, someone reached over and disconnected my mask following the mechanic's direction while they were still in the process of servicing/refilling the system. i just confirmed the relief pilot disconnected my mask directed by the mechanic. almost simultaneously, both relief pilot's o2 masks were leaking. i then smelled what seemed like burning protein and realized the tip of my hair had burned. i looked back and observed smoke, sparks, and heard a loud explosion.due to the high concentration of oxygen in a confined area, i was concerned about the potential for a fire and wanted to evacuate the flight deck immediately. however, the relief pilot was positioned behind my seat and i did not want to block the escape route by moving my seat aft, nor did i want to move closer to my oxygen mask cavity. i attempted to exit by squeezing between the center console and my seat. my right ankle became caught in the narrow space, causing me to lose balance and sustain a scratch to my right arm. i was able to move clear. the captain directed the #1 fa to initiate a rapid deplaning of passengers.cause: follow sop. do not conduct any procedures outside of established protocol unless specifically directed to do so.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B767-300 flight crew reported multiple EICAS and status advisory messages during cruise. Crew referenced QRH and landed without incident.
text: while in cruise, we received three eicas advisory messages:eicas monitorcpt primary flight display (pfd) monitorfo pfd monitoralong with eight status messages:cpt pfd monitor, display unit (du) interface, first officer pfd monitor, eicas monitor, r electronic flight instrument system (efis) control panel, graphic generator unit (ggu) sw configuration, du degraded, and l ggu.we ran the qrh and continued, as all indications remained normal.while on vectors for the visual approach to runway xx into redacted, we called the field in sight. the captain (pf) began to maneuver the airplane on the base leg. around 2000' msl, all three large display screens (lds) went blank, except for a gray line down the middle.the captain continued to hand-fly using the head-up display (hud), which remained unaffected and displayed good data. the crew requested a vector out to a longer final from air traffic control since, in the confusion, we had lost the airport. air traffic control placed us in a left downwind extended position for runway xx. after being established on a roughly 10-mile final, the captain first advised the first officer to press his own pfd transfer button, but nothing happened. next, the captain asked the first officer to press the pfd transfer button on the captain's digital cockpit panel (dcp). after that, the center screen data reappeared with the eicas information, however, neither pilot's lds returned.we discussed declaring an emergency, but since we were on a final, with good standby data, good hud data, and a cavok day with crystal clear skies, and now on a 5-mile final, we decided against it. we felt it would create more work and communication and take away from the task at hand, which was safely landing the airplane. we were focused on getting on the ground in case more cascading failures were forthcoming.the captain landed the aircraft without incident and taxied to the gate uneventfully.after landing, we noted additional status messages, including terrain sys and tcas fail, and made an additional write to record losing the screens and those messages.cause: aircraft sytem failuresuggestions: likely unavoidable due to failed aircraft system.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a UAS during approach. The crew was made aware by ATC and no evasive action was taken.
text: while on the instrument landing system 25l approach into lax, our flight experienced a near midair collision (nmac) with a drone aircraft. the previous aircraft reported a drone sighting to socal approach. we were advised of the drone sighting by socal with about 30 seconds advanced notice. so, i as the non-flying pilot, was focused on looking for the traffic. i was able to sight the drone about 5 seconds before the aircraft passed about 50 feet off our left wing at about 10, 400msl. our position was just west of the krain intersection. i immediately pointed the aircraft out to the flying pilot. because of the size of the drone, and the brevity of the encounter, initially, it was difficult to tell how far away, what altitude, or exactly what the object was. but at the time of the initial sighting, it was obvious that we would not collide with the drone. as the drone passed off the left wing and slightly higher than our altitude, the drone maneuvered on its side. i could clearly see (either the top or bottom) that the aircraft was in the shape of an x and about 1 meter in size. after the encounter, i reported the nmac to socal approach. the aircraft following ours also reported the sighting, so i knew that our aircraft did not collide with the drone. it was still flying at the same position about 1 minute later.suggestions: better adherence to regulations regarding the operation and separation of drone aircraft, by the drone operator.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury
synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported an NMAC with a departing airplane at destination. Crew took evasive action and continued to a landing.
text: on approach into redacted airport, we were descending to 7000 and noticed traffic flying towards us from below that was climbing out of redacted. the crew had briefed prior to arrival that there would likely be lots of ga traffic in the area that may or may not be transmitting on radios. we had the tcas mode set to above and below to allow us to see all traffic around us, so we spotted the aircraft that was headed towards us at least 20 miles out. after observing the clouds with the understanding that we would have to descend into the airport visual flight rules and remain clear of clouds, the crew came up with a game plan to make a slight left turn where there was much more blue sky versus the broken layer to the right, and after the left turn, proceed to fly over the airport above traffic pattern altitude and enter the left down for runway xx. after we had the airport in view within 50 miles, we requested to cancel instrument flight rules with redacted center, and before they approved our cancellation, they notified us of the traffic that we had on tcas, but were not talking to them and did not have an idea where they would be going. we did not have them insight at this point, but decided to continue with the instrument flight rules cancellation and focus our efforts on traffic avoidance with what we could see on tcas while also looking for the traffic visually. as soon as we canceled instrument flight rules, i initiated a descent to 3000 feet and started a left turn to avoid the traffic, as they were climbing out and at this point, were about 5 miles ahead of us and about 1500 feet below our current altitude. we could not initiate a right turn due to the cloud layer that would not allow us to descend to the airport visual flight rules. the left turn would give us plenty of clear sky to descend, while also taking us away from the oncoming traffic. soon after we initiated the left turn and the decent to 3000, we both noticed that the traffic started a right turn towards us, and we attempted to continue more to the left to avoid the traffic. we then got a tcas traffic advisory, and soon after received an resolution advisory to climb, noticing that the aircraft was 400 feet below us at this point and still heading towards our direction, even though we had started the turn away from their anticipated path. i immediately and promptly disconnected the autopilot and initiated max thrust and a pitch up attitude to comply with the resolution advisory that was commanding between a 1500 and 2000 ft./min. climb to avoid the traffic that was climbing below us. as i pitched up (we were at 210 kts. at the time in clean config), we experienced the stick shaker for one second which i respected with a slight relief in pitch up to stay below shaker aoa while keeping climbing. this happened in the few seconds that it took for the engines to spool up to apr thrust, and once thrust was achieved, there was no issue with maintaining the climb to meet resolution advisory requirements. the resolution advisory only lasted a few seconds as we climbed up to 7600 feet from 6500 feet. after we were clear of conflict, the first officer (first officer) got a short visual on the traffic out his right window below us. we were tuned into the afis at this point, but they did not provide any traffic avoidance. the first officer let them know that we had performed a traffic avoidance maneuver and had been giving position reports to them since we were 60 miles out from the airport periodically. after we were clear of the conflict, we reset our altitude to descend to 3000 as planned to fly over the airport and eventually enter the pattern on the left downwind. all three pilots in the flight deck were fully strapped in via five point seatbelt, and did not feel that the maneuver was overly aggressive, but instead was an appropriate reaction to the resolution advisory. about one minute after the maneuver, we received a call from the cabin that the first officer answered. the flight attendant called and asked what had happened, and the first officer responded that we had performed a traffic avoidance maneuver. the first officer asked if everyone was ok, explained that we would be landing in five minutes, and asked how the flight attendants were doing. the flight attendants mentioned that they had taken a stumble, but that they were ok at that point and they occupied their jump seats for landing. they also mentioned that all of the passengers were seated, and there were no reported injuries. at this point, we were glad that everyone was ok, and continued into the airport and landed uneventfully. we did not declare an emergency, since at this point everyone was doing ok and we were clear of any conflicts. after parking at the gate and starting the deplaning process, the forward flight attendant person a let us know that he was feeling dizzy and was having some pain in his ankle and requested to sit down. we also got a better picture of how person b was feeling, and she said she fell against a wall and had some scratches and soreness on her body from the maneuver. person a said he had fallen and hit his head during the maneuver, and twisted his ankle. i asked them if they would like to be evaluated by medical personnel, to which they both responded that they would. i immediately asked operations if they could arrange for medical personnel to give the flight attendants an evaluation on any injuries they may have sustained, as well as to hold boarding for the next flight. there were no customer reported injuries, but the flight attendants said that they felt unable to continue to work back to redacted. the station felt that the quickest and safest way to arrange medical personnel to see them would be to have a taxi service take them to the nearest clinic, which they done promptly. myself and the line check airman that was with us riding the jump seat down to redacted stayed with the plane, while the first officer went with the flight attendants to the clinic. over the next hour or two, i as the captain talked with the dispatch coordinators, maintenance, operations personnel, and the first officer talked with the chief pilots, providing a rundown and answering any questions that they had. we followed the procedures outlined in the fom, and the airplane required further inspection due to our abrupt maneuver after fdr download. i made a write up in the aml (aircraft maintenance logbook) and logged it with maintenance control, making sure to explain that we had achieved apr thrust in the maneuver. we continually received updates on how the flight attendants were doing, despite the poor facilities in the area and lack of good cell service. the flight attendants were given some pain medicine for their muscle soreness, but were not diagnosed with any serious injuries besides what has been described as soreness and bodily scratches. the entire crew was on the same page that the maneuver was necessary to avoid the oncoming traffic, and everyone worked extremely well and professionally together, including dispatch, scheduling, maintenance and management teams. the redacted operations station was extremely helpful throughout the whole process in arranging all of the logistics. there were no customer reported injuries during this entire incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737 Captain reported the right pack was inoperative and while following the after-takeoff checklist with the bleeds off as required by the MEL; the aircraft was depressurized for a short period of time while climbing.
text: this aircraft had a right air conditioning (ac) pack that was inoperative. the release had several steps associated with configuring this panel during several phases of flight. the minimum equipment list required takeoff and landing to be bleeds off.the operation was normal until the after takeoff checklist. following the steps for the right pack inoperative, there was a short period of time that the aircraft was climbing while depressurized.maybe boeing did a copy/paste and didn't think about reversing switches? the left pack inoperative would have a slightly different procedure, however, because the isolation valve remains open. so it's not exactly a mirror image procedure.following the minimum equipment list steps for the right pack inoperative, the isolation valve is closed, so when i turn the engine 2 bleed air on, it doesn't do anything. the next step is turning the apu bleed air off, which is what started the depressurization. i paused for a couple seconds to allow some stabilization like would be done in a normal bleeds off takeoff.after realizing the issue, i quickly turned the engine 1 bleed air switch on. the aircraft began pressurizing again, and there was no further issue.for the right pack inoperative after takeoff checklist, the engine bleed air switches should've been reversed. yes, engine 1 bleed air and apu bleed air would be on at the same time potentially causing the dual bleed air light. however, this is addressed in the notes of the minimum equipment list already so boeing is aware and is ok with this light for a few seconds that it might be illuminated.the risk here is something like this happening at a high elevation airport and triggering the cabin altitude warning.there's one other minor issue that could be addressed as well. for the landing checklist, it tells us to turn the apu bleed air on. however, there's no mention of turning the apu on prior to that point. so here's another potential of depressurization.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: Fractional First Officer reported it was difficult to see the hold short markings for Runway 11 at TQPF at night.
text: we started our duty day at xa:30 with a live leg from redacted to tqpf. we were fuel limited due to potential showers in the area and wet runway. we were forced to divert to redacted when approach refused the hand-off from center and were vectored 100 miles south of redacted which put us in a fuel critical situation and made the crew decision to land at redacted. upon landing in redacted fuel recorded was roughly 1900 lb. after deciding with passengers and company we took fuel and departed for tqpf. flight to tqpf was uneventful, passengers left and we turned the aircraft for our 91 position to redacted to clear customs then 91 position to redacted to get me home.as we were taxiing out of the fbo in tqpf, tower advised us to hold short of runway 11 on taxiway a due to a departing aircraft on the runway. tower asked us if we were holding short of the runway on alpha taxiway to which i acknowledged we were, tower advised us we had passed the hold short markings and told traffic on runway to cancel takeoff clearance and we proceeded down runway 11 to taxiway e and hold short of taxiway d to give clearance for departing traffic. tower controller was extremely friendly and we explained to him that due to it being almost" dark we had a hard time locating the hold short markings.air traffic control notified us of aircraft position on taxiway.cause: tqpf has an fbo ramp right off of runway 11 and had very poor lighting due to it being almost dark it was extremely hard to see the hold short markings for runway 11. fatigue was also an issue as we diverted and had to deal with customs in redacted and tqpf and also knowing the airport was only a day only airport when night time was fast approaching at tqpf.we moved to a different taxiway on the airport.we should have stopped the flight in redacted when we diverted but due to passengers "need" to get to tqpf we decided to take them to tqpf only to realize we were feeling rushed when we waited over an hour to get out clearance to redacted with night time operations fast approaching."

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported during their approach in IMC conditions descending below the FAF altitude resulting in a GPWS terrain alert and the flight crew executing a go around.  The flight crew's second approach also resulted in a go around and the flight returned to the departure airport.
text: before departing, weather reports at the destination were already deteriorating. we knew we would be flying an instrument approach and because of the short flight briefed the instrument landing system on the ground. once on descent into the destination, the approach controller notified us that the rnav to the opposite runway was in use. we asked to use the instrument landing system but the controller notified us that instrument landing system approach end tower visibility was reported as being poorer. we accepted the rnav and briefed and set up for the approach. this was compressed due to our closeness to the field and the fact that the approach was now straight in vs opposite direction. however, we completed required checklists and briefings and upon reaching the faf altitude everything seemed to be in order and the aircraft was properly configured. i remember seeing the autopilot capture the faf altitude at 8700msl, at which point the captain rolled in the missed approach altitude. we verified gps appr at 2 miles, computed a groundspeed at 1 mi, and at .2 prior to the faf the captain rolled in a vsi and began his descent. i noticed that the vnav snowflake was at full top deflection already, at which point i cross checked our altitude and noticed that we were already quite a bit lower than faf altitude, in the vicinity of 8200msl. at first i told the captain to level off, but i quickly realized we had probably been below faf altitude since before the faf, almost simultaneously the gpws issued a 'terrain, terrain' alert, so i called for a missed approach. the captain executed the missed and we took vectors out to check our fuel and elect whether or not to try another approach. after discussing the incident and thoroughly preparing for another approach, we attempted the rnav again. this time it proceeded without incident, though we did not see the runway at minimums due to poorer than reported visibility and performed another missed approach, ultimately diverting to our alternate. cause: i believe causal factors included being rushed on the arrival/approach, which gave us little time to set up and probably caused us to become task saturated and more likely to miss errors. we did not complete all checklists until on the approach, which tied up our attention on non-flight path items. also at the time, due to rapidly changing conditions, tower was not recording the full atis which required us to receive the complete weather report from the controller once on tower frequency, another source of distraction during a critical phase of flight. we probably became too fixated on the 3-2-1 checks prior to the faf at the expense of a more complete cross-check. although i do not know exactly where the descent below faf altitude was actually initiated, i suspect it was slow and gradual, making it easier to miss.suggestions: we could have built time for ourselves on the approach by requesting delay vectors or slowing earlier, which would have eased the pace and given us mental headroom. we should have considered discontinuing the approach when we were still running checklists while commencing it. as flight path management is always primary, we should have been incorporating the altitude more regularly into the crosscheck just prior to the faf to detect a deviation, and were probably too trusting that the autopilot would keep us at the previously captured altitude (assuming we actually captured it and did not misinterpret indications).

text: while returning from a solo cross country, my student suffered a lateral runway excursion upon landing on runway xx at redacted. surface winds at redacted were below 5 knots so crosswinds were not deemed a factor by me. prior to commencing his flight, i reviewed his cross country planning and determined that the entire route would be visual flight rules, and the winds would stay well within his demonstrated capability. my student had previously completed two other solo cross countries, and had demonstrated safe practices during dual cross countries with me in the airplane. after the excursion, my student secured and shut down the airplane and called me for assistance. during a post incident discussion, my student admitted that he landed in a side loaded condition which caused a loss of directional control. he also further admitted to me that he knew he should have gone around. this incident further illustrates the importance of not only landing with the longitudinal axis parallel to the centerline of the runway, but also the importance of commencing a go around if the parameters of a stable approach and landing are not met. it is not unusual for incidents such as this to occur in the training environment, especially at a student pilot level. however, i plan on taking corrective action by having him file a report, obtain further training through the wings program, and extensive flight training focusing on maintaining directional control on landing, with and without a crosswind component.
