synopsis: General aviation pilot reported on go around; conflicting traffic also made a go around resulted in taking evasive action and a NMAC event.
text: day 0, xa:13-31, hdc after-hours uncontrolled class gaircraft x, aircraft yreference: faa advisory circular no: 90-66b related to the right-of-way rules under title 14 of the code of federal regulations (14 cfr) part 1, § 1.1 (traffic pattern), and part 91, §§ 91.113 and 91.126 regarding safe entry into part-time non-towered operating airspace.aircraft y operating under company demonstrated unsafe adm at hdc during non-controlled hours on day 0, xa:25. aircraft y came in on a visual flight rules straight-in for runway 13, interrupted established traffic (3 planes) on runway 18 despite atis reported winds favoring runway 18 (180 degrees at 4kts). aircraft y claimed 10 mile straight-in final for runway 13 less than 7 miles out. they did not state any instrument flight rules approach nor appropriate fix callouts, did not enter left downwind for the established runway in use, and did not request any delay of established traffic to allow them to priority land-- which i would have happily done so for them. i was visual flight rules when preparing to land and only looking outside and listening to the callouts and assumed at supposed 10 miles or 5-6 miles as they stated incorrectly, i was getting out of their way quickly.when aircraft y called short final on runway 13 as i was about to land on runway 18, i immediately called 'going around for landing traffic, ' as i did not feel comfortable since they were coming in faster than anticipated. in which they responded also, 'going around, ' after i had already called going around… then i immediately called out, 'left 360, ' in order not to merge with aircraft y on our go-arounds. terrifyingly, aircraft y then also called a left 360 into me and my runway 18… this was completely baffling and unsafe, especially at 500'… and there is absolutely no reason for aircraft y on runway 13 to be doing a left 360 into my runway 18 space… at the very least they could have done a right 360 away from runway 18 traffic or proceeded on their official missed approach of climbing 2000' straight to cobim and hold per the hdc rnav runway 13 procedure if they were in fact on a practice approach, which they never claimed to be on until after their go-around.this was a very unsafe scenario, and i hope that such situations can be avoided in the future. i continue to reflect on what else could've been done to have avoided this situation, and i'm personally very grateful it didn't end in tragedy.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: C560 Captain reported that while they were distracted; they taxied off the taxiway and resulted in the main gear being stuck in the mud.
text: while taxiing to the active runway, i was momentarily distracted and looked down and thus removed my focus from the task of steering the airplane on the taxiway. when i looked back up i saw that the airplane was about to taxi off the pavement and into the grass. i tried to correct but the grass was wet and the ground was soft due to a rain storm the past evening and the right main wheel went onto the grass. because the ground was soft, the wheel immediately sunk into the mud. i stopped the airplane but it was stuck and was not going to move back onto the taxiway. the lesson learned is that when taxiing an airplane the pilot's focus should be 100% on the task of taxiing. the pilot should not try to look at the checklist, tune a radio or do anything other than focus on taxiing. fortunately the airplane was not damaged nor was any equipment or other aircraft involved or damaged. distraction can be a very dangerous thing. pilots must remain focused on the task at hand at all times.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: CL 650 flight crew reported during cruise flight experiencing an un-commanded climb from their assigned altitude. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft and descended back to their assigned altitude.
text: we were flying a red eye oceanic crossing from redacted to redacted at fl280. we were in the vicinity of a nearby storm and on top of a layer. we were getting a wave like action approximately 1hour 39 minutes into the flight which was about 150 nm west of redacted in redacted airspace and suddenly the plane performed an uncommanded climb abruptly. we disconnected the autopilot and immediately descended back down to fl280. so much happened in a matter of seconds. no cas message was announced. air traffic control said they noticed we climbed to fl290 during this event. no tcas event happened. no other aircraft were involved. (note local time of event was based off of redacted local departure time)

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: C172N instructor reported miscommunication between aircraft in practice area resulted in evasive action and a NMAC event.
text: my student was flying the aircraft in the left seat and i was observing from the right in aircraft x. we took off from xxl at redacted and a piper seminole, aircraft y, took off after us. they proceeded to climb above us after departure, overtaking us but not passing on the right. after just having departed the class d, redacted tower advised traffic overhead and we confirmed and halted our climb to 7, 500' and soon thereafter our intended 8, 500' for maneuvers. at this point, after the seminole had flown over top of us, i told my student to resume their climb to 8, 500'. considering the seminole was climbing and going southeast away from the multi-engine practices areas to the southwest, i figured they were enroute to another airport or with redacted approach. however, once we got near the practice areas we turned south to follow the road and the seminole was in the practice box with another 172 maneuvering nearby. i scanned for the seminole, noting on my foreflight efb that we only had around 300' separation, and once they seemed on a converging path flying west, i called them out by tail number on the practice area frequency by stating our geographic position, altitude, and intentions and asked what they were doing in the area. a pilot responded 'west side of the box and we're doing steep turns' before proceeding to turn right into us, which was when i actually saw the seminole as it banked. i had my student start a descent from 8, 500' out of caution and estimate we were around 8, 300-8, 200' before i took over. initially by sight i thought they were turning south - away from us - but then realized the opposite. our garmin 430 with ads-b in also alerted us, and foreflight audibly warned me of aircraft at the same altitude in my headset. i took controls from my student, cut our power to idle, and dove down to 7, 800' as the seminole went overhead before then proceeding southeast. i maintained visual separation until distance dictated otherwise. due to the sudden and dangerous nature of the situation i did not call on frequency in the moment while i tried to get the aircraft under control and i do not believe the seminole made any practice area calls thereafter.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported that due to the student's excessive speed and panic; resulted in student's loss of control and taxiway excursion.
text: the student was taxiing to runway xx via taxiway 1. i brought the throttle to idle and told him to smoothly apply the brakes. the aircraft suddenly turned to the right. i asked for the controls and applied the left brake but the student froze and remained on the brakes preventing me from overriding his inputs. all three wheels went into the grass. no damage was done to the plane or any airport equipment. the problem was caused by not beginning the braking action sooner. to prevent this from happening again. i will have the student practice slowing down at lower speeds.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: M-20 R Ovation pilot reported flying an unstable approach resulting in multiple bounces on the runway and a prop strike. The pilot was able to taxi to the ramp.
text: landing redacted runway xx. approach to the runway was stable, but i carried excess speed over the threshold (approximately 10 kts). initial touchdown resulted in a bounce due to the extra energy. i applied power in an attempt to minimize bounce but failed to execute an immediate go-around which is the proper recovery procedure. this resulted in a pilot induced oscillation. the aircraft contacted the runway multiple times, resulting in a propellor strike.winds were calm and there were no other extenuating circumstances. the engine remained running and i was able to taxi off the runway and to parking. upon engine shutdown i observed each of the 3 blades of the propeller were bent. the landing gear also appeared compressed from what i can only assume is the impact from porpoising. i have reviewed the mooney poh and recovery procedures for bounced landings. should this happen in the future i will execute an immediate go-around if the aircraft bounces or if my airspeed is not on target at the runway threshold.this incident, to the best of my knowledge, does not meet the reporting requirement for an accident per 49 cfar 830.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A general aviation pilot cleared direct to SUS airport reported ATC assigned them an altitude below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: while being vectored to sus, i believe i was left on the wrong frequency from central illinois. the controller gave me instructions to descend to 2000 feet. to which i read back 2000 feet. i was also told to go direct to the airport. i was aware of the towers in the area and was going to cross directly over the top of one. i decided to halt my descent at 2300 feet and ask air traffic control. he responded that i needed to climb to 2600 feet. i also realized i could barely hear him. he gave me the correct frequency of 126.5. there was clearly a misunderstanding of the correct altitude. i'm not sure what happened but the tower was very apparent in my synthetic vision and in the window. had this been in instrument conditions or if i was less aware of the area the situation could have been closer. also it seems weird that stl approach routinely assigns altitudes with hundreds of feet like 3500 and 2600. most other controlled airspace operate at regular thousand foot intervals.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Corporate pilot reported on the initial climb not meeting a crossing restriction resulting in flight towards terrain. ATC issued a low altitude alert and the pilot climbed the aircraft away from the terrain.
text: after initial takeoff i was focused on terrain ahead and staying below 1750 as per sid but was short of my next waypoint at or above on the sid (i believe above 3300 required)we were visual vmc and air traffic control advised i was low as i was turning and climbingno other response from air traffic control and a non-eventful flight

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: GA pilot reported during cruise flight having an NMAC with another aircraft that was being controlled by ATC. Both pilots took evasive action to avoid a collision.
text: i was flying my cessna 182 departing from redacted westbound. i was cruising at 6500 msl which was my chosen cruise altitude. i was not on flight following but i was monitoring redacted approach redacted.x. on foreflight i noticed that a jet that i now know was an embraer erj-145lr, flight abc, was headed in my direction head on. the jet was descending while i was cruising level. i noticed the jet at xa:45, maybe a distance of 10 miles away. since it was headed toward me, i decided to follow standard faa recommended advice and turn right to avoid the traffic, around that same time of xa:45:00. at xa:45:10 the replay indicates that approach instructed the jet to turn left. this put the jet into direct and continuing conflict with me despite my having changed course. approach was warning the jet about me so i heard the jet state that it had me in sight. approach also called out to see if i was on frequency which i was, and i responded. i also gained a visual sight of the jet albeit when it was quite close to me. ultimately i watched it pass in front and below me by about 500 feet below. the embraer pilot mentioned that an resolution advisory was triggered.our approach controllers do excellent work and do the best they can under tough circumstances. in this case i view the controller's decision to turn the jet left as a mistake that contradicts aviation safety principles, which should be discussed at redacted tracon so as to reduce the chances of a mishap. i don't view myself or the embraer pilot as having committed any errors in this situation.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: C560 Captain reported trying to obtain IFR clearance in the air after being unable to while on the ground and shortly after departing there was an RA that the reporter responded to but resulted in the aircraft overshooting into Bravo airspace.
text: i filed an instrument flight rules flight plan redacted to redacted. i was unable to raise redacted departure on the ground despite numerous attempts. no notam was present regarding the frequency redacted.x being unusable, and this was the frequency listed on foreflight which was current. i troubleshot the radios, connections and headphones, but still unable to contact redacted departure to open my instrument flight rules flight plan. there was no phone number in my foreflight info page to call except for fss redacted. i decided to depart visual flight rules and pick up instrument flight rules in the air. i departed runway xx, conditions were clear visual flight rules weather, with a fair amount of ga traffic. after takeoff, i called redacted departure but no answer. shortly after departing, i received a resolution advisory instructing me to climb, climb, climb. i increased power to full power and climbed and saw a cessna 172 or 152 close enough that i could see the pilot. i estimated 500 feet away, 200 feet vertical separation. it was the closest i had been to a collision, and it was very unsettling causing an adrenaline response. i climbed to avoid a collision with full power. i overshot into the bravo airspace and immediately attempted to contact air traffic control at the departure frequency in foreflight redacted.x. i tried both radios, confirmed switch on headphones was on and not to the oxygen mask, but still unable to contact. i went to 121.5 and asked for any pilot to provide redacted departure control frequency and was able to reach redacted departure.this was a preventable situation, and if i had been more persistent in calling fss i believe they would have been able to find a phone number for me to call air traffic control before departure. given the busy ga traffic on a nice day, it would have been much safer to obtain instrument flight rules clearance on the ground prior to departure. the second factor is that after climbing out at full power in response to the resolution advisory, i should have focused not on calling air traffic control but on getting the aircraft out of bravo airspace. this was a very preventable event which should not happen again if i follow these recommendations.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A Cessna Skynight 320 pilot reported a rough running engine and a return to the departure airport.
text: normal operations observed during taxi, run up and take off up to 1000 ft. agl. at 1000 ft. agl, when pulling the power back for cruise climb, the right engine manifold dropped more than usual with given throttle input and immediate engine roughness occurred. power was added back to take off power and the roughness subsided. a second attempt at reducing power gave the same results. it was at this time that i noticed the fuel flow on the right engine was excessive at 45 gph and cht's at 150 degrees. i told air traffic control i wanted to return to redacted. air traffic control asked me if i would like to have priority handling and i said not at this time. i left my take off power in turning back to the airport, but once i got closer to the pattern i started to slowly reduce the power. the engine roughness got worse with the reduction of power, and i needed to decrease and increase power repeatedly to prevent the manifold from dropping significantly. the right engine manifold would fluctuate from matching the left engine to 4-5 inches below the left engine. fuel flow remained excessive even with slight leaning. i decided not to continue to lean the engine after entering the pattern. when i was handed off to tower, i decided to request priority handling since i could not reduce my power without the roughness and yawing getting worse. i landed with no incident or injury to myself or my passenger.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: Light aircraft instructor and student reported a taxiway excursion after landing at RST and clearing the runway; during a training flight; resulting in the aircraft becoming stuck in the mud. The crew called ATC to get help in removing the aircraft; no injury or damage occurred.
text: night flight from redacted to rst. cleared for the option runway 13 by rst tower. after landing instructed by air traffic control to exit on a8, taxi to 13 via a, and remain on tower frequency. once exiting 13 on a8, the left main gear became stuck in mud beside the taxiway. the taxiway and the color of the mud were similar so it was difficult to distinguish the taxiway from the mud. once the left main became stuck the mud pulled the right main in as well. attempted to exit the mud but were unable. no visible damage was done to the aircraft. upon post flight inspection, mud on tires, struts, and leading edge. no evidence of prop strike or flat tire upon inspection.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A C1 flight instructor demonstrating a power off 180 landing lost control of the aircraft resulting in a tail strike.
text: while practicing power off 180s with my student, i took the controls to demonstrate. we were landing runway xxr, and the wind was 120 at 14 gusting 24 knots. i lined up the aircraft over the runway and descended into ground effect. as we were floating to the 1000 footers, i continued to increase back pressure on the yoke to increase our angle of attack to make it to the 1000 foot markers. just before touchdown, the wind decreased, and we fell toward the ground. due to the nose-high attitude, the tail struck the ground before the main gear. the nose came down smoothly, and we taxied off the runway. we inspected the tail and saw that the tail tie-down ring had been sheared off. no other structural damage was noted at the time. i downed the aircraft in flight schedule and called our school's mechanic to inspect the aircraft before others could fly it.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: operating a small uas on day 0 in my neighborhood taking recreational video. attempted to unlock the airspace via the app and the site said it was not required. i was under the impression that this area (this side of the river) was under 200 feet. per the laanc website, this area is 100 feet. will unlock via laanc when flying from this location in the future. there was no near miss or conflict with any people, vehicles or aircraft.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying in a restricted military alert area without authorization.
text: on day 0, i operated a small uas for approximately 15-20 minutes along the coastline of the trail. my flight path was primarily over the coastline and occasionally over the water. while my maximum altitude reached approximately 80m (262 ft) agl, i spent the majority of the flight at a much lower altitude, well below the 400 ft recreational limit. i was accompanied by three friends who acted as informal visual observers. during the flight, they spotted a manned aircraft flying at a much higher altitude. although the aircraft was well clear of my position and way above me, i proactively lowered the uas even further as a safety precaution until the aircraft passed.after landing, i realized i had inadvertently entered the nas whidbey class c / alert area 680 without prior authorization. while i typically verify airspace restrictions on a planning app before every flight, this instance was a complete oversight due to being distracted by the scenic beauty of the landscape. no safety hazards, property damage, or injuries occurred.corrective action and prevention: to prevent recurrence, i have updated my physical pre-flight checklist to include a mandatory 'airspace go/no-go' step. i will now use a dual-verification method by checking two independent airspace awareness applications (e.g., laanc and drone buddy). furthermore, i have adjusted my drone's flight software settings to permanently limit the maximum altitude to 60m (197 ft) to provide an automatic safety buffer below the legal limit. i have also briefed my frequent flying companions on how to assist with identifying potential 'no drone zones' using these apps before we launch.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: TRACON controller reported having an NMAC with one of the aircraft being an airspace violator and additionally their STARS display background settings preventing them from observing all targets on the STARS display resulting in the controller's inability to provide safe ATC services.
text: ii noticed earlier a untracked target transitioning from east to west over the sna c. i vectored aircraft x around it to the north and then a couple of minutes later i cleared them for the va (visual approach) to 20r. as they started turning south, that previous target had blended into the hazy background and turned toward them about 3 miles away. i eventually noticed the conflict and issued a safety alert to aircraft x who quickly reported them in sight. i consider this to be a near mid air. since the recent implementation of stars update, the screen background was arbitrarily increased to maximum which made the black background white, fuzzy and gray. because of this ridiculous change, i am now unable to clearly observe and identify aircraft. all of the contrast has been lost and all definition has been removed. my eye muscles continue to be in pain due to having to strain to see the information on the display through the white fog.the black background is now a gray haze with a white halo around the edges which severely elevates the distraction and takes away from focus and scanning.recommendationif the faa wants to continue to lock out the controllers from adjusting their own settings, these dangerous events will most likely continue at an alarmingly increasing rate.the faa is still on notice that this change was not discussed with the controllers here at sct and no input or feedback was solicited.the faa is on notice that they continue to make safety of the nas a low priority and that the decisions of others, that don't operate these workstations, are more important.the faa is on notice that these events are being documented and that the faa is ignoring the warning signs that safety is at risk.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B777 Captain reported returning to departure airport after receiving a forward cargo door warning in cruise flight.
text: shortly after leveling off at fl330 we received an eicas message, door fwd cargo.we pulled up the checklist and immediately. released we were not going to redacted. i advised air traffic control, requested a descent to 8000 feet, per the checklist, and requested a turn back to redacted. since we could not continue the checklist until reaching 8000 feet. we called for the relief pilot to return to the flight deck, briefed the lead flight attendant, contacted dispatch and maintenance control. we decided rather than land at redacted over weight in gusty crosswind conditions we would dump fuel. we coordinated with air traffic control and began dumping fuel. at xa:52z 8000 feet n41.xx.x w070.xx.x 138.7 pounds on board. and completed at.xb:21z 8000 feet at n41.xx.y w073.xx.y 42.2 pounds remaining. we completed the door fwd cargo checklist and fuel dump checklist preceded to redacted via redacted redacted vxxx redacted direct. landed without further incident and continued to the gate. the crew was excellent, we completed the many tasks in a timely manner.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Fractional jet First Officer reported GPS jamming issue during cruise flight in domestic airspace. The GPS signal returned to normal after a period of time; and the flight was cleared to a fix on the arrival.
text: while in cruise at fl430 over northern nevada we experienced gps interference and/or gps jamming near w-ar641a and the reveille north moa. we, along with several other jets on frequency reported our outages and requested headings to ensure that we did not somehow end up in special use airspace. there was at least one other company aircraft also affected, possibly at least one other tail from a different fleet. signal returned approximately 15 minutes later. we were 5-10 miles from where the jps thought we should be by that time. we told air traffic control and they cleared us to a fix on the arrival. flight landed uneventfully.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a momentary stick shaker occurred on departure following a wake turbulence encounter.
text: upon climb out, the sid obaka 3d, out of fra, after being released as requested for relief of (250 below 10k) we were accelerating and cleaning up - retracting flaps on schedule. when the first officer commanded flaps up" we were accelerating and above flaps up maneuvering speed. the flaps had not yet reached full up and we encountered apparent wake turbulence. our bank angle at that time on the sid was approximately 5 degrees.. we encountered a brief stick shaker, immediately the stick shaker subsided and we continued op's normal.cause: either a glitch in vnav or we were heavier than what the table represented."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B-777 pilot reported a low oil quantity then a low oil pressure EICAS message on one of the engines during cruise. The flight diverted to an alternate airport.
text: at approximately xa:30z on day 0, during cruise at fl300 west of redacted, the eng synoptic automatically populated on the lower display unit and indicated 2 quarts oil and a lo flag on the #2 (right) engine. all other parameters were normal. we reviewed the aml (aircraft maintenance logbook) and contacted dispatch via sat phone with maintenance control joining the conference call. the aml showed a previous in flight zero quantity indication on the same engine that returned to normal after landing.we continued while monitoring the engine. a slight decrease in #2 (right) engine oil pressure was noted, followed by continued incremental decreases. we contacted dispatch and maintenance control a second time and advised of our decision to divert to redacted. center was notified.we were cleared to redacted via initial heading then joining the redacted for runway xx. approach was normal except for the #2 (right) engine showing lower oil pressure than the #1 (left). a precautionary flaps 30 landing was planned and executed. at approximately 4, 500 feet on final, an eng oil pres r" eicas message appeared. with landing imminent, we continued the approach and reviewed actions in the event of an engine failure or commanded shutdown, including confirming and commanding flaps 20 vref.a precautionary landing was completed and we stopped on the runway for cfr (crash fire rescue) inspection and were escorted to the gate.cause: major oil leak"

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a critical ground conflict after exiting the landing runway with an aircraft on an intersecting taxiway.  Reporters stated the second aircraft was on ramp frequency and that this configuration risks a potential collision.
text: we were flying to phl i was pf and made a routine landing on runway 35. we exited the runways at the proper speed on to the e3 as tower instructed us to do and contact ramp at spot 14. we had transferred controls to the captain at 60 knots on the runway. as exciting on e3 we heard tower instruct an aircraft y to hold short of us exiting the runway. they were northbound on e. they were already on the ramp frequency and entering the ramp at spot 14. they did not stop and we were forced to stop on e3 to prevent a ground collision.cause: using spot 14 as a entry spot to the ramp when planes are landing 35 and exiting onto e3suggestion: if planes are landing 35 we should not have planes taxing north on e to enter the ramp past spot 13. it's hard to see the planes exiting the runway and they are going to already be on the ramp frequency.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a critical ground conflict at CLT while entering their company ramp.
text: we were holding on the orange line at 27e in clt which is a transition point to the next ramp control. we contacted the next ramp control (north ramp) who told us to continue on the orange line to our gate xx. we started our taxi when suddenly aircraft y came screaming in [gate] xy directly in front of us at a high rate speed without talking on the frequency and we immediately both slammed on the brakes to avoid a collision. we queried ramp control about the aircraft y that cut in front of us and she just repeated our clearance to taxi to the gate. we asked again what had happened and she said she would investigate. we were on the north ramp frequency at approximately xa:30 local time day 0 as aircraft x. i am assuming that aircraft y had been cleared into their gate on the east ramp frequency but they were moving quite quickly for entering a ramp nonetheless.miscommunication at ramp control nearly caused a collision at [gate] xy.suggestion: investigate this incident and educate controllers on how to coordinate better at transition points.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A220 pilot reported engine vibration and Hydraulic Pump malfunction and diversion to nearby airport.
text: cruising at 39, 000 we started to get a vibration. we got a l eng thrust reverser fail caution message that came on momentarily followed by hyd edp 1a fill caution msg. at this time the vibration got louder. we ran the checklist for edp (engine driven pump) 1a fail caution. as we followed the checklist, when turning off the ptu (power thrust unit) the hydraulic pressure started to drop off. the checklist drives us shut down the edp and use the ptu (power transfer unit). with this accomplished we still had a loud vibration going on. we discussed it and with the fa's (which they had already called up for the vibration) and made the decision to divert. we got on with dispatch/ maintenance to discuss the situation. we chose to divert to redacted as it was the most reasonable station in front of us. we made the decision to divert due to the continued loud vibration that was still going on. hyd system 1 continued to work normally with the use of only the ptu. the landing gear was put down 4-5 miles early to make sure we had no issues with its operation working solely on the ptu. flaps were moved separately from gear to not overload the system. landing was normal and performed by the first officer as he was pf. redacted center gave priority handling for us after initial contact about the situation.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported a ground conflict with a large UAS during taxi.
text: we had just operated flt abcd into redacted and we were in the process of turning the aircraft to operate flt abce back to redacted when we heard an unfamiliar call sign on the ctaf making traffic pattern announcements (redacted tower was closed for the night). the callsign in question was a little difficult to make out. shortly thereafter the flight was closed out and we announced our pushback onto taxiway 1 and our intent to use runway xx for departure. during the pushback the mysterious aircraft announced that he was back taxiing on runway xx and would clear at taxiway 2. at that point we were abeam taxiway 2. i looked out of my left window and was more than a little surprised to see a military mq-9 reaper drone sitting on the active runway, waiting to exit onto taxiway 2. i instructed my pushback crew to push us deep past taxiway 2 so the drone would have enough room to clear the runway. in addition, i warned my pushback crew to use caution as the drone would be operating in close proximity to us. we announced our intention to push past taxiway 2 and the drone operator responded that he had us in sight and would clear the runway. i did then observe that the sensor turret on the chin of the drone was pointed at us which seemed to be how the drone operator was able to see us. the drone then proceeded down taxiway 1 ahead of us. we disconnected from the pushback and announced our taxi. as we started down the taxiway we contacted redacted center for instrument flight rules release. redacted center advised that he was unable to release us as the drone had not yet cancelled its instrument flight rules flight plan. we contacted the drone operator over the ctaf and requested that he cancel with redacted. he complied with our request and redacted released us. we continue to follow the drone down taxiway 1, assuming that he was going to pull into one of the hangars to the right of the taxiway. this was an incorrect assumption as the drone proceeded all the way down to the approach end of runway xx and came to a stop short of the runway. we pulled up behind the drone at which point my taxi lights illuminated the drone and gave us our first really good look at it. i was quite alarmed to discover that the drone had two underwing weapon pylons with each pylon occupied by a brace of anti-tank missiles and here i was pulled up short directly behind this fully armed and un-safed aircraft. i could, at this point, clearly identify the yellow markings on the missiles indicating that they were live ordinance with a high explosive fill. after a brief halt, the drone crossed the active runway and appeared to head for a small, partially lit parking area on the far side of the runway. we then announced our departure and took off uneventfully from runway xx.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: B737 Captain reported they continued their takeoff roll after Takeoff Hold Lights illuminated and they observed an aircraft on short final for the intersecting runway.
text: i was the pilot monitoring while the first officer performed the take off from redacted xxl. we were aware of the 787 on final to xxr as the controller had made reference to it in the take off clearance. we were above 80 kts call as the last lights of the runway status lights/take off hold system illuminated just as the last light elements disappeared under the nose. i recall seeing 96 knots in the hud (heads up display) as we were well into the takeoff roll just past 1 intersection. i looked and saw the 787 was on very short final, looked ahead and could not see any other threats entering the runway and decided it was best to continue. as we flew through the intersection the tower was already telling the 787 to go around, i again looked right and could see the 787 was in the flare and low enough that it was causing mist and water to displace out from the jet blast and wing downwash. they appeared to be just short of 2 intersection on xxr. we continued our departure with no other issue or anything being said by air traffic control.the illumination of the lights so late in the take off caused me some confusion as to perform an rto (rejected takeoff) or continue. i quickly was thinking it is not a condition we brief to reject for above 80 kts, and if i did reject it might put us stopped right in the intersection of the runways possibly in the path of the 787. continuing seemed best but what if the lights were for a threat of another vehicle or aircraft we did not see yet and not the 787. in the end i believe it was the best decision given the circumstances but it brings up some deficiency in our awareness and reaction to these lights. had the lights illuminated earlier with more in view, i would have been more inclined to stop. however, only seeing the last lights illuminate in a split second as they disappeared from view created great uncertainty. i tried searching our company documents for reference to these lights and could only find one article from an report, day 0that discussed a similar event with a crew out of redacted. this leaves us with the guidance that is found in the aim as our only reference. inclusion of the thl lights in the take off rejection considerations section of the aom/fom and training would be appropriate.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A C172 Flight Instructor reported a NMAC when they were entering the pattern at a non towered airport.
text: cessna 150m flying back to redacted airport, heard radio call from aircraft on a final approach, aircraft #2 called turning crosswind for runway xx and aircraft #3 on a left base runway xx. cessna 150m called 4 miles southwest of redacted inbound for a left downwind runway xx. visual flight rules day, using visual avoidance, cessna 150m flew at 900 ft. entering in downwind runway xx, made radio call entering left downwind runway xx. roughly 30 seconds later a 172l calls for a position clarification of the downwind aircraft. 150m calls that we are on the downwind for runway xx with the local high school directly to our right, calls that we see the upwind traffic in sight to our left. traffic of 172l above and off to our left, called to confirm we had 172 traffic in sight. the 172l next call gets blocked intermittently but states they are extending their upwind. after 150m lands, the 172l landed as 150m was clearing the hold line. after the 172l takes back off the pilot makes a call that their transponder is not working and is remaining in the pattern, will make radio calls. 150m - should have entered the 45 downwind at more of a 45 rather than straight in. come in at 1000ft instead of being below traffic pattern altitude. 172l- if they were concerned about intermittent transponder, they should have stayed grounded to fix the issue, called their upwind, extended their upwind for entering downwind traffic, slowed down in the pattern to allow for spacing for landing traffic. 150m was visually trying to avoid crosswind traffic, did not immediately see upwind traffic. pilot in 172l seemed flustered due to transponder issue, there were 4-5 aircraft in the pattern and making radio calls. contributing factors were stress with the amount of aircraft in the pattern, 150m was on training flight with new student which is also a distraction, both pilots in incident are aware how how close they got to each other. in the future for the 150m we will enter in on downwind using a true 45 degree. take a wider route coming in from the east to avoid upwind traffic. continue to monitor frequency and see and avoid other traffic.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: A Cessna 310 pilot reported an electrical failure while in cruise due to improper maintenance procedures and continued to their destination.
text: during a visual flight rules flight from redacted to redacted at 10, 500 feet msl. as described above, the avionics began failing. first the garmin 430 then the aperro transponder. i transmitted to redacted approach, as i had been using visual flight rules flight following and informed them of an electrical problem. i received a broken acknowledgement after which all of the avionics failed except for the garmin g5 ai (attitude indicator) and dg which continued to operate on internal battery. the aircraft ammeter indicated in the center position, no charge or discharge and the aircraft had no way to monitor bus voltage. i descended to 8500 to stay out of the adsb required airspace and proceeded to my destination, avoiding all airspace requiring a transponder. upon arrival in the destination area i manually extended the landing gear and made an otherwise uneventful landing. the problem was found to be the left generator output wire being secured directly to the intake manifold by a plastic zip tie. the wire chaffed through and shorted to ground. this was in front of the ammeter so gave no discharge indication. the right hand 35 amp generator accepted the load but it was later found that a 50 amp regulator had been installed causing the generator to exceed its output rating, overheat and fail. after this, the battery drained and the system failed altogether. this is a maintenance failure. improper securing of electrical cabling and installation of the incorrect regulator for the installed generator. the cessna service manual even makes it clear not to mismatch these components in a precautionary note.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Epic E1000 pilot reported a malfunction of the #1 Air Data Computer and Primary Flight Display altimeter.
text: during a routine climb in imc, the aircraft's adc1 altitude indication froze at fl230. prior to the freeze, the altitude had intermittently lagged and the vsi had shown abnormal spikes. shortly thereafter, the indicated airspeed on (primary flight display) pfd1 froze, began declining, displayed a yellow caution, and was eventually flagged invalid with red x's on both pfd1 and the standby gi275.we were assigned fl270. pfd2, operating on its independent adc, continued to indicate a normal climb consistent with reaching fl270. based on the instrument behavior, i suspected a static system blockage or freeze affecting adc1. i transitioned to hand flying using pfd2 indications and advised air traffic control that our instruments appeared unreliable. i informed them that pfd1 was frozen at fl230 while we were continuing the climb to fl270 based on the alternate adc. air traffic control confirmed they were observing fl230 via mode c.during this time, the autothrottle was responding to the erroneous low indicated airspeed by attempting to add power. esp protections in the g1000 nxi attempted to re-engage, increasing workload during a high-task phase of flight. i eventually disconnected the autothrottle and used my free hand to disable esp in order to reduce automation interference and maintain stable manual control. there was an airbus aircraft behind us requiring vertical separation. i stated that we were climbing to fl270. some confusion developed regarding whether we were maintaining fl230 or climbing to fl270 due to the discrepancy between what air traffic control was observing on their display (derived primarily from mode c) and what we were indicating on pfd2.i had previously understood that air traffic control altitude depiction was derived from both radar returns and mode c, and that discrepancies between the two would be readily apparent. in this case, air traffic control was primarily referencing mode c altitude, which remained fixed at fl230. although separation was ultimately maintained and no loss of separation occurred, the mismatch between actual altitude and transmitted mode c altitude created the potential for reduced situational awareness and separation risk from both pilot and controller. the issue resolved later in the flight. post-flight, maintenance evaluation of the static system was requested.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: GA pilot reported they initiated a go-around from short final to a non towered airport when they observed a business jet on the runway taxiing opposite direction.
text: the awos-3 at redacted is out of service (notam). winds at nearby airports to the west southwest of redacted had winds around 240 -270 degrees. nearby airports to the north were reporting gusty winds from 300 degrees. to get a better sense of the winds at redacted, i stayed in the traffic pattern and made several approaches looking for flags or wind socks as i passed over the runway xx before executing a missed approach. there was no intention to land on the first three passes down the runway at usually at 25-50 feet agl, ending in missed approaches to stay in the pattern. on perhaps the third approach on final approach, a business jet was seen moving slowly towards and less than a couple hundred feet from the approach end of runway xx closer to the south side of the runway. he passed an exit taxiway. i assumed he was back taxiing to the approach and of runway xx or alternatively he had just landed. less likely in my mind considering the winds.i added power and went missed approach at a couple hundred feet above the runway and went around the pattern again. sensing no cross winds on the low passes in the pattern for runway xx, i proceeded to land uneventfully. when i parked on the ramp, two men approached and falsely claimed i almost hit them on the runway after they landed on runway xy. i told the jet pilots, i was a little surprised they landed on runway xy considering the winds clearly favored runway xx. the jet pilots then stated the winds had just turned around. the reports i later printed out showed the winds had not changed and favored runway xx for 40 minutes.a representative of the airport later called me to ascertain my perspective of the events. i sent him the wind data on which i had based my decisions. when it was apparent he was not going to clear the runway prior to my landing, i executed a missed approach back up to pattern altitude.i called out my position reports, crosswind, downwind, base and finals. i never heard the jet pilots announce position reports for an apparent straight in approach.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: PA28 pilot reported engine vibration during approach.  The pilot continued the approach and landing.
text: we were instrument flight rules and popped out of the clouds and had an aggressive engine shudder. i cancelled instrument flight rules and requested to go to tower to land as soon as possible out of precaution. they were landing runway xx but i requested opposite runway which i was closer to (runway xyl). i was cleared to land by tower on runway xyl and landed without incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737 Captain reported First Officer side airspeed indicator failure and return to departure airport.
text: climbing through 16, 000 feet the first officer's (first officer's) airspeed indicator failed with a red flag. after checking all my instruments i determined my airspeed indications and engine indications were completely normal. i then told the first officer that i had the flight controls and the radios and to get out the qrh and go to the back of any tabbed page and look for 'airspeed'. the only checklist for our situation is the known as the 'airspeed unreliable' checklist. having done many sim sessions i am very aware of this 8 page checklist that covers a myriad of possible airspeed malfunctions and things can get extremely confusing when trying to navigate this checklist, and how our relatively stable situation could be easily rectified by doing a simple test. i have seen the exact malfunction on the ground perhaps over a hundred times during my career.it is a very common maintenance issue. maintenance will be called out to the plane and will simply recycle the airspeed circuit breaker. my intention was to return to redacted regardless of whether the first officer's airspeed was working or not and then write it up upon arrival. but if we could get the first officer's airspeed indicator working again i would most likely not need to request priority handling. so, i instructed the first officer to find the first officers airspeed circuit breaker but not to pull it yet. when the circuit beaker was found and we both agreed that that circuit breaker was, absolutely in fact for his airspeed indicator, i instructed him to pull it and reset it. the result was exactly what happens on the ground. the airspeed indicator reset and went to the appropriate airspeed. in our case it went to 296 kts., the same as my airspeed indicator. i then tested if his airspeed indicator would follow mine by simply accelerating to 320 kts. as we accelerated my airspeed indicator increased normally and his stayed frozen on 296. i knew immediately that we would need to request priority handling. moments later, due to the discrepancy between our airspeeds, his airspeed indicator again flagged out.we requested to return to redacted and requested priority handling. we landed on runway xxr with no incidents, returned to gate and wrote up the maintenance issue in the logbook. i recognize, as a captain i am to simply followed the qrh checklist, however, given the circumstances, i was very concerned about making a relatively simple problem far worse by trying to navigate a very complex checklist in our qrh and end up possibly making our situation more dangerous.

anomaly: Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: B747-400 flight crew reported they turned the wrong direction on initial climb and received a Low Altitude Alert from ATC.
text: it was a 2-man crew redacted- redacted. we got to the airplane, and i got my vest to do the walk around, and then of course the security check when i went upstairs. by the time i got to the flight deck, it seemed like almost nothing had been taken care of. the captain (pf) was sitting in his seat with the paperwork and not doing anything. i sat down, and he handed it all to me, said the route wouldn't uplink and to please type it in manually and then verify the routing. i told him i would, but he also needed to verify it. i had to ask him a few more times before i saw him take the flight plan and verify everything. in doing this, i saw they still had xx closed (there had been discussion about it being reopened prior to departure because we were expecting the zzzx sid), departures were off xyl, and we needed a new clearance. i asked the captain to join me for a voice clearance, it was again an argument from him, almost hostile, and he told me not to call and ask. i did as he said, keeping it in the back of my mind for closer to departure.thankfully, the captain noticed a few trucks were driving up and down the runway (xx) and asked me to go ahead and check to see if our departure would be changed. i asked him again to join me on voice, where we were given the zzzzzx from xyl. i loaded it into the box and had him verify it. after this, he sent for performance, and when it came up, he asked me to load it in the box, but would not let me verify the zfw from the document- yet again, i had to ask multiple times, and at this point i thought to myself 'how much more of this before i should get off the airplane?'. i did not put in the performance since he would not hand me the document. he ended up doing it himself and then getting up. i then looked over the document and performance numbers to verify it was correct.with no further issues, we got the setup done, and he gave a correct briefing, accurately highlighting the left turn to heading redacted in our departure, contingencies including 2000 or 4.0, whichever comes first. i very clearly remember watching him put everything in the mcp (mode control panel), including arming lnav and vnav, because he did not do it before the briefing, and i was trying to think of a way to ask him or do it myself without making him upset again. i also clearly remember verifying on the nd (navigation display), the sid looked accurate, because after the redacted heading, it was vectors then redacted, so the magenta lines looked a little odd at 5 scale.we did the appropriate checklists and procedures and eventually ended up at xyl, cleared for takeoff. after reaching 2000, the fd (flight director) indicated a left turn, and he stayed on runway heading. he then asked me if it was a right or left turn. i told him left, but could not recall the exact heading, and the legs page had already sequenced, so i grabbed my ipad to see. at this point, he had already started a turn to the right, and air traffic control asked what we were doing. i told them a turn to the south, and they gave us a low altitude warning as we were rapidly approaching the mountains off xyl.for the remainder of the flight, i felt i could not get up and leave him alone in the flight deck, as even after this event, he operated in a nonstandard manner. he would want to get up to get food, etc., and i had to strongly tell him multiple times to give me control of the aircraft instead of just saying 'i am going to the back'. after each time, i told him, 'okay, go ahead and give me the airplane first'. he eventually started doing so without me telling him.the pf should have entered the route, and this likely would have helped him remember which way to turn, and kept the operation standard. the pf also should have followed his command bars or automated when he realized he wasn't sure what to do, after verifying the fmas (flight mode annunciators).after the nonstandard events leading to the deviation, i should have worked harder to better anticipate the next nonstandard thing, be it from the fom or an air traffic control instruction, and been stronger in my stance to stay within the clear lines we are given to operate. which i did for the remainder of the flight, as given in the last part of my description narrative.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported encountering wake turbulence just after touchdown at CLT from a preceding heavy jet that resulted in the nose of the aircraft veering sharply to the left.
text: we were informed by air traffic control that we were following a heavy for the instrument landing system 36r. we followed assigned speeds. we stayed at or above glide path breaking out at about 700 feet. we touched down just past the aiming point numbers. just as the nose wheel touched down, the nose veered hard to the left. i added right rudder nearly to the the stops, bringing it back on centerline. i believe that wake turbulence from the heavy in front of us hit the tail causing a weathervane effect.suggestion: not knowing the exact separation from the heavy, it's hard to say. i noticed a slight right quartering tailwind on final that turned to more of a headwind on landing. perhaps the vortices were pushed forward by the tailwind and then across the runway as it settled with more of a crosswind.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Air carrier technician reported while troubleshooting a crew oxygen leak; they noticed smoke coming from the electronics bay.
text: my partner and i were assigned an etops [inspection] on aircraft x. during our inspection, we found the crew o2 bottle was reading 1300 psi. we then replaced the bottle, no leaks noted, sitting in the cockpit and completed the etops check, and went to sign off paperwork. we received a gate call, from the flight crew, that the captain's mask was leaking after he tested it. when we arrived at the cockpit, the captain had disconnected the mask from the box and explained to us that it wouldn't stop leaking. we then connected the mask, and saw that the mask was leaking, and disconnected it again, due to safety reasons and not wanting to leave the mask connected and leaking. we went and ordered a mask and replaced the mask, and no help. at that point we decided to change the stowage box, and at that point, i went downstairs, turned off the bottle, went back, replaced the box and mask, and when i turned the bottle back on to leak check, all the other masks started leaking as well. my partner told me to turn the bottle off, which i did. at that point, we contacted our lead technician, to let him know what was going on. he came out, and i went back downstairs to the o2 bottle, saw smoke in the e&e area, and called our crew chief. at that point i called upstairs, and found out that there was an issue there. after the flashover, i then removed the o2 bottle from the plane.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported the UAS flew above the authorized ceiling during an automated mission due to the automated app being set to meters; not feet.
text: i was flying a spexi automated mapping flight and the drone went higher than authorized. my laanc authorization was only good to 200 ft agl. (drone autonomously flew to 270 feet agl). i expected the automated mission to be under 200 feet agl, since i had already obtained laanc authorization for 200 ft agl in that grid zone. i immediately cancelled the flight and returned the drone to homepoint. (the drone was above 200 feet for less than 2 minutes i estimate). i reported the problem to spexi for bug consideration after cancelling the flight.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A B787 First Officer reported temporary uncommanded speed increases while in cruise due to severe mountain wave turbulence.
text: we were in a cruise descent from 40, 000 feet to 36, 000 feet in lnav / vnav at .853. strong winds from the west over 120 kts. at approximately 38, 500 feet, i noticed the air speed was increasing at a rapid rate. i mentioned to the captain watch your air speed. at that moment he was distracted putting on his headset as the airspeed was increasing even more rapidly, whereas i reached up made sure the throttle's were at idle and grabbed for the speed brake. as i began to deploy them, the captain at the same time grabbed the speed brake handle and he pulled towards full deployment. he grabbed the controls at that point, clicked off the auto pilot as vmo was exceeded and not trending towards a correction. this caused the entire speed tape to show full red. i called out climbing, and the captain mentioned still descending as there was a conflict between the altitude tape and the vsi. vmo was exceeded by about 15 kts for a duration of about 20 seconds. once we were stabilized at 36, 000 feet and the autopilot was reengaged, i made a report to air traffic control that we had just experienced a very strong mountain wave. a maintenance write up was then reported for this exceedance. maintenance met us upon reaching the gate.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a lightning strike on final approach that resulted in significant damage to the aircraft.
text: while on approach we experienced a lightning strike. at the time we were imc in moderate rain. radar did not indicate thunderstorms in the area. no systems were lost and all indications remained normal. we continued the approach and landed. we notified maintenance upon arrival, and they noted significant related damage to the aircraft. the aircraft was taken out of service.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported that a lightning strike caused the Captain side instruments to fail which resulted in a return to the departure airport.
text: on climb out from redacted the aircraft was struck by lightning at approximately 10, 000ft. immediately the auto pilot disconnected, the stick shaker on capt side activated continuously, airspeed disagree message and aoa disagree message appeared. we determined fo instruments were more reliable and fo was now flying pilot. priority handling was requested and return to redacted was requested. dispatch was notified, ias disagree check list was accomplished, and fas were briefed. there were no noticeable control issues. an approach and landing were accomplished uneventfully. airport fire rescue inspected the aircraft after landing noting no visible damage was noted. we returned to the gate and the aircraft was written up. at this time the aircraft log write up is still open noting damage to the capt aoa, capt pitot, radome and surrounding area.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B777 Captain reported a loss of control due to severe mountain waves and wind shear at cruise altitude.
text: at fl370 experienced moderate to severe mountain wave. aircraft had an uncommanded climb of 400 feet with speed 5 knots into red over speed band for 10 seconds with idle thrust and full speed brake having no affect. then an uncommanded loss of 500 feet and 20 knots below commanded speed of mach .85 with max continuous thrust. aircraft could not accelerate to normal airspeed and we requested fl350.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: ERJ 175 flight crew reported that after takeoff; they disregarded ATC instructions to turn right due to another aircraft on their right side which was a missed approach from a parallel runway.
text: taking off rwy xxl redacted on the redacted sid tower instructions were to turn to heading 110 and climb to 10000 ft and cleared for takeoff. at approximately 40 kias i heard another aircraft on tower frequency declare a missed approach so i was mentally prepared to hear tower instructions to the aircraft to deconflict us as i knew the missed approach would place the aircraft in our previously cleared path. upon rotation and climbing out i noticed the tcas indicated a target at +300 feet above and in amber. at approximately 700 to 800 feet the tcas issued an resolution advisory to descend which i did immediately as i had already almost leveled off so as not to hit the missed approach aircraft. i also chose to fly the runway heading initially vs tower instructed heading as the latter would have placed us even closer. tower never once issued any instructions to myself to do anything other than the initial one to fly 110 heading and climb to 10000 ft. the missed approach aircraft came as close as .08 nm and within 100 feet according to info i have been told.cause: the lack of subsequent missed approach procedures to allow separation from a previously cleared departing aircraft and one executing a map.suggestions: improve air traffic control handling and plan for the possibility of a missed approach for every arriving aircraft and its consequences in re to previously assigned instructions to departing aircraft.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air taxi pilot reported the MYNN Runway 10 hold line markings are in an odd spot and are too close together for a jet aircraft to fit between them without hanging over into the runway area.
text: landed runway 14 at mynn. my pm and i had briefed a long rollout to avoid a lengthy wait for runway crossing into the ramp. we were instructed by air traffic control to exit the runway at taxiway b and hold short of runway 10. we exited the runway and immediately realized that the hold point for 10 was much further back than we anticipated, and that the space between the hold short line for 14 and 10 was only about 20 to 30 feet apart. there was insufficient room for our airplane to fit between the two lines without hanging over them. additionally there were planes landing on both 14 and 10 so we were unable to cross the runway.we noticed when exiting the runway that the hold short lines were so close together it was hard to decipher which one was for what runway. and very easily could have been crossed if we were not as attentive as we were. a fatigued crew likely would have crossed unknowingly due to the expectation of the hold line for 10 to be closer to the runway.cause: the runway hold line markings are in an odd spot and are too close together for a jet aircraft to fit between them without hanging over into the runway area.we taxied in as far as we could to maintain a safe distance from both runways. this probably meant that we were hanging over each line by approximately 5 feet. but we were unable to notify air traffic control due to frequency congestion and the fact that there was an aircraft landing on runway 10 and runway 14.suggestions: a note in company app to alert crews of the odd placement of the hold line and the insufficient space for aircraft to safely clear both runways.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Ramp
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported Ground Control did not advise the flight crew the intentions of another aircraft and that aircraft then proceeded to turn into a closed spot. The closure of this spot as well as another spot is not indicated on the AMM nor is there any signage.
text: taxi out terminal, ramp cleared us to spot 23. ground control cleared us 17r ek - l. approaching spot 23 first officer noted 2 aircraft approaching on the right. ground did not tell us the intentions of the aircraft approaching from south on k. we held at spot 23 watching traffic approaching from south on k as we were unsure of where they were going. first aircraft turned into the ramp next to us at the (non-existent/closed due to construction) spot 24. captain set the brake.from the time we saw the aircraft was turning into spot 24 until they were already committed and past us was a very short time, approximately 5 seconds. we could not alert the aircraft or controllers as we were on ground frequency and they were on ramp control. the aircraft did not contact (impact) our aircraft. the second aircraft stopped on k.relief pilot called ramp to query whether the first aircraft was cleared into the ramp, they said no" and that spot 24 was not a spot due to closure for construction. it was unclear what their actual clearance was.10-9 airport moving map (amm) chart does not depict closures. as it is, the chart leads one to believe spots 22 and 24 are open. this is contradicted by jepps chart dfw 60-7a-4t which shows construction closures.change amm chart to show closure of spots 22 and 24 in alignment with jepps chart dfw 60-7a-4t. spots 22 and 24 closure signage in the field is inadequate. add clear, large signage on field indicating spots 22 and 24 are closed.ground control did not advise us of the taxi intentions of the two aircraft. ground control should advise fellow aircraft of the intentions of those around them."

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported they had to stop suddenly to avoid a collision with a vehicle crossing their path while taxiing at CLT.
text: after push back was complete from gate xx in clt we were given clearance for a right turnout and to join the line outbound. after clearing both sides we began turning right. there is an access road that passes close to the drop point and a truck was approaching us from behind on this road. as we made the turn the truck sped up and sped past us. he wasn't visible till half way through the turn, i needed to slam on the brakes to avoid colliding with the truck. i called back to the fa's to make sure they were ok. after conferring with everyone we decided to continue the flight. the driver of the truck needs to be addressed and the ground staff who use the access roads at clt need to be reminded that aircraft always have the right of way.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B767-300 Captain reported a lightning strike on initial climb resulted in the autopilot and HUD malfunctioning and a return to departure airport.
text: we were climbing out on the redacted departure. there was a radar return at our 1-2 o'clock in the vicinity of our turn to the south. as we climbed out, we could see clearly underneath the clouds and there was no precipitation from the return. aircraft y had departed just before us and went through the area with no complaints. as we entered the cloud, the total air temperature (tat) jumped up to +14c. as we secured the engine anti-ice we got a small flash of st. elmo's fire followed by an explosion and brilliant flash of blue light. the head-up display briefly turned a blue color from the normal green. it sounded like a stick of dynamite going off rather than a crack of nearby lightning. my hands and teeth felt like i had briefly grabbed a bare wire and my ears felt like they did when i was too close to a grenade simulator explosion. the explosion came from somewhere around the tat/pitot probes. i coupled the autopilot so i could gather my composure and it seemed to have a hard time holding airspeed. given all of this information the first officer and i decided that the most prudent course of action was to return to redacted to have the aircraft inspected. the prospect of continuing to redacted at fl400 (our flight plan alt) did not seem worth the risk if we had sustained damage to the nose of the airplane. cause: air traffic control vectoring us near the radar return caused this to occur. i thought about asking for an early turn, but given all the other information, it seemed like the turn was acceptable. suggestions: insisting on turning early would have prevented the incident. next time i find myself in a scenario like this, i will be more insistent on an early turn. just because it is cold outside doesn't mean there's not sufficient energy inside a radar return to cause something like this to occur.

anomaly: Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported Ground Proximity Warning during initial climb out of HOB airport.
text: at hobs airport, the tower cleared us to redacted airport as filed. on takeoff, tower cleared us on a left turn course which is what we complied with. afterwards, we retracted flaps and checked in with center, and he gave us direct to diesel at 6000ft and to climb and maintain fl230. at the same time, the egpws went off while we were climbing out. once we were 20mins into the arrival, air traffic control asked us where we were going. i responded, that we were direct to chlly for the mscot4. air traffic control then vectored us off the arrival and told us to expect the drllr5 from mport. after clearing us direct to mport air traffic control notified us of a possible pilot deviation.cause: some contributing factors was that we had momentarily leveled off while accelerating to 200kts after retracting flaps.suggestions: i should have confirmed the clearance with air traffic control after the egwps went off and we should have kept at least a 500ft per min climb.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: CRJ-900 pilot reported losing braking power on the icy ramp approaching the gate and striking a baggage cart.
text: flight diversion recovery flight to redacted. on the recovery flight to redacted after landing poor taxi conditions lead to very slow taxi to the gate. approaching gate xx the captain lined up with what we thought was the lead in line for the gate as the ground crew scrambled to get vehicles out of the gate area. the line was completely obscured by snow and ice. once we were lined up we started to taxi into position almost immediately the left wing walker threw up an x with his wands because they had missed a baggage cart that was in the safety area. the captain stopped and we waited as two of the walkers tried to push it out of the way by hand. they moved it and signaled that we were clear to start pulling in again. we were moving super slowly, cautious of the ice and trying to find the line the whole taxi but especially when entering the gate area. as we were pulling in the captain noticed the wing walker on his side throw up the x again as we had gotten close to the baggage cart they attempted moving. the captain stepped on the brakes in an attempt to stop the aircraft but we started sliding on the ice and slid to the left bumping the baggage cart.the aircraft only came to rest after the captain cracked the thrust reversers. after investigation and coordination with the ground crew and airport ops with clearance we decided it was best to have the tug back us out and tow us in rather than doing it under our own power. which was a good decision because even the ground ops tow vehicle was not able to get traction with us. the ramp was sprayed and sanded twice before they got the grip to get us to the gate. after we arrived to the gate we ran all procedures as necessary. on post-flight walk around it was found to have a cracked nav light cover with no other damage to aircrafti believe the cause for this event was primarily the poor ramp conditions first and foremost. had the ramp not been icy, or snow covered the aircraft would likely have been much closer to centerline to start and would not have slid further towards the cart during braking. i think that had either the ground or flight crew stopped and said that the ramp needed to be cleared first that would have saved this event from happening. this is very easy in hindsight but is something i will pay more attention to in the future and not be afraid to refuse a parking spot. i think a secondary cause was the ground crew giving little to no directions as we were entering the ramp area while having better reference to where we should and should not have been, the marshaller had sticks up and was waving straight in until the walker signed the x.in the future i will be more forward about refusing a parking spot if ramp conditions are poor or at minimum request extra caution from the ground crew. better training for ground and flight crews about what are and are not acceptable ramp conditions would also likely result in better safety and fewer events like this happening in the future

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the BUF Runway 5 ILS was intermittently unreliable.
text: during the instrument landing system runway 5 into buf, we noticed the morse code identifier was hard to hear, but we had positive localizer and glideslope indications. during intercept we decided to disengage the autopilot because it was notam'd to not be flown coupled but we noticed we were losing localizer indication intermittently. we struggled to maintain lateral course and when we were about to report it to the approach controller, he noticed we were off course and he offered us to break off and come back and try it again. we accepted it and performed a soft go-around. we notified the fa and passengers.on the second attempt, we also lost localizer indication intermittently and brought it up to the controller and in conjunction with him, we decided to attempt the instrument landing system one more time but this time to do it from outside the (if) zobso. in that second attempt, during the soft go-around, since we were hand-flying and got task saturated during the climb, we missed our assigned altitude of 3000 feet for a few hundred feet and during that correction we were also given a lower altitude of 2300 feet, and during descent we were late to perform our soft go-around profile and when doing so we noticed our speed was at around 221 when we retracted the flaps from 22 to 9 degrees. we completed the checklists and with the high workload also thinking about a plan b, we decided as a crew to back up the instrument landing system with the rnav 5 since the ceilings at that moment were just above mda. the aircraft was landed safely.due to high workload, we didn't contact dispatch until at the gate.suggestion: next time, perform the soft go-around in a timely manner.
