anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: A Piper Saratoga pilot reported loss of directional control during landing resulting in a runway excursion.
text: during a landing rollout in a piper pa-32r (saratoga), the aircraft experienced a violent, high-frequency vibration and a sharp pull to the left, resulting in a low-speed runway excursion into the grass. no damage was sustained to the aircraft or airport property.initial assessment. initial symptoms, including a 'humming' noise during taxi and an apparent lack of symmetric braking, suggested a mechanical hydraulic failure or master cylinder bypass.post-event analysis and corrective actions. i have taken the following proactive steps to ensure this does not happen again:technical consultation. i consulted with a certified a&p mechanic to inspect the braking system. while the hardware was found to be within limits, the inspection highlighted the extreme sensitivity of this specific aircraft's braking system compared to other models in the fleet.diagnosis of human factors. through diagnostic taxi testing with the mechanic, i identified that a subconscious 'left-leaning' posture during the flare, combined with an off-center seating position, led to unintended 'brake pressure' on the left toe brake.instructional intervention: i have scheduled additional proficiency training with a flight instructor recognized as a subject matter expert in this specific airframe. sop implementation: i am incorporating a standardized 'cockpit stance checklist' into my landing flow, which includes seat positioning. ensuring specific seat-track notches for optimal leg angle.neutral position check: a 'heels-on-the-ground' verification callout during the flare to ensure zero brake engagement. conclusion. this event was a combination of aircraft-specific sensitivity and a subtle ergonomic error in pilot posture. by standardizing my 'stance' and enhancing my tactile connection to the machine, i have mitigated the risk of future directional control issues. and currently doing instruction with the cfi that is also most proficient with this particular type of aircraft for proficiency and familiarization before i use this particular aircraft for personal uses. my goal is proficiency and safety. i took the time to fully investigate the matter cooperatively with the club, a&p and other cfi, to address the issues and make sure that we resolved the problem.

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: A Citation pilot and PA28 flight instructor reported the Citation was overtaking the PA28 on final to a non towered airport. The instructor pilot reported a NMAC. The Citation pilot reported they had the PA28 in sight and maneuvered to avoid.
text: during a cfii training flight in my aircraft, i was teaching my student how to give vectors to final for the rnav xx approach into redacted with waas (wide area augmentation system) disabled. we, aircraft x, a piper pa-28 gave ourselves vtf (vectors to final) at 2000ft msl approximately 8nm ne from the airport. we turned into and captured the fac (flight augmentation computer) of rnav xx with no other traffic on an approach into redacted for runway xx. we descended 500fpm until reaching 1500ft msl, the faf altitude listed on the approach plate. we were driving to the final approach fix, level at 1500msl approx 6nm from the airport when aircraft y made a 10nm final call over the redacted ctaf frequency. the citation did not appear on our traffic map on the g1000 nxi mfd (multi-funcion flight display) until he was nearly 1000ft above us and i saw the traffic on the mfd display a downward arrow, indicating the citation's descent. in a matter of less than 30 seconds, the citation was approximately less than 1 mile behind aircraft x, and 500ft above me. this is when i got the tcas alert and immediately grabbed flight controls and took evasive action, banking the aircraft nearly 60 degrees and turning 90 degrees to avoid a collision from the citation.my airspeed at the time of the evasion was 78kts and the citation, aircraft y was 201kts according to ads-b exchange data. i started the evasion at xa:36:30. if i had not taken the aggressive and immediately maneuver, i confidently believe the citation would have crashed into me, aircraft x and killing myself and my student. no radio contact was established with the pilot of aircraft y outside of his initial 10nm final call over ctaf and a short final radio call that i could pick up. after rolling wings level i made a radio call telling the pilot of aircraft y that i had to break off the approach to avoid being hit by him. he never replied to the radio call. i gave vtf again for the approach into redacted and landed safely. prevailing conditions of the flight were visual flight rules, cloud ceilings were approximately 3000-4000agl. my aircraft, aircraft x maintained visual flight rules cloud clearance requirements of 500ft below cloud layers at all times during this flight. i do not believe the pilot of aircraft y ever saw us on the approach. if the pilot of aircraft y was on an instrument flight rules flight plan shooting an approach into an airport with a known flight school, with pilots making radio calls at every phase of flight, i question why he would shoot an iap going that fast, or why air traffic control would clear him for the approach while my aircraft is on the final approach segment.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A TRACON controller reported a fractional pilot on a visual approach experienced an NMAC with an unidentified VFR aircraft.
text: redacted tower called me and asked for a heading for aircraft x. i was preoccupied with my other arrivals and i didn't understand why they couldn't keep aircraft x in the pattern when they had 1 aircraft, so i verified that they 'could not keep the aircraft in the pattern, ' to which they replied that they could not. this is often confusing because of the rules of what a visual approach go-around is supposed to do - enter the traffic pattern. i issued a 290 heading and 6000 just to get the aircraft going so i can go back to my other traffic. during this time, i recognized that i could either get aircraft x back now, ahead of other arrivals or they would have to climb and go back out to the back of the line, causing a delay and another potential issue with all of the visual flight rules targets flying out there. i opted to get the aircraft back to the airport now. so i issued a downwind turn (210 heading) ensured the field was in sight still and issued a visual approach clearance. meanwhile, i had 2 other instrument flight rules aircraft on converging courses with visual flight rules targets that i was doing my best to separate. while focusing on the other instrument flight rules aircraft and making sure they were avoiding the random visual flight rules targets out there, i noticed a visual flight rules target seemingly appearing to depart redacted's class d. however, this target was several hundred feet below aircraft x and i had no indication that the visual flight rules target would continue their climb, and at this moment, aircraft x appeared to be in the safest position compared to my other instrument flight rules targets. i shipped aircraft x to the tower so they could work them in. recommendation: we need controlled / protected airspace north of redacted. this area is a mid-air waiting to happen. we've been told that we can't lower the bravo airspace out there. nor can we create a satr or otherwise. we just seem to be in this unsafe situation in perpetuity. we all see the solution, but the faa is silent and does not seem to care about fixing the problem. every controller can tell you the solution, but only the faa can act on it, and unfortunately, they sit idle until two airplanes collide. i'm not talking local faa. i'm talking big faa... the only ones who can make the airspace safer.get some protected airspace out there in that area asap - two airplanes will collide at some point without it.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported the glideslope for CLT ILS 36C is out of service and instead of this being referenced within a NOTAM for RNAV 36C; it should have its own NOTAM for ILS 36C.
text: this topic could have been raised before but i thought i would bring it to your attention. in day 0 the faa issued notam for the clt rnav (gps) y runway 36c. it is a notam telling you to disregard the note about lnav procedure na during simultaneous operations. the issue i have is imbedded later on within the same notam text it indirectly addresses a totally different approach, the instrument landing system 36c. it says the i-dqg instrument landing system or glideslope out of service. there are at least 2 or 3 other notams for runway 36c but none of them call out the glideslope except for the rnav notam. you do not use the i-dqs instrument landing system for the rnav approach.last night we were given a late runway change to the visual to 36c after setting up for and briefing the approach to 36l. the standard is usually to back up a visual approach with an instrument landing system. we quickly reviewed the notams for 36c and the first officer set it up and we briefed the visual backed up by the instrument landing system 36c. we were vectored across the field coming in from the north to a right downwind for 36c. in the downwind vector, from a previous flight, i remembered there was a trick" with 36c. as i re-reviewed the notams i caught the imbedded instrument landing system glideslope note within the rnav 36c notam. we changed the approach again in the box to the rnav 36c, re-briefed, and except for the tower controller talking to us during the touchdown and high speed rollout, we made an uneventful landing.my question is, why is this not a separate notam for the instrument landing system 36c highlighting the instrument landing system or glideslope out of service and how can this concern be relayed to the faa?cause: the instrument landing system 36c i-dqs instrument landing system or glideslope out of service should be its own notam for the instrument landing system 36c, not imbedded within the rnav 36c notam."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported spoiler malfunction on approach and continued to land.
text: may be coincidence, but at top of descent into redacted, we were experiencing light turbulence. at this time, we received a splr 6 fault alert on the ecam, accompanied by a significant yaw of the airplane. upon examination of the flight control page, we discovered that spoiler 6 had fully deployed, creating a airflow/drag issue over the left wing.the captain was the pm at the time, electing the first officer maintain control of the airplane while running the qrh.qrh procedures were unsuccessful in recovering the spoiler. the spoiler remained deployed. this resulted in a cross control scenario to compensate for the increased drag. at this time, it was determined that the captain would assume pf responsibilities.once descending below 10k feet, the crew did a flight control check to assess maneuverability and control. at this time, we requested priority handling. qrh procedures drove a non-standard configuration/speed for landing. the approach was conducted in cat i weather, acquiring the runway shortly before minimums. landing was uneventful and the request for priority handling was cancelled. cause: malfunction of the flight controls.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier B737 flight crew reported number one engine hydraulic pump failure and a return to the departure airport.
text: on climb out, the engine driven hydraulic pump light for the #1 engine illuminated. this aircraft had previously diverted into redacted for the same issue and was reflected on the release. before pushback we had briefed this as a technical threat since it was the first flight after this was supposed to be fixed. when the light illuminated, the captain /pf passed the controls to the first officer and ran the qrh, which instructed us to turn the pump off and rely solely on the electrical pump. the capt and first officer discussed, continuing vs returning to redacted, contacted dispatch and maintenance control, and ultimately decided to bring it back to redacted for maintenance instead of risking running a backup system for a 4 hour flight. we were in holding just north of redacted while figuring this out, level at 18000 ft. once all checklists were performed and the approach brief into redacted was completed we proceeded back to redacted. since we were going to be landing about 10000lbs overweight we told air traffic control we'd like cfr (crash fire rescue) to check our brakes after landing. they told us to do this we would have to be a priority aircraft, at which point they provided priority handling for us. we landed on xxr, exited [taxiway] 1, and had the trucks inspect us. they said the brakes were hot but not quite in a caution range. we single engine taxied back to the gate without issue.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 Captain reported push crew headset failure and incorrect hand signals resulted in uncommanded aircraft movement with momentary loss of aircraft control.
text: the first officer (first officer) and i had completed the before push checklist and were waiting to hear from the tug driver that they were ready for brake release. the group crew seemed to be having problems with their headset. i then saw a ramper come into view from the captain's side window. he pointed to his ears, shook his head no, and gave a broken or no good type of hand signal. he then held up both arms with his hands clenched into fists. i said to the first officer, it seems like they're having headset issues... it looks like they're ready for brake release, why don't you call for push. i then held my hands up for the ramper to see my clenched fists and i opened both fists to show all 10 fingers and i released the aircraft brakes. saw the ramper repeat my hand signal to the tug driver. almost immediately, the aircraft began to slowly move rearward. i said out loud to the first officer, we may have an uncommanded aircraft movement here. i then noticed the ramper who was giving me hand signals move hurriedly toward the tug driver. i immediately moved my feet up on the toe brakes and gently applied pressure to slow the aircraft movement and bring it to a stop. if i had to guess, the aircraft moved somewhere between 5 and 8 feet before i brought it to a stop.i set the parking brake and we waited until the ground crew found an operable headset. upon completion of our ensuing pushback, i asked the ramper to submit a safety report to document this event and told him that i would do the same.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Tecnam P2012 Captain reported left engine malfunction resulted in an expeditious return to departure airport.
text: - this was a two captain flight crew operating flight #redacted, with service from redacted to redacted. this was the second flight of the day in the airplane and no major mechanical abnormalities were experienced during the first flight. the only notable event was a tlo light (left side) that illuminated during cruise. person a served as the first officer and pilot monitoring during both the first and second flights. i had not flown in 18 days as a result of a previous reported incident and person a was helping me regain proficiency in the airplane.- in redacted, the aircraft started up normally and we taxied to the runup area on the 1 taxiway. upon completing the before takeoff checklist, and with both engines within all parameters, we were given taxi instructions to runway xx and then cleared for departure. - both engines eventually developed full power at 103 percent and we rotated around 72 knots. i noted that the engines were surging at times but appeared to smooth out with more airspeed and prior to rotation. when we were around 200 feet above the runway, the left engine began to make a loud popping noise and the power reduced to around 70%.- there was a substantial amount of runway left in front of us as runway xx is 10, 400 feet long. since we had a headwind and variable crosswind gusting to 22 knots, i initially pulled back power in order to land back on the runway. this is what i had briefed in the takeoff briefing.- at this point, person a stated that we should keep flying and to continue our climb straight ahead. i considered it and then moved both throttles back to full power. we started climbing again. the engine popped one more time but did not lose power. - we were able to climb without incident to 1, 000 ft and person a notified air traffic control that we needed to return to the airport for landing. air traffic control was able to accommodate us immediately back for a left pattern for a return landing on runway xx. the landing and rollout were uneventful and we notified redacted ops that we had returned. we also informed them that aircraft x needed maintenance attention and was not airworthy. we also told them that we would need another aircraft to fly our passengers to redacted.- person a contacted maintenance control while i wrote up the incident in the aircraft maintenance log. person a then contacted operations to inform them of the situation. he was then instructed to contact person b, the on-call duty manager. he did so and we both chatted with person b on speaker phone. he supported our decision to return and guided us through the process.- we obtained another aircraft and were able to fly our passengers to redacted without incident. we remained in our same crew positions for the second attempt of this flight, with myself as pilot flying and person a as pilot monitoring.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported engine oil pressurization warning resulted in engine shutdown with expeditious handling to a safe landing.
text: while at the gate in redacted the aircraft displayed a l oil lvl low status message, with the left engine at shut off prior to blocking out. we (the first officer and i) checked the oil level on the menu page. it indicated that the left engine oil level was at 51%. after referencing the crj 900 qrh 0-xx table 0-1: oil level indication and duration table, we determined to be in the 10 hour flight range and above the do not dispatch" minimum. we continued with the flight as normal. the apu was deferred on this flight so we executed a right engine start at the gate using ground supply air and electrical power. after the right engine start was complete, we pushed back from the gate and taxied to the xxr deice pad on a single engine using all standard procedures. completed type 1 deicing process and then began our taxi to runway xxl for departure via taxiway 1. while on taxiway 1, the first officer and i completed a cross bleed start to the left engine using bleed air from the right engine as directed by the qrh. once the left engine start was complete, all normal delayed start and before takeoff checklist and procedures were completed. in addition to that, the oil level of both engines were check via the menu page and found to be at an acceptable level for departure. departed runway xxl at redacted with no adverse indications. completed a normal climb to our cruise altitude synopsis: A320 crew reported numerous transient 'ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE'  ECAMS during climb-out. During descent for return to departure airport ENG 1 failed to accelerate when commanded; but the flight continued to a safe landing.
text: during engine start, we received eng1 gen fault. we followed ecam procedures and it came back online. i entered it in the elb (electronic logbook), called dispatch, and finished the procedure with maintenance control. we called for taxi, was cleared to runway xx, taxied out, and departed. at approximately 1500' both the first officer (first officer) and i noticed a sort of shimmy, as though the gear was still down, flaps were down, or maybe the speed brakes were out, but all was normal. it did not seem to me like an engine vibration and we didn't notice any parameters showing high vibes, so we continued. on climb out, beginning at ~3000', received multiple transient eng 1 thrust lever disagree ecams. all engine parameters were normal on both engines and the thrust levers were perfectly aligned, so i felt that continuing was the best plan. on the 4th or 5th ecam, it stayed up almost long enough to run the full procedure, but then it went away again. it came back again as we were passing ~23, 000'. it was no longer transient and i decided we needed to start back to the field. i asked the first officer to pass the info to dispatch. they messaged back that they would get the ball rolling. air traffic control turned us back and began our descent. the ecam cleared, but we had already started turning back so we continued. we requested priority handling in the turn back to redacted. to this point, both engines had been performing normally and it seemed like it may have been an indication issue. on level off, eng 1 did not spool up, staying at flight idle. the plane commanded lever mct (maximum continuous thrust), and performance went into eo (engine-out). at this point, i asked the first officer to request arff (airport rescue and firefighting) support upon arrival. they said the trucks would be ready. we revisited procedures and both agreed that everything had been completed, to include a report to the (lfa) lead flight attendant. we were vectored to the instrument landing system xx, but the tailwind during the return pushed us too much and we were vectored around for further descent. upon the next vectors, i thought air traffic control had requested a ten degree turn to the left, which i did and then our course was promptly blown too close to the localizer - apparently they had given me a right course correction. they vectored us out once again and gave us much more room to catch the localizer. we commenced the approach, and landed without any further issues. at some point, when were exiting the runway i smelled something odd, so i requested arff scan eng 1 just in case there was something internal to the nacelle. arff completed the entire aircraft scan and reported no further issues with the flir. i requested to continue into the terminal, to which we were given clearance. at this point, a passenger got up and used the bathroom before the fas could stop them. once they sat back down, we continued to taxi to the gate, shut down normally, and deplaned the pax. i'm fairly certain, with everything going on and the previously transient ecam, something was missed in the approach. we revisited the procedures, although we briefed the passengers later than i would have liked, making sure all the information was covered. i feel like everything was covered, maybe poorly and out of sequence, but so many things were happening that i was doing a lot just staying in front of the problem and making sure that i was prioritizing flying the aircraft. we were constantly checking in with each other to make sure each of us were up to speed and also sa.

text: departing redacted redacted arrival in convective weather we were given vectors off the sid then direct fix speed 290 or greater.we could visually see the build ups to our right, below us, and to the left, but the vector looked good. we were attempting to adjust the radar to get a good view but the radar was not showing anything. at times the radar would show returns indicative of contamination on the nose cone for one sweep but the screens didn't match and then the return would show nothing again.climbing out of 15, 000 ft we began to experience moderate turbulence and airspeed variations +\- 10 to 15 kts. approximately fl180 the air speed variations became stronger and more rapid at which time the auto pilot disconnected.i took control of aircraft and did my best to manage the gains and losses while keeping the climb going while the first officer reported it to air traffic control. the airspeed trend vector was shooting rapidly in both directions so i maintained my climb careful not to over control. in doing so i observed an airspeed between 270-310 knots with airspeed trend vector near maxed back and worth in both directions.i observed the trend vector rapidly rise to the top and the max airspeed reach 310 kts when we received a master warning over speed one time.shortly thereafter we were above the layers and ride was smooth. upon reaching our destination i notified maintenance and they stated no writeup was required. i sent them a picture of the radar return at fl330 in the clear that would show up randomly on my screen, then go away and show up on the first officer screen. maintenance elected to apply the minimum equipment list to the weather radar.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a Cabin High Altitude warning during climb. Crew notified ATC; stabilized the condition by closing multiple cabin door vent flaps; and continued the flight.
text: i am submitting this report to document an event that occurred during a ferry flight from redacted.i was assigned to reserve availability period 1 and was called in for standby position 1. i received a call from customer service indicating that there was a ferry flight from gate xx that needed to proceed. upon arriving at the gate, i met captain a, who informed me that he was still awaiting a flight release and that there was no gate agent available. i sought assistance from the neighboring gate to gain access to the aircraft, and we both began our duties to prepare for the flight. after completing my walk-around, i performed the cabin equipment check. with our duties completed, we both proceeded to close the main cabin door using the checklist, and we confirmed the door status as green on the eicas status page.we did not realize that the vent flaps on the remaining three cabin doors were not closed and secured. being new to ferry operations, i initially interpreted the eicas messages for the remaining doors as indicating that the slides were not armed, which i mistook for the vent flap issue. we continued to set up for our flight, and on departure we received clearance to climb and maintain fl210.during the climb through 10, 500 feet, we encountered a cabin high alt warning. captain a immediately advised air traffic control that we would level off at 10, 000 feet to address the issue. i, as the first officer and pilot flying, disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to halt the climb and descend to 10, 000 feet. i did not reset the altitude selector to 10, 000 feet, and the aircraft briefly accelerated to 325 knots while descending from 11, 500 feet to 10, 000 feet. captain a then held the throttles at idle to assist with deceleration and directed me to set 10, 000 feet in the altitude selector. the aircraft returned to a normal speed, and the over-speed condition lasted approximately 3-5 seconds.air traffic control asked about our intentions three times, we confirmed that we would remain at 10, 000 feet while we assessed and addressed the issue. after the third inquiry, air traffic control vectored us to our assigned heading. following stabilization, i conducted a positive exchange of controls so that i could proceed to close the vent flaps on the remaining doors. cabin altitude subsequently returned to normal, and we continued the flight without further incident.cause: i am providing a cause narrative for the ferry flight from redacted to document the factors that contributed to the cabin pressurization event and to outline corrective actions. the sequence of events revealed a chain of contributing factors centered on ferry-flight procedures, crew experience, and situational awareness during the abnormal situation.the root cause began with an incomplete preflight and door-status verification for ferry operations. vent flaps on the three non-primary cabin doors were not closed and secured, a condition that went unidentified prior to departure. this oversight stemmed from a lack of ferry-specific checks and limited experience, which led to the misinterpretation of eicas messages as indicating slide arming rather than the actual vent flap status. i initially assumed that eicas messages related to the other cabin doors pertained to slide arming, causing the vent flap issue to be overlooked until the event unfolded.during the climb, i disconnected the autopilot and did not reset the altitude selector to 10, 000 feet, allowing a brief overspeed condition as we descended from 11, 500 feet toward 10, 000 feet. this indicated a delay in crew coordination and procedures during a high-workload, time-critical event. the situation was further stressed by limited ferry-flight experience and delayed identification of the vent flap closure issue and misreading of cues from the eicas system. in addition, the preflight process did not include a definitive check of vent flap status on all cabin doors, increasing the likelihood of an undetected vent-flap exposure. communication with air traffic control under stress also highlighted the need for clear, decisive actions, as initial exchanges were hampered by moments of uncertainty before we could present a unified plan.immediate corrective actions were taken once the situation was stabilized. a positive exchange of controls allowed me to close the vent flaps on the remaining doors, after which cabin pressure returned to normal and the flight proceeded without further incident. the aircraft was stabilized at 10, 000 feet, and air traffic control vectored us to a safe heading, ensuring continued safe operations.suggestions: during the recent operation, we faced pressure to expedite departure, but we determined that slowing the pace was necessary to maintain safety and accuracy. we also recognize that we could have leveraged available resources more effectively, including maintenance, dispatch, and company operations, to aid decision-making and risk assessment.going forward, i have learned that when any aspect of a procedure or condition is in question, it is essential to slow down and seek clarification before proceeding. this approach will help ensure we address potential issues thoroughly and maintain safe, compliant operations.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Fractional First Officer reported a NMAC during final approach. Flight continued to a landing.
text: on approach into bfi, we were cleared for the visual approach to runway 32l. at about 1, 000' agl, the bfi tower controller issued us a traffic advisory for aircraft y in right closed traffic for runway 32r, the close parallel runway, and reported that we 'might see him when he turns base.' i recall seeing aircraft y turning right crosswind but i can't recall if the captain reported 'traffic in sight' to air traffic control or not. when we were at about 400' agl, i saw aircraft y turn right base directly at us, about 200' above us, and probably 0.25 nm to our east (right side). aircraft y continued to descend, momentarily leveled off on base, and then turned final for runway 32r. i estimate that aircraft y got within 100' vertically and 400' horizontally of us. i had visual contact with aircraft y the entire time but when aircraft y turned right onto final, the aircraft y pilot could not see us due to the aircraft's low-wing design. it was very concerning that the aircraft y pilot decided to turn base directly at us instead of extending downwind until passing us. trying to hand-fly the aircraft on the visual approach and continually watch aircraft y as it flew directly at us was very distracting and was not safe.suggestions: the parallel runways at bfi are spaced only 375' apart, centerline to centerline. with that in mind, the bfi tower controller should have instructed aircraft y to extend downwind in an effort to stagger arrivals to the closely-spaced parallel runways. it should be standard operating procedure for bfi air traffic control to ensure that arrivals are staggered and separation is maintained. 'maintain visual separation' continues to provide subjective distances of adequate separation for pilots to maintain. the aircraft y pilot should have maintained adequate visual separation with us and extended their downwind or slowed down in order to do so because we were on a straight-in approach. more education for ga pilots on flying traffic patterns at airports with closely-spaced parallel runways could help.

synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported landing safely after experiencing inflight engine shutdown due to low oil pressure.
text: we started our day two of the trip with two legs on day 0 in redacted. this day we were scheduled to operate redacted-redacted then from redacted to redacted. initially the inbound aircraft to redacted was delayed. shortly after we claimed the aircraft and started the trip we found the apu to be inop and minimum equipment list-ed (49-xx-redacted). this was observed both in the engineering change request form as well as informed by the incoming crew. aside from that minimum equipment list the aircraft didn't have any issues or malfunctions. on the ground at redacted we observed ' l oil level lo' status message. after confirming the indication we checked with qrh and confirmed that the aircraft was still good to go and within the limitations specified in the table in qrh . the flight from redacted into redacted was operated as normal and without any issues. after getting to redacted and preparing for the second and last flight of the day, a preflight inspection was conducted by me (first officer) and nothing out of the ordinary was found. no leakages of either engines or any other fluids were observed. after boarding and getting ready for pushback, we once again checked the left oil level and it showed 51% (engine off), once again we checked the table and found that the duration of available oil until next service is 10 hours for that quantity. we made a mental note and discussed to let maintenance know once we got to redacted. shortly before pushback, we observed snow flurries starting to fall and decided to get de-iced prior to departure. we taxied single engine onto the de-ice pad (xxr), after getting done with de-icing we started our taxi for runway xyl in redacted and did a cross-bleed start on the left engine. before, during and after the engine start all indications were showing within the normal parameters. after going through our procedures and checklists we then continued onto the runway and prepared for take off. during the take off and climb phases all indications were showing operations within normal parameters. shortly after reaching our cruising altitude of fl310 ( approximately 10-12 minutes ) we once again checked the oil level, at this time we observed 15% on the l side quantity. after checking with the qrh table, we followed as written and continued the flight while monitoring the oil temperature and pressure. during this time the oil temperature was stable and good while the pressure was flickering and slowly dropping (at this time it was still green and within limits). shortly after this observation we got a 'l eng oil press' warning (approximately 3 minutes after initial observation of pressure flickering). we then confirmed the warning and followed qrh. while running through the qrh, we had two of the three specified indications ( l eng oil press warning and affected engine oil pressure below limits). we double and triple checked that oil pressure was indeed below limits and referenced the table in the manual. while running the qrh and having pulled back the affected thrust lever to idle (qrh), the left oil pressure was showing 20 psi (while 25 psi being the minimum per the manual). we then again quickly saw the pressure dropping again to 19 psi. we confirmed displayed indications and followed the qrh for an 'engine failure/in-flight engine shutdown'. while running the qrh and just before engine shutdown, left oil pressure was at 19 psi. while going through the qrh we communicated with air traffic control and let them know that we were working with an engine issue we than advised air traffic control once it was clear that an inflight engine shutdown was imminant. we also continued to communicated with dispatch, and maintenance via acars, and informed them of our situation and that we were still planning to continue to redacted unless thay would suggest otherwise. we continued the flight to redacted and completed qrh for a single engine approach and landing without any other issues. during the approach bit, we had already set up and briefed for runway xz into redacted ( per atis at the time) as we got closer they informed us to expect xa, after receiving this information we communicated amongst ourself and both agreed that runway xz would be preferred due to its longer length, favoring winds, and reduced workload on us with it already being programmed and briefed i then asked the approach for the current winds in redacted ( winds were 280 at 7 knots), we then requested xz and got vectored for the instrument landing system runway xz into redacted. approach and landing were conducted successfully without any further complications. cause: after reaching the cruising altitude we check the engine oil level and found it to be 15% for the left engine. shortly after we got a 'l eng oil press' warning due to the pressure dropping below limits. during the post flight walk around, i observed leakage on the l eng exhaust cone (pictures attached).

o-rings slot but sitting on top of the filter, the safety wire was installed loosening and i was able to remove the filter bowl by hand. i corrected both issues by replacing the module and replacing the filters, packings and backup rings. reference logbook deferral sheet redacted and xxxxxxy. this is the fifth time in two weeks i have noticed in the wheel well of case drain bowls being safetied to hydraulic lines and second time of the packing being installed on the outside of the bowl and not inside the unit.cause: in these instances i was on walkaround while on a-check and pointed it out to the individuals on gear which we corrected these issues, but for aircraft x, i was on gear and did not have task cards assigned to service these case drain filters. suggestions: i feel that the company needs to have a junior mechanic program for individuals who are fresh out of a&p school with no previous experience working at any airline. this is a recipe for disaster and a huge safety hazard. when i started in aviation over xx years ago, we had a ojt program where you were paired with a senior technician and had to accomplish ojt before graduating to the floor. before arriving at air carrier x i worked at the regional airlines and did contract maintenance heavy jet until i was hired at air carrier x. there cannot be inexperienced technicians out on the floor without any prior airline experience with only school under their belt which is the basics. their should be a minimum of two years mandatory as a junior technician paired up with a senior technician for safety reasons. in the past years with air carrier x hiring people fresh out of school, i have seen too many things which can lead to a safety issue, whether the inexperienced individual doesn't ask, doesn't care, or just does a job any type of way without consulting and referencing the aircraft maintenance manual. something has to be done because i see a huge safety issue and i don't want anything to happen, i am very worried about the lack of experience from people fresh out of school without at least 2 years of hands on experience working at a fbo or airline. the low seniority resides on night shift, this is where i feel 85% of the maintenance is being taken place, this is also where new hires mostly fresh out of school are placed due the airlines demand to hire anyone due to the shortage of mechanics and future demands. an airline must hire qualified and experienced technicians or have in place a junior technician program. since around the time of retiring some of our fleet, the overall workmanship, quality, professionalism of maintaining our aircraft has hugely diminished, this is what i see, this is what a passenger see's as well because our interiors of our aircraft is a reflection of our maintenance program to any passenger that flies on our aircraft. it is absolutely necessary that a junior program be set in place before senior mechanics with great experience, military experience that has served for this company for over 40 years pass down their knowledge before its too late so that the incoming generation of technicians understand the expectancy level and the requirements of their job qualification as well as performance to be able to provide safety and a quality product to our passengers and the many people we serve across the world. a lot of work is needed in our maintenance program regardless of how much profit we make. in the end, i don't want to hear something on the news and then the company reacts. it will be too late! i also don't want to see aircraft get damaged or someone get hurt which recently i've seen many close calls. with this being said, we have to do better when it come to safety and quality whether in house or outsourced technicians that provide maintenance to our aircraft.

synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported encountering turbulence and subsequent altitude deviation during cruise. Pilot requested higher altitude and continued.
text: was on an instrument flight rules flight plan to davidson executive airport. there was 60 knot cross wind component slowing me down at 7000 ft msl the flight was smooth at 7000 with occasional minor turbulence to this point. i requested a decent to 5000 ft msl in an effort to fly in decreased winds. upon reaching approximately 6000 ft msl the turbulence was severe and i requested a return to 7000 ft. upon reaching 7000 ft msl i was instructed to contact columbia approach, i acknowledged the frequency change and entered it into the com radio standby mode. the aircraft was then stuck by turbulence again and i experienced heavy down drafts and updraft causing altitude variations. an updraft came that put the aircraft in a rapid climb and i was not able to maintain altitude. i saw that i had exceeded 7300 ft msl and i contacted air traffic control to request a block altitude and reported difficulty maintaining level flight. jacksonville air traffic control responded and acknowledged i was higher than 7300 feet msl, provided me a block altitude of 6000-9000 feet and reminded me to contact columbia approach and acknowledge the block altitude assigned. i acknowledged the assigned block altitude and switched the standby frequency and checked in with columbia approach and informed them of my block altitude assignment. shortly after i requested and climbed to a higher altitude, accepted the head wind impact for smoother conditions.there were no aircraft in the vicinity of my aircraft, no evasive maneuvers were required to avoid other aircraft. the remainder of the flight continued without further incidents.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Corporate Jet Captain reported a NMAC on final approach. Pilot executed a missed approach and returned for a second landing.
text: on day 0 at xa:45, a mid-air collision nearly occurred between aircraft i was piloting and aircraft y. the event occurred on the final approach corridor to runway 35 at trm at an estimated distance of 1 mile, and an estimated altitude of 750 feet. the weather was vmc, light winds, clear skies, and unrestricted visibility.participating traffic were a small aircraft in left closed traffic for runway 17 executing a rh 360 on the lh downwind for spacing, another aircraft 6 miles east inbound to runway 35, a jet holding short of runway 35 for instrument flight rules takeoff. another jet taxiing from the ramp to runway 35, myself in overhead left traffic for runway 35 having clearly called number 1 for landing during coordination with the small aircraft on the other downwind and the jet holding short for takeoff, and last----aircraft y coming straight-in to runway 35 making distance calls inbound to 'cochran.' i didn't clearly hear the jet make a radio call. but i don't doubt the word of the other crew at debriefing given the factors described below. in any case, the crew did not recognize that the pattern was full at the airport they were approaching, and they did not coordinate their plan to come straight-in with any of the other aircraft using the airport.as i was descending from base to final, i was a bit high on approach. i received a tcas traffic advisory while turning final. after rolling out on final the displayed threat aircraft was 100 feet directly beneath me (solid-yellow circle -100).no tcas resolution advisory was issued since both aircraft were configured for landing below 1000 feet. this situation was something like a perfect storm that somewhat defanged the tcas. since the initial traffic advisory showed yellow and stayed yellow (20-48 seconds), the urgency of the situation was confused, and my initial reflex was to think that there was another aircraft in the vicinity of the airport, but not one on approach. it took me a moment after establishing myself on final to note that the threat symbol, and myself were collocated on the tcas screen with only 100 feet of separation.since i did not have full sa or visual contact with the threat aircraft, i was sufficiently confused by the situation to abandon the approach. i executed a go-around and re-entered the left downwind as aircraft y landed and rolled out on the runway.a second approach was safely completed without incident.all local traffic were coordinating using the phrase 'thermal area traffic' to identify the airport and operations. this is normal at this airport even though the airport is called 'jaqueline cochrane regional' airport. the word thermal contains 2 syllables. the official name of the airport contains 7. this ctaf frequency is often very congested due to the uncontrolled traffic volume at this airport. it was congested at the time of this event.the crew was unfamiliar(first-time to the airport), and did not associate 'thermal' with the airport they were landing at. as a consequence, they didn't participate in coordination efforts with the other aircraft using the airport. they rightly pointed out on debriefing that 'thermal' is not printed on any of the airport plates. thus, local habituated knowledge and telephony understandably contributed to all affected crews' loss of sa.also a contributing factor was the inhibition of a tcas resolution advisory at low altitude. the yellow-circle symbol did not reflexively indicate the proximate danger present during this event. even so, without the traffic advisory advisory, i am confident that a catastrophic collision would have occurred. this can go up as a tcas save----if a somewhat confusing one.the traffic situation surrounding this event, and every day at this airport during the snow-bird season can produce a situational-picture that is way too much for any single-pilot in a jet to safely keep track of. i'm a pilot not an air-traffic controller.at 100 feet of vertical separation, and no visual contact made, this was a very close call. this is my second traffic related go-around at this airport in x years due to jet-aircraft coming straight-in to a full-pattern without participating in effective self-coordination.this airport needs an air traffic control tower----like yesterday!

synopsis: DA20 Flight Instructor pilot reported engine lost power on short final to a non towered airport and they landed in a nearby field.
text: i had a flight scheduled with a student pilot. the plane was aircraft x. we both completed a preflight and had a full tank of fuel. everything seemed normal. we taxied to the runway at redacted and did our run up. the magnetos showed around 50rpm drop each, as expected. fuel pressure was normal, oil pressure was in the green arc. everything was looking normal. we were cleared for takeoff on runway xx and my student applied full throttle rapidly. immediately we both felt a sputter in the engine and i called for an aborted takeoff. we exited the runway on taxiway 1 and returned to the run up area. i wanted to try to diagnose the issue. i triple checked everything and went through the run up checklist another time. i completed a fouled spark plug checklist just in case that was the issue but i did not believe it was. i concluded that the sputter was due to the aggressive application of the throttle. we agreed to attempt the takeoff again with a smoother application of the throttle but if there was any sign of an issue, we would cancel and taxi back. the second attempt was normal and the engine had no issue so we took off. we took off. the rest of the flight was uneventful. we stayed on flight following while we did a cross country to redacted with the plan to return to redacted after. based on traffic and our direction of flight, we elected to do a straight in for runway xy. we started our descent checklist and began descending to pattern altitude. we transferred over the redacted [ctaf] and began announcing our position. when we had just passed a 1 mile final, we were a little low for the approach and i instructed my student to add more power. i looked at her hand and noticed she had already added power but we weren't getting much power out of the engine. i didn't look at the tachometer but could tell based on the sound that we did not have a high rpm. additionally, we were not gaining altitude and were still descending. i realized we had an issue and immediately say 'my controls' while trying to do quick troubleshooting. i checked the mixture and the fuel pump were both full rich and turned on. i attempted different throttle settings but had no change in rpm and heard more sputtering in the engine. i hadn't heard this before on this flight but sounded similar to when we aborted takeoff. the engine was still making noise and the propeller was still spinning but we had a partial power loss and would not be able to make it to the runway. at this point we were descending toward trees. i made a right turn for a field and did a soft field landing in this field. there was not more than 30 seconds from telling my student to add throttle and then landing in the field. there was no damage to person, property, or aircraft.

synopsis: C172 pilot reported aircraft broadcasted entry and position incorrectly as they entered the traffic pattern resulted in a NMAC event.
text: on day 0, at approximately xa:35, while operating at redacted during non-operational tower hours (ctaf in use), i (aircraft x) was conducting closed left traffic pattern work for runway xxl and performed a touch-and-go.another aircraft from my flight school (aircraft y) was also operating in the pattern. an inbound aircraft (aircraft z) announced that he was several miles out and would be entering on a 45-degree entry to the left downwind for runway xxl. he also stated he was aware of traffic already operating in the pattern.after departure, aircraft y announced he would extend his downwind for spacing. i announced that i would extend my departure leg for additional spacing.based on the inbound aircraft's announced 45-degree entry to left downwind, i anticipated a standard left downwind entry. during my climb from runway xxl, however, the inbound aircraft executed a turn that placed him on a northbound track intersecting the extended runway xxl departure path, resulting in a flight path geometry different from what he had a indicated.i did not initially have the aircraft in sight on the takeoff climb. approaching the west boundary of the pattern near the redacted delta airspace, i initiated a left crosswind turn and announced the turn on ctaf.while turning left downwind for runway xxl, the inbound aircraft told me he could not see me and ask me if i have him in sight. at that time, i acquired visual contact. the aircraft was approximately 75 feet below me and to my left in close proximity.upon recognizing the proximity, i announced that i would extend further toward the border to allow additional spacing and sequencing. i initiated a climb to increase vertical separation and allowed the inbound aircraft to land first. no contact occurred and both aircraft continued normal operations.post-flight review of ads-b track data clarified the inbound aircraft's turning path and the intersecting geometry.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: PA46 Malibu pilot reported touchdown on snow contaminated runway resulted in aircraft loss of control and a runway excursion.
text: i left redacted at approximately xa:30 on day 0 on an instrument flight rules flight plan and was cleared on route direct to redacted. i was the sole occupant of the airplane. i climbed to 16, 000 feet and the flight was very normal. approximately 50 miles from redacted i was turned over to redacted approach and requested the rnav xx via redacted iaf. the weather was clear, light winds that were variable, and good visibility. i elected to use the instrument approach since redacted is surrounded by high terrain. the most recent metar had 3 knot winds that equaled a 2 knot tail wind but i elected to land on runway xx because the landing roll would be shorter due to the upslope. my approach and approach speed were very normal and at 500 feet i confirmed that i met all of my stable approach criteria. the most recent ficon was 100% 1/8' dry snow 5/5/5.my airspeed was approximately 85 kts. when i started to flare. my flaps were at 20 degrees i had three green landing gear indicators. i had a very smooth touchdown just after the papi. the runway markings were obscured by snow but i landed on or very near the center line. i touched down first on the main landing gear and when the nose gear touched down, the nose veered left. i attempted to correct this with right rudder. the airplane began to fishtail and i continued to try to correct with rudder. after a couple of attempts to correct, the fishtails became worse and i attempted to initiate a go-around. at that time my right main landing gear caught the edge of the snow on the right side of the runway which caused the airplane to turn to the right and exit the runway into the snow. the snow caused the nose gear to collapse which caused a prop strike. i was not injured in any way.

synopsis: B757 First Officer reported the aircraft initiated an uncommanded aggressive pitch downwards while descending on the arrival but the flight crew were able to regain control and landed safely.
text: while descending on the redacted arrival into redacted, around 8000 feet, we received an eicas warning: unschd stab trim. simultaneously the airplane initiated an aggressive 4-degree nose down. the autopilot disconnected and the autopilot disengage alarm sounded. i silenced the alarm and read the associated message while the captain immediately regained control and started hand flying the aircraft. we estimated a 400 to 600 foot loss, but did not exceed any published altitude or airspeed restrictions on the arrival. i reviewed the associated non-normal checklist and we discussed the next steps. once the autopilot was off, the eicas message extinguished, and the aircraft was under control. the captain mentioned the only degradation was slightly heavier control inputs were needed. with that determined, we both agreed running the checklist and identifying which specific system was inoperative would unnecessarily add to our workload. we concurred that best course of action was to continue the approach, hand flown, and land. a normal approach and landing was accomplished, followed by a normal taxi to the gate. upon arrival, maintenance control was notified, an electronic log book (elb) entry was made, and the captain filed a report as well as contacted the chief pilot.

synopsis: EWR Tower Controller reported ongoing construction within the tower is causing visual obstructions and health hazards; impacting safe operations.
text: i am writing to formally express serious safety concerns regarding the ongoing construction within the newark liberty international airport (ewr) tower.as controllers, we rely heavily on unobstructed visual access to aircraft movement areas to ensure the safe and efficient handling of traffic. currently, construction activity has significantly obstructed our ability to clearly observe traffic at romeo mike while actively working aircraft. the obstruction of the tower windows directly impacts our situational awareness and compromises operational safety.although it has been stated that plastic barriers were installed to contain dust and debris, visibility through these materials still allows a clear view of ongoing construction activity. this creates both distraction and concern, in addition to raising questions about the effectiveness of the containment measures. furthermore, the continued exposure to construction dust and airborne debris presents potential health hazards to employees working in the tower environment.the current conditions are unsafe for both operational and health-related reasons. as safety professionals, we are held to the highest standards in protecting the flying public. we must also ensure that our own working environment meets appropriate safety standards.what immediate corrective actions are being taken to eliminate these hazards? how will management ensure that operational visibility is fully restored and that employee health is not compromised?we request that this matter be addressed urgently, with clear communication outlining a mitigation plan and timeline for resolution.
