text: for the instrument landing system z 24l to osaka, the flight management system states at or above" altitudes for to points on the approach, whereas the fd pro approach charts indicate hard altitudes."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B777 Captain reported a high engine vibration indication on take off. Crew elected to return to departure airport for an uneventful landing.
text: this aircraft had a l engine exceedance and engine swap prior to report time. this was the first flight after engine change with a minimum equipment list deferral it required an etops verification flight (1 hour cruise, all systems normal per fom 5.60.2) before legal to enter the etops area of operation. showing at aircraft about an hour before departure, three maintenance personnel were working in the cockpit. the crew gained cockpit access around the departure time. after a few maintenance issues were resolved on the ground (l thrust rev status message, auto spoiler eicas, and previous exceedance that wasn't cleared), we pushed about an hour late. all was normal until takeoff roll. around 80-100 knts, the left engine n1 vibration indicator was higher than normal and the box inverted to white with black digits in the 4.0 range. takeoff was continued (no eicas indications) and vibrations weren't felt on the throttle and airframe until past the low-speed abort phase and into initial climb. one of the relief pilots also thought he smelled something not normal. the first officer noted an additional vibration surge above 5.0 occurred during power reduction at 1500 agl. the non-normal engine indications made etops entry illegal, so the decision was to hold over water and dump 200, 000 lbs. of fuel or land overweight dumping fuel would delay landing an additional 45 minutes. aas the engine was not working normally on its first flight, i decided landing overweight to be the safer option to get on the ground sooner with long runways available back in redacted. this had been coordinated previously with dispatch regarding the etops verification options. after initial climb out, we completed the after takeoff checklist as i wanted to clean up and get some altitude to discuss the issue. the crew concurred to return to redacted per our plan with dispatch on the etops verification.we requested a level off with air traffic control and were assigned 14, 000msl on the redacted sid, then a request to return to redacted. air traffic control cleared us direct redacted and descent to 11, 000 msl and to expect the instrument landing system xxr. while i (pf) and the first officer (pm) prepared for the approach, the relief pilots assisted by getting a satcom with dispatch. i had them inform the fas and passengers of our plan to return to redacted. we run the electronic overweight landing checklist and determined we had to use flaps 25 for landing as the target speed was over 161kts. i believe the final target speed was 167kts. the first officer pulled up acars landing data for runway xxr that we knew was slightly longer than the takeoff runway xxl. brakes 4 selected. approach was brief and descent checklist completed. air traffic control vectored us similar to a redacted star down the bay as we slowed and descended. the approach was uneventful on the instrument landing system to xxr. landing checklist and callouts per sop. touchdown was smooth rolling to the end and exiting runway xxr. after crossing xxl on taxiway 1, the brake temps began to increase, so we coordinated with ground to hold on taxiway 1 and have the ear inspected for hot brakes. apu was started and engines shutdown to allow the parking brake to be released with no aircraft movement. brakes began to cool and we verified no fire or fuse plug issues from fire rescue vehicles. we requested to be towed back to gate to avoid using brakes or need to restart engines. after the brakes had cooled around 30 min and began going from amber back to normal, maintenance and tug crews connected and towed aircraft back to gate xx. normal checklists completed at gate and passengers deplaned. maintenance write-ups for the engine vibration experienced on the left engine and the brake temp eicas.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier jumpseating Captain reported the flight crew misinterpreted ATC's nonstandard clearance of speed at your discretion" and accelerated above 250 KIAS below 10;000 feet."
text: i was jumpseating sfo - redacted. during climb below 5, 000 ft., norcal departure cleared the pilots speed at your discretion." i observed the captain tell the first officer to delete the 250/10000 line on vnav climb page. then he started to accelerate. i was sitting in the second jumpseat so i asked the first officer why we were accelerating above 250 kias below 10, 000 ft. he said that air traffic control had given them high speed. i told him that we are never authorized to exceed 250 kias or clean maneuvering (if higher) in the us airspace. the first officer did not correct the captain, so i spoke up and advised the captain not to exceed 250 below 10, 000 ft. he too told me that air traffic control had given us high speed. i corrected him as well. we did have a thorough discussion of the applicable far 91.117(a).this is a regular occurrence climbing out of sfo as norcal is in the dangerous habit of giving the nonstandard clearance of "speed at your discretion." this has been occurring for years and i observe it regularly giving line checks and on line flights where the pilots mistakenly interpret that instruction as a clearance for high speed below 10, 000 ft. several of us line check pilots (lcps) have been reporting this and have called norcal tracon to try to get them to stop this practice. we have had no effect on stopping this from happening."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: B737 Captain reported Ground Control issuing urgent call to stop taxi due to conflict with aircraft pushing from gate.
text: after push and start, we received clearance from the ramp to taxi to the top of the alley and switch ground. approximately 30 feet before the dashed line (south of spot xx), i began smoothly applying brakes to stop the aircraft five feet prior to the dashed line, while awaiting ground clearance for taxi. at this time, ground control urgently called stop." so i applied more brake pressure and smoothly stopped our plane ~12 feet in front of the dashed line. this radio call was due to a boeing 787 pushing from gate xx that presented a significant conflict if we were to taxi beyond the dashed line. normally, gate xx traffic push (more or less ) directly onto taxiway 1, but presently there is construction on 1 which blocks this option. shortly after we stopped, ground queried the 787 if he was able to continue pushing, but he responded he was unable due to a (now) broken tow bar. more than likely, a 787 crew member or tug driver aggressively applied brakes due the urgent radio call to prevent a ground collision, resulting in a broken tow bar. at this point, ground asked if we were ready to taxi and we continued the flight without further incident."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B777 First Officer reported high engine vibration during takeoff and climb. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: relief pilot on a flight. left engine was replaced prior to our report due to an egt exceedance the flight prior. an etops certification was required before we coasted out. during the takeoff roll, the left engine displayed engine vibrations exceeding 4.5 with a clearly felt vibration in the airframe. at thrust reduction, the vibration increased temporarily to 5.0+ as displayed by the engine instrumentation. vibrations were also felt by the flight attendants. the flying crew determined this was not normal as part of the etops engine check and opted to return to redacted. no emergency was declared and a normal, but overweight, landing was performed by the pilot flying (captain). also, during the takeoff roll after power up, a faint smell of burning oil was detected, possible from the environmental control system.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757-200 pilot reported a Cabin Altitude warning during cruise. Crew advised ATC; descended; referenced checklist and continued to landing.
text: at 24, 000 feet, we received a cabin altitude warning with the left pack off. i immediately turned the pack back on, but the warning remained. we notified redacted center, donned our oxygen masks and began a descent to 8, 000 feet while i ran the checklist. the cabin altitude was pegged at 10, 000 feet, the differential pressure varied, and the rate of descent was approximately 300 fpm. the warning extinguished as we passed through roughly 14, 000 feet. we continued to redacted with no further issues. dispatch did a nice job working with the other agencies and being proactive asking if i needed new fuel numbers. i declined because we were tankering fuel and expected to land close to the planned weight. the mechanics on the ground mentioned that this particular aircraft has had a history of similar issues in the recent past.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: B757-200 First Officer reported receiving an ATC low altitude alert during approach to FAT. Crew corrected altitude deviation and continued approach.
text: while on the star inbound to instrument landing system29r at fat the weather dropped below cat1 minimums. i was pilot flying, but the captain would have to fly the cat3 approach now required. we requested and entered holding at the point outside the faf (sango). i continued to be pilot flying until the captain had completed the cat3 instrument landing system and associated briefing guide. with the captain as pilot flying he selected flight change for a pitch mode and set the altitude for sango (2800) in the mcp (mode control panel) altitude window. he and i have a discrepancy in what we remember being set in the altitude window. i remember confirming 2800 and he remembers setting the altitude for the faf (1800). the best way to fly this segment of the approach would have been to stay in vnav to ensure the altitude restriction at sango was protected. i didn't realize the wrong altitude was in the mcp until approach gave us a low altitude warning. at this time we climbed and corrected the altitude deviation. i reset the appropriate altitude in the mcp and the rest of the approach was uneventful. lessens learned are taking more time in holding to prepare for approach, verifying what you see, and use of vnav.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Inflight Event / Encounter Bird / Animal
synopsis: B747-400F pilot reported an engine failure and fire indication during climb. Crew advised ATC; referenced checklist and returned to departure airport where evidence of multiple bird strikes was found.
text: initial takeoff on xxl was uneventful until the landing gear was selected up. at that time, we heard and felt what was believed to be the nose landing gear spinning down after retraction. the associated noise and slight vibration lasted longer than normal. shortly thereafter, the engine 2 vibration indication appeared.at approximately 1, 500 feet agl, an engine 2 failure indication was received. air traffic control was notified. at approximately 2, 500 feet agl, an engine 2 fire indication was subsequently received. the engine fire checklist was completed, and the fire indication was extinguished.after completion of the checklist, preparations were made to return to redacted. firefighting services were requested. the landing on xxl was uneventful, and the aircraft was brought to a stop on the runway. fire department personnel inspected the aircraft on the runway and found no active fire or unsafe conditions. the aircraft then taxied to parking. after inspection of the aircraft, maintenance found multiple bird strikes.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Inflight Event / Encounter Bird / Animal
synopsis: B747-8F Captain and Relief Pilot reported an engine failure; engine fire; and hydraulic failure EICAS messages during the climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and landed where maintenance identified bird damage to the engine.
text: a series of systems failures led to an engine fire shortly after takeoff.just after raising the landing gear after lift off we, the crew, heard and felt a vibration that was very much like a nose wheel rubbing on the scrubbers, and we smelled what we thought was burnt rubber. we all thought that a nose tire had perhaps failed and was disintegrating against the scrubbers. each of us had experienced this before. however, this vibration went on too long. at this point we were at around 1000 afe and the #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity.the #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity to the standpipe level, but we still had hydraulic pressure. i decided to wait until we were in a lower threat phase of flight to deal with this issue. we were perhaps now at 1500 afe and i noticed that the #2 engine vibration was very high. i called this out to the crew. i don't remember the exact number. all other engine indications were normal, and the n1 and egt matched the other engines (as far as i can recall). then, the #2 engine failed. the relief pilot called out #2 engine failure. i decided to run the engine failure checklist. the first officer advised me to wait until flaps were up. this is the correct procedure following a v1 cut, but i felt that in this case we were high enough to begin the checklist. however, i agreed to the first officer's suggestion. at this point we were probably 2000 afe. i notified air traffic control and the engine caught fire. the #2 engine caught fire and i ran the fire checklist while the first officer flew. at this point the vibration was gone and we knew what the problem actually was. the fire went out after the first fire bottle.i now took over pilot flying duties. we returned to redacted for a landing and the fire department checked the aircraft while we were on the runway. the fire was out and we had the necessary hydraulics to taxi back to the ramp so we taxied back and shut down.maintenance later showed me that we had multiple bird strikes all over the aircraft and much damage as a result, including a hole in the right wing root.perhaps i could have ran the severe engine damage checklist before the engine failed. however, all engine indications except the vibration were normal. i would have expected a high egt, surging n1 and banging noises if we had severe engine damage, and we had none of these.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC on initial approach to DFW because their altimeter was improperly set.
text: during transition into dfw from fl310 we executed the appropriate 'descent checklist' and set the altimeters to 30.57. throughout the arrival there was no indication of error from air traffic control. upon reaching delmo at what we believed to be 12, 000 msl we were given a frequency change to 118.42 and instructed to continue our descent to 6000 msl. during the descent we were instructed to expedite and given additional clearances to 5000msl while turning base, 4000 msl on base, and 3000 msl on base to final. while rolling out on a 160 heading to intercept the 18r loc for the visual approach. air traffic control asked us to verify our altitude. at this point we were still descending to 3000 msl indicated. air traffic control then verified the altimeter setting of 29.57 and instructed us to level at 2300 msl. nearly simultaneously air traffic control issued a 'low altitude alert'. i immediately disengaged the auto pilot and pitched slightly nose high to level and reduce speed from 210 kts. while maneuvering the aircraft the pm was able to get the appropriate altimeter setting and we were able to use his pfd (primary flight display) to verify altitude. once acceptable altitude and heading for the approach was achieved i was able to set my altimeter to the appropriate setting and proceed with a stable approach to landing. cause: multiple factors contributed to causing this incident. pilot complacency with higher altimeter settings associated with cooler climate therefore not being alerted to the significant change when arriving in a warmer environment. misinterpretation of the atis altimeter setting, failure to verify the altimeter setting, and lastly a lack of warning from air traffic control that previous altitude restrictions at altitude had been missed by nearly 1, 000 msl. suggestions: apply common sense when returning to warmer climates after conducting consecutive operations in cooler weather.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Inflight Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported GPS jamming caused by military doing broad and unannounced jamming operations led to the loss of GPS; and failure of ADS-B; clocks; terrain displays; and EGPWS during cruise near ELP.
text: during cruising approaching elp, lost position on both gps receivers. anp degraded as we approached el paso eventually reaching approximately 0.5. notified air traffic control our loss of gps and air traffic control confirmed that jamming operations were being conducted in the area. several other aircraft in the area also stated they lost gps. a transponder fail light illuminated. following the procedure i inquired with air traffic control on the status of our transponder, and as expected our transponder was still working full mode s but it was our ads-b that was no longer working. utc clocks, terrain displays, and enhanced ground proximity warning system (egpws) also ceased operation. to mitigate the loss of navigation performance, we requested to shoot a vor approach to a runway that would keep us over the city of el paso and away from terrain. this allowed us to navigate to a position to get visual contact of the runway and perform a visual approach. upon landing some gps functionality started to return such as terrain displays and the first officer's clock.caused by the military doing broad and unannounced jamming operations. either the military adequately warns of such activity or cease them all together. disruption of civilian air traffic into terrain sensitive airports is not acceptable.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported APN airport was not accurately reporting the runway conditions as evidenced by the discovery of ice over the entire runway surface that was not reported.
text: we were in constant contact with dispatch throughout the flight to apn about the weather and runway conditions. while in route the first report was 2/2/2 with 3 inches of wet snow on the runway of intended use. we were informed that they were currently working on the runway to improve conditions. we continued the flight to the iaf and held over jegob while we awaited the newest update. 5 minutes before bingo fuel the report came in as 3/3/3 with 1/4-inch dry compacted snow. so with the weather still being about minimums we began the approach and made a landing. in was night so it was impossible for us to tell the actual runway conditions until after touchdown and on roll out when we discovered the braking action was nil and there was at least 1 inch of visible snow on the surface. with full thrust reverse almost any application of the brakes cause the airplane to slide on the runway. we managed to eventually slow the aircraft and had to come to a complete stop before attempting to turn off at the very end of the runway but still slid a great deal while attempting the turn. taxiing very slowing back to the gate the taxiways were no better causing us to slide with any attempt to slow the aircraft. out of safety concerns we did not operate the flight back to redacted that night.the next day we returned to the airport to attempt to return to redacted. the trucks worked on the runway conditions for several hours and the reported to us 3/3/3 with 1/8-inch dry compacted snow. after the events of the previous evening we asked if they would take us out to see the runway conditions for ourselves. it was at the time we discovered that it was 1/8-inch or more of 100% ice with 1/8-inch or more snow on top over the entire runway surface. the truck taking us to the runway slide every time doing a brake check going only 20 mph. he allowed us to get out the truck and confirm it was ice which was difficult to even walk on. the ice was obvious yet the station did not want to report it.cause: the airport not accurately reporting the runway conditions.suggestions: audit the airport and their runway condition reporting procedures.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the inaccurate taxi diagram and lack of markings and mapping of additional pavement that was caused by the ongoing construction at the airport led to the flight crew getting stuck and needing a tug for re-positioning after making the wrong turn.
text: redacted - ags. upon landing in ags on runway 17 at approximately xa:00, we slowed to make our taxi off at the end of the runway onto taxiway foxtrot. it was difficult to identify a taxiway lead-off line as it was not painted entirely onto the runway. additionally, because of airport construction there appeared to be an extra piece of pavement prior to taxiway foxtrot that was not accurately depicted on the airport diagram. due to this misinterpretation and dark conditions, my captain preemptively made the turn onto the additional concrete before the taxiway. we both realized that we had initiated the turn too early and immediately came to a stop. we explained to tower that we had made the turn too early but were still on the runway. in communication with tower, we attempted to make a 180-degree turn to get ourselves back into a position to enter the taxiway. however, the taxiway lights were positioned into the runway and prevented us from making a turn. my captain then attempted to make a turn in the other direction. however, i had to ask him to stop as one of the runway marking signs was in the way of our expected path. we decided as a crew that it was best to come to a stop and have a tug come out to push us back. tower helped us to coordinate with operations to have a tug enter the runway and assist in pushing us back. communication was made with the passengers and flight attendants before the tug pushed us back about 20 feet. this was enough for us to then disconnect and move under our own power. we then back-taxied down the runway and finally to our gate.cause: i think both my captain and i could have done a better job of confidently identifying the taxiway before making the turn using the taxiway lights as cues. overall, i believe the cause of the mistake was the lack of markings and mapping of this additional pavement caused by the ongoing construction. once we had initiated this turn, there was no way of straightening back out to correct the mistake as the taxiway lights protruded far into the runway and the runway marking sign impeded our path in the other direction.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the push back crew disconnected the tow bar without advising the flight crew; and the aircraft rolled forward until the brakes were applied.
text: while operating as pilot in command from far to redacted, we prepared for push. we had good communications with ramp crew. during pushback, we were cleared to start engines. my first officer started the right engine. the push crew pushed us, stopped, and continued the push several times. i had been told my previous trip to fargo that they were still creating the proper procedures to push aircraft off of the new gates, so we attributed the several stops to the push crew being unfamiliar with the new area and push procedures.at one point, we stopped for a longer period of time. i asked the push operator if we were complete with the push, but got no response. i then noticed we seemed to be moving forward. i asked why we were moving forward and got no response. i looked further down below the nose while trying to determine why we were getting no response and saw what looked like people working near the nosewheel while my first officer announced that we were definitely moving forwards.i chose to slam on the brakes to avoid possibly running over the ground grew who appeared to be near the nosewheel. i then told the tug operator to stop everything and tell me what was going on before we continued. he informed me that they had disconnected my aircraft from the tug without telling us or asking for the brakes to be set. after reminding them that communicating this with the crew was a vital safety measure, the tug operator apologized for forgetting and admitted it was his first time pushing an aircraft. there was no training supervisor present.fortunately, my first officer and i were paying attention during the push and i was able to stop the aircraft and prevent anybody from being hurt or any equipment from being damaged.this incident reinforced to our crew the importance of keeping high situational awareness and not relying on the ground crew, even when using reliable headsets. in the future, we will be even more alert during pushback having seen how quickly a bad situation can develop.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a light jet flew over them without communication as they taxied into position for takeoff at ZZZZ.
text: after we taxied short of the runway, we called the ctaf and heard 2 aircraft coming in on final runway xx. we waited till the second aircraft landed, made a radio call and asked if anyone else was on final as we didn't see anyone on tcas. there was another aircraft on a 15 mile final, which we had made several calls to and coordinating with them for our departure. prior to taking the runway, we checked final again and made our radio call stating that we are taking the runway to taxi back on runway xx, the only call we heard was the regional jet on 15 mile final. when we were 20 feet from the end of runway xx, we saw a jet on 1 mile final. i immediately turned to off right off center of the runway, the first officer (first officer) immediately made a radio call to tell the landing aircraft to go-around. no response from the aircraft on final . the jet landed over us and proceeded to taxi back on xx. i made a radio call stating that he almost hit us and didn't make any calls. the pilot of the jet stated priority, will tell you later.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported encountering severe turbulence resulting in altitude deviations and temporary loss of control on a flight to MYR.
text: we were on our way back from a standard training lesson, and in between redacted and myr, we began experiencing moderate - severe turbulence. we reduced power to fly around 110kts, yet we were still getting full deflections of the ailerons, and losses of altitude resulting in our heads hitting the ceiling to the point where flight instructor (ip) headset was falling off. the airplane was full on fuel, yet the turbulence was still causing temporary loss of control. ip took controls on the way back and took the landing in the interest of safety.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Air carrier Technician reported during an engine replacement on a A300F4-620R; they found corrosion on the aft pylon mount that exceeded the Aircraft Maintenance Manual limits.
text: on day 0 i was put on the engine change crew to continue with the remove & replace of #2 engine on aircraft x. my first job was to apply the protective coating on the bottom of the aft engine mount due to corrosion that was found during the after removal of engine lower pylon inspection. upon first application of the primer i noticed that the bottom outboard mating surface of the aft engine mount had in my opinion a substantial amount of pitting. i ceased operation and notified the inspector of my finding. the inspector did a visual of the area and told me that it was ok to continue the application of the second coat and the area was within limits.the initial found fault of corrosion found during the engine inspection was already documented and signed off as removed corrosion per the applicable aircraft maintenance manual (amm). i initially took his word for it and continued because i was just coming to a somewhat extensive and lengthy job and assumed that everything had been researched and performed per any applicable amm or structural repair manual (srm). while waiting on the paint to cure enough for work to be performed i did start research in the srm to look for limitations on corrosion in certain areas. i found a few items in the srm that went over engine mounts and brought it to the inspectors attention. there were some limits that we went over and came to agreement that .020 was a max allowable limit on certain areas. i do recall looking mainly in the srm i did also eventually look in the amm and found a ref for the inspection of the aft engine mount. at this point i was still taking into consideration that he is a quality control inspector and that he has more extensive training in limits and expectations of repairs of damaged areas on the aircraft as well as the experience of seeing discrepancies like this on a more regular basis. after we had hung the engine and installed engine mount bolts i looked back at the task card and noticed that the engine install( the task the inspector said was used for the inspection) referenced the removal of corrosion amm for both the inspection of the lower pylon fwd and aft fittings as well as the lower longeron and the remove corrosion if found item. in my opinion i could not see how you can use a reference to remove corrosion as a reference for doing an inspection. i went to the amm for the inspection of the aft engine mount and found that it calls out for the removal of the mount itself to do the inspection. i then brought it up to everybody i believe and pressed the issue until we were instructed to remove the engine by our manager. we subsequently found a substantial amount of corrosion in the pylon bolt holes at the point where i went off shift. i was questioned as to why, if i believed that the pitting corrosion was not in limits then why would i assist in the engine install up to the point of where i called for the removal. the only answer i can give is that i was trusting of the judgement of my fellow mechanic/inspector but for my sake and the safety of the aircraft/lives i was still going to continue research until i was either satisfied with the inspectors signoff or i found documented evidence that disputed him. i was concerned about flight safety and my fellow union members that were working on it and was willing to call for the engine removal no matter what step of the install we were on. for the human factors i believe i can attribute: 1: lack of communication on my part by not communicating my concern to someone outside like technical support/engineering/maintenance control, 2 lack of knowledge: not knowing the corrosion limits and stopping the job until everybody was in agreement that the aircraft was safe in a timely manner, 3 lack of assertiveness: not injecting my concerns severity sooner., this report has been submitted in good faith and the events/timeline that happened have been reported to the best of my recollection.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: C182 pilot reported oil on the windscreen during the initial climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and landed where it was discovered the oil cap had come loose.
text: upon take off at redacted we noticed oil coming up on the windscreen called air traffic control and told him we needed to land immediately because we have oil on windscreen. he responded back and we landed on xxr. we taxied back to the hangars and inspected for leak. what i found was that the oil filler cap had come loose and was allowing oil to escape out in the engine compartment as well as left side cowling. we cleaned up the engine compartment test and found that the problem was fixed. corrective action will be to check oil filler cap before take off wether i open the filler cap or not.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Cessna 172 instructor reported landing safely after a throttle malfunction limited engine power in the traffic pattern.
text: event: pilot a (instructor) and pilot b (member tasked to look after the plane 'mx officer') took the c172s for a maintenance checkout flight after the 100hr inspection with maintenance at redacted. the fuel tanks had no visible debris. the left tank had 15 gal and the right tank had 16 gal of 100ll. the right tank had tiny water droplets (about 1 mm), which were poured away. no water observed in the left tank. three laps in the pattern (.6 of hobbs time) were completed without issue. the plane was placed back in service. no fuel was added given that there was a line at the fuel pumps and the fuel truck was not available. the next flight was scheduled right after the end of this flight. the next flight was an aircraft transition training flight with pilot a (instructor) and pilot c (ppl only with about 240hrs). three laps in the pattern were completed. the first lap was go around due to a gust during flare making the aircraft climb. pilot c initiated a go around. the second lap was a normal landing and takeoff (touch and go). during the third lap, pilot c completed a gumpss flow: fuel selector both, mixture full rich, light switches on and seat and seat belts secured. once abeam the numbers, pilot c reduced the power and aimed for 1500 rpms. the rpms showed 1200 rpms. pilot c realized the difference and slightly added power. the mfd (multi-function flight display) displayed 1700 rpms. pilot c was distracted by the rpm settings and started to extend the downwind leg while descending. pilot a noticed a change in propeller sound different from the usual increase in rpms and similar to an rudder only turn during cruise. pilot a checked the position of the 'ball' in the pfd (primary flight display) and confirmed it was centered. pilot a then noticed the altitude of about 600' msl and prompted a turn to base. pilot c noticed higher than usual rpm changes and asked pilot a to take over to rule out pilot c's improper throttle changes. pilot a took controls during the base turn and confirmed the propeller sound was still present and decided to do a full stop landing to troubleshoot on the ground. pilot c agreed. pilot a turned final and confirmed the fuel selector was both, fuel shut off was in, mixture was full rich, and magnetos were on both. oil pressure was in the green arc, oil temperature was in the green arc and fuel flow was still in the green arc. when pilot a confirmed the aircraft could glide to the runway, he reduced the throttle to idle. the propeller slowed down more than usual. over the numbers, pilot a set the flaps to 20 degrees (10 degrees already added on downwind). after touchdown the propeller stopped windmilling and came to a complete stop. pilot a used the energy remaining to let the aircraft roll to the first exit, ([taxiway] 1) and called [clear of the runway attempting to roll all the way clear]. after crossing the taxi intersection, pilot a applied brakes and brought the aircraft to a complete stop. pilot a called pilot b and reported the issue. pilot a restarted the plane without prime and the aircraft started without a problem. the aircraft was taxied to its parking spot and shutdown. a magneto ground check did not show any issues. pilot b met the aircraft with a representative of maintenance. the aircraft was secured and was not refueled. what i believed caused the problem:i believe the throttle control settings may caused the problem. after repeated use of the throttle controls the settings inside the cowling may have come loose and caused the engine to stop. i believe something was not properly secured during the 100hr inspection. no debris or water was found after inspection of the fuel sumps (left, right and engine). there were no changes in the mixture during flight. the aircraft restarted and taxied without problems on the ground. not sure what can be done to prevent the recurrence

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC

text: while instructing and conducting simulated single engine emergency training, during a vmc practice instrument approach to rnav17r. hooks tower did not advise of any traffic directly to my west. i heard them on the radio tell another aircraft to turn due north immediately. i looked to my right and was able to read the tail number they were that close. thank you hooks tower for keeping us safe you avoided a mid air, i do feel that they were too close though.

anomaly: No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: Pilot reported the FAA Hotline is inoperative and needs to be fixed or removed.
text: the faa aviation safety hotline is broken - fix it or kill it. i tried calling the faa aviation safety hotline (1-800-255-1111) to report a concern. what i got instead:first prompt: a long sermon on the whistleblower protection program. then four menu options - safety isn't even #1. you hit #4. then #2 to speak to someone." only to hear: "due to high call volume, we no longer accept telemetric data. please use the online form."bottom line: there is no hotline. it's a voicemail trap that punts you online after wasting your time.this isn't just annoying - it's dangerous. aviation safety shouldn't hide behind bureaucracy. if the faa can't staff a real line for urgent reports, they should stop pretending. scrap the number, update every manual and website, and funnel people straight to asrs or a live system that listens.right now, it screams: "process over people." that's not safety. that kills trust.thanks for being the real outlet."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Pilot reported landing on a closed runway at LFK but did not know until the following day. The closed runway was not mentioned in the ASOS broadcast; NOTAMs; and there were no visible runway closure lighting signs.
text: before landing at lfk i listened to asos and checked weather and notams. no notam for runway 16 that i landed safely in. but the following day i learned that runway 16 was closed. also no runway (x) closure visible lighting signs on runway or on the asos broadcast. i feel that all of this could have been avoided if more safety precautions from the fbo had been taken. moving forward i would recommend for the fbo to enhance safety measures by providing pilots with more information and (x) lighting signs on each end of the runway.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC while on a circling segment of the approach to MWC.
text: we were enroute to mwc. we were eventually cleared direct to mwc. we were in between layers at 6000 ft with an overcast deck about 2000 ft below. handed off to mke approach. we rejected a descent to lower stating that we wanted to stay above the deck as long as possible to avoid any potential icing. air traffic control cleared us direct ivaly, cross at or above 2600 ft, cleared the rnav 4l approach to mwc, circle to runway 33r. we descended to 4500 ft just above the deck, crossed ivaly and began an expedited descent to the next step down of 2300 ft at owyal. we broke out at about 3000 ft and advised approach with a report of light rime ice at about 3500 and our break out altitude just above 3000. approach instructed us to contact tower. at this point we were still about 3 miles from owyal. we contacted tower with position reported as outside owyal. tower asked if we wanted to land runway 4l or circle to 33r, winds 300 at 10kts. we elected to circle and tower said 'circle southwest of the airport and enter left base for 33r.' we had the airport in sight and began to maneuver to enter an extended left base for 33r descending to pattern altitude of 1745 ft. tower calls out an altitude alert saying 'we don't have a standard approach altitude.' we believe we were cleared on a visual segment of the approach via circling instructions. we replied that we were entering an extended left base for 33r and asked tower to confirm that we were cleared to land. cleared to land 33r ahead of traffic from the ne. landed and cleared at taxiway c, b, b1 with no further comment or issue. why the altitude alert? tower may have been tracking the profile for a straight in approach to 4l which would have alerted the altitude below the stepdown floor of 2300 prior to reaching owyal. raises another question: when should you break off your approach and begin circling? wait until the map? or proceed visual when cleared to circle while maintaining visual contact with the airport? wait until within the circling radius for your category? at the mda the protected area at the circling altitude for category a aircraft is 1.1 nm radius from the approach end of the runway. but at pattern altitude the whole class d area should be ok.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: SR22 pilot reported a loss of engine power and fuel flow on initial climb from a non towered airport that resulted in a returned to the airport.
text: with aircraft x, sr22t, flight plan from redacted, following completion of pre-flight inspection and normal before-takeoff checks, i departed redacted runway xx. all engine parameters were within normal limits during takeoff and initial climb.at approximately 900-1000 ft agl, a partial power loss was observed where rpm decreased, and a reduction in fuel flow and manifold pressure was observed.i requested priority handling and initiated a left turn with the intention to position for downwind runway xx. the power continued to decay and caused the inability to maintain altitude for a standard traffic pattern for runway xx. familiar with the airport redacted, i therefore conducted a landing on the former runway, currently designated as taxiway 1.there were no injuries, damage to property and no external aircraft damage. aircraft was handed over to local maintenance facility for inspection.

synopsis: SR20 Flight Instructor on short final to a non towered airport reported a NMAC when an aircraft not communicating taxied on to the runway and departed in front of them.
text: aircraft x was on a training flight. i was the instructor in the right seat. we were on short final and had made previous crosswind, downwind, base, and final traffic calls as appropriate. aircraft y entered the runway while we were very short final and i called them on the radio and they did not respond. as we performed a go-around, aircraft y began their takeoff roll and departed. we took evasive action and attempted to reach them on the radio with no success while others in the area confirmed they had us on the radio. we tried to reach them no less than seven or 8 times to no avail.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: Gulfstream IV First Officer reported an inflight upset resulted after encountering wake turbulence from a preceding Boeing aircraft inbound to PHX in descent through FL250.
text: we were flying along at fl410 and given a descent clearance to cross scole at fl250 maintain 300 its or greater in transition. i advised we were unable altitude but will give best rate as descent clearance was given late. we were descending 4000ft per minute and vnav was still dropping indicating us needing a greater descent. air traffic control cleared us to be higher and to give best rate, we were given a frequency change and leveled at spink with 300kts and changed frequency. at the moment of leveling the autopilot kicked off and plane banked 60plus degrees to the left and right while dropping altitude. both captain and copilot grab the controls to counteract the roll together and we're fighting it. air traffic control had leveled us 5nm in trail of what appeared to be a boeing and we were encountering major wake turbulence. we were having a hard time maintaining wings level and altitude and called air traffic control letting them know we are offsetting to the right due to wake turbulence as we turned to gain controllability of the aircraft. air traffic control then instructed a 120 degree heading which was maintained for a while. after being cleared direct geela and given frequency change the controller told us it was an issue offsetting due to restricted airspace and it was our responsibility to fly the plane. i informed him it was major wake turbulence and it was needed for control ability. it's air traffic control responsibility to maintain a separation distance and not following arrival speed and altitude procedures cause this deviation from our flight course.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A DA40 instructor pilot reported they had a near miss with a military aircraft on short final when the reporter approached the wrong runway.
text: we were extended downwind xxr. then tower instructed us to turn right base which we read back. then we heard the tower controller say aircraft x cleared to land xxl. we repeated back cleared to land xxl aircraft x. the t-38 had a similar sounding callsign when listened to. i thought the other callsign on the radio was a da42 aircraft x which was actually a t-38 aircraft y. the controller's rapid pronunciation of 'x' on the audio sounds exactly like 'y' on the audio recording vs 'x'.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air Traffic Control instructor reported the developmental controller descended two aircraft on merging headings resulting in ATC issuing a traffic alert and one aircraft descending below the MVA to avoid a collision with the other aircraft.  ATC climbed the aircraft to a safe altitude.
text: i was the instructor. aircraft x was on a downwind vector of 040 and descending to 065 for the instrument landing system approach. there was visual flight rules aircraft y approx. 10 miles ne of aircraft x moving westbound at 070. aircraft x was descending slower than the trainee expected and when they were both at 071 msl and merging i instructed the trainee to issue a traffic alert. he issued the alert exactly as we were taught in the simulators, 'traffic alert aircraft x suggest you descend immediately. traffic 2 o'clock 2 miles 7000 aircraft y westbound.' aircraft x descended quickly and descended through the previous assigned altitude of 065 to 054. the mva in the area is 059. the trainee issued a low altitude alert and climbed them back up to 060. we were trained in the simulators on traffic alerts and low altitude alerts multiple times. each time we were instructed to not issue an altitude when we gave a traffic alert as is would be the pilots prerogative. i recommend that management and staff support go through training to know which way the correct way is to issue traffic advisory and then re-run all the controllers through the simulator to make sure it is taught correctly so this miscommunication doesn't happen again.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported pressurization system failure and continued flight to their destination at 10;000 feet.
text: during the climb from redacted, we were cleared up to 16, 000 feet. while performing my climb flow as pilot monitoring, i noticed that the cabin rate of change was rapidly increasing, up to 2, 500 feet per minute, and the delta pressure was very small. this was outside our standard pressurization schedule. i relayed this to the captain during my climb flow, and he monitored and cross-checked the indications. we both agreed this was abnormal and decided to level off to diagnose the issue and run the qrh. we requested a level off with air traffic control and stopped the climb at approximately 10, 000 feet, which was approved. the captain then transferred control to me and began running the qrh. we determined that we had lost both the automatic and manual pressurization systems. after discussions with dispatch via acars and coordination with air traffic control and the flight attendant, we decided to continue to redacted.for descent planning, we remained in communication with air traffic control regarding the pressurization issue and advised that a gentle rate of descent would provide improved passenger comfort. air traffic control accommodated this request and provided vectors for a longer final approach into redacted. i remained on the controls for the remainder of the flight so the captain could monitor the pressurization system, as he was the one who previously ran the qrh. the remainder of the flight was safe and uneventful.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: A300 Captain reported both pilots smelled fumes during the initial descent with no equipment malfunctions or warnings. The flight continued the descent to the destination.
text: in cruise at fl350, .8mach, we descended to fl330 per air traffic control. once leveled at fl330, we both smelled an abrupt burning sulphur odor, similar to expended fireworks. we donned oxygen masks, established comms, and designated duties. communications were troublesome with the masks on with lots of background noise, speaker static, and breathing over the intercom. there were no indications of malfunctions with any systems.the first officer was given flying, navigation, and radios and the ca did qrh, procedures, and normal checklists. the first officer got a descent down to 10, 000 feet and direct to the redacted fix for the briefed approach of instrument landing system-xxr. the ca did the smoke/fumes quick reaction checklist, in-range checklist, and reconfigured the aircraft from the planned 15/20 flaps to 30/40 for a shorter landing roll and quicker stop.the ca and the first officer swapped duties with the first officer taking pilot monitoring and the ca taking pilot flying for the approach and landing. the crew requested priority handling with airspeed to 300 knots and air traffic control approved. approach and landing were uneventful followed by clearing off the runway to a full stop and egress.cause: the cause of the fumes is unknown as there were no indications of malfunctions with any systems.suggestions: investigate aircraft systems for cause of the fumes, repair, and report the cause to pilots for safety awareness if similar event occurs.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: CRJ-700 First Officer reported Captain conducting a Visual Approach descended below the Minimum Safe Altitude and Glideslope and they received a Low Altitude Alert from ATC.
text: on this night we were on approach to the redacted airport. my ca was high mins so i was pilot monitoring for the flight. roughly 20 miles out we were given direct to redacted and pilots discretion to descend and maintain 2000' which we complied with given we were doing the visual approach to rwy xx backed up by the instrument landing system. within 10 miles we began to slow and configure and within 5 miles the captain began to hand fly the approach as we were cleared for the visual but on a 90 degree intercept of the final approach course. as we were switched to tower and i was completing the final configuration and before landing check the captain had bugged 1000 feet and asked me to confirm which i did, however i also advised we were still below gs intercept and can remain level. we did begin our descent to 1000 feet still which prior to alts cap air traffic control had advised us of a low altitude alert which we corrected immediately and recaptured to the proper gp on the papi. we landed uneventfully and no gpws event was triggered as well. looking back at the situation i realize as the pm and first officer i should have been more assertive with my ca to level off the aircraft and capture the gs before descending and i should not have confirmed 1000 feet as we were already below msa and the lowest we could have descended to was 1700 feet for the tpa. in the future i will make sure to be more assertive in ensuring the pf makes the proper corrective action regardless of position and be more aware of tpa and msa's when setting altitudes to descend to on visual approaches.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier pilot conducting an RNAV approach reported aircraft terrain warning even though they were slightly high on glidepath and within PAPI guidance.
text: while on approach into redacted on the rnav xx in day vmc we got the 'too low terrain' followed by 'landing gear.' while we were clear of terrain and the gear was in transit going down. we were doing a 900 fpm descent and i brought the nose up in response to the warnings and they went away quickly. this happened around the redacted fix on the approach about 6 miles from the airport and we were roughly 2000 feet agl. we were actually slightly high on the flight path angle and were 2 white 2 red on the papi. i had visual of terrain which we were clear of and continued the approach and landed safely.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A PA24 pilot reported they were on final approach to an airport after the Tower closed with an electrical power failure resulting in radio failure and they had an NMAC with another aircraft on final.
text: flight was to redacted along location x with visual flight rules flight following. another plane was following me into the airport environment. approximately 8 nm southeast of redacted i had a partial panel loss. i lost all comms, gps and transponder. the tower was closed so the airport was class g with unicom reporting on the tower frequency. air traffic control ended flight following and i attempted to switched from redacted [tracon] to redacted [unicom] at which time i had the partial loss of panel (radio stack bus). i lost comms so i was unable to make position calls. i also lost ads-b out so the airplane following was unable to see me on ads-b in. i was on final for landing and the other plane saw me and maneuvered (climbed) to avoid a possible collision. i am reporting this because i was inside the redacted mode c veil when i lot my transponder. i was also unable to communicate position or intention causing the close encounter with another aircraft.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a near miss with another aircraft while flying an extended downwind in the traffic pattern. The other aircraft maneuvered sharply to avoid the pilot's aircraft when they turned early.
text: tonight around i was involved in a near aircraft collision. i was cleared into the delta and was informed to get behind aircraft y on a crosswind, entering into a downwind. i followed that aircraft. air traffic control was trying to get a faster aircraft in before aircraft y and myself landed. after a prolonged downwind, i asked air traffic control would they like for me to continue, they said yes. i then continued what appeared to be straight and naturally my training kicked in to follow xx flying south. i continued that direction and short after i saw the plane coming in my direction and he turned sharply and descended to avoid me. i am a new ppl and currently in instrument training and was getting night flight time in. i will be reading the far/aim and looking for certifications regarding situational awareness and mid air collisions. i accept responsibility for drifting to the right and following xx as a reference point to ensure that i did not loose the airport.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an aural terrain warning during a visual approach to DEN. Crew executed a missed approach.
text: while flying day, vmc to den runway34r, we were cleared for the visual approach on a dogleg heading and 9000' with instructions to maintain 170 kts to corde (faf). first officer had a 2 mile ring around corde for sa, and as a spot where he briefed he would drop the gear and call for flaps 15. first officer armed the approach but we did not set a lower altitude. corde altitude is 7000' or above. just outside of the 2 mile ring from the faf i mentioned that we were high and needed a lower altitude set with the autopilot on, did he want 7000? we then set 7000' and the plane began a shallow descent, but we were still high. just inside the 2 mile ring (1.5 miles from corde) we were 600-700' high and going higher on the path. we lowered the gear, he called for flaps 15, and began to slow to his target speed of 160. we were now over 800' high, and i mentioned that it would be helpful to keep his speed up to lose the required altitude. he responded by increasing the mcp speed back toward 170 with the autopilot on. when i saw that we were over 1000' high on the path deviation scale i told him we that wasn't going to do it, we needed to get the nose down and increase our rate of descent, whereupon he disengaged the autopilot and pitched down a bit. we also went flaps 25 at this point. i assessed that we were too high to use v/s to capture glideslope from above in time to make the stabilization windows, but we were nearing glideslope as he hand flew the plane, at between 165-170 kts. i told him that the 1000' window was coming up, we should reduce the descent rate from what i recall was reading over 1800 fpm.big failure on my part was that, as i was distracted with helping correct the descent rate and glideslope, i failed to mention that we still did not have final flaps at the 1000' window.first officer was able to arrest the rate of descent, but, as we were nearing 600', i recall that the papi was displaying 4 red (low), and we got a couple of 'glideslope' calls. as we were still slowing to our target speed i felt that by leveling off he would recapture glideslope from below about the same time we would hit our target speed, so i figured we'd be able to achieve the 500' stability window. however, as we neared the 500' window we received a 'too low, terrain' call and went around. the 'too low, terrain' call surprised me, as we were completely vmc and nowhere near dangerous terrain on final, but i then realized that we were not at flaps 30. i know that will sometimes cause a 'too low, terrain' call instead of a 'too low, flaps' call, which would've been more obvious as to what was wrong.in hindsight a 'too low, terrain' callout should be followed by a terrain escape maneuver instead of the go-around that we did.the go-around was uneventful, as was the subsequent landing on runway35r.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported having to immediately brake to avoid traffic during taxi. Taxi continued uneventfully.
text: during taxi out of sfo on taxiway a, the ca and i noted a widebody jet taxiing abeam us on taxiway b. we both noted that we liked the livery and that the plane looked very nice. as we were single engine taxiing, the ca called for the delayed engine start. while performing the delayed engine start, i heard the ca state something like 'woah!' and engage the brakes. i looked up to see the widebody aircraft had used taxiway g to turn directly in front of our aircraft on taxiway a. after the widebody aircraft turned, sfo ground control informed us to give way to the widebody aircraft. i stated something like 'we definitely see them, giving way' to ground. the taxi speed prior to braking was not noteworthy to me and i'm estimating that we were around 15 kias of ground speed. i cannot be certain as i was performing the delayed engine start procedure but nothing felt 'fast.' the remaining taxi and takeoff were uneventful.at xa:05, just prior to the top of descent, the fa called the flight deck informing us of back pain during a braking moment in san francisco. the ca directed the fa to cease duties and file a report.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B757-200 Captain reported a loss of an engine during climb. Flight crew returned to the departure airport.
text: passing through 4000, the r eng (engine) press eicas and light intermittently displayed. the first officer continued to fly the aircraft throughout the flight. i ran the eng press and subsequent engine shutdown checklists. the right engine was shutdown, priority handling was requested, and an uneventful air turn back completed. after landing, the crash fire rescue crew observed oil dripping from the right engine.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-175 First Officer reported loss of a hydraulic system during descent. Flight continued to landing.
text: on day 0, i was pilot flying redacted-redacted. when descending on the redacted arrival between 10, 000-11, 000 ms, we got an eicas message of hyd 2 lo pressure. i looked on the hydraulics page and there was no hydraulic pressure in system 2. the captain requested air traffic control assistance and advised approach that we had xx souls on board and 4900 pounds of fuel. the captain requested vectors so that we could stay out of the way of other aircraft and could run the checklist per the qrh. once the captain located the checklist he started going through it and while doing it, we also got the spoiler fault eicas message. the captain completed the hyd 2 lo pressure checklist items and hyd 2 lo pressure remained annunciated, after that he worked on the spoiler fault checklist and once that was completed, spoiler fault extinguished. the captain then calculated the landing numbers to get the appropriate v-speeds and landing distance. once he got those numbers we transferred controls and he became the flying pilot and i became pilot monitoring.when the captain called for gear down i moved the gear selector and the gear did not come down and we got the lg lever disagree eicas message. after completing this checklist, it called to go to the alternate landing gear extension checklist which we completed and the gear came down. after this, we notified air traffic control that we were ready to come in for landing, they gave us runway xx l which is up sloping. this was the most ideal choice as it would aid in stopping the aircraft. the landing was successful and soft but the plane did not have nose wheel steering, so differential braking was used to keep directional control. the captain was able to slow the aircraft enough to make the high speed exit and clear the runway and make a slight right turn onto taxiway 1. once on taxiway 1, the aircraft was stopped and we notified tower that we would need to stay there until we could get tugged in.once tower was notified, the captain notified the passengers, operations, and dispatch of the issue. we left the plane in the landing configuration, started the apu and left both engines running until the tug arrived. after waiting 25-30 minutes, tug came and we secured both engines and got towed. once at the gate, all passengers deplaned and the captain spoke to the dispatch supervisor and maintenance control and made the appropriate logbook entries.cause: aircraft loss of hydraulic system 2.suggestions: as second in command, i could've done a better job suggesting that we get in contact with dispatch, the passengers, and the flight attendants to keep everyone informed on the situation.

synopsis: EMB-175 Captain reported loss of a hydraulic system on descent. Flight landed successfully.

checklist.additionally, because of the feeling stress, i failed to inform the dispatcher, the flight attendants, and the passengers of the situation at hand. looking back at the situation, i had synopsis: CRJ 700 flight crew reported temporary loss of aircraft control due to moderate to severe turbulence encountered during cruise.

power!" to the first officer. he rapidly responded by applying toga power and asked if apr was necessary. i said no as airspeed was rapidly recovering. it is important to note the weather radar had previously showed no weather at or beneath the location where this happened at any point leading up to or at this location. moments later, the autopilot disconnected as the airplane lurched suddenly into approximately 20 degrees of left bank and 7 degrees of pitch up accompanied by a rapid loss of airspeed. i took control of the airplane and called, "my aircraft." i leveled the nose immediately and leveled the wings while simultaneously reapplying toga thrust. focused on maintaining attitude, i allowed deviations in altitude but remained very conscious of airspeed as it fell. i ordered the first officer to call a descent to fl340 to air traffic control as a means of maintaining airspeed as the airspeed was initially completely unresponsive to the increased thrust and i felt a descent necessary to stay on the correct side of the power curve. in approximately negative 2 degrees of pitch, the airplane initially began descending to approx fl355 and then rapidly climbed to approx fl365 while still pitched down as the airspeed rapidly recovered before the first officer could inform air traffic control. the airplane came back under positive control and i modified my instructions to the first officer, 'inform air traffic control of a severe turbulence encounter with deviations +/-500 feet.' the airplane remained under positive control thereafter, although for 5 or 10 minutes a very high thrust setting (clb) was frequently necessary to maintain .75m, which we had been flying at before, during, and after the encounter. i returned control to the first officer and the rest of the flight proceeded as normal except for a later stall fail caution message in the descent to redacted. no one was injured and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft."

synopsis: B-737-800 flight crew reported returning to departure airport after the aircraft failed to pressurize during climb out.
text: on day 0 while operating from redacted to redacted. we experienced a pressurization issue shortly after departure. during the climb, the cabin was not pressurizing as expected and cabin altitude indications were not responding normally.we had a rapid rate of cabin altitude ascent. we proceed to stop the climb out and stop at 7, 000 feet to stop the cabin from climbing.prior to departure we did write up that the n1 gauges were showing a big split between each other on the ground at the gate. maintaience came and looked at the issue which was written up a similar way for this aircraft earlier. maintaience put the right pack back on mel even though it had been cleared in redacted just prior to this flight. i questioned that choice and spoke with the dispatcher, duty pilot and maintenance control. maintenance control went through the previous write up and looked to see what was done. i was informed that the problem the aircraft had for the pressurization issue prior was not related with the pack and that they performed tests of pressurization in accordance with boeing standard procedures. after speaking with maintenance control my first officer and i were comfortable taking the aircraft as they said what test and checks were done by maintenance and the plane was safe to continue for service.once we leveled off and communicated with air traffic control. i immediately directed my attention to the abnormal indication and the first officer and i accomplished the applicable qrh procedure for pressurization malfunction. the aircraft was leveled off as required and we began coordinating a return to redacted.given the proximity to the departure airport, air traffic control coordination, aircraft configuration considerations, and time compression associated with the abnormal condition, my focus was primarily on safely flying the aircraft, completing the qrh, and setting up for the return and landing. the decision was made to return to redacted.during this period of high workload and compressed timeline, i overlooked referring the fom for additional considerations related to overweight landing and did not formally declare an emergency with air traffic control. air traffic control was informed about what the situation was and that we were doing a checklist and our plans to return to redacted. the qrh checklist was followed for the overweight landing and what to expect and to do a landing assessment. in that qrh under additional items which was after checklist completion it had a few lengthy paragraphs about overweight landing characteristics and a line about going to the fom for more guidance which i overlooked about the fom. in retrospect, referencing the fom would have prompted a formal emergency declaration due to the overweight landing condition.the approach and landing were uneventful. the aircraft landed safely without injury to passengers or crew and without aircraft damage. after clearing the runway, we coordinated with maintenance and completed the appropriate write-ups in the aircraft logbook regarding the pressurization malfunction and overweight landing.upon reflection, this event reinforced the importance of deliberate consideration of administrative and procedural follow-through such as emergency declaration requirements even when the operational outcome appears controlled and manageable. in the future, i will ensure that, workload permitting, i take a moment to cross-check fom guidance when abnormal situations involve potential overweight landings or other criteria requiring formal declaration.safety was maintained throughout the event, and all required documentation was completed.cause: aircraft had recent pressurization-related write-up. the right pack was re-minimum equipment list'd after being cleared.although maintenance stated issue was unrelated, prior history may have increased system vulnerability. there is also a potential normalization of repeat discrepancy.i think to mitigate this would be to not dispatch an aircraft with a repeat item in the same day with similar write up issues and investigate the problem closer.

degrees and cloudy. we had conditioned air prior to boarding and all necessary ground equipment standing by. at the time, i felt redacted should be a competent station to safely receive an aircraft without an apu. the cabin temperature got uncomfortably warm during the crossbleed start but cooled relatively quickly in flight. the apu was in the minimum equipment list and we felt redacted should worse, we had an faa representative on the jump seat witnessing the entire event.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a split duct pressure indication on take off. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: we took off xxc in redacted. it was a flaps 5 bleeds on nadp (noise abatement departure procedure) 1 dep. after calling flaps up after takeoff checklist, my first officer noticed during the checklist that we had a r duct pressure of 80 psi and that the l duct pressure was only at 40psi. we then told air traffic control that we wanted to level off. they gave us 15000ft to do so. at that time i transferred the controls over to my first officer as well as the radios and i started to focus on the issue. i remembered from previous flights that there is no real guidance on this issue other than a brief paragraph in the limitations section from the fm. which states ' a duct pressure difference of more than 8 psi may indicate a mechanicalmalfunction. if a duct pressure split is observed after bleeds are configured forflight, and the lowest indication is approximately 18 psi or less, contactmaintenance. text: there is a new landfill pit that garbage is being dumped into on a 1 mile final to runway 36l. we cross that point at 500 feet resolution advisory. i've noticed excavating on previous flights but on day 0 i saw that garbage was being dumped into this pit. landfills create thermals and attract large birds like seagulls. not a great idea just short of a runway. i again flew into aus the next day, day 1, and i saw more garbage being dumped into there. on the ground i mentioned to my first officer that this new landfill pit will cause thermals and attract birds, so be wary on upcoming flights. on our taxi out to 36r on our next flight on the same day, we heard planes landing on 36l telling tower that there were large birds at 200 feet. my first officer and i could see these birds.why in the world is a garbage pit allowed at the end of a runway? especially at a major airport? this should not be allowed.
