synopsis: Fractional First Officer reported while circling to land; the Captain descended below the minimum descent altitude and received a low altitude alert from tower. During the missed approach the flight received a bank angle warning.
text: headed to redacted with winter weather moving in. weather at destination had been a bit variable over the time period we had been watching it prior to our arrival.340 to 360 5-8kts visibility was reporting 6-7 miles ceilings were 600+ temp just above freezing around 2-3c. due to the high tail wind and decreasing weather conditions we were concerned with being able to land xx in redacted. weather in redacted had been similar however wind had been reporting higher. there was a lot of discussion about the pros and cons of shooting the instrument landing system to xx and landing with a tail wind vs loc xx circle xy. we did run our efb for both directions and they both worked with current conditions. however with the wind just below the limit at redacted made captain nervous with conditions worsening. he called tower directly over the radio and got a weather report. i don't remember what that report was i believe higher winds from the north. he also mentioned tower hadn't had any traffic in a while so no runway condition report. visibility was reporting plenty good so we opted for the loc xx circle xy. on the approach we broke out higher than i was expecting however visibility was not what was reported. in particular on the south end of the field. we circled at the published mda however we forgot about the notam with a mda 60ft higher. at the time we were both completely unaware we had made the mistake. around the downwind to base leg tower gave us a low level alert which we confirmed our altitude. shortly after we lost sight of the airport and went missed. which leads to the second error. the turn away from the airport. captain said i lost sight of the airport tell them we are going missed. i call tower and let them know, they acknowledged and told us to fly the published missed. captian hits the go around button brings power up then makes no call outs. i query him about setting flaps to setting two. he replied flaps two. then immediately calls gear up. i raised flaps to two and put the gear up. in the time period he started making a right turn away from the airport. i could tell he was behind the plane. i didn't want to cause more confusion or debate with correcting him at this point. so checked the chart for obstacles. when my eyes get back to the pfd (primary flight display) i notice we are well beyond 30 degrees of bank so i called out bank angle. he corrects however is a little aggressive with the controls when he does. at this point we continue on with the missed and divert to redacted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B777-300 pilot reported an engine oil quantity malfunction during cruise flight. The flight diverted to an alternate airport; dumped fuel; and landed.
text: at cruise flight engine #2 (right) had a complete loss of engine oil. oil quantity indicated zero quarts. coordinated with dispatch and maintenance and decided to divert to redacted. we requested priority handling with air traffic control. in the interest of safety we dumped fuel to get below max landing weight. finished up all checklists on the way to redacted and landed non eventful. cause: the event resulted from an unexpected mechanical malfunction of an engine component, likely due to wear. no prior indications were noted during preflight.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported GRI Tower informed the flight crew of pushing into the movement area without clearance and that this is a recurring issue.
text: after an engine start at the gate we pushed back for a crossbleed start and taxi out. we completed the tasks and received taxi instructions from tower (they were handling everything on tower frequency). when we started to taxi, i believe it was a tower manager or supervisor told us that we had pushed into the movement area. we apologized. i mentioned we used to power out and this was the first time i had pushed out. he stated that he was aware that we had once powered out and said something to the effect that this has happened a lot lately. also that the people that were pushing us were instructed to inform us to call for push, which we didn't get. despite that, ultimately it is my fault for allowing the aircraft to push into the movement area. tower informed us no harm, no foul" which was kind, but there was a foul. my fault. biggest reason to write the report is so perhaps pilots can be given a bulletin to watch out for this issue, only because the tower stated it has been happening lately (pushes into the movement area). i incorrectly thought there was space to push but was incorrect and it appears others have had the same issue."

text: we were cleared for takeoff from runway xxr from redacted. all pre take off checks were normal, take off config was ok and brake temps were in green. we were on a normal take off roll, with normal acceleration. at about 90kts, we had a warning message- no take off config, with take off brakes" aural warning. emergency brake was stowed and nothing looked out of normal. this was followed with brake degradation and brake overheat cautions messages. at 95kts ca rejected takeoff. we reported to the tower and exited the runway. ca called the maintenance and decided to taxi back to the gate to deplane."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: ERJ 145 Captain reported smoke in the cabin at the gate prior to push back. Captain refused the aircraft.
text: during pre-departure preparations for flight abcd (redacted-redacted), maintenance personnel entered the flight deck approximately ten minutes before door closure to check oil levels and advised us they would service the no. 2 engine. we acknowledged and continued normal duties. after receiving matching passenger counts from the flight attendant and release, i authorized door closure. both packs were operating at that time, and no abnormal odors were present.seconds after the door closed, while awaiting the flight attendant's cabin secure" report, i detected an acrid, "old socks/burning" odor on the flight deck with no visible smoke. i immediately turned both packs off and opened the dv (direct vision) windows to ventilate. the flight attendant confirmed the odor was also present in the cabin. with windows open and recirculation fans on, the smell began to dissipate. i contacted maintenance control and described the situation. they requested that we turn each pack on individually to isolate the source. i expressed concern about reintroducing fumes, but they advised the effect should be minimal with ventilation.we briefed the flight attendant and instructed her to open the service door if the odor returned. pack 1 produced no abnormal smell. upon selecting pack 2 on, the same strong acrid odor immediately returned, prompting us to turn pack 2 off. the flight attendant opened the service door due to the intensity of the smell. at this point, i determined the aircraft was no longer safe for passengers or crew. i instructed the first officer to contact operations and request the jet bridge be reconnected for deplaning. i informed maintenance control that i was refusing the aircraft and contacted dispatch to advise that a new aircraft would be required.after all passengers deplaned, the crew elected to seek medical evaluation out of caution. vitals and blood samples were taken, no abnormalities were found. i experienced a scratchy throat, and medical staff advised it should resolve within 24 hours.cause: i believe somehow the oil vapors or oil drippings got into the apu bleed system when they were servicing the engine number 2.suggestions: use o2 mask whenever it is needed. i didn't use it because i thought the ventilation with the windows open was enough. i ended up with a scratchy throat."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B717 flight crew reported an engine compressor stall that resulted in a diversion.
text: rh engine compressor stall on takeoff out of redacted runway xx. at 1200ft, heard a loud repetitive bang coming from right engine, which was confirmed by rh engine tgt (turbine gas temperature), n1, and epr (engine pressure ratio) gauges. ca was pf. crew acknowledged the situation and ran appropriate memory items, qrh checklist, and procedures. pf pulled power to idle on rh engine. per the brief that was accomplished at the first flight of the day, crew decided to divert to redacted for longer runway, familiar terrain, and facilities availability. pf decided to request priority handling and state intentions to divert to redacted with air traffic control. pf tried to climb again after the checklist was done, but the compressor stall came back. pf decided to keep both engines below 80% n1 and accomplished a shallow climb to cruise alt. ran appropriate checklists and managed workload, communication, and positive aircraft control between pf and pm. landed in redacted runway xyl. stopped on the runway to get inspected by fire trucks. then proceeded to taxi to the ramp after the fire chief gave us confirmation that no external damage was suspected. filled out maintenance logbook and notified maintenance of the situation.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air carrier technician reported while taxiing aircraft from the gate to the hangar; they inadvertently crossed a runway hold short line and ATC instructed a landing aircraft to go around.
text: i was taxing aircraft x from the terminal to the hanger. i was told by air traffic control to cross runway xxl at taxiway 1. i think i was told to 'operate without delay' or 'expedite'. the aircraft was much heavier than usual due to extra fuel onboard. i used more than usual thrust to cross runway xxl. once across runway xxl heading north on taxiway 1 i applied brakes to hold short of runway xxc. the aircraft brakes could not stop the jet like i was accustomed to. in addition to aircraft brakes, i was able to deploy left and right engine thrust reversers to get the plane to stop. the aircraft stopped beyond the hold bar causing a landing aircraft to do a 'go around'. cause: i believe the event occurred due to three reasons. one, the aircraft had approximately 20k lbs more fuel than normal. two, due to the weight of the aircraft, it's performance both on accelerating and braking was not what i have experienced in the past. three, i was following direction to 'expedite'.suggestions: in the future, i will tell air traffic control i'm unable to expedite if an aircraft is too heavy.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: C172 pilot reported a gust on landing resulted in a runway excursion; momentary loss of control; and a prop strike.
text: normal preflight at redacted. filled both tanks. departed runway xx closed pattern for excellent landing - slight crosswind. back taxi then departed rwy xx and departed area to north. turned west after clear of redacted airspace toward redacted. on unicom call to redacted, faster traffic behind me. i radioed intention to circle to the north and follow him in. he reported clear of active as i entered downwind for rwy xy. i had obtained awos enroute. usual pattern for me - 10 deg flap abeam and 20 degrees on base and final. cross threshold 75 mph and idle. slight left crosswind. round out and flare over centerline. immediately before wheels touch, abrupt gust pushing me to the right causing change of heading and right wheel touch first. correction applied to bring left wheel down. was offline and left concrete onto grass. i allowed speed to slow then applied left steering to return to concrete. able to apply brakes and back taxi to ramp to inspect. engine did not stop until shutdown on ramp. inspection all normal except prop ends curled. airport manager and i drove down runway and noted where airplane exited concrete and then returned. he noted approx 5 cm area on concrete edge where plane returned to rwy that appeared to be where prop skimmed concrete. i think there was significant crosswind gust right at wheel touch that contributed to exiting runway. i would plan review flighttime with instructor.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Corporate Captain reported flying direct to destination Knoxville instead of the fix OCATL due to both sounding similar.
text: we received a clearance to proceed direct to what we heard was knoxville, tn (tys) from air traffic control. upon receiving this clearance, we read back proceed directed to knoxville and ended the readback with thank you. after the readback we input the turn into the flight management system and proceeded directed to knoxville. after approximately 3 to 5 minutes air traffic control came back on and said we were not cleared to knoxville and to turn to a head of 280. at which time air traffic control sent a new route via cpdlc with the first fix, ocatl. after proceeding direct to ocatl, we clarified with air traffic control that we heard and read back clear to knoxville." they said no we were clear to ocatl. it appeared that there was a miscommunication between air traffic control and the crew. they cleared us directed to ocatl and we heard and read back directed to knoxville. when we read back to proceed to knoxville and air traffic control never corrected us, apparently hearing that we said directed ocatl. we feel that the closeness of how the fix's name (ocatl) and our destination name (knoxville) sounds led to both the crew and air traffic control missing the clearance and readback."

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a NMAC during departure climb with an aircraft that had previously departed.
text: on day 0, i was flying with another time-building pilot, person a. we departed from runway 03 at igm.while taxiing for run-up, there was another low-wing aircraft ahead of us. i was not certain whether it was a aircraft y or aircraft z, but it appeared to have retractable landing gear.the pilot announced on ctaf that he would conduct his run-up outside runway 03. i then transmitted on ctaf that we would be number two behind him for run-up.after completing his run-up, the pilot announced on ctaf that he would depart runway 03 with a straight-out departure. once he began his takeoff roll and became airborne, no further position reports were made by that aircraft.i also did not see his aircraft displayed on foreflight, although my sentry device was operating normally and i was able to see other aircraft traffic. therefore, i believed the aircraft likely did not have ads-b out.after visually observing him climb to approximately 300 feet agl, i made a ctaf transmission stating that we would be departing runway 03 with a left crosswind departure returning to redacted.after takeoff, i announced on ctaf that we were on the go from runway 03 and would be making a left crosswind departure. during the left crosswind turn, i again reported our position, altitude, and intention to return to redacted.the previously departed aircraft made no additional ctaf transmissions.we continued climbing, and while passing approximately 5, 000-6, 000 feet, i suddenly noticed an object very close to us on our right side about 200ft horizontally and same altitude. i immediately looked to the right with my safety pilot and observed a low-wing aircraft passing nearby at what appeared to be a similar altitude and nearly parallel but opposite direction flight path, and still nothing displayed on our foreflight. because the aircraft appeared to be moving roughly parallel and separation was increasing, i made only a slight left deviation to increase spacing rather than performing an aggressive avoidance maneuver.i cannot confirm with certainty that it was the same aircraft that departed before us, however, based on its appearance, it was likely the same airplane.we continued making position and altitude reports on ctaf and then proceeded to depart the area and return to redacted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported throttle failure during takeoff roll resulted in rejected takeoff.
text: i was practicing touch and goes with my student pilot. on our ninth touch and go, we were cleared for the option on xx r. the student completed the landing and set throttle to full for takeoff. the throttle moved to the full position but no change in power. i took controls and tried as well with the same result. the engine was stuck on idle with no way for us to control the throttle. i requested from tower to make it a full stop and we taxied straight in to the ramp. from the ramp we taxied to our maintenance hangar where we proceeded to shut down as normal. there was no injury to people or property during the incident.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a critical ground conflict during takeoff roll with a helicopter that was hovering over the runway.
text: i was taking off at aun a helicopter announced he was short final and 'simulated engine out.' when the helicopter passed overhead, he was very high and not over the runway...he was over the taxi way. every time i have flown with helicopters in the vicinity, they have flown over taxi ways and landed on helipads in between taxi ways and the runways. i am unfamiliar with and have rec'd no formal training on helicopter operations.when i began my takeoff roll-after seeing the runway clear-i lowered my eyes to check my gauges and looking up, i saw the helicopter hovering about 200 feet over the runway just short of midfield. by that time, i was already almost at rotation speed, and felt like if i were to stop, and if the helicopter landed, i might not stop in time and hit him or go on the grass. at that point, i decided to expedite and proceed with my take off, and use the far left side of the runway as he was hovering over the right side of the runway. in the moment that seemed like the best chance for avoiding a collision or injury.i passed under him to his left as quickly as i could (15 mph over vr) to get out of the way. once clear, i rotated safely and took off. i apologized and proceeded to redacted.i probably should have watched and made sure the helicopter was doing what i expected before my take off roll. i really have never seen a helicopter use the runway or airspace directly over the runway. it was a busy day at aun with many people coming and going.

synopsis: Air taxi Captain reported flying direct to HAGEL instead of the cleared HAGAL and did not realize this mistake until ATC inquired.
text: just after leveling at 26, 000 feet i crossed bamma waypoint and made a left turn towards hagal waypoint. two minutes after turning air traffic control calls me and asks are you sure you are heading to hagal? i checked the gps - it shows direct hagel not direct hagal. it is a heading difference of 23 degrees. there was a left direct crosswind of over 130 kt. so i really didn't notice the extra turn towards the west. i have flown this route a number of times recently and have the route pre-stored in the gps. unfortunately, i didn't realize that there were two stored routes for this trip and one of them had the waypoint hagel instead of hagal. i failed to double-check the stored routed after selecting it. that is a mistake i will not make again.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported the aircraft's engine failed just after landing.
text: incident occured shortly after landing on runway xx at redacted. pattern at the time was empty. after an uneventful ladning i took controls to taxi off the runway. upon idling the engine to slow to make a turn onto the taxiway, the engine sputtered and died. the aircraft came to a stop about 1 foot away from crossing the hold short bars. attempted a quick restart that failed, ended up having to shut down the aircraft and push. in all, the aircraft was stuck within the runway environment for about 30 seconds until i pushed it out. luckly no one was in the pattern at the time. the failure seemed to be a result of spark plug fouling. once clear of the runway, i was able to properly start the engine and troubleshoot the issue. overall, the issue was resolved and did not result in any further incidents, and other traffic was still absent from the airport throughout the timeframe during which this incident occurred. i wanted to submit a report given the position the aircraft initially came to a stop at, prior to being pushed out.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: C177 pilot on an RNAV approach reported a NMAC with a light sport aircraft climbing from a nearby non towered airport.
text: i was flying under call sign x on approach to redacted. i was flying the rnav xx on an instrument flight rules flight plan. i was handed off from redacted app to tower. on the handoff i was advised of traffic in the pattern at redacted. checking on with redacted tower they told me there was two in the pattern at redacted and i said i had both in sight (one on final and one on the go). shortly my gps alerted me to traffic 500 below. i had lost sight of the departing aircraft as it had gone under my nose, but at 500 below and based on the track presented to me it appeared to be in the pattern that i was overflying. seconds later i saw an aircraft same altitude heading directly at me in a climb. this aircraft never leveled off or cleared the area. i took evasive action diving and braking away to the right to avoid the midair collision. i would estimate we were 100 ft or less. i let tower know i was maneuvering aggressively to avoid traffic and they told me they understood. no other issues on the flight.after landing i looked up the flight and found it to be aircraft y from company.looking at the departure of the aircraft they took off in a normal pattern, then climbed through downwind before departing. after following the highway for several miles. this was not a normal departure from that airport nor was it one following the aim. it is also clear to me they never cleared the climb and i saw the aircraft take no action to avoid the conflict. this was a clear unsafe maneuver that almost ended the life of both myself and my daughter. i believe this could have been avoided with departing the airport per normal aim procedures as the aircraft did on the next flight of the day. i believe there is an unsafe culture at redacted and more so out of the flight school that is operating there. this is not the first time i have heard of conflicts and i'm worried someone is going to get hurt.

text: i was conducting a training flight with a student. i was on short final .5 nm from the runway threshold, established on a straight in for runway xx with a private pilot student, when a cub making a 300 ft agl (500 ft) msl pattern caused a near miss. while i was established on final and he was on downwind for runway xx '300 agl', he proceeds to fly directly over the approach end of xx causing a near miss at the end of the runway. as i realized this hazard i made the prompt decision to take controls and perform a maximum performance climbing right turn to avoid him by roughly 200 feet. his friend argued on frequency that no comms or transponder are required in class 'g' airspace, which he is correct about, however he flew direct opposite of the final approach course of the active runway head on with myself. his pilot in command decision making consistently poses a threat to the safety of myself and other aircraft.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: C182 pilot reported smoke and fumes in the cockpit during cruise. Pilot diverted and landed safely.
text: while operating a 2020 cessna 182t (g1000 nxi), under visual flight rules with flight following, i experienced an in-flight electrical smoke event.en route with one practice landing at redacted. after departing redacted, i was established in cruise at 6, 500 feet msl in clear vmc conditions. i had completed the cruise checklist shortly before the event, and all indications were normal at that time.while in cruise, i observed a light puff of white smoke emanating from the left side of the instrument panel accompanied by a strong electrical odor. no visible flame was observed. at approximately the same time, the multi-function flight display (mfd) went blank, the primary flight display (pfd) and radio panel flickered intermittently, and the secondary radio became inoperative. no circuit breakers were found popped.i immediately requested priority handling with redacted [tracon] and diverted to the nearest suitable airport, redacted. i pulled the mfd circuit breaker. the master and alternator were left on in order to retain primary radio communications during the diversion. no windows were opened, and no oxygen was used. the aircraft landed approximately 5-10 minutes after onset without further incident. there were no injuries.after landing, the avionics switches were observed to be heat-deformed/melted. no additional smoke was observed after the initial puff.post-flight maintenance inspection reported no evidence of active fire. a malfunctioning avionics switch on bus 2 was identified and replaced. wiring behind the panel was inspected by maintenance personnel, and an independent avionics shop conducted an additional inspection prior to return to service.this report is submitted in the interest of safety documentation and analysis of an electrical smoke event involving heat deformation of panel components and partial avionics failure in flight.the problem arose in cruise flight at 6, 500 feet msl, shortly after completing the cruise checklist with normal indications, a light puff of white smoke was observed from the left side of the instrument panel accompanied by a strong electrical odor. avionics degradation followed immediately.the event was first identified visually (smoke) and by smell (electrical odor), followed by loss of the mfd and intermittent operation of other avionics.the precise initiating failure is undetermined from the pilot's perspective. post-flight maintenance identified a malfunctioning avionics switch on bus 2. the relationship between that component and the in-flight smoke event was not independently determined by the reporting pilot.the presence of smoke in the cockpit was assessed as a potentially time-critical situation. immediate priorities were aircraft control, communication, and expeditious landing. priority handling was requested promptly. a decision was made to pull the mfd circuit breaker while leaving the master and alternator on in order to retain primary radio communication capability during the diversion.the event occurred unexpectedly during routine cruise flight. the presence of smoke created a heightened workload environment requiring rapid prioritization of tasks. maintaining situational awareness and communication while managing a partial avionics degradation required focused attention.the aircraft was diverted to the nearest suitable airport (redacted) and landed within approximately 5-10 minutes of onset. the mfd circuit breaker was pulled. other electrical components were not de-energized in order to preserve communication capability during the emergency descent and landing.the aircraft was removed from service pending maintenance evaluation. maintenance reported no evidence of active fire. a faulty avionics switch on bus 2 was replaced, wiring was inspected, and an independent avionics inspection was conducted prior to return to service.

text: in month 2, while i was off duty, my peer redacted qc (quality control) inspector person a completed a borescope re-inspection on aircraft x #1 engine, s/n redacted. she determined that the previously deferred (logbook deferral sheet redacted) burn holes had grown axially but remained on the same 150-hour re-inspection interval.two days later, maintenance control technician person b forwarded an email to the list of the redacted qc shop. the email was between person c a powerplant engineer and person d, an engineer. the email explained they did not agree with the axial measurements and the worst radial measurements appeared to be 0.177 inch and per the amm (72-xx-xx-redacted-redacted-redacted-x) the item should be on a 750-hour re-inspection interval.upon my return to work, i read the email and checked the online system to find that maintenance person b had changed the re-inspection interval to the 750-hour limit from the 150-hour re-inspection interval applied in redacted on month 1due to power plant engineer person e conferring with person d. it is my understanding that maintenance control is not to change inspection department findings without an approved document. a review of the facts found that redacted had originally placed this deferral on a 300-hour re-inspection. however, under redacted, deferral reference, dated month 0, identified a 150 hour re-inspect but a 750-hour re-inspection per the engineer.in month 1, redacted inspector person f dropped the original limit from its initial 300-hour re-inspection to a 150-hour inspection. following this change, redacted, redacted and redacted qc inspectors completing re-inspections all determined the limit should remain on a 150-hour inspection interval the amm (72-xx-xx-redacted-redacted-redacted-y) states accept with an inspection each 750 hours if the le hole beyond the 50 percent span is less than 0.10 in. (2.54 mm) axially and less than 0.20 in. (5.08 mm) radially.there are multiple pictures on the qc borescope file showing that the radial holes are larger than 0.20 in. to me, this would be either a 30- hour re-inspection or a 150- hour re-inspection depending on how the axial dimensions are measured. we have a measurement training guide that shows the way all of our inspectors measured it, we also have the email from person d stating to measure from where the nose of the leading-edge airfoil would have been back the end of the damage. i emailed maintenance to have the deferral revised. however, to date, i have not received a response except from our supervisor person g who suggested he will investigate this matter. but is currently training at another station.cause: maintenance changed a re-inspection interval without advising the staff involved with the limit, without having supporting technical data.suggestions: prohibit having maintenance changing discrepancies and limits entered by others.

xx at about 700 ft agl, my student suddenly yelled 'traffic!!' and made abrupt control inputs, climbing and banking left. before i had a chance to react, i saw the helicopter pass in front and below us through the lower right corner of the windscreen, and then out my side window maybe 50-100 feet below. we regained our composure and the student decided to continue with the flight.i would later ask the student when and where the helicopter was when he first saw it. he stated it was at about his ten o'clock and close enough to see the pilots face if it had been daylight.back in the office, i asked the line staff if they heard our radio calls and if he heard or saw the helicopter. he stated the helicopter came in and set down at their hanger, shut down for about thirty seconds, started back up and immediately took off. he said he heard our departure call on runway xx as the helicopter left the ground and started flying north through the two rows of hangers and passed by the office at high speed and rooftop level. he said he has never heard a helicopter take off that loud before. he thought to himself that the helicopter was going to fly right through (our) departure path. he the landings, i departed redacted for my return to redacted. my eta at redacted was approximately xa:00, and, based on the weather data available through my efb, my expectation was an arrival on runway xx at redacted. the flight from redacted to redacted was unremarkable in all regards. approximately 10 miles east of redacted, i obtained the weather via the redacted awos system, which indicated winds from 020 at 9 kts. as expected, the winds favored an arrival on runway xx, so i set up for a slightly wider than normal righthand base entry for runway xx. there was no local traffic in the pattern, and the only radio traffic was from a single inbound plane approximately 10 miles out for runway xx.i descended to pattern altitude at approximately 5 miles from redacted, added 10 degrees of flaps, and entered the right base for runway xx pitched to approximately 90 kts. upon turning north for final, approximately 2-3 miles south of redacted, i noted the winds aloft at pattern altitude seemed brisker than the awos report and i felt slight gusting, which was consistent with my prior experience at altitude and generally unremarkable. because of the ground level crosswind and the gusting at pattern altitude, i decided to make my landing with 20 degrees flaps, rather than my normal 30 degrees, and adjust my final approach speed up from my normal 65-70 kts to something in the low to mid 70 kts range.during final approach, i added the second 10 degrees of flaps approximately one mile from the threshold and i maintained a crab angle into the wind, which meant my heading was east of the runway heading, as expected. i adjusted my pitch after adding the second notch of flaps and was holding a pretty steady 72 kts airspeed with 20 degrees of flaps. upon reaching short final, i added left rudder to transition from a crab heading to runway heading using a 'right wing low slip technique' and continued to hold approximately 72 kts. the slight gusting i had experienced at pattern altitude was no longer evident at short final altitude. overall, the final approach felt stable and my airspeed and heading varied very little from the initial turn final until the threshold, except for the intentional airspeed adjustment associated with adding the second notch of flaps.as i crossed the threshold, i pulled power to idle, compensated for the slight nose down action associated with the 182 when power is brought to idle, and entered the ground effect. flight in the ground effect was stable, and my runway placement was slightly left of center but certainly within the middle third of the runway.when my airspeed dissipated sufficiently, i began my flare for touchdown. at this point, i experienced a gust (presumably) that caused the plane to yaw noticeably and abruptly to the left, which resulted in me being in a 'right wing low' bank with the right main leading the left main. i was expecting to touchdown any moment, so my reaction was to correct the left yaw by adding right aileron to bring the nose to the right and toward the center of the runway. in doing so, i believe i overcorrected for the left yaw and ended up pointing too far to the right when i touched down, which occurred immediately after making my correction.the touchdown led with the right main, which would have been oriented farthest to the south at this point due to the overcorrection. after the right main touched down, the left main and nose gear followed, either at the same time or perhaps with the left main slightly ahead of the nose. the touchdown itself was not particularly hard, although i wouldn't hold it out as my smoothest landing by any means.at this point, elapsed time became a little difficult to judge, but it seems like within a second or two after touchdown, i felt a force acting on the plane that i hadn't experienced before, and that caused me to pause for another second or two in order to evaluate what i was experiencing. i determined the force was sideloading toward my left, and i also noticed the left wing of the plane was dipping and the right main had come off the runway, resulting in the plane rolling only on the left main and the nose gear. i responded to the side loading by adding what little remaining right aileron i had left and pressing the left rudder pedal aggressively. unfortunately, neither control input seemed to help, and i believe the sideloading actually caused the nose wheel to turn to the right because the plane began rolling across the runway in a right arc. the tilt to the left gradually increased to the point where i actually leaned to the passenger side of the plane in an attempt to offset it. at some point, i heard a rubbing noise i didn't recognize, and my first reaction was to look out the left window to see if the left wingtip was dragging the ground. it did not seem to be close to dragging, so i assumed the rubbing noise was coming from the nose gear being in a bind or something along those lines (i later learned the noise was the prop contacting the runway surface).after arcing to the right across the runway for a couple seconds (which felt like an hour) with all the right aileron and left rudder i had to provide, the plane leaned back to the right and settled on all three gears. at this point, i engaged the brakes pretty aggressively and came to a stop about three feet from the right edge of runway xx with the engine running smoothly at idle. i'm guessing at this point, but it seems the nose of the plane was pointing about 040 or 050 at the time. suffice it to say, the rightward arc i traveled across the runway was significant in any event.i looked out the windows of the plane and noted a runway light less than a wing width away toward my left, and, based on my proximity to the runway edge, i didn't think i had enough room to attempt a left turn on the runway without risking an impact with the runway light. as a result, i elected to exit the runway to the east, make a lefthand arc through the rsa, and reenter the runway between the next set of runway lights, so that's how i proceeded. the exit and reentry of the runway was smooth and uneventful, so i proceeded north down runway xx to the next taxiway intersection and exited the runway. while taxiing down the runway, i heard the plane behind me call a five-mile final, so i announced myself upon exiting the runway and noted the traffic was on short final at that point.i taxied uneventfully back to the hangar and shut down the engine, and when the propeller came to a stop, i realized the tips were all curled, hence the unexplained noise i heard while arcing across the runway. this was the first time i realized a prop strike had occurred.at the time of the occurrence, i held a private pilot license with an instrument rating, as well as high performance and complex endorsements. i had 314.9 hours of total time, with 287.2 as pilot in command. specific to c182 time, i had a total of 81.0 hours and 100 landings, 40 of which were night landings. in the last 180 days, i had 20.8 hours in a c182 and 18 landings, 7 of which were night landings. in the last 90 days, i had 5.6 hours in a c182 and 11 landings, 6 of which were night landings. eight of the eleven landings in the prior 90 days, including all six of the night landings, took place one week before the occurrence, and those practice landings took place at redacted in nighttime crosswind conditions comparable to the date of the occurrence.i believe the occurrence was ultimately caused by pilot error, and better pilot actions at a couple different points in time could have potentially avoided the outcome. the initial opportunity could have been when i first experienced the gust (if it was a gust) and the resulting left yaw immediately before touchdown. had my reaction been to add full power at that point, rather than attempt to correct the heading, the outcome might have been avoided. likewise, had i not overcorrected with right aileron / under corrected with left rudder during the correction, i may have touched down aligned with the runway and avoided the sideloading upon touchdown. additionally, had i immediately recognized the side loading force when it occurred and added the remaining available right aileron and left rudder without a couple seconds of delay, i may have timely offset the force and corrected the track of the rollout before the side loading became so strong that the right main gear left the runway pavement. in terms of future corrective actions, i plan to schedule some instructor time under crosswind conditions so the instructor can make a fresh evaluation of my crosswind landing technique to see if there are deficiencies i haven't recognized. as an additional step, i believe i'm going to obtain a tail wheel endorsement because i've heard and read that tailwheel training really enhances rudder skills during landing and taxi operations.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Learjet 60 flight crew reported a runway excursion during landing on a slippery runway.
text: day 0, learjet 60, departed redacted for redacted. the forecast for redacted indicated ¼ mile in fzfg which caused the crew to delay takeoff for 1 hour to allow our arrival at redacted for the estimated forecast at xa:00z to be 200 and ½ mile visibility. the crew departed redacted at xb:51z and arrived in the area at approximately xc:06z just after the control tower opened. the crew acknowledged the new atis '1' indicating winds calm, ¼ fg, ceiling 100, temp -1c/dewpoint -1c, and altimeter 30.17. there was no mention of freezing fog. rnav (gps) rwy xx was in use. the instrument landing system rwy xx glidepath is notam'd out of service. as a crew, we decided to 'take a look' and performed the approach. at minimums, the approach lights came into sight and then the runway was in sight. however, due to a loss of visual to the runway missed approach was conducted. during the missed approach the crew noticed the weather seemed to be improving. we talked about it and thought that we would be able to complete an approach and land. after being vectored to the final approach course by redacted approach control, we performed a second rnav (gps rwy xx approach. on this approach, we again had the approach light system in sight at minimums and then the runway in sight. the flying pilot maintained a stabilized approach speed of approximately 140 knots based on a calculated vref speed of 137 knots. during the landing flare the plane floated for about 2 to 3 seconds before touching down. the flying pilot immediately deployed the thrust reverser system and began braking. the pilot monitoring noticed the 1000 foot marker quickly approaching and made the callout. the pilot flying went to maximum braking and the aircraft overran the end of the runway approximately 20 feet in soft mud.the calculations from the aircrafts aircraft performance program indicated that based on the criteria of a wet runway and flaps 40° and using 115% performance numbers, our landing distance based on a 18, 361 pounds was 3794 feet. unfortunately, because of the 3 second of floating time, much of the runway was used up during the landing.after shutting down the engines and notifying the tower of the incident, we exited the runway to assess any damage and coordinate with our company to recover the aircraft. i noticed that the runway was very slick in spite of being grooved which i believed contributed to the overrun. no obvious damage was noticed and recovery efforts were accomplished with no further problems.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: BK117 (EC-145) pilot reported there was a failure of the bus tie control relay in the overhead panel that rendered the bus tie switch inoperative; but the preflight procedures for the aircraft do not include checking the bus tie open caution lights.
text: potential electrical hazard in the bk117c2/c2e. while checking aircraft battery voltage, i noticed the caution and advisory display (cad) had asymmetrical caution lights with the left side bus tie opn caution not illuminated. after troubleshooting, i was able to determine the #1 main bus was hot when it should have been cold in this state. the cause was determined by maintenance after extensive troubleshooting and effort to be a failure of the bus tie control relay in the overhead panel as it was generating power at all times causing the bus tie relay to be closed at all times and rendering the bus tie switch inoperative. my concern is that our base pilots operating per the checklist for everyday operations close both bus ties and never noticed, nor should they have noticed, the anomaly with the aircraft. there are multiple electrical emergency procedures that would be affected by such an anomaly and i feel airbus should consult as to whether or not they wish to change their guidance for preflight procedures as they did when they added the dc system check" to the rotorcraft flight manual (rfm) for the ec135 in the early 2000's. they should add a step in the normal procedures section of the rfm to pause when turning power on via the bat mstr switch in the "on" position until the central panel display system (cpds) self-test is complete and ensure both bus tie opn caution lights are illuminated before cycling the switch to the "engage" position."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Champ 7EC pilot submitted follow up report on incident concerning losing a main wheel during take off. Cotter pin was re-installed.
text: after losing the left wheel on takeoff and successfully landing back at redacted airport the missing wheel was recovered. on inspection of the wheel it was noticed that the cotter pin for the wheel retaining collar was missing. i had removed the wheels recently to clean and check the brake linings and shoes to improve brake performance after a few flights and it appears that i did not replace the cotter pin on the left side. with the anti-clockwise rotation of the left wheel against the retaining collar it appears the collar became unscrewed causing the wheel to come off the axle.i do not know how i missed this when installing the wheel hub cap and dust plate.lesson learned is to double check critical installations and even have a second person check the work.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Gear Up Landing
synopsis: Diamond DA42 pilot reported failure of a main landing gear to extend during landing. Pilot landed gear up.
text: i arrived and began preflight planning for a maintenance flight to test a diode on the right engine. i conducted a weight and balance form, a dispatch sheet and spoke with maintenance about what had been done to the aircraft in order to plan accordingly. i planned to travel to the midway practice area and perform basic maneuvers to include steep turns, slow flight, and stalls at 3, 000 feet over water southeast of redacted. i conducted a preflight and noted no defects with the airplane, all fluids were filled to an acceptable level and no notable damage was found. i got into the airplane and started the engines, taxied to the runup, completed the before takeoff check checklist and taxied to the runway without any issues. i did a normal takeoff from runway xx full length at redacted and noted no issues on the takeoff roll. approach let me know that there were two other airplanes in the practice area so i talked to them and determined i would work the east side north south at 3, 000 ft. i got into the practice area, got set up for maneuvers and started with steep turns. no issues with steep turns so i moved on to slow flight. once i began slow flight i pulled the power to 25% load on each engine and lowered the landing gear handle. upon landing gear extension i noticed a strange yaw to the left and looked down and noticed my right main landing gear position indicator light was not illuminated and my gear unsafe light was illuminated.i continued to fly south and i began to trouble shoot starting with the gear fire test button which illuminated all landing gear position indicator lights and proved that all lights were working. i then called aircraft y and asked if they could fly below me and check if my gear was down. they did and confirmed the right main was in the wheel well. i then asked if they noted any change as i ran the manual extension of landing gear checklist and pulled the manual extension handle. the pilot of aircraft y confirmed that the landing gear was still stuck in the up position. this confirmed that there was a real problem and i began to maneuver with the gear handle down in an effort to try to pull the landing gear out of the wheel well. once i had tried this a few times i determined that it was not working and wanted an official answer from the tower confirming that the right main landing gear was stuck up. i swapped frequencies to approach control and requested priority handling requesting to return to redacted for a low pass. i did and the tower confirmed that the right main appeared to be in the wheel well.i responded to the tower that i would return to the midway practice area to troubleshoot and burn off fuel. i returned to the midway practice area, continued to maneuver the aircraft and asked over our company frequency if anyone could get maintenance on the radio. maintenance had me try a few different methods to lower the gear including going 180 kts and lowering the landing gear, pushing the manual gear extension handle back in and cycling the gear a few different times and adding constant g forces in a 60 degree banked steep turn. none of these methods worked. eventually aircraft z, containing a representative of the fsdo and my chief pilot, departed redacted and flew close to me while i troubleshot the problem. once i had tried everything and burned 10 or more gallons of fuel, i determined that the gear was not going to come down. i then returned to redacted. i entered left traffic xx. on short final for xx ~100' i pulled the power to idle and turned off the left then right engine masters and landed. i opened the canopy as i was coming to a stop. once stopped i turned off the electric master and departed the aircraft.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Air carrier Technician reported while troubleshooting a crew oxygen leak in the flight deck; they had a flash over as they reconnected the second observers oxygen mask.
text: my partner and i were assigned an etops on aircraft x. during our inspection, we found the crew o2 bottle was reading 1300 psi. we then replaced the bottle, no leaks noted, sitting in the cockpit and completed the etops check, and went to sign off paperwork. we received a gate call, from the flight crew, that the captains mask was leaking after he tested it. when we arrived to the cockpit, the captain had disconnected the mask, from the box, and explained to us that it wouldn't stop leaking. we then connected the mask, and saw that the mask was leaking, and disconnected it again, due to safety reasons, and not wanting to leave the mask connected and leaking. we went and ordered a mask, and replaced the mask, and no help. at that point we decided to change the stowage box, and at that point, i went downstairs, turned off the bottle, went back, replaced the box, and when i turned the bottle back on to leak check, all the other masks started leaking as well. when all 4 masks started leaking, the flight crew assisted me in disconnecting all the masks by the quick disconnects. the captain disconnected his, i disconnected the first and second observers mask, and the other was disconnected by the relief pilot. i then contacted my crew chief, and when he came out, i wanted to show him what we had as a problem. when i reconnected the second observers mask, we had the flashover.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Fractional jet Captain reported a failure in CRM along with flying pilot's lack of familiarization resulted in two GPWS terrain alerts on approach to VNY.
text: after listening to the atis while in descent into vny, i advised the pf that winds were from the north and visual approaches where being conducted to 34l. no approaches are available for that runway so i loaded a visual approach with a 5nm final. after gaining sight of the airport, air traffic control cleared us for the visual. we enter a base for a 5 mile final and began our descent. i check my ipad to find the altitude of the terrain we were over and determined the obstacles in the area were at about 2100' msl, and we were currently a 3500' in a descent. approach handed us off to tower and as i was about to make my initial call to tower, we received a caution terrain" aural alert. pf added power and and slowed his rate of descent. shortly after, we received a "terrain, pull up" aural alert. pf added power and started a climb away from the terrain. the lowest altitude i saw was about 2600. after clearing the terrain, we were able to continue a normal descent into landing.detection was from the aural alert and pfd message of the terrain. after landing, i learned that the the pf had not landing on runway 34 before and was not aware of the terrain. while i was aware of the terrain, i did not realize our proximity to it.we conducted an escape maneuver until we were clear of the terrainsuggestions: stronger briefings for myself"

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Aircraft inspector reported they observed a crack indication on the right-hand main landing gear door actuator lug. They incorrectly initiated a non-routine for the left-hand door actuator.
text: while accomplishing an ultrasound inspection of the mlg door actuator fittings in accordance with task card #redacted on day 0, i observed a crack indication on the rh mlg fwd. lug beneath the flanged bushing, inbound., at approximately the 9 o'clock position. i informed my supervisor and requested we have another qualified inspector double check my findings before initiating a non-routine. person a was assigned the verification. person a checked it and verified there was a suspected crack. i then initiated the non-routine.i was subsequently informed by person b, approximately two weeks later that he had accomplished a follow-up inspection of the suspected crack, and that he had signed it off as no crack found. he also commented that he thought i had made a mistake on the paperwork, but that he had fixed it. it later occurred to me that i should follow up to review the task card and non-routine to make sure all was in order. when i reviewed the paperwork this evening, i discovered that i had signed off the task card correctly, indicating that the rh mlg fitting had a suspected crack, but when i initiated non-routine # redacted /xxy, i incorrectly called out the lh mlg lug as having the suspected crack. my concern is that due to this error, when it was re-checked and signed off, the incorrect fitting was checked, and the rh mlg actuator fitting still has a potential crack.suggestions: the only thing which could prevent this from happening, is better focused attention to detail. also, if someone had contacted me to verify the discrepancy between the lh/rh position on the non-routine vs. the discrepant position indicated on the task card, i could have immediately clarified i had made a mistake, and the correct fitting could have been re-inspected before releasing the aircraft back into service.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: A319 Captain reported smoke in the passenger cabin after exiting the landing runway and starting the APU. Flight crew proceeded to the gate after shutting down the APU with Airport Rescue and Firefighting oversight.
text: exited runway, smelled odor, got a call from fa of smoke in cabin. coincided with starting of apu. immediately directed first officer to secure apu. called tower to roll airport rescue and firefighting. elected to continue taxi to gate. arrived at gate under 3 min. smoke in cabin dissipated.cause: suspect apu

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported descending too early on a visual approach into GUC.  Crew climbed back to previous altitude and continued the approach per SOP.
text: i was the pilot flying from redacted to guc i believe it was our third day doing the same redacted/guc flight on a visual flight rules day with strong west winds. i had setup the 052 radial and 9 mile arc for the west visual approach. we were approaching from the south and i believed due to my previous 2 days going in to guc that i had the airport environment in sight. (a hill normally obscures the runway from the south).we received a visual clearance and i started a decent based on visual cues. at 12000 feet i realized i had started down early and the valley i was looking at was incorrect. i climbed back to 14000 informed center and we continued to complete the normal company visual procedure.during this event safety was never in doubt and we were not close to terrain.cause: caused by my misjudging mountainous terrain and not backing up visual cues with instruments/ vor location.suggestions: rely and verify with instruments what we are seeing visually, especially in mountainous terrain.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury
synopsis: ERJ 145 Flight Attendant reported pressurization failure during climb and a return to the departure airport.
text: clearly from my end i didn't know what was happening until communication with the flight deck. after take off i immediately felt my head hurting and feeling ill. as we continued to climb up i kept feeling bad. flight deck made an announcement once they got a chance, i remained seated the entire flight. passengers complained about major headaches and noise once we landed. in redacted we switched aircraft and went to redacted i tried ti sleep when i woke up i still had the headache and felt dizzy. i told the pilots how i felt then called out. cause: auto pressurization failure. suggestion: turn that aircraft into a plane tag.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Flight instructor reported during training flight experiencing a reduction in engine RPM resulting in the flight instructor taking control of the aircraft and returning to the departure airport where they landed safely.
text: the engine startup, taxi, takeoff and climb out were all normal/standard. we headed south to the practice area and stayed a few miles south of location x for the main body of the lesson. we performed basic attitude instrument (bai) maneuvers, gps and vor tracking and then climbed up to 6, 500 feet. we performed 3 spins with climbs back to altitude in between with no engine changes. afterwards we performed two unusual attitude recoveries. after the second recovery the engine rpm was unable to be recovered back to full power. it remained at 1, 700 rpm at full throttle for the remainder of our flight back to redacted. as we noticed the problem, i took control from my student and turned direct to redacted. we began trouble shooting by activating the fuel prime, exercising the throttle and changing to the alternate air source. we pitched for best glide airspeed and continued to the airport. we were unable to maintain altitude and remained in a constant descent at around 100 feet per minute. the wind was very light so we took the left base for runway xxl when offered by the tower, as it was closer than entering for xyr. we held our altitude from 3, 500 to 3, 000 as we continued to the left base. upon reaching the left base we descended and entered a slip to make the runway while keeping as much altitude as possible. on the base to final turn with the power reduced we heard a slight knocking noise coming from the engine. we asked the tower if they could make out any loose parts on our nose but they reported nothing. the landing was standard with no issue. upon landing the rpm fell well below the normal 1, 000 rpm idle to only 600 rpm. we saw no other issues so we taxied to the ramp and shut down. after landing we saw oil coating the starboard side of our belly and the landing strut.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B767-300 First Officer reported a fuel gauge failure shortly after takeoff.  Flight crew elected to return to departure field but was concerned about documentation related to the event.
text: shortly after takeoff and just prior to sending the ops normal message, the captain alerted me to a fuel quantity indicator failure. after troubleshooting for a few minutes we realized the malfunction wasn't intermittent. we looked at the weather at our destination redacted and the forecast. the current weather was poor and the forecast wasn't improving. the weather at redacted where we just departed was visual flight rules. captain made the decision and i concurred that the safest option was to return to redacted since we knew the weather there and weren't far away. we coordinated with air traffic control for a level off and leveled at fl230. the captain coordinated with dispatch our situation and plan to return to redacted. after concurrence with dispatch we coordinated with air traffic control our return to redacted. we landed at redacted without any issues. in the relatively quick flight we never inquired if an amended release was needed or filed. it wasn't until days after the flight we were informed that because we didn't request priority handling an amended release is required to change the destination and one was not filed for our flight.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier technician reported they were assigned to build a PW 4060 turbine assembly and noticed that several parts were damaged. The parts were determined to be not serviceable.
text: on day 2, i was assigned to build pratt & whitney 4060 hpt (hight pressure turbine) module. there were three cardboard boxes stacked on a wooden pallet. the lowest box contained the t2 rotating airseal, the middle box contained the t1 outer airseal, and the top box contained the t2 retaining plate. the boxes were not secured to the pallet, which has not been an issue in the past.previously, on day 0, i had opened the top box containing the t2 retaining plate (p/n redacted), installed the plate and placed the empty box back on top of the other two. on day 2, i opened the box containing the t1 outer airseal, visually inspected the part and noticed an area on the edge that was dented and had raised metal. looking closer i noticed it was cracked. inspection looked at the damage, rejected the part and placed the item on pending engineering review. on day 3, i removed the bottom box containing the t2 rotating airseal and immediately noticed a grey powder near the edge of the part. the edge had what appeared to be a dent approx. 2' long and a rough, jagged area about the same length as the dent. inspection looked at the damage, rejected the part and placed the part on pending engineering review. it appears that both parts suffered impact damage with a hard surface, probably concrete. all three items were made serviceable on different dates, so it is unlikely that they were damaged before or during their short stay in the stockroom. the logical conclusion is that the parts were pulled from stock, placed on the pallet and then fell off the pallet during transport from the stockroom to the build area. the cardboard box for the t2 rotating airseal had grey powder along the cut in the box, indicating the part came through the box, impacted, and then was pushed back into the box.although having damaged parts is never a good thing, i am more concerned with the fact that someone knew these parts had fallen off the pallet and then placed them back inside the box and there was no follow-up to ensure the items were still serviceable. was this accident brought to management's attention or did the employee, fearing loss of his job, try and hide what happened? once inspection looked at the parts, it was immediately clear the parts were not serviceable, so i highly doubt anyone bothered to get inspection involved. furthermore, these parts still had serviceable tags on them, meaning the inspectors who made them serviceable were placed in jeopardy by someone else's deliberate carelessness. lastly, if i had not seen the damage and installed the parts, then my job would have been in jeopardy also. if i sound upset, it's because i am: hiding damaged parts is crossing the line and doing so endangers other employee's careers and puts our passenger's safety at risk.suggested resolution: the company needs to do a better job communicating that damaged parts must be brought to the attention of management, and management must get inspection or engineering involved before proceeding. early in my career it was drilled into me that you won't get fired for damaging a part, but you will get fired if you try and hide it. it appears the company is not doing a good enough job of ensuring this is well known amongst all employees.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC during departure from IZA; a non-towered airport; requiring evasive action to avoid a possible collision.
text: during departure from iza, there was no other traffic in the pattern. i announced my intentions to depart runway26 and depart via the noise abatement procedure for an eastbound departure, which states to turn left heading 210 until airport boundary and 1500' msl, traffic pattern is published at 1700' msl. after rotation, i announced my turn to 210 degrees to comply with the noise abatement. shortly after turning to 210, another aircraft gave an initial radio call that they were entering the pattern in a standard 45 degree downwind entry. i responded with indication that i was on the noise abatement procedure, heading 210, and will make a right turn to avoid traffic in my climb. opposing traffic indicated confusion as to why i was heading towards him and also turned right to deconflict. both aircraft shortly gained visual on the other aircraft and were able to maintain separation. once lateral and vertical separation were assured, i turned eastbound to resume my flight. the remainder of the flight was completed without issue.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: M20E pilot reported communication and navigation failure resulted in divert utilizing backup system.
text: while en route from redacted to redacted on flight following with redacted center, i experienced a total loss of electrical power approximately 20 nm from redacted while direct redacted. at the time of the failure, i suddenly lost all radios and navigators. my garmin g5 backup batteries remained available, which allowed me to maintain attitude and heading information. i also retained traffic awareness on my ipad through my sentry.i evaluated my options and descended toward redacted after acquiring the airport in sight. once low enough to regain cell service, i called redacted tower on my iphone and advised them of the situation. the tower controller issued me landing clearance by phone and remained on the line with me until i was on final. after landing on runway xx, the controller provided taxi instructions to parking via 1 and 2. i landed without further incident, taxied in, and the aircraft was subsequently repaired on the ground.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a critical ground conflict at a non-towered airport.
text: this is about the dubious practice of 'line up and wait' at an uncontrolled airport. the pattern was busy. i was on downwind and heard a twin on the radio inbound, pretty close. as #1 on downwind, i offered to extend my downwind. in the meantime, a c172 pulled onto the runway to 'line up and wait.' the twin was a bit slower than i anticipated, so after it passed i was way downwind, so i told to aircraft behind me to go ahead and turn base and i'd turn in on final behind him. the pilot waiting on the runway clearly lost situational awareness and, because he was facing the wrong way, had no way to check final before he started his takeoff roll. although i called short final, the plane on the runway began to move just as i passed over to land. i stopped my descent at 100 ft, sidestepped to the right, and let the departing aircraft pull ahead and climb above me as i went around.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Small aircraft flight instructor reported receiving low altitude alert from ATC during cruise. Flight returned to assigned altitude.
text: we were operating on an instrument flight rules flight plan returning from gyr, with an assigned altitude of 6, 500 feet near the bxk vor. i observed traffic approaching from the southeast at a distance and identified it as an aerobatic aircraft inbound to bxk. the aircraft's altitude and heading appeared unpredictable, as it was descending and turning toward our flight path. i attempted to contact the aircraft and also monitored and transmitted on the buckeye frequency but received no response. phoenix approach frequency was congested at the time due to weather conditions, and i could hear them actively vectoring jet traffic in the area. i advised phoenix approach that i would be descending to a lower altitude to avoid a potential collision with visual flight rules traffic. approach acknowledged and assigned us 6, 000 feet. during the descent, it became apparent that further descent was necessary to ensure separation, and we descended below 5, 500 feet, advising approach as we continued further descend to avoid collision. approach then issued a low altitude alert and instructed us to return to our previously assigned altitude. once we confirmed the traffic had passed and there was no longer a conflict, we climbed back to assigned altitude.no further instructions or concerns were communicated by approach at that time. we were subsequently vectored back to goodyear without issue. the tower was open upon arrival, so no flight plan closure was required.

synopsis: Agricultural UAS pilot reported spray drifted onto a neighboring field and possibly damaged crops in that field.
text: when conducting an agricultural operation, spray drifted off-target several hundred feet into an adjacent field, resulting in damage. it was discovered weeks after the operation that damage had occurred- symptoms of damage were slow to present themselves. the operator was informed of the damage by the landowner. it is possible, but has not been determined, that a temperature inversion was present despite wind conditions indicating otherwise. no injuries to persons occurred. corrective actions are currently being discussed with the involved parties as of the time of this report being submitted.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: Cessna 172 Student Pilot reported experiencing an NMAC and a rotor wash encounter during approach at JYO airport.
text: i was a student solo. i had informed tower before my initial takeoff with callsign 'student solo aircraft x holding short, runway 17.' after receiving clearance for takeoff and my readback, i said, 'wish me luck.' on my third landing to complete my solo, i was on short final about 150ft above the ground and about 0.25 miles from the runway threshold for runway 17. when the controller told me to 'make a left three-sixty.' he informed me that he wanted me to make space for inbound traffic behind me that was a faster plane and was not in the closed traffic. as he described to me, in his thinking, inbound traffic should have priority over pattern work. i reminded him that the lowest aircraft has right of way, and i was on short final for landing. as i turned, i attempted to arrest my descent, increase airspeed, reconfigure the aircraft (flaps, carb heat), turn, and climb all at a very low altitude and slow airspeed (approximately 60kts). the maneuver caused a loss of airspeed (as low as 50kts), nearly stalling the plane. i leveled the wings (at approximately 360 heading) to regain vertical lift and lowered the nose to allow the airspeed to increase. once i felt the plane was safe, i continued my 360-turn to the left. as i resumed my left turn and reached approximately a 280 heading, i observed aircraft y approaching from my right, and it was evident that continuing my turn would result in a mid-air collision. i took evasive action by turning to the right. within a few seconds of my evasive maneuver the controller asked me to 'turn a little to the northeast' which would be a right turn from my current heading. as indicated above, i had already initiated that turn to the right/ne. after this near miss, i was instructed to resume landing following a helicopter. i knew the rotor would create heavy turbulence, so i extended my downwind significantly to allow time for the turbulence to dissipate. however, i still experienced significant turbulence on final approach and chose to go-around. i believe that this controller made several mistakes that endangered me as a student. i believe it would have been unacceptable even for an experienced pilot to be turned away on short final like that.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air Taxi Captain reported that readback and compliance of an ATC altitude assignment resulted in an ATC low altitude alert and a CFTT event.
text: we operated aircraft x to den in vmc conditions. all required checklists and briefings were completed. we conducted the sskii 4 rnav arrival into den and was subsequently being vectored for the rnav y runway 16r approach.while being vectored, air traffic control issued a descent instruction. we believed the clearance was to descend to 5, 000 feet msl. the assigned altitude was read back as 5, 000 feet msl, and no correction was provided by air traffic control. we believed the altitude assignment had been correctly received and acknowledged. we did not question the clearance at the time because it was acknowledged when received. additionally, based on the altitude to lose and the phase of flight, 5, 000 feet msl appeared reasonable at that moment.the flight remained in vmc conditions. it was at that point while descending through approximately 6, 500 feet msl, we began discussing that the assigned altitude and how it seemed lower than expected given the aircraft's distance from the den airport (which was in sight during the descent). before we could query air traffic control regarding the altitude assignment, air traffic control made contact, stated they received a low altitude alert, and instructed the us to level off at 6, 000 feet msl and asked whether the airport was in sight. the flight was thereafter cleared for a visual approach to runway 16r and landed without further incident.this event served as a learning experience. although thorough arrival and approach briefings had been conducted, in the future i will place additional emphasis on reviewing and cross-checking instrument approach procedure altitudes, even when operating in vmc. this includes recognizing the significance of published altitudes, as well as maintaining heightened awareness of airport elevation and surrounding terrain. as a captain, i will continue to promote effective crew resource management by encouraging open communication on the flight deck and maintaining a strong focus on situational awareness and operational safety.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: DA42 Twin Star Flight Instructor and student reported that the student lost control during landing causing a main gear flat tire.
text: lh main gear flat tire at redacted. upon landing during a simulated one engine inoperative landing at redacted, braking and later a yaw was was felt towards the left during the rollout on the left main tire. the instructor took controls and kept the airplane from veering off the runway and coming to a complete stop about 100 feet from taxiways 1 on runway xx. a traffic call was made to alert other pilots and aircraft of the distressed situation. a few airplanes initiated go-arounds. the crew is safe. other pilots on the ground in the vicinity of redacted were able to help the crew move the airplane off to taxiway 1 to clear the runway.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 172 Flight Instructor with student reported loss of engine power during initial climb and landed on remaining runway available.
text: on day 0, i began a dual training flight departing out of redacted as the pilot in command instructor. preflight, runup and taxi to runway xxl was unremarkable. on takeoff for runway xxl, everything was normal until reaching 400 agl on the initial climb. at that point, i observed an audible 'pop' from the engine, moderate vibrations, and an immediate reduction in rpms. i called for the controls from my student, and requested priority handling with redacted tower. i was able to land on the remaining runway available on xxl, then returned to the ramp without further incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: C162 Skycatcher pilot reported a rejected takeoff due to airspeed indicator failure.
text: on takeoff roll, i observered no airspeed indication. informed the tower controller i was aborting takeoff. tower controller instructed me to exit the runway, when able, at the next available taxiway. i exited the runway at taxiway 1 and cleared the runway. the tower controller asked me the reason for aborting the take off to which i replied no airspeed indication. the tower controller asked me of my intentions to which i replied, taxi to parking. the tower controller instructed me to contact ground control. i contacted ground control and requested taxi to parking. the ground controller gave me clearance to taxi to parking. i taxied to parking without incident.
