synopsis: Flight instructor reported an NMAC with a UAS in the traffic pattern.
text: on day 0, cfi/cfii/mei person a was flying with a commercial pilot working on cfi rating. we were practicing takeoffs and landings. at about xa:13 cfi person a observed a drone flying below south of the airport at about 500 feet agl in the traffic pattern. no evasive action was required to avoid the drone. cfi person a reported the sighting to tower air traffic control. tower processed the reported sighting as per their protocols.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A TRACON controller reported a B737 descended below their assigned altitude and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: aircraft x was on the redacted arrival and requested the rnav xxl. i cleared aircraft x to descend via the arrival at redacted cleared rnav xxl approach. i continued my scan to confirm other instrument flight rules departures were clear and when i returned my scan to aircraft x he was descending through 12700 in a 13000 mva. redacted intersection is a hard alt of 14000. i asked aircraft x to confirm he was descending via the arrival for the approach but did not issue a low alt alert because he had already passed through to the 110 mva and was above it now. he replied affirmative and when we discussed the approach profile further he said his autopilot had judged him high for redacted and increased the rate of descent. i reiterated the 140 crossing restriction.notice the descent rate sooner and issue a low altitude alert if aircraft is below crossing restriction of 14000 ft.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: B737 Captain taxiing after push back reported sudden stop to avoid colliding with a catering truck crossing their path. Reporter stated aircraft-vehicle conflicts on the ramp occur daily.
text: we pushed back tail south off [gate] xx. after given taxi clearance we cleared left and right, i applied power to eng2 for the right turn out single engine taxi. as i turned to look back to the left to ensure it was clear, a catering truck was driving towards us with no intention of stopping. i applied brakes and stopped the aircraft abruptly. two additional vehicles followed the catering truck. we continued the turn out and taxied out. this happens regularly at redacted more than any other airport. the push is incredibly shallow and the ground vehicles refuse to give way to aircraft trying to turn out. when it appears a vehicle is stopping and you proceed to begin moving then find the vehicle is not stopping causing the need to quickly stop the aircraft this causes significant risk to our flight attendants that are up walking in cabin as well as potential aircraft damage if a vehicle is contacted. i know many pilots have reported this issue, we hear it daily on the frequency and have discussed it regularly. nothing has changed and redacted appears to not take this as a serious issue. i personally have reported this exact issue several times.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported they refused a takeoff clearance due to an aircraft on landing roll which had not exited the runway. Crew reported after receiving subsequent takeoff clearance an aircraft on final approach was issued go around instructions.
text: columbus tower cleared us into position and hold on runway 10l. we pulled into position after a corporate jet landed. while the corporate jet was still visibly on the runway rolling out in a snow storm, tower cleared us to take off. as pilot monitoring, i immediately grabbed for the push to talk switch and advised the tower that we could still see aircraft on the runway and we were not going to take off. this action momentarily set off duel input of side-stick. as tower responded we could hear someone in background of frequency yelling 'no no no'! when that corporate jet finally cleared the runway we received another takeoff clearance. as we were complying with this clearance we heard the tower initiated a go around for aircraft behind us on short final. initially we were given runway heading on takeoff clearance. go around aircraft was given the same heading then received a turn to the north. we completed the takeoff and flew to redacted with no further incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported an uncommanded aircraft roll on climb. Crew disengaged and reengaged autopilot and continued flight.
text: while climbing through fl180 command b was engaged by the first officer who was flying. fd (flight director) modes were n1 lnav and vnav spd. approximately 5 seconds after autopilot being engaged the aircraft rolled abruptly left with no turn commanded in the fmc navigation. the yoke was deflected approximately 45 degrees and the aircraft banked between 10 and 30 degrees before the autopilot could be disengaged and an upset recovery performed. after the aircraft was stabilized autopilot a was engaged without further issue.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Fractional flight crew reported First Officer flying did not comply with the required climb gradient at EGE and deviated off course resulting in a terrain warning.
text: we were cleared for the bevvr1 rnav departure. first officer was conducting the take off. normal rotation occurred at vr but rate of climb was reduced due to pitch only reaching 3deg. bevvr1 requires a climbing left turn as soon as practicable but no later than der heading 206deg. the turn began at approximately 150 feet and we received a terrain warning. i asked the first officer to increase the rate of climb which was complied with however the flight director was not followed and we were diverging away from the correct path. i took control and regained the flight directors commands and regained the sid.the first officer in my opinion had lost situational awareness which required input to correct. we debriefed the occurrence and i believe a positive outcome was achieved.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: DA40 Flight Instructor and Student Pilot reported there was engine roughness during climb and opted to return to departure airport.
text: during our turn to crosswind in the traffic pattern, both myself and student noticed engine roughness, and what felt like a loss of power as our performance decreased. upon inspection, no load percentage or rpm changes were noted and no annunciations were seen. i then took controls and made a return to land on the opposite runway. after landing, runup was ran with no abnormalities and a return to ramp was made.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: PA-44 Flight Instructor reported the Student Pilot noticed there was another aircraft that turned away to evade and later learned that the transponder was inoperative.
text: while maneuvering for a one-engine-out procedure, the student and i were maintaining 10, 000 msl altitude and a north heading. i never saw the airplane coming directly towards us from the north. the student said the aircraft made a sharp turn away from us towards the west approximately 500 feet below our airplane. we do not know whether the other aircraft descended to evade us.we continued our maneuvers. we entered the redacted airspace and made proper communication calls on unicom. there were other aircraft at the airport. no one advised us that our ads-b was not seen.after making a touch-and-go at redacted, we continued to redacted, our home airport. at ten miles out, north, we contacted the redacted tower. they asked us to reset our transponder. after resetting, air traffic control reported that our transponder was not sending a signal. air traffic control found us on radar and gave directions to come into the airport. we noticed upon arrival that air traffic control was instructing other aircraft to remain out of the airspace. air traffic control asked us our position several times, and we reported. while turning final, we did see the aircraft air traffic control told us to watch for above us, and that aircraft reported seeing us. we continued for a successful landing.i am reporting this because we may have been closer to the aircraft near redacted than we realized, and because we were inside the 30-mile ads-b mode c circle for redacted airport. the transponder issue was reported to maintenance upon our arrival at the flight school. during the one-engine-out procedure, the student had his head down, reading the checklist, and i had mine down, verifying that he was using it. one pilot's attention must be outside the aircraft when flying in vmc.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: PA-28R pilot reported cancelling takeoff per instruction from ATC as there was traffic on the runway.
text: this morning i was having issues with my electrical system in the arrow i was flying. my radio comms failed and i had talked with the tower over the phone about me receiving my takeoff clearance over the cell phone and using that as two way comms until i was out of the airspace. i was proceeding to an uncontrolled field as my final destination. during my first takeoff attempt i was nervous and accidentally turned left onto runway xx instead of right onto xy. as i began to throttle up to take off, tower told me cancel takeoff clearance so i immediately idled the power and applied brakes. that was my evasive action when told to cancel my takeoff. tower told me to make a 180 so i did and taxied off the runway. there was traffic using runway xz.after taxiing back to the ramp and recomposing myself, i attempted again but using the correct runway and proceeded to my final destination safely. all while using the telephone to get my takeoff clearance.the series of events that led up to this event was as followed: i had to spend the night due to an electrical issue the night prior where seemingly my battery died. mind you i had no issues with the electrical system prior to the evening startup attempt. after having it looked at by an airframe and power plant mechanic the next day (today), we addressed the issue and all seemed as normal. i went to take off and when i went to bring my wheels up, lost all electrics in the plane. so i landed and had the system examined again. it was returned to service and i had talked to tower on the telephone about taking off, maintaining visual flight rules, and proceeding to my destination without talking to anyone. i held short of the runway and was handed off to tower and that's when the bit where i am filing this report happened. i was noting my departure instructions, trying to maintain contact via telephone, and get myself going back home so the plane could be examined by the mechanic at my home field. task saturation and nerves occurred here. i should have remained more calm and just taken one step at a time and thought through the situation more thoroughly instead of trying to be in a hurry to get home as soon as possible trying to avoid weather that would envelope my home field for the next week judging by the forecast.after another attempt, i was able to safely take off and proceed enroute as planned.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Cessna 172 Flight Instructor reported having to evade another aircraft that entered the incorrect pattern to the wrong runway.
text: aircraft y approached the pattern at awo from the southwest and made no radio calls until within a very close distance of the airport. entered the 45° leg to the wrong runway 16 although making radio calls for 45° leg for 34. runway 34 was in use. upon reaching midfield on the incorrect 45° leg proceeded to turn directly into us in aircraft x established in the downwind although we had been making all standard traffic calls and flying the pattern properly. evasive action was needed to avoid aircraft y turning directly into us. the pilot of this aircraft demonstrated a large lapse in situational awareness and proper pattern entry procedures almost causing an aircraft collision. this airport is unfortunately known by flight schools in the area to have bad pilots frequent it with terrible radio calls and traffic procedures.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Controller in Charge reported there was miscommunication with a trainee and as a result; a helicopter had to take evasive action to avoid another aircraft.
text: aircraft x was northbound over the freeway inbound to redacted airport. aircraft y was inbound to runway xx on left downwind. i was monitoring the lc (local control) frequency and training, in addition to monitoring the gc training since a discussion was taking place. aircraft y was turning base and i was unsure if traffic had been issued. the trainer on lc asked the trainee are they in sight" and the trainee replied in the affirmative. this left me with the impression that traffic was in sight, so i monitored gc's training again. as i looked out the window i saw aircraft x make an abrupt maneuver, then the pilot came on frequency and advised tower that they had to make a right turn, and i interpreted that to mean it was a near midair. it became clear after entering an mor, the trainee had to clarify that he did not issue traffic.more management oversight so cpcs can do their job. less overtime for those on the no list. we are all fatigued and burnt out in that respect. as for the situation itself, our trainers need to take better care of holding helicopters and issuing traffic in a timely manner. the trainee that worked this has had many issues some that were attempted to be addressed while i was his trainer. the trainer asking the question of the trainee above left me feeling that our diligence had been done since the trainee had answered in the affirmative reference traffic issuance and aircraft in sight. the trainee needs more training or something to better serve their situational awareness. as a controller in charge (cic), i need better serve my team by being more active in being thorough with making sure all positions have done their job correctly. even at the expense of our rapport."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: S46 Trainee reported getting distracted and by the time the reporter remembered about the aircraft; it had descended below MVA and was also in another airport's airspace.
text: i was training, the weather was visual flight rules all day. pae was advertising for visual approaches so when aircraft x checked in on the devyn star, i descended him immediately to 030 to get him set up for a visual approach. the aircraft came back and asked for the instrument landing system. i affirmed his request, but left him descending to 030 (where normally i would leave them at 050 for the terrain) and let him fly the path of the arrival which sets the aircraft up for a downwind to 16 at pae. i didn't amend his altitude because that's what the aircraft would need to before the instrument landing system anyways. i got distracted with an aircraft y arrival that was tangled up with some visual flight rules traffic and forgot about aircraft x and had an mva violation. the aircraft was at 3000 in a 5000 feet mca and a couple miles in whidbey's airspace, instrument flight rules, without a point out. another controller reminded us of aircraft x. my trainer took the frequency and turned the aircraft immediately and got the point out with nuw. a low altitude alert was never issued.the only recommendations i have on my own skill set and to have better operating practices for aircraft landing pae and to not be in a huge hurry to descend them.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Vehicle
synopsis: Air carrier First Officers reported the de-icing truck made contact with the aircraft and after returning to the gate and getting the aircraft inspected; Maintenance confirmed damage had occurred.
text: after de-icing was completed, de-ice crew notified the pilots that they had contacted the aircraft with their equipment. we coordinated a return to gate. maintenance found damage on the leading edge of the rudder.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Vehicle; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported a tug with a baggage cart went between the aircraft and jet bridge; narrowly missing both.
text: after door closure, the jet bridge was moved approximately 15 feet from the aircraft. the ground crew was unable to verify that it was in the painted circle due to ice and snow on the ramp obscuring the lines, but it appeared to be a safe distance for pushback.while waiting for ramp clearance, prior to pushback, a tug pulling a baggage cart drove out from the terminal garage at [gate] xx and went between the aircraft and the jet bridge, narrowly missing both. the tug and baggage cart then continued, passing underneath the left wing before disappearing from view.the event was reported to ramp control and local operations, and the ground crew verified that no contact was made with the aircraft before beginning the pushback. the flight continued without incident.intentional non-compliance with sops and a lack of concern for safety are the main contributors to this event. the driver's actions would have been considered reckless on the best of days, but an even greater margin of safety is required on a snow covered ramp.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CRJ-700 flight crew reported a pressurization malfunction occurred just as the aircraft leveled off at cruise level and the flight crew performed an air turnback.
text: operating aircraft x redacted - redacted on day 0. departed gate around xa:00. just after reaching cruise altitude at fl260 got cabin alt caution message and almost at the same time noticed cabin altitude climbing through 8500 feet and continuing at steady pace. immediately asked first officer to request descent to 10000 feet and request priority handling. at the same time prepared for descent and immediately after receiving clearance started descending. at that time cabin altitude climbed to 9700 feet. put oxygen masks and established communication. after that i asked my first officer to run qrc for cabin alt. in a meantime we requested diversion back redacted, briefly informed fas about situation and contacted dispatch. once enroute back to redacted finished checklists, completed fa's brief and made announcement informing passengers about diversion, cause of it and that situation is under control, we are safe and our landing in redacted will be a normal, safe landing plus that gate agent and/or company representatives will be working with them after we arrive at the gate.don't have any suggestions. this experience gave me a very important teaching moment and i will be a better pilot learning from how i handled it and things i now think i would have done slightly differently.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-170 First Officer reported AVNX MAU 1A FAIL EICAS during approach resulting in missed approach. Crew returned for a safe landing.
text: as we were being vectored to final on xxl, i was pm and ca was pf. just as we were leaving 4, 000' descending 3, 000', ca called flaps 1. soon after flaps 1 extended avnx mau 1a fail appeared on eicas. the approach was discontinued as i requested for delayed vectors to run a checklist. following the discontinuation of the approach the ca called for and i initiated (per company procedure) the 'avnx mau 1a fail' qrh. while running the qrh ca opted for priority handling to be requested due to the possibility of anti-skid and normal braking not operating normally. along with lh brake fault and rh brake fault appearing on eicas. after completing the avnx mau 1a fail qrh i initiated the flight control malfunction descent checklist as directed by the qrh. in accordance to that checklist we briefed for a flaps full approach and adjusted our v speeds per the checklist. just before the final approach fix, we conducted the flight control malfunction landing checklist. ca called for gear down and as i swung the gear down, there was no response. almost 2 seconds later the gear came down albeit at a very slow rate. no eicas messege associated with that appeared. after landing, we were met with airport crash fire and rescue (cfr) out of an abundance of caution and continued to taxi to the gate where maintenance and cfr chief met us on the jet bridge who advised of no signs of smoke, fire, or over-brake temp. concluding, no further issue transpired.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported an NMAC while in the pattern at BXK during training.
text: during pattern work at bxk, aircraft z departed runway 17 extending upwind and communicating on ctaf, our aircraft following on departure extended upwind and communicated the extension of pattern leg on ctaf. crosswind and downwind turns were as normal. third aircraft (aircraft y) took off runway 17 and turned crosswind without extending for traffic in the pattern (myself and other airplane ahead). they proceeded to turn and climb towards us as we continued the downwind to try to avoid them. it was first noted by me, the instructor and secondly by a tcas alert from the airplane. i advised my student to accelerate past as any other deviation would put us in the path of the conflict aircraft. no attempt to correct was seen by me regarding the conflict aircraft as they continued to climb into us. they disappeared behind my right wing. our aircraft's adsb data showed aircraft y being within 100 ft vertically as they passed below and slightly behind us. they then proceeded to turn downwind very close behind us and perform a full stop landing at bxk. this is not the first time i have witnessed pattern conflict issues from their flights and some safety changes need to be made to prevent future occurances.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier ground personnel reported uncommanded aircraft movement during push back procedures. Crew set the brakes.
text: riding in the tug for the first time in accordance with the new operations manual rules. we started pushback. we started engine #2 during push back. once the tug changed direction, and started moving the aircraft forward. the flight crew asked for clearance on #1 engine. they immediately told me that they had an apu bleed leak. it was right as we were stopping to disconnect the towbar. i remember telling the flight crew to set parking brake. they asked if we could spool up at that location to cross-start if needed. i told them that we could. i told them that i was disconnecting temporarily. i unplugged then plugged in outside the door. then i fumbled around with the orange cord to see how to best fold it up to disconnect it and give it to the ground crew. then i told flight crew that i was disconnecting temporarily. i unplugged the orange cord, and plugged directly into the aircraft with my headset, and as i took a couple steps back to the place that i always stand when launching a plane. i noticed that the aircraft was moving with the towbar still connected to the plane. i was confused because i didn't know that they had disconnected from the tug. the ground side later claimed that i gave them the brake set hand signal. i do not remember showing that sign. usually i would be standing in position looking back at the tug, and would verify that the parking brake light is on at the nlg before giving that signal. i would never give that hand signal until i saw the light illuminated. i immediately and urgently said set parking brake. i saw the parking brake indicator go from no light to illuminated. i was clear of the towbar when they set the brake. the aircraft stopped immediately. the tug had already reversed a good long way before the aircraft started to move. once brakes were set. i disconnected the towbar from the aircraft side. after that the ground crew removed it. the flight crew then stated that the bleed leak cleared, and i cleared them to start #1 engine. flight dispatched without further incident

synopsis: Air carrier lead technician reported that an aircraft arrived with an oil leak from the fuel-oil cooler unit. They found the gasket seals for the integrated drive generator cooling tubes were not installed.

synopsis: B737 flight crew reported diverting to an alternate airport after experiencing a malfunction with the cabin pressurization system during climb out.

synopsis: B767 pilot reported the Captain airspeed tape low and an Airspeed Too Low EICAS message during the climb; along with other autoflight malfunctions.The flight returned to the departure airport; landed overweight; where maintenance discovered damage to the AOA probe.
text: we departed redacted on runway xxl with a clearance to 5000 with a heading of 110 degrees after takeoff. i was the pilot flying and shortly after vnav was selected at 1000 agl the airspeed tape appeared abnormal as it showed yellow caution tape on the airspeed indicator while well above flaps maneuvering speed. all three airspeed indicators were indicating the same airspeed and it was reasonable but my airspeed tape was indicating yellow and an eicas message of airspeed too low displayed. the first officers airspeed tape was indicating correctly. we got a momentary stick shaker even though we were well above the flap maneuvering speed. also during this time the captains and first officers flight director pitch bar disappeared. cycling the flight deck switches brought them back but only momentary. once the flaps were retracted and accelerated to 250 kts i selected the alternate air data computer which eliminated the airspeed too low message. we continued to climb and continue to a safe altitude to attempt to resolve the issue. at this point i suspected that the captain air data computer had failed but as we continued it was apparent there was more to the situation. the aircraft would level off about 150 low on every altitude captured. in addition to that the autothrottle flight mode annunciator (fma) would indicate alpha at level off and then change to spd.i transferred control to the first officer with the relief pilot backing him up while i contacted dispatch and maintenance control via satcom. after a discussion we jointly determined that a return to redacted was the best option. we then requested priority handling with air traffic control and were cleared direct to the airport. we planned for an overweight landing but it was only projected to be approximately 5500lbs overweight. during the descent we noted that using flch caused a aggressive nose down pitch and added power. the fma for the auto throttles displayed alpha. after some experimenting it was noted that with the auto throttles off and use of v/s the autopilot worked normally. we were vectored for the instrument landing system z xxr and landed with no further issues. upon block in we were met by maintenance personnel and they informed us that the captain side aoa probe was broken. there was a previous write up from the inbound leg that the crew stairs hit the aircraft and the aoa probe was likely damaged but not detected. no one was aware that the probe had been compromised by the crew stairs. it was likely cracked and not detected and once airborne it failed. the aoa vane was replaced by maintenance and we departed redacted with no further issues.the success of the safe return and landing rests on the tremendous job of the first officer and relief pilot who were indispensable in making this happen.

synopsis: A319 flight crew reported an unstabilized approach and a low altitude alert from ATC when the autopilot reacted with an excessive pitch down moment below the glide path after a late flap configuration change. The autopilot recaptured the glide path; stabilized; and landed.
text: air traffic control cleared us for 170 kias to the final approach fix. ca called flaps 2-to-3 at the fix, then flaps 3-to-full as we slowed toward approach speed. while flaps were transitioning from 3 to full at ~155 kias, the aircraft pitched down significantly- first officer called out an instantaneous vsi of ~2, 200 fpm. this happened as we descended through 1, 200 ft agl, with intermittent ground contact.by ~1, 100 ft agl, we gained intermittent visual contact with the runway and started correcting toward the glideslope (about 3/4 dot low). at ~800 ft agl, tower issued a low-altitude alert, we acknowledged and continued. no gpws warnings sounded--likely because the deviation stemmed from the earlier pitch excursion rather than terrain proximity. go around was not called at 1000 ft agl because the aircraft was correcting and we gain visual reference. the aircraft was stable with runway insight at 500 ft agl.cause: it is believed the rapid flap extension from 2-to-full, combined with high deceleration, created a strong nose-down moment that overwhelmed auto pilot pitch control momentarily. in future, especially in intermittent imc conditions, earlier and slower flap transitions will help create better conditions for a smoother approach.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Cessna 340 pilot reported discovering that the aircraft was non-compliant with a FAA Airworthiness Directive. Pilot grounded the aircraft.
text: i had purchased a cessna 340a on day 0. the same mechanic who performed the annual inspection also performed the pre-buy inspection as well. everything appeared to be in order and we took ownership and ferried the aircraft from redacted to redacted. over the next few months i had accumulated approximately 27 hours in the aircraft from training and familiarization flights to and from various airports. all were uneventful. however, as i continued to log more and more time in the aircraft, i endeavored to continue to familiarize myself with the specific maintenance requirements of the cessna 340a as well as keeping track of relevant airworthiness directives, that i would need to accomplish to maintain airworthiness of the aircraft. however, in my studies, i discovered a discrepancy a few days ago with the propellers - i found that both propellers are listed in an ad - which indicates that the lag screws, which are a vital component in securing the propeller blades to the propeller hub, are defective in certain mt composite propellers manufactured/installed between certain years. as it turns out, both of the propellers on aircraft x are flagged under this airworthiness directive as having the defective lag screws. under certain high-load conditions such as heavy turbulence or maneuvers, these defective screws can fail, leading to potential inflight blade separation and severe damage to the engine and airframe. continuing to go through the propeller logbooks, there is no evidence that this ad was ever complied with whatsoever. the aircraft mechanic who performed most of the maintenance on aircraft x in the 4 years prior to our purchase of the plane, made no mention of it either.because of this, the aircraft is not airworthy and has not been for several years at the earliest, and the previous owner flew it during this time as well. immediate corrective actions had begun the moment i discovered the propellers had an outstanding ad. the aircraft was immediately grounded. first, the aircraft will have its propellers removed and shipped to an authorized repair facility, and the aircraft will have another annual inspection performed to rectify these issues. i exercised poor judgment in assuming that everything was in order with the aircraft and did not do enough due-diligence on the aircraft logs or ad records, as i perceived the aircraft to be in excellent shape with everything else in order on the pre-buy inspection. ultimately, it falls to the pilot in command to ensure the aircraft is airworthy, and i incorrectly placed the entirety of my faith in the mechanic that did the annual and pre-buy, as well as the previous owner. said corrective actions will continue as swiftly as possible to correct this oversight and return the aircraft to a fully airworthy condition. in addition, going forward, i will heavily scrutinize and cross-check any and all maintenance performed on this airframe, ensuring everything is in order for each flight and not allowing any assumptions to fall into place.

text: this incident occurred during takeoff at redacted at approximately xa:24 on day 0. i was taking off runway xx with calm winds, >10sm visibility, and skies clear. once airborne, i encountered mist, but it did not impact actions on the ground during takeoff. i initiated a rolling takeoff and accelerated to my published vr speed of 86. i rotated and leveled the aircraft to accelerate in side of the aircraft popped open. prior to takeoff, i had verified the door was secure twice: once before taxi (personal technique), and again short of the runway in accordance with the before takeoff checklist.due to the increased airflow and noise within the cockpit from the door popping open, i lost situational awareness of the aircraft and failed to continue my climb out. the nose of the but had lost enough altitude that resulted in the right propeller struck the runway, causing damage. indications of the ground contact were a spark-like flash and a scraping sound loud enough to be heard over the engine and airflow noise.following the ground contact, i recognized that my gear was retracted and there was insufficient runway, so i continued my takeoff and executed a left traffic pattern to land back on runway xx. i did not receive any cockpit warnings, cautions, or advisories. while in-flight and during my deceleration to land, i noticed a mild vibration that further indicated damage to the propeller, but i felt no significant loss in controllability or performance. upon landing, i immediately taxied to the fbo ramp and shut down the plane.after parking, i completed a thorough inspection of the aircraft. i found that all three blades of the right engine propeller were damaged, curled up about 3-4 inches each, with some pieces of the propeller broken off. i found the passenger's footstep aft of the right wing was bent upwards with a crack in the tubing and abrasion damage on the bottom. additionally, i found punctures to the fuselage skin on the right nose, inboard of the right nacelle, and below the nose baggage compartment, moving towards the leading edge of the right wing. i did not find evidence of the right wing, or any part of the fuselage, including the nose, belly, and tail, making contact with the ground. the left propeller also appeared free of damage.i immediately notified my flight controller, who notified the director of operations, and then notified my director of maintenance, who initiated recovery. after debriefing my company's safety officer on the events, it was determined that the takeoff profile i used did not align with published procedures, but was corroborated by other be58 pilots as what was taught in our training. contributing factors: this was my first time flying in and out of this airport. runway illusions induced by an unfamiliar runway at night may have given me the perception that i was higher off the runway surface than i actually was when i retracted the gear during my level acceleration.human performance considerations: i had received approximately 16 hours of rest following my previous duty, and about 7-8 hours of broken sleep in the preceding 24 hours, but had been awake for approximately 11-12 hours by the time the event occurred. an additional factor affecting performance was that the cargo pickup was delayed by an additional hour, resulting in almost 2 hours of waiting on the ground at redacted in the dark and cooler weather. actions/inactions: i failed to maintain aircraft awareness and was distracted by the door pop event, despite knowing from training that it could not be resolved while airborne. i also believethat the pitch trim, set during ground checklists, had been set slightly nose-low within the takeoff range indicated on the trim indicator wheel, which required more effort to keep the nose up, rather than nose down during the takeoff, so when my focus was pulled from flying, the nose was able to dip. after the takeoff, while returning to the airport, i assessed the condition of the aircraft, mostly certain of the propeller strike, but unconfirmed, and determined the aircraft was still flyable and therefore did not shut down the engine to avoid complicating the scenario and requiring a single-engine landing.

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported an airborne conflict with crewed aircraft during a mission. The UAS pilot took evasive action and descended the UAS.
text: the airport is in uncontrolled airspace. there was a ton of snow in the area so i thought the airport was closed. flew a couple of hours without issue. as my last mission for the day was wrapping up 90% completion, 2 planes took off from redacted. i noticed they were launching right into my flight path so i paused the automated mission, dropped altitude, let them pass, and continued mission after. i am unsure about the distance between aircraft as it happened quickly and i was focused on maneuvering out of their path. note added to internal documentation as a preventive measure moving forward that includes airport's contact information.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: CNO Tower Controller reported the Stand Alone Weather System has been out of service for over a year.
text: aircraft was over the runway attempting to land during santa ana wind event with multiple reports of windshear. our stand alone weather system has been out of service for over a year. the asos wind reading will go missing intermittently, but always more so on days with the sustained strong east winds the santa ana winds bring to the entire area. the wind was reading m/m" for around 10 minutes and during the small jet's approach. it appeared the jet was losing control while over the runway on approach when the pilot recovered the aircraft and it safely landed but well left of centerline and barely inside the runway edge line. the small jet's left wing was definitely over the north runway edge line of runway 08l. while the pilot was on landing roll-out the wind reading on the asos finally came up and was showing the winds strongly favoring runway 03.recommendation: we need to get the stand alone weather system working again for the pilots' safety and accurately lining up for the best suitable runway. we are in the middle of getting our radios and voice switches swapped out when there was absolutely no need to and we cannot reliably issue wind readouts to pilots operating in the airspace, let alone passing them along to approach."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A TRACON controller reported a departing IFR aircraft deviated off course to avoid a VFR aircraft and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: aircraft x departed redacted visual flight rules to redacted, climbed to about 020 on about a 120 heading. right after that, aircraft y departed redacted on an instrument flight rules flight plan but flying the visual flight rules departure procedure. this procedure treats the instrument flight rules departure as visual flight rules climbing to 011 on a right turn to a 120 heading until passing the redacted [vor] 165 radial then climb to 021.aircraft y was faster and overtaking aircraft x, aircraft y failed to climb out of 010 due to aircraft x above. i called redacted tower to ask why aircraft y was stopped at 010 and they replied that he should be climbing. i tried to climb aircraft y and then he turned south below the mva, at almost the same time aircraft x turned south too. as this was happening the two data blocks were overlapping and it was difficult for me to determine which aircraft was doing what. as i noticed the turn, i asked aircraft y if he was in fact turning and he said yes he was maneuvering due to the traffic above. i stated that he was instrument flight rules. i issued a low altitude alert and turned to get out of the lower mva and issued another climb. i would not launch a fast guy right behind a slower aircraft when they are both flying the same route

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A319 pilots reported a lightning strike during descent to the airport and an electrical odor with no cockpit indications. The flight landed safely and Maintenance could not identify transient cockpit warnings and the Captain refused the aircraft.
text: this incident report is for flight abcd which was later flown and completed on a different aircraft with a different aircrew following our refusal for the reasons as detailed below.our duty day began at xa:13 in redacted beginning with a deadhead to redacted followed by three flying legs scheduled afterward: redacted-redacted, redacted-redacted, redacted-zzz3on the second flying leg (redacted-redacted) we encountered a possible (what i believe to be likely) lightning strike during the descent into redacted. initial reaction was surprise but thankfully all aircraft systems appeared to continue functioning without fault or issue. we did note a brief but apparent smell of burning electrical cable or wire, which dissipated within several minutes. there was no associated smoke or fumes beyond that. after querying the cabin crew if they saw anything irregular they also noted the brief smell but otherwise cabin and occupants were not experiencing anything out of the ordinary during our descent. given no aircraft faults, we were able to continue the arrival and landing uneventfully and arrived at redacted for a normal shutdown and deplaning. during the flight we notified maintenance of the observed lightning strike by submitting a maintenance request requiring a post-flight inspection. the maintenance team was able to meet us at the aircraft shortly after the cabin door was opened and we described the incident and they conducted their exterior inspection. the conditions at the time were light periodic rain, at night with marginal ramp lighting. i also conducted a thorough inspection during my routine exterior walk-around to see if i could find evidence of a lightning strike. with our limited visibility from the ground using only handheld flashlights, both the maintenance personnel and myself were unable to find specific evidence of a strike with only a visual inspection. so we continued our preflight, maintenance cleared the forms and we planned to continue the next leg redacted-redacted.however, during the flight deck preparation, shortly before our preflight checklist and briefing, an ecam fault appeared that was either tcas or resolution advisory related. we noted that was unusual but maybe just a system fault that may automatically reset or require a procedural reset. before we could evaluate further, a second ecam appeared within 60 seconds or so, followed by a complete array of faults that would normally only be visible in flight. some of these were cautions and several were warnings including 'all engines failed' with a continuous bell ringing in the cockpit (during boarding), in addition to 'stall, stall, stall' and other significant warnings and aural alerts. this was all while we were still completing boarding, with passengers walking right behind us. we were only able to silence these alerts and alarms by continuously holding the 'emer cancel' button on the ecam system selection panel. this continued for at least 3-4 minutes, at which time maintenance was able to observe some of these indications.eventually, after about 5 more minutes, the faults cleared and the ecam screen went back to normal, but there was clearly something abnormal to trigger those warnings during ground operations. while our exterior inspection was inconclusive, maintenance had done their check and recommended a full system power down and reset, with passengers aboard. this took about 5-10 minutes. upon power up, the aircraft did not seem to have any faults noted, so maintenance again cleared the forms and gave us a clean release. shortly thereafter, we got one additional ecam fault (at xa:36, picture attached), reducing our confidence that the issue was fully corrected or otherwise absent. at this time we suspected there might be something deeper within the avionics that got damaged but without a further inspection we could not be certain. for this reason the captain and i agreed that it constituted an unreasonable flight safety concern, which we did not feel comfortable accepting. we decided to refuse the aircraft and return it to maintenance.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737 Captain reported engine anti ice failure warning during cruise that necessitated operating that engine at idle. Flight diverted and landed uneventfully.
text: during cruise flight at fl380 with anti-ice selected off, the amber cowl anti-ice light as well as the master caution light illuminated. transfer of controls took place while i ran the respective qrh procedure. in accordance with the checklist the left engine was brought to idle. due to the engine being at idle we were unable to maintain fl380 so a drift down to fl240 was initiated. after coordinating with dispatch and maintenance control we concluded that a diversion to redacted was appropriate and our best option. we advised air traffic control for the one engine being at idle and an overweight landing. the diversion, overweight landing, and taxi in were uneventful.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a TCAS RA during climb out of DEN in conflict with an aircraft executing a go-around.
text: departed 34r in snow and fog on the epkee7 departure. takeoff roll, gear retraction, and initial right turn per the sid were normal. passing approximately 5700 feet, tower advised of traffic to our right climbing through 6000. i advised we were imc but would look. i noted the yellow tcas indicator as tower directed a turn to a 025 heading. as i was replying and dialing the heading into the selector, we received a tcas resolution advisory alert requiring a climb. the first officer immediately increased climb to place the resolution advisory at the top of the green zone as i relayed the alert to tower. the first officer continued the turn while climbing and the closure of the aircraft dots slowed and stopped although vertical separation indicated 100 feet briefly. once we received the clear of traffic alert, we notified tower and began leveling at 10600 feet. tower advised the other aircraft had been a go-around and gave us a new heading of 105 before handing us off to departure. at that point we raised the flaps and completed the after takeoff checks.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: B767-300 First Officer reported multiple system warnings during climb. Crew returned to departure airport where a damaged AOA probe was discovered.
text: on takeoff rwy xxl redacted, capt flying pilot, i was the first officer, at approximately 1000 instrument pitch bars disappeared followed by yellow caution airspeed tape displayed on the capt side. we were above flap maneuvering speed. airspeed indicators (all 3) were indicating the same speed and seemed normal. airspeed too low eicas msg followed. momentary stick shaker occurred. we continued the departure climb to a safe altitude and when flaps were retracted the capt selected alternate air data. after level off it was noticed the acft was approx. 150 low and the a/t (auto throttle) fma (flight mode annunciator) would change to alpha then back to spd.i became the pilot flying as the capt coordinated with operations to troubleshoot and determine our course of action. we then advised air traffic control, returned to redacted for a 5500# overweight landing by the capt.during descent we found that v/s was the better choice since flc caused unusual pitch down movement followed by alpha displaying again.we received vectors for the instrument landing system z xxl redacted and capt made an uneventful landing. after block in maintenance told us the capt side aoa probe was damaged possibly by ground crew positioning the stairs during the previous flights block in. earlier in the day, during our pre flight walk-around when we initially arrived at the acft there was no indication that this aoa probe was damaged. the aoa probe was replaced, ops checked and we departed for our leg to redacted.i'd like to say the capt set the tone during this unusual occurrence to bring it to a positive outcome. and the relief pilot was outstanding in backing us up multiple times having the big picture from his observers seat.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Inflight Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported GPS jamming and spoofing after departing LTFM/IST. Reliable GPS signals returned later in the flight.
text: almost immediately after takeo' from istanbul, we experienced gps jamming. by top of climb, we suspected gps spoofing. the checklist was run and gps updating was turned o'. i had the first rest so i went back to the bunk. when i returned later and signed in as pilot in command i reviewed the status of the aircraft and noticed that the fmc time was four minutes and 36 seconds faster than the aircraft clock time. at about four hours into the flight we started to receive a gps signal, but it was unreliable showing the gps position between 38 to 45 nautical miles ahead of our iru (inertial reference unit) position with dme/dme updating (this position was also checked against land based vor signals). by the time we crossed into the astana fir we were receiving a reliable gps signal to the captain's ipad the first officer's ipad started to receive a reliable signal about an hour later. we kept gps updating turned o' and let air traffic control know about our situation. with our 3 irus updating our anp was between 0.38 to 0.45nm. crossing position sarin entering chinese airspace (urumqi fir) we began a turn to tch on airway a368. we then received the eicas caution message unable rnp. our anp was noted at 15.4nm and fluctuating. i was about to call urumqi control when they called with a heading of 130. again we let air traffic control know of our spoofing encounter. within two minutes our anp showed 0.39nm. after a few minutes on the heading, urumqi control asked if we were able our own navigation and gave us direct position salmo. about 25 minutes later we were alerted to the eicas caution message autopilot, with lnav and vnav faults shown. we also noted an anp of 12.3 that almost immediately decreased to 0.43nm. we selected hdg (heading) sel and flch and the re-engaged lnav and vnav, with no disruption to the flight path. the flight continued to destination with no other anomalies.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported during push back observing ground personnel giving an X signal and could not establish communication with the tug driver. The aircraft rolled a few feet before the brakes were applied.
text: on push back to spot xx i was informed that i was cleared to start the engine. i had first officer start the engine and at the same time i look out the window and notice that the wing walker is holding up an x. i asked push tug if wanted to set brake. no answer and i noticed the plane was rolling and since no one was communicating with me and i see an x i apply brakes gently but it made the plane jerk and ramp comes on and tells me that i was only to start the engine not brakes. i didn't want to start an argument for no communication when i asked a question. as all this was happening i noticed the ramper was no longer showing me an x. disconnected the tug and did our checklist. i had first officer and call for taxi and advise ground that we needed somewhere to park to address the situation. i called maintenance control and advised them of the situation and they asked me if the shear pin had been broken and i advised them they had use an electrode. i was told there isn't an inspection for my issue. only asked me if it was a violent reaction or stoppage. i said no at best it was jerky.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported encountering severe turbulence resulting in the loss of control of the aircraft; the flight crew regained control of the aircraft and continued to their destination.
text: center asked us if we could climb from fl350 to fl360 for a direction of flight change ahead and coordination with redacted. center also reported smooth rides at fl360. we checked the vnav cruise page and determined that fl360 would work at 0.78m with a 400 foot buffer. we had a discussion about lower level weather topping around fl280-300 and decided together that with the weather and air traffic control ride reports to accept fl360.the radar was on to depict weather, we were running our efb and wsi (weather stress index) as well. we made the decision while going over the weather by greater than 5000 feet to seat the passengers and flight attendants prior to approaching it. i made the required announcements. we also noted some taller thunderstorm activity about 30-40 ssw of our position and blow off might cause a few bumps.at approximately xa30 we encountered an immediate and sudden area of severe turbulence. there were no radar returns, nothing at our altitude on wsi, and our efb showed no adverse rides. the duration lasted approximately 10 seconds. initially we encountered a strong updraft showing a rapid airspeed increase from 0.78m to an overspeed of approximately 10 knots and a vertical speed showing +2000fpm. the aircraft climbed to approximately fl362. suddenly the trend reversed, autopilot disconnected, and we experienced decreasing performance, airspeed decreasing, vertical speed -2000 fpm and we descended to fl358. i immediately took manual control of the aircraft, instructed the first officer to report the severe turbulence to air traffic control, and request fl340. they instructed us to standby and at nearly the same time we were through the isolated severe turbulence and maintained fl360 until given a descent few minutes later. automation was re-engaged me no further issues happened.we checked in on the flight attendants and they reported no injuries, and that the cabin was good.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury
synopsis: Global 5500 First Officer reported during taxi experiencing a vehicle that did not give way to their aircraft resulting in the flight crew taking evasive action to avoid a collision with the vehicle.
text: we received aircraft services on the remote ramp used by the fbo. after fueling was finished, i entered the updated fuel load and adjusted the passenger seating from zone 1 to zone 2 as they had moved from when they got on the plane. i do not recall if i actually heard the lead fa say 'cabin secure'. we were marshaled from our parking spot and began our taxi. the lighting from the surrounding area and the wetness of the ramp made it difficult to see obstructions on the ramp so all of the forward lights were turned on. as we came out of the back of the remote ramp i noticed a vehicle on the right side of the aircraft driving parallel to the aircraft. we were taxiing a little slower than you would on an unobstructed taxiway. as we approached the hold bar at taxiway 1, i called ground to get taxi clearance, at this time the vehicle was still driving parallel to the aircraft. redacted ground gave us the clearance to join taxiway 2 and hold short of 3. we noticed the vehicle in the vehicle road make a left turn and not stop at the intersection, and the now continue towards our aircraft. the pilot in command started to apply the brakes to slow the aircraft in case the vehicle did not stop. the vehicle, now clearly a van, continued at speed not slowing and crossed in front of the aircraft. the pilot in command applied full braking in order to avoid a collision, and the van passed approximately 20 feet in front of the aircraft. the flight attendant fell during the braking and hit the floor near the jumpseat and the aft of the center pedestal. the pilot in command stopped the taxi and checked with the flight attendants to confirm that everyone was ok. we received confirmation from the flight attendants that they felt ok to continue, and that the owners were safe. i notified redacted ground that we had a near collision with the vehicle and received a secondary taxi clearance. after entering taxiway 2, the aircraft lighting was reduced. redacted ground was also notified that the flight attendant fell due to the near collision, but was not injured. as the flight continued the flight attendant that fell indicated that his ankle and side were sore. the pilot in command went to check on the flight attendant and to talk to the owners. it was determined everyone was okay to continue to the destination of redacted. out of an abundance of caution the flight attendant went to get checked out after landing.suggestions: we could have had a better confirmation of cabin secure. due to waiting for fuel i was mindful that the passengers may have changed seats. my mind may have associated the fa telling me the new seating positions with the cabin being secure as these are usually stated together.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A321 flight crew reported loss of both electrical generators during climb. Flight diverted and landed safely.
text: time: day 0, approx time of event xa:45weather: night imc, navigating rain storms with minor convection imbedded.location(s): approximately at waypoint redacted on the redacted departureairspeed about 300 kias, altitude fl260aircraft: aircraft xca: person a (pf)first officer: person b (pm)first officer's narrative:departing out of redacted to redacted at fl260 crew experienced a dual generator failure. ca retained control of the aircraft by using the standby instruments, he remained on altitude and maintain a safe airspeed, manually adjusting the thrust and 'hand flying'. he also turned on the dome light immediately. first officer, referenced the qrc and stated this is not a 'quick action item or an ecam exception'. the crew had to wait as the rat (ram air turbine) deployed and this took approximately 2 to 5 minutes to provide emergency power. when the upper ecam became available, the crew was reassured the engines were operating normally, which was evident in the ability of the ca to maintain altitude and airspeed, and the crew had situational awareness that the aircraft control was being maintained in altn law (alternate law) with no auto thrust. after the audio panel initiated a boot up sequence, the first officer requested priority handling with air traffic control and began coordinating with air traffic control to proceed back to redacted. weather at redacted was received from air traffic control and reported ovc 200' 1/2 mile visibility. ca instructed first officer to get weather at redacted, which was better with ovc 600', with light easterly winds. ca instructed first officer to begin coordination to divert to redacted. after the aircraft was safely moving in the direction of the divert field, the first officer began ecam actions which regained generator 1 after one attempted reset and did not regain number 2 generator after one attempted reset. ecam did not direct the crew to disconnect the bus tie to attempt a second generator reset on the number 2 generator. other ecam actions were to reset the facs (flight augmentation computer) and eng (engine) n1 mode off (1/2). the autopilot was functioning now in direct law after the fac reset but the auto thrust wasn't functioning after eng n1 mode was selected off, as expected by the crew. at this time the crew elected to not address any ecam follow ups due to conditions and crew workload. during system initialization, after restoration of aircraft power, the first officer didn't have a map on his side and primary instruments were unreliable. the ca regained full functionality of the pfd (primary flight display) and map, and the first officer regained pfd, but the map did not function on his side. this condition persisted for the reminder of the flight. ca/fo elected to not run the apu because the crew was satisfied with the electrical power being supplied from the rat and gen 1, and the cause of the elec malfunction was unable to be immediately identified by the crew with the information presented. the crew didn't want to introduce another electrical component to the system if they didn't know the exact cause of the malfunction. additionally, no immediate procedure drove the crew to turn on the apu, it is in the ecam follow ups. during the decent into redacted, the crew addressed all remaining non-normal and normal checklist, ran the land app using the 'normal' tab for the overweight landing. in the land app the non-normal tab, under the failure tab, did not have an 'additional system failure...' selection that fit the current condition. additionally, the crew accomplished the overweight landing checklist in its entirety. the only communication with dispatch was through the acars diversion message, which the first officer accomplished. the ca maintained pf duties for the whole duration of the event and the rest of the flight. the first officer maintained pm duties for the event, and briefed the fas about the nature of the event and the crew's plan to divert into redacted. of note, the #1 fa has enhanced systems knowledge of the airbus fleet and understood the rat was deployed because she heard the 'humming' of the turbine. she knew the flight crewwas dealing with an electrical problem and/or a hydraulic problem and was able to relay to the first officer during this conversation of her situational awareness. this is above and beyond for her position and her actions need to be commended. she enhanced the other fas awareness of the gravity of the situation and maintained passenger confidence that the pilots had the situation under control. the ca directed the first officer to address the passengers that we experienced a 'power interruption' and brief them of our plan to divert into redacted where there will be company assistance to continue their travel to redacted. the crew was vectored by air traffic control to 4, 000' msl on final for runway xx at redacted. the crew set up and briefed the instrument landing system to runway xx after a few turns in holding on final. this gave the crew time to reassure themselves the aircraft was in a safe configuration to accomplish a safe recovery to the runway and taxi to the gate. additionally, this low holding help reduce the aircraft weight. the crew flew a non-eventful instrument landing system to a min rate of descent to touch down, and taxi to gate with no additional malfunctions. after safely at the gate, the ca turned on the apu and shut down the engines. the apu started and functioned normally. no additional ecam displays were noted after shutdown.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reported a situation where ground personnel used non-standard signals while the aircraft was attempting to park at the gate. The flight crew released the brake resulting in the aircraft rolling backwards. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft and was tugged back to the gate.
text: while working the flight there was a situation that arose from ground crew-to-flight deck communications. upon reaching the gate, the ground workers gave us the 'stop' message with the batons in the shape of an 'x.' the manor in which we received this signal was abrupt and nonchalantly given. our original thoughts in the flight deck were about the idea that we had rolled too far on the parking job and that it could potentially be possible that a tug would have to push us back. we deducted that this was a possibility due to the nature in which we were told to stop. the abrupt order to stop from the ground crew helped us draw this as a potential conclusion. the head ground personnel had given us the 'x' and stood stationary for almost 2 minutes while the captain and myself later assumed he had forgotten to give us a 'chocks-in' signal. we proceeded to run shutdown flows and checklists because of the ground workers approaching the airplane for post flight duties despite the forgotten chocks in gesture. it was at this moment that we received hand signals from the lead ground marshaller, to disconnect our parking break. this was later found out to be the ground controller signaling us about the beacon light still being on. the hand signals he gave us were incorrect and were interpreted as a 'release brakes' message.in some scenarios, it had been known that being pushed back from the stopping point is a possibility at some airports because of the lack of motion in some gate docking devices. we assumed this was the case, and that a tug had been hooked up as well to the nose, to also prepare for the next quick turn on this aircraft.with the assumptions made, that we were asked to release brakes, and that the tug could be connected, like it possibly, and many times is after shut down, we elected to turn the parking brake off after the shutdown checklists. our thoughts were that we had received word from ground that we were too far forward and needed a small push from ground crew to correct this. so we complied with what we thought was happening, which was a small pushback correction. we had wing walkers come to the wings as if we were actually pushing back from a gate to fuel the idea that this was a serious possibility. so as the brakes were disarmed, the captain and i were attentive to the controls. we were ready to act at any moment in this sterile environment.we were both under the impression that we were in an active push back discussed via the common sign language used between flight decks and ramp crew. it was at this moment that we also realized the wing walkers followed us back as if we were getting pushed. at about 10 feet back from where we had originally stopped, we became alarmed to see that the tug was still at the stopping line at the gate, and began to immediately question why we were moving and why there was crew doing nothing to stop us or explain what was occurring. i had opened my window on the first officer's side to inquire about why were still moving with ground crew if there actually was no tug attached. the same moment, we came to an abrupt stop, which was a required action as we had realized that the plane was rolling backwards with no indication from ground crew that, that was our reality. the parking break was pulled in an effort to immediately stop the potentially dangerous roll, and thankfully, no damage, injury, or potential to put someone else in serious danger had occurred. the seatbelt sign was unfortunately off due to the shutdown flow being completed. the events that had unfolded happened in a very short time frame, that the primary consideration was with what was happening to the state of the aircraft.the nature of this entanglement with the parking situation was grounded in miscommunication from the start. the nonchalant nature of the ground crew made it near impossible to realize that we were in an entirely dangerous scenario where we thought they signaled to push in a non-controlled ramp. we were able to quickly act by stopping the aircraft, and having a direct verbal conversation with ground personnel to get towed back in to the gate.cause: miscommunication, no action taken by ramp workers.suggestions: to avoid this event again, my suggestion would be to emphasize the need to not move the aircraft until absolutely certain the message received was correct and based on fact. it would be beneficial to also emphasize the idea that ground ramp personnel can't always be trusted and that a pilot's judgement needs to be separate from what ramp may indicate.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: ERJ-175 flight crew reported an inflight upset resulted when they encountered wake turbulence on descent into PHX in trail of a heavy aircraft. ATC was not helpful when they requested a track deviation prior to the encounter.
text: while flying the hydrr one arrival into phx, we were following a heavy aircraft y. the first officer was the pf and the ca was the pm. when becoming aware that we were following an aircraft y, 5 miles in trail, we requested to sidestep upwind in order to mitigate the threat of wake turbulence. air traffic control was unable to accommodate since we were not yet experiencing the wake turbulence. the ca and the first officer created a shared mental model that if we experienced wake turbulence we would use emergency authority to deviate upwind and away from the wake turbulence. along with that, the ca made an announcement to have everyone seated, including the flight attendants, as a preemptive measure. once passing judth on the arrival, air traffic control cleared us direct geela and to descend via the arrival. while descending through fl230, the aircraft began to experience minor oscillations similar to light turbulence. the first officer put their hands on the controls and shortly after the aircraft experienced the full wake of the aircraft y, banking left between 15 and 20 degrees and slight nose up attitude. the first officer disconnected ap (autopilot) and recovered by pushing the nose down, rolling the wings level, increasing thrust, and stabilizing the aircraft. during the recovery, the ca requested priority handling and stated that we were experiencing wake turbulence and deviating course to evade the wake. once stable, the first officer flight upwind which was left of course and leveled the pitch in order to stop the descent into further wake. the first officer then called for heading, altitude, and autopilot which the ca armed on the fma (flight mode annunciator). once fully recovered and away from the wake, the ca called the flight attendants to see if there were any injuries, which there were not as everyone was seated and buckled in. air traffic control clarified if we still needed priority handling and if there were any injuries. we responded negative, cancelled priority handling, and continued on course with the arrival begin directed to fly direct geela and to continue the arrival descent. we created space between the aircraft y and ourselves and landed uneventfully. debriefed on the ground.cause: the cause of this was due to lack of separation from a heavy aircraft y and lack of accommodation when preemptive actions were requested by the pilots. suggestions: in order to avoid this in the future, further separation from a heavy aircraft y is needed. if air traffic control will not accommodate, we must be more assertive in how it is necessary for safety.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported that during initial approach after they disconnected the autopilot; they observed the aileron controls were ineffective until the control column was displaced more than 10 degrees to the left or right.
text: during outbound flight redacted-redacted first officer's leg and first officer engaged autopilot at 600 feet, disengaged autopilot at 400 feet on approach in redacted. during takeoff this flight, ca leg, left aileron trim was applied (approximately halfway between neutral index and first index mark left of neutral - approx 1/4 of available aileron trim) to reduce control forces and autopilot engaged at 600 feet. during approach at 1500 afe, autopilot disengaged and observed aileron controls 'loose' or ineffective until control wheel displaced more than 10 degrees left or right of neutral. essentially within 10 degrees of neutral - left or right control wheel aileron input had no artificial feel or self-centering/resistance and produced no rolling effect.after shutdown checklist and debrief was complete i contacted the chief pilot to expand the team and seek his thoughts. it was determined that i should contact maintenance control and explain the situation to them.cause: unknown why. no caution messages received.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported departing with weather all around the departure airport and during the climb; the aircraft experienced a lightning strike. This resulted in the flight diverting to another airport where they landed safely.
text: weather over and around redacted. we waited until the cells have passed east to start making our way to the runway for departure. we saw other aircraft depart and head south to avoid the weather and nothing was reported prior to our departure. we decided it was okay to continue and we departed runway xx. we had continuous ignition on along with the radars for takeoff. i was pilot flying for this leg. we did not depict any large cells on departure but air traffic control advised us of extreme precipitation 12 o'clock. we requested deviations and it was approved. shortly after, climbing through around 15, 000ft, we were struck by lightning. we continued the climb to get over/around the weather. all systems, pressurization, and flight controls were operating normal. we also contacted flight attendants to make sure everything was okay. they had nothing to note. at this point we made the decision to continue. at cruise we did notice a loud thud or popping sound and decided to divert to redacted. we did not declare an emergency and the flight landed uneventful. damage was found on the aircraft from the strike.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported receiving a nose gear disagree alert during intial climb.  Flight crew returned to departure airport and landed safely.
text: during walk around, found nlg strut completely compressed (bottomed-out). contract maintenance serviced it to in-range extension with n2. taxi and takeoff were uneventful until gear retracted. nlg green down and locked extinguished, red unlocked light illuminated and remained illuminated. pilots ran gear disagree checklist. noise level and vibration seemed nearly normal on climb out and fuel flow was nominal for phase of flight. after weighing options, captain decided to continue to redacted and continue troubleshooting on way to redacted. manual landing gear extension checklist was reviewed just in case it would be needed. contacted dispatch and maintenance control to determine any other possible action. maintenance control informed us that the maintenance tech in redacted left his flashlight in the nlg compartment. this was the most likely cause of the problem. pilots agreed to extend the landing gear early for landing since fuel state was not a concern. during approach, when the gear handle was moved to the down position, the nlg red unlocked light remained illuminated. the green down and locked light remained extinguished. overhead panel nlg green light also was extinguished. both mlg lights indicated down and locked. pm (at this point it was the captain) referred to the manual landing gear checklist and attempted a manual extension. this was unsuccessful. nlg indications did not change. pf abandoned the approach and called for the go-around. redacted [tracon] vectored us northwest of the airport at 12, 000. crew referred to the landing with partial landing gear checklist. dispatch and maintenance control were consulted. briefing with brace instructions was provided to the flight attendants. after running all applicable checklists the captain performed a normal approach and light landing while reducing loads on the nose gear for as long as possible. the nose settled on to the extended nlg. ops and airport rescue and firefighting inspected the aircraft, pinned all landing gear before exiting runway. the flashlight was located in the nlg compartment. a normal taxi to the arrival gate occurred without further incident.
