anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported during taxi the cabin became extremely hot. Flight returned to the gate and everyone deplaned.
text: we pushed off the gate on time for a departure from redacted. there was a front to the west of the airfield approaching quickly. we were up with ground and got a full reroute which added quite a bit of fuel required. we taxied to a spot to get in touch with dispatch and come up with a plan. we decided to drop the alternate so we could takeoff legally as there were many good options along the route clear of the weather.we taxied to the runway and were number 6 for departure. redacted was doing 20 in tail spacing for departures. as we waiting for turn the weather hit the field, with wind shear of over 25 kts at 500 being reported. tower stopped all departures and was estimating a minimum of an hour till the weather was going to clear.around this time the flight attendant called me and said it was pretty hot in the back. i asked the first officer to use the max cooling procedure from the flight manual. we talked again to dispatch and decided a return to the gate was necessary due to fuel and the weather.as we were taxing back the fas called again and said it was very hot. we switched the pack temperature controllers to manual and full cold (737-700). we parked the plane after a long delay to get the self park system to operate. the jetway driver would not bring the jetway to the aircraft due to the ramp being closed. i called ops, ramp, dispatch and the chief pilot to get my passengers off the plane. i requested priority handling at the gate due to heat, it was approximately 95 degrees in the back. after around 30 minutes the jetway was driven to the aircraft and passengers were deplaned.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported an engine failure.
text: previous flight that we flew in for assigned (737 ng) aircraft y had a pneumatic maintenance issue. i was unhappy with maintenance effort to rectify problem. they cleared the warning electronically and did a leak check of right acm (air cycle machine) bay. basically, they turned on apu and told us to call them back if light came on again, but would not check the wing strut or leading edge despite our requests and explanation of system. after a discussion with dispatch, she agreed it was a problem, and offered a solution of another aircraft, aircraft x, that was scheduled to ferry to redacted with two pilots we had deadheaded in. this plan was put in motion. i was told the ferry paperwork needed to be changed to a revenue flight and aircraft brought from hangar. deadheading crew was to fly back with us.while we waited, we reviewed the aircraft history. apparently on day 0 aircraft x (737ng) experienced a #2 engine failure that tore up the turbine blades and sent debris into the horizontal stabilizer. the logbook documented that the engine was replaced at redacted, ground run only, and horizontal tail holes speed taped. first officer and i discussed concern on putting revenue pax on aircraft with new engine that had never been flown, and concluded this was indeed faa approved company policy and all paperwork appeared in order.when we arrived at aircraft, it was clear it had never flown, and cockpit was in configuration of last single engine landing (flap inhibit up, trim adjusted). duty day was beginning to become concern due to delays and it was brought to my attention that customs closing was an issue. at some time dispatch notified me that customs would stay open, but we needed to hurry up. the usual delays of switching aircraft (bags and catering) occurred, and i was notified some bags had to come off for pax that had not re-boarded. start up and push was normal, but upon after start check we discovered that eecs (electronic engine controls) were in altn. called dispatch and conferenced in maintenance control to discuss (item is flight crew placardable). discovered eec were not on, first officer said he must have missed on pre-flight flow (very easy to do). maintenance control could find no reason they were off, but i asked about ground run test card that was in logbook and on a hunch she got the actual mechanic that did the ground run (he was still in redacted) who admitted it was part of the test and that he left them off. maintenance control then cleared us to turn them on and proceed and with concurrence with dispatch, first officer did so. dispatch then had to check to see if customs would still stay open at redacted for our late arrival, which they did and she gave clearance to proceed.taxi, takeoff, and initial climbout was normal for night vmc at redacted. we had just negotiated a isolated line of thunderstorms that were putting out a little light turbulence and first officer as pf had slowed the aircraft for turbulence when he decided to speed up to econ speed at about 31000 ft. i felt a rumbling vibration and a slight yaw as pm and asked 'did you feel that?' before he could answer i felt more vibrations and looked over to the engine instruments to see #2 engine rolling back and 'eng fail' displayed. he said 'my aircraft' at same time i said 'your aircraft' and clicked off autopilot as aircraft was slowing and yawing. i realized that we would immediately be drifting down, and requested priority handling with redacted control asking for lower and a return to redacted (we were 20-30 min out and this was closest suitable airport). immediately started getting calls from back of aircraft saying they had seen a flash and 'sparks'. executed qrc eng severe damage or separation checklist due to prior vibrations, and subsequent one eng inop landing and nonroutine landing checklist while first officer navigated back through weather towards redacted and i followed along with charts monitoring minimum safe altitudes (low chart and 20-1 page) as identified threat was also terrain. communication was difficult dueto constant communication with cabin and language barriers with air traffic control. air traffic control told us to expect instrument landing system y xx which is a teardrop turn from redacted vor to the instrument landing system xx. neither the first officer nor i could get it to load without placing a discontinuity in the middle of the approach. we tried numerous techniques but it kept leaving a discontinuity in middle of approach. normal checklists also completed sometime in here. i am familiar with redacted and knew they vector on one side of the airport, so asked for vectors for the instrument landing system z which they approved. this removed a major distraction. first officer flew the aircraft on fd1 (flight director) and ap1 (autopilot) (cmd 1) to downwind as i briefed the approach, and set up for flaps 15, brakes 3. i decided to fly the approach as i had just done a flaps 15 in there that morning and was more experienced in the aircraft. took aircraft on base leg and intercepted loc on vectors at 2, 500 ft. for some unknown reason, i saw flight director disappear in hud and looked down at pfd (primary flight display) to see lateral disappear and shortly after vertical to disappear. immediately transitioned to hud raw data and continued hand flying while asking first officer to troubleshoot by resetting fds. field was in sight and papis operational.flew overweight landing to a smooth touchdown about 1, 500-1, 700 ft down and stopped short of a taxiway (1 maybe) about 8, 000 ft down 10, 500 ft runway. first officer moved flaps 40 and spoilers down while i spoke to people in back. arff (airport rescue and firefighting) rolled up to inspect aircraft. we quickly discovered we had no contact with arff and tower wanted to relay all communications to them which became really awkward as we relayed our condition, what we wanted checked, and tried to warn them to stay clear of operating #1 engine. additionally, we checked brake energy and discovered for our weight and speed were in 'caution zone'. through a series of awkward communications (language barrier and 'pass the message' barrier) we asked tower to have fire chief aware and eventually we got back info that one tire/brake was indeed smoking. i asked tower to have arff chock nose so i could release brakes with a plan of allowing brakes to cool some and eventually taxi to gate. this seemed to not be understood or confusing to those on ground. first officer at this time was also trying to get hold of ops for gate assignment and to notify maintenance. we attempted visual signals but mostly just got quizzical looks. at some point a random individual showed up on first officer side and he believed this individual (which was not a uniformed fireman) was asking us to shutdown. since we had not gotten hold of anyone at company yet and fire chief had not cleared us off, i was reluctant to do so. i told him to signal the fellow to come over to my side and tried to communicate to this very animated individual who was not responding to my chocks signal either. had to shut down in order to hear him. turns out he was company maintenance of some sorts and basically just took over from fire chief telling me he would get tug to tow us in. i told him we had hot brakes (assuming he might not want us immediately in a gate area) but he did not seem to care. tug showed up and we towed to gate area. once at gate and checklist complete, i sent first officer down to ensure wheels were chocked twice and released brakes to cool. first officer told me that maintenance got a bit aggressive downstairs stating he was in charge and how we should have listened to him immediately (even though we had no idea who he was or why he was there). my first officer says he corrected him in the conversation as to who was in charge-us and arff at that point in the situation. later i found out that they had run from hangar straight out to us, but had no headsets, radio, or chocks with them. i am not sure they were communicating at all with fire chief on ground. ops never answered on radio. i called dispatcher, who had gone home, asked replacement for chief pilot, who could not be found, so called safety. filled out logbookfor engine failure and overweight landing. after that, things seemed to move along. through ops coordination and the app eventually secured 8 rooms for crew. assigned to fly aircraft y (original aircraft) home next morning. my original refusal write-up as signed off with requested inspections when we showed up.cause: what started out as a simple 'turn' ended up being very long day. the length of day and darkness exuberant the 'startle affect' for all involved, but front and back end of crew worked well together. terrain, weather, and communication barriers were a constant distraction. first officer and i reviewed/debriefed with safety software. i discovered a few errors and pointed that out for us both to learn. i found out that when i asked for flight directors to be reset, he did not turn his off (just mine) as he was afraid he would lose his flight director. i suspect had we recycled, that problem would have gone away. we are not sure why approach would not load. i suspect it was some combination of direct to iaf and constraints somewhere. the next day i was able to put in the flight management system for aircraft y no problem.maintenance in redacted seems to have a bit of attitude working with aircrews and arff. if they are going to insert themselves with arff they really need comm gear (radio/headsets) and if planning on towing, chocks. arff at redacted really needs comm capability with priority aircraft. finally, i really don't think the first flight after an engine change needs to be with revenue pax on board.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Check Pilot reported loss of hydraulic system during cruise. Flight continued.
text: approximately half an hour into the cruise, while resting in the cabin, i heard the master caution chime, and autopilot disconnect alert. upon entering the cockpit and seating in the observers seat i saw the captain reading a qrh checklist and observed the eicas caution message 'hyd press sys 1' along with the lower eicas displaying the hyd sd page, and the number 1 hydraulic tank indication empty. i then opened the hyd prees sys 1 checklist on my ipad and monitored the actions of the pm and pf. following the selection of the alternate gear extension, the right hand wing gear indicated hashed/in transit, and an eicas gear disagree message was displayed. the crew actioned the gear disagree checklist and that did not remedy the situation. i contacted maintenance control, deputy chief pilot and the supervisor on the sat phone. i asked the question to the supervisor if, (as we had used the alternate gear selection ) would there be any negative repercussions with selecting the landing gear handle down, as this was not a step that the gear disagree checklist advocated. upon receiving the 'no objection' from the supervisor the gear handle was selected down and the right wing gear indicated green. we then landed in accordance with the loss of hyd 1 system, and were towed to the ramp following shut down on the runway.i wish to commend the captain on his excellent crew management and command handling of this malfunction.suggestions: i suggest that the b744 qrh gear disagree checklist be amended to direct the crew to step xx (landing gear lever (if possible)…dn. currently the checklist directs crew to step xy bypassing the gear lever down selection.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the approach end of PVU's Runway 31 is dangerously close to the departure end of SPK's active runway and presents a risk of midair collision.
text: experienced a traffic conflict (tcas traffic advisory) due to another airport's traffic while circling to land in pvu. commenced a vmc circle maneuver from the rnav runway 13, to land runway 31. winds required landing runway 31, and the rnav visual runway 31 was not an option due to marginal ceiling that would have prevented us from maintaining required visual contact and cloud clearance. while maneuvering base-to-final for runway 31, we received a traffic advisory, and the target appeared to be within 2 miles (possibly closer) and less than 700 feet below us. shortly after the traffic advisory sounded, we heard a traffic call on the other airport's ctaf, which we were monitoring in accordance with company chart recommendations. as we were in a very high workload moment, i don't recall how close the target ultimately became. we never acquired visual contact with the conflicting traffic. already in a turn away from the conflicting traffic, we continued the circling maneuver to landing. cause: spanish fork municipal (spk) lies less than 5 nm from the approach end of pvu's runway 31, with a similarly-aligned runway. pvu's class d airspace has a cutout for this airport, such that the only way to keep a circling maneuver within the class d would be to fly less than a 2.5 nm final to runway 31. utilizing the protected circling radius of 4 nm, we were well outside of pvu's class d during the maneuver, placing our base-to-final nearly over the departure end of spk's active runway. the layout of these two airports, especially with one being uncontrolled, presents a unique risk of midair collision.suggestions: for my part, i would have made a traffic call on spk's ctaf during the circling maneuver, though doing so would need to be carefully balanced with the need to manage the flight path during a high workload situation. having monitored the ctaf since well before commencing the approach, i would have hoped for a traffic call from the other aircraft before they were airborne, but it seemed that their first ctaf call was made after departing. besides mutual ctaf communication, i'm unsure how to mitigate the risk of midair collision between these two airports, but there must be an in-depth discussion of how to do so. of all the places i operate, landing on pvu runway 31, especially when the rnav visual 31 is unavailable, presents a unique risk. enough repeats of this flight's circumstances, in my view, will eventually lead to an accident.

text: lna is a non-towered airport under pbi airspace. there was heavy single engine training traffic in the pattern. aircraft y departed ahead of me. my intention was to depart to the east under the pbi class c airspace until clear of it. after departure there was traffic in front of me so i turned south. aircraft y that had departed before me was in sight about 500 feet below. as i lost sight of him my ads-b showed he started climbing and i got a traffic alert that he was 200 feet directly below me so i quickly climbed to avoid him. i entered the class c airspace to avoid the traffic. i saw there wasn't any traffic in front of me so i continued south while avoiding some clouds to get out of the airspace as quickly as possible.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported an NMAC with what was possibly a UAS during final approach.
text: i was performing the duty of an instructor in the right seat of a small aircraft. talking to bjc tower, we were making right traffic for 30l at bjc. upon rolling out on our right base i noticed an object off our right wing, same altitude (about 6, 300' msl), estimated to be between 100' and 200' directly west of us, and situated just north of the extended centerline for 30r. the object was roughly in the shape of a 'miniature hot air balloon'. i estimate this 'drone' to be roughly 3' x 3' feet in size. it was red in color and had a distinctly visible bright red pulsing beacon, pulsing approximately the same rate as one from an aircraft. i did not notice any rotors, but did not see it long enough to inspect further. no evasive maneuvers were required based on the timing of when it was spotted. the object appeared stationary in the air.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: R22 instructor reported conflicting traffic entered landing zone area resulted in taking evasive action and a critical ground conflict.
text: during autorotation practice, a plane was holding short of the taxiway. at our airport we run dual patterns with fixed wing on one side to the runway and the rotor wing on the other to the taxiway. we saw the aircraft holding short of the taxiway and erroneously thought they were remaining there. we entered the autorotation and ~150' from our flare and recovery from the maneuver, the fixed wing pulled out onto the taxiway. cfi took controls and executed a go around by ~75'-100'. no damage occurred, but decision had to be swift and proximity was close. reflecting on the situation i would have elected to forgo the maneuver and go around to reset given the proximity of the aircraft and the possibility for a close call. a secondary communication with the aircraft would have helped to avoid confusion as well.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a NMAC in the pattern. Flight continued.
text: arriving from the west i elected to enter the left hand pattern for runway 10 from approximately 1.5 mile north of the runway. due to the current traffic in the pattern i decided to do a 180° rh turn onto the downwind leg- i was at the pattern altitude of 5400 feet msl. aircraft y had called in from the south for a midfield crosswind entry to a lh downwind for landing at the same airport. normal pattern speeds would have given the aircraft in the pattern, and myself, over the airport plenty of time to position them selves for a normal pattern and landing with a larger aircraft in the pattern. however, aircraft y came from the south at 6000 ft. msl and entered the traffic pattern at over 231 knots (from adsb data) straight over the top of my aircraft and just in front of aircraft z 1.5 miles to the east climbing through 7000msl westbound over the same runway. vertical separation with my aircraft was 600 feet but the speed of aircraft y left no one in the pattern any time to maneuver for better separation horizontally. there was no time for corrective action. the aircraft y pilot was very arrogant and non-cooperative when questioned over ctaf on the speed and flight path they had flown, blaming others for 'coming at me'. recurrence preventative: hopefully, in the future the aircraft will approach at legal speeds (<200kts) and altitudes (1500 agl for turbine). otherwise, the safety margin is greatly decreased or even eliminated. in the future, i will make sure that when i'm landing at gxy, that i stay well clear of that particular aircraft until i see the pilots behavior and attitude have changed.

text: nmac - tower cleared aircraft x to enter airspace at aproximately xa:35 to make left traffic rwy xxl. upon joining the downwind an r22 helicopter was cleared for a transition from redacted to the heli port and was advised of 2 fixed wing aircraft on the downwind. no other transmissions were observed regarding conflict. the r22 was inbound at 1900' msl heading ~220 and the cessna was begining descent from tpa of 2300 feet heading ~040. this dual evaluation mission had the student flying and beginning configuration unaware of the head on conflict. the conflict was mitigated after the instructing pilot took controls and began a vx climb and left bank to avoid the head on conflict with the traffic in sight. crew landed safely at redacted.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: First Officer reported a low altitude alert during approach from ATC. Crew adjusted and continued approach.
text: during the approach for instrument landing system z runway 6 into teb the glideslope was not captured at intercept altitude of 1300. i do not believe it was working. the captain initiated a descent to about 350 feet. (localizer only minimums are 600ft) tower alerted us that we had a low altitude alert and to maintain our altitude, they mentioned to altimeter setting with 30.33 and that is what we had in the altimeter. while we were at this low altitude, the localizer cdi what's showing two dots deflection, i called this out. at about 300 feet we finally saw the field and we were high. the captain then put us in a descent of about 1400 fpm around 200 ft agl with vref +20 (145 kts) we had a firm but ok landing followed by hard braking and thrust reversers. the correct action here would have been to go around.

text: busy pattern activity, had visual of traffic aircraft y and aircraft z in pattern. and aircraft a on take off. did not have visual of aircraft b. i believe when banking into the downwind my wing was masking my view. when entering the downwind, aircraft y reported being 'cut off by aircraft x'. did not know the details of this event until after checking ads-b tracking.lessons learned:changing my landing traffic maximum to 3 and looking to add ads-b in.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Aeronca 7EC pilot reported main wheel departed aircraft during take off. Pilot returned to departure airport.
text: left wheel hub and tire departed the aircraft on take-off from redacted on route to redacted to practice touch and go landings. missing wheel noticed by aircraft on ground at redacted and verified by visual inspection out of left window. decided to fly back to redacted as they have full emergency services. di a low pass with the tower at redacted to verify missing wheel and agreed on a slow landing on runway xxl as this minimizes the impact to the airport and has a smooth runway without the rain grooves that are part of the main runway xyr.decided to land on the concrete runway rather than the grass to minimize the effect of the left brake hub digging into the ground. wind was at 220 at around 10+ kts so flew a slow approach and put right gear down and let the aircraft slow down until the left gear touched down then kept the aircraft straight with rudder and right brake.only damage was to the brake shoe hub and lower brake shoe which were both ground down a little.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: PA-28 Cherokee Flight Instructor reported oil pressure decreasing during cruise. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: so uneventful flight, preflighted noted no abnormalities, filled up 2 quarts of oil as level was below 6 on the dipstick. everything looked normal. did about an hour of manuevers in air, at first it did have struggles of power holding altitude in steep turns but nothing noticeable that seemed abnormal it was the first warm day of winter. did 2 steep spirals then planned to do eights on pylons. as we begin to setup, the student makes a turn and adds power and thats when i noticed the engine not making the power it should've and i noted the engine instruments and oil pressure was around 65 and dropping. thats when i took controls and immediately started turning towards redacted. i figured i had power still enough right now so i elected to climb as much as i could to gain some altitude an use the tailwind to at least get us away from trees and give better gliding distance to a field. told my student to run the loss of oil pressure checklist and sqauwk redacted while i handled comms and advise on redacted ctaf. at about 2400ft is when i pulled the power back to prevent overheating of the engine and kept just enough to try and hold altitude but temps kept climbing so i reduced more which eseentially gave us a drift down with some power. we were about 14 miles southeast ish away from redacted when i noticed the oil pressure dropping. by about 6 miles away the engine began losing more rpms but by then i had a good feeling we'll make the runway but it'll have to be a tailwind landing. there wasn't enough power to get into the pattern so i just elected for a straight in runway xx at redacted. after we landed we still had some power to roll off the runway and started rolling towards the ramp by then temps were really hot so i shutoff the engine and continued rolling on to the ramp. as we get out there's oil all over the bottom and noticed no oil in the dipstick. shutdown terminated and then made some calls.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: PA-28 Cherokee Flight Instructor reported a close encounter with another aircraft during training maneuvers. Flight climbed and continued the training flight.
text: while practicing chandelles with my cfi student, we noticed another aircraft in the area that appeared to be maneuvering west of location x. we attempted to take a proactive approach stating our intentions on the local practice area frequency (redacted.xx) and keeping an eye on our ads-b while trying to locate him visually. we started maneuvering at 4500' msl and gradually climbed throughout our maneuvers to 5500 msl, keeping an eye on the rv that was just west of us. we established visual contact and saw that he was rapidly climbing and descending with no apparent pattern. we attempted to contact him on frequency as he came closer to us with no response. we tried bailing to the southeast to get away from him and he made no apparent attempt to take evasive action for us. i think this could have been avoided if we were able to communicate with the rv, without being able to do so it was impossible to predict his next move and if any action we took would cause further conflict. that area is known for high-volume student training and it's important that everyone is on the same page to ensure we can continue flying safely.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: i am writing this report on behalf of my company's request for a mistake i made on a utility inspection contract outside of redacted airport.the company i work for is company x. as a contractor for company x i am responsible for utility inspections.on day 0 i was operating, doing utility inspections on distribution telecommunication poles outside of redacted.i misread the map and made a mistake of operating outside of our authorized waiver.my mistake was going outside of the certificate of waiver or authorization.i did not realize that these poles i collected were not a part of the waiver even though this contract has those poles to inspect. i understand this is a serious infraction, i did make a mistake and there was no danger involved.i do apologize for this mistake, and i will be more conscious of my flight planning on my daily operations, especially around restricted airspaces.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: A Tower Controller in Charge reported they observed an aircraft on short final initiate a go around due to an aircraft holding position on the runway.
text: i was controller in charge listening to local control 1. local control 1 was correcting an instrument flight rules departure who asked 'are we supposed to turn to 220?' local control 1 asked if they received their instrument flight rules flight plan and then to follow their flight plan, then switched the aircraft to departure. local control 1 called redacted [tracon] to let them know that the instrument flight rules was late on their turn, but redacted [tracon] didn't answer. local control 1 turned to ground control to say something about the instrument flight rules then turned to final, i was watching the instrument flight rules on local control 2's certified tower radar display (ctrd) to ensure the instrument flight rules was identing and talking to approach. then, i looked at the threshold and the sr22 that was in the pattern was going around and that aircraft x was lined up on the runway. local control 1 had lined up aircraft x after the instrument flight rules departure and the sr22 was in the pattern for multiple. we both got distracted by the instrument flight rules's confusion. i didn't hear them clear the sr22 for a touch-and-go, but found out after that he was cleared while aircraft x was in position. i was focused on closing the instrument flight rules loop being closed, instead of helping local control 1 scan their runway knowing their focus was on another task. training for controller in charge on how to scan to aid the locals to prevent unsafe situations.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: TPA TRACON Controller reported the departure procedures out of LAL are unusable due to VFR aircraft flying just outside the D airspace. Controller had to maneuver an airline away from traffic as there were VFR aircraft in direct conflict with the SBOAT departure procedure.
text: aircraft x departed lal on the sboat departure. there were visual flight rules aircraft at 2500 and 4000 who were in direct conflict with the sboat. i stopped aircraft x at 2000 and turned him. not only is the sboat (and the owayy) departure usually unusable due to visual flight rules aircraft just outside the d airspace, the entire sector is a safety nightmare. aircraft approach lal from any and all directions and at any altitude. there is zero safety net protecting approaches and departures in and out of lal.if measures aren't taken to protect aircraft in and out of lal there is going to be a midair. lal should have been a charlie years ago.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported red nose landing gear light illuminated during climb. Flight continued to destination and landed uneventfully.
text: on the walk-around prior to the flight the captain noticed that the nose landing gear strut was fully compressed. maintenance was called to fix the issue and it was resolved so we taxied out and took off. i (first officer) was the pilot-flying and the captain noticed upon retracting the gear that the red nose landing gear light illuminated. we let redacted [tower] know that we had a gear malfunction and may need to remain in the airspace. although there was a very slight vibration difference we agreed the gear was up and potentially not locked. we decided to continue on to redacted and we maintained the slowest practical airspeed during the flight as to not exceed gear limitations. we briefed the arrival and approach into redacted and elected to configure early in case the gear did not operate properly. when the gear handle was extended the unsafe indication remained and i called for the go-around. we climbed and were vectored north or the airport where we ran necessary checklists in an attempt to get the gear down and locked. our efforts to get a safe gear indication failed so we prepared for landing and decided it would be best to swap flight controls so the captain could control the tiller in the event the nose landing gear operated abnormally. the landing was uneventful and the gear pin was inserted before we taxied to the gate.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier ground personnel reported uncommanded aircraft movement at the gate.
text: aircraft came to get after passengers deplaned and ready to push aircraft to remote stand. aircraft slides backward and i told the ramp on the radio the aircraft is sliding before we pull the jet bridge. when i came down the line was at the dot, i turned on to operate and lifted canopy and was waiting for ramp guidance to pull the bridge and saw the aircraft sliding back.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Pilot reported HYA's ATIS has been unreadable for weeks.
text: 35 miles from destination, flight listened to atis 1, which was almost unreadable and excessively long with notams, taking up too much time to hear the entire broadcast. bos approach advised info 2 had just been posted so pilot attempted to listen to 2. info 1 was still on the air so pilot had to ask approach to read the new atis. hya atis has been almost unreadable for weeks now and has bleed-over from previous broadcasts.cause: atis broadcast from hya poor quality and almost unreadable. it is so hard to understand that it takes excessive time and effort by the pilots to copy it. often approach has to read it to the pilot. this degrades safety in a single pilot instrument flight rules environment where the pilot attempts to copy the atis info while listening to two radios at the same time. atis broadcast is too long with too many notams.suggestions: install new atis system at hya to provide clear broadcast and only pertinent notams.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a loss of pressurization during cruise. Flight diverted and landed safely.
text: leveling off at 36000 feet, i made a pa to the passengers, and turned off the seatbelt sign. a few minutes later we heard the cabin altitude horn going off. we immediately donned our oxygen masked, accomplished the qrc procedures, and silenced the horn. the first officer called air traffic control, requested priority handling, and he began a descent to 10, 000 feet. the cabin was uncontrollable after accomplishing the qrc for rapid cabin depressurization, so i began the descent checklist. i advised the fa's and passengers to get on oxygen and to fasten their seatbelts. later i called the fa's to find out how everyone was doing and that we would be landing in redacted in 15 minutes. after speaking with the flight attendants, i made a pa to the passengers updating them on the situation. i let dispatch know through acars of our situation and that we would be diverting to redacted. the first officer as pilot flying did an excellent job coordinating with air traffic control and setting up for our approach to xxl in redacted. after landing, we stopped the plane, reassured the passengers that we were safe, and taxied to the gate.cause: we lost pressurization and i have no recommendations. our training prepared us for this day.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a terrain alert and high winds during approach. Flight crew missed the approach and returned for a safe landing.
text: during a visual approach to runway 30 into hts, strong winds made challenging to control de airspeed so rapid changes were made on the trust levers which made the glide slope slide down for a second and made the aircraft chased it. this change put the plane on a nose down attitude and due to the mountainous terrain activated the egpws terrain alert. we were aware and pull up a little more up. we decided to continue with the approach since we were aware of the terrain and have the runway insight and we were stable. once we were over the runway gusty winds and high power settings made the aircraft gain a lot of airspeed and made the approach unstable so we executed a go around. once on the climb we stayed on the traffic pattern and attempted a second try which resulted on a safe landing with no issues.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: C152 pilot reported high winds causing the aircraft to drift off the runway when lining up for takeoff; and tire became stuck off the runway surface. The pilot coordinated with ATC; shut the aircraft down; pushed the aircraft back onto the runway; and took off without issue.
text: at redacted, i was attempting to taxi to runway xx at redacted for a cross country flight when winds caused the plane to drift off the runway to the left when perpendicular to the runway prior to lining up with the centerlines. of note, the flight had been delayed one hour due to gusting winds. winds had reduced prior to taxi and were predicting to continue to decrease according to regulated weather sources. the rate of drift was slow, but rudder control was reduced, leading the tires of the plane to be slightly to the left off of the runway when control was re-established. due to the position, the tire was stuck and the plane was unable to move forward to be re-established on the runway. the pilot communicated the issue to air traffic control, who directed upcoming landing traffic to go around. due to the plane's inability to move backways (due to the manufacturing limits of the plane), i communicated with air traffic control that i would need to physically push the plane backways. i then turned off the plane, pushed the plane backward and then in line with the runway. after starting up the plane, i regained contact with air traffic control and let them know that the plane was now in line for takeoff. i was able to takeoff without any issues with winds or gusts. the plane was landed without incident at redacted. there was no damage to person or aircraft during the incident. incident occurred due to wind gusts and the pilot underestimating the extent of the effects of the gusts when perpendicular to the runway prior to lining up on centerline. corrective action includes further training on effects of wind, especially in cessna 152. in addition, although the flight was delayed due to the wind, further delay or cancellation would have avoided the incident completely.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a heading deviation from the published departure procedure; due to a communication problem that resulted in an ATC low altitude warning. The pilot resolved the communication issue; received vectors; and continued the flight.
text: i was departing bur from runway 15 on an instrument flight rules flight plan. as i lifted off, my passenger in the front seat, who is also the owner, switched the radio from tower to departure just as i was asking tower if they were going to call my right turn because they have done this in the past. i then realized that my passenger had switched the radio to departure on me. i then switched back to tower, but i was just starting my right hand turn to head to twine intersection. tower then said to switch to departure and i did. he then called out a low altitude but i told him that i was headed back on course and i was already past 3000 ft in altitude. he then gave me vectors to join the sid and i did. i explained that i had a radio issue but that i was able to join the sid. he continued to give me vectors and then he said cleared direct sli, which i did. my destination was redacted and i cancelled instrument flight rules 13 miles from city x. once on the ground, i called air traffic control. i explained the above to him, but i forgot to mention that i also had traffic in the area that i was support to turn towards on the sid. i did not want to turn into that traffic that was on my mfd (multi-function flight display) screen. this could have been avoided if my radios had not been messed with on take off.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: General aviation instructor reported a near miss with another aircraft while performing training maneuvers with a student in a designated practice area.
text: date: day 0location: practice area east/northeast of redacted near the redacted fixaircraft: aircraft x, aircraft yother aircraft involved: rv-4 on day 0, during a training flight operating in the practice area northeast of redacted, a near midair collision occurred between our aircraft and an rv-4 near the redacted fix. the conflict developed as both aircraft converged while climbing and maneuvering in the same airspace. evasive action was required to avoid the other aircraft.during a training flight on day 0, i was instructing my student pilot departing from redacted. they are working on their private pilot airplane single engine land training in the cessna 172 skyhawk. they have nearly 100 hours and was doing one last flight to prepare for their end-of-course progress check. after departure, we transitioned northbound from redacted and proceeded into the local practice areas commonly referred to as city x and city y at 7, 500 msl. these practice boxes are below redacted class bravo.we remained in the practice area for a short while, conducting normal training maneuvers for a private pilot. after completing those maneuvers, we transitioned eastbound, positioning ourselves slightly south of redacted.while in this area, we conducted two ground reference maneuvers: turns around a point and s-turns across a road. these maneuvers were performed at approximately 1, 000 feet above ground level. which, for this given area, was roughly 5, 900 msl. we were making routine traffic calls on the north practice area frequency of redacted.redacted throughout the entire flight. we made sure to comply with 91.119 and maintain an altitude allowing for an emergency landing without power, without undue hazards to person or property on the surface. this is a sparsely populated area consisting mostly farmlands underneath the redacted class bravo.upon completion of the ground reference maneuvers, we began a climb to 6, 500 feet msl while turning westbound to return to redacted. this put us roughly 1, 500 ft agl.while en route westbound at approximately 6, 500 feet msl, shortly after, i observed a traffic advisory on the aircraft's mfd (multi-function flight display) indicating traffic off our right side. the traffic was identified on ads-b, an rv-4, and was initially displayed approximately 500 feet below our altitude.because i did not yet have visual contact with the aircraft, i instructed my student to initiate a climb to 7, 000 feet msl in order to increase vertical separation. the student began the climb, and the aircraft reached approximately 6, 770 feet msl when i observed the aircraft passing below. i pointed out the traffic to my student and notified them that it should soon be passing under the nose and appearing on their side (left) of the aircraft. we continued climbing to increase separation. i monitored the traffic information on the mfd and observed the altitude separation decreasing rapidly. the traffic indication changed from 500 feet below to 400 feet below, then 200 feet below, and eventually indicated the same altitude and the same position.at that point, it became clear the other aircraft was climbing directly toward our altitude. i immediately took control of the aircraft and initiated a right-hand evasive turn to the north.as i initiated the right turn, the rv-4 also began a right-hand turn toward the north, indicating the same altitude the whole time, further reducing the lateral separation between the aircraft.based on the maneuvering and flight profile, it appeared the rv-4 was performing aerobatic maneuvering in the area and was likely unaware that we were operating nearby.i personally did not obtain visual contact with the rv-4 during the conflict. however, my student, who was seated in the left seat, did acquire visual contact and estimated the aircraft passed approximately '3-5 feet off our wing'. they told me, 'they are right next to us and turning into us'. i then steepened the bank to roughly 50 degrees and pushed the nose forward to accelerate us to 129 kias.we lost roughly 1, 000 ft attempting to break away from this aircraft and were still indicating the same altitude throughout the evasive action. this lasted almost a minute.following the evasive maneuver, we successfully separated from the traffic. we then continued east briefly before turning northbound to reestablish our route back toward redacted while maintaining separation from the other aircraft. we then went north of the class bravo and climbed up to 8, 000 msl. the aircraft continued to the south. we attempted to contact the aircraft on both practice area frequencies of redacted.redacted and redacted.y. we received no communication back from the traffic. no further traffic conflicts occurred during the remainder of the flight.this event is concerning because the practice areas northeast of redacted are routinely used by student pilots from multiple training organizations. many students conduct solo operations in these areas and routinely transition through the same airspace.the behavior and maneuvering of the rv-4 suggested the pilot was likely conducting aerobatic maneuvers and may not have been aware of other aircraft operating nearby. the lack of apparent situational awareness by the rv-4 created a hazardous situation in an area that regularly contains high volumes of training traffic.given the frequency of student pilot operations in this region, this type of maneuvering presents a significant risk for future conflicts. given the maneuverability of the rv-4 and the spontaneous maneuvering, it was extremely difficult to decipher which direction/altitude would clear us of traffic. no contact was made with the aircraft.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Small transport aircraft pilot reported a resolution advisory during descent. Flight crew complied with advisory and landed safely.
text: 10 to 15 miles ne of danville (dan), air traffic control was hesitant to lower us below 12, 000 feet because another aircraft (aircraft y) did not close out the flight plan and air traffic control needed to figure that out first. eventually, they descended us to 6000 feet but kept us there because of traffic below at 4000 feet. the captain was very concerned about making the runway so he prioritized making the descent and canceled instrument flight rules with air traffic control to enable us to go lower - the field was in sight (cavu day). the captain instructed me as the first officer, and as the pilot flying, to descend at a high rate and he recommended 4000 ft./min. i asked about the traffic and he said 'it's ok, start the descent'. thinking he was clear on where the traffic was i complied, especially as the captain was reaching for the vs knob to scroll it down (though i was the one to command the v/s knob). i started the decent while looking to gain perspective on where the traffic was. i looked down at the mfd (multi-function flight display) and as i did that, we received an resolution advisory which required us to pull up. we complied with the resolution advisory and added power. the next resolution advisory was to level. we complied at 4000 ft, and the traffic was clear after that. at our closest point, (to my recollection), we were 400 ft from the traffic. from there, we descended in plenty of time to make a normal approach into danville with a safe landing.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported taking off with aircraft on short final which executed a missed approach. Pilot continued the take-off.
text: i was getting a flight review from a cfi since i was out of currency at erie airport, erie, co. runway 16 was the active runway. the pattern was full, and an incoming plane announced they were on a straight-in for runway 16. the last transmission from the plane i heard was 3 miles out. the plane in front of us took off on runway 16. after the plane in front of us took off, i saw the plane on approach and judged i had enough time to take off and clear the runway before they arrived for landing. i announced i was taking off on runway 16 and entered the runway. the straight-in traffic announced on the ctaf that they were on short final and a plane had entered the runway. i continued my takeoff roll, believing we would be clear of the runway in time for the landing aircraft. the landing aircraft announced they were going around and side-stepping to the left. we briefed this incident on the ground and agreed the better course of action would be to announce your intention to take off and give enough time for someone you may not see to respond before crossing the hold short lines. the next best course of action would have been to stop or clear the runway as soon as possible without taking off.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: PA28 pilot reported ATC failure to provide separation resulted in a NMAC event.
text: on a visual flight rules flight returning from near redacted (flight originated from redacted, overflew redacted then returned to redacted). using visual flight rules flight following in contact with redacted approach. approximately 20nm north north west of redacted at 5, 225 msl i noted traffic enter the 4nm ring in the app on my ipad +300 ft above and slightly ahead on my right on a course crossing mine at approx 90 degrees from mine. i asked my passenger if he heard a traffic alert from air traffic control that i missed but he had not. i looked for the traffic but could not see it. i noted that the traffic was descending to within 200 ft above and now approx 3mn and still slightly ahead intersecting my course. i called air traffic control and notified them that i was descending to avoid traffic. i did not hear a reply. i could not yet see the traffic. when i did see the traffic it was approx 200 ft above nearly even with my right wingtip and approx 250 feet away. i continued my decent and the traffic passed barely above and slightly behind me. i noted that the traffic continued descending toward redacted. ads-b showed the traffic id as aircraft y. at that time i recalled that a couple minutes before this incident i heard a pilot discuss an instrument approach to redacted and connected that this might be the same plane. moments later air traffic control asked me if i had redacted atis information. i told him that i did not. i tuned redacted atis for their information then informed air traffic control that i had redacted information 1. air traffic control then instructed me to squack visual flight rules and contact redacted tower. i waited a couple of minutes to all as i was still 19 miles from redacted and well away from their airspace recalling that in the past redacted tower has requested that i contact them again when i was closer. the rest of the flight to redacted was without incident.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: who, what, where, when, why?on day 0, at approximately xa:40 local time, i operated a small uas (under 250g) at a park in layton, ut. the location is within a 0ft laanc grid for hill afb. my intent was a short local flight in a public park. at the time, i was unaware the park was in a 0ft laanc grid for hill afb.i flew for approximately 3 minutes and at maximum altitude of 45 feet agl. i landed the drone and powered it down completely. shortly after i had finished the flight and the drone was secured, i observed a military aircraft taking off from hill afb. i immediately realized the proximity of my flight to active military operations and the potential safety risk i had inadvertently created. at no point was the drone in the air while manned military aircraft were operating.contributing factors:i am a new hobbyist and misunderstood that even micro-drones require laanc in a 0ft grid. i incorrectly assumed that recreational flight in a city park was permitted without checking the specific uas facility map (uasfm) for that gps location.corrective action:immediately following the event, i researched faa regulations and successfully completed the trust completion certificate (the recreational uas safety test) to ensure full compliance with hobbyist rules. i have downloaded a laanc-integrated app (b4ufly) and will ensure all future flights are conducted in permitted airspace with proper authorization.i am filing this report to document the incident and demonstrate my commitment to following all faa safety guidelines and respecting national defense airspace in the future.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B777 flight crew reported unforecasted turbulence resulted in an aircraft overspeed; altitude excursion; and momentary lose of control
text: we were level at fl390 ride mostly smooth with occasional light chop and with light mountain wave. we had the airspeed window open at mach .82. (+airspeed +/-10knots.) suddenly at the above location experienced moderate mountain wave with airspeed gain of 30 kts. and altitude gain of 400 feet. the flying pilot extended the speed brakes and slowed the aircraft the initiated a descent to fl390. flight conditions remained smooth throughout and all indications of mountain wave disappeared. there was no forecasts or reports of moderate mountain wave. wsi (weather app) showed light with occasional moderate turbulence along our route. another weather app showed only light turbulence.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: B777 First Officer reported lav smoke detector repeatedly activating during cruise. Flight returned to the departure airport.
text: i was serving as the relief pilot on flight # from redacted to redacted. while on crew rest in the bunk, i heard a pa announcement from the captain advising that we would be returning to redacted to have the aircraft checked due to a maintenance issue.i returned to the flight deck and was briefed that the aft lavatory smoke detector had been repeatedly activating. the flight crew discussed the situation with dispatch, maintenance control, and flight attendants. based on those discussions and in the interest of safety of flight, the decision was made to divert back to redacted.fuel jettison was conducted in order to arrive below maximum landing weight. the aircraft returned to redacted and landed without further issue.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: B737 Captain reported they had to unexpectedly swerve to avoid collision with a vehicle while taxiing on the ramp.
text: was taxiing out on the '1' line when a van darted towards us, swerved a bit at the last minute and sped towards the terminal. i had to come to an abrupt stop to avoid colliding with him, no fa injuries.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported being low on the approach. Flight crew momentarily leveled off and continued to an uneventful landing.
text: was assigned tiptoe 28l, with initial clearance for course only at 6, 000ft. was cleared to 3, 000ft where level change was selected by pf. after visual contact with field, was cleared for the visual tiptoe 28l approach. was past iaf eddyy, where pf instructed pm to set touch down elevation (100ft). plane was configured for landing appropriately and continued to descend, where around 1, 000ft, pm recognized below vertical path and lack of engagement of vnav when we cleared the visual approach. due to error, level change was still engaged below 1, 000ft. pf disconnected ap (autopilot), and corrected/regained flight path. approach was continued to uneventful landing. debriefed. determined both pm/pf could have used better monitor/crosscheck and automation management when cleared for the approach to prevent error.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Jet Blast
synopsis: A EMB-505 Captain reported that the rudder was malfunctioning during a preflight test on an aircraft that had experienced jet blast on the ramp the day before.
text: aircraft x was jet blasted by a challenger 350 yesterday in redacted at the fbo. that crew in aircraft x was about to start engines and experienced first hand the violent jet blast. they wrote up the aircraft for an inspection and it was inspected and signed off later yesterday afternoon. this morning given the history of the aircraft we felt it prudent to do a flight control check with each of us outside to observe the control surfaces. this is when we discovered the rudder making a loud distinctive clunking/binding noise with a lack of smooth travel moving in the pedals themselves. another aircraft was parked next to us (another phenom) we had that crew do a full rudder deflection. we noted no noise coming from this aircraft and the difference was night and day compared to aircraft x. i do not believe the engines were inspected either for fod ingestion.

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported a fuel leak during boarding process. Captain refused the aircraft.
text: on day 2 at approximately xa:00 prior to aircraft door closure i was informed by the ground crew that they had observed an uncontrolled fuel leak coming from the right main wing tank on the outer edge of the tank towards the winglet.immediately i grabbed my safety vest and air protection, exited the flight deck, and went out to the ramp to confirm that yes indeed there is a pencil width sized leak coming from the vent hole on the fuel tank. this leak was uncontrolled, could not be stopped, and required immediate attention. i returned to the flight deck and made a pa and told the passengers the situation and mentioned that because it was a fuel spill that had not been contained yet it was advantageous for everyone to grab their belongings and exit the aircraft as soon as possible. i then called my dispatcher and told them exactly what i had done and the event that had occurred outside. he was in agreement, deplaning the aircraft was a good idea. in the meantime, the redacted ground crew flawlessly contain the spill so that there is minimal impact to ramp safety.i got off the phone with the dispatcher so that i can make the appropriate entries into the aircraft electronic logbook. my first entry into the logbook, stated that there was a new leak coming from the main wing tank. this issue had previously been written up and addressed on day 0.after making the logbook entry, i called back dispatch and asked to be connected with the maintenance desk. the tone of the maintenance technician on the phone sounded frustrated, but eager to help. they simply said without any investigation or asking me any questions that i had just been over fueled and the situation was normal. the situation was not normal. we were already at our recommended fuel release load. between us inspecting the leak and approximately 10 minutes later we had lost almost 200 pounds of gas due to a leak. when i advised the technician of this they did not change their judgment. they simply said yes that happened because you were over fueled, even though we are at the correct fuel load given our flight conditions as a matter of fact, we took off out of redacted with a higher fuel load on the previous flight and never encountered a leak.once i was finally able to make my point across the technician on the other end of the phone, they decided it would be worth calling contract maintenance to come out and look at the aircraft.roughly about an hour later maintenance arrived to the aircraft and began inspecting the wing for leaks . maintenance personnel asked me to fully extend the flaps and slats so that they can fully inspect the wing to find other leaks. the contract maintenance technician then asked me to move fuel from the fuel control panel inside the aircraft to different tanks. i told him i was not comfortable doing that because it violated our sop's. and i was not fully taught how to do this. less than one month prior to this incident i remember an email being sent to all pilots asking us not to perform maintenance functions on the aircraft.the contract maintenance person was frustrated with me after i politely told him that i would not be able to comply with that request. i offered him my seat so that he could do it himself. the contract maintenance personnel moved roughly 1000 pounds from the right main wing tank to the left main wing tank and told me that the leak has stopped and that we were good to go. he became very frustrated with me when i told him that that doesn't comply with company sops. and that we are not allowed to take off with a 1000 pound and balance between the wings. i also informed him that both main tanks had to be full of fuel before the center tank could be filled. the leak simply stopped because we moved gas away from the hole not that we did not actually solve the problem or find the source of the leak.after this diagnosis and attempt to fix the problem, i refused the aircraft and made a corresponding info item notation in theelectronic logic book. i had lost faith that this problem was gonna be solved to a satisfactory and safe nature and i elected that it would be best to remove myself from the situation. and not fly an unsafe aircraft.i then received a call from the chief pilot. the chief pilot did not give me their name and immediately became a line of questioning that seem to escalate and tone and speed, spinning a tighter and tighter web trying to find a fault in my story and trying to find a weakness in the narrative that i had told them. the told me not worry, the aircraft was actually fine and i was being overly cautious. i was told we had just been over fueled and it happens sometimes. for the record, i have almost 6, 000 hours in this aircraft and that has never happened. i also informed them that we were at the correct few release number. this fuel release number is also not very large and it's very normal for this route and altitude.their line of questioning seemed to invalidate my concerns for safety. had i not been so confident in my judgment and prior experience, i could've easily been manipulated into making an unsafe decision that merely would've only benefited the company by moving an aircraft. this line and reasoning for questioning is very concerning to me. it seems unsafe, unprofessional, and against the norms that i had become to expect from company.thankfully, the first officer had taken a video of us finding the leak. i sent the video to a number that texted me saying that they were with the management team and they needed to talk to me immediately. i wanted to also let it be known that every contact attempt by the company did not include the dispatcher. i found that very concerning because any communication with the dispatcher is on a recorded line.i talked to a new maintenance control supervisor named person a. he told me that the contract maintenance personnel also found a fuel leak coming from the fuel service panel on the right wing. person a then asked me to perform more function checks on the aircraft. i told him i did not feel comfortable doing that. although person a seem frustrated, he did not seem frustrated with me. merely just at the situation. i fully understand the inconvenience and impact this maintenance issue caused, but unfortunately the facts are undeniable. taking an aircraft off the ground full of people that is leaking fuel is unsafe.a new contract maintenance personnel member came out to the aircraft approximately 2 1/2 hours after our initial report of the fuel leak at this point the leak had stopped, but we had lost approximately 400 pounds of fuel. the maintenance technician went to the flight deck, asked to sit in my seat and begin working with the fuel panel. the technician moved fuel from both wing tanks into the center tank and claimed that he had fixed the leak and that everything was good to go. i asked him how he fixed the leak and he said he had moved fuel from the wing tank to the center tank and you should be fine while both tanks were balanced. the center tank was grossly overloaded. this goes against company standard operating procedure of fueling the wing tanks first then fueling the center. i asked if the hole and leak had been located and fixed he said no.despite and obviously known outcome, i remained on duty to ensure that the maintenance situation was dealt with accordingly, i was fearful that another pilot would be given this aircraft with it fully not fixed and have an issue. at approximately xe:45 the dispatcher working my flight had called me and said 'hey, i am at shift change. i just wanted to call and see why things were and how things were going.'i informed him that nothing really changed. there is still a leak. there is fuel moved away from it, which is simply why it stopped leaking. i still don't fully understand how this is deemed a reliable and practical fix. i then told him for a third time i am still refusing the aircraft. i will not go into crew rest only to come back out to the airport and fly the same aircraft home if nothing had been fixed. i noted that i had said this for three times, and put it according info item in the electronic logbook hours ago. it was at that point we were finally released from duty given a min rest overnight and a new aircraft to fly home the following morning. cause: safety can at times be inconvenient, however should not cut corners to find a substandard resolution.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B747-400 flight crew reported non compliant push crew commands resulting in uncommanded movement striking tow bar. Aircraft returned to gate.
text: during the pushback sequence from gate xx, engines 4 and 3 were started in accordance with approved company procedures. ground handling personnel failed to adhere to standard operating procedures in several critical respects:-they did not issue any verbal instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake prior to initiating disconnection of the tow bar and tug.-without prior authorization from the pilot in command (pilot in command), and while engines 1 and 2 had not yet been started, they proceeded with disconnection of the towing equipment.with the parking brake unset and the nose wheel steering bypass pin installed (disabling hydraulic steering), as engines 4 and 3 stabilized at idle thrust, the aircraft began to move forward and yaw uncontrollably to the left.ground personnel immediately shouted instructions to 'release the parking brake, ' to which the pilot in command promptly responded, 'parking brake is released.' shortly thereafter, ground personnel urgently directed the crew to 'set parking brake.' the pilot in command applied the brakes without hesitation upon observing the aircraft's forward and leftward movement.despite the immediate brake application, the aircraft's residual momentum caused the nose landing gear to strike the tow bar, resulting in damage to the scissor link (torque link).immediately following the incident, the flight crew overheard, via the interphone, the headset operator (ground personnel) state: 'i [expletive] up.'upon return to the gate and subsequent opening of the aircraft door, the flight crew promptly disembarked to inspect the damage and assess the situation. the headset operator involved in the pushback was no longer present in the vicinity.the root cause of the incident was procedural non-compliance by ground handling personnel, specifically:failure to follow the standard pushback sequence, including the omission of any instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake.initiation of towing equipment disconnection without clearance from the pilot in command.premature disconnection attempt while two engines (1 and 2) remained unstarted.no injuries were reported.suggestions: reinforce ground personnel procedures and communications.

text: after departing redacted on the redacted departure, center gave us climb and maintain then climb to fl210. we had a busy depart due to heaving precip and lighting in the area that we were avoiding. at approving 15000-16000' we received the aural warning for cabin pressure and noticed the cabin pressure illuminating red indicating 10400' and holding maybe slowling increasing, we immediately requested a descent to 10000', center gave us and initial descent to 13000' then followed by 10000'. the pm went to the qrc followed by the qrh to lookup the procedure. as pf i noticed the #1 & #2 packs closed advisory message on the eicas, i looked to check if the buttons for the valves were in the closed position but they were in the open position. i asked the pm if he reset the #1 & #2 packs on the after takeoff flow since we did a to-1 takeoff due to weather, and said they couldn't remember. i further noticed that none of the after takeoff flow/checklist was completed. we reset the #1 & #2 packs valves and the aircraft pressurized as designed with no further issues. flight was continued as normal.

synopsis: Air taxi Captain reported initiating approach to wrong airport during landing. Crew executed missed approach and continued to destination.
text: flight was clear and visibility unrestricted. flight was made to ont west to east at 5000 msl. moderate to severe chop and turbulence persisted enroute. windshear was forecasted and reported in the area.approximately 10 minutes into the flight the copilot-pilot monitoring (pm) announced airport 12 oclock and we're too high. the pm called air traffic control for a 360 turn to lose altitude. atc gave us descend to 4000. we turned right to lose altitude and lined up on the airport poc which has two parallel runways similar to ont.i asked the (pm) how far is ont because the runways and my perception of the runways were not long enough and we arrived to soon. the (pm) stated this is the wrong airport. immediately at 1000 agl we executed a go around, began climbing and simultaneously-atc called us, announcing a low altitude warning which the atc's aural warning could be heard in the transmission. the pm announced to air traffic control we had lined up on the wrong airport. no landing at poc was executed. we continued climbing to 4000 msl and proceeded direct to ont without incident or further comment from atc.pilot in command relied on the pm statements and this action caused an inaccurate decision identifying the wrong airport.corrective action would be to have distance of destination airport prominently displayed for situational awareness. double check the pm by the pilot in command.turbulence and forecasted windshear affected flight comfort.at the end of the previous day of flying certainly had affected the pilot in command. the actions of an irate and verbal abusive passenger was experienced by the pilot in command due to a customer service issue. perceived violent and intimidating body language was displayed by that passenger towards the pilot in command. many appologies were given and all were not accepted by the passenger along with snide remarks directed to the pilot in command.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Decathlon pilot reported a NMAC with a helicopter while in the pattern. Pilot took evasive action.
text: immediately after executing a base leg turn from downwind for runway xx, inside long downwind base traffic, at approximately 400-500ft agl, i observed helicopter final traffic to my immediate right, west of the field at approximately 300ft agl. last i saw this traffic i was ahead of them and from my sight view there would be no traffic conflict caused by my early base turn to final. i did not hear the helicopter traffic's base and final radio calls for the midfield grass area for landing, due to my passenger stepping on the radio call over intercommunications systems (ics).my early turn to base/final, coupled with the missed radio calls created the potential for a midair collision between my aircraft and the helicopter final traffic. early turns to final with potential conflicting traffic should be avoided at all times if traffic is not seen. additionally, no turn to base should be initiated until final traffic is clear. it is better to avoid the early turn to final and extend the downwind than risk a potential for midair collision.enhance lookout doctrine for traffic closer into to the field, especially helicopter traffic routinely operating at the field, not just the traffic you are attempting to turn inside of. additionally, avoid turns inside of other traffic, even if sufficient space is available.brief the importance of a sterile cockpit for ics communications with passengers to avoid blocked radio calls from other traffic, emergency calls only.even though in the landing phase minimize overflight of airport hangars and buildings. to minimize risk for other personnel and equipment in the event of unexpected aircraft emergencies.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported descending to an unsafe altitude while doing a simulated engine failure during training.
text: during a private pilot training flight i guided the student over the petaluma airport. i was monitoring the ctaf and verified there was no traffic in the area. i gave the student an engine failure and the student determined the petaluma airport would be a good place to land. we entered a downwind for runway 29 and i made the appropriate radio call on the ctaf. i verified visually that there was no traffic in the area. the student was on a high and close downwind and turned base at 1300 feet msl. the student determined that we were too high on the approach and we wouldn't make the field. i scanned the area to confirm no traffic was present and i took the flight controls. the altitude was 1100 feet. i started a right 360 turn to lose altitude. i verified we were not over any houses or people before performing the turn. while in the turn we lost more altitude then expected and exited on final around 500 feet. in the debrief i discussed that this maneuver was a nonstandard maneuver and shouldn't have been done unless we had actually had an engine failure. this maneuver could have been dangerous given how low we were. in the future i will advise students that the 360 could be an option but i won't demonstrate it at those altitudes. i got too low because i started the 360 from too low of an altitude initially. this discussion was caused by my fixation on demonstrating the importance of flying the aircraft, setting up for a good approach, and hitting your desired touchdown area under positive control during an emergency scenario. i also felt that the student had resignation over being high and i wanted to prove that there were still things we could do to get a positive outcome.

synopsis: Small aircraft flight instructor reported an NMAC in the pattern during landing phase. Pilot took evasive action.
text: avl approach asked us to make a left base turn and handed us to tower. tower informed us we were number 3 to land. we informed them we did not see other traffic. tower then asked aircraft y to make a right base turn. we informed tower we still did not see the traffic. as we neared the position to make our turn into final, i asked tower if we could turn final and if we were still cleared to land as we did not see the other inbound traffic. they said yes. following this they asked the other aircraft (supposedly #2) to abort landing clearance and make and immediate left turn to 090. at this moment, that aircraft y came into view as it flew out from right under us, approximately 300 feet below. it's concerning that two planes were turned on base from opposite directions at the same time and that we did not have adequate spacing here. i believe the handoff from approach to tower created the problem and that tower confused some of the planes since it was a busy afternoon with 4 aircraft in the pattern. in the future, pilots should not accept the base turn until the other traffic is in sight.
