synopsis: Cessna Caravan pilot reported an engine surge during climb. Pilot returned to departure airport.
text: proceeded to taxi to runway-xx for takeoff. did the normal set for takeoff power (1700 of ft/lbs approximately). noticed that at the full travel of the power lever it barely reach the 1700 ft/lbs like we normally do. proceeded to cancel the takeoff and exited the runway and went to taxiway 1 to troubleshoot. did another run-up there and at full power lever travel this time the engine gave about 1800 of ft/lbs which seems normal to me the only thing i notice out of the ordinary was a slight higher temperature in the oil temp but still inside the green arc range.proceeded back for takeoff after the run-up. on the upwind leg of the takeoff i started to hear a slight surge on the turbine, looked at the torque gauge and i can see minimal fluctuation of the torque values, and also notice a high oil temp on top of the green arc oscillating between the top of the green arc and the red limit. that was when i decided to turn back to the airport (informed air traffic control about the situation) approximately 1 minute after that i felt a big engine surge on the turbine and i could notice that the torque was decreasing towards the 1000 ft/lbs mark, i immediately started my turn back towards the first available runway (runway xy in this case) and proceeded to request priority handling and landed without any incident on runway xy at redacted.

synopsis: Citationjet C525 Captain reported an uncommanded autopilot deviation during cruise. Flight crew re-engaged the autopilot and continued.
text: while in cruise at fl430, approximately 30 nm north of redacted, the aircraft experienced an uncommanded autopilot deviation.the autopilot initiated a 20-30° descending right turn without pilot input. during recovery, we lost approximately 1, 000 feet of altitude.i disconnected the autopilot and recovered manually. we advised air traffic control immediately of the deviation and the flight continued.during the event, the flight director indications did not correspond with the flight management system or the flight mode annunciator annunciations. after the event, the flight director indications returned to normal.when the autopilot disconnected, there was no audible 'autopilot' disconnect aural warning, although the physical snap of the autopilot switch moving to the off position was heard. the trim switch was used to disconnect, not the red autopilot disconnect button.the autopilot was subsequently re-engaged and functioned normally for the remainder of the flight, with no recurrence of the issue.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a NMAC in practice area and took evasive action. Instruction flight continued.
text: during a part 91 training flight, a nmac occurred during maneuver training. prior to the flight maneuver, a clearing turn along with visual scanning of the flight path was performed. a radio call including approximate position, altitude, direction of flight, and type of maneuver to be performed was made approximately 50-60 seconds before occurrence. the student was in control of the airplane at the time, and was attempting to perform a power off stall. as the stall was about to become fully developed, a traffic conflict with another ga airplane heading southeast was detected. i immediately assumed control of the aircraft and began the stall recovery procedure. the conflicting aircraft passed underneath, and the conflict was over at that point. i did not observe evasive action or alteration of flight path or altitude from the other aircraft. i find contributing human factors to be inadequate scan of the maneuver area, failure of other aircraft to announce position and intentions on relevant ctaf, distraction during observation of the learner pilot performing the maneuver leading to decayed traffic scan. it is worth mentioning that i did not have access to an ads-b in receiver, which i believe would have provided an early warning of traffic conflict, which would have prevented the nmac. even though i have significant experience flying in the highly congested long beach practice area, in the future i will ensure to exercise increased vigilance in ensuring all areas around are thoroughly clear of conflicts prior to initiating a flight maneuver.

text: after a normal landing on runway xx we turned off on taxiway 1 and were given taxi instruction by tower back to the ramp. when bringing the power to idle before completing the after engine checklist, the engine sputtered and shut down. there were no indications or engine malfunction in flight and the carburetor heat was on for the entire approach, landing, and rollout. multiple unsuccessful attempts were made to restart the engine and the aircraft was towed back to the ramp. a post-flight inspection revealed no obvious fluid leaks or damage. on the post-flight inspection, it was determined that there were 18 gallons of fuel on board. the aircraft was grounded and referred to maintenance for further inspection.

synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a low altitude alert from ATC as a result of a traffic conflict. Pilot took evasive action and continued flight.
text: i was cleared for the visual flight rules-to-instrument flight rules transition departing sql runway 30. clearance was to turn right within 2nm of the airport to heading 120, intercept the oak radial, and climb to 2, 100 feet. after departure, while below 1, 100 feet msl and still operating visual flight rules, i visually identified aircraft y directly above my aircraft. air traffic control had also issued a traffic advisory to aircraft y calling traffic at their 6 o'clock low, aircraft x overtaking, confirming awareness of the proximity of both aircraft. climbing as cleared would have created an immediate collision hazard. i exercised my authority as pilot in command under 14 cfr 91.3 to maintain 1, 000 feet msl to ensure safe separation. i reported to air traffic control that i had traffic directly above me and requested an amended heading. air traffic control responded that my altitude was unacceptable and instructed me to climb immediately. i began climbing. air traffic control then issued a low altitude alert and instructed me to turn right to heading 300 immediately. shortly after, air traffic control questioned why i was turning despite having just issued the heading change. i again reported i was avoiding traffic. the primary contributing factor was conflicting visual flight rules traffic in the climb corridor during the visual flight rules-to-instrument flight rules transition, combined with contradictory air traffic control instructions during the traffic avoidance. improved traffic sequencing and coordination during visual flight rules-to-instrument flight rules transitions at sql could help prevent recurrence.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A320 Captain reported high velocity and gusty crosswind conditions during landing phase. Crew diverted to alternate and landed.
text: the flight diverted to redacted due to increasing crosswind gusts at the destination and a developing fuel margin concern.during preflight planning, a threat-forward approach was used. the first officer, dispatcher, and i evaluated the original flight plan, which had us landing near maximum gross weight with no alternate listed. additionally, forecast gusts at the destination were near the aircraft's flight manual maximum crosswind limits. given these conditions, we coordinated with dispatch to revise the plan to include a suitable alternate with improved margins. a thorough fuel and performance discussion was conducted during the approach briefing, including crosswind limits, landing performance with gust factors, and contingency planning should a go-around become necessary.the approach was conducted in high velocity, gusty crosswind conditions. the approach was primarily in imc. appropriate precautions were taken to balance gust additives with stopping distance considerations. the approach was turbulent, careful automation management was utilized to maximize pilot situational awareness. below approximately 500 feet agl, high crosswind gusts appeared to increase significantly and momentarily, requiring large control inputs, to maintain the desired flight path while remaining within stabilized approach criteria. during the flare, at approximately 20-10 feet agl, with thrust just brought to idle, the aircraft encountered a strong sustained lateral gust that required substantial control inputs to maintain runway centerline. simultaneously, the gust produced a noticeable performance increase, resulting in altitude gain of 20-30 feet. based on recent performance training and anticipating the potential for an equally rapid loss of performance as the gust potentially subsided, along with the risk of airspeed decreasing below lowest selectable speed, i immediately initiated a go-around. the gust began to subside and the aircraft did appear to momentarily descend.during the maneuver, careful attention was paid to pitch attitude to mitigate tail strike risk. flap retraction and pitch changes were managed deliberately, ensuring a positive rate of climb prior to significant changes.given that a possible go-around scenario had been thoroughly briefed in the context of our general fuel state, the wind conditions, and considering the largely imc conditions associated with lower ceilings on the approach end of the field, the crew recognized that a second attempt (if unsuccessful) would introduce downstream fuel concerns. after coordinating and assessing the situation, we elected to divert to redacted.the diversion was conducted in a smooth and controlled manner. the fom diversion guide was utilized. dispatch was notified. the crew was very efficient, having thoroughly discussed and prepared for this possibility during the threat forward departure and approach briefing. threat forward briefings, and recent performance training were pillars in insuring a safe outcome. the diversion recovery guide was utilized upon landing. we departed redacted with additional fuel, and landed in redacted uneventfully.

text: the crew of aircraft x flight to mtj descended from their cleared altitude after being cleared to fly the mtj instrument landing system 17 approach from gejyu but before being established at gejyu.this was the crew's first flight of the day, both pilots were well rested, and the approach was briefed, loaded, and checked in the flight computer. the ca was flying and the first officer was monitoring. conditions were vmc and the flight was under instrument flight rules control by denver center. the crew had been working well together over the previous days and continued to after this event.on extended vectors after the previous aircraft had not canceled their clearance upon landing, aircraft x was level at 14, 000 feet to the north west of gejyu flying direct to gejyu when cleared the approach instrument landing system 17. not expecting to be vectored as far north as they were, the crew had loaded the approach starting at meyrs which included a crossing restriction at gejyu of +12, 300. about 6nm prior to reaching gejyu the crew initiated a descent to cross gejyu at 12, 300 in approach mode with 8100 selected in the altitude window. about 3nm prior to gejyu center asked if the crew was established on the approach. the ca matched the aircraft's course to the course on the approach plate and believed the aircraft to be within the rnp 1 bounds of the dirdy to geyju leg and its lower +11, 000 restriction. the ca replied in the affirmative and confirmed that terrain was in sight, which the first officer relayed to center. center then directed the crew to maintain 14, 000 until reaching gejyu. the crew immediately commanded a level-off passing 12, 800 and was level at 12, 500. the ca momentarily selected a positive vsi to initiate a climb before canceling it as the plane neared gejyu where a further descent would be required to fly the approach. the approach and landing was conducted without event after gejyu.after parking the aircraft the crew discussed the event and concluded that, even if the aircraft was on the dirdy-gejyu leg, the approach clearance began at gejyu and so they should not have descended until crossing gejyu (as required by far 121.659(a) and fom. moreover, even if they had been cleared the approach from dirdy, the flight computer was not loaded with dirdy as the feeder fix so determining when established on the rnav portion of the approach would be, at best, difficult and counter to the fom which directs that rnav procedures be selectable in the fmc and flown using autopilot or flight director guidance. in heat of the moment, while monitoring area traffic at a non-towered airport, with the field and terrain well in sight the crew inadvertently got head of themselves did not comply the instrument flight rules established approach requirements.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A300 flight crew reported multiple ECAM messages climbing through FL200 accompanied by a change of pressure in the cabin. Crew safely diverted to a nearby airport.
text: after climbing through fl200 we were checking our systems pages and noticed there were xx in place of the volts reading for both generators. with anti ice on we received a bleed air 1 fault. we were able to reset the fault. shortly after in cruise the yaw damp 2 paddle tripped off and we were unable to reset it. shortly after, the first officer noticed his flight director had failed as well as some data on the pfd and nd. we came to the conclusion that it could be an adc fault even though it was unannounced. he selected the fd and adc switches on the switching panel to recover data. having lost the adc, we found we were unable rvsm and began a descent to fl270. during descent we heard a boom and looked at each other thinking it could be a load shift, however, the lower forward cargo door light came on as well as the lower forward cargo door ecam message. we felt an irregular cabin pressure. we also received a pack 1 fault and bleed air fault with the cargo door ecam message. we donned our oxygen masks and requested priority handling and diverted to redacted where we landed uneventfully. we performed all required checklists and my decision was the cargo door was not safe. per the checklist one of two choices, abnormal cabin rate, with accompanying door light confirmed diverting was the safest option.

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Light jet pilot reported a low altitude warning from ATC during climb out of VNY; citing a conflict with a GA aircraft as contributing to their late call to ATC.
text: just after takeoff on canog3 departure, we complied with first level off of 1750ft. after that, due to traffic, we were late on climbing to initial altitude. when we switched from tower to departure, air traffic control mentioned we were low, due to terrain. the non flying pilot mentioned we were visual flight rules and had the terrain in sight. at the same time our attention was diverted on the climb due to ga traffic. we were asking for vectors to avoid traffic. we had the traffic in sight and were clear of the traffic. it was a little late, but we finally got a climb and a turn from air traffic control. noticed immediately upon switching from tower to socal.cause: late communication in a traffic saturated air space, on a short flight from vny to zzzidentified traffic visually, and remained clear, and complied with air traffic control vector and climbsuggestions: upon debriefing with other pilot, we recognized lack of communication between pilots and air traffic control. air traffic control was busy with ga traffic, and we were distracted by identifying traffic to remain clear of.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Small jet flight crew reported an EGPWS warning during a night visual approach. Crew corrected and continued approach.
text: arriving in darkness after tower closed into redacted we were cleared for the rnav visual xxr as we requested direct redacted. this to avoid the no transgression upwind runway xx/r area. 2 things happened that could have been done better. we approached a bit fast for being under the class b shelf of 5000 and this contributed to a steeper than normal descent rate to get down to at or above 4500 at redacted to establish on the glide path for the approach. not exactly sure what transpired with the mode control as i was more concerned with being outside the aircraft for terrain and traffic avoidance and my co-pilot was flying. additionally i was canceling with approach, getting a phone number to contact them for clearance/cancellation on the ground and preparing to switch to ctaf. my co-pilot was being proactive to get us down and capture the glide path and get us slowed down. at one point the descent angle and rate increased to a steeper than stabilized value which, to no surprise to both of us, activated the egpws (enhanced ground proximity warning system) sink rate, too low, pull up, to correct, which my co-pilot disconnected the autopilot. we were still on the downwind so we elected to continue the approach, which we completed without incident. however, with the appr armed vnav armed flight management system showing captured we could not get a capture of the glidepath until 700 or so agl. and we think this was also a contributing factor to why the plane did not arrest the rapid descent rate that set off the egpws previously. again flight management system was capture on the mode selector scoreboard, but perhaps we were not close enough to the course to capture the vertical guidance. either way, vmc prevailed and there was never the perception that there was a cfit risk. however we could have done better not to set off the egpws and that our speed may have been slightly above 200 under the class b at one point or another during the descent. and we were a bit confused as to why the plane did not capture the vertical guidance and why it steepened its descent rate right before the egpws warning.suggestions: we will endeavor to approach redacted from the south at a slower speed for the class b shelfs and to allow for more time to descend and capture. additionally, we tried to adhere to the attention all users guidance to avoid the xxr/l upwind. but i couldn't help thinking that it might have been better to track the course completely from redacted off the arrival and cut through this non transgression zone, especially since it was after tower was closed with little to no traffic. that way we could have been flying a prescribed course and altitude from the get go, giving us more time to concentrate on configuring etc. as it was my primary focus was cfit awareness given the fact that we were maneuvering visually to the direct redacted to avoid the no transgression zone. we were on frequency and the egpws occurred around xa:29. incidentally we offered to to preposition earlier than scheduled during daylight and prior to the 3 hour sit in redacted, but we were backing up trips on the coast and it was determined best to wait to ferry from redacted to avoid possible double ferry legs.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a ground conflict during taxi at CLT resulting in firm braking during taxi. Two flight attendants reported minor injuries.
text: taxiing on inner line to spot xx at clt west ramp our clearance was spot xx to join the line to 5w. approaching the spot i looked left and didn't see anything. we were slowing to make a right turn and the first officer said clear right. i looked left to say clear left and saw aircraft y approaching which appeared close and i applied brakes. firm at first then eased off. we sat at the spot for a minute and the aircraft y pilot asked ramp controller what going on. who was giving way and why weren't they notified. ramp controller said that she didn't think aircraft y was going to turn the corner that fast and it wasn't going to be an issue. well it was. the ramp controller told aircraft y to give way to us and we proceeded to take off. i didn't call the cabin to see if everyone was ok. i thought they would call us if something was wrong. we flew to redacted without incident and had normal communications with the cabin. after shut down and leaving the flight deck a couple of f/a's asked what happened taxiing in clt. when we got to the top of the bridge by the gate we told them what happened. the number 1 said she bumped her arm in the galley and the number 3 bumped her head. the number 2 said her back hit the galley wall. i asked why they didn't call us in clt. they were preparing for takeoff was the answer i got. i asked if anyone needed medical attention and was told not yet. i called dispatch per the fom for a follow up since everyone was able to preform their duties.cause: ramp control to give specific instructions as to who is following who. communication from the cabin telling us they were injured before we depart. not after completing the flight.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: A319-100 flight crew reported safely diverting to an alternate airport after experiencing yellow hydraulic system failure in cruise.
text: we experienced a total loss of the yellow hydraulic system and accomplished appropriate procedures. after coordinating with dispatch and maintenance we elected to divert to redacted for an overweight landing.cause: random mechanical failure

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A321 flight crew reported loss of both Integrated Drive Generators and APU requiring diversion to nearest suitable airport.
text: flight was dispatched with minimum equipment list 24-redacted (inoperative idg (integrated drive generator)) configuration requiring use of apu during flight as a secondary electrical power source. approx 120 west of redacted apu failed in flight. qrh requires land asap with one power source, several attempts to restart apu were unsuccessful. while discussing our diversion a acars was sent to our dispatcher to coordinate/discuss our intentions. after receiving an additional ecam (ecam idg 1 oil overheat) and noted idg#1 temperature increasing, idg#1 was disconnected per the second ecam and we requested priority handling with the decision that we would be diverting to redacted. during the descent dispatch acknowledged our status and suggested a diversion to redacted but in the interest of safety (after the overheat msg) we decided to not fly further than required. a normal precautionary landing was made with a taxi to the gate. first officer was the flying pilot and did an excellent job having the diversion airport/approach and a few air traffic control calls handled during time period i briefed the flight attendants and advised the passengers about our diversion, his efficiency was very much appreciated and he completely reduced my workload during a very short time frame from cruise at altitude to landing.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported activation of the stick shaker during approach. Crew lowered flaps and continued to a safe landing.
text: we were on a heading of 065 between two lines of weather to intercept the xxl localizer between redacted and redacted at 7-8, 000 feet with an assigned speed of 200 knots configured to flap 1. we were assigned 4, 000 feet with at least a 45 knot tailwind trending high. i advised the first officer to keep coming down due to the tailwind. he extended the speed brakes fully. air traffic control then assigned us 180 knots. i acknowledged the clearance then got distracted by something. the first officer slowed to 180 knots which was about 5 knots below flaps 1 maneuvering speed. we hit a gust and had a momentary stick shaker which i called out. i realized the situation and moved the flaps to 5. the rest of the flight was relatively uneventful. (llws advisories).

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: CRJ900 flight crew reported a cabin altitude warning during climb. Flight crew returned to the departure airport.
text: maintenance had signed off the aircraft for an intermittent pax (passenger) door indication which was written up by the previous crew. during the climb out we noticed our ears continuously popping and that the pressure didn't seem normal. ca asked me to reduce my rate of climb as we had been cleared to climb to 18, 000 ft. at 10, 000 we got the cabin alt caution message, this is when ca advise air traffic control we would need to level off. ca assumed pf duties and we advised air traffic control we would need to run our checklist which is when we entered the hold. after running the qrh for cabin alt we determined we would return to redacted. we staid in the hold while we re configured the aircraft for an approach into redacted. after getting our data and briefing the approach and fas we made our way back to the field. since we caught the pressurization issue early and did not continue climbing, we did not declare an emergency. our return to redacted was uneventful and maintenance met us at the gate. after correcting the issue and running a few verification test we were able to depart a few hours later.cause: the aircraft did not pressurize during the climb out.suggestion: maintenance could have verified the pressurization prior to signing off.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: PA-44-Flight Instructor reported abnormal engine indications during flight. Flight crew secured engine and returned to the departure airport.
text: a routine instructional flight was being conducted to practice airwork and maneuvers in a multi-engine training aircraft. while maneuvering in an area of moderate turbulence, we experienced erratic rpm indications on the left engine. the tachometer rapidly fluctuated, momentarily indicating approximately 4000 rpm (overspeed) before dropping to zero rpm and then returning to a normal reading. the indications continued to fluctuate unpredictably. simultaneously, the manifold pressure indication decreased to approximately 3 inches and fuel flow reduced significantly. at the time the anomaly first occurred, my student had the controls and the aircraft was in a bank while exiting moderate turbulence. due to the turbulence and aircraft attitude, it was initially difficult to determine whether the aircraft itself was responding abnormally. aurally, the engine did not sound significantly different from normal operation. i took control of the aircraft and began running the appropriate checklist procedures with the student. we verified each step and monitored engine indications. due to the continued erratic indications and the possibility of an engine malfunction, i made the decision to secure the left engine. after completing the engine shutdown procedure, i contacted redacted approach and advised them that we had secured the left engine and would be returning to redacted. an emergency was not declared. the aircraft was configured for single-engine operation and we conducted a precautionary return to the airport.the remainder of the flight was uneventful and we landed safely at redacted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL
synopsis: B73-700 Captain reported unreliable airspeed indications on climb. Flight crew returned to the departure airport and landed uneventfully.
text: during a flight from redacted to redacted, i was the pilot in command and pilot monitoring, with the first officer serving as pilot flying. after pushback we received an engine indication light and identified a soft mode failure of the eec (electronic engine control). dispatch and maintenance control were contacted, and the issue was coordinated via phone. a maintenance deferral was applied and a placard was placed in the cockpit per maintenance guidance. minimum required fuel was amended to account for the delay.during taxi we experienced a short takeoff delay due to traffic back-taxiing on the runway.after takeoff, at approximately 500 feet agl, the autothrottle disconnected and we experienced unreliable airspeed indications on the captain's side. we began troubleshooting while maintaining aircraft control. departure assigned 2, 000 feet initially, then 4, 000 feet, and provided extended vectors while we completed the qrh. we accomplished qrh (ias disagree), which led into qrh procedures.after completing the qrh and coordinating with dispatch via acars, we elected to return to redacted and i requested priority handling with air traffic control. we initially planned the rnav approach, however, due to fmc issues we transitioned to a visual approach.on short final we received an airspeed low" alert as noted in the qrh. the aircraft landed uneventfully and arff (airport rescue and firefighting) was standing by."

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: An air taxi Captain reported a low altitude alert from ATC on approach. Flight crew corrected and landed safely at the field.
text: when we were approximately 20 miles from the airport the approach controller said he had received word from the tower that the winds had shifted and he suggested we switch from the rnav 25 to either the visual or rnav for rwy 18. we accepted the rnav 18 and were told to proceed direct to the iaf pakte and cross it at 5000 and were cleared for the approach. after crossing pakte at 5000 we failed to capture 4700 en route to jikor and the controller said he received a low altitude alert and cancelled our approach clearance and gave us a climb back to 5000. contributing factors were the last minute change of approach and the proximity of some rough weather that was headed towards the field. conditions were visual at the field and we had the field in sight from pakte. after a short vector we received a visual approach clearance and landed at the field safely.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported their student taking the runway with aircraft of final approach. Landing aircraft executed a missed approach.
text: i was giving a flight review to a pilot who was out of currency at erie airport, erie, co. runway 15 was the active runway. the pattern was full, and an incoming plane announced they were on a straight-in for runway 15. the last transmission from the plane i heard was 3 miles out. the plane in front of us took off on runway 15. after the plane in front of us took off, my student saw the plane on approach and judged he had enough time to take off and clear the runway before they arrived for landing. he announced he was taking off on runway 15 and entered the runway. the straight-in traffic announced on the ctaf that they were on short final and a plane had entered the runway. my student continued his takeoff roll, believing we would be clear of the runway in time for the landing aircraft. the landing aircraft announced they were going around and side-stepping to the left. we briefed this incident on the ground and agreed the better course of action would be to announce your intention to take off and give enough time for someone you may not see to respond before crossing the hold short lines. the next best course of action would have been to stop or clear the runway as soon as possible without taking off.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: PA-28 Flight Instructor and their student reported that they turned to follow the wrong aircraft on downwind resulting in a NMAC with a subsequent downwind aircraft.
text: after overflying runway xxr at redacted we were instructed by tower to follow a sling traffic that was going to be on the left downwind and enter left downwind for runway xxl. we knew this traffic to be a ga aircraft and after scanning found a ga aircraft on the left downwind and proceeded to follow them. as we were joining the left downwind we saw another traffic close to us also entering the left downwind and identified it as the sling we were instructed to follow, and also heard a call from the controller to that traffic to start a circle to avoid traffic which was us. we also immediately started to correct to stay away from that traffic and advised to tower we made a mistake misidentified the traffic to follow for similar looking traffic, and they advised us to continue on downwind.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Light transport pilot reported encountering an aircraft taking the opposite end of the runway during landing rollout. Both aircraft took evasive action.
text: i landed runway 36 from the instrument landing system approach. i turned the lights on at the airport 10 miles out and made a radio call on ctaf on a 5 mile final after getting switched from center frequency. the other aircraft lined up on runway 18 and started their takeoff roll while i was still on the runway on my landing rollout. i didn't notice them until after i was on the ground. once i saw them coming toward me, i moved to the far right side of the runway and it looked like they moved right as well. the aircraft made no calls on ctaf before, after or during the incident.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported the UAS flew above authorized altitude twice when switching to automated return to home. The pilot took manual control of the UAS to bring it back down and land.
text: i was conducting a uav flight to capture images of a residential property at location x around xa00 hours on day 0. the flight path remained directly over or in close proximity of the property's boundaries. prior to the mission, i received laanc approval to fly up to 100' (within the boundaries of redacted class c airspace). i maintained an altitude below 100' during the duration of the flight, and was at approximately 70-80' directly over the structure when a battery alert began to annunciate. knowing i had ample battery power to complete the mission, i chose to capture my last image prior to manually landing the aircraft. when the battery power reached a pre-determined level, the uav software initiated an automatic 'return to home' sequence i was not expecting. at this time, the aircraft automatically began a rapid climb to begin the sequence. knowing i was relatively close to the 100' approval ceiling, i manually overrode the sequence, which i had to accomplish twice within an approximately 15 second window. for approximately 2 seconds, the aircraft traveled up to approximately 112' before i could manually lower it, then again, for approximately 3 seconds, it traveled up to approximately 119' before i could manually lower it. it was at these maximum altitudes for approximately 1 second each prior to being manually flown lower, below the 100' approval ceiling. i landed the aircraft without further issue. no injuries or aircraft damage resulted from this incident. in the future, i will consider landing the aircraft prior to the initiation of the 'return to home' sequence, and will maintain increased situation awareness regarding the return to home sequence/ altitude and the aircraft's remaining battery power.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A Center Controller reported an IFR aircraft climbing on a missed approach could not climb to their assigned altitude due to icing and flew below the Minimum IFR Altitude.
text: aircraft x was on approach (rnavxx) into redacted followed by aircraft y. aircraft x reported on the missed approach and said they had severe icing and would like to head back to redacted at the lowest altitude they could get, i told aircraft x to execute the published missed and climb and maintain 027 which is the minimum instrument flight rules altitude (mia) in the area they were in they said they were unable, i pulled up the rnavxy, redacted is the missed approach fix for the rnavxx and the middle fix for the rnavxy with a terminal arrival altitude (taa) of 020 so i gave them 020 and a clearance after redacted direct redacted airport as the terrain is more flat to the east of redacted all the way to redacted they said they were unable to climb to 020 the visual flight rules chart states that in their current location 010 was a safe altitude i gave them a pirep for redacted that i had received from their company and told them they could try for redacted, i gave aircraft y holding instructions and they asked to go back to redacted as well, i used aircraft y and another aircraft to relay until the aircraft x got clear of the icing and in visual flight rules conditions and cancelled ifrchange the phraseology for low altitude alert. 'low altitude alert check your altitude immediately air traffic control services unnavailable below mia'

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A TRACON Controller reported that a Cessna 441 descended below their assigned altitude due to turbulence and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude
text: aircraft x was on the redacted arrival going to redacted. when he checked on at 16000, i told him about turbulence in the descent. i assigned him 12000 when i could after he passed redacted. i saw him descending below 12000, and began issuing multiple low altitude alerts and instructions to climb immediately. i didn't get any response from the pilot. the lowest i observed him reaching was 10400 just as he exited the 12000 mva and entered the 11000 mva. eventually the pilot responded and climbed, but his transmissions were very difficult to understand. i was able to barely get a report from aircraft x saying severe downdraft with extreme turbulence. neither of those were known at the time. he hit the turbulence and downdraft which made holding altitude impossible, and he was too busy to respond to me until he got the aircraft under control. i had a few redacted departures that i was issuing climbs and weather reports to. redacted departures were getting moderate turbulence and mountain wave. while i was trying to get the pirep from aircraft x, a redacted departure on another frequency was telling me about severe on climb out. turbulence reports were everywhere, and the severe was not known to the southwest. not much could have been changed here. i could have issued better low altitude alerts, but aircraft x encountered turbulence that made it impossible to respond to me or comply with any instructions.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757 First Officer reported IAS disagreement during cruise. Flight crew landed uneventfully.
text: in cruise at fl360 on the redacted arrival just before starting our descent we got an eicas message ias disagree. we accomplished the checklist and determined the reliable sources to be the captain's airspeed and also the standby airspeed indicator, and that the first officer's side was unreliable. we decided not to use the pitch power combination in the immediate action items because we were stable at the pitch and power we had in cruise, which was a good match for the information in the tables once we got to that part of the checklist. we advised air traffic control. we did a flaps 20 landing in redacted as directed by the checklist. the landing was uneventful.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Other / Unknown; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the lead-in line for a gate at MSP was completely faded and the red safety line was also badly faded with most of the safety zone unmarked.
text: the lead-in line for e gate at msp was non-existent, it was almost 100% faded. the only part of the line that was visible was the actual t at the end of the lead-in line for the nose wheel stopping position. additionally, the red safety line was also very badly faded/with most of the safety zone unmarked completely. in addition, there looked like an old lead-in line had been removed adjacent to the faded line which created a shadow and confusion. we were able to slow down and just take directions from the marshaller and parked in the appropriate spot/angle. i would imagine that other gates in the area are in the same condition.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the aircraft's tires got stuck in 6-inch divots or sinkholes while taxiing to the gate.
text: the gate was occupied upon landing and we were cleared to taxi to the apron between h5 and h4. after waiting about 10 minutes we were clear to taxi to our gate. when i released the parking brake the aircraft lurched forward and stopped. i attempted to single engine taxi but the aircraft did not move at 45% n1. the first officer started the number 2 engine and the aircraft still didn't move with 2 engines at 45% n1. ground cleared the area behind the aircraft and i increased thrust to 50% n1 and were still not able to achieve breakaway thrust.we suspected a locked brake and called station ops to request maintenance and a push crew meet the aircraft. when they arrived the tug connected and maintenance confirmed the brakes were operating normally. ground personnel examined the area around the main gear and stated the tires were in a pair of 6-inch divots or sinkholes. the tug even had trouble moving the aircraft initially. after being freed i decided to have the tug tow us to the gate.the first officer reported the sinkholes to ground and airfield ops arrived to inspect as we were towed away. i sent an electronic log book (elb) report to inspect the gear to ensure there was no damage. there was no notam about this area before we taxied there nor was there one the following day for our flight out. there are two notes on the 10-9a page about this area restricting it to code c/d aircraft, but aircraft x is a code c aircraft.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 Captain reported poor communication with ground personnel led to uncommanded aircraft movement after push back was completed.
text: on pushback from gate xx the pushback appeared to have stopped. there was no communication via headset. i was alert waiting for 'pushback complete, set parking break command' it never came. i noticed the airplane starting to roll forward and jerking noises coming from the nose gear. i said ' radio check' over the intercom. no response. i told my first officer i think we are rolling i'm not sure if we are still pushing or if he is disconnecting us. he opened his window and yelled to the ramp and told me to set the break they were disconnecting the aircraft. at this time i was holding the breaks and trying to flash my light at one of the rampers. the first officer had a quick interaction through the window. i finally got him on headset and he asked me to disconnect headset. i asked why did you disconnect if you never heard me say 'parking break, set pressure normal'. he didn't answer and asked again if we could disconnect headset. i said no. and repeated my question. he said he thought he heard 'brake set'.i never said brake set. furthermore i asked if he ever heard the words pressure normal. he said no. i firmly explained to him never disconnect the aircraft until you have clear and full sop verbiage from the captain. we were rolling forward and were close to contacting the tug or ground personnel. i do not believe he had confirmation bias either. i never said radio check until well after the push stopped for 20 seconds or so and i noticed the plane rolling and jerking noises before i even verbalized 'radio check'

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier ramp employee reported chocking the aircraft after the aircraft parked with the engines spooling down; then further aircraft movement occurred resulting in the chock jamming under the front tire. Reporter stated it appeared the self-park system was not properly aligned.
text: i chocked the plane exactly on the line. the plane stopped, spooled down and then started to move forward again. the chock was jammed under the front tire with the rope under the wheel as a result. it would seem the self-park guided the pilot to move off the line.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reported a cabin door EICAS message during descent. The crew continued to the destination airport and landed.
text: as we were descending through fl190 we received an alert eicas message 'door pax aft open' that kept disappearing and re-appearing, we immediately ran the qrh and had flight attendant #2 check the 3 indicators and one of the indicators was half green and half white. as per qrh upon leveling off at 11, 000ft we dumped the pressure and continued on to redacted since it was our nearest suitable airport. from the first moment we received the alert message we monitored the pressure and it was good the entire time. once on the ground we advised maintenance of what happened and also briefed the next crew that was taking the plane.cause: alert message 'door pax aft open'suggestions: should have declared emergency even though the qrh didn't call for it but it was stated to land at the nearest suitable airport.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported an electrical odor during the climb; the flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed. After landing; Maintenance discovered the cockpit emergency flashlight had indications of internal burning.
text: during climb phase out of redacted, i started to smell something that smelt like electrical wires burning. i asked first officer if she smelt anything and after a few moments, she said she did. we started searching the flight deck for any indications of any wires, burning or smoke or fire we could not find anything. at this point, i contacted the flight attendant to see if she smelt anything and she confirmed she smelt something coming from the flight deck door area. i had her search the area to see if she could find any indications of smoke or fire anywhere and again there were none. smell grew stronger overtime during our climb at this point we were now level at flight level 240. air traffic control radio an additional climb to 330 at which time i advise them we were unable as we were working through an issue. after discussing the situation with the crew, we decided we would deviate at this time. i texted dispatch to inform them of the situation and of the deviation. i then radioed air traffic control and advise them, we would now be deviating to redacted and requesting priority handling. at this point, i gave the flight attendant a report and asked her to make an announcement to the passengers. during the descent he situation did not escalate, but the smell continued. upon landing in redacted, crash, fire, and rescue was standing by and available. ground resources did not report seeing any smoke or fire upon landing. crash fire and rescue followed us to the gate where all passengers were evacuated onto the jet bridge and into the terminal safely. fire department entered the aircraft, checked for sources of fire and reported all clear. ground crew reported a strong burning smell, smell inside the cargo bay when they opened the cargo door, but again no fire was detected or visible. after some time when contract maintenance showed up, they reported the captain side, emergency equipment, flashlight was burning up inside. he had me smell. it had a strong smell of burning plastic consistent with the smell in the fight deck. passengers in the front of the aircraft later advised flight attendant. they smelt it as well, and some were covering their mouths and nose. passengers in the back of the aircraft had not smelt anything until after landing in the deployment of the thrust reversers. no passengers or crew required medical attention.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported an apparent compressor stall during climb-out. Flight crew returned to the departure airport for a normal landing.
text: during initial climbout from redacted and passing approximately 11, 000 feet the aircraft suddenly experienced a single airframe shudder, abruptly yawing to the left momentarily. i was the pilot flying and the autopilot was engaged and remained so. i transferred aircraft control to the first officer. i immediately looked at all engine instruments and they were normal. the flight attendants then called informing me they and some of the passengers reporting seeing a brief spark on the left side of the aircraft near the engine. i told them everything was functioning normally and to let me know if they saw any other visual indications. the first officer and i discussed the situation and determined it was most likely a single compressor stall on the number one engine and the first officer began coordination with air traffic control to return to redacted. i began running the non routine landing considerations checklist in the qrh along with the overweight landing checklist, which included sending a company message about the air interrupt and briefing the flight attendants on a precautionary landing. we were vectored for an instrument landing system to xxc and requested thru air traffic control for arff (airport rescue and firefighting) equipment to meet us after landing in order to inspect the aircraft. the approach and landing were uneventful and we cleared the runway and stopped on the parallel taxiway to be inspected. no damage was noted and we then taxiied to the gate uneventfully.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Air carrier Lead Technician reported that during a Wi-Fi modification on an ERJ-175; they could not inspect the cap and stowage of the wiring due to it being covered with heat shrink.
text: working in redacted during the partial wifi demod, i do verify that wires are cap and stow after the technician has completed the job, and an inspector i can not see the quality of the work done because the wires have the heat shrink over them already.this same condition is possible on other aircrafts including aircraft y and aircraft zcause: during the process of cutting a couple wires in the twisted pair, the technician incorrectly cap and stow the wires and the shielding shorted out the wires. the insulation of the wires was damaged and the inspection of the cap and stow was done after the heat shrink was over them.suggestions: we need to be more vigilant, and check step by step during the process of cap and stow the wires, and inspect them more closely for any damaged of the wires.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Person / Animal / Bird
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported a rejected takeoff at a non-towered airport due to a person on the runway.
text: performed a stop and go landing with my student after making radio calls prior to entering redacted's airspace and pattern. on landing we slowed to stop around just prior to the thousand footers in order to configure for a short field takeoff practice. as we began to speed up, we saw a pilot run over to the runway. my sp (student pilot) began to prepare to abort as we saw him near but slow to a stop within the grass between the runway and taxiway. another pilot in aircraft y then called that they were going to grab some debris from the runway that they struck after we takeoff, however the pilot suddenly entered the runway leading to my sp immediately aborting takeoff and cutting throttle to idle and applying maximum available braking. we had just passed taxiway '1' at redacted leading to us exiting on '2' which is roughly where the pilot entered the runway. the two pilots were in the same plane as on taxiing back i saw him re-enter that aircraft.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Metroliner Captain reported that the First Officer accidentally put the left hand engine in reverse just prior to the landing flare; but successfully landed the aircraft.
text: first officer was pilot flying. just prior to landing flare she pulled the left hand engine into reverse and immediately stalled the left wing causing it to drop suddenly. we were within a few feet of the ground and the main landing gear absorbed the shock preventing us from striking a wingtip. had we been a few feet higher the airplane would have sustained damage.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Decathlon Student Pilot and their Flight Instructor reported a loss of control during landing that resulted in a prop strike.
text: i was working on my tailwheel endorsement, and this was my third flight in the aircraft. everything felt pretty normal until we tried our second landing. i ended up forcing the nose of the plane down, and after the third bounce, the prop hit the ground just as we were trying to go around. at that point the instructor took over flight controls. there wasn't enough runway left to safely abort, so we continued with the go around climbed out normally, and kept our pattern tight. after we landed and shut down we found out the propeller had struck the ground. looking back i realize i shouldn't have pushed the nose down so hard trying to stay on the runway and i wish i'd recognized the need to let my instructor take over after the bounces to prevent the prop strike.
