anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: EMB-505 pilot reported on departure using FMS and the aircraft executed a shallow wide turn resulting in ATC issuing a low altitude alert.
text: departed runway xx on the redacted departure. initial heading was 282°, followed by a climbing left turn to 090°. the flight management system was armed for the departure, and during the turn the aircraft executed a very shallow, wide turn while in flight management system mode. air traffic control subsequently issued a low altitude and terrain alert.we were visual with the terrain throughout the departure and terrain clearance was never in question. the aircraft did not generate any terrain warnings.on future departures from this airport, i will plan to fly the initial turn in heading mode rather than flight management system. the flight management system-commanded turn radius appears too shallow for the terrain west of the airport on this procedure.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: ERJ 145 Captain reported a deviation from the published missed approach procedure after a temporary loss of control on short final due to a wind shear encounter.
text: setting up for the approach, field conditions and aircraft status (wet runway, ice encountered, thrust reversers yes) we could not generate flaps 22 numbers. flaps 45 was our only option for an attempt. tower reported conditions initially winds 270 @ 30g45 and updated to 280 @38g60 as we past faf. ceiling and visibility were not a factor. during approach and subsequent go-around, we experienced continuous moderate turbulence and wind shear resulting in a stick shaker just as we intercepted glide slope, uncommanded autopilot disconnect, wind shear indication just after 500' call out, flaps 45 speed exceedance of 168 kias. maintaining a stabilized approach was extremely difficult as large airspeed swings of 15-25knots. on the missed approach, instructions from tower were to fly the published. the flight management system was not in sequence and i switched to runway heading for about 30 seconds as i had to assist my pilot monitoring with reprogramming the flight management system. i flew past the assigned altitude by about 600' during my efforts to assist the pilot monitoring. i corrected both lateral vertical paths, assessed our fuel status and proceeded back to redacted. the rest of the flight was uneventful.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a critical ground conflict while taxing to the assigned gate.
text: after landing on xxl at redacted, we exited the runway at [taxiway] 1 and we were cleared to taxi to our gate via taxiway 2. we entered the ramp and i was taxiing slower than normal because it was wet and dark. both the first officer and i called clear (left/right)" and we turned onto 3 and started to enter the ramp. very shortly thereafter the first officer yelled "stop". i abruptly stopped the aircraft and then aircraft y appeared out of nowhere taxiing at excessive speed (especially considering the conditions). there was no communication from air traffic control or aircraft y aircraft regarding the conflict. aircraft y entered the ramp and was clearly trying to beat us to the gate so they would get parked first (apparently there is only one ramp crew at that time of night). if my first officer had not seen aircraft y when he did, i believe a collision was likely because if we had not stopped immediately there was no way aircraft y would have been able to stop in time to prevent a collision.cause: this near miss should have never happened had aircraft y slowed down and not tried to beat us to the gate. in my 25 years at my company i have never seen such a brazen and cavalier action by another pilot. the aircraft y captain (a check pilot) completely disregarded safety and unnecessarily put his aircraft, passengers and crew in jeopardy just so he could get to the gate before us. it is very concerning that the aircraft y captain is a check pilot and is normalizing unsafe practices such as this to the next generation of airline pilots."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A321 First Officer reported a low oil pressure indication that resulted in a return to the departure airport.
text: on day 0, from redacted to redacted, we received an ecam indicating low oil pressure in our number one engine, and we requested priority handling. i was the pilot flying, and the captain decided to let me continue to have the flight controls and radios while he worked with the ecams, checklists, and follow-ups. we decided that we needed to return to the redacted, but we were overweight, so the captain ran the overweight checklist. at about 3000ft msl during our approach to runway xxr, our oil pressure indicators returned to normal. i landed aircraft x with a soft landing using medium brake. the safety equipment was already waiting for us to inspect the aircraft once it was finished, they escorted us into the gate xx.cause: in a situation like we just had, i believe it is very important to have a good crm with clear communication involving everyone (fas, first officer, ca, air traffic control, dispatch, operations, passengers etc.). finally, this is what makes a difference.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: Challenger 300 Captain reported a wake turbulence encounter on descent to HHR in trail of a B747-800 inbound to LAX that resulted in an inflight upset with bank angle exceeding 70 degrees. Control was regained and the flight landed safely.
text: aircraft was on the irnmn two rnav arrival descending via the star. the autopilot was engaged with nav, and vnav modes selected. weather conditions were clear skies and smooth flight conditions, light winds. passenger sign was turned on just prior to passing through 10, 000 ft. we had 8 passengers and a short flight. fa (flight attendant) came to the cockpit to inform us cabin was secure. the passengers were seated with their seat belts fastened. the flight attendant was then returning to her seat.air traffic control informed us we were in trail of a b747-8. we did not report the traffic in sight. air traffic control then requested a descent from 6, 000 ft directly to 2, 600 ft as they were going to take us under the approach path for lax.at this time, we did have the b747-8 in sight ahead and below our altitude. we did not report this to air traffic control as we wanted air traffic control to apply the required wake separation. descending through 5, 000 ft with the autopilot engaged, nav or hdg (heading) and vs mode selected, we encountered the wake turbulence of the b747-8. the aircraft rolled abruptly and aggressively to the right. captain, pf, immediately disconnected the autopilot and initiated the upset recovery" maneuver. pm informed air traffic control of the wake encounter. at this time, we encountered a second wake with another strong roll to the right. again, captain initiated the 'upset recovery' maneuver and the captain informed air traffic control we wanted to maintain 5, 000 ft and reduced our airspeed from the assigned speed due to wake turbulence encounter. air traffic control approved our request and informed us they would vector us around the flight path for the approaches into lax.no further wake turbulence was encountered. the approach and landing into hhr were normal.during the wake encounter, the fa was returning to her seat. fortunately, she was bracing herself with the ceiling as she returned to her seat. during the roll, the fa did hit her head on the ceiling. this caused neck and back muscle stress.the max bank angle may have exceeded 70 to 80 degrees. no negative or positive wing loading was encountered. it was an abrupt strong roll to the right in both indications.cause: the cause was air traffic control not providing wake separation for a light aircraft following a heavy.an early descent below the flight path for aircraft arriving into lax, not keeping the arriving aircraft for another airport clear of the arriving traffic for laxsuggestions: vectoring the aircraft around the approach area for lax and not under the arriving aircraft into lax."

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported encountering wake turbulence departing CLT in trail of an A320 that resulted in uncommanded bank in both directions and a stick shaker. Control was regained and the flight continued to destination.
text: departing 18c in clt, we encountered wake turbulence at approximately 1, 500 msl from an a320 that departed before us. the aircraft banked approximately 30 degrees in both directions and the stick shaker activated. stall recovery procedure was applied and the bank angles corrected. flaps were up and speed was approximately 210 kts. we notified air traffic control and confirmed with the fa that no one was injured. the flight continued as normal with no other events.assuming proper air traffic control separation minimums, i think this was just a rare occurrence.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: EMB 145 pilot reported the aircraft veered to the right during landing roll; requiring crew to stop on the runway briefly.
text: approach and initial landing were standard and within limits. landed on centerline. after initial touchdown the aircraft began to turn right. this happened almost immediately after nose wheel touched down. pf applied full left rudder to correct, and the aircraft continued to veer towards the right. captain then assumed aircraft control and after disengaging tiller the aircraft stopped its right motion. we informed tower we were stopping on the runway to assess the ability to taxi further. after contacting maintenance and exiting the runway we slowly taxied back to parking. logbook entry was added. no further malfunction was detected.cause: we narrowed it down to the nose wheel steering issue as both trs were placed back to reverse idle and full left rudder was applied to try to correct to center line.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: ERJ 170 First Officer reported a Hydraulic System 2; Autopilot; and Captain's side Automatic Data System failure during cruise. The flight continued to the destination airport and landed safely.
text: it was my leg to fly, going to redacted, cruising fl230, we got hyd 2 low pressure, ads1 (automatic data system) fail, and autopilot fail. i started hand flying while the captain handled the checklists and talking to air traffic control. as the captain followed the checklists, we both would confirm the checklist in the qrh and confirm anytime he turned on /off a switch/button. as doing the checklist we got hydraulic 2 elec pump fail, we requested priority handling. hand flew until final configuration then captain took the landing because we were not going to have steering. we took the high speed, called ops for a tug. when we got to the gate, captain and i did in depth debrief. the captain has also submitted a in detail report.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: SR20 Flight Instructor and Student Pilot reported an inflight upset resulted shortly after takeoff when they encountered rotor wash from a helicopter that departed ahead of them. Control was regained and they continued the flight.
text: we were following instructions to line up and wait while a helicopter departed ahead of us. we were cleared to take off soon afterwards. on takeoff, we experienced low altitude rotor wash departing from goodyear runway 21. we experienced an uncommanded left roll about 30-35 degrees while below 200 feet. banked right more than intended afterwards, also possibly due to rotorwash. continued climb out and flight as normal. contacted goodyear tower and alerted them to the issue while in downwind.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757 Captain reported an engine failed during final approach and the crew continued approach to landing.
text: air traffic control cleared us for a visual approach xxr at redacted. shortly after selecting gear down and flaps 25 the left engine egt spiked and failed. because it was a visual approach and we were both heads up neither one of us noticed the egt spiking. it wasn't till the eicas messages appeared associated with the engine failure that we realized what happened. i added power to the right engine to maintain speed and pulled the left engine to idle. no fire indication in the flight deck. the first officer requested priority handling, started the apu, and we focused on maintaining a stable approach to landing. after an uneventful landing we cleared the runway and stopped on a parallel taxiway. i shut the engine down and the first officer ran thru the engine failure qrc to make sure we didn't miss anything. the fire marshal inspected the aircraft and noted no visible fire or smoke. we could confirm that with the egt decreasing. the fire marshal confirmed that at the time it was safe to taxi to the gate and that they would follow us. while i was coordinating with air traffic control and the fire marshal the first officer was coordinating with the purser and redacted operations. he also made a quick pa to the passengers. operations confirmed what gate they wanted us at and we taxied to the gate uneventfully. it wasn't till after gate arrival that we heard we had what i'm assuming was a tailpipe fire. the fire marshal pulled some security video of flames coming out of the back of the engine. we never did get a fire warning in the flight deck and there was no fire once the trucks got to us on the ground.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B747 pilot reported main gear would not retract on initial climb resulting in return to departure airport.
text: normal operations until after the takeoff when the right-wing main landing gear did not retract. the eicas msg. gear disagree displayed along with the gear synoptic display showing that the aforementioned gear was still down. the status msg. gear monitor also displayed enroute.after the speed up and clean-up of the aircraft the pm accomplished the gear disagree qrh checklist. upon completion of said checklist we contacted maintenance control via dispatch for guidance, and it was agreed on to return to redacted. we jettisoned the necessary fuel to allow us to land below maximum landing weight and proceeded to receive vectors for an uneventful landing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B767 flight crew reported a tail strike while initiating a go around after the auto spoilers did not deploy during landing.
text: during touchdown after a stable approach flown by the first officer (pf) to runway xxr, auto spoilers did not deploy automatically which caused the aircraft to pitch up. a balked landing recovery was performed. during climb out, momentary tailskid message was displayed. we returned for a second approach followed by an uneventful landing with normal automatic deployment of the ground spoilers. during post-flight inspection, noticed some paint missing from the tail-skids plate. the finding was entered in the logbook.we will continue to focus our awareness on the limited pitch attitude range during all these critical phases of flight since they can be easily exceeded.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported they shut down an engine and diverted to a nearby airport due to engine banging noises; vibration and a stall warning.
text: i was the captain and pilot monitoring on flight abcd redacted to redacted. during cruise at fl 360 we were requested to slow from mach .77 to .75. as the engines started reducing thrust i felt a sudden shaking/ thudding in the aircraft, along with some banging sounds. at the same time i noticed that the number one n1 was fluctuating, and then it rolled all the way back to idle. we then received an eng 1 stall ecam that lasted for a few seconds, and then went away after the n1 recovered. however, there was still some jolts/thudding, and bang noises that i could feel in the cockpit. the first officer and i discussed the situation and decided to do a precautionary engine shut down. i then requested priority handling, and requested a lower altitude. in the descent, even with the engine at idle, i still felt the vibration and bang noises. the first officer and i decided to divert to redacted. the first officer continued flying duties, setting up for the approach to runway xxl, and with air traffic control comms while i ran the appropriate checklists. after accomplishing the procedure to shut down eng 1, the noise and vibration stopped. once all checklist and non-normal landing procedures were accomplished, i communicated with air traffic control that we would make a full stop on runway xxl, and wanted arf (airport rescue and firefighting) to do an inspection of the number one engine. we asked for any indications of, smoke, leaks, fire, and damage. after landing the inspections were completed, and after checking with my flight attendants that there were no signs of fumes or smoke in the cabin, i made the decision to taxi to the gate. engine number one had a prior history of problems. that flight crew also experienced an eng 1 stall message.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Hazardous Material Violation; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Air carrier flight attendant crew reported an offensive urine smell in the cabin.
text: upon arriving to gate in redacted, we were alerted by crew of flight abc that they had 'taken out a/c because the a/c they originally had a strong urine smell in cabin.' they wanted to give us a heads up. once we checked in with the agent, she said that 'maintenance and cleaners were working on it.' after about 30-40 min, the agent said the plane was good. they asked us to 'check the smell and let them know.' we agreed and proceeded one by one to enter the a/c to see if we could smell the odor. we did and it was a strong urine smell. we then, proceeded to wait in the jetway. at that time, the capt asked if we could smell it and we all said 'yes.' she said that she needed to contact 'her boss and let him know.' after a few minutes, both the agent and lead agent came to ask what we wanted to do. we advised her to ask the capt. at first, the capt asked us if the odor was too strong and we told her yes so, she said she would attempt to turn the air on strong and hope the odor would dissipate. we waited. after a few minutes, capt also said that the maintenance log didn't show anything so, she needed to ask them if they did anything to remove the odor. the agent chimed in and stated that the cleaners sprayed the aft lav carpet area with coffee grinds and lemon juice. maintenance said they 'could not locate the source of the urine leak' and that the same a/c had a leak a couple months earler but, the carpet was cleaned. nonetheless, the a/c stil smelled like urine. capt asked if we were 'comfortable taking this plane with the urine odor?' we said 'no.' she said she would advise 'her boss.' the agents were making comments such as 'i've been here since xa:00 and someone needs to take this plane out of here!'...'there is absolutely nothing compromising the integrity of this a/c!' by this time, both the purser and i had reached out to the managers. after several back and forths, the capt said that 'her boss' advised her that 'although the urine odor is offensive, it is not a safety issue.' with what felt like no one backing our concerns, we were made to feel like we had no choice other than to get on the plane and prepare to board. once boarding began, the capt and the purser came to the boarding door to advise me that 'if even one pax complains about the urine smell, that we will not be going.' as pax began to board, one by one, each started either making comments or asking questions about the 'bad smell on this plane.' frazzled, i asked the capt if the agents had made some sort of announcement describing our issue. she wanted to know as well and so, we asked both the lead agent and agent if there was an announcement made to the paxs and they said no. this, was one of many disconnects that occurred during this entire experience. one of the most difficult things that our crew encountered was the pure aloofness that was presented by the agents regarding the strong urine odor. it's as if, the fact that urine, which is considered a biohazard and unsanitary was completely disregarded. and when attempting to speak to the lead agent about it, she laughed as if it wasn't being taken seriously and i attempted to explain to her that 'this is not funny.' the entire incident was just heightened by the disconnect between our pilots, crew and redacted agents. and, it should be stressed that the biggest issue (problem) which was the urine leak from the aft toilets was never resolved. in the end, no one seemed to care about how unsanitary and unsafe having urine (biohazard) soaked into the carpet and contaminating the cabin air was.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Air carrier technicians reported they attended to a pilot report for the thrust reverser failure to deploy.  Upon investigation they found the lockout bolts installed and the hydraulic control unit unlocked.
text: we performed a gate call for the aircraft related to a thrust reverser failure to deploy. upon arrival to the aircraft we determined that the inhibition bolts were still installed. on further investigation, we found that the isolation control unit (icu) was unlocked. an minimum equipment list for the tr in question had been cleared for the aircraft that morning.the manual procedures to clear the minimum equipment list had not been followed, which left it in the state where we discovered the aircraft. procedures to clear an minimum equipment list should be properly followed.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier technicians reported while taxiing aircraft to the maintenance hangar; the aircraft slid on the taxiway due to heavy coating of algae; grime and mildew on the surface of the taxiway.
text: on the recorded date and time, upon taxi of said aircraft for hangar input, while all required ground personnel were present and being marshalled forward, engines at idle with controlled forward movement, hydraulics and brake pressure normal, aircraft began to skid when attempt was made to straighten from initial left turn. due to idle power speed, we were able to recover intended straight steering position which caused a safe and terminating of taxi hangar input intention.tarmac surface of the greater area of ramp in heavily coated with algae, grime and mildew making the area significantly slippery for even walking let alone taxiing an aircraft during damp to saturated conditions. removal and the continuous assurance of the absence of algae, grime and mildew (maintenance) is imperative so that said or worse conditions do not occur.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Ground Event / Encounter Fuel Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: PA-32 pilot reported taxing into a pole which damaged the wing tip and caused a fuel leak.
text: i had stopped for a refueling on a cross country flight.after fueling the aircraft, i clipped the right wingtip on a concrete pole resulting in a splintering of the fiberglass and a leak of the fuel in the wingtip. i used the airport fuel spill equipment to collect the leaking fuel and further drained the right wingtip fuel tank using the quick drain. the attendants at the airport assisted in collecting and moving the drained fuel and the fire department dispatched a truck to monitor the fuel spill but left noting no fuel on the surface as it was contained. i patched the wingtip with speed tape and test flew it around the pattern. the repair was satisfactory and i proceeded to continue to my destination. aircraft performance was nominal as the fuel imbalance toward the full left wingtip lessened.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Bird / Animal
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported entering an active parachute jump area and taking evasive action to avoid the jumpers.
text: i was departing redacted and heading to redacted, initially following a route below redacted's class c shelf (at about 1500 ft msl) and between redacted's class d airspace and redacted's class c inner airspace. about 4 miles from redacted i switched the radio to redacted.xx to listen for traffic heading to redacted. within a few minutes i switched the standby frequency to redacted.y and enabled monitoring on it to listen for traffic at redacted since i would be overflying it and knew they sometimes have parachute activity there.about 4 miles east of redacted i cleared the redacted class c shelf and started climbing to cruise altitude (4500 ft msl). about 1 mile east of redacted i noticed two parachutes directly ahead and about 500 ft above me. i immediately turned hard right to avoid them but after turning about 70 degrees i noticed two more parachutes slightly to might right and above me so i turned hard left to avoid them. no more parachutes were observed so i continued on course to redacted. a short time later their pilot called my tail number on the radio and i explained that i might have been late getting on their frequency, that i didn't hear the warning about the jumpers, and i did my best to avoid them once i saw them.there are two main things i will do to avoid this problem in the future:1. avoid overflying redacted in the future. i just had one route that takes me over redacted so i will no longer use that one.2. when approaching airports with jumpers, make sure the primary radio frequency is tuned to that airport at least 10 miles away.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Global Express First Officer reported encountering extreme mountain wave conditions during cruise flight resulting in loss of control. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft during stall recovery; and the flight continued to its destination.
text: while flying from redacted to redacted, aircraft x encountered extreme mountain wave activity and was unable to maintain fl470.at fl450 pf and pm noticed slight to moderate turbulence started to begin. noticing another airplane crossing above us, we asked air traffic control for a ride report at fl470. the aircraft at fl470 reported a smooth ride and we decided to step up to fl470.once level at fl470 pm heard on the radio another pilot at a different altitude report mountain wave activity. shortly after pm saw an increase in altitude of about 100 feet with some oscillations in the airspeed. pm made a comment that increase in altitude may have been the mountain wave that the other aircraft had reported. moments after the speed went from .80 to .72 and the stall aural warning came on. pf announced, 'stall recovery' and initiated the stall recovery procedure. pm told air traffic control we were in mountain wave and we were going to be descending to another attitude and we were assigned to descend to something in the low 40s. at one point pm noticed a descent in excess of 3500 fpm and notified air traffic control we were going to need even lower. air traffic control assigned fl380. when it looked like we were going to need lower as the descent continued air traffic control assigned fl300. the descent started to stabilize around fl395 and we were able to descend and maintain fl380 for the rest of the flight without incident.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Cessna 185 pilot reported they manually started the engine without setting the parking brake and before they could get into the aircraft it rolled forward into a snow berm.
text: -36 f initial engine startup manually due to a weak battery. aircraft tires were chocked by pinching the tires with the hydraulically-operated snow skis. after manually starting the engine, and as the pilot entered the cabin door, the aircraft began to slowly move forward and caused the pilot to slip and fall next to the cabin door. the aircraft moving forward, the propeller contacted a snow berm. the engine continued to run after contacting the snow berm, and was shut down in the normal procedure. the problem arose from not using the aircraft parking brake. contributing factors were the extremely cold temperature and un-willingness to use the normal parking brake and the extreme cold not allowing the pinching factor of the snow skis to deform the tires and provide braking action such as has been demonstrated in less-cold (warmer) temperatures. additionally, the contributing factor of a weak battery due to extreme cold, and the necessity of manually starting the engine were significant.the pilot believes that manually starting an aircraft engine is not an abnormal operation, but understands that the perceptions of individuals who do not regularly perform this action will be significantly different. the ranking of contributing factors would be re-arranged by those individuals. extreme cold, and a desire to perform a start-up, run-up, charging system check, and shutdown and engine blanket coverup in order to allow time for the engine compartment to 'heat soak' while the pilot enjoyed a warm mug of coffee are a very real human factor consideration. thank you

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Global Express BD700 Flight crew reported encounter with mountain wave activity and loss of aircraft control.
text: whilst in the cruise at fl470 we encountered some fairly severe mountain wave activity. this caused a loss of airspeed from m0.80 to m0.72 and with it a stall warning, stick shaker and auto pilot disconnect.the pf ( i, as the pilot in command was on my crew rest), applied full power and reduced the pitch attitude of the aircraft and started a descent. the pm spoke to redacted air traffic control and requested an immediate descent. the stall warnings, almost immediately went to an over speed warning. we eventually leveled at fl380 and away from the mountain wave activity settled down into the cruise once more.whilst this was happening, i managed to get from crew rest and into a kneeled position between, the pilot's seats to observe what was happening. immediately i was satisfied that we were not stalled, as it was the stall wanring and stick shaker that had alerted me to the problem. i could see that the pitch of the aircraft was at about 1 degree below the horizon with wings level and the power was at full. the airspeed was showing above mmo (maximum mach operating speed) and we were descend8ng at about 3, 700ft per min. i reassured the pf that his actions were correct and that we could now re-engage the autopilot and cruise at the lower level. i returned to the galley and assured the flight attendant and when to talk to the passenger. we landed at destination about two hours later, without incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: G100 Captain reported a Battery Overheat Warning on one of the two aircraft batteries during climb resulted in a divert.
text: during climb to altitude on a route from redacted to redacted, at approximately 35000' we experienced a 'battery overheat warning' on our number two battery. both batteries are located at the back of the wheel wells. the temperature rapidly increased beyond the top limit of a 160 degrees. it quickly climbed to a peak reading of 197 degrees. due to the imminent risk of an uncontained thermal runaway and/or battery fire, i advised air traffic control, initiated an decent and requested vectors to the nearest airport (redacted) for landing. i also requested the fire services be on standby for the landing. the aircraft landed without incident. upon investigation it was found that the temperature sensor was faulty. due to the design of the aircraft there is no way to ascertain if it is a fault or potential fire, therefore the pilot has to assume the worst case and react accordingly. the service provided by air traffic control during what was a very high workload was exemplary and much appreciated.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a near miss with during final approach with an aircraft departing opposite direction.
text: chain of eventshow the problem arose / contributing factorsi am a cfii and was conducting instrument training at m54 while flying a practice rnav (gps) runway 19 approach with a student. the airport was using runway 01 for traffic pattern operations at the time. our intention was to fly the rnav 19 approach to lnav minimums and perform a low approach while yielding to all traffic operating in the pattern.throughout the approach, i made multiple ctaf position and intention reports advising traffic that we were conducting the rnav 19 approach for a low approach only and that we would give way to all traffic in the pattern. i recall specifically making calls at approximately 9 nm, 6 nm, 4 nm, 2 nm, and again at approximately 1.5 nm final.at the time of the incident, there was only one aircraft in the traffic pattern, which was turning left base for runway 01.while descending on a 1.5-mile final toward lnav minimums, an aircraft identifying as aircraft y announced on ctaf that he intended to depart runway 01 from the a1 intersection. immediately after hearing that transmission, i announced that we were on a 1.5-mile final for the rnav runway 19 approach.the departing aircraft replied that he was 'rolling' and began the takeoff roll on runway 01. the aircraft departed directly toward our position on opposite headings while we were established on final.from our perspective on final, the aircraft initially appeared to be a small single-engine aircraft. i did not recognize the aircraft type until after passing. after liftoff, the aircraft accelerated rapidly and continued climbing toward us.how the problem was discoveredthe conflict became apparent when the departing aircraft announced he was rolling for departure while we were already established on a 1.5-mile final for the rnav 19 approach.corrective actionsas the aircraft climbed toward our flight path, i initiated a right turn to ensure separation before resuming the runway course. the departing aircraft then began a right turn away from our position.at the closest point of approach, the aircraft appeared to pass approximately 200 feet below our altitude with an estimated 300-400 feet of horizontal separation.after passing, the departing pilot asked over ctaf why we were flying an opposite-direction rnav approach while runway 01 was in use. he further indicated that he believed we were flying the rnav (gps) 01 approach and that i was making calls for runway 01 instead of runway 19. i responded that multiple ctaf calls had been made advising traffic that we were flying the rnav 19 approach as a low approach only.there were no injuries and no damage to either aircraft.human performance considerationsperceptions, judgements, and decisionsbased on the limited traffic in the pattern and the multiple ctaf advisories made during the approach, i assessed that the practice rnav 19 approach could be conducted safely while yielding to traffic in the pattern.when the departing aircraft announced his intention to depart, i immediately transmitted our position on a 1.5-mile final. when the aircraft began climbing toward our flight path after departure, i determined that initiating a right turn would provide additional separation.factors affecting the quality of human performancethis event occurred at a non-towered airport where aircraft were operating both in the traffic pattern and conducting a straight-in instrument training approach opposite the runway in use.the departing aircraft was aircraft y, which has high acceleration and climb performance. this reduced the time available to resolve the situation once the aircraft began its takeoff roll.actions or inactionsmultiple ctaf calls were made throughout the approach advising traffic that we were conducting the rnav 19 low approach. an additional call was made when the departing aircraft announced his departure.when the departing aircraft climbed toward our position, a right turn was initiated to ensure separation while continuing to monitor the aircraft's climb and trajectory.note: after completing the final approach segment and the map, my student maneuvered our aircraft to the right, then back to the left. this movement was not the evasive action taken earlier during the final approach to runway 19.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Learjet 60 Captain reported encountering turbulence on departure resulting in the flight crew being unable to stop their climb at the assigned altitude. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft and continued to their destination.
text: i was the pilot in command and pilot flying a learjet lr-60 departing runway xx at redacted. we obtained our instrument flight rules clearance via telephone from redacted departure and were released for departure with instructions to climb and maintain 5, 000 msl. weather at the airport was mvfr with strong gusting winds (270/g40+), snow flurries, and very cold temperatures (later determined to be approximately isa -18). based on the conditions, i anticipated entering imc and encountering turbulence shortly after departure. my sic and i conducted a thorough briefing of the takeoff and climb profile. i executed a crosswind takeoff on runway xx without incident. after takeoff i established a climb at 250 kias. the sic completed the after-takeoff checklist. moderate turbulence was encountered shortly after departure.at approximately 2, 500 msl, just prior to entering imc, i engaged the autopilot in heading mode (laterally) and level change (vertically) to continue the climb at 250 kias to the assigned altitude of 5, 000 msl. we entered solid imc and continued climbing in moderate turbulence. approaching the assigned altitude, i observed that the aircraft climb rate had increased to approximately 3, 000-4, 000 fpm and was continuing to increase. the increase in climb rate occurred without a corresponding pitch increase or thrust change, suggesting the aircraft had encountered strong vertical air movement. it became apparent that the autopilot would not capture the assigned altitude. i reduced thrust and disconnected the autopilot to manually level the aircraft. although airspeed decreased as expected, the aircraft continued climbing at a significant rate. i reduced thrust to flight idle and lowered the pitch attitude, however, the aircraft continued to climb while the speed decreased to about 170 kias. the aircraft was experiencing moderate turbulence and control responses seemed atypical. i suspected a strong updraft or unstable air mass. due to concern about imposing excessive negative-g loads on the aircraft structure, i elected not to force an abrupt level-off and instead allowed the aircraft to 'ride it out, ' and stabilize. we subsequently exceeded the assigned altitude. the redacted departure controller queried our status and i advised that we were 'correcting.' air traffic control then issued a climb to 8, 000 msl. at approximately 7, 000 msl the rate of climb began to decrease and the aircraft stabilized. i re-established a normal climb profile. as we approached 8, 000 msl i re-engaged the autopilot, however, the autopilot again failed to capture the altitude. in retrospect i suspect this occurred because i engaged the auto pilot too close to the level off, not allowing sufficient time to capture. i again disconnected the autopilot and manually leveled the aircraft as we exited imc into vmc on top. the aircraft leveled at approximately 8, 500 msl. air traffic control again queried our status and i advised that we appeared to be experiencing an autopilot issue and were working the problem. we were instructed to climb to 10, 000 msl and proceed on course and were then handed off to artcc. the artcc controller asked if we required assistance or had an emergency. we advised that we were not declaring an emergency and that the aircraft was under control. we were subsequently cleared to climb to 17, 000 msl. i hand-flew the aircraft to that altitude and leveled off.after completing the cruise checklist and confirming that all systems appeared normal, i re-engaged the autopilot. the autopilot then appeared to function normally for the remainder of the flight. lessons learned: this event caused me to give serious consideration to the fact that, in conditions involving strong winds, turbulence, and cold temperatures, significant vertical air movement may be present even outside of convective activity. this highlighted the importance of more closely monitoring climb performance and autopilot modes before, during, and after altitude capture. if the aircraft energy state becomes excessive or automation behavior is unexpected, transitioning more promptly to manual control and managing the aircraft more conservatively would help prevent future altitude deviations or structural loading concerns. the sic and i debriefed this incident at length after the flight and discussed strategies for prevention of such occurrences in the future.

anomaly: Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Corporate jet Captain reported it was difficult during approach to tell apart the runway and taxiway at MYAM due to the faint runway markings and wet runway surface. Captain stated other aircraft on approach experienced the same issue.
text: on day 0, in aircraft x, i was the pf on an empty leg from redacted to myam. the initial plan was a visual approach to runway 09 using the rnav as a backup, as runway 09 tends to be more commonly used runway at this airport. this airport does not report the weather, and we were unable to pick up any other nearby weather stations. upon arrival in the area, traffic in the pattern was operating for runway 27, so i asked the first officer what the correct downwind is. he looked it up and found the correct pattern is left traffic for runway 27. so we joined the correct downwind for runway 27 to integrate with existing traffic and planned to fly a visual approach to runway 27. we did load the rnav approach for 27 into the flight management system, but with the last minute change, we did not have time to brief it. there was a small plane in the pattern and i believe two other jets making callouts further away. on the downwind on the near side of the final approach fix, i disconnected the autopilot to fly the remainder of the approach manually, as there were people lining up and back-taxiing, and the timing required that we have a short base before the faf.while turning onto final for runway 27, we observed what appeared to be an aircraft positioned on the taxiway that looked as though it was holding short of the runway, as we had heard on the frequency that someone announced they were holding short. it appeared that the aircraft was waiting for traffic to land.as the approach continued, the runway and taxiway surfaces were difficult to distinguish due to very faint runway markings and the runway surface appearing slightly wet. at approximately 200 - 300 feet, we initiated a go-around due to the lack of complete certainty about the runway markings. the aircraft remained airborne during the entire maneuver and did not touch down at any point. while our go-around was in progress, and while we were on crosswind, another pilot in the sequence directly behind us transmitted on the radio asking which surface was the runway, specifically asking whether the runway was the one on the right or the left. we believed him to be joking and responded with, that's why we went around." he then responded, "no, seriously, i can't tell, is it the right or the left?" we responded that it was the left one, and he proceeded to sidestep and land on runway 27. shortly afterward, the third aircraft in the landing sequence (two aircraft behind us and a jet) landed on the taxiway.during our approach it became apparent that the runway markings were very faint, and with the runway surface wet the contrast between the runway and taxiway was reduced. one of the cues that helped clarify the situation was the ability to begin seeing yellow taxiway markings through the water, which helped distinguish the taxiway from the runway.after parking, we went to the airport office. we spoke with airport personnel as they initially believed the aircraft may have touched down based on the amount of fuselage visible above the surrounding tree/shrub line. we clarified to the airport manager that the aircraft did not touch the ground on go-around and that the go-around had been initiated at approximately 200 - 300 feet agl.during the go-around and pattern activity, the aircraft immediately behind sidestepped and also went around, while the jet behind that ultimately landed on the taxiway. the only reason we were able to perform a go-around is because my first officer was vigilant, and spoke up.the runway markings at myam appeared very faint, and with a wet surface the distinction between the runway and taxiway was reduced. also the jet we believed was holding short when we began our approach was actually a disabled aircraft that had turned clear of runway 09 at the end, and was positioned to look like it was holding short. given the radio transmissions questioning runway identification and the report of an aircraft landing on the taxiway, the condition of the markings may contribute to runway and taxiway misidentification, particularly during busy traffic periods.we are lucky we went around and are safe, but this is clearly a problem if three aircraft in a row, two of which were operated by professional pilots, had mistaken a taxiway for a runway at an uncontrolled airport. this could have ended completely differently and tragically."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: PA-31 pilot reported on the climb out experiencing trim issues resulting in the aircraft porpoising. Pilot regained aircraft control and returned to departure airport.
text: below is a summary of the unforeseen malfunction with the autopilot/trim that caused the pilot deviation while transporting 6 passengers to include infant today. this event occurred after takeoff on the initial climb out of redacted visual flight rules. as i proceeded to climb to 1000ft under the bravo shelf, i received a blinking trim error notification on the autopilot display panel and the plane began gradually porpoising. i followed the standard operating procedure by disconnecting the autopilot to reset the system. it worked initially, however, after 10-15 seconds and activating autopilot again, the trim gave an error indication, once more, and the plane began an abrupt nose up pitch. after disconnecting the autopilot again, in an attempt to recover the aircraft, the trim wheel was still rolling aft and the plane kept increasing the rate of climb. i ran the system reset flow and recovered the aircraft after approximately 2-4min. while regaining full control of the aircraft by hand flying, i attempted to make contact with redacted app on redacted.x to inform them of my flight deviation, however due to the high volume of radio calls they were handling at the time because of severe weather, i never got a reply from air traffic control. after receiving no response, i switched frequencies and contacted redacted app xxy.xx to explain what had just occurred. this can be verified by the squawk code that i received to get visual flight rules flight following. by this time, i was able to resolve the issue with the trim and eventually land the plane safely . after deplaning the passengers, i immediately contacted our lead mechanic to inform him about the event that had just occurred while in flight. i explained that this was my first time experiencing something like this and he recommended additional measures to take in the event that this ever happens again. i, in no way, had any intention of this happening and sincerely apologize for the deviation or possible inconvenience this may have caused. i pray this type of malfunction or incident does not occur again. thank you for your time.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported the UAS collided with a street lamp during automated return-to-home.
text: i was conducting the pre-made mission. the mission was nearing its end and the end of its in-flight battery life when it reached the approximate area of the intersection location x. that is east of the parking lot. at that time, the battery life indicator in the head-up display (hud) indicated 18%. the x10 entered its auto return-to-home program and began its flight path back. as the x10 moved along its return-to-home path, i noticed something in its way as it approached the parking deck. because the parking deck was unlit, the object was hard to see. as the x10 moved closer, the object appeared to be tall and slender, black or dark in color. it quickly became apparent that the object in question was a street lamp. i stopped the mission, adjusted the altitude to put the x10 higher than the street lamp. i click the return to home button on the screen. i watched the aircraft start to move forward, but it also auto-adjusted its altitude, lowering itself. as i went to stop the x10 again to prevent the descent, a second street light appeared in view of the camera, and i lost connection with the aircraft. i immediately notified my immediate supervisor and launched a secondary x10 to access the scene and find the downed x10. i was the only one involved as the remote pilot in command. during the initial incident and the scene sweep, i did not observe any people in the area of the incident. i did observe a deployed chute from the x10, and the downed x10 appeared to be lying on the ground halfway between the dock and the light pole that was struck.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: Government UAS pilot reported the UAS struck power lines during a training flight.
text: i was flying a mavic 3 drone as part of my initial training to become qualified to fly drones. while flying around, i believed i was at 60ft agl when i was actually at 48ft agl and while piloting the drone, i approached power lines that were southeast of my location. i thought i had enough altitude to clear the power lines when i did not. in the future, i will slow down and scan the environment as i fly and ensure i have enough altitude to clear any obstacle or hazard that maybe present during flight.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude
synopsis: Center Controller reported an aircraft had an issue while in cruise flight and requested a lower altitude but due to another aircraft in the vicinity; the controller was unable to provide a lower altitude due to separation requirements.
text: i was side training on sector xx and aircraft x was flying south from redacted to redacted at fl330. just checked in at fl330 and requested fl310. i responded unable due to traffic. there was aircraft y 4 nm off his right wing and at fl310. aircraft x asked if fl290 was available and i said i could give him an off course vector and get it for him if he would like. the response was ok sure. i did a few things and then turned aircraft x 10 degrees to the left to work on lower and get the required 5 nm separation. as i made another few calls aircraft x requested priority handling. aircraft x needing lower. i replied aircraft x roger are you experiencing severe turbulence or something. aircraft x responded with we are having a pressurization issue and need lower. i said aircraft x i have your request. he said how about the requested priority handling. i said roger i cannot issue lower for traffic within 5 nm of you. aircraft x said that we are having a communication issue and i said i do not believe we are. aircraft y still has not checked on and i was unsure at this moment if i could turn aircraft x more if he was having this issue as we typically turn other aircraft.aircraft x immediately said you need to turn the other aircraft. i told aircraft x i am not talking to the other aircraft yet and that i cannot issue lower due to separation requirements and that aircraft x is the pilot in command of the aircraft and to take control of his aircraft as i am unable to issue lower. aircraft x said that he was descending. i said roger. while this was happening the instructor was coordinating with sector xy who was talking to aircraft y to see if they were there and if they could turn him. they did not have the aircraft. i heard all this with my other ear and then called in the blind to aircraft y. aircraft y was sitting on frequency and i had them turn xxr as by this point i had 4.8 nm and [runway] xx would get them clear in 5 seconds and a bigger turn would not have accomplished it faster. there was never a loss of separation and all the rest of the coordination was done without land line as they knew we were busy. i issued fl290 as soon as they were clear and then sector xz gave me control to fl190 and i asked if they wanted me to turn the aircraft x on course and they said they would take care of it and i gave control to sector xz and then shipped aircraft x to sector xz.this is a tough one. are we allowed to turn an aircraft that is an emergency hydraulic problem that is screaming for lower? the communication between the aircraft and controller needed to be better and more clear on what is going on as they checked on just requesting and were very short and not helpful for me to understand to gravity of his situation. the frequency tied up for this did make it to where aircraft y did not check on and had he i would have turned them sooner and did everything in a more timely manner to ensure the safe travel of aircraft x.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a cabin altitude warning occurred after descending from cruise flight that resulted in inaccurate cabin altitude indications as the checklists did not fully resolve the issue.
text: we were level at fl330 after descending from fl370 and the cabin altitude warning started sounding. both pilots accomplished their memory items for the associated checklist. communication was established quickly. when i looked at the cabin altitude indication, we were indicating 10, 000 ft. cabin altitude. we initiated an emergency descent to 10, 000 ft. msl and requested priority handling with redacted center. during the descent, i did notice at one point in the descent the pf had gone from lvl chng to vs and our ias was increasing. i commanded the pf back to lvl chng and to reduce speed back to 280 kt. ias as that is when the warning occurred and i knew the checklist would later say not to increase speed if structural damage is suspected. we had not reached that point in the checklist yet and had not made that determination. the cabin altitude warning checklist did not regain pressurization. according to the cabin altitude needle, we remained at 10, 000 ft. cabin altitude. later on when we were level at 10, 000 ft., the cabin altitude needle indicated as high as 50, 000 ft. the cabin altitude needle changed multiple times during the rest of the flight making indications that didn't make logical sense and i suspected it was an indication problem. my theory was further reinforced that prior to the event, there were no physiological symptoms reported by any crew member. regardless of this theory we still treated the problem as an actual depressurization. physiological symptoms of ear and sinus pain did occur for some crew members as a result of directions for manual control of pressurization from the checklist. the cabin oxygen masks never deployed. an uneventful approach and landing occurred. emergency personnel followed our aircraft to the gate.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 First Officer reported experiencing right engine EGT in caution range on initial climb resulting in the flight returning to the departure airport.
text: during initial climb right engine egt in caution range (highest obsered was 928) and was increasing. i was the pm of the flight, called out the condition when it was obsered. we monitor the condition for couple more seconds and the egt seems to be increasing so captain, the pf, disconected the autothrottle and pulled power back so that the egt stays in normal range. talked to the dispatch and maintenance control, decided to return to redacted.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737 Captain reported encountering continuous moderate and some severe turbulence on departure resulting in the aircraft making uncommanded turns. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft and proceeded to their destination.
text: after takeoff climbing on redacted sid encountered continuous mdt (moderate) turbulence initially as expected. as climb progressed ride was not improving, past redacted selected n1 max continuous thrust and climbed at 270kts for better climb performance. at redacted intersection for less then 30 seconds encountered sever turbulence, first officer was flying and airplane rolled up to 10 left bank uncommanded then right to 10 degree bank several times with turbulence making it hard to read flight instruments. i almost hit my head on my side window frame it was so abrupt. during this time airspeed rapidly decreased to about 260 and increased to about 280 several times. after about 30 seconds the severe turbulence subsided and went to moderate and then light turbulence. after the encounter i called back to the flight attendants to check on them and the cabin and they said they were all in their jump seats and everyone was in their seats. upon reaching cruise altitude when the lgt turbulence subsided i did a fa (flight attendant) check in call over the pa. response was fas and cabin were okay with no injuries. continued on to destination.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B737 Captain reported the flight crew did not notice the left start lever inadvertently moved to the cutoff position during cruise flight but was able to successfully restart the engine for an uneventful landing.
text: at approximately 90 minutes prior to touchdown, we completed the descent checklist and briefings. at about 40 minutes out, while maintaining fl360, i reached for the sun visor to detach and stow it. the visor fell inadvertently and landed on the aft section of the center console. while the visor struck the left start lever, neither pilot immediately realized the lever had been moved to the cutoff position.we noticed a discrepancy a few seconds later, a thrust lever split developed and the autothrottle disconnect light began flashing. initial diagnosis suggested a mechanical issue with the left thrust lever, i attempted to prevent the lever from retarding and tried to re-engage the autothrottle, but the system would not engage and the lever would not maintain its position.the first officer identified that the left start lever was in the cutoff position and verbalized the state while i observed the airspeed dropping. recognizing the engine loss, i reiterated that i had control of the aircraft and radios, and commanded the first officer to perform the appropriate checklist. we requested priority handling and initiated a descent. when the first officer requested to return the start lever to idle, i concurred, however, upon observing an engine egt over-temp, the first officer correctly returned the lever to cutoff to protect the engine.while the first officer was waiting for the apu to start, he contacted the flight attendants (fas) to inform them of the engine shutdown, they were instructed to wait for further guidance, though no brief was conducted at that time. we both agreed to delay the passenger announcement until the results of the engine restart were known.in accordance with the checklist, once we descended below fl240 and accelerated toward 300 kt., we initiated the engine restart. the engine restarted successfully at fl220 and 300 kt. once the engine stabilized and checklists were complete, the fas were updated and a passenger announcement was made stating that we had experienced abnormal engine indications which were successfully resolved.dispatch was notified of the engine shutdown and subsequent restart. i transferred radio communications back to the first officer and directed him to cancel the priority handling. we continued for an uneventful landing in redacted. following the shutdown checklist, we conducted a crew debrief. maintenance received a full briefing on the flight deck, and an entry was made in the electronic logbook (elb). we then briefed the chief pilot and dispatch. although we initially felt fit to continue our deadhead to redacted, the chief pilot later informed us of a schedule change for review, and we were released to go home.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter FOD
synopsis: Air carrier ground personnel reported poor lighting at SFO Taxiway K.
text: while towing a plane during night shift, which we normally do not do, we were coming down the dark kilo taxiway at the hangar and as we were struggling to view our kilo parking spot due to the post light within the vicinity being inoperative causing the area to be too dark, we unfortunately ran over an unknown wheel chock which was within our path. there were also large puddles that sit on top of the kilo line and also hurt the visibility of any fod within the area of travel.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: E175 flight crew reported there was miscommunication with the ground crew regarding brake release that led to the brakes not being set and the aircraft rolling back after being released from the tug.
text: while preparing to push back we had released the brake to be captured and once they had lifted us they realized that the tug was broken and that they would have to lower us and grab a new tug. during the lowering process they advised they will let us know when to set the brake. however they released us from the tug and we had rolled back about two feet and were never instructed to set the brakes until they gave us hand signals after they had moved the tug back.cause: lack of communication from the ground crew telling us to set the parking brake prior to releasing us from the tug even though we had asked multiple times.suggestions: if no response from ground we should have rung the horn to make they can hear us to make sure that they inform us to set the brake.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Fractional Captain reported the aircraft started to turn inbound while on the visual approach to follow a 'ghost localizer' and the flight crew intervened.
text: visual 13r: on a few occasions while vectored from the east for a visual approach to 13r the garmin captured a ghost localizer a few miles east of the localizer and the aircraft started to turn inbound. we intervened of course.suggestions: maybe a faa verification flight.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: A319 Captain reported smoke/fumes during departure climb. Flight crew returned to departure airport.
text: during climb out the first officer and i noticed a strong smell of burning oil. as we continued the climb the smell got stronger. at an intermediate level off below 10, 000 feet i called the flight attendants and asked if they smelled anything. all three flight attendants indicated that they we smelling the same thing and that the smell was getting stronger. at 10, 000 feet i handed the aircraft and radios to the first officer, she assumed pilot flying duties and i began gathering data to come up with a plan of action. we ( the first officer and i ) determined that it would be most prudent to return to redacted. i attempted to contact dispatch through the crew phone app over the flight deck wi-fi, even though the wi-fi was connected and working the crew phone app continued to give me errors so i sent a few messages to dispatch through acars. i advised dispatch of what was happening and eventually informed them that we would be returning to redacted. our initial plan was to burn down some fuel to get under max landing weight, after evaluating that i elected to return with an overweight landing. the first officer requested priority handling with air traffic control and coordinated a return to the field while i ran the appropriate checklist. we returned to the field on runway xxr, stopped on the runway, arff (airport rescue and firefighting) inspected the brake temperatures and after getting the all clear we taxied to gate xx, where the aircraft was taken out of service.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: E170 flight crew reported the weather and turbulence was more severe than expected and after executing a missed approach; diverted to an alternate airport.
text: this event happened while on the instrument landing system runway xx approach at approximately the redacted intersection or right around 10, 000 ft. we had just maneuvered around a heavy return on the radar for precipitation and we were cleared direct back to redacted [vor] to resume the approach. at this time we were only in moderate turbulence and moderate rain. as we descended on the approach the turbulence started to increase in intensity to the point where the stability of the aircraft was in question and the turbulence became severe in intensity. we elected then to conduct the missed approach, we informed tower of the missed approach and they told us to contact center. as we switched to center frequency the severe turbulence that we encountered became a windshear escape procedure. we conducted the escape procedure with the thrust levers set to maximum thrust and we were still descending. center was trying to contact us to get a pilot report but we had become task saturated in the recovery of the aircraft. the aircraft did eventually start to climb again but the severe turbulence existed through the missed approach altitude and through 16, 000 ft., making it difficult to determine if we were out of windshear. when we were able to resume communications again air traffic control finally cleared us to fl200 and asked of our intentions. we then informed air traffic control that we were diverting to redacted. we conducted the recovery exactly as trained. we flew the aircraft first, we navigated the aircraft in a tight mountainous area, and finally when
