intermediate altitude to attempt to continue to redacted. the crew stated that, based on the known bleed air malfunction, rising cabin altitude, terrain considerations, forecast turbulence, and passenger factors, they believed returning to redacted was the safest course of action.the chief pilot verbally stated the crew had not violated any regulations or company procedures. when the sic asked whether a report should be filed, the chief pilot advised against it because no regulatory violations had occurred. after further review, the crew determined the event met the criteria for voluntary safety reporting. in the 48 hours following the event, the sic developed a symptomatic sinus infection/cold. this suggests that during the flight, the sic was operating with an unknown yet underlying medical deficiency that, when combined with the prior heat exposure, likely accelerated the onset of hypoxia symptoms and exacerbated the physiological recovery time, further validating the decision to decline further flight duty under 14 cfr 61.53.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft
synopsis: Beech 76 instructor pilot reported the right engine throttle was not working and the engine was at full power; so the instructor shut down the engine prior to landing. Aircraft landed short of runway when the prop was not feathered.
text: after takeoff from redacted and leveling off at 8, 500 msl in the north practice area, we noticed the right throttle was not working and power stayed at full power. we decided to divert to redacted and planned on shutting down the right engine before landing. my multiengine student was the pilot flying in the left seat, and i was the instructor pilot not flying in the right seat. on extended right base to runway xxr i shutdown the right engine with the mixture control. i read through the engine securing checklist. before turning final it appeared we were on a normal glide path to runway xxr and extended the landing gear. on short final, approximately 300 feet agl, we realized we were going to land short of the runway. i selected the gear up to increase our glide, and we landed on the airport property approximately 75 feet right of runway centerline and approximately 500 feet short of the runway. when shutting down and securing systems, that is when i realized the right prop was not in the feathered position.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: PC12 pilot reported the loss of the left brake resulted in loss of aircraft control and taxiway excursion.
text: on day 0, during taxi for take-off, down taxiway 1, just past 2, taxing to runway xx, approaching the s turn in the taxiway with strong winds on the tail, i attempted to make the left turn and realized i lost my left brake with full left rudder deflection in i was still unable to make the left turn. once i realized i was not making the turn, i killed the power and maneuvered myself to the right to miss the taxi light and stopped in the grass. i notified the tower immediately that i was stopped in the grass and then with permission from the tower i got out of the aircraft and inspected the aircraft to confirm there was no damage to the aircraft, taxi lights, and grass. i got back in the aircraft and told the tower i was going to need a tug to remove the aircraft from the grass. then i contacted an fbo, they brought a tug down and pulled aircraft back to their ramp. during the initial taxi, just after park brake release, i confirmed both brakes were operating properly. i taxied for roughly 1 mile with both brakes working properly, before this incident occurred.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported while in hover on station at NYL had to take evasive action to avoid a converging agricultural aircraft during an NMAC event.
text: aircraft x was a customs and border protection, air and marine operations helicopter engaged in law enforcement duties. aircraft x had 3 personnel onboard, a pilot in command, a tactical flight operator (tfo) and a pilot in the passenger seat for observation training. aircraft x was responding a pursuit / rescue effort of 1 individual.at approximately xa:50l aircraft x was cleared into class d airspace from the northwest after requesting access to the northern portion of the airspace below 700msl. aircraft x then entered the class d airspace and proceeded direct to the canal to provide support for law enforcement. aircraft x was established in an out of ground effect hover to provide overwatch and video recording for law enforcement in pursuit of an individual hiding in a dam. aircraft x established an approximate hover altitude of 500msl/350agl. aircraft x was positioned in this specific hover location due to a small angle to view the individual resisting rescue efforts.at approximately xb:15l while pointing the aircraft northwest on a heading of approximately 340°, aircraft's pilot in command noticed an aircraft inbound from the west at the same altitude. the pilot in command waited a few moments to see what the aircraft was doing but noticed no change in altitude or direction. the pilot in command then decided to sidestep to the left/south and climb altitude to gain a better visual of the aircraft and make himself known. the sidestep to the south was to align with wind, and the climb was to get a downward angle on the aircraft and make aircraft x easily visible to the other aircraft, and lastly for obstacle avoidance. the pilot in command noticed it to be an agricultural aircraft but was unsure if the aircraft was in communication with tower. additionally, had aircraft x moved from its original hover position the aircraft may have passed overhead at either co-altitude or 100ft overhead. after the aircraft passed, aircraft x reestablished its previous position. the pilot in command then called nyl tower to request the tail number of an aircraft that just passed on the north side of the class d airspace. tower initially reported no contacts, however, shortly after tower reported it may have been aircraft y. aircraft x stated 'someone almost flew into me.' at which point another unknown pilot over the frequency stated, 'aircraft x i saw you.' aircraft x did not respond to the unknown pilot. shortly after, aircraft x was cleared to go off station and returned to nyl.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter FOD
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the Captain discovered during walkaround in PIT that a large amount of rock salt that was used for traction and grip in the gate area was ingested in the #2 engine; necessitating an engine change.
text: i worked a trip ending at xd:50 on day 0. i drove home at xf:15. i repacked for my current trip and received about 7 - 8 hours rest. i was active all day day 1. we started the current pairing with a scheduled redeye to redacted. the aircraft was late arriving. the ca was assigned a line check and we had a deferred acars/atsu (air traffic services unit) system. redacted was experiencing bad weather and high winds on arrival, with reduced visibility and a contaminated runway with reduced braking action. we then waited for a gate. we had to debrief the line check and did not leave the aircraft until 20 minutes or so after block in. we then missed the shuttle to the hotel and took a cab. our 10:51 rest turned into about 9 at the hotel - after having been awake all day day 1 and flying all night with elevated threats. even after 5:30 minutes of sleep i was still tired. we had 1 scheduled leg to redacted at xa:10. we had a short 12 - 13-hour layover, landing just before xd:00. the ca and i wanted to go.upon arrival we preflighted the aircraft. the weather in pit was 1/4 sm 200 vv in heavy snow with some lingering freezing precipitation and winds gusting above 30 kt. the rvr was at cat 1 mins as pit was just getting hit with the winter storm redacted had experienced. we discussed getting in, autolanding and possibly diverting to dtw. not ideal conditions, but we still were optimistic and wanted to try. it was my leg. while walking around the ca discovered a large amount of rock salt (used for traction and grip in gate area) ingested in the #2 engine. we called maintenance. they asked us to run the engine with passengers on board, we declined due to safety reasons and potential damage to the engine with people on board. the mechanic told us upon further inspection the engine had ingested those particles into the core and would need to be pulled. while waiting for a swap, we assumed that even if we left at xc:00 best case scenario (roughly an hour from when we deplaned) we would be on another min rest layover.already on a sleep deficit after a stressful redeye into stormy conditions and 9-hour day sleep layover, i did not feel safe operating into the same weather facing another min rest layover and almost guaranteed trip disruption in pit. i called fatigued. when i left the airport, the plane had been located but was not going to be ready for departure at xc:00 and was still in maintenance getting ready to be towed out. upon arrival at hotel - the hotel had not received my voucher even though it was reflecting in my schedule 30+ minutes after assignment. i was then on hold for 20 minutes with the hotel desk to no avail. i called the chief pilot who promptly assisted and i checked into the hotel at about xc:45, 50 minutes after arriving at the hotel.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Flight instructor with student on short final approach to RBL airport reported an NMAC with a helicopter on base leg.
text: operating visual flight rules short final had to take evasive action to the right in a turn away from helicopter operated in rbl.as we approached rbl airport made several calls that we were doing practice instrument flight rules approach to runway 33. we had several aircraft in pattern and departing. helicopter was doing touch and goes left down wind as we got within less than a mile the helicopter reported short approach and turned directly at us at which time i told pilot to start a right turn away from helicopter. i communicated on ctaf that your situational awareness was poor. never heard another word from helicopter. i'm always mindful of slower aircraft in pattern at uncontrolled airports but the timing was so fast form helicopter saying short approach then turning directly at us just enough time to power up and turn away from it.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: CL65 flight crew reported wingtip ground strike during landing due to windshear encounter.
text: on the date of the event, the flight departed redacted en route to redacted. during the initial climb, at approximately 1, 300 feet agl, the aircraft received a windshear warning. the windshear escape maneuver was executed in accordance with company procedures, including the application of maximum thrust. i assumed control of the aircraft from the first officer during the maneuver. once the aircraft was clear of the windshear condition and stabilized, air traffic control was notified of the event, and a pirep was issued for traffic in the area. control was then returned to the first officer.during the enroute phase, weather conditions along the route and at the destination were continuously monitored. given the reported gusty winds, i elected to assume pilot flying duties for the landing.transfer of control occurred during cruise flight. at that time, the autopilot was transferred to the captain's flight director, and the transponder was switched from position 2 to position 1, allowing adc 1 to provide the associated data.the approach to runway xx at redacted was stabilized by 1, 000 feet agl. surface winds were reported as approximately 160 degrees at 13 knots, gusting to 23 knots. the runway was wet, with braking action reported as good (5/5/5). the calculated gust crosswind component for runway xx remained within the crj-200 published crosswind limitations of 27 knots throughout the approach and landing attempt.during the flare at approximately 10 feet agl, with thrust at idle per normal procedure, the aircraft encountered a sudden and severe wind disturbance consistent with windshear or a strong localized microburst. this resulted in a rapid uncommand roll displacement, with the left wing rising and the right wing dropping. control inputs were applied as trained to counteract the roll and maintain alignment with the runway. within approximately less than 2 seconds, a second abrupt wind disturbance occurred during the same low-altitude flare regime.as a direct result of these sequential, uncommand wind disturbances in the flare, the left wingtip contacted the runway surface momentarily. the landing was completed without further incident, the aircraft was decelerated normally, and it taxied to the fbo at redacted under its own power.a post-flight walkaround inspection revealed damage to the left wingtip.this report is submitted solely to document the sequence of events, the prevailing environmental conditions (including low-level wind disturbances/gusts), and to support identification and mitigation of potential hazards associated with similar windshear/gust encounters during the critical flare phase on the crj-200 in gusty, wet runway conditions.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: GA pilot at cruise altitude reported an NMAC with another aircraft climbing into its path.
text: while cruising at 5500 ft on a heading of 110 i noticed an aircraft, aircraft y, on ads-b that was traveling on an approximately 150-180 heading and would appear to be on an intercept to my course. ads-b data showed the plane had come from the direction of n82, i noticed that the aircraft was continuing to climb on that course, as i was 'on the right' i would have had the right of way in this scenario. when i gained a visual they were approx. 500 ft below with no change in course or climb rate, with this i began an emergency climb to avoid this aircraft when the gtn650 collision avoidance began to alert. i also took evasive action and turned to position myself out of their path. this aircraft ended up flying directly under me, about 300ft below and horizontally by approx. 2-300 ft. then continued at an altitude of 5500. i am sure that we could have been extremely close to or could have collided if no action was taken and i did not have adsb-in. i believe that the other aircraft's lack of situational, or visual awareness was a direct factor, and if not, a blatant disregard for, or perhaps a lack of knowledge of, aviation collision avoidance rules. i confidently say that ads-b, and particularly adsb-in was responsible for the safe and uneventful outcome of the situation. maintaining visual and situational awareness at all times is extremely important for all aviators as well as knowledge of how to handle close encounters such as these.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A pilot outside their aircraft at the ramp fuel pump reported an arriving helicopter flew near them and the rotorwash caused the reporter's aircraft to move and a ladder to fall.
text: this is a description of dangerous and reckless helicopter operation that nearly resulted in substantial damage to my airplane, and could have severely injured me. the incident involved helicopter aircraft x at the redacted.i had parked my airplane in front of fuel pump #1 at the fuel island, had electrostatically grounded the aircraft, set the ladder in front of the wing in preparation for fueling, and had opened the pilot's door completely. i was at the fuel island terminal activating the pump when i noticed helicopter aircraft x approaching. the helicopter approached from taxiway 1 and proceeded towards its landing area at the fbo on a northerly track behind my aircraft. the helicopter flew within approximately 70 feet of my aircraft in the non movement area carrying substantial power which created significant rotor wash that started rocking and moving my aircraft. as i ran to my aircraft to stop its movement, the ladder in front of the wing began to fall forward. i caught the ladder and grabbed the wing strut to stop the aircraft's movement. the helicopter then pivoted to face east and land behind my aircraft, generating even more rotor wash and blasting my aircraft while i braced against the strut to prevent the aircraft from moving further. i could barely hold it and the aircraft moved about five feet forward and pivoted sideways due to the rotor wash. had i not caught the ladder, it would have struck my propeller causing substantial damage.had i been on the ladder, i would have been knocked off, and could be seriously injured. had i not been able to stabilize and stop the movement of my aircraft, substantial damage could have resulted. it was fortunate that the open door does not appear to have been damaged by the rotor wash (i will have a mechanic inspect it).after the helicopter landed and shut down i approached the pilot to discuss the incident. she stated that she saw my aircraft, and she explicitly said she saw the ladder and the open door, but proceeded anyway. when i pointed out the effect of her flight on my aircraft she said 'what am i supposed to do?' she maintained that she was perfectly justified in flying the way she did. i informed her that in more than forty years of flying i have never had a helicopter or any other aircraft operate in such a way as to endanger my aircraft with their rotor or prop or jet blast. she kept asking 'what am i supposed to do?' i asked why she did not avoid my airplane, and she stated that the helicopter is an emergency response vehicle. i asked if she was responding to an emergency, and she stated that she was not. she also said i should take it up with the fbo.i related the incident to an experienced helicopter flight instructor at redacted, who was appalled by the incident and stated that the helicopter operation was totally inappropriate and hazardous. he stated that the proper procedure would have been to set the helicopter down far from my aircraft and come in under low power on the skids. i suggest that [helicopter pilot] requires some remedial training on operations in the proximity of other aircraft, and have greater consideration for safe operations.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Repairman reported there has been a recent increase in shops using liquid Teflon tape; which acts as a lubricant; and causes the fittings to back off under aircraft vibrations and start leaking.
text: i run a pitot-static repair station and have recently found an increase in previous shops using liquid teflon tape and pipe dope" to seal their national pipe thread pitot-static fittings. when i do the 91.411 test years later, these fittings are failing the leak checks because the liquid sealant acts as a lubricant, causing the fittings to back off under aircraft vibrations and start leaking. the leak is immediately fixed when we remove the liquid sealant and replace it with the proper sealant tape. since we were able to fix the leak, we leased the aircraft for service. on the most recent aircraft, we told the owner about this, and he stated that the shop that did his pitot-static test years prior was telling him about how they had recently switched to using liquid teflon tape, "because it was so much easier to use." since we have been able to fix the leaks, we have been returning the aircraft to service, but wanted to make sure safety folks are aware of this issue and maybe help get the word out about the issue with using these liquid sealants. we did directly notify the shop that did the recent aircraft where we found the issue."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Tower controllers reported the SOP was amended without any input from the controllers with a new staffing procedure for local and local assist positions that has then led to a safety issue.
text: beginning on day 0, management implemented a new procedure for staffing the local and local assist positions. emphasizing the importance of local 2 (lc2) being staffed instead of the local assist (la) position regardless of situation. this involved amending the sop without any input from controllers of how this would affect operations.on day 9, there was a scheduled closure for runway xxr from xe:00 to xs:00 local. under current sop, the lc2 is responsible for all departures. however, since the primary departure runway was closed lc2 handed off control to lc1 for all departures. essentially, lc2 had zero traffic, but we were instructed to keep the position open instead of opening la to assist lc1 with arrivals and departures of runway xxl. we didn't have the staffing to open both lc2 and la and under current mandate we are to staff the lc2 position before la. as you can see this is an unsafe operation giving all the traffic to lc1 with no assistance and standing at a position with zero traffic to control. this opposes the intent of the new change to make the tower a safer environment.i recommend that the supervisor or controller in charge (cic) have the discretion to open and close the lc2 position based on the staffing and current traffic, focusing on the safety of the tower and airport instead of enforcing their new change.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported executing a missed approach after twice encountering wake turbulence on approach to SFO in trail of two heavy jets.
text: flying the approach following heavies for 28l and r we encountered wake turbulence. the right wing dropped, i wasn't sure what my control input was, however it felt approximately 90 degrees of control column deflection. no aural bank angle was heard either, so i assume it was not more than 30 degrees. in addition, i added thrust and applied forward pressure to the control column while regaining control. after we felt out of the wake, we continued the approach and i verbalized we would fly it higher to remain clear of the wake. maybe 15 seconds later while indicating 500 feet higher than the vpi (vertical path indicator) we encountered wake turbulence a second time. this time we informed air traffic control we will not continue the approach and were vectored back around for a visual approach to 28l.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A Lektro tug driver reported that the aircraft became disengaged from the tug during push back and rolled back into the chocks.
text: there was a breakaway on [gate] xx during the capture of an erj 175 and the lektro pushback. after receiving confirmation that the aircraft brakes were released via headset and proper hand signals were reciprocated, i proceeded to capture the aircraft to the lektro push tractor. upon the aircraft being pulled onto the nose gear cradle, the strap slipped off the hook of the winch. the aircraft rolled back into the chock placed at the aft of the nose wheel.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Tecnam P2012 pilot reported that during the initial climb the flight controls were stiff and did not feel correct.
text: when taking off controlled were stiff and was hard to push the yoke back. during climb making turns were stiff as well. my first officer was flying and i took controls to see how it felt. i confirmed that something didn't feel right and decided to return to land.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL
synopsis: A319 pilot reported a cabin pressurization malfunction during climb. Flight crew diverted.
text: the skin air outlet valve was placed on minimum equipment list 21-xx. we complied with the minimum equipment list procedure and verified that it had been signed off prior to flight in the logbook and cleared the fault on the engine warning display (e/wd). while climbing out we noticed that cabin was climbing faster than normal. we stopped climbing and requested a lower altitude. we advised air traffic control, descended, and diverted to redacted.cause: the initial logbook entry was made several hours earlier by a previous crew. while it was signed off appropriately we could have asked to speak to a mechanic to reverify the valve position and minimum equipment list procedures.we should have leveled off at 10, 000 when we noticed the cabin altitude climbing faster than normal. there was a brief discussion about the minimum equipment list 21-xx and if a higher cabin altitude was normal given the minimum equipment list. when it became clear that the rate was not slowing and the cabin altitude would exceed 10, 000 if we did not intervene we requested a got a descent.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported loss of aircraft control during push-back procedure.
text: started number 1 engine at the gate due to inoperative apu. began pushback using normal procedures and communication. after pushback to designated position, i was waiting for breaks set communication that i never received. called ground crew multiple times to ask if they wanted the breaks set, but no answer. tried to get the guide persons attention with breaks set hand signal and hand waving, but he was looking toward the tug, (which was not visible to me) and never saw me. next the aircraft began moving forward slightly which i acknowledged to the first officer they are still pulling us forward. about that same instant the first officer said break break, to which i applied the breaks immediately. the first officer was able to see the tug moving away from his side. at that time the guide person gives the breaks set hand signal to which i acknowledged. i gave the guide person a thumbs up to which he responded with thumbs up and salute and walked away.in an abundance of caution i decided not to move the aircraft and requested the crew chief return to the aircraft and establish communication. i wanted to confirm there was no damage to personnel or equipment to which he confirmed there was no damage and no issues. cause: i have no idea why they would disconnect the tow bar and disconnect communication before saying breaks set and hearing breaks set clear to disconnect interphone. there definitely needs to be some additional training for the pushback crew.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reported being low on approach from using an incorrect altimeter setting.  FO visually recognized this and adjusted flight path on the PAPI for a normal landing.
text: when cleared to descend via redacted arrival to redacted, i read back the clearance and the altimeter setting and subsequently entered the altimeter setting in the standby attitude indicator. when we completed the descent checklist we used the altimeter setting set in the standby attitude indicator for each pfd (primary flight display). just outside of the faf the first officer disconnected the autopilot and the auto throttle as was previously briefed. inside the final approach fix and somewhere between approximately 500 and 1000 feet the first officer asked me if i thought it looked like the automation was bringing us in on a very shallow approach. i agreed and instructed the first officer to maintain our altitude and transition to the papi. the first officer re-intercepted the glideslope and landed without incident.cause: when we were on the ground we realized that i had input a much higher altimeter setting in the standby attitude indicator which we later used for both pfd altimeter settings thus causing us to fly lower than the automation believed we were at.suggestions:--in the future i'll write down the altimeter setting from the atis or weather request and cross check it with the altimeter setting given on the arrival. if the setting is close then i'll use it for reference in the standby attitude indicator. if it's significantly off then i'll use the predetermined altimeter setting and query the controller.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported loud noise coming from cabin service door during cruise and cabin altitude climbing.  Pilots failed to transfer autopilot to the PF side which led to being high on the approach but landed normally at the diversion airport.
text: flight normal until incident. cruising at fl290 heard loud sound from flight deck door. checked pressurization and doors page then called fa. fa reported sound coming door, noticed cabin altitude increasing, called air traffic control and initialized a descent. advised air traffic control and diverted to redacted. upon 17000 feet noise ceased and pressurization stabilized. ca transferred controls to me (first officer) while he ran through qrh and communication with fa, pax and dispatch. when controls were transferred, unintentionally against standard operating procedure, autopilot and transponder were not switched to first officer side. this was due to high workload. which caused issues later on approach. after reaching 4000 feet with stable cabin pressure we entered a hold to burn gas to get below max landing weight. during which time checklists, communications and procedures were completed. the ca who was initially pf for the flight had me as pm take over due to his recent time off. the autopilot was on the ca side after exchange of controls. during the approach i had the autopilot captured the localizer in white needles due to the crosswind, and at approx 12 mile final switched to green needles and the loc captured. at the minimum glide slope intersect the gs captured but the autopilot did not descend despite the gs mode being captured which causes the aircraft to be high on approach. as pf i disconnected the autopilot and flew the approach visually which allowed for the aircraft to be back on the glide path and stabilized by 1000 feet for stabilized approach criteria.cause: high workload and task saturation due to high stress from pressurization loss and diversion. the transfer of controls should have included the autopilot and transponder as required by standard operating procedure.suggestions: in the future despite workload i will make sure to check the autopilot side in my scan.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air Taxi pilot reported a critical ground conflict involving an airport runway sweeper.
text: i was holding short of xxl and tower cleared me to cross xxl and continue taxi 1, 2 and to switch to redacted.x. i proceeded to cross xxl and made the switch, after crossing the runway i notice a yellow runway sweeper to my left on 3 moving a high rate of speed. after crossing 4 i notice the sweeper speed and direction was unchanged and we were on a collision course. immediately i held the power lever down and started threshold breaking, the aircraft successfully came to a halt allowing the sweeper to cross in front of the aircraft. air traffic control asked if i got the plow/sweeper number and i told them i was unable to.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Regional jet Captain reported being low on a visual approach into GSP while hand flying after autopilot failed to capture approach course.  Crew had received a late runway change and the navaid's were not operating which increased the crews workload.
text: during the arrival phase and landing in gsp. we received a runway change with the new weather of calm winds and clear skies. we initially planned for runway four, but it was changed to runway 22. during the vector, we were told to go direct to the final approach fix. once we were 3-4 miles from the final approach fix we were cleared for the approach and the aircraft did not auto transfer. the localizer. the first officer called it out and i switched to green needles. there were no id for the approach. i disconnected the autopilot and was visually flying the approach using the papi. while configuring for the approach. we were fully configured at 948 ft agl and landing checklist done at approximately 800 ft. at one point on the approach we got low with 4 red indication on the papis. the first officer, call it out, and i immediately started correcting and continued the approach to a normal landing. once on the ground we asked air traffic control if the instrument landing system was working they then said they will cycle the switch. cause:--lack of the localizer and glide slope increase work load and task saturation.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported a critical ground conflict with a de-ice truck.
text: while departing redacted on aircraft x a de-ice truck cut off the airplane, causing injury to both flight attendants. cause: we pushed back off gate xx and advised operations that we would need de-ice due to light snow and freezing conditions. the ramp crew pushed us back just past the 'zipper road' and onto the ramp area. the ramp is uncontrolled and the ground crew did not push us back far enough that we were able to make the turn without crossing the zipper road.once we completed the after start checklist, we advised ground and confirmed taxi instructions to the de-ice are. i looked and cleared right, looked left, then checked to make sure the radio tuning unit (rtu) was on the correct frequency. as i looked back to the right, a de-ice truck was approximately 30-45 degrees off the right side of the airplane. i called 'deice truck right side' and started to put my feet on the pedals when the captain hit the brakes. the deice truck went off the zipper road into the gate area to avoid us, and was traveling approximately 25-30 mph.as the airplane came to an abrupt stop, i heard a grunting noise from the cabin. we immediately advised ground control of the incident and the captain called the flight attendants to see if they were injured. i could overhear the captain ask about how the flight attendants hit the ground, and we started the process of deciding to gate return.after confirming with several people from ops, duty pilot, and the flight attendants, the flight went on without further incident. it should be noted that both flight attendants were the ones who had and made the final decision to continue the flight. upon arrival at our destination we asked that paramedics meet us at the gate to ensure there was not any unseen injuries, or any other medical issues that could arise.one flight attendant was taken to the hospital and the other was released and continued on with the rest of their flying schedule. suggestions: push the airplane back further, retrain the driver of the truck.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: DA40 Instructor and student pilot reported their aircraft was cut off on a taxiway by a service truck.
text: taxing back to ramp from xxl on taxiway 1 when a ground vehicle pulled out in front of us on the roadway by taxiway 2, requiring student pilot and i to completely stop taxiing. the vehicle was in sight the entire time so we didn't have to come to a sudden stop but we did have to come to a complete stop before continuing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Corporate Captain reported diverting to a suitable airport because the fuel temperature was below the limitation.
text: fuel tank red crew alerting system message in flight at fl410cause: fuel temperature fell below -40 degrees celsiussuggestions: followed checklist and interest of safety diverted

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types
synopsis: Military pilot reported communication difficulties with ATL Center due to frequency bleed-over and interference from TYS Tower and GMU Tower.
text: aircraft x ferry flight originating from redacted enroute to little rock afb, ar at fl360. atl center assigned frequency was 257.775 which also interferes with tys tower (257.8) and causes center frequency bleed-over. missed multiple calls from center due to being stepped on by tys tower transmissions.this exact situation replicated itself with atl center assigned frequency 257.675 interfering with gmu tower (257.7) causing missed calls and comms from center being stepped on by tower transmissions. recommend de-conflicting these frequencies by a margin greater than .025.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported an NMAC with an aircraft arriving at the same airport. GA pilot took evasive action.
text: i was pilot in command in aircraft x enroute to sbp cruising at 10, 500ft approximately 40nm east of sbp. flight conditions were clear visual flight rules in stable air. i received an adsb traffic warning 6 o'clock high. observing the garmin display, and recorecting the zoom it appeared an aircraft was overtaking my position while descending from above me, with less than 700ft of vertical separation, and a 80knot closing rate. i identified the aircraft from it's adsb transponder and made a radio call on 121.5 to that tail number, which received no response. i made a 45degree descending left turn down to 10, 000ft until making visual contact with the aircraft. due to the aircraft proximity during the evasive maneuver i did not have high fidelity situational awareness of the other aircraft's location until making visual contact. aircraft y had been enroute visual flight rules from redacted to sbp on what appears to be a direct course at 12, 500ft. aircraft y began its decent into sbp, at 174kt. at this time aircraft x was 1.6nm ahead, 1000ft below and at 130kt. aircraft y accelerated to 210kt in the decent, making the closing speed at the incident 80kt.aircraft x made an evasive descending right turn. there was a less than 200ft of vertical separation, less than 200ft of horizontal separation and aircraft x was unable to make contact with aircraft y on 121.5. the evasive action allowed visual contact to be made, and both aircraft arrived without incident to sbp. in summary: aircraft y began an enroute decent, and accelerated during the denent. uncertain of obstruction or telemetry inside the aircraft y aircraft, the pilot was likely unaware of the high speed overtake on the same course and position. aircraft x was only able to identify the situation through adsp and garmin 275 display, and made evasive action avoiding a mid-air collision. it is recommended contact be made to the operator of aircraft y to discuss if the onboard adsb equipment was able to identify the imminent collision, and if so were warning systems functional, to ensure the operator scans the airspace in front of the aircraft when making course/altitude changes, and to remind the operator maintaining auxiliary radios on 121.5 could have allowed air-to-air deconfliction over radio communications.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A Cessna 175 pilot reported an intermittently rough running engine; resulting in a successful diversion to a nearby suitable airport.
text: enroute from redacted to redacted, at 6500 in class b talking to redacted approach on redacted.x, engine experienced sudden loss of power. ran through standard skylark emergency procedure. engine restarted after adjusting power/mixture/carb heat, but started cycling in a pattern of running 5-10 seconds, not running 5-10 seconds. pointed towards redacted and made a precautionary landing. not carb icing or fuel venting. suspect carburetor issues.no injuries or damage.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Small transport pilot reported a NMAC with a helicopter while in the traffic pattern.
text: approaching redacted crossing south of runway xx-xy a position report was made with the intention of entering a left downwind. a left downwind was entered at 2000 ft agl and a second position report was made descending to 1550 ft. a third position report was made turning left base at 1300 ft. no traffic reports by other aircraft were heard. as the aircraft was about to turn final a helicopter was spotted slightly below the left wing and about 200 ft to the left. both aircraft took evasive action and contact was averted. the aircraft x traffic alert system (tas) did not give any alerts. a safe landing was completed and the helicopter made a low pass over the runway and continued doing pattern work. after the roll out was completed comm 2 was noted to not be on the correct frequency. i believe the problem was having the incorrect frequency in comm 2. although i made position reports, they went unheard. through vigilance of both pilots an accident was averted. the tas system in the aircraft x from time to time will give a crew alerting system (cas) message that it is has failed. i don't recall seeing a cas message to that effect. i will ask my mechanic to check on this and in the future will use the pneumonic 'w.i.r.e.' for weather, instruments, radios, environment and will also ensure that is added to my check list.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported an NMAC with inbound traffic that flew over them on final approach.
text: i am an instructor doing a pattern lesson with one of my students using runway xx at redacted airport. my student had just turned left base for runway xx when the pilot of aircraft y (vans rv8q) made a radio call for a '5 mile initial' for runway xy at redacted. runway xy is a grass strip that is parallel to runway xx. i clarified over ctaf frequency that they are landing runway xy, which the rv8 pilot confirmed. my student continued to fly the pattern while i scanned for the inbound traffic. i noticed on adsb that the rv8 looked like it was lining up for runway xx, and was flying 200 feet above our current altitude less than a mile behind us(according to adsb). at this point we were on short final for runway xx, and i took controls from my student. i dove to lose altitude and watched the rv8 fly ~200 feet over us. i told the rv8 pilot over ctaf that he was lined up for runway xx, not runway xy. he responded over ctaf by saying 'we don't have a runway xy'. i informed him that we do, to which he responded 'whatever'. i performed a go-around and the rv-8 did a left break-to-land on runway xx. the rest of the flight continued without incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: B737 Captain reported failure of fire detection system and return to departure airport.
text: the aircraft operated was under minimum equipment list for a failed b fire detection loop. a loop only selected per the minimum equipment list and tested ok on preflight. shortly before reaching cruise altitude we noticed the fire loop a fault light flashing intermittently. a message was sent to dispatch and we were patched through to maintenance control. after some confusion in relaying the system failure due to poor radio connectivity we sent an acars to maintenance control explaining that we had a failed b fire loop and now a fault in the remaining a fire loop. maintenance control advised it was captain's discretion whether to continue the flight or not. after conferring with the first officer we decided it would be better to divert back to redacted because we had no working engine fire detection system on either loop. our thinking is that we had another 4 hours of flying ahead and it would be bad to continue since it would be possible to have an engine fire with no flight deck indication. we coordinated with air traffic control for a return to redacted and ran the appropriate checklists. flight attendants and passengers were notified. we ran the checklist for overweight landing and opted to land on the longest runway, xxl, with auto brakes 2 to avoid hot brakes. we advised air traffic control that we wanted fire and rescue to examine the aircraft after landing to verify no smoke or fire on the brakes and no signs of an engine problem. air traffic control advised that if we wanted the trucks they would have to request priority handling for us. we agreed out of an abundance of caution to have fire and rescue look us over after landing. subsequent approach and landing were uneventful. upon exiting the runway post flight inspection showed no signs of engine problems or hot brakes. we taxied uneventfully to the gate. maintenance entries were made for an overweight landing at 174, 000 pounds and the failed fire detection loops.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Citation Excel Captain reported a landing gear handle malfunction where the gear would not retract during the climb; then the handle would not return to the down position. The handle was forced into the down position; then returned to the departure airport and landed safely.
text: redacted was meant to be a fuel stop on our trip. when we fueled up and departed redacted, called for gear up, the gear handle raised but the gear did not retract. we continued to climb to a safe altitude of 6000 feet and get vectors from the controller while we ran the checklist. the gear handle would not go back down to the 'gear down 'position for some time. upon reaching the point of the 'gear will not retract' checklist, it called for gear handle down and with some force, the handle finally moved to the down position. the gear indicators throughout the entire time remained 'three green' down and locked. there was never a 'gear unsafe' red light illuminated. there was never a hyd pressure light illuminated to indicate pressure to gear . never received any other abnormal indications. once sufficient fuel had been burnt off to make landing weight, we returned to redacted with airport rescue and firefighting positioned just in case. the landing was uneventful. two days later we ferried plane for maintenance on a ferry permit. crew was fine and passengers were sent another aircraft for remainder of their trip.suggestions: the checklist for 'gear will not retract' addressed some of what we were seeing but not everything. our concern was that the gear handle being left in the up position might cause a gear collapse on landing if left in that position. luckily, we were able to move it back to the down and locked position. with the gear handle down and the gear never having retracted, the checklist was complete. i believe that ultimately the entire gear handle mechanism got replaced but would like to know for sure what failed in the system to cause this problem.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: CL-350 Captain reported hearing a loud abnormal noise coming from the cabin door area during climb and returned to departure airport. The reporter stated there needs to be a more specific MEL for a malfunctioning main cabin door.
text: door minimum equipment list for door that would only close halfway. departing redacted at around 3000 feet loud abnormal noise coming from cabin door area, continued climb to 5000 per air traffic control instructions monitored noise level. no cas message displayed, door was locked. because the pressurization appeared to be working hard and not pressurizing combined with ears sensing pressure changes with a pulsating feel diverted we decided to return to base (rtb) due to the traffic volume and task saturation we could only send a very brief acars message to a chief pilot. landed at redacted xxl without incident. upon arrival at fbo, line personnel who had assisted us with the door told us he could see a cable protruding along the side of the main cabin door that wasn't there when we left.we debriefed the flight. we made a good call to return based on the information available to us. upon closing the aircraft we did note that the metal retraction cable for the door retraction system seemed jammed and was not retracting. we did discuss that as a result of this experience a possible safety suggestion it seems there needs to be a more specific minimum equipment list for a main cabin door that is only closing halfway and binding vs. the electric motor burned out so as to identify binding or parts within the retraction system that are not operating according to design.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL
synopsis: A319 pilot reported a VENT SKIN VALVE FAULT ECAM message during climb; resulting in the cabin altitude climbing above 10000 ft. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed.
text: after takeoff, ecam of vent skin valve fault which was already under minimum equipment list. ran ecam. climbing through 10000 ft, cabin altitude above 10000 ft and donned o2 masks and requested priority handling to descend to 10000. conferred with dispatch and diverted. put into logbook

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported setting an improper altitude below the FAF in the autopilot system while descending on a visual approach resulting in a terrain warning. The flight crew immediately climbed to the FAF altitude.
text: descending into tri cities we were cleared a visual approach early. we were making a downwind turn when i referenced the chart to set the bottom altitude. inadvertently the faf was not chosen and a different lower and larger(appearing on the chart) altitude that was next to it was chosen. this lead to a lower altitude bugged than should have been. when we started looking low, we referenced the chart which is when we heard the terrain alarm. we climbed immediately to the faf altitude.cause: inadvertently bugging the incorrect altitude referenced from the chart.suggestion: verify selected altitudes that are put in with the chart more than once. recognize and correct sooner with visual outside references.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: SR20 Flight Instructor and their student conducting a touch and go at a non-towered airport reported a conflict with opposite direction aircraft on short final.
text: on rnav xx approach at redacted, landing runway xx. >5kt tailwind, which per recommended procedure, we are to use runway xx. two aircraft ahead circle xy. first aircraft was not as big of an issue, as we were still 2 mile final when they were in the upwind of runway xy. the second aircraft aircraft y was still breaking off of the rwy xx approach, so should have been a non-factor. we make our short final call, and shortly after, aircraft y makes a base call. i call again clarifying we're lower and closer to the airport (implying that we have the right of way per 91.113 (g)). we touch down, and prepare for the go around, and they turn final and continue to descend. i have to call on the frequency several times that we were already on the runway before they went around. traffic got within 300' of us, as they barely offset to the side of the runway performing their go around. we continued our touch and go once they were clear, and departed to finish the lesson.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: ERJ 175 First Officer reported multiple avionics failure during departure climb. Flight crew returned to the departure airport and landed safely.
text: around 6, 000 feet the auto throttle failed and i called for the captain to cancel and identify. i asked the captain to delay running the checklist until we got to 10, 000 feet as it was busy. i was in controlling the throttle while monitoring the airspeed and the other instruments. after reaching 10, 000 feet, the captain completed the after take-off checklist and i took the radios and flight controls so he could focus on running the qrh. the captain ran the qrh for auto throttle fail" and we waited 10 seconds and attempted to reengage the auto throttles which remained failed. we decided to continue the flight to our destination without the use of the auto throttles. i gave the radios back to the captain. the captain notified air traffic control that we would need to amend our final cruising altitude as we were no longer able to enter rvsm. air traffic control then asked if we needed any assistance and the captain replied "no". as we continued to climb and at approximately 14, 000 to 15, 000 feet the aircraft switched into flight path angle (fpa) mode from flch mode. i tried re-engaging flch mode, with no success. i changed the fpa to 3 degrees up and started monitoring the vsi and asi. next the aircraft went into roll mode. i attempted to engage hdg (heading) mode, with no success. then the auto pilot disengaged. as we continued climbing through 16, 000 feet, we received a total air temperature (tat) 2 failure message on the eicas and we lost the flight management system speeds. we entered imc and we received an icing conditions eicas message. we were having multiple cascading failures that were increasing our workload while heading to our destination. we decided to return to the field. i leveled us off at 17, 000 feet and the captain requested a descent to exit icing conditions with vectors back to redacted. we were given a descent to 13, 000 feet and a heading to return to the field. the captain briefed the flight attendants and built, bugged and briefed the rnav approach to runway xxl into redacted. we regained flight management system airspeed, while descending through 10, 000 feet.i hand flew the aircraft for the remainder of the flight and completed a successful landing without further incidence. the emergency equipment had not been requested, but they rolled the trucks as a precaution."

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported receiving erratic glideslope movements and glideslope aural warnings despite the flight crew following the PAPI with a perfect path and stated that the ILS equipment at POB Airport needs to be checked and calibrated.
text: arrival into pob airport we were cleared for a visual approach for runway 23. it was day visual flight rules with calm winds and we briefed for a visual approach backed up by the instrument landing system for runway 23. once cleared i selected direct aceno what is the iaf for the approach and about 2 miles from aceno i selected direct nayin. the first officer flew a visual approach and once the localizer and glideslope were captured the glideslope showed erratic movements 2 degrees up and down and we got the glideslope aural warnings. the first officer continued following the papi with a perfect path. at about 300 feet we had continuous glideslope aural warnings all the way to the flare being on the papi path.cause: i think the instrument landing system equipment at the airport needs to checked and calibrated, i don't think our airplane instrument landing system equipment was the cause.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported engine vibrations and return to departure airport.
text: during climbout from redacted, #1 engine vibrations fluctuated wildly, oscillating between 2.0 and 3.5. high vibrations continued until power was reduced to maintain cruise altitude. i contacted dispatch through vhf radio and we did a 3 way call between myself, dispatch, and maintenance control. maintenance informed us during the conference that the #1 engine had a recent history of several writeups for high vibrations and that there was a technical item assigned to that engine to track its performance. i expressed my concern that this aircraft was assigned to a destination like redacted (our original destination) given its history. the three of us agreed that it would be prudent to return to redacted given the limited contract maintenance available in redacted and the high terrain in the area that places a high demand on the engines in the event of a go-around or takeoff from runway xx. at the time we were about 6, 000 lbs over max landing weight, so we coordinated with air traffic control to hold until we were under max landing and we returned to redacted. known history of bad performance on an engine that was also assigned to a destination which has limited contract maintenance.aircraft with engines that have a recent history of questionable performance should not be assigned. the lower display in the 737 should be turned on during the after takeoff checklist so that all secondary engine indications are displayed to catch this and other engine situations that slowly creep up on the crew. the time to be prepared and do something is early before the situation arises, not when the display automatically pops up. this should be standardized across all boeing fleets.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported hydraulic system malfunction and diversion to a nearby suitable airport.
text: just prior to beginning our descent we noticed the green hydraulic quantity was very low just above the amber. once we started the descent just prior to the fix redacted on the zzzzzx arrival, we got an amber hyd g eng 1 pump lo pr ecam. i continued as pf while my captain ran through the ecam procedure. he had me fly the aircraft and run radios while he dealt with this procedure. we elected to level off and enter a hold over redacted to develop and analyze a plan. the ecam had us shut down the green eng 1 pump which displayed numerous inop systems, including the possibility of manual gear extension, gear retraction, nosewheel steering, etc. after advising maintenance, dispatch, and fa's we determined the best course of action was to request priority handling and divert to redacted. i continued flying while my captain contacted redacted ops, reviewed procedure manual pages and briefed fa's of a precautionary landing in redacted. we notified redacted tower we would be stopping on the runway and would need possible tow off runway as well as airport rescue and firefighting (arff) to give a quick inspection. joining final for runway xxl, we turned on green eng 1 pump as directed by the status page appr procedure. we regained back all our inop systems and the aircraft was operating as normal. we landed as normal, came to a stop, and the captain made a pa to the passenger notifying that arff would be inspecting the aircraft out of caution. we were able to taxi back to the gate under our own power with no further issues. event was caused by hydraulic abnormalities. only mitigation is to continue to be proficient in emergency procedures.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Cessna Citation Sovereign First Officer reported an uncommanded descent from the auto pilot while changing automation modes.
text: during descent on the redacted arrival at redacted, i selected vertical speed (vs) mode from vnav in preparation for transitioning altimeter settings. upon disengaging vnav while maintaining vs mode, the aircraft began an uncommanded rapid descent.i immediately disengaged the autopilot and manually corrected the flight path. after crossing redacted, i was able to stabilize the aircraft and regain full control. i then completed the necessary transitions and subsequently re-engaged vnav without further incident.cause: creating a comfortable transition for passengers.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported cabin door seal failure in cruise and return to departure airport.
text: just after reaching cruise altitude at 36, 000ft with the first officer as pf, a fa called from the aft galley saying there was a loud wind noise coming from door 2l in the back of the aircraft. i checked the overhead panel and verified no door lights were on, the cabin altitude was steady at 8000ft with a differential 7.8psi. i had the fa verify the door 2l handle was secure in the latched position and she verified the door was secure mechanically. the fa said the ambient noise was so loud that they would need ear plugs to continue the flight. i could also hear the loud ambient noise through the intercom as we talked.i told the fas that the door seal most likely failed or did not engage properly, and that the door was mechanically secure so there was no safety risk of it opening inflight. i told the fas that i would have a conference call with maintenance control and dispatch to come up with a plan, but most likely we would be returning to redacted.i informed the fo/pf who had been listening in what the situation was and had the first officer continue to manage the aircraft and air traffic control coms while i talked to dispatch and maintenance control. after establishing a phone patch with dispatch and maintenance control i relayed the information from the fa and maintenance control had me verify the cabin altitude and dif pressure readings. ultimately a decision was made to return to redacted and that the airplane would be landing about 7500-8000lbs over the max structure landing weight. i had the first officer coordinate with air traffic control new clearance to return to redacted and to request lowest altitude possible to burn off as much fuel as possible on the return as well as attempted to lower the cabin alt and reduce the ambient noise if possible. an emergency was not declared at the time.i did a brief with the purser, then made a cabin pa for the passengers explaining the situation. after referencing the 737 flight manual for overweight landing i ultimately decided that due to our landing weight being close to 8, 000lbs over the max structure the need for runway xxr in redacted (longest available) as well as the possibility of hot brakes after landing that requesting priority handling and having fire trucks on standby for the brakes was the most conservative plan of action. i informed air traffic control of the change of status to priority handling and why, then requested runway xxr and to have the fire trucks on standby for a brake check once clear of the runway. air traffic control passed along all the information and verified our fob and sob. i did another briefing revision with the purser due to the change to priority handling status. i then made a pa to the cabin about the reason for the fire tucks meeting the aircraft after landing.after the fmc was set up, briefings and checklists were complete i took over pf duties of the aircraft. i did this due to the need for a soft landing and the first officer was coming back form a leave as we were conducting the first officer's requalification training on this trip.a soft landing was made with a vsi of about -210fpm (3.5fps) at 153, 800lbs landing weight. after clearing the runway the fire crew did a circle around the aircraft and reported the brakes looked normal with no glowing or any signs of overheating. a normal taxi to gate xx was made and aircraft parked and passengers deplaned. maintenance techs met the aircraft and took the details from me after i sent in the log book reports for the door and overweight landing. flight redacted continued out of gate xx with a different aircraft 90 min later.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a galley fire occurred during climb; but was extinguished by the flight attendants. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: approximately 15 minutes after departing redacted and climbing through 28, 000 for fl330 over location x the cabin interphone call chimed. as pilot monitoring i took the call and was alerted by a very panicked flight attendant that there was a fire in the forward galley. details were not very clear but i understood they were getting fire extinguishers and starting to fight the fire. without delay i hung up the phone and took control of the aircraft. the first officer immediately informed air traffic control and we began a turn and descent back towards redacted. once the aircraft was on the desired path towards redacted we were able to speak with the purser and found that the fire was contained to the forward galley oven and had been extinguished using one halon extinguisher. control was transferred back to the first officer.we communicated with air traffic control the fire was out but since there was no way to be sure it wouldn't reignite we continued to redacted and informed them that it would be an overweight landing. dispatch was notified via satcom.a pa was made advising the passengers that we were heading back to redacted.the fas were briefed.a normal approach and landing was made on xxl.we were met by airport vehicles to ensure no issues with brakes or tires.after inspection we taxied to the gate without incident, crash fire rescue (cfr) boarded the aircraft and ensured the fire had been fully extinguished.passengers were deplaned and a new aircraft took them to redacted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported hydraulic system failure and continued to their destination. Hydraulic failure resulted in inoperative nosewheel steering.
text: in cruise observed master caution followed by yellow hydraulic reservoir low level ecam on aircraft x ( a319 ). ecam was accomplished, maintenance notified by calling dispatch and patched through. maintenance advised that nose wheel steering was on the yellow system for this aircraft as opposed to our classic a319/320. however the aircraft was not showing it as in-op system but i deferred to maintenance control. requested priority handling, advised we would be stopping on the runway and would need a tow. maintenance coordinated the tug to be standing by. worked through remaining checklists and landing performance, i took over as the flying pilot and we landed on xxr in redacted without incident and stopped the aircraft roughly halfway down the runway, the nose wheel steering was in fact inoperative. emergency vehicles checked us out and mentioned fluid all down right side of aircraft, maintenance hooked up the tug and towed us in to gate xx. maintenance came on board and verified fluid all over the aircraft. called the chief pilot and continued on duty for our next flight to redacted.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Vehicle; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A wingwalker reported during pushback maneuvers; the towbar bypass snapped and the aircraft rolled forward into the pushback tug.
text: crew was pushing out flight redacted heading to redacted. while our driver was pushing the plane back he was told to reverse to make space for other aircraft. this flight was leaving from gate xx. the towbar snapped on the alley way. while the driver reversed the towbar began to snap and plane kept on going forward towards pushback until it came to a complete stop. at no moment did the towbar cross the red line so it was odd how the towbar just gave out and snapped. this is what i saw as i was wingwalking the flight. the moment i realized the event occured was when i heard the by pass pin snapped. cause: i don't know exactly why this occurred as i was not the driver. as i was wingwalking from my vantage point the towbar never crossed the red line, i believe the towbar gave out due to the weight pushing back towards the towbar and it snapped. once the plane had stopped, maintenance and managers came out to observe what had happened. suggestion: i would suggest that we due monthly check ups on all towbars to make sure they are still in good shape to withstand the weight of the planes.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Air carrier Lead Technician and Inspector reported they failed to connect a cannon plug during a fuel pump replacement and failed to inspect the pump prior to installation; which caused a fuel leak on the subsequent flight.
text: on day 0, we had aircraft x enter ron (routine overnight) with pump 2a on minimum equipment list and pump 2b requiring removal due to high time. the mechanics removed and installed the two pumps, and the aircraft flew to redacted. when the aircraft landed, they noticed fuel leaking from the belly of the aircraft. redacted says fuel pump 2b canon plug was not connected and pump 2a was missing an o-ring which caused the leak. the mechanics states that the pump comes with o rings already pre-installed and that they remember connecting the canon plug. per the maintenance manual the fuel pumps are not rii (required inspection item) since they are internal tank components which internal tank components do not require leak check and no item under ata 28 requires rii for operational check (system check). the maintenance manual states that the preinstall and leak check on fuel tanks panels is rii. i watched one of the techs prep the panels and installed new o rings and lubricants that the amm (aircraft maintenance manual) called for. i did an area check prior to panels being installed to verify no tools or unwanted materials were inside of the tanks. i then stayed nearby to watch the install of the panels and watched the panels be torqued. after, the mechanic finished torquing the panel i verified each bolt by physically going over every bolt with the torque wrench. i then watched the leak check for the panels and after transferring fuel into the center tank there were no leaks noted from the fuel panels.we have one specific mechanic that works here that is a danger to our hanger and he needs to be spoken to because he is constantly messing things up.suggestions: mechanics need to do a better job when it comes to working on the aircraft. they need to make sure they are following the amm tasks references to ensure this does not happen again.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a near miss during final approach with two ground vehicles sitting on the runway. Flight Instructor performed a go-around.
text: me and my student turned final for runway 17 at ela, we began to notice some red lights that were out of place on the runway. we made calls on frequency asking if anyone was on the runway and decided to do a low pass after no answer. as we were passing at about 300' agl we began to see 2 vehicles move and exit the runway, as they exited we could see that these vehicles were police vehicles. there were 2 police vehicles sitting on the runway with no red/blue or hazard lights. the only reason we saw them was because one car had its brake lights on. after the pass and watching them both clear the runway we decided to land. under slightly different circumstances something like this could end bad quick, say we were landing on the side of the runway closer to them and then our landing light not work this could have ended very bad very quick. summary is that 2 law enforcement vehicles were sitting on a dark runway at night with no hazard lights on.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A pilot entering the traffic pattern to a non-towered airport reported a NMAC with an aircraft performing aerobatic maneuvers.
text: i was flying a short cross country training flight. i was on an instrument flight rules flight plan for the entire flight. prior to the flight, i checked the notams for my destination and was made aware of aerobatic activity within 1nm of the airport. i was cleared by redacted center for the visual approach and switched to the ctaf. i made my intentions to overfly midfield 500 feet above pattern altitude to enter the left downwind for runway xx clear. i re stated my intentions multiple times 10nm out, 5nm out, 3nm out, and 1nm out. i did not hear any communication of an aircraft doing aerobatic activity above the airport. as i overflew midfield, i saw an aerobatic plane approximately 500 feet from me. as we saw each other, the pilot said that i was not supposed to be flying west of the field. i continued a teardrop entry into the left downwind making all appropriate radio calls, did a touch and go, and departed back north. neither the notam or the chart supplement prohibited me from overflying midfield from the west or using left pattern for xx. chart supplement does state that runway xy is right traffic when aerobatic activity is in effect.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: C152 Flight Instructor reported while training traffic pattern operations encountering another aircraft in close proximity resulting in the Flight Instructor taking evasive action to avoid a collision with the other aircraft.
text: while conducting instructional traffic pattern operations at redacted in a c152, we were established in the standard left traffic pattern at approximately 1000 feet agl.we were flying a normal pattern sequence. during the turn from crosswind runway xx to downwin runway xx, another aircraft (c172) approached from the west and entered the pattern area on a converging path.the aircraft appeared suddenly in my left-front quadrant, which is a known blind spot during a left turning maneuver. the distance was estimated to be approximately 200-300 feet, creating an immediate traffic conflict.at the time of the event, a student pilot was flying the aircraft. i immediately took control and executed evasive action to ensure safe separation.it was unclear whether the other aircraft was established in the pattern or had made appropriate radio calls. the aircraft did not appear to follow a standard 45-degree entry or otherwise integrate into the established traffic flow.no collision occurred, however, the proximity was significantly closer than expected for normal traffic pattern operations.this event highlights the importance of proper traffic pattern entry procedures, vigilant visual scanning, and clear radio communication at non-towered airports, especially during instructional flights.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
