anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported experiencing fuel exhaustion resulting in the pilot making an off airport landing in a field and reporting no injuries or damage to the aircraft.
text: in the interest of safety, i am writing this report to help pilots be more aware of the risks of improper fuel planning. on day 0, a passenger and i made our way to redacted for a joyride. when we arrived at the airport, i immediately began my preflight with aircraft x. my standard walk-around includes checking all control surfaces, propeller, tires, brakes, oil, and fuel. fuel is always my last task. on this particular day, i visually verified that both tanks were full. i also strained the fuel to ensure no contaminants were present. since this was a day visual flight rules joyride, i calculated the distance and time we would be flying, and it was agreed we would just go where we wanted to.the flight was uneventful for the first portion as we made our way from redacted to redacted at 4, 500 feet, where we conducted a landing and then flew up to location x for pictures. we then flew from location x to redacted, where i flew the rnav xx approach. at that point, i decided not to stop and check the fuel and performed a low approach, believing i had plenty of fuel to make it back to redacted.i knew the aircraft held 38 gallons of usable fuel and estimated a burn rate of 8 gph. at the time we executed the low approach at redacted, we had only been flying for approximately 3 hours, which i believed was sufficient to return to redacted.i then began setting up for a practice rnav xy approach into redacted. after crossing redacted on approximately an 8-mile final and descending through about 2, 500 feet, the engine began to sputter. i checked the total flight time, which was approximately 4 hours and 5 minutes. i immediately looked for the nearest airport on the gps and initiated a 180-degree turn to attempt to return to redacted, which was approximately 4 miles behind us.the engine continued to sputter and then completely lost power shortly after leveling the turn. at that point, it was clear we did not have the altitude or power to reach an airport. i immediately began running the emergency checklist and pitched for best glide and began looking for a suitable field.around 100 feet agl, i noticed the airspeed decreasing and added full flaps. the selected field was clear of crops, and i executed a soft-field landing. there were no injuries and no damage to the aircraft.upon review of the aircraft, it was determined that both fuel tanks were empty due to higher-than-expected fuel consumption during the flight. even though we departed with full fuel, i did not adequately calculate the fuel required for the flight we ultimately conducted.additionally, the mixture was not properly adjusted during portions of the flight, which likely contributed to increased fuel consumption. the decision to continue from redacted without verifying fuel quantity was also a contributing factor and, in hindsight, could have prevented the situation.as pilot in command, i take responsibility for the outcome of this flight and the planning decisions that led to this situation. this experience highlighted a lapse in judgment that resulted in a scenario i had not intended.i am proud of how the situation was handled. i remained calm, followed established procedures, and relied on my training to safely land the aircraft without injury or damage.i learned more from this experience than any single flight lesson. it reinforced the importance of thorough planning and disciplined decision-making.in the future i will ensure fuel requirements are properly calculated, including legal reserves, even on shorter or 'joyride' flights. properly adjust the mixture throughout all phases of flight. stop and verify fuel status rather than relying on assumptions.this is an experience i will not forget, and it has reinforced the importance of completing all calculations thoroughly and maintaining situational awareness throughout the entire flight.

text: for the past several years i have flown my employer to view the preparations of grounds for the event. this flight entailed 3-4 circular orbits at 500-600 ft with airspeeds ranging from 60-80 knots before departing south to redacted. approximately 15 minutes later we departed redacted, enroute back to the hanger. while in cruise, we overflew location x from south to north at an altitude of 500 ft and 100 knots airspeed. within 1.5 hours of landing at the hanger we were approached by (2) sheriff's deputies who informed us that they were operating drones overhead as part of their security detail. he said we flew at an altitude below one of the drones, which was at 200ft. we vehemently denied the possibility. before leaving one deputy stated that there was no active tfr, but there is a heightened security risk, due to conflicts abroad. had we been aware of these facts we would not have conducted the flight. drones are increasingly being used by law enforcement due to low cost and are less intrusive from the ground (low noise and visibility). before drones, law enforcement helicopters were deployed for this type of surveillance. they were easily seen by other helicopters in the vicinity and monitored an air-to-air frequency to communicate with other aircraft. unfortunately, this level of safety does not exist with drones. they are invisible to aircraft and are most often stationary. corrective actions: local law enforcement when operating security/surveillance drones at events should be required to depict times and location on aircraft navigation equipment via ads-b. drones should be required to have a highly reflective surface in addition to higher intensity anti-collision lights. due to possible inaccurate altitude indications, drone maximum altitude should be reduced below 400ft to increase vertical separation. tfr's should be required when any level of additional security is needed at an outdoor event when security drones are in operation.

synopsis: CRJ900 First Officer reported a temporary loss of control while landing in wind gusts which resulted in a bounced landing.
text: on approach into redacted flying the approach winds were light but there were updrafts/downdrafts. while correcting for the gusts descending pass 100ft captain announced to add power. on adding power the descent rate increased where the resolution advisory callouts were rapid hence cutting power to idle and flaring late that resulted in a bounced. through the entire approach vref was maintained at/above with small deviations.as briefed the advice of adding power was due to reduction of n1 settings in the 40% after crossing 100ft due to correcting for gusts. upon bounce the ca took controls and initiated a balked landing. cause: adding too much power with nose down trim which led to an increased in descent rate.suggestion: minimal power changes/corrections below 100ft

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: EMB145 First Officer reported pack failure on initial climb caused smoke in the cockpit and a return to the departure airport.
text: flight proceeded normally during our pre-flight duties. we were slightly delayed pushing waiting for wing walkers. once pushed, we were cleared to start engine 1. upon starting engine one i had noticed the eicas message 'pack 2 vlv clsd'. i ran the qrh, which did not resolve the issue. captain and i decided that we needed to go to a hard stand and call maintenance for further troubleshooting/possible deferral of the pack. during our taxi, (starting from gate xx, to the west hard stand) as a means of troubleshooting and isolating variables, we decided to start engine 2, and see if the message would persist with engine bleed air instead of apu bleed air. after starting engine 2, the message persisted. we informed ramp of our issue, pulled into the handstand and the captain proceeded to call maintenance.pack 2 inop is flight crew deferrable item, so we followed maintenance's procedures for the deferral and then worked on the next task. as part of the deferral, we were restricted to fl250 (originally fl360) and since this was an minimum equipment list affecting our performance and fuel consumption calculations we needed to call dispatch and see if we have enough fuel, and if so, get a new release. upon calling dispatch we were able to continue with our current fuel on-board, and obtain a new release. after getting our new release we rejoined the departures and the taxi-take off was completely uneventful. the take off was normal until the climb portion where i had noticed the eicas message 'eng 2 blv vlv clsd' during my after take off flow. i consulted the captain on the appropriate qrh procedure and conducted the qrh procedure. upon completion of the procedure the message had cleared and we continued. as we leveled off at fl240 (our final filed altitude), i smelled a burning smell, simultaneously the captain had noticed the same thing. as we looked at each other, i noticed smoke coming above the captain's head. we then dawned our o2 masks, and we informed air traffic control that we needed to immediately return to redacted due to 'smoke in the cockpit'. the flight attendant also contacted us about a burning smell. the captain flew and coordinated our return while i ran the qrh, during this time i transferred radios to the captain while i continued the qrh. we then descended and received vectors back to redacted, we joined the localizer for xxc. since i was not fully caught up on setting up approach/speeds, i informed the captain that i 'needed more time' we informed air traffic control. we continued on that heading for a brief minute, then the captain determined that the safest course of action was to continue for xxl instead of delay vectors, as we did not know the source, nor the severity of the possible smoke and fumes. i was able to load in the approach speeds and we joined the localizer xxl. he landed very smoothly, we pulled off the runway and asked crash, fire, rescue to confirm that there was not any visible smoke or fire on the exterior of the aircraft. they confirmed that it was clear on the exterior. we then determined that it was not necessary to evacuate the aircraft as there were no signs of persisting smoke or fumes and the flight attendant also did not have any signs of smoke in the cabin. we elected to taxi to the gate. from our brief acars message, i said that we were told to go to gate xy. as we taxied into the ramp, ramp control informed us that it was occupied. we then stressed that we need a gate asap ! they then directed us to another gate on the concourse. i cannot remember the exact gate, possibly xz or xa. we then taxied over to the 'vacant' gate, but there was a fuel truck in the way and no rampers. we immediately called operations and informed them that we needed it moved immediately, we proceeded to wait for another few minutes, despite another call. however, we confirmed that there were still no signs of smoke or fumes from the aircraft during the taxi and waiting period, and had a fire truck follow us. we pulled into the gate, deplaned the passengers in an organize manner, and shut down the aircraft.maintenance determined pack 1 exhaust duct had blown, and it was ingesting pack exhaust into the cabin (preliminary)

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: B737 First Officer reported the autopilot disconnected and the First Officer's flight director failed on final approach resulting in descent below glidepath and minimum vectoring altitude.
text: holding for runway xx in redacted for weather to improve to have a better chance of getting in for landing at waypoint redacted at 4, 000ft. after 20 minutes of holding (estimate) weather improves and approach descends us to 3, 000ft to proceed inbound. it was my leg (first officer) and began to configure for the approach that would be near minimums. once inbound, i recognize that the plane ahead of us (corporate) is relatively close but approach permitted us to continue. i would estimate we were in trail by 4-5 miles. fully configured prior to gs intercept, as we cross redacted, the autopilot disconnects, and i lose guidance from the flight directors (fd) but continue raw data. captain and i recognize he still has guidance, and so we transfer the controls at around 1, 400ft with the autopilot off. we are stable at this event. approach then directs us to break off the approach and turn left 90 degrees (cannot remember the specific heading) and climb to 3, 000ft. as pm, i turn off the fd's, spin the heading bug and altitude bug while clicking lvl change and heading (hdg) select. i believe i did this with the flight directors off, but due to the subsequent events, i am not so sure. as i am doing this, the captain is calling for flaps 15 and gear up. it is during this that i realize, the captain is still descending because of the flight directors giving him an improper guidance. the captain was following the gs down but had began the turn to the requested heading. after setting the flaps to 15, i tell the captain to climb" repeatedly. he recognizes what he is doing, and corrects to our assigned heading and altitude. the lowest we got was approximately 1, 050ft. we also got an audible callout of which i assume was "sink rate" and approach asking us to check our altitude and notified us of the mva. i cannot recall those 10 seconds exactly, but i assume those were the events that occurred to my best knowledge. from there we cleaned up the plane, and set up for the approach again. to get proper automation, i flipped the nav frequencies from the loc to the vor, and then clicked hdg and lvl change. captain asked if i wanted to take the plane back, and i did. after i had controls, we both decided leaving the autopilot on the captains side would allow for better situational awareness and we proceeded as such, and landed the plane with that configuration. we saw the approach lights at around 400ft. there weren't many things that i felt went right if i were to do the situation again. i believe that handing the plane to the captain at 1500ft, albeit low, was the right decision at the time. i tried to be preventative and cycle the fd's to get to the proper automation, but that did not work as planned. only once the nav frequencies were flipped, a preventative action was taken. i also believe the captain handing the plane back to me for the second approach was a containment action from him, i do not know if he was shaken up or had gotten disoriented by what had just occurred, but i felt very comfortable with flying the plane from the position we were in and do believe it was safe to do so given what had just happened. not once do i think that crm had fallen apart, in fact, i think we both excelled at communicating what was happening once the event had happened. i want to bring up that after we had completed our duties as flight crew-members, the captain did not waste time asking about what happened, what went wrong, etc. again, i want to emphasize that i never felt that crm was an issue and the captain was very approachable about the event afterwards."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Flight Attendant reported galley oven caught fire; was extinguished; and flight returned to departure airport.
text: 6 minutes after the sterile light went off the forward galley oven closest to the flight deck caught on fire. i was getting ready to take the food out of the oven to put in meals from the mid galley when i noticed the oven fully illuminated orange. at this point i didn't realize it was fire. when i went to pull the tray out a piece of the ember flew back on me. as i jumped back, that's when i realized there was fire. the purser was coming back to the galley. i couldn't make out the words to tell him fire, but he realized what i was pointing at. i called pilots right away and said fire. the captain told us he was turning around. we closed the oven until we got the halon. at this point i waving for the fa in the mid galley to come up. i told the purser to let the others know what was happening as we were trying to put the fire out. the fa from the mid galley closed the curtains before we opened the oven so that passengers couldn't see what we were doing. the purser opened the oven while i extinguished the oven. after some time i stopped because i wasn't sure if i should keep going. the purser told me to keep going until it was empty. at that point the captain called back and asked the purser all of the questions about the fire. he then gave the purser brief information for a land emergency since we were landing overweight. i forgot to mention the aft fa brought up a halon just in case after the purser let the others know what had happened. we all met in the mid galley for the information and had about 10 minutes or less until landing. we were told we didn't need to do an evacuation at that point and if anything changed they'd let us know. after we landed the captain told us our brakes were okay to continue to the gate so no evacuation needed. once we got to the gate it was determined that everyone would deplane and the aircraft would be taken out of service. the captain also acknowledged a part outside of the oven where i believe got burned. one of the maintenance workers also said the fan probably caused the spark on the aircraft.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor with a student reported a runway excursion and propeller strike during an attempted takeoff.
text: we decided to do a few grass landings at redacted for practice and i demonstrated a landing on runway xx and took off runway xy then my student performed a landing and a takeoff and then asked if we could do more so i decided to instead of landing with a tailwind land with a headwind and land xy. we landed and went all the way down to the beginning of xx and took off. we got to about midfield and just started to get off the ground and we would ended up going off the end of the runway and the prop struck the asphalt while it was not moving. there was people on the left side of the runway so the only option was either go off the end where it was steep or go to the left. we made the decision to abort the takeoff in order to prevent going into the trees and power lines that were at our same altitude.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: DA20 Student Pilot reported a runway excursion after landing in a quartering tailwind and over-correcting.
text: while i was landing at redacted, i realized there was a quartering tailwind. i performed the ideal corrections and landed on runway xx. i made the landing but over-corrected and rolled into the grass. no damage was done to the plane and i made it to the other taxi way safely. i took off again and headed back to redacted with no problems.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Flight Instructor with student on a taxiway awaiting departure from a non-towered airport reported they observed a NMAC between two aircraft on base leg.
text: i decided, for the safety of flight, and perhaps a good discussion, to post a little educational rant about a very close midair my student and i watched happen on day 0 at xa:20 at redacted. we were holding short of runway xx and watched a prior plane on a somewhat long final make a touch and go. a cherokee then turned their base behind them appropriately and i pointed out to the traffic to my student. interestingly, we then noticed a subsequent cessna turn a very low tight left base. the cherokee by this time was already on final, and had made their call. they then asked if the cessna had them in sight. they replied in the affirmative and that they would 'extend their base.' for the record, they were already on their base leg. i watched as both planes continued on a collision course right above the street x intersection with the cherokee finally climbing and side stepping and the cessna staying low and flying due south probably about 50 feet of separation between them, then making a radio call 'that was close!' i spoke to the cherokee pilot afterwards and fortunately they did have the cessna traffic in sight throughout the incident, so i suspect while it looked close that it would have had a safe outcome regardless of how it looked from my vantage point. a few thoughts for all of us to ponder. i am convinced that the cessna never had the cherokee in sight. i presume, perhaps falsely, that they were looking at an adsb return rather than out the window. we all need a reminder that adsb is not visual separation. when air traffic control asks you if you have traffic in sight, they mean with your eye balls. not on your 'fish finder'. please, for the love of god, do not call it that. even more importantly, when another pilot asks if you have them in sight, do not reply in the affirmative if you do not. instead, take action immediately to increase the separation between you. in formation flying when you lose sight of your wingman, you immediately call blind and increase the separation between the aircraft. this isn't checkers, it's flying. and a simple screw up will kill you, or much worse, someone else. adsb isn't perfect. it has a lag. sometimes a fraction of a second and sometimes 20 seconds. are you using a third party device that then wirelessly connects to your foreflight app to show you? are you holding a phone in your lap? or is your system installed in the plane and displayed on a multi-function flight display (mfd)? even primary radar has a lag. nothing is perfect. more importantly not everyone has adsb. it's not required. i don't have it in my plane. it is for situational awareness. it is not meant to replace your eyeballs. when someone on the frequency calls a position you should look outside the plane first, not at your panel or your phone. i presume we all know 91.113 about right of way. read it again if you haven't this year. landing traffic has the right of way. if someone is already on final, turn your left base once they are at your 9'o'clock, not while they are still at 11 o'clock. the c210 on day 0 turned their base low at least a half mile before the cherokee. in the left seat, low, with a high wing, they had no chance of seeing that cherokee. why then did they say traffic was in sight? and what does extending your base leg even mean when you are already on your base?the question i pose to myself, sitting at the threshold, is should i have been empowered to play air traffic control and demand a go around? my thought was to not clog the frequency while these two worked it out. however in hindsight, there was no negotiation between them. i would have felt very guilty if i had not said something. kudos to both pilots afterwards for being kind and professional. neither of them got nasty on the radio (something that i hear too frequently these days) and neither of them chastised each other. the cessna exited the area and the cherokee got back in the pattern. i presume both had honest debriefs when they got home. however, the rest of us can stand to learnsomething from this close call before the flying season gets busy. every year in our country someone dies due to this situation because of two reasons: 1.) they misinterpret 91.113 or 2.) they are too hard headed to realize that even though they are in the right, they neglect to knock off their approach and create separation because - dang-it - they have the right away!!! i argue that this cherokee, due to the fact that they could see the cessna making a mistake, could have aborted their touch and go 30 seconds earlier. they could have sidestepped on an upwind to keep the cessna in sight and learned a valuable lesson that being courteous, even when you were the one that was wronged, is the right thing, and the safe thing, to do. don't think this thing happens a lot? how many classic 91.113 see and avoid mishaps come to mind right off the bat? dca accident? centennial accident between the metro liner and cirrus. or maybe all of us need to have a little common sense and remind ourselves to be courteous. this means if you are working with a student on instrument work and the pattern is really full, it's not the time to do your circling maneuver. this means if it's clear and a million and you're on an instrument plan in a single engine piston, you shouldn't fly a 10 mile straight in and you should join the pattern in a visual flight rules manner - even if your bladder is about to explode! it means if a turbine is arriving, that the rest of us make way and let them land. we only have one sand box to play in. we should keep it pleasant for every user…we all have a right to be there.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Flight Instructor and trainee pilot reported an engine failure during cruise. The flight landed safely at a nearby airport.
text: i was providing flight instruction near redacted airport when we experienced a total engine failure at approximately 2, 500 feet msl and about 4 nm from the airport. the engine failure occurred without prior warning. the engine abruptly made an abnormal sound and then lost all power completely. a review of the engine indications confirmed a full loss of power, with the engine instruments showing a significant drop.at the onset of the emergency, the student transferred flight controls to me. i confirmed there was no useful engine power and no meaningful response from the engine. i immediately began evaluating available landing options and determined that redacted airport was the best available landing site.once the airport was selected, the student and i coordinated duties. the student assisted with navigation and frequency management for redacted, while i maintained aircraft control, maneuvered toward the airport, and executed the in-flight engine restart checklist. during the restart attempt, the engine tried to relight but did not successfully restart. instead, it produced backfire-type sounds without developing usable power.i then transmitted on the redacted unicom frequency that we were experiencing an engine failure and intended to land on runway xx. at approximately 500 feet agl, the engine attempted to produce power again and momentarily developed approximately 1, 200 to 1, 400 rpm for about 10 seconds, but then lost power completely once more.i continued the forced landing and landed the aircraft safely on runway xx at redacted airport. there was no injury to either occupant and no damage to the aircraft or other property. after touchdown, using the remaining landing energy, i was able to clear the runway and stop on the taxiway.while on the taxiway, i evaluated whether the engine would produce any usable power. with full throttle applied, the engine produced only approximately 400 to 650 rpm, which was unstable and accompanied by significant vibration. using that limited power, i was able to taxi the aircraft to the fbo area.maintenance personnel responded and conducted a full inspection of the aircraft. the discrepancies were addressed, documented in the aircraft maintenance records, and the aircraft was subsequently returned to service later that same day.this event involved a sudden and unexpected total engine failure without meaningful prior warning indications. positive crew coordination between instructor and student, prompt identification of a suitable landing site, emergency checklist execution, and timely radio communication contributed to a safe outcome.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor and Local Controller reported conflicting traffic failed to maintain assigned altitude resulted in evasive action and an NMAC.
text: myself and a student were doing touch and go pattern work at redacted for a stage check. about our 4th lap, we were in thedownwind at traffic pattern altitude (tpa). i noticed an aircraft entering from the south on the multi-function flight display (mfd), myself and the student made positive contact with the incoming plane. i could tell he was not following instructions from tower. as the aircraft got closer i could se he was descending right towards us. i eventually took controls while keeping eyes on the aircraft, pulled power and started a steep descent to avoid. once clear of the aircraft we climbed back up to tpa and decided to exit the airspace.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported an engine failure on takeoff that resulted in an expeditious return and a runway excursion.
text: on day 0 at approximately xa:25, aircraft x with person a as instructing pilot in command with a student pilot on board experienced a sudden and total loss of power upon turning crosswind after taking off xxl. the engine restarted after a turn back toward the airport had been initiated, but person a continued his return to the airport, not trusting that the engine would continue to run.during the departure, a turn was initiated at the pilot's request to accommodate traffic departing runway xxr. the engine interruption occurred during this turn.person a communicated with air traffic control, advising that aircraft x was returning to the field due to a loss of engine power. an emergency was not formally declared. air traffic control cleared other traffic and subsequently issued a landing clearance for runway xyr.during the approach, flaps were extended to 30 degrees at approximately 90 kias to reduce airspeed. with approximately 500 feet of runway remaining, flaps were retracted and full braking was applied. the aircraft exited the end of the runway at approximately 58 knots, came to a stop, and then taxied onto extended taxiway 1. there were no injuries or damage to the aircraft.after exiting the runway, the aircraft was instructed to contact ground control and was cleared to taxi via taxiway 2 to parking. during taxi, the engine initially operated roughly, then smoothed out, but began running rough again as the aircraft approached the ramp before ultimately stopping. the mixture was placed in cutoff, and all electrical systems were secured.subsequent sumping of the fuel system revealed no visible deficiencies with the fuel on board.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Pilot reported near miss with traffic departing opposite direction same runway.
text: i arrived at redacted and observed an aircraft at the end of runway xx i completed preflight in the hanger and assumed that runway xx was in use. once aircraft was started and i gathered the atis which stated that winds where calm. atis instructions are runway xx is calm winds runway. i did not hear any aircraft talking on ctaf due to being on guard 121.500, while doing the before takeoff checklist i noticed this and put in the ctaf. i announced that i was departing with no other traffic heard. once i lined up on the runway xx i observed an aircraft heading towards me approximately 250 ft above me and 300 feet away climbing. once it was clear i committed to a take off since i made a radio call and was on the runway. once i took off i observed two more aircraft running up for runway xy. once i saw this i immediately sidestepped to the right incase any other aircraft were in the pattern for xy. no radio call were made by any other aircraft about my actions. after i departed the area approximately 15 mins the traffic pattern went back to runway xx.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Pilot reported many airports within the vicinity of CRP do not have reliable weather reporting stations.
text: the area east of corpus christi to victoria is without reliable weather reporting stations. both tfp and rkp have inoperative weather stations. the nearest station is ras. ras is on the beach and has different weather than inland airports. we have about 15 airports within a 50-mile radius of crp. for 15 airports we have less than 6 that could be considered reliable weather stations. tfp, t69, and rkp are very unreliable. on the east half of the crp area only ras is reliable and its location makes it a poor choice for weather inland of the coast. not having wind data in an area known for 30 knots on almost a daily basis, and no ceilings data for a coastal environment is a major safety concern consideration. lack of maintenance funds is poor reason for not having these stations in good working condition.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported an NMAC during cruise flight with what appeared to be two UAS. No evasive action was taken.
text: i was flying with 3 passengers on an instrument flight rules flight plan from redacted to 1v6. when passing approximately 8 miles west of apa (location and time is approximate, i did not mark it on the chart) at 9000ft msl, we encountered two objects that appeared to be drones flying very near our position.i spotted the first object a few hundred feet ahead of us. it reminded me of encountering a bird in flight. it was clear it was slightly lower and to the right of us, so i left the autopilot engaged and didn't take any evasive action. i pointed it out to a passenger (my wife, who is not a pilot, but is familiar with ga due to several hundred hours as a passenger with me). our initial reaction was 'what was that?' the object was grey/silver, reflected a fair bit of light, but was much more boxy and angular than a mylar balloon would be. it did not look like a typical quadcopter, but was also far enough away that we couldn't really identify any means of flight (wings, propellers, etc). the object was a 1-2ft across, similar in size to a medium bird, but much more metallic/machine looking.several seconds later, i spotted a second object ahead of us. it was at approximately the same altitude as the first object, but this time to the left of our flight path. i pointed it out as it went by. the passenger in the back seat behind me saw it go by as well. it appeared similar to the first object.given our groundspeed of around 150kt, we passed by both objects very quickly. it was as if they were standing still. given the large difference in our speeds, i could not tell whether the objects were moving, or their direction of flight, except that it was much slower than us.i can't think of anything different that i or air traffic control should have done. assuming that the objects were drones, whoever was operating them should not have been flying them there without significant coordination with air traffic control. given how busy the airspace around denver is, the danger this kind of operation poses is obvious.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported ATC failure to provide separation resulted in a NMAC event.
text: i was advised by bwi tower to climb to 2500 msl after requesting a mid-field crossing while heading back to redacted. while at that altitude, a commercial airliner departed bwi from runway 28. the controller advised me of the departing aircraft and i acknowledged. the airliner was handed off to potomac departure, and it was seen making an ascending left turn in our direction. i notified bwi tower that the aircraft was heading in our direction and asked if they wanted me to descend or change course. the controller initial advised that was not needed, but seconds later told me to descend. while quickly descending, i noticed that the tcas showed the airliner as yellow and that it was approximately 500 feet from my altitude as it continued to the southeast in my direction.the new faa policy in order to separate airplanes and helicopters went into effect. at an altitude of 2500 msl, helicopter are often in the departure corridor as airliners ascent to their initial assigned altitude.in this case, it would have been safer to hold my aircraft south of bwi at a lower altitude until it was safe to cross the field. additionally, i could have been vectored to the east behind arriving aircraft.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Center controller reported a military aircraft exiting a MOA was at the same altitude as a large military UAS operating in the vicinity and climbed without a clearance.
text: aircraft x was working in the redacted moas. they then departed the moa and when they depart are assigned fl230 as a final altitude. aircraft y was proceeding to work along the border level at fl230. aircraft x contacted me who was in the turn direct the redacted waypoint. i called the aircraft y traffic to aircraft x who acknowledged the traffic call then proceeded to climb after the fact. he then also reported a resolution advisory. i told him he was not issued a climb and to maintain fl230. he then proceeded to climb again without a climbing clearance. i then told the pilot to contact redacted for a pilot deviation.recommendation: honestly, there was really nothing except maybe emphasize maintain fl230. without a climb clearance aircraft aren't allowed to climb but maybe just ensure that the military pilot will maintain an altitude even after a traffic call.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that taxiing to the gate at night in FSD is difficult due to inadequate lighting.
text: i have filed reports on this particular subject before. taxiing in to the gate in fsd at night is a real challenge. after speaking with the gate agent it sounds like there has been multiple complaints for pilots. the ramp is extremely dark. there's no lighting. you cannot see the numbers on the buildings and in addition gate xx which is company x, leaves the jet bridge lights on which are blinding. gate xy is completely pitch black and if the rampers are not there which they were not tonight, then it's very difficult to see the correct gate. the gate agent told me that she gets complaints almost every evening from the crews about this particular issue. right next to the ramp is the de-ice pad, which is also right next to the tower and the de-ice pad is extremely well lit with a lot of bright lights which also makes it more difficult because it creates a lot of glare and you cannot see the poorly lit ramp area. in addition to the lighting issue, it's a very tight taxi around the ramp and into our gate, which makes this a real safety issue. the ramp again is completely black. we're gonna wind up having a problem somebody's gonna hit something going into this ramp. the agent has said she's complained multiple times, but nothing has happened. i feel like this needs to be addressed as soon as possible.

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an airborne conflict during approach to SFO resulting in a TCAS RA to descend which triggered an ATC low altitude alert.
text: at approximately 1800 feet we got a descending tcas resolution advisory due to the aircraft next to us not flying the flight management system bridge visual to 28r. we followed the resolution advisory and told air traffic control. at about 1000 feet we got a low altitude warning from tower. seconds after that the resolution advisory went away and we continued to an uneventful landing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: B767-300 Captain reported returning to departure airport after the right engine did not produce full power during takeoff and initial climb.
text: during the takeoff roll, at approximately 100 knots and prior to v1, we experienced a reduction in thrust on the right engine, with n1 indicating approximately 8485%. additional thrust was applied and appropriate rudder input used to maintain directional control, however, there was no increase in power on the right engine. airspeed continued to increase and was verified by both crew members. as we were approaching v1, we elected to continue the takeoff rather than initiate a high-speed rejected takeoff.after liftoff, the right engine stabilized at approximately 85.6% n1 with the thrust lever at the forward limit. we sent a divert message to the company and elected to return to the departure airport. during the assessment, the first officer determined that landing weight was approximately 2, 000 lbs above maximum landing weight, so we entered a hold to burn fuel prior to the approach.we coordinated with air traffic control, requested emergency equipment, and conducted an uneventful return and landing on runway xx in redacted. the first officer performed exceptionally well and contributed to a safe and professional outcome.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported a compressor stall and return to departure airport.
text: after a regular departure and climb out from redacted to redacted over approximately redacted the aircraft leveled off at fl310. right after level several loud bangs were heard from the left side of the aircraft as well as indications of a surging engine or compressor stall. flight attendants then made contact as they had heard and felt the bangs and saw sparks from engine 1. control was established and the duties of flying were then given to the first officer and the captain then ran the qrc and qrh checklists. after the autothrottles were disconnected in accordance with the checklist the engine then ran normally. decision was made to return to redacted in the interest of safety and a turn and declaration was made. checklists were then completed as we returned to redacted for a normal landing on runway xxc. crash and fire inspected the engine and aircraft found no damage and as it was deemed safe we taxied to the gate and parked. casual factors include long day, multiple legs and maintenance write ups as well as delays. mitigation was good crm and use of any and all information available to us to make the safest decision possible.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A319 Captain reported a loud banging noise emanating from the right wheel well and diversion to nearby airport.
text: upon aircraft pickup in redacted previous flight deck and cabin crew reported a loud banging noise coming from right wheel well area in cabin on landing. passengers were heard remarking about this as well. maintenance discrepancy entered in logbook and maintenance notified. inspection was performed at gate. no irregularities noticed at time and maintenance writeup closed. proceeded for a normal takeoff. climbing through 10000 ft cabin crew calls and reports loud banging sound coming from right wheel well area in cabin. i request deadheading airbus pilot with maintenance background to get involved with troubleshooting from cabin. he describes sound as loud popcorn popping sound. all flight deck indications normal and i request level off. cabin crew reports sound getting louder. were look at pressurization page on ecam and at max differential cabin pressure so unsure if cabin pressure being held properly so we request a descent. sound continued in the descent. passengers we noted being visibly upset at this time and priority handling requested with air traffic control and we requested a diversion to redacted right off our nose. we descended to 8000 ft and proceeded to burn off 3000 lbs of fuel to get under landing weight. made a normal landing. arff (airport rescue and firefighting) inspected plane visually and proceeded to gate. logbook was filled out on aircraft. no masks were dropped cabin never rose above 10000.unknown but suspect a seal/hull pressurization problem.

text: on approach in redacted (visual xxl using instrument landing system xxl as guidance), we received a gnd (ground) prox (proximity) message. this happened within 500 feet of the ground, after the captain had switched to outside references. we showed one white and three red on the papi. the captain continued the approach and landed within the touchdown zone without incident.cause: i believe the deviation was caused by gusty winds which caused us to briefly lose altitude.

synopsis: B767-300 flight crew reported the right engine lost power during departure; resulting in an engine shutdown and a return to the departure airport.
text: on departure climbing out of approximately 7000 we heard a 'pop'. then observed the right engine rolling back. we advised air traffic control and ran through the engine shutdown checklist. attempted a restart n1 was 16-19 percent. engine did not relight. continue back to redacted and landed without incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported a ENG 2 BLD VLV CLSD EICAS message during climb and cockpit smoke resulted in a return to the airport.
text: pushed from the gate and started engine one. engine started normally. eicas message appeared indicating 'pack 2 vlv fail'. first officer ran qrh and we were unable to resolve the message. i instructed the first officer to start the second engine to see if that resolved the pack issue. it did not resolve it. proceeded to hard stand to contact maintenance to troubleshoot. maintenance concluded the issue could not be resolved immediately so we minimum equipment list'd pack 2. we then contacted dispatch to get a new flight release below fl250 and see if we could continue the flight with our current fuel load. dispatch ran the numbers and we were able to continue the flight on current fuel with a new flight release.after receiving and signing the new release, we contacted redacted ground to let them know we would be restricted below fl 250. we proceeded to the runway and were cleared for takeoff. while running the after takeoff checklist, first officer noted eicas message 'eng 2 bld vlv clsd'. first officer ran the qrh procedure, which cleared the message.we were cleared to climb up to fl240, and as we were leveling, i smelled an unusual smell and asked first officer if he smelled it too. he said he smelled it and then stated 'smoke in cockpit!'. i instructed him to don his oxygen mask immediately at 100%, and we both did so. we immediately notified air traffic control and they provided priority handling for us. first officer ran qrh for smoke in cockpit while i took radios and asked for an immediate return to redacted. we were given a descent and vectors. i notified the flight attendant of what was going on. she briefed the passengers that we were returning to redacted. air traffic control asked if an approach to xx center was acceptable. i accepted it, and continued to descend. air traffic control asked if we required airport rescue and firefighting (arff) to meet us upon landing, and i said yes. as we got close to the airport, the first officer was still running landing distances and speeds, and was not yet ready for the approach. we notified air traffic control and they gave us a vector to the east to finish setting up. in order to minimize time to land in order to reduce the possibility of a fire occurring inside the aircraft, i then requested vectors for the instrument landing system xxl. air traffic control cleared us for the visual to xxl and we descended and landed normally. we taxiied clear of the runway, turned northbound on taxiway 1 and stopped the aircraft. i set the parking brake and began to communicate with arff, telling them we needed the aircraft visually inspected before we proceded to the gate. they obliged and told us the aircraft showed no evidence of smoke or fire. we then taxiied to gate xx, parked, and shut down the aircraft. passengers deplaned and arff boarded the aircraft.cause: after inspecting the aircraft, maintenance, notified us that one of the couplers had disintegrated on the pack, and the exhaust from the pack was entering the air system for the aircraft.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: ERJ145 Captain reported low airspeed resulted after encountering wake turbulence on short final at PHL from a heavy aircraft landing on an intersecting runway. Stabilized approach criteria was regained and the flight landed safely.
text: on visual approach to runway 35 backed up with the rnav into phl. upon reaching 500 feet i kicked off the autopilot to continue the approach. we were informed by air traffic control twice to caution wake turbulence from a heavy aircraft landing ahead on crossing runway 27r". i was concerned for the proximity of the aircraft and slowed between ref (137 kts.) and approach speed (157 kts.) to help with spacing. upon reaching 450 feet msl we had a decrease in performance and the pli (pitch limit indicator) rose to yellow briefly but immediately. i pushed over the nose and increased throttle to 70% n2 (estimated) simultaneously and increased airspeed back to approach speed after ensuring the aircraft crossed in front and landed. we heard a quick rumble but could not tell if the stick shaker officially. there was no push over and we were stable and above vref the entire time. gusty conditions 340 at 22 gusting 32.cause: slowing within 5 knots of vref to prevent spacing issue during a gusty day.suggestion: with seeing the pli and hearing the potential shake, we should have executed a go around as per the aom."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier pilot departing a foreign airport reported they were issued takeoff clearance from an intersection while another aircraft was beginning takeoff from the end of the runway.
text: due to the busy time frame in the late afternoon, redacted tower was issuing line up and wait behind clearances for arriving and departing traffic. after crossing runway xx on taxiway 1, which was closed and not in use, we were instructed by redacted tower to run numbers for taxiway 2 intersection departure for runway xy. we also asked about our sequence to the runway due to enroute spacing over the departure fixes mentioned to us while getting our clearance at the gate, and was told we were 'behind an aircraft.' after receiving this information, efb returned good performance numbers for our intersection and the first officer went through the departure changes checklist. after several inbound arrivals landed, we were now sequenced in front of said 737 who was holding short of runway xy full length from taxiway 1, while aircraft x, another 737, was given a line up and wait for runway -full length.as we approached the runway xy/2 hold short line we were instructed to line up and wait. my first officer read back the clearance 'aircraft x, runway xy, line up and wait' and i realized this would put us in front of the aircraft y 737 in position, but still give us adequate separation on the runway. he remarked to me 'i guess we're going to cut him off' and i said, 'yeah this is definitely a new one for me.' while we were speaking to each other about the odd nuances of this scenario, redacted tower issued, in spanish - what we can now later assume - a takeoff clearance to aircraft y. i continued to very slowly taxi the aircraft towards the hold short line, attempting to visualize how far in front of them we'd be and wondering how much we'd be jet-blasting them when the inevitable takeoff clearance was given to us as the preceding aircraft. while paying close attention to aircraft y, i noticed their strobe lights were flashing, which, at least per our procedures, is a normal requirement when on an active runway. due to our angle, in daylight conditions, and approaching at 90 degrees from their right, i wasn't able to detect whether or not the landing lights were on, which would've been a more obvious clue they were issued a takeoff clearance. after visually confirming the approach path of runway xy was clear, my first officer again queried tower to confirm our line up and wait instruction, to which tower replied 'affirm.' about the time the aircraft radome crossed the hold short line, my first officer noticed the wheels of the 737 moving. he announced 'stop. stop!' i looked over at him and simultaneously pressed the toe brakes and set the parking brake once the aircraft stopped. i said to him 'i didn't hear line up and wait behind, i heard line up and wait.' he acknowledged to me he heard the same thing from air traffic control. he again asked redacted tower to clarify the clearance and tower said it was a 'line up and wait **behind**' instruction. my first officer informed him that he issued us a 'line up and wait' **only** clearance to which the controller responded, 'ohh oops, my bad.' we were then instructed to line up and wait from taxiway 2 and departed shortly afterwards without further incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown
synopsis: A320 pilot reported a Pressurization System 1 malfunction while leveling at cruise altitude resulting in intermittent cabin warnings while the backup pressurization system maintained cabin pressure with system 2. Due to the intermittent audible and visual warnings; the flight returned to the departure airport.
text: shortly after climbout and reaching cruise phase of flight out of redacted, experienced an amber ecam cab pr 1.ran ecam which were all advisory messages along with qrh, determined cabin pressure 1 was inop but sys 2 was holding.would have been fine to continue on the leg if this was the case, but shortly after amber ecam cab pr 1, associated with this we experienced a red ecam of cab pr excess cabin alt.obviously this was in error as we were holding can pressure within normal limits with normal delta pressure, the problem we faced was the constant audible and visual warning in the main cabin where the customers/passengers were experiencing every time this ecam occurred on the flt deck. this occurred a total of 4 times.in the interest of safety and passenger comfort and safety, i decided to precautionary return to base back to redacted, after completing a sat call to discuss with maintenance and dispatch.emergency was not declared not to add to the unusual circumstances and conditions we were facing, and sys 2 pressure held normal. again the aural and emergency light visual indications in the main cabin along with the ecam warning messages deemed necessary to accomplish an air return, along with the possibility of sys 2 failing where we would have had no choice but to declare an emergency and execute rapid descent on our 2.5 hr flight.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an EGPWS caution obstacle alert while on final approach in visual conditions at night in turbulent conditions. The flight continued the approach.
text: i was called in for a reserve assignment to lga. we departed after numerous delays at approximately xl:00pm. my reserve period began that morning at xa:00am. as we progressed through the flight we started preparing and briefing for the rnav z runway 31 at lga. this was the only leg me and my captain flew that day. i was pilot monitoring and the captain was pilot flying, this was also the first time i flew this approach. as we approached the airport from the south air traffic control vectored us to the ne through the final approach course. then followed by a short right hand turn onto an approximately 8 mile final. this short vector resulted in overshooting the final approach course but was quickly corrected. the aircraft was fully configured and stabilized with the landing checklist completed prior to 1000 feet above tdze. while on short final 3-4 miles we received a enhanced ground proximity warning system (egpws) 'caution obstacle' alert. it was gusting between 25-30 knots that evening and we encountered a downdraft at the time the egpws occurred, which may have been the trigger for the alert. the aircraft remained stable the entire approach and it was vmc conditions so we continued the approach. after the flight during our debrief looking back on the situation the captain and i both agreed a go around would have been the more prudent decision. by the time i thought to call for a go around the egpws alert had stopped, and again we were still stable on the approach. during the last 30 minutes of the flight i could feel the onset of fatigue starting to take place. this may have been a contibuting factor as to why i didn't react more quickly and call for a go around. if i could do it again i would call for the go around immediately after hearing the first obstacle caution, especially considering it was night time.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude
synopsis: C172 flight crew reported during VFR practice approach a traffic conflict resulted in taking evasive action and an NMAC event.
text: while receiving advisories from redacted [tracon], there was a near miss event between two opposite direction traffic. traveling southeast bound direct redacted [vor] for the practice vorxx full procedure into redacted. the other involved aircraft was already inbound the vor course at 3, 000 feet. i was eastbound doing the parallel entry at 3, 500 as advised by the redacted [tracon] controller. i was given a traffic call for the other aircraft while they were still in the outbound leg of the hold at redacted [vor], i advised traffic insight. i was given an additional traffic call for an aircraft not talking on the frequency roughly 2 miles southeast of me, also traveling east at 3, 500. at the time i had the east bound traffic insight but not the vor traffic in the outbound. i proceeded to scan and eventually saw the vor traffic still in the outbound portion of the hold. shortly thereafter, i observed the previously no factor eastbound traffic at 3, 500 make a left 180-degree turn on a collision course toward us (head-on). while observing this traffic, i lost sight of the vorxx traffic which was at this point off our nose 500 below. i began to descend as we were converging with the aircraft making the left 180-degree turn at 3, 500. i descended toward the vor traffic and shortly before collision both head on aircraft took evasive action (both turning right). no collision occurred and both aircraft returned to the airport safely.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Gear Up Landing; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: C182RG Flight Instructor on training flight with student reported landing gear failure on approach.
text: when coming into land on a 45 degree entry to the traffic pattern, the gear was placed into the down position after making the callout of 'below 140, gear down'. the gear motor light lit up, and then turned off once the gear was cycled down. the gear position indicator did not show green nor orange. **the landing gear malfunction checklist was referenced and executed to the extent possible.** air traffic control had already given landing clearance at this point so i instructed my fellow pilot to let air traffic control know we were having gear issues and to ask for a low approach and i was going to troubleshoot while he continued to fly the airplane. he did so and we were given an extended downwind to account for airliner traffic as well as troubleshoot. i cycled the gear four separate times to determine if it was a one off incidence or there was another cause. at this rate, we continued with the low approach and asked air traffic control to verify that the nose gear was facing the correct direction while doing the low approach. we could see it in the mirror but i determined based on audible of the sounds of the gear that it was not locking into position but simply cycling and the nose was the issue. due to the fact that the 182 has one indicator for three pieces of gear it could have been any of them but i decided it was the nose because of the audibles of the tradition of the gear based on hundreds of hours in the airplane. after verification from air traffic control and another aircraft that the nose gear was the correct direction we continued on the upwind. the other pilot and i had a short discussion on weather or not to attempt to put the airplane on this runway or the airport it was based out of and i made the decision to keep it at redacted due to the availability of emergency services and long and wide runway. in the downwind leg of the traffic patter, we tried varying airspeeds and bank angles to get the gear down. we were unsuccessful. we considered pulling the emergency gear extender but having knowledge of the system and being aware that if it was a locking issue that the application of this would not help we continued. this is because this would have simply made the gear motor manual and we were not having issues with the motor. after this, i briefed my fellow pilot on if the nose were to collapse that i would pull the mixture, throttle, and bring the fuel selector to off and that he would turn off the mags and master and we would both hit the brakes. following that i **guarded the controls and assisted my student** on the controls and it was a soft touchdown and roll out. on the roll out approximately 10 seconds after landings the nose collapsed, almost simultaneously i pulled the throttle mixture and hit the fuel selector as well as applying the brakes. while doing this, i reminded him to turn off the starter and master. all were off before reaching a complete stop. we then exited the airplane and waited for emergency services.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: SR20 flight crew reported following ATC instructions in the pattern resulted in taking evasive action and an NMAC event.
text: during this flight, person a was the sole manipulator of the controls, and i was acting in an instructional capacity, providing guidance as needed to ensure the safety, legality, and overall proficiency of the flight. person a is an instrument rated pilot, but has not flown for several years except with me for the past few weeks to get proficient again. person a is a very knowledgeable and capable pilot, although he is a bit rusty from time off of flying. after departing, we proceeded toward redacted. approximately 12 miles south of redacted, person a contacted the tower with the current atis information and was instructed to 'join right traffic for runway xxr, maintain 7, 000 feet.'we both found this instruction somewhat ambiguous in terms of the expected pattern entry. based on our understanding, and in consideration of the previously published letter to airmen regarding traffic flow at redacted, i advised person a to proceed toward midfield to facilitate entry into the pattern.after proceeding on this heading for approximately one to two minutes, i observed multiple aircraft in potentially conflicting positions. i was actively scanning for traffic and monitoring the situation while anticipating additional instructions or clarification from the tower. during this time, i observed a cessna 172, believed to be operated by a flight school on a converging flight path.as we anticipated initiating a turn to enter the downwind, the tower instructed us to 'turn right 20 degrees for sequencing.' person a complied with this instruction, however, we remained uncertain as to which aircraft we were being sequenced behind, as no immediate clarification was provided.while maintaining visual separation and focusing outside the cockpit on traffic avoidance, our aircraft briefly descended below the assigned altitude of 7, 000 feet. this deviation was unintentional, and i did not recognize it at the time, as my attention was directed toward identifying and avoiding nearby traffic.shortly thereafter, the cessna 172 passed below us, and the tower advised us to look for that traffic. the assigned right turn for sequencing placed us in close proximity to the airport, after which we were instructed to make a right 270-degree turn over the approach end of runway xx. this sequence of instructions was unexpected and contributed to our uncertainty regarding the intended traffic flow and sequencing.it appeared that the other aircraft was already established on the downwind, which added to our confusion as to why we were directed to turn right, potentially contrary to the established traffic pattern flow, rather than being instructed to enter the pattern via a standard left turn.ultimately, we acknowledge that we did not maintain the assigned altitude, with a deviation of approximately 200 feet below 7, 000 feet. in retrospect, i recognize that i should have requested clarification from the tower regarding their sequencing intentions and pattern entry instructions. at the time, due to the frequency being busy, i hesitated to add additional radio traffic.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Light transport Captain reported radio communication failure between aircraft resulted in a NMAC event.
text: this is an addition / correction to a previous report regarding this incident involving aircraft x. a previous report i submitted that the pilot of the aircraft y that we nearly hit did not communicate over ctaf. we were able to locate a recording and the aircraft y was transmitting and made all of the appropriate calls and are clearly understood on the recording even though they were muffled / static ridden when the single transmission we did receive was misheard in our aircraft. also, they indicated that we did not make calls but they are audible on the recording which indicates that he was not receiving our transmissions as well. we have grounded the aircraft for maintenance on the radio stack.in addition to the discovery of the hardware issue which must be resolved before further flight.the event could have been avoided by the publication of a phone number for departure during off hours at ixd, which could be called rather than departing visual flight rules, or by contacting departure via the phone number available at ojc which is near by but was not considered until after the incident.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported dimly lit traffic on expected taxiway required progressing to next exit which resulted in a ground conflict and a go around.  First Officer also reported ATC remarks to crew was unnecessary; distracting and becoming a pattern.
text: upon landing at night on 28r in sfo i applied braking consistent with an exit at t. during transfer of controls to the captain toward the end of the landing rollout, poorly illuminated aircraft y became visible holding on t between the runways and the captain increased braking force to instead make the exit at e. it quickly became apparent that we weren't going to be able to make the e exit and that's when the obviously annoyed tower controller instructed us to exit at d, and we had to add power to regain some speed to hurry down to d. we exited quickly and the additional time we were on the runway was very minimal.after exiting 28r and crossing 28l at d without stopping, and contacting ground, a snarky controller instructed us to taxi to our gate and watch the go around (that we had presumably caused). aircraft z was passing right behind us in their takeoff roll on 28r, another aircraft on final for 28r was going around, and aircraft y was still holding between the runways on t.aircraft y on t was difficult to see in the dark. if we had been given a heads up by the tower controller that it was there, we would have planned on exiting at e. regardless, our time spent on the runway was not excessive and should not have caused a go around. departing and landing traffic was too compressed behind us.and, significantly, the flippant remark made by the ground controller was inappropriate, distracting, and unprofessional. sfo controllers are packing us together as tightly as ever in a highly chaotic environment with the slimmest margin for error. verbal attitude on the radio only adds to the chaosand erodes safety. with all of the routine havoc in sfo - being held high on approach by air traffic control, then slow down and get down, needing to pick out conflicting traffic on approach among many similar targets which blend in to the background, converging aircraft turning on to final, the resulting resolution advisory's from flying wingtip to wingtip, departing traffic on crossing runways passing right in front of landing traffic, etc… for many years it has felt like sfo is continuously on the verge of a catastrophe. there is a pattern, or a culture, of controllers venting frustrations on the radio with immature remarks and public beratement that we hear regularly around the country, usually at the busiest and most stressful airports. it always adds an unnecessary distraction to all of us on the frequency and it needs to stop. we all work best and safest when we are civil with each other and this needs to be ingrained in the air traffic control environment. this is a simple human factors component and one change to our system that can and should be made immediately.

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported a NMAC with a helicopter on final approach. Pilot maneuvered off course and continued approach.
text: we were on the pbg rnav 17 approach, past faf inbound at ~1500ft, we noticed an adsb target moving from our 1 o'clock moving to 11 o'clock on the almost reciprocal course. we had negative visual with is target, so i advised pilot flying to turn off the approach course to our right side to avoid the target. we continued our descent. we sighted a helicopter. based on the foreflight adsb track moved from right downwind of pbg runway 17 across approach course of rnav 17 at a 30 degree angle to cross the final approach course at nupiy at 1000 ft. it is exactly on the glide path of rnav 17. on a nice day with wind 170 / 8-10 kts, numerous aircrafts are conducting approaches. this helicopter should cross the pbg midfield from west to east bound travel. for us, we probably should have leveled off at avoid the wake turbulence underneath the helicopter.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: C-150 Flight Instructor on training flight with student reported engine malfunction on climb out. Returned to departure airport.
text: after taxi and engine run up, everything seemed normal. we received our takeoff clearance from the temporary tower at redacted airport. on our climb out, after turning a left crosswind to the east we lost 150-200 rpm. turned on carb heat, lost some more rpm as expected, then rpm recovered. about 30-45 seconds after that we lost 250-300 rpm and let redacted tower know we're turning back for engine roughness. tower provided priority handling. rpm losses were not constant, but in waves.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: C421 pilot reported right main landing gear collapse on landing resulted in runway excursion and loss of control on landing.
text: i was pilot in command of aircraft x, a 1975 cessna 421b, operating under 14 cfr part 91 on a personal flight. on board were myself as pilot in command, my family as passengers -- six souls on board total.i conducted a normal preflight inspection prior to departure. the aircraft had a current annual inspection completed a couple months prior, at which time landing gear work, repair, and rigging was performed by a certificated repair station. all required inspections and maintenance were current at the time of the accident.during landing rollout at redacted, the right main landing gear collapsed without warning. the collapse resulted in a propeller strike on the right engine, and the aircraft departed the right side of the runway coming to rest in the grass adjacent to the runway. all occupants exited the aircraft without serious injury.upon inspection of the runway and aircraft following the accident, a broken metal component identified as part of the right main gear assembly was recovered from the runway surface near the touchdown area, and an additional broken component was recovered from the aircraft itself. these components appeared to have suffered a sudden fracture failure. both components have been preserved as physical evidence.the aircraft had been maintained in accordance with manufacturer recommendations and applicable fars. i am reporting this occurrence in the interest of aviation safety and to document the circumstances surrounding what appears to be a landing gear structural component failure following recent maintenance and rigging by a certificated repair facility.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Flight Instructor and student reported a near miss during landing roll with an aircraft that crossed the runway in front of them.
text: i was doing pattern work with a commercial student. the other airplane (aircraft y) was not making any radio calls and landed on runway 18 when we were using runway 14. upon touchdown, aircraft y crossed the runway without making a radio call and without looking. i had to take the flight controls and apply heavy brakes to not hit aircraft y crossing the runway.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Cessna Citation flight crew reported an NMAC during takeoff and initial climb. Crew continued the departure.
text: this is a follow-up to our earlier submission concerning the incident involving aircraft y and aircraft x.we have now listened to the air traffic control recording. it confirms that the pilatus pilot made several radio correct calls on ctaf, which the citation crew did not hear.our sequence of events was as follows:- we departed the hangar and taxied toward runway xx.- radio 1 was set to monitor ctaf.- radio 2 was set to clearance delivery (redacted.x).- we were unable to establish contact on redacted.x.we did not receive nor recognize any in coming calls from ctaf- upon reaching the end of taxiway '1' at runway xx, we switched both radios to redacted.x in an attempt to contact clearance.- when we still could not reach redacted clearance, we elected to obtain our clearance in the air.- prior to commencing our takeoff roll, we made a radio call stating our intentions.the recording shows that we did transmit a call before takeoff. however, the pilatus pilot stated that he did not hear any calls from the citation crew.based on the recording and other factors encountered during the flight, our conclusion is that we have a bad radio which had a malfunctioning radio (or radios) that prevented effective communication on the appropriate frequencies. due to other factors before reviewing the content of the recording we communicated that there is an issue with the radios

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported being informed over the radio that they had caused a NMAC with an aircraft on final approach.
text: at approximately xa:47 my passenger i were training in the pattern at cco and i heard a transmission telling us we were within 100 feet of another aircraft. we asked them where that happened and they said landing. we tried to get some more details, but didn't want to hog the radio and proceeded to make the next landing a full stop taxi back to gain clarity. we did not talk further with the aircraft telling us we had a near miss. after training, i reviewed flight aware data and pieced together from their break off point that the following may have occurred: as we were practicing a power off 180 maneuver, we made a turn towards the runway almost immediately after pulling power to idle. in doing so, we cut off a plane and as we were higher than normal for that position in the pattern, we did not see any traffic thus seemed to have almost flown ontop of the other aircraft. we were making calls in the pattern, but did not specifically call out a short approach, just downwind, base, final calls. we did not hear calls from the other traffic. the pooer than normal visibility may have contributed to our inability to see the other traffic as well. after the other aircraft took evasive measures, we did hear them key up the radio to tell us we cut them off and they had to break off of final to avoid us. we got a few calls with them, but did not continue to take up radio time discussing the matter in greater details. my passenger and i made a full stop taxi back on our next pattern lap to discuss and try and decifer what happened. we did one additional lap in the pattern before terminating the flight. in that final lap, the aircraft took the runway without making any audible calls to us, but we were hearing other local traffic and another airport's traffic just fine. we were on a longer final and did not have any spacing issues, but the event added to our evaluation that the other aircraft were difficult/impossible to hear at times and may have had radio issues of their own, decreasing our awareness of their position. additional situational awareness tools such as foreflight and traffic may have helped us in completing the maneuver safely which i will be more diligent about checking before completing short approaches in the future.
