synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a near miss with an aircraft in the traffic pattern which required evasive action.
text: before flight i saw notams redacted xx/redacted and xx/xxy so i chose a normal route to redacted over zzz1at 2300 feet msl, at redacted tower said to go to redacted [tower] frequency and start decent and helicopter traffic below. i changed freq and announced my position descending from over redacted on 45 to downwind at redacted. there was 1 aircraft in the pattern (champ i think) and one had turned crosswind heading toward redacted. i was descending from 1900 to 1400 over the riverbed toward the mountain. during decent some aircraft said they were on downwind, i lifted the left wing and saw an aircraft about my 7 or 8 o'clock position behind and above my altitude. i think i said i saw the aircraft. the aircraft was behind me and i assumed my entry was fine. i continued the pattern descending to turn base before the mountain, then saw the other aircraft overhead, started slipping and announced i was landing on the grass runway--- leaving the paved runway clear.i landed on the grass and turned off about 1 third down the runway and parked in front of the restaurant. i feel i had no choice other than hitting the mountain or the other aircraftwhen i did the short approach.awhile later a person said i cut him off and made him go around twice before landing. the notam said between 1000 and 2000 agl helicoptertraffic caution. aircraft y descended from 3475 msl into the pattern at redacted and wasabove my altitude at an airspeed of 123 to 67 knots while i was below at 57 to 61 knots.i do not know if the other aircraft had talked to redacted [tower].there may be a lack of training for pilots that use air traffic control at towered airports relying onatc instructions not available at non towered landing strips, as well as pilots not landing on the numbers but using the instrument flight rules past the numbers, expected at towered or ifrairports.

text: cruising @ 3500' msl the engine ran rough for 2-3 seconds - i checked engine instruments and all was normal. 5-10 seconds later there were 6-7 'pops' of small backfires & then no thrust. i ensured throttle, prop, mixture full - no change. changed fuel tanks no change - prop was windmilling. advised air traffic control & asked for nearest airfield - redacted 10 nm. turned toward redacted & saw w/ current alt & sink rate we would not make it. 10 nm - asked for next airport - redacted, 9 nm - again alt/sink rate would not allow redacted. i looked for an open field w/o trees etc and set up for a landing. i left gear up to avoid any cartwheeling, lowered flaps to get slower anspd (airspeed), had passenger open door so it wouldn't become jammed - at approx 150' agl, had passenger 2 say a prayer. leveled off to bleed off airspeed at 2-3 ft agl. we touched down in grass field & hit small bump - went airborne for 60 ft (approx) touched back down in plowed field and skidded to a stop. all occupants were ok. i made a radio call that we had landed safely and we all egressed the aircraft.

synopsis: B737-800 pilot reported refusing an aircraft that had a deferred APU and a history of pack malfunctions.
text: on day 0, i was scheduled to operate flight abcd from redacted to redacted. during my review of the aircraft maintenance history, i noted multiple recent write-ups involving the left air conditioning pack, including pack lights illuminating during climb and high power settings. several prior crews documented that qrh procedures were performed, with the issue either not resetting or recurring.the apu was deferred inoperative under minimum equipment list, reducing system redundancy. based on the recurring nature of the discrepancies, the recent history of repeat write-ups, and the minimum equipment list condition, i assessed an increased likelihood of a pack-related issue recurring during climb or high power phases of flight.given the planned 4.5-hour flight and the operating environment into redacted, including high elevation and terrain considerations, i determined the overall operational risk was elevated. based on this assessment, i elected to decline the aircraft.this decision was made using available maintenance history, operational factors, and a conservative risk assessment.some of the contributing factors included repeated left pack discrepancies, prior unsuccessful qrh resets, and reduced system redundancy with the apu inoperative. additional considerations included flight length and the operating environment into redacted. risk mitigation includes continued review of maintenance trends, clear communication of repeat discrepancies, and use of conservative decision-making when multiple risk factors are present.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B777 pilot reported that maintenance had discovered a fuel leak while the aircraft was parked at the gate prior to flight; resulting in a steady drip of fuel to the ground. The pilot refused to operate the aircraft.
text: walking down the jet bridge a mechanic from company x was waiting for me. he told me that they were working on a fuel leak on the left engine and that it might take approximately 30 minutes. we carried on with our flight preparation, and i relayed the maintenance information to the relief pilot who was about to start the walk around. i called dispatch to keep them in the loop. he patched we into maintenance control and they started working on it with maintenance. maintenance came to the cockpit to explain. he was saying it was just a small amount but with the language barrier he decided to draw me a picture. his depiction showed a depression in the pylon area that fills with fuel, and when it reaches the top, it spills over and results in the leak. he also showed me a picture he took on his phone, of a bolt where the fuel seems to be coming from. he wasn't sure what was on the other side of that bolt or the source of the fuel, but possibly the main tank. i spoke several times with dispatch and maintenance control said to call back because they were still working on it. the maintenance guy came to the cockpit to inform me that he spoke to company y maintenance and that we can accept the aircraft if it is a stain and not a leak. company y maintenance confirmed this. i told maintenance that i was concerned about our twelve and half hour flight home and that pylon collecting fuel. he thought it would be 'no more than a cup'. all four pilots went to look at the area in question. i could see fuel around the bolt and a grease fitting. i wiped the fuel away and it immediately re-appeared. it was at this time that the relief pilot informed me that when he did the walk around, he observed a steady drip of fuel, almost a steady stream, traveling towards the rear of the pylon and dripping to the ground aft of the combustion section. it was at this point that i refused the aircraft.cause: the aircraft came in a couple of hours before our arrival. maintenance found the leak on their walk around. how long had this leak been dripping and how much fuel was actually up there leaking, before my relief pilot saw it, to when it became a 'small drip'. they wrote up a 'leak' and then added a 'stain' so they could find a way for someone to accept this aircraft. it has been a couple of days, and the write up is still not in the software app. is this because they don't want the pilots to know what is happening with the aircraft until they actually get in the cockpit and read the book? if so, why else would you do this unless you want to apply added pressure to the captain to accept an unsafe aircraft. i recommended an engine run-up to see if the leak reappears. to my knowledge, this still has not been done. in the write up, in the book, it says 'leak is considered stain'. these two are mutually exclusive. a leak cannot be a stain.it's sad that we are playing semantics when safety is involved.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL
synopsis: A321 pilot reported receiving an ECAM for cabin pressurization during cruise. After landing; maintenance technicians reportedly cleared the ECAM write-up without issuing the required MEL.
text: aircraft x upon reaching cruise altitude of fl350 received an ecam for cab pr sys 1 fault. ran ecam, qrh, follow ups (none) and ecam supplemental. item was listed as 'crew awareness, ' as suspected. wrote up the ecam as it was listed in the status page as an inop system. logbook deferral sheet #redacted. continued to redacted without further incident. maintenance met the aircraft at the gate in redacted. they needed to run resets and computer checks so flight crew exited the cockpit. item was cleared with a final action of ok, message cleared. upon returning to the flight deck, i reviewed the sign off in the log book. the troubleshooting took some time and we were about done boarding. i checked the status and the inop system, cab pr 1 in amber was still in box 4 of the ecam. i called station maintenance and asked for the mechanics to return. the junior mechanic came back to the aircraft and i showed him the status message. he then saw that the system was indeed, not fixed. he said he needed to run the resets again. first officer stayed in the cockpit while i vacated the area so the mechanic could use my multipurpose control display unit (mcdu) and seat. he proceeded to troubleshoot the same issue for about 45 minutes. after some time passed, the more senior mechanic arrived back to the aircraft and joined his partner in the cockpit. the first officer exited the aircraft and joined me on the jetbridge. he was listening to the mechanics talk about the issue and basically realize that the system that they signed off, message cleared was in fact, not cleared. they were essentially attempting to fix the system this time without entering anything else into the maintenance logbook to cover up the fact that they didn't actually clear my write up. eventually, they gave up and decided to minimum equipment list the system. something that should have been done from the very start so that we could have had an on time departure out of redacted as this system was allowed on the minimum equipment list. they wrote up a new discrepency of cab press sys 1 fault logbook deferral sheet #xxxxxxy and applied minimum equipment list 21-redacted. they pulled and collared circuit breaker d9 and x23. we waited for the sign off to clear the logbook and reviewed an procedure that needed to be accomplished during pre flight to satisfy the minimum equipment list. upon review of the procedure, i saw that we needed to open circuit breaker x23 that controls the residual pressure control unit (rpcu) on step 1. step 6 states to close circuit breaker x23. this circuit breaker had been pulled and collared by redacted station maintenance. at this time i had lost all faith in these two mechanics. they were rushing to complete a task. i called air carrier x maintenance control and conferred with them about what to do. i asked if i had permission to remove the circuit breaker collar since the pre flight pilot procedure was to manipulate the circuit breaker and that it needed to be in the closed/in position for flight. after looking up the minimum equipment list and procedure, maintenance control agreed with me that the circuit breaker collar needed to be removed and left off to remain in compliance with the minimum equipment list. maintenance control mentioned that they station maintenance might have been using an old revision of their repair manuals. at this point, neither the first officer or i trusted that station maintenance complied with the maintenance procedures listed in the minimum equipment list so i had maintenance control go over them with me and he confirmed that by having circuit breaker d9 pulled, the aircraft maintenance manual (amm) procedures were in compliance. at this same time, the station maintenance called up to the flight deck using the ramp head set and told us to remove the circuit breaker collar at x23 and that they were using the wrong amm repair manual. he apologized. after reconfiguring the aircraft to the state that was in compliance with the minimum equipment list and performing the pre flight tasks associated with it, we deemed the flight safe to continue and left for our destination without further incident. i take this event to be a serious safety infraction as an expired manual was used in the application of an minimum equipment list that required circuit breakers to be pulled for flight. station maintenance's attempt to cover up the fact that they had cleared the write up instead of issuing the minimum equipment list was unacceptable. cause: use of expired repair, amm, and minimum equipment list manuals by redacted station maintenance. rushing to complete the task by redacted station maintenance. signing off a write up that shouldn't have been signed off. applying the wrong minimum equipment list procedure by redacted station maintenance. air carrier x's pressure of middle managers to push mechanics, pilots, and other staff to rush, overlooking a safe operation such that they achieve their quarterly bonuses is an egregious causal factor. it should never have come to the pilots needing to check the work of mechanics and fixing these mistakes as the last barrier to safety. these mistakes should never have been made and it shakes the foundation of safety culture and our trust in our peers' ability to perform their jobs safely and correctly. i do not appreciate being pushed to the limits of safety in the name of on time performance. i have a life outside of flying as a father and husband and i take those jobs extremely seriously and they are more important than any job flying airplanes. i intend on making it home to them every time i leave for work. this airline needs a serious look at other work group safety, i'm so tired of the onus being laid upon us time after time, risking our licenses and lives, for what? bonuses and stock prices. nasa, the faa, and whomever else has a stake in safety needs to have a look at practices here at air carrier x and really push safety first. we say it every day, it's time everyone actually lives it.

synopsis: Citation 560XLS flight crew reported cabin pressurization malfunction during climb. Flight descended and continued to destination.
text: during the climb, around 20, 000, the pilot in command and i heard and felt a 'bang'. i looked back and noticed that the aft seated passenger appeared to have just shut the lav door and i thought he slammed the door shut, thus causing the 'bang.' i glanced at the cabin pressure differential gauge and noted there was a split in the differential pressure and that it appeared normal.just after leveling off at 38, 000 the crew alerting system (cas) message 'cabin altitude' appeared. we donned our masks, requested priority handling, and started to descend. i pulled out and began to run the checklist. the pilot in command took the radios and requested a lower altitude and a clearance direct back to our home base. after running the checklist, i took note that the cabin pressure differential gauge still showed a split in differential pressure, and that cabin altitude showed 10, 000. the pilot in command advised the passengers of what happened and one passenger requested the oxygen masks, which the pilot in command then manually deployed.once we descended below 8, 000 the cas message 'cabin altitude' shut off. we canceled priority handling request and landed uneventfully back at our homebase.what i believe really caused the problem is that the outflow valve or some of the pressurization piping malfunctioned or blew a seal during climbout. to better respond to this issue in the future we could have requested priority handling soon after hearing the 'bang'. i now plan to monitor the cabin pressure differential gauge more closely during the climb and more frequently during level off and cruise.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Light twin pilot reported during cruse flight in the Grand Canyon SFRA encountering another aircraft not flying at the appropriate altitude for direction of flight resulting in taking evasive action to avoid a collision.
text: i was flying with my friend in his airplane during a visual flight rules sightseeing tour through the grand canyon special flight rules area (sfra). we were northbound in the corridor when we observed traffic at our altitude on an eastbound heading from our left on the adsb, resulting in a converging situation. the other aircraft subsequently turned southbound while remaining at the same altitude. per the applicable section of 14 cfr pertaining to this sfra, direction of flight within the grand canyon sfra corresponds to specific altitude assignments.as the traffic continued to close, we attempted multiple times to establish radio contact with the other aircraft on the ctaf to determine if they had us in sight. no response was received. the applicable section of 14 cfr requires all pilots operating within the sfra to monitor the designated ctaf frequency.as the closure rate increased and radio contact was not established, i disconnected the autopilot and began maneuvering a descent and right turn to create separation. at that moment, the right seat pilot called 'my controls.' to avoid a dual-input situation during an already time-critical event, i relinquished. the right seat pilot executed a left descend turn. the other aircraft passed at very close range. to my knowledge, i was the only crew member with a visual on the traffic throughout the encounter.following the incident, i recommended discontinuing the tour and landing. i also attempted to conduct an informal debrief with the other crew members on board, the conversation did not take place at that time.the next day, i identified the pilots from the other aircraft and approached them to discuss the incident and review the applicable sfra regulations. one pilot engaged in the conversation and indicated they had been receiving flight following services and had been attempting to descend at the time of the encounter. the remaining pilots from that aircraft did not engage in the discussion.contributing factors were the converging traffic at the same altitude within the sfra, no radio communication established on ctaf prior to close proximity, cockpit workload and crew coordination dynamics during the avoidance maneuver.continued pilot education on the grand canyon sfra requirements is recommended, particularly altitude assignments under the applicable section of 14 cfr and ctaf monitoring requirements. review of crm protocols for dual-pilot operations during traffic conflict situations, including clear pre-flight agreements on control transfer procedures.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Baron 55 Flight Instructor reported during training flight they experienced a stuck right throttle resulting in the Flight Instructor taking control of the aircraft and returning to the departure airport where they landed safely.
text: i was acting as pilot-in-command (pilot in command)/mei for an instructional flight at redacted. during our seventh lap of the traffic pattern, the student reported that the right engine manifold pressure (map) failed to decrease when the throttle lever was retarded. i verified that while the throttle lever could increase power, it would not respond to downward input.upon identifying the malfunction, the student relinquished the controls. i contacted redacted [tower], requested an immediate departure from the pattern, and diverted to redacted. redacted [tower] cleared us for a northwest departure and coordinated visual flight rules flight following with redacted [tracon].upon transitioning to redacted [tower], i advised them of the stuck throttle. redacted [tower] vectored traffic to accommodate our entry, allowing for a right downwind for xxr. i requested an extended downwind to ensure a lengthy stabilized final approach.during the descent, i briefed the student on our options. i determined that shutting down and feathering the right engine would severely diminish aircraft performance and negate our ability to perform a go-around. instead, i elected to conduct an approach using the stuck left engine at approximately 20' map, while managing the right engine's power via the throttle control as necessary. to ensure a safe, predictable landing, i planned to pull both mixtures to idle cut-off in the flare, thereby eliminating the risk of asymmetric thrust during the rollout.as we neared the landing phase, redacted [tower] moved a departing aircraft from xxr to xxl, clearing us to land. recognizing the presence of traffic behind us, i notified redacted [tower] of the mechanical issue and my intention to secure both engines via the mixtures upon landing, noting that we would likely be unable to clear the runway under our own power. when redacted [tower] inquired if i wished to request priority handling, i confirmed in the affirmative and requested that a tug be dispatched to our location.the landing was executed as planned. after the flare i pulled both mixtures to idle cut-off. the landing was uneventful and the aircraft retained sufficient momentum to turn onto taxiway 1 and clear the runway. once off the active surface, i secured the fuel and electrical systems and exited the aircraft. the aircraft was met by ground personnel and towed to the school's hangar. i performed a thorough post-flight debrief with the student regarding the incident and our aeronautical decision making process.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: PA-28 flight instructor reported taking controls of aircraft from student during the takeoff phase. Remainder of flight was uneventful.
text: at approximately xa:00 local at redacted, my student and i were departing for a fly-in event at redacted. the student had approximately 10 hours of private pilot training at the time.preflight and taxi to runway xx were uneventful. after receiving takeoff clearance, the student began the takeoff roll and applied power. during the roll, the aircraft began drifting to the right--either due to excessive right rudder input or a crosswind from the east causing a weathervaning effect.in an attempt to avoid departing the runway into the grass, the student rotated early and aggressively, placing the aircraft in approximately a 15-30 degree nose-high attitude.i verbalized, 'i have the controls, ' and attempted to lower the nose to reduce the angle of attack for a standard climbout. the student was unresponsive, his fight-or-flight response appeared fully active, and he was fighting me on the controls with both hands.i had to physically remove his arms and hands from the controls in order to regain control. i was then able to lower the nose enough for the stall warning to cease.the remainder of the flight was uneventful.contributing factors may have included slight complacency during the takeoff phase. in hindsight, more active rudder coaching--such as prompting or assisting with left rudder during the takeoff roll--may have helped prevent the initial deviation.after the flight, we conducted a debrief. the student understood what occurred and recognized that he had placed the aircraft in a potential power-on stall situation.after further discussion with other instructors, an alternative technique was suggested: temporarily blocking the student's visual reference (e.g., covering their eyes) to interrupt the startle/freeze response and regain control of the aircraft. i plan to evaluate this technique and incorporate it into future training as appropriate.the purpose of this report is to recommend that flight instructors incorporate a mandatory simulated takeoff upset prevention scenario, including techniques to ensure the student releases the controls when necessary. i believe this should be a required task in the cfi acs (airman certification standards).lighter or less physically strong instructors may be at a disadvantage when a student resists. a dpe could simulate early rotation and/or poor directional control during the takeoff roll, transitioning into a high but still safe climb. the instructor should emphasize a clear positive exchange of flight controls, and be prepared to take immediate, decisive action such as covering their eyes to regain control of the aircraft if the student does not comply.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a NMAC while entering the traffic pattern at EUL non-towered airport. Flight continued to a landing.
text: traffic at eul was using runway 12. we made an initial inbound call 5 nm sw stating our intention to cross midfield at 4, 000 msl, then set up to enter the pattern runway 12. we noted the presence of two fixed wing aircraft in the pattern, but did not hear any calls from aircraft on the 45, or intending to enter the pattern as such. we crossed midfield at 4, 000 and made a call stating our position and intention to enter the pattern via teardrop.approximately 2.5 miles ne of eul we cleared the area to the right in the direction of the teardrop, then began a descending right turn to join the 45 left downwind 12. aircraft y made a radio call saying, 'did you see the aircraft y you just flew over, trying to get on the 45?' i (instructor, right seat) looked right and low, and saw aircraft y behind us on what appeared to be a 180 heading 2 nm due e of the runway. it appeared aircraft y was trying to join the 45 from the north, and made a tight turn to enter the pattern. upon reviewing the event, my student and i agreed aircraft y made no advisories calls prior to the one above. aircraft y appeared to be attempting a 45 degree entry very close to the airport from the n, which put us on a course where aircraft y was in our blind spot below.after reviewing ac 90-66c, we determined the best course of action for the future when crossing midfield for a teardrop entry on the 45, is to cross, fly outbound at least 2 miles, and descend prior to turning inbound on the 45. we also determined to be more clear when stating intentions to enter the pattern on the 45, so as to provide more situational awareness for fellow aviators. we recognize that advisory calls on the ctaf are not mandatory, but crucial for safety.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: GA Flight Instructor reported a conflict with ground vehicle on takeoff from EIK non-towered airport. Instructor continued take off to avoid traffic.
text: while i was teaching my student untowered airport communications at eik we had just completed a full stop taxi back landing on runway 34, exiting via a4, taxing via a back to runway 34 and using radio calls with each segment.we visually cleared base, final, and the runway before departing and called our departure on runway 34 via iek ctaf, at ~48 knots a side by side vehicle going from the left to right blew through a3 around ~500 feet in front of us.at this point i deemed it not possible to stop the aircraft and pulled the aircraft off the runway to clear the conflict, recovering airspeed once airborne.while looking outside to ensure i was clear of the side by side vehicle i noted that if we where not off the ground it looked like we would have collided with the side by side and injury may have resulted.the side by side vehicle made no attempt to stop / hold short of runway 16-34 on a3, it seemed like it made no attempt to speed up or slow down while crossing, it did not make any radio calls, and it did not respond to my request if they where listening/ on eik ctaf - there where 2 passengers in side side by side.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Other / Unknown; Ground Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: Commander Lark pilot reported engine failure due to fuel starvation during takeoff. Aircraft was pulled back to FBO by tug.
text: after during runup checks, i moved the fuel selector switch to off instead of both. approached the hold short line, told to hold short for landing traffic. cleared by tower to lineup and wait, was given takeoff clearance, started to accelerate, engine quit due to fuel starvation. battery was too weak to restart the airplane due to minimal flying in previous weeks. tug was called from fbo to pull plane back to hangar.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Cessna 150 pilot reported unstabilized approach due to crosswinds. Pilot executed missed approach and returned to departure airport.
text: i was entering a straight-in approach to runway xx at redacted, intending to practice crosswind landing. i believe winds were 300 @15kt, and knowing it was a strong crosswind i wanted to test this specific airplane in those winds. this was the first contributing factor, not having done crosswind landing in some time, and not in this airplane. i was not strongly considering my minimums.i had significant right-rudder input, as well as moderate left aileron, lined up with the runway and doing fine until i hit a strong downdraft over the highway. i had expected this downdraft having flown this approach before, but the downdraft felt much stronger than what i'd prepared for and i elected to go-around. not having a solid plan for the go-around and aerodynamic effects of full power from the crosswind landing configuration into a climb was my second contributing factor. i knew i may go-around, but i hadn't visualized it and prepared for it sufficiently. as power was added, i failed to maintain left aileron and the plane began to yaw to the right. i failed remove rudder and maintain runway heading, and panic started to set in. i failed to notice my right leg was still mashing the right rudder for several seconds.at this point i was doing everything i could to maintain airspeed well above stall, instinctually pushing the nose down and for some reason i let the airplane turn to the right as i struggled to maintain level flight and airspeed. i realized my foot was heavily or possibly full right rudder once i had significantly deviated from runway heading and neutralized the rudder after at this point. i stabilized the climb and headed south, maintaining separation from the tree line south of the airport. at this time i was close to heading 140, roughly 2000ft to the west side of the xy approach, low, headed downwind. i elected to head straight back to my departure airport redacted and end the flight.my performance in this flight was definitely inadequate. i did not take appropriate action to train on this specific flight condition in my aircraft with a cfi, or refresh with a cfi in recent months on higher crosswinds, and my skillset has obviously diminished, or i overestimated my minimums for this aircraft, a c150d with a horton stol kit. my judgement to take a leisurely scenic flight and 'throw in some crosswind practice' on my way north created risks due to insufficient planning and contingency planning for 'whatifs' and i was not prepared to react properly in my go-around. i hope my experience will help others to not make the same mistake. practicing crosswind landings is crucial, briefing phases of flight, and their resultant phases of flight, whether it be landing or going around, is crucial. i made a decision to challenge myself, without preparing myself. i had to work very hard to recover from what should have been an ordinary crosswind practice approach and landing, and this is largely due to the startle effect and subsequent panic when my right leg became frozen subconsciously. i'm happy nobody was hurt.in the future i will practice in a simulator and with a cfi, and refresh my personal minimums to better judge what i can do safely. i will review proper crosswind technique, and go-arounds in crosswinds. i will also research what i can do to avoid freezing any particular control in urgent situations. i think making sure i am in the best condition to fly is also imperative, as being dehydrated, tired, or less than optimal overall can have dire effects when stressors are added.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A ZDV Controller reported their sector assumed the CYS TRACON airspace and they were not sure of the requirements to maintain terrain separation for departures from CYS.
text: cheyenne tower was open with no approach control yet. they called for release on aircraft x and i said 'aircraft x is released.' when aircraft x called me, they said they were 'climbing to one one thousand, runway heading' and they were only out of about 8, 000 ft. heading westbound. the mia (minimum instrument flight rules altitude) in that area is ten thousand and increases to eleven thousand. i wasn't sure if there was a tower procedure i didn't know about so i said, 'leaving one zero thousand, cleared on course direct denver vor.'having cheyenne function as a tower only has created a lot of confusion. i'm not sure if this is a contributing factor because i don't know rules between tower and approach controllers. i do know that it didn't seem safe for an airplane to be flying below my mia without being on a departure procedure or taking responsibility for his own terrain and obstruction clearance.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: ZMA Enroute Air Traffic Controller reported a situation where another sector implemented a no notice airspace closure resulting in making their sector overloaded and highly complex with no plan of action to resolve the issue and others allowing more aircraft to enter the airspace.
text: on day 0, while working a very busy sector xx, i was placed in an operational situation that i believed was unsafe due to traffic saturation, excessive workload, and the lack of safe alternatives. i was advised by the controller in charge that sector xy was going to shut me off and that, if not, i would need to hold and/or vector aircraft because of the traffic volume. i immediately stated that, given the complexity of the operation, the safest course of action was to ground stop departures rather than continue feeding traffic into an overloaded sector or require tactical vectoring in already saturated airspace.i was then advised that, at managements request, i was expected to spin aircraft. i stated that i would not do so because, in my judgment, vectoring aircraft in close proximity at the same altitudes during a high-workload saturated operation was unsafe and created unacceptable risk. i advised that i would instead descend aircraft and call them to the sector that owned fl240 through fl340, which i believed was the safer alternative under the circumstances.the aircraft i specifically recall being involved were aircraft x and aircraft y at fl310 and fl330. aircraft z may also have been involved in the overall situation, although i do not specifically recall shipping that aircraft without a handoff.as aircraft x and aircraft y approached the sector boundary, my radar associate initiated a handoff to sector xz. the receiving controller advised that he was unable and would not take the handoff. i then got on the line myself as the radar position and explained that we were extremely busy, that sector xy was shutting us off, and that we needed assistance. the receiving controller again refused to accept the aircraft. at that point, i believed i had been left without a safe operational alternative. in my judgment, additional vectoring or spinning of aircraft in that environment would have created a greater and more immediate hazard. i therefore advised that i was going to ship the aircraft without handoffs because no safe alternative was being made available to me.in my judgment, the more dangerous action would have been to vector and spin aircraft at the same altitude during a saturated, high-workload operation, as i had been directed to do. there was an expectation of compliance even where safety concerns had been raised.i am concerned that this event reflects a broader pattern in which unsafe operational situations are allowed to develop and persist without sufficient corrective action. when controllers raise legitimate safety concerns and are met with pressure rather than support and mitigation, operational risk is normalized instead of corrected. if these conditions are allowed to continue unchecked, unfortunate consequences may result.i am submitting this report because i believe i was placed in an unsafe operational situation, was directed to take action that i believed increased risk, and refused to compromise safety. a stronger stand for safety must be taken by management to ensure controllers are supported in making safe operational decisions and to protect and preserve human life.establish clear procedures for sector saturation events so departures are stopped, sectors are shut off, or other traffic management initiatives are implemented before controllers are forced into unsafe tactical situations.controllers should not be directed to use tactics they identify in real time as unsafe. when a controller raises a safety objection, management should be required to assess and mitigate the hazard rather than pressure compliance.require immediate supervisory escalation when a receiving sector refuses handoffs during a saturation event so the controller is not left without a safe operational outlet.provide additional training for management and supervisory personnel on safety culture, operational risk management, and response to controller-raised safety concerns, with emphasis on supporting safe decisions.conduct a review of staffing, traffic flow practices, workload management, and recurring saturation events to determine whether unsafe conditions are being allowed to develop without timely corrective action.reinforce through policy and practice that protecting human life and operational safety takes priority over production pressure or unquestioned compliance with management direction.i respectfully recommend that this event be reviewed not as an isolated occurrence, but as a warning of broader workload, coordination, and safety-culture issues that require corrective action before a more serious incident occurs.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Tower Controller reported an air carrier pilot questioned the bright lights about a quarter of the way down PWM Runway 29; saying they were overly bright and confusing.
text: aircraft x was on final approach to land runway 29. since they were the only aircraft on frequency, they asked what the lights were about 1/4 down the runway were. they made the comment that the lights looked like a vehicle. i told them that they were the runway lead on lights. they responded saying 'well they are very bright'. the aircraft landed without incident. i do not know exactly what needs to change so pilots don't get these lights confused with a vehicle. i would think all pilots are much more on edge watching for vehicles on the runway. some pilots in the future might elect to just go around without asking, potentially putting them in an unexpected unsafe situation, or just wasting their time / gas over nothing. something should change so this situation doesn't happen.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported ORD Taxiway T center line is very faded and hard to see.
text: taxiway t is relatively new at ord, yet the center taxiway line is almost completed faded /gone, making it very difficult to see, especially at night or when it is wet. this is compounded by the fact that the taxiway zigzags left and right, making the issue worse. on top of this, taxiway k leading to taxiway t has multiple old joining taxiway lines that are still somewhat visible and have not been removed fully, which again at night or when wet makes it difficult to discern which centerline is the correct one.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported crossing hold short line during taxi for takeoff. Crew continued taxi per ATC instructions.
text: clearance by tower to taxi to runway xx via 1 and 2 and i understood the instructions to be to backtrack to holding point of runway xx and hold short of runway xx at that point, a common taxi instruction to runway xx. i am very familiar with redacted and have been doing redacted turns all month. i read back taxi instructions to the first officer 1, 2, backtrack xx and hold short. obviously there was a miscommunication. we completed the before takeoff checklist to the line before taxiing to try and avoid threats and distractions. i then called for 'final items' which i will never do again in this particular area because it brought the first officer heads down at a critical point. i would say the majority of the time i finish the entire before takeoff checklist before taxiing out of redacted due to this particular threat. just as we crossed the hold short line tower told us to stop which we did but nose of aircraft was across the hold short line. there was an aircraft on final that was sent around, guessing approximately 1000-1500 feet. i did clear left and right and saw no aircraft before proceeding across hold short line.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported fuel leak in cruise flight. Diverted and landing uneventfully.
text: while at cruise at fl330, upon turning off the center fuel tank pumps, an imbalance of between 500-600 lbs low was observed in the right tank. we ran the crossfeed checklist to balance the tanks. we referenced the flight progress tool and noted we were about 1000 lbs lighter than our planned fuel should have been. we ran the suspected fuel leak checklist. once balanced we started a timer. per the checklist if in 30 minutes a difference of 500 lbs is observed a fuel leak is verified. we reached the 500 lbs difference in in 9 minutes. our fuel projected at landing was continuing to decrease.we coordinated with dispatch, our flight attendants, made announcements to the passengers, requested priority handling with air traffic control, started a decent, and diverted directly for redacted. per the checklist we shut down the engine number 2 on the side with the confirmed fuel leak. we observed a stop in the loss of fuel post engine 2 shutdown. we also ran the overweight landing checklist as we landed about 2, 000 lbs overweight. upon landing on runway xxr at redacted, we cleared the runway and had airport rescue and firefighting inspect the aircraft. after no abnormalities were observed we single engine taxied to the gate. proper logbook entries for the fuel leak and overweight landing were made post shutdown at the gate.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B767 First Officer reported that the EFB Jet Pro APP is prone to lockups; is unresponsive; and unusable since an update that resulted in a loss of a navigation resource.
text: i have noticed since updating to ios 26.x that the jepp pro app on the efb is prone to lockup, becoming frozen and unresponsive. it seems to happen most often while using moving map on the high ifr chart, where the map will freeze and the screen becomes distorted. at that point the jeppesen pro app becomes unresponsive and must be restarted again. no other apps seem to be effected, nor data lost on the restart. thankfully it hasn't happened while in a critical phase of flight while in a flying seat, though i have heard reports of other crew members saying they've had the same issue.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A319 Captain reported uncommanded aircraft movement after releasing brakes to begin the pushback. The Captain applied the brakes with no damage or injury to ramp personnel.
text: before pushback i was talking to ramp. they said they were 'ready for the brakes' and the before pushback checklist was complete. i replied with 'brakes released, standby.' the aircraft rolled approximately 5 feet backwards when ramp told me to 'stop the airplane.' i applied brakes and stopped the aircraft. i coordinated with ramp and reset the parking brake, i told ramp that we needed to reset the pushback and started over 'from the beginning because we had an uncommanded aircraft movement.' the rest of the pushback was uneventful.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: B787 First Officer reported the weather application froze up and restarted a couple of times while attempting to use it and was showing different information from the Captain's.
text: the weather app froze up multiple times, while attempting to use it. it even restarted a couple of times. also, it appears that it is constantly trying to update, as indicated in the lower left corner. it also, almost continually shows that it is attempting to connect, as indicated at the top of the screen. furthermore, there were multiple times throughout the flight where my map layers were showing different data than the captain's electronic device, despite our settings being the same. for example, multiple missing flight planning guidance (fpgs) or sigmets. this instability does not inspire confidence in the app.multiple times during the flight the flitedeck pro screen would freeze and become unresponsive (other electronic device functions continued to work normally). several times actually restarted. fortunately, none of this occurred during a critical phase of flight. it appears that the new version is not stable and contains bugs.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B767 Captain reported a RT HYD QTY EICAS message during cruise after coasting in from oceanic airspace. The flight continued to the destination and landed.
text: approaching the coast of location x, eicas rt hyd qty. status page was selected and quantity was depleting at a fairly rapid pace. ran hyd qty (r) checklist. hyd quantity continued to deplete at a slower pace. eicas r hyd sys press on and then ran hyd sys press (r) checklist. dispatch, maintenance control, and chief pilot notified. all were in agreement to recommend continuing to redacted, as other two hydraulic systems were normal and aircraft handling characteristics were normal. after conferring with flight crew, we agreed to continue to redacted. flight attendants were advised of the situation and told to prepare for a normal landing. passengers were advised as well. air traffic control was advised and a normal landing was accomplished without event.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: Ramp agent reported an uncommanded aircraft movement when starting the pushback for a reposition tow from the gate. There was no injury or damage to the aircraft and the reposition tow was completed to the new gate.
text: my partner and i were in tug xx. we approached the nose of the aircraft to pin it and capture it. we were also going to hook up the ground power because it was not hooked up, but lying on the ground. my partner then pointed out the stairs that were resting and wedged in between the aircraft and the ground. we had to wait for a decision from management to start the rest of our assignment.i went through my sop and checklist for shutting down the apu. i released the brakes and then my partner helped me guide the jet bridge to its painted marking. once the aircraft went wheels up, i signaled to a ramp agent in [gate] xx that it was ok to grab the chocks. i helped him put a chock in the chock cart. i went back to the tug to grab the wands. i walked out to the service road. my partner gave me the horn sound and he turned the tow lights on. i thought that he should be moving by now. my partner said on the radio that it is not moving. i came to the tug and asked what the issue is. he said it's just not moving. i mentioned to him maybe try and reset it by turning it off and on. i didn't realize that the paddles on tug xx were open and the aircraft started to roll. i froze for a second before i started looking for chocks on the ground. there weren't any. the plane stopped rolling then i saw the ramp supervisor chock the back tire. there was a lot going on before all of this with other employees trying to intervene. after my partner was able to recapture the aircraft, the tug (xx) would not lift up the aircraft. my partner finally got it to lift up and was able to move it back a few feet. before this happened, i asked the ramp supervisor if we can move the aircraft, he said it was ok to do so. we then proceeded to finish our tow to [gate] xy.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier push crew member reported pilots failure to set brakes after push back was complete resulting in aircraft movement. Brakes were then set.
text: i was pushing plane out when the pilot ask me to push him deep. i told him another plane was getting ready to push and i didn't want to block them from coming out. he told me to push him deep again and it pushed him a little pass next gate so i wouldn't block the plane that was getting ready to push. once i stop pushing, i ask was that good he said yes and it was a great push. i said thanks and set brakes. waited to give the hand signal to the wingwalker, but then the plane started to roll. the pilot said i didn't set brakes, so i said it again. no one got hurt but the plane did roll a few feet.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier push crew member reported uncommanded movement of the aircraft at the gate prior to push back. Aircraft was stopped.
text: upon arrival to assigned gate (xx), a service ladder was discovered wedged up against the front of the plane on the captain's side. this caused a delay with our process to move the plane from the gate by the assigned time. once ready to push back and having received clearance, the push tractor gave a system error warning and would not move. i notified my partner and ramp tower to cancel push. i then proceeded to lower the cradle in order to reset the push tractor. in error, i released the tire paddles without securing the aircraft rear tires and therefore the aircraft rolled back 10 to 15 feet. pressure to get the aircraft off the gate by ramp tower and company agents waiting for the gate for a company aircraft in sight and waiting on the taxiway, led me to a major lapse in judgement resulting to this incident. this was my mistake and i take full responsibility. the good news, there was no damage nor injuries, but the possibility was certainly immanent.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Pilatus PC-12 pilot reported receiving a Central Advisory and Warming System caution during take off. Pilot returned to departure airport and landed uneventfully.
text: on day 0 at approximately xa:40 hrs i was pilot in command of aircraft x conducting a maintenance check at redacted. i was cleared for takeoff from xxr and upon rotation and with positive rate of climb i retracting the gear and immediately received a caws (central advisory and warning system) caution light for 'bus tie' and 'non essential bus'. i advised the tower that i wanted to remain in the pattern and land due to an unknown electrical issue. while downwind for xxr i selected the gear handle in the 'down' position and immediately received a 'hyd' indication on my caws panel with (2) green indicator lights advising that my main wheels were extended and locked but my nose wheel had a red light indication. i contacted tower and to request priority and a request for a low approach for the tower to inspect my nose wheel. prior to passing the tower i utilized the manual gear extension handle allowing for the nose gear to fully extend and i confirmed with a 'green' nose gear indicator light. i conducted a low approach near the tower and i was advised that my nose gear appeared down and locked in place. based on the information i received from the tower, information received from indications in the airplane, and my prior training and experience with this make and model of airplane, i formed the opinion that my landing gear was in the down and locked position, and that it was safe to conduct attempt a landing on xxr. the landing was uneventful and the airplane was in good condition to taxi back to the hangar without incident. i was the sole occupant on board and there was no injuries or damage to the airplane.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported possible open nose gear door during climb. Crew returned to departure airport for a normal landing.
text: while at approximately 15, 000 feet and a little over 300 kias while in the climb to redacted we heard a very loud noise and felt a thud along with some vibrations. in the second the passed we determined that it was likely the nose gear doors deploying. i then disengaged the autopilot, put thrust to idle, deployed speed breaks, and leveled our attitude to bleed speed quickly to get below 250 kias to reduce aerodynamic load on the doors. during this maneuver the captain and i verified via the eicas that the nose gear had not deployed. upon reaching a reasonable speed for our new configuration we referred to the qrh 'nose landing gear up door open'. the captain decided that it was best to request priority handling and commence a return to redacted out of precaution. i flew and worked comms while the captain worked through notifying air traffic control, dispatch, the fa (to include the special procedures), and the pax. we then reconvened and completed the necessary cruise, descent, and approach checks and briefings. i had two major threats i included in the brief. my concerns were structural damage to the door that may impede the operation and deployment of the nose gear door and thus secondly a chance that the nose gear would deploy properly. for these reasons i decided that i would deploy the gear prior to commencing the approach to verify a three green, down and locked condition. if we did not get that, we had a plan to hold and execute the procedures for that condition. due to our concerns of structural damage to the doors we felt it appropriate and precautions to have arff (airport rescue and firefighting) respond.following an uneventful landing, we were escorted to our gate by operations and arff. the post flight inspection revealed no noticeable deformities to the nose gear doors.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: A319 Captain reported a ground conflict with baggage cart at end of push back phase.
text: our pushback clearance was 'tail west, drop point' from gate xx in redacted. just prior to the 'brake set, cleared to disconnect interphone', i noticed that the nose was over the roadway for the vehicles to use. i believe the nose wheel was directly on the drop point spot. after the salute, i noticed a baggage cart moving from right to left go under the nose of the airplane. all traffic that uses this road was yielding. the baggage cart stopped at gate xy to drop off his passenger and he continued on. we continued on to destination.cause: i guess some people are in a hurry to make sure they either get to were they need to go. what if i started to apply power and hit the baggage cart. they were completely out of my view. i only saw them out of the corner of my eye. either people need to be more serious about their surroundings or we need more time to move passengers and bags between banks. maybe there is not enough emphasis on what can go wrong. i guess a person needs to be fatally injured for change.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A319 Captain reported a brake system fault message during takeoff roll that resulted in a rejected takeoff.
text: cleared for takeoff runway xxl at redacted the pf (the first officer) began pushing the power toward takeoff power (flex) when an ecam for brake sys 2 fault was triggered. the first officer called reject and brought the power back toward idle. the captain called reject my aircraft and initiated the reject procedure. the first officer noted 18kts as the max speed. there was no immediate danger or serious concern. the aircraft taxied clear of the runway without declaring an emergency or requiring assistance. at a stop the crew talked to mx (maintenance) who recommended a return to gate for further inspection. the crew coordinated with mx, dispatcher, and ops for a return to gate. the fas and passengers were informed and the aircraft returned to the gate without incident. cause: the ecam for brake sys 2 fault caused the immediate takeoff rejection and return to gate. the aircraft had a history of the same malfunction. possibly addressing the reoccurring malfunction sooner could have prevented the reject.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CRJ-550 pilot reported after receiving their takeoff clearance experiencing IB FLT SPLRS and SPOILERONS caution messages resulting in the flight crew rejecting the takeoff and returning to the gate.
text: i was the pf on this flight. after receiving takeoff clearance for runway xxl, we selected toga and began advancing the thrust levers. immediately upon application of thrust, we received ib flt splrs and ib spoilerons caution messages.given the abnormal indications at the start of the takeoff roll, we elected to discontinue the takeoff while at very low speed. we notified air traffic control and were instructed to exit runway xxl at 1, then turn right on taxiway 2 short of 3.once clear of the runway, we accomplished the applicable qrh procedures and contacted maintenance control. based on their guidance, we returned to the gate, where maintenance personnel met the aircraft. the discrepancy was entered in the aircraft logbook, and the aircraft was subsequently placed aog.both the captain and i later called fatigue, with reports on file.while this event could be categorized as a rejected takeoff, the aircraft was at minimal speed with negligible acceleration. additionally, this is not typically a condition that would warrant a high-speed reject. however, due to the unexpected caution messages at the initiation of the takeoff roll, we elected to abort in the interest of safety.cause: this occurred near the end of a long duty day following an early report. the first half of the trip involved duty periods extending close to midnight, which may have contributed to cumulative fatigue and influenced our decision-making.suggestions: overall, i feel like we handled this situation appropriately and in the interest of passenger safety. had we had been at a high speed, an aborted takeoff might not have been appropriate however we were at minimal speed.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CRJ-700 Captain reported Steering Inop caution message on climb. Flight continued to destination and landed safely.
text: steering inop caution message after take off. followed qrh. advised air traffic control. landed safely at redacted.cause: steering inopsuggestions: need better mx (maintenance)

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported lack of aileron feel resistance during flight. Flight continued to destination.
text: during takeoff from redacted runway xx, with 12 knot winds reported from 70 degrees right of centerline, slight r aileron was applied into the wind. during takeoff roll above 80 knots observed some lateral controllability issues - as if the slight right aileron input applied was too much.during the climb observed all three slip/skid indicators showed the brick slightly left of center and some l rudder trim was applied to bring the slip/skid 'bricks' into neutral alignment.engaged ap (autopilot) at 600 feet. no ap trim messages during flight. during approach, disengaged ap at 2200 msl and observed aircraft wanting to roll uncommanded to the right. applied nearly one index mark of l aileron trim (approx ½ of total l aileron trim available). after applying this trim to reduce workload, observed a slop (dead band) in the control wheel between neutral and approx 20 degrees left of neutral. there was 'feel' (resistance) immediately from neutral to any control wheel position to the right of neutral, but no 'feel' (resistance) was felt between neutral and 15 to 20 degrees control wheel rotation left of neutral. essential there is nothing to prevent the pilot from overcontrolling the aircraft between neutral and any input between 0 and 15 degrees left of neutral. from 15 degrees left of neutral and beyond there is feel (resistance).the aircraft had seen a successful functional check flight in the past four days for a disconnected l and r aileron cables / replaced cable guide if i recall. cause: unknown.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: BE-95 Travel Air flight instructor reported an engine fire after landing. Fire was extinguished.
text: returning to redacted, <10nm noticed egt temps were high on right engine. ensured mixtures were set to rich, and cowl flaps were open. reduced power settings and temps returned to a normal state. all other indications were showing normal for operations. proceeded to fly and land the aircraft with no issues. upon exiting the runway, right engine shut down. i proceeded to restart the engine and keep taxiing to the non-movement area with no faulty indications. while pulling in to parking t-spot right engine shut off again. to continue taxi, i attempted to restart the engine again, without hearing, seeing or smelling any news of a fire, tower announced to us that we had a fire. a few seconds later, flames surrounded the sides of the right cowling. i immediately pulled all throttles to idle and mixtures to cutoff. grabbed the extinguisher, and evacuated the aircraft with my student. the extinguisher in the aircraft was not strong enough for the flame, so student went to obtain larger extinguisher from fuel truck, i returned to the plane to double check everything was off. student arrived with the extinguisher 20-30 seconds later, and we put the fire completely out. no damage was done to any persons or souls on board, nor any property other than the right engine.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Aero Commander AC50 pilot reported a loss of hydraulic system during takeoff.  Flight returned to departure airport.
text: after takeoff from redacted, the gear was selected up but it took a bit longer than normal for the gear to swing. the nose gear never came up because it is held up by hydraulic pressure. we cycled the gear to the down position where we could now see hydraulic fluid spraying out of the right hand gear well. we ran the appropriate checklists and came back to land at redacted without flaps. the emergency aux hydraulic system was used for braking and then we shut down the engines on the runway, and were towed back to the fbo.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: PA 28 pilot reported a main gear collapse on runway during landing resulting in a runway excursion.
text: while conducting a flight for the purpose of completing a certificated flight instructor (cfi) practical test, the incident aircraft (pa28r-200) experienced retractable gear malfunction/collapse and erroneous indications. while approaching the right downwind for runway xxr and after contacting redacted tower, both the designated pilot examiner (dpe) and cfi candidate on board the incident aircraft witnessed the two main gear lights illuminated and the nose-wheel indicator light off after setting the gear selector switch in the 'down' position. both pilots onboard immediately established appropriate crm and began troubleshooting efforts. these efforts included: several pass-by's for a controller/tower visual inspection of the landing gear, multiple usage of the 'emergency landing gear extension' checklist and yawing maneuvers, and one final tower confirmation that the gear was down prior to landing. throughout the 'troubleshooting' phase of the flight, the 'gear in transit' light would remain illuminated and a whining noise (suspected by the pilots to be a hydraulic pump) was audibly heard. after the incident aircraft made the several low passes, the redacted tower controller stated that the gear appeared to be down and that he was unsure the gear was locked. ultimately, the decision was made between both pilots on-board to make a landing on runway xxl (longer and wider runway). understanding that the nose wheel indicator light remained off, the landing was briefed in the flight-deck by the pilots. it would be a smooth landing (using similar techniques as required for a soft-field landing) and the aircraft would be allowed to 'roll' with no braking as necessary in order to prevent the nose gear from collapsing in the event it was not locked and uncontrollably-lowered by itself. priority handling was [given] by the tower and fire-emergency services were requested by the pilots prior to landing. approximately 20-30 minutes after first responders were contacted, emergency vehicles and airport personnel were ready. it was decided that the dpe would land the aircraft on runway xxl and the cfi candidate would operate the only exit door located at the right side of the aircraft. upon landing, the aircraft's main landing gears touched down smoothly and within seconds of landing the right main gear slowly collapsed by itself. upon feeling this unexpected condition, the dpe corrected by deflecting the control wheel to the left in an effort to prevent the hard impact of the right (lowering) wingtip with the runway. eventually, the right wing/wingtip would impact the runway causing the right wing to drift aft and the aircraft to veer off the runway and into the dirt just off the right side of runway xxl. as the aircraft came to a stop, the engine was immediately isolated/starved of fuel and the aircraft's right door was opened. an immediate evacuation was initiated and no injuries or fire occurred. emergency services and airport personnel responded in a quick manner and were ready to assist pilots as necessary. in retrospect, this incident showed me how critical crew resource management (crm) is in the event of an emergency. despite having large differences in experience between the dpe and cfi candidate, both pilots communicated, split tasks, and assessed the situation continuously. aside from the crm found in the flight-deck, it is my opinion that the assistance/communication that redacted tower provided was concise and necessary to the outcome of the best case scenario of this incident. with this in mind, it was emphasized/learned that communication and clear actions both inside and outside the flight-deck are necessary in the event of an emergency.

text: while conducting the visual xxl into redacted on final tower asked if we could switch to land runway xxr. the ca (pm) told tower we could and as the pf i disconnected the autopilot & autothrottle with the airfield insight to proceed visually for xxr. the ca tuned up the xxr instrument landing system frequency and selected approach mode to give me a good flight director for the new runway. shortly thereafter we continued configuring the aircraft for landing. after the flaps 30 landing checklist call the captain noticed the flap position indication was stopped between flaps 25 & flaps 30. we were on course and on glide slope in a safe position to land. the ca stated continue. still on course and glide slope closer to the ground we got the aural 'too low terrain & too low flaps' callouts. the ca again stated continue. we safely landed the aircraft. after landing and clearing the runway the ca wrote up the irregular flap condition and we notified maintenance requesting that they meet us at the gate. we left the flaps at the selected position 30 for taxi in with the indication still displaying between 25 and 30 for maintenance personnel to see. maintenance said they were going to work the problem.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: A321 flight crew reported a hard landing which resulted in a bounce upon touchdown and a Pitch; Pitch; Pitch aural warning. The Captain took control of the aircraft and completed the landing with no damage or injury reported.
text: everything was normal until very short final below 50 feet. winds were a little gusty but the first officer was handling the plane well and we were stable. the first concern i got was coming through 30 feet and the first officer had not begun a sufficient flare rotation, so i said something to the effect of 'round it out.' this began a period of just 3-4 seconds where everything happened, starting with a very firm touchdown mains first. the plane either bounced or fully extended the gear shocks, but movement was definitely upward and i called for a go-around. as the aircraft settled back down onto the runway i looked down at the thrust levers and in that instant it appeared that the first officer had started the reverse process part of the landing sequence, and then went up to toga mode after my go around call. since i thought i had seen thrust reversers activated, i said something like 'forget it. i have the aircraft', and control was immediately relinquished to me. i went into full reverse with approximately 7000ft of runway remaining and the aircraft was fully settled and under control. again, this sequence of events happened very quickly, just a couple of seconds, during which i was working off of outside visual cues and a brief glance at the thrust levers. i did not see the vsi or primary flight display (pfd) and cannot say what they were reading at touchdown, but got some info after parking from the jumpseater who helped us debrief and break down what went wrong. rollout and taxi-in were normal, and after the parking checklist, the first officer and i debriefed the landing and requested input from the jumpseater, who was performing a faa line operations safety assessment (losa). knowing that losa observers don't normally debrief, i felt like this event was important enough to request his input just as a fellow air carrier captain. he pointed out two things that in the moment i did not even realize had occurred: our touchdown pitch had approached 10 degrees, and we got the 'pitch pitch pitch' aural. in those few seconds where everything was coming at us fast, i must have had a tunnel vision effect that did not allow that cue into my thought process. had he not told us, i would not have know that occurred. after the debrief, the first officer and i went outside to check for any indications of a tail strike and found none.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A320 Captain reported a hydraulic quantity malfunction during cruise. The flight returned to the departure airport; landed; and required a tow to the gate where maintenance found a leaking hydraulic line.
text: normal climb out of redacted. kept the flight attendants seated a little longer for turbulence. finally found some smooth air and let everyone up. we had done our cruise checks and all systems looked normal. was in cruise flight nearly an hour into the flight when we got an ecam for hyd g sys lo pr, g rsvr lo lvl, g eng 1 pump lo pr. the hydraulic system page showed no fluid in the green system. we followed the ecam. we referenced the flight manual (fm). we alerted dispatch and the fa's. we talked to operations about best divert options. i didn't want to attempt a landing in redacted because we would be a fixed gear aircraft in the event of a go-around and the mountains and night time special airport was a concern. we talked about redacted, redacted and redacted. operations said that redacted would be best for the operation. the first officer and i discussed that if any other systems degraded we would drop immediately back to redacted but we felt ok to return to redacted for the best resources. we did a brief with the fa's but elected not to brace and no evacuation planned. we told the passengers the plan. we requested priority handling and returned to redacted. descent was normal. we asked air traffic control for a 20 mile final for xxr so we could do the gravity extension. all went according to plan. landed, only 1 reverser but stopped using alternate braking. set the parking brake, apu on, engines off. airport rescue and firefighting checked us out. brake temps were just under 500c on the left side and cooler on the right. tow team came out quickly. we did the tow-in checklist. advised all parties. towed into gate xx and it took us about 40 minutes to get to the gate. per the electronic log book, maintenance found a blown out hydraulic supply line near the engine 1 pylon.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported stopping abruptly to avoid a conflict with another aircraft during taxi at ORD.
text: after pushback, start-up, and checklist completion, we called ramp for taxi and were told to contact chicago ground. we called ground and were assigned runway 10l@dd and to taxi via u g tt a a10 n. we cleared left and right and started our turn to the left and when we did aircraft y was directly off of our left taxiing passed us on taxiway u. air traffic control never told us to give way to aircraft y nor did they tell aircraft y to give way to us. aircraft y came to a quick stop which we did as well. aircraft y queried air traffic control, thinking that we had already crossed over the ramp line into the taxiway. i looked out of the left window and noticed that we were still within the ramp safety zone and communicated with ground that aircraft y was clear to continue and that there was sufficient wing clearance. further, we mentioned to the controller that they never told us to give way or gave a clearance to aircraft y to give way to us. air traffic control responded that they 'thought' we would have had plenty of room to get in front of them before they got to us. this practice of chicago air traffic control not giving specific instructions to hold for, or give way to, or follow any specific traffic is a continued problem at o'hare. doing this air traffic control puts their separation on the backs of the pilots operating the airplanes and guessing who gets to go first at any given intersection.
