synopsis: A320 First Officer reported loss of the G hydraulic system at FL350 resulted in return to departure airport.
text: take off and departure out of redacted was uneventful. we were filed at fl330, however there was continuous light turbulence so we opted to climb to fl350. once getting to cruise, the crew completed the cruise checklist and there was nothing notable. about 20 minutes later (over redacted), we received the ecam: hyd g rsvr lo lvl and hyd g eng 1 pump lo pr and g sys lo pr. the captain gave the controls and radios to me and started working through the ecam. we discussed the failure as well as the status page before stating ecam complete screens normal". once the ecam was complete, we used radio to contact dispatch to determine our best course of action. with this failure needing a landing gear gravity extension and with redacted being a special qualification airport, we decided we didn't want to continue to our destination in case of executing a missed approach, where the gear would be left out and would make our climb more difficult in a mountainous terrain environment. at this point, we had 18, 300 lbs of fuel remaining, which was plenty for any of those diversion options. dispatch and maintenance control recommended to return back to redacted. we notified air traffic control and returned back to redacted with vectors direct to the airport. we set up and briefed the approach, reviewed the landing gear gravity extension procedure, as well as the towing procedure. with the failure of the g hyd system, we had to stop on the runway (xxr) due to no nose wheel steering. airport rescue and firefighting was standing by and cleared the aircraft of any imminent threat. the tow was hooked up on the runway after completing the towing procedure checklist and we were towed back to gate xx."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B747-800 F/O reported loss of hydraulic system 4 in cruise phase. Flight continued to destination.
text: midway through the flight to redacted, hydraulic pressure system 4 failed. our first indication was multiple brake source alerts, both as an eicas advisory and aural caution alert. checking the hydraulic schematic, the pilot flying and pilot monitoring noticed a loss of hydraulic fluid quantity in hydraulic reservoir 4. we called the captain to the flight deck. after four brake source alerts, hyd press sys 4 checklist appeared on the eicas. the pm ran the electronic checklist to completion. we then started an acars conversation with dispatch, notifying them we lost hydraulic system 4. concerns at this time: low weather minimums into redacted and loss of ability to legally perform cat2/cat3 auto-land, fuel in the event of a missed approach or go around (with hyd sys 4 off, landing gear would not retract once down) rendering a higher than planned fuel burn to our alternate airport, possibility of diverting in an area surrounded by hostile airspace and with few viable available options for diversion airports, planning a longer than normal landing configuration set up while keeping compliance with air traffic control, manual brake landing as well as manual speed brake deployment and reverse thrust only on 2 and 3 as recommended by the checklist notes, and finally only having one runway available in redacted (the longer runway is under construction and closed).the captain patched in a satcom call to dispatch and discussed the condition of our flight. the weather at redacted improved to cat 1 forecasted so the decision was made to continue to and land at redacted, runway xx.the landing was completed by the captain, following all alternate procedures in accordance with the qrh and associated notes. the manual brake landing caused for higher than planned brake temperatures, several brakes in the 7's brake temperature monitoring system and one brake pad peaking briefly at 8. no damage, no melted fuse plugs, and no observable problems resulted. after shut down, ground crew and maintenance was advised of the hydraulic system 4 failure and the hot brake condition.suspected failure of engine driven hydraulic pump for hydraulic system 4. possible associated hydraulic fluid leak resulted in a gradual total loss of reservoir fluid.consider improving the quality of headsets provided on the aircraft. normally, i have my own. however, my baggage was lost day one of my pattern and i am traveling these two weeks without. i have had to resort to using the headsets provided on the aircraft. unfortunately, they are of such low quality that communication with air traffic control and my other crew members was a major challenge and inconvenience which added only another (but fixable) layer of complexity to an already busy, and complex non-normal situation.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported the main and backup stabilizer trim systems failed during climb. Flight diverted to alternate airport.
text: while hand flying through 12, 000 feet, i commanded nose-down trim and observed trim not responding with increasing control pressure. eicas indicated 2° nose up with no movement, warnings, or aural activity. both primary and backup trim systems, including first officer inputs, were unresponsive.we leveled off with air traffic control and requested a block altitude to troubleshoot. with no trim runaway indications, the first officer ran the qrh pitch trim inoperative procedure. aircraft remained controllable, so we proceeded with landing planning.we requested priority handling, coordinated with dispatch, and diverted to redacted. i briefed the fa and passengers, emphasizing a precautionary landing. all required checklists, including overweight and non-routine procedures, were completed.during descent, a slight pitch-down tendency developed, we referenced the qrh and briefed a two-pilot control strategy if needed. approach remained stable. landing was smooth and within limits. we taxied to the gate without further issue.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reported total loss of AC electrical power during taxi when they were starting the APU. Power returned to normal after APU reached full operating parameters.
text: full duration of flight was normal with no 'noted' issues - departure, enroute, arrival, approach, and landing were are normal with no abnormalities noted - normal turn off at intersection of runway xx and taxiway 1, right turn, with another right turn onto taxiway 2 for gate xx as instructed by air traffic control - as passing across the hold short lines, i called for 'flaps up' and requested the apu to be started as the taxi was short to gate xx - after completing the turn onto taxiway 2, the aircraft was doing approx 2 to 3 kts across the ground with the nosewheel on the yellow taxiway centerline as the post flight check was completed by the first officer - as the apu reached 75% of n1 the aircraft ac power completely shut down - both idg's (integrated drive generators) from both running engines were deactivated - the aircraft lost nose wheel steering as well as all displays reverted to battery operation - i immediately stopped the aircraft on the taxiway and set the parking brake - first officer called the fa's to check their status while i evaluated what was going on - the apu reached 100% and became the source of ac power - asked the first officer to make announcement to the passengers to remain seated as the fa's indicated people were getting up to grab bags (although the aircraft was not at the gate but all signage was turned off) - while i notified air traffic control that we needed to sit in place without the need for assistance while we determined the best course of action - as the aircraft was technically 'rebooting' itself, we awaited for all eicas messages to clear - after approx 90 seconds, the aircraft was fully powered up (note, both engines were still running) - 2 eicas messages were left on - idg 1 (and 2) fail caution messages - i called for the qrh for both - after following the procedure - the idg's were cleared and reset and back online - we checked other eicas status pages (including hyd and power) to ensure we were both reassured the aircraft was safe to move under its own power with the note 'if it happens again we will call for ops to tow us to the gate' - we notified air traffic control we could continue and was cleared to continue our taxi - parked at xx without any further issues - we noted prior to departure the apu had previous write ups' but did not seem to be related to what we experienced. both the first officer and myself agreed to call maintenance control to discuss what happened and to see what they wanted - after that conversation with maintenance control they agreed we did what was necessary and asked for write up in the logbook. i completed the info to maintenance as instructed. post flight walk-around inspection was normal. the station was not going to relocate the aircraft to a ron spot, so a normal shutdown and power off was completed with no issues. post brief with the first officer resulted in all crm decisions were approprate and did not pose any risk to the safety of passengers, crew, or aircraft. the cause of the power failure is unknown by myself at this time.suggestions: all aspects of the issue were handled without issue. maintenance will need to continue to investigate what might have caused this post landing during the taxi.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: A319 Captain discovered an unresolved hydraulic leak during preflight. Captain refused the aircraft.
text: during preflight inspection, i observed a large area of hydraulic fluid on the belly of the aircraft. maintenance initially reported it as residual" and wiped the belly clean. shortly afterward, hydraulic fluid reappeared through panel seams and drain holes.i contacted maintenance a second time and requested they locate the source of the leak or perform an appropriate leak test, such as a leak measurement manifold (lmm) test. maintenance instead cleaned the interior belly with alcohol and stated that the belly would be clean upon landing. i re-inspected the belly and confirmed that hydraulic fluid had reappeared.maintenance refused to identify the source of the leak or conduct a proper leak test. as captain, i determined that the aircraft was not airworthy due to an unresolved hydraulic leak. in the interest of safety, i refused the aircraft.cause: unresolved hydraulic leak on the aircraft belly. maintenance repeatedly classified reappearing fluid (through panel seams and drain holes) as "residual, " cleaned the area with alcohol, but refused to locate the source or perform a diagnostic leak test (e.g., lmm test).suggestions: require full identification and resolution of hydraulic leaks before aircraft release, rather than cleaning only.mandate diagnostic testing when fluid reappears after cleaning.ensure prompt escalation and engineering involvement when captain raises unresolved leak concerns.reinforce captain authority on aircraft acceptance for safety."

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier incident Captain reported beginning taxi from gate prior to salute from ground personnel. Reports from flight crew thought to be the incident flight crew reported they did not taxi before salute.
text: began taxi before receiving all clear salute, with tug and marshallers below field of vision. preconception that a salute was received. no damage or injuries. stopped airplane. completed salute. remainder of flight completed without issue.cause: received 'clear to start engines' immediately after clear to push instructions given. this caused both engine starts to be completed relatively early. as occurs regularly in redacted, when i don't immediately see the salute, marshallers sometimes return to the gate - usually before engine starts are complete. ran the after start tasks and checklist. first officer and i did not see the marshaller or lektro cart (my seat is in the highest position while in ramp areas. this operation was run with one lektro cart driver and one marshaller. first officer sent taxi request command. waited some time and did not hear from ramp, so first officer radioed for taxi and we received a taxi clearance. we cleared left and right sides, turned on taxi light, and began to move the airplane in a right turn. the lektro cart driver ran out from under the airplane giving the stop signal, and i stopped the airplane - realizing we had not actually received an all clear salute. the marshaller also moved to a visible position with the headset bag. i opened the window to confirm that we had not hit the tug or a marshaller, which was confirmed that we did not. lektro cart driver moved the cart to a visible position and we received the all clear salute. notified ramp that we needed 5 minutes in position, and received the ok. we called for and received a new taxi clearance and proceeded to the runway. remainder of flight completed with no issue. suggestions: one marshaller to remain visible between 10 and 2 o'clock positions. lektro cart driver retrieve the headset if there are only two marshallers. preferably use three marshallers. use a pole or lighted antenna on low/small lektro carts, to remain visible from flight desk. confirm via call-out with first officer that both of us have seen the salute. avoid distractions until the all clear salute is received. if unsure, stop or open the window to see below.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor

text: the left alternator light on the annunciator panel began flashing intermittently accompanied by a burning smell, we turned off the left alternator and the heater to isolate both from the system. we ran the qrh for alternator abnormalities and briefed the cabin electrical fire or smoke procedures as well, diversion was not required. we notified operations and landed without incident then wrote up the plane.cause: there were previous write ups with the alternators last week in aircraft x. it had a dual alternator failure. when the left alternator was showing intermittent indications again and we smelled burning we isolated it and the smell quickly dissipated. i suspect it to be the left alternator. the heater was turned back on after and no odors occurred.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B747-400 Captain reported a ENG 3 OIL PRESS EICAS message during cruise. The flight diverted to an alternate airport.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a concern an incorrect MEL was applied to unrelated system. Aircraft was removed from service.
text: upon arrival at the aircraft, i was advised the aircraft had experienced a significant maintenance event involving the hydraulic system. while reviewing the aircraft status in the logbook, no minimum equipment list had yet been issued, and i was awaiting clarification on which minimum equipment list, if any, would be applied in order to properly evaluate its applicability and associated safety margin.after discussing the discrepancy with the previous captain who made the original write-up, as well as dispatch / maintenance control, i developed concern that an incorrect minimum equipment list could be applied to the discrepancy, potentially masking the actual system involved. specifically, maintenance control referenced the yellow hydraulic electric pump, while the original discrepancy involved the yellow engine-driven pump, indicating a possible misalignment between the reported condition and the anticipated minimum equipment list application.given the potential for an incorrect minimum equipment list application to inappropriately authorize dispatch of an aircraft with an unresolved or non-deferrable condition, i determined it was necessary to delay boarding until the discrepancy and maintenance action could be fully verified.i proceeded to the gate area and instructed the gate agent, person a, to hold boarding until i could verify the maintenance status with local maintenance, dispatch, and maintenance control.the agent responded that boarding would continue, stating, 'no, the tower instructed us to board.' i reiterated my instruction to stop boarding, emphasizing the need to confirm the aircraft's airworthiness. the agent again refused and stated that i was 'not in charge of boarding.'i issued a third and final instruction to not board the aircraft, then returned to the flight deck and contacted station operations via radio to request a supervisor.a supervisor subsequently arrived at the flight deck and acknowledged concerns regarding the gate agent's conduct. i requested a reassignment of the gate agent, which was completed.following coordination with maintenance control, it was confirmed that an incorrect minimum equipment list had been applied to the discrepancy, and the actual system affected was not eligible for minimum equipment list deferral. as a result, the aircraft was removed from service and a replacement aircraft was assigned. the flight was completed successfully. as of the time of this report submission, aircraft x remains out of service for the hydraulic system discrepancy, now exceeding approximately 34 hours, further reinforcing the significance of the original maintenance issue and the importance of delaying boarding pending proper evaluation.this event highlights multiple breakdowns in communication, coordination, and adherence to established authority during an active maintenance situation:the gate agent's immediate refusal to comply with direction to hold boarding introduced undue time pressure to accept a maintenance action without proper evaluation. this type of operational pressure can lead to rushed decision-making by flight crews. given that this was a known recurring issue from the prior leg, which manifested shortly after takeoff, there was a credible risk that proceeding under these conditions could have resulted in an in-flight abnormal or escalation.the gate agent's behavior became a distraction from a higher-priority safety issue, specifically the need to correctly diagnose and resolve the hydraulic discrepancy. this diverted attention and resources away from critical troubleshooting.the agent's unwillingness to follow direct instructions from the captain raised concern regarding reliability in time-critical situations, including the ability to execute essential duties during an emergency (e.g., evacuation or emergency deplaning).local redacted maintenance demonstrated a misunderstanding of the original discrepancy and appeared to pursue a path focused on expediency rather than full verification of the write-up in the logbook. this created risk of applying an incorrect minimum equipment list to an unrelated system.there was a lack of direct communication from local maintenance to the flight crew. i spent approximately 15-20 minutes attempting to gather information independently, as no maintenance personnel initially made contact at the aircraft to discuss the discrepancy.initial coordination with maintenance control was also ineffective. maintenance control declined to engage in discussion regarding minimum equipment list applicability, citing local maintenance authority. this was inconsistent with standard practice, as maintenance control is typically involved in minimum equipment list evaluation and troubleshooting coordination. after further effort, i was able to establish direct communication with the responsible a320 maintenance control team member, at which point it was confirmed that the incorrect procedure was being considered.overall, these combined factors--external pressure to board, lack of coordinated communication, recurrence of the discrepancy, and misapplication risk of maintenance procedures--significantly increased operational complexity and reduced safety margins during a critical phase of aircraft evaluation.cause: • breakdown in adherence to captain's authority: gate agent refusal to comply with explicit instruction to hold boarding during an active safety evaluation. • operational time pressure ('get-there-itis' at the gate): immediate push to board created pressure to accept a maintenance action without adequate verification. • maintenance misdiagnosis risk: local maintenance did not fully verify the original discrepancy in the logbook and appeared to pursue an expedient corrective path, increasing the likelihood of incorrect minimum equipment list application. • ineffective communication and coordination: lack of timely, direct communication between flight crew, local maintenance, and maintenance control, initial reluctance from maintenance control to engage in minimum equipment list discussion further delayed accurate assessment. • distraction from critical task: gate agent interaction diverted attention from troubleshooting and evaluating a known recurring hydraulic issue from the prior leg. • lack of standardized escalation: no clear or immediate pathway to pause operations (boarding) while resolving conflicting maintenance information. • reinforce captain's authority: ensure all gate/customer service personnel understand that boarding must stop when directed by the captain for safety-related reasons. • establish a formal 'boarding hold' protocol: create a standardized procedure that clearly pauses boarding when an aircraft is under active maintenance review or airworthiness uncertainty. • improve maintenance verification procedures: require local maintenance to validate discrepancies against the original write-up prior to minimum equipment list application, especially for system-specific issues. • strengthen maintenance control involvement: reinforce expectation that maintenance control actively participates in minimum equipment list determination and troubleshooting coordination, regardless of station-level activity. • enhance communication standards: require direct, timely communication between maintenance and flight crew during active discrepancies before operational decisions (e.g., boarding) proceed. • training on operational risk awareness: educate gate and maintenance personnel on the risks associated with time pressure and recurring discrepancies, emphasizing safety over schedule. • standardize escalation pathways: ensure flight crews have a clear, rapid method to involve station leadership when operational conflicts arise that impact safety decisions.

text: following a recent engine overhaul, i was conducting a cross-country flight in aircraft x. prior to departure, an interior ceiling panel fell in the cabin, exposing hanging wires. i had to the master red switch and avionics master being in the 'off' position, the electrical bus remained 'hot.' the engine monitor and radio stack remained powered, indicating a bypassed or stuck master contactor.additionally, the primary garmin g5 electronic flight instrument was discovered to be defective, the barometric/altimeter adjustment knob was inoperable, rendering the aircraft unairworthy representative. per their instructions, i aborted the return leg of the trip. i secured the aircraft, and left the keys with a representative of the fbo at redacted. i coordinated third-party text: on day 0, my private pilot level student and i took off from redacted airport at approximately xa:40. our intended lesson was to fly to the practice area where i would introduce stalls, slow was at a normal range. during the run up we leaned the mixture out for best power. both magnetos had a normal drop of less than 175 rpms and the difference between the two drops did not exceed 50 rpms. on takeoff, we received normal rpm output and our temperature and pressures all remained in the green, normal range. on climb out we maintained a normal climb out rate with normal airspeed, we continued to climb on a northern heading until we reached 5, 500'. at 5, 500' we leveled the plane out and brought our rpms back to 2300. shortly after bringing the rpms back to 2300 we heard a loud noise from the engine. the noise sounded like a boom. we immediately lost all rpms and both the vacuum and oil light illuminated. i increased the throttle to see if we could maintain altitude or climb but we could not. i then turned us to the south to circle to keep us close to the small airpark west of us. while i attempted to restart the engine by ensuring that the fuel pump was on, putting the mixture full, and switching the fuel tanks. i then cranked the starter but there was no indication that the engine would turn over and restart. at this point i knew that we would not make it back to the airport, we were 7 miles north and we did not have adequate altitude to return back to our original point of departure. i knew that we were going to have to land at redacted airpark so we turned northwest to head directly to the airpark. i did not have adequate time to advise air traffic control. we started a slow descent at our gliding speed of 76 kts. i added in the first notch of flaps (10°) when we were a mile away from the airport. i added another notch of flaps (25°) when we were short final. we didn't have excess altitude so we had to come in low. on our approach, our right wing grazed through shrubs but it did not cause us to falter off of our path. we touched down on the runway and the plane veered to the right slightly because of the gravel but we maintained control and brought the plane to a stop in the center of the runway. we then shut down the engine and performed the engine securing checklist.

synopsis: SA-227 Metroliner First Officer reported right engine indicated erratic torque indications resulted in two aborted takeoff attempts.
text: on day 0, we were conducting a flight from redacted to redacted in aircraft x. i was serving as pilot monitoring (pm) for the departure from runway xxl.due to ambient temperature and aircraft weight, continuous alcohol water injection (cawi) was required for takeoff performance. prior to takeoff, the before takeoff checklist was completed.during the initial takeoff roll, upon reaching approximately 35% torque, the pilot flying (pf) called for water injection. i confirmed activation of the cawi system, including pump indications and an initial increase in torque on both engines. shortly thereafter, the right (no. 2) engine torque indication began fluctuating, with uncommanded decreases and increases observed. i announced the abnormal indication, and the crew elected to reject the takeoff. the rejected takeoff was completed without further incident, and the aircraft exited the runway.after clearing the runway and completing applicable checklists, the crew assessed the situation. a potential contributing factor considered was improper positioning of the right engine speed lever. based on this assessment and normal indications at that time, a second takeoff attempt was initiated.during the second takeoff roll, the right (no. 2) engine again did not produce expected torque with cawi activated. the crew rejected the takeoff a second time. the aircraft was brought to a safe stop, exited the runway, and returned to the ramp for further evaluation. no injuries occurred.this event highlights the challenges associated with diagnosing abnormal engine indications during high-workload phases of flight such as takeoff. the fluctuating torque indication on the first attempt created ambiguity regarding whether the issue was mechanical or related to configuration.the decision to attempt a second takeoff was influenced by a perceived, correctable configuration issue and the absence of persistent abnormal indications while stopped. however, recurrence of insufficient torque on the second attempt suggests the possibility of an underlying mechanical or system-related issue.this event also underscores the importance of conservative decision-making when abnormal engine indications are observed during takeoff, even if a potential explanation is identified.

text: during the final approach phase of the flight, air traffic control was vectoring us on a 140 degree base leg to 13l, which made it very hard to maintain the airport in sight.first officer was pf and i, the captain, was the pnf.lone star approach initially cleared us for the approach into ads, a nearby airport, which prompted clarification from me telling them we were landing love field. after a few seconds air traffic control corrected himself clearing us for the approach into love field, rwy 13l, unfortunately by that time we had traveled some ground distance and a very tight turn was required to align ourselves with the runway.upon switching to tower, we received a low altitude alert, as the first officer was trying to align with the runway with a bank angle of 45 degrees and descending to an altitude of 1350ft when we should have been at 1900 feet.i promptly corrected and helped the first officer gain back altitude and adjust the flight path where we proceeded to land without further incident.in this chain of event, air traffic control technique (very common in dal) to vector on diverging modified base of 140 degree makes the timing of the visual approach clearance paramount and the delay in giving such clearance created a situation in which the first officer had to bank beyond the normal maneuvering to avoid overshooting final.my suggestion is to limit base legs to 90 or 100 degrees to avoid issues like these in the future.better monitoring of the first officer from my end was necessary as well.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A light sport aircraft pilot reported nose gear collapse while landing at a non-towered airport.
text: a normal takeoff, normal pattern, and otherwise normal landing was performed in ranger aircraft x at redacted. upon landing, both main gear wheels touched the ground first. as soon as the nose wheel was lowered and contacted the ground, a severe 'shimmy' and vibration was felt. i held the control stick aft to keep the nose wheel pressure to a minimum which reduced the shimmy until airspeed bled off. the shimmy returned and then a loud snap was heard and the airplane fell forward and slid to a stop. the airplane was kept on the runway. once out of the aircraft, it was evident that the main axle bolt for the nose wheel had snapped and the wheel collapsed under the gear. no one was injured and no other part of the aircraft was damaged. the airplane was removed from the runway immediately and then towed back to the hangar.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization and flew above 400 ft.
text: i was recently on vacation with my wife and we made a stop in location x. while there, i flew two, almost identical flights back-to-back over to location y. during those flights, my signal was getting spotty, and i climbed higher to maintain a solid link. at the time, i was so focused on my connection and camera that i didn't realize i had drifted over 400 feet (max was 134m on the 1st flight and 136m on the second, and for just a short duration for both- most of the flights were below 400) during both flights, no other aircraft were observed, and there were no near misses or conflicts of any kind. the flights were uneventful in that regard. i also honestly didn't know about laanc or authorization for that spot. i didn't even realize i had made these mistakes until a couple days later, during a different flight in location z where i had a similar experience and realization. after that, i went back through my logs and seen my flight data from location x and realized my mistakes. this was a huge wake up call for me. since then i have locked my dji settings at 120m so it can't happen again. i've also downloaded the aloft app to check for restricted airspace before i fly. i found out about aloft during a google search after these flights. i also plan on taking the trust test as soon as time permits. as a relatively new drone owner, i had a limited understanding of the full scope of regulations. this experience was a wake up call for me regarding the importance of pre flight planning.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: B737 flight crew were advised of fumes in the forward galley area by FA. Crew continued to an uneventful landing.
text: at the beginning of our approach into redacted, at 12, 000', the purser notified me of an electrical burning smell coming from the forward galley coffee pot. i provided her awareness that we would be on the ground shortly and gave her instruction to notify me if smoke or fire was seen. my first officer and i briefly reviewed the qrc/qrh and we landed uneventfully. taxiing to the gate the purser notified us that the smell was intensifying. we requested priority handling and requested fire trucks meet us at the gate. we continued to the gate under our own power and parked uneventfully. dispatch and chief pilot were notified. an electronic log book was sent and maintenance had us fill out a smoke/fire form.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported while on final approach to MROC/SJO ATC advised them of traffic ahead of them. On short final the Captain executed a go around due to the preceding traffic being on the runway.
text: while on approach we were handed off to sjo tower, they responded with 'continue approach arriving aircraft'. we were perplexed because we heard no one on approach frequency ahead of us. finally at just below 1000' we saw aircraft y on a very short arcing base to final ahead of us. the first officer called 500', aircraft y was just touching down, so we called the go around. there was absolutely no way this was going to work and the tower should have never, in our opinion, allowed that aircraft in so close to us. on the plus side, the complexity of the go around was briefed as a threat in the arrival brief and flown as briefed.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B767 F/O reported on rotation experiencing an unusual noise and aircraft vibration resulting in the flight crew returning to the departure airport where they landed safely. Post flight inspection revealed a nose gear door stuck open.
text: upon rotation, pm (ca), heard unusual 'bang' noise. positive rate of climb, gear up selected. pf continued climb out however immediately upon accelerating beyond v2, airframe vibration, accompanied by commensurate increase in ambient noise, was noticeable and objectionable. vibration and noise increased with airspeed. 'doors' light was illuminated and aircrew recognized that the vibe/noise was correlated with the doors light. the noise and vibe were moderate at gear retraction, increasing to extreme at 230kias. after allowing a fair amount of time for gear door to close (hoping issue may resolve itself), aircrew advised departure control and received priority handling, ceasing climb at 6, 000ft and maintaining airspeed at 215kias. aircrew ran appropriate checklist with no resolution and proceeded to return to redacted for uneventful landing. postflight inspection revealed right nose gear door was stuck open, causing the airframe vibration and noise.

anomaly: Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Citation Latitude Captain reported that an inflight upset occurred when they encountered wake turbulence on approach to LAX in trail of a B737. Control was regained and the flight continued to a safe landing.
text: due to circumstances beyond my control, this is the first chance i have had to finish this report and review it before submission.while flying the arrival to lax and programing the flight management system for the assigned runway, my finger accidental touched the vectors to final button on the garmin gtc (garmin touch screen) which immediately caused lost of flight management system sequencing. air traffic control was notified immediately that a wrong button had been pressed and a heading and altitude to descend to was needed. socal assisted in the request. i managed to get the arrival reloaded and told air traffic control that we could resume the arrival again. unfortunately, my copilot did not press the nav button on the mode control panel and while was busy trying to reloaded the correct approach procedure for runway24r, i hadn't noticed the course deviation. i saw what was happening and brought the error to my coworkers attention and immediately confirmed the error with the socal controller when he said that we appeared to be off course. we corrected and got the flight management system capture for lateral navigation.we were told we were following aircraft y that was turning right base. we saw aircraft y and advised the traffic in sight. it wasn't more than a few seconds later that aircraft x began to receive light turbulence when all of sudden, the airplane was rolled to the left uncontrollably. i can only estimate the roll to the left felt like 45-50 degrees of bank. our aircraft was not subjected to any unusual of out tolerance g forces, just a significant roll due to strong vortices. the aircraft upset was eventual corrected but we were both shaken up. we just didn't know if it was over. i communicated the event to the socal controller. he asked if we wanted to change to the south complex and fly to 25l behind a jet. both of us agreed to flying to 25l instead.unfortunately, i programmed the flight management system for 24l, not 25l. so when the vector heading of 220 degrees to join caused the aircraft to intercept the 24l loc, we inadvertently flew in the flight track of another flight. realizing the error, i was able to program 25l correctly and we were able to get onto the correct flight path eventually. suggestions: 1. obviously, the garmin screen is very touchy. it's critical to go slow when programming.2. an aircraft upset event requires notification followed by possible delay vectors to regain mental clarity and composure, especially behind a commercial airliner. you have to slow down cockpit tasks.3. even during a traumatic event, standard sop and mode confirmation along dual verification must happen so that future errors can be trapped.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: Medium Transport Captain reported an altitude overshoot occurred following a wake turbulence encounter departing IAH in trail of an ERJ175.
text: iah-zzzcaptain pf, first officer pm. climbing out of iah runway 15l, departing on the mmugs4, air traffic control instructed us to maintain 4000. just prior to leveling off at 4000 we encountered wake turbulence from an e-175 that took off in front of us. as we were fighting to keep the wings level and exit the wake turbulence, we inadvertently climbed through our assigned altitude. as we exited the worst of the wake turbulence we asked air traffic control for a short cut or vector to get us away from the area of wake turbulence and the controller called out that we were 300 feet above the assigned altitude. we immediately corrected our altitude and as we were correcting he cleared us to 16000 feet and gave us a shortcut. the flight resumed without further incident.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported encountering wind shear with subsequent rapid fluctuations in airspeed during climb. Crew recovered and continued flight.
text: i (first officer) was pilot flying with ap (autopilot) and at (autothrottles) engaged during the climb to cruise altitude of fl370. climbing through fl355, through clear and smooth air, we experienced sudden windshear causing airspeed to increase 20-30 kts and vsi increasing to around 4500fpm. as i saw the airspeed approaching redline i reduced thrust and as the clacker sounded the ca took the controls, disengaged ap and at, continued to reduce speed below red line and began to level off. ca returned flight controls to me just before we got to the back side of the windshear and quickly lost 20-30kt and approached minimum maneuver speed. i told the ca i will be descending to fl 360 in order to reduce pitch and regain airspeed at that altitude and he made the request to air traffic control. air traffic control continued our descent to fl350 where we leveled off on airspeed and reengaged ap and at. ca made an airplane maintenance logbook entry for the over speed. flight continued to redacted with no issues. cause: the event's main causal factor was meteorological. unknown windshear at altitude. i would say another causal factor could be my monitoring of speed as i could have noticed the speed increase slightly sooner, however the dramatic performance increase and decrease would have occurred regardless of reaction time. proper training and execution of that training were essential in regaining airspeed control. performance demonstrations at high altitude in the simulator were helpful during this event. because of those demonstrations and knowledge it was clear that after the loss of performance on the back side of the windshear, a decrease in altitude was necessary for proper and timely airspeed recovery. more of these demonstrations and relating this meteorological/performance possibility to other factors that we talk about, such as microbursts, will help in mitigating risk by helping pilots with timely recognition and recovery.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported GPS interference consistent with jamming/spoofing during cruise in Turkish airspace. Flight continued to destination.
text: flight experienced gps interference consistent with jamming/spoofing while operating in the turkey region. during this phase, one or both gps receivers were intermittently lost or unreliable. standard degradation of navigation capability was observed and managed.continuing for the remainder of the flight, or nearly the remainder of the flight, after exiting the interference region, anomalous system behavior continued while one gps remained offline. the aircraft clock began oscillating between correct time and an offset of approximately five minutes. this was not a steady offset but a repeating switching between time sources.this time instability resulted in multiple downstream effects:• cpdlc instability, including repeated logoff/logon requests from air traffic control (lppo), likely due to message timing/sequence issues.• ads-c / ads-b discrepancies. (on a prior flight) air traffic control reported position inconsistency on approach to del, with the aircraft depicted approximately 0.5-1.0 nm north of actual position while established on the instrument landing system. approach and tower control seemed to think we were not on the localizer, and maybe believed we were lining up for the wrong runway. they seemed very concerned. other crew members on the flight related being directed to go around on a prior flight to del for the same reason.• nat ads position reporting becoming unusable due to reporting over a fix at a time in the future. we reverted to hf voice position reports for the entire crossing.• nuisance egpws alert (whoop whoop pull up") at cruise altitude (fl360). (prior flight)the aircraft flagged the gpws terr pos, however, nuisance alerts continued to be generated. in the absence of company guidance addressing this condition, i selected terr override to suppress repeated false warnings and reduce distraction during flight. various conditions persisted well beyond the geographic area of known interference, and one gps position never recovered. mitigation actions included increased cross-checking of navigation sources, use of procedural separation techniques (including hf position reporting when appropriate), and cautious use of datalink functions. however, no flight deck intervention was available to isolate or reset the affected time source.cause: this condition presents more than a nuisance. incorrect time and position outputs can lead to:• misleading air traffic control surveillance displays• cpdlc communication failures or delays• false terrain warnings, including at cruise altitude• increased crew workload and distraction during critical and non-critical phases of flight.consider system-level mitigation to prevent corrupted gps-derived time and position from being intermittently accepted after initial rejection. a more robust isolation of unreliable inputs, or a crew-selectable means to inhibit gps-derived time and/or terrain alerting when flagged unreliable, may improve resilience.a means for resetting an individual gps receiver inflight. with the incidence of jamming/spoofing likely to increase, there needs to be an emphasis on making our aircraft more resilient. another aircraft type flew through the jamming/spoofing areas with considerably less bother."

anomaly: Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Passenger Electronic Device
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported passenger electronic device battery caught fire and was extinguished by flight attendants.
text: during cruise at fl330 we were descending to fl310 for traffic, the flight attendant emergency call button illuminated. fa stated there was a fire from a lithium battery in seat pocket and that they were attempting to put it out. they state smoke in the cabin and that the passenger threw water and a soda on it and they would call back once secure or had further info. i transferred controls to pm and alerted both air traffic control and also sent the same message to dispatch. we referenced the smoke emergency card and discussed donning oxygen masks if the emergency elevated to its requirement and continued towards redacted. within approximately 2-3 minutes the fa called to inform me the fire was out and that it was secure in the containment bag and that they did not use any pbe (protective breathing equipment) and the passengers were ok and smoke was clearing. in that time air traffic control called and said they were giving us priority. we told them the fire was out and the battery was in the containment bag. they said trucks would be waiting and follow us to the gate to dispose of any hazmat. landed runway xx without further incident on runway xx and arff (airport rescue and firefighting) followed us to the gate and personnel confirmed battery was out and no threat continued to exist and we deplaned with no issues. i engaged every passenger as they deplaned and also confirmed that all passengers and passenger affected needed no assistance. deplaning was per normal.cause: lithium battery overheat fire

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: BE-99 pilot reported ATC advised aircraft on same runway approaching at a high speed while crossing the runway. Aircraft continued to taxi.
text: i was cleared to cross runway xx at taxiway 1. as i approached the hold short line i looked left for approximately 3 seconds then shifted my view to the right for another approximately 3 seconds. in my scan both directions i saw no traffic and made my normal clear left and clear right calls to myself in the flight deck. during this time i was moving towards and crossed the hold short line at approximately 10 knots. at this time air traffic control told me to use caution as aircraft y was on runway xx that was told to stop before the intersection. the ground controller let me know that aircraft y was still at a high rate of speed and they were concerned if aircraft y would stop before running into me. as soon as i heard the ground controller key up i looked back to the left and saw aircraft y rapidly slowing down and coming to a stop before the intersection about 30-50 feet off my left wing. after this event i have made an effort to look more closely for aircraft on the runway and or on final approach. i am unsure why i did not see aircraft y on final approach as i looked in that direction for several seconds. air traffic control also did not let me know prior to or after giving me the clearance to cross the runway that there was traffic using the runway.
