synopsis: General aviation pilot reported an NMAC during cruise flight in the vicinity of 50R airport. Pilot took evasive action and continued flight.
text: in cruise flight on a deadhead from pipeline patrol, aircraft a, a training aircraft, was maneuvering approximately 1, 800 feet above us. they abruptly turned directly towards us and rapidly descended to our altitude (~1, 000 ft agl). they then proceeded to follow us at level flight within ~500ft of separation. they followed us for about 1 minute while we tried to accelerate, climb, and turn away from their heading. they proceeded to follow us in the same direction.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor ground observer and student on a solo flight reported student encountering a gust of wind on landing that resulted in loss of directional control and a runway excursion.
text: my student who is training to become a private pilot was planning to solo today. they had completed the initial solo, but this flight was supposed to be a pattern solo. it had been some time since they had flown solo, we had flown a pattern lesson the previous week with ten landings to smooth out their landing flare technique (tended to not flare enough leading to hard landings), and towards the end of the lesson the landings were pretty good. so today just to make sure everything was good i decided to run a few laps in the pattern with them before they went solo today. we did three laps in the pattern and had no concerns with their takeoffs and landings. after the third lap in the pattern, i had my student drop me off at the fbo and i was going to observe the rest of the lesson from the ground. the student then proceeded to complete seven laps in the traffic pattern using runway xx at redacted with no issues. the weather was 10sm visibility, sky clr, with winds 220 at 7kts. after the seventh landing the student then proceeded to take off. i was told by the student that after they increased the power, they were rolling down the runway and glanced over to the right side of the cockpit to make sure the oil temperature and oil pressure was in the green. at that time the right wing started to roll moving the plane to the left on the runway. the student then proceeded to pull power and tried to maintain control and drove the plane into the grass on the left side of the runway. i then ran over to make sure the student was okay and that the plane was okay. after assessing the situation and seeing my student was okay and the plane seemed to be fine, i taxied the plane out of the grass and back to the main ramp. plane had no damage and the taxiway, lights, and signs on the side of the runway by [taxiway] 1 had not been damaged. upon review from what i saw on the ground and from what i was told by my student the contributing factor to this accident was an incorrect input of the flight controls and not correcting for the crosswind on takeoff. as the flight instructor i need to be more vigilant on teaching cross wind corrections and make sure my students know the importance of them. also to keep their eyes down the runway during the takeoff roll to see the trends and movement of the aircraft so the correct crosswind corrections can be made.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: Taylorcraft F-19 pilot reported the Statux ADS-B receiver does not provide reliable traffic alerting when paired to the Garmin Pilot EFB.
text: while using a stratux ads-b in receiver paired to the garmin pilot efb, the traffic display will repeatedly disappear for several seconds or up to a minute, and lose individual targets. on at least one occasion, the stratux system did not show an aircraft that was so close i could see the paint scheme and identify the operator, yet the panel-mounted system had no problem displaying the target. on this occasion, the stratux had line-of-sight from its antenna to the aircraft in question.on the flight mentioned above, multiple targets maneuvered and changed direction and altitude to become potential conflicts while disappeared" from the traffic display. this was in very congested airspace (from redacted to redacted). the stratux has been verified to be assembled correctly, and both stratux and garmin pilot software are up to date. this problem does not appear when garmin pilot is paired with commercially assembled receivers such as the gdl 52 or panel-mount units such as the gtx 345.i am filing this report to alert the flying public that the stratux ads-b receiver should not be considered reliable for traffic alerting in busy airspace. i am taking the corrective action of disposing of mine and replacing it with a commercially built unit. unfortunately it is positioned as a budget-friendly alternative to much more expensive commercial receivers, as such, i believe awareness should be raised that the stratux does not nearly meet the same standards of safety or reliability as other units."

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Light aircraft flight instructor reported a CFTT event while entering the pattern at FFZ. Flight landed uneventfully.
text: descending into ffz after training flight, in contact with ffz n tower on 119.7. being followed closely behind on our left by another aircraft. instructions into ffz were 'make left traffic 4r'. student had controls, initiated a descent into kffz, from 3500 as expected on normal arrival. tower reported traffic off to our left, 'possibly a helicopter', closing at our altitude. we saw the traffic 100 ft above, closing quickly, so at my instruction the student increased out rate of descent to evade the traffic. the helicopter, according to adsb onboard our aircraft, was aircraft y. we missed the helicopter, and again at my instruction the student leveled off, about 150-200 ft below ffz tpa of 2400. we immediately climbed back up to 2400. we likely clipped the populated area overlaying fountain hills, that appears to have a southern limit of 'e shea blvd', below 1000 agl. the terrain changes pretty rapidly, but i'd estimate we were 800agl for 10 seconds, just about over, if not just past, e shea blvd. i would have liked to have entered to the east of the populated area, but we were being closed in by traffic descending above us, a dangerous situation for a high-wing aircraft, and my decision was to remain clear of and not cross his path. after reaching pattern altitude, we continued on with an uneventful landing to ffz.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Light aircraft flight instructor reported an NMAC with a helicopter while in the pattern for landing at PMV.
text: while in the traffic pattern at plattsmouth we began our initial descent from pattern altitude down to begin the downwind to base turn for runway 16. at the time of the turn we had a traffic advisory go off in the airplane of traffic 12 o'clock and low. less than 1 mile. upon visual scanning it was found the helicopter at its lowest was 150 directly below us and traveling south to cross the midfield as we were set up in a downwind just in the beginnings of a base turn for runway 16 at kpmv. evasive action was taken to avoid the helicopter and a rapid climb was initiated. prior to this conflict we had been reporting crosswind legs, downwind, base, and final legs for situational awareness of another plane in the pattern at the time. the helicopter made one call that they were to the northeast inbound at 2500. that was the last call made before the conflict occurred. the helicopter was actually at 1500 feet. no damage was found on the airplane and the flight was finished as normal. the helicopter would cross kpmv at 1500 and procced south bound following the conflict with another plane in the downwind at that time. multiple calls were made to the helicopter pilot following the incident about the danger of the situation that unfolded on 122.700.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: FBO A&P reported Beech Musketeer pilot making an off field landing due to fuel starvation. Aircraft was flown back to airport.
text: pilot made an landing on highway x just east of city x due to fuel starvation. no damage occurred and it was a safe landing. upon inspection of the engine found the fuel line coming off the carburetor had the fitting backed off and was not connected. that carburetor and fuel line had not been worked on recently. the fuel line was reconnected and torqued down. 10 gallons of fuel was added. operationally checked the engine running for any other issues and for leaks. no leaks noted and engine functionally ran normal. the county sheriff blocked off highway x from traffic in that area and the plane took off south bound and flew to city x/redacted. the plane flew normal with no issues.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization. They were also unaware they needed a Part 107 license for the operations being conducted.
text: i am a video editor by trade. i was recently hired as a social media and content coordinator. my role is to manage social media channels for them and gather content and edit it to post to social media. i was informed that the company owned a drone, so i waited until there was an opportunity to use it. i have never flown a drone before and i have never been trained to. today, i operated the drone at a residential site from about xa:25 - xa:55. the goal was to capture photos or videos of a completed backyard that has been designed and built by the landscaping firm. i did not have any issues with operating the drone and i did not fly above 300 feet, and that was only for a brief moment to begin descent of the property. most of the flying was close to the ground. while i was operating the drone within 10-20 feet in the air, i did hear and notice a helicopter overhead. by reflex, i soon landed the drone. when the helicopter returned (or it may have been another), i had already ceased operating the drone. i did not believe that i was doing anything improper at the time. still, it prompted me to conduct an online search about laws regarding drone usage. i then learned that i am required to be licensed to operate the drone, and also that i cannot fly within 5 miles of an airport. i performed a google search and realized that this address was within 5 miles of redacted airport. this news brought me anxiety, for i did not intend to violate any faa laws and i had no idea that the airport was so close to the job site. i do not know if my inadvertent action was discovered or reported to or by the faa, as it could have just been routine helicopter operation, but i did later learn that my drone has a digital id that can appear and be noticed. i informed my employers right away about this, in case they are contacted. the drone belongs to the business owners and i was using their drone on site, operating alone with no training or awareness of the laws. i regret operating the drone today and i wish i had been aware of the requirements. i do not plan on operating the drone again until i am licensed and have obtained approval to fly in any airspace requiring it.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying a UAS in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: unintentional uas operation in class d airspace (first flight experience)during my first-ever recreational drone flight, which occurred at approximately xa:00, i unintentionally operated within class d airspace without prior authorization.the flight took place in an area that i later learned corresponds to a 100-foot laanc grid within class d airspace. at the time, i was not aware of airspace classifications or that authorization is required even when operating below the published grid altitude. the flight was brief, and the drone did not exceed approximately 50 feet agl. no other aircraft were observed in the area, and no unsafe interactions occurred.following the flight, i researched the airspace and became aware of faa requirements regarding controlled airspace and laanc authorization. i also learned that my home location is within class d airspace that extends to the surface (0 feet agl) during tower operating hours, meaning authorization is required prior to any flight regardless of altitude when the airspace is active.since this event, i have not conducted any additional flights. i have begun educating myself on faa uas regulations, including airspace classifications, laanc authorization procedures, and safe operating practices. i intend to ensure that all future flights are conducted in full compliance with applicable regulations and will obtain proper authorization prior to operating in controlled airspace.lessons learned:authorization is required in controlled airspace regardless of altitude, including areas with published grid ceilings.airspace classifications and laanc grids must be reviewed prior to any flight.understanding local airspace (including home location) is essential before operating a uas.corrective actions:ceased all drone operations after recognizing the issue.reviewing faa uas rules and airspace requirements.planning to use laanc authorization before any future operations in controlled airspace.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Vehicle
synopsis: MAF Tower controllers reported having to cancel an aircraft's takeoff clearance after realizing there was a vehicle still parked on the runway.
text: runway 16r was the active. i (training on local control) had control of runway 16r. ground control (gc) had control of runways 16l, 10, and 4. gc had a vehicle that needed to mow the area immediately surrounding the intersection of runways 16r and 10. ground would request permission from me to have the vehicle enter the intersection. when i needed runway 16r clear, i would inform ground, and they would have the vehicle exit runway 16r and remain on runway 10 for quick re-entry. each time i give gc permission to enter the runway, i put my memory aid up on the runway incursion device (rid), as required by our sop. i had a visual flight rules helicopter maneuvering about 300 feet above ground level (agl) several miles south of the field inspecting a power line. i had aircraft x ready for takeoff at runway 16r at taxiway papa. another aircraft was taxiing northbound on papa and would be ready to depart shortly. because the helicopter was in the way of the departing aircraft, i coordinated with the departure controller and received a left turn heading 100 or heading 110, which would get the departure well east of the helicopter. i wrote the coordinated heading on the flight strip as a not-required memory aid to give the aircraft the turn when clearing it for takeoff. at that time, the vehicle was in the intersection of runways 16r and 10, and my memory aid was where it should have been. after seeing the helicopter out the window to the south and turning to look at aircraft x to the north ready to depart, i cleared aircraft x for takeoff. i issued the left turn and gave the aircraft the wind and the position of the helicopter. aircraft x then entered the runway and began powering their engines up, all the while the pickup truck is parked on the runway. the ground controller noticed aircraft x moving and mentioned it to me, then exclaimed that the vehicle was still where i had coordinated that it could be: halfway down the runway directly ahead of the departing aircraft x. i told aircraft x to cancel takeoff clearance and turn right at taxiway mike. the pilot promptly read back my instructions, slowed the aircraft, and exited the runway at mike. the pilot then asked me why their takeoff clearance was cancelled. i informed them that there was a vehicle on the runway. the ground controller had the vehicle exit runway 16r. the other departing aircraft was ahead of aircraft x at this point and departed first. aircraft x next, but this time runway heading because the helicopter was not a factor. aircraft x never got closer than 3, 250 feet to the vehicle.if i had had direct communication with the vehicle, rather than the vehicle being on gc's frequency, i would likely have been more aware and would have talked to the vehicle before talking to the aircraft. i need to ensure my normal scan (including the rid and runways) does not get compromised when i have additional things to include in my scan (in this case, the helicopter in a specific place out the window and the heading in a small box on the flight strip). if i had looked at the rid and seen the memory aid or looked at the runway and seen the truck, i would not have cleared the aircraft x for takeoff.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the flight crew forgot to set the brakes due to miscommunication with the ramp crew and the First Officer and when the aircraft began to move forward; the reporter applied and set the parking brake.
text: ramp crew pushed us back using mostly standard phraseology, including the clearance to start engines. they did not, however, report pushback complete, set parking brake." their next communication was "towbar disconnected, pin removed, " at which point i directed "disconnect headset." we continued with engine start, and neither i nor the first officer noticed the discrepancy, and i returned the marshaler's salute. during the after start checklist we both noticed the aircraft creeping forward on the taxiway. i applied brakes and set the parking brake. the first officer did not monitor the interphone during this pushback, but stated he did not hear me read back the call "parking brake set, pressure normal." during debrief, we discovered that he was under the impression that he could not monitor the pushback. we reviewed the flight manual (fm) pushback section."

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A320 Captain reported the flight crew realized the FMA was in the wrong mode and received a terrain warning; leveled off which caused a flap overspeed; and then corrected the path to an uneventful landing.
text: in visual flight rules conditions on approach to [runway] xx. air traffic control asked if we had visual on terrain, we said yes and proceeded to descend to 2900 and subsequently were cleared approach. we armed approach and set faf in window. as we started down visually we realized our flight mode annunciator (fma) was in open descent instead of descent mode. aircraft warned of terrain and i allowed the airspeed to creep up from 180 flaps 2 to 200 while it's fixing descent issue. leveled off, corrected the path and made an uneventful landing.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A320 First Officer reported the flight crew realized the FMA was in the wrong mode and received a terrain warning; leveled off which caused a flap overspeed; and then corrected the path to an uneventful landing.
text: while on rnp xx, air traffic control gave instruction to descend visually to 2900 msl on rnp xx. we were in open descent mode on the approach. after being cleared for the approach, we set 2000 feet as the faf altitude on the flight control unit (fcu). while starting down visually and noticed we were in open descent mode. we were fully aware of nearby terrain and closure rate. the airplane warned of terrain closure, and pf arrested descent. this caused a flap overspeed that was immediately corrected by disconnecting ap and autothrust. the aircraft leveled off and continued the approach to an uneventful landing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported an engine failure in cruise. Diverted and landed uneventfully.
text: while operating aircraft x from redacted to redacted, at approximately xa:15 utc and in cruise at fl360, we heard a bang from the left side of the aircraft and felt a slight disturbance. prior to that event, the flight had been normal, with me acting as pf and the captain acting as pm.immediately after the noise, we observed an eng 1 out message on eicas and verified that we had a no. 1 engine failure. the flight attendant contacted the flight deck and reported that passengers had heard the noise and that some appeared concerned. we advised the flight attendant to stand by while we focused on aircraft control and the immediate abnormal procedures.i remained pf and continued flying the aircraft. the captain requested priority handling with air traffic control and requested descent to fl230. the captain set began the applicable engine-out qrh, and turned the apu on. during the procedure, i monitored aircraft control, guarded and confirmed the required actions as appropriate, and continued the descent.after the no. 1 engine was safely secured, the captain coordinated with dispatch and we elected to divert to redacted. air traffic control then cleared us direct redacted and issued descend and maintain 11, 000 feet. during the descent, the captain made a pa advising the passengers that we had experienced an engine failure and were diverting to redacted for a safe landing, while i set up the flight management system and prepared for the approach.during the descent, we also observed a pack 1 ovht (overheat) message. the captain selected pack 1 off. later, we observed a rudder hardover protection fail message. after ensuring the aircraft remained stable in the engine-out condition, i transferred control of the aircraft to the captain, and the related qrh was completed while continuing the diversion.the flight attendant continued her procedures and kept the cabin under control. the approach and single-engine landing at redacted were completed without further difficulty by the captain. after clearing the runway, engine 2 was shut down and fire/rescue personnel performed an external inspection of engine 1. we were advised that there was no visible external fire or smoke. afterward, engine 2 was restarted and the aircraft taxied to gate xx.at no point did i perceive a loss of aircraft controllability. workload was elevated but manageable, and crm among the captain, myself, the flight attendant, air traffic control, and dispatch was effective throughout the event.suggestions: the company's engine-out training was very helpful during this event. continued emphasis on maintaining proficiency and currency in engine-out scenarios would be beneficial.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported an unusually loud rushing air noise coming from main cabin door. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: after departing redacted for redacted we received a call from the number one flight attendant climbing through approximately 10, 000ft. the number one stated that there was an extreme amount of noise coming from the forward entry door. as he was speaking to me on the inter phone i could audibly hear the loud rushing air noise and the flight attendant was having to yell to communicate with me. the pressurization was on schedule and there was nothing on the gauges to alert us of any kind of issue with the system. we discussed with the number one that we were going to climb a little higher to see if the door will get a seal on it. some aircraft need a little more pressure to create a good seal. as we climbed we contacted the number one and he stated that there was no change it was still loud. i then called dispatch and maintenance control and went over the issue with them. they all agreed this was not normal. as i was talking to them the cabin crew was calling to let us know the passengers were uncomfortable. it was at this point we decided to take the plane back to redacted instead of continuing over the ocean to redacted. we discussed that the plane would be slightly overweight for landing and given the unknown situation with the door we advised air traffic control and started coordinating with air traffic control for a return to redacted. on our way in to redacted we ran the overweight landing qrh procedure and the non routine landing checklist. the rest of the flight was unremarkable and we made our way to the gate for a normal deplaning via jet bridge. at the gate i made the entries in the logbook for the pressurization issue and the over weight landing. cause: casual factors in this event are mechanical failures as well as communication and crew coordination. this is the type of event that could really only be discovered during flight as the ac is not pressurized enough on the ground to know. i did follow up with the actions of the mechanics and it seems there was a tear in the door pressurization seal. mitigation may have to occur on overnight maintenance checks of door pressurization seals.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: B777-200 relief pilot reported a hydraulic leak during cruise which resulted in a diversion to an alternate airport.
text: we had a delayed flight due to a reported hydraulic leak from the left wing. this was visible from the ground during the preflight walk around(see pictures). the mechanics balancing entry stated that they found the leak, but it was in the normal range. normal takeoff and climb other than an inoperative printer in the cockpit leading to a higher workload. as relief pilot, i took the first break. after an hour or so, i received a call from the cockpit with news that there was a hydraulic fluid leak and it didn't look good. paraphrasing. i returned to the cockpit and saw the hand written table showing a steady decrease in hydraulic fluid quantity on the left side and an estimate of a low quantity upon reaching redacted. also, notes from maintenance control conversation were they agreed that it was not normal and a probable leak. the decision was made to divert and redacted was chosen. a normal, overweight landing was performed following by a normal taxi to the gate.cause: not sending an aircraft with a possible hydraulic leak for an ocean crossing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A320 pilot reported parking brake pressure lost and aircraft rolled forward uncommanded into the chocks.
text: the flight crew arrived at redacted to operate aircraft x to redacted on-time on day 0. while completing our receiving checklist, the ca noticed that the ca's oxygen mask (interphone) would not test properly, and that there was not a proper 'switch over, ' to the mask-microphone function. after confirming that the first officer's mask was working properly, and attempting to resolve the issue multiple times, dispatch was informed and maintenance was called to the aicraft. maintenance confirmed that the ca's mask was not working properly, and upon further investgiation, damage was found to the cables connecting the mask to the aicraft in the flight deck. maintenance informed us that they would 'swap, ' the mask assembly box with the second observer's mask to resolve the issue. this process took several hours as it proved to be a difficult task to accomplish due to the ergonomics of the assemblies. after the procedure was complete, the maintenance technicians proceeded to begin the 'sign off, ' process, and took the logbook to 'close out, ' the open write-up. while this was happening, the aircraft unexpectedly rolled forward completely uncommanded into the chocks. the captain first noticed this, and it was confirmed by the remaining maintenance crew still onboard the aicraft. we verified that the parking brake was still engaged by first looking at the e/wd, and then looked at the 'triple indicator, ' to see that both the accumulator and both brake pressure indicators were showing zero pressure. after coordinating with maintenance, the yellow pump was turned on which immediately pressurized the yellow system. hydraulic cavitations were felt and heard, and the 'triple indicator, ' immediatley showed tha the system was pressurized. at this point, we realized that there may be an issue with the accumulator. at no point did we suspect that the indicator was incorrectly reporting the pressure, as it was confirmed on two separate 'known states, ' that the pressure was first 'lost, ' and then 'recharged.' during the next 35-40 minutes of troubleshooting and invesgitation, we noticed that the presure in the accumulator was dropping rapidly, and the brake pressure indicators were also showing a loss of pressure. the manual states that 'effective on a/c all - accumulators maintain the parking pressure for at least 12 hours. yellow accumulators can be pressurized by pressuring the yellow electric pump switch. brake and accumulator pressure are indiciated on the triple indicator.' the total time elapsed from first parking brake application (aircraft block-in from redacted) to the aircraft moving into the chocks was approxmately 3 hours -- clearly outside of the normal expectation for the system. at this point, we were notified that the airport authority had instructed us to move the aicraft off of the gate because it was needed for another aircraft. we proceeded to 'deplane, ' the customers, and maintenance moved the aicraft to another suitable gate. this process took several hours, and during this time, on-site maintenance worked to test the aicraft and seek a resolution. ultimately, the flight was cancelled due to the extended delay as the inflight crew had worked the incoming flight from redacted, and we were rapidly approaching our mot (minimum off time). we were notified that we would be operating an extra section for the route, aircraft y on day 1.the next morning, after waking up in redacted, i noticed that the schedule stated that the flight would be operated with the same tail number, aircraft x and there was an minimum equipment list applied -- minimum equipment list 32-xx-redacted. in my opinion, after reviewing the minimum equipment list details, this was an incorrect minimum equipment list for the situation, instead referencing the indicator not being correct. at this time, i felt that maintenance control was attempting to apply the minimum equipment list that would allow us to depart while the aicraft was still in an unsafe condition to fly. ultimately, the issue was resolved via a 'tail swap, ' to another aicraft, and aircraftx was grounded.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A320 Captain reported air conditioning system issues resulting in very high ambient temperatures and return to departure airport.
text: i was assigned from reserve to operate aircraft x from redacted to redacted.during preflight, the first officer and i reviewed the aircraft logbook and mels. multiple mels were noted, including two related to the air conditioning system. neither minimum equipment list contained operations procedures or notes indicating degraded cabin temperature performance. during cockpit preparation, i observed the pack flow selector in the high position. as this was not required by any minimum equipment list or procedure, it was returned to norm.pushback was slightly delayed due to ramp congestion. taxi and takeoff were uneventful. during climb, passing approximately 10, 000 feet, the flight attendants reported increasing cabin temperatures in the aft cabin. in response, i selected all temperature zones to full cold and set pack flow to high. a subsequent report from the cabin indicated that conditions were worsening, with very hot air from the vents.the cond page was reviewed and indicated increasing cabin temperatures and elevated trim air temperature (approximately 150°c). i made a pa to inform passengers that we were working to address the situation. at that point, i transferred aircraft control to the first officer and requested a level-off from air traffic control to allow time for system evaluation and troubleshooting.no ecam messages were present, and no applicable non-annunciated procedures were identified in the qrh. based on system indications, we selected the hot air pushbutton off, no improvement was observed.i established communication with maintenance control via satcom and provided a summary of system indications and cabin reports. in coordination with maintenance control, we selected the hot air push button off and performed a pack reset. these actions did not result in any sustained improvement. cabin temperatures continued to increase, reaching approximately 105°f forward and 100°f aft. concurrently, the cabin crew continued to report worsening conditions and increasing passenger discomfort.given the lack of response to corrective actions, continued adverse temperature indications, and ongoing cabin reports, the first officer and i assessed the situation as a safety concern and elected to discontinue the flight and return to redacted.the first officer coordinated the return with air traffic control while i remained in communication with maintenance control. during the return, trim air temperature briefly decreased, however, cabin temperatures remained elevated and subsequently increased again. based on this trend, the decision to return was reaffirmed.i advised the cabin crew and passengers of the return. due to workload during the approach phase, i contacted redacted operations via vhf to advise of the return and request notification to dispatch.the approach and landing were uneventful. after arrival at the gate, a logbook entry was made and the aircraft was subsequently removed from service.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A320 Captain on initial climb reported the handle broke off the rear door and it did not seal properly so they returned to departure airport.
text: shortly after departure from redacted airport, while climbing through approximately 1, 500 feet agl, the crew received an amber ecam message: door r aft emergency exit.the message appeared after the takeoff inhibit phase, at which point we leveled at 5, 000 feet and requested vectors to troubleshoot. ecam and qrh procedures were initiated.per qrh guidance, continuation of flight may be considered if pressurization is confirmed normal. however, during coordination with the cabin crew, a physical inspection of the door revealed that the handle had become detached and the door appeared unsecured (unlocked"/not properly seated).this created a discrepancy between: system indications and qrh conditional guidance, and direct physical observation from the cabin crew indicating a potential door integrity issue.additionally, due to the early phase of flight in which the ecam message occurred (approximately 1, 500 feet agl), there was limited opportunity to reliably assess cabin pressurization performance prior to reaching higher altitudes where any degradation could become operationally significant.given: the uncertainty regarding the mechanical status of the emergency exit, the abnormal condition of a detached handle, the limited ability to confirm stable pressurization early in the climb, the planned routing over the redacted/oceanic segment, where diversion options are more limited, i assessed that continuing the flight would introduce unnecessary risk, particularly in the event of a pressurization or structural issue. given these factors, delaying the decision until further climb would have reduced available margins and increased exposure to risk in a less favorable operational environment. after completing the qrh, i coordinated with dispatch via satcom, briefed the passengers, and elected to return to redacted for a precautionary landing. the aircraft landed without further incident."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A220 Captain reported stabilizer pitch trim was not responding correctly to inputs. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: shortly after liftoff, we raised the landing gear, noticed the nose pitch trim was not corresponding correctly to the flying pilots (captain) input. as the aircraft accelerated through 800' feet, both pilots recognized the excessive pressure it took for me to keep the nose at the proper pitch angle for climb. although i could command the blue" electronic pitch trim speed bug forward, there was no airspeed trim vector "green" indicated. as the airspeed increased and the aircraft continued, it was harder to keep the nose down at the proper climb angle. upon level off at 5, 000, i was forcefully pushing forward pressure constantly to keep the aircraft nose from pitching back up. i was able to control and eventually level the aircraft and reduce the speed, as the speed trim bug was 30-40 kts above the flight management system preselected climb speed in the climb. i was able to eventually ease the forward pressure on the stick and level the aircraft off. the first officers side seemed unaffected by the problem. we both made the decision that he would fly the aircraft and i would handle air traffic control and programming the flight management system for the approach back into redacted. i elected to return the aircraft back to redacted, rw xxr. i did not declare an emergency, simply because i did not feel assistance on the ground was warranted at the time. i did not brief my inflight, as time was a virtue. however, all items of a briefing were accomplished. getting the aircraft back on the ground safely was my main priority. we were cleared back to join the instrument landing system approach for runway xxr and to descend to 3, 000. my inflight was instructed to prep the cabin for landing. i made an announcement over the pa to the passengers. the aircraft did not auto-call 1, 000 resolution advisory while on final approach. the aircraft handled as expected through flare & touchdown, while the first officer flew the approach. once on the ground, i contacted dispatch, maintenance control and the duty chief pilot."

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: TMB 940 pilot reported gusty wind conditions resulting in a runway excursion during landing.
text: i was arriving at redacted in gusty southerly wind conditions. the reported winds were approximately 170° at 11 knots, gusting to 18 knots. visual observation of the windsock indicated variable and gusty conditions.on the first approach, i experienced instability on short final related to gusty conditions and airspeed management. recognizing the unstable condition, i executed a go-around.on the second approach, i increased my approach speed and initially maintained runway alignment. however, during the landing phase near touchdown, i encountered a gust while applying significant control input to maintain directional control in the crosswind. the aircraft deviated left of centerline and exited the runway into the grass, where it came to a stop in soft ground.there were no injuries, and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft. the aircraft is being inspected prior to return to service.this event highlighted the importance of maintaining adequate control margin in gusty crosswind conditions. while the reported winds were within expected limits, the variability and gusts resulted in higher control input requirements than anticipated on short final.in reviewing the event, i recognize that increasing control demand earlier on final approach was an indicator of reduced margin. continuing the approach into the flare under those conditions reduced my ability to respond effectively to a gust at touchdown.going forward, i will use earlier decision points based on control input and stability, and will discontinue the approach if increasing control demand indicates diminishing margin. i will also ensure appropriate energy margin is maintained in gusty conditions.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: Cessna 172 Student Pilot reported an engine failure on takeoff resulting in a runway excursion. Student secured the aircraft.
text: initial student pilot solo: i was cleared for take off and rolled out on to runway. checked all gauges and went to full power, i was applying right rudder to counteract left turning tendencies, engine lost power and the plane moved rapidly to the right when plane moved to right i added left rudder to counteract act that and the engine regained power turing meback to left while left rudder was applied. i was attempting to make it onto taxi way 1 while avoiding planes on active taxiway. the plane was carrying too much speed and rolled into the grass and stopped. i was unable to move throttle so i shut plane down via mixture knob. there was no damage/harm to the airplane or persons.

text: my aircraft, the c172n was cleared and established on rnav xx into redacted. we were following traffic ahead of us to land on runway xx. throughout the approach we had traffic alerts and could not see any other traffic than the aircraft we were following. at about 700ft msl i was able to see a c172s about 400ft below us and to the left based on my estimate. tower told the c172s to go around to the right, the aircraft requested to bear left and was approved to do so on the go around. we continued the approach and landed runway xx.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: PA-28 pilot reported runway excursion after landing in crosswind.
text: i checked awos at approximately xa:20. i checked weather again at approximately xa:30 there were no pireps or notams relevant to landing visual flight rules on runway xx. the winds on the reported awos were 230@4 and 200@5 respectively. runway in use was xx. i called ctaf/unicom and reported approaching and landing. there was no other traffic, or no other reports regarding airport conditions.i approached rwy xx carrying approximately 85 knots on final approach speed, which allowed for 5 knots above no-wind final approach speed of 80 kias. approach and landing were uneventful. after landing on runway xx at redacted after all wheels were on the ground, i began deceleration with aerodynamic braking. landed with crosswind controls into the wind. at approximately xa:43 the plane swerved to the right. on correcting with nose wheel steering and with flight controls for assist the plane swerved the other direction and then off of the runway.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A TRACON Controller Trainee reported a military flight of two F/A 18's descended below the assigned altitude and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: aircraft x and aircraft y were participants flying in standard formation entering the rxxxx complex from redacted [artcc] redacted intersection. normally when rxxxx participants are entering the sua their instrument flight rules flight plan is cancelled and they are given a visual flight rules clearance to operate within the complex. however, in this situation when they checked in to enter rxxxx they were still in imc conditions so i gave them a conditional short range instrument flight rules clearance to find vmc sky. the phraseology was, 'aircraft x, after redacted you're cleared to redacted airport via radar vectors, fly present heading, then descend and maintain one six thousand, correction one seven thousand. report reaching vmc conditions.' i thought i heard the proper read back but i was wrong because listening back the pilot read back 'one six thousand'. the mva in that area is 16, 200 and the aircraft descended very rapidly all the way to 16, 100 before my trainer stepped in to handle the situation. the only recommendation i have to prevent the re-occurence of this event is to listen very carefully to every pilot read back. especially since i corrected the original altitude assignment i must be extra vigilant to ensure the pilot reads back the correct one.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737 Captain reported a lack of inspection accomplished to diagnose specific maintenance item. Aircraft was refused.
text: we were supposed to operate flight to redacted with a good 737-8 tail. moments before boarding the crew is notified of an aircraft swap and gate change, next door to aircraft x. the gate agent for the new gate briefs the crew that the aircraft was a return to gate and rejected by the previous captain over an 'apu issue'. we board the aircraft with a good release stating the apu was minimum equipment list'd. i call dispatch to confirm what is the history of the jet, and the reason for the return to gate and denial of the aircraft. the dispatcher calls the previously operating dispatcher, discovering that during push back and engine start, the apu fire light illuminated, resulting in oil on the tail of the aircraft and the ramp. dispatch then discovers that the maintenance team came out to disconnect the apu from the reset of the system, cleaned up the oil on the tail and ramp, but could never diagnose what the cause of the fire illumination. with concurrence of dispatch, the chief pilot, and my first officer, i elected that this aircraft was not air worthy for operation due to the lack of inspections accomplished to diagnose the underlying cause for a fire illumination in the flight deck.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 First Officer reported nose wheel steering malfunction during takeoff roll. Flight crew rejected the takeoff.
text: initially pushed back from gate and after engine start and permission to taxi, the ca began to taxi but the nose wheel went completely full left and was unable to move it back to the right with the tiller. aircraft was stopped and maintenance called. was eventually towed back to the gate. maintenance informed us this occurred due to a stuck pin as a result of how the ground crew disconnected the bypass pin. we were informed that the issue was repaired and the release was cleared. pushed back again and was able to taxi with no observable issue. when cleared for takeoff, ca transferred controls to me (pf/fo) and began the takeoff roll as normal. at approximately 50 knots, the plane began pulling to the left but corrected with rudder input. however, as we continued to increase speed the aircraft continued to pull left (winds were less than 10 knots), but increase rudder pressure would not bring the aircraft back to centerline. at approximately 80 knots, the ca took controls and performed a rejected takeoff. i announced to tower that we were rejecting the takeoff, however, i failed to verify speed brake and rejected takeoff were engaged. as the plane slowed the rudder and tiller became effective again and taxied back to the gate without further incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B767 First Officer reported a malfunction with the pressurization system at cruise altitude.
text: i was the pilot flying. we had a right pack deferred and verified all procedures needed were done in accordance to the minimum equipment list before departure. departed with a cruise of fl330 and maximum was fl350. as we reached cruise we appeared to pressurizing normal. then our jumpseater noticed the cabin vsi was fluctuating up to neutral and told us. i began to watch it and we slowly creep to a cabin altitude of 10k and we got altitude high. we ran the qrc while i flew left and set up for a descent. air traffic control was notified initially since the altitude was not rapidly rising it was sitting at 10k. we were denied descent and deemed we need to get down soon as still rising so priority handling was used and we dropped to fl210 and pressurization began to stabilize and cabin altitude high went away. we got maintenance control and dispatch on the line to talk while i flew and talked on the radio. then the jumpseater appeared to get nervous stating we need to go down to 10k. i pushed as to why because our cabin altitude at 3k now and slowly going to sea level and how was that an issue as we do not have a chart for standard pressurization due to the auto 1/2 system. no faults were shown at fl210 to those systems. i was confused how it would be an issue at 2000 cabin altitude. he continued to use appropriate cuss" words to the point where it felt better to be at 10k and analyze the situation because flying with him touching me and signaling to go down while the captain ran checklists and talked to dispatch and maintenance control was becoming a distraction despite both of our efforts efforts to clear the question with valid explanations. we ultimately re requested priority handling choosing the safest action to keep crm and safety of flight and went to 10k feet terrain and gas were no issues and landed uneventfully in redacted with plenty of gas."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported fuel leak in cruise. Diverted and landed uneventfully.
text: while climbing in the higher flight levels (about 270-330) some time had past since turning off the center fuel pumps by this point, i the first officer and pm noticed the right side fuel indicator was yellow and showed the word imbalance underneath the quantity. i pointed it out to the ca who was pf. we tried to balance the fuel and after about 10 minutes, the right side was still decreasing more quickly than the left side. we suspended trying to transfer fuel and began to run the fuel leak engine qrh procedure. we stopped it short of shutting down the engine because we were not concerned with suspected leak enough to justify shutting down an engine, making things more complicated than they had to be. we deemed it safe and appropriate to request priority handling and divert to redacted giving us a reasonable amount of time to safely execute the diversion while monitoring our fuel situation. as we continued the right side continued to decrease fuel more than the left with no other outlying indications. upon landing we had airport rescue and firefighting (arff) check out the aircraft to make a visual inspection, they reported nothing noticeable and so we continued to the gate and had arff follow us until we were shut down at the gate and cancelled the priority handling.cause: suspected mechanical issue, we ran appropriate qrh procedure.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A320 Captain reported returning to departure airport after experiencing an engine EGT over-temp on climb out.
text: our flight was from redacted. we boarded aircraft x and found the flight deck and forward galley in a bit of disarray, with gear pins, papers, and rags on the cockpit floor and a mechanic's headset and pitot tube covers in the galley. the aircraft had been sitting in redacted for what i recall was a few days from the logbook. we requested that a mechanic come to retrieve any items that didn't belong on the airplane and ensure that everything that was required to be onboard was accounted for, which they did. my first officer verified that no gear-pins, collars, reverser locking pins, etc. were in place on the exterior of the aircraft.we departed on time and taxied to runway xxl for takeoff. the takeoff was normal and we received a vector of 230 and clearance to 10, 000 feet from redacted departure. passing through approximately 6, 000 feet, an ecam message appeared, eng 2 egt over-temp" with engine parameters in agreement. i was the pilot monitoring and began the non-normal plan strategy, which led us to reducing thrust to see if the egt would come below the high-limit. it did, but after a brief discussion of our situation and about how such a reduction in thrust didn't make flying all the way to our destination seem very practical or wise, we decided that returning to redacted would be prudent. this discussion was cut short by a second ecam, "eng2 epr mode fail", so the plan strategy began once again. the ecam action led us to a reversion to n1 mode of thrust control and subsequent loss of auto-thrust, and that went smoothly. my first officer, whose capacity to fly the aircraft extraordinarily well and handle high task-loading with apparent ease (while i was quite busy with qrh followups, status page updates, the ecam supplemental manual, diversion notification, etc.), was able to observe that increasing the thrust on the affected engine close to climb would cause another over temperature condition while decreasing the thrust to idle also caused a sharp increase in temperature up to the limit. unusual. i notified the flight attendants and passengers of the need to return to redacted for a mechanical discrepancy. we notified air traffic control for a more immediate return to the airport, although the situation was quite under control, the strange behavior of the egt on the affected engine gave us enough reason to think being on the ground sooner than later would be a good idea. we performed an overweight landing checklist for what would be a landing at approximately 4, 000 pounds over maximum landing weight. during landing the #2 engine thrust reverser didn't deploy, and displayed amber when selected to reverse. after clearing the runway we noticed that the #2 engine, when at idle, was approximately 150 degrees hotter than the #1 engine at idle, but within limits. after shutdown, we also noted an "eng2 fadec" class 2 status message. before i had the chance to pick up my ipad to begin making all of the necessary logbook entries, we were greeted on the flight deck by two mechanics who noted that they weren't very surprised by our return because the airplane had "quite a history". they mentioned that the work done on the airplane over the last day or two involved replacing pieces of a wiring harness, but the reality was that the airplane simply needed an engine change. i can't speak to the veracity of that statement, but it was said to me. i spoke with our dispatcher, chief pilot. we swapped to another a-320 at the neighboring gate and departed about 2 hours late for a successful flight.cause: the specific causal factors, at least in so far as what caused the egt to over-temp in such a way with the follow-on failures (engine pressure ratio mode failure, thrust reverser failure, full authority digital engine control fault) aren't available to me at this point, so i could only speculate. my decades of experience flying turbine engines would lead me to believe that the engine's turbine tolerances had become excessive and the engine was simply out of time. that would agree with the statement the mechanics made to me, but i can't verify that. as i sit writing this, it's not immediately apparent to me why an egt exceedance (at least one that's not severe) would cause the other issues, too. concerning this, i don't have any recommendations for this situation to be prevented, but i can speak to the effectiveness of the planned strategy and of course recommend the reinforcement of its teaching. an egt over-temp on a high-time engine for a brief period during takeoff isn't exactly unheard of, and in fact is even allowed in some cases with a maintenance discrepancy item, but this event unfolded in a rather unexpected way after the over-temp occurred, and the planned strategy is indispensable in such a situation."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Cessna Citation flight crew reported receiving an ENG Exceedance CAS during take off. Crew rejected takeoff and returned to the ramp.
text: on departure out of redacted we received an engine exceedance crew alerting system (cas) message briefly. pm observed the message and called for the low speed abort. we cleared the runway and taxied back to ramp to contact maintenance and company.cause: tail wind component was within limits and winds were variable in direction. we determined we were within safe and legal tailwind component limit of ten knots. we believe the tailwind component may have shifted which generated the momentary cas.suggestions: crew will be even more conservative below the published tail wind component maximum to help ensure the possibility a shifting tail wind component does not necessitate another low speed abort.

synopsis: Aircraft technicians reported they discovered damage on the CE-700 left outboard flap during an R3 check. They documented the discrepancies and turned it over to the incoming shift.
text: day 23statement on aircraft x lh outboard flap maintenance. on day 0/1 aircraft x was input at redacted for r3. my crew accomplished the base checklist in which we discovered, and i created found faults for.1) lh wing otbd (outboard) upper split flap panel otbd edge rubbing on bottom of aileron panel (day 1)2) lh wing otbd flap at inbd (inboard) actuator fairing has excessive play in fairing. (day 1) at the end of the shift, i gave a turnover about the damaged flap, and the actuator play at the fairing, to management during the shift turnover meeting and to the oncoming lead tech at the aircraft (as per sop). as i recall now, i had even shown one of the on-coming managers the damaged flap and the play in the actuator at the inboard fairing. on the evening of day 7, our first night back i was informed at the lead turnover meeting, that the flap needed to be removed for evaluation since the etic (estimated time in commission) was day 10. my crew consisted of 5 technicians, 3 of maintenance manual procedure, and the illustrated parts manual for removal of the flaps. at which point my focus was then on the wing leading edges of which were found numerous cracks in the inner skins, and the inspection of the fuel tanks. the flap was removed and i was told that there appeared to be damage to the actual hinge assembly, and that numerous spacers appeared to have been damaged by the play, and possibly some were missing. me and the qc (quality control) tech looked over the flap and agreed with the techs that this did appear to be what was occurring. i then created a found fault (lh otbd flap removed fom (maintenance facility) day 7) linking it to the actuator play fault. i was going to order the parts that appeared to be needed but had seen that the day shift lead tech back order which were the shims and bolts.this was the last time that me and my crew had any interaction with aircraft x until our meeting to discuss why the flap was removed the way that it was.suggestions: management not wait 7 days to have technicians investigate a discrepancy if the due out time is in 10 days to where they are putting any shift/technician in a hurry up and get it done framework. also when turnovers are given in meetings instead of the normal management shaking their heads and doing nothing, that they actually listen assigning someone in management to these large discrepancies to coordinate the way that these are worked from investigating the fault, through ordering of the parts, then verifying and expediting the acquisition of said parts instead of waiting to the last minute. lead techs can only do so much with the resources that we have, and sometimes there are things that the resources available to management allow them to achieve at a more adequate/positive outcome.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft
synopsis: Mooney M20K pilot reported collapsing of the nose wheel during landing. Aircraft was removed from runway and pulled to the ramp.
text: i departed in mooney with a destination of redacted. the weather was exceptionally favorable--clear and sunny, with some ground fog in the region. i climbed to an altitude of 13, 000 feet, enjoying a smooth instrument flight rules flight.as i began my descent towards redacted, everything seemed normal. i arrived and made my approach for landing. during the landing phase, i touched down at the typical speed of 55 to 60 knots. upon landing, the steering did not feel normal, and the aircraft began to veer left of centerline. my first thought was that i might have a flat nose wheel tire. i provided control input to correct the course, and while the aircraft initially responded, it soon began to veer to the right. it wasn't long before the nose gear collapsed, causing the nose to drop and the propeller to strike the pavement at an approximate ground speed of 30 to 35 knots, resulting in the engine shutting down.after communicating with the tower about the collapse of the nose gear and informing them that i was evacuating the aircraft on the runway, i pulled the mixture knob, switched the fuel selector to the off position, turned the master switch off, switched the ignition to the off position, removed the keys, and placed them on the dashboard. i then grabbed my handheld radio to remain in contact with the control tower before evacuating the airplane.once outside, i conducted a visual inspection of the aircraft and noticed no damage other than the collapsed nose gear and bent propeller. additionally, there were no fuel leaks or indications of leaking oil. the nose landing gear doors remained unscathed, as they did not contact the pavement due to the collapsed nose gear's ability to keep the aircraft elevated. i also noted that the nose tire was fully inflated.soon after, personnel arrived to assist me. a forklift was utilized to lift the nose of the aircraft using cargo straps attached to the propeller and to pull it to the ramp.

synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying a UAS outside of the boundaries of their LAANC authorization.
text: while conducting a commercial mission for company x, i utilized a 100 ft laanc approval for an area adjacent to a 0 ft class d grid. my operational plan was to remain within the 100 ft zone and utilize the aircraft's zoom capabilities to capture the target property.throughout the flight, the remote controller interface froze on multiple occasions, significantly hindering my ability to monitor real-time telemetry and positioning. additionally, the flight app's visual map depicted the class d boundary incorrectly. these technical issues, combined with sustained strong wind conditions (documented by multiple controller warnings), resulted in the aircraft operating within the 0 ft class d boundary for the majority of the 9-minute and 28-second flight.based on the delayed and inconsistent data provided by the frozen interface and the inaccurate map, i believed the aircraft remained within the approved 100 ft ceiling during the operation. this deviation was confirmed during a routine post-flight review of the recorded flight path on day 0, which revealed that the actual coordinates of the aircraft had overlapped the restricted boundary despite the real-time map interface showing it as clear.at approximately xa:17 into the flight, the controller issued a 'manned aircraft warning.' upon receiving this alert and recognizing a potential conflict, i immediately initiated a manual override to exit the unauthorized airspace and performed an expedited landing, touching down at xb:28. i am filing this report to document how a combination of interface failures, mapping inconsistencies, and environmental factors led to this unintentional deviation, and to record the immediate corrective action taken upon discovery

synopsis: EMB-175 First Officer reported a dual failure of both FMS's during cruise. Flight continued to destination and landed uneventfully.

vectors for navigation.the crew attempted to navigate using raw data via the redacted [vor] by selecting v/l (green needles) and tuning nav radios, however, no reliable lateral guidance was received. situational awareness. fuel status was manually calculated and monitored, confirming sufficient fuel to continue to destination. an emergency was not declared.approximately 200 nm from redacted, the crew manually computed top of descent and landing performance data. weather at redacted was visual flight rules. as the aircraft approached the terminal area, vor navigation became available, and the anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B777-200 Captain reported a hydraulic system quantity decrease during cruise flight before entering ETOPS airspace. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed overweight.
text: aircraft x was placed on a maintenance hold prior to boarding when maintenance discovered a hydraulic leak on the left wing. maintenance cleared the issue, and we proceeded with an approximately 45-minute delay. the crew briefed the issue as a potential threat that would be mitigated by monitoring the hydraulic system prior to entering etops airspace.shortly before level off, the first officer initiated a log to monitor the hydraulic system quantity and pressure. very quickly, the hyd synoptic showed a steady decrease in hydraulic quantity on the left side at a loss of .01 every 8-9 minutes.if that rate were to remain steady, we calculated that the left hydraulic quantity would read 55% by the time we reach redacted. complicating the matter was that the flight plan release included a redacted field report that indicated a wet runway, with a 500/500/500. as a restricted captain, i am not authorized for a cat iii approach. if those conditions had persisted, we would have been eligible for a cat ii approach using the exemption. however, during our previous threat briefing, it was discussed that fog at redacted tends to be the most intense at dawn rather than around midnight, which was the time of the field report.as we typically do not monitor the hyd synoptic page in flight, we initially reviewed the aircraft systems manual (asm), quick reference handbook (qrh), and aircraft operating manual (aom) to determine if a continued decrease in hydraulic quantity on the left side is normal in flight. we could not find any information in the manuals that indicated it was normal. at this time, we were near redacted airspace and initiated a satcom call to dispatch to confer with the maintenance control. at the conclusion of the initial call with maintenance control, we determined the best course of action to be to continue monitoring the hydraulic quantity to see if the trend persisted and to call back on satcom prior to the etops entry point if the trend continued.upon entering redacted [artcc] airspace, the trend of decreasing hyd quantity on the left system continued at the same rate. we subsequently contacted dispatch and requested a second conference call with maintenance control. during the second call with maintenance control, we inquired about the normalcy of the decreasing loss of indicated hyd quantity on the left side. maintenance control informed us that this situation was not normal. at this juncture, as a crew, we determined the most suitable course of action to be to divert prior to the etops entry point. redacted was the closest option, but considering redundancy in the hyd system, maintenance facility, and the ease of rebooking passengers, we concluded that redacted was a more appropriate diversion field. upon arrival at redacted, we executed an overweight landing (23, 000 lbs. above the maximum landing weight) without incident.cause: causal factor for the divert was a steadily decreasing hydraulic quantity on the a system.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A319 Captain reported a loud bang during takeoff and a ENG 1 STALL; followed by ENG 1 FIRE ECAM messages. The Captain took control of the aircraft; rejected the takeoff; then taxied to the gate after an inspection by ARFF.
text: received takeoff clearance on runway xxr @ redacted. aircraft lined up and first officer was given control. normal engine spool up and normal thrust setting technique applied. as engines were placed into flex detent and just as first officer called out flex, loud bang from #1 engine with aircraft immediately veering left. i commanded control of the aircraft, brought aircraft to a complete stop while first officer issued radio call to air traffic control to inform. i applied brakes and made pa to passengers to remain seated. initial ecam messages was eng 1 stall, followed just after bringing aircraft to stop to eng 1 fire. simultaneously with both crew members calling out engine fire, a air carrier x aircraft that was given line up and wait behind us on runway xxr made a radio call that our left engine (#1) was on fire and that they could see flames from their position under and behind the engine. first officer began the qrc proceeding with quick action item for eng fire (on the ground). i moved to start apu and establish contact with cabin. it was at this time, that i realized that due differences in button location between basic and enhanced aircraft and multiple versions of both, that i may not have actually broadcast initial remain seated" pa using the proper function on audio control panel. after placing #1 fa into loop and asking for them to look from windows to see if we were missing anything, i used handset to make addition pa to passengers to explain our situation, that they were to remain seated and that equipment was approaching aircraft. dispatch was notified of our situation. first officer finished checklist, initiated contact with airport rescue and firefighting (arff), maintained contact with air traffic control and then did the most important thing, added a pause to our procedure to make sure we were still working towards the completion together. arff contacted, stated no further fire or flames noticed and that the temperature, that had been upwards of 1000c, was in fact reducing. they also inspected left landing gear. i kept the #2 engine running during event while we completed checklist and determined if an evac would be required. i felt evac was not required so we agreed and coordinated with arff, air traffic control and cabin to taxi back to gate under our own power with arff following. no further issues and passengers deplaned normally.cause: i felt we as a crew performed well, but the multiple configurations of radios and switches to include multiple locations that we face on the a319/320/321 can cause confusion especially when task saturated."

synopsis: C340A Captain reported left engine wastegate failure resulted in a divert due to lose power and engine efficiency.
text: during climb phase.left manifold gauge dropped from 31' to xx'.autopilot changed pitch and vsi whilst maintaining ias.there was no rpm change indicated on the left engine.neither was there any audible rpm change detectable nor sudden change of yaw.i concluded that we still had something weird happening to the left engine.decided that instead of continuing the flight.it would be smarter to return and have the manifold pressure discrepancy diagnosed by our mechanic.thus requested to divert to redacted.expected to land on rwyxx in redacted but found myself on top of a thin broken layer.thus requested for the gps rwyxy approach.approach and landing occurred without further incident.our mechanic diagnosed the issue as a stuck/ceased turbo wastegate.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: BE55 pilot reported on landing a left brake failure during landing. Pilot safely exited runway.
text: flight plan was direct from redacted to redacted. everything was normal and responsive on the ground at redacted, including taxi, run up, and takeoff. i didn't notice anything abnormal on the preflight inspection. i landed at redacted and realized my left break was completely unresponsive and went straight to the floor when trying to apply breaks. i pulled the mixtures when i realized and was able to get the plane off the runway safely onto a taxiway. the plane did not go off the runway and there was no damage to anyone or anything. the breaks were just serviced at redacted when this same issue happened, but it was on the ground before the flight and the engines weren't started yet. the fbo replaced both of the master cylinders for the breaks after they found a leak but it turns out upon closer examination it was discovered that there was a leak coming from the parking break valve. after disassembly of the valve, a damaged o-ring was discovered as the cause of the hydraulic leak causing the break to fail. the parking break wouldn't leak with the plane sitting on the ground even while applying break pressure. it is suspected that while the airplane is flying, considering the vibrations and movement, a significant hydraulic leak develops while the airplane is flying. there was no hydraulic fluid leaking on the ground under the landing gear on any occasion. the plane only flew approximately 10 hours after being serviced by the fbo before this occurred.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported receiving an ATC low altitude alert and a traffic advisory for nearby general aviation traffic during final approach to ISP. Flight crew performed a go-around and returned to land.
text: on day 0, on our flight to isp i, the first officer, was the pf and the ca was the pm.after dealing with an inflight issue, we prepared for the approach and started our descent into our destination. both the ca and i had never been to isp, and after a careful review of the airport company pages, we briefed what to expect. we prepared, per the atis and the airport company pages, for the instrument landing system for runway 24, expecting vectors to the if coram. in addition, as the airport company pages informed us of increased ga traffic in the area, we exercised extra caution scanning for aircrafts.once on frequency with the final approach controller and at 3000 feet, we were given a final vector for the approach between the faf ukege (1400 feet) and if coram (2000 feet), while being instructed to descend to 2000 feet. we were asked to call for the airport in sight. as soon as we made visual contact with the field, we communicated it to air traffic control, which cleared us for the visual approach to runway 24 and handed us over to tower, at around 2500 feet, on a relatively short base leg.the aircraft was now on a shorter than expected base leg, too high for appropriate glide slope intercept between the faf (at 1400 feet) and the if (at 2000 feet), additionally requiring to slow down for an appropriate descent and approach intercept. at 210 knots, with flaps 1 configuration, i elected to pre-select 180 knots, asked the ca to lower the gear and to accomplish a descent to 1500 feet. being cleared to fly the visual approach i requested the ca to select direct to the faf, with the intention of intercepting vertical and lateral guidance to runway 24 at the faf, at 1500 feet.we descended from 2500 feet to 1500 feet, while slowing from 210 knots down to 180 knots. just prior to level off i noticed a momentary descent rate of -2100 fpm. during the level off, air traffic control advised us of a low altitude alert, most likely caused by the momentary descent rate of -2100fpm, to which the ca replied roger, we are leveling out". as we were approaching the faf at 1500 feet, i asked the ca for flaps 2, continued to slow down and asked for flaps 3. the low altitude alert was also followed by a traffic advisory from air traffic control, which paired with workload saturation, contributed to distracting us from realizing the aircraft did not capture the glideslope.upon recognition of the unsuccessful gs intercept, i promptly disconnected the autopilot and attempted, while maintaining an appropriate rate of descent and speed, to re-intercept the gs or go back on a 2 red 2 white papi configuration. the aircraft was on a flaps full landing configuration at this point. while safely getting close to re-intercept, at 500 feet agl we initiated a go around for unstable approach, and advised air traffic control, which vectored us back on final. we landed safely following the second approach.the first approach which ended with a go around, was the result of multiple factors. firstly, the faf altitude was 1400 feet, and preselecting 1500 feet while going direct to the faf resulted in reaching the faf 100 feet above gs intercept. in addition, higher workload resulted from expecting an instrument landing system and vectors outside the if, to then being unexpectedly vectored between the faf and the if, on a shorter base and a visual approach. lastly, the increased presence of ga traffic contributed to air traffic control calling us for ga traffic on our right as we were passing the faf. at the same time, traffic appeared on our display to our left. these events greatly contributed as the distractions that ultimately resulted in not realizing that the aircraft did not intercept the gs."
