anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported two near misses at W28; a non-towered airport.
text: on day 0 starting at approximately xa:50 local, two near-collision events occurred within a short amount of time at sequim valley airport (w28), involving myself (aircraft x), an aircraft y, and aircraft z.incident 1 -- runway incursion by aircraft y causing me to abort takeoff.(the conflict data entered above on this form refers to this specific incident. the 2nd incident described below, concerns a 3rd plane, has even smaller margins for their near-miss.)i was operating aircraft x and had completed all pre-departure checks. i made radio calls on ctaf 122.7 announcing my intention to taxi onto and depart runway 09. after lining up at the runway 09 threshold, i observed aircraft y move from the parking area to the runway edge at midfield (2100' ahead from me), then taxi onto the runway and proceed toward runway 27 -- the opposite end from where i was positioned. no radio calls were made by the aircraft at any point during this time. i made multiple calls to the aircraft and multiple radio checks, no response was received. i elected to abort my intended takeoff and vacate the runway rather than risk departure with an aircraft of unknown intent on the runway.after i vacated, the aircraft y pilot then disclosed he had been on the wrong frequency the entire time. despite this, his first action upon returning to the correct frequency was to announce his departure without first assessing the traffic situation or acknowledging the conflict he had caused.incident 2 -- near midair collision between aircraft y and aircraft z:at approximately xb:04 local, while aircraft y was positioned at the runway 27 threshold preparing to depart, aircraft z executed what appeared to be a go-around or touch-and-go on runway 09 and climbed out directly over aircraft y at an estimated vertical separation of no more than 100 feet. aircraft y appeared unaware that aircraft z had passed overhead. aircraft z subsequently called on ctaf to apologize, disclosing they had also been on the wrong frequency throughout their approach and pattern.contributing factors:two of three aircraft at the airport were simultaneously tuned to the wrong ctaf frequency, rendering the standard self-announce separation system ineffective.w28's runway configuration requires prolonged runway occupancy to reach thresholds, increasing exposure time and collision risk.the aircraft y pilot, after discovering his frequency error, did not pause to assess the traffic situation before proceeding with departure.the narrow runway (40 ft) with no parallel taxiway significantly reduces margins for error.what prevented a worse outcome:i visually detected aircraft y before initiating my takeoff roll and held position.i elected to vacate the runway rather than assume the other pilot's intentions.aircraft z's go-around (likely triggered by sighting aircraft y on the runway) provided vertical separation.recommended preventive measures:encourage pilots who discover a frequency error to pause, listen, and build situational awareness of the existing traffic situation before taking any further action.at narrow runways like w28 where no parallel taxiway exists, hold-short lines should be positioned to provide greater lateral clearance from the runway edge, and pilots should be explicitly encouraged -- through signage or chart supplement notes -- to perform a thorough visual check for aircraft already on the runway before entering.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported the engine quit during take off roll.
text: chain of events and discovery: during an introduction flight i followed checklist usage, however after the run-up i demonstrated to the student that it is important to lean out the mixture while waiting to take off to prevent the spark plugs from fouling. i aggressively leaned the mixture as prescribed, but forgot to re-apply the appropriate mixture for takeoff (full in this case with a density altitude in the negatives). as the aircraft began to accelerate with the student's full application of power, the engine stuttered and stopped on the takeoff roll. i scanned the cockpit and noted the problem. i immediately felt a sinking feeling in my stomach, but was simultaneously struck with fear for how dangerous that situation could have been if we were off the ground. i notified other airplanes on the ctaf that we were stopped on the runway, re-started the engine and taxied off the runway. this event shook me up. as a new instructor, it was a wake up call that it is harder to diagnose issues without my hands on the controls. it was also a shock for how fast everything occurred. i have replayed the event many times in my mind and considered what i should have done differently. i am so thankful that we both walked away safely, and for the instructors that demonstrated aggressive lean procedures to me. this technique caused the engine to stop on the ground rather than in flight.contributing factors: as a new instructor i was undoubtedly focused on the new students performance during the takeoff. the previous mental space that i would have devoted to re-applying mixture was now distracted with my student. this inadvertently and unnecessarily lowered my situation awareness. another causing factor was lack of a final flow or adequate takeoff checklist before applying full power.correcting actions: a learning lesson for me from this was to always use the demonstrate / performance method. an external factor at play was me trying to make the introduction flight as fun as possible by letting the student takeoff. in retrospect, i should have simply let the student put his hands on the controls to feel the correct application. if i would have focused on the demonstrating the correct configuration, the next time the student would also have knowledge of the correct mixture configuration. additionally, my attention would be less on the students control inputs and more on an overall scan for improved safety. another learning lesson is two fold: 1) updating the takeoff checklist in the airplane to include mixture configuration (3rd party checklist and manufacturer's didn't include this). 2) performing a final takeoff flow in all airplanes to cover the most important items, especially ones like mixture that might have changed. for example, once on centerline, i will callout as i confirm: mixture set, props forward (if applicable), throttle forward. closing notes: this was a very humbling event for me. i feel thankful that nothing serious happened, and i hope to do the most learning i can do from this to prevent another occurrence like this from happening. i also hope that others can learn from my mistake. i apologized for/debriefed my mistake hope that it does not negatively influence his training.

synopsis: Public safety UAS pilot reported an NMAC with a public safety helicopter during a mission. Neither crew were informed the other would be operating at the same location. The UAS pilot landed the UAS after the NMAC as a precaution.
text: who: a public safety unmanned aircraft system and a responding public safety helicopter operating during a multi-agency incident. uas operations were already in progress under the existing incident command structure. a secondary command officer from an assisting agency independently requested the helicopter.what: a near midair conflict occurred when the helicopter entered the incident airspace below 400 feet agl without prior coordination. the uas was operating in an orbit around the incident at approximately 250 feet agl. the helicopter's initial pass appeared below 400 feet agl and likely below the uas altitude at the time of entry. the uas pilot visually identified the aircraft and initiated lateral and altitude deconfliction. during repositioning, return-to-home was initiated and the aircraft climbed toward a programmed rth altitude of approximately 397 feet agl. communication was then established and safe separation maintained.when: day 0 at approximately xa:08.where: rural uncontrolled airspace, outside controlled surface airspace. operations occurred below 400 feet agl within the incident footprint.why: the helicopter was requested and entered the incident airspace while uas operations were already underway. the responding aircraft was not advised of the active uas, and the request was made independently without coordination with command personnel managing uas operations. this resulted in simultaneous low-altitude operations without prior airspace coordination.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported multiple systems issues shortly after departure; including an unreliable air speed indication.
text: when departing redacted, we experienced an airspeed unreliable due to speed limitation followed by mach trim fail and auto slat fail. during the diversion planning phase, i was the pm. while trying to contact dispatch to coordinate diversion, i inadvertently caused a communications gap with air traffic control and had incomplete communication my dispatcher. only after we were on the the satcom system on the aircraft worked fine, but the operations phone would only ring for several calls without an answer. finally, on one call the dispatcher answered, but i only got a few words in before the call dropped. after the failed satcom attempts, i went to the call me" button on acars. the dispatcher messaged me to come up on the company x vhf frequency. when i dialed in the company x frequency on vhf2 (i thought it was vhf2), i was able to hear them but they couldn't hear me. this compounded the mess, as not only were we unable to communicate on vhf2, but a new distraction was normally. after arriving at the gate, i called the dispatcher by cellphone and learned that he couldn't hear any of my transmissions on the company x frequency (but i could hear him). at that point, i synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a ground conflict while on final approach with an aircraft on the runway. Pilot performed a go around.
text: i was conducting touch-and-go practice at ccr in aircraft x, visual flight rules in vmc. i was in contact with concord tower on 119.7.tower cleared me for the option on runway 19l. after completing the touch-and-go and climbing on the upwind leg of 19l, tower advised that winds had shifted and they were switching to runways 32l/r. they instructed me to turn left and join the left traffic pattern for runway 32l and cleared me for the option on 32l. i acknowledged 'cleared for the option 32l.'while on the base-to-final turn for 32l, i heard tower clear another aircraft for takeoff on runway 19l. the other pilot acknowledged the clearance. on short final for 32l, i observed the departing aircraft beginning its takeoff roll on the intersecting runway 19l. (xa:30) to avoid a potential collision at the intersection, i immediately initiated a go-around.tower then instructed me to 'continue downwind for 32l' and said they would call my base. i replied 'negative, i am on short final 32l, going around.' tower responded with 'sorry' and stated they 'did not see where i was.'after the go-around, i re-entered the left pattern for 32l and completed two uneventful touch-and-goes.later, while on the upwind from runway 32l, i heard a jet request landing on runway 1l and receive clearance to land on 1l. i offered to tower that i could switch my next touch-and-go to runway 1r to avoid being on an intersecting runway with the arriving jet. tower replied that it would not be necessary and instructed me to enter a right pattern for runway 32r.on downwind for 32r, abeam the numbers, tower instructed a short approach to 32r, then immediately said 'negative, that is not going to work' and directed me to make a left 360 for spacing. it appeared tower had not accounted for the proximity of the jet on final to 1l (intersecting runways). (xa:38)after completing the 360, i was cleared for the option on runway 1r as the jet landed on 1l. i completed the touch-and-go on 1r followed by a full-stop on 32r without further incident.contributing factors i observed: multiple rapid runway configuration changes, intersecting active runways (19/32 and 1/32), controller apparently losing situational awareness of my position twice, and instructions that created potential conflicts with departing and arriving traffic on intersecting runways. i had to initiate evasive action (go-around) on my own the first time, and the second event required an unplanned 360 due to spacing issues with the jet.

synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported a significant wind shear event during cruise resulting in a course deviation. Pilot corrected and continued flight.
text: during departure from gnv, i was cleared for takeoff from runway 7 and instructed to maintain runway heading to 3, 000 feet. tower also provided wind direction and velocity information. the takeoff was normal. at approximately 700-900 feet, i was instructed to contact jacksonville approach. i complied and continued the climb to 3, 000 feet as assigned, applying wind correction while operating in imc conditions.at approximately 2, 000 feet, i encountered a significant wind shear event which caused an abrupt lift of the left wing, resulting in a strong right bank. the combination of the bank angle and climb angle of attack brought the aircraft close to a stall condition due to increased stall speed at higher angles of attack.i immediately prioritized aircraft control (aviate), leveling the wings with left control input and reducing angle of attack to regain airspeed and prevent a stall. after regaining full control of the aircraft, i transitioned to navigation (navigate), where i verified heading, altitude, and vertical speed, and observed a deviation from the assigned runway heading. i initiated corrective action to return to the assigned heading.while correcting, jacksonville approach contacted me and inquired about the heading . i advised that the deviation was caused by wind shear. after a few minutes approach then issued new heading and altitude instructions, which i followed, and i continued the climb to the assigned altitude.

text: \while in holding south of chicago at roughly 12, 000 feet, developed severe icing in under 2 minutes cumulative time with all aircraft anti ice already on. asked air traffic control for lower to descend out of the severe. as the engines spooled up, received severe vibrations in air frame, 9.9 flashing on #2 engine n1. requested priority handling and requested lower altitudes to sublime or melt off the ice that the anti ice was not preventing. asked for a turn back to indianapolis. maintained engine #2 at idle as any spool up caused high engine and airframe vibrations. no ecams were present as it was an annunciated issue. notified dispatch accordingly. entered into vmc and landing in visual conditions to a straight in landing on 23r. only bringing thrust up on #2 engine as needed on short final. landed without incident. notified chief pilot and maintenance accordingly. #2 engine continued running the entire time and at no time did we secure the engine.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported the engine malfunctioned during a flight and was possibly flown without required maintenance inspections.
text: i was operating cessna 150. prior to the flight, my scheduled flights were canceled because the owner/operator stated that the aircraft needed a 100-hour inspection. based on that explanation, i understood that the aircraft would be unavailable until the required inspection was completed and the aircraft was confirmed airworthy.however, during the same weekend when i was told the aircraft would be down for the 100-hour inspection, the aircraft was operated for approximately 40 additional hours. this made me question whether the 100-hour inspection was actually performed at that time, whether it was properly completed before the aircraft was returned to service, or whether the aircraft was being operated beyond its inspection status. no clear maintenance log entry or inspection signoff was provided to me before i flew the aircraft.during the flight, the aircraft experienced an engine failure or serious engine malfunction involving a cylinder failure. i monitored the available engine instruments. oil pressure and oil temperature indications appeared normal, including after the event when troubleshooting was performed, and the engine was restarted, but only limited to 2100 rpm under full throttle. however, the aircraft's cylinder head temperature indication was not available to the pilot because the cht system had reportedly been disconnected. there was no clear cockpit indication available to me that would have warned of the developing cylinder problem.after the incident, i was informed that a mechanic had previously heard the aircraft backfire on the ground and attempted to stop it, but the aircraft was not stopped before the flight. this information was not communicated to me, the pilot, before departure. if i had been told that the aircraft had backfired or showed signs of abnormal engine operation, i would not have accepted or continued the flight without further maintenance inspection and written confirmation that the aircraft was airworthy.my safety concern is that the aircraft may have been released for flight even though the stated 100-hour inspection was not performed, not properly completed, or not properly communicated to the pilots. if the inspection had been performed correctly, the cylinder condition, compression, ignition system, spark plugs, and related engine components should have been checked before the aircraft was returned to service. the later cylinder failure and the report of prior backfiring raise concern that an existing mechanical issue may have been missed or not addressed.another safety concern is cockpit instrumentation and placarding. if an engine monitoring system, such as cht, is installed but disconnected, the pilot should have clear information on its status, including proper inop placarding if required. in this event, the normal oil pressure and oil temperature indications did not provide warning of the cylinder-related failure, and the unavailable cht indication reduced my ability as pilot to detect abnormal engine conditions before the failure became serious.in addition, the aircraft was operated under a dry lease structure, where operational control should rest with the renter. however, scheduling and maintenance availability were controlled by the owner/operator. my flights were canceled for the stated purpose of maintenance, but the aircraft was reportedly still operated by others during the same general period. this created confusion about who had operational control, whether the aircraft was actually down for inspection, and whether the aircraft had been properly inspected before being released.the main lesson from this event is that a pilot should not rely solely on verbal statements about maintenance status. any required inspection, especially a 100-hour inspection, should be clearly documented and communicated before the aircraft is returned to service. any reported engine abnormality, including backfire, rough running, abnormal sound, or suspected cylinder/ignition issue, should be immediately communicated to the pilot, documented as a discrepancy, inspected by qualified maintenance personnel, and resolved before further flight.in the future, i will personally request confirmation of the maintenance log after any major inspection or maintenance-related cancellation, verify the status of any inoperative instruments before accepting the aircraft, and decline the aircraft if there is any report of abnormal engine operation that has not been clearly inspected, documented, and resolved.to prevent recurrence, aircraft owners, lease operators, and maintenance personnel should establish a clear process that requires written confirmation when a required inspection is completed. aircraft should not be released for flight based only on verbal statements. any abnormal engine operation observed on the ground should be immediately communicated to the pilot and entered as a maintenance discrepancy. the aircraft should remain grounded until the discrepancy is inspected, corrected, and signed off by qualified maintenance personnel.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an NMAC during descent into LGA. Crew followed RA commands and flight continued normally.
text: while descending into lga we had a very close resolution advisory. we were level at 10, 000 feet at roughly 290 knots when air traffic control gave us a traffic advisory as well as a descent to 8, 000 feet. captain was pf and immediately began slowing to 250knots in order to go below 10, 000. maybe two seconds after the air traffic control communication we were notified of traffic on the pfd (primary flight display) immediately followed by the resolution advisory. i quickly notified air traffic control that we were responding while i was looking for traffic. captain did a great job following the resolution advisory and making prompt control inputs. if i remember correctly that aircraft was within 300 feet of us and i was never able to make visual contract. we also accelerated over 260 knots while executing the descent resolution advisory. after completion, i notified air traffic control and asked if they still wanted the descent to 8, 000 which they did and the flight continued normally.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude
synopsis: GA pilot reported a loss of separation with traffic during takeoff. Pilot momentarily leveled off then continued climb.
text: i was flying aircraft x on a practice approach into chs (vor 21) and had been cleared for the option for runway 21. i had a view limiting device on until approach minimums (440 ft) but was flying with an instructor acting as a safety pilot. upon reaching minimums i removed the view limiting device and executed a touch a go landing. shortly after rotation at roughly 100-200 ft agl, i spotted aircraft y on the southeast side of runway 21 at approximately 400-500agl. when i initially made visual contact with aircraft y it was on a course to cross the runway directly in front of our path of flight. i immediately leveled off to avoid further loss of separation and at about this time contacted tower to advise them that aircraft y was overflying the runway. i received no response to this radio call and continued to visually avoid aircraft y. aircraft y passed across the centerline of runway 21 and i subsequently began to reestablish a climb and once again contacted tower to advise of the near miss. the tower controller then told aircraft y that they 'were supposed to remain south of 21'. upon hearing this, aircraft y began to turn back towards runway 21 (and our flight path) to cross back over to the south side. we once again had minimal separation as aircraft y flew directly in front of us a second time to return to the south side of the runway. after aircraft y transitioned to the south side of the runway no further loss of separation occurred and we returned to our original point of departure uneventfully.at no point before, during, or after the incident were we advised of any helicopter traffic to be aware of nor did the controller seem to realize aircraft y's error until well after our first report of the loss of separation.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier FO reported a rejected takeoff was caused by another aircraft crossing the active runway.
text: got to the airplane about an hour before a scheduled departure and maintenance was on board fixing a problem with our elevator aileron computer (elac) system. this caused a delay of about an hour. flight was not very full but we were boarded up and had to stay at the gate until maintenance finished their job and paperwork was signed. we eventually pushed back and everything was normal. 2 engine taxi out to runway xxr for departure. there were 2 other planes waiting at the end to takeoff but we were given a takeoff clearance by tower since they were waiting for en-trail spacing. i remember thinking that our takeoff clearance was given a little early, as we were still probably 500'-800' or so from the end of the runway. ca was pf and i was pm on this leg, our first flight together. ca pushed the throttles up and we began the takeoff roll. everything was normal up until about the 50-65kt range when the takeoff hold lights suddenly changed from green to red. at this point i was looking at the engine pages but i remember seeing the change from green to red happen out of my peripheral vision. i also remember looking down the runway and even though it was dark, i saw an airplane crossing downfield. the captain immediately used max braking to slowed the plane to a stop. we skidded a little bit due to the wet runway. he set the parking brake and made a pa in the back. at the same time, i advised redacted tower that we were aborting the takeoff on the runway. they seemed a little confused but one thing that stuck with me is that they never asked us why we discontinued the takeoff. i asked tower to roll the fire trucks in case our brakes were hot or locked up or there was any other outside damage they were able to see. we were able to taxi so we decided to turn off the runway on an upcoming taxiway and that's where airport rescue and firefighting met us. they could see no such damage and our brakes were not on fire or anything like that. we sat on the taxiway for a while to gather ourselves and to run appropriate checklists. we decided that it was best to go back to the gate because we were getting close to our min fuel for takeoff and we also wanted maintenance to do a quick inspection of the plane in case one of the wheels locked up since we skidded during the abort. we taxied back to the gate without issue and myself and the captain walked up to the terminal to debrief what had happened.in my opinion, there needs to be better communication between controllers and pilots. i'm still not sure if this was a case where redacted ground cleared a plane to cross xxr while redacted tower cleared us for takeoff, or if the crossing plane did so without a clearance, or what exactly happened. it was very strange (in my opinion) for tower not to ask us a reason for the abort. they never recognized the reason why we had to abort the takeoff or maybe they did and said nothing about it. either way, there was a massive communication breakdown between ground, tower, us, and another aircraft.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A ZAB Center Controller reported an aircraft reported an NMAC with an unmanned non-transponder equipped balloon.
text: i was working sector 79 to provide relief to sector 94's higher volume. during this session, aircraft x reported seeing what they believed to be a balloon at 'eye level' with their aircraft, estimated 100-200 ft off their left wing (est at oto165018). i immediately notified the supervisor, who then went to a few of the different balloon tracking websites available. the supervisor did have paperwork on a balloon, but it was never made clear whether the balloon launched or not. the balloon did not have a transponder on it. at the time of the incident, the supervisor found on the tracker website that the balloon was estimated well above fl410 (estimated around fl700), and a bit further north than where the report was made. aircraft x also made it seem like the balloon was unusually small for being at that altitude, so it may not have been the same balloon/object that was known and being tracked. i made the announcement over frequency regarding the unmanned derelict balloon, and made it known more specifically to some aircraft nearby at varying altitudes (fl380, fl400, and another one further north at fl410) and no other aircraft was able to identify/spot the balloon. aircraft x wasn't able to tell if the object/balloon was in a climb or a descent as they just caught it out of their peripheral. the aircraft and pilots were unharmed, and they requested an estimated location of the event for their reporting as well.i have heard it suggested several times, and agree, that any balloon that is being knowingly launched into class a airspace needs to have a transponder attached so that we can more accurately know its location and altitude. it's incredibly unsafe to have something climbing uncontrolled/untracked through controlled airspace that could cause an accident should it get draped over a windshield/engine/control surface etc. i don't think balloons should be allowed to be launched without a transponder, period.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported loss of hydraulic system during approach. Crew landed without incident and taxied to the gate.
text: working to redacted. once we joined downwind for runway xxl at redacted, we're assigned a speed reduction from 210 kias to 180 kias. i called for flaps 5. shortly after this speed reduction and configuration changed we noticed a hyd master caution followed by an uncommanded autopilot disengage. i was pilot flying so i continued to fly the plane. my captain requested priority handling and ran the non normal checklist. we let company, fas, and passengers know about the issue and delay. captain took the landing. we landed uneventfully on xyc redacted.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported windshear encounter during landing. Crew initiated missed approach and returned for an uneventful landing.
text: i was the pilot flying on flight to lbb.the flight and approach to landing on runway 26 in lbb were all standard and normal. atis was reporting gusty winds about 25-35 kts. right down the runway and low level wind shear advisories.we briefed the go-around procedure in case we did get a wind shear advisory.the weather for lbb was reporting visual flight rules.i turned the autopilot off around 200 ft above the minimums. at approximately 200-300 agl we received a wind shear warning. i called for a go around and pushed the thrust levers forward and pitched up for the recovery.i initially pushed the auto throttle button when i pushed the thrust levers forward on the go around. while the plane was climbing i realized i hadn't pushed the toga button so i did, and at the same time while i was doing that my first officer said push the toga button.tower instructed us to climb runway heading to 5000 ft.during the climb out around 1200 ft the airspeed got slow and the shaker went off. i lowered the nose and my first officer assisted in pushing the thrust levers forward.after we recovered, the first officer re-engaged the auto throttle and engaged the autopilot. we climbed to 5000ft and cleaned up the aircraft. we got vectored back around for runway 26.we landed uneventfully with no further encounters of wind shear.suggestions: i should of had my finger on the toga button.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Undershoot; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an autopilot degradation during the climb in IMC conditions; resulting in a loss of airspeed and high pitch attitude. The Captain took control; stabilized the aircraft; then continued the flight.
text: i was the pilot monitoring for this flight. toward the end of the climbout of redacted, somewhere above 2000 feet, flaps had been retracted on schedule and we were climbing at 240 kias. weather was imc. i was prompted to switch to departure, then we were given direct to redacted [vor]. i was about to call '3000 feet' and prompt for the after takeoff when this occurred. after i had got confirmation and executed the direct, my first officer said something about the autopilot being degraded. i then looked at the flight mode annunciator (fma) and saw 'alt hold' with an amber line through it indicating a degraded vertical mode, then noticed our airspeed was quickly rolling below 200 kts and nearing 180 kts. we were in the amber airspeed band with the performance limiting indicator (pli) visible. there was a startle effect and a moment of disbelief or confusion in what i was seeing, but i called out the speed, and prompted the first officer to accelerate as the pli was floating near the limit. i remember saying something like 'lower the nose'. when the pli contacted, i called 'stall' took control, and rolled wings level to initiate the recovery. it took a few seconds for me to realize we were not accelerating at which point i realized i was unconsciously working against the auto throttle at which point i pushed the throttles all the way forward and clicked the autothrottles off. the aircraft began accelerating, the descent arrested and began climbing. during this i also had to tell air traffic control we were responding to a situation and we'd get back to them. they gave us a vector to 270 and to advise them when everything was okay. airspeed reached approximately 270 kts as we were climbing again where i started to easy the climb and the airspeed to re-automate. i called for autopilot center command, and once it engaged it resumed the turn to the heading we had been assigned (270). however we immediately got a 'bank angle' aural alert, which confused us because although the autopilot was banking slightly beyond the flight director, the angle was not any higher than 25 degrees while at about 240 knots. nevertheless, i disconnected the automation again, eased the bank and hand flew with the autothrottles engaged at 240 kts. once rolled onto our heading of 270 and steadily climbing to our altitude (we had gotten 7000 and then 11000 assigned during this), i called for the autopilot again, and then never had another issue. i asked the first officer if they were ready to retake the controls, and they took over just before 10, 000. we then accomplished the after takeoff checklist. i did not notice at what point we went into altitude capture, when the vertical mode degraded, or when airspeed began rolling back as i was in the middle of air traffic control responses etc as is typical for this phase of flight. the events all happened very quickly. i only remember seeing the degraded mode, and then the pitch and airspeed which i was immediately fixated on along with the vsi and the altitude, the usual instrument scan. automation modes were secondary to me at the time as they were being disconnected. i did not think to reset flight directors or try other autopilots since i was focused on the recovery and keeping the plane flying. we descended about 700' during recovery starting from about 3700' regaining altitude at about 3000' and climbing. we talk about, and practice upset recovery in every sim session. we talk about startle effect in crm every year and in sims. we are trained to expect the unexpected, but it's not until it happens to you in the real environment where you fully realize the effect it has on you.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: GA pilot reported a main gear tire failure as power was applied for takeoff. The aircraft stopped and communicated with airport operations.
text: i was flying with a friend, he is a private pilot and was acting as pilot in command. we were holding short awaiting departure. after receiving takeoff clearance, power was increased only slightly--just enough to start the aircraft rolling. within only a few feet of movement, before any substantial takeoff roll had developed, the left main wheel assembly separated. from an initial visual look, the hardware appeared to still be in place, and the condition seemed consistent with a wheel/rim-related failure. the aircraft was stopped immediately. tower was notified of aborted takeoff and we maintained communication until airport ops was on sight and avionics shutdown was approved as requested.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Eclipse 550 pilot reported several autopilot and FMS failures resulted in momentary loss of control with uncommanded altitude changes and drifting.
text: i was flying my personal airplane to redacted for repair of intermittent right engine not starting issue and occasional auto pilot disconnects. during the flight at flight level 390 while in cruise with a 75 kt tail wind, the auto pilot suddenly disconnected. the airplane immediately started to drift and climb. the flight management system also disconnected and i lost the flight command level bars, i manually took control of the side stick and tried to reengage the autopilot with no success, i was successful in engaging the flight management system system, and the flight bars returned, i immediately leveled the wings and stabilized the attitude, during this 30 second or so the airplane climbed approximately 500 to 700 feet. i stopped the climb and arrested the sudden climb and immediately started to descend at the same time that air traffic control called and asked me what the problem was and i told them i had an auto pilot failure and they said to immediately turn 40° to the left and descend to 390 which i immediately complied. my copilot pulled the qrh manual and looked up the procedure for auto pilot failure and i flew the airplane manually while he troubleshot the issue. he continually tried to turn the autopilot on and within a few minutes it reengaged. along the route we had 3 other similar disengagements but did not have a severe up draft and altitude issue. i was able to immediately engage the flight management system and fly the command bars and keep the altitude and track constant, especially after the first unexpected incident, i was prepared for this potential issue. the auto pilot disconnected one more of the times while in rvsm airspace but it reconnected fairly quickly so i continued the flight in rvsm. it disconnected several more times below rvsm on the way to redacted. the airplane is at the service center currently, i spent time with maintenance going over the issues. i also downloaded the computer data storage unit (dsu) of the flight and gave it to maintenance dsu so they could trace the cause of the autopilot failures.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: B737 First Officer reported a loss of engine oil pressure caused by a tail pipe fire during taxi in. Flight crew shut down engine and parked normally.
text: on the ground taxi in we lost oil pressure in the number 2 engine. ca called for the engine to be shut down. on the taxi in we noticed smoke, but had no indication of fire. we parked and maintenance came aboard and explained we had a tailpipe fire

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Jet Blast; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported receiving a sink rate" warning after encountering wake turbulence from an A330 that was taking off from SAN."
text: we were on rnav z approach for runway 27 into san. tower cleared airbus 330 for takeoff as we were less than two miles from the runway and told us caution wake turbulence." we had reviewed the bulletin and briefed that a go-around would be mandatory in case the "sink rate" aural warning activated. we were also landing with flaps 40 and following vnav guidance all the way down.we were at approximately 200 feet when i started to feel the wake from the a330 that was taking off. i adjusted the path and heard the "sink rate" aural warning. the first officer called for a go-around, and i looked at the heavy and thought it was too close and doing a go-around would cause us to encounter significant wake turbulence. i practiced my best judgement and said "we are landing." i also didn't think that we were unstable or too high."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: ERJ 145 flight crew reported a loss of Hydraulic System 1 during taxi in and elected to be towed to the gate versus using differential braking as per the checklist.
text: after landing at redacted on aircraft x, we received taxi instructions to proceed via taxiway 1, 2, 3, and 4 to gate xx. we turned off engine no. 1 after 2 minutes and continued taxi on a single engine.as we approached the turn from taxiway 1 onto taxiway 2, the eicas displayed a hyd 1 fail message. this was followed by rudder sys 1-2 inop, ail sys 1-2 inop, and steer inop indications. upon recognizing the messages, we stopped the aircraft and advised ground that we needed time to accomplish the checklist due to a maintenance issue.the captain and i reviewed the qrh and confirmed that the procedure called for directional control using differential braking. after evaluating the situation, we determined that towing the aircraft to the gate would be the safest course of action.while i handled radio communications and coordination with air traffic control and airport personnel, the captain kept the flight attendants and passengers informed of the situation and provided updates as needed. airport operations coordinated for a tug to respond, and once it arrived, we accomplished the tow in accordance with the aom gate tow-in procedure. the aircraft was then safely towed to the gate without further incident.suggestions: crew coordination and communication were effective throughout the event. given the loss of hydraulic system 1, the decision to discontinue taxi and request a tow helped reduce operational risk and ensured a safe arrival at the gate. continued emphasis on prompt checklist use, clear crm, and conservative decision-making during abnormal ground operations would be beneficial.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that during taxi; they had to take evasive action to prevent a collision with another aircraft that turned onto the wrong taxiway.
text: during taxi in, we were on d taxiway and cleared to the gate via c5 after aircraft y that was passing us on c and remaining on c until c7. aircraft y however, incorrectly turned on c5 requiring us to slow to avoid a collision. air traffic control told aircraft y they turned on c5 (the wrong taxiway) and to get back on d taxiway. cause: i slowed to have traffic in sight prior to beginning the turn and also in case they created a issue (which they did). there was enough room to avoid contact.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: ERJ 145 First Officer reported an EICAS failure that resulted in a rejected takeoff.
text: on take off roll runway xx the eicas went completely blank after 80knts but prior to v1(132). i believe the speed was 120knts. the take off was rejected by the captain, and captain took controls. cleared the runway taxied off and ran appropriate checklist, and called appropriate people (maintenance/dispatch/crew scheduling). we returned to gate and maintenance came.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: A330F flight crew reported burning acrid smell resulted in crew illness and divert to a safe landing.
text: reaching cruise on flight abcd enroute to redacted, the captain and i became aware of a burnt plastic/acrid smell in the courier compartment. after conferring with duty officer, dispatch and maintenance, we as the crew decided to air return out of precaution. later, while holding to burn off fuel to get under max landing weight, we noticed that the smell was bit of a dirty sock smell and we both felt light-headed at various points of exposure. we then noticed the severity of the incident, we donned our oxygen masks, requested priority handling and performed the smoke/fumes removal procedure in the qrh.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: B737 Captain reported #2 engine low oil pressure and low oil quantity after landing. Flight taxied to gate and deplaned.
text: as we were rolling out on the final landing of the day and exiting the runway, the first officer and i were alerted by the low oil pressure" annunciation on the upper engine panel with all three yellow annunciators blinking. after looking down at the lower engine panel, we both noticed the oil quantity very low and the oil pressure very low. the oil quantity was eventually replaced with a "lo" annunciation, and the oil pressure was outlined with a red box and read 7 psi. at that moment, we had already started the apu and decided to immediately shut down the engine. the relief pilot referenced the low oil pressure qrh, but there was no further guidance in that checklist other than to reference the "engine failure or shut down" checklist. all steps were already accomplished in the "engine fire or failure shut down" checklist for the conditions of the flight. as we taxied into parking spot, i noticed a large amount of smoke coming from behind our plane. i directed the first officer to call operations to see if we could have anyone do a visual inspection of our aircraft. the ground crew was already in place, and they marshaled us into parking where we set the brakes and shut down the remaining motor uneventfully. the maintenance representative came on board and told us that he saw a tailpipe fire as we were taxiing with a lot of oil underneath the number two engine on the ramp. we both concluded it was the oil that was dripping on the hot engine and exhaust area that caused the smoke and tail pipe fire. we had no indications of any type of fire or high egt inside of the aircraft since the tailpipe fire was outside of the internal core of the engine. the maintenance representative left and returned telling us that the fire had reignited and he wanted to get everyone off of the aircraft quickly. we were already in the process of deplaning the aircraft, but i made an announcement over the pa that we had smoked coming from the right side of the aircraft and we needed to expedite the disembarking of the aircraft. all passengers exited through the primary door attached to the jet bridge without incident. after all of the passengers had deplaned, i, along with the purser, exited the aircraft. i was unable to enter a logbook entry through my ipad because more than 10 minutes had elapsed since the flight closed out, so i contacted maintenance control and explained the situation and he said that he would enter the write up into the logbook."

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier captain reported during taxi they took evasive action to avoid a collision with a vehicle that failed to stop and yield for them.
text: after pushing back from gate x, we were getting ready to taxi out towards the north line at the gates. the pushback crew put us at a standard 45 degree angle. we started engine #2 and configured for a standard single engine taxi. after completing the after start checklist, scanning for traffic, and turning on our taxi lights, we commenced our taxi with a right hand turn (towards the operating engine) towards the north line. due to the adverse yaw, forward momentum was required to make the right turn. as the airplane moved forward and i began my right turn, a baggage truck with two individuals came from my left side and failed to stop. i abruptly brought the plane to a stop to avoid contact with the ground personnel. the cart identifier was noticed and this happened at around xa:15 local time. after watching the baggage cart drive away, i cleared for traffic and commenced (again) the process of inching forward to gain momentum to make my right turn. since i had already moved forward a few feet, my left wing encroached the service road as i made the right turn. as i completed the right turn, i observed a catering truck driving on the service road towards my wingtip, again, without stopping. i began to bring the airplane to a stop and observed the truck completely go off the service road to avoid my wingtip. even with all my lights on, not a single car / truck stopped to give way. as we taxied north, i observed another aircraft that had just pushed back from gate y make the right turn towards the north line. even without inching forward much, their left wing tip encroached, although slightly, the service road. i observed multiple catering trucks drive around the service road instead of stopping and waiting for the aircraft to exit. this is an incredibly unsafe situation that apparently has become normal practice for the ground handlers to drive in such a careless way in one of the most congested ramp areas in the world.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a baggage cart tug stopped beyond their clearance point requiring flight crew to stop suddenly to avoid a potential collision.
text: while taxiing i toward the ramp on taxiway b, a tug driver pulling two luggage carts stopped on a crossing service road far past the stop sign causing the captain to stop the aircraft suddenly to avoid a potential collision with our wing tip. when we informed ground control, the controller issued instructions that i understood to mean to give way to aircraft y if we were going to be stuck and aircraft y taxied in across our path. we decided to slowly proceed and slightly depart the taxi centerline to ensure clearance from the cart. aircraft y didn't move but as we taxied past aircraft z reported that we did not properly yield to them. we understood the yield was conditional and in reference to aircraft y, so we proceeded.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported ATC handling led to unstable approach which resulted in low altitude alert while regaining glide slope.
text: during visual approach to sfo 28 r we were held high 3000ft and 190 knots till the bay bridge. we asked multiple times for descent but told to maintain 3000/190. finally they cleared us for the approach right at the san mateo bridge, normal crossing altitude is about 1800 and 180 knots. we had the gear down and began slowing and descending as quickly as possible. just prior to 1000ft tower called aircraft x altitude alert, altimeter 30.13" as we were descending and slowing. passing 1000 feet we had flaps 25, planning for 30 so i said "set missed approach altitude, not cleared for approach, final flaps to go". we then set final flaps and were on speed, landing check complete by 500 ft. then an uneventful smooth landing. as we talked and debriefed on the ground we can only assume the altitude alert call was because of higher than normal descent rate to capture the glide slope."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Citation Longitude flight crew reported a GPWS alert on approach.
text: on the visual approach to xxl at redacted, we received a gpws warning to pull up. it was clear and a million and we were vmc for the entirety of the flight. we were given vectors and told to square the base turn. the airplane was fully configured and we were above the glide path on the company visual which was loaded in the box. in the descent on the base leg we received a pull up" and i shallowed the descent. the warning disappeared immediately, we were well above terrain, and we were still in a normal position to land. the approach was continued to a landing.suggestions: make the gpws less sensitive in this area."

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Fractional flight crew reported receiving an aural taxiway notification during takeoff and later noticed the small yellow chevrons that were impossible to see from the hold-short area of the runway at MTN airport.
text: departing runway 15 at martin state airport. given takeoff clearance after holding short of runway for several minutes. after lining up and confirming runway, controls were handed to sic and i was pilot monitoring. upon sic applying power we received aural taxiway" notification while accelerating. power was instantly pulled back instinctually but we thought the warning was in error because we thought the runway was simply displaced for landing operations. we did not see any sort of large yellow chevron markings indicating that we were on a taxi only portion of the runway surface before reaching the runway threshold. air traffic control had not given us any sort of instruction to taxi forward and then depart either. we did not want to remain on an active runway longer than was necessary or cause a timing or separation problem for the tower controller so elected to continue takeoff. as we later approached what we thought was the displaced threshold for landing only, not takeoff, we did see small yellow chevrons which were impossible to see from where we were previously holding short of the runway. remainder of the takeoff, departure and flight was normal after that.i would suggest better markings or signage at martin state airport. have large yellow chevrons painted on the taxiway portion leading to the threshold or a sign indicating the nonstandard displaced threshold that can give pilots a heads-up while they hold short of the runway. i also don't recall seeing any sort of hotspot circle in that area on the jeppesen airport diagram. a notation on the company flight planning brief or notation in the flight release package from dispatch would also be helpful. i would think this is a relatively common mistake made at this airport and that it could be better addressed and mitigated."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Challenger 350 flight crew reported a possible compressor stall during the initial climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and landed safely.
text: during takeoff, at about 400' agl, both crew members observed 3 loud bangs" and a momentary yaw of the aircraft. the event occurred just as the landing gear was in transition, leading both crew members to assume it was a landing gear malfunction. after requesting a heading and altitude, the crew accomplished a cycle of the landing gear malfunction the landing gear cycled without issue. both crew members then deduced that it was possibly a compressor stall. a phone call was placed to the chief pilot and a collective decision was made to return to redacted. there were no passengers onboard. a successful instrument landing system approach and landing was conducted to runway xxl in visual conditions. upon exiting the aircraft, line personnel stated that they observed the audible "bangs" from the ramp. after a post flight inspection by both crew members, there appeared to be no visual evidence of bird strikes, or any other fod damage to the airframe or power plants."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 Captain reported loss of 'B' hydraulic system while on approach.  Crew continued to landing.
text: our flight from redacted to redacted was uneventful until we started our approach. the first officer and i planned and briefed our approach to runway xxr. when we got handed over to redacted approach, we were advised to expect runway xyr. after a runway change and new briefing, we completed the before landing checklist to the line. shortly after we were instructed to descend to 4000 feet and fly direct to redacted to intercept the xyr localizer. we were instructed to cross redacted at 4, 000 feet and cleared for the instrument landing system. at 4, 000 feet, i selected lnav/vnav and closed the speed window to engage vnav pth but remained in vnav spd. approach instructed us to reduce speed to 170 knots. i opened the speed window to reduce speed. while slowing down, i requested flaps 1, vnav pth engaged and i selected 2, 300 feet for the faf altitude. at this point, the master caution light illuminated, extinguished and then illuminated again, we saw the hyd light illuminate of the right annunciator panel. the aircraft had already started a descent on the approach path but no more that 100 to 200 feet, we requested to abandon the approach and maintain 4, 000 feet as well as a vector to the right. autopilot was disengaged momentarily and then re-engaged when established on an altitude and heading. we selected the systems page on the lower du (display unit), at this time we noticed that the hydraulic quantity was zero and we had lost pressure in hydraulic system b. at this time the low-pressure lights on the overhead panel also illuminated. i declared my aircraft and communications and requested the loss of system b qrh procedure. while completing the qrh procedure, we noticed the flap indicator needle was between the flaps up and flaps 1 position. we requested priority handling with air traffic control and advised them of the aircraft status and intentions, we requested arff (airport rescue and firefighting) shortly after.we completed the qrh procedure, i then transferred control and communications to the first officer, i proceeded to complete the non-normal landing considerations procedure contacting dispatch and maintenance control and informing our cabin crew and our passengers of the current situation. air traffic control advised us to expect the instrument landing system to runway xxl, we selected and briefed the new approach. air traffic control vectored us for the approach, we lowered the gear and landing flaps while on base leg and completed the before landing checklist.our landing on runway xxl was normal, we vacated the runway and were able to vacate to the left and stopped on taxiway 1. we asked fire command to inspect the aircraft exterior and were informed of smoke coming from the right landing gear but did not detect excessive temperatures with their thermal imaging. arff requested we shut down the right engine which we did after the 3-minute cool down period, at which time they advised smoke was no longer detected. we decided to continue our taxi to our assigned gate as we were confident in our ability to stop the aircraft normally. even though we had no issues stopping the aircraft, we requested to stop on the ramp short of the gate area and have the aircraft towed to our parking position. after parking, we completed the shutdown checklist, completed the logbook and our maintenance team took over the aircraft.cause: mechanical failure of the onboard hydraulic system. i believe the airlines training for non-normal procedures was evident in this situation. a recommendation for myself as a new captain was to have let the first officer fly the aircraft and communicate and i complete the qrh procedures.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter FOD
synopsis: B737-800 pilot reported a thud sound after landing while taxiing to the gate; then the aircraft stopped short of the gate without braking. After shutdown an inspection discovered one main tire shredded with rubber pieces in the tire area and damage to the wing fairing.
text: normal takeoff, cruise and approach. no anomalies and completely routine. rnav xx. normal touchdown and roll out. taxi off runway on taxiway 1, joined taxiway 2 east bound. ground advised taxiway 2 to right on taxiway 3 to taxi to gate xx. upon turning onto taxiway 3 we heard a faint thud. i suspected a *single* tire failure. the gate was approximately 200 yards away. as we approached the gate we noticed the airplane seemed a little tilted to the left. following the marshallers commands, i got the takeoff config warning inadvertently. i immediately pulled the engines back to 40% n1. at 40% n1 the aircraft came to a stop on its own without brakes. completed the shutdown checklist. the jet bridge could not reach the airplane. once stairs were placed, i went outside to find the number 2 main was shredded and the number 1 tire was off the rim bead. once passengers deplaned a visual inspection found multiple tire marks on the top of the engine cowl, under wing, flaps, fuselage, gear arm and elevator. pieces of rubber were found inside the fuselage wheel well area. a hole around 5 inches was found in the rear wing fairing. closer inspection found the trailing edge of the flap to be cracked at a stringer. during a conversation with company officials, i recommended a runway inspection of xxl in redacted. remains of a tire were found mid field on runway xxl in redacted at the approximate rotation point. i suspect this tire failed at rotation although there were no indications to the flight attendants or flight crew. the fact that a large tire mark was found on the top of the left engine cowl near the inlet this event could have played out very differently. i suspect the number 1 tire was the only wheel doing the braking on the left side during landing and the blow out plugs popped due to overheating on the taxi in on the remaining tire. cause: better tires.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 MAX 9 flight crew reported a takeoff configuration warning during initial take off. Takeoff was rejected and flight returned to the gate.
text: we had a normal departure from the gate and a normal taxi out to runway xxl. when it came time to do the before takeoff final items checklist i tested the takeoff warning horn by advancing both throttles individually. our aircraft did not have a takeoff warning horn button to test it. when i advanced both throttles individually the takeoff warning horn did not sound. my first officer tested the master caution system during his flow and we did not have any caution lights stay illuminated.we were cleared for takeoff off runway xxl. i advanced the throttles to approximately 40 % and let the engines stabilize. as soon as i started advancing the throttles again toward the takeoff setting the takeoff waning horn sounded. i immediately said reject and reduced the throttles to idle. we did not get above 30 knots. i estimated it was about 20 knots. my first officer informed the tower and we exited the runway at taxiway 1. this was more of a discontinued takeoff at a normal taxi speed.we had a master caution light and two door lights on the overhead were illuminated. the left fwd overwing and left aft overwing both were illuminated.we exited the runway and came to a stop on taxiway 1. my first officer informed tower that we were addressing a maintenance issue. i made an announcement to the passengers that we had to exit the runway to address a maintenance issue and that i would give them more information when i could.my first officer ran the rejected takeoff checklist as i followed along. we then ran the abnormal checklist for the overwing exit lights illuminated. then with the parking brake set i called dispatch on my phone and explained to him what happened and asked for a conference call with maintenance control. maintenance control came on the line and i explained to him what happened and what we had. he informed me we would have to return to a gate and he would advised station maintenance. i asked the dispatcher to inform the station that we would be a gate return and he said he would. i informed my first officer and then i called my purser and informed them. i then made a pa to the passengers and told them i had some unfortunate news and that we needed to return to the gate and have maintenance address the issue and that i would have more information for them when we got back to a gate. we coordinated with station ops and we returned to gate xx. station maintenance came on board and we briefed them on what happened. i entered two separate elb (electronic log book) entries, one for each overwing door light, and informed station maintenance over the radio. i then made a pa and informed the passengers and gave them an explanation of what happened.maintenance informed us that they found a servo that was malfunctioning that would need to be replaced and gave us a time estimate of over an hour and once they replaced the servo they would need to pressurize the aircraft. i informed the gate agent of this information and we both agreed to deplaned the passengers. after the passengers deplaned i called the chief pilot on the phone and briefed them of what happened. i then debriefed my entire crew in first class before we left the aircraft. they found us a new aircraft to take to redacted. the aircraft this event happened in was a b737 max 9.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reported severe turbulence in cruise resulted in temporary loss of aircraft control.
text: redacted-redacted flight, i was flying as pf. while cruising at fl350, after returning from a bathroom break, the captain briefed me on any changes. he was currently on heading mode deviating to the left from a vertical developed cloud after requesting and receiving authorization from air traffic control to do so. we accomplished positive exchange of controls. the captain made a pa telling the flight attendants to take their seats. a few moments later, we started hitting turbulence while flying to the left of the cloud. i had my hands on the thrust levers and yoke ready to take over. as the turbulence became severe, the ca told me to hand fly, because ap would most likely disengage. at this point, the turbulence was severe. my focus, as discussed with the ca, was to try my best to maintain wings level and control over aircraft. we caught a strong updraft and hit fl356. once the turbulence became less, as i was recovering to initial heading and altitude, air traffic control called us that he saw us 600ft above our altitude. captain answered, explained we hit severe turbulence and were unable to maintain heading or altitude, but were already out of that area and correcting. air traffic control didn't say anything else about it. we reengaged the ap once conditions no longer showed any turbulence. ca called the flights attendants, who notified us that everyone in the back was ok with no injuries. cause: squall line passing by redacted. our route took us south, then west before heading back toward redacted. we were monitoring radar, but had a lot of distance from any thunderstorm cells. cause of severe turbulence was the vertical build up that we were deviating from.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported ground spoiler and anti skid caution messages after take off. Flight crew returned to departure airport.
text: aircraft x conducted an air return due to a maintenance issue on day 0 during a a planned redacted-redacted flight.immediately after takeoff the ib gnd spoiler fault status message and the a/skid inbd caution message posted. the crew ran the qrh which required an additional 110% addition to the actual landing distance, leading to a requirement for >7, 000ft against redacted runway xx available runway length.after communicating with dispatch a joint decision to return to redacted was made, due to poor weather in redacted and good, long runways and maintenance available in redacted.air return was initiated with air traffic control center, and aircraft returned to redacted successfully.crew did not declare an emergency, but air traffic control ensured fire trucks were available near the landing runway on our arrival. after a safe, normal landing the fire crew returned to station without being needed.cause: air return required per qrh procedure due to lack of available runway distance at redacted with a/skid inbd caution. required>7000ft vs max 6549ft available.joint decision made with dispatch to air return to redacted.caused by aircraft system malfunction, and qrh procedures as well as poor weather in redacted (wet runways increased required landing distance, and low ceilings due to stationary front).suggestions: this was in response to an eicas message and qrh procedure. no maintenance mels were active prior to the flight.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Citation Longitude Aircraft Maintenance Technician reported that during installation of an engine fuel nozzle; they inadvertently damaged the nozzle due to the burner can boss being misaligned.
text: during installation of the rh engine upper outboard start fuel nozzle, the new nozzle assembly was damaged. during installation of the new nozzle the mounting ears of the nozzle got bent due to an unseen misalignment of the nozzle. it was found that either during removal of the old nozzle or during insertion of the new one that there is a tapered boss on the burner can internal to the engine that floats in a flange, this boss was shifted and causing the new nozzle to not correctly engage into the engine. from the aft edge that is visible the nozzle was sitting flush with the engine case but it was lifted on the backside (fwd) edge where you couldn't see without a mirror. the mounting nuts were run down and damaged the mount ears of the new nozzle during this process. no damage occurred to the engine mounting boss. the nozzle was removed and after researching found that the floating tapered boss can be moved back into position and another replacement fuel nozzle was inserted without issue.suggestions: add a warning note in the mx (maintenance) manual to notate that the internal alignment of the floating tapered burner can boss can be moved if pushed on during removal/install causing the reinstallation of the nozzle to not align in its bore correctly. suggest a process to realign the tapered boss if it inadvertently gets shifted.

text: filed an instrument flight rules instructional flight from redacted to redacted. after completing the second approach and landing without issue, the engine shut down during the landing roll on the runway (runway xx). i verified mixture and fuel pump and concluded they were in the right position as set during the pre-landing checklist. the throttle was in the idle position. while still rolling on the runway, i advised redacted tower of the engine shutdown. once we stopped on the runway, we restarted the engine successfully. tower instructed us to exit via taxiway 1 and contact ground.on taxiway 2, ground requested details, and we reported the incident. taxi to the hangar was completed without further issues. upon arrival, we notified the aircraft owner, and the aircraft was placed in maintenance status pending inspection.additional details:fuel on departure - 17 gallons left tank / 16 gallons right tank - total 33 gallons estimatedflight duration - 1.2 hours departing tank - left tank landing tank - right tank weather conditions - instrument flight rules

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported poor climb performance and stall warning during take off. Pilot rejected take off.
text: on day 0, at approximately xa:20, i was pilot in command of aircraft x, a cessna 172s nav iii, departing runway xxr at redacted on a personal flight with one passenger. i hold a private pilot certificate, asel, with approximately 163.5 total flight hours, all in cessna 172 aircraft, and 16.6 hours in the preceding 90 days. i was well-rested, of sound mind, and had completed the imsafe checklist prior to flight with no concerns. no hazardous attitudes were recognized.the aircraft was rented from the fbo at redacted. prior to flight, i taxied to the fuel tank where the fbo personnel topped off the fuel. a preflight inspection and walkaround were completed with no abnormalities. fuel was sumped with normal results. engine oil was observed at approximately 6.5 quarts, one quart was requested and added. a weight and balance computation was completed and confirmed the aircraft was within limits. the fuel selector was verified on both. aircraft loading was as follows: pilot in command at 180 lbs, one passenger at 255 lbs, and approximately 20 lbs of baggage in the rear seat area, with full fuel.atis information 1 was current at xd:53, reporting winds 120 at 10 gusting 18, variable between 070 and 140, visibility 10 statute miles, ceiling broken at 4, 000 ft, broken at 7, 500 ft, temperature 27°c, dew point 17°c, altimeter 30.18. increased bird activity was noted in the vicinity of the airport. the wind presented a right crosswind component on runway xxr. density altitude was elevated due to the 27°c temperature, however, the conditions were within the normal operating envelope for the aircraft type and loading.during the engine run-up at 2, 000 rpm, a magneto check was performed. the left magneto dropped to 1, 930 rpm and ran smoothly. the right magneto dropped to 1, 910 rpm and ran rough. the idle check was satisfactory at 840 rpm. a second magneto check was performed, during which the right magneto ran smoothly. both drops and the differential were within limits.i contacted redacted tower and reported holding short of runway xxr at taxiway 1, ready for departure. tower instructed line up and wait due to traffic on the downwind. subsequently, tower cleared me for takeoff on runway xxr with an assigned heading of 080.i began the takeoff roll from the full length of runway xxr. full throttle was applied with mixture full rich, flaps up, and trim set for takeoff. engine instruments were checked and indicated in the green. airspeed was confirmed alive. the takeoff roll felt normal in terms of acceleration. i noticed the crosswind component during the roll consistent with the reported winds.rotation was initiated at 55 kias with approximately 10 degrees of pitch. immediately after liftoff, climb performance was sub-optimal and the aircraft was barely gaining altitude. at a few feet agl, the stall warning horn activated. i reduced the angle of attack, but airspeed was not increasing. i observed the engine rpm between 2, 400 and 2, 500. the engine sounded smooth and was not surging or running rough. the aircraft drifted left of the runway centerline.within a few seconds, recognizing the aircraft was not climbing and was drifting off centerline, i made the decision to abort the takeoff rather than risk running out of usable runway or being forced to land off-surface. i pulled the throttle and mixture fully out, shutting down the engine. the aircraft touched down on the remaining runway approximately abeam taxiway 2, roughly 1, 600 feet from the runway xxr threshold. i continued on runway xxr, slowing down and turning right onto runway xy, where i came to a full stop.i transmitted to tower that i was aborting the takeoff. tower initially instructed a right turn at taxiway 3 to contact ground, then corrected to exit on runway xy and contact ground. i acknowledged and advised that the engine was off. i contacted redacted ground and reported engine-off on runway xy after the aborted takeoff. ground asked if i needed assistance, i requested a moment to assess. after confirmingeverything was in order, i successfully restarted the engine and requested taxi back to the southeast ramp. ground cleared me to taxi via runway xy and taxiway 3.upon return to the ramp, i completed a squawk write-up documenting the event. maintenance was contacted. the aircraft is pending inspection and the cause of the degraded takeoff performance has not yet been determined. no injuries were sustained by either occupant. no aircraft damage was observed.chain of events and contributing factors:the problem first arose during the run-up when the right magneto ran rough on the initial check. although the second check was smooth and within limits, this may have been an early indication of a fouled spark plug or developing magneto issue. the problem became apparent immediately after rotation when the aircraft failed to achieve a normal climb rate despite full throttle application, and the stall warning activated at a few feet agl. engine rpm was observed at 2, 400-2, 500, which, combined with the initial rough magneto, suggests a possible partial power issue such as a fouled spark plug or intermittent magneto malfunction.human performance considerations:i was well-rested and had passed the imsafe checklist with no concerns. my perception of the initial rough right magneto was that it had cleared on the second check, and i judged the engine fit for flight based on the smooth recheck and all indications being within limits. in hindsight, the initial rough magneto warranted additional scrutiny. my decision to abort was made quickly once i recognized the convergence of poor climb performance, stall warning activation, and lateral drift from centerline. i prioritized remaining on the runway surface and bringing the aircraft to a safe stop over attempting to continue a climb that the aircraft was not performing.corrective actions and prevention:the aircraft has been squawked and is pending maintenance inspection, which should identify the mechanical cause. in future operations, if a magneto runs rough during the initial check -- even if a recheck is smooth -- i will perform an additional magneto verification while holding short prior to takeoff to confirm the issue has truly resolved rather than accepting a single smooth recheck. this additional step adds minimal time and could catch an intermittent ignition issue before committing to a takeoff. i will also establish a more deliberate go/no-go gate at the hold-short line for any anomaly observed during run-up, treating an initial rough magneto with greater caution.
