synopsis: Cessna 172 Flight Instructor reported an over flare by the student resulting in a tail strike during landing.
text: on day 0 i had a morning flight. intentions of the flight were to go north from redacted to redacted and do pattern work to work on take offs and landings. winds were 210 at 7. after completing several laps in the pattern and working together on improving the round out and flare portion of the approach to land, we were a little high in the round out and ended up high in ground effect. this led to us sinking through ground effect (this was not severe enough to justify a go-around). i said, 'we need slightly more flare'. student then pulled the yoke back and the best way i can describe it is he 'over-flared' by pulling the yoke back too far too quickly. this resulted in a tail strike. i was not fully certain of a tail strike at first due to landing on the mains seemingly simultaneously, so we continued the flight while i took flight controls and felt for any abnormalities, i also looked back and checked in our next pattern for any fod on the runway. after i checked these items and determined the plane felt as it should, we returned to redacted. after the student tied down and debriefed with me, i completed a post flight walk around and confirmed the tail strike.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: A helicopter pilot reported they were hovering near the intersection of two runways when an arriving aircraft landed and rolled past them.
text: while conducting flight instruction in a helicopter (cfi positioned left seat, pilot-student right seat) at the local high traffic-use un-towered airport, we had conducted our approach to the predominant wind use runway xx, making the ctaf radio report of the approach, and runway xx mid-field intersection termination point. the mid-point area of the runways intersect, with runways xx and xy crossing, with the winds indicated by windsock on the airfield of 350-010°, 10 knots with occasional gusts during our traffic pattern training. the runway alignment angle of runways xx and xy does not allow a direct view on final for runway xy if positioned near the intersection or north on runway xx for reference. this positioning makes it necessary to verify conflicting approach path is clear of course, if directly holding short (responsibly announced) or prior to an initial departure intention from runway xx, neither of which was the case in this situation. upon completing our approach to the mid-field intersection on runway xx, i was allowing the student pilot to stabilize their hover in the wind prior to our take-off checks and prepare for next departure / right traffic pattern. i heard an aircraft in-bound over the ctaf, making a call with the intent to use runway xy, despite the winds and traffic pattern in use already, so as to avoid back-taxing to parking, as only runway xy has a parallel taxiway directly accessible easily to & from the apron / ramp area. i made another ctaf call stating we were a momentary delay, midfield intersection runway xx. i did not hear another ctaf call, however just a few moments later the american a-5 tiger landed in front on us on runway xy, (from my right, angled and blocked by the pilot-student / door) rolling directly by within 50' or less from our hovering position on runway xx, just south of the intersection. the pilot while, rolling out after landing, proceeded to chastise us over ctaf, stating we 'were too close to the runway and shouldn't be there'. i restated we literally had called our position on our approach and again just prior to his approach, stating we were still occupying the predominant wind runway at the intersection, using the crossing runway xx as established by us and other aircraft in the recent traffic pattern operations. the other pilot continued to berate us over the radio, saying we should have moved 'off to the side' since he 'was landing', insisting that despite the crossing runway in use, the runway stated as occupied and he saw us in position on runway (xx), implied it was his right of way to continue his approach regardless apparently in lieu of considering a ctaf call about our holding position or the option to go-around since the runway area was already occupied. there was no inquiry about if we were holding short on runway xy, or if we could reposition away from the crossing runway (which we can & will do routinely), nor any attempt to abort his landing approach, despite knowing we were still there. this continues to pose an hazard to flight operations at the airport, where airplane traffic will force repeated runway changes during established traffic pattern operations, in order to simplify their ground taxi to parking. the airplane traffic continues to demonstrate no intention of clearing final approach or the runway environment on multiple occasions, insisting their landing gives them the right of way to an occupied runway, regardless of any aircraft already present. this has developed into a stigma, instead of addressing the core safety issues of communication, runway / pattern operations in use, traffic flow courtesy and clarifying intentions or going around versus forcing a situation into a near mid-air collision or runway incursion to a known occupied runway.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported the engine started shaking and RPMs decreased during cruise. Pilot diverted and landed safely.
text: arrived at redacted for preflight. preflight was normal with no abnormalities. oil level was at 4 quarts, which led me to add 2 more quarts to bring it above the normal 6 quart range. no contaminants found in fuel during sump. no oil leaks in or around the engine. aircraft had full fuel tanks and i was the only occupant in the aircraft for this flight.started the engine, contacted clearance and ground frequencies for taxi to run-up area. the taxi was normal with no abnormalities.the run-up went smoothly with no abnormalities. magneto checks were very smooth and well within range. the engine sounded normal and i continued my taxi to the runway.departed redacted with no abnormalities. the engine sounded completely normal during climb out. i exited the airspace and started to head north-west towards redacted, which was my destination for this flight. 4 minutes after my departure, i reached my cruising altitude of 2, 000 feet due to a cloud layer above me and my relatively short flight plan to redacted. my rpm setting for the flight was 2300 rpm's, and the mixture was leaned slightly due to the high density altitude for the day. 12 minutes after my departure, i noticed a steady decrease in rpm's. the drop started at 2300 rpm's and decreased on its own to about 1500 rpm's. i checked to make sure that the throttle did not back itself out. everything looked normal. the engine started to shake violently. i immediately added full mixture and pulled the carburetor heat. neither of those inputs made the problem any better. i backed off the throttle enough that the shaking wasn't as violent, but kept it high enough that i could mostly maintain altitude. i first thought that the propeller could have been knocked out of balance, however i decided that that was more than likely not the issue. there was too much shaking for it to be a normal bad magneto, so i also ruled that out. however, in case there was a bad magneto, i did not attempt a magneto check. i checked my engine gauges and the fuel pressure was green, the oil pressure was green, but the oil temperature was gradually decreasing. i monitored the gauges throughout the remainder of the flight. i was monitoring guard on 121.5 as soon as i had gotten the frequency change call from redacted tower. redacted approach responded to me on 121.5 and asked what kind of aircraft, how many souls were on board, and how much fuel i had. i responded that i was a cessna 172, 1 soul on board, and full fuel as i had just departed redacted. i did my best to report my location before i was contacted by approach, however they made radar contact with me fairly quickly. they eventually asked me to switch to their frequency.i started to look for somewhere to land near me in case my engine decided to quit. i eventually made my way to the highway that leads into the bay and the city. i observed traffic patterns of the vehicles on the highway to see if it would be a safe option to land on. traffic was relatively light, so i stayed over top of the highway until i could find a possible landing location at an airport. approach gave me a few options to the north. those airports were private strips. after hearing my options, i decided that redacted was the best option. approach informed me of runway length, width, and winds available to the best of their knowledge. about 6 miles away from redacted, i started to turn towards the airfield. i utilized the 3d imaging on foreflight to see what the strip would look like since it was private. i made visual contact with the field and continued my flight towards it. approach informed me that an aircraft was above me and following me in case i had to ditch elsewhere.i had enough power to maintain my altitude for a normal left downwind entry for the field. i added 10 degrees of flaps to help me maintain my altitude while the aircraft slowed down. once i was confident that i could make the short runway, i added full flaps. there was nearly a 90 degree crosswind for the runway (runway xx). the landing was smooth and did not require any substantial abnormal procedures. i taxied the aircraft off of the runway and shut down immediately. postflight inspection resulted in seeing that there was a substantial amount of oil pooling on the ground on the right side of the nose wheel coming from the cowling and around the exhaust. i was not able to take the cowling off of the aircraft due to the amount of screws and lack of tools. nothing looked abnormal in the engine other than the obvious oil leak. i believe that most of the oil leak came after the engine stopped, or at least when i was on the ground. the oil pressure never fell out of the green range and the engine stayed on throughout the flight until i was on the ground and shut it down myself. to my knowledge, i do not believe that any far's were broken or deviated from.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air taxi Captain reported GPS jamming while on RNAV GPS approach to JAC. GPS recovered and crew completed a second approach attempt.
text: i was flying left seat and was the pilot flying on the approach into jac. my first officer and i were on the rnav gps x into runway 01 approach. from my memory, we were near the cileg intersection or in between cileg and homva. we started seeing some 'flags' appear on our primary flight display (pfd) and flight management system that notified us that we no longer had lpv and the required rnp for this approach. we then had no terrain map. we heard air carrier x on frequency complaining of the same issues. there were plenty of us on frequency who then could not commence this approach because of the gps spoofing/jamming. air traffic control then notified us that they were jamming the gps systems. we were all going to have to go back around to get sequenced for the vor approach into jac, when finally everything started working normally again. we requested and received vectors to come back around and re-commence the rnav gps x to runway 01 into jac. we received the required rnp value of 0.3 and had lpv guidance like we normally do. we were able to commence the approach successfully and had a successful landing.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported unknowingly flying a UAS in a TFR area that restricted UAS operations.
text: on day 1 at approximately xa:50, i was conducting a commercial video production flight operating a dji mavic 2 pro under part 107 certification.i was hired by a private company to film a private event at this location. the sole purpose of the flight was to capture aerial photographs of the event venue building from a favorable angle. i launched from the 5th floor of a nearby parking structure to achieve the necessary vantage point for the shot.prior to the flight, i checked my drone application for airspace restrictions. the application did not clearly indicate that a tfr was active in the area. based on this, i proceeded with the flight.i was flying at approximately 100-200 feet agl for less than 10 minutes when local law enforcement approached and instructed me to land immediately. i complied without hesitation and landed the aircraft promptly.after landing, i checked my application again and discovered the active tfr restricting uas operations from day 0 to day 4. the client/property owner was present, confirmed the nature of the work, and spoke with officers. no further enforcement action was taken on scene.contributing factors: inadequate pre-flight airspace verification. the application did not provide a clear alert prior to flight. i failed to independently verify tfr status through official faa sources such as tfr.faa.gov.corrective action: i will implement a pre-flight checklist that includes direct verification at tfr.faa.gov before every flight, regardless of what third-party applications indicate.

text: our approach to 4r in ewr was preceded by a 767. suffering from intermittent wake turbulence as pf, i was focused on the approach and flight path. at around 1700 ft. agl flaps 30, set final reference, landing checklist" was called. upon completion of that checklist, the approach continued till approximately 300 ft. agl when the aural "too low, flaps" was annunciated. a go-around was immediately commenced to another subsequent approach and uneventful landing.my conclusion is the fo/pm set the flaps to 25 thinking they were in the 30 detent and was not verified via the flap display in accordance with the checklist."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Fractional Captain reported GPS spoofing during cruise. Flight continued to destination.
text: at fl380, the synthetic vision system (svs) failed, then the global navigation satellite system (gnss) not available message showed in the flight management system scratch pad. checking the gps status page on the flight management system it was confirmed the gps was failed. the ads-b out fail crew alerting system (cas) message appeared on the left multi-function flight display (mfd). mazatlan air traffic control was notified of the nav failure and we were given a heading to tenay intersection. ten minutes into the failure, the course guidance on both pilots primary flight displays (pfd) conflicted, one showing left of course the other showing right of course. both pilot and copilot mfd screens flickered too, momentarily. all this took place approaching the sea of cortez from the east heading west bound at fl380 vmc conditions. it lasted until approximately half way across the sea of cortez. a total of 18 minutes of outages were noted. on the jeppesen charts, it showed there were or has been previous spoofing in mexican airspace. we briefed this in our crew briefing.suggestions: plan for extra fueling and review all approaches in cabo.

anomaly: Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence departing DFW in trail of an A321 that resulted in a 45-degree bank and required full aileron deflection to recover.
text: on takeoff out of dallas, we encountered wake turbulence from the previous aircraft at around 1000 feet causing the aircraft to bank to around 45°. i held full aileron deflection for a few seconds before i got the aircraft to right itself. we then encountered it a second time and i turned 15° off course to get out of the path of the wake turbulence and immediately informed air traffic control of the corrective action. once clear, they gave us a heading to rejoin the departure, and advised us that they lost separation with additional departing traffic. we did not receive any tcas advisories in the cockpit. the rest of the flight was without incident.cause: wake turbulent encounter. more vigilance in noting the wind that pushes wake turbulence into the flight path.

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported while on short final to DRO; a non-towered airport; they became aware of an aircraft on short final landing opposite direction. Reporter expressed concern about the traffic volume at DRO and suggested a Tower would enhance safety.
text: while coming into dro today we started making our calls to come into the visual for runway 3 50nm out. there was a plane doing traffic pattern work on 21 in durango when we first made our call. there was also another plane with plans to land runway 3 as well as another plane that both announced on ctaf. as we got closer, i asked aircraft y in the pattern to switch to 21 since that's what everyone else was doing. he refused, as we continued the approach, i continued making calls of our intentions as well as the other plane did. we ended up turning final for runway 3 while the other went into the crosswind for 21 and stopped making radio calls. as we were short final, he made a call that he was turning final for the opposite direction runway right in our go around path. we landed as we felt it was the safest option. the other plane ended up going around because of this aircraft.cause: uncontrolled airport operations were a big factor. as well as macho attitude from the aircraft y pilot that was incredibly dangerous.suggestions: i would implement a tower in dro as soon as possible due to the constant traffic there with airline travel.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B767-200 flight crew reported a cabin depressurization during cruise; resulting in an immediate descent. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed.
text: in cruise flight at fl400 we received a cabin alt high warning, and physical indications of decompression. i called to don o2 masks and we both did. the first officer (pm) told air traffic control we needed an immediate descent which air traffic control granted to 10000. i started the descent then added spoilers, and the pm ran the checklist. i made the decision to request priority handling to descend rapidly. after leveling at 8000, we ran all checklists, verified that the cabin altitude was stable and started to come up with a plan. due to the fact that we did not believe we had fuel to fly to destination at 8000 feet. i made the decision to head for redacted or redacted area and contacted the company through acars and decided redacted was the nearest suitable airport and we requested vectors for an approach into redacted. the rest of the flight was uneventful and safely landed. i also wrote up the incident in the logbook.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Commercial rated pilot reported post flight confirmation of a chip in the propeller possibly caused by contacting snowbank at departure airport.
text: during taxi out from ramp to runway xx the instructions were taxiway 1, 2 to taxiway 3 cross runway xy to depart runway xx. pireps were saying poor braking on taxiway 2. the pilot in command complied with instructions and was taxiing very slowly on taxiway 3. there was a lot of blowing snow which made visibility limited. the plow trucks were clearing the center portions of the taxiways and leaving behind snow banks. the ground controller called them windrows. braking action on taxiway 3 was poor. it was slippery that the plane shifted from 180 degree to 150 degree heading. the pilot in command had both brakes to the floor and r engine in full reverse to help from drifting into the windrow. the l propeller went into the windrow. the pilot in command was able to correct the position and begin to proceed slowly on taxiway towards runway xx. i could not see sitting in the r seat that the propeller made contact with anything but saw extra blowing snow assuming that we made contact with the snowbank. we were both concerned so the pilot in command shut down the l engine and looked at the props from inside the cockpit. we couldn't see any damage so the pilot in command started up the l engine and took off to our destination. once we landed we both took a look at the props and noticed a chip. we informed the chief pilot and he took a look as well. the pilot in command made a maintenance write up that the prop may have hit ice during the taxi out of redacted.cause: slippery taxiways and winds.suggestions: i don't think there was much i could have done as second in command (sic) as i was not the one in control or taxiing the airplane. i think the pilot in command acted promptly.

synopsis: EMB-145 pilot reported Battery Overheating indication and diversion to a nearby airport.
text: at fl330, received a batt1 off bus caution that quickly went away. approximately 15 mins later, received a batt1 ovtemp master warning and batt 1 off bus caution. observed temperature at 65c rising as high as 90c. ran and complied with qrc/qrh procedures. decided best course of action in the interest of safety was to get the airplane on the ground. requested priority handling and landed at redacted without incident.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a GPWS alert during approach. Captain performed a go-around.
text: while flying into tri turning base to final for a visual approach for runway 23 we received a an gpws alert for 'too low terrain' around 2, 400 to 2, 500 feet within less than a 5 mile final. we were flaps 22 with the gear down, fully configured for landing. there was still sunlight out so the first officer and i could see there was no terrain in front of us on the approach path. my descent rate was shallow at about 1, 000 fpm as well during turn and when the gpws gave us caution. we were within mocca and eaver at the time. the approach plate also does not show terrain within the vicinity of where we were turning base to final. when the caution sounded it confused me at first due to not seeing any obstacles or terrain on our flight path. i adjusted my flight path and slightly climbed the aircraft and it stopped. i opted to continue the approach, but i was still confused on how i got the caution. i then decided to do a go-around for a reset and do the approach again just for good measure. i have never had a gpws event in the aircraft before and felt i was not within vicinity of obstacles when it occurred, but i followed the system's guidance for the safe measure.suggestion: i think as a crew we made the proper actions to follow the gpws caution to avoid the conflict and to execute a go around for a better piece of mind. i think potentially fixing in mocca would probably be a better avenue of approach for runway 23. however, i still do not recall any terrain or obstacles during this event.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance
synopsis: Air carrier technicians reported while accomplishing a biweekly service check on an EMB 170; they inadvertently serviced the # 1 engine with hydraulic fluid.
text: on day 0, at about xa:30 i was on airplane aircraft x. i was doing an outside biweekly. i was working the hydraulics 1 and 2. i bleed the pressure in hyd 1 and was opening all the panels making sure everything was ok. i noticed that ecology bottle #2 on that side was full. so i got an empty can of oil with pig mats, and cut a big hole in the can so i can drain it better and put pig mats in case anything spills. we also don't have any specific equipment to dump hydraulic fluid when we're up on the line. that's why i usually use an empty oil can. when i was finished dumping it, i took speed tape and put 2 big strips over it to cover it up. i do that 1 so people know not to use it and 2 so it won't spill in the van. at the end of the day when we had back down to the hanger i always make sure i dump it in the proper manner in the correct bucket. after a few hours go by and me and my co-worker head over to plane aircraft y at around xc:30 am. i am doing the walk around on the plane as he is filling oil in the engines. i walk back over to the van to grab my ipad to head up to the plane to start doing paperwork. he comes over and asks me why the oil looks like that. and told me he dumped it into the engine. i saw that he took the speed tape off of it and i told him to call the leads now. at that point he called the lead, and then we had to bring the plane down to the hanger.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: SA-227 AC Metro III Captain reported a nosewheel steering failure during landing that resulted in a taxiway excursion.
text: while operating a flight to redacted, upon the touchdown and roll-out phase at approximately 80 to 85 knots while speed was decelerating, i experienced an uncommanded hard left turn of the nose wheel steering mechanism on my aircraft.the initial roll out and deceleration in ground speed was normal and straight forward, however, at around 85 to 80 knots, the aircraft started careening to the left. i attempted to correct the loss of control by first, selecting the prop condition/speed levers to low, thinking that the side throttle stick button was the defective item and that normal operations would be restored. nevertheless, that proved ineffective. i was pressing hard right rudder, brakes and using right reverse thrust for differential breaking while leaving the left throttle at idle, however, i was losing the battle at maintaining directional control and the aircraft wanted to veer hard left into the grass.i realized that taxiway 1 was quickly approaching and since the aircraft was already veering left, i tried my best to guide it towards the appropriate taxiway 1 left turn exit. i successfully made it halfway on the taxiway pavement, but, the nosewheel and left main gear came to rest onto the gravel area adjacent to the asphalt taxiway. no airport signage nor lighting was damaged, neither was any damage done to the aircraft.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: SONX pilot reported loss of directional control resulted in a taxiway excursion and subsequent damage to a taxiway light and propeller strike during taxi.
text: i was taxiing south along taxiway 1 to runway xx at redacted. wind heading was approximately 320, shown by the visible windsocks - awos not reporting at time of incident. as such i was using crosswind controls - forward elevator and ailerons away from(left) the right quartering tailwind. i was using a portable adsb device in conjunction with foreflight. my reported groundspeed in app was 15mph.as i passed taxiway intersection 1 / 2, the aircraft yawed hard right and proceeded to exit the taxiway into the grass and nose over, damaging a taxiway edge light and resulting in a prop-strike. i shut everything off and exited the aircraft.inspection of main gear wheel hubs/brakes and tailwheel assembly showed normal functionality and no flat tires.its possible my crosswind control configuration was unwarranted and resulted in loss of control caused by airflow over a down elevator and gusting wind against the rudder from the right rear quartering tailwind.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor and student reported that the left main tire became flat during landing and came off the wheel.
text: during a routine training flight, instructor and student were practicing landing attempts. it was the second landing attempt of the flight. upon landing, aircraft touched down on centerline, pilot flying reported directional yaw to the left. instructor applied additional right rudder to counteract the directional turn. as the aircraft deaccelerated and eventually came to a stop, the pilot flying looked out the left seat window to discover the left main tire had seemingly came off the rim. no sideloading was experienced as the aircraft touched down.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Small transport Captain reported control difficulties related to moderate turbulence and subsequently penetrated BNA Class C airspace during climb.
text: soon after departing vfr from runway 02 at john tune airport, nashville, having been previously cleared on course to the southwest, reaching approximately 600-800 feet agl, i encountered moderate to heavy turbulence and began a shallow turn to approximately 240 magnetic.as i did so, the aircraft's heading turned me directly into the sun, approximately 35 degrees above the horizon. the turbulence intensity was such that attempting to engage the autopilot was pointless. as i alternated using my right hand to shield my eyes from the sun and retard the power levers, i was immediately concerned with antennas and tv/radio towers close to my flight path atop the rising terrain west and southwest of the airport.amid all this difficulty and distractions, attempting to level the aircraft and remain below the class charlie airspace, i finally managed control approximately 3, 500 feet (msl) though still climbing slightly.after being handed off to nashville approach/departure, the controller queried my position and altitude. i stated i was still having difficulty controlling the aircraft, asking if he could standby.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported that while on short final to a non-towered airport; they initiated a go around to avoid a near collision with a faster aircraft overtaking them.
text: aircraft y came in to redacted from the north and was going to enter right traffic for xx. another pilot came over the radio and told them it was left traffic. instead they crossed the departure end of xx and entered on the crosswind following us (aircraft x) in the downwind. we called left base xx and final xx. after that, they called left base xx. they never made a final call. we were very short final xx (past the threshold) when the bonanza came over the radio and asked if we could do a go around because they were ' right on our [expletive]'. i was confused for a second because they never made a final call. i decided i would do a go around just in case. after i had my student execute the go around i turned around and they were close enough i could see their faces and they flew beneath me and landed. after they cleared the runway i asked if they could give more separation next time. they told me it was as slow as they could go. there was nothing preventing them from extending downwind to give better separation. we were the slower and lower aircraft, therefore having right of way. i believe they turned final without having me in sight and only got me in sight when they asked me to do a go around. i also believe that me doing a go around was the less safe because our flight paths would have crossed between them continuing their descent and us climbing out. there is no reason that they shouldn't have decided to do a go around as soon as they realized they were too close to me.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Light aircraft pilot reported another aircraft on short final on the opposite runway during take off at RYW. Pilot rejected take off.
text: the flight began at the fuel ramp at ryw. i had fueled and preflighted the aircraft and started the engine. after performing the pre-taxi checklist, i listened to the awos and observed the nearest windsock. the windsock pointed to a departure on runway 33 but the winds were light and variable. i called austin (tx) approach for my instrument flight rules clearance to ksat and indicated that i intended to depart on runway 33. i was given my instrument flight rules clearance and was told to call back when i was number 1 for departure. i then broadcast my intentions to taxi to runway 33 for departure on the ryw unicom frequency and monitored that frequency until i was ready to depart. i completed my preflight checklist at the departure end holding area of 33 and then called austin approach for my release. after a few moments on the phone i was given my departure instructions and release. i then broadcast my departure from runway 33 on the unicom frequency, again hearing and seeing no other traffic. part way down the runway i saw another single engine aircraft on short final for the opposite runway (15). at nearly the same time i also noticed the traffic warning on my tis-b unit. i broadcasted on the unicom frequency that i was aborting my take off. the landing pilot acknowledged and executed a missed approach and left the area without further incident. i subsequently departed kryw without further incident.potential contributing factors:1. i might have missed any communications from the other pilot while i was on the phone communicating with austin approach and getting my clearance and release.2. the calm wind runway is 15 and any landing pilot might reasonably expect to land on 15 irrespective of any conflicting information provided by a windsock on the ground.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: A P50 TRACON Controller reported a VFR aircraft flew in unsafe proximity to an air carrier on approach to IWA. Reporter stated VFR aircraft not required to contact ATC routinely conflict with arriving air carriers to IWA.
text: aircraft x cleared for the rnav-visual runway 12c into iwa. aircraft y squawking 1200 not in communication with air traffic control maneuvering outside the class b. in my opinion. aircraft x came into an unsafe proximity to aircraft y. traffic was issued, and the pilot had aircraft y in sight and maintaining visual separation. no tcas-resolution advisory was announced. the rnav-visual approach into iwa barely touches the phx class b airspace. it provides minimal protection from visual flight rules aircraft not in communication with air traffic control. the majority of this procedure is in class e airspace. there is high intensity training activity in the area of the approach. this area is a known 'hot-spot' to controllers due to the frequency of tcas-resolution advisory's and traffic alerts. maneuvering aircraft routinely change trajectory and/or altitude placing them into unsafe proximity into airliners descending or departing from iwa airport. there is a huge risk currently of unpredictable, non-participating aircraft intersecting with high-speed traffic flows. i propose 3 solutions to help mitigate this safety issue. listed from most effective to least effective:1) implement class c airspace at iwa. a standard class c airspace design would fully contain the approach procedure. iwa meets the faa requirements to become class c. in 2025, iwa recorded 15, 309 air carrier operations, presumably all of which were instrument flight rules, and 95, 618 air taxi operations, unknown with publicly available information how many were instrument flight rules. the threshold is 75, 000 instrument flight rules operations. additionally, iwa had 2, 036, 218 passengers in 2025, dramatically above the threshold of 250, 000 enplaned passengers. 2) expand the class b airspace to more fully encompass the approaches at iwa. this may be difficult because iwa is not the primary airport, but the airspace should be studied to more fully accommodate jet traffic in the phoenix area. 3) implement a special flight rules area (sfra) or special air traffic rule (satr). mandate that pilots communicate with air traffic control near the iwa airport. 4). charted hot spot on the sectional/tac chart. the current traffic mix near gateway airport presents a systemic and increasing safety risk. proactive mitigation now reduces the likelihood of a future serious incident or accident.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: P50 TRACON controller reported SDL Tower allowed a high performance military jet aircraft to depart with no coordination with the TRACON; and a delay in radar ID of the aircraft resulted in a NMAC with another aircraft.
text: an aircraft x departed sdl requesting visual flight rules flight following. aircraft x established communications with me approximately 10 miles northwest of sdl in a slow climb and moving quickly. i radar identified aircraft x and issued traffic. relevant traffic was aircraft y, who just terminated flight following a couple minutes earlier and was off my frequency. the pilot of aircraft x said 'radar contact'. i subsequently issued a traffic alert and the pilot indicated he had the other aircraft in sight. in my recollection, the aircraft at the closest proximity were target merge and 200 feet. in my opinion, this is a 'near mid-air'. recommendation: there are several things at play here. firstly, aircraft x called me in the blind for flight following. uhf radio stepping on the vhf frequency. it took several transmissions for me to determine his callsign and type aircraft. contributing to this difficulty was poor radio and reception quality making it difficult on first listen to determine the callsign if you aren't expecting it. secondly, aircraft x was not transmitting an ads-b callsign. if the aircraft was transmitting the ads-b callsign, i would have determined his callsign much quicker. ads-b is required to operate in the airspace aircraft x was flying in. because of the delay in inputting the necessary information into stars, i was unable to issue the aircraft control instructions to more effectively avoid traffic. recommendation: sdl tower should solicit high performing aircraft for flight following and input, or have biltmore input flight plan information into stars/nas. this would eliminate the back and forth the radar controller has to do to determine the pilots callsign and intentions. in turn, we could provide a much better service. iwa tower does this already and it is very helpful. sdl tower should too. alternatively, sdl tower can give the biltmore controller a heads up of what's about to happen.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: A Center controller reported HLN non radar TRACON issued a VFR aircraft a frequency change to advisory frequency instead of the Center frequency contrary to established procedure.
text: aircraft x was on visual flight rules flight following at 10, 500 and transiting through helena (hln) non radar approach control airspace. the sector xx controller told them radar service terminated and shipped them to hln approach frequency per loa (letter of agreement), when the aircraft was exiting west of hlns airspace the aircraft never checked in.i was training a trainee on d xx and we had him call hln approach to have them try the aircraft again. they responded that they didn't even know the aircraft was on visual flight rules flight following so they never shipped the aircraft to us. this resulted in a lot of coordination trying to get a hold of the aircraft, which we never did. multiple phone calls were made to spokane approach to advise them of the situation and let them know the aircraft is nordo. we called hln approach again to see exactly what the controller told the pilot. hln told us that they told the aircraft to report 20 miles west of hln vor and at that time told the aircraft change to advisory frequency approved. the supervisor had to call the omic (operations manager in charge) and discuss whether or not this warranted us being able to remove strips on the aircraft. the aircraft was still on their squawk code the entire flight, because they were never told to squawk visual flight rules. the pilot did nothing wrong.there has been talk with recent meetings with helena approach to discuss other issues that the controllers there often throw away active flight progress strips. i'm not sure if this happened in this situation, but if hln approach had seen the strip for the aircraft they would realize the aircraft was on flight following and needed to be shipped back to center once leaving their airspace. the aircraft was transiting westbound from the bil area through hln airspace and landing at 7s0, ronan airport.have helena approach keep strips to ensure this doesn't happen again and maintain clarity of which aircraft are or aren't on flight following. this required a lot of extra coordination for the controllers. i have also heard that hln approach has discussed that they sometimes don't receive all of the strips they need for aircraft, so perhaps there is an issue with their fdio (flight data input/output). they have had several fdio outages lately which have required a lot of manual coordination.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a near collision with a service truck while taxiing from the ramp.
text: we were cleared to taxi from ramp to the taxiway. ramp asked us to stop and wait for another aircraft so we stopped, which put the nose in the service road. we were then cleared to resume taxi in sequence. as i add power to taxi i thankfully saw truck x or truck y running down the road. when he crossed in front of us we had to sit up to see past the nose to see him, he was that close. he had to exit his lane to be able to pass us.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B767 Captain reported the aircraft began to roll after the Captain failed to set brakes during the before start checklist.
text: we were on hardstand xx at redacted. this is the first time in the decades i've operated a normal revenue flight like this stand. we were free to taxi straight out, which unlike other hardstand we have pushback. everything was normal with ground personnel, all pushback procedures completed. after before pushback checklist complete the brakes were released. i did not reset the brake. the aircraft rolled approximately 2 feet. ground personnel had disconnected and i was just receiving a salute. i should have reset the brake after the brake release. at other hardstand cities i've always been pushed back from parking from hardstands. expectation bias i guess won out. this is a huge threat as it is different from normal ops. four pilots missed it on the flight deck, i take sole responsibility. huge learning event for this pilot as safety was in jeopardy as was the aircraft. my situational awareness was 100 percent but the pushback sequence from this type of hardstand was very different. no injuries or aircraft damage. salute received then aircraft rolled.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported aircraft parked on taxiway off the extended center line of IAH Runway 33R posed a safety risk in the event of a rejected takeoff. Flight crew notified ATC which moved aircraft off taxiway.
text: this report is to point out a safety concern we as a crew of this flight experienced and would like to bring to attention.distributing factors: iah-redacted flight close to maximum takeoff weight.during our departure from iah on runway 33r, we experienced a situation that presented a significant safety risk, which we believe warrants attention.after being cleared to line up and wait, and subsequently cleared for takeoff, we observed two aircraft stopped at the far end of runway 33r, appearing to be positioned on taxiway nb in direct alignment with the takeoff runway. a subsequent query with air traffic control confirmed these aircraft were indeed on taxiway nb.both aircraft remained in that position during the takeoff roll of the preceding aircraft. given our aircraft was near maximum takeoff weight, these stationary aircraft were directly in line with the runway overrun area in the event of a rejected takeoff. this created a completely avoidable additional risk factor that could have resulted in a serious incident.as a precaution, we elected to not accept our takeoff clearance(prior to initiating the takeoff roll), until the aircraft could be moved. air traffic control instructed us to taxi off runway 33r via wl and proceed back down wa for resequencing. ground control successfully contacted the stationary aircraft, which were moved clear of the potential overrun area before any further departures. we were resequenced and departed runway 33r a few minutes later without incident.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the font size of the AVDGS (Advanced Visual Docking Guidance System) at SLC is too small to be easily read.
text: both the first officer and i observed that in our collective opinion the gate xx avdgs (advanced visual docking guidance system) system distance countdown in feet font size if that's the term was a bit small thus not easy to read as we got to the close in range. referencing the same type of system in ewr terminal a the feet countdown digits are bigger and then i believe turn even bigger once close in like say 20 feet? this is very useful functionality regardless of one's vision. case in point my first officer doesn't need corrective lenses whereas i do.i'd advise seeing if the airport owner or manager can see if such a system modification is possible as the digits really could stand to be bigger for flight crew clarity. thanks for your time.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: A319 flight crew on an approach and a helicopter pilot reported an NMAC between their aircraft.
text: during the initial climb-out from runway xx at redacted, redacted tower attempted to contact aircraft y (a helicopter) to establish visual contact with our aircraft. aircraft y did not initially respond to tower.upon hearing the call, i initiated an immediate visual scan. i located the target on the tcas display off the right side and subsequently acquired visual contact with aircraft y. at that time, the helicopter appeared to be in a stationary hover. we continued our climb via the sid.shortly thereafter, the helicopter began a turn toward our flight path before abruptly maneuvering to pass behind us. this maneuver triggered a tcas resolution advisory (resolution advisory) to 'descend'we received a 'clear of conflict' shortly after the descent was initiated. after clear of conflict, we resumed our climb on the redacted x departure.the captain, the pilot monitoring, notified redacted tower that we were responding to a tcas resolution advisory. at this point, aircraft y responded on the frequency, however, the audio quality and timing suggested the helicopter may have been on a different frequency or experiencing a communication lag with redacted tower during the initial conflict.
