anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported an NMAC on descent into LGB. Pilot took evasive action and continued flight.
text: i was completing a round trip flight from lgb in aircraft x. my right-seat passenger was an instrument-rated private pilot. we were descending to land at long beach 26l with visual flight rules flight following, on socal approach. route of flight was direct from the southeast, descending through 3000 on a 303 degree heading, descent to 2500 authorized. air traffic control issued a traffic alert for a converging aircraft at 2500 feet indicated. i added power and held 3000 feet until further advised. i never saw the other traffic, so turning away was not an option. as the other aircraft (aircraft y) passed directly beneath us, my copilot snapped a foreflight screenshot showing the tracks crossing, the other aircraft was shown at 2600' on adsb-in.the other aircraft was not in communication with socal so far as i could tell. it is possible the other pilot was on the practice area ctaf, though i was not. the near-miss happened very fast. collision was avoided due to my evasive action of aborting descent in response to the air traffic control alert. my analysis is that my choice to use air traffic control flight following, and a quick response to the air traffic control traffic alert, likely saved our lives. my attention was divided between managing the descent, visually scanning outside, descent checklist, navigation, and communications. my ipad was not showing traffic consistently, as it would not maintain a steady wifi connection to my sentry plus. yet i should have been able to note the conflicting traffic on my own adsb-in on the g1000 multi-function flight display (mfd). had the other aircraft been on frequency, likely there would have been air traffic control intervention to deconflict. had i been monitoring the ctaf, i might have heard the other aircraft make a position announcement, but the extra radio work would have increased my workload and delayed my imminent handover to lgb tower.see-and-avoid is a fantasy in situations like this one. again, though i was actively looking, i never saw the other traffic. i will redouble my own efforts to maintain situational awareness of traffic using all resources available. i would support a requirement for all aircraft to transmit adsb-out in all us airspace. i would also support a change in the fars to allow general aviation copilots to log second in command (sic) time, in order to encourage pilot-passengers to serve as pilot monitoring. thank you.

anomaly: Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported a course deviation during climb out of HEF that resulted in a CFTT event.
text: i took off instrument flight rules from hef, the departure procedure was to climb to 800 ft and continue a climbing right turn toward csn. the tight turn was required because of r-6608a. when i reached 800 ft i began my left turn by turning the heading bug. the heading bug did not respond. at the same time i was a full power and clean for the climb. i got disoriented briefly because the heading plane wasn't responding and failed to increase the altitude to the next altitude of 2000. so i was 800 ft off the ground and gaining speed. i focused ouside for obstacle clearance i called air traffic control, let them know i was having trouble. the gave me vectors and prompted a climb. those controller are so great!anyway. i was very well prepared for the departure procedure. i don't do them very often so i studied it hard and set up the nav properly. the first mistake was setting the altitude to 800 ft, the first point the climb was supposed to stop was 2000 ft. the second mistake was turning the wrong knob for heading change (two identical knobs - one does altimeter the other heading). the third mistake was trouble shooting the autopilot. i should have disconnected it and hand flown. if i had done that i would not have veered far off course. what i did well was call air traffic control quickly and they helped me get my head back on straight.i discussed with two respected atp/cfi's and gained additional insight. i've shared my story with other pilots.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Small transport pilot reported seeing a helicopter at the end of the runway while on short final to TBR. Pilot executed a missed approach.
text: we were being vectored to the final approach course for instrument landing system 32 at tbr, and i cancelled instrument flight rules when the field was in sight as there was no other traffic in sight or indicated on my traffic display (ads-b and garmin 800). i switched to visual flight rules on the transponder and switched to the ctaf to report my position and intention to land on runway 32. a few seconds after i reported my position and intentions on ctaf the runway lights came on bright. i had not activated that so i concluded that someone at the non-towered airport had heard me and out of courtesy turned the lights up bright.as i turned onto the final approach course at the final approach fix i noticed a single white strobe light at the departure end of the runway. i wondered if it was an aircraft on the runway or a single runway end identifier light. since i had not heard any other transmissions or position reports on the ctaf and observed no traffic on my traffic display i concluded it must be a single reil, even though i had never seen such a thing.i made a short-final position report but still was unsure what the strobe like was. just before crossing the runway threshold i looked down and saw what i thought was an aircraft at the end of the runway--the source of the single strobe light.i immediately added power and initiated a go-around. i climbed out and turned to a left downwind. at that point i questioned if i had tuned the correct ctaf, so i checked airport info on foreflight and discovered i had tuned 122.75 instead of the correct frequency, 122.72. i reported my position and intention to land on 32. a helicopter pilot responded and said they had been on the runway. i explained my frequency mistake and apologized. the pilot said something to the effect of 'no problem.' i saw the strobe light move off the runway onto a closed diagonal runway so i continued my downwind.just before touching down another voice transmitted, saying he was the instructor in the helicopter and claimed we were just 10 feet above them when i initiated the go-around. given that i was busy with the landing i did not respond. and that was it. no other transmissions from the helicopter.the next day i attempted to find out who was flying the helicopter so i could discuss the situation with the instructor, but the airport said they do not know of anyone who is training there in a helicopter.my mistake in tuning the incorrect ctaf frequency was obvious. but the sudden change in runway lighting made me think someone heard me and turned up the lights, so i had no reason to think i had the incorrect ctaf. plus, i wasn't surprised that no other aircraft responded to my initial calls because it was nighttime and there was no traffic shown on my traffic display. i've learned from that to double check every frequency input. but i wonder why the helicopter would remain at the very end of the departure runway for several minutes without any movement, and why they did not appear on my traffic display. that's what i wanted to talk to the helicopter instructor about.that experience was a dramatic and sobering example of how an unrelated series of events and circumstances can lead to a disaster. pay attention to details!

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: E550 Captain reported losing three of four flight display units after takeoff.  All units returned on to online status during climb.
text: redacted. runway in use xx sid redacted day 0 xa:47. we have on board 4 display units (dus) (screens) but as soon as we took off we lost without any warning 3 out 4 dus, with only the right front du working but the information that we were getting was limited and not accurate in terms of speed, altitude and heading... the altitude indication showed 5, 000 ft. but we were absolutely positive that was a wrong indication so we were not able to comply with the sid right away, we managed to turn right using the magnetic compass, but altitude indications continued not being reliable at all, our main concern at that time was to promptly to recover our failed dus in order to have accurate navigation info. so we executed the proper check list for each du and we were able to recover all of them one at the time, when we reached about 7 or 8, 000 ft. everything was working in perfect order again, and we were able to continue our 2:30 hour flight to redacted without any further malfunction at all.up to now we still don't know what was the cause of the problem, the embraer legacy 500 is very computer and technologically fly by wire aircraft, i have talked to a couple of mechanics and their best guess is that after being parked for 9 days in the cold humid and rainy weather there was some kind of glitch in any of the computers that cause the problem when the aircraft was airborne. i must mention that the departure redacted controller did in fact a great job that day he was completely busy at that time, we didn't have any tcas advisory or resolution at all mainly thanks to him. i have been flying for over several decades and my co-captain for over more than several decades and this was for me the most stressful situation i have ever encountered in the cockpit as a pilot in command, we even thought for a brief moment to declaring an emergency but the frequency was so busy and crowded, so meanwhile we focused on recover our dus and being as safe as possible!!

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported briefly exceeding their authorized altitude.
text: while flying the drone, i mistakenly flew the drone around 100 feet over the permitted altitude. this happened because as i was setting up the drone, i wasn't fully aware of the altitude i was putting on the drone and mistook the max altitude for the max distance. as soon as i realized the mistake, i took down the drone as soon as i could and i changed my max altitude to 100 feet.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported during takeoff roll; a business jet flew overhead 200 - 300 feet from the opposite direction on the same runway.
text: on day 0 at xa:55 (calm winds and clear) while departing the redacted airport in my bonanza, i had a very close encounter with a business jet departing in the opposite direction on the same runway. to back up a little, i started the engine in front of the hangar and set up the nav along with some of the other preflight items while the engine was warming up. on taxi out, i made a radio call announcing that i was on the south ramp taxiing to runway xx for departure via taxiway 1. a mooney immediately came back saying he was doing the same thing. i saw him taxi out from between a row of t-hangars and followed him to the run-up area. while taxiing, a cub announced that he was departing (opposite direction) on runway xy. it is worth noting that a zenith experimental aircraft had previously departed runway xx and was on a downwind departure. after completing my run-up checks, i continued taxiing to the runway checking for traffic in the pattern and announced that i was departing runway xx with a left crosswind departure. on the takeoff roll at about 40 to 50 mph a business jet came flashing overhead, opposite direction, about 200 or 300 feet above me. way too close! the traffic traffic alert went off after the jet had passed overhead. i continued the takeoff and as i was turning crosswind, the mooney announced his takeoff. i called him and asked if he heard the jet make a takeoff call. he said no. i never heard any communication from the jet before, during, or after the encounter. did he not make a call or was he on a different frequency? at the redacted airport most of the aircraft are parked or hangared at the opposite end. runway xy is the most convenient runway for departure. the remarks section of the airport information states that runway xx is the preferred calm wind runway. almost nobody pays any attention to this. aircraft in the runway xy run-up area are difficult to see from runway xx. turbine aircraft on the ramp departing runway xy typically taxi from the ramp right onto the runway and depart without stopping, traffic permitting. what could i have done better? look harder at the opposite end for traffic? if the jet had been on ctaf, perhaps a second call that i was rolling on runway xx for takeoff would have helped.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: SCT Approach Controller reported a small jet aircraft not communicating with ATC had an NMAC with a light aircraft.
text: while working springs [tracon] i noticed a target climbing on a converging course with aircraft x. i issued multiple traffic alerts. the pilot asked what course of action they should take but i couldn't determine a safe action that would ensure separation. the pilot initiated a turn and very likely prevented a collision. aircraft y never contacted me. in my opinion aircraft y was aware of the traffic because they turned slightly approximately 3-4 miles before converging with the traffic. looking at the replay it looks like aircraft y was aware of the traffic but continued to fly a course that was extremely unsafe and put lives in jeopardy. additionally the ground speed indicated 300 knots below 10000 ft.recommendation:due to the complexity, volume and wide range of aircraft in congested airspace i feel that instrument flight rules airways should be protected class b airspace.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported they had to brake abruptly to avoid a collision with a ground vehicle during taxi at EWR.
text: we were cleared by ground to taxi to the ramp by a9. ramp cleared us to taxi to gate xx via a9. we were taxiing behind a aircraft y and approaching a9 we noticed a vehicle stopped in the area between a9, a8, f and a, facing south. after aircraft y made the turn towards the x gates on a9, the vehicle started moving south across a9. we had started our turn and had to stop aggressively. the vehicle made a u turn on a9 and returned to their original location. thankfully, all passengers and fas were seated with their seatbelts on, and no one was hurt. if this had happened on taxi out when fas may be standing, we could have had an injury.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew departing IAH reported ATC failure to provide separation resulted in an NMAC event.
text: shortly after takeoff 33r we received a tcas resolution advisory at approximately 1, 800 msl, after thrust reduction altitude, but still climbing at flaps 1. with no prior tcas symbology, with received an instantaneous traffic" (single), superseded by a corrective "level off, level off, level off". as pf i executed the maneuver while disconnecting auto thrust, at approximately .3 g. upon leveling off, i glanced at the nav display and it indicated that there was an aircraft 300 feet (relative) above us, red square +03. the first officer reported the tcas event. the controller acknowledged. approximately 20 seconds later, the controller asked if we "responded" to the resolution advisory and the first officer replied affirmative. we never discussed the event again and proceeded to to our destination."

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported braking abruptly to avoid a collision with a truck while taxing in to the gate at IAH.
text: after landing and approaching gate xx at iah with the apis self park system activated, safety zone clear, and wing-walkers in position, just as the aircraft was approaching the top of the yellow lead-in line, a pick-up truck approached from the right without stopping and drove right in front of the aircraft. the captain was forced to hit the brakes and stop the aircraft to avoid a collision. the driver of the truck somehow was totally oblivious to the commercial jet pulling into the gate area! due to an emergency vehicle stopping traffic near gate xy, (one gate over), the offending pick-up truck was stationary and stuck behind other traffic. we then completed our gate arrival without further incident for an on time arrival.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL
synopsis: A300 Captain reported engine 2 fire loop ECAM on departure. Decision was made to return to the departure airport.
text: during departure from redacted, the aircraft was operating with a deferred item: eng 2 fire loop (no indication as to which loop) along with other unrelated deferrals.shortly after departure, we received multiple intermittent ecam alerts for eng 2 fire loop b. the alert appeared and cleared several times, prompting further review of the aircrafts maintenance history and current status.upon re-examining the aircraft logbook, i noted that a similar discrepancy involving eng 2 fire loop b had been recorded two pages prior out of redacted. the associated maintenance comment indicated the issue had been entered into the maintenance software, however, there was no clear documentation specifying the corrective action taken and if that was the current deferral we had. this lack of clarity made it difficult to determine whether the previously recorded issue corresponded to the currently deferred loop a, or if there had been an error in deferral.i cross-checked the deferred item (di) list and logbook entries and discussed the situation with my first officer. to clarify information, i contacted dispatch, who confirmed that loop a was the deferred system. however, due to the ambiguity in the maintenance records and absence of a clear timeline or action history, uncertainty remained as to whether the correct loop had been deferred or if both loops were potentially inoperative.given the possibility that both fire detection loops on eng 2 could be non-functional, effectively leaving the engine without fire detection capability, we assessed this as a potential safety-of-flight concern. we communicated our concerns to dispatch, including the possibility of an incorrect deferral and the operational implication of having no fire detection on eng 2.dispatch concurred with our assessment and requested a return to redacted, with an amended release issued. the return was conducted uneventfully.upon arrival, we coordinated with maintenance to clarify the discrepancy. after additional review, maintenance confirmed that the deferral was correct and that both fire detection loops on eng 2 were inoperative, loop a having been placed on deferral a while ago, and loop b being inoperative now without deferral. to me this event highlighted a significant gap in flight crew access to detailed and time-stamped maintenance actions and deferral history. the absence of clear documentation regarding when a system was deferred, what exact corrective actions were taken, or whether previous discrepancies were related to current deferrals. it created uncertainty during an in-flight abnormal situation.in my opinion this lack of transparency led to an unnecessary increased cockpit workload during a critical phase of flight by the difficulty of verifying a system status and minimum equipment list applicability.i would like to see an improvement of flight crew access to detailed maintenance records, to enhance our situational awareness and support more informed and timely decision-making.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757-200 flight crew member reported EQPT OVRHT and MAIN BATT DISCH messages in cruise. Flight diverted and landed uneventfully.
text: cruising at fl390 an eicas message popped up that said eqpt ovrht. we ran the qrh with no change in message. then main batt dsch popped up. we ran that qrh procedure and made the decision to divert to the closest suitable field which was redacted. the rest of the divert process was uneventful and efficiently completed.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: EMB-170 flight crew reported uncommanded aircraft movement after arrival to the gate when the Captain failed to properly set the parking brake.
text: leg was briefed and flown as first flight of the day. flight was uneventful until parked at gate. upon stopping, i neglected to set the parking brake (although i thought i had), gave the marshaller the parking brake set sign, and proceeded with the shutdown flow. upon calling for the shutdown checklist, i noticed unusual movement peripherally at the same time the marshaller also noticed the aircraft rolling backward. i immediately applied the toe brakes and brought the aircraft to a stop. i made a pa to request the passengers return to their seats. the aircraft had rolled approximately 10 feet backward and needed to be repositioned. in coordination with the ground crew, we attempted a start of the #1engine. when it failed to start, we started the #2 engine, turned on the #1 hydraulic pump and repositioned the aircraft. i set the parking brake, shut down the engine, and accomplished the shutdown checklist without further incident. cause: this event was caused by my inattention, distraction, and lack of attention to detail. inwardly, i was focused on other shutdown tasks and confirming my next assignment (deadhead to redacted).suggestions: continue to maintain situational awareness until all shutdown tasks are complete. no matter how many times a task in a shutdown sequence has been repeated, confirm switch position and indication after accomplishing a task. always be cognizant of parking brake position and indication. do not pay lip service to checklists!

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: CE-680A Captain reported GPS jamming at cruise in Mexican airspace.
text: enroute mmsl aus, we experienced what was potentially gps spoofing/jamming. we were about 50mi from the coast, ne bound crossing back into mexico when then right pfd (primary flight display) began to tumble and the aircraft began small turns left and right. we immediately put the plane in heading mode to stop the shallow banking and received the following messages: amber both in gps 1, amber adsb out fail, and white att/hdg 1 and 2 fail system messages. i ran the appropriate qrh for the adsb out fail cas, changed transponders, and the cas cleared. after checking the gps sensor statuses, it was determined that the gps 2 sensor was not receiving any information. we asked mazatlan center if they had any reports of gps jamming/spoofing activities, as there had been reports earlier that morning. he was unsure, so i reported it and we continued on. about 4mins after the initial issue, the green path marker on our pfds started roaming around aimlessly and we then received a white surface watch fail cas that went away after a few seconds. since we were actively navigating to a vor, we placed the frequency in and monitored it as a back up in case we lost all gps sensing. approximately 100mi from the coast, all messages cleared and gps 2 began getting information again. we continued with no further issues or erroneous information. upon checking the gps jamming/spoofing website, we found that we had crossed along the edge of an active area.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the UNV Runway 24 PAPI does not align with the instrument approach glideslope.
text: flight abcd, redacted to sce, flew into unv. the weather was ceiling 300 and visibility was 3 miles. the instrument landing system approach requires 1/2 and the dh was 1418 which shows 200. new york center brought us in on the instrument landing system and the previous 2 airplanes ahead of us got in. i've seen this before even in visual flight rules conditions. i saw on the notams that an amendment 10a coupled approaches na below 230ft. on the approach we picked up the lights around dh and descended 100ft down and after that we had the runway environment in sight and landed safely. i have noticed in the past the papis didn't align with the g/s and i did mention that to the unv/atc tower and they said they would get airport maintenance to look in to that. also they mentioned the terrain is a factor as well. from looking at the airport /runway chart i saw that the approach end elevation of runway 24 is 1192 and the approach end of runway 06 is 1231ft and the slope is .06% up from runway 24 side. after we landed and parked at the gate i spoke with the dispatcher about that notam pertaining to no coupled approaches below 230ft and they stated that was good information and would put that information on the release to let other crews know just in case it gets overlooked. suggestions: every release has the notam section which has good information and sometimes i've noticed that the jepp chart has something that the paperwork doesn't and so i would call the dispatcher to see if they see that notam. now dealing with the amendment notam 10a, coupled approaches below 230 ft are not authorized and it's not on the jepp plate of runway 24 but there is a notam for it which might be overlooked especially during instrument flight rules weather conditions. i've noticed at airports such as norfolk they have that on the jepp plate for instrument landing system 05 for no coupled not authorized below 1180ft.maybe this information can be put on the company page or the dispatcher can put that on the release because that notam probably can be overlooked but again i wrote this to bring attention to that threat.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: ERJ 145 First Officer reported that the Captain felt the controls were heavy on take off. Flight continued to destination.
text: we flew an aircraft that had recently had a heavy check inspection and the aircraft was operated normally. the control check was completed and gave no indication to me or the captain that there was something wrong. we had other unrelated maintenance write ups including my seat back and the stab anti-ice inop in icing conditions. the captain after the flight, days later, mentioned to me that on rotation the controls felt heavy." i did not perceive that to mean the controls were improperly placed. it was discovered from the write ups that the elevator cable was misrouted on the aircraft."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported engine high oil temperature indications. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: flight abcd (redacted-redacted) departed at xa:40z with 53 passengers. approximately 12 minutes after departure while climbing through fl220 we encountered a high oil temperature on engine #1. we stopped our climb and ran the qrh n ann engine oil overtemperature procedure. oil temperature continued to rise and decision was made to shut down the engine. we advised air traffic control and requested vectors back to redacted.we accomplished one engine inoperative approach and landing.flight attendants were briefed and passengers were informed.aircraft landed uneventfully on runway xxr at redacted.per request of arff (airport rescue and firefighting) the other engine was shutdown in order for them to safely inspect the aircraft. no abnormalities observed and no evacuation required.operations towed us to the gate with no further incident.here is the maintenance history of this aircraft on the few months preceding this event:day 0 eng 1 exceedance high oil temp - removed and replaced eng 1 oil temp sensorday 5 eng exceedance on landing - r&r (remove and replace) gen i/o mod in mau1day 8 eng 1 exceedance upon landing - removed and replaced w5 harness on lh engday 87 eng 1 no dispatch caution - performed gvi (general visual inspection) of the fmu (fuel metering unit) connector removed and cleaned performed 2 engine runsday 111 eng 1 exceedance on landing - followed fim (fault isolation manual) to clear exceedance messageday 115 eng 1 high exceedance 25 seconds at 255c - performed fim to clear exceedance message, cleaned oil temp sensor, ran engine and monitored oil tempday 116 eng 1 exceedance message on eicas - r&r generic i/o module 1 per ref amm (aircraft maintenance manual). no faults on eicas ops check i/o mod 1 goodday 119 eng 1 exceedance oil temp - r&r oil level/temperature sensor iaw (in accordance with) lmm (light maintenance manual) ops check goodday 121 eng 1 exceedance chronic - cleaned oil temp sensor per lmm performed high power run ops check goodday 142 high oil temp increased while climbing // eng 1 exceedance (pilot action: return to field and landed single engine) - r&r oil level temp sensor and w5 red/green harness

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Aircraft Captain reported a ground vehicle on the runway during approach. Pilot executed a missed approach.
text: i was on the approach into ook airport, already cleared for the approach from on the ground in redacted. i was in contact with another aircraft in the vicinity that was staying out of my way for the approach. as i was inbound, i started making a 10-mile, 5-mile, and 3-mile final call. at minimums, i continued the approach as i had runway environment in sight, as i continued the descent and prepared for landing, i made out a large grader in the middle of the runway on the first third. i immediately did a go around and went missed. after getting myself sorted, i called up the center and explained that i was on the published missed approach. they asked why i went missed, and i said there was a grader on the runway, and asked if i would like to shoot the approach again. the grader then came on the radio and let me know that he was now clear of the runway, and that he had his radio volume turned down, so he didn't hear our calls. on my second approach, i landed without issue and took off without incident.cause: the cause of this incident was the grader's radios being turned down to where he did not hear my inbound radio calls. this, paired with low visibility and ceilings, left me in the dark about whether he was in the runway environment.suggestions: suggestions that could prevent this event from occurring again would be to make sure that the grader's are required to have their radios on and turned up when on the runway, or moving in the runway environment.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: ERJ 145 Captain reported a loss of the EICAS screen during take off. Captain rejected the takeoff and returned to the gate.
text: i am the pilot monitoring, v1 is 132. we were rolling on xx, when reached around 120kts, eicas went blank. i was not sure if we lost all eicas information or just the screens. i saw that we had long runway, so i called 'reject, my aircraft', we did all the check list and made pa, then i called dispatch and the maintenance adviced to return to the gate to have open write up.suggestion: maybe continue rolling taking off then come back and land?

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: EMB-170 Captain reported the flight crew encountered wake turbulence on arrival into EWR in trail of an Airbus.
text: when we passed patrn for instrument landing system 22l we caught a wake from the airbus in front of us and it was enough to click off the autopilot without our actions. we were never informed the traffic we were following. we notify air traffic control about the wake turbulence and was then informed about the airbus and immediately got vectored for heading 190 and received the instruction to maintain 2500 until established. cleared for instrument landing system runway 22l. i had to immediately extend line off of gimme and then capture the localizer from that point. my first officer initiated a timer to time the wake from the preceding aircraft which was an outstanding course of action. when we were short final the timer read :45 seconds therefore it was my decision that we touch down past the airbus's touchdown point which we were unsure if it was past tdz. however, we were able to safely bring the aircraft into a complete stop and vacate at taxiway n.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: DA40 Flight Instructor reported a propeller overspeed on takeoff roll and rejected the takeoff.
text: i am a stage check instructor and person a, a student pilot, had been given a line-up-and-wait clearance for xxr at redacted. person a completed the before takeoff checklist. person a applied takeoff power and called 'takeoff power set'. i observed the rpms reach approximately 2360 rpms and turn red. i advised person a to reduce power to get it out of the red. person a did, and as he returned takeoff power the rpm's went to 2400 and went red. i took controls and advised we would reject takeoff. i notified air traffic control of the rejected takeoff and we were given clearance to turn off of xxr onto taxiway 1. we returned to the ramp without further incident.we did not notice anything abnormal while conducting the runup checklist. the gearbox oil did appear to be at the top of the 'dot' during preflight.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: DA40 Flight Instructor reported engine knocking after takeoff and returned to the departure airport.
text: after rotation out of redacted, we were climbing out when at 300 agl engine knocking and extreme roughness were experienced. rpm stabilized at overspeed 2360, power was reduced. pf and pm continued a climb to 700 agl then immediately reduced power to 50% and flew a low pattern to return to land. previous cleared squawk on the aircraft was for engine knocking as well.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a NMAC while on an instrument approach.
text: coming inbound on the instrument landing system runway xx at redacted, we intercepted glideslope at 3200 at/around redacted faf and aircraft y was at about 3000 feet crossing redacted heading westbound. i saw this and told my student to level off and forget about the approach because if we were to fly the approach how we should have been, we would have had a mid-air collision. i (the instructor) called them up on frequency and there was no response. i called them up on the southwest practice area frequency and there was also no response. i tried again a few minutes later and still no response. when i landed, i looked up their tail number and it looks like they landed at redacted and are a c172 skyhawk.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a NMAC in a Special Flight Rules Area.
text: climbing out of redacted in a left box climb to enter the redacted sfra to the north. at about 4200 ft msl, while making a left turn in the box climb to the east, another aircraft already at 4500 ft msl was entering the redacted sfra to the north as well. we had the traffic in sight at all times but separation was merely 200-300 ft vertically, and about 100-200 ft horizontally. they passed over us and we continued our climb and intercepted the 132 degree radial from redacted vor to continue into redacted sfra behind them.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Light transport pilot reported a NMAC with a non-communicating small aircraft without ADSB when they entered the traffic pattern.
text: upon making several traffic calls beginning from 20 miles south of the burnet airport, we observed another aircraft making calls, this aircraft had no adsb and our tcas was unable to detect it. after several more calls from us about making a left downwind entry to runway 19, we had a near miss with aircraft y who i can presume departed the burnet airport and failed to make traffic calls. evasive action was taken. we made traffic calls 20, 15, 10, 5 and 3 miles before entering the downwind at burnet. i believe that the aircraft was not using ctaf at the time of the incident and the ctaf frequency was clogged by traffic at other nearby airports making it difficult to hear transmissions around the burnet airport. aircraft y made a departure call when taking off on runway 19, then no other calls were observed by us. we could hear other traffic at burnet making radio calls without an issue.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Cirrus SR22 pilot reported entering the runway for takeoff with another aircraft on short final that resulted in a go around.
text: i was holding short of rwy xx at redacted getting my ifr clearance/release for a flight. the field was 1000 overcast. i was on the phone (through my headset) with redacted clearance delivery and radio background noise and poor telephone connection were very distracting and makde for difficult communication. i turned the volume on comm 1 way down to hear redacted. once i got my release, i heard no traffic on ctaf (i didn't realize that comm 1 volume was at zero), and i announced my taxi onto the runway for departure. with a quick glance, i saw no traffic on final and taxied onto the runway. sight of the traffic on final was blocked by the airframe and i gave a cursory, at best, visual check of final. i didn't expect to see any traffic and therefore i didn't. as i turned on the runway, i saw a flash of an airplane overhead and stopped immediately. after a few seconds to analyze what i'd done, i realized that comm 1's volume was at zero. therefore, i hadn't heard the traffice making their calls. unbelievably, i had taxied onto the runway with an aircraft on short final. i realized my mistake, corrected my comm 1 volume, and taked with the aricraft that was on the go and going back into the pattern. i told them of my error and thanked them for being aware and taking corrective action for my mistake. they were quite gracious. i then took quick second to analyze things and decided to proceed with my departure. the rest of the flight was uneventful. background distractions with comm 1 and the telephone both in my headset caused communication difficulties and i turned comm 1 volume to zero. there was a failure to check comm 1 volume before taxiing onto the runway. i felt rushed (self imposed) because of a 5 minute void time, and my connecting flight pilot (leg 3) was up against a tfr at the final destination. i was trying to gain as much time for him as possible. i allowed myself to feel rushed in the moment and made a critical error that could have had terrible consequences. only a cursory glance of final was a factor since i didn't expect to see any traffic because i hadn't heard any radio calls in several minutes. i will not turn the volume on comm 1 or 2 to zero ever again. turn it down a bit perhaps, but never to zero. i have an acute awareness now of the issues with being rushed in the cockpit. i will be very careful to not allow myself to rush. i am incorporating a slow and methodical final cockpit check before taking the runway.a slower and more intentional check of final before proceeding onto the runway will also be a corrective action. i never imagined (wiht my varied experience) that i'd make such stupid and compounding mistakes leading to such an incident. i believe that i am a more diligent, aware and intentional pilot moving forward.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: PA28 Flight Instructor reported an engine failure resulting in a safe return to departure airport.
text: when departing redacted airport in cherokee, an engine incident occurred during the initial climb out. during taxi from the ramp to the runup area just off of runway xxr at taxiway 1, there were no bad engine indications on either the standard engine gauges or the installed engine monitor. the engine runup was conducted, and all indications were normal and in the green, including fuel pressure, oil pressure, oil temperature, and cylinder head temperature. magnetos were also checked and were within specifications. after the runup, we were told to cross xxr at taxiway 1 and hold short of xxl at taxiway 1. before we entered xxl for departure, i verified that the aircraft was properly set up, including the electric fuel pump on, the fuel selector on the fullest tank, and the mixture full rich. we were then cleared for takeoff on xxl at taxiway 1. we rolled onto the runway centerline and smoothly increased power to take off. my student is fairly new, so i pointed to each engine indication and called out each of the following for him. fuel pressure in the green, oil temperature in the green, oil pressure in the green. i then verified with the digital engine monitor. we climbed on the departure leg to 1, 100 feet indicated, then started our left climbing turn out to the southeast. up to this point, there were no indications on the engine gauges other than positive indications. while in the left-hand turn, there was a loud bang and a thump that i felt through my seat. this was followed by shaking throughout the aircraft and the flight controls. oil began spraying onto the windshield. this was followed by smoke filling the cockpit. my first action was to turn downwind and reduce power. i contacted redacted tower and requested a short approach to land on runway xxl. the tower responded, saying they were unable due to landing traffic. i then responded to the tower, informing them that i would need a short approach to runway xxl. the tower then told the landing traffic to go around. i made a left turn toward the runway and landed safely. at the time of the landing, i did not know if there was a fire due to the smoke in the cockpit, so i used full braking power using the parking brake handle and exited runway xxl at taxiway 2. as i was rolling off the runway, i brought the mixture lever back to idle cut, turned the magnetos off, and removed the key. at this point, i saw that there was no fire, and smoke was coming from the hot oil and exhaust gas. i notified tower that we would not be needing emergency services. i then turned off the master switch, opened the door, and my student and i exited the airplane. i, as pilot in command, did everything in my power to properly pre-flight the aircraft, including verifying that the required inspections were complete, required documents were in the aircraft, and the aircraft was airworthy, verifying the engine was running properly before takeoff, and swiftly and safely returning to the airport when the incident occurred. after landing, i inspected the engine and found that the #1 cylinder had cracked and the pushrods had been forced from their seat. there was nothing further i could have done to prevent this issue from occurring.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: E145 Captain reported the flight crew felt it was hard to pull the yoke during takeoff and during the climb in icing conditions; the flight crew received EICAS warnings. It was later discovered that Maintenance had misrouted an elevator cable.
text: hello to respond to the misrouted elevator cable of aircraft x. on day 0 redacted - redacted on the takeoff roll my first officer calls v1 rotate. as i try to rotate the yoke, it was harder to rotate than normal. i pulled my normal weight and we didn't rotate. so i pulled harder which rotated the plane. i told my first officer in the climb-out wow the yoke is hard to pull up." i honestly thought maybe it was just me not trying hard enough or the plane needed more trim. as i moved the trim it was easier to pull up.during our climb we get into icing and got an eicas warning of "ice cond a/i inop" and "stab a/i fail." we ran the qrh which advised us to exit icing conditions which we did. we get to cruise with no further issues. once we land into redacted we wrote the plane up for the icing issues and a couple non-related issues to the elevator. i didn't think much of the elevator. we are writing this report to advise what happened, and since the plane was noncompliant without our knowledge.suggestions: no way us flight crew could have known maintenance have misrouted an elevator cable. i hope this is looked into to see how this could have happened, it could have been serious."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported receiving notification that previous aircraft flown was found to have misrouted elevator cable.
text: on day 0 we flew redacted to redacted and redacted to redacted on aircraft x, as scheduled. both the first officer and captain completed all preflight duties and the flight was commenced. there was no issues on both flights. all flight control surfaces were inspected preflight, all checklists were completed, and flight controls were checked prior to departure. the turn was completed at xa:56 with no issues. on day 0 both the captain and first officer were contacted by a safety manager and were informed that aircraft x had been 'identified to have a misrouted elevator cable, ' which occurred during a heavy check prior to our scheduled flight. there was no sign of flight control issues or capability during our time on this tail number. all logbooks were checked, signed off, and on board the aircraft.suggestions: as the first officer i completed both the pre-flight exterior inspection and the flight control check prior to takeoff. during these normal checks i did not notice any issues with the capabilities of the flight controls. i did not notice any binding or difference to normal operations. the flight was conducted with no abnormal events and we later found out from a safety manager that the plane had an issue 2 days after our flight was commenced.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A320 Captain reported multiple ECAM indications during cruise. Flight diverted and landed without incident.
text: immediately after starting descent from fl340 multiple ecams illuminated: eng 2 epr mode fault n1 degraded mode along with auto flt a/thr off. we had a third ecam but i can't remember what it was. we lost #2 egt and engine pressure ratio (epr). we executed the qrc and then proceeded with the ecam action. i immediately formulated a plan to not go to redacted due to the #2 thrust reverser being inop coupled with a short runway, the current epr issue and fuel possibly becoming an issue, i communicated this with the first officer for his input and he concurred, so i coordinated with air traffic control and asked for holding at fl300 to give more time to work the issue. i was the pilot flying and the first officer was monitoring so we maintained those positions for the remainder of the flight. after finishing ecam actions i had the first officer go to the follow up items as i continued to fly and communicate to air traffic control. after a brief discussion with the first officer i favored the notifying air traffic control option and communicated that with air traffic control followed with souls on board and 1.5 hours of fuel. we did three turns in holding which allowed for us to finish everything we needed to do inside and outside the aircraft to include the comms to dispatch, fas, the passengers and redacted ops to make sure they were ready for us. we setup the arrival and approach and slowly worked towards redacted. we completed all checklists and landed without incident. tower wasn't sure as to our plan for leaving the runway after landing so we told them we would clear immediately after landing. fire trucks still responded even though they weren't requested, followed us to the gate and we shutdown the engines.the first officer and i did a post flight inspection walk around of the aircraft specifically the right engine and saw no anomalies. i communicated with chief pilot who passed on the info to the ioc duty pilot, dispatch informing them the plane was grounded awaiting contract maintenance, and maintenance control due to the out of base write up.the first officer did a great job of remaining calm and helping me work the issue. his input and dedication to the task at hand was perfect and the interaction between us was seamless. side note: major issue with the wording on the ecam vs what's on the switch- wording is mismatched which caused an unnecessary distraction and wasted time in proceeding to the 2nd ecam which was turning off autothrust, which almost led to an mmo overspeed. the ecam says: eng 2 n1 mode oneng 1 n1 mode onwhile we presumed this was actually the full authority digital engine control (fadec)s it doesn't say that and i was concerned about the result of turning them on during flight (it's labeled ground power and a guarded switch for a reason?!) and possibly exacerbating this issue or creating another issue. so i had the first officer scrub the manual to confirm that n1 mode= fadec during holding in an attempt to complete the first ecam action. meanwhile the airspeed was slowly creeping up as we delayed doing the third item of the 1st ecam - move the thrust levers, since we hadn't resolved the 1st two items of the first ecam . this distraction brought us real close to an mmo overspeed but i caught it prior to it occurring. i retarded the thrust levers appropriate to the speed needed. we then circled back to the 1st two items of the first ecam and the search for n1 mode.cause: there seems to be a mismatch of ecam procedures and the name of the switch which should be looked into further.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Diamond DA-40 Flight Instructor reported an NMAC with an aircraft on a crossing runway during final approach.
text: i was the instructor on a visual flight rules instrument training flight flying the rnav runway xx approach to lpv minimums into redacted my student was flying the aircraft under the hood as i operated as safety pilot and instructor in the right seat. before hitting minimums about 2 miles from the airport we were cleared the option runway xx and after the option we were told to fly runway heading. it was very busy at the airport, from the atis i knew they were landing and departing runways xy and xx which intersect. as we continued passed minimums i told my student that he had the airport in sight simulating breaking through the clouds. since we were cleared the option i decided to have my student continue the approach to landing where we would touch and go then continue as cleared on runway heading. as we descended to the runway i noticed a cessna on the ground to our aircraft right rolling down runway xy. i had not been told about any traffic though i had been listening to the tower frequency and had known that the primary runway in use was runway xy. i made the snap judgment that the aircraft had possibly just landed and was about to taxi off the runway which seemed odd since we were so low on the approach. as i continued to watch the cessna on runway xy i noticed it was accelerating and clearly about to take off which would have been right throughout our landing path. i glanced at my ipad which has ads-b traffic information and saw that the plane was company traffic. i told my student the go missed and climb immediately. i then told my student to turn right to avoid the cessna, my student had not seen the cessna as from his prospective the aircraft was to his right and under the nose. my student responded to my command to side step to the right telling me we had been instructed to fly runway heading. i grabbed the stick bumping it right while telling my student there is aircraft below us we need to side step. i keyed the mic announcing we had gone missed. the tower frequency was extremely busy and it was clear the controller was having a difficult time. i chose not to ask what had gone wrong in that moment as i knew it would do no one any good. my student finally saw the cessna as it climbed to our altitude as it passed behind us and to the left. it was clear from the angle that we had been right over each other at some point over the runways and could not have had a separation more than 200 feet. while side stepping to the right i lost visual with the cessna due to the low wing of our da40. after talking to the instructor of the cessna and his student i came to find he was unaware of my presence landing runway xx and did not see us at any point. the classic high wing, low wing conundrum played a roll in this event as i could not adequately maintain visual separation and take evasive action at the same time.if i had not seen the cessna or taken corrective action the separation between our aircraft and the cessna would have been extremely close.i have a few takeaways first for myself, i should have been listening more intently on the radio of what other traffic was cleared to do. i did not know what the cessna was doing until i saw it on the ground accelerating i should have had a better mental picture of the traffic around me.we should not have been cleared the option for runway xx, in my opinion we should have been told to break off and been given a heading prior to the threshold that would have avoided overflying runway xy. i have received this kind of clearance at redacted before and would have accepted it. if we could not fit into the traffic flow we should not have been cleared the approach or not have been told to continue when checking in with tower. it would be frustrating but i would rather be told that we need to break off early than be put into a situation such as this. there is no substitute for looking outside. i have heard this countless times as a pilot and i now fully appreciate why.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: ZTL Center Controller reported being overloaded during a special event with an extremely high volume of traffic that was not predicted or well managed.
text: yet again i have to write a report because the safety culture of management, traffic management unit (tmu), and the command center is severely lacking. the faa does not have safety as its number one priority. they care more about efficiency and running plans to keep stakeholders happy than controller workload and safe sector flow.on day 0 multiple areas in ztl worked extremely high volume traffic that was not predicted or well managed due to the special event. i had already been working steady traffic flow at spartanburg with clt departures and arrivals, and atl departures as well as numerous point outs on ags/aik/dnl/hqu arrivals going into east departure. i was called by the macon sector to say that east 16 had told them to hold ags and i would need to hold one in my airspace, once i got them in the hold i called east to let them know atl departures would be delayed climbing due to the holding pattern, east said we're not holding ags put them on a 180" which i did. not two minutes later macon called again to say we are holding aik, put another in the hold and then the supervisor said were running aik but 25 miles in trail (mit). i called east and they said that they had never been holding aik. this was just the start of an extremely chaotic and unsafe 45 minutes where it became clear that tmu and oms were not aware of the traffic volume and did not have a plan to appropriately mitigate it. the sector spartanburg has a monitor alert parameter (map) value of 14, we started at a 20 and briefly went up to a 24 which is absolutely not safe, an unacceptable risk for no reason.when i finished up with the holding mess i looked back to the east side to see about 8 ags area departures flashing at me all looking for higher and with a mess over overtakes and bad speeds. all of these departures would cross the standard atl departures with everyone wanting higher. i had to vector a few to maintain separation but this was an absolute disaster where my d-side and me were barely holding on to the sector. i left that session feeling extremely stressed and frustrated that we did not get support from tmu and ztl management to stop sectors from being overloaded.this happened because the command center, facility management, and tmu do not care about safety and do not care about sector overload. their number one priority seems to be keeping as many aircraft moving as possible, especially when it involves special events. tmu is forcing normal atl and clt traffic flows which already put our sectors near capacity and then adding significant event volume on top of that, is not a safe combination.additionally we do not have the staffing to support overloaded sectors with d-sides and trackers. we had xx people on this shift and needed two more than that positions open but we couldn't do it.recommendation: when there are special events regular traffic flow must be reduced to not overload sectors, even something like 30 mit off atl and clt would have helped in this case. it is unsafe for a controller to work normal traffic flow plus 100s of additional flights for the special events.from what i can discern tmu has no tools to plan for departures pushes off of smaller airports, especially with a special event they need to be able to see these departures and meter them to manage sector overload. when a sector starts getting overloaded the first move should be shut off departures, re-evaluate the situation and then resume with needed restrictions in place, this did not happen in this event.local facilities need more say on what restrictions to implement from the command center, especially when it involves safety. i can't count how many times i have told an operations supervisor (os) or om that some situation is unsafe but the answer is that's what the command center wants so we have to do it.traffic volume needs to match controller staffing, we need to reduce traffic on low staffed days and this needs to be variable depending on numbers. if we have 9/12 then we should have 75% of traffic volume, this way demand can better meet capacity as opposed to the current method of we will put in a staffing trigger if you are at 50%."no notice holding" needs to be an absolute last resort, we should have the tools to see when too many aircraft will get to an airport at the same time and manage that well in advance to reduce last minute holding and vectors which increase risk.the map is a useful tool but it is too slow to update and does not properly capture departures from small airports. today 32 spartanburg was showing green for most of the day with the exception of the current block that was a red +5 - 10 above map. how can we use this tool to manage sectors if it can't accurately look at departures?overall i cannot wrap my head around the fact that on a normal day if we are 1 over the map number on a combined sector they will split it, if a sector appears red on the board they will add a d-side but on a day like today where we exceeded the map values on multiple sectors we are just a "little busy" and managers say "well we made it through, thanks for the hard work" this is unacceptable we cannot have it both ways. if exceeding map values is a big deal on a normal day than it also needs to be a big deal on special events and weather days. we cannot keep working sectors that are too overloaded to safely separate traffic, someday there will be an error that is unrecoverable."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: ZAB Center Controller reported one of their receivers is unreliable and needs maintenance.
text: 132.8 qow site has gotten progressively worse in last 2 months. transmission that can only be picked up by the site is completely unintelligible, even for aircraft departing from saf. the reliance on the receiver is incredibly high, as it is the only site that can pick up transmissions from the aircraft at low altitude (at or below (aob) fl200). in current state of the audio quality, the controllers on sector 16 can't be expected to provide any meaningful services in the aforementioned area. the transmitter/receiver needs urgent maintenance work.the site needs maintenance. if the site is left in its current condition, it is only a matter of time before an incident happens due to it.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air traffic controller and corporate flight crew reported receiving an ATC low altitude alert when aircraft descended below the MVA during approach.
text: i was training on sector 40/41. during the session, aircraft x was handed off to us from nct with destination to apc. the pilot stated he had the atis for apc. i cleared the pilot direct rribt, a transition fix on the rnav 19r.the pilot said he could not find rribt on the approach plate, i spelled it for him and he was able to find it and go direct. i then cleared him to cross rribt aoa 060 and cleared him for the approach. during this time we were sequencing for sts and went into holding for sfo. we were also discussing sector operations and procedures given that sfo/norcal was in an unusual/uncommon configuration (landing se). at some point my trainer observed aircraft x descending below 059, which was low for the segment of the approach he was on, but still above the mva. my trainer brought it to my attention, at which point the pilot descends below the mva, and we issued a safety alert. the pilot climbs to 045 as instructed, but does not follow the lateral guidance of the approach, at which point i canceled the approach clearance. i vectored him back around for the approach, he flew it with no problems this time and landed at apc.recommendation: confirm pilot is familiar with approach being given. notify pilot of deviation from approach segment altitude prior to it requiring a safety alert.better low altitude alert phraseology. wouldn't have prevented it, but could've been better regardless.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B757 flight crew reported a lead edge and trailing edge flap malfunction.
text: on visual approach to approach to runway xx at redacted, i was pm(pilot monitoring) and line check pilot (lcp) conducting operating evaluation (oe) training for my first officer(first officer) who was pf.(pilot flying). during the approach we were slowing and configuring to land. upon calling for flaps 30, we encountered a wind gust that increased our airspeed and caused a 'flap relief' eicas caution message. i return returned the flap handle to flaps 25 until we got out of the gust and slowed back to return the flaps to 30. at this time we received a 'le slat disagree' and 'te flap asym' eicas caution messages. we executed a go around and per sop retracted the flap handle to flaps 20. the flaps retracted to about 21 degrees and stayed stuck there as we tried to retract them on the go-around. i returned the flap handle to correspond with the flaps at the '20' detent. we retracted the gear and flew the missed approach per air traffic control instructions and remained at 180 kias. we advised air traffic control of our condition and requested priority handling. after completing after takeoff checks we ran the qrh procedures for the above listed malfunctions. they directed us to accomplish an approach and landing using flaps 20 ref + target speeds. we completed all checklists. i spoke to the flight attendants and advised them of our situation and used our brief model. i then spoke to the passengers and advised them of the situation. i sent an acars message to dispatch to advise them of the situation and we were in the pattern for landing and would speak on ground if needed. we finished our briefs and checklists and i took over the aircraft as pf due to my first officer being a student on oe . we then advised air traffic control we were ready to return for landing. they vectored us to a visual approach to runway xyc as we had requested that as a longer runway per our configuration. we landed uneventfully and cleared the runway where we spoke to and were followed to the gate by the airport responding vehicles. we taxied safely to the gate without further incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757 flight crew reported a malfunction of the weight-off-wheels switch and returned to the origin airport.
text: while completing cruise duties at initial level-off and preparing for etops entry, the pm checked the status page on the lower eicas as part of normal system checks. it was then that both pilots noticed the status message 'air/gnd disagree'. after checking circuit breakers, we discussed the meaning of the message and the fact that status messages are not controlling in-flight and do not require crew action. however, we discussed the possibility of the issue developing into an 'air/gnd sys' eicas advisory which drives a non-normal checklist. we considered about 10 minutes into discovering the discrepancy that we may need to air return. we considered the weather forecast at redacted, redacted, and redacted. redacted and redacted were forecasting rainy and gusty conditions with thunderstorms in the vicinity, redacted was dry with light winds. we also considered that if we received the eicas advisory that our auto brakes, auto speed brakes, and thrust reversers would be inop all while navigating near thunderstorms approaching redacted. we completed an hf phone patch to maintenance control to discuss the issue, attempt to gain more awareness about this message, and rope in dispatch to get their latest information about local weather. we researched more and discussed the risks which worked in our favor to burn more fuel to get our gross weight below max landing weight. at about 1+30 into the flight, we decided that the workload to take this potential issue into the islands with unfavorable weather would not be the safest course of action. additionally, the minimum equipment list mentioned that the issue does not have minimum equipment list solutions once on the ground. we coordinated with dispatch, air traffic control, and flight attendants to start heading back to redacted. on the approach, we configured early including gear to see if the ground/flight mode anomaly would appear and force the air/gnd sys advisory. it was a normal approach, however, i noticed that the aircraft sank faster than usual while pulling power during the flare. this may have been because the jet allowed the engines to go to ground idle before touchdown, but i added power to re-establish a normal flare and descent rate then gradually reduced power to idle as the jet touched down. while deploying thrust reversers, the eicas advisory 'air/gnd sys' appeared and remained on until we cleared the runway. we passed all this info to maintenance who was able to capture it in the write up.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported there are too many unsorted NOTAMs for alternate missed approach instructions for the runways at SFO.
text: the sfo vor has been notamed out of service for a while and will continue to be due to construction. because of this, there are also notams for alternate missed approach instructions for instrument landing system 28l and instrument landing system 28r.in my experience, very few pilots are briefing these or even know they exist - because thoroughly reviewing notams is not one of our strong suits. this is partially the fault of the pilots, but primarily the fault of the system. there are way too many notams, many of which are irrelevant to pilots, and they aren't sorted at all. today there are 66 active notams (5 pages) for sfo, and the majority of them are about construction cranes. it's no wonder people miss the important ones.so how can we make this easier, specifically in sfo?i suggest modifying these two notams so they say right at the top applies only to non-rnav aircraft" or equivalent. every jet landing at sfo is capable of using rnav as a primary means of navigation in the terminal area. why are we briefing (or not briefing, as is usually the case) some alternate procedure when we are fully capable of flying the published procedure even with the vor out of service? furthermore, i bet if a jet actually flew the alternate procedure in accordance with the notam, air traffic control might be surprised because they're not expecting that.please forward this to the responsible people in air traffic control. let's work together to simplify things where possible. make these two notams apply only to non-rnav aircraft."

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the airspace around PVU and SPK is congested and the flight crew received an RA and two TAs while on visual approach into PVU.
text: on arrival on the rnav visual runway 31 into provo we got a resolution advisory (resolution advisory) between sivrt and rtchl waypoints. approach controller was alerting us to the traffic and told us he wasn't talking to the aircraft. we obtained visual contact and our paths appeared to be diverging but the airplane was below us and we were descending on the approach in a managed descent. the tcas gave us a level off" resolution advisory so the pf did the memory items, etc. we notified approach that we got an resolution advisory, he asked if we wanted to discontinue the approach and the pf determined that the approach was still feasible without any aggressive maneuvering so we told approach we were going to continue once we were clear of conflict. after clear of conflict we reported that to approach and he switched us over to tower frequency. between the resolution advisory and landing we got two more traffic advisories (traffic advisory). an aircraft was taking off from spanish fork airport, just south of provo, and he must have had an extended upwind leg to trigger the traffic advisory. once we were on final, we got another traffic advisory from an aircraft in the traffic pattern for runway 31. he started turning his right base a bit early and triggered a traffic advisory for us. we landed with no further issues. the airspace around provo and spanish fork is so congested and half the ga aircraft are not talking to anyone. the airspace type needs to be changed to a class c or get a tower at spk to help mitigate a little more."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Challenger 300 Captain reported an inflight shutdown of #1 engine when abnormal noises were heard.
text: we were about 30 miles from destination redacted we were descending through 6000ft spoilers were fully deployed and engines were at idle speed was around 230kts. when i looked at the speed i wanted 250 until 10nm from destination so i slowly brought in power. this was first sign of a problem. we got a weird fluttering noise. brought power back.. i looked at the other pilot said that's not right. i proceeded to stow the spoilers to see if they had anything to do with the noise but they did not. the i slowly added engine power same noise. back to idle. then i added power on the number 2 engine no noise power smooth. next i added power to number 1 engine and it made a lot of noise like a helicopter. at that moment i smelled oil in the cabin. i looked all the engine parameters and both engines in the green and matched up. i then made a decision having the runway in sight and a good number 2 engine to shut number 1 down as to avoid fire or damage . i told person a to use the fuel cut off. he let approach know that we had and engine issue and we shut it down and that we would like straight in to runaway xx. . i joined the ils and on autopilot made the approach even though we were cleared for the visual. we made a safe and secure landing..cause: the aircraft is at maintenance at redacted they have not told me yet what exactly went wrong with the engine.suggestions: stay calm focus on flying the aircraft which i did.
