synopsis: PA-32 flight instructor reported the loss of brakes during landing resulting in a runway excursion.
text: it was a normal introduction training flight with a new student. we did maneuvers heading north from redacted. after introducing the high altitude maneuvers we went into redacted for a few landings. on his first landing he landed past the thousand footers and i told him if he had gone much further i would have had him go around. the brakes didn't indicate a problem and had perfect braking action. we only do full stop taxi backs in the multi at my school per my schools sops. the second lap in the pattern i said we should probably switch runways but someone entered the pattern ahead of us and i didn't stick with my decision so i wouldn't disrupt the other traffic. my student landed well before the thousand footers on the second landing and i told him good work. the brakes initially worked then my student called out that he lost the left brake. i took over after that and i did my best to keep us on the runway while trying to slow us down. by the time i took over i didn't think a go around would be safe so i tried to get us as slow as possible while keeping directional control. at the end of the runway i saw we were going to go off so i gave it full aerodynamic braking and any brakes we had left before going off the runway and i killed the engine with the mixture. we went off the runway, hit a runway edge light and skid into a snow berm the only thing i can see that i could have done better right now is stick to my decision to change runways and avoid a tailwind.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757 flight crew reported door seal failure during climb resulting in loud squeal. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: we departed redacted as normal. there was an minimum equipment list on the aircraft for the aircraft door 4l in which maintenance needed to check the door before flight. on climb out around 17, 000 the rear flight attendant called and said door 4l was making a loud, unbearable sound. i could hear this high pitch squeal from the door on the phone, making it difficult to hear the flight attendant. i took the aircraft controls from the captain so he could assess the situation and talk to dispatch and maintenance control. i stopped the climb at fl270 and coordinated a hold so we could prepare for a return to redacted and burn some fuel, we were overweight for a landing. the captain frequently updated me on details from dispatch and maintenance control. we subsequently requested priority handling and were vectored back to redacted. as a crew, we decided it would be prudent for the captain to fly the approach and landing. we ran the overweight checklist and completed deferred items and landing checklist before landing on xxr (longest runway). crash and fire rescue were standing by at our request. the landing was uneventful. a post flight debrief with the entire crew was carried out. maintenance also inspected the door and informed the captain and i there was a rubber seal protruding from the door.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B777 Captain reported indications of GPS jamming/spoofing. Crew referenced checklist and continued to destination.
text: while on my rest break, one of the relief first officers came back to brief me that the aircraft had lost gps navigation capability. they had experienced several symptomatic indications of a gps jamming or spoofing event but had not received the gps l or r icas messages. symptoms included transponder faults, adsb fault icas, and irs nav only messages on the fmc and the loss of the gps nav indication on the nds (navigation displays). he briefed that they had actioned all checklists and also ran the gps nav data unreliable unannunciated checklist which directed them to select gps nav data off. they also advised dispatch via acars, air traffic control via cpdlc and contacted maintenance. anp drift went to a maximum of 6 and then corrected back to less than 1 once dme dme became available over japan. the decision was made to continue to our destination pek and monitor the system while informing each air traffic control fir of the failure. upon my return to the flight deck, i was briefed that nothing had changed with the gps system and anp was good everywhere we had dme dme reception. we briefed the threats of the downgraded nav capability would have on the approach emphasizing a detailed brief of terrain around the airport. as expected the terrain display was not available. we decided to leave the egpws (enhanced ground proximity warning system) active, but be aware that we may get false warnings and if they became a distraction we'd override that system. we received no warnings during the approach and landing in pek.while we suspect this was a gps jamming/spoofing event, we can't verify that and this may have also been some sort of system fault.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B767 First Officer reported uncommanded aircraft movement during engine start at the gate.
text: we were parked at the hard stand in redacted, which required no pushback, just a straight taxi out. the ground crew told us over headset that they were ready for brake release and engine start. we called ramp control to find out that we just call when ready for taxi. we started one engine, gave the ground crew the all ready and we received the all clear salute. shortly after running the after start flow, i noticed we were slowly rolling forward. i called it out in plain language and immediately the captain applied brakes to stop the roll. once in route, we realized how the error occurred. we were expecting a pushback from the ground crew, so we never reapplied the brakes after they said they were ready for brake release.

synopsis: B737 Captain and Dispatcher reported the flight returned to departure airport after loss of a generator and the APU in cruise.

synopsis: CKB ground personnel reported aircraft guided in right of lead in line to accommodate the jet bridge; bringing into question the design of the painted line.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Mooney M20R pilot reported an alternator failure during cruise. Flight continued to destination and landed safely.
text: was in a cross country trip from redacted to redacted when we experienced an alternator failure. with the reserve battery on board we decided shedding avionics load, and continuing was our best course of action. safer continue to a known airport, with better wx, than force a partial panel into imc conditions. we made our radio calls to redacted [tracon], redacted [tracon], redacted [tracon] letting them know we were gonna lose comms and our plan of action. we lost comms about 30 minutes out from redacted. continue accordingly to the plan made with air traffic control. after we lost comes we maintained vfr until close to our destination. where we swapped to reserve battery, got our gear down, reestablished comms with redacted [tracon] got a vector for our descent through imc. lost comms again, broke out in hole around 3000 foot, then maintained vfr from that point into redacted. called redacted on the cell phone got cleared to land, taxi instructions etc. landed safely at xa:40amno incidents or accidents, no further complication arose.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported taking evasive action to avoid another aircraft during climb.
text: the goal was the transition from san carlos area to the north at 2000'. we had flight following with norcal approach. we requested the oakland transition and were asked if we were planning on proceeding over the oak runway 30 numbers. we confirmed and were told to proceed. as we were northbound to the numbers, aircraft y departed hwd runway 28l below us. they made a climbing left turn (likely per their instrument flight rules clearance) which put them head on with us. when they checked in with approach, approach immediately gave them a traffic call out, and then relayed it to us. at that point we were approximately 1-1.5 miles apart when i made visual contact. the aircraft y crew then advised norcal that they were complying with a tcas resolution advisory. since aircraft y was head-on with us turning left, i also turned left to avoid a closer call.i am not sure what lead up to the problem, as the oakland transition is a common route. we were on flight following and in class c airspace at the time. i believe aircraft y's instrument flight rules clearance/release put them in a position where a midair would be possible despite norcals knowledge of our position.i will give extra attention to aircraft departing satellite airports in busy airspace, especially when transitioning an area commonly used for departures. i fly out of hwd under instrument flight rules frequently so i am aware jet aircraft may be climbing out on the west side of the field.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a NMAC in the traffic pattern at a non-towered airport. Instructor took evasive action.
text: i was in an aircraft that had just completed a touch and go at lvj. we were about 200' agl when i noticed an aircraft tracking eastbound towards the departure end of 14. i began making calls to aircraft y which was the aircraft according to adsb. i received no response despite 3 attempts to make contact on lvj ctaf. after no response and no change in their course i had to break off of the departure leg of 14 at lvj to the right to avoid a collision. they crossed the runway departure end at 700' maybe .5-1nm south of the airport when there were about 5 people in the pattern at the time. they proceeded straight across the departure end with no calls into efd airspace. pearland regional has become a hot spot for near misses like this due to volume of traffic and confinement of airspace. something needs to change such as a control tower to improve the safety of an area that commonly has these kind of avoidable near misses.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Flight instructor reported engine failure in the traffic pattern resulting in the flight instructor landing the aircraft at the airport.
text: engine failure in the traffic pattern. i was the cfi on a training flight with a private pilot student. the whole flight was normal until the final lap in the traffic pattern. we were in the downwind leg abeam the runway and the engine ran rough and lost power. i told air traffic control we need to land asap. as i turned final, the propellor completely stopped and i glided the airplane safely down and made a normal landing and exited the runway on taxiway 1 before coming to a complete stop. no physical damage to the airplane or injuries whatsoever. i think my actions and experience helped me land the airplane safely on the runway preventing any injuries or damage to the airplane.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported an NMAC with a UAS during final approach. The pilot took evasive action.
text: at the end of the second traffic pattern at rnt north flow (rwy 34), we spotted a drone hovering at around 200-300 ft, <0.5 mi from the runway threshold. we had to dive away, passing under by <5 ft. it was a dark grey quadcopter, and it was difficult to spot against the ground clutter until it was just a few seconds away. i don't see much we could've done to identify it sooner or avoid the situation - if i had been scanning my instruments at that point we would've collided. since the uas has remote id broadcast, i believe it would have improved safety if the tower had access to a receiver, even if not all drones would have the transmitter.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: ZDV Air Traffic Controller reported releasing an aircraft off CYS airport without understanding the departure procedures and turning the aircraft on a flight towards terrain.
text: cys usually has an approach, they were tower only. this has become more common and procedures are not spelled out sufficiently. can tower issue rh (runway heading)? can i issue rh? i don't believe so but tower regularly issues rh without requesting or coordinating. it is ambiguous and it is the only airport in my airspace like this and it is an odd configuration that has become more frequent. aircraft was released and cleared as filed after tower requested release. then aircraft checked on asking if they could continue on course and advised they were flying runway heading. i asked the cys controller if the aircraft was issued rh and they weren't sure. then the pilot wasn't sure if that's what he was issued. i cleared the aircraft on course once more, directly, and he turned on course but under the mia. i did not issue a low alt alert. i should have and that is obvious to me now. in the moment it felt very confusing.recommendation: get qa (quality assurance) involved discuss this face to face with those of us who work this airspace, provide clarity on what we are supposed to do and make that same communication with cys tower. cys tower are not faa controllers, they are a dod facility and their knowledge of procedures seems less than ideal.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: ZDV ARTCC reported a situation where two air carriers reported airborne conflicts with weather balloons at FL350 and FL360; resulting in an unsafe environment with ATC not being advised of this balloon activity.
text: at approximately xa:20 on day 0, aircraft x at fl350 reported passing a weather balloon that passed about 1000 ft above them. they later said they were not sure of the exact altitude, but it was 'too close for comfort' they described it as a large white balloon with strings holding a payload underneath it. this was around the ako270010 fix. later aircraft y passed the same balloon at fl360 but described its color as black. this would be about the ako340010 fix. there was another balloon launch earlier in the day which was known and had a transponder on it which was tracked by zdv. this balloon was not reported to zdv, nor did it have a operating transponder. this was also occurring in the arrival corridor for den arrivals on the lawgr starrecommendation: i would recommend that if an organization is going to launch a large free unmanned balloon that they would notify the faa of this launch, especially if it is right in the arrival corridor for den arrivals.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported while flying into an airport with known GPS signal loss flying the GPS approach and losing the signal resulting in the flight crew advising ATC and being cleared for a VOR approach. The flight arrived safely at the airport.
text: shortly before beginning the descent for arrival into pvr, we lost the gps-r and then the gps-l signal (gps-r/l invalid fmc messages). over the last many (6+?) months, i have seen loss of usually one, occasionally both, gps signals in this same vicinity, en route to pvr. the ca and i discussed that we'd both seen it before and that it was a known issue for local air traffic control, and that the signal(s) usually returned shortly. that i am aware of, this is general knowledge only and cannot be found in any jeppesen company pages, pilot bulletin, manual entry, etc. yesterday, the event lasted longer than usual, and in addition to the unable reqd nav perf - rnp message in the scratchpad, it also displayed this message on the navigation display, and the utc time on the clocks was blanked out. we ran the unable reqd nav perf - rnp non-normal checklist and the gps data unreliable checklist, notified air traffic control of our equipment loss, and requested a vor approach. while flying direct to the vor to be vectored to vor final and at approximately 19, 000 feet msl the gps-r returned. we notified air traffic control and were directed to the iaf for the rnav approach. somewhere on the approach the gps-l returned as well and the approach and landing were uneventful. we spoke with a maintenance representative, who was also aware of this issue happening, but he said a good gps reset would just get the gpss back to where they were - there was no indication of an issue on the ground. dispatch was notified. the ca and i definitely had expectation bias that the gpss would come back before we started our descent, which delayed our running of checklists and briefing the vor approach. this gave us a high task load during an already busy time and we needed to pay special attention to briefing the vor approach, which is not an approach we normally do, and has specific safety considerations mentioned on the mmpr company page.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving taxi instructions and not being able to read the instructions back to ATC due to frequency congestion resulting in the flight crew taking evasive action to avoid a collision with another aircraft.
text: after disconnecting from the push crew at the gate, we were given a re-route while waiting for our taxi instructions. i was inspecting the route and coordinating with the dispatcher. during this time we received our taxi instructions from ground but were not given a chance to read back our clearance as ground was extremely busy. many other aircraft were not given an opportunity to respond either. i did not hear the clearance but my first officer did. he read it to me a few times as i missed the call and wanted to make sure i fully understood the instructions. i asked him to try to get a call in to ground to verify it since i hadn't heard it myself. i started my turn to the left after ensuring it was clear. it appeared to be clear at first and i continued the turn as my first officer tried unsuccessfully to call ground. as i continued the turn i saw aircraft y coming down taxiway uniform with no intention on stopping. i had to firmly apply the brakes and was able to stop still on the ramp. we were not given instructions to give way from ground so this caught me off guard. aircraft y did not need to deviate off the taxiway centerline as we were still on the ramp. after they passed we confirmed with ground that the original taxi instructions were correct which they verified. the rest of the flight continued without further incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported on the initial climb experiencing cabin over pressurize situation resulting in the flight crew stopping the climb and returning to the departure airport.
text: during climbout, all indications were normal until right at 8, 000 feet, at which point the cabin began to rapidly over pressurize. initially, the condition was physically noticeable through ear discomfort and a message on the eicas: pressn auto fail. we then referenced the cabin pressure acquisition module (cpam) indications on the bottom of the eicas and became fully aware of the situation.at one point, i observed approximately -3000 fpm on the cabin vsi. eventually the cabin altitude and cabin vsi indications are dashing out yellow on the eicas and the delta pressure rapidly went to 8.0 psi. due to the increasingly uncomfortable and mildly disorienting conditions, i elected to engage alt hold before we even reached 8100 feet and stop the climb. at this point the first officer took over the radios as well and began to inform air traffic control of our intention to hold 8000 feet and for the moment continue on course. manual control of the digital controller was unresponsive and inoperative which led to a cabin dump. after completion of the qrh i knew we would have to return.we were in contact with air traffic control and advised them of the situation, stating our intent to return to redacted. we requested delay vectors in order to reduce weight and arrive within landing limits. the flight attendant had contacted the flight deck when we were still running the qrh and still in sterile, clearly recognizing that something was abnormal with the obvious ear pain and expressed concern from himself and the passengers. i advised him i would provide a special procedure shortly, as we were still managing a high workload at the moment. once workload permitted, with the first officer handling flying duties and radios, i provided the flight attendant with a proper report, explaining that we were experiencing a pressurization issue and would require approximately 30 minutes to land, because we needed to burn fuel, i instructed him to prepare the cabin for a normal landing and deplaning, with no special instructions or brace commands anticipated.i made a pa to the passengers advising that the situation was under control, that the aircraft was safe, and that we would be unable to continue to redacted and would instead be returning to redacted.no cabin aural warnings were triggered, as the event occurred at 8, 000 feet. passenger oxygen masks did not deploy. at no point did i or the first officer declare an emergency, rather, we communicated to air traffic control that we were returning to the field and requested delay vectors to reduce weight. as this was not assessed to be a time-critical emergency, i exercised judgment to avoid an unnecessary overweight landing. we elected to drop flaps 9 and gear significantly early to increase drag and fuel burn to get on the ground sooner and there were no exceedances of any limitations.on final approach, i observed the fire trucks had rolled out. i queried ground regarding this, as no emergency had been declared from the flight deck. it is possible that air traffic control provided priority handling on our behalf, however, this was not communicated to us. after landing, we contacted the fire chief on their assigned frequency and advised that no assistance was required. we then taxied to the gate, parked, and deplaned normally.suggestions: it would be nice to get confirmation from air traffic control on if priority handling was provided on their behalf.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: ERJ 145 First Officer reported receiving a FLAP FAIL notification during approach. Flight crew executed a go-around.
text: after being cleared for the visual approach for runway xxl at redacted airport we were instructed by tower to slow to 170 kts. i selected flaps 9 and extended the landing gear while we were slowing down we received a icas notification stating flap fail". the captain called the go around and i alerted tower we were told to climb and maintain 3, 000 feet. at this time we were around 2, 500 feet so we began our climb and cleaned up the aircraft. we told the tower the reason for the go around was for a flap failure we were then switched to redacted departure. we received vectors to join the down wind while we got set up for another approach. the captain gave flight attendant a a special procedures brief as well as alerted the passengers what the situation was. after that was completed i began to run the flap fail checklist in the qrh. once that was completed we alerted air traffic control and they gave us vector to join the localizer for runway xxl again. the captain also told them we would like to have the fire trucks ready just in case our breaks overheated and caused a fire. once landing we pulled off on taxiway 1 where we waited for the fire trucks to inspect our breaks. they told us they looked to be okay and from our break temp indication they were only slightly in the orange indication. we shut down 1 engine so we wouldn't need to use as much breaks and began our taxi to our gate as normal."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported while flying an approach in gusty crosswind conditions experiencing an unstable approach resulting in a go-around and returning to airport where they landed safely.
text: i was the first officer and pilot flying to redacted, operating aircraft x. during the approach to runway xxl, winds were reported from 160-170 degrees at 10-12 knots, gusting to approximately 18-20 knots.prior to initiating the approach, i briefed the captain that i had limited experience landing in gusty crosswind conditions in this aircraft, as i am new to it. the captain acknowledged this and suggested that completing the approach would provide a valuable learning opportunity, which i agreed to.at approximately 1000 feet agl, i disconnected the autopilot. i noted that the crosswind effects felt stronger than anticipated, requiring continuous aileron inputs to maintain alignment with the extended runway centerline. at 500 feet agl, the aircraft was stabilized in accordance with company criteria.at approximately 200 feet agl, a gust resulted in a brief loss of energy and a slight deviation below the glide path, which was promptly corrected. the correction caused the aircraft to pick up energy. as the aircraft approached approximately 50 feet agl, i assessed that the approach could result in an undesirably firm touchdown. i initiated a go-around, however, during the initiation, the main landing gear made brief contact with the runway, followed by a bounce. i called going around, flaps 9, check thrust while advancing the thrust levers. the captain who was the pilot monitoring said ok but the flaps were still at 45. i reached for the flaps to avoid over speeding them and was intending to retract them to 9 but accidentally got them to 0. landing gear horn started going off. captain took flight controls. a positive rate of climb was established, and the landing gear was retracted. tower was advised of the go-around, and we were instructed to maintain runway heading and 1700 feet, followed by a climb to 3000 feet. climb check was done at acceleration altitude. we were subsequently vectored for another approach and cleared to land on runway xxr. the captain conducted the second approach and landed it. after parking, both pilots visually inspected the landing gear with no visible abnormalities noted. maintenance was contacted regarding a brief, less than 2 minutes, eto reserve thrust, which was reported to have been within allowable limits by maintenance who said it didn't require inspection.suggestions: providing additional guidance on how gust factors should be applied in conjunction with published crosswind limitations for pilots with less than 100 hours in type. clearer interpretation may help crews better assess overall crosswind risk in variable wind conditions.reinforcing collaborative decision-making between pilot flying and pilot monitoring when evaluating approach conditions may further enhance safety margins.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 402 pilot reported on departure the gear did not retract resulting in the flight crew blowing down the gear and returning to the departure airport.
text: i, (captain) was pf. person a (first officer) was pm. captain made a takeoff briefing with the first officer. captain ran the before start checklist and started the engines. startup was normal. during taxi to rwxx, first officer ran before takeoff checklist to the line. captain did the runup holding short of rwxx @taxiway 1. first officer completed below the line. no abnormalities were noted. captain performed takeoff. normal call outs were used by first officer. after first officer called positive rate at around 100 feet, captain put the gear handle up. first officer called out that the gear did not retract. captain confirmed gear did not retract. captain briefed first officer and let them know that they would stabilize the aircraft at traffic pattern altitude and exchange controls with the first officer in order to run the qrh since all circuit breakers (cb) and gear switches were on captain side. captain instructed first officer to tell tower there was an issue and that we would like a south heading in order to troubleshoot the issue. tower approved this. captain commenced a positive change of controls with first officer. first officer flew south heading. captain ran qrh 5.4 and 5.5. captain also briefed the passengers. tower cleared us for right traffic at this point. captain requested we stay in the pattern to continue running the checklist. captain discussed with first officer the checklist that was being ran, and briefed each qrh item before running it. checklist was completed, and within qrh 5.5 the blowdown handle was pulled out. once checklist was completed, captain briefed the first officer to let them know that they would exchange controls again so the captain could make the landing. captain and first officer briefed and decided that there was no need to declare an emergency as the gear was down and locked. first officer commenced a positive exchange of controls with the captain, and an uneventful landing was made. upon landing, captain briefed passengers on the issue being non-emergent. passengers deplaned. captain and first officer completed a walkaround and did not note any abnormalities.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Tecnam P2012 pilot reported on final approach experiencing a right fuel pressure issue resulting in vectors off the approach where the situation stabilized and they landed safely at the airport.
text: arriving into redacted the rvr for xxr dropped to 1000 rvr and i requested for delayed vector. once the rvr improved above 1800, redacted approach was sequencing us for the final. after redacted approach gave the heading of 130 degree near the final approach segment, the right fuel pressure started fluctuating in and out of the red with a rh fuel prs hi crew alerting system (cas) message, the aircraft also yawed towards the right momentarily. the right temporary limited operations (tlo) illuminated. at this point, i informed redacted approach that i was receiving indication of high fuel pressure on my right engine. they asked if i wanted to declared an emergency and that i was next in the approach to land. i informed approach that i would like to hold out and turn in for final. the aircraft system stabilized after awhile at 2300 rpm. i informed air traffic control that the system had stabilized and they asked for souls and fuel on board.cause: mechanical issue with aircraft x.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air taxi pilot reported the crew hatch door opened during final approach. Post-flight; the pilot found the door had separated from the aircraft.
text: i was pilot moniting sitting in the first officers seat. departed with no issues, everything normal. redacted approach instructed us to hold present position for sequencing, approximately 10 miles to the east of redacted. at some point whille holding the door warning light illuminated. there were no signs that any of the doors were open. our initial thought was an indication issue. we did not inform redacted of the door warning light. shortly after the light illumincated redacted started to give us vectors to runway xx. on the base leg approach sent us over to tower. on the first call from tower, they said that we were following another aircraft and that company will be holding in position and to continue. a little bit later tower told us 's' turns were approved for spacing. a few moments later, approximately 1/2 mile to a mile from the runway we heard a popping sound and air rushing into the plane. we noticed the crew hatch had opened. shorlty after that tower gave us the landing clearance for runway xx. we read back the clearance. tower then reapeated the clearance roughly 3 more times. we did not realize it at the time however, the door had knocked off the antenna for comm 1. i pressed the ident button to acknowledge the landing clearance. i tried to quickly set up comm 2 with tower however that wasnt until the landing roll out. i told tower that we were exiting at taxiway 1 and that our door popped open on short final. we taxied to the gate with no other issues. upond exiting the aircraft i noticed that the crew hatch was completely missing. i then turned the radios back on and contacted ground and told them that on short final our door came off.the crew hatch popped open on short final. some how the locking system on the door failed in flight and the pressure caused the door to open.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported experiencing engine performance degradation during climbout resulting in the Captain diverting to another airport where they landed safely.
text: while operating the flight in a tecnam p2012 traveller from redacted, i experienced an approximate 20% loss of power on the left engine shortly after departure. during climbout, i observed degraded climb performance compared to expected aircraft performance.engine indications showed approximately 2450 rpm on both engines, however, the left engine was not producing normal power output. the aircraft remained fully controllable, and no abnormal vibrations or warning indications were noted. the right engine continued to operate normally.as the climb continued, the reduced performance persisted, requiring adjustments to the climb profile. upon reaching cruise power settings, the left engine continued to under perform despite indicating approximately 2100 rpm, confirming that the issue was not transient.due to the sustained nature of the power deficiency and in the interest of safety, i elected to divert to redacted. the diversion, approach, and landing were conducted without further incident, and the aircraft landed safely at redacted. no injuries to passengers or crew were reported.cause: the exact cause of the left engine power loss is unknown at this time and requires further maintenance evaluation. based on the observed symptoms--normal rpm indication with reduced power output--the condition is consistent with a partial loss of engine efficiency or thrust production.a comprehensive inspection and troubleshooting of the left engine and associated systems is required to determine the root cause.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer reported receiving an 'obstacle' EGPWS warning while hand flying an approach in visual conditions after a dual MFD failure. Pilot reported being task saturated resulting in an unstable approach but landed safely.
text: initial descent into redacted, i was pf (first officer) and the ca multi-function flight display (mfd) went black. as we were descending through below 18k ish, my mfd also went black. so now we had no mfds in the airplane. ahead was a few buildups, we did our best visually to avoid these. that being said the ca were both pretty task saturated due to us both losing our usual info. things just felt off when you are missing all mfd info. as we got closer we got our runway assignment, as briefed. we were getting vectors for the visual. all looked okay, as we got our final intercept turn, i noticed the ca never sequenced the flight management system. so this autopilot (ap) was going to blow through the course. as i was visual at around 3k, i disconnected the ap because it was going to be a lot of button pushing rather than just turn and line up. ca cleaned up box, and we were back on track. air traffic control then told us 180kts until 5 mile final. this was a challenge with no mfd and my localizer(i was green needles) not giving me any dme. the ca did something in flight management system to get us distance from runway threshold. in the meantime i am 'heads down' trying to get info from my ipad about what altitude is the faf at and such. obviously this was all briefed in cruise but it isn't something that i had memorized . so we get 6 miles from runway and call gear down. i start slowing and get the flaps 30 just after 5 miles. as i can visually see us close to runway, as soon as possible. i called for final flaps. at this point things are happening really quickly as i am hand flying and very busy. but i recall hearing '1000' prior to having the before landing check completed. i am not sure what our true msl altitude was at the time in relation to height above touchdown (hat). i flew an ugly hand flown approach. as i was mainly following the papi, most of my scan was outside. the ca called 'vertical speed' and i said correcting. when i looked i was at 1.3vs. shortly there after we heard 'obstacle' enhanced ground proximity warning system (egwps) callout. i corrected vs and had an unobstructed clear path to the runway so we continued. the last few hundred feet of the approach stabled out and had an uneventful landing. cause: task saturation, due to dual mfd failure. poor vertical path control by me, pf. in an already busy airport environment, i should have reconnected the ap while on the approach to alleviate task saturation. the faf redacted is relatively low (i guess from what i'm used to). so i thought we had more time than we did. suggestions: use ap for approaches when necessary. make stronger mental notes of charted altitudes/gs intercepts (maybe write them down). incorporate the vsi into my scan below 1k more often. most importantly, go around!

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a loss of aircraft control while the ground personnel were attempting to connect the aircraft to the tug. The flight crew took evasive action to stop the aircraft.
text: we were ready for push and the ground crew said to release brakes. there were two people working on loading the plane onto the electric tug. i released brakes and confirmed green light with them. they loaded the nose wheels onto the tug and raised it. the ground crew did not like the way the nose wheels loaded onto the tug and told me to set brakes. i set the brakes and they lowered the plane and backed up the tug. they repositioned the tug to straighten up their approach. they pulled the tug up to the nose and prepared for another attempt. they said to release brakes and the plane started to coast backwards. i informed them we were rolling backwards and asked if i should set brakes. they said yes and i promptly set the parking brake. it was an abrupt stop. i asked if everyone was okay on the ground and they said yes. i checked with the flight attendants and they said everyone was okay in the cabin. there was miscommunication between the ground crew about when to release brakes.cause: it seemed as though the ground crew did not have a shared mental model about when ready to release brakes.suggestions: when the ground crew reset the tug for another attempt it seemed to flow normally and seemed like enough time for them to prepare the strap and wheel chocks for another attempt. i will be extra cautious next time and double check when ready for brake release especially when the ground crew gets out of their routine.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Pilot reported a NMAC with an aircraft not under ATC control while being vectored for runway 9 at TIX. Pilot mentioned misunderstanding after clearing runway between ATC and pilot.
text: i was being vectored for runway 9 at tix. i had a visual as it looked like air traffic control (orlando) was oversaturated and going to send me past final. i make the call to orlando approach that i had the field and received no response. i finally made contact after a second attempt but i was already crossing the final approach course. as i was cleared for the visual i had to over correct for the late vector by maybe 10 degrees in order to get established for the visual approach. as i was on final i received a traffic advisory resolution advisory to climb. i disconnected the autopilot but had the training aircraft y passing off my left wing by maybe 500 feet and radar showed -100 below. i had flew the rest of the approach with no incident. i asked tower if they had been talking to the training aircraft y and they responded they had not. i told them i had received a conflict but had a visual resolution. after landing tower told me to turn right on runway 18 and contact ground. after exiting runway 9 and turning right onto runway 18 i contacted ground. after several attempts i was able to get a response. they asked why i kept moving on a closed runway. i told them i had been told to turn right on runway 18 and contact ground which i had done. they told me i was supposed to stop and contact ground. no notams showed runway 18 had been closed and as far as i knew it was still an active runway and i made my was to taxiway echo to come to a stop once cleared of 18. i don't recall seeing a runway clearance line on runway 18 showing i had cleared runway 9. i debated sending in this report but safety is my absolute number one priority and i want to be the best aviator i can be.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: DHC-6 pilot reported gusty crosswinds for landing resulted in a runway excursion. Aircraft was taxied to the ramp.
text: runway xx. last reported wind: 250 at 10, gusting 20. demonstrated crosswind component and company standard for captains is 25 kts.we were hit by significant crosswind on landing. initially added slight power while in flare to stabilize before touchdown. touched down on centerline and corrected a slight swerve. was then hit by a significant crosswind component from the left. despite left aileron deflection, right rudder, differential power (right engine in deep reverse), and right brake applied, the aircraft tilted forward and to the right, traveling on the nose-wheel and right main tire. the aircraft slowly moved to the left and exited the runway. the left main then came down. shortly afterwards, i applied full reverse on both engines and locked both brakes in the soft ground, bringing the aircraft to a stop between the runway and parallel taxiway. we crew-members checked that each other were ok. we then confirmed that the passengers were ok. both engines appeared to be running normally. after confirming that both main tires were intact, i added power and aft elevator, entered taxiway 1 near the midpoint, and taxied to the ramp. checklists and shutdown were completed normally, and the passengers disembarked. a walk around inspection revealed that the right wingtip sustained damage, including the outboard flap bracket. subsequent observation of the tire marks on the runway asphalt and in the dirt confirmed that the aircraft was sliding at an angle pointed towards the left, towards the wind, for a significant distance.other considerations:1. crosswinds from the west can be partially blocked by a large hangar west of the touchdown point. from there, continuing the landing touchdown and rollout northward can be followed by a very abrupt return of a 'slotted' crosswind.2. runway xy-xz was permanently closed last year.3. the general opinion of those who fly this make and model for my employer is that it has particularly challenging ground handling characteristics.

synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor reported an NMAC while in the traffic pattern. Flight continued to a landing.
text: i was conducting flight training in a cessna 172 at redacted under visual flight rules flight conditions in the downwind leg of the traffic pattern for runway xx. the other aircraft, a t-6 texan appeared overhead approximately 200 to 300 feet above our altitude of 1000 msl. prior to his entry above us and inside of our traffic pattern, i did not observe the aircraft on ads-b or hear any instructions for the other aircraft to overtake us in the traffic pattern. due to the observed close proximity of the texan, i prompted my student to take evasive action and decrease altitude in order to provide separation from the texan. after redacted tower confirmed location and aircraft type, the t-6 texan radioed their entry into the pattern and was then immediately instructed to conduct a right hand 360 in the left downwind as we were cleared to land immediately after the near collision. this near collision did have contributing factors due to the nature of aircraft build as the 172's upward visibility is limited due to its wing location, and also the similar aspect of the t6 texans, low wing configuration contributing to its lack of downward visibility.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported vacuum driven heading indicator was failing resulted in heading deviations and loss of situational awareness. Pilot also mentioned ATC displayed lack of professionalism and concern by making disparaging remarks.
text: i was operating aircraft x on an instrument flight rules flight departing sna on a leg of a personal instrument flight rules proficiency flight. during the initial climb, i experienced a loss of situational awareness resulting in a heading deviation.prior to takeoff, during the run-up, all instruments appeared operational. however, approximately 3-5 minutes later, while holding short of the runway, i observed that the vacuum-driven heading indicator had drifted. i reset the heading indicator to the runway heading prior to takeoff and set the heading bug to the assigned departure heading of 220°.aircraft instrument lighting was suboptimal. the magnetic compass was difficult to read due to inadequate illumination.after takeoff, i conducted a normal climb. at approximately 800 feet agl, i requested and received approval from the tower to begin a right turn and was subsequently handed off to socal tracon. during the turn, i misinterpreted the heading indicator. instead of recognizing that the heading indicator was indicating that 220° was to the left, i initiated a right turn as previously instructed by the clearance delivery controller, resulting in a 100° deviation towards a heading of approximately 020°, effectively creating a 360-degree turn in the wrong direction.the controller identified the problem and issued corrective headings. during this time, i recognized that the heading indicator was no longer providing reliable information. i informed air traffic control that i was experiencing issues with the directional gyro. at this point the controller engaged in a series of disparaging remarks over the radio adding to the stress of the situation. the controller responded to my notification of the loss of directional gyro with 'i do not care'. this took me aback because this should have let the controller know that for the moment i had no idea of what heading i was truly on. the controller also asked if 'do you know how to fly the airplane?' followed by 'i have to hold departures for you.' conditions were vmc therefore, i switched from instrument flight momentarily to looking outside to gain some sort of bearing on course.due to the poor cockpit lighting, the magnetic compass was not readily usable without additional illumination, requiring the use of a handheld light. this increased workload during a critical phase of flight. after some back and forth with the operation of the aircraft and the controller, air traffic control continued issuing vectors, and i complied using gps-derived heading information. the controller also issued multiple instructions in rapid succession while managing other traffic and attempting to correct my course. i experienced elevated workload and stress while troubleshooting the instrument issue, maintaining aircraft control, and complying with air traffic control instructions. i managed task saturation by focusing on aircraft control and navigation until situational awareness was regained. i transitioned to using the garmin 650 gps display as my primary source of heading information, as it was the most immediately legible and reliable instrument available.the flight continued to the destination without further incident.contributing factors included heading indicator drift and unreliability of the vacuum-driven system. inadequate instrument lighting, particularly affecting compass readability. night instrument flight rules conditions during initial climb, increasing workload. misinterpretation of heading indication leading to incorrect turn direction and increased workload and task saturation during instrument failure and air traffic control vectoring.

text: i was flying towards redacted after overflying redacted approximately 8 miles south of the airport. i called redacted [tower] and was given a recommendation of flying 310 for xxl.i turned to 310 and flew at approximately 2400 un der the bravo west of redacted. i was then told to change to the redacted [tower] frequency which was controlling traffic for xxl. i contacted the controller and advised that i was 310 for xxl. the controller acknowledged this. i was approximately 6 miles sw of the field at 2400 feet under a bravo shelf and outside the redacted delta airspace. redacted was using two runways, xxl and xxr.at about the same time air traffic control was trying to verify if an aircraft was having an emergency. it sounds as though there was a plane was squawking 7700. air traffic control was trying to verify if there was an emergency. it sounds as though there was not an emergency, but a plane was squawking the 7700 code. nevertheless, there was a great deal of radio traffic, and i was unable to communicate with redacted [tower] for further direction. i noted that i was approaching final for xxl. i turned to final approximately 4 miles from the runway. i also descended 400'. i beleive i may have overshot the final by approximately 1000' from the center line. i noted multiple planes in front of me visually and on ads-b.redacted [tower] asked if i was turning final. i indicated that i was. at about the same time, another voice on the frequency advised an altitude alert. another plane that had been directed to turn base was advised to manuever away from me.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: C25B Flight crew reported multiple system failure and engine failure inflight. Landed at destination uneventfully.
text: date: day 0time: approximately xa:10pm location near / before fix zzzzzflight stage: beginning decent description: we had just begun decent from redacted. defog and bleed air was on, and maybe a few minutes after, i got alert to multiple failures: generator, oil pressure, hydraulic, master cautions and warnings. noted right side had no thrust. pushed throttle to test, confirmed. we ran the engine failure checklist. after securing the engine, we notified atc of the engine loss and requested priority handling. they suggested diversion points to our south. i postponed diverting as there is better and known crash fire response at destination, as well as a longer available runway for the next stage of checklist, which is a flap 15 landing. also, weather in area meant we needed to correct course more towards the north. we elected to continue. we were only 15-20 minutes out and had plenty of altitude. i began transfer of fuel at 200lb imbalance, and also utilized anti ice and cross flow as we had to decent through precip. as we descended, i continued to asses the situation. i briefed passengers that we'd had an engine rollback, but all remaining systems are normal and explained our intentions to continue. i initially opted to not attempt a restart for fear of taxing unknown systems faults with the starter sequence, but once we were given our discretion for altitude, i realized i could remain higher, conserve speed, and utilize the steeper decent to get to required restart parameters. i discussed with my copilot, and we agreed to the attempt in decent. we built excess speed of 230kts, and followed air restart procedures. they were successful. i asked her to notify atc we successfully restarted motor, but remained cautious and continued to monitor for any faults. (pic) after restart we got another warning that said 'n1 ref cic' on the fms. we were unable to get a photo before it went away.we made a normal landing, briefing for if the issue returned at any stage of the approach. i then taxied to and parked at vip parking, where we were asked to present documentation for the flight to local officials. i inspected what i could of the motor, and did not note any leaking fluids or score marks on nacel. oil was checked, and was over the minimum line (pic). i contacted our maintenance in redacted to make sure he was in loop, and we'll start prepping plans for either a flight to the service center or on site maintenance.

text: during the times of around xb:00z, there was 2 near misses from aircraft y. the first was easily avoided (xa:54z), as we were on our way direct to redacted. we noticed them on our right side (2500ft, heading southbound. our action of avoidance was to climb to an higher altitude, other a/c continued on course with no change. i broadcasted on the local training frequency multiple times, on redacted.x, with intentions of talking to the pilots but they were not on frequency. 2nd near miss occurred at xb:06z, while we were holding at redacted as published (visual flight rules at 2500ft). aircraft y was on route for a head on collision. tcas alerted us, blaring red for both instances. our course of action was breaking off from our hold course, then climb. after changing course, we observed on our traffic map, aircraft y started a climb into our direction. i took controls from my student and preformed a chandelle to avoid a collision. aircraft y continued to climb, at this point, i proceeded to perform an descent away from the other aircraft's general direction, to gain distance away from them. the other aircraft never changed their course or steered away from our direction in the entire interaction. i broadcasted on frequency more than 3 times and no response.

synopsis: PRC Tower Controller reported an aircraft on short final initiated a go around to avoid an aircraft in position and holding on the runway.
text: aircraft x was in my traffic pattern and was told to continue for traffic holding in position. aircraft y had called up ready at r21r, i told aircraft y to luaw and but before i could give the associated final traffic i realized aircraft x was too close to the runway for a departure to work, so i then said disregard, disregard hold short of r21r. i then went and cleared aircraft x to land, he read back his landing clearance. unbeknownst to me aircraft y had taken and read back the luaw clearance, i did not hear that. a few moments later aircraft x said they were going around for an aircraft on the runway. from the tower to the approach end of r21r it is almost impossible to see a small aircraft on the runway's approach end, so i got my binoculars and at that time i could see what appeared to be a c172 on the runway, and then i had to check the ground radar to see who exactly was on the runway and that is when i realized that aircraft y had luawed. aircraft x reentered the pattern and landed safely and aircraft y took off without incident. recommendation==============we use to have a camera at the approach end of r21r and that helped a lot when it came to actually seeing the approach end of the runway. it was removed after the tower was remodeled in the winter of 2024-25 and was never replaced. because the visibility at the approach end of r21r to the proximity of the tower having a camera placed there is highly beneficial.

text: i am operations supervisor (os) in area during a weather event. our frequency 123.72 has been notoriously bad. the sector that belongs to that frequency is fl240-350. in normal day to day there has been issues with coverage on the north and northwest side. synopsis: B737 F/O reported severe turbulence in cruise resulting in passenger injuries.
text: on an otherwise uneventful flight from redacted to redacted, severe turbulence was encountered south or in the redacted fir. there were no forecast indications in cockpit weather radar or wsi (weather app) of this event. redacted assigned fl 330 for our final altitude. there was a forecast fpg (flight plan guidance) along our route of flight and low level radar returns on both wsi and the onboard weather radar. all indications were that we were topping any radar returns by approximately 20, 000 feet. both captain and first officer determined that actual ride conditions allowed for the seat belt sign to be off and flight attendant up and about the cabin. approximately 80% of the way through this forecast fpg, the aircraft encountered severe turbulence. what started as appearance of mountain wave (i.e. small fluctuations in speed and altitude) quickly progressed into rapid airspeed and altitude changes. unexpectedly the aircraft accelerated into the mmo (maximum operating mach number) tape while simultaneously gaining approximately 1500 feet of altitude. the captain as pilot flying quickly disengaged the auto pilot to more precisely control the aircraft. during the event, i as pilot monitoring instructed the flight attendants to be seated immediately and turned on the passenger seat belt sign. in addition to air speed and altitude fluctuations it was noted that the aircraft entered imc conditions with intense static discharge and fire observed on the windscreens. the captain was able to level the aircraft at approximately fl350. once radio traffic permitted i advised air traffic control of our deviations and requested a block altitude. turbulent conditions continued so we requested and were approved for a turn to the south, as this seemed like the most expeditious manner of exiting turbulent conditions. once the aircraft was again under control, the captain re-engaged the auto pilot system. after a short amount of time of smoother air flight attendants were advised to take their jump seats. after a few minutes of smoother ride conditions, the captain request requested a check-in from the flight attendants who noted that they were all without injury and in their jump seats. a pa was made by the captain asking any passengers who needed medical attention to ring their flight attendant call button, there was no initial response. sometime later closer to our top of descent point a flight attendant called forward advising of a potential injury as a result of the turbulence. medical advisory services procedures were initiated but unable to establish voice contact due to poor connectivity. during descent flight attendant advised of another possible injury. both injured passengers requested no immediate medical assistance but asked for ems personnel at the gate. dispatch was advised of both potential injuries. an elb (electronic flight book) report was submitted via the acars system to advise of the over speed.flight proceeded without incident and landed safely in redacted. ems personnel met passengers at the gate. captain established phone contact with maintenance control.

synopsis: Fractional jet Captain reported making an emergency stop during taxi to avoid a general aviation aircraft operated by a student pilot on a solo flight.
text: after landing on runway xxl at redacted, we vacated south on taxiway 1 and was given a clearance to taxi via 2 eastbound and held short of runway xy. while on 2 approaching the 3 intersection (an over 90-degree intersection), i saw a piper warrior taxiing south at a high rate of speed. i performed a stop and the warrior swerved and continued taxiing on 3 coming to a stop about 100 yards past the intersection. in my estimation, the warrior's right wing came well within 5 feet of the nose of our aircraft narrowly missing us. i couldn't see part of their wing because of how close they were. it is by far the closest call i've ever had and surely would've caused some significant damage had we collided because of the warrior's speed. after a phone call with the tower after the incident, i learned that the student pilot solo in the warrior had been cleared across runway xxl on 3 and into their ramp by the tower controller who was working a lot of traffic in the air on three active runways. we were on ground frequency and did not hear any of the communications with the warrior.this scenario seems to spawn from 1.) the tower controller giving taxi clearances while not running ground and being very busy with in-air traffic 2.) the warrior and ourselves not being on the same frequency 3.) the warrior being behind and left of us in an obscured area not in the direction we were traveling 4.) the warrior being a student pilot.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 402 pilot flying reported a door warning light illuminated on short final and moments later the crew door departed the aircraft. Aircraft landed safely.
text: while on final approach to runway xx at redacted, my crew door suddenly and explosively departed. the door warning" light had come on approximately 10 minutes before while holding between redacted and redacted for traffic to land. captain person a was sitting on the copilot seat and we both verified that the door lock was latched correctly. after three turns in holding, we were cleared by redacted tower to land on runway xx. the crew door departed approximately 500 feet above ground on short final approach. we were flying over the redacted at the time, close to the bridge and the runway. person a tried to assist with radio calls, but when the door departed the aircraft, it took out the top communication antenna and then hit the vertical stabilizer. i did not notice any adverse flying characteristics of the airplane, so i continued straight ahead and landed as close to the runway numbers as possible. only then we had a chance to switch radios and contact tower to let them know what happened.cause: the crew door was properly closed and locked as per the before take off checklist. all annunciator lights were verified off by both of us. the "door warning" light came on approximately 10 minutes before landing. crew door departed the aircraft on short final to redacted runway xx, about 1 minute before landing.suggestions: given this event, i strongly suggest that request priority handling if the door warning light comes on and land. we were lucky that no more serious damage occurred."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Global Express pilot reported either a aircraft avionics or GPS signal malfunction during an RNAV GPS approach.
text: rnav (gps) y runway xx. the approach coupled normally with the correct indications on the scoreboard. the flight director and the fpv (flight path vector) were aligned and looking through the hud (heads-up display) the picture looked good, we were pointed at the aiming point and once we passed redacted at 1500 feet and we started down. at some point i noticed that the picture from my side view did not look correct and i noticed the glide slope move up the hud, i announced this and as i disconnected we got a grd prox warning. i got back on profile immediately but was taken aback by how quickly this happened whilst still being coupled to the approach. we landed normally and taxied to the fbo. on the way out we heard air traffic control call an aircraft who was on the same approach runway being advised that air traffic control was getting a low level alt warning and that pilot copied the transmission.suggestions: i don't know if this was our aircraft system or the gps approach itself. we had apprfms and vgp (visual glide path) all in green, the missed approach alt was set at 1500 feet. but it has given me concern about using vnav or an rnav approach. we flew to redacted and flew a visual approach backed up with the instrument landing system and there was no issues. we are going to fly again this coming week for a pilots landing currency and i'm going to monitor the approaches carefully to see if we have any more vnav or rnav issues.

text: during cruise we heard a loud pop and hissing sound in the flight deck. we called the flight attendant and it was audible on their side of the flight deck door as well. we figured out it was the flight deck observer mask leaking o2. we contacted air traffic control and requested a descent to 10, 000 fee msl and notified dispatch.we were given a diversion airport of redacted. upon getting the oxy lo press the qrh was complied with and we continued the diversion to redacted. we notified the flight attendant of the diversion and landing airport in the descent. the passenger announcement was made upon arrival to redacted and all the passengers were deplaned. aircraft was written up and moved to the cargo ramp in redacted for maintenance to work on the airplane.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue

text: while conducting an instructor standardization flight for instructor candidate person a, i observed a liquid substance emanating from the right fuel cap area, which was highlighted by the position of the sun. i checked the left fuel cap area and did not notice a similar glistening region behind the fuel cap. i asked the instructor candidate his thoughts and he looked at it. the instructor candidate reported that he was able to see bubbling from behind the most rear screw area that secures the fuel lid to the wing. the instructor candidate decided that a return to redacted would be the most prudent course of action considering the circumstances. the instructor candidate called air traffic control and requested to return to the field. i took controls momentarily while the instructor candidate looked through the qrh to confirm that there was no specific action to be taken to resolve this issue in flight. we both continued to observe the amount of fuel in the right tank via the mfd (multi-function flight display) and confirmed continued leakage during the remainder of the flight. upon landing and securing the aircraft a squawk was entered in accordance with policies and procedures. no further action taken.

descent to start upon which we started descending. the first officer noticed the airspeed dropping with a descent on both pilots pfd's (primary flight display). i heard the aircraft accelerating and is the only thing that will facilitate positive change a mass casualty event? suggestions:-close one of the 3 [expletive] airports in city x, take 20% of air traffic out of that airspace, and completely redo the approach/departure corridors. -hire more air traffic control, and not just based on how they look. that is old and we no longer need to pretend that's okay. -stop wearing the complicated nature of city x airspace as a badge of honor. there is no reason to continue to operate with high complexity. i promise, normal humans would be okay if less flights were stacked on top of each other. and don't give me that 'well we need to maximize profit' corporate ghoul speak.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that during initial approach the EGPWS sounded for terrain; too low; gear not down; and more warnings.
text: on vmc approach into redacted, on left downwind for rwy xx, cleared to descend from 5000 to 3000. msa for the area is 3400 feet, and no obstacles on the chart near us. first officer was pilot flying. began descent at 1500 fpm. approximately 4500 feet, received a series of enhanced ground proximity warning system (egpws) alerts - (1) landing gear, (2) too low, terrain, (3) sink rate. first officer executed escape / climb to return to 5000 feet. both crew members had full visual reference at all times and did not see anything or any indication of terrain or obstacles. communicated to air traffic control what happened, resumed descent, and completed normal approach and landing into redacted rwy xx. upon landing, called maintenance, and under guidance, reset egpws circuit breaker, in case it was a fault in the system. to be honest, entire thing seemed like a false alarm, however we complied with necessary procedure.unclear if it was a gpws malfunction or incorrect charts.unclear if it was a valid alert or not. if not, then crew complied with necessary procedure, completed flight under vmc and had no further issues. if the alert was valid, then the charts should be revised to reflect the obstacle or terrain.unclear if there was an unknown obstacle or if there was a fault in the egpws system. reset circuit breaker on ground to mitigate system issues. if valid callouts, then advise revision of charts / safe altitudes because there was no indication that our altitude or trajectory could be a problem. had clear visual references at all times.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the aircraft rolled without the assistance of a tug.
text: this was our first flight of the day and this was my first time operating out of this airport.we had completed our preflight procedures, closed the doors, and began getting ready to pushback. the captain turned on his ramp button and began the process of calling the ground crew for pushback (this is an uncontrolled ramp). after making a couple calls we looked to the lead marshaller who patted his ear twice with a flat hand, and gave us a thumbs down, indicating to us that there was no audio connection and we would need to continue without headsets. we did not receive a briefing beforehand on hand signals.i saw the marshaller give the signal for remove chocks, the captain acknowledged. i then saw the captain signal for brake release. i did not see what the marshaller did in return, but the captain mentioned that we were good to release brakes. the captain then gave the hand signal to initiate the pushback procedure. i did not see what the marshaller did in return as i was heads down continuing to set up some of our radios. at this point i was heads up. the head marshaller then put his hands and wands behind his back, and watched the following unfold without giving us any indication that anything was wrong.the captain and i both believed that we were under tow at this point. we came back what i estimate to be 20 feet, and then came forward what i estimate to be 10 feet, we then came back maybe another couple of feet before coming to a stop. the captain then gave the hand signal to set his parking brake, and the marshaller gave us the return hand signal to set our parking brake, and the parking brake was then set. we then sat there for a couple minutes for the ground crew to disconnect the tug, but couldn't feel or hear anything. finally the captain opened his window to discuss with the marshaller if the tug had been disconnected. the marshaller responded, there is no tug here, you guys rolled back." the captain asked, "we rolled back? there was no tug?" to which the marshaller said, "yes, most people here will either powerout, or rollback and then powerout." the marshaller implied that people before us had done the same thing, which i believe is a major safety violation, and we have no written procedure for.we then started both our engines and continued our flight to redacted without further incident.cause: there were a few main breakdowns in communications between the flightdeck and the groundcrews. the ground crew did not brief us that there was no tug, and that this would be a powerout. the hand signals were not briefed in person prior to event.suggestions: next time if we cannot establish communication via headset with the groundcrews i will follow company procedures, stop what we are doing, and talk face to face with groundcrews. if groundcrews have not talked to us before gate departure, we will go find them and make proper plans. a company page or note about powerout procedures at this airport would be helpful."
