visual flight rules flight following to redacted. i was going a runup, everything was completely normal, mag drop was checked within limits, carb heat was checked, fuel tanks were swapped, all performed by flow, backed up with checklist, nothing was missed in runup. on departure i was cleared into redacted class b airspace at or below 2, 000, however i stayed at 1, 500 to stay away from cloud layers near my intended route of flight. i was cruising at a low power setting, around 100mph indicated and 2, 200 rpm. at approximately xa:00 local, i felt a small amount of engine roughness, which was typical for that specific aircraft. normally, that issue can be fixed by adjusting the power setting, so i did. as a precaution, i also applied carb heat, as well as turning the fuel pump on. the problem went away for a little while. shortly after that, approximately at xa:06 local, the engine started running extremely rough, as well as the rpm fluctuation between 1800 and 2400. the throttle lever immediately became unresponsive, so i immediately started a turn back to the departure airport and advised air traffic control of the amended destination. air traffic control requested fuel and souls on board, as well as asking if i needed any assistance, so i provided the information and declined assistance. i turned back to redacted and started troubleshooting the issue. i made sure my memory items were compete and they were. i referenced the checklist, and everything was complete. i turned the carb heat off, and the roughness went away. i advised air traffic control that the issue had ceased, however, i was still going back to the original airport to troubleshoot more on the ground. i got cleared to redacted right downwind rw xxl for a full stop landing. i exited the runway and parked the aircraft, and completed my shutdown checklist items. i got the airplane put to bed and went home. if i could be in the situation again, i should've requested priority handling due to the immediate threat to safety of flight. i believe a root cause could have been spark plug fouling, because after inspection of the maintenance logbook, it had been approximately 60 hours since the last spark plug service. in the future i feel like there isn't much that can be done to prevent this from happening just due to the fact that there are so many issues that just end up happening with very little control being had from a pilot's point of view.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor reported an NMAC during cruise phase requiring evasive action to avoid a possible collision.
text: i was returning to the airport with my student, we were within 50 feet of a mid air collision with cessna 182, aircraft y. the pilot int he other airplane was person a (ppl). he had 2 kids in the back seats and an adult male in the front seat. we had just announced our position on the radio since we were doing a simulation of an emergency descent. we completed the maneuver and the student started to fly heading east. at this point we had climbed to around 4, 500' and i told him to start turning towards the airport. we tuned into the awos to determine which runway to use and proceeded to go towards the airport. just as i was about to make the next position report, the student banked sharply to the left. i looked to the right and saw aircraft y at the same level on a collision course no farther away than 50'. both my student and i were looking outside the cockpit. i was looking to the left and he was looking towards the front and he was able to spot the other plane coming towards us an oblique angle from our right hand side. i later spoke with person a on the ground. he had just taken off on runway xx and had made a right turn towards the east. he admitted he didn't make radio calls but did say he had heard us make the radio call about the emergency descent simulation. he also said his front passenger was flying the airplane. the other aircraft made no evasive maneuvers. at this time, my student and i decided to discontinue the lesson instead of proceeding to do touch and goes at the airport. i had another cfi get involved and we made sure the student was okay and she also was present during the conversation with person a. person a is known for taking people on flights around the area. he said he did not see us and that his passenger was flying the airplane at the time of the near miss. he did not have ads-b out and we had a conversation about it. he said he was going to look into having it installed in his airplane. he did say that near miss had been too close for comfort but did not seem to be too concerned about what had just happened.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Helicopter flight instructor reported a NMAC with a kite while in the pattern. Pilot took evasive action.
text: on day 0 at xa:25pm (local time) i was conducting a training lesson at wvi - we were practicing normal approaches using a left traffic pattern on taxiway a - parallel runway 20. the pattern was being flown at ~500 agl or 700 msl, inside the fixed wing pattern. on the third lap in the pattern approximately abeam mid field my student and i both noticed an obstruction in front, at or above our altitude, and slightly left. immediately upon seeing the object i took controls and entered a steep evasive bank to the right. passing the object i identified the object as a kite - this kite has been spotted in this spot on other occasions.after evasive action i reestablished stable flight and entered a spiraling approach back to the taxiway and parking area i operate out of.i estimate the kite was within 50 ft of the helicopter and appeared to be overhead as we flew by.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: RV-12 pilot reported a mechanical issue with the engine exhaust manifold separating from the header.
text: the aircraft is used for flight training, but i am the owner and not a student pilot. we had a report of a c0 alert in the aircraft and so the pilot in command made a precautionary landing at redacted on the day 0. when our mechanic was available, we went out to the aircraft on the day 2 and i assisted in his repair of the issue, which was an exhaust manifold separating from the header due to the bolts coming off. we inspected the remainder of our fleet and discovered that the other aircraft also had loose or missing bolts also on the rear exhaust headers, these were accordingly tightened and will be routinely checked.after the repair, i performed a run-up and, satisfied that the engine was operating normally, obtained clearances to taxi out and depart runway xx. just after takeoff, i heard a noise from the engine, and almost immediately started seeing the c0 numbers climb and an alert warning (as the aircraft is equipped with a monitoring system). as the numbers were quickly approaching 100ppm (and did pass them before landing), i opted to return to the field immediately. i had been assigned a straight-out heading, and was unable to reach tower due to communication congestion, but given the situation started my turn anyways, at which point tower contacted me and asked the situation. i explained that we were having engine problems, as we did not yet know what they were, and he cleared me to land. i landed and taxied in without further incident.upon examining the engine, we determined that the exhaust springs had stretched, allowing the muffler to separate from the right side exhaust headers when full power was applied quickly for takeoff (we believe the more gradual application of power in the run-up had not done this). the following day, our mechanic replaced all exhaust springs and re-sealed the system, we performed extensive run-up testing, and i flew the aircraft home without incident and returned it to service.due to the occurrence of loose exhaust header bolts across all the rv12 aircraft, which we believe is being exacerbated by an existing gearbox issue impacting the rotax 912is motor, we are implementing a regular inspection interval of 50 hours on all exhaust header nuts. i believe this should be expanded via an sb (service bulletin) or ad, as applicable, to all 912is-equipped rv12 aircraft, until the situation is better understood. the rv12 has an exhaust system manufactured by/for van's aircraft, and not the stock rotax exhaust, so we have no reason to believe that this issue necessarily affects other models using the same engine.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a UAS during descent on approach. No evasive action was taken.
text: during descent on the rokkr 3 arrival into bur we passed by a blue and white drone within 500ft laterally and less than 100 feet vertically. it passed by our left side and was traveling nw bound, opposite of our direction. once spotted there was no time to react or maneuver the aircraft to avoid the drone if it had become necessary. the location was approximately 10 miles south east of the fillmore vor, just prior to the mikei fix on the instrument landing system z 8 approach into bur. we were at 7000 feet and slowing from 250 kts to 210 kts. it was 2-3ft in size.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757-200 Captain reported loss of the EICAS system during cruise. Flight continued to destination and landed uneventfully.
text: about 12 min before top of descent, at fl290 and 13.0 lbs of fuel. planning to land with 9.6 lbs of fuel, 90 min. the eicas began to flicker before finally just turning off. no message, no warning lights. just no eicas. power remained on the center display, so the standby engine indications were not triggered to turn on. and selecting eicas would transfer the primary navigation to the center screen (showing it worked). however the eicas did not appear on the primary display. it was pretty clear the computer failed. however, the only qrh checklist i found was eicas monitor and eicas display. neither seemed to actually be correct for our exact situation. but after discussing with my first officer, we decided that with no fuel flow indications, and unable to safely determine length of time we could hold. also, no things like oil quantity, hydraulic quantity, no air traffic control indications. we decided that in clear visual flight rules conditions. it was safer to continue and land and not spend excessive time in the qrh or attempt a sat phone call to include company. the manual code that seemed correct was 31-90-05-00. we continued and landed uneventfully and without delay.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a GPWS warning during approach to ELP. Crew executed a go-around and returned for a safe landing.
text: coming into el paso landing east, runway 08r. tower breaks us off the arrival and assigns a 260 heading for the visual. from the arrival and assigned vector, we were arriving on the north side of the airport. during the flight, i warned my first officer of the threats involved with el paso and being known for unstable approaches. this was his first time in el paso, and my first time landing east. on downwind, we tried to slow but the winds at altitude kept us fast leading to the gear being dropped to slow down. both pilots had the terrain feature pulled up for visual reference due to the blinding sun and low level haze layer obscuring the mountain directly ahead. once the sun dropped below the mountain the fog immediate disappeared and the mountain was only several miles away. i recognize it and immediately start a mountain escape with vectors and altitude from air traffic control after i successfully escaped. we came around from the south side and had zero issues and landed 8r.cause: gpws message for terrain west of el paso airport.suggestions: being cleared the visual from the north side for runway 8r is not safe. i have lost sleep realizing how close i actually was. there is zero warning of terrain regarding el paso, no published app procedures for 8r, (due to mountains), but no company pages for suggestions, the aom suggests creating a pbd of 5nm (faf) and 1500 afe to keep a standard 3.0 glideslope. (this is the procedure of a visual approach per the book). that was what i followed, and due to the lack of general company pages on jepp, i had no idea terrain was inside of 5nm. due to the terrain feature being pulled up on my own, it saved us from the mountain. there was no warning, no prior training in visual app, no company pages, new pilots with no experience landing east, and sunlight blinding us as it set were definitely factors. i hope this almost crazy accident is investigated further to realize that landing from the north for runway 8r is way too close for comfort.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported stopping abruptly to avoid a conflict with two airport vehicles driving in front of aircraft during taxi at CLT.
text: we had just finished the pushback procedure and the tug had left from the front of the aircraft. due to a 30 minute departure delay for redacted i opted for a single engine taxi.i called for flaps 1 and we both completed our flows. after the first officer called ramp for taxi clearance i said clear left and the first officer said clear right. we definitely looked both ways before i brought the power up. i then completed the brake check. about a second or 2 after this quick check the first officer said hold on .. stop". or something similar to that. i immediately and abruptly stopped the aircraft while looking over and to my right. to my surprise 2 charlotte operations trucks were in movement in front of us down the painted roadway and kept moving and did not stop. they directly cut us off. if it wasn't for the quick reaction from my copilot i'm pretty sure we would have impacted one of the trucks. the trucks kept moving as if nothing happened. i immediately set the parking brake and got in touch with ramp expressing my frustration and explained to them what happened.cause: it's possible, due to the slow nature of starting off taxiing single engine followed by a brake check, that the driver of the truck either assumed we were not moving or had stopped. i do not remember if i had my taxi light on as i normally do.i think it's always important to keep looking both ways when crossing a painted roadway on a ramp.one should never assume a vehicle is going to stop for you, always anticipate there is a chance they might not be paying attention."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier pilots reported a GPWS obstacle alert and a terrain warning on a visual approach to BOI with temporary cranes near the airport. The pilots performed a go-around then returned for another approach and landing.
text: on day 0, while operating aircraft x from redacted to boi, we were initially planning the rnav (rnp) z runway 28l. my prior examination of the boi notams were confusing for this approach as it stated procedure na" and later provided adjusted specific altitudes for specific legs of the approach. during descent toward the end of the kourt 4 arrival toward littl, air traffic control informed us that the rnp z was out of service due to crane operations. the approach controller offered us a visual to 28l or the rnav (gps) y 28l. the first officer quickly pointed out on our company arrival pages that the rnav (gps) y 28l was not listed as an authorized procedure. finding out it was completely out of service, given our location and workload in mountainous terrain, lack of destination framiliarity/procedures and the offered approach not being authorized, i elected for the radar vectors to a visual approach 28l given the favorable vmc conditions. we accepted radar vectors for a visual approach to runway 28l. to ensure a stabilized approach and maintain terrain awareness in the mountainous environment, i elected to retain the hobsi fix in the mcdu (multipurpose control display unit). i programmed a hard altitude constraint of 3, 900 ft at hobsi (the published faf altitude for the rnp z) to serve as a safety barrier and provide vertical guidance for a 3-degree glidepath. again, we were being radar vectored on to the visual approach in vmc conditions with a final vectors of 260 descend to 3900ft. these vectors pointed us directly to hobsi fix.we conducted the arrival using a managed descent profile toward hobsi with 3, 900 ft set in the fcu (flight control unit). the aircraft was fully configured and on speed just prior to reaching hobsi to meet fom stabilized approach standards and to account for a lack of local airport familiarity. as we were in the managed descent approaching 4, 000 ft, just prior to hobsi, the egpws (enhanced ground proximity warning system) issued an 'obstacle' alert. i immediately verified our position visually and confirmed we were clear of all terrain while the aircraft leveled at the 3, 900 ft fcu altitude. shortly after, at or around hobsi, the system issued a 'terrain, terrain, pull up' warning. although we were in visual conditions and clear of obstacles, we immediately executed the full egpws escape maneuver in accordance with sops. at the start and during the maneuver, i noted that no prominent guidance was displayed on the pfd (primary flight display) vsi.during the climb we made air traffic control aware of the go-around actions, received a heading/altitude assignment and cleaned the aircraft up. we then conducted a briefing to discuss the event and plan the next arrival. we subsequently flew the rnav (rnp) x runway 28l to an uneventful approach and landing. it is my assessment that the crane operations near the approach path likely triggered the egpws logic.cause: a significant factor in this event was the late-stage transition to a visual approach in an unfamiliar, high-terrain environment, which was made more challenging by confusing notam information. the decision to keep the hobsi fix and a 3, 900-foot altitude constraint in the system was a proactive effort to ensure a stabilized descent and maintain safety margins. the election for a visual 28l inadvertently brought the air carrier into egpws threshold for the temporary crane operations even though we were well clear with of any conflict. the limited selection of authorized backup procedures also added to our workload, as we had to quickly adapt our plan while navigating mountainous terrain. based on the timing, unclear notams, mountainous terrain if we had more time at altitude with the issues at hand we could have researched the rnav (gps) y 28l, found it to be legal and optimum to fly. this was discussed post flight with the first officer on how and why we could have flown the rnav (gps) y 28l. again, he did a stellar job looking at the company arrival pages and i was focused on descent inmountainous terrain. it was my decision for the radar vectors to 28l approach based on workload, timing, terrain.to help manage these types of situations in the future, it may be beneficial to clarify ambiguous notams with dispatch or air traffic control as early as possible. when a primary approach is out of service due to temporary obstacles, using a slightly higher vertical buffer than the published faf altitude can provide extra peace of mind during a visual approach. additionally, identifying and briefing a secondary authorized procedure, like the rnav (rnp) x, can help keep the workload manageable if the primary plan changes and in this case if flown would have mitigated this event. a thorough debrief was conducted and the lessons learned in this write up as well as additional items were noted between the two of us."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: A320 flight crew executed an ATC directed go-around and overshot cleared altitude on go-around.
text: we were on approach to xxc when tower cleared an aircraft to takeoff ahead of our landing. we had been given approach and landing clearance but saw it was going to be tight with departing aircraft. tower obviously felt the same and commanded a go around which we did. we were told to turn left to 270 and i heard climb to 6000 which i read back. they was no correction from air traffic control but apparently they had said 4000 feet rather than 6000. after going from tower to approach i feel certain i checked in climbing to 6000 but never received correction or had any idea of there being an altitude deviation at any time.cause: go around are always last second and time compressed. obviously there was a miscommunication. the fact that i heard and read back 6000 instead of the published 4000 should have been a cue. always verify twice an altitude that is different from a published altitude

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: A319 Captain reported executing a go-around to avoid a traffic conflict with an aircraft on the runway; they then experienced a flap overspeed and altitude deviation.
text: during this flight i was the captain and pilot monitoring. on final approach to runway xx at redacted the departing aircraft on the runway began their takeoff roll, momentarily stopped, then began rolling again. tower cancelled their takeoff clearance and directed us to go around. the first officer (pf) had disconnected the autopilot in the descent at 1000ft agl and was hand flying the aircraft during the approach and go around. the first officer immediately initiated a go around at 400ft agl as directed. all initial go around procedures were executed and call outs made. the aircraft was established in a climb, gear up, flaps 3.the aircraft had established a very high rate of climb and we were on the way to the published missed approach altitude of 3000ft. at 1000ft msl the pf moved the thrust levers to the climb detent. also, at 1000ft msl tower switched us to departure frequency. immediately upon establishing radio contact with departure they told us to maintain 2000ft. given our very high rate of climb, both of us immediately focused on altitude awareness and the need to level at 2000ft. both of us reached for the altitude set knob to put 2000ft in the window. eventually, it was set, and 200kts was set in the speed window. the pf began to lower the nose and rate of climb in an attempt to catch 2000ft. at that time, we heard the flap overspeed warning. i immediately set the flaps to 2 and the pf manually reduced thrust and raised the nose to control the speed. the aircraft slowed below flap overspeed and the pf placed the thrust levers back in the climb detent. shortly after that we reached 2000ft, still in a climb. the pf pushed the nose over at 2200ft and began a descent to 2000ft. the aircraft began accelerating again towards a flap overspeed. i raised the flaps to 1 and the pf once again manually reduced thrust. once level at 2000ft and safely below flap overspeed the thrust levers were again placed in the climb detent, and the autopilot was engaged.the flap overspeed was approximately 5 knots, which was confirmed by maintenance during their inspection.cause: the causal factors for this event were a combination of human error, automation management, and task saturation. the initial go around procedures were executed in accordance with sop, but the maneuver got away from both of us at 1000ft with the radio switch to departure. the unexpected level-off clearance at 2000ft was the first distraction that took my attention away from aircraft configuration and speed monitoring. it had the same effect on the pf whose full attention went to altitude control. the high rate of climb and proximity to the new level-off altitude became the primary concern of both of us. so much so that the pf reached for the altitude knob to make sure 2000ft was set in the window as quickly as possible. there was a moment where we both were reaching for the altitude knob and had to establish whose responsibility it was to set it. this momentarily took us both away from the primary flight instruments at a critical time. the result was that we did not configure the aircraft to flaps to2 on cleanup schedule.this failure to continue to maintain the normal configuration schedule was a direct result of task saturation and monitoring error on my part. i allowed my attention to be drawn to the altitude issue and away from monitoring the aircraft configuration and aircraft performance. so, task saturation led to an error in monitoring.additionally, the pf's decision to hand fly the entire go-around with no autopilot added significantly to the workload for both of us. not engaging the auto pilot earlier in the maneuver required significant attention to be paid to basic flight control and added to the task saturation.the first recommendation i have is to utilize the autopilot as much as possible during a busy maneuver like a go around. that allows both crew members to focus on aircraft trajectory, performance, and configuration, rather than monitoring basic aircraft control.the other recommendation is for me as pm to establish crew duties immediately as soon as it gets busy like that. as captain and pm i should have told the pf, since he was hand flying, to concentrate solely on the primary flight instruments and let me listen to departure, set altitude/speed window parameters, and keep him informed of any necessary changes. had i focused his attention back to flying the aircraft immediately, he probably would have caught the overspeed before it happened. i also should have recommended that the autopilot be engaged early in the process.the lesson learned for me is that i need to ensure a very thorough brief on pilot duties and automation management during a go-around. i also need to take a more involved approach during the maneuver to make sure that the pf is solely concentrating on flying the aircraft and controlling its trajectory, velocity, and configuration.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A319-100 flight crew reported ECAM message on departure with notification of nose wheel steering failure.
text: we departed redacted and experienced an ecam: wheel n/w strg fault after takeoff. the first officer and i followed sops in accordance with the fom and aom. i advised our dispatch and we both agreed to continue to redacted. once in-range of destination, we requested priority handling and advised tracon that we would not be able to vacate the runway after landing. we advised operations that we would need a pushback tug to retrieve us. the landing was uneventful and after we came to a complete stop, we coordinated with air traffic control, arff (airport rescue and firefighting), and operations to assist in our transit to the gate without further incident. i wrote up the ecam in the aircraft logbook and advised maintenance control.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Relief B787 First Officer reported uncontrolled aircraft movement after parking at the gate and setting the parking brake. The Captain stopped the aircraft from rolling backwards; no injury or damage was reported.
text: normal flight, arrived at the gate. captain parked the aircraft, set the brake, instructed first officer to shutdown engine l and r and called for the shutdown checklist. ca then stopped the aircraft from rolling backwards. apparently the aircraft rolled backward a few feet and a tug was used to pull us back to parking position. i was the relief pilot for the flight.cause: ensure the 787 fleet parking brake is operating as certified and intended.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported non compliant push back verbiage resulting in nose wheel shear pin damage. Lack of communication then resulted in the aircraft rolling forward because the 'set brakes' command was never given.
text: during pushback i notified the push crew first to standby, " then when cleared by ramp i said "cleared to push tail north". i did not release the brake and i failed to say "brakes released." an unusual sound was heard and i immediately realized that the brake was still set. the push crew stopped the push and investigated for any damage - i informed him that the brake had not been released. they advised that tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. i released the brake and the push continued. about 50 yards into the push the crew stopped and had me set brakes. something was not right with the tow bar and they had to swap it out. once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push. nearing the desired drop point, the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as i waited for the driver to advise me to "set brakes." just then the tug and the aircraft began to roll forward and the driver said "captain brakes brakes." i immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes and stated "brakes set, cleared to disconnect inter phone." i had assumed the aircraft was still being positioned by the tug driver, but perhaps we had been disconnected without brakes being set. on taxiout we entered the hardstand. the first officer researched tow bar pin shear (fom requires inspection) as we both began to wonder if that may have occurred. since we were off gate we contacted dispatch and were patched through to maintenance control. maintenance control did great work to coordinate with redacted maintenance and ops to find out if there was a shear. while we waited in the hardstand the first officer and i decided it best to taxi back to gate and get the nose gear inspected just in case there was a pin shear. we taxied back to gate xx, shutdown and entered an logbook entry. there was notably good collaboration at the gate from our maintenance team including the original ground crew providing their inputs so that the inspection could be done properly. with the inspection complete we departed without further issue.cause: causal was my failure to release the parking brake prior to authorizing the push. my normal habit is to say "standby" after receiving the guide person's "all secure below" advisory, which i did. but when i reviewed the ecam just prior to clearing the pushback i only noted the nw strg disc memo and failed to note the park brake memo. and i didn't state "brakes released" nor did i release the brakes. i am going to add a technique of pointing to the parking brake handle and then to the ecam prior to stating "brakes released, cleared to push." this was suggested by the first officer who has seen other cas using this technique. and while i didn't feel rushed, i think making this process a slower and more deliberate execution will do me well in the future. i'm certain that the drop point rolling issue was part of this cascade from the non standard pushback. the guide person was very quick to catch the issue and call for brakes."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported slow spool up of an engine on takeoff resulting in directional control difficulties and a rejected take off.
text: first officer takeoff. as he spooled the engines up the number 2 engine spooled normal the number 1 lagged. as he went to takeoff thrust aircraft started to veer to the left. i called my aircraft rejected the takeoff and the speed was 18 knotscause: the number one engine took more than normal to spool up and didn't give me enough time to let the first officer know to give it more time

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported loss of a hydraulic system during descent. Crew continued to destination and landed safely.
text: around redacted intersection on the redacted arrival we received an ecam message hyd y rsvr lo lvl. we did an assessment, followed by qrc, ecam actions, qrh follow-ups, and the procedure. we advised air traffic control and requested arff (airport rescue and firefighting) standing by on runway xxl. i notified dispatch of the situation and briefed the flight attendants for a precautionary landing. lastly, i made a pa notifying the passengers of the precautionary landing that would be followed by an exterior inspection from safety vehicles. the subsequent approach and landing went uneventful. after landing arff inspected the aircraft and told us there was hydraulic fluid on the right landing gear. i decided to have arff follow us to the gate for safety and to avoid a possible similar situation as a recent incident. before starting the taxi, i made another passenger announcement to reassure the passengers. after arriving at the gate, the fire marshal came in the flightdeck and updated us on the break temperatures. during deplaning i stood and greeted all the passengers as i do during most flights and i did not observe any distraught persons.cause: i don't have any further recommendations. our training worked great in this instance.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B787 flight crew reported uncommanded aircraft movement after arriving at the gate. Aircraft was brought to a stop and the brakes set.
text: upon arrival at gate, i set parking brake. moments later it was noted that aircraft was rolling backwards. i applied brakes and reset parking brake. ground personnel hooked up tow bar and towed us back to parking spot.cause: assure aircraft completely secured prior to finishing parking/securing check list

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: B737-800 pilot reported engine oil leak during cruise. Crew diverted and landed safely.
text: before departing redacted, i noticed the oil quantity of the left engine to be 16 quarts and the right engine 12 quarts. after we took off, the oil quantity in the right engine dropped to 9 quarts, which i just attributed to oil gulping on the cfm-56 engines. it stayed steady for a while and then fell to 7 quarts, stayed steady there, and then fell yet again to 5 quarts. engine ran normal with good pressure and good temperature. it was at this point i started tracking it. from 5 quarts it dropped 1 quart for approximately every 20 minutes. once it hit 3, we initiated a conference call with dispatch and maintenance control and the decision was made to not enter redacted [artcc] airspace, and turn around and divert to redacted. once turned around, we requested priority handling and requested arff (airport rescue and firefighting). landed overweight, stopped on the runway while the arff vehicles checked out the engine. once given the all clear, we taxied to the gate under our own power via the other engine without further incident. cause: oil leak

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 MAX 8 pilot reported uncommanded continuous roll with autopilot engaged. Pilot disconnected autopilot and landed safely.
text: during descent at approximately 7000 msl and 240 kias in the clean configuration and autopilot b engaged, the aircraft experienced an uncommanded continuous roll to the left. the autopilot turned the yoke to try to stop the roll however it was unable to due to lack of roll authority. roll authority was displayed on the attitude indicator followed by a bank angle annunciation. autopilot was immediately disconnected. full right aileron was used and very slight rudder to correct the cond ition. this initially appeared as if we had experienced severe wake turbulence but atc informed us we were 6 miles in trail of a 737 max. autopilot was re-engaged with the same result shortly thereafter. in each instance, when the autopilot was disconnected, it appeared as if the autopilot had been commanding a continuous control input (perhaps rudder) that then released when the autopilot was disengaged. manual control of the aircraft was used to touchdown.no aircraft limitations were exceeded.cause: unknown cause. suspected mechanical anomally with the flight control or auto pilot system. crew assumed immediate manual control of the aircraft to prevent further upset of intended flight path. i believe this is an example of where the crew immediately maintained control of the aircraft, analyzed the situation and took appropriate corrective action to safely land the aircraft during a transitional period between end of decent phase and beginning of approach phase.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain on short final to SNA Runway 20R reported a small aircraft turned final in front of them for Runway 20L with no advisory from Tower. Reporter expressed concern about the mix of general aviation and commercial traffic.
text: we were cleared from the disnee arrival onto the final for runway 20r and subsequently cleared for the visual approach after calling the airport in sight. i was on the instrument landing system to back us up with automation fully on. somewhere around 1000 feet i visual saw aircraft y, wing up turning final onto 20l. we both dont recall having this traffic pointed out to us. i saw that it appeared they had joined the final. it startled the first officer at first as at first glance it was not clear to him that the aircraft was turning onto final, although i could tell his wing was 'up' and joining. we were dealing with turbulent conditions and a tailwind that at somepoint was supposed to shift to a slight headwind for a landing on a very short runway for us. we quickly overtook the aircraft that was on our wingtip and it became a non factor. we received one tcas traffic advisory for the aircraft at some altitude and possibly too low for an resolution advisory to take place. the speed of aircraft vs a small single engine airplane that it would be really difficult to measure closure rates and to avoid abruptly. we proceeded to have a normal landing. perhaps that one of the most troubling things of all, this was a normal day at sna with an experienced crew that has been to the airport before. we had briefed these multiple threats, were ready for them, and everything went uneventfully. however, it is honestly shocking to me that this is sop at the airport. we are running large aircraft at 160knots on a final to a challenging runway, while very close on our wingtip we have student pilots doing multiple approaches in visual flight rules traffic patterns. if aircraft y had misaligned for final approach, i would have had little time to avoid.cause: i understand that this airport has been operating this way for a long time and to my knowledge mostly uneventful. however, under 'see something, say something' i feel compelled to file this report after having similar experiences in my recent trips to the airport, including at night. with recent revocation of the side by side approaches at sfo, sna to me, is a far bigger safety risk than sfo. we are now reliant on low experience pilots to join onto final in front of aircraft traveling twice their speed. we are putting to much trust in a private pilot to not overshoot the final. student activity and traffic pattern work should not be permitted at the airport. i do not even think 20l should be operational when 20r approaches are being conducted. we have some mentions of the ga activity along coastline in the company pages, but that really does little to express what the first time pilot could expect flying to sna as the traffic isn't isolated to the coastline, it is joining up on your wing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported tail pipe fire after gate arrival and engine shut down. ARFF personnel foamed the engine to extinguish the flames.
text: after aircraft shut down and parking checklist accomplished, the first officer and i had begun disembarking the aircraft.while the first officer was exiting the aircraft during deplaning, and i stood with my bags at the flightdeck door, i heard 4 (or more) chimes which could be either the fas calling the front or the ground crew. i did not see any indication of a call from the fa's, and noticed the ground crew trying to get my attention on the right side of the aircraft. the first officer must have heard these chimes as well as he managed to make his way back to the flightdeck.i opened first officer's side window to talk to ground crew from the flight deck. after about 20 seconds i realized they were indicating a fire in the right engine. looking back toward the #2 engine there was no indication of any fire. no smoke was noted and no flames were visible. routinely, the ground crew will see something and think it is a problem when in fact it is not. the first officer left to investigate from the ground.i saw the first officer return to the right side of the aircraft where i was still located and he indicated there was a fire back there. i still could see no visible smoke or fire from my viewpoint. i queried if he thought fire trucks should be called. the first officer indicated that he believed it would be a good idea to call them out and assess the situation.i immediately grabbed the hand mic (as all our belongings had been stowed and some were on the jetbridge) to call ground and ask them to send the trucks out due to a fire that the ground crew had told us about. i also advised it was the #2 engine that was in question. ground asked a passing by jet if they saw any fire from our #2 engine. the jet confirmed they did see some fire located at the 6 o'clock position of the back of the motor.with still zero visual evidence from the flightdeck of smoke or fire, i proceeded to call the air carrier x maintenance control office to let them know of a possible fire and give them a heads up" of an upcoming aircraft maintenance logbook (aml) entry. by this time, while on the phone with maintenance, my first officer returned to show me a picture he had taken of the fire. it was, in my opinion, not anything major, but had been now burning for approximately 10 minutes. i described the fire to the mechanic through the phone as being between the exhaust nozzle and the rear blades. the mechanic indicated he thought it was a "candle flame". right about the same time, i herd the first officer say, "they're foaming the engine". a quick glance out the window, and i could see foam flying by the first officer's side window. when i indicated this to the mechanic he said that the action of foaming was a big problem and that i needed to find out what type was used for my aml entry. at this point we were nearly deplaned. i did not make any special pa's to the passengers since most the people were already off and all remaining passengers were in the aisle with their bags in hand. the two forward fa's were made aware of the situation by the first officer. the cleaning crew that had tried to come onto the aircraft were told, by me, to leave the aircraft. i had contemplated making a pa but feared at our current point in the deplaning process, the pa could create some unnecessary panic and do more harm than good. i allowed the deplaning to continue normally which took another couple of minutes.after the passengers were off, i got word from the first officer, that the fire chief wanted the apu shut down. all the passengers were off the aircraft at this time and the fa's were gathering their belongings for their layover. we did not have any ground power attached, the apu was shut down as if it was the last flight of the day.the first officer and i went down to the aircraft to talk with the firefighters. we ended up talking to the firefighter that sprayed the aircraft. he mentioned that he had never seen that type of fire and did attempt to spray it with water first, this did not yield the desired result. i assume this to mean that the fire would not extinguishby water alone. he then resorted to the foam and mentioned he also foamed the wing as an extra precaution. when asked the type of foam used for my aml entry, he said it was the "latest and greatest f-3 foam". later he indicated the new foam being used was non-corrosive.having the information we needed and the aml entry complete, the first officer and i grabbed our already packed bags and proceeded to the hotel for our scheduled layover. while walking up the jetbridge i contacted our assigned dispatch at air carrier x to make them aware of the aircraft state and that maintenance had been contacted.cause: during the event a tailpipe fire never entered the conversation. on our return flight we discussed about the potential being there and that neither of us had really witnessed a persistent tailpipe fire, if one exists. myself, i've flown for decades and a majority of that has been in jets. pictures of tailpipe fires and possible expansion of qrc to include all steps if this occurs well after engine shutdown."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 MAX 8 First Officer reported uncommanded roll during descent. Crew disconnected autopilot and continued to an uneventful landing.
text: while near the end of the zzzzzx arrival, runway xx transition, we experienced two uncommanded roll events to the left while autopilot b was engaged. the aircraft was below 10, 000' on the segment of the zzzzzx before the slight left turn at redacted, on the straight-ahead sequence of fixes between redacted and redacted when both of these uncommanded roll events occurred. neither event could be attributed to any change in aircraft configuration, input, or other factor that i can identify, both happened without any identifiable cause. before the first uncommanded roll event, we were descending via the arrival in lnav and vnav with autopilot b engaged. without warning or identifiable reason, the aircraft suddenly began rolling to the left. the autopilot initially stayed connected, and the autopilot system turned the yoke significantly to the right in an attempt to counter the roll. however, the autopilot was unable to stop the roll, the aircraft continued rolling, an amber 'roll authority' displayed on the attitude indicator, and an aural alert sounded (this all happened very quickly--i cannot clearly remember what the aural alert was, since at that point i was already reaching for the disconnect to take recovery actions. my captain later said that he recalled it being a 'bank angle' aural alert). i called out 'my aircraft, ' disconnected the autopilot, and applied right aileron and some right rudder to stop the roll and return the aircraft to level flight. since the aircraft was notifying us that the autopilot's aileron authority alone was insufficient to keep control of the aircraft's bank angle ('roll authority' annunciation), i determined that some amount of rudder was necessary to ensure we could overcome whatever unusual force was causing this uncommanded roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron alone. my inputs successfully stopped the roll, and i returned the aircraft to level flight and re-established the aircraft on the flight path. feeling that the aircraft was now under control, my captain and i searched for any reason why that might have happened and couldn't identify anything. for that reason, we initially suspected wake turbulence. the captain asked air traffic control if we were following a heavy aircraft on the arrival, but air traffic control responded that we were following another 737 max. we did not think that a fellow max miles ahead would cause such an aggressive effect on our aircraft. since the aircraft was stable and showing no further signs of control issues, we elected to re-engage autopilot b to monitor its response. shortly thereafter, the same thing happened: an uncommanded continuous roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron input. i was already prepared to disconnect the autopilot quickly at the first sign of a recurrence, so i did so, applying the necessary inputs to stop the roll and re-stabilize the aircraft. in both instances of this uncommanded roll, it felt as if the autopilot had been commanding some sort of continuous control input that then released when i disengaged the autopilot, because the aircraft was responsive to my control inputs and recovered without difficulty after the autopilot was disengaged each time. since the aircraft annunciated 'roll authority' on the attitude indicator, indicating that 100% of the autopilot's roll authority was insufficient to control the aircraft's roll, i wondered if perhaps the aircraft had experienced an uncommanded rudder deflection that the autopilot was unable to overcome with ailerons, which then released when the autopilot was disconnected. however, that is just a possibility that crossed my mind, we could not identify any cause, nor did i feel any sort of yawing or rudder pedal movement prior to each event. after two uncommanded roll events in a row on autopilot b, we were convinced that we had a genuine problem with something in the autopilot system, as two events in a row like that did not seem like a wake turbulence encounter with anaircraft of the same type that was miles ahead. at that point, we were about to make the turn to redacted to join the instrument landing system course to runway xx, so i continued to hand-fly the aircraft to a safe and otherwise uneventful landing. i experienced no control issues while hand-flying the aircraft. the captain made a logbook entry and notified dispatch after gate arrival, in accordance with company sop.cause: causal factors unknown. recommend thorough maintenance investigation.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported a near miss with another aircraft during taxi at JFK as a result of not being notified by ATC of the crossing traffic. Reporter stated this is a frequent occurrence at JFK.
text: after clearing runway22l after landing, we were giving taxi instructions to proceed down runway 31l to hold short of mb. approaching taxiway ke which goes across runway 31l, we observed aircraft y proceeding across runway 31l in front of us, not slowing down. i braked to a stop, and we asked air traffic control if we should give way to aircraft y, the response was 'uhh, yessssss' we were not told to give way to any aircraft. we did not hear aircraft y receive clearance to cross or to give way to us. until we observed the aircraft cross in front of us we had not situational awareness there would be an aircraft crossing our runway in front of us.cause: this is the third time in 8 weeks that jfk air traffic control has lost track of either my aircraft or others that impede traffic flow until air traffic control is queried for clarification. we have had a mid-air collision and a runway fatal accident due to air traffic control losing situational awareness. what i often hear is 'well, it's jfk', 'it's jfk, that the way it is'. the pilots and air traffic control at jfk are operating under an extreme setting of a systematic normalization of deviation of safe practices, policies, and procedures. it is a daily occurrence to hear colloquial language, american slang, incomplete clearances where the pilot is expected to interpolate what ground control is wanting them to do and were to go, and losing track of aircraft completely. this is not new. reports for years have been filed by pilots. it is time to act. it is time for industry, faa, and air traffic control to make the needed changes.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a Pitot Heat caution message on climb. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: took off of xxl at redacted assigned a 080 heading. right after takeoff, around 2500 feet, we recieved a l pitot heat caution message on engine display 1. the captain flew the airplane while i ran the qrc and qrh. the qrh lead us to the source selector panel and changing the air data source to 2, which created a plethora of red xs on the captain side primary flight display (pfd). the plane briefly climbed through our assigned altitude of 10, 000 feet at this point (reaching 10, 400) so the captain disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the plane back down to 10, 000 and stayed at 250 knots. i asked air traffic control for present heading and present altitude while we troubleshoot an issue. the captain handed me the airplane, transferred flight directors, and ran the qrh themself, leading to the same issue. the end of that checklist led us to the air data failure qrh which led us to the unreliable air speed qrh. it was at this point that we decided it would be best to return to the field. the captain notified dispatch, and then flew the airplane while i briefed the flight attendant on the brief items. we asked air traffic control for vectors back to redacted airport. in my recollection, air traffic control didn't tell us what runway to expect, so the ca directed me to load the rnav for xxl in. i started working on setting up the approach and getting landing performance. as we received further vectors, air traffic control informed us that we can expect runway xxr, so i reloaded the correct approach. at this point, the captain handed me the aircraft while they double checked my work, double checked the unreliable airspeed qrh to make sure there were no signs of discrepancies, and i was given instructions to intercept the approach and a clearance for the visual approach to xxr. instead of clicking approach mode, i accidentally clicked the speed mode button. this prompted the captain to take controls, disconnect the auto pilot, and hand fly the intercept. it initially looked like the captain was lining up for runway xxl, so i clarified with them, and we corrected to the correct runway, xxr. the captain kept a buffer above vref as a precaution for unreliable air speed. once we landed safely and got off the runway, i called operations to get us a gate. once we were stopped with the parking brake set, the captain delivered a pa to the passengers. a taxi to the gate without issue and had maintenance meet us there.cause: i believe the lightning strike that the aircraft suffered the day prior may have affected certain systems that led to this failure. however, i'm not certain.'suggestion: i should've discussed with the captain about declaring an emergency, and taking a little bit more time up in the air to set up the aircraft properly and calmly before commencing the approach. i should've also flown the airplane the entire time while the captain managed the aircraft and the situation. tunnel vision and adrenaline were running high in this situation and i failed to speak up and instead deferred to the captain for decision-making.

synopsis: Cessna 206 pilot reported intermittent radio function. Pilot diverted and landed safely.
text: noticed the 750 navigator start blinking and freaking out. radio became intermittent, i made a call out to traffic in the area that i was loosing electrical power and was coming into land at redacted. the reply was that i was on guard. oops. but a good thing.i lost all electric gauges .on downwind i noticed a plane doing a touch n go and one on the run up area. made a no flap landing turned off the runway with no radio calls, stopped on the ramp and started the diagnosis. found the alt breaker tripped, turned off the master, reset the breaker, turned on the master and saw the amp gauge hit +60, waited till it came down to +30 then turned on the radio and heard someone calling for me saying that center was wondering if i was down and safe. i said yes and thank you. my alt breaker is below the yoke shaft and hard to see and i didn't see the volt amp gauge till later.

text: passing around 27, 000 feet in the descent on the zzzzzx arrival near the redacted point, the aircraft was on command b and in fmc spd, lnav, vnav path. aircraft initiated a very rapid roll to the left and an annunciation of 'roll authority' was given. the aircraft was maintaining around 30 degrees angle of bank but struggling to do so. both pilots recognized the annunciation and called upset. while this does not meet the strict definition of an upset from the company guidance criteria, it was an abnormal situation that the aircraft was struggling to keep up with. automation was disengaged, push and roll inputs were made and thrust was checked. autothrust was reengaged first then command b. the rest of the flight was uneventful and the aircraft was controllable with both autopilot on and off after the event.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier ramp personnel reported uncommanded movement of the aircraft at the gate prior to push back. Chocks were put in place.
text: none of us where familiar with gate xx. so, after loading the aircraft, our lead went to find a push back tractor and in what direction we need to push back. this took a while, and when the lead came back, he told us that the tail of the aircraft is pushed to the left. however, when the lead moved to hook up the aircraft to the push back tractor, he left the nose gear chocks in place. this meant the plane did not move. when our lead saw that, he removed the front chock, and the plane rolled forward uncontrollably. the other ramp agent i was working with immediately placed the chock back. it was then that i learned that the brakes where released, and the aircraft would move freely. in fact, i think the brakes were released before our lead went searching for a push back tractor.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: Air carrier ground personnel reported an indicated lack of braking system for two baggage carts on the ramp that resulting in an uncommanded cart movement.
text: while operations were ongoing on the ramp, two baggage carts that were staged on gate xx became mobile due to strong wind conditions. the carts were not properly secured and had no functioning braking systems. as a result, both carts rolled from gate xx toward gate xy.ramp personnel responded immediately and ran to intercept the carts, successfully stopping them before they entered the non-movement area (nma). no aircraft were parked on gate xy at the time. had an aircraft been present, the situation could have resulted in significant aircraft damage and potential personnel injury.upon inspection, both carts were found to have no operational brakes whatsoever. it is currently unclear whether these carts have been properly serviced or inspected, however, their condition indicates they were not compliant with ramp equipment safety standards.this incident highlights a serious safety gap regarding staged ground equipment on the ramp. sop requires all ramp equipment to be serviceable, secured, and routinely inspected to prevent uncontrolled movement, accidents, or injuries. failure to comply puts all ramp personnel, aircraft, and partner operations at risk.it is imperative that all staged ramp equipmentregardless of vendor or partnerundergo periodic servicing and brake inspections in accordance with sop. additionally, equipment must be properly parked and secured at all times, especially under adverse weather conditions.this event underscores the need for consistent sop enforcement across all vendors and partners operating on the ramp. a lack of compliance by one party creates unsafe conditions for everyone and increases the risk of serious incidents or injuries.

synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported severe turbulence and stick shaker activation during climbout.
text: incident occurred on the climb out passing roughly 9000 feet msl, the ride was constant moderate turbulence all the way from takeoff to cruise with pockets of severe turbulence. passing 9000 feet the captain elected to put the auto pilot in vertical speed mode and climb the plane at a higher rate of climb to climb above the rough air. after doing this, the speed deteriorated close to 205 knots. upon reaching the speed, we encountered a pocket of rough air, which made the pitch limit indicator turn red in the stick shaker engaged for roughly half a second. after this, the auto pilot kicked off, and the captain lowered the nose and gained control of the aircraft. we continued our climb with no more events the rest of the flight.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported ground vehicles on the runway prior to take off. Vehicles exited and flight departed.
text: runway xx-xy was notamed closed till xa:00 with a planned departure of xa:10. asos was advertising ils xx available at approximately xa:08 when we started taxing .we noticed trucks on the runway and called to asked when the runway would be available for use and they reported it would be opened in 5 minutes.we waited, and after approximately 7 minutes later, crew working on the runway radioed that they were clearing the runway. we called center, picked up clearance, and made a call on ctaf that we would taking runway xx.as we were taxing the runway there still appeared to be airport vehicle on the runway and it was dark. they quickly keyed in on the mic an apologized as they exit the runway. as we lined up on the runway i noticed another vehicle on the runway towards the departure end. i stopped and applied the parking brake and the first officer made another call on ctaf. the airport truck got on frequency cleared cleared the runway. we took off with no further incidents.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A320 pilot reported a ENG 2 thrust lever angle ECAM warning on climb. Crew continued to destination and landed with the engine operating at idle thrust.
text: we were #1 for departure and holding short in redacted when we noticed eng2 tla fault on ecam. as i was preparing to call maintenance control, we selected status page and message went away and the navigation display had nothing except normal indication. we cleared status page and ecam no longer appeared and to configuration page was present where all green no blue was present. no sts white flag was present and we selected status page to verify one last time and there were no indications of abnormalities. page was cleared and all was normal. we decided message cleared itself and there was no longer a need to contact maintenance control. we proceeded with a toga to and all went normal. after takeoff from redacted, at 2000ft after flap retraction we had en eng2 thr lvr disagree ecam. we complied with ecam actions qrh. also sat com with dispatch, mx was performed. requested priority handling with air traffic control and a fas were briefed. we continued to redacted as we were 10 minutes away. we landed with eng 2 thr at idle per the qrh and proceeded to gate where a normal deplaning occurred. mx write-ups were performed.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: PIAT pilot reported an engine failure during cruise; probably related to fuel exhaustion.  Flight landed safely off-airport.
text: we planned a time building flight from redacted to redacted to redacted to redacted to redacted to redacted to redacted. this flight took place around xa:00 and was the second flight of the evening, the first went well with no issues. on the return trip around 20 minutes from redacted we decided to proceed to redacted and do a practice approach before continuing on to redacted. we decided on this course of action after verifying with the fuel gauge that we still had roughly 9 gallons of fuel (estimate of around 2.5 hours of flight). after completing an approach at redacted we then planned and flew directly towards redacted. however, on the flight at about 10 nm from redacted at 8000 msl we experienced engine failure. over the course of less then a minute our engine became very rough and had a large drop in rpm, we increased throttle and had no change, and then the engine fully died. we verified that the gauge still read 4 gallons of fuel, the battery still had 13.1v but the oil pressure read 0. the pilot in command for this flight contacted air traffic control and landed in a field close to redacted when it became clear we would not make it to the runway. after landing we verified that we were both unharmed and then contacted emergency services. the main factors that contributed to these events were unfamiliarity with the plane and over reliance on fuel gauges rather than our planning. both the pilot in command and i had flown this plane before but neither of us were 'experienced' in it and while we had both read the poh neither of us were knowledgeable in it. additionally, we should have trusted the flight plan and calculated fuel burn and trusted it rather then our instruments mid flight. what can be done in the future is ensure that pre flight planning is the number one source of planning information and that it is stuck to unless forced to change.

synopsis: Cessna 177 pilot reported suspected static system failure on climb. Pilot utilized alternate static source and returned to the departure airport.
text: on the upwind leg immediately after takeoff from redacted on an sfra/flight restriction zone visual flight rules flight plan with my flight instructor, during initial climb out i noticed lower than usual airspeed. as the airspeed continued to fall below stall speed despite pitching down to recover, i also noticed a frozen altimeter and therefore we suspected static system failure. i then opened the alternate static source, which appeared to restore function to the airspeed indicator and altimeter. we elected to discontinue the flight due to the failure and made closed traffic and returned to redacted. the issue was reported to the flying club's maintenance and the aircraft is undergoing repairs.

text: i launched my drone from the roof of my home and failed to check for tfr. i flew near my home to capture photographs of nearby, emerging weather conditions. after about 20 minutes of flight i noticed stadium lights in the distance and realized there was an ongoing game at the stadium, and i was within the 3 mile radius of a tfr. i immediately returned home to land the craft. law enforcement had arrived on my block and was looking for the craft operator. i talked with law enforcement regarding the missed tfr.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported an NMAC with a light twin in the vicinity of 0A3 airport.
text: departed 0a3 enroute to my home field i was heading west on an approximate heading of 280 in cruise and level at 4500 feet. i observed aircraft y on adsb level at 4500 feet on an eastbound heading of about 050. i was ahead of him and to his right but he never attempted to change course to pass behind me or to seek a proper eastbound cruising altitude. i picked him up visually and realized that he was not going to change course or altitude so i had to take immediate evasive action with a 3g hard left descending turn. i was not able to identify the aircraft i observed. when i attempted to return on course and back to 4500 feet aircraft y decided to turn back into me while heading west and once again i had to take evasive action with a hard right turn. i was monitoring bna approach as well as 0a3's ctaf frequency and never once heard him make a radio call.clearly this pilot had no clue as to what the proper visual flight rules cruising altitudes are or the right of way rules for converging traffic. upon return to base i tried to look up his call-sign but it does not match any registered aircraft so apparently it has no relation to their actual n number.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Object; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Balloon pilot reported noticing single strand power lines shortly before landing. Pilot contacted the power lines; sustaining damage to the balloon but no personal injuries were reported.
text: i was piloting a hot air balloon on a passenger flight. we launched from a field just west of redacted, and our flight path took us approximately 8 miles to the northwest.i was flying a cameron z105 with passengers.weather was clear with visibility greater than 10 miles. surface winds were 7 mph at launch and approximately 6 mph at landing, both from the southeast.the takeoff and flight were uneventful. i approached a large open grass field (approximately 7 acres) to land near the driveway leading from the road to the house. i was approximately 5 to 10 feet above ground level, moving about 6 mph toward the driveway. the passengers and i scanned the area for power lines and poles but did not see any in the field. we did see and discuss the power lines along the road, and we agreed the area between us and the driveway was clear.as we approached the driveway, a passenger and i noticed two single-strand power lines running from the road on our left to another pole north of the house. the lines were about 80 feet in front of us. this occurred at about xa:40 pm, sunset was xb:43 pm. factors affecting the visibility of the power lines would have been background clutter with the background field and trees. the balloon chase crew was also turning onto the driveway at the same time and called out the power lines over the radio. this occurred just seconds after the pilot and passenger noticed the power lines. i immediately opened the parachute valve to put the basket on the ground short of the power lines and allow the balloon envelope to lay over the lines. this is considered a 'rip out' situation as described in the flight manual and the faa balloon flying handbook (faa-h-8083-11b). this is the safest maneuver to perform when contact with power lines is inevitable. if not performed, the basket could have contacted the power lines and injuries, or further damage could have occurred.there were three electrical arcs with two power lines. on the third arc, the fuse on the street power pole opened. the basket came to rest on its side, and all occupants were uninjured. we were able to exit the basket on our own. the balloon remained draped over the power line. there were no injuries to the pilot or passengers.a power company removed the balloon envelope. the power was restored to one residential property. the balloon and equipment were packed and transported to our storage facility. the next morning, i inspected the aircraft. four panels within the first 10 feet of nylon fabric had burns and holes. no load tapes or structural members of the aircraft were damaged. per the continued airworthiness manual, the holes were not required to be repaired because they were below the first 10 feet of nylon fabric.i plan to develop a near-miss presentation to share with fellow pilots and balloon crew members.the envelope has been repaired by an authorized repairman and returned to service. the event arose from late identification of two single-strand power lines along the intended landing path. the balloon was already very low and moving toward the driveway when the lines were recognized, leaving limited time and distance to fully avoid contact.contributing factors- low-visibility hazard: the wires were single-strand and therefore harder to see.- background clutter: trees and the field behind the wires reduced contrast/visibility.- operating environment: landing near a road/driveway/house increases the likelihood of utility spans and service runs that are not as obvious as roadside distribution lines.- expectation/attention: attention was drawn to and discussion occurred about the roadside power lines, reinforcing the assessment that the area between the balloon and driveway was clear.- time/distance constraints: wires were detected at close range (~80 ft) during a low-altitude, high-workload phase of flight.the wires were discovered visually on short final when the pilot and a passenger noticed two single-strand lines spanning from the road to a pole north of the house, approximately 80 feet ahead. the chase crew also called out the lines over the road seconds later as they turned onto the driveway.corrective actions- immediate operational action: pilot opened the parachute valve to execute a stop-short landing ('rip out' procedure) intended to keep the basket short of the lines and reduce occupant risk.- utility coordination: local power company responded, removed the envelope from the lines, and restored power to one residential property.- recovery and inspection: with permission, balloon and equipment were packed and transported to storage.- maintenance disposition: damage assessed, envelope repaired by an authorized repairman and returned.- lessons learned dissemination: plan to develop a near-miss presentation for pilots and crew members.human performance considerations- high-workload phase: approach and landing require continuous control decisions while scanning for obstacles, time available to detect/confirm thin hazards can be limited.- attention management: visual attention may narrow toward the touchdown zone, making small, low-contrast hazards (single-strand wires) easier to miss until close.- team scanning and shared assumptions: having passengers assist with scanning can increase coverage, but agreement that the area was clear can also reduce continued challenge/verification.- lighting/angle considerations: late-day conditions and low sun angle can reduce contrast and increase glare risk (sun angle noted in the report).

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported beginning the take off roll with an aircraft on short final. Pilot rejected take off.
text: i was waiting to take off behind the hold short line for runway xx. i heard on the radio that someone was on final for runway xx but had no visual. i did see another airplane about turn to the left base for runway xx. i looked multiple times and did not see a plane on final. i then heard a plane announce their turn to the left base. i looked again and still did not see anyone on final.assuming (incorrectly) that the plane turning to base had mis-announced final, i announce i was departing on xx and taxied onto the runway and started my roll. the plane on final saw me proceeding and announced an abort. they passed over me about 500 ft in the air and continued down the runway while climing. i cut my engine and exited xx at the first exit.this was my fault. i don't think i looked high enough when searching for the plane on final. i should have trusted what i had heard and waited for the traffic to land and/or asked again to confirm a plane on final.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Diamond DA40 Flight Instructor and student reported propeller over-speed during takeoff resulting in a rejected takeoff.
text: run up was completed with no issues. during takeoff, power was applied smoothly to full throttle and the rpms went into the red, power was reduced but the rpms continued to stay in the red. instructor took the controls and adjusted the power setting but rpms stayed in the red. the takeoff was rejected, power was reduced to idle, and we exited the runway to return to the ramp.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Cessna 172 Flight Instructor reported the throttle cable became dislodged from the forward panel. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: while performing a training flight, i pulled power to simulate an engine out scenario for my student. throttle came out entirely from the assembly. i immediately tried to push it back in but there was no response. power was stuck around 2300 rpm. i immediately took controls and advised to my origin airports tower. i then began preparing for landing. to help with the decent i deployed flaps 10 to help slow down by creating some drag. this worked initially but as we got closer to the airport i realized i was still too high. i deployed flaps full to increase my decent rate. i then decided to take it back a notch to 20 but realized the flaps were stuck. on the ground i could see that the breaker was popped for the flap motor. i landed on runway xxr at redacted l with a strong gusting tailwind. i cut the mixture and pulled the fuel shutoff when landing was assured and landed dead stick. i was able to keep the aircraft rolling and exited xxr at taxiway 1 between xxl and xxr. maintenance personnel told me after the fact that it seemed like the throttle cable snapped giving me no control over the rpm setting. no injuries to myself or my student and no damage other than the cable and possibly the flaps from an overspeed condition.

text: i was flying a general atomics mq-9a uav. after a training event in a restricted area, i was transiting from the restricted area back to redacted, in preparation to land at redacted. i was on an active instrument flight rules flight plan and in communications with redacted center. as we were getting closer to redacted airspace, redacted center requested we descend to and maintain 16, 000, which i complied with. several minutes later i realized we were not yet in the restricted airspace of redacted. i asked redacted center for a climb back above 18, 000, so we would be in compliance with our certificate of authorization (coa). the controller handed me off to redacted control and i made my climb request with them. we climbed back above 18, 000 until we were established in redacted airspace. we then were cleared to descend, and landed at redacted.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: A PCT TRACON Controller reported reoccurring frequency outages on 126.1.
