synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a UAS during final approach.
text: large black quad copter drone was spotted flying north bound approximately one hundred feet above our altitude turning base to final. incident occurred while level at 3, 000 feet, in class b airspace, over the 710 freeway, on visual with instrument landing system back-up to runway 24r at lax.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported failure of aircraft to pressurize during takeoff. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: during takeoff roll started to have popping in ears at high speed. after rotation it got worse and heard wind noise until gear retraction. ears get having to be popped multiple times. i knew something was not normal so i asked to level at 3000 feet so we could check things out. once leveled off we asked for vectors around. we noticed that the cabin pressure matched altitude which indicated no pressurization. we looked for checklists. we had no annunciations on the overhead nor on the recall. after running the cabin depressurization checklist we noticed that everything was normal and the pressurization panel was in the normal operating position. i contacted dispatch and got maintenance control on the line and we exhausted everything. told dispatch that we will be going back to redacted and would be landing overweight. i burned as much fuel as i could before heading back and we had tower roll trucks for precaution. we never declared an emergency. went over the overweight landing section and used the guidance to come in and land on xxr. as soon as we put the gear down the noise intensified beyond normal which further indicated something was wrong. we shot the instrument landing system down and had a smooth landing. we taxied off the runway and had the fire department check the brakes. no hot brakes so we taxied to the gate. wrote up the aircraft pressurization and the overweight landing. at the gate mx (maintenance) came aboard and asked if we had the equip door light on. which we told them we had not seen that light on the entire operation including no door annunciations on recall. they told us that the e/e (electronics/equipment bay) door was open. they then determined that the door annunciation switch was not working and that they needed to replace it.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported multiple bleed duct leaks during cruise. Crew descended and continued to a normal approach.
text: while in cruise at fl300 just prior to top of descent, bleed leak l, c and r eicas messages displayed. associated non-normal checklist bleed leak l, c and r accomplished leading to closing all bleeds and turning off all packs. descent was requested prior to final pack being turned off. clearance was only to fl280. notified air traffic control and clearance received to descend 3000m. during descent max cabin altitude was approximately 6000ft. after descent to 3000m air traffic control was updated and approach and landing flown in accordance with checklists to a normal landing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported strong cabin fumes during climb. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: climbing through 400' after takeoff, there was a very strong fume event in the flight deck which caused a strong burning sensation in our eyes, nose, throat and chest. we donned our oxygen masks and engaged the autopilot. we established communication with the flight attendants and they were experiencing similar conditions. we requested air traffic control assistance, ran the appropriate checklists and did an overweight landing.cause: more maintenance inspections as there seems to be an increased rate of fume events.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: B767-300 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence departing SEA in trail of a large transport that resulted in an abrupt bank angle and a momentary stick shaker. Control was regained and the flight continued normally.
text: on departure from sea the takeoff and initial climb out were normal. while climbing out at normal pitch attitude shortly after flap retraction on schedule we encountered wake turbulence from previous departure aircraft y.the aircraft jerked and instantly banked 20-25 degrees left wing low (my estimation) and the stick shaker momentarily (less than 1 second ) activated. before i could reach for controls the first officer (pf) had already recovered following all company procedures. the entire event lasted 3-4 seconds and the rest of the flight was normal. the first officer (pf) did an excellent job.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown; Ground Incursion Ramp
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a ground conflict with a tug during taxi. Captain brought the aircraft to a stop.
text: upon approaching spot xx on the south ramp in clt, we had a dangerously close call with a tug that was pulling a trailer that crossed the service road in front of us. we had been given instructions from ramp control to proceed on the blue line from spot 16s to spot xy. as we approached the service road near spot xx at approximately xa:28, the tug crossed in front of us. we came to a stop and turned on all of our lights to alert the driver as well as advised ramp control of the incident.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a 'bank angle' warning during climb.  Crew corrected and continued climb.
text: on departure from redacted runway xx l, we were initially given runway heading. after the switch to departure, we were given a clearance to climb and maintain 10, 000 and turn left direct to redacted. i moved redacted to l2 while simultaneously spinning the altitude bug to 10, 000 and asked the captain to confirm the flight management system. he said execute" after verifying, but i mistakenly pressed the wrong button and it never executed. the captain brought my attention to it and while doing so he inadvertently continued banking the aircraft until we heard a bank angle callout which was quickly corrected. the flight continued normally."

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor reported an NMAC during cruise. Crew took evasive action and continued flight.
text: was returning with a student to redacted after doing maneuvers training adjacent to redacted. noticed an aircraft on ads-b to the northwest several miles out. was receiving visual flight rules flight following from redacted [tracon] air traffic control. complied with air traffic control instructions to climb to 4000 feet to avoid traffic. other aircraft was not talking to air traffic control. aircraft disappeared from ads-b but took controls from the student as a precaution and began looking for aircraft. it then reappeared a few moments later, now much closer and less than 500 feet vertical separation. was unable to make visual contact. air traffic control immediately gave me vectors and an altitude to avoid the aircraft, which i attempted, but aircraft continued to converge on me. tried climbing and turning, but aircraft began climbing and following me too. with less than 100' indicated of vertical separation, i reduced power and began a descending right turn per guidelines that converging aircraft shall yield to the right. mindful of not getting too close to the terrain, i leveled out and worked with air traffic control to travel out to the west to avoid any additional encounters with this traffic. in retrospect, i will be a lot more aggressive with modifying my travel direction to avoid non-communicative traffic. instead of making a slight adjustment to my flight path, i plan to more intentionally alter my direction of flight to avoid any close encounters with such aircraft. additionally, i will be more intentional with planning lessons to try to avoid being near untowered airports that may have a greater preponderance of non-communicative traffic.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Cirrus SR20 flight instructor reported a ground conflict with an aircraft on final during takeoff. Flight continued takeoff.
text: a student and i were on a post solo flight to check their work regarding maneuvers and pattern work at an uncontrolled field. we had already completed the maneuvers being evaluated at this point and picked redacted as the uncontrolled field to use for today's lesson. the student executed a pattern entry recommended by the faa in which they overflew the field by 500' agl and enter on a 45 degree to the downwind. the student and i proceeded to continue in the pattern making appropriate radio calls and normal landings/takeoffs while in the pattern. after our first full trip in the pattern another aircraft i noticed had shown up on adsb, aircraft y. i proceeded to have visual contact with the other aircraft as they were cutting through the approach corridor for the runway the winds were favoring and we were using. the current winds at the time were 070 9kts from the redacted atis and the wind sock at the field confirmed this. we had quite a bit of lateral separation from this aircraft due to us being mid-field downwind for runway xx at this point and elected to have the student side-step to provide additional separation just in case. i watched the aircraft turn southbound and was 200' above pattern altitude. this led me to believe it was transient and it was transitioning through the airspace. i lost visual contact with the other aircraft after we turned final and they did not make any radio calls on the ctaf frequency for redacted. focusing on the remainder of the pattern the student and i turned base and final completing a successful landing. upon powering up the aircraft to initiate our takeoff i noticed aircraft y was short-final committing to their landing. the student and i exchanged flight controls. we were already close to our rotation speed roughly 3/4ths down the runway to which i took off and side-stepped to the left to de-conflict with the traffic. there was no adsb traffic indication on our end showing this traffic and no conflict advisory. given this situation i would likely believe if we had tried to stop it would've created a runway excursion or accident as the other aircraft continued to land behind us giving no indication of a go-around on their part.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Government UAS pilot reported an NMAC with a helicopter. The UAS pilot also reported the ADSB signal for the helicopter was repeatedly turning on and off; so they were not able to track its position accurately.
text: i was flying in the area of location x. my altitude was 149 agl. i had person a as a visual observer and the entire flight was in visual line of sight. at the time we were mapping an auto pedestrian accident for law enforcement. our rc controller indicated there was manned aviation in the area, then the warning disappeared. it did this a couple of times and i did not see the distance or altitude relative to mine because the alert turned on and off. because there were a few alerts that turned on and off quickly over an approximately 30 second period, i attempted to pull up flight radar on my phone and as soon as i did that aircraft y flew west of us, by approximately 100' and above our altitude somewhere between 350-500' above us, (this is an estimate from how close they looked, but their barometric altitude on flight radar would have them more than 700' above us). the exact time they passed near us was xa:42. according to flight radar, aircraft y passed us at 5088' barometric alt and 140 mph ground speed. we were on the street and near a multi-story apartment building. on the road was a construction crew actively working with heavy machinery, so we did not hear aircraft y.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: i failed to request airspace authorization for redacted (via laanc) for flight scheduled at xa:00 on day 0. had originally researched that the planned flight was in a 200-ft ceiling zone and authorization could be requested through laanc with automatic approval. the phone app used to make the request is 'airhub portal'. met up with client, set up equipment, and proceeded with the mission. flight elapsed approximately 15 minutes. it wasn't until the second planned flight at xf:00 that i realized i forgot to request authorization. second flight is postponed while i reflect and report the event. this was a failure to follow our pre-flight checklist, which includes checking airspace. airspace was checked the prior day, but the request should have also been made. the decision to hold off on the request because it would be 'quick and easy' the morning of the flight led to forgetting submission. i was in too big a rush to complete the flight and head off to the next project that i neglected a very important safety requirement.in order to help eliminate the risk for future flights, i will make a physical checklist that can be looped around the uav and will serve as a reminder before the device can be set up for flight.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: N90 TRACON controller reported they issued an incorrect altitude to an aircraft and it descended into another sector's airspace without coordination. Controller stated they were responding to multiple reports of TCAS RAs reportedly caused by radio interference from a drone operator which is an ongoing safety hazard.
text: the airspace around the primary airport has been experiencing phantom resolution advisory reports from arriving instrument flight rules aircraft. this has caused frequency congestion and is a distraction from safe operations. although the reason for these aircraft ras remains unclear, it is believed to be from a remote drone operator in the area. the ras are not related to a drone, however, it seems to be a radio interference glitch. the faa has been aware of this for some time but as of now has not taken any corrective action.aircraft x was an arrival to lga at 10000 feet. i had meant to issue a descent to 080 but due to confusion with aircraft advising me of the ras and the extraneous verbiage i was now required to use, i accidentally issued aircraft x an altitude of 050. (note, 050 is not a usual altitude that we use but it was the altitude that an aircraft had just reported the resolution advisory at)aircraft x read back 050 and initiated the descent. due to my focus on the resolution advisory zone and my reports to subsequent aircraft and reporting to the front line manager (flm) i missed the readback. aircraft x entered another facilities airspace but did not conflict with any other aircraft or go below the mva. we routinely report anomalies to management, but it seems as though our reports go unanswered until there is a serious incident or accident. this situation could have been avoided if the faa had withdrawn the approval for the drone operation or by the issuing of a notam.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the aircraft got stuck because of pavement conditions while taxiing to the gate on Taxiway A10 at EWR.
text: when taxiing to gate xx after landing on 4r, we entered on a10 and were holding on a10 just about at taxiway f" behind aircraft y, which was holding short of f2. when aircraft y resumed taxiing, i released the parking brake, and felt what seemed the be the brake re-engaging momentarily after i released the brake. i added some power, and the aircraft did not move. both the first officer and i agreed that we felt the brake had re-engaged, although the brakes and accumulator pressure indicator showed that parking brake pressure had been released. we cycled the parking brake, and again added breakaway power, again without the aircraft moving. we tried this 2 more times, and then opted to call maintenance. maintenance advised that it appeared as though we were at a known spot on a10 where the asphalt meets the concrete, and there is a ridge in the taxiway, which the main landing gear had settled up against. maintenance advised, they would prefer to have us towed to the gate. we were towed uneventfully to the gate. upon deplaning, maintenance did some brake checks, and confirmed that the brakes were ok. they also verbally advised me that they had run into this situation before, and were aware of this spot on a10, and have advised the port authority."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from the Control Tower during approach. Flight continued.
text: on visual approach 35r, i selected open descent to cross fronz at 7000' and 180kt. i was at 250kt since we were off the arrival on vectors. once they cleared us for the visual approach, i wanted to get down first then slow down. we leveled at 7000' 5 miles prior to fronz and was able to smoothly slow to 180k. but received a low altitude alert from tower. we confirmed we still had the runway inside and they told us to continue. the ca looked on the 10-1b to confirm we were inside class b airspace. we had a nice stable approach to a smooth landing.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an NMAC with a UAS while being vectored to the approach.
text: on vectors to approach instrument landing system 4 into lga at 9500 feet a drone was approximately 100 below. no tcas or resolution advisory. proceeded to land successfully at lga.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B787 Captain reported the loss of nose wheel steering during taxi. Flight was towed back to gate.
text: in redacted taxing on 1 and making a left turn onto 2, lost nose wheel steering in turn and had to use brakes to stop aircraft from leaving taxiway. remained on taxiway, shut down, and was towed back to gate.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Fractional flight crew reported incorrect NOTAM information on a runway closure was discovered during descent into LFSB/BSL.
text: no documentation available to the crew during pre-flight preparation or in flight (e.g., master flight document/release/flitedeck pro notam information) gave any indication that the longer runway (15/33) was closed for construction work. in fact, reviewed notam information indicated runway 25 was closed (7 not approved for landing). it was only during atis review did we find out the airport was landing runway 25... this runway was not closed after all...therefore, during our last 8 to 10 minutes of the flight, the two-pilot crew (having flown 7.5 hours over our normal rest time and previously set up for and briefed for landing runway 15) had to set up and brief/conduct an approach to runway 15 with a circle to runway 25 for landing. even though the weather was cavok on this day, this last-minute adjustment created a significant gap in safety because a very tired crew had to review for obstacles, and brief a circling approach at an unfamiliar airport in a tight timeframe.suggestions: any runway closure should be a critical highlighted note in the performance section for any departure or landing airport. more to the point, company x needs to adjust its dispatch review process when operating internationally to scoop up the aeronautical information publication (aip) supplemental information.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 402 pilot reported trailing edge flaps failed to retract during test flight in cruise. Flight diverted.
text: performing fcf (functional check flight) for stall vane check. intended to perform stall in clean configuration. performed first steps of procedure lowering flaps and gear. attempted to bring flaps up and immediately observed that flaps would not retract from fully extended position. we did not hear any sounds indicating a problem with the flap motor and observed the flap motor cb (circuit breaker) had not tripped. cycled the flap lever and observed that had no effect in retracting flaps. we were able to maintain approximately 120 knots in airspeed and notified air traffic control and operations of our situation. we elected to divert to redacted as were closer there than redacted. i also did not want to fly back to redacted with our slow airspeed. notified air traffic control we were diverting to redacted and landed without incident. wrote up aircraft and contacted maintenance control. needless to say, aircraft did not pass fcf.cause: tbd by maintenance. possible broken wire.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: A320 pilot reported significant asymmetric thrust during takeoff roll resulting in a rejected takeoff.
text: low speed rto (rejected takeoff) due to significant asymmetric thrust during thrust application.. aircraft speed was below 60 kts. eng 1 appeared to have spooled normally but eng 2 very little if any sign of spooling.flight returned to the gate for maintenance action

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B787-800 Captain reported uncommanded nose wheel steering input during taxi. Flight returned to gate.
text: uncommanded nose wheel steering turn event.we had a normal pushback from redacted gate xx into the west alley and were cleared to start both engines. during the engine start the ground crew reported some difficulty removing the tow bar (not uncommon event) and during the process, a 'nose wheel steering' message displayed briefly on the upper eicas. the message disappeared shortly after both engines completed the start process which happened just as the ground crew were able to disconnect the tow bar. the entire pushback seemed smoother than most without any sharp movements, turns or noises.we were cleared by redacted ramp to right on taxiway 1 to spot xx, at spot xx we were cleared by redacted air traffic control ground for an immediate left onto taxiway 2, right on taxiway 3 for a full length departure off runway xxl.this was a very short taxi and required two immediate 90 degree turns after initial taxi. my estimated speed was approximately 5 knots or less due to the planned short taxi and other traffic. nose wheel steering and feel was normal for the first right 90 degree turn. approaching the second left turn for 2 after passing spot xx the aircraft performed an uncommanded hard right turn to a 45 degree angle along with an immediate total loss of nose wheel tiller authority. i immediately applied full braking to a stop and notified ground control followed by redacted operations and maintenance.i would describe the right turn like as quick as one could turn right 45 degree with the tiller. it wasn't a gradual failure. even with an immediate braking response, it appeared our nose position ended up 10 -15 feet right of the taxiway centerline. nose wheel steering remained non responsive and tiller movement felt stiff, maybe 2x-3x normal force required to move the tiller. the tug lined up at the approximate nose wheel steering angle for tow back.we were eventually towed back to gate xx where the aircraft was taken out of service.cause: none.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a ground conflict during taxi with an aircraft that ATC had not pointed out.  Captain applied brakes.
text: ord ground control is overwhelmed and periodically loses track of aircraft positions and clearances issued, failing to provide ground separation.i was issued a clearance from spot he turn left on b, cross 9r, taxi e hold short of 4l".while on b i had to suddenly stop as aircraft y joined b out of v1 directly in front of me. ground control never mentioned that aircraft to me - before or after.few minutes later we were told to follow aircraft z joining e from m. shortly afterwards aircraft z was told to follow us on e. as the result we both stopped at the intersection of e and m unable to proceed, while the frequency was non stop occupied and neither of us was able to get clearance clarification.today was the second time in a week when - while taxiing at ord, following my taxi clearance - i had another aircraft turn and pass right in front of me forcing me to brake - with no mention of that aircraft from air traffic control before of after.this is an aircraft collision waiting to happen.cause: overwhelmed, insufficiently staffed air traffic control at ord"

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: General aviation jet Captain reported a temporary loss of aircraft control during cruise due to nearby convective activity.
text: in cruise at fl400 light chop. heavy thunderstorm activity 56 nm to west of our position, with tops estimated at 45, 000.position was south of nav point ohlaa off coast of florida. heading 210 due to 56 kts wind from 287/52kts.experiences what felt like a mountain wave which i assumed was due to the the upper level winds caused by the ++thr [severe thunderstorm] activity 56nm to the west of us.in anticipation of an increase in speed i informed the pm i was selecting manual speed, and reduced our mach # from m.85 to m.83. there was a 39 kt spread between our ias and the barber pole. airspeed continued to increase and auto throttles slowly started to reduce. as it was evident that the speed was increasing faster than the auto throttles were responding i again informed pm i was disengaging the auto throttles and manually reduced the power back further and then to idle!. within a second the airspeed increased into red line activating the aural overspeed warning.i extended the air brakes ab1, and the speed stopped increasing but was still within overspeed regime by 10 kts. i decided not to disengage the autopilot but rather press the touch control steering (tcs) button to raise the nose as the only option to reduce the speed out of the overspeed envelope. this did reduced the speed to below the barber pole causing the aural overspeed to cease.i released the tcs button allowing the autopilot to immediately engage selected vs mode on the guidance panel to descend back to our assigned flight level, and manually took command of the throttles manually. i instructed the pm (second in command) to inform miami center what had happened and explained why.miami asked if it was due to severe turbulence, to which we replied no, it was type of mountain wave or rather severe thunderstorm wind turbulence wave that caused uncontrolled speed deviation most likely caused from the severe thunderstorm 56 nm west of our position.other aircraft were also experiencing the same type of effects after our encounter.once things had settled down and i felt we were away from any possible reoccurrence, i engaged the auto throttles keeping the m.83 (our turbulence penetration speed) set to manual. we then verily reviewed the automation confirming we would keep the autothrottles (at) / manual m.83 set until we both felt we were away for the area of concern. miami air traffic control seemed fine with our immediate explanation and we were not asked to call anyone, nor have we been asked to explain further to anyone.suggestions: i have experienced mountain waves around the world many times as well as thunderstorm rotor turbulence. however after many hours i have never encountered such a rapid uncontrolled speed increase (within seconds) as i experienced with this one. on reviewing our actions to control the rapid speed increase, i don't think we could have done anything different. hindsight is always 20/20 and one could say had we waited with power at idle and ab1 (air brakes) extended, the speed would eventually certainly started to reduce.although on reflection this might very well have been so, yet i could not be sure that the speed might not have continued to increased into a very critical regime where structural damage might have been encountered. therefore utilizing the tcs and using pitch as a last resort to control the speed was, i think the best cause of action.56 miles away from a ++thr is generally considered ample distance.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported temporary loss of aircraft control during approach resulted in a missed approach
text: ca pm first officer pfwe were cleared for the visual approach xx backed up with the instrument landing system. the first officer had briefed me that he was just off low-time hours in type. we had done one leg together which i flew. on the approach we identified the traffic to follow and proceeded inbound. the first officer was delayed in calling for configuration as we became established on the loc. i am not the type of ca to micromanage speed reductions and flap configurations as long as it does not affect stabilized approach criteria. however, i prompted that we need to begin configuring as we are getting close to the aircraft ahead and do not know their ground speed. i believe we were at flaps 3 gear down when air traffic control notified us of a 60kt overtake and that s-turns to the right were approved. we slowed to final landing configuration and were stabilized at 1000'. i told the first officer to perform s-turns and he proceeded, reaching 1000 fpm momentarily and getting low - hitting 3 red lights on the papi before he rejoined the course and corrected - but otherwise we continued to remain stable through 500'. air traffic control told us at about 200-300' to go around and the first officer hit the toga button but i did not hear him make the call-out as he was a very soft-spoken individual. i looked down to make sure the throttles were in toga detent and made the call-out myself then retracted the flaps to position 2. we performed the gear retraction properly and at that time air traffic control told us to climb 2000' and turn heading (i believe) 270. i bugged the panel and selected heading and was monitoring the first officer hand flying when i prompted him to take the autopilot (ap) to reduce our workload, which we engaged. it is hard to remember the exact sequence of events that followed because of the momentary stress but after i engaged the ap, we received another instruction to climb 3000' and turn heading (i believe) 330. it was at this time i noticed our speed reducing and realized we missed the flch 210 call out and were still bugged at our vap of 131. i noticed the speed around 140kts approaching 131 quickly and because we were in a turn, the low speed tape was higher, buffering vap speed. i called out speed 210 speed 210" as the speed turned amber and instead of spinning the speed bug the first officer disconnected the ap and pushed the nose down, which threw me off since i was not expecting the action and now i was back to manipulating the control panel. we did not receive a stick shaker. i spun the speed to 210 and at the same time i saw we were in a nearly 40-45 degree bank and approaching 3000' with a high rate of climb. i told the first officer "altitude" "bank". i pressed forward on the controls and we managed to level and the first officer reduced the bank angle. i engaged the ap once more and we continued to speed up and clean up the aircraft. we came back for a second approach without incident and landed uneventfully. we parked and debriefed the event. it was the first officer's first go-around. we discussed fixation which led to the omission of speed on both our ends and the importance of aviate-navigate-communicate. we discussed the speed tape and how at higher bank angles it can lead to accelerated stalls and that there was no need to turn to the heading so aggressively. i also encouraged him to call for ap early in order to reduce workload."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: C72 Flight Instructor with student reported a complete electrical failure during cruise. Flight diverted and landed.
text: preflighted the aircraft normally and performed initial start up and run up checklists as usual. no unusual readouts or abnormalities. on takeoff and climb out all indications were normal. outside of the airport environment i had my student put on the goggles and directed us to a gps fix for some simulated imc practice. upon leveling out at cruise i took controls and had my student remove the foggles, handed control back and had him run through his initial checklist for maneuvers. we loaded in the nearest fields frequency and made a call that we would be maneuvering 15nm nw of the field at 5, 700. i demonstrated a set of steep turns and then we went over the importance of running our cruise checklist and scanning all instruments every time in between. student attempted a set of steep turns and requested to practice another set. we ran through the cruise and instrument scan and noted no abnormalities. we went over the importance of finding good visual reference points, and he attempted a steep turn to the left. after completing and leveling back off, i re-scanned the instruments and noted the ammeter read out was low (around 2 or 3). i looked to the annunciator panel and noticed there was no illumination and the engine instruments digital screen was flickering and dim. upon noticing this i took controls and had my student get his checklist to check the alternator low / inop checklist. at this time the primary flight display (pfd) gave an ahrs failure notification and inop readouts for our attitude indicator and heading. simultaneously both of our g430s went black and our pfd /multi-function flight display (mfd) flashed off and back on. we ran the troubleshoot checklist and verified circuit breakers had not popped, they hadn't, attempted to reduce the load by shutting off the fan, shutting off lights, tried turning battery master and alternator off and back on, turned on the power for the standby attitude indicator and it worked alright for a couple minutes before flagging that it was inop. nothing worked, and at this time we were a little over what looked like 10nm from the closest airport redacted. i made the decision to head to redacted and as it was an untoward field and g430s were black screened, i squawked 7600 for loss of comms and attempted to transmit in the blind. called that we were approximately 10nm nw of the field and inbound for a landing with no electrical power. redacted center responded asking if we could hear them, if we needed assistance, and informing us we were transmitting on guard. i responded with our location and intentions and that was when we lost our standby attitude and our pfd / mfd went black. redacted center asked if we were able to swap and transmit on the local ctaf. i responded unable as we still did not have the 430s. a nearby aircraft also on guard called center and offered to transmit on our behalf on the local ctaf. center agreed and we continued inbound to redacted prior to landing we lost all electrical. we landed, taxied to the ramp, secured and post flight inspected the aircraft. the only abnormality we found was a significant drop in oil level. in pre-flight it was 6.5 and in post flight it was 5.5 at most

text: i was with my student taking off runway 5 at vdf. the winds were favoring 5 and numerous planes were in the traffic pattern. while on take off, we heard a call from aircraft y that they were on a 2.5 mile final 23. at an altitude of 100 feet, i directed my student to side step the runway to the right. we then passed aircraft y at the same altitude around 200 feet with a horizontal separation of 200 feet. aircraft y then did a missed approach and came back in on runway 5. this could have been avoided if they had circled to runway 5 or done an approach for 5 from the start. the initial call at 2.5 miles was also a contributing factor since it reduced situational awareness of the traffic in the pattern.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Taxiway; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported a critical ground conflict while landing.
text: redacted is turning into a very hazardous operation. the amount of airline enplanements and new foreign student starts has made a very difficult airport that was already overloaded with competing traffic a complete nightmare.although i respect the controllers wish to serve as many planes as possible, providing traffic separation services outside of the class d and using shortened non-standard radio phraseology is making matters worse. there will be legal consequences for controllers making pilots outside of the zone follow instrument flight rules aircraft with the help of vectors and other references if it ends in a collision. this is not the purpose of a class d facility which is to serve the landing and take-off separation inside of class d airspace. it has also created a distraction for the tower controller today.we were on a short final to runway xxr and told to expect a late landing clearance. subsequently another piper cherokee warrior was cleared to 'line up and wait'. at approximately 300 feet my student performed a go-around and offset to the right. the tower gave us instructions to commence a right downwind at 500 feet after clearing the tower safely and we were then told to make a three mile final after confirming that we had a landing aircraft in sight. the tower then sarcastically chastised us for believing that the final was closer to two miles. i then asked him to confirm landing clearance and was again belittled for him believing that the clearance had already been given.we landed uneventfully and exited at taxiway 1.i called ground frequency multiple times without response. believing it safer to move the aircraft then occupy an exit point of the runway, we made a right turn on taxiway 2 and exited the first left turn onto the ramp, the total distance being about 150 yards.the voice had changed from a male to a female voice on the frequency and no notification was made of a controller-change over the frequency prior to this.there's a lot to unravel here, and it pains me to have to report the inadequacies of this facility. first of all, i am a current large transport aircraft pilot with decades of experience, many type ratings, licensed in several different countries. as a former chief pilot and check airman and former chief flight instructor, i have never seen anything so dangerous, unprofessional and poorly run as the facility at redacted, nor have i seen such a wrong allocation of class d airspace when quite clearly, class c airspace as a bare minimum should be applied.there is no flow for departures and arrivals by sector, no reporting points, no entry or exit altitudes. this is unheard of in any other high volume training airspace anywhere else in the world.quite clearly, a midair collision is imminent.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a critical ground conflict during approach with an aircraft landing opposite direction runway.
text: i was on short final at redacted for runway xx. it was sunset. the entire runway was in shadow. the sun was in my eyes from the sunset at my right. i had repeatedly tried to activate the papi using 5 clicks on the radio, but it was not activating and was discussing with my pilot/passenger in the right seat why it was not activating. i did not realize that i was on the wrong frequency and not on redacted ctaf. i made a call that i was on final runway xx at redacted about 3 miles out. i did not see any other aircraft on adsb north of the field, and i'm not sure i looked south of the field on the map to see if there was anyone on adsb. the wind was calm, so either runway was a candidate for takeoffs and landings. at about 500 feet agl/msl my right-seater and i both noticed at the same time an aircraft's landing lights on the runway. i was doing a short field landing, so was slow, and so i carefully broke off to the left without adding g loading, adding full power, and gently entered a climb with full flaps, gradually working the flaps out. the aircraft must have just landed on runway xy without me hearing them on the radio because i was on the wrong frequency, and without realizing i was on final for xx because they didn't hear my transmission, and they probably didn't notice me on adsb, if they even have it. once i was in a stable climb, i realized i wasn't on frequency and changed to ctaf and heard the other pilot calling me. i replied explaining it was entirely my fault because i had been on the wrong frequency, and the other pilot was gracious about the situation. i'm assuming the other plane must have taxied off the runway and to the ramp because i didn't see them after that. we set up for another landing, which was uneventful.the problem was that i don't have a correct-frequency check as a checklist item, and skipped verifying that i was on the correct ctaf. this was compounded by the runway being entirely in shadow and the sun in my eyes. the papi not turning on should have alerted me to the fact that i was on the wrong frequency. the short field landing i was doing also had me in a nose-high attitude behind the power curve, which made it slightly harder to see down the runway. i was also focused on maintaining the plane at a low airspeed, lined up for landing, during the slow approach, which is a bit more demanding and may have been an additional distraction from the issue unfolding. the plane that had just landed on xx may have turned on their landing lights on the runway to alert me of their presence, because neither my right seat pilot/passenger or i noticed them until the plane appeared halfway down the runway. to avoid this in future i plan to add a frequency check to my checklists, make sure i run my checklists every time, make sure my landing lights are on for takeoffs and landings, and consider what else may be wrong when i notice something 'weird' like a papi not activating.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Safety pilot reported the pilot flying barely cleared obstacles during initial climb resulting in a CFTT event.
text: i was acting as a safety pilot for another private pilot. we were coming in to land at redacted airport and we were making left traffic for runway xx. the pilot flying made a base turn that was closer to the airport than usual and this put us up for a high and fast final. we landed after using up most of the runway. this was a touch and go so we immediately took off again. after takeoff, the pilot flying pitched up for our best rate of climb speed and we continued climbing. however, i can see obstacles at a distance. we were going to clear them. however, after reaching those obstacles and climbing over them i realized we were uncomfortably close to them. if i were in this position again i would have asked the pilot flying to initiate a go around after recognizing we were going to be high and fast. this would have prevented us from landing long. if we did land i would have told the pilot flying to make this a full stop and do a standard takeoff. upon climbout after our landing, instead of climbing at the best rate of climb, i should have told the pilot flying to climb at the best angle of climb. these actions would have prevented the issue. while i did recognize the issues, i did not speak up since we were both private pilots and i felt i wasn't in a position of authority to tell another pilot how to fly. i should have spoken up when i recognized the issue and will do so next time.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported temporary loss of aircraft control during approach. Flight crew executed missed approach.
text: the captain and i were doing a leg of a multiple day trip. it was a flight to redacted. captain was the pf and i was the pm. we were setting up for the instrument landing system xxr into redacted. weather was about 4sm and overcast around 1500'. we were vectored for the approach around redacted at 2500' and cleared for the approach. captain armed the approach. the max9 captured the loc and gs roughly at the same time causing the airplane to aggressively pitch down attempting to catch the glideslope. airspeed was increasing rapidly toward the barber pole, decent rate was increasing rapidly and captain attempted to override the autopilot by pulling back on the yoke. he did not disconnect the autopilot. as he saw the airspeed increasing he extended the speed brakes. airspeed is at the barber pole, aircraft pitching down aggressively and we hear sink rate, sink rate." captain disconnects the autopilot (ap), pitches up very slightly and banks right. i said "roll wings level" he rolled wings level momentarily, still high on the gs and turned to the right again, ignoring the flight directors. i said again, "wings level" and put a little pressure on the yoke to get the airplane level. captain said "upset!" we were not in an upset condition and i was afraid captain was going to pitch the aircraft down, i said "my controls". i took control of the aircraft and executed a go around procedure at 1200 agl in imc. we got runway heading up to 4000', cleaned up the airplane and i asked the captain if he wanted the controls back, he said "yes". i gave him the controls and requested vectors for the approach again with an extended final. once on the ground we debriefed the situation. the captain admitted he was disoriented and was very confused about what had happened. we talked in depth about what happened and i made it clear how scary the situation was. the captain just came off the 777 and just completed 737 ioe."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Security; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a cabin altitude warning during climb. Flight descended and diverted.
text: while operating flight from redacted, we received a cabin altitude warning indication and associated master warning and horn. we were passing fl260 to our assigned cruising altitude of fl320. we performed the immediate action items (o2 masks, established communications, seatbelt sign on) and first officer advised air traffic control that we had a pressurization issue and requested an immediate descent lower and then clarified 10, 000 ft. the autopilot and auto throttles were disconnected and i requested lvl change and 300 kias. the speed brake was utilized as well. while descending i observed that the cabin pressure was slightly above 10, 000 ft and it didn't get much higher than that. it got very busy due to initial difficulty communicating (mask and volume issues), air traffic control requesting details and the fas immediately trying to contact us multiple times as well. we didn't initially request priority handling since the focus was flying the airplane first and dealing with our issue, but we eventually did due to the fact that we were going to land overweight. when first officer was performing the cabin altitude warning or rapid depressurization/ descent qrc he discovered that the pressurization switch was already in manual when he got to step 6. while he was performing the checklist, i was still hand flying in the descent to 10, 000 ft. the fas were concerned that we were concerned about our well being and tried to enter the flight deck (fd) utilizing the fd door emergency entry button. this occurred after they attempted to call the flight deck a few times and knocking on the door as well. what they didn't know was that we were very busy dealing with the checklist and air traffic control concurrently. when we heard the door door door audio, first officer performed the immediate action item for the flight deck door and pressed the hard lock switch. we were able to eventually advise them that we were very busy and that we'd contact them when we get a chance. after completing up to step 17 of the cabin altitude warning non-normal, we discussed diverting to redacted. we informed dispatch of our issue and our intentions to go to redacted. they eventually replied and asked if we requested priority handling and we informed them that we did. i slowed the aircraft to 250 kias at 10, 000 ft as to not feel rushed dealing with our issue. the fas were contacted and the brief was performed. the passengers were also briefed of our issue and our intentions to divert to redacted. everyone was also informed about the emergency equipment on standby and they were going to be there as a precaution. the divert* function had been completed, aircraft re-cruised and set up for the arrival into redacted. since we were landing overweight, we calculated our landing distance utilizing the landing distance normal configuration - flaps 30 (800) table. we were given vectors for instrument landing system xxl and conducted a flaps 30/auto brakes 3 landing. after landing, we exited runway xxl and came to a complete stop so airport rescue and firefighting (arff) could inspect the aircraft exterior for any damage. after none was noted, they departed the scene and returned to their base of operation. we eventually taxied to the gate. after we completed the parking checklist, we spoke to one of the maintenance technicians. they were debriefed. afterwords, i contacted the chief pilot and advised him that we were ok to continue. electronic log book entries were made for the cabin altitude (occurrence altitude and cabin altitude indication noted) and overweight landing (smooth landing and weight noted (…approximately 8200 lbs overweight). outside the flight deck, we had to opportunity to conduct a thorough debrief. we discussed aspects of how we handled the situation (workload management and situational awareness) and the fact that we were able to cover all the steps dealing with our issue and safely divert to redacted. communication is what could've gone better. we discussed how the warning horn was a distraction before cutout was selected, establishing communication with masks on, air traffic control callingus while we were doing checklists and the fas immediately trying to contact us numerous times as well. the primary issue though was how we both missed the pressurization switch in the manual position. we discussed about the possibility of confirmation bias regarding the switch position, but we also discussed ways to prevent a repeat of undesired outcome of events.

synopsis: B737 flight crew reported cabin pressurization system failure. Diverted and landed uneventfully.
text: during climb, all systems normal, the auto fail light on the pressurization system lit up. we stopped our climb at 25, 000 ft. while i flew the plane, the pf proceeded with the checklist. in alternate control, it looked to have the pressurization under control so we asked air traffic control to continue our climb to flight level 350. during the climb around 31, 000 feet the cabin rake spiked and we asked air traffic control to stop the climb. the cabin was increasing up to 3000 ft./min. during descent, the cabin alt did exceed 14, 000 feet so the passenger masks did deploy. we could not control the presentation on manual so we requested priority handling and deviated to redacted. in was an overweight landing.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an unstabilized approach with a high rate of descent resulting in ATC issuing a low altitude alert. The flight corrected to the glideslope; continued the approach; and landed.
text: on approach into sfo we were cleared to 'maintain 3100 (for visual flight rules traffic below) until established, cleared the instrument landing system.' as acting pm i was partially heads down to switch frequencies, and make flap changes while also monitoring the aircraft state. after looking up from switching to tower, i noticed we had not captured the glide slope and were now quite high on our approach. i immediately notified the captain (pilot flying) by clearly saying 'we are high' and he promptly corrected by asking for more flaps and gear down. this resulted in a high energy descent from about 3000 to 1500 feet when we fully established on the glide slope. shortly after, air traffic control stated 'aircraft x low altitude alert, check altitude immediately' i responded with 'roger aircraft x' and noticed we were slightly below the glide slope now at approximately 1500 feet (no more than a half dot low) and the pf corrected immediately. i believe the alert was more a factor of the descent rate than the altitude itself. we met all stabilized approach criteria and landed without incident.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported severe turbulence during the descent; resulting in large airspeed excursions. The Captain called the cabin and was informed a Flight Attendant had sustained an injury due to the turbulence.
text: at the start of the descent into ord, i advised the captain of weather notifications of moderate/severe turbulence ahead of us at 190 and 200. he then told the fas to prepare the cabin for landing in order to get them seated before the turbulence. approximately 5-8 minutes after that, he spoke to a fa inquiring if he had told them to prepare the cabin, to which he responded that yes he had. shortly after that, we encountered sudden and severe turbulence passing through fl220-200, with airspeed excursions +/- 20 knots. the captain gave them be seated immediately, be seated immediately." air traffic control had received no information regarding turbulence, and expressed surprise when the captain reported it. once stabilized, the ca told them to take their jumpseats. once they checked in, they reported that one fa had sustained an injury to her wrist and potentially her ankle as well."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a ground conflict during taxiout at MIA airport resulting in an aircraft having to execute a go-around.
text: contacted mia ground for taxi. controller advised expect rwy 8l for takeoff and to taxi via txy k to holding point for rwy 8l. we had loaded rwy 8r during preflight, so during the taxi, i loaded rwy 8l, entered the takeoff data, and confirmed waypoints. the ca called for the runway change checklist and it was completed halfway to the holding point. ground then directed us to monitor tower frequency approaching the holding point. when tower contacted us, they directed us to cross runway 8l and hold short rwy 8r and expedite for traffic on 5-mile final. as we crossed the hold short line for rwy 8l, tower advised us to proceed onto hold for rwy 8r. i advised that we would need a few minutes to run checklists. tower replied with hold short rwy 8l and the ca applied brakes, but we were past the hold short line by about 50 feet. i advised tower and he said to then expedite and hold short rwy 8r, traffic on 2 mile final. ca advanced throttles, but we did not clear rwy 8l in time and traffic on final was directed to go around. holding short of rwy 8r we completed all the runway change items one last time and rest of departure was uneventful.cause: change of runway assignment followed by expedited instructions to cross and then on to the new runway and hold before crew could run required checklists. i also should have been more vocal about our requirements before attempting to cross rwy 8l, but with the hold short instructions initially provided for the other side, i thought we would have time while holding short of rwy 8r.suggestions: when workload is high and expedited instructions are received to cross an active runway, request hold short of that runway to ensure all requirements are completed to prevent conflicts.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported tug driver coming to an abrupt stop during push back resulting in a broken shear pin.
text: on day 0 around xa:37 in redacted, aircraft x blocked out for its flight to redacted. weight of aircraft on pushback: 75, 100 lbsi communicated with tug driver to confirm that she and the rest of her ramp crew were ready for pushback off gate xx. she confirmed that they were ready. i called for the pushback checklist, which my first officer and i then completed. my first officer then called ramp for push clearance. we received push clearance straight back off [gate] xx. once we received push clearance, i turned the beacon on, released the parking brake, and verified once more the nose wheel steering was off. at this point i stated to the tug driver, beacon on, brakes released, nose wheel steering off. you are cleared to push straight back." if i had to venture a guess, it was maybe 10 yards off the gate when the tug driver brought the push to a very abrupt stop. there was a very sharp jolt to the airplane associated with this abrupt stop. i queried the tug driver as to what happened and she relayed to me that a wing walker had given her the signal to stop the push due to traffic on the roadway behind the aircraft. once the traffic was clear, she attempted to restart the push and gave us clearance to start the right engine. however, shortly after the push started it was evident that something did not feel or sound right. we stopped the engine start attempt and the tug driver brought the aircraft to a stop. she got off the tug to inspect the nose gear and tow bar and told us that something was not right and the tow bar was possibly broke. at this point i told her i would set the parking brake, which i then did. i immediately called maintenance control through my dispatcher. my first officer then told ramp control our situation and then called local maintenance in redacted. maintenance came to the aircraft and conducted their inspection. fortunately, it was a shear pin on the tow bar itself that broke and the inspection of the nose gear was satisfactory per maintenance personnel. once the paperwork was completed and the logbook returned, we proceeded on our way to redacted.cause: the tug driver stopped the push too abruptly resulting in a shear pin event on the tow bar."

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Ramp
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a ground conflict with another aircraft shortly after landing. Captain immediately stopped the aircraft.
text: after landing in redacted ground instructed us to hold short of taxiway 1 on taxiway 2 to wait for our alley to clear. aircraft y was on taxiway 3 also holding short of 2 waiting for their gate. after a short wait ground cleared us to taxi 1, 2 to gate xx. before i started taxiing the first officer and i cleared left and right and saw no conflict so i released the parking brake and started taxiing. as i started moving i double checked again that i was clear left and aircraft y had not started moving. when i started making the turn on 1 i began looking down towards where our gate was and my first officer shouted stop stop. aircraft y had quickly started taxiing and immediately cut us off on 1 forcing me to stomp on the brakes as hard as i could activating the anti skid to avoid a collision. after stopping and making sure the passengers and fa's were okay i continued taxiing toward our alley. aircraft y had also turned into our alley and stopped and told ground uh i don't think we're parking at [gate] xx anymore". they then communicated with ops and parked at [gate] xy. if my first officer hadn't spoken up it most likely would have led to a collision. by the time i stopped their wingtip was probably 10 feet from our nose.cause: not confirming with ops after landing to confirm gate assignment leading to expectation bias assuming another aircraft's taxi instruction was their own.suggestion: reinforce the importance of clearing left and right before taxi and communicating with ops on gate assignment after landing in redacted"

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: Tecnam P2006T flight instructor and student reported right wing striking a light pole during taxi. Maintenance assessed damage.
text: after completing the training flight with the student, we were was taxiing the aircraft back to the hangar to be parked. the student was on the control taxing. there is a light pole by the fuel pumps at the flight school that we have to clear on the right side for a turn. there is usually cars parked along on the left side that we also have to clear, but due to the timing of the lesson, there were less cars. this is a tight spot the aircraft has to clear. during this time, there were conversations in the flight deck which caused a distraction to both the student and instructor resulting the right side of the wing running into the light pole.there is structural damage towards the end of the wing. maintenance observed the damage and reported that the dented parts will need replacement. no spars were damaged but would need to inspect to see if there are internal damages along with the root of the wing as there were small wrinkles observed.the student is a current commercial applicant that is also training for their commercial multi-engine training at the same time. to prevent this, instructor should never get complacent with any student and what rating they hold. also need to make sure to follow the taxi lines to ensure the clearance and not have expectation bias as aircraft wing spans all differ. during taxi, should always still practice sterile flight deck while engine is still on.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC while descending towards the airport pattern requiring evasive action to avoid a possible collision.
text: i was flying aircraft x from eul for solo training under part 91. i departed eul and flew westbound in a continuous climb to 12500 msl approximately 15 miles south of ono. after maneuvering at 12500, i began a descent eastbound to 08500 msl approximately 12 miles west-northwest of eul, where i performed several standard maneuvers. upon termination of those maneuvers, i began a descent on a 090 heading from 07500 msl to a planned altitude of 03400 msl with intent to join the 45 entry to the runway 30 right-downwind at eul. during this descent i made standard radio calls on eul ctaf mhz including my callsign, type, location, altitude, heading and intentions. no radio calls were received which would have indicated conflicting traffic. at an altitude of 05700 msl, i noticed a traffic alert on my efb. the traffic was located at my one o'clock, 300 feet low, opposite direction, climbing, at approximately 1 nm range. i immediately applied full power, initiated a climb, and briskly rolled the aircraft into a 35 degree right-hand turn. upon taking evasive action, i visually identified the conflicting traffic. the conflicting traffic was observed visually and via ads-b in an approximately 30 degree left-hand climbing turn. observing the conflicting traffic in a left-hand turn, i increased my angle of bank to 45 degrees in the climbing turn. after observing traffic pass below me, i continued the right-hand turn to re-join my original course. during the evasive action, i climbed to a maximum altitude of 06200 msl. the minimum observed vertical separation from ads-b data on my efb was 200 feet.an attempt to raise the conflicting traffic was made on caf and unicom mhz after the conflict was resolved. no response was received.at the time of the incident, my aircraft was equipped with ads-b in and out, and i was utilizing an efb with live ads-b traffic data from the aircraft superimposed over the sectional chart. at the time of the incident i was relying on visual traffic scanning and pilot-to-pilot radio communications to avoid other traffic. i was not actively scanning my efb for traffic. if i had used my efb more proactively during this descent, i likely would have noticed the conflict sooner and been able to avoid the conflict without aggressive maneuvers. during this incident, the conflicting traffic utilized non-standard collision avoidance technique by initiating a left-hand turn and continuing a climb to avoid opposite direction, higher altitude traffic. because of this, a collision hazard existed throughout the evasive maneuvers, and altitude alone prevented a collision.during this incident, i do not recall hearing radio calls which would have indicated a collision hazard from the conflicting traffic. i was also unable to raise the conflicting traffic on the eul ctaf after the incident. this serves as a reminder to actively listen to the ctaf when operating in the vicinity of an airport, and to make standard radio calls regarding your position, altitude and intentions.the conflicting traffic is owned and operated by a flight school. this raises questions of traffic awareness and avoidance while instructing, and ensuring that a competent person is actively looking for traffic.

text: roughly around xa:00, i went to a park in location x to fly my drone-'dji neo 2'. i flew the drone 4-different times, the first 3-times were around 2-3 mins, the 4th-time was about 8 mins. on the 4th time- i flew the drone further than i intended, though still at the line of sight. shortly after, above the trees, i lost sight. i was stressing a bit at this point. generally flying blind, with only about 3-weeks of experience flying, i pushed the home return button, apparently it didn't work, so i'm still flying blind trying to navigate back home using the camera screen through my controller knobs for a couple more mins. i then pushed the return to home button again, this time i held it down for a few seconds, then it worked. the drone then returned within about 2-mins, safely landed on a bench table i was sitting at. i left shortly after thinking i'm in violation of code 107.31. naturally, my conscience kicked in. i researched what to do, so here i am. not sure if necessary but wanted to be 'safe'. thank you.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach

text: on day 0, i was the pilot in command of a cessna 172 conducting a student solo cross-country flight under visual flight rules to redacted airport.approximately 2 nm from the airport, i was at 3, 000 feet msl and was advised by air traffic control that i was high and instructed to proceed westbound to descend for landing.i entered the traffic pattern for runway xx with atis information. i was established on downwind at approximately 1, 000 feet msl. i turned base at approximately 800 feet msl and continued on final approach.on final approach, the aircraft was configured with full flaps. airspeed was approximately 65 knots with engine power set around 1, 100 rpm. the approach appeared stable and no stall warning was observed prior to the event.during the landing flare/short final phase, the aircraft experienced an aerodynamic stall, resulting in a hard landing.after landing, i requested priority handling with air traffic control and confirmed i was not injured. fuel leakage was observed from the aircraft, with no fire or smoke present. airport operations and fire response personnel responded and secured the aircraft and mitigated the fuel leak.weather conditions were visual flight rules with clear skies, 10 statute miles visibility, wind 240° at 6 knots, and altimeter 30.03.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Instructor pilot reported misjudging spacing with aircraft on the runway during final approach. Pilot performed go-around.
text: returning to cxp after a discovery flight with multiple ac in the pattern and transiting the area north and south at cxp. we approached the field from the south to enter the 45 for runway 27. we entered the 45 with aircraft y turning left downwind. we established and made frequent radio calls x 2 on the 45 at 3 miles and two miles, at left downwind midfield and abeam the numbers 27. sometime and almost 'stepping on another radio call i heard 'i'll be slow' assuming the call was associated/from aircraft y. not aware of what class or type aircraft y is, i interpreted ' i'll be slow' as i need to slow ourselves down or create space. i radioed that i would extend our down wind, i slowed ac further by lowering more flaps than normal and waited for aircraft y to pass my left wing (they were on final) and waited another 3-5 seconds to turn base. as i turned left base i also was slightly high. i then turned final to see comfortable spacing between our ac and aircraft y. we were about 0.5 to 1 mile from the numbers, aircraft y appeared almost halfway down the runway. i was a bit high and utilized a slip to establish on glideslope, as soon as i saw pink(red) over white i removed the slip, maintained a stabilized approach. with good spacing i felt we could continue to landing. aircraft y appeared to be at least if not more than half way down the runway and landed with what appeared slow to no movement. less than 5-10 seconds the spacing became uncomfortable and a go around was performed. full power with carb heat off nose pitched for increasing as. the ac didn't feel as thought it was increasing speed or climbing as it normally does, i performed a flow check and found the flaps still full. the flap setting was set to 10 degrees and the as and eventually the altitude increase. as the we climbed out two radio transmissions announced concern for the proximity of my ac. we performed the go-around in the pattern and landed without further events. i did attempt to find the aircraft y pilot for purposes of a debrief without success. i believe was ignorant to the type of aircraft y and how slow it really can be, and its normal taxi operation. i could have asked but the radio traffic was heavy enough i felt pressured to be short and succinct. i also believed i had enough spacing initially. i could have given more spacing than i thought i needed or performed a go around immediately. i felt i hesitated on my decision due to perceived spacing, the extended time needing to enter the traffic pattern. possibly 'get there itis' was a factor due to another reservation behind ours, and we were running late due to the heavy traffic and maneuvering required. last but not least having a goal of remaining minimum 500 feet from now landing aircraft and setting new personal minimums to 1500 feet horizontally with landing ac seems to be a good start, possibly increasing to 2000 feet. also my muscle memory didn't automatically go to the flaps on the go around. i teach my students it verbally but i didn't automatically reach for flaps. so my going to go do go-around training with a flight instructor and build that muscle memory back into my routine.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: GA pilot reported post flight review of flight during cruise may have been conducted at altitudes with reduced margins to terrain.
text: during a night avionics familiarization and instructional flight, i was providing complex endorsement training to a new aircraft owner in an aircraft equipped with an avidyne ifd440 that i had limited prior experience operating.while returning to the departure airport via a route over downtown los angeles, i devoted attention to programming and interpreting the avionics system. during this period, i directed the pilot receiving instruction to maintain course over interstate 10 while i managed cockpit tasks.at the time of flight, i did not observe any terrain or obstacle alerts or hazard indications on the installed avionics. post-flight review the following day using foreflight track log data suggested that portions of the flight may have been conducted at altitudes with reduced margins relative to surrounding obstacles or terrain.the flight was conducted beneath the class b airspace shelf in the los angeles area, and altitude selection was intended to balance airspace compliance with terrain and obstacle clearance considerations. however, task saturation associated with avionics management and instruction may have reduced my overall situational awareness during this phase of flight.contributing factors:night operations in a high-density urban environment.limited familiarity with installed avionics system.instructional workload combined with avionics programming tasks.reliance on pilot receiving instruction for aircraft control during head-down tasks.corrective actions:increased emphasis on avionics proficiency prior to instructional use in-flight.avoidance of combined high-workload scenarios (instruction + unfamiliar avionics + night operations).reinforcement of minimum altitude buffers beyond regulatory requirements in urban environments.prioritization of 'aviate, navigate, communicate, ' with stricter limits on head-down time during critical phases.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: B767 flight crew reported an IAS disagree EICAS message during climb. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: i was scheduled to operate flight from redacted on aircraft x. as part of my preflight duties, i reviewed the aircraft logbook history for the preceding days and noted that the 'ias disagree' eicas message had occurred multiple times within the past couple days. during the threat-forward preflight briefing with first officers a and b, i highlighted this recurring discrepancy and reviewed the applicable memory items.pushback, taxi, and takeoff were uneventful. this was first officer a's leg. after gear and flap retraction and completion of the takeoff checklist, between approximately 5, 000 and 6, 000 feet during the climb, we received an ias disagree eicas message. we immediately accomplished the applicable memory items. as we transitioned from the quick reference checklist (qrc) to the non-normal checklist, the eicas message cleared, however, the captain's adi speed tape continued to display a 'spd lim' flag.we discussed the situation and agreed to initiate a three-way conference with dispatch and maintenance control. following coordination with both parties, we elected to return to redacted. this decision was based on the recurring nature of the discrepancy and the potential for re-occurrence, which could lead to an undesired aircraft state, including unreliable airspeed indications, nuisance or erroneous warnings (e.g., stick shaker, overspeed), and abnormal handling characteristics, as outlined in qrh 2.100.21.i requested priority handling with air traffic control and advised them of our intention to return to redacted. crew duties were clearly assigned: first officer a remained the pilot flying, international relief officer b handled air traffic control communications, and i coordinated the return with dispatch while also updating the flight attendants and passengers.at the time of the decision, the aircraft was approximately 16, 000 pounds above maximum landing weight. with no fuel in the center tank available for jettison, burning down to landing weight would have required approximately one hour. given the operational risk associated with the recurring ias disagree condition, i exercised my authority and elected to proceed with an overweight landing.air traffic control provided priority handling for our return. first officer a executed a safe and stabilized landing on runway xxr, with a touchdown rate of approximately 200-300 feet per minute.once at the gate, we conducted a debrief among ourselves and afterwards provided a detailed briefing to maintenance personnel regarding the event.
