anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Light Transport Captain reported receiving 'landing gear' annunciation during final approach. Crew pitched up and continued approach.
text: on descent into ixd we were given the option by air traffic control to fly the instrument landing system 36 approach or fly a visual approach. we had briefed the instrument landing system prior, but having the field insight i elected for the visual. we were cleared for the visual and told to contact tower. we switched frequency and cleared to land. i glanced at the approach plate and saw the glide slope intercept at 1580. being visual i asked for 1500 in the alt select. i began my a gradual descent and adjusted my heading to intercept final. as we leveled at 1500 i noticed that we appeared much lower than anticipated and further away than i initially believed. i elected to stay at 1500 and intercept the glide slope as we got closer in.as we were looking outside at the field as we got closer, the terrain actually was beginning rise, triggering the aircraft to alert landing gear, landing gear. i asked for the gear. the gear was selected and i began requesting flaps. flaps 1 and 2 were selected as we began to configure to land. as we were configuring i looked down at the pfd (primary flight display) just in time to see the terrain turn yellow and get a terrain proximity alert then a pull up command.cause: after shutdown, we debriefed the incident. after reviewing the approach plate i saw i had mistakenly seen and requested the altitude at zixat not the altitude at the faf skini. complacency stemming from a nice early morning flying into a scenic area. not reacting to multiple clues of rising terrain. no additional advisories from approach or tower to check altitude. not excusing my mistakes or complacency, but may have triggered us to take action sooner.i pitched up adding power to climb. i leveled off still at roughly 2000 were i waited to intercept the glideslope before continuing descent on the approach. once on the glideslope i continued the approach to land.suggestions: moving forward if an approach has been programmed and briefed, given the option to fly the approach or take a visual i will elect to continue on the approach as the difference would have been a few additional vectors to final. with regard to visual approaches i will continue to back them up with vertical guidance when available and be more cognizant of both information available to me on approach plates, airport information, and visual cues.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CE-680 Captain reported a Gear Disagree advisory during final approach. Crew executed a go-around.
text: at xa:30pm while conducting the visual approach into xxr at redacted i called for the landing gear down. at that time we received a gear disagree r cas (crew alerting system) message and the right amber x on the gear indication for the right main. i decided to go around when i saw the indications. after the after takeoff checklist we asked for delay vectors to run the appropriate qrh checklist for the cas message. after running the checklist we still had an amber x for the right main gear indication and the cas message. we then climbed to 10, 000 ft where i was able to get a hold of the chief pilot who was person a at the time. he confirmed with me that all of the items were done on the checklist. he then stated we should request priority handling since we still had the amber x for the right main gear indication. we did request priority handling. we then discussed the landing and the threats associated with a potential unsafe gear and also an emergency evacuation if needed. after the approach checklist i requested a low approach to see if the right main was out. it was dark but i thought i would try. when the flaps were selected full, the amber x turned to a red x and we received the audible 'landing gear' warning that was very loud and continued which made it hard to communicate between us and tower. the first attempt the emergency vehicles could not tell because of the runway light reflection. they asked if we could do it again and they would aim spotlights at the landing gear. on the second low approach they were able to see that the right main was down. we then came back around and ran the approach checklist again and landed. the plane landed without incident but i elected to stop on the runway until emergency vehicles could inspect the airplane for any anomalies with the landing gear. they saw none so made a left turn on 1 and exited the runway and shut the plane down on 1 and was towed in from there. person a the chief pilot was helpful along with redacted tower and emergency vehicles.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported a loss of all navigation instrumentation.
text: during takeoff from redacted in vmc conditions and lnav deselected due to vectors from air traffic control, the ca nav display and flight director (fd) lost heading guidance. i (ca) was flying. following completion of the after takeoff checklist and once at a safe altitude, it was determined that the first officer had full fd and nav guidance, so controls were transferred and command b selected while i referred to the qrh. there were no fault indications on the overhead, and no procedures in the qrh to address the loss of heading guidance. no circuit breakers were tripped. i assumed control of the aircraft to allow the first officer to search the qrh for an applicable procedure with the same negative result.i transferred control back to the first officer, did a thorough scan of the overhead and discovered that that the inertial reference system (irs) 1 selector switch was in att vice nav. with concurrence from first officer, decided to switch the irs to nav mode, which led to a complete loss of navigation data on both sides and autopilot disconnect. we had attitude guidance and altitude guidance from the fd, but were down to magnetic compass for heading. notified air traffic control, and let them know we were trouble shooting the issue. there were no procedures in the qrh or aom to restore the nav. we coordinated through dispatch with maintenance control (crew phone was down due to loss of wifi), but maintenance control only asked if there were and circuit breakers tripped and had no alternative solutions. we decided that proceeding to our destination without navigation was a poor choice so requested priority handling and diverted to redacted, which was reporting vmc. with vectors from air traffic control, we hand flew the aircraft to an ils/visual intercept where we regained fd guidance for the approach using raw data and landed without incident.cause: the major factors that we identified as a crew that led to this were the inadvertent selection of att during preflight by the first officer, not catching the lack of flight mode annunciator 'hdg sel' annunciation, lack of fd guidance at toga during the takeoff roll and selection of nav inflight after the original issue was identified. there is a procedure in the aom for inadvertent selection of att during pre-flight on the ground, but nothing for discovering the condition once airborne. in retrospect, without guidance we should have left the switch in the att position with the good data on the first officer side, but it would be helpful if there were procedural guidance for this condition inflight.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported braking abruptly to avoid another aircraft.
text: near runway incident involving aircraft x and a ga aircraft upon exiting runway. aircraft x was exiting xxr onto the high speed taxiway 1 upon landing, and was advised to contact ground upon exiting. nearing the hold short line, captain noticed first a ga aircraft taxing southwest on 2 and created a conflict with aircraft x exiting the runway. the aircraft was a similar color to the taxiway, so the first officer did not notice it at first, but did after captain applied aggressive braking and pointed out the traffic. aircraft x was not made aware of the potential taxiing conflict by tower controller when advised to contact ground. had aircraft x been exiting onto the high speed at a higher energy state it would have likely been an incident.cause: probable cause related to air traffic control not notifying landing aircraft of potential conflicting traffic while exiting runway.high workload involved while exiting runway.similar color of ga aircraft to taxiway made it challenging to spot.suggestions: suggest communication between tower and ground controllers of potential conflicting aircraft while aircraft are taxiing for departure and exiting runways, especially high speed exits.suggest exiting runway as slowly as possible, even a high speed since the lower energy state of the exiting aircraft aided in the mitigation of the threat.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Flight Attendant reported a pressurization issue during climb phase. Flight diverted and landed safely.
text: crew briefing with captain prior to boarding included expected turbulence 27-30 min after takeoff. however, fas were good to get up at the audible signal. at the audible signal, 10, 000 feet, there were some light bumps as we were still climbing, so we sat briefly for a few more minutes before prepping for service.once we felt it safe to get up, we settled into normal service routine. person a, my fwd galley, began to set up the galley while i worked on creating an order sheet for first class.while i was creating the order sheet, person a and i both noticed an alarm sound that was continuously going off. at first we thought it was a pax (passenger) phone alarm and i stuck my head out in the aisle to pinpoint the sound. that was when i realized the sound was coming from the flight deck. i listened in with my ear to the door, as this was an abnormal alarm sound that was constantly blaring. as i was listening, a few moments later, i heard what sounded like a release of oxygen followed by a loud air sound. person a and i both looked to each other and confirmed we both heard the same thing. i could not hear the pilots--there was no sign nor indication of them moving or talking in the flight deck. i immediately called them. after a few minutes of no answer i called them again. while waiting on the phone for their contact, i noticed the plane descending back down. after several minutes of no contact with the pilots (5 minutes or more), no sounds or indications of them being conscious, paired with a continuous blaring alarm and air sounds coming from the cockpit, and the plane still descending… i began to be suspicious they could be unconscious and/or incapacitated whether it was due to a decompression or some other abnormality. at that point, my main priority was to make contact with the pilots. i kept calling, with no answer. pressed for time, and aware of the incident surrounding the demise of another air carrier, i determined the best course of action was to use the emergency entrance system to enter the flight deck and wake them up/respond to any medical attention they may need in case of unconsciousness/incapacitation. i proceeded by calling the back galley, asking my senior co-worker, to come to the front immediately for assistance. when she came up i set up the cart barrier for normal flight deck entry/exit procedures. with the three of us now in the galley to assist in the emergency, i called the flight deck again. there was still no answer and all i could hear was a loud air noise in the background. this is when i proceeded to knock and attempt to enter the flight deck via emergency entrance system and the assistance of my coworkers.however, after thinking we knew how to enter the flight deck via emergency entrance system, the door would not open. i was a bit panicked by this because i couldn't understand what we were doing wrong. i banged on the door in hopes that, even if i couldn't enter the flight deck to check on them, maybe i could be loud enough to wake them up. however, i still could not hear anything on the other side--there was still no indication of them being conscious. at that point there was nothing more we could do other than me continuing to call and stay on the phone in hopes of making positive contact with the pilots. eventually, after 15 minutes or so (from what i can recall) since the initial alarm and air sounds, we finally received contact from the pilots. all that was said was something like, 'hey sorry we've been busy up here, but we are ok. just standby for more info and we will call back.' with positive contact from the pilots in the flight deck, i was so relieved and instructed my crew to put everything away and take their jumpseats while we stood by for an update.while waiting for the update, the cabin temperature dropped--we were very cold and our ears began to pop/hurt. i confirmed with my crew they were experiencing the same cold temperatures and ear popping. the next form of contact/update we received from the pilots was via pa. they notified the entire cabin that they had requested priority handling and we would be diverting to redacted. they confirmed we would be conducting an emergency landing and would have emergency equipment/authorities meeting us on the ground.followed by the cabin pa, i received a call to the front from the pilots. captain began by informing us that they had donned their oxygen masks and confirmed there was a depressurization. the captain asked me if our oxygen masks had deployed, i informed him they had not. since they had advised air traffic control and we would be conducting an emergency landing, i proceeded with standard brief information and procedures.after providing me with brief information, the captain's tone seemed to be unalarmed and when i inquired about preparing the cabin, he said to prepare the cabin like normal. i inquired again, if he meant like a normal final/standard landing, and he confirmed yes. after receiving the update/information regarding our emergency landing and diversion to redacted, i proceeded by preparing the cabin like normal and did not perform emergency demonstrations. as i walked through the cabin for compliance, i made sure to talk to my exit rows and confirm they were aware of us landing and to be alert for further instructions. i also asked them to review their safety card again prior to landing. despite cabin announcements, pax seemed to be unaware of the emergency landing and/or were incredibly calm by our updates. our landing was incredibly smooth and did not cause alarm. once we were on the ground, we could see emergency crews outside of the plane with sirens and lights. when we got to the gate and the seatbelt sign went off, i called the flight deck to confirm we were clear to disarm all doors (i had not received any instructions since being on the ground about what to expect). the pilot responded with 'we are at the gate aren't we?' i took his comment as a sign that it was clear for us to proceed with standard procedures and made the announcement instructing fas to disarm doors for arrival and standby for all-call. we disarmed all of our doors, cross-checked, and all-called before the gate agent knocked like usual.once the door was opened, all pax remained seated based on our instructions and supervisors boarded. with the help of staff, pax were instructed to deplane while i conducted a briefing with supervisor and her colleagues.there was no further conversation conducted between myself, my crew and the pilots beyond them apologizing for the lack of communication. i am still unaware of the circumstances surrounding the depressurization and what occurred in the flight deck.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown
synopsis: Cessna 150 pilot reported starting the takeoff roll with an aircraft on final approach. Pilot rejected the takeoff.
text: at about xa:0xx local time on day 0 my son and i taxi to runway xx at redacted for a sight seeing flight. i heard a sportsman in the pattern (multiple take offs and landings). i performed my run up at the instrument landing system hold short line on taxi way 1/2. i thought i heard the sportsman call turning crosswind for xx and taxied to the runway. before crossing the movement/non-movement line for runway xx, i turned the plane toward the approach end to look for traffic. no traffic was seen and made the call i was departing runway xx. a second later i heard the sportsman say he was side stepping and asked if the cessna departing would delay the take off for spacing. i pulled the throttle back to idle and confirmed i was delaying my take off roll. the sportsman said he was just behind us about 200' above. i then saw him above and to the left as he performed his go around. i then commenced my take off and departed the area to the north. the problem: i did not see landing traffic and took runway xx for departure with landing traffic on final.causes: 1. when i made my turn towards the approach end of runway xx, the sun was setting and right in line with any landing traffic, which probably obstructed my view of the landing traffic. 2. perhaps the landing traffic calling crosswind when on base - which in my mind put him at the other end of the runway?3. i did not hear the call of the landing traffic of turning final. i may have missed it while explaining to my son what would happen on takeoff. prevention:1. when checking for traffic before taking a runway and the sun is right in line with the approach end, wait a few more seconds while looking for traffic. 2.verify/double check where known traffic is before taking the runway. even a crosswind could be shorter than expected.3. when with passengers, have a sterile cockpit during pre-takeoff checklists.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor reported an NMAC while departing the pattern with student. Flight continued normally.
text: while finishing up pattern work at redacted with a student, student turns crosswind and announces to traffic 'aircraft x left cw runway xx, we will be a left downwind departure to redacted.' while student was making this call i noticed on ads-b traffic (aircraft y) northbound 1/2 mile or less from the pattern(which is a southbound pattern- left pattern xx) and at an altitude about 800 feet above pattern altitude.student turns downwind and announces 'left downwind xx, we will be a downwind departure to the south.'on this turn i quickly pulled up the conflicting head on traffic call sign and radioed up 'is aircraft y on frequency?'seeing traffic now at our altitude and looking to be heading directly for us- i began a right turn- aircraft y did respond saying 'he was making a right turn to enter the downwind (less than 500ft away at my altitude) he thought we (aircraft x) would be higher.' his turn to the downwind was between mid field and the approach end of xx- less than 1 mile west of runway.his choice to fly directly into downwind traffic at pattern altitude was a shock to me.there was multiple planes within the 7 minutes prior announcing and joining the pattern from the nw on a 45 deg entry for a left midfield downwind- when i originally noticed this traffic on ads-b i thought they would fly further west of the field to do what all the other pilots were doing to join the pattern.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Landing Without Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported an engine EGT in the caution range.
text: enroute to redacted, requested cruise climb from f340 to f360 per flight plan. at approximately f352 the number 2 engine egt surged into caution range. checklists were accomplished (autothrottle was disengaged and thrust lever retarded until back within normal egt range). red line was not exceeded. qrc and qrh were accomplished. continued climb and leveled off at f360 and autothrottles were re-engaged. egt was in normal range but was 100c greater than number 1 engine egt. radio was contacted and phone patch requested to dispatch and maintenance control. as we discussed options, number 2 engine egt climbed up to 115c greater than number 1 engine. due to warmer trending egt, captain and i decided to request priority handling and divert to redacted. preparations were made for an overweight landing (approximately 10, 000 lbs over maximum landing weight.) emergency vehicles were asked to standby. descent, approach and landing were normal and uneventful. taxied to the gate under own power.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757 flight crew reported a flight deck window arching and crack resulting in a diversion.
text: the flight began with a normal and smooth pushback, taxi and take off. as we were climbing through 18, 000 feet, relief pilot left for his rest break and as he closed the door behind him first officer noticed a significant long spark on r2 window. at the time i was checking in with redacted [artcc] on a newly assigned frequency. first officer brought into my attention about the spark on r2 and as we started to ascertain if that could have been st. elmo's fire, eicas suddenly displayed 'window heat (r)' message. i advised the first officer to continue flying and i would do the window heat non-normal checklist procedure. the checklist directed us to check the window in question if it had any visible arcing or cracking. since it was night time and the cockpit was too pitch dark, i advised the first officer turn on the flash light and see if there was any damage to the window. on doing so we both discovered large arcing on left bottom side of the window. checklist dictated to land at a nearest suitable airport if such damage was visible. i immediately decided to call relief pilot back and as he was stepping back into the flight deck he observed a large crack had also developed on right bottom side of the window. we decided to request priority handling and land back asap. roles were delegated as per the sop, first officer was asked to continue flying while i and relief pilot completed the necessary checklists including diversion guidelines, obtaining weather and performances data. i advised the air traffic control of our intention, spoke to dispatch and maintenance control. we decided to return to redacted and air traffic control offered us rw xxl for landing considering it was longer than xxr and we were going to make an overweight landing. i asked the purser to pull up his briefing card and briefed him accordingly. made an announcement over the pa and apprised passengers of the safety concern and that we were returning to redacted. told them upon reaching the gate customer service would be there to arrange for their alternate travel. also gave heads up to them they would be noticing emergency vehicles on the ground and they didn't need to worry about it as their presence was totally going to be out of abundance of caution. due to heavy weight, high vref approach and potential liability issues i decided to land the plane. an uneventful landing was conducted at the end. briefed local maintenance and chief pilot thereafter.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A300 Captain reported that after arriving at the gate; setting the parking brake; and shutting down the engines; the aircraft began to roll.
text: after landing we taxied to our parking spot. i followed the marshallers direction into the spot and after receiving the stop signal i reached down and set the parking brake as i always do. after setting the brake i secured both engines and called for the shutdown checklist. as we got down to parking brake i looked at the pressure gauge and noticed the pressure was not set and the handle retracted. at that same moment the first officer called out we are moving. we both immediately hit the brakes and reset the parking brake. we established contact with ramp to make sure everyone was ok. thankfully ramp replied and told us all personnel were clear. we rolled what appeared to be less than 10ft. once parking brake was set, and verified set, we finished the shut down checklist. we were pushed back into the spot and completed the secure checklist without further incident. i firmly believe that i set the brake after stopping the aircraft as i have done every single time prior, but i suppose i could have missed it or possibly pulled it and not set it properly or somehow inadvertently knocked it loose during fuel cutoff. my first officer said he saw me pull the handle as he normally does before starting the checklist. regardless, it did not get set properly and i did not verify the brake was set by immediately checking the pressure gauge upon pulling the handle. this is an item i will not miss in the future. this is the first time this has ever happened to me and needless to say it has spooked me pretty bad. i feel we were extremely lucky today.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Tecnam P2012 Traveller Captain reported that the left engine began to lose power during cruise. The Captain returned to the departure airport and landed safely.
text: shortly after reaching cruising altitude of 9500 feet and setting cruise power, the left engine began to intermittently lose 15 to 30% power. there was a noticeable yaw to the left and and tone change in the engine. i was about 50 miles from redacted so i turned around and went back to redacted and landed.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported low altitude alert was issued by ATC during a visual approach.
text: during a night visual approach to runway xxr in redacted with the first officer flying while i monitored, we received a low altitude alert from air traffic control and elected to abandon the approach and try again. we were initially expecting runway xxr, but when the atis was advertising that runway xyl was in use, we changed the approach in the flight management system and briefed for runway xyl. upon contacting approach control, the controller advised that the winds were from the south and gave us the option of xz or xxr. we chose xxr, due to the runway being longer, and a runway assessment indicated we had adequate runway to land with a slight tailwind. as we descended to 2000 feet for the approach, we picked up the runway visually and were cleared for a visual approach. the final approach fix altitude was 1600 feet, and the first officer selected 1600 as the next altitude while arming the instrument landing system xxr approach. however, when the autopilot captured the instrument landing system signal, it turned away from the runway and paralleled the course instead. it was then that i realized that the instrument landing system signal must have still been set to runway xyl. the instrument landing system frequency for both xxr and xyl were the same, and i had not seen the ident displayed on the primary flight display (pfd). the other issue was that the papi for that runway was out of service, so it was difficult to determine our glide path. the first officer disconnected the autopilot and tried to return the aircraft to the centerline while i disengaged the flight directors. while i was trying to find an rnav approach to quickly load into the flight management system, air traffic control alerted us to our low altitude, and i saw we were at 1000 feet and still outside the final approach fix. we attempted to regain altitude to salvage the approach, but air traffic control offered to vector us back for another approach, and we agreed. at this point, we had already been configuring for landing, and we had the gear down and the flaps were at config 3. as we continued to climb, we were slow to reconfigure, and the aircraft was still at approach speed (160-170 knots) when i instructed the first officer to select toga, and we were finally able to climb to 2000 feet and reconfigure the aircraft. on the next approach, i noted the correct ident on the pdf for runway xxr, and we were able to successfully land. in hindsight, i should have known something was wrong with the instrument landing system signal when i did not see the ident displayed. i also should have been monitoring the approach better and corrected the altitude deviation sooner, or at least commanded a full go-around once air traffic control alerted us.cause: it has been many years since i've seen a situation where the instrument landing system frequency is the same for both runways. i did not consider that multiple runways changes might cause the wrong runway to be selected by air traffic control, and i should have confirmed the correct ident before allowing the first officer to arm the approach.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation instructor pilot reported a traffic coordination conflict while back taxiing on a runway at a non-towered airport with another aircraft on final approach. The aircraft on final performed a go-around to provide separation.
text: we were conducting stop and gos, but did not have enough runway to take off, so we got clear of the runway because aircraft y was on final (we had been coordinating with them the entire time in the traffic pattern). as we entered the runway to begin our back taxi, aircraft y made a call on ctaf that an aircraft (aircraft z) was on final. aircraft z had not made a single radio call on the d56 ctaf, which we had noticed and aircraft y confirmed that aircraft z had not made a single one. we didn't see them turn base to final and when we heard aircraft y make that call and then saw aircraft z on final, we swiftly exited the runway. we were off of the runway by the time aircraft z would've touched down, but aircraft z executed a go-around out of precaution.cause: lack of coordination from aircraft z, and i didn't zoom out on the mfd (multi-function flight display) because i still had it zoomed in to determine if we had 2000ft to take off. it was a fault on both ends. certain fatigue on my end too since this was a late afternoon flight and the second consecutive day where i had an early morning flight and a late afternoon flight in the same day.suggestions: all aircraft in the traffic pattern should be coordinating with each other. also checking the mfd before entering a runway, because traffic might not be talking. i was scanning final as aircraft y was coming in to land but at the time, aircraft z was likely on base which i didn't see.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: B737 pilot reported a caution light during the takeoff roll and an autothrottle disconnect with an associated red light. The pilot rejected the takeoff with no injury or damage; and the Engine Electronic Controls; were found in the alternate mode.
text: around 80 kts caution light with associated engine light occurred on takeoff. autothrottles clicked off with flashing red lights. rejected takeoff was performed. when completing rejected takeoff checklist after clearing the runway - electronic engine controls (eec) were found to be in the alt mode. maintenance control notified. gate return performed.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported a discrepancy with the location of Spot 25 at DFW.
text: on day 0, approximately xa:30. aircraft x. dfw - redacted. aircraft x pushed from dfw gate xx and was released at the 'x' by the ground crew. ramp cleared aircraft x to taxi out to spot 25. using the jeppesen airport moving map (amm) on page 10-9 of the 'taxi' tab, spot 25 appeared to be south of the three light poles.construction, light poles and spot locations are accurately depicted on company page. ramp notified the crew that spot 25 was to the left and that we were the second aircraft to taxi towards spot 26 in lieu of 25. there was plenty of space to turn left back to spot 25. the aircraft's magenta dot is on the line for spot 25, but north of the number 25 on the amm. the chart depicts 25 in a non-taxi area with light poles and construction staging equipment.cause: geospatial data is not slewed precisely between the gps position and the jeppesen chart. perspective taxiing from xx alley made spot 25 looked precariously close to the three light posts and more maneuvering space was open near spot 26.recommendations: resync or recalibrate the gps signal accuracy for electronic devices if needed. paint the number 25 with arrow on taxi line where the fork is to clarify. update the jeppesen chart by moving spot 25 exactly adjacent to the line. limit use of spot 25 until construction is complete or discrepancies listed above are resolved.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Other / Unknown; Ground Event / Encounter Aircraft
synopsis: Flight crew reported while on the ramp another aircraft was parked very close to their aircraft and began to taxi resulting in the other aircraft striking their wing.
text: our aircraft was parked at the fbo in teb. it had been towed into place and backed into a spot alongside other aircraft with our tail facing a hangar. aircraft y, was parked slightly behind us and to our right. we had a clear path in front of us to taxi out, and we discussed the nose of aircraft y being a little close but that we would keep an eye on the distance and taxi slow in case we needed a wing walker.with pax (passengers) onboard, we cleared the area and started engines, ran the after start checklist, and got our taxi clearance. before we started moving, the captain announced 'clear left, ' and when i looked to clear the right side, i was alarmed to see that aircraft y, parked with it's left wing behind our right wing, had begun to taxi forward. i immediately notified my captain and threw up my arms to the window in an x signal to the other crew as it didn't look like they would clear. my captain did the same. the other crew appeared to see us motioning and stopped briefly, but then started moving again and subsequently struck our wing. to our surprise they continued taxing out toward the runway and we called them on ground to inform them that they had hit us. they said they didn't realize they had hit us, and we asked if they saw us motioning them to stop. they said that they saw us motioning but their marshaler signaled them to go. they aborted their taxi and returned to the ramp.we shut down our aircraft and tended to our passengers. no one was injured.suggestions: suggest that the fbo use wider spacing with no overlap when positioning aircraft. it is already a tight ramp with a high incidence of collisions. crew of aircraft y should use wing walkers when necessary and confirm wingtip clearance before moving. it seems they were in a hurry, and i believe a slower pace could have helped them avoid this as well.

synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported experiencing a flight with no VNAV resulting in flight towards terrain on the final approach; ATC issued a low altitude and the flight crew returned to the correct altitude.
text: i was operating a flight from to redacted. the aircraft was a crj-700 without vnav and with a single flight management system. we experienced a low-altitude event during the rnav xx y approach into redacted. i was pilot monitoring and the captain was pilot flying. conditions were vme from the initial approach fix until landing. at 4000 ft msl, we were cleared direct redacted for the approach. shortly after, we were told to switch to the tower frequency. at 4000 ft, prior to redacted, the vertical guidance snowflake had not populated, so the pf initiated a descent to 2700 ft using constant speed mode for the crossing restriction at redacted. the pf then reached up to set 900 ft in the altitude pre-selector for minimums and i confirmed the altitude. vertical guidance populated shortly after, and the pf adjusted the vs mode descent to track the snowflake. i cross-checked the altitude at the next fix to verify we would meet the crossing restriction. at redacted, the approach was stable. the captain then asked what the ref speed was for the approach. i did not remember off the top of my head, so the captain used the flight management system to find the ref speed on the legs page. i was also heads down, looking at the flight management system with him. he found the speed and verbalized it. at that moment, we received a caution obstacle alert. i scanned the primary flight display (pfd), and we were at 1080 msl crossing redacted. the crossing restriction was 1500. at the same time, tower called with a 'low altitude alert, please check altimeter 29.76'. i responded '29.76, aircraft x'. the captain disconnected the autopilot and initiated a climb. as soon as i finished responding to tower, i stated that we should be at 1500 ft. after climbing and reestablishing a stable approach, we continued the approach to landing uneventfully.

text: on day 0, at approximately xa:40, a student pilot under my supervision was conducting his first solo flight. the student pilot was instructed to perform three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop. the first two landings were performed without incident. on the third landing, the airplane, a cessna 172s, bounced, then began porpoising with the nose gear striking the runway multiple times. the student initiated a go-around and landed without incident and taxied the airplane back to the ramp. the airplane was immediately grounded. subsequent inspection identified visible buckling of the lower firewall consistent with repeated nose gear contact with the runway during the landing sequence.there were no injuries to the pilot or any persons on the ground. there was no damage to property, only what was observed on the aircraft. weather conditions at the time of the incident were visual flight rules with light winds

synopsis: General aviation pilot reported having to avoid gliders in the area and stated that glider activities near 89TA conflict with IFR traffic descending to IWS and SGR.
text: i was flying aircraft x on an instrument flight rules flight plan from redacted to iws. my initial clearance was radar vectors/as filed (which was direct from redacted to iws), and shortly after takeoff was cleared direct to west houston airport and climbed to my filed altitude of 9000 ft., which was above the clouds. the ceilings were around 4000 - 5000 ft. for the entire flight, although the visibility was somewhat poor at iws but still above 3 miles according to the unofficial awos that the airport has. the direct route from redacted to iws puts traffic almost directly above 89traffic advisory. i used to tow and occasionally fly gliders, so i was familiar with their operations and local frequencies. on this particular day, iah was landing east and therefore traffic had to be lower than the jets on the east finals. i was given a descent to lower altitudes and i had been hand flying these descents, but my atp rated passenger (although not familiar with the century 4 autopilot) stated the autopilot could do the descents. for some reason it kept keeping us around a 300 - 400 fpm descent rate. after struggling with the autopilot for the descents, air traffic control advised for us to pick up the rate of descent. we then tried to get the autopilot to expedite the descent, at which time i decided to hand fly the descent as i had almost every time flying this plane in the past. as we started coming down, air traffic control advised multiple targets (possibly gliders) in the area. i then switched to the local soaring frequency, 123.3, on the secondary radio and made traffic reports for us. at around 4500 ft., we went vmc through the clouds and immediately in front of us was a glider without ads-b/transponder as it would normally show up on the display. i took evasive action by leveling off with a turn to the east, knowing that it was likely there were more gliders just below the clouds (likely the legal 500 ft. below, but still in the 3500 - 4000 ft. range). air traffic control then started getting on us about how we needed to descend. i told them i was leveling off due to glider traffic, and they started giving us vectors to the east and north to take us away from iah finals while pushing us to descend. it was difficult to comply with the clearances while also trying to maintain visual contact with the gliders. eventually we descended away from the glider field then landed safely at iws.i believe the issue is that the glider field is right in the way of descending instrument flight rules traffic to iws and sgr. i looked at procedures in the houston area and the only arrival available to iws/sgr is the snday1 arrival that keeps traffic 15 nm west of the 89traffic advisory soaring operation. flying instrument flight rules traffic between 2000 - 4000 ft. within a 3 nm radius of 89traffic advisory is not safe due to the gliders being towed anywhere up to 4000 ft. in that area. i would therefore highly recommend not flying instrument flight rules traffic over the top of 89traffic advisory with altitudes below 5000 ft. on saturdays and sundays during daylight hours. i am filing this report for the information of air traffic control and also in the event that i did not comply with a clearance in the interest of flight safety.

synopsis: Tecnam P2006T flight instructor reported being unable to restart the engine after feathering and securing it during training. Instructor and student returned to departure airport and safely performed a single engine landing.
text: dual instruction being given, specifically within the part 61 multi-engine course for students seeking to add their multi-engine rating to existing commercial certificate.conducting flight lesson with student practicing both visual flight rules maneuvers (e.g., steep turns, stalls) as well as engine inoperative maneuvers. as part of course, instructors can demonstrate, while at a safe minimum altitude, the actual shutdown and feathering/securing of an engine on the twin-tecnam aircraft being used.flight instructor was flying the aircraft while the student was walking through each step of both the securing checklist as well as the engine restart checklist procedure. followed the engine securing checklist (with the exception of leaving the right engine fuel selector on the right tank) to a shutdown of the right engine followed by the restart checklist procedure, but the engine did not relight / restart. checklist offers a continuation of the procedure if the engine restart was not successful with a few additional items to follow. this was accomplished using the additional on-board aircraft battery to assist, but the engine still would not restart. the checklist was reviewed for completion and no steps were observed to have been missed. the right engine would not restart and at that time the aircraft proceeded directly back to redacted for an actual one-engine inoperative landing on runway xx. to avoid any populated areas and for time-consideration, the aircraft entered a wide left-base to runway xx. there was no other observed traffic in the pattern or in the vicinity of the airport, only one aircraft holding short of runway xx in a ready-for-takeoff position (again, holding short of the runway). tecnam aircraft landed without any incident and proceeded single-engine taxi to parking.

synopsis: Sling 2 flight crew reported miss communication between aircraft in traffic pattern at a non-towered airport resulted in an NMAC event.
text: i was doing visual flight rules practice approaches into redacted with an instructor while under the hood. we went missed from the instrument landing system runway xx but could only climb to 2, 000 ft because of cloud cover. another pilot entered the airspace and radioed on the ctaf that he intended to take the instrument landing system approach. i made a traffic call communicating my altitude and my intended course. instead of taking the instrument landing system, the other pilot began descending and turned inbound along the shoreline for a normal visual flight rules pattern approach without making any announcements. i was task saturated and under the hood and too busy trying to keep the plane level while fighting my own disorientation caused by the weather to make note of the other pilot's deviation. when my instructor saw that we were on a collision course, they instructed me to remove the foggles so that i could see the incoming threat. the aircraft was descending into me perpendicularly, so i took evasive action to avoid the incoming aircraft which got close enough for me to identify the shape and color of the plane (a small twin engine). the other pilot realized the danger at the last moment and climbed to avoid me as well. this encounter and encounters like this that have occurred and will continue to occur at this airport can be avoided if it became a towered airport. there is far too much traffic at this location for it to remain untowered.

synopsis: Cessna Citation pilot reported several engine surges after turning on the engine anti-ice resulted in a return to the departure airport.
text: during climbout from redacted entered imc icing conditions around 10 thousand feet. just after turning on the engine anti ice the right engine compressor stalled numerous times. looking at the engine instruments the right itt (interstage turbine temperature) was over temperature limits and i brought the power back to get below limits. the engine throttle split was significant to keep the right engine below itt limits, so decided to request priority handling and return to redacted. the approach and landing was uneventful and taxied to the fbo to shutdown for inspection.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: C172 flight crews reported practice area location and lack of communication resulted in an NMAC event.
text: i departed redacted headed towards redacted flying visual flight rules. approximately 15 miles away from redacted, on an approximate heading of 110 degrees at 7, 500 feet, i observed an aircraft (n passing in front of me from left to right approximately 1 mile ahead at the same altitude. the aircraft then began a 360 turn to its right, which put the aircraft directly into my flight path.i took evasive action and avoided a collision. in reviewing the ads-b data, the aircraft appeared to be less than 500 feet of horizontal separation and 25 feet or less of vertical separation.i believe the primary factor was the aircraft's lack of performing clearing turns before maneuvering. however, i also believe that having designated student training areas below the bravo shelf contribute to congested airspace for aircraft departing redacted to the east.

synopsis: PA-24 pilot reported a partial loss of engine power during initial climb. Pilot returned to departure airport and landed.
text: i had a visual flight rules flight plan from redacted to redacted and had been given a squawk code for flight following as well as a departure frequency for redacted center. pre-flight was uneventful, run up was uneventful, and i was cleared for a right downwind departure on runway xx. the take off roll was uneventful, take off was uneventful, gear was up, auxiliary fuel pump was still on. at approximately 300 msl, the engine rpms went from full power (approximately 2600) down several hundred to somewhere between 2000 and 2200 rpm for 2 to 3 seconds, then back up to full power. approximately 4 to 5 seconds later, the same drop occurred again for another 2 to 3 seconds. i immediately initiated a right crosswind turn and requested priority handling and asked for any available runway to land. i continued to slowly climb as the rpm oscillation continued. i was cleared for xyr but was in the right downwind too close to make a base and final turn. i asked for and was cleared for xyl, but was unable to make that base and final turn quickly enough. once turned, i had made it just above 900 msl and was too high for either xyl or xyr. i asked for and was cleared to land with a tailwind on runway xz. i informed air traffic control that i was comfortable with the 11 knot tailwind and was able to touchdown on runway xz somewhere between the first 1/3 and 1/2 of the runway. i was given taxi instructions to allow aircraft y to depart xx before returning to parking.

text: hnd - redacted. i was captain and pilot flying of this flight. my first officers had warned me about the runway conditions on runway 34 right for takeoff at haneda airport. as we took the runway and started takeoff run, we started feeling bumps from the potholes on the runway. at one point, the runway was so rough. i actually made a comment during the takeoff run. it was the opinion of the entire crew that a report should be written to bring it to the attention of the review team. it would be a good idea for the union and the company to inspect the runway and actually ride in the jump seat to see and feel the actual roughness of the takeoff. it would be unfortunate to have another accident similar to the dc-10 tire failures, which caused the concorde's fuel system to fail in the subsequent loss of the concorde aircraft and the passengers on board. i certainly hope that that the review team will take this report seriously and do something to mitigate a possibility of tire failure during takeoff.

synopsis: B767-300 pilot reported the brakes were not set before the tow bar was removed.
text: during pushback i started the right engine then asked the mechanic if we were clear to start the left engine. we were told the left engine was clear to start. i began the engine start and shortly after the mechanic asked me did i tell you to set the parking brake? i replied no and then i was told to set the parking brake. i felt the airplane was moving as i set the brake and asked if everyone was okay on the ground and then asked if the aircraft was okay. i did not know the tow bar had been disconnected. i do not know if the mechanic was in the tug or not during pushback but i have noticed the mechanic riding in the tug vs not in the tug has changed the level of transparency of what i/we see as pilots. perhaps their routine is affected as well and the habits they are used to are affected when they ride or do not ride in the tug. i know many times the mechanic goes through steps during the pushback where headset communication is interrupted and i am not aware of when they are or are not in communication with us. i get uncomfortable with this period especially when we are starting an engine or the towbar is being disconnected. there are so many things that could happen while the mechanic is unplugged from us. i do greatly appreciate when they let me know the are going to disconnect and when the reconnect their headset and i hold everything associated with the pushback and start during this time period. i certainly know this is an ongoing issue of brakes not being set during starts. i'm not sure what i could have done other than perhaps noticing the sounds of the tow at being manipulated during disconnect. i was focusing on the start, thinking of, the weather we had, and a runway change all at the same time. i look forward to any suggestions to keep this from happening in the future.

synopsis: B747 flight crew reported an EICAS warning for the Captain's pitot-static heat.
text: after block out and engines started with after start checklist complete. we had an icass message heat p/s captain. after contacting dispatch and maintenance control it was agreed we return to parking.maintenance ran tests and advised us that it appeared to be a captain pitot failure. the captains pitot static probe was deferred under 747-8 minimum equipment list 30-xx-x-x.we blocked out after maintenance cleared the logbook. we briefed prior to takeoff that there may be a discrepancy of airspeed since the system had been worked on. on takeoff roll the captains airspeed indicator was up to 20kts less than the first officer airspeed indicator prior to 100kts. above 80 kts and approaching 100kts the airspeed indicators matched within 2 kts. i elected to continue weather was cavu and the airspeeds were within reasonable match to continue a normal takeoff. we had no icass messages during takeoff roll.in cruise the capt and first officer airspeeds stayed within 2-5 kts indicated. in the descent airspeed indicators also stayed within 2kts approach and landing were normal. during deceleration on landing again below 100kts the airspeed indicators began to separate between the capt and first officer up to 20 kt difference as we slowed to turn off the runway. the captains airspeed was again the lower airspeed indicator. aircraft was written up in redacted after block in stating the discrepancy in speeds reference above.in redacted with the initial write up of heat p/s captain. we observed the maintenance crew unbolting, cutting the seal and attempting to remove the captains pitot static tube. is it normal procedure to defer the captain pitot under minimum equipment list 30-xx-x-x by just reattaching the failed pitot tube and no further testing or action required?

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Vehicle; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported SFO Runways 1L and 1R do not have hold short lines due to ongoing construction and a tug was observed driving right to the edge of Runway 28L during takeoff roll.
text: while on the takeoff roll on runway 28l at sfo at xa:00, a super tug with an aircraft attached taxied from one of the runway 1s (relatively confident it was 1r) directly up to the edge of our active runway. the speed and timing of their approach left us with essentially zero margin to initiate a safe rejected takeoff had the vehicle/aircraft not stopped in time.the tug was not on tower frequency, so i did not hear any clearance or acknowledgment. given the circumstances, i believe a rejected takeoff would have been fully justified. i elected not to call for one only because of trust in the air traffic control system - a trust that has been called into question recently.there is no hold-short line painted on the runway 1s. as a result, the tug proceeded all the way to the edge of the white runway designation line for 28l. this created another serious time/distance dilemma for deciding whether to reject. runway monitoring systems and stop-bar lights on the runway 1s are presumably inoperative due to ongoing construction and vehicle traffic. had they been active, the lights on 28l probably could have illuminated given the tug's rate of closure.sfo's runway width is published as 200 feet. aircraft x exceeds this, as do larger aircraft. while it was impossible to accurately judge lateral separation at night during the takeoff roll, the absence of a hold-short line raises legitimate concerns about wingtip clearance. from my observation, the tug and attached aircraft stopped right at the edge of the 28l runway line.

synopsis: A319 Captain reported cabin fumes that resulted in crewmember illness symptoms after pushback and a return to the gate. After engine shutdown oil was found in the APU inlet.
text: boarded in redacted. passengers were the first to notice and report the smell to the flight attendant. as i came on board i also smelled something that was faint but smelled like potential burning oil. i called a mechanic out for a second opinion before writing it up and he came out and said it was definitely not coming from the plane and instead was caused by the belt loader near the aircraft and that once we started engines and pushed back from the gate the smell would go away. we agreed to that plan but once we had pushed back from the gate the smell was still present so we returned to the gate. as far as symptoms go, i had a headache pretty much as soon as i stepped on the aircraft. after taxing out the first officer and i both had a strange sensation of a metallic taste which later the #1 fa also commented she had. upon return to the gate the #1 fa also said she felt slightly nauseous. the crew agreed that we were no longer fit to fly and needed to be seen by medical personnel due to our symptoms. i called the emergency line first who then directed me to call a medical advisory service. the medical advisory service asked about my symptoms during the event and that of the crew members which i explained in detail. then the medical advisory service asked if any of us were still experiencing symptoms which none of us were. then the medical advisory service said that in their professional opinion since no one was still having symptoms they would like to medically clear us to fly and continue on the sequence. i explained that we would still be seeking medical care. it took about 20 min with each crew member answering questions before they directed us to go to the hospital. i was removed from the rest of the sequence and deadheaded home although my schedule does not reflect that at all. it simply shows me ending in redacted with no way home. i was told by my chief pilot that it was as if i were removed due to a family emergency. i explained that my schedule was altered due to a company failure to maintain its aircraft, not because i called in sick or with a family emergency. however, due to the lack of contractual language i learned i will not be getting paid for the extra day of the trip. not only did i lose pay but my schedule for the purpose of far 117 work and rest schedules is completely inaccurate.cause: oil was found in apu inlet after the fact. this is a known problem with airbus and the mechanic should have recognized it and backed me up in writing it up. instead he dissuaded me from writing it up and instead convinced me it had nothing to do with fumes coming from the aircraft. in the future i will immediately deboard if i smell anything even slightly abnormal.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a NMAC while on final approach. Flight crew performed a go around and returned to the departure airport.
text: my student and i departed for dyl for pattern work for our block time. runway 23 was in use at dyl. we had two close calls in the pattern. the first involved aircraft z. while doing pattern work, we heard this aircraft making calls they were inbound to the field. they entered the pattern in the crosswind. my student and i were turning upwind to crosswind when this aircraft entered the crosswind in front of us, cutting us off in the pattern. my student and i were following the departure procedures for this runway and were about two miles from the airport. the other aircraft entered the crosswind closer to the airport. there was plenty of separation with this aircraft, but had i not been in the airplane, my student would not have spotted them. the second incident, involved another airplane in our fleet aircraft y. my student and i were on short final for the runway. we were within one mile of the runway. we saw on our avionics there was an aircraft off to our left, 400ft above us and descending. the closest vertical separation this aircraft got to us was 200ft above our aircraft in the pattern. my student announced our position on each leg of the traffic pattern. as we noticed this aircraft coming towards us, i took to the radios and called out this traffic. they did eventually see us and then continued to fly the base, through the final approach for the runway. on this approach, we performed a go around. aircraft y was flying parallel with us off to our right as we flew in the upwind. i asked aircraft y was on the frequency and asked what happened. they stated that they did not hear our radio transmissions and apologized for the mistake. at this point, my student and i departed to our original point of departure as we were running low on time for our block.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC while being vectored for approach. Pilot took evasive action and continued flight.
text: on vectors for the rnav for cdw runway 22 at 4, 000, i was alerted to unidentified visual flight rules traffic at my 1 o clock climbing from 500 feet below my assigned altitude of 4, 000. my avionics units (avidyne entegra mfd (multi-function flight display), avidyne ifd 550 and 440 also identified the traffic). i responded to approach that i did not have visual on the traffic. no assignment was made by air traffic control to avoid the traffic. i took evasive maneuvers, applying full power and initiating an immediate climb. after i had climbed 200 feet, i identified the traffic at 12 o clock at 4, 000 feet, indicating that a collision was possible had i maintained my assigned attitude without deviating. air traffic control provided a climb advisory after i had initiated my climb but i believe it would have been too late to avoid a collision.the visual flight rules traffic made a left turn and continued to climb and passed off my left wing at the same altitude at a distance of less than 500 feet.loss of separation continues to plague the newark sector within 50 miles of ewr. whether i am instrument flight rules avoiding visual flight rules traffic, or visual flight rules avoiding instrument flight rules traffic, i have had far too many traffic advisories in a short time span. newark needs to hire additional controllers or redesign the approach paths to reduce the likelihood of conflicts between instrument flight rules and visual flight rules traffic.i strongly recommend the newark bravo shelf is expanded horizontally to the south, west and north, to require visual flight rules traffic to remain below 3, 500 feet between 30 and 50 miles of the ewr airport. this would provide visual flight rules traffic with adequate obstacle clearance while avoiding mandated instrument flight rules descents into visual flight rules traffic without adequate attention from controllers to separate instrument flight rules traffic.

synopsis: A319 First Officer reported exceeding bank angle while on final approach in IMC.
text: redacted, instrument landing system xx. altitude 10000'. visibility was full imc. a/p (autopilot), a/t (auto throttles) engaged. established on the approach procedure, inside of redacted intersection approaching redacted, we were cleared for the approach to instrument landing system xx and contact tower. i was pf. as the pm was switching to contact tower, i armed the approach. after arming approach, aircraft banked left about 30 degrees and started a track toward the airport. i disengaged the autopilot and banked right to recapture an inbound course for redacted. i advised pm that the automation did not respond appropriately and i took over. as i was banking right, i called for direct to the fix and looked at my nd (navigation display) for a distance from redacted. during the time i was looking at the nd, i became unaware that my bank angle exceeded the normal range. after the pm said bank angle, i corrected immediately. i re-engaged the automation and we landed without further incident. i did not arm the approach until i was inbound on the runway heading.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Multiengine aircraft pilot reported a left engine failure during initial climb. Pilot returned to the departure airport and landed.
text: aircraft x was delivered to the fbo for annual inspection. after initial completion of the annual inspection, a pre-return to service run-up about a month later revealed a fuel leak on the right engine. both engines' throttle controls and fuel assemblies, because they were the same vintage, were removed and sent to company x for overhaul. both throttle controls and fuel assemblies were overhauled and reinstalled, and the aircraft was returned to service on day 0. i arrived at redacted to pick up aircraft x on day 8. after an extended pre-flight, i executed a runup to the tarmac. all engine indications were normal, oil pressures, oil temperatures, cylinder-head temperatures (cht), fuel flows and exhaust gas temperatures (egt). the runup was as usual with appropriate indications of oil-pressure and rpm drops as the propellers were exercised. i requested a taxi for full-length of the runway xx, but changed to an intersection take-off at taxiway 1. take-off procedures were normal, i.e., brakes held until released and engines' indications in the green. take off roll was normal with full rpm's, manifold pressures, and fuel flows. i extended my upwind flight along the runway center to 500' agl, then entered a turn crosswind. that is a point at which i normally start another check of the engine instruments, starting with the egt on the far right of the panel and working left across the rpm, throttle, and mixture in the middle of the panel, then to the lower left for the triple gauges and oil pressures, oil temperatures, and cylinder head temperatures, briefly before a normal rpm reduction to 2500 rpm at traffic pattern altitude or about 1000' agl. that check showed the left engine egt spiking to maximum temperature. i called redacted tower for a return to the runway stating i had an instrument problem. the crosswind turn required additional right rudder to correct a slight roll, which keyed me to check the other indications for the left engine. they showed low rpm, low mp (manifold pressure), and zero fuel flow. i then automatically pushed all engine controls forward, which they mostly were anyway at that stage of flight. because of the aircraft's known single-engine climb capability at redacted's elevation, i was able to obtain 800' agl to 1000' agl on downwind. after executing the emergency checklist, i adjusted the downwind-to base and base-to-dual turns to accommodate the critical engine out, extended the landing gear and flaps and landed on runway xx, rolling out to taxiway 1 and eventually taxiing to taxiway 2 to exit the runway. the aircraft is undamaged and no one sustained an injury. another aircraft on taxiway 2 reversed and exited the taxiway as redacted personnel and the fire truck arrived. after shutting down both engines and securing the aircraft, i was handed paperwork by the redacted airport personnel, which i filled out. the maintenance shop was notified and came out to tow the aircraft back to the shop. post event, the maintenance shop found a loose connection on a left engine fuel system hose which may have admitted air enough to disrupt normal mixture control. further, after the event and after additional runups, the left engine boost pump was found to exhibit low pressure and is being replaced. currently the aircraft is still in the shop awaiting the new left engine boost pump. an additional flight test upon return to service is anticipated. on the human performance considerations, a positive factor is my more than 1000 hours in this aircraft and regular participation in type, make and model specific re-currency training programs. these programs over the years made my responses to this event practically automatic.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Global 5500 Captain reported inadvertent release of parking brake resulted in uncommanded aircraft movement and momentary loss of aircraft control.
text: at approximately xa:00 in redacted. i was occupying the right seat of aircraft x with my partner that day in the left seat. we have completed dual route verification and we doing our pre-departure briefing. we got up to the before start checklist. at that time ground control called us and told us one of our globals was returning to the ramp and they might need to switch airplanes with us. at that point we got out of the cockpit. the parking brake was inadvertently turned off during this process. next we were standing in the back waiting for the company airplane to park. then at or around this time aircraft x started to roll forward down the sloped ramp. the airplane rolled approximately 30 to 50 feet where my partner reoccupied the left seat and applied the brakes. no damage to the aircraft or any other aircraft was done.suggestions: this was classic case of task interruption. our company has very specific procedures on the removal of chocks and the occupying of the pilot seats during the removal of chocks. proper and immediate adherence to these procedures would've prevented this from happening. i would recommend in training we talk about the procedures we do every day and verify if we're actually doing procedures correctly. i would respectfully suggest covering procedures such as towing, jet blast on the ramp, chock removal, the discharging of coffee or ice and other liquids on the ramp. also vehicle operations on the ramp around our airplanes, these but a few things that might be covered and reminded during training. i would further suggest some additional day to day operations that need covered include uncontrolled airport ops, standard instrument departures with an engine failure after the divergent point.i am not trying to shift blame from what was most probably my error. what i am suggesting is sometimes we need to reaffirm the day-to-day operation and make sure we're doing things correctly.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B747-400 Captain reported engine oil quantity and pressure decrease after takeoff; followed by hydraulic system malfunction. Flight continued to destination.
text: soon after takeoff from rwy xx in redacted, the secondary eicas came on to show a partial compact engine indication. eng #1 oil quantity was down to 1.we were not surprised. the previous crew had reported their engine oil quantity having dropped after heir takeoff from redacted and maintenance in redacted had topped off the #1 oil by 11 qts.the oil pressure was slowly decreasing, but without any eicas msgs i decided to continue climbing as much as we could because of the mountains ahead and below us. we were very heavy, about 355 tons.some time later, the eng 1 oil press advisory msg came on. with oil p below the red line limit, the qrh directed us to shut the #1 engine down. we continued to climb but only to 29, 000 ft to comply with the fmc engine out drift down guidance.15 or minutes later, i was in the process of telling the crew that i preferred not to return to redacted (rvrs reporting around 2000) and were about to call dispatch, when the hyd press dem 1 msg came on. the hyd quantity was good, so i suspected a failed pump perhaps.some time later and without an operating eng #1, the hyd press sys 1 msg came on.i was familiar with this qrh procedure, having done it at the training center a few times. gravity landing gear extension would be needed and the flaps would be on secondary mode. my mind was then made up to continue to redacted where i was very familiar with the airport. the weather forecasts i had obtained at the hotel before departure were good and were now checked again to be great. no threat of nearby mountains like redacted and the winds would be almost lined up with the long redacted rwys.we sat-called dispatch/maintenance and after explaining our predicament, they were in agreement that continuing was the better option. i was concerned that if redacted refused to handle our emergency arrival, we'd have to go to redacted or redacted (our planned alternate) but redacted fortunately agreed to handle us. i insisted with the dispatcher that we'd need a tug to tow us off the rwy.it was at about this time that i took over pf duties from my first officer. i was going to let him fly and land the plane with an engine inop, but not with the #1 hyd system gone also.the former pf first officer, now pm then did an amazing job of balancing fuel which became the real focus and hassle for the rest of the flight.we had advised air traffic control after shutting the engine down much earlier, but the redacted center controller took it upon himself to give us priority handling. i was glad he had done so, as i suspected that priority handling to still be better understood to everyone, as opposed to our declared advising".redacted had reserved their longest rwy, xxr for our arrival. i managed to keep the plane on the rwy cl with the rudder and an occasional tap on the left or right brake as needed, but was happy at how steady the 747 remained without nose wheel steering.the good people of the redacted fd (fire department) had dispatched 4-5 trucks and did a visual inspection of our plane and #1 engine. they reported seeing nothing unusual.the tug pre-arranged by the dispatcher and ground operations was waiting and promptly towed us to the ramp.after blocking in, the mechanics opened the nacelle on engine #1 and saw a lot of oil (or hydraulic fluid, they said they didn't' know which) pour onto the ground.i called ground operations the next day to ask if someone had determined by now why we had also lost hyd system 1 after losing the #1 engine. they said they really couldn't be sure. they suspected either a failed demand pump or the entire accessory gear box having failed. they were considering changing the entire engine.cause: not sure. the engine had a massive leak of oil to the outside of the engine, not inside. the previous crew experienced a loss of engine oil in redacted, but never got an eicas msg, so didn't shut the engine down and continued all the way.i thought operations was closely monitoring the engines and trends remotely from their office. maybe everyone was off.suggestions: i was concerned that in secondary mode the flaps would take longer to deploy than in the simulator. i voiced my concern to my fos and briefed that i would slow down early. i really didn't want to go around because i had not allowed enough time for the gear and flaps.the qrh says to allow extra time for flap extension from 1 to 5 (4 minutes). i slowed down and asked for flaps much too soon, before downwind. i timed the flap extension with the stop watch. it took only 3 minutes and 30 seconds. the gear came down in alternate mode with all greens indicated in about a minute, or so. if this ever happens to me again, i won't slow down and configure so early."

synopsis: ERJ 175 First Officer reported returning to departure airport after experiencing multiple compressor stalls in #2 engine.
text: leaving 10k feet as we begin accelerating, we heard multiple loud bangs which felt to be under the right side of the cockpit. the captain was pilot flying, and he immediately turned off the auto pilot and auto throttle to begin leveling and slowing the airplane. we requested to level off at 12000ft and begin trouble shooting the issue. we had no indications on the eicas, and the engines were within normal parameters. we requested priority handling and informed that we would be returning to the field. the loud bangs continued ever few minutes in intervals of 2 or 3 bangs. we initially believed that it was a panel or door because it occurring during the acceleration period and seemed to occur when in turns. we decided to do a airport fly by to see if it could possibly be a gear door, but tower said they did not see anything. the flight attendant in the rear also stated that they felt the same sensation from the rear of the plane which led us to believe it had to be something different. we returned to the field with the bangs only occurring normally in turns. we landed below max landing weight and exited the runway. the fire trucks did not see anything of note, so we taxied back to the gate. we also received a remote circuit breaker trip, 'taxi lt rh'. during the walk around everything seemed normal until 3 passengers seated behind the number 2 engine said they saw flames shooting out the rear of the engine every time the loud bangs occurred. this led us to believe that the number 2 engine was having intermittent compressor stalls that were not severe enough to show and create surges in thrust.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported confusion about the crossing altitude at CADAB on the approach to SBP airport.
text: we were flying the rnav (gps) runway 29 approach into sbp this evening from kikii, which requires a hold in lieu of procedure turn (hilpt). we were cleared for the approach prior to crossing cadab. the approach had been armed, and we were on the vertical descent path when we crossed cadab at approximately 6800 ft. msl. it wasn't until just prior to cadab that we noticed there is a published maximum holding altitude of 6000 ft. msl. we expedited our descent to below 6000 ft. msl and continued the approach as normal. what we did notice was that as soon as we crossed cadab, the vertical deviation bar went from being on the path to being high. we were surprised that the aircraft didn't realize we needed to cross cadab no higher than 6000 ft. msl. looking back at the constraints in the navigation database in the aircraft, all it shows is that we needed to cross cadab at or above 5700 ft. msl (no mention of the following maximum holding altitude). nothing was mentioned to us by air traffic control, and the remainder of the approach was uneventful.
