synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported unexpected GPS jamming near ABQ during cruise flight. Flight crew continued the flight to their destination.
text: during cruise, near albuquerque, we began to lose gps due to jamming in the area. several other aircraft in the area were complaining of the same issue to air traffic control. the nav data page showed gps 2 completely lost, and gps 1 degraded to an aided" status and momentarily back to "nav" status before completely being lost. with the autopilot engaged, the aircraft began a standard bank turn to the left, upon which i quickly selected "hdg" mode to regain the plotted nd (navigation display) course to our next fix within .2 nm laterally. after reporting the incident to air traffic control, we completed the approved qrh procedure for gps interference. after being unable to regain gps accuracy, we deselected navaid function to continue to redacted. we were able to utilize irs (inertial reference system)/dme/dme for the remainder of the flight, as our gps remained jammed until landing. we also lost onboard wifi connectivity after the jamming event. the flight management system waypoint sequencing never was lost, and we landed without further incident in redacted. a logbook entry was made upon gate arrival in redacted.an unexpected jamming of our onboard gps equipment. my sole recommendation is for a more appropriate method to conduct electromagnetic/gps testing which respects the integrity of onboard navigation equipment used by the flying public."

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported an NMAC during cruise required evasive action.
text: i was pilot of aircraft x, enroute visual flight rules at approximately 7, 500 feet msl. at approximately xa42z on day 0, my ads-b in traffic system generated a traffic alert for nearby traffic.the traffic alert indicated an aircraft at my 3 o'clock position and 0 miles. based on the alert indicating immediate proximity, i immediately initiated a left turn away from the reported traffic to increase separation. i did not have enough time to positively identify the other aircraft visually or determine its aircraft type or registration.the traffic target appeared on ads-b exchange replay as target id x. the target appeared to be a non-icao / dynamic / radar-track type target rather than a normal ads-b target with a displayed n-number or aircraft type. i was unable to determine the aircraft registration or type from the cockpit display or public ads-b replay.the alert occurred near my altitude and close enough to create concern for a possible near-midair collision or unsafe proximity. i do not know whether the other aircraft was civilian or military. given the location near the patuxent river operating area and the non-icao nature of the target, i am reporting this event for safety awareness and possible atc/radar correlation.contributing factors may have included lack of visible or identifiable ads-b registration information for the target, possible radar/tis-b rebroadcast traffic, and operation near an area with military and civilian traffic.i maintained aircraft control, continued to monitor the traffic display, and continued the flight. i am submitting this report to document the ads-b traffic alert and possible near-midair event.

synopsis: Aircraft wheel technician reported an aircraft had a gate return with a brake locking problem due to a missing wheel bearing that was not installed.
text: on the day in question during build we were starting to get in our heavy summer volume of wheels in. we were short staffed including the trainer that was supposed to be training a new guy that day, so the asst. manager who also inspects the wheels put the new guy with person a who's only been there a little over 6 months and myself that's 2 weeks away of being there 6 months. we ended up building around 20 or 21 big mains while having to watch the new guy. later when we were done i asked the supervisor if he was going to check my work and he told me he would do it later. later that day when it was time to put on dust covers we put them on and continued cleaning of parts and shop keep and our usual daily tasks. fast forward to day 1 a plane gets taxied back in with brake locking problems. come to find out it was a missing bearing. mind you i'm not used to this kind of volume of wheels and didn't need to get put with a trainee. fast forward to day 5, the shop manager comes in and puts only me on administrative leave for a month pending the investigation of what happened. thru the whole month i emailed person b wondering why nobody needs a statement for me, and from speaking with others that i work with that not one thing happened to inspector and 2 ap mechanics not to mention ant one else that could possibly inspect after it got put on said aircraft. in a result i have been laid off and nobody else has been reprimanded. this could happen again which from what i hear it's happened before. but if it's the same people with credentials that it's getting by, who's to say it won't due to negligence.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Piper PA-22 pilot reported an NMAC with a Cessna 172 while in the pattern for landing.
text: i was flying patterns at redacted. at approximately xa:30, i was on left downwind for runway xx. there were several aircraft in the pattern. i was unable to get the air traffic control recording but to my recollection i had been cleared to land. air traffic control called me as traffic to a 172.air traffic control informed them they were gaining on me, 20kts faster and to widen their pattern. i was unable to see them at this point. i do not recall if they acknowledged having me in sight. liveatc.com was incomplete and i have not heard any other recordings. i confirmed later the 172 did veer slightly right.i was flying consistent patterns and having heard the instruction for them to widen, i proceeded normally to reduce power abeam the numbers, reduce speed, deploy 1st flaps, then began my base turn about 1nm to the west of the runway and about 1.5nm southwest of the intersection of xy/xx.as i rolled out of my turn on cross wind and looked left as my wing raised, i saw the 172 coming what appeared to be straight at me. simultaneously air traffic control directed them to 'climb immediately!' i received no instruction. there was really no time for me to do anything but stay my course as they passed directly above me. close enough to make out the landing gear.i finished my stop and go and completed one more pattern to finish my flight. i do not recall any further radio communication about the near miss.cause? the 172 was flying faster than typical for a 172 and my pa-22 is slower to begin with. knowing they were gaining on me and inside i would have expected them to make a sharper turn to the right and slow down. i suspect they did not have me in sight.air traffic control could have been less vague with them. they also could have cancelled my landing clearance, extended my downwind, and let the 172 go first. or they could have had the 172 do a right 360. but i do not know what traffic was behind them.for my part i might have had a closer look at adsb, however at that critical phase i try to keep my eyes outside and not let the ipad interfere with my night vision.i also could have made a radio call to ask if the 172 was clear before i made my base turn.things added up for potentially a very bad night for all. i feel like we all got lucky.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: A ZAB Center Controller reported they were unable to hear read backs of clearances while vectoring an aircraft for an approach to SAF on 132.8. Reporter states this frequency problem is a recurring issue that has not been addressed.
text: multiple aircraft inbound to saf airport. radar controller managing sequence by vectoring aircraft into the valley north of saf. audio quality of the frequency was serviceable until aircraft x. when the aircraft was approximately 15nw of the airport, the pilot was given descent to 13000 feet. the read back was barely intelligible. after the preceding aircraft was reported to have arrived, radar controller issued the approach clearance. once again, barely intelligible. as the aircraft is getting vectored and descended through the valley, and subsequently issued approach clearance, such frequency issue is unacceptable.the frequency quality (132.8) needs to be addressed as soon as possible. the spot where the receiver quality issues present, is around saf airport and the valley to the north of it. with high terrain and volume of traffic in the area, the frequency is an urgent safety issue.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: A ZAB Center Controller reported poor radio quality on 133.65 with two aircraft above FL410. Reporter stated poor radio reception on 133.65 and 132.8 is a recurring problem that has not been addressed.
text: sector 94, frequency 133.65 with poor radio quality. persistent issue for the sector for better part of last 6 months. transmission from aircraft at fl450 and fl410 are received with extremely poor quality despite the aircraft were at high altitude. p70 site (clines corner) for 132.8 has been suspected of poor reception quality that has not been addressed yet. 133.65 showing signs of reception quality is troubling. considering that there were minimal factor for disruption (no precipitation, no line of sight issue), i must suspect that the issue lies with the site itself. any rcag (remote communication air to ground site) issue needs to be resolved as soon as possible, especially with adverse wx approaching.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: A Tower Local Controller also working as Controller in Charge reported they became distracted and cleared a taxiing aircraft to cross a runway with an arriving aircraft on short final.
text: aircraft x was in the pattern doing full stop taxi backs on rwy xx. they exited at taxiway 1 and i issued them instructions to taxi via taxiway 2 to rwy xx and to cross rwy xy and rwy xz. numerous aircraft were in the pattern on xx both touch and goes and full stop. aircraft y was on a right downwind for rwy xz, just entering the downwind, the only aircraft assigned rwy xz. i anticipated there was ample time for aircraft x to cross rwy xz prior to aircraft y turning base. the pattern was complex with a mix of performance in the aircraft needing constant control, and extending upwinds/downwinds on rwy xx to make it work. i got tunnel vision on rwy xx ops. my ground controller (new cpc) spoke up and said 'he should have probably had held short' and i scanned my rwy xx ops thinking they meant that, when they clarified they meant rwy xz, i saw aircraft x clearing the rwy xz hold short bars with aircraft y short final, i am not sure if they were passed the displaced threshold. i did not observe when aircraft x entered the runway reference my aircraft on final. they were also unable to say when the threshold was crossed. neither pilot said anything.that taxi route usually takes just a moment and i anticipated they would clear of the intersection well before my arrival as the arrival was only entering the downwind when i issued the instructions. aircraft x must have taken closer to several minutes to cover the distance. we were short staffed this day and i was working controller in charge (cic) as well as local.my tunnel vision led to me not verifying aircraft x's position during my rwy xz operation. i was shocked at the slow speed of the taxi. i will recommend to my fellow controllers that we issue paper stops during these increased volume sessions when we have control of both runways. i also spoke with my ground controller and mentored them to be assertive if they suspect their local controller has missed something, even if they aren't cic qualified. perhaps in future configurations like today we should have the cic only combined with ground.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a traffic coordination conflict on final approach when ATC cleared a heavy transport for takeoff on an intersecting runway at night. The Captain could not locate the departing traffic and confirm separation; then executed a go-around to de-conflict from the traffic.
text: while we were less than 1000 feet off the ground air traffic control cleared aircraft y for take off from runway 15r. the atis did not say anything about using 15r only landing 04r and departing 9 with winds 320 at 05 knots. we were not told when we checked in about traffic holding 9n multiple intersecting runways nor were we expecting 15r to be in use with a tailwind. after aircraft y was cleared for takeoff both me and my first officer questioned each other where the airplane was where the intersection of the two runways were, and how this would work with our location to the runway. i queried air traffic control about them clearing some one to take off with us that close and air traffic control said yes they were cleared. having never seen this operation in over a decade of operating in boston and mixed with a voice i have never heard working the tower in boston before i told the first officer i don't like this and he agreed. with it being night and our location to the threshold of 15 r we could not see the departing traffic and i told the first officer let's go around. he agreed it was bad and we initiated a go around. air traffic control seemed surprised we were going around but mixed with the surprise of a departure from a runway we were not expecting in an unknown operation with air traffic control's less than stellar recent performance throughout the country recently we were not going to hang around and see if it would work. we went around then landed shortly there after with no issues.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Fractional pilot reported a near miss with a glider aircraft while descending on a published arrival in daylight visual conditions while communicating with ATC. The flight did not receive a TCAS warning and was not identified until passing behind the aircraft.
text: near mid air collision.while on the dryye two arrival into dal between scops and sway at 5000, i noticed and airfield off the right side of the airplane as i sat right seat. pf had autopilot on, alt was level and being maintained while navigating laterally with lnav on the star. i glanced over at the mfd (multi-function flight display) to see what the identifier of the airport was. it was not listed. when i looked back outside, a glider appeared 2-3 o'clock about 100 feet off the right wing, same altitude! i notified air traffic control immediately. no evasive action taken as the event happened so fast and the glider was behind the airplane by the time i'd be able to grab the stick. on the ground i was able to find out the airport was traffic advisory11, tsa midlothian tx a private strip that has a glider program. airfield is less than 1 mile from mode c veil and one mile south of the arrival center line. pf never saw the glider.cause: no tcas indications no ta/ra, glider must not have had adsb. no air traffic control radar alert or traffic advisory.response: notified air traffic control, immediately assigned a heading that turned us about 10 deg left.suggestions: only visual flight rules chart reveals caution area for intense glider activity.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported a nose wheel steering malfunction during landing. The Captain disconnected the steering; used differential braking and rudder to clear the runway; then called for a tow to the gate.
text: uncommanded nose wheel steering upon landing in redacted xxr. transferred controls at 60 kts. attempted to taxi taxiway 1. aircraft jerked hard right. captain advised he was disconnecting steering. unable to steer. differential braking and rudder was required to vacate taxiway 1 at xxr. required tow team to arrive at gate.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Citation Sovereign flight crew reported an engine malfunction and a fuel boost pump CAS message when leveling off at FL410. The crew diverted to an alternate airport and landed.
text: during the level off at fl410, person a and i heard a loud thump. i initially suspected an issue with the front nose gear while checking whether the nose door had opened, the auto throttles immediately disengaged. person a had observed that the left motor had rolled back and was at approximately 50% n1, and the left amber boost pump crew alerting system (cas) message illuminated, which then caused the motor to relight. we consulted the checklist, landed as soon as practical, and i notified the company. the copilot and i both agreed to divert to redacted and discussed the details with the company.cause: engine fuel pump.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A321 flight crew reported tread separation from main gear tire resulted in expeditious handling to a safe landing.
text: flight from redacted. upon reaching cruise altitude, we were contacted by redacted [artcc] of a possible blown tire. a report from the departing aircraft behind us stated they saw tire debris on the runway during their takeoff. we had no indications from the flight deck of a tire issue as we did not hear or feel anything abnormal. coordinated with dispatch via satcom to include maintenance control and the chief pilot for best course of action. station ops and maintenance control were to gather additional information as to the origin on the tire debris and get back to us. no conclusive data was determined except that it was a air carrier x main landing gear re-tread tire. the first officer and i had an extensive discussion of multiple outcomes and possibilities. reviewed flight manual procedures for tire damage, gear extension malfunctions, expedited landing, and evacuation procedures. we descended to a lower altitude to reduce landing weight and continued to redacted. briefed with the flight attendants was conducted. requested priority handling with redacted [artcc]. a soft landing was made followed by a fire and rescue inspection at the end of the runway that revealed damage to the left main landing gear outboard tire. the outer tread had separated from the tire leaving marks under the wing and flaps. with an all clear from airport rescue and firefighting and the tire still inflated., we taxied to the gate without further incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported during the climb experiencing an EICAS for bleed 1 over pressure resulting in the flight crew returning to the departure airport where they landed safely.
text: on climb out at about 8000 feet, we received a eicas message that we had bleed 1 over pressure. we followed the qrh procedure and the message was cleared. once we got to about 15, 000 feet, the message of bleed 1 over pressure reappeared and we once again followed the qrh procedure. this time the message did not extinguish so we were forced to follow the rest of the procedure. once we realized that we were going to have to do a single engine approach and landing, we requested priority handling and told air traffic control we wanted to return to redacted. we followed our checklists. we advised dispatch through acars of our situation, we notified the fas and passengers, and we set up the aircraft for the instrument landing system xxl and ran the qrh checklist for single engine approach and landing. we requested the emergency vehicles to be on standby by the runway just to be safe. we landed safely and had no issues returning to the gate and deplaned the passengers safely and normally through the jet bridge.suggestions: all crew members should be removed from duty for 24 hours following a situation like this. i think it's critical to crm and crew well being.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: A319 pilot reported while at the gate ground crew reported a propane like odor resulting in the flight crew evacuating the aircraft at the gate.
text: pre-departure (doors closed, jet bridge retracted).after cabin doors were closed and the jet bridge was retracted, ground personnel notified the flight deck of a 'propane-like' odor detected near the aircraft. the source of the odor could not be immediately identified by the ground crew.i immediately briefed the flight attendants on the situation and instructed them to disarm all doors in anticipation of a possible emergency deplaning.contacted maintenance control to report the odor and seek technical guidance. logged the discrepancy in the aircraft maintenance logbook as: 'ground crew reported propane smell, source undetermined.'maintenance personnel arrived for an initial assessment and reported that no odor was detectable at that time. however, to comply with fume protocols, maintenance determined the aircraft needed to be taken out of service for a more thorough investigation.based on the lack of any detectable odor or smoke in the cabin, i determined that an emergency deplaning/evacuation was not required. i maintained frequent communication with the passengers, explaining that the delay to push was a proactive safety measure to allow maintenance to investigate an external report. we coordinated with operations to reconnect the jet bridge, deplaned via normal procedures, and completed a ship change. the flight subsequently departed without further incident.cause: an unidentified odor reported by ground personnel created a potential safety hazard. the fact that the source was not determined warranted further investigation. the threat of having a fume event in the cabin remained until the source was positively identified.maintenance requirements necessitated removing the aircraft from service to ensure airworthiness, despite the odor being transient.early notification to the cabin crew and passengers prevented alarm, primed the crew and passengers to be able to detect any abnormal smell in the cabin, and ensured the crew was prepared for a rapid deplanement if the situation escalated.staying at the gate and performing a ship change was the most appropriate course of action when the source of a reported combustible smell could not be verified.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported flight deck fumes and odor resulted in use of oxygen masks and return to departure airport.
text: while climbing through 10, 000ft we noticed a bad smell which became stronger and began to bother us. given our path ahead we talked about a return to redacted as it was only becoming more bothersome. we stopped our climb at 25, 000ft and decided to don our oxygen masks and notify air traffic control of our intentions along with requesting priority handling. we ran all appropriate checklists and set up for the longest runway due to an overweight landing of around 153, 000lbs. we planned on meeting arff (airport rescue and firefighting) to inspect our brakes on the runway upon landing. the landing was uneventful and when we came to a complete stop i opened my window and we removed our masks and continued communications via headset / hand mic. this helped to greatly dissipate the odor. with the aid of the fire chief we calculated that we were not in the caution range with our brakes and vacated the runway. we took a few minutes to coordinate some things with the cabin and return to a gate. we requested arff to follow us due to a long taxi and check our brakes upon shutdown. they simply said that we were 'ok'. paramedics met us at the gate as our flight attendant was feeling ill. both captain and i were not feeling great as well and could taste this strong odor in our throats and elected not to continue with a new aircraft.cause: the aircraft underwent a check for severe turbulence upon landing and we were told the stick shaker was activated on the previous leg. possibly this had something to do with the odor.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported during the climb experiencing left engine oil pressure message resulting in the flight crew returning to the departure airport where they landed safely.
text: on departure from redacted and climbing through approximately 14, 000 feet, the crew received a left engine oil pressure high crew alerting system (cas) message (which was intermittent twice more) and there was a positive exchange of controls to the captain as we went through the process to troubleshoot with the qrh2. shortly after, this was followed by a left bleed leak. crew reduced thrust on the left engine and performed the immediate action item per the qrh2 of addressing the bleeds. we advised air traffic control of our desire to run a few checklists and need to level off at a lower altitude. following our checklist (and having known previously that the aircraft had just come out of maintenance for a left engine remove & replace), crew opted to return to redacted and advised dispatch, air traffic control, and the passengers of the return. no emergency was declared. air traffic control recleared crew to redacted via vectors and crew continued in for the ilsxxr with no further issues excluding the possibility of an overweight landing. landing was made smoothly and thrust reversers were applied. once on the ground, crew advised dispatch, chief pilot, as well as maintenance. the passengers were offloaded as well and kept informed of the situation. suggestions: we can always use events like these, to improve in many facets, whether it be operationally, procedural, etc..even with events that are caused by a malfunction in the aircraft equipment or system.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a NMAC in the pattern at a non-towered airport.
text: i was flying aircraft x doing flight test. the final phase of my flight included multiple pattern operations where i flew right closed patterns at redacted. i was continuously communicating on ctaf with other traffic in the patterj, primarily a pilatus who i let ahead of me. as i was turning base to final, i saw traffic appear low on my display. at first, i thought it was a helicopter because of how low it was and that nothing in that vicinity had made a radio call. the traffic alert turned yellow and then i got visual on aircraft y who had made a wrong direction base turn to final and was on a collision course. i added power and made a left turn to clear over the top of aircraft y and re-entered the pattern after aircraft y landed. likely cause: pilot of aircraft y was inattentive to ctaf, and not making radio calls, and flew wrong direction pattern.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported loss of directional control after landing that led to a runway excursion.
text: i was flying touch and goes at redacted airport, in class d airspace. as i was taking off on runway xxr to do the touch and gos on xxl, 2 other planes already in the pattern has just reported significant wind shear on the approach to xxl, in the order of 10-15 knots. the tower when reported 'calm winds' along with the wind shear pilot report. as i came in on final for my first touch and go, i strongly felt the wind shear at about 500 agl, about 100 yards from the runway. i initiated a go around on the first approach and let the tower know the wind shear was still there.on the 2cd and 3rd approaches, i was able to complete the touch and go without a lot of difficulty-the wind shear was still there but i felt it moving farther south away from the approach end of xxl.on the final approach, again i felt the wind shear about 400 yards south of xxl, but is seemed to calm down by the time i was over the runway threshold. the landing was very smooth without any significant crosswind. as was was rolling out preparing to do another touch and go, i reached to raise the flaps, i was going maybe 40-45 knots on the runway at that moment. very suddenly the aircraft veered hard to the right. i felt if i tried to brake or try too much left rudder the aircraft would tip over, as the plane was moving quite hard and fast. i elected to accept the fact i was going to go into the grass off the right side of the runway. i did not hit any landing lights as i entered the grass. once in the grass the plane slowed considerably, and i gave it left rudder and a little power and was able to exit the grass and get back on the runway without damaging the plane or any runway lights. the area of the grass i was in was flat and almost level with the runway, so the propeller did not hit the ground during this event.i then contacted the tower, told them i had entered the grass and was back on the runway, and was done doing any more touch and goes. i taxied down the runway to an taxiway and then the tower asked if i needed to stop and check the aircraft for damage. i told them no and was going back to my parking area. they gave my taxi instructions.once back at the tie down, i inspected the aircraft and it looked undamaged.as to why this happened, i am just not sure. i did not feel i had a significant crosswind on the last landing. i also do not recall my right foot hitting the rudder pedal hard enough to swerve the plane over to the right like it did. i have recorded over 1, 000 landings and that has never happened to me before. i also felt like the wind shear was moving away from the airport on the prior landings. the weather was partly cloudy with good visibility and reported light winds, save for the wind shear. the plane taxied with out difficulty and the brakes appeared to be functioning normally before this event. i guess it must have been something i did, but i can not determine what that was. i did have a passenger with me- an old friend who is also an old pilot, he was uninjured.

anomaly: Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: GA pilot reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC during approach to HAF.
text: i was continuing my instrument flight rules currency by doing an rnav approach into redacted. the controller asked what my intentions were. i stated i would like to go direct redacted on the missed. they said 'on the missed contact redacted [tracon]. the ceilings were pretty high at 2500 feet, so i did the missed and remained visual flight rules until contacting departure. the new controller said climb and maintain 4000 feet and then said 'terrain alert, you should be going west'. i went west and he had me climb to 4000 feet than sent me direct redacted.i should have done the standard missed, and not assumed that my request was approved.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: PA28 pilot reported during initial climb the engine began to lose power.
text: during takeoff/departure, i departed runway xxr. during the crosswind turn at approximately 450 feet agl, the engine began to experience intermittent power loss and nearly quit. i immediately lowered the nose to maintain airspeed and turned back toward the airport. i switched fuel tanks and requested priority handling with tower with a distress call.i initially positioned toward runway xyr because i was turning back toward the airport and wanted to get the aircraft on the ground as soon as practical. the engine was still producing power and i had excess airspeed. based on the aircraft's position and speed, i determined that continuing the turn and landing on runway xxr was the safer option. i completed the landing on runway xxr without further incident.after landing, i taxied clear of the runway as instructed. there were no injuries and no known aircraft damage. the aircraft has not been flown again and is awaiting mechanic evaluation to determine the cause of the intermittent power loss.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a rejected takeoff due to no airspeed indication.
text: prior to the incident, the pilot in command (instructor) conducted all appropriate checks on the aircraft, including run-up procedures, to ensure it was in an airworthy condition. after the pre-flight checks were completed, the student (acting pilot in command) conducted a takeoff briefing with the pilot in command. this briefing included all required items, including what would be done in the event of an aborted takeoff. after concluding the briefing, takeoff clearance was requested by the student. takeoff clearance was shortly received, and the aircraft lined up for departure. the student then increased the throttles to verify correct engine performance and that all gauges indicated normal. the student then applied takeoff power and began to accelerate the aircraft down the runway. both the pilot in command and the student expected to see the airspeed indicator begin to increase after releasing the brakes. however, the airspeed did not increase. the pilot in command immediately called 'reject' to abort the takeoff, notified the tower, executed a positive exchange of flight controls, and slowed the aircraft back to safe taxi speeds. the aircraft was then taxied clear of the runway and back to parking. once the aircraft was fully shut down, the pilot in command exited the aircraft and performed a visual inspection. there was no damage to the aircraft and no hot brake condition. the pilot then continued the visual inspection of the aircraft and was able to identify that the pitot cover had been left on the pitot tube. while the student and pilot in command did conduct a preflight inspection, both missed the pitot tube cover. while the student is in training and is expected to know how to check for these items, the pilot in command ultimately is the one responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft and determining airworthiness. the corrective action is for both the student (but more importantly) the pilot in command to ensure that they are conducting a thorough inspection of the aircraft prior to accepting it for flight using approved checklists. the pilot in command elected to terminate flight operations for the day to allow the student and pilot in command the chance to debrief, reflect, and try again on another day.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported severe engine vibration resulted in expeditious handling to a safe landing. First Officer also added possible cause was due to metal fatigue in engine.
text: climbing through about 34, 500 msl, we felt a sudden jolt and then pretty severe airframe vibration. we initially thought it may have been a flight control issue. engine instruments were normal until we scanned down to the vibration (vib) gauge and noted it was pegged at 5.0. there was definitely a startle factor to the whole thing but upon noting the vib, we both said we needed to reduce thrust on the left side. i started pulling the power back slowly but the vib stayed high until i got all the way to idle. then it settled around 1.8. we noted an odor but it fairly quickly dissipated. i asked the captain to ask for a lower altitude and he found the engine out page in the flight management system to get our driftdown speed and altitude. once we had it i set that in the mode control panel and set max continuous thrust on the right engine. i think at this point i had the autopilot off because it had gone into control wheel steering (cws) at some point so i just took over until i could get it set back up. we decided to go back to redacted so we coordinated that with air traffic control. we elected to go there because the captain and i both fly in there a lot so we are very familiar, and because we have air carrier x ops there. the right engine had all normal indications. we briefly discussed redacted which was almost directly under us, but felt more comfortable going back to redacted. that would also give us more time to run checklists and get set up without rushing through things. around this time i took over the radios and the captain got into the qrh for engine vibration. i believe he sent a quick message to dispatch that we were turning back to redacted and had also answered a call from the fas. i got us all set up for our approach and landing in redacted, and after running the vib checklist we decided to request priority handling so we would have airport rescue and firefighting (arff) standing by. we discussed brake temps and our planned overweight landing and that we were unsure what was going on with the engine or how much damage it had. at this time we also decided to put on our oxygen masks for the remainder of the flight. i think this was after speaking with the fas and asking if there was any odor in the back and they said there was a little bit. the initial odor we smelled up front lasted for less than a minute and then we were kind of distracted by the immediate issue of the vibrations and possible damage. then the smell dissipated. but since the fas said there was an odor and to play it safe, we donned our masks and established communications, and the captain ran the one engine approach and landing qrh. we never shut down the left motor as the vibration stayed below 2.0 at idle. he asked if i was comfortable landing it and i said i was as long as he would back me up with any info from the head-up display (hud) as far as trends. we discussed the high ref speed due to flaps 15 at just above max landing weight. we completed that checklist and flew the rnp xx. landed without incident just a few knots above ref, rolled down to the end of the runway and had arff check our engine and brake temps before taxiing back to a hard stand. after shutdown, mechanics came up to the flight deck and said there was severe fan blade damage. it appeared that a piece of the spinner hub broke off and was ingested by the engine. it damaged about 5 fan blades and took a quarter sized chunk out of the trailing edge of at least one of them. to prevent in future: maybe mechanics should be checking for metal fatigue in these older 737-800s. i know we also have engines that run at a high vib level but below 4.0 and we're requested to let maintenance know about that but just continue operations. sometimes it's audibly noticeable like your old prop sync is out of whack and i've even had flight attendants call saying it sounds abnormally loud in back. i guess in hindsight we sort of treated this like 'engine severe damage' initially and ran the memory items for that rather than getting the qrh out for high vibration first. maybe this was the right call and we saved the engine from shredding itself by leaving it at high rpm for too long. i don't think we ever attempted to increase the power on it again after going to idle. the sudden jolt we felt seemed to indicate that something had broken internally and i know we briefly discussed that out loud. we probably should have donned our oxygen masks right away and in the future i would do that as soon as an odor is noted. if it had not almost immediately dissipated i'm sure we would have donned them sooner and i realize that we should have because a fume could've still been lingering in the air. other things we could have done better - probably should've started the apu in flight and had it ready to use in case the left motor fully seized at some point.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a traffic conflict with another aircraft that was descending for an adjacent airport resulted in a NMAC event.
text: my student rotated off runway 26 for anotherpattern. immediately after rotation, i observed an object directly off our 12 o'clockposition that rapidly resolved into a large aircraft--consistent in size and speedwith a corporate jet--apparently on final approach to runway 8 at rei. theaircraft was approaching head-on, and its apparent size was growing rapidly, indicating closure at high speed.i immediately called 'my plane, ' assumed control of the aircraft, and turnedsouthbound to escape the conflict. we continued to climb on an offset upwindtrack, south of the runway centerline, clearing the west ramp area byapproximately 100-200 feet. throughout this maneuver i monitored ads-b trafficon my ipad, the conflicting aircraft displayed a northeasterly heading, indicatingit was passing through the rei environment at an angle. we remainedsouthwest of the airport to maintain separation.at no point during this encounter did the conflicting aircraft make any radio callson the rei ctaf frequency. vertical separation between the two aircraft wasestimated at approximately 200-400 feet--an unacceptably small margin givenour low altitude immediately after rotation.several seconds later, the aircraft initiated a gradual left turn northbound, whichappeared consistent with a left base leg entry for san bernardino internationalairport (sbd). this maneuver confirmed the aircraft had penetrated well outsidethe sbd class d airspace boundary and deep into the rei traffic environmentwithout any coordination or traffic advisories.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: A320 flight crew reported receiving a TA and RA.
text: on arrival into redacted, redacted approach vectored us on a downwind for runway xx. descending down to 4, 000 we got a traffic advisory for ga traffic that was in sight and pointed out to us by approach. we then received an resolution advisory as it looked like he was climbing within 500 feet of us as we passed over. i disconnected autopilot, flew into the green [band] and climbed no higher than 4, 300 feet before clear of conflict. engaged automation and continued the arrival after notifying approach.cause: ga traffic wasn't in contact with approach as he was under the shelf. the only mitigation would be to maybe have leveled off at a higher altitude, but overall i believe all parties did what they should have, it was just an unusual case of ga traffic flying near a downwind without communication.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: CRJ-550 pilot reported on departure experiencing an EFIS COMP MON failure resulting in the flight crew being able to reestablish directional control and continued to their destination.
text: during a line check departure from runway xxl at redacted airport, the crew experienced an unexpected efis (electronic flight instrument system) comp mon failure shortly after takeoff. this resulted in significant compass discrepancies, with the captain's heading indication approximately 180° in error and the first officer's approximately 90° in error.during level-off at 5, 000 feet, which occurred rapidly due to a light aircraft weight (approximately 12 passengers) and a climb rate exceeding 4, 000 feet per minute, the first officer initially began a turn to the indicated heading of 180°. in reality, the aircraft was turning toward approximately 090° due to the erroneous heading indications.recognizing the developing situation and degraded situational awareness, the pilot in command assumed control of the aircraft. the crew transitioned to visual references, using known north-south ground features (roadways) along with standby compass indications to maintain proper orientation and stabilize the flight path.air traffic control subsequently issued direct routing to redacted, however, the clearance could not be accepted immediately due to unreliable heading information and the need to reestablish accurate directional control.the situation was stabilized without further incident through effective intervention, use of external visual cues, and crew resource management.cause: runway xxl has massive magnetic deviations if left sitting on the runway. we were holding in position for approximately 2 minutes and received the efis late on takeoff roll.suggestions: avoid prolonged line up and waits on redacted runway xxl.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported on vectors to final experiencing a terrain warning resulting in the flight crew climbing and advising ATC.
text: in level flight at 5, 400ft, while being vectored outside of redacted for the rnav y xx at redacted as we were issued a turn towards redacted, we noticed the radio altimeter suddenly come alive and then very quickly rise from 2500 to approximately 1500. i immediately disconnected the autopilot and climbed back up to 6, 000 feet. we advised air traffic control, who told us that his mva in the area was 5400 ft so 'there was nothing there'. i replied to him that we were complying with company procedures to advise him, not blaming him. and we continued to a nominal landing on runway xx. we had briefed the terrain escape maneuver and reviewed the company pages on the ground in redacted, and reviewed both again enroute to redacted. i believe the aircraft generated a spurious caution based on the resolution advisory closure rate it perceived as we turned and exposed the belly to the terrain on the right side of the aircraft. while we did receive the 'caution, terrain' we did not receive any of the other indicators associated with that, namely the highlighted terrain on the mfd (multi-function flight display).

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: ERJ 145 flight crew reported a flight spoiler would not retract when commanded during approach.
text: during descent through 10, 000 ft, the captain attempted to stow the spoilers. the aircraft immediately rolled to the right, and the autopilot had difficulty maintaining the commanded flight path for approximately 10 seconds. shortly thereafter, the autopilot recovered, and an eicas message, spoiler fail, " was annunciated.the captain retained control of the aircraft and assumed communications. as pilot monitoring, i completed the applicable qrc and qrh procedures. we advised air traffic control and requested arff (airport rescue and firefighting) to be placed on standby. the flight attendant and passengers were briefed accordingly.we elected to continue with runway xxl, as the aircraft was already configured for the instrument landing system xxl approach. landing performance was calculated in accordance with the qrh, and the available landing distance was determined to be more than adequate. to avoid unnecessary workload, no runway change was requested.during the approach, the right spoiler returned to the stowed position. an uneventful landing was accomplished on runway xxl. after landing, the aircraft taxied to the gate without further incident.cause: mechanical failure."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Cirrus SF50 instructor reported right main wheel locked up on landing resulted in tire failure. Instructor also reported Cirrus Vision jet should have anti-lock brakes.
text: during an attempt at a short-field landing the right main wheel locked up, causing the tire to wear through completely and the tire deflated. i have performed numerous short-field landings and applied similar brake pressure while have no issues of this type. no squealing sound was heard from the tire, so i had no indication that the wheel was locked up until the tire deflated. the blown tire cause drag that pulled the aircraft to the right, but i maintained control and was able to turn the aircraft onto a concrete driveway surface in order to clear the runway. a tug arrived within 10 minutes to pull the aircraft further away from the runway.cirrus maintenance was contacted with a request for aircraft grounding support and they sent a technician to the location who was able to replace the wheel tire assembly. he stated that the sign-off for the repair would be sent electronically as he had no access to print a label version at that time. i believe that this met the requirement for a sign-off of maintenance performed.we advised the technician that we would be taking off to return to our home base. this technician acted as a runway observer to watch out for deer known to be in the area as i conducted the takeoff.as for the locked wheel, i have long believed that cirrus aircraft should install anti-lock brakes on the vision jet. this would have prevented this event from occurring.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Small transport Captain reported clearance confusion and ATC procedure at night resulted in airborne conflicts.
text: flight event was for night currency at srq. i needed three takeoffs and landings by myself, before i could legally complete a later flight event with a crewmember to reestablish night vision goggles (nvg) currency. knowing runway 4/22 is difficult to see/use at night, when i called air traffic control (all positions combined on tower) for clearance, i requested runway 32 for closed traffic with full stop/taxi backs. i was immediately asked by the controller if i could use the short runway instead. since i didn't hear anybody else using 4/22, i reluctantly accepted. they also confirmed the type of aircraft i was. clearance was given with a reduced pattern altitude at or below 1, 100'. taxi and runups were uneventful, however, traffic at the airport started to increase with a small surge of arriving practice approaches/night currency aircraft and airliners on runway 32.upon being cleared for takeoff i was told to enter left closed traffic. i thought this was odd because i would be operating towards incoming approach aircraft. takeoff and initial upwind leg was uneventful. right as i was leveling off on upwind, before turning crosswind, the controller called and i heard the instructions of 'make sure downwind is over approach end 32 please.' i read back 'downwind over approach end 32'. workload was high with level off, configuration changes, check lists, turns, etc all happening quickly at the same time. it is also worth noting this location and flight direction is difficult at night due to facing the blackness of the intercoastal/bay and gulf. i was relying heavily on the gps 530 and horizontal situation indicator (hsi) to make sure upwind and crosswind leg headings were correct and instruments to make sure i was level. upon turning crosswind, approximately 2.3 miles away from runway 32 centerline, i couldn't see the runway edge lights. i knew the general location but couldn't identify the beginning of the runway. the lights for the runways are pretty directional and there are numerous buildings as well as trees on the west/southwest, so visibility from that position was pretty hard from that sideways angle. additionally, runway 32 has a long displaced threshold and the sequenced flashing lights (rabbit) is blocked by trees just southwest of their location. until you get south or high enough, especially when they are on low intensity, they can be difficult to see. i finally got sight of the rabbit off my left and started my turn downwind. after rolling out on downwind, i could see that i was slightly south of the southernmost rabbit light. a few seconds later, i started putting in flaps when air traffic control called, 'aircraft x yeah………turn heading 090 now'. this was about 2 miles from crossing the centerline of runway 32. i thought this was odd as they were turning me head on into approaching traffic. i quickly executed an aggressive sharp turn to the right. the introduction of flaps, sharp turn, and not being trimmed for this new configuration/input contributed to an inadvertent balloon above assigned altitude that i corrected as fast as i could. after reading back 090, they then angrily responds back 'i have advised you to have the uh…your downwind over the approach end -numbers- for runway 32, traffic at your 1 o'clock, two miles, is aircraft y descending out of 1, 400'.' i can't remember if i responded. i believe i read back simply 'looking' as i was trying to identify the correct traffic and get the airplane trimmed for level so i could safely be eyes outside. they called back to immediately descend at or below 500 immediately now. they then pointed me out to aircraft y at 1, 200' and told them to maintain at or above 1, 600. i had pulled power back to idle and dropped the nose aggressively to level off at 500'. they called they were going missed (on training instrument approach) and had traffic in sight below them. i also called back that i had traffic in sight as well. i do not believe the garmin 530 had issued a traffic advisory at any point, but i was diving and eyes outside, so i can't recall if i saw or heard it.at this point it was becoming clear from their previous transmission that they and i were working on different instruction expectations/situation awareness. i had heard approach end 32 and they had claimed to have said approach end numbers 32. my readback also did not include it, which was not noticed or challenged.) the controller then responded back upset 'aircraft x, you can expect a full stop after this one'. trying not to be confrontational and make a bad situation worse after having gone through a roller coaster ride, i simply responded 'sorry about that'.i was then given instructions to enter the left downwind runway 22. at this moment i was not stabilized in the pattern (45 degrees diverging away), low at 500', and runway 4/22 is still hard to see at night unless you are pointing at it. on my readback, i advised them that i might need to extend out to see the runway. their response was 'yep, that's okay, uh were you confused on the instructions to keep your downwind over the approach end numbers runway 32?' at this point i am behind trying to fly the plane, reenter the pattern and not start any kind of disagreement over the radio. i responded back, 'i heard approach end, but i didn't hear numbers.' their response was 'yeah, that wasn't approach end though.' again, with the high workload and not wanting to argue, i simply responded back 'roger'.i was then cleared to land on runway 22. on final they notified me that there was traffic on 1-mile final runway 32. i slowed down as much as i could and asked them on short final if spacing was good. they called for me to do a go around and to extend upwind. they told me to make right closed traffic this time and advised of traffic that was transiting the intercoastal at 500' that i would be pointing at. right as i crossed behind the traffic they gave me a turn for crosswind. to keep them happy, i proactively kept the pattern tighter than i'd like (~1.1 nm) and made an uneventful approach/landing. upon slowing they cleared me to exit and taxi to the ramp. during taxi in, they didn't mention anything further about what had happened on the flight. i didn't attempt any further flight events and called it a night.reviewing and digesting the data on the ground, i feel i was pretty much set up for failure. in the air and in the moment, based on the conditions previously mentioned, i was not able to identify this. had they had given me a distance instead on their initial instruction, i might have been able to promptly decline, negotiate, or adjust my turns accordingly (assuming reasonable request). looking at centerline distances from runway 4/22, their last-minute request of flying downwind over the numbers of runway 32 would have put me on a 0.46 nm downwind cross track. i am familiar with steep turns in this aircraft so to make that work, i would have to bank on both upwind/downwind and downwind/final turns nonstop at about 50-55 degrees. this is obviously impractical and unsafe in the pattern for a turboprop multiengine aircraft x. even if they had given the approach end of runway 32, as i had heard/perceived, this was still unreasonable as it was at 0.89 nm cross track from the farthest southernmost sequencing (rabbit) light. looking at my actual upwind/crosswind turn, using normal 30-degree bank, i rolled wings approximately abeam of this 0.89 nm distance point. i still needed the extra distance to regain sight of the runway and turn downwind. the reality is even if i had kept the turn going from upwind straight to downwind, i couldn't have complied with that request. assuming on my turn to downwind that night that i made no correction attempts after going wings level and just paralleled runway 4/22, i would have been on a 1.6 nm downwind.additionally, it is worth noting:due to company pressures, i flew again the next night to finish my night currency takeoff and landing requirements. the same controller was working all frequencies again. before i called for clearance, an aircraft called for pattern work for runway 22. i then called and requested pattern work for runway 32, which was granted. i noted the controller told the other pilot to make sure their downwind leg was 1 nm. while i am happy they used distance this time and not a ground fix in the dark, it really stuck out to me how unrealistic their expectations were of my aircraft/performance the prior night in comparison.night currency flight was uneventful. subsequent nvg currency flight was also completed without any issues. after both flights, i reviewed the downwind data for both pilots, and our downwind legs averaged 1.3 nm - 1.8 nm cross track distance using standard turns and procedures.moving forward on future pattern night currency flights, i will be on higher defense to prevent events like this from happening again. additionally, due to poor lighting and visibility i will probably never accept night pattern work on runway 22 again for safety and liability concerns. i will only accept runway 14/32 or go to a different airport.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Corporate Captain reported signage at Taxiway E and K at GSO were nonstandard; and led to a taxi deviation.
text: atis information: 300 10g17 few120 few250 22/4 3003 landing departing 23r expect visual 23r. called ground. from fbo taxi runway 23r via c m m4 cross 23l k e h. taxiing out. fast forward to after crossing 23l on m4. turned right on taxiway k. continued down k looking for e for the left turn. had my taxi chart up on garmin g3000 multi-function flight display (mfd) screen. had it zoomed in. then zoomed back out to see exact location of taxiway e. had left the zoom out. looking for taxiway e out the window. some activity had grabbed my attention by the cargo aircraft. the taxiway k and e sign was nonstandard on the right side of the aircraft/taxiway. taxiway e sign on the left side was far off to the left closer to juliet taxiway which at my angle was momentarily blocked by the a frame pilot of the door and windscreen. then realized that i had passed echo. immediately called ground and said i missed echo. ground stated that is okay to just make a 180 on the taxiway then hold short of echo on kilo for my company traffic that was behind me by about 1 - 2 minutes. then continued to follow traffic e h to hold short 23r.to prevent this from happening again will just have to remember to zoom the taxi mfd screen in closer to keep a closer eye on exact location. will also stay more focused on signage that is on opposite sides of the taxiway.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a conflict while landing with FOD placed near the runway threshold to identify the runway as closed by NOTAM at a non-towered airport.
text: i conducted a routine flight form my home base (redacted) to (3n6) old bridge airport. as part of my routine flight preparation, i failed this day to do a complete check of notams when reviewing the airport information before takeoff. upon what seemed a normal arrival and announcement into the airport pattern, i could see some localized work being conducted next to the t hangers at the far end of the runway. the runway was clear, unobstructed, and did not appear to have visible markings. approach was normal and without event. in preparation to flare as i crossed over the runway end i observed what i first believed to be a cover/possible aircraft cover of sorts wrapped and balled up near the end of the asphalt near the grass edge. with the intent to land and report the debris near the field, i continued. the entire runway was clear and unobstructed. as i was beginning my flare crossing the threshold, i overserved sandbags and quickly realized the airport was likely closed and the debris was likely a fabric x placed originally on the threshold. given the current wind conditions at the time, (10/12 gusting to 18/20) and the short field i felt the safest course of action was to land and immediately stop as opposed to aborting the landing. once stopped i shut down and walked down to make contact with personal working to advise them of the condition of the temporary airport marking as well as to arrange to restart and taxi safely to the ramp which were both conducted without incident.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Government UAS pilot reported an NMAC with a helicopter during a mission. The UAS pilot took evasive action.
text: on day 0 at xa:30, i was operating a small unmanned aircraft system (suas) in support of an emergency public safety call. the operation was conducted within autonomous / fully automated at an altitude of approximately 125 feet agl.during the operation, i observed a manned helicopter operating in the vicinity at an estimated altitude of approximately 150 feet agl. upon recognizing the potential conflict and limited vertical separation, i immediately initiated risk mitigation procedures.i executed a controlled descent to increase vertical separation and clear the helicopter's flight path. the descent was conducted in a safe and predictable manner. no evasive action appeared to be required by the helicopter, and no loss of control or unsafe operation occurred.once the helicopter was clear of the area and sufficient separation was established, i reassessed the airspace prior to continuing the mission. at all times, i prioritized yielding the right of way to the manned aircraft in accordance with faa regulations.no injuries, damage, or further incidents resulted from this occurrence.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air traffic controller reported an aircraft descended below the arrival procedure in an area of poor radar and radio communications. The controller issued a low altitude alert and a vector away from the terrain.
text: aircraft x checked in on the subky arrival. he requested the visual approach. the aircraft was descending via the arrival on my west frequency of 119.55. i switched the aircraft to my other frequency of 118.97 at the appropriate time. the pilot was having trouble hearing me on the frequency so i began trouble shooting and using different transmitter and receivers and then changed to an emergency backup frequency. i did notice that the pilot had continued to descend but they were well above the mva so i did not have concern. (in hindsight i should have questioned the pilot on his altitude sooner.) i eventually lost radar on the aircraft in a spot that we normally lose radar. i asked the pilot to report his altitude and that i had lost radar. he stated that he was at 085 which was below the mva, but because i did not have radar i could not tell where he was. i advised the pilot of this and gave him a low altitude alert with instructions to climb immediately. once i saw that he was in the 110 mva i pulled up the eovm (emergency obstruction video map) map and vectored him away from high terrain with an emergency vector.there have been several reported events at this sector where aircraft have been in close proximity to terrain. because we do not have primary radar we cannot see these aircraft at all times. we are only using secondary radar and adsb. having primary radar would improve air traffic control services and increase safety. we have also had issues with the two frequencies at this sector and being able to properly communicate with the pilots.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a UAS while being vectored onto final approach. No evasive action was taken.
text: on a vector to join the final to 22l in ewr, about 1 nm west of gimme (1-2 nm w-sw of teb airport), i experienced a near miss with a drone at 2600'. the drone was small, approximately 10 lbs, black, and appeared to be a quad rotor. it passed just under my right wing. i made my debriefing with dispatch and the chief pilot.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: A321 First Officer reported shortly after starting taxi they received a call from the cabin indicating smoke and a burning odor. The crew stopped; shut down the engines; and received a tow back to the gate.
text: we pushed off the gate and started both engines. we completed the after start checklist and requested our taxi clearance. upon increasing power on both engines the captain and i heard a loud whirring noise but assumed it was just the engines spooling or coming from the nose wheel steering but we both commented that it was louder than normal if it were the engines. shortly after the noise, the flight attendants called and informed us that white smoke and a burning odor is filling the mid cabin. i informed the captain and we immediately stopped the aircraft. i informed ramp we were stopping and to standby then pulled out the smoke/fumes qrc and ran that. during that, the captain elected to turn on the apu and shut down both engines as we didn't have any abnormal flight deck indications and assumed the smoke was engine related because the noise we heard got louder as power increased. after the qrc was completed, i informed ramp and ops we needed a tow back to the gate due to the event. i also informed maintenance of the smoke event and gate return. the captain handled coms with the cabin until his radio panel quit working and he was unreadable over the mic. i then handled all coms inside and outside after that point. a few minutes after engines were shut down we received a pack 2 ovht ecam but we were unsure if that was related to cutting out all airflow into the cabin. we were also receiving a nuisance rmp 1 fail ecam that would chime every few seconds leading to the failure of the captains coms. after a few minutes, i checked back in with ops to determine the time for a tug to show up because it was getting extremely warm in the cabin with zero airflow. they indicated no more than 5 minutes. maybe 2 minutes later the tow crew arrived and hooked up to the aircraft. once they established communication with me, i queried ramp for clearance back to the gate. once cleared, i gave the clear to tow to the ground crew. i then informed ops that we would like the paramedics to meet us at the gate in case any passengers or crew experienced any symptoms from the smoke inhalation. we returned back to the gate and deplaned the aircraft.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: LIH ramp agent reported a ground conflict with another aircraft that started taxi behind an aircraft that was pushing back. The ramp agent stopped the pushback to prevent a collision.
text: i witnessed what was almost a near miss, where aircraft x was pushing out of gate xx and aircraft y started to taxi right after on the taxiway passing behind aircraft x. fortunately, ground crew was able to give signal to stop immediately to give way for aircraft y. during debrief, pushback driver was given clearance to push, the plan was to push tail north as aircraft y was in the south direction. while pushing out of gate xx, aircraft y started taxiing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported engine vibration exceeding limits. Diverted and landed uneventfully.
text: we took off from redacted normally, and climbing through 13, 000' or so we both noticed the secondary engine instruments screen turn on, which only happens when an engine parameter has been exceeded. we both noticed it right away and looked at what limit was exceeded. upon seeing the #1 engine vibrations exceeding 4.0 and varying between .3 and over 4.0 i called for my aircraft and the captain began working on the qrh for the high engine vibrations. we never felt any vibrations from the flight deck. i reduced thrust in the #1 engine until the vibrations remained within limits, as called for by the qrh. i had to reduce thrust back to near idle to keep the vibrations low enough. the captain and i then discussed the situation and decided to return to redacted. he had me continue to fly the airplane while he talked to dispatch, air traffic control, the flight attendants, and the passengers. while he did this i accepted vectors to a star and set up for an rnav approach to runway xxl. we discussed an overweight landing, briefed the approach, and landed normally. we taxied off the runway and then stopped to get checked out by airport rescue and firefighting (arff). they told us they saw no damage so we taxied back to the gate as they followed. no further abnormalities.cause: it seemed like just a maintenance issue. a couple of years back we changed procedure to blank out the screen with the secondary engine instruments with the idea being that when one is exceeded the screen suddenly turning on would get the pilot's attention. i have personally flown with captains that both like and dislike this idea. in this instance the screen popping back up worked very well and immediately got both of our attention.
