synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported flap malfunction on approach to land.
text: flats did not extend past 10 degrees with normal procedure. it stopped at around 12 degrees. we requested priority handling and followed the procedure for the alt flap extension method. landing was done normal with flaps 15.cause: we requested priority handling and followed sop and crm. steps were accomplished by both pilots and good teamwork.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737-800 pilot reported experiencing a hydraulic system loss during landing resulting in aircraft being towed to the gate.
text: at 200 feet a master caution light flickered. light did not stick. then in landing flare the light flickered again and did not stick. decelerating on the landing roll the master caution illuminated and stayed on for a hydraulic issue. we stopped on the runway and ran the qrh for loss of system a hydraulics. ops met the aircraft and towed us off the runway.cause: hydraulic leak/burst line. mitigate risks by following the checklist and qrh

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported there was no NOTAM issued for inoperable PAPIs for Runway 16L at JAN.
text: on day 0, i was the pilot flying on aircraft x from redacted to jan. on the visual approach for runway 16l, we started configuring the aircraft with flaps 8 and 20 at about 10 nm on a right base leg. we slowed to the maneuvering speed for flaps 20. we then intercepted final in white needles (rnav) at about 7 nm from the runway. then we put the landing gear down, configured flaps 30, and slowed to the straight in speed. we started descending on the approach using vertical speed 0.2 nm prior to the fix harag. we then noticed that the papis for 16l were not visible. this caught us off guard because there wasn't a notam saying they were inoperative. the captain tried to turn the lights on using the radios without success. we decided to continue the approach since it was visual conditions and we had an electronic glideslope from the instrument landing system. reaching 1000 feet, i called out one thousand, " and the captain replied "stabilized, cleared to land." on short final, at about 300 feet above ground level, we got a "terrain" enhanced ground proximity warning system (egpws) callout, which confused us since we were on the glideslope. a couple seconds later, we got a flaps aural alert, which made us realize we were still at flaps 30. we immediately initiated a go-around. we were then vectored back to a 10 nm final by approach control. we continued to a landing without further incident. at the gate, we debriefed the reasons for the go-around.the primary contributing factor for the unstabilized approach was fixation / distraction by the unexpected inoperable papis for 16l. this caused us to forget the final flaps configuration and the before landing checklist. a secondary contributing factor would be complacency with the 1000 feet stabilized call. it can become habitual to say the callout without fully verifying all of the stabilized approach criteria.going forward, i will focus on preventing distractions and fixation during critical phases of flight, and i will verify all of the stabilized approach criteria at the 1000 foot call. a helpful tool would be to use the "1, 2, 3, 4, 5" memory aid to verify proper aircraft configuration. 1 is cleared to land, 2 are the two thrust reversers, 3 is down three green, 4 and 5 are flaps 45."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported inadvertently taxiing onto a taxiway without the proper clearance from ATC due to poor signage and markings.
text: leaving our gate xx in ord, we were told by ramp to taxi on e, left on sp, hold short of a, and contact metering. while taxiing east on sp, my right-side view of a was blocked due to active construction. i continued taxiing on the solid yellow line marked sp until i saw a sign ahead that said a, where i stopped abeam a6. there was no indication of where sp ended and where a began. it appears that sp merges into a.the cause was complicated and inefficient taxi instructions, the sign markings not showing where sp ends and where a begins, and active construction obstructing views of taxiways.suggestions: better taxi instruction from ramp would be to say taxi on sp and hold short of a6. another suggestion would be to paint a line showing where sp ends and where a begins. additionally, put a clear upright sign that says when you are on a leaving sp.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CL-350 flight crew reported diverting to an alternate airport after the inflight failure of IRS and yaw damper.
text: over redacted [vor], we were settled in at fl450 almost to our destination at redacted. we had just received a reroute due to weather and were proceeding to redacted [vor]. the aircraft gave a small wag, then the autopilot kicked off. i received an electronic flight instrument system (efis) comparator inop and yaw damp fail simultaneously. we knew we could not sustain fl450 for long without making an immediate descent to a safe altitude. we requested priority handling and began a descent to fl300. that way we could control the aircraft and run the appropriate checklist. at this time, i also noticed that my heading and attitude indicator were also inoperative. we ran the appropriate checklist, and notified ops. we decided as a crew to divert to redacted.cause: there was a significant maintenance event that caused the yaw damper and the inertial reference system (irs) to fail in flight.suggestions: suggest that the irs does not fail in flight.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a helicopter while maneuvering on initial approach to LGA in visual conditions.
text: on the proud2 arrival to lga for landing on runway 22, the flight crew was instructed to follow the hudson river northbound at an assigned altitude of 4, 000 feet msl.while flying midway over the river, the aircraft's traffic collision avoidance system (tcas) triggered a resolution advisory (resolution advisory) to 'monitor vertical speed.' the crew initiated the appropriate flight maneuvers in response to the resolution advisory. during the event, the crew sighted the conflicting traffic and identified it as a helicopter flying southbound, located east of the aircraft's position, and approximately 500 feet above the aircraft's altitude (4, 500 ft msl).prior to the resolution advisory, the flight crew received no traffic advisories (tas) or notifications from approach control regarding the helicopter's proximity. following the resolution advisory, once separation was established and the conflict was resolved, the crew contacted approach control to advise them that an resolution advisory maneuver had been performed.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor reported landing with reported wind shear and dust storm resulting in a runway excursion and contact with signage.
text: i am writing this to explain the series of events that led me to run off the left side of the runway on xxl at redacted airport on day 0 at approximately xa:00 and strike a taxiway sign in aircraft x.weather at the time of airplane dispatch was 310@13g18. i decided to do a landing lesson with a ppl student pilot to prepare him for his upcoming prog check. winds throughout our instruction had been variable, gusting up to 24 during our laps in the pattern. during instruction, i was teaching the student how to execute crosswind correction during landing.on the sixth lap in the pattern, while we were in the downwind, the weather conditions at the airport deteriorated rapidly. at this point, redacted tower released a weather report stating severe low level windshear, winds 250@20g35, and a dust storm at the departure end of the runway.at this point, redacted tower had cleared us for the touch and go, and i instructed my student to turn base for runway xxl. while turning onto the base for xxl, i saw the massive dust storm that redacted tower had reported quickly approaching the departure end of runway xxl, blowing left to right. at this point, my student dropped flaps 10.turning base to final, i instructed my student to come in at 70kts due the excessive wind. he dropped flaps 20. after this, i instructed him to maintain flaps 20 and emphasized coming in at a higher approach speed.now on short final, i could feel the crab angle required for our ground track to run parallel with the runway increasing as we were descending. the idea for a go around had entered my head, however looking down the end of the runway, i could see the dust storm, at least 800ft tall, moving toward the approach end of runway xxl. seeing this, i knew going around at our current trajectory would involve penetrating the dust strom at a low airspeed and altitude, and i immediately took the controls with the understanding that i needed to get the airplane on the ground.i was able to use a crosswind landing technique to touch the airplane down on the centerline of runway xxl. i immediately initiated flaps zero and instructed redacted tower that this was going to be a full stop. as i was attempting to slow the airplane down on the runway, the nose of the airplane began to drift from the center line to the left at a rapid rate. i immediately acted by exercising full aileron correction left, and full rudder deflection to the right in an attempt to prevent the airplane from weathervaning into the wind. i had reached the control limit of both the aileron and the rudder while still on the runway, but i had lost complete directional control at this point.now completely at the mercy of the wind, i could see that our direction of movement was veering us off the runway and into a taxiway sign. i initiated full back pressure to reduce as much kinetic energy as possible, causing the airplane's nose to rise. we struck the taxiway sign with the underside of the airplane.now at a reduced airspeed, i was able to get the nose of the airplane pointed back toward the runway. i allowed the airplane to coast back in the direction of the runway. i did not apply toe break pressure for the sake of preventing the nose landing gear from digging into the grass. we came to a full stop with the right main landing gear on the runway, and the nose wheel and left main landing gear in the grass.the first thing that i did was turn to the student and ask if he was okay. he told me he was. i called up to the tower and told him that everyone on the airplane was okay. i asked tower if we should taxi onto a taxi way. he told me to shut down and stay where i was, and i complied.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: ATC controller reported a military large UAS had a malfunctioning radio which made communication with the UAS crew difficult.
text: aircraft x, military q9 drone from redacted to redacted, radios are not airworthy, cannot communicate safely with this aircraft at all. very difficult to understand or hear the drone operator. drone operator continuously responded to radio calls that were not for them. delay of 15 seconds or more for them to respond to calls. cluttered frequencies the entire time they were in our airspace. eventually they went completely nordo and looked like they held in redacted [artcc] airspace because they didn't have clearance for lower into redacted [airport]. this aircraft is operating unsafely and should not be allowed in air traffic control controlled airspace until its radios are fixed and thoroughly tested.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported EWR Tower Controllers provided incomplete weather information by omitting gusts and had to specifically ask for it.
text: this report is informational as an observed trend that ewr tower controllers, as experienced on this flight, are, many times, not stating the gusts when broadcasting the winds. in this instance, and this is approximate because i can't recall the exact numbers, he called winds at 290/8. i then asked if there were any gusts, since the atis stated gusts and the rough ride confirmed it. the controller then said gusting 14. in a subsequent call to another jet, the controller again stated the wind without the gust. perhaps this report could be used to, perhaps, change the air traffic control wind calls or tools for the controller to include gusts consistently. as you likely know, the gust factor is an integral part of our target speed calculation that serves as an important vref buffer for gusty winds.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 Captain reported a traffic conflict on final approach with an aircraft on the runway resulting in an ATC directed go-around. The go-around resulted in an undesired aircraft state before regaining aircraft control and a return for another approach and landing.
text: a complex go-around created by an air traffic control landing/take-off conflict led to an undesired aircraft state in which the pm perceived safety was in jeopardy and took control of the aircraft.the flight began eventfully with a passenger and service animal issue that caused a delayed departure. once resolved, the taxi out through initial approach was unremarkable. the workload and complexity began during the latter stages of the arrival and clearance for the approach.the weather was approximately overcast010 to few050 and there was a notam for our landing runway (xxr) that advised 'special authorization cat 1 (instrument landing system) procedure not authorized, unless advised by air traffic control that cranes are down.' as we were cleared for the approach and above the glideslope (~2000' agl), i directed the pm to inquire on the status of the cranes. we were informed multiple times that the 'cranes are up' and there was an unfamiliarity from air traffic control about this notam, but eventually a declaration that 'we are authorized for the approach.' meanwhile, i had disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle, accelerating about five knots, but intercepted the glideslope configured gear/f15, slowing from 165kts to target speed at the faf/1500' agl. we briefly discussed that we felt safe continuing the approach, completing the landing checklist prior to 1000' agl and entering imc. this phase was the first element of complexity during this approach.upon breaking out of the weather at approximately 800' agl, i observed an airplane on the runway and queried the pm if he saw the same thing. he confirmed there was an airplane there, followed by air traffic control providing instructions to it and the preceding aircraft. next, we verified stable at 500' agl and were discussing the probability of a go-around as the aircraft was slow to begin the takeoff roll. air traffic control instructed us to go around at approximately 300' agl, but with noticeable closure on the impending lift-off of the other aircraft. i initiated the go around in accordance with the sop, while offsetting to the right (away from the other runway) and remaining under the weather layer, keeping the departing aircraft in sight. i was unable to verify any of the pm go-around actions as i was primarily concerned about flightpath deconfliction with the other aircraft and verbally said 'what does he want us to do' as i estimated our distance to the other aircraft nearing 3000' nose-tail separation. air traffic control then gave us a left turn to 060 (nearly across the taking off aircraft's flight path) and climb to 3000' msl, and after a slight delay, i complied with that instruction, beginning the climb back into imc. this phase was the second element of complexity during this approach.as we climbed into the weather and i transitioned to instruments, i observed the aircraft passing through approximately 1200' msl at approximately 12 degrees nose high pitch, but with an airspeed of approximately 190 kias and decreasing rapidly with the trend arrow approaching 160 kias. i immediately lowered the nose towards 5 degrees nose high as i scanned across the other side of the cockpit to analyze the poor aircraft performance. during this time, i believe i said '(check) flaps' or possibly 'level change, set climb speed (cms), flaps 5, ' but more attention was narrowly focused on determining the throttle setting/engine performance and aircraft gear/flap configuration. i continued to lower the flight path towards level flight, advanced the throttles slightly, and did observe increasing airspeed, as well as a momentary sink rate of approximately 500' fpm. there was comm from both air traffic control and the pm during this point that i did not fully interpret while focused on precisely controlling the flight path, while also still attempting to diagnose the performance degradation. at this point, without any enhanced ground proximity warning system (egpws) aural warnings, the pm perceived 'red terrain' on the navigation display and said 'climb' and then 'i have the aircraft.' obviously, this was also startling, but i released control of the aircraft and tried to make the mental shift to gain situational awareness (sa) as the new pm. i did not immediately notice any 'red terrain', but did perceive a significant increase in pitch attitude. still without certainty of the flap position, i begin moving the flaps to a lower setting, neither the first officer nor i can definitively say who moved the flaps to 5, though we know he did press lvl change and set cms at some point in this immediate sequence of transitioning pf/pm roles. while still gaining sa, i observed 'yellow terrain' on our nose starting at approximately five nautical miles and made a request to air traffic control that 'we need a turn away.' air traffic control subsequently provided a frequency change, the new pf also said things during this time that i did not fully comprehend. i observed the aircraft continuing to accelerate, nearing 250 knots and i raised the flaps to up, the 'flaps, flaps' aural warning also sounded at some point during this sequence of me functioning as the pm. the pf at some point engaged command b and we cleared the weather back into vmc. this phase was the third element of complexity during this approach.now on top of the weather with a stable aircraft and on a good vector and altitude, we were able to restore normal crm, and executed the after take-off checklist. we double checked each other and the aircraft, returned to the original pf/pm roles, completed a descent check, and uneventful landing and taxi-in (though there was still concern/uncertainty regarding the notams referencing the cranes, but we had not noticed any on the previous approach). due to being late, we only very briefly debriefed in the airplane after completing the parking checklist and i said we would discuss prior to the next flight. the first officer left the jet as i stayed to wish passengers farewell and apologize again for the inconvenience. upon exiting, i saw the ca of the next flight on the jetbridge and we discussed the passenger service animal and notam issue for several minutes. i arrived to the next aircraft and began a deliberate debrief with the first officer, recognizing that we will probably be late departing. during our discussions, it became apparent to me that we may have oversped the flaps, i then left the middle of our debrief to go back to the other aircraft to inform the captain of our suspicion, stating that it was less than 10 knots, for less than 10 seconds, at flaps 5 or less at ~2000' msl. i returned to satisfactorily continue our debrief, double checking on the fitness of both the first officer and my own fitness for duty for the next flight. he stated that he was, i agreed with his assessment, and did not have concerns regarding my fitness. the next flight was conducted uneventfully.to recap and summarize, the slightly varied and out-of-sync sa among the pf, pm, and air traffic control resulted in multiple missed/delayed comm and lack of shared mental model on the flight deck (degraded crm), ultimately producing a poorly executed go around.

synopsis: A321 flight crew reported landing safely after experiencing cabin depressurization on descent.
text: descending on the zzzzzx approaching redacted at 26000 ft pressurization page presented itself showing cabin altitude 9000 blinking. noticed delta p was around 5.2 less than what it should have been and outflow valve open. became distracted didn't cross redacted at required altitude distracted with conversation about emergency status with captain. we realized depressurization was happening. i was instructed to fly the plane and communicate with air traffic control. we donned our masks and established crew communication per iac (immediate action checklist). i expedited descent as i noticed delta p descending and cabin altitude climbing which peaked at 11150. once established on vectors for xxr and at 10000 ft with cabin altitude mirroring ambient conditions i removed my o2 mask donned my headset, transferred controls to the captain for a cat 3 approach with a subsequent uneventful landing and taxi to the gate.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported information on LEBL/BCN Jeppesen charts are outdated and needs to be updated with the current departure procedures.
text: company chart 10-7 for bcn in the jeppesen manual is no longer correct and requires an immediate update. it should read as follows:all current 24l rnav sids state, maintain runway heading to 410... the initial turn shall begin no later than upon reaching 500." the state rules and procedures, 10-1 pages no longer include any of the verbiage referenced in 10-7.i would further recommend the entire section under "turn compliance" be deleted or completely rewritten. the current wording states we "must" violate our opspecs and begin the turn below 400 feet. air traffic control does not require this and this circumstance does not meet the other 2 exceptions to our minimum turns after takeoff (fom).furthermore, there's a superfluous statement: "hand fly or autopilot engaged (minimum of 200 feet)." is there another way to fly an airplane?as one who has regularly flown this departure, it is unnecessary to fly this departure in heading if hand flying. by leaving lnav engaged and beginning the turn at 410 feet, lnav magenta path will automatically update directly to the first fix on the departure. it's far simpler and less likely to be flown incorrectly. a far more useful suggestion would be to verify all speed and altitude restrictions on the sid. i have yet to load any of the sids at bcn that didn't require manually entering at least one speed restriction not coded in the database. in addition, at the weights we usually depart bcn some of the altitude restrictions are difficult if not impossible to make, especially at higher ambient temperatures. under these conditions use of noise abatement departure procedures 1 (nadp1) is required. lastly, this station frequently publishes variable wind direction in the body of the metar, often resulting in a tailwind component that prevents us from using the shorter runway 24l/06r. many crew members seem unfamiliar with the calculations necessary to ensure performance data performance. perhaps a training module would help?i assume the information on the page was written some time ago and never updated resulting in low altitude turns and overly complicated and unnecessary departure "technique.""

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Speed All Types
synopsis: B737-800 pilot reported an NMAC during a climb at FL350. The flight crew responded to the RA and ATC issued a turn.
text: i was flying at fl350 with fl370 as final. redacted center was the controlling sector during this time. i was given a climb to fl370 at 1, 000 fpm or greater. i set the fma (flight mode annunciator) to vs +1000 and told the first officer that we will monitor the airspeed and bleed off as much as we feel comfortable with or make it to fl370-but not going to get too slow or be dangerous. we started the climb with an indicated mach of .752at approximately 36400 i was 10-12 knots above 1.3vso and decide thats enough. the first officer told redacted center that we can no longer maintain 1, 000 feet per minute but can take a turn. we were given 10 degrees left. then told to turn right 090. we start the turn and almost immediately told then turn left 300. when turning left the first officer goes oh thats because another plane is right below us. i then look at the mfd (multi-function flight display) and see they are 400 feet below. immediately we get a tcas resolution advisory to climb. i disengage the automation, go full power and comply with the resolution advisory per the procedure in our 737 aom. when we were clear of conflict i reengaged the automation and continued our climb to fl370. the other aircraft also got a tcas resolution advisory to descend. then given clear back to redacted [vor].cause: the climb to 370 was not that imperative-we could have just waited for the other aircraft to pass and climb then. also there was a sigmet on the weather app for mod turbulence up to 350 shortly after top of climb. to get above it faster for flight attendant safety and passenger comfort i flew the climb at max rate on the vnav page which was 256 indicated and that become .752 mach when we started our climb to 370. typically we fly 280-300 and then .76-78 so if the conditions allowed a faster climb perhaps i could have had more speed to bleed off to get to fl370. also with the price of fuel i know we are really paying attention to econ speeds and everything where our usual 300 and .78 may not be the more desirable speed anymore-but that could have given me more speed to bleed off.

synopsis: C182 Flight Instructor reported partial power loss on departure that resulted in an expeditious return to the departure airport.
text: partial power loss on takeoff successful return to the runway. took off from rwy xx and all engine instruments were green and everything seemed normal. at about 100' to 200' we noticed that the plane was barely maintaining 70kts and about 100 fpm but all engine indications were normal and power sounded normal. shortly after we weren't able to climb at all so i turned back towards the runway. had just enough power to drag back to rwy xy and landed.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported a situation where their student flew to another airport and had a runway excursion due to crosswinds.
text: my student pilot flew to redacted. before he departed we checked the weather and i reviewed his flight planning. i endorsed his logbook and he departed. post arrival he told me that he had landed in a strong crosswind and had run off of the side of the runway and gotten stuck in the mud. the tower had him land on the longer runway which had a strong crosswind 10 gusting into the 20s. my student announced 'student pilot'. redacted tends to use runway xx since it's longer runway due to a lot of military and jet training, even in a strong crosswind. the other runway xy would probably have been a better option for a student pilot in a cessna 172. the wind would have been a quartering crosswind and much easier to deal with. the student pilot did not have the experience to know that he could ask for the other runway. the tower did not offer the other runway. i myself am going to make sure my students know that they can request a different runway. tower should be aware of student pilot limitations in crosswinds.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a critical ground conflict with an aircraft on approach.
text: pa30 was approaching the airport and announced a 5 mile final. cessna proceeded to runway xx hold short line and completed final checks for departure. the cessna crew scanned the sky for traffic but did not see the pa30 on final. the pa30 announced a 2-mile final, the cessna pilots visually scanned the final approach, did not see traffic and immediately proceeded towards the runway for departure. the cessna pilot made a radio call 'taking runway xx for departure'. the pa30 pilot shouted 'hey we are on short final, what are you doing!' the cessna pilot immediately stopped the aircraft approximately 150 feet from the runway edge but beyond the hold short line. the left seat pilot looked again, saw the pa30 and judged the aircraft to be about 1 inch wide on the windscreen. the pilots exchange dialogue for a few moments to verify positions, and eventually the pa30 executed a go-around which seemed to be several hundred feet above the threshold, contributing factors: overcast, grey sky, and cessna was position perpendicular to the departing runway. lessons learned: angle the aircraft prior to the hold short line as appropriate to get a clear view of the final approach course. it may have been possible to see the pa30's landing lights.human factors: cessna crew was alert, fatigue was not a factor. cessna crew used pre-takeoff checklist, and briefed the takeoff prior to departure. the crew heard the distance calls and judged and concurred the separation to be safe and sufficient for departure.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Cessna 182 pilot reported that oil sprayed onto the windscreen during departure resulting in the pilot returning to the airport where they landed safely.
text: while performing a normal take off for a flight to redacted oil sprayed onto my windscreen. at the time i was unsure of what the issue was so i began to prepare to land straight ahead. my passenger, another pilot, assisted me by stating that we still had good oil pressure and that perhaps we should go around and land on the same departing runway xx. i agreed, increased power to full, climbed to pattern altitude and told tower that i'd like to land xx. they asked me if i was requesting priority handling and i responded that i was, and that i had oil spray across my windscreen. i was cleared to land on xx, and i landed on xx. other traffic on final to xx was directed to clear out of the way. i landed, exited via taxiway 1 to the ramp and taxied back to the hangar. i was met by airport fire / rescue. upon inspection after shutdown it was found that the oil filler cap wasn't secured or came loose during takeoff / flight. sop procedures are currently being updated to stop the practice of taking the cap off after flight to allow the crankcase to exhaust. the positives of this practice seem to me to be far outweighed by the negatives. i also have altered my procedures to never fly an airplane that i haven't physically checked that the oil cap and any other removable caps are secure. i've also discussed with cfis to update my abort briefing to be adjusted that i only land straight ahead or turn back to land in the event of a power plant failure. if i am able to still safely climb, i will do that and return to land on the departing runway.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Citation Excel (C560XL) Captain reported encountering turbulence that resulted in a momentary loss of altitude and aircraft control.
text: we were flying along the top of some stormy weather at fl 390, as the cloud tops began to rise we asked to climb to fl 410 to be above the clouds and weather. once we did that we were vmc above the weather with pockets of occasional light chop. we saw on the radar that we were approaching a cell ahead of us, however there was no cloud build up that we could see and it was indicating that the building cell was beneath us. we decided to ask for a deviation to the right just to make sure we wouldn't fly directly above it, even though continuing straight or turning would have remained clear of any clouds and we be above the cloud tops by at least a couple thousand feet. in our turn to the right we encountered turbulence that began to build rapidly and ultimately pitched the aircraft up and down so violently, that the autopilot disconnected and the aircraft pitched down losing about 300 feet rapidly, by the time i was able to regain control of the aircraft, apply power, and pitch up, we had sunk below our cruising altitude to about 40600 feet. we reported the loss of altitude to air traffic control and then stated that we were back on course, completed with our deviation. besides the continuation of moderate chop we continued on to our destination with no other events

synopsis: Mooney M-20 F Flight Instructor reported green gear light not illuminated yet other aircraft indications and visual showed gear down; resulting in a landing gear collapse on landing.
text: flying back from redacted to redacted entering the left downwind for runway xxl... ran gear down before landing checklist and noticed no green light on dash to indicate gear was down. went through checklist and tried to troubleshoot. we did have gear down indication on the floor of the aircraft and no gear horn when power below 12 inches of manifold pressure. called tower to ask if they could see gear down and tower said 'gear appears to be down'touched down normally on mains and the gear collapsed a second or so after touchdown and we came to a stop in the middle of the runway on the belly of aircraft. no injuries. on preflight inspection gear was checked and appeared to be in normal working condition. we did do a full stop taxi back and multiple touch and go landings at redacted before returning. im thinking that the gear much have been damaged on the last landing at redacted which is the reason it did not lock down back at redacted.

synopsis: General aviation pilot reported the noise abatement sign at PWM airport distracts pilots from the hold-short line.
text: in low light, high commercial traffic, and intersecting runways in use setting, ground and clearance frequency were same guy and they were trying to get planes out and in as weather worsened. there was confusion on my call for clearance, then a rushed taxi instruction. taxiing to runway 18, there is a noise abatement sign, which when read, distracts pilot from displaced hold short line well before the turn to the runway from taxiway c. easy to miss hold short line. moving the noise abatement sign and making the hold short line distinct from it would lessen confusion, as would staffing ground and clearance delivery frequencies.

synopsis: Government UAS pilot reported learning post-flight they flew in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: reporter (pilot) and volunteer crew of 2 extra people flew a drone to capture imagery of the area along a road at location x. as the pilot, i was unaware that redacted airport airspace extended as far south as it does and i unintentionally flew the drone into class e2 [class e surface airspace] airspace at an altitude of 97 feet without prior authorization from the faa/atc. the drone software would not allow me to fly over 97 feet in altitude but did not issue any warnings. i did not realize the airspace was class e2 until i began doing research later, at which time i found the faa online web map. i have since found the sectional maps for the airport mentioned, as well as familiarized myself with laanc. there was no interference with manned aircraft, private property, and no damage incurred.

synopsis: A Center Controller reported a departing aircraft did not turn in a timely manner and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: i was training a developmental who is competent, we had light traffic only one departure at the time. i overheard the supervisor mention a runway change and noticed we still had a strong south wind. i turned to discuss thee runway change with the supervisor and then heard my developmental issue a 350 heading to aircraft x. the aircraft had been issued at 295 heading and the pilot had correctly the 295 heading however he was slow in the turn and enter entered 3 mvas below the mva. we should've issued an expedite instruction, and expedite climb instruction and a low altitude alert.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: ZMP Controller reported poorly coordinated IFR releases off a non-tower airport resulted in a loss of separation with clearance issued below MVA.
text: i was working the r-side with a d-side training team with me as well. at sectors xx/xy combined. aircraft y called requesting their clearance from mkt to redacted. my d-side coordinated the approval request with m98 approach and with their approval i read aircraft y their clearance and released them for departure. during this time, i was having a discussion with the d-side trainee and trainer about the coordination they just did. i also had to have my d-side coordinate and altitude with m98 as well as point outs that were required for another aircraft. during this time aircraft x called airborne off of mkt and i thought they said they were 3 miles northwest of the airport. the flight plan they had to redacted airport. with what i thought i heard for their distance from mkt and the airport they were flying to being roughly a 320-heading vs aircraft y's route which was roughly a 360 heading. i used the code for aircraft x they were below the mia when radar identified them. so my clearance was 'aircraft x climb and maintain 6, 000 leaving 2, 800 cleared to the redacted airport via direct. at this time the d-side trainer said you probably should have just told them to maintain visual flight rules. but it was too late. mkt is a class e airspace, and they were less than 3 miles from the airport. seconds later aircraft y called airborne. as soon as their tag came up i turned aircraft x to a 270 heading and amended their altitude to 4, 000. i did not radar identify aircraft y but asked them is they could maintain visual flight rules i know this legally doesn't change a thing, but it was the first thought that came to mind. when aircraft x was at 2, 800 and aircraft y was at 3, 100 their courses were diverging, however the separation was only 2.02 miles apart. once aircraft y was level at 5, 000 feet i radar identified them. then switched them to m98 approach. after this i cleared aircraft x back on course. i told my supervisor and had him pull up the replay. then got out of position to fill this out.recommendation: ensuring the separation could have been done by simply not issuing a clearance to aircraft x and telling them to maintain visual flight rules. this scenario happens often at mkt being a busy airport while several aircraft will call up airborne picking up instrument flight rules. i should have done what i did in the past and not issue the clearance. i misjudged the distance aircraft x was from the airport and misheard them. the aircraft type difference was a large factor in performance, and i should have known better than to issue the clearance. a tower at mkt has been in the talks and would greatly improve the safety of the aircraft going in and out.

synopsis: Air carrier Ground Personnel reported a ground conflict during push back. Push back direction was altered and continued.
text: upon pushback on gate xx, our lead was denied the checkout of the gate's box due to him having one previously checked out still in his name on a different gate. this forced us to borrow a box from xy to obtain headsets and wands. there was only one set of wands in this box. i gave the wands to the other wing walker since he was the one who would be disconnecting the aircraft from the tug and saluting the pilot. as we began to wing walk, the pusher began to turn the plane to go around xz. this is a very strange and difficult push, and our lead/pusher was not used to pushing this particular gate. when i saw the tail of our aircraft come dangerously close to the tail of the aircraft parked in xz's gate, i spoke into the mouthpiece of my headset to 'stop.' however, it was windy on this day and the mouthpiece wasn't picking up my command. i used hand signals with my arms/hands by making an 'x' to stop the push. the other wingwalker saw this and relayed the command to the pusher, resulting in him stopping. i proceeded to motion him to pull the aircraft straight back so he would clear the tail of xz's aircraft. he followed suit until i motioned for him to turn the nose of the aircraft the appropriate way for that push. as i was walking back to the gate, i approached a supervisor in his van and told him what had happened.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Fractional Captain reported AXH departure procedures should reflect ODP and instruct to turn to the right and not to the left for obstacle avoidance.
text: this narrative is regarding the events that occurred on the morning of day 0 at approximately xa:28. this report is being filed to bring awareness to a potentially dangerous situation. it is my hope that a more detailed analysis will be conducted to help alleviate any further issues.on the morning of day 0, at the non-towered axh airport for a repositioning fight to redacted, the crew was issued an air traffic control clearance from houston approach. the clearance was issued on the ground and is as follows: aircraft x enter controlled airspace heading 220, climb and maintain 2000." before departure the crew referenced the obstacle departure procedure for runway 9 instructing a climb to 2000 feet before turning left. crew briefing included the air traffic control instructions, obstacle departure procedure (odp) procedure, and nothing indicating an other than standard traffic pattern direction. there was no mention of obstacles on the airport chart and after completing the briefing the crew elected to continue with normal operations and depart instrument flight rules. the crew complied with the listed odp by climbing to 2000 feet and then turning left to then comply with the air traffic control issued heading of 220. radio contact was initiated with houston approach, questioning why we had turned left. air traffic control went on to indicate the proximity of the aircraft to an antenna farm on the left downwind leg that had an altitude of 2000 feet. air traffic control instructed a climb to 3000 and a turn to a new heading. there were constructive discussions regarding omissions of chart data and misleading odp instructions. in conclusion, the crew followed all directions, to the best of their knowledge and attempted to operate the aircraft in the safest manner possible.suggestions: it is imperative that the axh jeppesen chart 10-9 reflect obstacle departure instructions to climb to 2000 before turning right and not left. in addition, conduct an analysis and change the direction of runway 9 traffic to the right for obstacle avoidance. going forward, when air traffic control issues a clearance off of runway 9 they need to specify, turn right heading - - -. if a right turn is not specified the crew assumes a left turn is expected as indicated by the left turn on the odp and direction of the standard left traffic pattern. dangerous obstacles exist north of the airport and there needs to be a modification to either the chart or the air traffic control procedures when issuing clearances."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported GSP Approach and Tower closed without notifying the crew during descent.
text: arriving into gsp with no arrival routing at a top altitude of 10, 000 feet, atlanta center handed us off to greer approach. greer approach then instructed us to maintain present heading and descend to 4, 000 ft and expect runway 22, our heading was going direct the airport. we noted in jeppesen charts that the tower closed at 0445z. however, that time is wrong for daylight savings time and it really closes at 0345 z and is the consistent closure time year round, locally.after leveling at 4, 000 feet a couple minutes passed and we needed further instruction. we queried greer approach a couple times for further instruction and received no answer. greer approach and tower had closed. we were still on an instrument flight rules clearance and we had no turn to intercept or anything. they just left us hanging on a heading at 4, 000 ft. no further clearance. we switched to tower frequency, also ctaf, and announced our intentions. it was visual flight rules and continued forward with an approach to runway 22 while announcing our position on ctaf. after landing we cancelled instrument flight rules with atlanta center. no further events noted. radios operated just fine the entire time. greer approach and tower just signed off without notice.cause: greer approach closing and leaving us on a heading and altitude for approach without any further clearance or instructions prior to closing. just silence. the charts publishing tower closure time incorrectly during daylight savings time. this is true of all our charts, not just gsp, for tower closures. publishing zulu times does not account for daylight savings time.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported GPS jamming during descent to MUHA airport.
text: during decent onto arrival into havana cuba we received nav fm/gps pos disagree ecam. the message kept popping and disappearing throughout the decent. we suspected gps jamming going on in the area. we were able to check the position of the aircraft and continued on. we were set up for the visual approach backed up by the instrument landing system to runway 06 in havana. the gps position began to drift more and we got terrain warning message during landing close to the runway. since we were on a visual approach in a stable position to land we continued and made a normal landing. by the time we taxied the position error had fixed itself. we wrote up the discrepancy in the log book. everything went back to normal and we continued on the next leg with no issues.cause: i think if cuba is jamming gps signals they should let us know ahead of time. i think multiple flights were having position errors that day into havana. we shouldn't fly there during the times they are gps jamming.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported executing a VMC missed approach versus the cleared RNAV procedure to SGU airport due to traffic.
text: air traffic control cleared us for the rnav runway 19 into sgu. we were given the frequency change and everything was normal. there were numerous aircraft around sgu including on the ground, in the traffic pattern, and inbound to the traffic pattern. when we were at about a 10 mile final, aircraft y turned base. we immediately started discussing the possibility of a go-around because of the proximity and probability that we were going to catch up to them. once we confirmed the aircraft wouldn't be clear of the runway, we initiated the go-around. we made left traffic and landed with no further issues. when on the ground i remembered that we were cleared for the rnav and i believe we technically should have flown the missed approach. i believe we made the safest decision flying the traffic pattern as we did because of the amount of traffic in the area and because it was vmc below 10, 000 msl. cause: large amounts of traffic on and around the airport. uncontrolled airport. a pilot who may not have understood how fast we would catch up to them turning base in front of us.suggestions: in the future, i plan on talking to aircraft which i believe will possibly cause a conflict so we can coordinate arrivals more effectively. we could also cancel instrument flight rules when we know we meet all requirements to stay and operate in vmc in accordance with company policy

synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported a GPWS terrain warning while on an assigned heading in visual conditions. The Captain stopped the descent and climbed until the warning stopped; then continued the approach.
text: we were flying along trying to navigate through thunderstorms in which our radar was not depicting very well at all. while in some of the roughest bumps, our radios were overcome with static screeching and we were able to hear air traffic control maybe 1x5. this bout of turbulence was likely the worst i have encountered thus far as a pilot.while in the midst of this we received a cab emer call from our fa. she explained to us that a older male pax was on our emergency o2 since his personal o2 was depleted. with the distraction of the radio and heavy turbulence we herd that the o2 bottle has a 15 minute supply on it. with these factors in play i decided to immediately request priority handling and proceeded to redacted asap. we advised air traffic control as well as dispatch and requested emt personnel to meet the aircraft at the gate.redacted approach cleared us for a visual approach to rwxx. however, they them advised us to turn in order for them to squeeze in one aircraft ahead of us. this did not make me happy to say the least. during this approach we received a terrain followed by pull up gpws which is described in my previous report. upon landing we quickly got to the gate and the emt came onboard to check on the pax before the rest of the plane deplaned. i was told the pax was ok and he was take into the terminal via wheelchair. after this event ended, i called maintenance and minimum equipment list'd the portable oxygen bottle as it was used and still indicating 1000 psi.once we returned to redacted. i had enough time to talk with our flight attendant. she described the situation and told me how the passenger had two portable oxygen (batteries) that are personal. the first tank was depleted on his previous flights and the tank used for our flight became depleted because of the turbulence and his heavy breathing during the flight. our flight attendant described the actions she took and i think she did a fantastic job in addressing the situation. she was filling out her medical form to provide us. however, the turbulence was so strong. it was not feasible to complete that task or for us to reach out to medlink. there were no medical professionals onboard the aircraft.during this flight we had previously requested priority handling. we had the field in sight and cleared for the visual to rw xx. i had selected 2100 which was the faf altituded and was pointing the plane towards the fix to land asap due to situation. air traffic control gave us traffic to follow and instructed us to turn right an additional 15-30 degrees. we were in a decent at 1000fpm and the 'terrain terrain' caution alarmed followed by a warning 'pull up'. we were visual with the ground so i disconnected autopilot and climbed to 3000. the alert went away. this occurred about 10 miles east of the final approach course. i then hand flew the rest of the approach and landed without any further issue.cause: pax o2 supply became depleted due to heavy breathing with associated turbulence. the actual descent rate exceeded the planes threshold for issuing the warning.suggestion: inform pax requiring o2 to come with a greater supply if possible. priority aircraft should have priority to the field, especially medical in nature. pax was on o2 with a breathing issue.

synopsis: Bonanza 35 pilot reported loss of the engine during flight resulting in an off airport landing. Aircraft was towed back to the airport.
text: had been descending through a cloud layer from cruise at 11, 500. picked up small amount of rime icing on windshield. came out into vmc at 6700 feet and began maneuvering in vmc while holding assigned altitude of 5000 feet. initially noticed some engine vibrations increasing. adjusted mixture and throttle but continued to worsen. losing power so tried to adjust rpms. vibrations increased to shaking. then noticed severe engine overspeed to 3100 rpm. attempted more propellor controlled adjustments but had effect. then noticed oil pressure had gone to zero. began looking for a spot to land. puff of smoke came into cockpit though not thick and temporary. requested priority handling and asked for vectors to nearest runway.engined shook and seized. followed vectors toward redacted but could see it would not be feasible located a reasonable looking farmfield and lined up for landing. lowered landing gear and landed on field. no damage to airframe and no injury. airplane was then towed to redacted.glider training was very useful in this circumstance.

synopsis: A321 flight crew reported landing gear extension malfunction during approach.
text: over the final approach fix (ilsxxc redacted redacted), the landing gear was attempted to be extended for landing and upon lever extension ecam lcgiu 1+2 fault was illuminated and there was no gear movement. we attempted to recycle the gear handle, that was not successful. a normal soft go-around was conducted and we rejoined the traffic pattern to work the ecam procedure. a normal ecam procedure was executed followed by usage of the flight manual for actions for the manual gear extension. the manual gear extension was successful with 3 green lights on the panel (lower ecam gear displays were amber due to the failure of the lgcius (landing gear control interface units)). after completing the procedure, air traffic control was advised as a precaution. a normal configuration and landing was accomplished. aircraft vacated on a high speed and came to a stop on taxiway 1. emergency vehicles inspected the aircraft and noted that the gear doors were extended with no other abnormalities. maintenance control was contacted to confirm we could taxi to the gate under our own power. a normal taxi was conducted and aircraft was parked at [gate] xx normally where maintenance met us at the jet bridge. normal shutdown procedures were accomplished. logbook entry was made for the manual gear extension.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Citation Latitude Captain reported a traffic conflict with an aircraft on downwind when crossing the hold short line at a non-towered airport.
text: we were holding short of runway xx at redacted on the east side of the runway. we had just received an instrument flight rules release from air traffic control who gave us a three minute void time. there was one aircraft on downwind for runway xx. we made a radio call to the common traffic advisory frequency to advise that we were going to take the runway for departure. as we began to power up past the hold short line, the first officer said stop stop. i stopped the aircraft with the nose just passed the hold short line for runway xx at the approach end. as i looked over the shoulder of my first officer towards the 3 o'clock of our airplane, i saw a c130 approaching low and fast on a severely short approach. the c130 operator had not advised us of his intention to make a short approach. due to the close proximity and high approach speed of the c130 i chose to stop and remain where we were and advise the c130 our nose was just passed the hold short line. the c130 made a radio call on the common traffic advisory frequency to say they were on left base. in the interest of safety and out of an abundance of caution, i chose to allow the c130 to execute his procedure first before taking the runway. the c130 accomplished a touch and go in front of us and then afterwards we departed without incident.suggestions: it's incredibly important, especially in an uncontrolled airport environment to be aware of the type of aircraft sharing the airspace. this particular c130 was a firefighting tanker out doing practice maneuvers. the aircraft commander of the c130 never indicated to us the type of aircraft they were or the nature of their fighter pilot type of approach that they were planning on accomplishing. the aircraft descended very quickly from 1600 feet above the runway on a downwind in a hard left bank straight to the runway threshold. this type of approach caught us off guard as we assumed a normal approaching landing which would have given us more than enough time to depart safely without conflict. i'm thankful to the first officer for having his head on a swivel and calling out the closure rate of the surprise maneuver.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a GPWS warning during approach. Flight crew configured and landed without further issue.
text: while on the visual approach for runway 24, we encountered a gpws warning. after entering the left downwind and cleared for the approach, my first officer set 2, 400' for the visual and began descending from previous altitude. after communicating with the tower and loading the flight management system for a 'pvor (pseudo vor), i noticed that we were descending towards a tower/obstacle at 2, 167' and had the pilot flying adjust course. we could see the obstacles and made a course correction away from it, but our gpws system alerted us with the 'landing gear'.aural warning. we configured and adjusted our downwind and base legs accordingly and landed runway 24 without further issue.cause: descent too soon while on the visual.suggestions: maintain vigilance as pilot monitoring."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A220 Captain reported a Bleed System failure during initial climb. Flight returned to the departure airport and landed safely.
text: the first officer was the pf. ca was pm and had just finished transition training a few weeks ago. we departed runway xxr in redacted, apu bleed on takeoff. shortly after takeoff we received an eicas message for l bleed fail. the fail light was also illuminated on the l bleed switch. we continued to climb out on zzzzzx departure, cleaned up the airplane and ran the after takeoff checklist. we decided to leave the apu on and start running the l bleed fail checklist in case the apu would be needed. the first officer continued to fly the departure and took over the radios while the ca ran the checklist. after closing the xbleed per the checklist and working through a few decision trees, the checklist asked if oceanic or high terrain is an issue. there was terrain along our route with the first critical point about 17 mins into the flight. since we were not there yet, we took that into consideration and continued with the checklist. the next step had us reducing the l thrust lever to idle. this step took us both by surprise. the ca tried to scroll thru the checklist to see what the next steps would be and if the engine would remain at idle or be shutdown, but it was too difficult to tell thru the checklist. we determined the best course of action was to contact mx (maintenance) via dispatch over satcom. we talked with mx to see what they showed and to verify that we needed to bring the engine to idle. they looked thru the qrh and verified the engine needed to be brought to idle, and the need to remain clear of icing conditions. they also showed that the prsov (pressure regulating shut off valve) was showing failed open. since dispatch was on, the told us a reroute would be needed to remain clear of icing and they were working with the duty pilot and chief pilot. while the ca was coordinating with mx and dispatch, the first officer had pulled up the minimum equipment list for the l bleed fail. it had a long note about the possibility of a duct burst that could cause a major event." the ca confirmed with mx that a duct burst was a possibility. we were now approaching the first terrain area. there was a broken layer of clouds out ahead of us that would prevent us from remaining out of icing. we were also unsure if we would get engine thrust back. we were dispatched method 2 and not yet at our cruise altitude. taking all of this information into account, ca and first officer decided the best course of action was to return to redacted so we could continue the checklist. the ca informed mx and dispatch of our intentions. mx agreed and dispatch worked on amending the release. the ca asked dispatch to notify redacted ops. the first officer notified air traffic control of our intentions and we were cleared back to redacted. once workload permitted, the ca continued the checklist, reducing the l engine to idle. the checklist permitted use of the left engine upon completion. we were overweight so the overweight checklist was also run. air traffic control worked us back into the arrival flow and we landed uneventfully in redacted. since air traffic control provided us with priority handling, cfr (crash fire rescue) was standing by but not needed. we taxied to the gate and wrote up the bleed fail and overweight landing."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: A321 Captain reported hydraulic green system with zero quantity and pressure on take off. Flight returned to the departure airport and landed uneventfully.
text: upon gear retraction after takeoff, we received an ecam caution message for hyd g eng 1 pump lo pr. the green system indicated zero pressure and zero quantity. additional ecam messages appeared that all seemed consistent with a loss of the green hydraulic system.we leveled off, advised air traffic control, ran the ecam and qrh procedures, and contacted dx (dispatch) and mx (maintenance) control via satcom. during this process, we determined that at least one main gear door remained open and our gear would not extend normally.after we addressed the non-normal and developed a plan, i briefed the inflight crew. we coordinated with air traffic control, dx, and mx control for an air return to redacted. before flying our approach, i informed the inflight crew and our customers of our status and our plan to make a normal landing back in redacted. after performing a manual gear extension, we experienced abnormal noises and vibrations. however, all indications showed the gear was now down and locked. we flew an instrument landing system approach to runway xxl. the first officer also asked the tower to verify that our landing gear appeared to be down. we landed about 10k pounds overweight with minimal vertical speed at touchdown. we dismissed arff (airport rescue and firefighting) services once it was clear we could continue to the gate normally.the qrh indicated that this specific aircraft would have nosewheel steering available upon landing. i verified this ability on the ground and checked in with redacted maintenance control before deciding to continue back to the gate under our own power.once parked at the gate, i made several logbook entries (hydraulic system failure, manual gear extension, and overweight landing). we deplaned and i was informed there was an aircraft waiting at the adjacent gate to continue the flight to redacted for our customers. redacted maintenance control showed us where a hydraulic line had become detached in the main landing gear bay, apparently leading to the loss of all green system fluid in flight.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier Captain departing on a SID reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC on initial climb.
text: departed xxr on the zzzzzx, first officer flying, bleeds off take off. the usual turbulence in the climb. uneventful initial climb out. after passing redacted he called for the after take off check about the same time as initiating the right turn in lnav/vnav. seeing that the aircraft was turning north away from terrain and meeting all vertical path requirements first (flight path forward priority here) thus far i diverted my attention to reconfiguring the bleed panel and ensuring we were pressurizing. all normal thus far. approaching redacted i completed the after take off check list and at the same time the controller called and said we were off course and asked if we needed assistance. this was both alarming and confusing, but at this time i did notice we were slightly left of the magenta line by maybe one half mile (.5) but he was correcting back. i checked our altitude to be 6, 200 feet - within vertical path limits. i responded with 'negative he is turning back.' controller came back with 'you are below the mva'. at this point we were passing redacted and on or above vertical path and returning to the magenta line heading east. normal ops at this point handed off to redacted center. i work a fair amount of flights out of redacted, i was surprised to hear this from the controller. we were absolutely never in any position of being in danger of terrain. it was day vmc and all vertical path criteria were met and as i said maybe 1/2 mile left but pointing where we should be. i will say this: in cruise the first officer and i de briefed this and he said to me 'maybe it's because i didn't use all the bank' to which when i queried this he mentioned we were heavy it was bumpy he didn't feel comfortable with 25 degrees of bank so he used less. intent to fly safely was there, but possibly this contributed to the controller seeing on his radar a slower rate of turn and slight track deviance. i told the first officer that unless we are single engine and below the shark tooth and in vnav/lnav we are protected for 25 degrees bank. the first officer is a stand up guy and has time in both seats at two other airlines previously but i do think the lower bank contributed possibly to this.

synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported a NMAC in the vicinity of a busy non-towered airport.
text: ip (flight instructor) (myself) was setting up the sp (student pilot) for vectors to the rnav xx redacted. as we were reaching about 2nm from the faf (~7nm from the airport), both the sp and i noted a large amount of aircraft on the ctaf and noted from ads-b on our mfd (multi-function flight display). we both agreed it would be a good decision to choose another airport to do an approach at instead, and i told the student to climb to 3000msl and visually fly over the ne side of the highway to avoid redacted airspace and stay sw of redacted. as we continued flying at 3000, we noticed on our mfd an aircraft departing from redacted aimed right at us, 500ft below, and climbing. i took controls, banked the plane to the left, and advanced the throttles to full to increase speed and deviate from this aircraft. because we were under the runway xy/xz transition zone from redacted and the xzs were in use at redacted, we were unable to climb above the altitude we were already at. shortly after i banked to the left, we got a 'traffic' callout from the g1000. we continued the turn away from the plane and got them in sight as they were about at our altitude ~1/2nm behind us. after visually confirming we were no factor, we turned back to the nw and continued the flight lesson as normal.

synopsis: Air carrier flight attendants reported experiencing a tail strike in the aircraft during takeoff.
text: during takeoff crew experienced a sudden jolt just after rotation that startled the crew, as this was not a normal type of takeoff. i was approached by a flight attendant that the flight deck had called the aft galley after take off inquiring as to whether they had experienced a jolt during takeoff. she explained that something was definitely not ok. i called the flight deck to understand what had happened, as i felt it too. they were very busy amongst checklist and contacting the company as i understand and they informed me that they would contact me momentarily and to suspend upcoming service until more information was received. after many minutes, i was called back and instructed to commence service as it was determined that we would continue our route to redacted. i only spoke with the captain one more time about the event, to which he explained that we may have a potential tail strike. i had previously instructed the crew that if we divert to be prepared and await instruction. no further communication as to the event were given to me, and only upon arrival was i made aware by ground maintenance/mechanics that we had indeed been involved in a tail strike upon takeoff. this was very concerning to the inflight crew as well as myself, as we were assuming a possible diversion and emergency landing following takeoff.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier technician reported during a scheduled engine change upon removal; they found the forward upper mount bolt missing a washer.
text: incorrect hardware stack-up on lh engine fwd upper mount boltwe were performing a scheduled engine change and upon removal of the lh engine we found that the fwd upper mount bolt was missing one of the two washers. aipc (aircraft illustrated parts catalog) 71-21-01-01 calls out for 3 washers to be installed on this bolt. one countersunk washer against the head of the bolt and two flat washers on the other end under the nut. by only having one washer installed it is unlikely that the torque was done correctly and the cotter pin hole was not properly aligned with the cutout in the nut leaving it possible for the nut to back off.cause: no idea other than lack of paying attention. on this job card these are the steps that reference the washers:step #xx tells you to remove the washers (plural) from the upper mount and references you to figure #xy for the picture.step #xz tells you to remove the washers (plural) from the lower mount and references you to figure #xy for the picture.step #xz tells the inspector to examine the washers (plural) and references you to figure #xa for the picture.step #xb tells you to install the washers (plural) and references you to figure #xy for the picture. there is also a note that specifically calls out that there are two washers installed under the nut as illustrated in figure xy.step #xc tells you to install the washers (plural) and references you to figure #xy for the picture. there is not a note here but there is nothing saying that you can just remove one of those washers.we replaced all the fwd upper and lower mounting hardware (i.e. bolts, flat washers, countersunk washers, and bushings) and moved on with installing the new engine.i have no suggestions for this one

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: C172 pilot reported electrical system malfunction during cruise and return to departure airport.
text: on a planned instrument flight rules flight from redacted to redacted, weather conditions at departure were visual flight rules with ceilings approximately 2, 800 feet agl and visibility around 6 statute miles. my planned route was direct from redacted to redacted. i received my instrument flight rules clearance on the ground from clearance delivery with a straight-out departure, radar vectors, maintain 3, 000 feet, and expect 6, 000 feet ten minutes after departure.after departure, redacted approach subsequently cleared me to 4, 000 feet and later to 6, 000 feet. the aircraft appeared to be operating normally during the climb. at approximately 2, 800 feet msl, i entered imc conditions. the operation was single-pilot, hand-flown, and conducted without autopilot assistance.while climbing through approximately 5, 000 feet msl and about 8 nm northwest of redacted, i heard an abnormal noise through the intercom/headset system. shortly afterward, i observed an undervoltage indication on com 2, and the ammeter showed a discharge condition consistent with a possible alternator or electrical system malfunction. immediately after observing these indications, i lost two-way radio communications with air traffic control.i attempted to reestablish communications with air traffic control and squawked transponder code 7600 for lost communications. due to concern over a potential alternator failure and possible continued degradation of electrical systems while operating in imc, i elected to begin a descending left turn toward known vmc conditions, which i knew existed below approximately 2, 800 feet. at the same time, i accomplished checklist procedures to reduce electrical load by turning off nonessential electrical equipment in an effort to conserve battery power and restore communications capability.at approximately 3, 500 feet msl, i was able to reestablish communications with air traffic control. air traffic control subsequently cleared me back to redacted via visual approach and assigned 3, 000 feet. shortly thereafter, i exited imc conditions. i advised air traffic control of my intention to cancel instrument flight rules in the air, however, full communications were lost again immediately afterward. i again squawked 7600 and proceeded to enter the traffic pattern at redacted, landing without further incident.in hindsight, i recognize that the published instrument flight rules lost communications procedures could have been followed after the initial communications failure. however, during a high-workload, single-pilot imc situation involving a suspected alternator failure, i prioritized returning to vmc conditions and landing as soon as practical. additionally, after communications were briefly restored, i believe it would have been beneficial to request priority handling and request direct routing back to redacted. at the time of the initial communications failure, i attempted to request priority handling but was unable to confirm transmissions were being received and therefore selected transponder code 7600 under the assumption air traffic control would recognize the abnormal situation.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: PA28 pilot and passengers reported engine roughness during approach resulted from fuel starvation and mismanagement. Pilot landed at destination.
text: during a recent cross-country flight, i departed with full fuel and conducted fuel tank changes approximately every hour after the initial 30 minutes of flight. en route, i continued monitoring fuel burn and engine operation, and no abnormal indications were observed during the flight. however, as the flight progressed and fuel levels decreased, i did not adjust my fuel management strategy to a more conservative approach. specifically, i should have switched tanks more frequently at lower fuel levels and should have more seriously considered making an additional precautionary fuel stop.while complying with air traffic control instructions during the arrival and landing phase into redacted, i began noticing engine roughness. recognizing the potential seriousness of the situation, i immediately contacted the tower and requested an immediate landing. air traffic control accommodated the request, and the aircraft landed safely without further incident. after landing, it was determined that approximately 10 gallons of fuel remained onboard.the issue arose primarily from inadequate conservatism in my fuel management decision-making. contributing factors included over-reliance on planned fuel burn calculations, confidence that the remaining fuel quantity was sufficient, and failure to fully appreciate the reduced margin for error as fuel levels became lower. although the aircraft landed safely with approximately 10 gallons of fuel remaining, i later recognized that my operational decisions unnecessarily reduced available safety margins.the concern was identified during post-flight reflection and review of the flight. after evaluating the circumstances, i realized that while regulatory fuel requirements may still have been met, my decisions did not reflect the level of conservatism and risk management expected for safe aeronautical decision-making. in hindsight, an additional fuel stop would have significantly improved the safety margin and reduced operational risk.from a human performance standpoint, several judgment and decision-making factors contributed to the situation. my perception during the flight was that fuel status remained acceptable based on calculations and expected fuel burn, however, this perception reduced my willingness to make more conservative operational choices. plan continuation bias and confidence in the original flight plan likely influenced my reluctance to stop for additional fuel. additionally, i recognize that i did not sufficiently account for the increased importance of proactive fuel management as usable fuel decreased.corrective actions taken since the event include additional study and review of aircraft performance data, fuel burn calculations, and fuel management procedures. i have reevaluated my personal minimums and fuel reserve standards and will adopt a significantly more conservative approach moving forward. in future operations, i will switch fuel tanks more proactively when fuel quantities become lower and will not hesitate to make additional fuel stops whenever they improve operational safety margins.this event served as an important learning experience regarding aeronautical decision-making, risk management, and fuel planning discipline. i take full responsibility for my decisions and will continue working to improve my judgment, situational awareness, and operational conservatism in order to become a safer and more professional pilot.
