anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: Sonex Waiex pilot reported losing control of the aircraft with subsequent runway excursion. Pilot later taxied aircraft back to hangar.
text: summary: i experienced a low speed runway excursion on landing, in a lightweight tailwheel airplane without differential brakes, due to the airplane weathervaning into the crosswind against a full opposite rudder input.i went for a 1.3 hour personal flight in a sonex waiex airplane out of redacted airport. due to preparations for an upcoming airshow, runway xx/xy was closed, and the airport was operating on runway xzl with winds from 200 degrees at 8 kts. when returning for landing, the atis stated the wind had increased to 12 gust 19, creating a significant left crosswind condition.the waiex is a tailwheel (conventional landing gear) airplane without differential brakes. it has a single hand brake, and the tailwheel is steered with a pushrod link to the rudder. it is an experimental amateur-built airplane.as i began the landing flare, i was using nearly full right rudder to align the aircraft heading with the runway, but was able to align it and opted to continue the landing. the landing roll initially stayed straight, then the airplane began to weathervane left into the crosswind as i slowed, and the airframe began to shudder due to the rightward deflected tailwheel skidding on the pavement (the crosswind on the tail surfaces overpowered the traction of the tailwheel). the airplane rolled off the edge into the grass at 20-25 kts and came to a stop about 30 feet from the edge of the runway, nearly aligned with runway heading.i notified tower that i had departed the runway into the grass due to crosswind gust exceeding my control authority, had not hit anything and would like to taxi clear, and tower cleared me to taxi back onto runway xzl and then exit at taxiway 1. from taxiway 1 i contacted ground control and taxied back to the hangars. there was no damage or evidence of the runway excursion on the airplane.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC

text: my student and i were conducting eights on pylons over three islands near the coast. we were at a pivotal altitude of roughly 900 feet msl. we had conducted about 5 eights on pylons and as we were rolling out of the turn heading northwest, we see a sea plane ahead and to the left of our aircraft. i immediately took evasive action turning the airplane to the right to avoid the traffic. it did not appear that the other plane took evasive action. my student and i conducted clearing turns prior to the maneuver to ensure there was no traffic, but the maneuver takes approximately 1 to 2 minutes, so that is enough time for traffic to arrive. we were unable to see the traffic due to our wing being raised and only saw the traffic as we started to level off. we concluded our eights on pylons after that plane passed by and continued with the flight lesson over the gulf. i believe low visual flight rules flying airplanes tend to lack situational awareness in this area due to sightseeing as they fly over the beaches. everyone needs to exercise caution because it is a popular area to conduct flight training as well.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot
synopsis: Small transport pilot reported a NMAC during descent. Pilot followed ATC vectors and continued flight.
text: was enroute to btl and starting my descent from fl360. had been held high for traffic. was told to descend and maintain fl240. i read back 'aircraft x descending flight level 240'. i started a 1000 fpm descent in vs mode while i waited to intercept the vnav profile for the approach to btl. i was then handed off to another sector and i checked in as 'aircraft x out of 340 descending fl240 direct [destination]'. the controller acknowledged. i then picked up the vnav profile and was descending at 1500fpm on vnav. shortly after, i noticed that there was going to be a traffic conflict with a climbing target directly ahead of me flying in the opposite direction. the controller asked the other target to turn right 25 degrees and then asked me to do the same, which i complied with. got a traffic alert at this point of 'same altitude twelve o'clock, 10miles'. this was then followed by a request from the controller to immediately turn right 90 degrees for traffic, which i complied with. switched to vs mode at 1000fpm while i scanned for traffic which i was unable to identify. fortunately, the other target had visual contact with me and passed off to my left. shortly afterwards was asked what altitude i was descending to (which i replied fl240).the remainder of the flight was unremarkable. apparently the data block had fl340 as my assigned altitude even though i had read back fl240 twice (to the assigning controller and then again when checking in with the next sector). this had created a conflict. he was very friendly and apologized profusely.

text: the flight was from redacted to teb on day 0aircraft x on an rnav arrival. i, captain, the flying pilot at approximately xa:22 do to weather that we were vector into by air traffic control. asked my first officer not one time but two times asked for slower from air traffic control. first time i believe they asked for slower, no response from air traffic control. next time i told them, tell them we are slowing down to 210 kts at that time. it was the worst turbulence. a thunderstorm!in thirty years of flying, i've never experienced that type of handling from air traffic control, to vector us in the middle of a cell, you can hear his voice it was almost like he was upset for us slowing down then i could not control the aircraft, and it was in an undesirable state of flight the autopilot kicked off multiple times and i was trying to do my best to hold altitude and heading was unfortunately unsuccessful do to the thermals in the thunderstorm that we were vector into.the air traffic control asked another aircraft if he was experiencing severe turbulence and he replied in the affirmative.

text: departing x14, runway 14. inbound aircraft y called 5 miles east inbound and asked what direction we would be departing, i responded northwest. announced departing runway 14 and commenced takeoff role. normal climb-out with good rate of climb. initiated standard left 45 degree turn as per recommendation of aim (aeronautical information manual) at which point aircraft y announced they were on the downwind and that we had turned in front of them. aircraft y passed several hundred feet below our aircraft already on the downwind beyond the departure end of runway 14 and parallel to the departure corridor. other aircraft stated 'you said you were departing northwest' to which i responded, 'that's on course, i am turning to a left downwind departure.' our aircraft was over 500 feet above pattern altitude when turned to downwind departure.aircraft y had made a long parallel downwind entry close in to the runway, and in my opinion, impeding standard pattern departure. if the aircraft y had made the recommended 45 degree entry to the left downwind there would have been no issue and i would have known where to expect them and made positive visual contact.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: Aeronca 7AC pilot reported a loss of aircraft control on landing; resulting in a ground loop and runway excursion. Pilot taxied aircraft to the hangar.
text: i was on a pleasure flight taking a pilot rated passenger who had never flown in a tailwheel aircraft. i was pf from the rear seat. it was a nice visual flight rules day, with winds reported by tower as 310/9 knots. we entered a right downwind for runway xx and i took control of the aircraft to make the landing. i flew a normal approach, compensating for the right crosswind, and touched down in a three-point attitude. during the rollout, i lost directional control and the aircraft ground looped to the right, exiting the right side of the runway. we stopped in the grass just off the edge of the runway. i estimate the speed at which point directional control was lost was less than thirty mph. tower asked if there were any injuries or damage, we replied negative and that we could re-enter the runway and taxi to the next intersection and exit. we did so, were handed off to ground control and then continued back to the hangar. after shutdown i did a visual inspection of the aircraft and noted no damage.contributing factors as i see them were a right quartering tailwind which was different than reported by the tower. as we taxied by the windsock i noticed the direction appeared to be northerly or northeasterly than the tower had reported. another factor was that i have limited time flying from the rear seat. the majority of my 7ac time has been from the front, this was only my second landing from the rear seat in several years.in retrospect, i should have requested runway xy or xz to mitigate the crosswind and tailwind components. i do not feel a go around would have been appropriate, as the speed at the initiation of the ground loop was very low.

text: boeing stearman landing rwyxxr, wind: 270/5, cavu. upon attempting three point landing, aircraft started to veer left, corrective flight controls were applied to stop the left wing from striking ground while simultaneously applying power to go around. left wing struck the runway. aircraft remained upright. upon attempting go-around right wing struck the runway. idle power was selected. aircraft did 180 degree turn on the runway in an upright position and came to a stop. damage to outer left and right wings. after ensuring no other damage aircraft was taxied to the ramp and secured. there was no injuries to the pilot or passenger. a more timely go around decision and not overcorrecting flight controls in the opposite direction might have helped. stearman is very susceptible to crosswinds. ensure pilot is aware of the winds and plan accordingly. since this aircraft can be difficult in cross winds staying as proficient, beyond what's legally required, will definitely help pilot in these situations.

synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying above the LAANC authorized altitude during a flight; causing an airborne conflict with a crewed aircraft. The UAS pilot landed the UAS upon realizing they had flown above the approved altitude.
text: on day 0, at approximately xa:45, i (the remote pilot) was operating a dji mini 5 pro small unmanned aircraft system (suas) from my residence. although i hold an active faa part 107 remote pilot certificate and have approximately 150 hours of small uas flight time, this flight was conducted recreationally as detailed in the laanc authorizations. the drone was equipped with the required anti-collision and navigation (nav) strobes: one top-mounted firehouse technology arc pro (flashing white on top) and four additional arc pros (flashing red on the port side and flashing green on the starboard side). these strobes and mounts increased the takeoff weight (tow) of the drone to 352 grams. i maintained visual line of sight (vlos) with the suas throughout the entire flight. my home is located just outside the controlled airspace of both redacted and redacted.i was flying under two active laanc authorizations (redacted) (redacted). both authorizations were valid from xa:00 to xm:00 and authorized a maximum altitude of 300 feet agl.purpose of the flight: i intended to take photographs of aircraft y that was on approach to runway xxl at redacted. the approach path passes almost directly over my house. i had not set the drone's maximum altitude limit to 300 feet agl before takeoff because i originally planned only a very short flight to capture the photos, land, and possibly fly again later (the laancs remained valid until xm:00. i climbed to approximately 385 feet agl. aircraft y was approximately 0.25 miles west of my location at 2175 feet agl when i was taking the photos. after taking several photos, i continued southeast to perform a loop. during this maneuver, i crossed into redacted airspace while still at 385 feet agl (where the authorized maximum was only 300 feet agl). i immediately turned north after crossing the highway and entered a grid with a 400-foot agl maximum, but i remained at 385 feet agl (still above my laanc clearance of 300 feet). continuing north, i then turned west at road x (crossing into class g airspace) and proceeded to the intersection of road x and road y. while circling south near road y, i realized i had been operating above the altitude authorized by my laanc. i immediately returned to my residence, landed safely, and began preparing this report. i am submitting this report voluntarily to promote aviation safety. i will provide my complete flight log and any additional information or data requested.

on the instrument landing system z rwy xx because of wind shear. aircraft x was a chinese speaker and definitely didn't understand english perfectly nor did he understand approach procedures correctly. more on that in a minute. after going missed, we vectored aircraft x and another aircraft toward rwy xy at redacted. aircraft x was then giving instructions to fly to redacted direct redacted direct redacted for the rnav x rwy xy. procedurally, if you do the approach over redacted, then there is no procedure turn authorized. well, aircraft x did the procedure turn! and as we had another aircraft right behind him, the complexity shot through the roof. i tried to handhold my trainee because i think i have a solid amount of experience and could help him through the situation. i think i did a pretty good job. so i was speaking to my trainee during most of his transmissions. i told my trainee to cancel the back aircrafts approach clearance, maintain 130 thousand, and make him do a left 360 for spacing. as soon as my trainee gives that clearance, tower calls us to switch the runway again! which in turn, brings more complexity to the situation. my trainee cancels the approach clearance of aircraft x. once that happens, the back aircraft requests something that we dont quite hear, and thats when i step in. i tell the back aircraft that tower just switched runways on us, and to fly back to runway xx, and climb him to 140 thousand knowing that my next move would be to climb aircraft x. then aircraft x asks if he should be on a heading. he was currently climbing through like 123 thousand, and flying through a 120 thousand mia box, but was going to momentarily be in a 129 thousand mia box. my trainee told aircraft x to fly heading 070 which i knew wouldnt be good in a moment. so i keyed up and told aircraft x reaching 130 thousand to fly heading 270 which would get him away from the other aircraft and be good with terrain. aircraft x never turned to the heading my trainee gave, and technically did go into the 129 mia box at 128 thousand briefly before reaching 130 thousand and turning northwest bound. the aircraft never turned below terrain and i felt that we handled the situation very well and the trainee and i both learned some things.recommendationmy trainee thought he was doing the correct thing by terminating the approach clearance for aircraft x, when in retrospect, we should have told him to fly the published missed approach and climb to an appropriate altitude to stay separated from our other aircraft and terrain. i think once we did cancel the clearance for aircraft x we had our hands tied and i think the next course of action we took was the correct one, except we should have issued a low altitude alert as well!my only other recommendation would be for aircraft x and that would be to correctly learn that procedure turns have to be authorized from a controlled if they are charted non-authorized in the pubs. we never had a chance to talk to aircraft x again about that as we needed to finish cleaning everything else up from all the missed approaches and runway changes.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A320 Captain reported discovering engine issues during preflight; resulting in the Captain refusing the aircraft.
text: on preflight, it was discovered that the spinner faring on engine 1 had cracks/fractures around one of the bolt fastening locations. the first officer and myself were not comfortable, continuing with a compromised faring that is under extreme stress at the front of the engine that could lead to possible failure and ingestion.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a momentary loss of control when they encountered wake turbulence while being vectored for final approach to LGA.
text: as we were turning from base to final at 3000ft msl for the rnav y 22 the aircraft encountered wake turbulence from the preceding aircraft on final. we were already in a roll to the right as we were intercepting the final approach course. upon entering the wake turbulence the aircraft rolled further right and the autopilot disconnected. i immediately took manual control however it was not before the aircraft reached the 'bank angle' aural warning.the flight path was recovered and command b was re selected. the rest of the approach was uneventful and concluded in a normal landing on runway 22.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: B737 Captain reported a momentary loss of control after encountering wake turbulence on descent into ORD in trail of a B777.
text: descent into ord via benky6, just past monkz given lower altitude by approach control. level at 6000, we were told to slow to speed 210, fly heading 360. just as we began to slow, we encountered wake turbulence. we both called 'upset' i was pm, my first officer was pf. he disconnected auto pilot/auto throttle and we recovered with approximate 30 degree roll in both directions. we gained about 100 ft in altitude, and continued on downwind heading. once stabilized, we turned to heading 360. we called air traffic control with a wake turbulence encounter, and air traffic control responded with 'there is no aircraft near you' which was incorrect because we could see the heavy jet turning base in front of us. in fact we even used vvm (verbalize, verify, monitor)/crm/tem (threat and error management) skills to say careful for potential wake behind the large aircraft. no mention of potential wake turbulence by air traffic control however. after encounter, upset, and recovery we told air traffic control of our wake turbulence encounter. air traffic control asked how much roll we had, and if there were any injuries. below 10000 ft/sterile it's kinda hard to get an instant injury report. we said no injuries, roll of 30degrees left/right. we continued approach landing 28c. by now heavy jet was 7-8 miles in front of us. approach handed us off to tower at seika, tower advised cleared to land 28c, caution wake turbulence. that was the first time air traffic control mentioned we were following a heavy jet. i acknowledged landing clearance and copy wake turbulence that we already encountered. landing/ taxi/parking all non-event. once parked, i was then able to ask flight attendants if there were any injuries/upset passengers. there were none.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B787 Captain reported experiencing clear air turbulence resulting in a loss of control of the aircraft. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft and landed safely.
text: clear air turbulence encountered on arrival at approximately 16000'. autopilot was engaged. the pilot flying trainee did not manage aircraft energy appropriately for the immediate actions required, undesired aircraft state. airspeed got down to 210 kts and momentarily the stick shaker, then increased to 280 kts. normal clouds on arrival. no moisture showing on radar with an increase in sensitivity of plus one. anticipating bumps, and to mitigation the threat, i had the flight attendants seated early. cabin was secured at the event.initially i reported to air traffic control moderate to severe turbulence, after evaluating the event, it was not severe turbulence. i updated the report to air traffic control. no maintenance write up was required. i checked with the flight attendants, and all passengers were all ok. other aircraft avoided the area and secured their cabins early from our immediate reports to air traffic control, crews told me that in operations afterwards. debriefed upset recovery, flight path management, and automation management. normal approach and landing.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B757 Captain reported landing safely after experiencing loss of the left hydraulic system.
text: departure and climb were routine. i was the captain/pm and the first officer was pf.after leveling off, we received an l hyd resv eicas message. we accomplished the applicable qrh non-normal checklist, which did not resolve the issue. a review of the status page indicated left hydraulic quantity decreasing, suggesting a system leak. based on indications, we anticipated progression to l hyd sys press.the leak appeared slow, and after reviewing the l hyd sys press non-normal checklist, we assessed that continuing to destination was acceptable. we contacted dispatch via satcom, requested maintenance be advised, and asked for concurrence on continuing. dispatch confirmed preference to continue to redacted.we advised dispatch that we would likely request priority handling in the terminal area and anticipated the need for a tow off the runway. requested they notify redacted operations.approximately 30 minutes later (about 90 minutes from redacted), we received l hyd eng pump. we accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the engine-driven pump within approximately 90 seconds of the eicas message.approximately 5 minutes later, we received l hyd sys press. we accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the electric pump within approximately 60 seconds. dispatch was updated and confirmed all parties had been notified.we requested priority handling with redacted center upon check-in and were vectored toward redacted. we requested direct redacted (final fix on the redacted arrival) to support our configuration planning.the first officer and i developed a configuration plan, including flaps 1 at redacted. subsequently, air traffic control issued a star change to redacted arrival, and we requested direct redacted, which supported our plan.we were initially advised to expect the instrument landing system xxl and completed the approach setup and briefing. approximately 20 nm from the airport, air traffic control reassigned us to instrument landing system xxr. i initially declined due to workload, but advised air traffic control we could accept xxr if doing otherwise would disrupt the redacted operation. after being cleared for the instrument landing system xxr, we were unable to obtain a valid localizer ident or glideslope. upon query, air traffic control advised the instrument landing system was out of service and offered the rnav approach. due to proximity to the airport and workload, we declined the rnav and advised we would need to execute a missed approach with the gear remaining down the rest of the flight. air traffic control issued a heading and climb to 3000 ft. redacted approach then offered the instrument landing system xxl, which we accepted. the remainder of the approach was uneventful.the first officer performed the landing. i assumed control at approximately 100 knots for rollout. rollout was uneventful. a company tug met the aircraft and towed us clear of the runway to parking.the crm training we received was extremely helpful to us in navigating the challenges we faced as a crew. we were task loaded with a complicated non-normal checklist. we had multiple changes by air traffic control on the arrival. specifically, reviewing the checklist before executing it, developing a what if plan such as considering an unanticipated missed approach with the landing gear down and the flaps in the alternate configuration, and using our resources such as air traffic control and dispatch to obtain support in the terminal area. the company procedures also prepared us well for this challenge. a recent intensified focus on fuel planning led to an enhanced awareness of our fuel status, which became critical on the missed approach. we both experienced this situation in the simulator many times so we felt very well prepared for this event and felt we, as a crew, maintained good situational awareness.for an aircraft operating under distress with a complex non-normal checklist, the number of late changes (arrival and runway assignment) significantly increased our workload. minimizing changes in the terminal area would improve safety and reduce crew task saturation.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: EMB-505 Captain reported a obstacle warning during approach.
text: on right down down wind at 3000ft assigned by air traffic control we were cleared for the visual approach runway xx. we defended to 2200ft to reach redacted faf at that altitude. we visually stayed cleared off the antennas south of us and upon decent we received altitude warning by both the aircraft and air traffic control due to the antennas.suggestions: suggest that if air traffic control clears you for the visual they will need to also issue a warning about the antennas and suggested altitude to maintain or don't clear for a visual without alerting the crew.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: Citation Excel Captain reported that an inflight upset occurred when they encountered wake turbulence on descent into PHX in trail of a commercial jet.
text: aircraft x was on the hydrr 1 arrival. we were cleared to descend via the hydrr 1 arrival. when we started the descent out of 37000 the pilot in command put the seat belt sign on. air traffic control gave us a speed restriction. my right hand was on the yoke. we were behind an airliner on the same arrival. we were at 25000 at scole and the airplane abruptly banked about 30 degrees to the left. the autopilot kicked off and i lost a couple of hundred feet. i leveled the wings first. there was a jolt when the airplane banked. i tried to gently climb back to altitude so i did not over stress the wings. we told approach that we had a wake turbulence encounter. we were assigned 210 knots before scole. after we were back at altitude we continued the arrival. we had a second wake turbulence encounter later in the arrival after transitioning to the local altimiter setting. now i'm trying to remember the exact altitude of the second wake turbulence encounter i think it was around 15000. it was not as severe as the first one. after the second wake encounter we were told to slow to 180. the pilot in command looked at his mfd (multi-function flight display) and saw that there was no wind. one passenger was not seated during the first encounter.suggestions: i will review the unusual attitude recoveries. i should have requested a slower speed. we should have checked on the passengers but we were both concerned with flying the plane.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: C402 flight crew reported loss of engine power on approach; and the engine failed completely on rollout.
text: on flight from redacted to redacted, i was the pf and the captain was the pm. departure, climb, and cruise were normal. we were cleared to descend from 4, 000ft to 3, 000ft. while descending into redacted at approximately 3, 500 feet, we were cleared for the visual approach to runway xx. during the approach, the left engine fuel flow indication displayed 0 pph. the left mixture was moved full forward. the pm referenced the qrh and no checklist item was identified specifically for a 0 fuel flow indication. the pm notified operations of the indication issue and potential write-up, and requested runway xy. air traffic control cleared us for landing on runway xy.at approximately 3, 000 feet, left engine roughness was noted. the pm selected the auxiliary fuel pumps to low. following an rpm drop, the pm selected the auxiliary fuel pumps to high. engine roughness continued. ran memory items. reduced thrust from the left engine was observed and additional right rudder was required to maintain coordinated flight. airspeed was maintained above vyse. the pm accomplished the engine inoperative in-range and approach checklists in the qrh. the crew briefed continuing the approach in the current configuration due to the left engine continuing to produce partial power. at that point the aircraft was turning base to final. the approach and landing on runway xy were otherwise normal. a positive exchange of controls took place and the captain assumed control of the aircraft during the landing rollout.after landing, i briefed the passengers regarding the presence of vehicles approaching the aircraft. the left engine subsequently lost all power after exiting the taxiway. the aircraft was secured without further incident.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported exceeding bank angle while in a turn to avoid turbulence.
text: we had received a last minute re-route now going east due to a pop up ts to the south, however during climb out of redacted we encountered another pop up ts with significant moderate turbulence from 4000 to 14000 ft. we used radar and air traffic control assistance trying to avoid but ended up with a rough ride regardless. i was pf and continued hand flying through about 15000 due to thinking the ap (autopilot) would shut off with the turbulence anyways, if engaged. in an attempt to get out of what we were in, air traffic control informed us out best bet was to turn to the right and gave a heading. in this right turn and effort to avoid the cell in front of us, i got a bank angle audio warning, immediately shallowed it to 30 degrees and continued, engaging ap shortly thereafter.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: CRJ700 flight crew reported a NMAC with another aircraft while on approach.
text: we were being vectored for the visual xxc. our clearance was intercept the final approach course and descend to 3000 from 3500 feet. we started the descent and then realized an aircraft was in front and below flying towards us. we got an resolution advisory and i clicked off the autopilot and leveled off. i got visual on the aircraft passing below and to our right side. i would estimate that we came within 500 feet of each other. we continued after letting air traffic control know that we got an resolution advisory, and landed without further incident.cause: aircraft separation.suggestions: more separation while being vectored by air traffic control.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: SR20 Flight Instructor and their student reported that the engine began to malfunction during takeoff at 600 feet AGL; resulting in a return to the departure airport.
text: 600 agl engine roughness during climb, run engine failure in flight check-list, cylinder 1 issue, pilot in command took controller requested priority landing, contacted air traffic control about the issue, power off 180 back to redacted, no error message on pfd (primary flight display).suggestions: strong vibrations during taxi back, cylinder 1 low temperature.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: PA-28 pilot reported a conflict with a stationary glider during takeoff from a non-towered airport requiring evasive action.
text: a glider was parked on south end of runway near the east edge. it was not visible from the north end due to its low profile and slight hump in runway. i made several radio calls on ctaf for taxi, holding short while performing run up, holding short again, entering runway to line up and wait, and departing. i heard the cessna behind me on the taxiway, number two for takeoff, making normal radio calls. nothing was heard from the glider or a tow plane. shortly after liftoff, i saw the parked glider and immediately side-stepped to the right. i continued my climb and departed the area to the east. i would suggest that one person in the glider ground team have a handheld radio, monitor ctaf, and respond keeping others apprised of glider intentions.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe
synopsis: Lancair Columbia 400 pilot reported engine malfunction during climbout resulting in a return to the departure airport.
text: first flight since annual and also my first flight in months. pre-flight checks were perfect so i proceeded onto runway xx. i took the runway and powered up half way well holding brakes to make sure engine data was good before releasing brakes and going full power. plane had lots of power and took off as expected with all engine data as expected. i turned cross wind at pattern altitude 2400 feet, raised the flaps and started reducing manifold pressure to 25'. i then started to reduce rpms as i started the downwind turn as i had climbed to 2600 feet. at this point the engine went to idle and fuel pump alarm came on. i turned on vapor suppression pump and switched tanks from left to right. this made no difference so i turned off vapor suppression and pressed the primer button. this brought the power back temporarily, at this point i announced aircraft in distress and intent to land runway xy and asked traffic starting on runway xx if they could clear runway xx. they were able abort takeoff and vacate . during call i had pressed fuel primer again this added power again and put me a little higher than expected and over xy. i did a s type descent deploying speed brakes and landing flaps to runway xy and engine died on rollout. i believe this because i forgot to turn on fuel vapor suppression on rollout.my first move should have been to turn back for runway xy and 2nd move to turn on backup fuel pump instead of vapor suppression and switching tanks. i need to review my emergency flight procedures well sitting in airplane so i can 'dry' practice as part of keeping current. i believe i did well. i had delayed this flight many days due to not feeling up to par, busy traffic pattern and sub optimal weather.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: C180 pilot reported an unstabilized approach resulting in a ground loop event and runway excursion.
text: landing runway xxl at redacted, ground looped to the right at low speed and exited the runway to the south with 180 degree change in direction. no damage to the airplane or grass. sky clear, 10+ sm visibility, light (~4 kts) direct crosswind from the south. touched down mis-aligned with the runway heading and failed to recover with proper control inputs following an unstabilized approach. initially air traffic control instructed to make a left base to enter a 3 mile final for xxl, and there was parallel landing traffic to xxr. before aligning on final was instructed to head for the numbers and cleared to land. this should have been easy, but i allowed the airspeed and sink rate to vary as i went to full flaps early as i was high for the shortened distance to the runway and now focused on turning final close to the threshold. was on speed over the threshold but not completely aligned. my mistake was not simply adding a little power and taking the little distance it would require to align with the centerline and touch down a little further down the runway.air traffic control local controller was excellent as usual, inquired if there was any damage, then cleared me to re-enter xxl, exit at taxiway 1 and contact ground.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: SR22 student pilot reported loss of directional control and runway excursion on takeoff related to a nose wheel steering malfunction.
text: i was practicing soft field takeoffs with variable wind. as i was giving back pressure to the stick to get into ground effect, i came back down to the ground and it felt like my front wheel was locked to the left, i tried to straighten the plane but was unable so i veered off the runway into the grass and slowed down. i nicked a taxi sign and came to a stop. no injuries and no further action required.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Learjet 60 flight crew reported PFD and FMS failure along with fumes resulted in an expeditious divert back to departure airport.
text: pilot flying - person a (pilot in command)pilot monitoring - person b (nfp/first officer)event:on day 0 lr 60 at approximately at or about xa:00 person a (pf) and nfp (person b, pm) executed an emergency descent from approximately fl270 for the smell of electrical fumes during climb on the zzzzzx sid direct to redacted intersection.while climbing in heading mode and deviating for weather, we were given direct redacted on the zzzzzx sid. pf and pm noticed flight management system1 was not working properly. pf/pic exchanged flight controls to first officer to continue climb direct to redacted intersection since his flight management system 2 was working properly and while pilot in command troubleshot flight management system1 and took the radio communications with air traffic control. we were then cleared to climb to fl310, when f.o's pfd (primary flight display) failed and immediately followed by the smell of electrical fumes. pilot in command requested flight controls from first officer, pilot in command took over the flight controls and requested priority handling for smoke or fumes in the cockpit and performed an emergency descent to assigned air traffic control altitude of 11, 000 and requested first officer to run the smoke and fumes emergency check list. no smoke was observed at any point in flight or in the cockpit. passengers were informed there was a maintenance issue by the pm and told to remain seated with their seatbelts on.pf and pm donned oxygen masks and began the appropriate checklist and emergency descent. pf then requested vectors back to redacted. the 'smoke and fumes in the cockpit' checklist was completed up to the first decision point where pf and pm then determined the fumes had dissipated. air traffic control provided vectors and altitudes for the emergency descent and return to redacted. pf continued flying the airplane, while pm set up the cockpit for the instrument landing system xxl. the descent, approach, and before landing checklists were completed. pf then executed a safe landing on runway xxl and taxied via 1, 2, 3, 4 to the ramp. pilot in command decided additional emergency assistance was unnecessary. the airplane was then parked by the pilot in command at the ramp, pm de- powered the aircraft and then pf opened the door for our 7 passengers. one female passenger received brief medical attention from emergency personnel and left the airport under her own power. after taking a moment to evaluate our performance both pilot in command & first officer in this situation, we felt we handled it well. however, we could have been more thorough with the appropriate emergency checklists. this was a highly stressful situation, and we were mainly focused on getting the aircraft on the ground as quickly and safely as possible.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Light aircraft pilot reported a non-communicating aircraft entered the opposite end of the runway while landing; resulting in a critical ground conflict.
text: at just past xa:00 on day 0 i was returning from redacted to lom and requested rnav 6 from phl approach control (123.8) for practicing my instrument flight rules flow (the field was visual). a request that was accepted by phl approach. i was directed to the lasbe (iaf-rnav 6) and cleared for the approach. on turning to the final approach course, i told phl approach that i had visual of the field. they advised me that there was no traffic observed. at this time, i canceled my instrument flight rules. i switched to ctaf and made a 9-mile final call on the ctaf, followed by a 5-mile final call, followed by a short final call. i did a quick scan of the runway on short final, and everything looked good to land.as i touched down, i see a plane on 24 at the opposite end of the runway, and that is the first time i heard him. his call was to warn me of his presence on the runway. he had just rolled on to 24 and was fortunately stationary at that end. there was no danger of any collision since i stopped within 1500 feet or so of touchdown and taxied off the runway. once the runway was clear, the other plane departed as soon as i was off the runway. when i walked into the fbo (there is a speaker tuned to ctaf), the people there told me that they heard my 3rd call - the short final call, but not the first two (or did not pay attention). they said they never heard the other plane till he piped up to warn me of his presence when i had already touched down and i was on my landing roll. what did i learn? when i am on a short final, i am generally focused on the touch down point, typically the numbers at lom, and once i pass the threshold and begin my level out and flare is when i raise my eyes to the end of the runway. i think that is what i did on this landing as well and by the time the presence of the plane at the other end registered with me, i was on the ground and slowing down. it was too late to go around. i should not assume that the runway is mine even if i have been making calls, scanning and hearing nothing on the radio. i should always be more watchful and continue scanning the entire runway environment, including at this late stage in my landings.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported conducting a UAS flight under a Certificate of Authorization that only applied to another pilot. The pilot landed the UAS upon realizing this error.
text: on day 0, i accompanied another drone pilot to conduct operations at a project site for company a. the other pilot has been operating at this location for approximately two years and had previously coordinated flight activities for the site.at the time of the operation, i was under the understanding that the required authorization/ certificate of authorization (coa) obtained for the project site applied to multiple pilots operating under the same organization. during the flight, i later realized that individual pilot authorization requirements may apply separately to each remote pilot conducting operations at the site.i operated the drone for approximately 20 minutes between xa:00 and xa:20. once i recognized that my understanding of the authorization requirements may have been incorrect, i immediately terminated the flight operation and informed my manager of the situation. following internal discussion, we decided to voluntarily submit this self-report in the interest of transparency and continued operational safety.no incidents, injuries, property damage, loss of control, or unsafe interactions with other aircraft occurred during the operation.to help prevent similar situations in the future, our team is implementing additional internal drone operation procedures and training measures. this includes the development of a structured drone training program for new pilots, with emphasis on:faa authorization and airspace requirementspilot-specific operational approvals and responsibilitiespre-flight compliance verification proceduresflight safety protocols and operational best practicesour intent is to strengthen awareness, standardize compliance procedures, and reinforce a proactive safety culture for all future drone operations.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 Captain reported flap malfunction during approach. Flight crew continued to landing after holding.
text: aircraft x had been cleared direct to redacted intersection (a transition fix to instrument landing system xx redacted). we were descending to cross redacted at or above 5000'. descending through 8500 and slowing to clean maneuvering i called for flaps 1. the flap needles on the flap indicator did not move. we continued the descent to 8000' and i selected alt hold. the first officer and i both confirmed a flap malfunction. i gave the aircraft to the first officer and i requested priority handling with redacted approach and asked to maintain 8000'. this was approved and approach clearance was cancelled and was issued a radar vector. i then stated fuel in minutes and pounds and souls on board. as we were vectored in the terminal area we agreed the we had a trailing edge flap disagreement issue. i ran the checklist, tested the flight attendants, made a pa and coordinated with approach control to head to the airport. i then took the airplane back to perform the landing. we coordinated with tower to stop the aircraft on a taxiway to have airport rescue and firefighting (arff) visually inspect the tires and brakes and any other abnormalities they could see. none were observed and we continued to the gate. we entered the abnormality in the aircraft electronic log book. upon completing the parking checklist we discussed all the details with maintenance personnel. next i completed the mandatory calls to chief pilot and dispatch."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported an autopilot disconnect during final approach and radar altimeter malfunction; loss of flight director; stabilizer trim; and ILS guidance on the First Officer's side.
text: on final approach into redacted while the first officer was flying the autopilot disconnected and the resolution advisory flag on the first officer side displayed. he then lost his flight director and instrument landing system guidance. this is also when he noticed that the electric trim stopped working on his control column. the ca then took control and was unable to have any success with the electric trim on his control column. since we were already flaps 5 and on the instrument landing system we decided the best option was to continue the approach and request priority handling as to mitigate the chance of a go-around which would have been harder to control while manually trimming. we continued landing with a normal approach and taxied off the runway to the gate with no further issues. we then remembered that the previous crew had seen an resolution advisory flag on their flight but they did not write it up as it did not come back.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported a near collision at DEN during taxi with an aircraft exiting the runway at high speed.
text: it was a busy day in denver, taxiway lima was full or airplanes and there seemed to be lot of airplanes taxiing in and out everywhere you looked. we were given the following taxi out instructions by ground. from 2e taxi to runway 8 via taxiway mike. as we turned left into mike aircraft y took a high speed exit on m7 after landing runway 35l. they appeared to be going really fast as they exited. i promptly told the captain to stop our airplane and i got ready to brake in case the captain didn't react. he did and once the aircraft y passed us still at a high speed is when we realized that this was almost a collision most certainly with severe consequences. we query air traffic control and they apologized. air traffic control did realize that he was really busy. aircraft y did not seemed to make an effort to slow down, i know they had thr right of way because they were exiting their landing runway, but doesn't matter whose fault it was we would have all been hurt.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported receiving a GPWS terrain warning on a visual approach to CHO.
text: flying the visual approach backed up by the instrument landing system 3. prior to commencing the approach, it was briefed with knowledge of terrain and obstacles, and i had my terrain display present on my mfd. i was pilot in command and pf.air traffic control provided us with a descent down to 3000' at midfield downwind, and then provided us with an initial base leg vector, prior to receiving clearance for the visual approach. being approximately 5 miles from the faf sipme and already on a tighter base leg, i requested 2600' to beset in the altitude selector, which is the minimum altitude at the faf sipme. after being cleared for the visual approach, the plan was to continue the descent down to the minimum altitude at the faf and capture the glideslope.at about 4600' and recognizing that we were slightly high turning into our base leg, i increased the descent rate briefly in order to trend towards the glide slope intercept altitude. after i recognized that we were trending towards it i began to intermittently shallow our descent out, ultimately setting less than -1000 fpm as the final vertical speed setting. at no point did we descend below the minimum segment altitude prior to the faf of 2600'.at approximately 3 miles from the faf sipme, and approximately 2700 - 2800 feet, we received terrain terrain pull up." i initiated the escape maneuver, but almost immediately after initiating it and having a pitch up attitude, the terrain caution concluded. since this message cleared almost instantly with a slight pitch up attitude, and no visual obstacles were in our path, it was determined that we were clear of the terrain threat. being in complete visual flight rules, and back to a desirable aircraft state at an appropriate speed prior to the faf, i determined we were in a safe position to continue and execute the approach. we proceeded inbound to complete the approach, having no exceedances or other events occur.afterwards, we had noted on the jeppesen approach plate that the approximate location just prior to receiving the terrain caution has terrain listed at 1785'. i had briefed terrain and the highest obstacles, but what could have been done better is to emphasize this specific point as it pertains to my descent plan for the approach. being in visual flight rules conditions, we had maintained a visual on the terrain prior to the base leg, and it wasn't until we were above it that it was out of sight.in hindsight as pilot in command and pf, recognizing that we were high and having been turned onto a shorter base leg, this could have been preemptively resolved by communicating with air traffic control, and potentially even requesting vectors to provide more time to descend.as a crew we debriefed this event on the ground, and talked in depth about exactly how this could've been prevented. we concluded that more in depth briefings on the terrain we will encounter at specific points, a more clear and shallowed descent plan, and avoidance ofcomplacency in visual flight rules conditions could've worked to prevent this from occurring."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 402 Captain reported #1 engine roughness on descent into destination. Flight landed safely and the engine failed after landing.
text: at about 3, 500 feet, we were cleared visual approach runway xx.switched to tower at ~3, 000, fuel flow was fluctuating then indicating 0 pph. indicator issue suspected.attempted qrh and no applicable qrh was noted. mixture on #1 was set to rich. operations was notified.contacted tower and requested runway xy, which was approved and cleared to land runway xy.descending out of ~3, 000 feet, aux fuel pumps low, #1 engine roughness noted, memory items ran, aux fuel pump set to high on #1. roughness continued up until landing.partial thrust on #1 verified with pilot flying, continued approach above vyse.engine inoperative in-range, approach, landing qrh ran.briefed abnormal approach with pilot flying and continued approach.priority handling requested, operations notified.normal landing.flight control transfer took place on roll-out, first officer briefed passengers. i taxied off runway xy on to taxiway 1.engine #1 failed on the ground at taxiway 1, 2 intersection. came to complete stop, notified tower and aircraft was secured.coordinated with ground crew and fire rescue.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported a GPWS terrain alert while maneuvering for a visual approach to RNO in mountainous terrain. The flight crew was visual with the terrain; and continued the approach.
text: during the arrival, air traffic control assigned vectors. our flight path took us several miles out on an extended downwind to an extended base. estimating 10 mile base leg. air traffic control cleared us for a visual 17l. we had rnav y in the box, and it was visual flight rules so we continued urate minimum altitude while flying direct urate. before reaching urate there is terrain. we came within 500 ft above the terrain and experienced gpws alerts for terrain, gear, and pull up. we could see and avoid the terrain and could see there wasn't a threat and no reason to execute a ga or escape maneuver. we continued the approach while visually avoiding terrain. we finished with a normal and stabilized final approach and landing.cause: being vectored far away from the field. then being cleared for a visual over 10 miles from the field. not choosing a better approach, in this case, rnav x.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a lack of designation of boundary line; and that taxiway lines were barely visible during taxi at ORD.
text: taxing on sp, and we were told to hold short of the boundary line. listening to traffic ahead, they are switching over near fw/a7. got clearance to go onto se and then told to continue sp and contact ground. contact ground and cleared to a13 with hold short v(this is the 3rd change to our clearance in about 3 minutes). at this point, ground tells us to hold short a7 (we're turning onto alpha). talked to tower and tower advised that we had missed an instruction to hold short of the boundary line. advised tower that we thought the boundary line was the communication boundary line abeam fw/a7(chart 20-9b). tower advised me that no the boundary line referenced is for the non-movement area on sp with implied instructions to hold short of alpha(ground markings not on the chart). asked for clarification on where the boundary line was they advised sp and alpha intersection. contributing factors was construction and taxiway lines barely visible at the intersection with construction on the north side of alpha taxiway. unfamiliar with where the non-movement boundary line starts, and taxiways begin, because we were on a taxiway (sp), we incorrectly assumed the communication boundary line on chart 20-9b was the non-movement boundary line and not a taxiway marking. suggestions: in chart 20-b, reference the boundary of where the non-movement area starts, it is not clear on any of the taxiway charts where the non-movement area ends. ramp control should also use standard phraseology. 'taxi sp hold short of alpha' instead of telling us to hold short of a boundary line that is marked on the taxiway and is faded from construction and aircraft movement.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Pilot reported GPS jamming and a malfunction of the Attitude Heading and Reference System; AHRS; resulting in loss of yaw damper; PFD's; and autopilot during cruise. The AHRS system and GPS were restored and the flight continued to destination.
text: at 31k feet approximately 50 nm north of flagstaff we had the auto pilot disengage as well as the ventral rudder and yaw damp. we had several red and amber cas messages and red x's on both pfd's (primary flight display). i immediately hit the quick disconnect and then person a grabbed the yoke as he was the one flying. when we realized what we had lost i contacted air traffic control (la center) and informed them we had lost autopilot and some other systems and needed to descend to 25k which is what our memory items are for the loss of systems mentioned. he asked if we were declaring an emergency and i advised air traffic control so we could get the priority handling. once we started i reminded person a of the possible dutch roll and then grabbed the qrh, person a said he felt vibrations in the thrust levers which i also felt. by this time most messages had cleared. around 25k i engaged the yaw damper. i then asked for lower at which point they gave us shock at 12k. we determined the system was back online and engaged the autopilot. at this point the system was still only using gps 1 and ahrs 2 was in backup gps and ahrs 1 was not online. we then told albuquerque we seemed to be back online and things seemed ok. we got cleared to yolow at 7k and i called the airport in sight and got cleared the visual. person a then hand flew the airplane the rest of the way in in case we had an autopilot issue again.suggestions: better information on gps jamming locations and do not use on known flight routes.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: DA-42 flight instructors reported dual ECU failure and suspected fuel leak during takeoff resulted in return to departure airport.
text: was conducting a repositions flight for aircraft x from redacted to redacted after dropping off a different diamond in redacted that same day. everything was routine/ normal / in limits until about 300 ft - 400 ft agl in the upwind. noticed an abnormal noise/ slight vibration/ engine roughness coming from the left engine. a few seconds later probably around 500agl received a left hand engine ecu (engine control unit) a and b caution. no change in performance or engine output/ engine indications noted. immediately after this communicated a decision to come back to land as a precaution. first coordinated with pilot monitoring (person a), then communicated to air traffic control that we were turning back to land xxr due to abnormal annunciation. person a then was helping run/ find checklists while i continued flying. they cleared us to land in the upwind. everything was normal until reaching midfield/ approach end of the downwind, when air traffic control advised that they potentially had seen a puff of 'smoke.' we then scanned and noticed in the left engine that we were leaking fluid pretty heavily. initially was thinking it was coolant due to location of leak (fins on the inboard side of the nacelle). other than ecu annunciations engine page looked normal and engine output felt normal. continued to setup for landing and focused on flying the aircraft while there was still available engine power. during the turn from downwind to final, we both realized that it smelled like fuel was potentially leaking. i continued to fly the aircraft and focus on landing when pm suggested we secure the engine just in case to negate a fire hazard. we then ran secure items and engine was feathered by about 300 agl on final. left gear down, but brought flaps back up to app in order to not lose airspeed, maintained approximately 85-90 knots down to the runway and landed safely. attempted to make turn off of runway, however was unable to continue due to asymmetric thrust overpowering steering. stopped on taxiway and requested a tow.suggestions: keep two pilots on reposition flights. it was infinitely helpful having a second set of eyes and hands assist with the problem.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Object; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: DA-40 Flight Instructor reported taking control from the student on approach when the speed and altitude got too low. The aircraft struck runway threshold lights.
text: training event at redacted in a da40ng, had successful touch and goes practicing short fields and normal precision landings to private pilot standards, used the 1, 000, 500 foot markers and runway centerline stripes as touchdown points. targeted advanced training by landing on the number xx for runway xx, student came too low. vso is 60 in the da40ng, a rule of thumb was 65 as no return for the da40 and i should take controls as or before that point. getting too low visually i called for a go-around, with no response i said 'my controls' and attempted to take controls at 70 knots, fighting controls with the student data shows full power was only added once hitting 60 knots. this led to a sink in altitude and struck the runway threshold lights on runway xx at redacted.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Light aircraft instructor pilot reported a critical conflict at SPK with another light aircraft landing opposite direction.
text: while landing on runway 12 at spk there were 5 other aircraft in the pattern for runway 12 and aircraft y made little to no radio calls that they were going to land runway 30. while in our flare on runway 12 someone called out on the radios that there was an aircraft short final for 30 and 12. us being the aircraft landing 12 we touched the ground and then initiated an immediate go around, upon reaching 20 feet agl the aircraft became visible to us and we maneuvered away to avoid them in case they took off again. the rest of the flight was uneventful.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported taking off and flying above the maximum altitude for one LAANC grid while transitioning to another LAANC grid.
text: situation 1:while operating from location x at the intersection of the 50 ft and 100 ft laanc grid, we moved the landing zone (lz) for safety reasons but failed to properly reassess the new location. i didn't account for the offset of the new lz being farther east than we originally calculated, and i failed to make the necessary adjustment in the field after relocating. after moving, we were positioned under the 50 ft grid but did not adjust our operational assumptions accordingly.situation 2:because the change in lz was not fully accounted for, we continued the flight using the 50 ft operating plan without adjusting for the offset. this resulted in operating at 100 ft when the correct authorization for that location was 50 ft.main cause:the primary issue was not fully re-verifying the updated laanc grid after relocating the lz. the offset shift was not recalculated in the field, leading to the incorrect assumption that we had exited the 50 ft grid when we were still inside it.going forward:anytime the lz is moved during operations, i will stop and fully reassess the new position before continuing flight. this includes confirming the exact grid location (especially 50 ft vs 100 ft boundaries), verifying any offsets in the field, and verbally calling out the corrected altitude limit before resuming operations.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported inadvertently flying without having met Remote Pilot recurrent training requirements.
text: during a review of my uas records, i discovered that i had inadvertently conducted commercial small uas operations while my recurrent training was overdue by approximately two months. at the time of the operations, i believed my remote pilot recurrent training status was current and that i had a reminder system in place to alert me before expiration. after reviewing my records, i realized the reminder had either failed or was not properly configured, which caused the lapse to go unnoticed.the flights conducted during this period were completed normally and safely, with no injury, property damage, airspace conflict, loss of control, or known hazard created. once i discovered the issue, i immediately stopped conducting commercial uas operations until the recurrent training requirement was corrected. i then completed the required recurrent course and updated my records.the primary contributing factor was overreliance on a single reminder system instead of actively verifying pilot currency before each commercial uas operation. as a corrective action, a new uas credential and training verification sop was introduced. this sop requires confirmation of remote pilot currency before accepting or conducting any commercial uas mission, periodic review of pilot credentials, redundant calendar reminders for recurrent training deadlines, and documentation of credential status in the mission file.additionally, as an extra safety and compliance measure, we will complete the faa alc-515 recurrent training course annually, even if the regulatory recurrent training interval allows a longer period. this annual review will help ensure continued familiarity with current part 107 requirements, operating limitations, airspace procedures, and uas safety responsibilities.this issue was unintentional and was corrected immediately upon discovery. the lesson learned is that currency requirements must be verified through a formal process, rather than relying only on memory or a single automated reminder.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)

synopsis: Air traffic controller reported working a light aircraft that descended below their assigned altitude due to encountering mountain wave resulting in flight towards terrain before climbing.
text: when i was getting the briefing the controller working noticed aircraft x descend below the terrain and attempted to issue a low altitude alert but the radio communications were poor in the area. a relay was used through aircraft y and the [aircraft x] pilot stated he was having a hard time holding altitude due to mountain wave. while i was working aircraft x again descended below the terrain and i issued a low altitude alert, the pilot again informed me he was having a hard time maintaining altitude. i did ask if he was vmc and he acknowledged he was. as he proceeded west he was able to climb and stay above the terrain, the terrain also dropped as he moved west towards redacted.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: SNA Tower controllers reported that a general aviation aircraft overshot the centerline of the parallel runway; creating a conflict with an air carrier aircraft who took evasive action to avoid a possible collision.
text: i was working aircraft x on final. i had previously handed off aircraft y who was inbound from the west for pattern work to the local control (lc2) controller. i had cleared him to land and told him about traffic on the downwind for the parallel runway. i told aircraft x that traffic had him in sight and would maintain visual separation when aircraft x was about 4 mile final and there was about 2 miles between him and aircraft y. i had heard the controller working aircraft y tell aircraft y to maintain visual separation and caution wake turbulence which is how i knew that aircraft y reported aircraft x in sight.i noticed that aircraft y was flying a shallower downwind than was usual and was doing about 120 kt. on the downwind which is considerable faster than what similar aircraft do on the downwind. i told the controller who was working aircraft y to 'watch for the slop over' because of the way aircraft y was flying. i then observed aircraft y turn base wide and 'slopped over' or veer into the path of aircraft x. i could not tell who was in front or behind from my perspective, but i then saw aircraft x turn sharply to the right as if he was afraid that aircraft y was going to impact his left side. i then told the controller that aircraft y was too close to aircraft x. the controller then proceeded to instruct aircraft y to start a climb and go around. aircraft x then said that aircraft y was way too close to which i just replied 'roger.' about 30 seconds later aircraft x said he was executing missed approach so i issued the standard missed approach instructions which is heading 195 and climb and maintain 3000.i would strongly recommend to suspend all flight training at sna. the runways at sna are 500 ft. apart which is extremely close. we are depending on low time or student pilots to turn the base in such a manner as to avoid colliding with airlines and jet traffic inbound on runway 20r. the afd instructs pilots to do a 15-degree offset dog leg for base to final turn. that is a lot to ask a pilot who is training or who just got the license. it's a complicated maneuver to begin with but it is a vital necessity due to the proximity of the runways.i see it constantly where the pattern workers on runway 20l will slop over and veer into the final for runway 20r. it happens constantly and no matter how many times we tell pilots not to do it or correct the pilots, it happens on a regular basis. luckily when there has been slop over, either nobody is on final for runway 20r or the inbound traffic is far enough in front or behind the pattern worker to take enough corrective action. it is my own personal belief that someday a small aircraft will slop over and collide with an airliner or business jet inbound on runway 20r. in my mind, if flight training is allowed to continue, it's not a question of 'if' but a question of 'when' a catastrophe will occur. mixing commercial jet traffic and visual flight rules pattern workers who are either learning or have low time at sna is a recipe for disaster that will cost a lot of people their lives. there are a number of neighboring airports where the student pilots can go and do their flight training without putting the lives of airline passengers at risk, i believe that right to live of 200 plus passengers on an airliner supersedes the right of a student pilot to learn to fly at sna.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: A student pilot and their Flight Instructor reported a brake failure while taxiing which resulted in a taxiway excursion.
text: student and cfi landed runway xx at redacted, taxied off the runway and taxied to the end of xx with no noticeable issues. holding short runway xx after running before takeoff checklist. student checked brakes before pulling onto xx. student noticed right brake had no pressure. student told cfi and cfi checked his brakes and noticed he still had brake pressure. cfi took controls and taxied us to the fbo. at the entrance to the fbo cfi lost all hydraulic pressure in right brake, due to slow airspeed rudder control was not enough to steer us right. aircraft turned left entering the grass left side of taxiway. cfi once aircraft had stopped, shut down the aircraft with no structural damage to the aircraft or damage to property at redacted. airport crew successfully towed aircraft out of grass and towed it back to the fbo where it is tied down currently.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Cessna Turbo Stationair 6 Flight Instructor reported during landing roll out at a non towered airport; they took evasive action to avoid an aircraft landing opposite direction.
text: during a company training flight we conducted pattern work at redacted on runway xx. after departing to the east for a simulated engine fire at 7, 500', we returned for a landing on runway xy. i monitored and announced on ctaf, no other traffic was heard or observed via ads-b in the vicinity during the descent or approach.upon touchdown on runway xy, i observed an unidentified aircraft on short final (approximately 5-10' agl) for runway xx, landing in the opposite direction. i immediately took flight controls, decelerated, and taxied clear of the runway to provide the other aircraft space to land or go around. given the length of the runway, the closest proximity between the two aircraft was approximately 4, 000'.i attempted to contact the aircraft on ctaf three times with no response. the aircraft taxied back and departed runway xx without making any radio transmissions. our radio was confirmed functional, as we had been in contact with other traffic 30 minutes prior. the registration number was not obtainable during the fly-over.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: C182 pilots reported a nose tire malfunction during the landing rollout at an non-towered airport. The pilots pushed the aircraft off the runway and serviced the tire with air.
text: upon landing my nose wheel went flat. no damage to persons, property or aircraft. came to full stop on runway due to flat tire. shutdown on runway and pushed aircraft off onto taxiway (to clear the runway). no other traffic nearby during this time, so no interruption to airport operations. local airport personnel provided air tank and i pumped up the tire to the poh specs. no observed leaks or indications of tire failure after pumping up the tire. restarted engine, taxi, takeoff with no further incident. my understanding is this is allowed under part 43 app a but may be misinterpreting and so now i understand i may should have had an a&p look at this before i took back off. i now understand and learned from this after the tire event occurred.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: PA28 pilot reported gusty winds during landing which caused a loss of control and runway excursion.
text: the xa:53 atis reported winds to be 340 at 6 kts. took off at xb:54, tower reported winds at 350/5 gusting to 17.at xb:55 tower reported winds to be 360/6 to 17.at xc:12 the incident occurred.at xc:17 winds were recorded to be 350/12 gusting to 24.after takeoff, i made three left pattern takeoffs and landings to runway xx. during the second and third, the wind gusts were erratic in speed and direction. on rollout of the third landing i was correcting for left crosswind when the gust abruptly shifted to come from the right and i was unable to reverse my correction fast enough. i began to swerve and slide to the left, off the runway. very soon after leaving the runway, the nose gear collapsed and the plane came to rest about 50 feet off the runway edge. i did not suffer any injuries.when i began losing control of the aircraft, i did not want to make any aggressive control inputs to remain on the runway out of fear of having either wing contact the runway, and so decided to stay in a level attitude even if it meant rolling off the runway.during the second and third circuits when the wind and gusts were increasing, it became more difficult to maintain a consistent approach airspeed on final approach, partly due to the quite irregular terrain south of the airport and topographic turbulence. my last glance at the airspeed near the threshold was about 85 mph, but the airspeed needle was bouncing back and forth and not stationary. on the last final approach, after round-out, i sensed that my airspeed was a little too fast as i seemed to be floating longer than usual. perhaps i should have opted to go around at this point. another thing that maybe i should have done is just ended the flight after first or second circuit, however how could i know that the last circuit's gusty conditions we going to worsen so quickly.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: LA-250 pilot reported that the left main gear collapsed during landing.
text: visual flight rules arrival to redacted, flying the profile of gps xx approach (straight it to xx). aircraft type: lake amphibian. normal pre-landing checks completed, gear down, green light, 3 wheels visually and hydraulic pressure up. normal landing was executed in the touchdown zone. on rollout, after cresting a hump in the runway (redacted runway is not flat, there are multiple large undulations), the left main gear collapsed and the left wing float contacted the runway. aircraft veered left and came to rest between the centerline and the left edge of runway, between taxiway 1 and 2. i shut down the engine and master switch, shocked and confused. gear handle appeared down, but hydraulic pressure was indicating zero. i turned the switches back on and pressed the gear handle down (it moved slightly further down) and saw hydraulic pressure coming back up.upon further investigation at the maintenance shop, it was discovered that the landing gear handle detent stop was misaligned and the gear handle was free to move up and was not held down by the mechanical stop as it should be. by design, the landing gear selector valve vents pressure back to the hydraulic reservoir if the handle is between detents. they were able to re-rig the mechanical stop to restore proper function.the benefit of being a lake with the engine on a pylon is that damage was minimal and limited to the wing float and scrapes on the lower fuselage keel where it also contacted the runway.
