synopsis: DA-40 Flight Instructor reported a dual ECU failure during cruise while returning to the airport. The flight landed safely.
text: my student and i had just finished shooting the rnav xx into redacted. we started flying back to redacted and as we began setting up for a dme arc, we saw and heard an ecu (engine control unit) b failure annunciation. as we started running through the checklist, it turned into a dual ecu failure annunciation. after going through the checklist, we had partial power, but we still had sufficient power to maintain altitude. we decided to continue towards redacted, and we called up air traffic control and requested priority handling about 12 miles se of the airport. they cleared us to land straight in on runway xyl shortened. we were grateful to make it back to the airport safely and for all the help from air traffic control and the crew on the ground.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported learning post-flight they conducted two UAS flights in an area where UAS flight is restricted.
text: on day 0, a friend and i were camping and doing photography and drone videography for fun. we had heard of this waterfall at location x and as we utilized the air control app, we saw that we could fly there as long as we did not take off from the road, so we took off from the overlook. two days later, i was sitting looking at the waterfall footage i had gotten and there was a no trespassing sign at the location that many people would often try to climb down from the observational overlook to the bottom of the falls. i started to do more research. though the airspace was class g and the air control app for drone airspace used said it was fine to fly in, i soon realized based on some research that flight is prohibited without a special use permit. there were no signs saying you cannot fly drones there and having used the air control app i thought i was okay as it only showed launching from the road would be an issue. we did not launch from the road. in the future, i will never allow myself to fly in an area without doing more research beyond what i see on the air control app for airspace but rather do more research if it's a popular recreational area that may have more rules and regulations.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: SCT TRACON Controller reported an airborne conflict at UDD airport and recommended the airspace become Class C and for ADS-B In and Out to be a requirement for all aircraft.
text: while working the sector i was asked by flight data (fd) for a release for aircraft x off udd. i asked they advise them of visual flight rules traffic south of the field at approximately 035 msl. the visual flight rules aircraft that wasn't imminent risk at first then continued northwest into the departure corridor so i began issuing traffic alerts before aircraft x even checked in. on the third traffic alert i suggested they stop their climb and they reported the traffic in sight so i climbed them at the pilot's discretion. the visual flight rules target stayed in the area at an altitude that directly conflicted with the approach aircraft y requested. so i advised them about the traffic and said that we needed a different plan / approach. they said they would take a visual approach so i gave vectors and altitudes to pass above the traffic. the traffic then tracked southeast out of the way and i gave aircraft y the visual approach. unfortunately because of the traffic delaying their descent aircraft y had to make a circling descent to land greatly increasing risk to the flying public in my opinion.considering the number of safety events that occur, the volume and complexity this airspace frequently receives, i am begging for a class c airspace to protect the flying public from unacceptable risks at critical phases of flight. the current trsa is completely outdated to adequately protect the flying public. i recommend all aircraft be required to have ads-b in and out for everyone's safety. additionally i recommend below 10000 msl procedures in and out of airports with considerable passenger volume have protected airspace.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: B-777 flight crew reported descending below a published altitude after being cleared for an approach at night in an area of mountainous terrain. ATC instructed a climb and the crew climbed to the charted altitude.
text: we were not given a star and i had to prompt air traffic control the star was a change from our plan. as we were changing it, controller cleared us direct redacted, instrument landing system xx, msa was 7200, alt past redacted 5100. pf requested 5100 for past redacted. i should not have accepted that but i think all 4 of us were confused by what air traffic control wanted. i realized the descent was a bit premature to what i wanted, but i could also see we were well clear of terrain. controller asked us to maintain 7200 and we climbed back up.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported engine vibration and abnormal engine temperature during takeoff resulting in a diversion to a nearby airport.
text: on flight abcd redacted-redacted while taxiing out to xxr both lh + rh tlo (temporary limited operations) illuminated. continued with takeoff after following qrh directive for tlo procedure. while on climb out from redacted we noticed less than normal climb performance and increased vibration. we scanned the engine page to look for any abnormalities and noticed the left tit (turbine inlet temperature) and cht were lower than right by a good amount. first officer turned on autopilot and once we leveled out at 5, 000 feet we tried different power settings to try and smooth out the vibrations. we also looked out at the engines, the right engine seemed to be running normal and the left engine was shaking a good amount. off of this we determined it to be the left engine with the issue. we had about a 45 knot tailwind at so we covered a lot of distance in a short time thus making returning to redacted a much longer diversion. after cruising for a few minutes the vibration got worse so i asked redacted approach for a 030 heading to stay closer to the coast which they then proceeded to ask if we were an emergency aircraft. i advised them negative emergency however left engine was running rough. after coordinating with dispatch about the diversion to redacted i asked approach to divert into redacted. we were given a discretion descent to 2500 and vectored in for a visual approach runway xx. air traffic control asked for souls plus fuel onboard and rolled the trucks as a precautionary measure. i advised them of the fuel and souls while also saying the situation has not improved nor gotten worse. first officer landed runway xx without issue we taxied to the ramp advised the passengers and received positive feedback from the passengers. myself and the first officer made phone calls to dispatch, maintenance control, and the chief pilot. recovery flight was sent up and took the passengers from redacted-redacted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported flap malfunction on final approach and ground agents detected a hydraulic leak after parking.
text: we were on final approach to runway xxl with flaps 2 selected. when we attempted to select flaps 5 the flaps did not move to the selected position. an attempt was made to get the flaps to move by selecting flaps 10 however, the flaps remained at the 2 position. at this pointed we executed a go-around and the flaps retracted normally. a second attempt was made to deploy the flaps and they got stuck between 5 and 10. a review of the trailing edge flap disagree checklist was completed. a 3rd attempt to deploy the flaps prior to executing the checklist and they worked normally. a landing on xxl was made using normal flap settings (30) and braking. we proceeded to the gate and after we parked the ground crew notified us of a significant leak emanating from the left wheel area. i went down to investigate and saw hydraulic fluid leaking from the union between the caliper and brake line onto the tire and brake assembly. i asked the ground crew to step back and went to the flight deck to contact operations to have them request arff (airport rescue and firefighting) assistance on my behalf. i then contacted maintenance control to advise them of the issue and entered the discrepancy into the logbook. i then noticed the sys a quantity decreasing fairly rapidly so i called maintenance control back to see if there was anything i could do to slow or stop the leak. i was advised the releasing the parking brake may help but i needed to ensure the aircraft was properly chocked prior to doing so. i went back under the aircraft to coordinate this with the crew chief and other ground personnel. after this was completed i went back to the flight deck to release the parking brake and observed that contract maintenance had arrived to the aircraft. i did not observe any arff presence during this process.time compression was a factor as we were on final approach when we noticed the flaps were stuck. in retrospect we should have not attempted to move the flaps, immediately executed a go-around, and executed the trailing edge flaps disagree checklist.in regards to our hydraulic leak after we arrived to the gate i should have contacted air traffic control instead of company operations. it is possible this could have generated a faster arff response to the aircraft.

synopsis: B777-300 flight crew reported pressurization failure during initial climb and a return to departure airport.
text: flight departed runway xxr and was turned right and given a climb. we continued being vectored and given progressive climb instructions. passing fl100 we received a red eicas warning and master warning bell cabin altitude. our cabin altitude was the same as flight altitude. we stopped climb and asked for lower altitude which was received. we donned oxygen and descended where the cabin altitude lowered below 10, 000 feet. we ran the appropriate checklists and asked control for vectoring and holding to accomplish them. air traffic control was advised.we decided to return to field for maintenance, and decided an overweight landing was appropriate since the necessity for dumping fuel was not necessary as there was no structural or flight control issue necessitating a lower landing weight. the landing field distance was appropriate for an overweight landing. priority handling was requested and we again accomplished all checklists in the hold for non-normal landing, overweight landing, etc. dispatch, passengers, flight attendants were all advised. landing distance computations were completed. we then commenced the return to field overweight landing.the landing and return to gate were all standard. the airport emergency services inspected the plane turning off the runway and reported no anomalies. we returned to gate.maintenance was advised of pressurization issue and the plane was removed from service.cause: aircraft mechanical.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A321 pilot reported partial electrical failure during approach. Flight continued to landing.
text: during departure i noticed the captains pfd blank out momentarily and come back. this happened once at cruise as well but after investigation i could find nothing abnormal with the aircraft. on base leg descending to 4, 000 msl in vmc conditions with the engines at idle, both the captain's pfd and nd went blank for at least 3 seconds, and we experienced partial electrical failure of a few other things. i specifically remember that the master caution light only had a few letters in the word 'caution' illuminated. i immediately started the apu. i called, 'my aircraft' and the first officer identified the ecam as 'elec gen 1 fault'. after confirming it was not a quick action or ecam exception i elected to continue to fly and have the first officer run the ecam. at this time air traffic control was also clearing us the visual approach xxc at redacted. i continued inbound while the first officer ran the ecam. after running the ecam we did not regain the number one generator, so we left the number one generator with the gen 1 switch off with the apu picking up the load. we requested priority handling and continued the approach through landing. we taxied clear on to taxiway p and had arff (airport rescue and firefighting) look at the left engine. arff reported seeing abnormal scorch/burn marks and possibly grease on the engine pylon and cowl. i then shut down the left engine as a precaution. with only the right engine running and there is no normal procedure for taxiing single engine with just the right engine i elected to call for a tug and get towed back in. of note, after the generator transfer of power the aircraft would not go to vapp in approach mode with the speed managed. i needed to manually select speed to vapp +5.recommend clear guidance on taxing single engine with just the right (number 2) engine operating.

text: passing redacted vor we were cleared for the rnav y approach via straight in from redacted for redacted xxl. after passing redacted our approach clearance was cancelled, we were given an altitude alert and told to climb to 5000 feet. we were given radar vectors for another attempt at the same approach. this approach lead to a successful landing on runway xxl.cause: i had flown this exact same clearance a few days earlier with no issues. i do not understand why today's flight lead to an altitude alert when the prior flight did not. all indications (during both flights) were normal - flight path, no egpws (enhanced ground proximity warning system) indications, airspeeds, etc.suggestions: in the future i will only fly this approach if vectored outside of redacted or fly the published course reversal at redacted. it would be helpful to understand why the two flights lead to two different outcomes.

synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported during takeoff an aircraft taxied onto the opposite end of the runway for departure; requiring evasive action.
text: my student and i taxied to runway 05 because the winds were out of 033. while performing run-up, i heard another aircraft call 'taxi to 23 from ramp'. i immediately said that there was an aircraft holding short of 5. when my student finished run-up, i call traffic again asking was there traffic taxiing to 23. the aircraft responded with twin is taxiing to 23. i advised him that we were holding short of 5 and would be headed out of the area so we wouldn't be in his way. after a brief inquiry from my student about not being able to see him on ads-b, i said he was communicating with us so we should be fine. my student then called taking runway 5 for departure to the nw. as we started moving the other aircraft started to display on our ads-b. as my student went full throttle i saw the traffic was positioned on 23. i called there was traffic rolling 5. knowing he was a twin, i took the controls from my student, got us in a better configuration to get off the ground, and immediately starting going right off the runway path when i got in the air. after a short spat on the radio, we both went our separate ways.

synopsis: General aviation pilot reported picking up ice during cruise and descending below minimum altitude to exit icing conditions.
text: i was at 7000 feet on direct routing to redacted to get north around a line of weather that was extending across my originally filed route. i was imc with light to mod rain with outside temp of 31 degrees. i started to pick up rime ice at a moderate to heavy rate. i asked the controller to turn around and descend. he said i could not descend because of where i was and to continue ahead for another 5 miles was the fastest way to get to an area where the minimum descent alt was 5100'. i descended 500 ft to 6500' and the icing stopped. the controller said because i was below 6900', the minimum for his area he was going to have to give me priority handling. after 5 miles there no icing accumulation and then i descended to 5100' still no icing accumulation. i am disappointed in myself for not fully evaluating the new enroute weather picture of my new routing around the weather. i knew where the icing air met was and filed below it for my original flight. the new route took me further north and into higher terrain that would reduce my exit options. the threat for me was a reroute that was off airway so i didn't put together the new mea's and the effect they would play with the icing levels. i never should have accepted the new route.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported LHW has unlit signs that are improperly located and the pavement markings are faded.
text: on day 0, i taxied to take off from runway 33 lhw in georgia. the hold short line is extremely faded, and is several hundred feet from the beginning of the runway. i overstepped it by about an airplane length. i stopped, called the tower and apologized. the tower cleared me for takeoff and instructed me to turn right to a heading less than one mile after departure end of runway (der). i was distracted by the passing of the line, the non-standard takeoff procedure, but believed all was ok.immediately after takeoff, when i looked at the engine parameters screen, i noticed something was unusual, but it was not immediately clear what that was - all indicators were in the green, but something seemed different than my usual picture. i was already in the air, committed to completing the takeoff, and under the instructions of very short turn clearance. i continued the climb and planned on identifying the issue and dealing with it once stabilized on the climb, after the turn, however, at that point i turned left instead of right. the tower directed my attention to the issue but gracefully said that there was no need to correct.the irregularity turned out to be higher than normal oil temperature indication. once that was clear, i performed a precautionary landing. it was an incorrect indication problem.lessons and conclusion: the initial hold short line crossing was irregular and got me a bit unsettled, and worried about consequences. in conjunction with the irregular indication, i made the second mistake. the conclusion is that i must make sure that i am 100% back to myself before accepting a clearance.another lesson is that the markings (throughout the field) in lhw are truly bad, and in my mind at an unacceptable level. signs are unlit, pavement markings are very faded, and the location of signs is improper. i would like to suggest that placing hold-short line locations on taxi diagrams is a good idea, especially when the hold-short line is so far from the actual runway (i estimate at least 250 ft.). i think that the average pilot will look for a hold-short line much closer to the runway and when the line is so faded will easily miss it. this however clearly does not release me from missing it.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Glider pilot reported the Jeppesen chart has misleading information regarding three grass runways located east of Runway 16/34 at AWO.
text: the jeppesen 10-26 new revision for awo 10-9 chart" (dated day 0 effective day 6) now has potentially hazardous misleading information note depicted and published, reference the runway 16/34 grass runway. however, note that the misleading information note may not necessarily be due to any jeppesen error, and may instead be traced back to either misleading airport published information, or misleading faa published source data? nonetheless, the depiction and related note may contain potentially hazardous and misleading information. the problem: the three runway 16/34 grass runways to the east of main runway 16/34 referenced by jeppesen in the note on the 10-9 diagram are actually 3 separate colinear grass runways that cannot be used as a single runway. it is not a single 3450 ft. x 145 ft. runway. note that there are deep terrain grading depressions now located between each of the three separate runways... due to (the arguably inappropriate) surface re-grading that was conducted years ago at awo. those grading depressions now preclude any aircraft from rolling at high speed from one grass runway to the next. it is only possible for any aircraft to transit those depressions at very slow taxi speed, as with a glider towing behind a golf cart. some powered aircraft, could now even risk a prop strike. note that the original navy design of the awo airfield since wwii (before the arguably inappropriate grading between those grass runways) was a much safer design, and actually originally allowed for aircraft contingency use, to safely roll across the crossing taxiways, in any non-normal situation, such as an overrun or underrun. however now, any grass runway overrun or underrun between those three grass runways would likely cause a serious accident. further, the new (inappropriately) revised geometry of the runway 34 departure threshold taxiways now places pre-departure holding-area aircraft obstructions in the immediate pre-threshold area of the first runway 34 grass glider runway when landing to the north, further shortening that grass runway's usable length. the usable runway 34 grass runway available distances and locations for each of those three separate grass runways should be depicted, and published, separately and individually."

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported a NMAC with a helicopter on final approach at a non-towered airport. The helicopter landed in front of the pilot on the same runway; no damage occurred.
text: there has been a good deal of helicopter training here over the last few years. generally we never have a problem with the helicopters, as they try to account for the normal traffic here and are rarely a problem. mind you, i'm not necessarily blaming the helicopter here, just trying to give some background about our particular airport.i made the usual radio calls at 10 and 5 miles, and i was following a cirrus in about as closely as prudent. there was a helicopter making right traffic above us, and he seemed to be a new guy, but we were all making the appropriate calls. because of the fact that i was hundreds of feet lower, had clearly announced final at a mile and a half out, and the helicopters are usually good about waiting for us to pass, i thought all was well. but he did descend fairly quickly, and landed on our end of the runway instead of the far end at about the same time i did.i thought it might be unwise to go around, since a helicopter could do almost anything. i always land at the start of the runway in a short distance -- since i always make the first turn-off -- so i did that, but did get a nasty comment from a pilot flying overhead. i don't think he was particularly blaming me. but i didn't like how it played out really, and i said at the time that it was probably my fault to mollify him.if you go by who is in front, well yes, he's a helicopter and he turned in front of me. if you go by who is lower, then i was. i think that i should have gotten a direct answer from him instead of just assuming that he was waiting for us both to land, but i was working with the cirrus so closely on the radio that i didn't think he would try to get in between us.the safety lesson? be careful around students? i'm not entirely sure, since i'm still thinking about it. i have always held that the helicopters have just as much of a right to be here as we do, but then again, they've been very considerate too. in this case, i probably figured that i had made radio calls and they would do as usual, and they probably figured that since they had made previous radio calls, it was all good.

synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor with student and passengers reported a loss of climb performance after takeoff; resulting in a descent back to runway and runway excursion.
text: during takeoff on a discovery flight i aborted a takeoff, overrunning the runway and rolling into the grass. we performed 2 takeoffs and landings. for the first take off of the day, the winds favored runway xx. the first takeoff went without incident. then the winds shifted to favor runway xy. the awos was reporting winds variable from 260-330 degrees 8g15kts. with that in mind, we decided to utilize runway xx. we rotated with a little extra speed (65vs60mph) to add an extra margin of safety if there were a sudden loss of lift due to a wind shift. after rotation the airplane climbed to 20-30 ft at which time the airspeed did not increase nor did the vertical speed. with the departure end of the runway fast approaching i elected to abort the takeoff and to descend back to the runway. the aircraft floated down past the 1, 000 ft markers on the departure end of the runway and eventually touched down. i applied max braking and maintained directional control and announced to the student/passengers that we would be rolling into the grass. there was no damage to the airplane, airport property, or injuries to report. at the time of the incident there were no other airplanes in the pattern or eye witnesses.

synopsis: B747-8 flight crew reported loss of aircraft bleed air/ aircraft depressurization during cruise. Flight continued to destination.
text: this was a scheduled cargo flight between redacted and redacted with two operating crew and two company jump-seaters. this event occurred within redacted firwhile operating redacted-redacted as first officer and pf we were established at initial cruise at 31100. we were continuously in and out of cloud tops during this portion. after a few minutes the wing and nacelle anti-ice systems automatically turned on. almost immediately we had a bleed #2 eicas alert with associated inop light in #2 bleed air switch. the pm ran the bleed #2 checklist, after complication we got l, r eicas msgs. while working that checklist we received bleed's 1, 3, 4 eicas alerts as well. this was followed shortly by the return of bleed 2 eicas alert. we noticed cabin altitude climbing and at an altitude of 5700' we elected to put on o2 masks and activated supernumerary o2 switch. the captain ran those checklists and managed to get two bleeds back on but we eventually lost all 4 bleeds a second time. unable to maintain cabin pressure, we advised air traffic control and coordinated a rapid descent to 3000 meters. during rapid descent the highest cabin altitude noted was 12000' and highest rate of cabin climb was 2000 fpm. once below 10000 we removed masks and continued running the litany of eicas generated non-normal checklists (cabin altitude, bleed 1, bleed 2, bleed 3, bleed 4, packs 1+2+3, cabin alt auto, outflow valve r/l, suprnmry oxy on, pack mode 2, pack mode 1, pack mode 3). once below 10000' we struggled to maintain communications with redacted control even using redacted.x, we required multiple relays with other aircraft. also during this low altitude cruise with center ap (auto pilot) engaged and no other crew engagement, power began to increase with a corresponding climb commanded by ap. pf disconnected auto-pilot and auto-throttles and returned aircraft to level flight at 3000 meters. we also noticed lights in mcp (mode control panel) flickering continuously bright to dim. once stabilized the left ap was selected and auto-throttles were re-engaged.after evaluating options and communicating with dispatch we elected to continue the short flight to redacted. once in terminal area we requested short delay vectors to allow for flaps to extend in secondary mode due to lack of bleed air to actuate leading edge in primary mode and landed safely off instrument landing system-z to runway xx. we maintained our air traffic control handling status until landing due to abnormal aircraft condition.this was a fairly challenging situation. time of day, complexity of system failures, communications with foreign controllers, cabin altitude and use of oxygen mask all contributed to high workload. i was surprised how much the o2 mask decreased our ability to effectively communicate and maintain a high level of situational awareness. i recently completed annual training which involved use of oxygen mask which definitely helped in this situation.

text: was given from what i understood to cross 5nm sw of lhs vor at 5, 000 feet. as i descended through 8, 000 i was given a terrain warning then told to remain at 8, 000 feet then told to climb to 9, 000 feet to which i promptly complied with and then i was asked if i had the terrain in sight, which i did and also had the cloud cover past the terrain in sight which was a few hundred feet below the tops of the mountains at the time. after landing, i was informed the controller had originally given me 9, 000 5nm sw of lhs and not 5, 000 which i read back to them as 5, 000 and wasn't corrected or asked to repeat again so i didn't give it much thought after that. i noticed the terrain and slowed the descent rate knowing about it and wanted to descend once i made the turn right to a 170 heading. no conflict with terrain or other aircraft was imminent at the time just a misunderstanding between myself and the controller.proper phraseology could've prevented this by the controller pronouncing niner thousand instead of nine thousand and also requested me to repeat the assigned altitude if he wasn't 100% sure i said niner thousand instead of five thousand.

text: student and instructor were on a practice instrument approach to runway xx at approximately 300-500' agl. student reduced power to set up to land. both student and instructor heard a snap followed by the engine revving up to full power. student pitched the plane for a go-around and began to climb. instructor took the flight controls and began troubleshooting, noticing that the throttle was loose and had no effect on engine power. instructor decided to circle back around and land using the mixture for power control. as we joined the downwind, we requested priority handling and let tower know our intentions. we made an extended downwind and adjusted the mixture as needed to descend on final. once we had the runway made instructor cut the mixture completely and added flaps landing without power. before landing we shut down the plane completely. i believe this was due to a throttle control cable failure. it should also be noted that the plane was due for a 100hr inspection soon after this flight.

synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in military restricted airspace without authorization.
text: before heading to the property, i checked the property and what restrictions there were at the property. weather was clear and wind was mild. i drove out to the property, and started my flight around the home. i went to the furthest distance to the south of the property to get the entire property in the shot, and made it to the 118m flight altitude. at that time, i noted that there were lots of birds in my flight area. i took the last picture at that farthest south position. i made the decision to avoid coming back through the birds circling in my flight area, and circled to the west to avoid them, crossing the road (no cars were present at the time of my crossover). i continued to fly north for less than .2 miles, and circled back over the road to the north (again it was empty). i continued my flight path around the property and safely landed. after landing i adjusted my position and did one more flight around the home at a lower flight altitude. the restricted area started at the west side of the road and led north, with the road being the red line. at the time when making that decision to go west, i was more concerned about avoiding the birds, that in that moment i mistook where the restricted area started. only after uploading images, and mapping property lines with aerial maps did i realize my error. for future flights, i need to recheck the aircontrol app when arriving at the location to visually see the lined areas in person, and set those reminders. when set to close restricted lines i need to visually run through scenarios and a plan of action of areas i can fly to in case i need to avoid issues like this in the future. i should have either turned east, came down in altitude to navigate around the birds, or returned home to wait until the area was clear.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported unintentionally flying out of the boundaries of their LAANC authorization.
text: subject: self-report of brief inadvertent airspace incursioni am writing to self-report a brief inadvertent entry into redacted zero grid airspace during a paid mapping mission around the redacted airport area. i was tasked with capturing cardinal direction photos of a newly constructed building. both google maps and aloft showed outdated imagery prior to construction, making ground reference difficult. my laanc authorization was approved to 200' agl. due to a positioning error of approximately 500 ft east of my intended orbit point (lack of usable landmarks), i briefly entered the restricted grid on two occasions while capturing east-facing images:xa:09 at ~100' agl (~30 seconds)xa:15 at ~200' agl (~30 seconds)i believed i was operating within the approved laanc area at the time. i discovered the incursion only after reviewing the photos post-flight. no other aircraft were observed, and there was no safety incident.i am reporting this proactively to help improve future operations in this area, particularly where new construction rapidly changes the visual environment. i take airspace compliance very seriously and have already adjusted my pre-flight planning procedures accordingly.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A Center controller working five sectors combined due to staffing reported they failed to notice an IFR PA28 filed on a route below the Minimum IFR Altitude.
text: aircraft x filed redacted. redacted to redacted and was level at 090. they were a p28a and not a jet or high-altitude aircraft so they should not have been on jet airways, which don't have an mea through the terrain around redacted. they should have filed a victor airway as they were not technically capable of flying jet airways. i had just taken over the sector from the previous controller. about 5 minutes later the msaw for aircraft x started flashing as they were about to hit an increased area of terrain where the mia (minimum instrument flight rules altitude) went up to 095.neither myself or the previous controller had noticed the aircraft was on a jet airway with no mea/moca and was headed towards higher terrain. i gave a low altitude alert and the aircraft climbed to 100.at the time this event happened i was completely task saturated. i was working 5, yes five, sectors combined over 3 different frequencies all by myself. i had multiple calls from approach, the missile range, fss clearances, redacted [center] calls, and other sectors. at one point an aircraft started broadcasting 'in the blind' because i was so busy answering other aircraft several hundred miles away from his position that he thought air traffic control was gone. i had numerous low altitude aircraft that i was providing approach control services for, 2 instrument flight rules drones that were hovering over the western arrival/departure corridor for redacted, and weather deviations, and high altitude overflights. in order to do all this i was essentially on a mid configuration and super zoomed out so i could see all the airspace under my control. i replayed the falcon. i had 23 data blocks on the scope at the moment the msaw started going off. i should have had a d-side just to help with all the data block separation, not to mention the phone calls.the cic (controller in charge) was planning to split off 2 sectors whenever someone came back from break or the xa:00 am people showed up, but that didn't happen fast enough. the tsd (traffic situation display) was obviously showing that my sectors were ready to get stupid busy. i told the cic i couldn't wait any longer and that they needed to abandon the cic desk and split off sectors x and y. they agreed and did so. it took probably about 5 min afterward for me to fully regain control of the sectors i had left: z, a, and b. safety was compromised without question.the combined configuration of c, z and a was already deemed unsafe for day shift operations and requires manager approval since we have had numerous safety events with that combination. the map number for when those sectors are combined is only 14. yet stupidly if you add even more sectors and complexity and combine up c, z, a, d, and b all together the map number jumps up to 20 and is not an illegal day shift combo. so we are actually incentivized not to split sectors. if we think it is unsafe to have more than 14 aircraft in the combined low sectors in what world does it make sense to allow 20 aircraft if we do all that plus add two additional high altitude sectors into the mix?!!this event 100% happened because myself and the controller before me were trying to do the job of 3 people and couldn't keep up. the manager was super busy dealing with all the other stuff and didn't notice we hadn't split anything off.we had a controller on break when this event happened, they should have been recalled. trying to provide approach control service to aircraft when you are looking at 300 miles of airspace is not safe on anything other than a slow mid shift. working 5 sectors combined on day shifts should not be allowed unless the volume is like 14 or lower like it is when only 3 of the sectors are combined.i should have shut off redacted [center] and redacted approach until i could get the sectors split off and safely take on more airplanes. i prioritized efficiency over safety.cics and flms (front line manager) need training to understand that the tsd (traffic situation display) is a predictor, and that it is not accurate tothe exact minute. sectors are not split in a timely manner because they wait because the tsd says the volume doesn't happen until xb:03am and will say i have someone coming back right at xc:00 am. ignoring the fact that it takes several minutes for a briefing to occur, but also not understanding that the tsd time is an estimate, a prediction, and can be of by 5-10 minutes, is a common problem is my specialty.due to staffing, we rarely have a supervisor in the morning. cics tend to take more risks and prioritize breaks and don't like to page someone back early because it is one of their peers and people complain. a supervisor in the area would have reduced the chance of this event happening..

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: A ZAB Center Controller reported that an aircraft at 36;000 ft. reported a balloon passed 1000 ft. below them.
text: an untethered balloon was launched from rio rancho, nm. zab was told when the balloon was launched and was given a website to track the balloons path and altitude. there was no flight plan filed through the nas and there was no transponder. the zab supervisor was trying their best to update where the balloon was and the altitude. however on the radar controller scope nothing was official. we could not see any target or altitude readout and had no official information on the balloon. aircraft y was at fl360 and westbound to phx at level flight. the aircraft y pilots reported seeing the balloon only 1000ft below them and just off their left wing. this is so unsafe that balloons can launch with no flight plan, no transponder, no way to track a target. i believe this could lead to a collision with an aircraft causing a loss of life. balloon should have a transponder with mode c and have a flight plan filed with the nas. there is no reason that in today's busy airspace we should have balloons flying through flight levels with no way of tracking the balloon. if the balloons have transponders with verified mode c altitude we could vector aircraft away from the balloon.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: B737 Captain reported conflicts with airport vehicles during taxi-out requiring the Captain to stop taxi to avoid a possible collision.
text: after engine start, both engines, first officer called for taxi clearance. we were pointed directly at our gate so had to make 180 turn to the left to get to taxi line. we got clearance for a left turnout, turned on taxi light, visually cleared left and right and started to slowly move forward. a fuel truck cut us off. he was on the vehicle road between us and the gate maybe going too fast but he certainly had time to see that we were moving and kept going. i had to stop the aircraft to avoid a collision. then a baggage cart also passed in front of us, he had to deviate off the road toward the gate to avoid us. i told ramp about the dangerous behavior of the ground vehicle drivers. my first officer and i both agreed it was pretty dangerous and would have resulted in a collision if i had not seen them early and stopped the aircraft.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B777 First Officer reported decreasing hydraulic quantity during cruise. Flight diverted with an uneventful landing.
text: prior to departure from redacted we incurred a couple hour delay to fix a broken hydraulic pump seal on the left engine. after performing a flight crew engine run at the gate the aircraft was signed off by maintenance. this fix required us to do an etops authorization flight prior to entering etops. special type certificate of operations was normal. at cruise we monitored our hydraulic quantity and noticed the left reservoir decreasing in quantity. for two hours we checked the quantity at 30 minute intervals. our quantity dropped from .80/.82 at start down to .61. the rate of decreasing quantity was roughly.03-.06 every hour. both the electric and right hydraulic reservoirs were normal and not decreasing. before entering etops we called maintenance control, dispatch and chief pilot to relayed our hydraulic fluid was decreasing and expressed our concern about authorizing etops. after a thorough discussion with all entities we came to an agreement to divert to redacted. we told air traffic control that we would like to divert to redacted and soon we were turned toward the redacted airport. we requested priority handing. we elected to dump fuel to get below max landing weight. we woke the relief pilots to assist with our recovery. we landed at redacted with an uneventful landing.

synopsis: B767-300 Captain reported a ground conflict during taxi with aircraft exiting the runway. Flight crew reported the event to ATC.
text: was standing on taxiway 1 waiting to cross both runways to head over to the parking area. but while waiting on landing cessna 206 stationair he landed then taxi'd off of the runway right onto 1 then 2 right in front of me. he didn't have enough clearance to get by me without edging over to the yellow line and almost into the grass while i fully had both engines still running. he was so close i couldn't even read the n numbers on the side of the airplane as he was passing. i called the tower to get the n number and discussed the nature of the safety of this. he agree and said they were dealing with and taking care of it. the aircraft has been apparently doing training in the area and may even be based there. the controller i talked to said they were training the controller that should have responded to the cessna but unfortunately didn't in time.suggestions: better communication instructions to the pilot from the controller. pilot needs to use better judgement when taxing and making aeronautical decisions while operating an aircraft.

synopsis: A320 Captain reported multiple ECAM messages during climb. Flight returned to departure airport and landed safely.
text: on flight to redacted, we were departing on redacted departure out of redacted at 7000 feet and climbing, we had a vent skin fault.we proceeded with the non normal procedures. as per checklist we controlled this item.following this item we had a air eng 2 bleed fault. we proceeded to do non normal procedures as per checklist, but did not reset. as we are getting this caution, we got the vent blower fault and extract fault again. i called fight attendant and explained the situation. at that time, we decided to hold on a fix. we called company, maintenance control and they recommended to reset items which did not reset. passengers were calm and explained of the situation. i did call again to the flight attendants and we decided to call a briefing. the reason i did not continue was, because for safety of the flight and pressurization abnormalities.we secure items with non normal procedures and we did a overweight qrh procedure following the divert guide. we landed safely. maintenance control came to the plane and i wrote up items and overweight landing on a/c (aircraft) book. we did not declare an emergency on that situation. passengers were calm and transferred to another aircraft. maintenance control told us that this aircraft was having the same issues, but in different phases of flight.this happened and reported in other previous flights.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: DA40 Diamond Star flight instructors reported dual ECU (Engine Control Unit) failures during take off. Flight returned to the departure airport.
text: there were two instructors in aircraft x. person a was pilot flying, i was monitoring. we had no abnormalities in preflight or in run up and during checklists. all was normal until during climb person a put fuel pumps off at 1, 000' agl... we had immediate red annunciation (i believe oil pressure), fuel pressure, and dual engine control unit (ecu) failures... along with significant engine roughness. person a pulled back power and put fuel pumps on as he turned back for redacted. red annunciation and ecus went away for a little. then person a notified tower we had engine roughness and needed to return to land. tower cleared us to land. person a flew a right downwind with ecu annunciations popping on and off. i was talking through situation with him, flaps position and feedback. person a performed great landing on original departure runway xx, and we didn't stop or do checklists as we taxied back to ramp. a few seconds after crossing nonmovement line the engine cutoff completely with fuel pumps still on. we turned off aircraft completely and walked over to get maintenance.

synopsis: A320 Captain reported a malfunction with air conditioning system inflight. Flight returned to the departure airport and landed uneventfully.
text: we were scheduled to operate from redacted-redacted in an aircraft with an inoperative hot air valve per minimum equipment list. after engine start the air conditioning system appeared to operate normally. we departed from runway xxr and passing 8000' the inflight crew contacted the flight deck with a report that the air is blowing very loud, all passengers are turning off gaspers, the air is surging and there is a loud whistling sound. they indicated it was not normal and something was wrong. at the same time the cockpit became uncomfortably hot and the air was not blowing from any cockpit vents. i briefed my first officer and we decided to level at 10000' enter into holding and troubleshoot the issue, for concerns of pressurization. after transferring control and radios to the first officer, the ca reviewed the system pages of the bleed air, which did not indicate any faults and reviewed the system pages of the pressurization which did not indicate any faults. the ca then contacted dispatch and maintenance control and discussed the malfunction. maintenance control could not find any issues on their end, however we clearly had a malfunction on our end that was not producing any ecam messages. after consulting with dispatch and maintenance control i advised them that we felt taking an aircraft into mountainous terrain, would not be the safest course of action. they both supported my decision to return to redacted. all checklists and procedures were conducted at this time, including diversion and overweight landing checklist. the ca setup a return to redacted and throughly briefed the first officer on our approach. the crew was briefed and passengers were advised. there were no issues with the return. once we completed parking checklist the ca made a logbook entry for the malfunction and overweight landing. the chief pilot and assistant chief pilot then made their way to the cockpit and asked for a detailed explanation of what occurred. a offline commercial pilot was in the cabin and commented as he deplaned that he knew that something was wrong with the system. we debriefed the inflight crew and they all heard the same loud noise, whistling, surging of air, and abnormal air pressure coming from the gaspers. we then debriefed with the chief pilots at the gate in the terminal.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Citation Latitude 680 First Officer reported a loss of aircraft control after noticing parking brake had not been set after repositioning on the ramp.
text: during our time on the ground at redacted, our aircraft was towed to another spot on the ramp. the aircraft was chocked and we continued our preparations for the flight, including tending to the cabin and loading passenger bags. passengers were boarded and we prepared to start engines. the captain gave the ramp crew the signal to pull chocks. once they were removed we began rolling. the captain turned on the aux hydraulic pump and pressed the brakes. we came to a stop after rolling about 20 feet. nothing was hit. we immediately realized the parking brake had not been set after the reposition.suggestions: we should always confirm that the parking brake is set after the aircraft has been moved. we should have also double checked before giving the ramp crew the signal to pull chocks.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported unusual handling and flight characteristics during rotation and later discovered the aircraft was overweight.
text: flight abcd was scheduled for departure at xa:40z from redacted to redacted. departure occurred 44 minutes behind schedule due to cargo loading delays in redacted.during the takeoff roll, the flight crew observed abnormal aircraft acceleration performance. additional thrust was applied in an effort to improve aircraft acceleration. the first officer was the pilot flying during departure.at rotation, crew experienced unusual handling and flight characteristics. the aircraft remained controllable and recovery actions were effective. no eicas messages, cautions, or warnings were generated during the event.after departure, the crew coordinated with dispatch regarding the abnormal takeoff performance. dispatch subsequently advised that the aircraft was approximately 56, 000 kg overweight. this information was later confirmed with redacted operations.the flight continued to redacted without further incident and landed safely.dispatch and flight crew coordinated effectively in flight after identifying abnormal aircraft performance. the faulty load sheet and resulting overweight departure condition created a potentially hazardous situation that required immediate operational assessment and risk management.captain a was dh (dead head). he assisted us through out the flight and sure be full paid for working the flight.cause: preliminary findingsaircraft departed significantly above allowable weight limits. initial indication of the issue was abnormal acceleration during takeoff roll. abnormal handling characteristics were experienced during rotation and initial climb. no onboard system warnings or eicas indications alerted the crew to the overweight condition. the issue appears related to an incorrect or faulty load sheet and/or load planning process.this event presented a significant operational and safety risk. an overweight takeoff condition of this magnitude could have resulted in: reduced takeoff performance, inability to meet required climb gradients, runway excursion or rejected takeoff complications, structural exceedances, loss of aircraft controllability during critical phases of flightimmediate coordination between the flight crew and dispatch was essential in identifying and managing the situation safely.suggestions: recommended follow-up actions1. conduct full investigation into load planning and load sheet generation procedures.2. audit cargo weight verification processes in redacted operations.3. review dispatch release validation procedures for overweight detection safeguards.4. evaluate communication and cross-check procedures between load control, dispatch, and flight crew.5. determine whether additional automated protections or alerts can be implemented to identify extreme weight discrepancies prior to departure.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Inflight Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported GPS jamming while in cruise flight.
text: about 30nm south of rsk we began getting indications that we were experiencing a gps anomaly/jamming event. on the flight management system cdu (control display unit) we had gps l invalid", "gps r invalid". while following company sop we began discussing the checklist and bulletin related to the messages. as the condition persisted we reported to both air traffic control and dispatch. both parties stated that other aircraft were experiencing similar issues. after about 10 minutes both clock indications blanked, terr pos message on the nd (navigation display), and the flight management system light on the irs (inertial reference system) panel illuminated, xndr fail, no wifi. after approximately 20 minutes we regained the l gps. throughout the event we didn't loose any navigation capability, we never regained use of the r gps. we selected an approach at redacted that didn't require 2 operational gps and landed without issue. after landing we made and aml (aircraft maintenance logbook) entry.cause: if gps jamming is anticipated a company message in the flight release would be helpful."

synopsis: B777 pilot reported engine failure during initial climb resulted in return to departure airport.
text: shortly after takeoff we experienced a left engine failure. after initial engine failure checklist items, we attempted to re start the engine as no damage was evident. attempt to re-start failed. we requested priority handling and returned redacted rw xx to land overweight. we stopped on the runway. safety fire rescue vehicles inspected the engine. after allowing the brakes to cool for 15 minutes we taxied to the gate and deplaned pax without incident. i was the relief pilot the captain was the pilot flying and the first officer was the other pilot monitoring.cause: more work on previous component failures.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B777 Captain reported that the First Officer's window shattered during cruise flight which resulted in a diversion to an alternate airport.
text: shortly after a point on the route the first officer's window shattered. we ran the checklist and briefly discussed our options. i choose to return the aircraft to our maintenance base in redacted as the best option considering good options fairly close by if the window condition changed. our flight and divert options continuing along our route are more challenging if the window condition changed.our 777 documents have a very good discussion of window failures and we were confident that this was the outer glass panel and not one of the structural panels.we coordinated with redacted who handed us back to redacted and they quickly gave us a turn back. redacted asked if were declaring an emergency and i replied that we were not. our only other request from redacted was to decend to fl300 and to slow to 280 ias / 440 tas. all controlling agencies were very helpful and several asked if we needed assistance but our situation was mostly routine.cause: i do not see any way to mitigate this type of problem going forward. i do commend our team for having a through document on this type of failure and although the exact details were not immediately in my memory the document was quickly found to support our decision.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC during final approach with what they believed to be a UAS.
text: location: lax (los angeles international airport)runway: 25l (25 left)flight phase: final approachaltitude: approximately 200 feet aglenvironmental conditions: nightduring night operations on short final for runway 25l at approximately 200 feet, the flight crew observed a small object quickly cross the front of the aircraft from left to right. the object operated in close proximity, estimated to be within 15 feet of the aircraft structure.the object exhibited a green light, or a distinct green reflection. while the reflection resembled a consumer-level mylar grocery balloon, its flight path and speed suggested an active propulsion system. both the captain and first officer observed the object and its green illumination. the flight crew assesses that the object was likely an unauthorized consumer-level drone (uas) operating illegally within the terminal airspace.

synopsis: Air carrier pilots reported a NMAC with a possible balloon during climb in Class A airspace resulting in a TCAS RA. The crew followed the TCAS command to avoid the traffic.
text: while passing fl180, air traffic control issued a 15-degree left vector to avoid 'balloon activity'. i complied with the vector before he issued a further 15 degrees to the left. i reported our new heading, and we continued the climb. at around fl200, i noticed a target pop up, indicating it was 300 ft above us, and received a traffic advisory shortly afterward. the relief pilot and i (captain stepped out to use the bathroom before the relief pilot went on break) started looking for the traffic, and i queried air traffic control about the target. air traffic control told us it might be a balloon at the same time we received a descending resolution advisory. i clicked off the automation, complied with the resolution advisory, and informed air traffic control of our maneuver while the relief pilot told the people in the back to take their seats (the seatbelt sign was on). once we were clear of the conflict, air traffic control gave us a heading and a clearance to climb.

synopsis: A321 pilot reported engine malfunctions on initial climb which resulted in a return to the departure airport.
text: upon wheels up we encountered an engine 1 overtemp along with an engine 1 bleed problem. we missed raising the gear and didn't catch it at clean up being we were dealing with the ecam issues. this resulted in us being low at redacted intersection by approximately 300' which was reported to air traffic control prior to reaching. we didn't catch the gear was down until we were at 250 knots with poor climb performance. i raised the gear to clean up where we should have slowed to 220 knots. the other issues with the aircraft had us return to redacted where a logbook entry was entered for the over speed.cause: following sops would have caught it on the after takeoff checklist at cleanup but we were distracted with working the multiple ecams. we should have followed standard procedures but i focused more on getting to climb power due to the engine overtemp.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A321 First Officer reported a generator failure on initial approach.
text: shortly after level off and once during cruise we experienced power transients. clicking and various screens blanking for quick moment (<1second).while on dogleg to final, there was a delayed power interruption (1-2 seconds) as the ca pfr (post flight report) or nav display was blank. with associated gen 1 fail ecam. we then ran through the non-normal methodology as ca did phenomenal job of intercepting loc. we reset the gen iaw (in accordance with) the ecam, faulted again so the ca directed to leave it off.i think we went follow-up in the qrh but do not recall. we discussed if we needed to go around and slowing, and configuring for approach and both thought okay to continue approach since we were so far out still. discussed taxi clear and have ground look at us to ensure no further damage.we discussed if needed to declare emergency and quick thoughts were advise air traffic control more appropriate. i advised upon transfer to frequency <30 later after our decision. i passed nature of situation, souls and lbs of fuel to tower and our intentions to clear the runway and have arf (airport rescue and firefighting) check us over.i inquired if tower preferred us to clear the runway and stop at a certain spot and they replied that it was our discretion.i think we kept both engines running. talked to arff and directed to inspect the left engine/generator area. they replied with 'lots of soot' and possible scorch marks on engine and pylon. we decided to shut down to apu and tow to gate since there was no guidance in the aom about single engine taxiing with the right engine running instead of the lefti#1). we relied on systems knowledge and discussed why - no redundant hydro system for bakes. luckily there was already a tug close so the response was likely 15-20 minutes quicker.tow to the gate was uneventful.there should be explicit guidance in aom or qrh about single engine taxi on left or right engine. this should not be left to interpretation and background knowledge.ca and i listened to another situation on the field and deplaning due to flat tire. we were dumbfounded that there is no better way to evacuate wheelchair bound passengers other than having them carried down by the firefighters. i was thinking of the occupational safety hazard of doing so. maybe a contingency plan of a catering type scissor lift truck to save neck/back injuries of firefighters. i am thinking worst case scenario of 350-400 pound person that cannot walk.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported a large concrete area at DCA has multiple taxi lines without adequate signage.
text: after landing runway 19 we slowed to exit the runway as instructed at f. we exited and switched to gc. they were busy. after a few moments we were instructed taxi to gate via right on j. i started to taxi and making shallow turn onto j but slightly overshot towards k. we immediately rejoined j and taxied to the gate uneventfully.cause: very busy in flight deck with after land duties. very large concrete area with multiple taxi lines. not very good signage. mainly ground paint.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported a Ground Proximity Warning while descending on a Visual Approach.
text: redacted - redacted. vmc weather. i was pm, first officer was pf. we had briefed the visual to xxl in cruise. shortly thereafter, redacted gave us xxr, and cleared us direct to the faf (redacted). the approach was loaded and re-briefed. xxr was our third choice, so i had to resend for landing data putting me heads down a bit longer than i would've liked during the short flight (we took off north and landed north). we then reran our descent check. given the clearance to go direct the faf - which had a bottom altitude of 7000 - and subsequently cleared for the visual, our shared mental model was that we needed to expedite our descent down to 7000 from 10000 to execute a stabilized approach. at about 7400 we briefly received an egpws audible 'too low terrain' and the associated amber switch light. almost simultaneously, air traffic control queried us regarding our altitude. the first officer immediately disconnected the ap and put us into a manual climb back up to 8000, which air traffic control had disclosed was the mva at our present position. air traffic control later said something to the effect of 'i see why you guys did that, ' before handing us off to tower. remainder of the flight was uneventful and we landed in redacted. i thought the first officer did an excellent job of making a very timely decision to disconnect the ap and executing a manual climb.clearance wasn't necessarily confusing but as the ca and pm, i could've done a better job maintaining sa and suggesting a shallower descent rate down to 7000. the short flight and subsequent runway change probably impacted my ability to effectively pm.perhaps an intermediate altitude assignment from approach control in this particular example.

synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported parking brake failed while parking at the gate and the aircraft rolled backwards.
text: i taxied the aircraft in to gate xx and stopped and set the parking brake. a couple of minutes later the plane rolled backward a couple a feet. i immediately stepped on the brakes and stopped the jet. the jet was then towed back on to the parking mark. called maintenance and told them. the said they would make a note of it. i also said i ran the hydraulic boost pump after that in case the accumulator pressure was insufficient. the parking brake held after that with no issues. maintenance asked if the plane had been chocked. it had not been.parking brake did not hold and no chocks. always be alert and verify that the plane gets chocked right away. it had not been in this case.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: DA42 flight instructor and student pilot reported experiencing engine problems during takeoff climb resulted in return to departure airport.
text: after being cleared for takeoff on runway xx at redacted, student pilot (sp) performed a short-field takeoff. after rotation, initial climb, callouts, and appropriate actions were made in accordance with sop. at around 700 feet agl, the lh engine began having rpm oscillations of around +-200 rpms, including going into the overspeed multiple times. at the same time, power of the left engine was reducing on its own and the yaw from the asymmetric thrust was setting in. during all of this, the engine was making a grinding noise, best described as it sounded like a handful of marbles were thrown into the prop. flight instructor (ip) took controls as soon as practical, and reduced the power setting on the left engine to 70%, where the roughness ended. after determining the engine was healthy enough to stay on, ip requested from tower to make a lap in the pattern and land back on runway xx. tower cleared us to land and asked if we were declaring an emergency, ip replied with negative", since the engine was operating normally at low power settings, and the flight was otherwise safe at this point. the rest of the traffic pattern went normally, sp helped flight instructor run checklists and the landing was normal. i'm currently unaware at this time if air traffic control provided priority handling on our behalf, as they never asked for fuel or souls on board, rather only asking what the issue with the airplane was. however, as we were turning base leg for runway xx, the airport rescue and firefighting trucks were sent to meet us at the runway, and one would follow us back to parking. upon post-flight inspection of the aircraft, nothing seemed visually wrong, and we never got any annunciations at any point from the primary flight display (pfd). airplane is now safely parked and secured on the ramp at redacted."

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported during departure experiencing an NMAC with another aircraft opposite direct to the runway and not broadcasting on the CTAF.
text: at approximately xa:00 at redacted on ctaf redacted.x, we departed runway xx and were in the initial climb at approximately 1, 200 feet msl. standard ctaf calls were made by our aircraft, with the last transmission being our takeoff announcement.shortly before turning crosswind, my student observed conflicting traffic pass approximately 200 feet below our aircraft. the traffic had not been visible prior to that moment and was not displayed on onboard traffic/ads-b equipment. the last transmission heard from the conflicting aircraft referenced beginning the rnav runway xy approach, despite runway xx being the active runway.due to the nose-high climb attitude after takeoff, the aircraft cowling obstructed a significant portion of the forward lower visual area, limiting our ability to visually acquire the traffic sooner. upon sighting the aircraft below us, we immediately initiated a right turn to increase separation and avoid a collision risk.it later appeared the conflicting aircraft was maneuvering/circling to side-step and join the downwind for runway xx. weather conditions were clear vmc.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported encountering another aircraft flying opposite direction to them resulting in an NMAC and the Flight instructor taking evasive action to avoid a collision.
text: at 2500 ft, instructor was talking a student through emergency landing profile (elp). while scanning instruments and then looking at the ipad for traffic to safely conduct the elp the instructors eyes then transitioned to the right and at this point observed a high wing aircraft at the same altitude, going the opposite direction, within 500 ft of the instructor's aircraft. instructor performed evasive maneuvers while the other aircraft maintained their original heading. no calls were made by the other aircraft on ctaf and the aircraft was not on ads-b. instructor had been making calls advising of the intended practice emergency landing. the rest of the flight was uneventful with the instructor and student landing safely. corrective actions would be requiring all aircraft to be on ads-b. most mid air collisions happen on clear days below 3000ft within 5 miles of an airport. all participating aircraft using ads-b-out would vastly aid in collision avoidance. the only other corrective action is using the see and avoid doctrine and diligently scanning in a figure 8 pattern 60 degrees to the left and right and 10 degrees up and down of the aircraft. a lapse of the scan pattern for 10 seconds while talking to a student and glancing at an ipad can mean the difference between a collision and an nmac.
