anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported loss of engine power during final approach resulted landing short of the runway and striking a runway light.
text: during local instructional flight operations in the airport traffic pattern, the aircraft experienced a total loss of engine power on short final at approximately 100 feet agl after full flap deployment (flaps 40). at the time of the event, the aircraft was configured for landing at low altitude and low airspeed consistent with normal final approach procedures.upon the loss of engine power, i, acting as the certificated flight instructor, assumed control of the aircraft. due to the aircraft's landing configuration and the significant drag associated with flaps 40, glide performance was substantially reduced and the aircraft was unable to reach the runway threshold.the aircraft subsequently touched down approximately 30-40 feet short of the paved runway surface, striking a runway end light prior to contacting the transition area leading onto the asphalt runway. the aircraft remained upright and controllable throughout the event.there was no operating control tower at the airport, and wind conditions were not considered a contributing factor. no injuries were sustained by either occupant. following the event, the aircraft was shut down and removed from service for maintenance inspection. no immediately apparent structural damage was observed by the flight crew at the time of the incident.subsequent maintenance inspection reportedly identified a leak in the engine induction system/induction lines, which may have resulted in the introduction of un-metered air and contributed to the total loss of engine power.the purpose of this report is to document the circumstances surrounding the engine power loss event and subsequent forced landing short of the runway.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: C182 pilot reported during departure having an NMAC by overflying a jet that was departing on the crossing runway; the pilot reported not hearing the other aircraft on the CTAF frequency.
text: arriving at redacted flight following was used with redacted and redacted centers and redacted ctaf and asos prior to arrival and landing. turbulence was a factor in all operations for landing, taxing and departure during the xa:45 landing period on runway. xx (wind 260@26g36) and the departure on rwy xy at xc:00 (wind 280@21g33). during our time on the ramp at the fbo, the ground crew chocked and tied down the plane due to the extreme turbulence on the surface. while landing, taxing in and out and departing we had the ctaf in the active position on the gtn 650xi and the center frequency in the standby position. conditions seemed to favor a departure on rwy xx, but at that runway hold line a recheck of the weather strongly indicated that xy had less of a crosswind component. i taxied to the 1 hold line of runway xy and did pre takeoff checks and setup the gtn 650xi for the departure route. on the takeoff i noticed over the intersection of rwys xx and xy that i was passing several hundred feet above a jet that had departed on runway xx.in analyzing the situation i discovered i had not heard any calls for the jet and that during my setup of the gtn 650xi at the runway hold line. i must have inadvertently touched the standby frequency block which brought the center frequency into the active position as the aircraft was rocking in the ground turbulence and thus not allowing me to hear the calls from the jet and the jet not hearing my departure calls either.the learning experience for me is recognizing how close the home and direct buttons are to the active and standby communication frequency selector on the 650, and to recheck the communication setup while at the hold line. this piece of navigation equipment is a relatively new addition to my aircraft. my previous radio equipment had a button which would exchange the standby and active frequencies. another thought would be to have the ctaf frequency in both the active and standby positions, and the center frequency on the number 2 com/nav unit.i fully understand how this kind of a human failure can cause a devastating accident and i will be more attentive to this detail.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: C172 pilot reported on a go-around having aircraft performance issue resulting in flight towards terrain; the aircraft was able to climb above the obstruction and continued to their destination.
text: i decided to land at the redacted airport while enroute. i had never landed there before so i gathered the airport information from my phone enroute. the runway is fairly short. there was another aircraft in the pattern as we were approaching and it was on the ground before we entered the pattern.my first mistake was with my radio calls. i was making calls stating the wrong runway end. i believe i was confused based on the calls the other pilot was making and the direction he said he was coming from. i should have verified with my chart. i didn't. i mention this because i realized that i was making the wrong calls on final and i think that the realization of this mistake just added to the situation. my pattern was a little tight and i ended up coming in fast. i was in landing configuration with 40 degrees of flaps. i felt i might not be able stop in time due to the short runway and decided a go around would be appropriate. however with a short runway with trees on the end and 40 degrees of flaps i ended up struggling to climb to clear the trees. i didn't want to start removing flaps as i was fairly slow and fairly low over the trees and didn't want to settle into the trees if i lost any lift. once clear of the trees i milked off the flaps as i began to accelerate and decided not to make a second attempt.i was too slow and too close to the trees for my comfort level and due to the short runway with obstacles really didn't feel i had many options other than keep the nose down and allow speed to build. had it been a warmer day with less aircraft performance it could have ended badly which is why i am filling out this report.there are several things that could have helped avoid this situation: 1. i should have done a more detailed review of the airport prior to landing there for the first time as printed resources don't always tell the whole story. perhaps i should have looked at some aerial photos or maps. 2. i should have made a better approach, because my pattern was tight i ended up high and ultimately too fast. a slightly wider pattern would have provided for a more stabilized slower approach. 3. i should have made the go around decision earlier. i ate up too much of the short runway trying to 'save' the landing. 4. i do think that some complacency and perhaps over confidence in flying a familiar airplane contributed to getting too far down the road before calling the go around. i did some additional go-around practice at a local airport with a much longer runway later in the flight and intend to do more specifically focused on seeing if letting some flaps out particularly in a 172 with 40 degrees would be more helpful or harmful in this scenario as the flaps are almost all drag at 40 degrees and provide very little if any additional lift.i did discuss this situation with some pilot friends to debrief the flight and brainstorm ways to improve and was given some helpful insight.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Mooney pilot reported an NMAC in the traffic pattern with an aircraft that was not transmitting on the CTAF frequency.
text: flying to redacted, aircraft x near miss with aircraft y who made no radio calls. 20 miles out i make radio call, 'redacted traffic, aircraft x, 20 south east, left downwind, xx, anyone in the area please advise.'15 miles out radio call, 'redacted traffic, aircraft x direct redacted, 9500, left downwind xx.'then i see traffic on screen, 11 o'clock, less than two miles -01 below. i instantly punch off autopilot, enter steep climb.traffic advisory alert goes off, 'traffic, 12 o'clock, one mile, same altitude.'i transmit, 'redacted traffic you on frequency?' response, 'yea we are at 9500 se bound.' i say, 'we are on a collision course, i am climbing'i then see the old twin off my right wing about 150 feet to my right and 350 feet below.i say, 'you know it would be good to provide some position reports.'i don't remember the lame response from aircraft y.aircraft y landed. stayed five min and left. no one heard any transmissions at all on taxi, take off or departure. i did not hear any radio calls.i was irritated for hours. this yahoo pilot should not be flying.not sure why adsb did not show him earlier, i am wondering if my tcas is the system that found him at less than two miles. i have both tcas and adsb in and out with garmin 3xi, 750 and 650.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: C172 Flight Instructor reported a NMAC in the traffic pattern required evasive action to avoid a collision.
text: on returning from a part 61 training flight in the practice area to the west of redacted, i instructed my student to pass to the south of the right downwind of runway xxr, in order to set up for a 45 degree entry. while sufficiently far enough south the downwind leg, i noticed an aircraft turn an early right crosswind and cut in front of another aircraft already on the crosswind. the traffic, a cirrus sr-22, announced via ctaf that they intended to depart to the south. they began tracing straight towards my aircraft, and at this time i took flight controls from my student. i attempted to reach the other pilot to coordinate via ctaf but was unable, or my calls were not acknowledged. at this time i began a descent and a turn towards the airport to allow the traffic to pass off my right side, to my south. the departing traffic, which originally was headed southwest bound, began a turn towards the west, again tracking towards my aircraft. seeing the other aircraft's ground speed of approximately 180 knots, and knowing my ground speed was approximately 100 knots, i knew it was only seconds until we would collide. at this time, both aircraft had descended to approximately 800 feet msl. to avoid the collision, and to avoid turning into other traffic established on the downwind to my north, i initiated an aggressive descent to pass beneath the opposite direction cirrus. during this descent, my altitude dropped to approximately 480 feet agl. after passing the cirrus, i resumed a climb back to pattern altitude of approximately 1022 msl, and conducted a normal 45 degree entry to the right downwind. the landing was uneventful. to avoid another near miss in the future, i will emphasize to other pilots the importance of departing the pattern in a manner consistent with the aim's guidance (downwind, then depart) instead of flying on course immediately.

anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Inflight Event / Encounter Aircraft
synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported there was no frequency listed for 00NC and was surprised to see live jumping operations occurring although there was no TFR or NOTAM.
text: checked for tfrs in pre-flight planning. none noted. my helicopter was flying at 500 feet agl northeast-ward from rdu airspace on a route segment offset 6 nm northwest of lhz, and one mile northwest of 00nc. aircrew noted no frequency listed for 00nc on the sectional. aircrew was then surprised to see a jump airplane and multiple parachutes in the sky while traversing northeast-ward. aircrew subsequently discovered that a foreflight user could see a notam overlayed for the live jumping operations, but that there was no tfr, and no notam could subsequently be found on the notam lookup service online.ideas for what could have prevented this situation: 1) allow a graphical notam layer to be overlayed on skyvector.com. 2) list a frequency for 00nc north raleigh (private) airport. it is unthinkable to me that an airport participating in commercial jump operations does not have its primary working frequency listed on the sectional. if you look up the airport in airnav.com, you can see the multicom frequency of 131.5, but it is not clear whether the parachute operations use this or perhaps use the lhz ctaf frequency instead. the inability to see the notam, an inability to view the jump operations in the same layer as a tfr layer, and a parachute operation not having their working frequency listed on the visual flight rules sectional all seem like areas of potential improvement to avoid a midair collision with either a parachutist or the jump airplane.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: GA pilot reported during landing experiencing a ground loop resulting in a runway excursion.
text: after landing rwy xxr during rollout, right crosswind gust yawed aircraft to the right. the aircraft veered to the right (ground looped) and left the paved runway into the gravel median at low speed. the aircraft completed a 180 degree turn in a wings level 3 point attitude. there was no damage and minimal side load to the landing gear and aircraft.my left shoe had caught on the rudder pedal preventing me from being able to apply the left toe brake to counter-act the right turning tendency caused by the wind gust.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot crew reported a near collision on the takeoff roll with an aircraft taking off on the crossing runway at a non-towered airport. The Captain delayed the rotation to avoid the other aircraft.
text: while operating a passenger flight from redacted to redacted we planned a departure on rw xx with a right forward quartering headwind /crosswind. we taxied to runway xx and announced our intentions on the unicom frequency. we received our instrument flight rules clearance on the ground via redacted ctr on the radio as well.we heard no other traffic on the unicom frequency of redacted.xx we saw no visible traffic during our taxi, in the air or on the ground. the cessna 182 had taxied much earlier than us so assumed he had departed on his flight to redacted. there were no radio transmissions from the cessna 182 and that was confirmed via the fbo audio recorded during that time period.our transmissions were on the recording stating our intentions to taxi to rw xx. we completed our taxi check and were holding short of rw xx. the co-pilot transmitted our departure intentions for redacted rw xx and we began our normal takeoff roll. the aircraft accelerated normally and the co-pilot called v1 and rotate, at that moment the c182 appeared at about 11 o clock in the windshield and approximately 50 to 75 ft. in the air. it was too late for an aborted takeoff as it appeared we would pass barely underneath the the c182. a rotation at that instant would have caused impact with the c182. i felt the safest option was to delay the rotation and remain on the runway for a couple of seconds as the traffic passed over us. it happened very quickly and we rotated and resumed the climb away from the runway. the remainder of the flight was normal and uneventful. the incident occurred due to lack of situational awareness resulting from a lack of radio communication. i was unaware visually of another aircraft positioned at rw xy prior to beginning the takeoff roll. this incident could have been avoided by pilots verifying correct unicom/ ctaf frequencies in use at uncontrolled airports. visually verifying other aircraft when possible and the use of all available appropriate aircraft lighting to enhance visibility.

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: C172 pilot reported a loss of control just before touchdown resulting in an aircraft stall; a hard landing; and a runway excursion.
text: in regards to the incident of a hard landing at redacted.this report is being written by the pilot in command of aircraft x at the time of the accident. the trip was intended to be a day trip into redacted, we had departed earlier that morning with a visual flight rules request from air traffic control to give us vectors in route to redacted. this request was canceled shortly after the plane was no longer under control of redacted's class c airspace. the intention behind this action was simply to take a more well defined route down the coast which we would follow south to redacted.the exact time of the event is not clear to me, i know that when i was roughly 25 miles to the north east of the field i had received the atis and information 1 was in effect. it stated that the active runway was runway xx and the winds were coming from 060 at 11kts, gusting to 18kts.upon contact with redacted tower, it was communicated the active pressure in inches of mercury and that i was to advise when i was established on a right downwind for runway xxprior to my advancement into the downwind the controller in the tower had called asking if i was setting myself up for a straight in approach into runway xy, as far as i was aware i was not only far east to the runway but also east of the tower that sits on the east of the runway. the tower communicated that from their perspective, i was in position for the unactive runway xy, however i was still at pattern altitude and at least a mile away from being lined up with the centerline for runway xy. i continued my approach into the right downwind and advised with midfield, everything seemed in order and even still, turning to base appeared normal, it wasn't until i had turned to final that it was clear to me that i had not adequately accounted for the wind correction due primarily to the gusts at 18kts. i was blown off to the west by roughly 0.5sm - 1sm, and with the gusts now coming in on the headwind, losing attitude on final proved itself to be a challenge, to the degree where this first approach resulted in missed/go around actions being taken. redacted tower at this point advised me to turn back into the right downwind for runway xx, however it was not advised that this turn was to be made while midfield with the runway, this required a sharper turn of of the runway heading, while working against the gusting 18kt headwind. my initial plan through this missed approach was to clean up the plane's flaps and trim while maintaining the runway heading until 700ft agl. this request from the tower, while not the primary cause of the hard landing, was in some key details a reason behind the unstable final approach that lead to the events regarded to in this report. i made the needed adjustments to clean up the plane, however i was only up to 800ft agl throughout the pattern instead of the pattern altitude of 1000ft agl. upon this second attempt at a right downwind i extended my downwind to allow for more room for adjustments on base and final. the turn to base was standard and by this point i had only applied 10 degrees of flaps and no trim. upon my second attempt for a final approach i had started off with 10 degrees of flaps but soon realized that i needed to lose more altitude than anticipated. this is because i knew i was below pattern altitude so i held off on the 500ft decent following the plane being abeam the runway numbers. by my approach into final the plane was still roughly 800ft agl, this prompted me to add in 20 degrees of flaps, however the trim stayed neutral. the plane was well pitched for 65-70kts on the decent because of the heavy use of flaps and everything was steady on the approach until around 150ft - 200ft agl the turbulence and gusts had rapidly gotten more intense. this pushed the plane back and while i was able to maintain a steady angle of attack until around 100ft agl, i was just barely crossing over the runway threshold when a final gust pushed the plane on an uneven angle and slowed it into a stall, the final airspeed i rememberseeing was 38kts right before the stall. this happened so close to the runway that i was unable to go around again or glide comfortably to the runway. aircraft x impacted with the runway and rolled in the grass between the runway and taxiway 1. it stopped in the grass and the mixture was leaned to idle before pulling out the throttle and turned off all electronics to the plane. the plane was swiftly evacuated and rescue crews arrived on the scene. no damage to property or injury to any body involved was found. the only known damage to be found was a chip to the front wheel's rim which was still able to hold air and the windshield had shattered leaving only half of the glass remaining in frame.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: CL600 air taxi pilot reported cabin smoke and a loss of pressurization during cruise flight. The aircraft diverted to an alternate airport and landed safely.
text: on a part 135 flight operating from redacted airport, the aircraft experienced an in-flight abnormal/critical event while in cruise flight.during cruise, smoke and an electrical burning odor were observed in the cabin area near the galley microwave. based on observations during the event, i believe the microwave inverter or associated electrical component may have shorted and produced smoke. i began troubleshooting and addressing the smoke source in the cabin.while dealing with the smoke the aircraft experienced a loss of cabin pressurization, resulting in the automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks. the combination of electrical smoke/fire indications and loss of pressurization significantly increased cockpit workload and created what i believed to be a critical situation requiring immediate priority handling.during the event, i was instructed to advise air traffic control that the passengers wished to change destinations rather than declare an emergency. the flight subsequently diverted to redacted airport. while enroute to redacted, repeated requests were made to air traffic control for lower altitude and direct routing to the instrument landing system approach. we were not given priority, instead we were given vectors and lower altitudes, but not direct to the approach.i believe we should have declared an emergency because we had: suspected electrical smoke/fire, loss of cabin pressurization, passenger oxygen mask deployment, and an increased cockpit workload and abnormal aircraft condition.had i been the pilot in command, i would have declared an emergency and requested priority handling to ensure expedited routing and appropriate emergency response coordination.the flight landed safely in redacted without further escalation. next time i believe the correct action would be to declare an emergency, especially if the source of the malfunction is not immediately confirmed.

synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a parachute jumper landed in front of the parked aircraft and the lines became entangled on the wing.
text: i was parked on the terminal ramp at hwy and loading a passenger in the front seat of my stearman when a solo parachute jumper was observed heading right toward the front of my plane from the right and he then landed on the ramp just in front of my right wing. his parachute lines and chute were blown over the top wing of my biplane and the jumper came to rest right in front of my right wings. i asked him if he was ok and he replied he was. i then got the passenger out of my plane and asked him to gather the chute together so it would not blow in the wind and possibly cause the lines to pull more on my wings. i then climbed on the nose of my plane and removed the lines that were stuck on my top wing and we were able to free the parachute and lines from my wing by walking it toward the wing tip. the jumper collected himself and was exiting the ramp when i called to him and asked if he was an instructor. he said no, he was a student. i met with the airport manager after this to make sure she knew what had happened and asked her to follow up with the jump operation who operates at the airport. my concern is my safety and the safety of my plane and passenger. it is my understanding that the faa allowed the commercial jump operation to operate at our airport but they had to comply with a set of rules or instructions which included no solo student jumps. there was only to be tandem jumps with experienced instructors or solo jumps by these instructors for their currency. this is a public use airport with many many flights per day which sometimes includes corporate jet traffic in addition several flight schools and one part 91 sightseeing ride operation. the jumper today came down on the terminal ramp, a good distance away from where their designated landing area is located.

synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor with their student reported experiencing a critical ground conflict and a NMAC during short final approach at BCV; a non-towered airport.
text: my student and i were conducting a training flight at pabv, with the objective of practicing landings. we were making appropriate radio calls and adhering to all guidance from the fars and acs on non-towered airport operations. we had discussed the relevant fars, acs, and potential hazards of non-towered airport operations during our preflight.my student and i were established in right traffic for 20r at pabv. we were conducting touch and go operations. the event i am reporting occurred after several circuits had uneventfully been completed.on short final for 20r, we observed that a taxiing aircraft had elected to cross 20r and the approach end of 20l at taxiway c. my student asked me if we should go-around. before i had time to advise, we observed aircraft y fly in front of us from the left, with the intent to land on 20l (the gravel runway). aircraft y had not made any radio calls, and had not been previously established in the established right traffic pattern. my student executed a go-around to avoid aircraft y and to avoid over-flying the taxiing aircraft.as my student executed the go-around, i observed aircraft y overfly the taxiing aircraft, land on 20l, and taxi to park.this is not the first time that i have personally witnessed aircraft flying in an opposing pattern, or opposite traffic pattern at pabv. my many of fellow cfi's have encountered dangerous pilots at pabv. myself and my co-workers have witnessed pilots (who appear to be based at pabv) being aggressive, heckling and rude to training aircraft on the radio. thank you for taking the time to read my account. please help stop this pattern of dangerous behavior. i am concerned that it will cause a fatality, and that nothing will be done to stop these dangerous pilots until it is too late.

synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported a runway excursion during landing.
text: during a routine training flight, my student and i were conducting closed traffic work at redacted focusing on landings and crosswind correction techniques. wind conditions were around 8 kts crosswind component on runway xxl. during our final landing of the lesson, the student applied the incorrect crosswind control and utilized the wrong rudder to align us with the runway centerline. this resulted in us deviating from the paved runway surface. i recognized the developing situation but was unable to correct it in time before the runway excursion occurred. the aircraft continued through the grass onto the next available taxiway and came to a full stop. i inspected the landing gear and propeller and found no apparent damage. no airport lighting, signs, or airport property were struck. the ground was solid and grass was short. i returned the aircraft to redacted where maintenance personnel inspected the aircraft and also didn't find any damage. in retrospect, several human factors likely contributed to the event, including possible student fatigue and frustration after repeated difficulty maintaining aircraft control in crosswind conditions. additionally, my instructional coaching and intervention were not sufficiently timely or effective to prevent the excursion. a go-around should have been initiated once the unstable landing and developing loss of directional control became apparent. this event reinforces the importance of an early go-around when landing stability becomes questionable. in the future, i will emphasize a greater importance on early go-arounds during training for myself and my students.

synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported conducting a UAS flight in an active TFR. The pilot landed the UAS upon realizing the TFR was active.
text: on the evening of day 0, i conducted a part 107 uas operation at location x in support of media coverage activities for a public event. the initial launch location was adjacent to the event area. the later portion of the operation was intended to capture concluding event activities and the final scheduled performer for the evening as part of the event media coverage scope.prior to the operation, i coordinated with event organizers, informed onsite event and public safety personnel that uas operations would be occurring in support of the event and conducted standard preflight planning activities. i obtained applicable laanc authorizations for the operational area, including authorization approved at approximately xa:08 and an extension authorization approved at approximately xb:32.during preflight planning, i reviewed applicable airspace information and mistakenly believed that no event was occurring at the nearby stadium during the planned operation window. receipt of the laanc authorizations and my incorrect understanding of the tfr schedule contributed to my mistaken assumption that all required airspace considerations affecting the operation had been adequately addressed.the aircraft was operated with additional safety considerations appropriate for a public event environment, including the use of propeller guards and operational procedures intended to minimize risk to persons on the ground. the operation was not intended to involve sustained flight directly over open-air assemblies of people.flight operations began at approximately xa:25. during the later portion of the operation, fireworks became visible and audible near approximately xc:28. this immediately prompted concern that a tfr was active. upon recognizing the possibility of an active tfr, i immediately terminated flight operations and safely recovered the aircraft without incident.following the operation, i reviewed the applicable notams and confirmed that a tfr was active. no injuries, property damage, loss of separation, or interference with manned aircraft occurred during the operation.contributing factors included incorrect assumption regarding incomplete verification of event-triggered tfr status, and confirmation bias after receipt of valid laanc authorizations for the operational area.as corrective action, i am implementing additional preflight verification procedures for all operations near stadiums or event venues, including direct verification of active schedules, final notam review immediately prior to takeoff, and secondary cross-checking through multiple planning sources to prevent recurrence.this report is submitted voluntarily in the interest of aviation safety and continued operational improvement.

text: climbing out of redacted passing through 18, 000 feet, a senior flight attendant called the captain in flight deck very distressed. she said the aircraft was vibrating significantly by door 2l. the captain had the relief pilots go check out the vibrations. they called the captain and said it was abnormally loud and you could feel the vibrations in their feet.at the same time the left vibration indicator on the engine instruments was steadily increasing from an indication of 1.1 to 1.7 as we continued climbing to fl320. the right vibration indicator stayed constant at 0.9. the crew elected to level off and as power came back the left vibration indication slowly reduced back to 1.1.the crew contacted dispatch on satcom and asked to be connected to maintenance control.there was no 787 mechanic available for over 10 minutes. at this time the crew decided to return to redacted as many of the crew and passengers were alarmed and the safest course of action was to get the engine evaluated before continuing a long flight over the ocean.maintenance control eventually came on the line and agreed with our course of action. the crew entered a holding pattern at fix redacted on the zzzzzx rnav arrival to runway xxc to redacted at 20, 000 ft and dumped 110, 000 pounds of fuel in approximately 40 minutes.we then landed uneventfully in redacted and continued to gate xx. the were unable to talk with a 787 mechanic through maintenance control for over 20 minutes as well. the inability to communicate with a 787 mechanic while troubleshooting multiple abnormalities stood out dramatically to the entire crew and dispatcher as a major breakdown for attempting to provide clear and timely information to our customers.after landing the captain and crew called the dispatcher, debriefed with maintenance control and with the chief pilot.

text: this was a scheduled flight between redacted and redacted with operating crews and company jump-seaters. this event occurred within redacted firwhile operating flight to redacted as first messages . while working that checklist we received bleeds 1, 3, 4 eicas alerts as well. this was followed shortly by the return of bleed 2 eicas alert. we noticed cabin altitude climbing and at an altitude of 5700 we elected to put on o2 masks and activated supernumerary o2 switch. the cpt ran those checklists and managed to get two bleeds back on but we eventually lost all 4 bleeds a second synopsis: Air carrier pilot Captain reported an altitude overshoot when descending on a published arrival in mountainous terrain. The Captain stopped the descent; climbed back to the charted altitude; then resumed the approach.
text: while descending into cyyc on the ebgal 7 arrival runway 36r, i was pm, and the first officer was pf. we had been held up due to traffic below us, and once cleared to descend to 9, 000 feet via the arrival, the pf chose to descend in open descent mode. we had a restriction to cross ebgal below 14, 000' and tiduk at 9, 000. i felt that descending in managed descent would have been more appropriate, but did not articulate that notion, because the altitude of 9, 000 was in the altitude preselect window, and the flight management system showed that we would cross ebgal below 14, 000. we requested the rnav y 35r with approach control and they cleared us for it via the tiduk transition. at that point the pf set 5200' in the altitude preselect window, and i reminded pf to select appr mode. when pf selected appr i noted that column 3 on the flight mode annunciator (fma) annunciated appr nav in green and column 2, line 2 showed alt final in blue. what i did not notice was that we were still in open descent in column 2, line 1.the pf chimed sterile at 13, 600, and got the exterior lights at 10, 000.i was reviewing my charts when i looked up and realized that we were at about 5, 800'. i immediately instructed pf to climb back to 9, 000' for the crossing restriction at tiduk, which we did make. we were not in dangerous proximity to the ground at that time, and in fact were in vmc, but we actually were between 200-500 feet below mea on that segment of the approach. after climbing to 9, 000', the remainder of the approach was flown correctly and we landed safely at cyyc.cause: i feel that while checking the fma was appropriate, my missing the open descent annunciation in my scan is what allowed this event to occur. i understand that open descent ignores constraints, but i did not realize that selecting appr would not cancel the open descent and capture the vertical path as i anticipated it would. we should have selected managed descent before arming appr.

i didn't request that authorization in advance because i was conducting four flights across a 100 mile radius that day and didn't think i could accurately predict my arrival time.this was my fourth and last property of the day for this client, most of which were smaller portions of larger building complexes. the actual amount of land owned by the client at location x ended up being much smaller than i had anticipated, and so was my operating zone. i picked my takeoff location and pulled up the aloft air control app, which said that laanc was not enabled for my operation. i misunderstood this to mean that my operation was outside of the zone requiring authorization as long as i stayed below the legal ceiling of 400 ft.i took off and conducted the flight, and halfway through i received a notification from dji that i had entered a warning zone. i used the dji map to navigate away from that area, take a few more shots outside of it, and land a few minutes later. i checked the aloft map again after landing and realized that there was a temporary flight restriction in place for the entire class d zone around redacted, and that i had entered that zone for maybe 1-3 minutes.primary cause is pilot error (hazardous attitude, inexperience and misinterpretation of maps and restrictions)-the operation zone i discovered when i arrived differed somewhat from what i had researched and planned in advance. -i was licensed several years ago, but i've only conducted about 6-10 commercial flights since then, and none in controlled airspace until day 0. i had submitted my first laanc request in location y earlier that morning. i wasn't familiar with how the map displayed temporary flight restrictions, i failed to reference the legend, and i misread the situation.-i covered multiple properties in a 100-mile radius that day, and this was the last of the day, leaving me somewhat fatigued and impulsive. i should've rescheduled the property when i realized i was confused instead of proceeding with my best, most convenient guess.secondary cause may be laanc software ambiguity. the language for laanc authorization not being available vs not being required is similar with the app i was using.this was my first experience with laanc and i have enough first-hand knowledge of the procedure now to significantly reduce my confusion in the future. i won't hesitate to reschedule in the future if i can't be sure i'm in compliance.

synopsis: B767 First Officer reported engine oil pressure issue during cruise resulted in an inflight shutdown and diversion.
text: flight abc from redacted to redacted. flight was late off the gate because of a tire change in the hangar then cleaning and catering once it got to the gate. pretty chaotic off the gate, so much so that someone mentioned it felt like a training exercise. there was also a delay in our final weights as we were taxiing due to an error with the initial weights we were pushed. something to do with an electric wheelchair.captain's leg, i was pilot monitoring. climb and level-off were normal. relief pilot calculated breaks and left for his rest period. received and ok'd etops wx. we had sent a message but were waiting on reply.almost exactly two hours after takeoff at xa:38, cruising at 35, 000 feet, about 110 miles almost due north of location x, the amber r eng oil press caution popped up and i pointed it out to the captain. looked at oil indications and right pressure was red, showing pressure of 0. i pulled up the fm non-normals for eng oil press l(r). pressure indication at or below red line limit: go to the engine failure or shutdown checklist." what!? a little bit of disbelief and surprise as i process the fact that this is an actual problem. the captain pulls up the non-normal emergency checklist on his side and verifies the issue. he directs me to request priority handling with redacted center and request lower altitude.i requested priority handling and get receive descent to 290. captain then directs me to take over flying duties so he can work the checklist engine shutdown. we transfer controls and i start down in vnav. i inform redacted of 170 sob and 7+48 fuel on board while ca shuts down right engine. he then calls fa to wake relief pilot and have him report to the flight deck immediately. i am speaking with redacted, descending, and receiving vectors to the south while the relief pilot joins us and ca works checklist and coordinates with dispatch and fas. i notice the r engine temperature indicator in the red. i feel the yaw in the plane but, admittedly, took too long to remember that i needed to step on the left rudder pedal since the right engine had been shut down. now in trim.a report from the cabin let us know a passenger noted flames coming from the right engine, though we had no indication of fire in the flight deck. the fire handle was decidedly pulled out of sequence from checklist but no extinguishing agent was discharged.i was working the radio and descending. i was trying to vnav down to 290, then 200, then 6, 000 feet, when i realized that was too many steps. i chose v/s out of fl200 because it was right in front of me on the panel. i realize after that i should have done flch, but it did what i needed done at the moment. kind of a frenzied blur of a descent but at some point coordinated for divert to redacted, put it in the fmc as alternate, ca activated instrument landing system approach runway xx, coordinated with dispatch, and fas, and control for arff (airport rescue and firefighting). through 10, 000 feet i was fast but recognized it and started slowing to 250 knots while continuing down. i was aware of but not focused on my distance from the airport and knew that i was high and fast. i was coming up on 6, 000 feet, but i was still at 250 knots and high. i was cleared to 3, 000 feet and direct to redacted (if) for straight in to runway xx, and shortly thereafter cleared for approach to runway xx. still high and 250 kts, though. the single biggest mistake of the night was my not arming app mode here when cleared for the approach. this led to me being below glide slope on final which was trapped at 1000 feet but could have been avoided had i armed when cleared for approach.we completed the checklist and had a quick brief. there was a question if i felt comfortable performing the landing. i was comfortable but offered if the captain wanted to take it. we stuck with sop, and i was going to make the landing and he was going to continue monitoring the situation. relief pilot was an invaluable extra set of eyes and mind offering timely advice and mental support. we were coming up on 3, 000 feet but hadn't fully restored our pm and pf rolls. i was worried about alt cap at 3, 000 because i misinterpreted the approach chart thinking the glideslope started at redacted. this error was not trapped and 700 was put into the altitude window because we were at redacted and cleared for the approach. altitude should have remained at 3000 since it was a level segment until gs intercept but definitely not lower than 1900 per the approach plate. this error when unrecognized and i ended up below gs with the runway in sight. gear went down around 3, 000 feet to help slow the plane and flaps were configured as we slowed through the flap speeds. the "glideslope" egpws warning went off and i shallowed my descent to catch the glideslope. at 1000 agl it was caught that i needed to level off to intercept the glide slope. i disconnected the ap, leveled off, and armed the approach. loc was captured right away, i stayed level and moments later intercepted the gs and then continued to follow it to the runway. i got right of course initially with a/p disconnect but worked my way back to the left for a stable approach at 500 ft and a 'buttery' landing, if not a little left of center line.pulled off the runway, got checked out by arff, and coordinated a gate. all cleared and taxied in for an otherwise normal shutdown."

synopsis: A320 First Officer reported temporary loss of aircraft control due to turbulence.
text: on the descent to redacted at 16000 ft we started encountering moderate to severe turbulence that resulted in at least 500-800 ft and bank of over 20 degrees. it smoothed out after. however during the approach the plane lost gps signal followed by loss of auto thrust and auto pilot around 11000-10000 feet. it was followed by thrust lock. the captain took over manually and we were fully stable with the landing checklist done by 1000 resolution advisory and landed safely and uneventful.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported a lightning strike while on initial approach resulting in an Eng 1 Reverse Unlocked ECAM message. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and after landing; damage was identified to the nacelle; flap; and static wick.
text: scheduled flight was redacted-redacted. the wi-fi was discovered to be inoperable on this flight and was not previously written up. dispatch was notified about this and did an excellent job of keeping us informed with the changing conditions and helping build our situational awareness. enroute to redacted, the flight experienced a rapid onset of moderate clear air turbulence which caused the airspeed to rapidly increase above vmo by 10-15 knots for about five seconds. the captain told the flight attendants to be seated immediately. the pf maneuvered the aircraft further away from enroute storms and the turbulence became consistent moderate. once the turbulence died down, the captain told the flight attendants to take their jump seats, followed by a check in. there were no injuries. redacted was calling for thunderstorms, hail and tornadoes at the eta. flight held over redacted [vor] at fl310 in smooth air to allow the storm to pass. after about an hour of holding, once the extreme precipitation was north and east of the field as reported by air traffic control and verified by the weather radar, the crew decided to begin the approach to runway xx. on the descent, at approximately 11, 000 ft msl the aircraft was struck by lightning and immediately showed an eng 1 reverse unlocked ecam message. the approach was aborted, the pf leveled off at 10, 000 and made a right turn direct to redacted. priority handling was requested and the ecam was actioned, resulting in bringing the eng 1 thrust lever to idle, where it remained for the rest of the flight. there was no buffeting so the engine was not shut down but it was treated as a single engine approach. the captain accomplished the brief with the flight attendants. the crew received vectors for the instrument landing system xyl at redacted. on approach, with flaps one selected, a momentary overspeed occurred due to gusty wind conditions. the overspeed lasted less than five seconds and exceeded vfe by approximately five kts. emergency equipment was standing by. a normal landing was accomplished followed by an uneventful taxi to the gate. postflight inspection revealed lightning strike damage to the left engine nacelle, right inboard trailing edge flap, and right sharklet and static wick.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Aircraft marshaller reported during gate arrival after disconnect from the tug; the aircraft rolled uncommanded until the pilot applied brakes.
text: i went out with one of my crew member to set up for the arrival on [gate] xx. when i see the aircraft approaching the gate i had doubt on the type of aircraft because of the size. when i go to look at the screen it had old information from earlier in the day. i marshalled in the plane slowly and when it was close i took a look at the nose for the aircraft type. i misread the type of plane and ended up parking it on the wrong line. after connecting the headset and talking with the pilot to let him know he needed to be adjusted i went to hook up the push tractor. when everything was ready, i asked the pilot to release the brake and i towed him to the right mark. when i go to talk to the pilot again my battery on the headset ran out before i can tell him to set the brake. i didnt notice that one of my crew members disconnected the aircraft from the push tractor so the aircraft started to roll forward. my crew member then goes on a tractor to give the pilot the hand signal for setting the brakes. i go to switch batteries to reestablish communication with the pilot and let him know that he needed to be moved again. after getting confirmation on brake release i pushed him to the right mark and let the pilot know to set the brake.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: EMB 170/175 flight crew reported during approach the autoflight system captured a false glideslope and descended the aircraft below approach path. Flight crew climbed back to charted altitude.
text: while operating flight abcd from redacted to redacted on day 0, at approximately xa:22, we were cleared direct to the final approach fix (redacted) by redacted tower for the visual approach and cleared to land on runway xx. visibility at the field was reported to be 10 statute miles and weather was vmc. we verified the instrument landing system frequency and course were tuned for runway xx at redacted. with preview selected on the guidance panel, the first officer selected approach mode with the autopilot still coupled and while still in magenta lateral and vertical modes. prior to the aircraft intercepting the localizer, the lateral and vertical modes both turned green and with the autopilot not yet captured on either the localizer or glideslope, autopilot performed an uncommanded descent from the assigned altitude and what appeared to be a smart turn inside the final approach course. the aircraft descended to approximately 800 feet agl. we heard the 'one thousand' aural altitude alert, which prompted immediate disconnect of the autopilot and the first officer climbed back to the charted altitude of the redacted (1, 600'). we suspect the aircraft may have inadvertently captured a false glideslope and the combination of prev mode active with app armed prior to localizer/glideslope capture may have caused the autopilot to respond to spurious vertical guidance.upon hearing the 'one thousand' alert, the pilot flying disconnected the autopilot and initiated an immediate climb back to faf altitude (1, 600'). shortly thereafter, air traffic control issued a low altitude alert. as pm, i acknowledged and noted that we were correcting.no terrain conflict, obstacle contact or loss of separation occurred. the remainder of the approach was well within company standards and the landing was completed uneventfully.cause: app mode selected prior to localizer and glideslope capturepotential false glideslope signal in the vicinity of the fafpossible smart turn intercept prior to localizer captureembraer 170/175 autopilot susceptibility to spurious instrument landing system signals prior to valid course captureautomation dependency automation responded to vertical guidance signal before established on the published instrument landing system pathsuggestions: consider company training emphasis on delaying approach mode selection until fully established on both localizer and glideslope, even when cleared direct to faf for situational awarenessconsider training emphasis on direct-to-faf clearances where autopilot and localizer/glideslope anomalies are most commonplaceconsider encouraging rnav approaches whenever cleared for visual approaches to avoid mode confusion (both on the part of the aircraft automation as well as on the part of the pilot)

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: EMB-175 pilot reported receiving a cargo fire extinguishing system message during cruise. Flight returned to departure airport.
text: we were assigned aircraft x to fly from redacted. when we arrived at the aircraft l was met by the first officer that had flown it in. he advised me they had received an eicas message about the cargo fire extinguishing system and that line maintenance was onboard working on the write-up they had made for the message they had received on landing. we continued to complete our preflight duties while line maintenance cleared the message and the aircraft was cleared by maintenance. we departed and all was normal operations until approximately 30 minutes into the flight at 34, 000 feet when we received a eicas message crg aft firex hi arm" advisory. the message was displayed for just over a minute and then extinguished. during that time we referenced the qrh for direction and it stated this was a "crew awareness" message. immediately after the "crg firex hi arm" message extinguished a second advisory message briefly appeared "crg firex lo arm" and was quickly replaced by a "crg firex hi disch" status message. the qrh states that this message means that the "cargo high-rate discharge fire extinguisher bottle has been discharged." we did not see any other indications of a cargo smoke warning (lights or eicas messages). at this point in the flight i opted to send an acars message to dispatch to advise maintenance control that the cargo high-rate bottle had discharged into the cargo compartment and asked them (dispatch and maintenance) if they wanted us to return to redacted. our thought being that we still had over 90 minutes remaining to fly to our destination, but we were now only approximately 30 minutes from redacted. i opted to establish a selcal phone patch with dispatch shortly after sending the acars message to expedite the communication that we needed to have due to the complexity of the possible decision to divert. while establishing the phone patch through company radio we received the message "maintenance says its crew difereable".once the phone patch was established with dispatch we discussed the message we received, what i thought was now the state of the compromised cargo fire suppression system, and some possible options with our dispatcher. the dispatcher again restated that maintenance said that we could continue to our destination and defer the cargo fire suppression system there. i told our dispatcher that this would mean we probably would not be able to carry cargo out of our destination. when a cargo bottle is used to respond to a "cargo fwd (aft) smoke" warning message and the contents are discharged the qrh states to land at the nearest suitable airport. while we did not have a cargo smoke indication (cargo smoke push lights, or eicas messages) our high rate bottle had been discharged and our ability to respond to any future cargo smoke messages during the flight was compromised. upon further discussion i opted to return to redacted to address the issue.my concerns regarding this particular in-flight event are the lack of safety minded real time decision making support from the team (dispatch and maintenance control) on the ground. a statement like "do what your qrh directs" does not help in this situation. especially considering the fact that the eicas messages we were referencing in the qrh did not expressly state what to do given this particular set of circumstances. if we had opted to continue to our destination we would have flown for over 90 minutes with a compromised cargo compartment fire suppression system to a destination that could probably not service (repair the system or replace the halon) on the aircraft while dealing with contract maintenance in a foreign country. according to the faa, inflight lithium battery fires and smoke incidents on domestic flights now occur at a rate of roughly two incidents per week. a fact that i was made aware of while attending recurrent ground school less than a month ago. we were carrying cargo and according to the eicas messages present we did not have a high rate bottle option available to fight a fire in either cargo compartment. guidance to continue to a foreign country destination and overlook the possible inflight risks, as well as deferring equipment that removes or seriously impacts the ability to carry cargo is at a minimum a bad business decision, or worse, our company is left trying to explain to the families of our passengers or the faa why we opted to continue if we had an actual cargo fire happen without the possibility to fight the fire in the remaining flight. the decision to return to redacted should have been made as a consensus by all parties involved. after returning and landing safely in redacted we were advised by line maintenance that this aircraft has a history of these types of messages occurring. a side note to this incident, after being reassigned another aircraft and completing the flight several passenger thanked us for getting them safely to their destination, despite arriving a couple of hours late."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Widebody Captain reported GPS jamming in Chinese airspace during cruise; resulting in a course and altitude deviation.
text: first shift pf and i were asleep in the bunk. when we emerged we were informed that there had been two fma (flight mode annunciator) and autopilot malfunctions possibly associated with the gps jamming we had encountered earlier in the flight near ukraine. this occured roughly 8 hours into the flight somewhere over china. the autopilot was disconnected and the flight path corrected during each event. possible altitude deviations of 200ft and course deviations of 2nm. a logbook entry was made after the flight.cause: system malfunction manually corrected after disconnecting the autopilot.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A321-NEO flight crew reported the aircraft rolled forward after setting the brakes at the gate because of a brake system malfunction.
text: upon blocking in at gate xx, i set the parking brake in accordance with (iaw) sop's and the triple indicator showed normal brake and accumulator pressure. i then took my feet off the toe brakes and the aircraft began to roll forward. the first officer promptly called 'we're rolling!' just as 'brake system fail' and multiple other ecam messages populated with aural alerts. i immediately applied maximum braking to stop the aircraft and noticed that the brake pressure indications in the triple indicator were at zero, with normal accumulator pressure. the airplane stopped abruptly as the ground personnel ran away from it. thankfully, the airplane stopped prior to impacting ground equipment, the jet bridge, or personnel. i estimate we were a maximum of 5' from impacting equipment in front of the airplane. i held the brakes until communications were established with ground personnel, the aircraft was chocked, and the tug was connected. at that time, both engines were shut down and the aircraft was pushed back by the tug to the appropriate parking position. shortly after the aircraft was pushed into the appropriate parking position and after the last engine spooled down, normal brake pressure indications returned to the triple indicator and the ecam faults cleared. a detailed discrepancy was entered in the logbook software. maintenance was called and i personally described the problem to the responding mechanic. note: i did discuss the situation with union safety and the committee volunteer who handled my call stated that this same problem had occurred with another airbus in the previous few days.cause: i have no idea what the causal factors were - there was clearly some issue with brake system of that particular airplane and based on my discussion with union safety, there may be an issue with the fleet. regarding mitigation, i sincerely hope maintenance, union safety, company safety, flight ops, and all other relevant departments investigate this situation thoroughly. as mentioned in my narrative above, the airplane was a maximum of 5' from impacting anything from ground equipment to a jet bridge, to a person. had the first officer not immediately noticed the unexpected forward motion of the airplane, we would be dealing with an accident, a damaged airplane, and almost certainly injured personnel / passengers.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier Captain taxiing for departure at ORD reported signage and markings in the area did not clearly identify where Taxiway SE or SP transitioned into Taxiway A .
text: crew received taxi instructions from ramp control while positioned in the ramp area at ord. during the initial transmission, the instructions were delivered rapidly and included multiple routing elements. the first officer, who was relatively junior, missed portions of the readback, and the controller requested the instructions be read back again.the revised taxi instructions were understood as follow another aircraft, taxi on the east side of the y, taxi via taxiway se, hold short of taxiway a, and contact ground metering.while complying with the instructions, the crew encountered several aircraft positioned on taxiway sp immediately ahead. additionally, aircraft y and aircraft z were oriented southeast on taxiway sp, limiting available maneuvering space and requiring the aircraft to continue further south on taxiway sp.as the aircraft proceeded, the crew attempted to identify the hold short point for taxiway a. however, the crew was unable to positively identify the transition point between taxiway se/sp and taxiway a due to limited signage and the absence of a clearly depicted taxiway se on available company taxi charts.uncertain whether the aircraft had stopped at the correct location, the crew contacted ramp control for clarification. ramp control advised that the aircraft had proceeded too far and instructed the crew to hold position and contact ground metering.after contacting ground metering, the crew was advised they were not expected to be in that location and were instructed to contact ground control. the primary contributing factor was confusion regarding the taxi routing and hold short location in a congested and operationally complex ramp environment. several factors contributed to the event:the routing issued differed significantly from normal and familiar procedures commonly used in that area in recent months. historically, crews typically remained on either side of the y and contacted ground metering prior to taxiing northwestbound on taxiway sp while monitoring 131.3. the routing issued during this event differed substantially from that normal flow. taxiway se was not clearly depicted on available company airport charts available to the crew. signage and markings in the area did not clearly identify where taxiway se or sp transitioned into taxiway a.multiple aircraft positioned in the area created congestion and reduced maneuvering clarity.rapid communication cadence and repeated radio exchanges increased cockpit workload during a critical phase of taxi operations.despite the confusion, the crew operated conservatively, taxied slowly, sought clarification when uncertain, and attempted to maintain clear and professional communication throughout the event.to help prevent similar events in the future, the following improvements should be considered:improve airport signage and surface markings in the southeast ramp/sp/a taxiway transition area to better identify taxiway boundaries and hold short locations.ensure all active taxiways and routing terminology used operationally are accurately depicted on company airport charts and electronic flight deck references.promote standardized taxi routing practices whenever possible to reduce confusion caused by frequent procedural changes.encourage clear, concise, and measured communication between controllers and flight crews, particularly during periods of high workload and congestion.consider additional coordination between ramp control, ground metering, and air traffic control to ensure consistent expectations regarding aircraft positioning and routing in this area.the crew believes the event resulted primarily from unfamiliar routing, unclear taxiway identification, and a congested operating environment rather than any intentional noncompliance with air traffic control instructions.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Incursion Ramp
synopsis: CRJ-700 First Officer reported a hydraulic system malfunction occurred while enroute and after diverting and waiting to be towed at the airport; the aircraft rolled forward on its own due to the loss of hydraulic pressure on the brakes after the engines were shut down.
text: while enroute, we had a system 3 hydraulic malfunction that required us to land at the nearest suitable airport. we found a spot on the ramp after exiting the runway. we contacted operations to send a tow team to tow us to the gate. in anticipation of the tow team's arrival, we shut down both engines. after waiting about 20 minutes for the tow team, suddenly the aircraft started to roll forward and then stopped. without realizing it, we had been parked in an area that had a slight pitch.in hindsight, we realized that by shutting down the number two engine, we lost hydraulic pressure on the brakes. due to the non-standard configuration of the hydraulic pumps with the hydraulic three malfunction, the normal brake pressure applied by that system was not on. keeping hydraulic two system on would have prevented this problem.cause: the non-standard configuration with the hydraulic system and the high workload related to an unplanned diversion both contributed to this event.suggestions: during non-standard operations with hydraulic system malfunctions, it would be great to have some kind of checklist or reminder to double-check the systems for any non-standard scenarios that might be anticipated. due to the nature of an unplanned diversion, and all the details that come with that non-standard scenario, it was difficult to remember the non-standard situations to expect with system malfunctions.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a temporary loss of aircraft control due to a severe turbulence encounter during cruise.
text: severe turbulence encounter over obk aboard aircraft x, redacted - redacted, xa:14 day 0.aircrew was aware of a large weather system along the route of flight and, on the previous flight (redacted - redacted), had coordinated a significant deviation from the originally filed flight plan due to this weather system. prior to departure, we reviewed the flight plan filed by dispatch, and assessed that, as the route of flight took us to the north of the weather pattern (as opposed to going through the south of it, as we had been filed on the previous leg), we would safely avoid the weather.i conduct all of my welcome aboard announcements via face-to-face communication at the galley. during my pa, i stressed that we would be encountering significant weather during the first 1 - 1.5 hours of the flight, and that it was very important for the passengers to remain seated while the seatbelt sign was on, for their safety, and that i anticipated turning the seatbelt sign off during the remaining hour of the flight.in flight, center (chicago center?) recommended that we add obk to our route to avoid the northernmost boundary of the weather. we entered obk into our weather application, assessed that this was a prudent route modification based on the developing weather, and accepted obk. i also communicated the change to dispatch. we observed an area of moderate turbulence over obk and did not see that as a significant threat, however it was enough for me to ensure that both fas were seated while we penetrated the turbulence in accordance with the fom.i initially directed the fas to remain seated during the initial climb based on other turbulence i observed we would encounter early in the flight, then i released the fas to perform service at their discretion. when i initially released them, i informed them that they would be able to be up for approximately 30 minutes, then they would need to be seated to penetrate an area of anticipated moderate turbulence (over obk). after approximately 30 minutes, and about 5 minutes until we reached obk, i called them to direct them to return to their seats.we had been operating in full imc for about 20 minutes prior to reaching obk. (the weather at obk was visually embedded from our perspective.) air traffic control advised that there was an area of moderate to heavy precipitation around obk, i was tracking this area via both the weather application and the onboard aircraft radar. i noted (via onboard radar) that there was an area of heavy precipitation depicted just south of obk, and that our route appeared to slightly bypass that area to the north. weather application still showed moderate turbulence.we encountered substantial turbulence as we reached obk. altitude and airspeed deviations were so violent that it was nearly impossible to keep up with them, i estimate that we had +- 500 ft. of altitude loss/gain at one point. first officer as pf slowed from mach .77 to .75, and i engaged both continuous ignition and the turbulence mode on the fcp.based on the information displayed on our weather application, i believed that we would not be in the worst of the turbulence for very long, so it was in our best interest to continue in our direction of flight instead of turn around. the event lasted approximately two minutes. after exiting the severe turbulence, i assessed that we had just experienced a severe turbulence encounter and called the fas to assess the conditions in the cabin. the fas reported no injuries or known damage. i then reported a severe turbulence encounter to air traffic control, consulted relevant guidance on the fom, notified dispatch of the encounter and requested maintenance to meet us at redacted.after reaching the western michigan area and exiting all turbulence, i turned off the seatbelt sign and the flight continued normally.in my opinion, the weather in the area around obk simply progressed worse / faster than forecast, and there just was not a viable means available to any of the relevant actors (flight crew, air traffic control and dispatch) to detect that area of severe turbulence.dispatch provided what appeared to be a safe route prior to departure (having immediately prior to that fight to initiate a route modification to that same departure point, i closely scrutinized the proposed route to avoid a repeat of that situation). air traffic control specifically recommended obk to further isolate us from the weather. dispatch was informed and did not object to the route modification. flight crew was actively monitoring the weather during our approach to obk via weather application and onboard radar, there was simply nothing to indicate an area of severe turbulence via the resources available to the crew, and likely dispatch or air traffic control.risks to passengers and crew were successfully mitigated by direct and constant communication and ensuring cabin preparation for turbulence penetration.suggestions: information only.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A320 Captain reported diverting after the flight crew received several ECAMs of a cabin pressurization malfunction.
text: aircraft was in cruise flight, 34, 000 ft., on a weather deviation approximately 35 miles east of route between the redacted and redacted intersections. flight was proceeding normally, we were anticipating a turn back on course to rejoin before redacted (turning back approximately abeam position redacted) as we tracked the weather via radar and satellite data from the weather app. aircraft was dispatched with 2 mels - 21-xx-redacted packs and a46-yy-yyy domestic enroute (usa) cpdlc restricted. the first minimum equipment list meant that we were operating with a single pack - #2. (pack #1 was off per the procedure of the minimum equipment list.)due to reported satcom outages - dispatch just happened to choose our flight to do a satcom voice check. as the non-normal unfolded this fortuitous satcom call from the company helped expedite communications to prep redacted operations for the divert. we were able to communicate our intentions and had both dispatch and maintenance control looped in on the issue as it was happening live. we received the following ecams: air pack 1+2 fault. cab pr lo diff pr. cab pr excess cab alt.we followed sop in accordance with an aeronautical decision-making model and worked the ecams as they presented themselves. i called for priority handling on 121.5 (guard) - announced our intentions to divert to redacted and we began an expedited descent to 10, 000 ft. redacted [artcc] air traffic control responded to our distress call - gave us a new frequency, established radar contact, and gave us a vector towards the airport (redacted). we donned our o2 masks and established flight deck communications. continued to work the non-normal while on the expedited descent. the situation continued to evolve as the associated ecams began appearing - i.e., cab pr lo diff pr & cab pr excess cab alt. i communicated to inflight via the call button - they answered right away. i told them that we were in a situation. explained the reason (loss of pressurization system) and told them our time to landing. i also made a pa to the passengers letting them know that we would be making an unscheduled stop, giving them a non-technical explanation of the problem, and that we'd have more information for them on the ground for how they would continue their journey to redacted. i was told during the post-flight debrief with the inflight crew that i did a stellar job pushing and pulling the information to both inflight and the passengers. inflight felt very calm about the whole non-normal as it evolved. (aside from the ear-popping) inflight told me that the passengers were very calm and nonplussed the whole time. my pa from the flight deck diffused any cabin stress that would have led to an undesirable outcome once on the ground.we continued working aspects of the non-normal and transited into the arrival and approach phase of the flight. our new destination was inputted, weather obtained, approach was built and briefed, charts and airport company pages reviewed. in this phase of flight - everything was stable. the cabin altitude was at a safe breathable level, we had removed our o2 masks and reestablished flight deck comms. important to note, the passenger o2 masks did not deploy from the passenger service units (psus) during the non-normal. we were proceeding on a vector to our approach - rvav xx into redacted. i took the time to review the overweight landing qrh checklist. (our landing weight was 147.8 - a couple of thousand pounds higher than max for that particular weight variant.) also, the divert checklist in the manual. i wanted to ensure that we were covering all of our bases and not missing anything. i also reviewed the steps we took during the non-normal up to this point - i talked out loud" while first officer and i discussed what got us from 34, 000 ft. to this approach into redacted and plainly asked, "did we forget anything?" the aircraft was expertly landed in redacted by first officer. he followed the guidance in accordance with the overweight checklist. "soft" touchdown and the brakes did not heat up above approximately 200 c. we taxied to the gate where we were met by station operations, local crash fire rescue (cfr), local customs and immigration, and local maintenance control representatives. times were noted and passed to dispatch. i made the following write-ups in the logbook: air pack 1+2 fault inflight - may have been due to ovht condition. cab pr excess cab alt ecam - associated with the above write-up. cab pr lo diff pr - associated with write-ups. overweight landing due to divert - landing weight: 147, 800 lb., soft touchdown, temperatures less than 210 c. nav tuning ls disagree inflight - reset as per qrh - continued normally. the 5th write-up was not associated with the situation, non-normal, or divert. after that i talked with the maintenance control representative, station operations, and made a pa for the passengers talking about next steps. passengers were deplaned and the non-normal was debriefed (informally) with all of the crew. aircraft was taken out of service and a flight was dispatched. any unintentional (or otherwise) deviations from sop were done under captain's authority under the appropriate fars. any errors were trapped using our threat and error management (tem) model. i would like to commend (and sincerely thank) the crew - first officer and fas - for their professionalism and skill during the event and divert to redacted. their quick thinking, calm demeanor, and adherence to sop made this a very easy problem to navigate. i may be the final authority and ultimately responsible for the flight, but we couldn't have done what we did without the support of the whole crew doing their jobs competently and without delay. they are all the best. i'd also like to thank the instructor pilots at company. every instructor that i interacted during every training event for the past years contributed to the safe outcome of this non-normal. in conclusion, we had a safe and successful outcome. i can tell you honestly that i will be debriefing this incident internally for the rest of my career - with many lessons learned. our flight had a serious mechanical problem and we stayed off social media and out of the news. the passengers seemed genuinely not annoyed with the outcome - they still got to their final destination, albeit a little later than they hoped. our training and the safety systems worked the way that they were designed. it wasn't perfect - no real world non-normal is. i'm very proud of my crew and it's ultimately because of them (and the whole company support structure) that we completed the flight as successfully as we did."
