synopsis: A220 First Officer reported the aircraft initiated an aggressive descent trying to catch the flight director and the flight crew disconnected the automation to regain control.
text: we were flying a220 into redacted on the redacted and had just leveled off at the bottom altitude of 5, 000 ft. at redacted. after passing the fix, the captain (pilot flying) selected heading mode and requested the route be cleaned up for the approach. as the pilot monitoring i cleaned up the approach by placing redacted as the from waypoint and executing. shortly thereafter we received a clearance to descend and maintain 2, 000 ft. the captain selected 2, 000 ft. and hit flc as usual. the plane initiated an aggressive descent trying to catch the flight director (fd) which was indicating a steep dive. the throttles also started to command a high power setting. the plane ended up in an accelerating nose low attitude increasing well above the bugged 250 kt. the captain attempted to troubleshoot the issue and confirm the selections on the fcp. as pm i was monitoring the rate of descent and our altitude and speed which was approaching 300 kt. and 2, 000 ft. rapidly. the captain removed all automation by turning the autothrottles and autopilot off. the aircraft was returned to level flight at 2, 200 ft. with a brief overspeed to 304 kt. we then proceeded to maintain our assigned altitude of 2, 000 ft. as the aircraft slowed. there was no air traffic control recognition of the excessive descent or high speed as we leveled by the assigned altitude of 2, 000 ft. automation was re-established and initially it looked like the fd was indicating another dive. automation was again disconnected and re-established and everything seemed to be functioning as usual. we completed the approach and landing without any further anomalies.

synopsis: DA42 Flight Instructor reported having to divert after the left engine would not restart after an intentional shutdown for training purposes.
text: during one engine inoperative demonstration, under flight instructor controls, aircraft was level, 6 - 7 nm away from redacted, at 3400 ft. msl (approximately 3350 ft. agl). lh engine intentionally shut down under flight instructor controls. when restarting lh engine after demonstration was over, lh engine master was turned on and starter engaged, lh engine did not unfeather or engage to start. when lh engine master was on, lh engine control unit (ecu) a/b annunciations appeared but did not latch. ran qrc/qrh checklists. lh engine still inoperative. flight instructor diverted to redacted and made landing. flight instructor was able to exit runway onto nearest taxiway, towed to parking. no injuries or damage. diversion due to mechanical failure. engine shutdown during flight, not related to single-engine training in a multi-engine airplane.

synopsis: EMB 170 Captain reported receiving a low fuel indication during approach. Flight continued to landing.
text: aircraft came out of maintenance with mel 28-xx-xx-x states that you could get fuel 1(2) lo level. on approach into redacted after leaving 10, 000ft and leveling at 7, 000 on the zzzx arrival. we received fuel 2 lo level indicators not knowing if it's a fuel quantity issue or fuel indication issue ran the qrh. we advised air traffic control as an abundance of caution as during this time if message was true we didn't have a lot of time to sort out and needed to get on the ground. being unsure if this associated with minimum equipment list or a different indication issue while having fuel lo level indicating on eicas we followed qrh. we were 5 min from landing at redacted landing xx called fa and told them we were a priority aircraft because of this indication did not issue brace command and there was no special considerations for them, did not have the emergency vehicles meet aircraft and landed at redacted with no incident. taxied to gate and called mx (maintenance).

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Flight instructor with student reported a NMAC during cruise required evasive action.
text: i was conducting flight training with a student over redacted waypoint, performing published holding practice for the rnav rwyxx approach at redacted. we were under radar services and maintaining active two-way radio communication with air traffic control. while established in the holding pattern, air traffic control advised us of a visual flight rules traffic (a beech debonair) flying erratically at an altitude that directly conflicted with our flight path. air traffic control repeatedly attempted to contact the target aircraft on the frequency to establish traffic separation, but the aircraft failed to respond to multiple radio calls, acting as a non-responsive traffic. as the target aircraft continued to tract directly into our holding airspace and intervened in our flight path, air traffic control instructed us to take immediate evasive action.we were unable to maintain a standard, squared holding track.evaluating the situation under aeronautical decision making (adm) principles, i determined that continuing the holding practice in the vicinity of a non-communicative and unpredictable aircraft posed an unacceptable hazard to flight safety. consequently, i chose to terminate the maneuver early and returned to redacted for a safe and uneventful landing.furthermore, a recent review of this specific aircraft's track logs indicates that it consistently utilizes this exact training area and fix for maneuvers. because this appears to be a recurring flight pattern rather than an isolated event, i am submitting this report to highlight a systemic risk and prevent identical hazardous conflicts from occurring in the future.

synopsis: Cirrus pilot reported a near miss during take off with an aircraft in position for takeoff at the other end of the runway.
text: today i was departing redacted runway xx when i had a near miss event with another aircraft. awos at redacted was reporting calm wind with metar an hour earlier reporting wind from 350 at 5. the designated calm wind runway at redacted is xx per chart supplement. i have been on the frequency while taxiing and doing the run-up. there were no communications on the frequency, which is usual for xa:20am. i did announce entering the runway and while speaking i cross-checked the tx annunciation on my idf440 radio. i do not always cross check it, but i did not hear the usual click on the radio when i keyed mic, so that caught my attention and i made sure i was transmitting. the departure was uneventful, however on the upwind another aircraft called me with 'radio check' and said that they were on runway xy when i was departing and i departed over them. i did not see the opposite side traffic while departing. this means i did not paid enough attention to check that the opposite side of runway is clear.

synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a NMAC at a non-towered airport.
text: i am the instructor of the da-40-40. practicing the vor xx circle xy into redacted. we made calls at redacted, xx nm final for rwy xx, 3 nm final, and 2 nm final, all mentioning vor xx circle xy. the other aircraft, aircraft y, did not make any calls, took off of rwy xy, and made a quick turn from upwind to crosswind at our altitude as my student went visual at minimums to circle. i took controls and descended to maintain visual whilst evading the traffic. after evasive action was taken, i asked traffic if they had us in sight. if i had not taken action, there would have been a collision with potential fatalities.

synopsis: PA-28 pilot reported the aircraft door opened at a low altitude; just after rotation. The pilot reduced power and landed on the remainder of the takeoff runway.
text: we experienced another unlatched door during take off. we have been careful with securing the latch during ground operations. this time the top latch opened up after rotation when aircraft is 10 feet airborne. luckily, we were on the long runway of xx at redacted. we idle the throttle, push nose over and returned to landing. we were not able to latch the door again while engine idle. so we taxi back to hanger. after engine shut down, we appears to be able to latch the door again. however, when we inspected the latching mechanism at its latched position, it was not secure. only the tip of the door hook was caught on the metal ring. we reported the problem to aircraft operator / owner / mechanic. they sent us a video on how to adjust the door latch. i do not feel that fixing in flight door latch problem is within my capacity.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Student pilot reported during landing experiencing a gust of wind resulting in the aircraft leaving the runway and coming to a stop on the aircraft's nose.
text: on day 0, i was undertaking flight training from my flight instructor in a piper super cub tailwheel aircraft, aircraft x, to pursue my tailwheel endorsement. the flight started off as any normal training does, we departed redacted to the east towards a training area so i could get a feel for the aircraft. after getting a feel of the aerodynamics of this aircraft, we proceeded to redacted. there we proceeded to enter the pattern and start landing practice.our first few landings were three point landings to get an understanding of the approach and landing of the aircraft. then we transitioned to wheel takeoffs and landings. on the second wheel takeoff, we proceeded as normal in the pattern with myself flying and making calls over the ctaf. as we turned base, the approach was stabilized on centerline and with a good descent rate. a gust on approach moved us left of centerline but was quickly corrected.on short final as we were crossing over the threshold, i brought the power to a position that would assist the wheel landing. on touchdown we started a rollout when a gust hit us on the right side of the aircraft causing us to weathervane into it. the flight instructor quickly hopped on the controls and verbalized his aircraft as the tail swung left into my gusting wind. as the plane started to turn it quickly turned into a ground loop that the flight instructor tried to correct for. suddenly we were pointed towards the grass on the edge of the runway. in an effort to stop the aircraft before rolling off my flight instructor tapped on the brakes in hopes of slowing us down but the plane instead stopped in its tracks causing the nose of the aircraft to fall over and onto the ground.after the aircraft stopped moving and the nose was positioned into the pavement i turned off the engine by cutting the mixture and throttle, turning off the fuel selector, turning off the magnetos and the electrical system. my flight instructor got out of the aircraft first and i followed getting away from the aircraft and assessing ourselves for any injuries. after confirming no injuries we proceeded to talk to the authorities.contributing factors for this event would be the gusting conditions, my little experience in a tailwheel aircraft, and the sensitivity of the aircraft brakes. my flight instructor performed to the best of his abilities and was focused on my safety throughout the incident.

synopsis: B737 First Officer reported a generator drive malfunction during cruise flight and was unable to start the APU to provide an additional back up power source. The flight diverted to an alternate airport.
text: after pushback and during taxi to the runway, the recall panel illuminated with electrical" and "flight control" cautions. we identified illumination of the right generator drive light, right generator source off light, and yaw damper light. ground control was notified and taxi was stopped while the aircraft was positioned in a suitable area to accomplish the appropriate checklists and coordinate with maintenance control.after completion of the applicable checklists and consultation with maintenance, it was determined that a return to the gate was necessary for further troubleshooting. an uneventful gate return was conducted and the appropriate maintenance write-ups were submitted. during troubleshooting, maintenance advised that the discrepancy could potentially be deferred under the minimum equipment list, however, due to the nature of the electrical indications, we were not comfortable accepting the aircraft without corrective action being taken. maintenance continued troubleshooting, subsequently cleared the write-up, and the aircraft was reboarded for departure. taxi, takeoff, climb, and initial cruise were uneventful.while in cruise at fl350, autopilot b disconnected and an additional "electrical" caution annunciated, again accompanied by illumination of the right generator drive light and right generator source off light. i assumed manual control of the aircraft and autopilot a was successfully engaged. the applicable non-normal checklist was accomplished, which directed an in-flight apu start. three in-flight apu start attempts were made at various altitudes, all attempts were unsuccessful.dispatch, maintenance control, and the flight attendants were notified of the situation. due to the unsuccessful in-flight apu start attempts, the checklist directed us to "land at nearest suitable airport." the decision was made to divert to redacted due to favorable weather conditions and the availability of maintenance and customer service support. air traffic control was advised of the diversion and electrical issue, and passengers were updated throughout the event.during diversion planning, we elected to request priority with air traffic control out of an abundance of caution due to the anticipated overweight landing of approximately 2, 100 pounds. an uneventful descent, approach, and landing were accomplished. after clearing the runway, no abnormal indications were observed, and tower and fire command were advised that no additional assistance was required. an uneventful taxi to the gate followed, and the appropriate maintenance write-ups were submitted."

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 Captain reported uncommanded aircraft movement after a headset communication malfunction with the ground crew while being pulled into a gate. The ground crew gave the Captain a signal to set the brakes; no injury or damage occurred.
text: guide man gave stop signal - i stopped the aircraft and set the parking brake. guide man walked towards the aircraft and out of view. i called for the number one engine to be shutdown. moments later the guide man came back into view and gave me the signals to taxi forward. realizing the engines were shut down he established communication with me - advising me he stopped the aircraft on the wrong nose wheel mark. a tug was connected and he requested that i release the parking brake. while adjusting the aircraft position the electronic headsets went out, and the tug driver disconnected the tug from the aircraft without asking for the parking brake to be set. the aircraft started rolling forward while my first officer and i were under the impression that the tug was moving us. a different ground crew personnel hurriedly gave me the signal to set the brakes - and they were set with no aircraft damage.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Tecnam P2012 pilot reported an engine malfunction during the climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and landed.
text: on flight abcd redacted - redacted in aircraft x i was operating as a single pilot. aircraft just came out of maintenance due to an air return the previous evening with the lh engine running rough. everything normal on taxi from gate to runway xxl as well as a standard takeoff. upon climbing through roughly 5-6 thousand feet the left engine started to cough with no tlo (temporary limited operations) or cas (crew alerting system) message. initially assuming it was engine protection mode i reduced the power slightly. for a moment the coughing stopped but then while i continued the climb the coughing returned. while viewing the engine page i noticed the lh oil pressure was in the yellow (low 50's psi) and the lh oil temp was getting close to the red line sitting just above 230 degrees f. once i leveled off i pulled the power to normal cruise settings which stopped the engine from coughing however the lh oil pressure stayed low and the lh oil temp stayed high. at this point i decided to ask air traffic control to return to redacted. air traffic control cleared me back to redacted and vectored me in for a visual xx. air traffic control inquired about the reason for coming back to redacted, which i informed them the left engine was not running properly at high power. air traffic control prioritized my aircraft and proceeded to get me back to redacted promptly. landing was normal and upon landing i was asked if i needed any assistance which i answered negative. engine did not cough after i asked to return to redacted. taxied into the gate uneventfully and passengers were taken care of. i then proceeded to contact maintenance control, operations, and the chief pilot.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A321 pilot reported while parked at the gate the aircraft began to roll resulting in the flight crew applying brakes to regain control of the aircraft.
text: on day 0 while operating aircraft x the flight crew experienced an un commanded movement of the aircraft during the shutdown portion of the flight. after being guided to a complete stop at the gate, the parking brake was set and park brk message verified along with normal pressure indications. the shutdown flow continued in sequence and during the portion of the flow while heads were down, the aircraft began to roll. once the un commanded movement was realized, the captain slammed on the brakes immediately. the aircraft came to an abrupt stop. at some point during the roll or just prior to toe brakes being applied the crew received a brakes park brk fault ecam message with zero pressure indicated on the accumulator. there were no injuries to ground crew, flight crew or passengers. there was no damage to either the aircraft or jet bridge. the crew followed standard operating procedures and maintained positive control of the aircraft to the best of their ability throughout the event. once the aircraft was confirmed chocked, the toe brakes were released and the parking brake recycled which then cleared the ecam and returned hydraulic pressure back to normal. the aircraft was subsequently repositioned via tug vehicle and secured. maintenance was contacted shortly after.cause: this event appears to be purely an aircraft systems failure. per the logbook, the aircraft has a history of this very same problem and clearly needs to be fixed permanently. one recommendation that the crew can add to help mitigate the risk of injury to the passengers would be to relocate the seat belt sign off to one of the last items on the shutdown flow and checklist. the passengers were thrown forward when the brakes were slammed on bc the seatbelt sign had been turned off per the second step of the flow. engines were still running which allowed the aircraft to move forward quickly. had the engines been shutdown prior to the seat belt sign being extinguished, we may not have had the high risk of injuring a passenger.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Ramp tower personnel reported a ground conflict with two aircraft.
text: i gave pushback approval to aircraft x off xx gate. no other aircraft cleared into the alley. aircraft x takes up the entire top half of the alley as it's a widebody. i noticed an e175 coming into the taxiway 1 north line and aircraft x made a hard stop as they were in pushback process. i could not get the e175, aircraft y, to stop before they entered as they were not on my frequency. they entered the wrong alley and did not attempt to stop as aircraft x clearly is halfway in pushback. they took it all the way into the alley stopping only at the very bottom were i had another aircraft, b737, taxing left to the taxiway 1 south line. i immediately notified management. there was no aircraft damage or personnal injured. aircraft y was assigned gate xy which is the next alley over.looking out the window tried reaching out to aircraft y aircraft x had already stopped.cause: aircraft y clearly did not know where they were going.notified management and as no one stated any damage/iinjury we filed a report.suggestions: better pilot training.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Citation I/SP Captain reported experiencing severe weather on the climb resulting in loss of control of the aircraft. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft and continued to their destination.
text: i was flying the zzzzzx departure on a charter flight on day 0 with many scattered thunderstorms at all altitudes. due to this, many planes were being vectored off of the departures to avoid severe weather. after taking a vector to the west to avoid a large storm i was assigned a climb up to fl230 but upon starting the climb realized it would climb me right into the bottom of a thunderstorm cell. i then requested a level off passing through 15500 ft and atc approved a level off at 16000 ft. by this time, we were already picking up moderate mixed icing and constant light to moderate chop as well as airspeed fluctuations. as i began to assign the level off to the autopilot, we began getting blown downward by downdrafts as well as moderate chop. by the end of all this we had descended back down to about 15400 ft and were then out of the storm cell. atc requested that i repeat my assigned altitude at which time i stated i was aware it was 16000 ft and then explained the situation described above. the controller understood and i was assigned to maintain 15000 ft.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter FOD
synopsis: Corporate Safety Officer reported a turbine engine starting event of abnormal high engine temperature after starting. The engine was shutdown and inspected where an engine cover was discovered ingested in one of the turboprop engine compressor blades.
text: rh engine start - engine started normally then abnormal indications of engine temperature noted. engine shut down & inspected, found engine plug positioned sideways having been ingested into engine compressor blades by about 4 inches. initial walkround conducted upon arrival to aircraft, with engine plugs left in due to expected delay. when decision to fly was made, another pre-flight carried out & 3 of 4 plugs removed. momentary lapse of attention when attending to rh engine meant plug was left in. not visible from flight deck when starting engines leading to ingestion.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: DA-900 flight crew reported a critical ground conflict with a vehicle entering the runway while they were near rotation speed on the takeoff roll.
text: we taxied unicom from the ramp to best suitable runway per the winds which was runway xxr. after all procedures were adhered per the faa procedures for unicom uncontrolled airport. we made sure we crossed all runways and advice in the unicom frequency that we were crossing and that we were cleared of the runways. when we received clearance for departure from redacted approach we lined up in runway xxr and informed again in the unicom frequency that we were lining up and that we were on the roll for takeoff. whilst on the roll i saw the vehicle approaching the hold short in taxiway 1 but the truck did not move further. near rotation speed the truck entered the runway from left to right and we cleared the truck by 50ft. we continued our flight and landed safely in our destination. thankfully no one suffered any damages.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported seeing people on the runway as they were taking off resulting in the pilot taking evasive action to avoid overflying the people on the runway.
text: i landed at x06 for fuel. the airport was busy with takeoffs and landings while i was refueling. upon taxiing out for departure on runway 06 there was a lull in traffic. after run up i checked for landing traffic then announced on 123.0 unicom that i was taking the active 06 runway for takeoff and departure. there were no aircraft on the runway so i lined up and did a final cockpit check. my aircraft is a taildragger so once lined up, you cannot see down the runway over the nose. the takeoff roll was short about 600 feet. once airborne, i could now see ahead and saw two people on the runway past the halfway point. they were walking off the runway to the left so i immediately initiated a climbing, right turn to avoid overflying them. i was about to make a radio call to warn that there were people on the runway when the ground operator began admonishing me for taking off. apparently the operator knew they were there, but never announced it or warned me when i called my intention to depart. this could have been avoided if a vehicle with a flashing light were present or if the people on the runway had a handheld radio to issue warnings. the runway could also have been closed. i have no idea why there were personnel on the runway.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Bonanza 33 Flight Instructor and student reported landing gear did not extend during approach for landing; requiring manual extension.
text: during an instrument flight plan for a commercial complex time building flight, there were no abnormalities noted enroute and no prior indications of electrical malfunction. air traffic control vectored us to a right downwind for runway xx, and the autopilot was engaged without issue. we were subsequently vectored onto base and then final approach. while being vectored onto final, the autopilot unexpectedly disconnected. tower cleared us for the visual approach and asked if we had the airport in sight. we responded, however tower advised they did not receive our transmission. a second attempt revealed that both com and nav equipment were intermittently powering off and attempting to reboot. we squawked 7600 immediately. tower then transmitted asking if we could hear them and requested to ident, which we complied with. we began running the appropriate checklist procedures to troubleshoot the electrical issue. upon attempting landing gear extension on final, the gear did not respond and we had no indication signaling the gear was down. we conducted a low approach and executed a climb out on runway heading while remaining in a right closed traffic pattern. during the downwind, we contacted redacted clearance delivery by telephone and obtained the tower phone number. we subsequently established communication with the tower while on right downwind for runway xx and advised them the situation. we requested another low approach for tower personnel to visually verify landing gear position. the landing gear was manually extended using the emergency extension procedure while we were downwind. tower advised that all three gear appeared down and locked. we remained in a right closed pattern for one additional circuit and subsequently landed on runway xx without further incident.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: C140 pilot reported loss of aircraft control during taxi resulted in runway excursion.
text: i am a private pilot considering pursuing a tailwheel endorsement. i was receiving dual instruction (dual received) from a certified flight instructor (cfi). this was my first lesson in a tailwheel aircraft, focusing on ground handling characteristics and directional control. while operating at a non-towered airport, we were practicing tight taxi turns and pivot maneuvers on an inactive runway to familiarize myself with tailwheel steering dynamics. during a turn, the aircraft began to drift further than anticipated due to my insufficient initial braking application. as the aircraft approached the edge of the pavement, i experienced momentary spatial disorientation and over-applied the wheel brakes in an effort to stop the aircraft. this sudden braking action created a nose-over tendency as the aircraft transitioned onto the grass area. the propeller struck the grass surface. the cfi immediately pulled the mixture control to cut the engine and secure the aircraft. there were no injuries to anyone on board or on the ground. the aircraft was grounded immediately for a thorough maintenance inspection. the event was entirely inadvertent during a dual training environment.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B757 flight crew reported miscommunication between the flight and ground crews led to the aircraft rolling a few feet during a gate arrival procedure.
text: upon arrival at redacted we taxied to gate xx. we kept the throttles at idle in/through the turn to parking per the company pages, however the aircraft momentum led us to stop short of the hold line and we required a tow in. i announced to the passengers to keep their seatbelts on and we would be towed to the gate. after brakes had been set the ground crew moved the tug in front of the aircraft beneath the line of sight from the cockpit. after a pause, one of the rampers on the captain side of the aircraft gave a hand signal quickly. i interpreted this as the opening hands signal to release brakes and did so. there was a short pause and the aircraft began moving. i initially perceived this as tug movement on the aircraft. the first officer said something expressing concern, which i first thought was due to him not having seen the signal directly. within another second or so we both applied brakes and i reset the parking brake. the aircraft had moved a few feet, but i couldn't give an exact distance. via interphone we resestablished positive comms with the ramper and the rest of the tow-in was uneventful. no aircraft damage or personnel injury occurred. i met with and debriefed with the rampers. i don't believe any passengers were alarmed by aircraft movement. i phoned the chief pilot and relayed the above information.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Ramp personnel reported while towing an aircraft into the gate the released the brakes unexpectedly resulting in aircraft rolling.
text: at gate xx the crew and i were receiving a flight. because of the slope at gate xx, the pilot could not reach all the way the parking spot, so the aircraft had to be towed all the way to the correct spot. person a gave the captain the hand signal of 'set brake'. afterwards the crew and i began the process of putting the parking chocks, connecting the bypass pin to the plane, and connecting the lektro to the plane. as i was in the process connecting the strap, the captain released brakes and the plane began to roll away to the side and the crew had to give the captain the hand signals to set brakes. we luckily were able to have the plane stop and than we proceeded to correct the error. during the offload, the captain spoke to us and stated he assumed we told to release brakes when in fact no one ever did

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported maximum braking was required to avoid a collision with a vehicle crossing their path at high speed.
text: specific location: ramp, spot 1sphase of flight: taxi outdescription of eventupon contacting atlanta ground, we received clearance to taxi behind aircraft y. after aircraft y passed and our sequence began, we initiated taxi. prior to aircraft movement, the taxi light was turned on to provide external visual indication of our intent to move. both the first officer and i conducted a thorough left-and-right clearing scan, confirming that the taxi path and surrounding area, including nearby ground trucks, were completely clear.immediately after commencing movement, while maintaining active outside vigilance, an airport ground vehicle crossed directly in front of our nose at an extremely high rate of speed. the vehicle's sudden crossing left zero reaction buffer. to prevent an imminent collision and preserve the safety integrity of the aircraft, crew, and passengers, i immediately applied maximum heavy braking. the vehicle did not stop, slow down, or yield right-of-way. once the conflict resolved, taxi was resumed normally.upon arrival at the destination, a flight attendant reported sustaining a back injury as a direct result of the sudden, abrupt braking required to avoid the reckless ground vehicle.causethis event represents a critical, high-risk safety breach caused entirely by the non-compliant operation of a ground vehicle. the excessive speed of the vehicle and its failure to yield to an aircraft with active taxi lights created an immediate hazard, directly causing a crew injury and narrowly avoiding a major collision.it is strongly recommended that airport authority telemetry, ramp surveillance footage, or gate cameras from atl at the specified date and time be reviewed to identify the vehicle and operator. ground vehicle operators must be held strictly accountable to airport driving regulations. failure to identify this operator and enforce compliance poses an ongoing, severe threat to ramp safety integrity.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Military helicopter unit safety officer reported a crew encountering two high wing aircraft opposite direction in ZAN airspace resulting in a NMAC.
text: a helicopter completed a search and rescue mission in the vicinity of herendeen bay. the helicopter was flying between 250-500' agl through a mountain pass to get to sand point, alaska (pasd) to drop off the survivor and to obtain fuel. enroute to sand point, near 5537.37n/16051.08w, approximately 200'-250' agl, two aircraft, described as high-wing, were traveling through the pass in the opposite direction. the helicopter took action and descended to the left. at the lowest point, the helicopter was at approximately 100' agl. it appeared that the two other aircraft were flying in a loose formation and they were banking left. one of the oncoming aircraft passed on the left side of the helicopter approximately co-altitude with 300' of separation, and the other flew directly overhead approximately 150' above the helicopter. the helicopter pilots reported the incident to air station kodiak as a 'serious near mid air collision.' there were no damage nor injuries reported to the helicopter crew. the crew is unsure if the other two aircraft were aware that they were flying through the area. there were no radio transmissions made or heard within the helicopter. visibility was reported from 1/2 to 2 miles. ceilings were reported as low as 500' within the pass.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported while in the traffic pattern; they were following ATC instructions that created airborne conflicts resulting in the pilot taking evasive action to avoid a collision.
text: good afternoon. during visual pattern operations for runway 26 at colorado air and space port, i observed two traffic sequencing and communication issues from tower control that reduced safety margins and required pilot corrective action.while intercepting final from the south on an approximate 360-degree heading, my aircraft was sequenced behind another aircraft on base to final. due to a significant closure rate, i assessed that spacing would become unsafe near or shortly after final approach intercept despite early speed reduction. i maintained visual contact and ads-b awareness of the traffic throughout the event.radio congestion limited the ability to clarify instructions with tower. to maintain safe separation, i offset slightly east of final approach course. tower communications and sequencing during the event indicated reduced situational awareness and ineffective traffic management consistent with degraded crew resource management and communication discipline.following the touch-and-go, additional pattern instructions resulted in a second developing overtaking conflict on right downwind. unable to safely match the slower aircraft's pattern speed and spacing, i extended upwind until constrained by the denver international airport class b airspace, then turned crosswind and maneuvered north of the expected pattern track to maintain safe separation.in both instances, corrective action by my aircraft was required to maintain safe separation and avoid an unsafe traffic conflict created by sequencing, tower desired ground track and communication deficiencies within the pattern. tower responses following both events suggested confusion and frustration regarding the evolving traffic situation. i departed the pattern visual flight rules to the east without further incident.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying a UAS during civil twilight without anti-collision lights.
text: i operated the dji mini 4 pro after sunset, during civil evening twilight, without operable anti-collision lights. i remembered the requirement in 14 cfr part 107.29(a) requiring anti-collision lights at 'night' (30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise), but forgot about the second requirement in 14 cfr part 107.29(b) requiring anti-collision lights during civil twilight.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: TRACON Controller reported they forgot to inform an aircraft to climb before it flew below the MVA.
text: during the time of this event, i was the on-the-job training instructor (ojti) for our radar east position training person a. we were on for about an hour already at the time. while traffic volume was not high, there had been increased complexity with parachute jump area (pja) happening, and multiple visual flight rules and primary targets that were a factor with our traffic that we were not in contact with. there was a visual identification tagged aircraft flying over redacted airport at 056 and local control (lc) (training in progress at the time) called asking if we wanted their next departure capped at 040 for them, which we said yes to. that cap was to stop a tcas-resolution advisory from happening. we were discussing at the time if the cap was necessary or not. aircraft x was put on course direct to redacted [vor]. we got distracted with other things, and aircraft x leveled at 040 towards the 044 mva and was not told to climb, by neither person a nor myself. aircraft x then requested higher as he was entering the 044 mva, which then person a told aircraft x to contact redacted [artcc]. it was at that time i realized he wasn't told to climb to 090 and keyed up to have him climb, though i did not issue a low altitude alert. he was 3 miles in the mva at the time.we should've put a focus on that aircraft and had continued their climb.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported encountering GPS jamming in cruise flight near ELP airport. Crew re-set a circuit breaker in an attempt to fix the issue; but multiple problems surfaced; and they diverted to an alternate airport.
text: while in flight around elp we experienced gps jamming. after a while we received gps and gls fmc alert messages. i verified rnp value of .24 and referenced the flight manual (fm). both left and right gps were failed at this time. it was anticipated that once clear of the gps jamming that all systems would return to normal. for some additional context at this point of the flight we had been navigating through thunderstorms and i had all the flight attendants seated. when approaching the portion of flight that was about to cross the gulf i reached out to dispatch and maintenance control to try to recover our gps as i was thinking about the gps issue more and was concerned that being away from land base nav aids for such a long time would cause the anp to drift to unacceptable levels for a long segment over water. maintenance control directed to pull the multi-mode receiver (mmr) instrument landing system-1 circuit breaker (cb) per fm. it was during this reset both fmc failed, autothrottle, autopilot, disengaged and the aircraft went into control wheel steering (cws). the first officer flew the aircraft and was able to recover and engage the cmd with alt hold/cws. we received radar vectors from air traffic control to stay over the houston shoreline at fl330. at this time chief pilot also was on the line and together we walked through a recovery of the right fmc was accomplished with the return of the control display unit (cdu) fmc functionality. it was at this time the options were discussed about how to proceed and i made the decision to divert due to the amounts of threats with the current aircraft maintenance status and external factors such as thunderstorms, overwater operations, international operations, remaining fuel on board, and weather upon arrival.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: Embraer 145 First Officer reported a cockpit smoke event from a communications panel during a cruise climb. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed overweight with no injuries.
text: the flight from redacted to redacted started off uneventful. everything was going smoothly and as expected. during our climb to fl330, at fl320 i noticed a faint amount of smoke coming from the ptt button panel. there was also a noticeable burning plastic smell. the smoke did not stick around very long and was gone in roughly 20 seconds. the burning smell did remain throughout the flight though. captain was the pilot flying when we noticed the smoke and smell. captain transferred controls to me and requested priority handling with air traffic control. it was a very small amount of smoke, but it was still smoke. so we did our smoke fire and fumes memory action items. we established communication but the captain was slightly hard to hear with the masks on. captain tried making another call to air traffic control but they could not understand anything he was saying due to the mask not being clear. we transferred controls back to him and i took over communications and checklists. i cleared up confusion with air traffic control that was present from captain not being understood. we established we were a priority aircraft and would like to divert to redacted. we were told to descend and we could expect vectors for the instrument landing system xx into redacted. while we started a fast descent, captain sent a message through acars to dispatch that we were diverting. i got out our qrh after confirming our memory action items from the qrc. i started the smoke fire or fumes qrh. while going through this checklist i did get interrupted a few times. i needed to relay to air traffic control our situation. i told them our fuel on board and the souls on board. i needed to make this call a couple times as they did not hear clearly the first time. once that was clear we called back to the flight attendant that we were diverting and seeing if he had any smoke in the cabin. he could not understand the captain and after a couple attempts, i told him we were diverting and learned he did not have any smoke in the back. while this conversation was happening air traffic control was giving us instructions to swap frequencies and to keep descending. i believe we got swapped to approach at roughly 14, 000 msl. approach gave us a heading to fly as well for the instrument landing system xx. while we were descending, and i was handling communications, the captain got the approach loaded and frequencies set up. communications were set up and the approach was loaded. i continued the qrh and got to the point of executing an emergency descent, at this point captain said to pause that checklist as we needed to focus on preparing for landing. we were also at roughly 10, 000 msl so we did not need any more of an emergency descent as we had acted quickly about getting lower. on our descent i called the fa for a briefing. i told him there was smoke and we are landing in redacted. i told him he had roughly 5 minutes or less until landing. no special instructions as we should be going to the gate as normal. no bracing signal. i had him report that back and he did so perfectly. continued our descent, we broke out of imc at roughly 8, 000 msl if i recall correctly, after having being in imc up until this point through the issue. captain gave a briefing on the approach. afterward, i ran the cruise, descent, and approach checklists. both of us verifying items were complete and accurate. after running the approach checklists, i checked our weight and told the captain we would be over max landing weight. we got swapped to tower and continued our approach. i ran the overweight landing checklist and we utilized the new landing distance that we were still in compliance with. we were cleared to land by tower on runway xx. with the landing, captain came in slightly below glide slope to have some time to arrest our descent. he did so very well and we touched down very smoothly. tower told us we could stop on taxi way 1 after exiting the runway but we elected to get to the ramp. while we taxied i gave a passenger announcement that we were in redacted due to a precautionary event and we would give them an update when we have one.i apologized about the inconvenience of the diversion and for not addressing them in the air as we were quite busy. tower gave us instructions to cross runway xy on 2. we got to the ramp and a fire truck was parked in front of the intersection, 3, that we took. the captain came to a stop as it seemed two firefighters were approaching us and wanted us to stop. the firefighters came up to the plane with both engines running. they did not appear to see anything abnormal as they were very calm. they wanted to communicate and gave us some hand motions to their ears. the captain and i opened our windows and i tried shouting to them that we could still smell the burning plastic. i had the goggles and mask still on which made this hard. they handed up a note pad to the captain and we coordinated to taxi to a gate with passing the note pad back and forth. i told the captain that we can still smell the smoke and mentioned evacuating there. he said no, it will be much better getting passengers off at the gate and i agreed. we did not confirm with the fa that everyone was seated before we started moving again. later, fa did tell me that everyone was seated when we started moving. we did not contact company ops in redacted, which looking back could have made the ground operations a bit smoother for us. while we taxied to the gate i addressed the passengers and apologized again about the inconvenience and thanked them for their understanding. while addressing the passengers i did not use an alarmed tone or emergency terminology. we parked the plane and continued to run all of our check lists on the ground as normal. the passengers started to deplane and while everyone was exiting, they were very grateful for keeping them safe. many expressed their thanks to our entire crew. no passengers reported any sort of illness or injuries. firefighters came aboard and utilized their heat camera and said they did not see anything triggering it. we assumed the source of the smoke was confirmed to be out. we talked with dispatch and maintenance and got everything situated for the day. the crew took a deadhead back to redacted.suggestions: i would suggest that during training there be a little more emphasis of what to do with issues when safely on the ground. our situation was time critical but did not constitute an emergency evacuation that would have drawn much more attention to the situation. the communications on the ground were lacking as well. i had assumed tower would have gotten a spot set up for us to go to when on the ground but they seemed very laid back with the mentality that we can go wherever we want.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported loss of directional control on landing roll that resulted in contact with a runway light. Upon parking at the gate; the APU failed and the aircraft went dark.
text: set up and departure from the gate at redacted was normal, however, i did notice that while taxiing the aircraft would veer to the left requiring right tiller and rudder inputs to remain straight. in spite of this i didn't consider the aircraft unsafe to fly with taxi and take off uneventful.weather en-route was stormy with storms moving through the redacted area, wx in redacted low instrument flight rules. by the time we arrived in the terminal area the storms had moved through with only light rain, winds at 010/8 and runway code at 555. flying the instrument landing system to runway xxr at redacted, the aircraft touched down on the runway centerline, however, just after the nose wheel contacted the runway the aircraft immediately veered to the left. my immediate thought was the aircraft was hydroplaning so i released brake pressure and applied right rudder. it felt like we were sliding towards the runway edge and i was concerned too much right rudder would exacerbate the slide. the reversers deployed but i don't think reverse thrust activated. as the aircraft slowed, i was able to regain control, return to the centerline and exit the runway. there was no shuddering or shimmy from the gear throughout the event.i slowly taxied to the gate with the aircraft still showing the left taxi bias we experienced in redacted. at this point the first officer mentioned he thought we may have hit one of the runway edge lights. it turned out we indeed had hit one of the runway lights between taxiway 1 and 2. there was no noticeable damage to the nose wheel or the aircraft. the only evidence was glass in the right nose-wheel rim. taxiing to the gate and once we started the apu the electrical system went haywire. master caution warnings and the eicas lit up like a christmas tree. the apu gen bus was offline, which would not reset. my pfd (primary flight display) and the first officer's mfd (multi-function flight display) went dark and it was like we were on essential power at the gate. an electrical reset completed under maintenance supervision fixed that issue. the passengers disembarked without any comment regarding the landing or the power outage at the gate. their only comments were regarding the turbulence enroute. my first officer is a low time pilot with just over 100 hrs on type, however, he was excellent throughout this event and was a tremendous help supporting me while i was communicating with maintenance and operations.suggestions: the event was typical of uncommanded steering and i probably should've disengaged the steering and called for a tow to the gate. i thought of this as i regained control however i think the startle factor played a role here. noticing the taxi trend to veer left maybe i should've considered a gate return, however the aircraft was late to the gate and i had a similar condition previously with the aircraft not tracking straight, however, previously it was not an issue. i didn't consider the aircraft unsafe to fly.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Maintenance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A321 flight crew reported an ENG 2 Reverser fault ECAM during the takeoff roll. The takeoff was rejected and the flight taxied back to the gate.
text: aircraft was being worked on at redacted for roughly 3-4 hours due to numerous logbook write-ups to include a thrust reverser issue. eventually logbook was balanced and minimum equipment list and cdl (configuration deviation list) were reviewed. i even called dispatch and was patched thru to maintenance control to review the maintenance actions which had taken place to give me more peace of mind. aircraft appeared airworthy. we boarded. taxi out normal. rejected the takeoff at redacted on runway xxl at 90 kts. due to thrust reverser 2 fault and epr 2 inop amber fault and aircraft yaw. it was suspected that the #2 reverser deployed during takeoff roll. complied with company rejected takeoff procedures.taxied back to the gate and completed required logbook write-ups and followed up with call to dispatch and also consulted maintenance control with debrief of rejected takeoff.cause: more thorough process of explaining the remedy to correct the original thrust reverser write up.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: Airbus A320 flight crew reported loss of hydraulic system during departure climb. Flight returned to departure airport and landed uneventfully.
text: shortly after retracting the gear on takeoff we received a hyd g eng 1 pump lo pr ecam. initially it was intermittent, with green pressure showing between 100 - 1100 psi. it shortly dropped to zero quantity. i delayed running the ecam until we had gained a little more altitude and completed the initial part of the zzzzzx departure. climbing through ~ 7, 000-8, 000 ft, i called for qrc. with no qrc, i transferred control to the first officer with instructions to tell air traffic control that we'd stop our climb at 11, 000 ft, which was our current assigned altitude. air traffic control was informed of the issue and that we'd need a few minutes to run some checklists and talk to company…with a likely return to redacted. i ran the ecam, and once that was complete, i began the qrh. once that was completed down to the emergency gear extension, we paused the qrh. i then contacted company via satcom (dispatch and maintenance control). the phone patch from dispatch to maintenance control took a while, so while we waited to be connected, we started to run the overweight landing checklist to make good use of our time. i also spoke to the cabin crew to bring them up to speed on what was happening and told them i'd get back to them when i knew what we were going to do. once connected with maintenance control, they confirmed that we had lost all green pressure. with thunderstorms forecasted for the redacted area, with the possibility of a divert, we agreed that the best course of action was to return to redacted. dispatch reminded me of the overweight checklist, which we had already begun. dispatch sent us the re-dispatch back to redacted, which we received via the printer as well as on the operations management system. once done with dispatch and maintenance control, we informed air traffic control with our intent to return to redacted, that we'd need about 20 minutes to finish checklists and to prepare for the return. i also requested priority handling, requested crash fire and rescue (cfr), and we notified air traffic control that once on the ground we would be unable to exit the runway due to the loss of nose wheel steering. with the aircraft ready for the return to redacted and having spoken to the customers as well as cabin crew, we informed air traffic control that we were ready for the approach. i briefed the cabin crew and made them aware it should be a normal landing with the exception of the cfr equipment meeting us and our inability to exit the runway/need for a tow to the gate. prior to returning to the airport we completed the overweight landing checklist and reviewed the remaining portion of the qrh from the emergency gear extension to the end, so that we had both seen it before needing to accomplish it.with everything prepared for the return, we notified air traffic control we were ready for the approach. i allowed ample time to get configured before the final approach fix. i instructed my first officer to note the touchdown rate of decent and we noted the landing weight as well. the touchdown rate was less than 50 fpm and i let the aircraft roll most of the length of runway xxl. brake temps initially were around 85 degrees, warming to roughly 160 degrees by the time the tug arrived. once stopped on the runway, i made a remain seated" pa and then spoke to cabin crew as well as made an announcement to the customers. cfr and airport operations met the aircraft. in roughly 10-15 minutes our tug arrived and we were escorted back to gate xx.one last component to mention was that we had an air carrier x pilot on the jumpseat. once the issue started, he got on the jumpseat headset and was a good help in monitoring radio calls while we got busy with checklists and briefing the course of action."

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A321 First Officer reported an inflight upset and sudden drop in speed occurred on descent when they encountered wind shear in a storm cell.
text: during descent into redacted as pilot monitoring (zzzzzx rnav arrival ) radar was showing weather to the west of redacted airport, most of it over the arrival route. deviation right of course was requested. air traffic control offered heading 170, i requested further right deviation due to weather but air traffic control denied it due to traffic over redacted and suggested again heading 170 stating that it was the best path around the weather. an aircraft in front of us had taken that heading minutes ago.although it was night we could see the cloud tops, captain shallowed the descent trying to avoid the rain cells but there was a point that inevitably we had to go through them. light to moderate turbulence was encountered but nothing out of normal range. minutes later due to wind shear the aircraft suddenly dropped the speed from 250kts to alpha prot speed disengaging the auto pilot, startle effect prevented us from calling out upset". because of that and being in doubt if the captain was flying the aircraft i pushed forward on my sidestick to prevent the speed to continue decaying, dual input was activated. captain stated i have the aircraft and correctly applied the upset recovery by lowering the nose and applying toga thrust. seconds later the speed came back to 250kts. after clearing the weather normal approach and landing was executed."

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a UAS during climb.
text: while in a climbing right turn to a 180 heading passing 4000' msl i spotted a drone just left of the nose and co altitude. i continued the turn and the drone passed off the left side about 300 feel laterally and 100 feet below. it looked similar to a model airplane but with engines underneath each wing. the drone was also in a right turn. the size was difficult to determine but my best guess is a 3-5 foot wingspan. the sun was reflecting off of the drone but it appeared to be metallic and light in color.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: CL-350 flight crew reported an engine failure during the climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and safely landed overweight.
text: after departing runway xx and at approximately 3000' we started getting a strong vibration that would change with thrust lever movement. shortly afterwards we received a l engine exceedance due to an over temp itt and a l engine vibration cas message. before we could run those checklists the engine shut itself down and we then had a l engine flameout cas. because i was already in the qrh i remained there and ran the engine flameout checklist that led to the engine shutdown in flight checklist and then the single engine landing checklist. we remained on approach control and he vectored us back to a visual approach to runway xyl and we landed without any further incident. i was the pilot in command and the pm. the sic was receiving ioe and was the pilot fly for the entire event.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: ERJ 145 First Officer reported an engine malfunction during the climb. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed.
text: on climb deviated around redacted due to convection between 15000 and fl210. prior to fl210 experienced a bump/turbulence that seemed similar to wake turbulence and shortly thereafter smelled burning ozone that dissipated within 15seconds. conditions were clear with convection all quadrants in vicinity. at fl260 climbing to fl280 eng1 out eicas illuminated coupled with rollback #1. leveling fl280 air traffic control issued direct redacted [vor]. we advised engine out and requested priority handling. conditions were imc no precipitation and no turbulence or chop. qrh engine out accomplished while coordinating redacted divert. acars did not work. eng out qrh lasted less than 7 min. we then accomplished relight qrh with no relight. attempted a second restart with no joy. eng oil 11qts both sides. no vibrations either engine. we then accomplished single engine approach and landing qrh while managing descent. coordinated with air traffic control to advise dispatch and acars were no comms. captain landed successfully xxr.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported experiencing GPS jamming in the ABQ area as reported by ATC.
text: approximately 100 nm east of abq we were advised by air traffic control of possible gps jamming activity on our route. few minutes later we did experience gps jamming which lasted about 8 minutes. our navigation was not affected.cause: we had adequate navigation and reviewed qrh interference . air traffic control was notified confirming that we were experiencing gps jamming.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A321 pilot reported during gate lead in; a reckless baggage cart operated within the safety area and stopped in front of the aircraft; resulting in a critical ground conflict.
text: when arriving to gate xx at redacted a baggage cart driver recklessly drove through the ground crew parking assisting our aircraft which was actively taxing in on the yellow to the jet bridge. what happened next is almost too egregious to believe, the driver of the cart, weaved around the right side wing walker and drove directly in front of the aircraft which was approximately 50 feet from arriving at the jet bridge, once in front of the airplane which was moving froward at the time, the cart driver stopped directly in front of the airplane on the yellow line. ca and first officer both in utter shock called out the intrusion, ca stopped aircraft in time to miss striking the cart. it took roughly 10 seconds for anyone to react to move this person from the active safety zone. of note the right side wing walker never flinched or attempted to stop or slow the driver as they violated the safety area.cause: a complete lack of situational awareness with ground personnel working at redacted. someone needs to pull the ramp tapes from this event and needs to be used as an example of how dangerous a flight line is. the only explanation is this driver was inebriated.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A321 Captain reported multiple ECAM indications of the takeoff thrust lever not being set correctly which resulted in rejected takeoffs and maintenance action.
text: on an etops flex power takeoff prior to 80kts ecam: t/l not set. rejected takeoff. cleared the runway, ran the qrh takeoff after rejected takeoff below 80 knots." discussed the possible causes of the ecam with the first officer. verified that the flex temperature had been properly entered and the requirement that the thrust levers (t/l) were in the flex detent. taxied out for a second flex power takeoff attempt. prior to taking the runway, verified flex temperature was on the perf page. first officer was pilot flying (pf) again. flex power was set, and immediately noticed man flex was not displayed in flight mode annunciator (fma) column 1 followed by ecam: t/l not set. rejected takeoff. cleared runway, called maintenance control and was instructed to return to the gate. aircraft removed from service. resulting maintenance action: replaced engine #1 & #2 t12 sensors and engine throttle control units.cause: the airbus aom discusses this ecam. the aom direction to select toga would only apply in the event that the flex temperature is not entered (or was inadvertently deleted due to runway change) on the perf page and a flex takeoff is attempted or when the t/ls are not in the flex detent. this being an etops departure, the decision was made to investigate further by rejecting the takeoff. this decision was validated after getting the same ecam on the next takeoff anttempt and the subsequent maintenance actions that were taken to return this aircraft to service. recommend the aom expound on the ecam recommended toga selection to include the possible reasons this ecam may be present. our experience and system knowledge prevented us from blindly selecting toga and flying an aircraft with a throttle control issue to destination."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737-800 crew reported a loss of A system hydraulics while on final approach.  Crew landed and was towed to the gate after clearing runway.
text: this report documents a loss of system a hydraulics on short final followed by a landing and qrh accomplishment. landing gear was pinned and aircraft towed to the gate. during the approach to redacted instrument landing system xx at 800 ft agl, a master caution light illuminated with an associated hydraulic elec 2 low pressure light (system a). pilot flying (pf) was the first officer and pilot monitoring (pm) was the captain. both pilots acknowledged the light. the pm announced the condition and the pf maintained aircraft control. based on the facts that we were fully configured, below 1000', had sufficient brake pressure, and were landing on a long runway well below required landing distance, we confirmed with each other and agreed to continue the approach to landing and delay the qrh until after landing. the pm subsequently extinguished the master caution light. at 500 ft agl the master caution light illuminated again with associated eng1 and elec2 hydraulic pump low pressure lights. the simultaneous illumination of both system a hydraulic pump low pressure lights indicated a probable loss of system a hydraulic fluid. at this point, since we were below 500 ft agl and conditions were still favorable for a safe landing, we once again confirmed with each other that to continue to a landing was the safest option. at this point in the approach, the pf noted that a small amount of increased right aileron input was required to maintain control. while abnormal, it was easily controllable. from this point on, both pilots focused on landing the aircraft safely. during touchdown and rollout the aircraft performed normally. automatic spoiler deployment occurred upon touchdown and the aircraft decelerated normally on autobrakes 3. manual braking was applied shortly after touchdown by the pf. the transfer of aircraft control to the captain occurred at approximately 70 knots. initially, nose wheel steering was operational and we cleared the runway on taxiway charlie cautiously and at a slow taxi speed. upon the completion of the turn on to taxiway charlie, the nosewheel steering failed. once clear of the runway the parking brake was set. at this point we determined that we had a complete loss of system a hydraulics. we informed tower that we needed to hold position to address a hydraulic leak. we did not declare an emergency, as the aircraft was on the ground and under control with the parking brake set. the captain then directed the loss of system a" qrh and the first officer read the checklist and we accomplished the applicable items. communication was established with the flight attendants by the captain and they confirmed that the situation was normal in the cabin. since the checklist calls for the gear pins to be installed prior to taxi, we determined the safest course of action would be to shut down the aircraft on the taxiway, have a ramp crew come out to the aircraft, install the gear pins, and tow us to the gate. the captain made a pa announcement explaining the situation to the passengers and informing them that we would be towed to the gate and all was under control. when the tow crew showed up, they plugged in to the intercom and we devised a plan to pin the gear and tow the aircraft to the gate, escorted by airport operations. we were advised us that they did not have gear pins available. we then briefed a plan to shut down the aircraft engines, and remain on apu power. once safe to approach the aircraft, we would drop the gear pins out of the flight deck window, then clear him to pin the gear. once the gear was pinned, we were towed to the gate by the ground crew. upon post-flight inspection it was noted that hydraulic fluid was leaking from the number one ground spoiler actuator on the left wing. also, airport operations said that there was hydraulic fluid on the runway.recommendations to mitigate the riskafter debriefing as a crew we discussed some other options. option 1: we could have gone around to run the checklist and to devise a plan. however, with the gear stuck down, we had a higher fuel burn rate and no alternate fuel (there is a warning in the checklist about this). we would have had to maneuver without the use of half the flight spoilers. we both believed that this option would have prolonged a dangerous airborne situation. we had the proper configuration for landing, adequate brake pressure, excess runway available (8700' avail). this option is worth discussing, but we both believed in this particular situation it was better to land. the difference between a normal landing and a non-normal with loss of a hydraulics is only 400'.option 2: stop straight ahead on the runway, pin the gear, get towed to the gate. we both agree that this may have been a better option. however, we would have been on an active runway at night, closing down the runway to other traffic. that being said, it would have been the most conservative action. option 3: coordinate with air traffic control to have arff available on site and follow us to the gate, since we had a hydraulic leak. at the time, we did not consider this. in retrospect, we believe it would have been a more conservative option. if we had accomplished the non-routine landing considerations qrh, it would have reminded us to do so."

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a NMAC with an unidentified VFR aircraft while on an ILS Approach to ORD at 2000 feet.
text: on approach to chicago, we were cleared for the instrument landing system 9 center. slowing the aircraft down commanded by air traffic control from 170 kn to 160 kn, diligently painted a mental model of the traffic around us. we were paired up with air carrier x on nine left, nine right, and behind a regional in front of us which i verbalized im actively looking for traffic. at approximately 2000 feet agl, i verbalize how there's traffic underneath us depicted on the navigation display (nd). as my attention went outside the aeroplane i physically saw aircraft y climb turn and descend underneath us for which i stated i had the aeroplane in sight within seconds if not tenth of seconds, my first officer was already manually flying the aeroplane preemptively in the best efforts to see and avoid. as as i proactively scan for traffic the only indication of an issue that i had was a second later when the tcas system alerted us of a traffic advisory. i had not checked in with tower as my attention was on guiding and managing the safety situation and near miss. laterally we flew above aircraft y vertically last indication i saw on the nd was a vertical separation of about 500 feet if not less. in the best efforts of avoiding further traffic separation my first officer went slightly above wide path if not shallow or decent. i checked in with tower, our checklist was complete and was clearanced to land and hold short of 9 center. we had another traffic advisory and on the end it was from the aeroplane that had already landed. we landed with no further incident.we had no advisory from air traffic control in protected airspace. factors that contributed to our success was a good qualified trained crew, pilot judgement, and crew resource management and coordination. i stated my pilot duties to properly and mentally picture our movement through the airspace and how conflicting traffic can be seen and avoided. my first officer assumed the flying duties as expected. i was 10th of a second from taking controls when i needed to however i relied on the good pilot judgement for my first officer to help manage the situation. i can't stress this enough that i could not have done what was required of us unless we properly coordinated as a crew like we did. the professionalism and experience of both of us in the cockpit is inimitable and irreplaceable to safety and security for an efficient and safe operation. my question still stands as far as where and why air traffic control had no idea of the situation. furthermore, where was the protected airspace and why was it intruded? the environment that we operated is dynamic so should the availability of protected airspace laterally and vertical. the dimensions should be and meet the operation to the fullest extent to extend bravo airspace if required and other air spaces for special use not just control airspace but specificly more restrictive requirements like bravo airspace. even if we had an orb of class bravo airspace around the aeroplane, nothing could have contributed more to a successful outcome then two pilots doing the job that was expected of us at all costs.
