anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: B737 crew reported Dutch Roll; lateral and altitude control issues during cruise in areas of turbulence. Crew observed Yaw Damper had disengaged and proceeded to destination after reengaging same.
text: on flight abcd from redacted to redacted on day 0, we encountered multiple areas of turbulence along our route of flight associated with convective and ride activity depicted on our weather and sky path information systems. prior to departure and throughout the flight, the first officer and i actively monitored ride reports, weather depictions, and turbulence forecasts in order to mitigate exposure to passengers, flight attendants, and the aircraft.after departure from redacted on the zzzzzx departure, we initially experienced intermittent light to moderate turbulence during climb and cruise. based on turbulence depictions along our route, particularly over portions of states x and y near the redacted vor area, i briefed the flight attendants in advance that we would likely require them to remain seated for an extended period in accordance with turbulence mitigation procedures.as we approached the area near redacted, we requested ride reports and altitude advisories from air traffic control in an effort to identify smoother ride conditions, however, air traffic control advised that aircraft in the area were reporting similar ride conditions at multiple altitudes. during this phase of flight, we encountered periods of light to moderate and occasional moderate turbulence, intermixed with smoother ride segments. due to the continuing ride conditions and forecasted turbulence ahead, i directed the flight attendants to take their jump seats and repeatedly advised passengers to remain seated with seat belts fastened.while operating east of the river and north of the redacted area, both the first officer and i began observing abnormal lateral/directional aircraft response characteristics during otherwise routine light to moderate turbulence encounters. specifically, the aircraft began exhibiting a dutch roll-type oscillation following even minor turbulence inputs. we noted that the oscillations appeared to amplify with time after turbulence encounters rather than dampen normally.the first officer, who was pilot flying, remained prepared to assume manual control if necessary while i continued monitoring aircraft systems, air traffic control communications, and cabin coordination. during this time, i made additional passenger announcements emphasizing the need for all passengers to remain seated due to ongoing turbulence. flight attendants also reported continued passenger movement in the cabin despite repeated announcements.shortly north of redacted, we again encountered light to moderate turbulence during which the aircraft's lateral oscillation increased further. the autopilot disconnected, and the first officer smoothly assumed manual control of the aircraft while intentionally avoiding abrupt control inputs in order to minimize unnecessary aircraft motion and provide the best ride possible for the cabin. during this event, the aircraft experienced an altitude deviation of approximately 600-700 feet while in turbulence. i immediately requested and received a block altitude clearance from air traffic control between fl350 and fl360 to safely manage aircraft control and ride conditions. other aircraft on frequency were simultaneously reporting similar turbulence-related issues and requesting altitude blocks in the same area.the first officer stabilized the aircraft promptly, and we returned to our assigned altitude shortly thereafter. while monitoring aircraft systems, i observed the yaw damper switch in the off position with the associated yaw damper light illuminated. i checked the annunciator panel and noted no associated flt cont annunciation. based on system knowledge and qrh guidance, i reengaged the yaw damper switch, at which time the yaw damper light extinguished and the aircraft's flight characteristics returned to normal. the first officer concurrently referenced and completed the applicable qrh non-normal procedures while i monitored aircraft performance and flight path.after the aircraft returned to normal handling characteristics, i contacted the flight attendants to assess cabin conditions. the flight attendants advised that there were no injuries among passengers or crew, although several passengers in the aft cabin and one flight attendant experienced nausea associated with the lateral oscillation and ride conditions. at no point did the aircraft experience severe vertical acceleration or abrupt up-and-down movement, the primary ride issue involved lateral oscillation and rolling motion that was particularly noticeable in the aft cabin.following coordination with air traffic control, stabilization of aircraft systems, and confirmation from the flight attendants that there were no injuries, we elected to continue the flight to redacted. an elb (electronic logbook) message was sent in flight to advise maintenance control of the event and to facilitate maintenance evaluation upon arrival. for passenger comfort, we subsequently reduced cruise speed to mach .75, and ride conditions improved significantly as we progressed north of state z. once conditions permitted, the flight attendants resumed cabin duties, and i made a passenger announcement apologizing for the turbulence and advising passengers that multiple aircraft in the area had experienced similar ride conditions.upon arrival in redacted, we coordinated with maintenance personnel to debrief maintenance control regarding the event and aircraft behavior observed during the turbulence encounter.

text: for our flight we had an observer in the back right seat. it was our first take off out of redacted, we got cleared to takeoff xxl and we were performing a soft field takeoff where we had a crosswind. as the student was initiating takeoff we started to veer to the left of center line so i appropriately added right rudder to get us back on course but when we lifted off, we heard the stall horn and my student added right aileron to get back on centerline. this caused us to drift to the right of centerline. i then appropriately took controls and added forward pressure to avoid a stall or spin and get us back on centerline. during this takeoff the wingtips briefly made contact with the ground. i then safely landed the aircraft on the runway aborting the takeoff and taxied back to the ramp with no further issues. during our walk around we saw there were scratches under both of the wingtips and scratches on the right side of the horizontal stabilizer. there were no injury's and we then wrote up the aircraft.cause: as the cfi/pic of the flight i understand that i am ultimately responsible for the correction and outcome of the flight. this was caused due to improper aileron input with the winds and not enough rudder usage.suggestions: in hindsight after having time to reflect on this event that occurred over the span of about 30 seconds as the cfi, i might have been able to take controls sooner and reacted to the aileron input faster. other solutions for this fast paced event could have been blocking the controls and better defensive positioning.

synopsis: EMB 170 First Officer reported a hydraulic system malfunction during cruise. Flight diverted and landed.
text: received the aircraft at redacted and determined it was airworthy after reviewing the documents and completing the preflight inspection. the flight departed redacted with no delays or issues. approximately 45 minutes into the flight, we received a hyd 2 lo qty" crew awareness message, but it disappeared quickly. by the time i opened the hyd synoptic page, it reappeared. when we first looked at it, the quantity in system 2 was at 20%, and we decided to monitor it for a couple of minutes. after 3-4 minutes, it dropped to 18%, and we realized it was actually leaking.we decided not to continue to redacted due to having roughly 450 miles remaining. the captain relayed this information to dispatch, and dispatch relayed it to maintenance. after a couple of minutes, we received a message directing us to divert to redacted. the captain and i discussed the situation and came up with a game plan: i would fly the airplane and handle the radios while he informed the flight attendants and passengers of the situation, handled the new release, calculated fuel, and programmed the box.i quickly got on the radio and advised air traffic control, "we have a minor hyd issue and would like to divert to redacted. we are not declaring an emergency at this time." air traffic control then gave me a heading and altitude toward redacted.by the time we were at 9, 000 feet, 250 knots, and approximately 50 miles from redacted, the airplane was fully set up. we decided to review the qrh item "loss of hydraulic system 2" to familiarize ourselves with it in case we lost all the fluid prior to landing. we came up with a plan to lower the landing gear early since we were close enough to the field and still had plenty of fuel remaining. one of the items we would lose according to the qrh was normal landing gear operation due to the hyd 2 loss, requiring use of the alternate gear extension lever. we also agreed that if we lost the system completely at any time prior to landing, we would discontinue the approach, run the qrh procedures, and return to land with the required items and equipment secured.i slowed to 230 knots, and we lowered the gear. approach vectored us for the instrument landing system xxr approach and asked about the nature of the problem. we advised them that we were not declaring an emergency at that time, but approach provided priority handling. from there, i joined the final approach course and flew the instrument landing system xxr approach into redacted.shortly after touchdown, we received several red and yellow eicas messages, and both the master warning and caution lights/buttons illuminated. i did not pay close attention to them because we were in a very critical phase of flight, but i only deployed the number 1 reverser, knowing the lights and messages were related to hyd system 2. we rolled to the end of the runway to avoid overheating the brakes, exited at taxiway 1, and stopped on taxiway 2 facing east.tower instructed us to switch frequencies to fire/rescue for communication. shortly after speaking with them, we noticed the right outboard brake temperature rising quickly, and we asked them to monitor it in case it caught fire. we waited there for approximately 25-30 minutes, and the brake temperature eventually cooled off. we then taxied to gate xx, and the remainder of the taxi to the gate was uneventful."

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported taking the runway for departure with an airplane on short final. Reporter stated the other aircraft was not communicating its intentions.
text: takeoff runway 35 bdn. as the aircraft departing ahead became airborne, and visually clearing the final approach course, i crossed the runway hold short line and announced on ctaf, 'taking runway 35 for westbound departure.' approximately 30 feet after crossing the hold short line another aircraft announced on ctaf, 'we're on short final.' i came to a complete stop, other aircraft announced going around. on ctaf i advised we'd heard no radio call and did not observe the other aircraft. other aircraft responded, 'i made three calls.' there was also some mention on frequency of a 'dogleg final.' i never saw the other aircraft until it was established on downwind after its go around. in my aircraft there were three (3) pilots, with a cumulative total of 35000+ hours. all of us were monitoring ctaf and no one heard a call from the other aircraft.suggested remedies: although radios are not required at non-towered airports, good procedure would be to make a call on ctaf/unicom and then pause for possible responses before crossing the hold short onto the runway. at non-towered airports, with other traffic observed on the ground and in the pattern, aircraft should fly a standard pattern so that they can be observed when on final approach.

synopsis: General aviation pilot on final approach to SEZ reported an aircraft departing in the opposite direction without transmitting their intentions. Pilot initiated a missed approach.
text: while receiving dual instruction in terrain flying from a cfi, i was acting as pilot flying from the left seat in aircraft x at sedona airport (sez). i hold a private pilot certificate with approximately 150 hours total flight time. operations were conducted under visual flight rules conditions at the non-towered airport.we were operating in the traffic pattern for runway 3 and we were making standard ctaf position reports while entering and flying the pattern. we selected runway 3 because of the variable winds and we preferred the uphill grade while landing. after turning final for runway 3, we visually observed another aircraft beginning a takeoff roll on runway 21 in the opposite direction.neither my instructor nor i recall hearing a transmission indicating the other aircraft's intention to depart runway 21. we are uncertain whether the transmission was not made, was not received, or we missed the transmission. possible contributing factors include radio congestion, overlapping ctaf transmissions, and the differing runway selection decisions (we selected runway 3, whereas the departing aircraft was operating on runway 21).after observing that the other aircraft had begun its takeoff roll, we initiated a go-around. we maneuvered to the right of the final approach course to provide separation and allow the departing aircraft to continue takeoff. once the conflict was resolved, we re-entered the traffic pattern and subsequently landed uneventfully.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a traffic conflict with an aircraft departing opposite direction while on final approach to DWA. Pilot initiated a missed approach.
text: while acting as safety pilot for a friend doing a practice instrument approach (rnav 34) at the yolo county airport (dwa), we were cleared for the approach and handed off by travis approach about 8-9 miles from the airport. i made my first radio call about 8 miles out, stating our distance in cardinal direction from the field and stated we were on a straight in traffic permitting doing a practice approach. we did not hear any traffic calls nor observe anything visually or on adsb data. i called a 3 mile final, and about a minute later when we were on short final an airplane says they are taking the opposite runway (16) and will turn out early to the west to avoid us. since we were basically on short final i cued up and said okay we will break off and turn out east to avoid the conflict. it appeared the aircraft was still barely rolling past the hold short line on the 16 side when i said this, so it seemed very obvious to me that he never made a hold short call and just decided to try to cut out in front of us. i would have happily broken off the approach early to accommodate him had i known he was holding but his first call did not come until he announced he was rolling opposite direction. he then berated me for turning east where the jump zone is. i am very familiar with this airport and know the hazards of the jump zone on the east side of the field but there were a few things going through my mind, #1 my first and immediate concern was avoiding the head on conflict created by the other pilot, #2 turning east was of course not my ideal choice but if my understanding was that he planned to turn west then i of course would not turn west myself and #3 i was very confident the jump zone was not active as i fly at this field regularly and am very vigilant regarding the warning calls the skydive pilots give prior to commencing a jump, so given all of these factors i made the decision to make an immediate turn to the east and continued the turn southbound out of the area. i think there should be some advisory circular or other relevant publication surrounding operations at the yolo county airport in the event an airplane needs to take evasive action and side step towards the east side of the field.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported loss of directional control after landing resulting in a runway excursion.
text: today i was renting aircraft x. after landing at low speed, with the power already reduced to idle over the runway, i initially used aerodynamic braking. when i applied wheel brakes, the aircraft veered off the runway and entered the grass by a short distance.i immediately informed the tower that the aircraft had veered off the runway. within seconds, i safely returned to the runway, exited as instructed via taxiway 1, and continued taxiing to the flight school in accordance with air traffic control instructions.while taxiing, i understood air traffic control to request that someone from my flight school contact the tower. since the school office was closed at the time, i attempted to reach the academy and also notified the office manager.shortly afterward, i contacted the tower directly. the tower requested my contact information and i explained the circumstances of the event.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported a NMAC during takeoff phase.
text: i was training solo as a student pilot in redacted, i cleared the take off from runway xx and followed upwind traffic, i acknowledged the instruction and took off from runway xx. after the initial climb i started to find the traffic and saw an airplane in the upwind turning crosswind, but that was not the traffic i was supposed to follow. the traffic i was supposed to follow was still upwind climbing. after the traffic i followed passed me i start turn crosswind while i heard air traffic control instructed me immediate right turn, i already in crosswind at that time and see traffic advisory on g1000 there was a traffic close to my right so i didn't follow air traffic control instruction, in the same time air traffic control instruct the other aircraft turn 360 and instruct me continue to downwind. the traffic alert was resolved after that.the first factor causing the near miss was i didn't follow air traffic control's traffic advice to find traffic in the upwind, and a contributing factor was i used to find traffic when it turns instead of when they are in front of me.one action i can do better is if i'm not sure, ask for air traffic control to confirm, ask air traffic control to call my crosswind. and look for traffic proactively

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: B737 First Officer reported an aircraft overspeed and altitude deviation during a weather encounter that resulted in a momentary loss of aircraft control.
text: cruising at 330, we were in and out of clouds and turbulence. as we started to find some smooth air, we asked the flight attendants to setup a lavatory break. i went first, and when i came back i became the pilot flying and monitoring as well. i received a frequency change, checked in with center. they called me and said to maintain my current heading for traffic. there were scattered clouds that didn't allow me to see buildups ahead. i finally saw it and called and ask for right deviation. they called me back and asked which way would you want to go. responded, whichever way, they gave me left deviation as much as i need. i was not able to avoid entering the buildup as i was getting closer to it. at xa:10, i started turning left and i was turning i got the high speed clacker and gained about 200ft. the plane approximately reached .823 for about 2-3 seconds. we returned to normal speed, cleared altitude, and eventually direct back to your fix, and the rest of the flight was uneventful.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an aircraft entered the runway and took off while the reporter's aircraft was on short final approach. Crew initiated a missed approach.
text: inbound to maf in vmc conditions we had been cleared for the visual approach to runway 10 and were using guidance from the instrument landing system rwy 10. we were instructed to switch to tower frequency at 5000' just outside farly. upon contacting tower we were cleared to land runway 10 with one departure prior to arrival. on the glide slope descending through 1000' afe i noticed aircraft y still on taxiway a. i asked the first officer (pm) to confirm we were cleared to land which he did and tower responded we were. aircraft y then must have asked to verify they were cleared to depart runway 10 after seeing us however we couldn't hear this transmission as they were likely still transmitting on ground frequency. we heard tower confirm to aircraft y they were cleared for takeoff runway 10 with no delay. at this point i made a remark on tower frequency attempting to alert tower that this would likely be a go around if aircraft y took the runway but heard no response. aircraft y entered the runway while we were on final between 750-500 feet afe. descending through approximately 300 feet afe while aircraft y was starting their takeoff roll it was clear to me that the spacing was too tight. i initiated a go-around and we were instructed to turn right to heading 180 and climb to 5000 feet. we subsequently made a visual approach to runway 10 and taxied to the gate without further incident.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: Air carrier Dispatcher reported the aircraft had a flap malfunction during cruise. Flight continued to the destination.
text: couple hundred nautical miles north east of redacted on flt lvl 380 crew informed about the non normal leading edge flaps transit light illuminated and roll is not encountered. patch with maintenance control was done on vhf and we both worked with crew through checklist 737 flight manual. complied with step 3 to go down to fl200 to recycle the flaps but light stayed illuminated. fuel calculation was made at fl200 and max airspeed of 300kts if we had the fuel to continue to redacted. maintenance control ok with continuing to redacted. fuel calculation showed remf (remaining fuel) of 6.0 and dispatch plus crew ok to continue. concerns came up from the crew after a couple minutes about the fmc showing remf of 3.1 with fl200 and max airspeed 300kts. advised the crew that after rerunning flight plan in fuel calculation remf showed 5.9 and that checklist note that fmc performance predictions are not accurate. after crew changed runway in fmc it showed remf 5.5 but was not the same runway as fuel calculations, but ok to continue.due to fuel burn concerns dispatch contacted maintenance control who said to contact chief pilot regarding if the flight needs to stay at fl200 after the flaps recycle with light still illuminated. checklist is not clear if you can go back to higher altitude to save fuel in this configuration after step 3. chief pilot contacted maintenance who said due to the unknown state of the flaps do not recommend to go higher than fl200 but checklist indeed unclear.based on position reports fuel burn seemed accurate with remf 5.7 and ok to continue to redacted.concerns to clarify:-in checklist to highlight the note about fmc predicted calculations not accurate for pilots. they almost wanted to divert based on fmc fuel calculations -in this aircraft configuration state how accurate are fuel burn calculations?-once you reach fl200 and recycle the flaps but light stays illuminated, is fl200 max altitude or can you go higher?

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Ground personnel reported a truck on the ramp; which almost collided with ground personnel and an aircraft taxiing to the gate.
text: the incident began when the inbound aircraft was entering the alleyway. because the ramp crew lacked the required number of wing walkers to safely guide the aircraft to the gate, the marshaller correctly held up an emergency 'stop' (x) signal to halt the aircraft's progress. the marshaller consulted with me, asking if we should proceed with only one wing walker or hold for a full crew. i directed the team to wait for a second wing walker to ensure total compliance with safety minimums.i immediately radioed operations to report the staffing shortage and request assistance. while waiting, i noticed extra personnel at the adjacent gate and asked if they could assist with wing-walking duties. they agreed, and as we were actively moving into our proper positions to safely bring the aircraft in, i observed one supervisor walking and another driving in our direction.once the team was fully in position and the aircraft was cleared to proceed, the ramp crew began actively marshalling the inbound aircraft into the gate. i was positioned as a wing walker, facing southbound toward the runway south of the airport, executing the standard 'proceed to next marshaller' signal. because of this positioning, my back was turned to the southbound oncoming traffic in the alleyway. the arrival proceeded normally until the opposite wing walker detected an immediate hazard and threw up an emergency 'stop' (x) signal with his wands. recognizing the urgency, i instantly mirrored the emergency 'x' signal to ensure the flight crew received a unified, immediate directive to halt. the flight crew reacted quickly and brought the aircraft to a stop.simultaneously, a truck traveling southbound in the alleyway failed to yield the absolute right-of-way to the arriving aircraft. the driver, seemingly unaware of the active arrival, breached the safety zone and braked heavily at the last possible second. the truck came to a sudden stop right next to my position, nearly driving past me and narrowly avoiding a catastrophic collision with both the aircraft and ground personnel. the immediate situational awareness and rapid communication of the wing-walking team successfully averted a major incident caused entirely by the vendor vehicle's failure to follow airport sops.afterwards, we directed the truck to back up and clear the area. once the hazard was removed, we attempted to resume the arrival, however, the pilot was unable or unwilling to apply enough engine power to get the aircraft moving again after the sudden stop. because the aircraft could not complete its forward momentum into the gate under its own power, the crew followed procedures to safely secure the flight.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy

text: push back at xa:21, after engine start successfully, cleared off mechanic, gave marshaller a light flash and pulled up to hold short, i waved and cleared the marshaller off. the marshaller affirmative/clear the entire time.ground was very busy, we also had to complete our takeoff brief and before t/o checklist due to the short distance between ramp and runway. i had pulled up to a safe position at the hold short. at approximately xa:30 we finally got a word with ground and were cleared to taxi.at this point, to my knowledge, we were not under marshaller control as i had cleared him off, i turned my taxi light on and began to clear left to right, the marshaller was still showing affirmative/clear and did not react to my taxi light, i didnt find this odd since to my knowledge i was no longer under marshaller control. as i cleared to my right and began to move forward a truck broke through the stop bar on the perimeter road at a high rate of speed (they had been previously stopped). i got on the brakes, confirmed idle and put as many lights on as i possibly could to notify of my movement. the vehicle immediately stopped.when i looked back to the left, the marshaller was gave me a normal stop signal.the truck that had jumped out began to reverse, but the traffic behind him also jumped and was occupying his previous space at the perimeter road stop bar. at this point both the marshaller and ramp individual were telling me to taxi on clear to move/taxi straight ahead, however, we could not as the truck was not clear. after much pointing and waving to the direction of the truck, ground crew allowed all vehicles to go in front of us.this entire situation was rather unsafe, had the crew not properly cleared an incursion and collision was imminent, especially when you consider the marshallese was indicating safe and clear (despite the fact we were not under marshaller controller). there seems to be significant confusion on the clearing off.we finally began taxiing at xa:33, 3 full minutes post taxi clearance. ground did not query, however, i shouldve reported the incident to ground control and did not, this didnt occur to me until cruise and was likely due to how busy the ground frequency was.re-training should be accomplished on what clearing off is. a safety notice should be posted in the airport company pages warning crews of this exact situation and to remain vigilant.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Aircraft

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Bird / Animal

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: EMB-145 First Officer reported an airspeed malfunction on the takeoff roll. The Captain rejected the takeoff and returned to the gate.
text: while on takeoff roll, as pilot monitoring, the airspeed readings on the first officer's and captain's pfd (primary flight display) were grossly off. i saw the first officer's pfd read an airspeed in the 40s while the captain's pfd read in the 60s. i also noticed the first officer's pfd did not read any airspeed until in the 40s. it seemed to be a delay not usual to any aircraft in the fleet. about the same time, the sps (stall protection system) advanced message dinged on the eicas. the captain called 'reject', slowed the aircraft down without any harsh braking, i called redacted tower and told them we were rejecting the takeoff. tower instructed us to make a right turnoff of the runway and to then stop on an adjacent taxiway to determine our next steps. the captain called the flight attendant and made a pa to the passengers. the captain also called maintenance and told them what happened, i overheard in the conversation that the captain was deciding to return to the gate to have the plane looked at by maintenance. i called operations and informed them we would need to return to the gate. i then called redacted tower and was given taxi instructions to return to the ramp and ultimately the gate. we parked at the same gate that we initially pushed off from. the passengers deplaned and we boarded a new aircraft which was taxing in to park next door to gate. i thought the captain handled the reject superbly especially with low ceilings and imc conditions. according to the captain the previous crew informed him that the airspeeds were reading unreliably. the captain included in his initial pre-takeoff brief a reference to what his intended action would be should he receive any abnormalities regarding any unreliable airspeed indications. the captain also stated he would see brief 'check eicas' indications on his pfd. i don't recall ever seeing this message appear on the first officer's pfd.cause: unknown mechanical fault causing the airspeed indicators onboard to be grossly off in cross reference to one another, making any reading unreliable.suggestion: repair the mechanical malfunction to the aircraft before placing it back into service.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: A320 Captain reported a hydraulic malfunction during the climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and was towed to a gate.
text: after departing redacted and approaching cruise altitude enroute to destination, we experienced a complete loss of the green hydraulic system. my first officer maintained control while i ran the ecam and qrh for the fault. i requested priority handling, notified dispatch and maintenance control of the situation and of our intentions. i notified the cabin crew of the urgent situation. i informed our customers that the aircraft was secure but that we could not continue, once all checklists and notifications were completei took control and landed in redacted with crash fire and rescue (cfr) on standby.once i made verbal contact with cfr we secured the aircraft with an after landing and a parking checklist. cfr gave us the all clear for any concerns we had. we were then pulled to the gate with a super tug and cfr trailed behind the aircraft to monitor us.

text: on climb out, heavy engine roughness began and rpm's shot into the red momentarily. ip (flight instructor) took controls, and slightly pulled back on power to stabilize rpm's. rpms went to normal ranges but roughness continued. ip asked for vectors to return to airport and safely landed without incidence. air traffic control had emergency vehicles follow aircraft to the ramp.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: B737 Flight Attendant reported fume event during takeoff and climb. Aircraft was removed from service at destination.
text: we had a fume event on this flight. during take off very strong odor came into the cabin and was smelled all through the cabin from front to rear. i informed the capt. he advised they were assessing and would call me back. they decided to keep going to redacted with the odor. it began to dissipate after about 15 to 20 min but returned on descent. i along with other fa's had scratchy throats and headaches. mechanic came on the plane once we landed and he was on the plane speaking with pilots roughly 5 to 10 min. i spoke to him on the jetbridge and he said just the short time he was on the plane he did not feel well. i told him being on this plane for multiple hours made us feel horrible and we still did. this plane had been at the hanger obviously not fixed and they took it out of service again when we landed in redacted i am still feeling the effects the day after and had to go to the hospital. i was even told there are daily fuming events experienced by air carrier x fa's. this needs to stop. our health and well being is at stake.suggestions: this needs to be studied and researched!! why are we having so many fume events. what solutions to solve this problem are being discussed. our long term health is on the line and should be considered. the toxic fumes we are forced to inhale daily contribute to cancer and neurological diseases.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Glider pilot reported during final approach an aircraft landed and stopped on the threshold. The glider pilot overflew over the aircraft by 20 feet.
text: i had a near miss while landing a glider on runway xx at redacted airport. there was a strong x-wind out of 280* that favored rwy xx for glider traffic. i had announced entry to left-hand traffic for runway xx and after my announcement, i heard a faint radio call from a powered aircraft announcing that they were on base leg to runway xy. i continued my downwind leg to the south believing that the other aircraft would be able to land on xy and clear the runway, especially since i was landing short and stopping at the 1000 foot marker, well before the turn off to taxiway 1. my base and final legs were normal, my passenger (a licensed glider piot) and i continued trying to locate the postion of the other aircraft, but we were unsuccessful. there were no further radio calls that we heard. it wasn't until we got closer to the threshold of xx when we realized the other plane was stopped on the west edge of the runway, right in the middle of the piano keys of the threshold. because of the small profile of the aircraft, (a rutan long-ez) he was virtually invisible as he blended into the piano keys. i took the necessary evasive actions to avoid a collision, landed, and rolled out to clear the runway with no damage to either aircraft. the other aircraft continued taxing on taxiway 2 back to his hanger where he put the airplane away. the pilot admitted that he had heard our radio calls but offered no explanation of why he had continued to the south end of the runway and rolled out to the end of the runway instead of vacating rwy xy at taxiway 1. the aircraft was pointing towards us as we overflew it by ~20 ft. by the time i was able to get back to the hangar the pilot had departed the airport so i was unable to discuss the incident with him. the other aircraft was a rutan long-ez.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
