text: while taxi from the ramp at marfa (mrf) wind was favoring runway 22 (wind 190 @8). i announced taxi using taxiway alpha to back taxi 22 to run-up area. upon completions of runup i announced lining up on runway22 to depart to the south. i saw aircraft y taxi before making the call for departure. it seemed like it stopped to which i assumed them holding short for my departure. as i increased throttle for takeoff i noticed the aircraft moving onto the runway. i then aborted take off which left me around the 1, 000' mark. i observed the aircraft continue to taxi on alpha. once cleared from runway i then proceeded with full throttle to commence takeoff. there was never any taxi announcements or advisories from the aircraft from taxi to line up and take off. the departed from runway 13 shortly after my departure.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a NMAC in the traffic pattern. Tower Controller reported the instructor caused the conflict.
text: i was doing pattern work with a commercial student on a visual flight rules day at fcm with a full pattern of about 4 planes. while about 6 or so laps in and making normal traffic acknowledgments when we had them in sight, we had the incident. on a touch and go we went upwind and got a traffic call to look for and follow aircraft y in the downwind. i called traffic was insight off our wing and waited a second for them to pass before turning crosswind. when halfway through crosswind and about to go downwind my garmin 750 showed a traffic alert and the controller asked to verify we still saw the previously called aircraft y. i then put the two together to look up about 300 feet and aircraft z was basically right above us so i dove down and did a 180 out of the pattern and alert the controller of my action and the issue. the controller said the fly out for a bit then rejoin the pattern with 180. i was very worried about the miss and getting in trouble. i keep thinking back and feel i wasn't wrong with my call based on the controller mentioning traffic in the downwind. one aircraft that i saw was downwind but the other the was missed and almost hit was in the crosswind and i don't called out. this miscommunication was unintentional but also risky and i plan to visit the tower to understand where i could improve next time and see where the mistake happened. if it was my error i believe a sense of being under their eye may have lulled me and also a confirmation bias from when i saw aircraft y he called. my garmin and ads b didn't show tail numbers so i was not able to visually confirm who was who as i normally can too.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Citation jet 525 Captain reported that during initial climb; they felt a noticeable thud and had a master caution for the right engine oil pressure. They shut down; secured the engine; and returned to the departure airport.
text: no abnormalities were noted during preflight inspection. the flight was a crew-only repositioning flight. we departed redacted and were cleared to climb to 3, 000 feet. upon leveling at 3, 000 feet and accelerating westbound, approximately 3 nm from redacted on a 245 heading, we felt a noticeable thud followed by a 'right engine oil pressure' audio alert and flashing master warning indication lasting approximately one second.due to the abnormal event, unknown aircraft condition, and engine-related warning, i reduced power, requested priority handling, and requested a return to redacted. we completed the engine precautionary shutdown checklist and shut down and secured the right engine.we conducted a single-engine landing in visual conditions at redacted without further complication. after clearing the runway, tower advised that the right engine cowling was missing. following shutdown on the ramp, a walkaround inspection revealed both the upper and lower right engine cowlings were missing.no injuries occurred.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: PA-32 pilot reported that during cruise in IMC; they had a partial loss of the audio panel and their Garmin 650 navigation equipment failed. They requested a deviation back to their home base instead of the destination airport which was authorized by ATC.
text: i was in cruise in imc when my garmin gtn 650 failed without warning and i also suffered partial loss of my audio panel, in that i could hear air traffic control, but i was unable to transmit a response. air traffic control established comms with me via text messages and once that was established, air traffic control gave commands and i would press the ident button to acknowledge the same. i am writing this report because after it was determined that all other systems in aircraft were operating correctly, i requested a deviation from redacted to my home base, redacted because i knew i could do so safely. additionally, this request for deviation was authorized by air traffic control and i have the text confirming the same, but i also acknowledge the fars require me to land at destination airport or to land immediately if i enter visual flight rules conditions. however, under the circumstances it made more sense to deviate to my home base since would not be able to fly the aircraft after landing and i could so safely.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported the push-to-talk button was functioning intermittently during cruise resulting in lost communications problems and return to departure airport.
text: training flight took place on xa:10 local on day 0, the lessons objective was to expose a privet student to fly the aircraft using the instruments under actual and simulated instrument. after a ground lesson we headed out to the plane to do a pre flight, upon completing the pre flight we proceeded to do the start up, pre taxi and run up procedures. after completing the checklist items i picked up instrument flight rules clearance for a flight plan i had earlier filed to 3 rnav waypoints then back to redacted departure and destination airport. about 35 minutes into the flight i noticed my push to talk was intermittently transmitting but thought it was an issue due to the distance and altitude i was away from redacted [tracon]. i was handed off to redacted [tracon] when, i went to check in i noticed the same problem, while trying to troubleshoot my student deviated west of course slowly which i didn't realize at the moment. after realizing i turned back on course and continued to troubleshooting after no success and briefly being in a hole of vmc about 2 miles in diameter and clear of clouds i decided to try to cancel instrument flight rules, go visual flight rules through the area of vmc and fly back to redacted beneath the layer. i was able to relay a message to redacted [tracon] on what i wanted to do and was able to cancel instrument flight rules but i wanted to remain with them for flight following. after an unsuccessful attempt to relay another read back i squaked 7600 for lost comms but remained a listing ear on frequency. the redacted [tracon] control verified with me thru ident that i was squaking 7600 intent ally, after being handed off to redacted [tracon] i was able to relay a 2 by 5 message to squak last assigned beacon code, and also cancel flight following closer to the destination. i de briefed my student who really didn't know what all had tooken place and we did a brief ground following up. that's all i really have on this report thanks.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: C172 pilot reported losing control of aircraft during landing and departing the runway surface.
text: i was inbound for landing at redacted after flying a 2 hour cross country flight with landings at redacted and redacted. i obtained the metar at approximately 10 miles south of redacted around xa:50. i did not realize the metar was nearly an hour old. the wind was reported as light and variable at 4 knots. i requested vectors to visually fly the rnav approach for runway xx from the approach controller as well as clearance for touch a touch and go. i was advised to fly heading 040. later i was advised to intercept and hold at redacted, the initial approach fix for the approach. during this interval i began experiencing heavy up and downdrafts which required more workload to maintain aircraft altitude. i was circling in the hold at redacted from approximately xc:05 until xc:20. during this time, i failed to obtain updated weather from the metar due to my increased workload maintaining altitude. i was cleared for the approach for runway xx. while on short final, the tower controller notified me the wind was at 060 at 4 knots. i realized i was going to have a crossing tailwind and briefly considered requesting to change runways. since the wind velocity was low i elected to proceed with the landing. i safely landed the aircraft on center line without issue. at this point i succumbed to plan continuation bias and applied full power, and raised the flaps to perform the touch and go. i did not take into account the full effects of the tail wind and slight crosswind component. as the aircraft accelerated, it began to excessively drift left of the runway center line. my airspeed slow to build and was not adequate to rotate. i aborted the takeoff, and simultaneously applied full brakes while setting the throttle to idle. i attempted to correct for the lateral drift however was nervous to make excessive rudder inputs considering my speed which was approximately 40-45 knots (airspeed) and higher (unknown) ground speed. once i realized the aircraft was going to depart the runway i cut the mixture, placed the fuel selector valve to off. i departed the left side of runway xx shortly after crossing taxiway 1 and entered the grass running parallel to the runway. the aircraft continued through the grass. the aircraft entered the displaced threshold for run xy where if finally came to a full stop. there factors associated with the incident started when i failed to get an updated metar. i did not realize how much time had elapsed or that my initial metar report was old. had i received updated weather before i was on short final i would have changed runways. i had committed to a plan and did not realized the changing conditions. additionally when the controlled advised me of the wind on final, i could have aborted the landing and requested to land on runway 090. finally after having the smooth and relatively easy landing, i had a confirmation bias that the take off would be the same. i did not consider the additional take off roll that would be required or the effect of the cross wind which pushed me left.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Small aircraft Flight Instructor reported a NMAC in the traffic pattern during a landing competition. ATC directed a go-around.
text: i was completing the competition landings flight for short field landing competition.everything seemed as normal throughout the flight. i completed my first attempt at landings as the 3rd aircraft in a heat of 4 airplanes. i had noted on my second climb out that my location with the second position aircraft had become less spaced out than on the initial lap in the pattern. to remedy this, i spaced on my upwind leg significantly so there would be no traffic conflicts on approach. i had waited until position one of the heat had made their mandatory base call to turn crosswind. from this point, i continued downwind as normal, remaining vigilant of the two aircraft ahead of me. as i was on the first quarter of the downwind leg, i heard position 2 call their base. i observed an aircraft head of me turning base to final at this time. i reduced power as normal, added flaps and turned base once i was 45 degrees off of the approach end. i cleared left and right final before commencing my turn. upon turning final, i had the runway xx numbers in sight and pitch for 70mph and added flaps 40. once i had been established on final for about 20 seconds, tower called and said 'position 2 and 3 you guys appear to be pretty close.' at this time, i looked ahead on runway xx to the aircraft taxi off the runway at 1 and beleived the controller was referring to this.seconds after the initial call, i heard 'position 3 go around.' i immedietly commenced the go around procedure. tower had asked if i had the aircraft in sight to which i responded 'i have them in sight now, apologies for not seeing them sooner.' i beleived he had been referring the aircraft i had seen taxiing off the runway. i then responded 'will this next lap count as my second attempt?' beleiving since tower called my go around i would be alloted another compeition landing attempt.after taxing back to the shutdown box, i was met by the cheif judge of competion who greeted me with 'hey.' i then said, 'hey, tower called my go around' to inform the to inform the judges to count my second attempt of landings after the go around. he then responded, 'tower did not call your go around, the judges did. do you have any idea why?' confused, and with the prior aircraft taxi off the runway in mind, i responded, 'spacing?' he then responded sharply and said, 'you came within 100 feet of another airplane.'shocked and confused, i stood next to the aircraft and was escorted over to speak with a pilot of another aircraft with the chief judge. the pilot had informed myself and the judge that i was so close, the pilot could see me through their sky light. i spent the rest of the evening confused and shocked until i heard more perspective from eye-witnesses. from what i understand now, the pilot in position 2 had extended their downwind base and final legs significantly. in fact, so far out that they had exceeded the competition pattern limitations by nearly 2.5 times. by the time i had turned based to final, they had extended so far out and were so low that they had become completely obscured to spectators on the ground, and invisible to myself in the aircraft. based on eyewitnesses, on final approach leg, i had become positioned over top of the position 2 aircraft within 50 feet. i assume they became completely obscured at this portion of the pattern as the aircraft cowling was blocking them. i believe at this point, i had mistaken the position one aircraft's location which aligned perfectly with when position 2 had called their base. competition landings operations are limited. for landings operations as a heat, only the lead aircraft is squawking and repeating clearances. this puts following aircraft at a disadvantage to identify the building of a near mid-air collision especially when aircraft competing leaves the published pattern limits which all competitors are thoroughly briefed on. this also limits tower's ability to identify this risk as well since only squawking aircraft appear on their scope. in a meeting with competition representatives, i brought up the possibility of having judges equipped with devices to allow a secondary location reference of aircraft other than visually. this would allow them to communicate with trailing aircraft when a aircraft ahead of them departs from the stringent pattern limits which would degrade not only an approach to landing, but safety in general. it is reiterated to pilots to space on the upwind leg, however this does not accommodate for aircraft who complete final leg segments twice the size of their upwind leg.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Part 107 UAS crew reported as the UAS lifted more hose during ascent; the increased weight caused the UAS to descend uncontrollably. Crew regained control and landed the UAS.
text: primary contributing factor was underestimation of hose weight increasing due to altitude gains. as the uav gained altitude, more hose was lifted and supported by the thrust of the uav. due to a lack of visual cues on the hose, too much weight was suspended under the craft. corrective actions taken include a precise measuring of the hose length and weight plus water weight. a visible ring of tape will be applied at the point of hose that indicates the airborne weight of the uav plus hose and water equaling 54 pounds (lbs). this solution should ensure a quick and accurate means of verifying that the weight does not exceed the maximum safe weight.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B747-400 First Officer reported aggressive auto braking during landing.  Crew reverted to manual braking to a normal taxi speed.
text: on rollout, with autobrakes 2 selected, the airplane suddenly jolted forward and began aggressively applying brakes. it seemed like the system knew it was stopping too quickly and then released all brakes. the airplane again aggressively applied brakes- all of this happened very quickly. since i did not know what the airplane was doing, i called out manually braking, no reversers since it was nonstandard. i gently applied the brakes and brought the airplane to a normal taxi speed. upon post-flight inspection, it appeared there was a large hydraulic leak. we put it in the logbook, and maintenance was still trying to determine the issue when the van came to take us to customs.cause: unsure at this time

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported loss of multiple avionics and auto systems resulted in fatigue; a higher fuel burn and divert.
text: it was my take off out of redacted. right as we were about to hit 100 knots or the high speed regime we got a master caution for and right side irs (inertial reference system) fault. captain said continue so i did. we rotated as normal. however as i started transitioning from flying visually to inside i looked down and realized i had the vert hdg and att flags as well as no flight director guidance. i glanced over and saw the captains instruments and flight director were there and working. being a more critical phase of flight i didn't say anything to the captain yet due to not wanting to startle him more than necessary and i knew i could fly based of his instruments and visually. once we got through 1000 ft and i knew we were safely away from the ground i stated that i didn't have any of that guidance. the captain said well let me take the plane and radios so you can run checklists to try to fix the issues. once we transferred the controls i started looking through the non normals. i started by trying to look for any checklist relating to my instrumentation failure. i looked and read through display failure but we both stated this didn't make sense cuz the display was fine. after talking we said the first indication was the irs fault light so let's start there. i started reading through that checklist and performing the actions it stated. it was around that time i realized we had performed a bleeds off to and we hadn't switched the bleeds to the engines yet. so i performed that action before we got into any type of unsafe situation. continuing that irs fault checklist it had me turn the irs selectors switch to both on left. as soon as i did that my side had all instrumentation and guidance once again. at this point we had leveled off at 270 because neither autopilot was working and they wouldn't let us into rvsm airspace without a working autopilot. i had sent a message to maintenance control stating our failures so that we could try to get the best guidance possible in trouble shooting. we transferred the controls back to me so he could talk to dispatch and manage the situation. due to being 10000 ft lower than planned we weren't sure we would make it to redacted. so we made a plan to go to redacted if needed based on how our fuel burn was going. we also made a plan to change controls back and forth so neither of us get too tired due to having to hand fly. we realized after a while we hadn't updated the cruise winds. once we did that we realized we were right above bingo fuel. then after flying a little while long we got below bingo so the decision was immediately made to go to redacted. this entire time we were conferring with dispatch and they agreed. on the descent into redacted every time we started descending my vertical guidance went out on the flight director. so i again just used other instruments to back up my descent and every time we leveled off the vertical guidance came back on my flight director. once we got on the approach both my vertical and lateral guidance went out. i was comfortable with flying it raw data and visually so continued flying to landing. due to the added stress of everything that had gone on the entire flight and having to hand fly for over 4 hours by the time we got to the gate both of us felt somewhat fatigued and weren't sure if we really felt safe to continue. i talked to maintenance to add the failures on decent and approach to our list of failures we had already reported. while i did that captain called the chief pilot about everything and why we needed to do now. the manager asked how we felt and he said we are both on the fence. he went through the fatigue questions and he said based on those answers you guys aren't fit to fly and you are fatigued and will not continue. i don't think we did anything wrong on the flight in any way and i think we worked together well to divide or manage the workload. all of that added stress to flying and having to do so much more work than normal i know drained me which lead to me being fatigued.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence departing SEA in trail of a heavy aircraft that resulted in 'intense' left and right rolls.
text: ahead of us for departure in sea was an aircraft y. they were not appended with a 'heavy' call sign. tower cleared them for takeoff and then subsequently instructed us to line up and wait. once their takeoff roll commenced we entered the runway. after taxiing onto the runway, our takeoff clearance was received almost immediately. there was no 'caution wake turbulence' advisory. flight controls were transferred to me (first officer) and takeoff power was applied. takeoff and initial climb out were completely within normal profile. upon acceleration i called for flaps retraction and after takeoff checklist. seconds later while the ca (pm) was performing the takeoff flow a large roll moment was observed which was countered with aileron. ca advised air traffic control and immediately had two more intense rolls, one left and then one to the right. the aircraft reached about 25 degrees of bank. i applied prompt and correct control inputs including decreasing climb rate to avoid remaining in the trail of the aircraft y, that ultimately avoided an upset condition. after recovery we were vectored off course to avoid further encounters. the after takeoff checklist was completed and no cabin injuries occurred.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 pilot reported a failure of the flaps to extend to the selected position. The flaps were successfully extended using the alternate method; and a safe landing was accomplished.
text: on approach onto redacted, we were max forward speed (320 kts) to redacted for the rnav yxxl. the captain was flying and we began slowing prior to redacted at 10, 000ft to 250kts. slowing normal to set up for the rnav he called for flaps to at 240kts. i moved the flap lever to 2. i wasn't really watching the dial move but it caught my eye as the l indicator needle flicked from 0 to 1.5 degrees and aligned with the r needle then they both stopped there. i looked at the overhead panel and back at the needles. there was no flap asymmetry but the flaps had stopped at 1.5 degrees on the indicator. i pointed this to out to the captain. we took a moment to decide what to do next. i then told approach that we needed delay vectors or a pattern to run a checklist. they told us to climb to 9, 000ft we were around 6000-7000'. the captain hit the toga button and complied with approach instructions. present heading and 9, 000ft. the captain handed the aircraft to me once level with the autopilot on. he then worked through the trailing edge flap disagree checklist while i handled the radios and flew the jet and followed him through the checklist. we determined that the flaps were not working normally and the checklist directed us to use alternate flap extension.we got to the deferred items after texting dispatch and telling the flight attendants the situation and that it would be a normal landing. the captain made a pa then i requested priority handling and handed the aircraft back to the captain. i then ran the deferred items on the checklist aloud then we initiated the approach and called the airport in sight prior to the final approach point (fap). we were fully configured for landing (flaps 15 and gear down) by 2500agl. landing was conducted normally in gusty winds with auto brakes max. we cleared the runway at taxiway 1 and released the emergency vehicles. we then taxied to the gate normally, leaving the flaps at 15 and the alternate flap switch in arm.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Pilot reported trees obscure view of traffic on final due to height resulted in a critical ground conflict.  Pilot stated the trees should be shortened.
text: as i taxied out to runway 14 i took note of 3 planes in the traffic pattern. these aircraft were doing touch and go's. after i completed my run up and before takeoff checklist, i counted 5 aircraft now in the pattern. complying with applicable far's and aim procedures i waited for my turn to depart. i was listening to multiple aircraft making position reports in the traffic pattern. one aircraft reported that they would extend their upwind. i presumed this was done to create spacing for me and another aircraft waiting to depart. i continued to monitor the pattern for traffic and their position. an aircraft on final stated that they were going to make a full stop. another aircraft reported turning left base. my perception was that they were about 3/4 to 1 mile away. after the aircraft on final landed i took position on the runway. once the aircraft cleared the runway i announced on ctaf and began my takeoff. about 700 feet into my takeoff roll i noticed another aircraft left of the runway on go around. i don't remember hearing and didn't see them on final for landing. once i noticed the situation i immediately aborted the takeoff for safety reasons and cleared the runway, and taxied back for another takeoff in sequence. my view from the hold short position for runway 14 is obscured by 60 to 80 foot tall trees. traffic on final is difficult to see especially if said traffic overshoots from base to final and or are low on the approach. the height of the nearby trees should be shortened to optimize viewing of traffic.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A TRACON Controller reported that they vectored an aircraft below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: i had been working the east position for 2 heavy pushes. i based aircraft x to a 180 heading and descended them to 040. i made several other transmissions, during one transmission the cic (controller in charge) stated to watch aircraft x's altitude. i saw that they had turned less sharply than i thought they would and were just inside the 5000 mva. i told aircraft x low altitude alert and issued the climb and turn. by then i had reentered the 3800 mva. i told aircraft x to when able maintain 4000 and i cleared them for the approach and shipped them to tower.i didn't issue the check your altitude immediately due to them following my instructions and to not make the recovery worse.i was busy and trying to combine transmissions, i usually descend after i have turned and i should have done that here.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported multiple autoflight equipment failures led to high workload and resulted in fatigue.
text: on the flight from redacted to redacted we had multiple system failures that lead to us having no autopilot or auto throttles. as a result we couldn't go into rvsm airspace which lead to a significantly higher than planned fuel burn. that fuel burn lead to us having to divert into redacted. as a result of having no autopilot or auto throttles we had to hand fly for over 4 hours which is significantly more draining than normal flying. when questioned by the chief pilot and their fatigue questions they determined we were fatigued.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that the Tower cancelled their takeoff clearance due to an aircraft on final approach. Flight crew rejected the takeoff.
text: we were taxiing eastbound on taxiway m to rw26r at m9 for takeoff. the tower cleared us to line up and wait 26r without delay as there was landing traffic approaching. we had not yet reached m9. i noted traffic was about 5 miles out from the runway. we were cleared for takeoff as we made the turn onto m9. as we made the turn to line up onto the runway i pushed to thrust levers up to begin the takeoff roll. the landing traffic then queried the tower about the separation between us. the tower controller immediately instructed the landing traffic to go around and cancelled our takeoff clearance. i had previously moved the thrust levers forward but had not yet selected takeoff thrust. i closed the thrust levers and stopped the aircraft at m7. tower instructed us to hold our position. we waited about two minutes for aircraft to go around an clear the departure path. while we waited we were able to request takeoff performance for 26r at m7 through acars. the new takeoff data message was received and uplinked data accepted. we reviewed the performance data. we were subsequently cleared for takeoff again by the tower.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: A319 Captain reported an air pack fault during cruise. Crew descended and continued to destination airport.
text: at cruise with pack 1 mel'd we received air pack 1+2 fault. we proceeded to descend to 10k feet per the ecam and monitored the pressurization and air systems. though pack 2 was faulted it seemed to be operating normally. we determined that there was no need to divert or declare an emergency as we could proceed to redacted with the fuel we had on board and preserve our 45 minute reserve. we could also proceed unpressurized should pack 2 fail entirely.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Person / Animal / Bird
synopsis: Ground personnel reported an aircraft began to taxi to the gate with the tug and crew in its path. Ground crew evacuated area.
text: after pushing an aircraft out of the gate, disconnecting coms and tow bar from aircraft, my lead and rest of my team and i returned to the break room to wait for our next inbound flight. after roughly ten minutes, my lead informed me and the rest of my team that the flight we just push out must return to the gate, for 'engine failure' my supervisor, in a panic to meet metrics rushed our team out to the taxi way in a push tug. i and my team were under the impression that the aircraft we just pushed out, was unable to return to the gate on its own due to said engine failure. once me and my team reached the aircraft in the push-tug i stepped out of the push-tug and walked behind the tug to disconnect the tow-bar. as i was doing so, engine 2 on the aircraft started spooling up and the aircraft started moving forward while the tug, my lead was driving, was directly inline with engine 2. suddenly the aircraft powered up and moved forward. my lead, in fear for his life instinctively accelerated the tug in reverse to avoid a collision with engine 2, unaware that i was directly behind the tug disconnecting the tow-bar. immediately, realizing i was about to be run over, i jumped back out of the way to avoid being run over. my lead reversed until he was clear of the aircraft as it whizzed right by us. i was informed policy would be changed because of the incident.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a NMAC with a helicopter during approach. Flight crew complied with RA guidance and continued approach.
text: we were flying into hpn at 3000 ft, receiving vectors for the rnav runway 34 approach. we received a traffic advisory followed by an resolution advisory due to helicopter traffic. the captain was the pf and followed the resolution advisory guidance on the primary flight display (pfd). the closest i remember seeing the traffic was 400 ft. below us. both the captain and i had visual with the traffic before the first traffic advisory triggered and throughout the resolution advisory. we never lost sight of the traffic. approach did not advise us of the traffic until after the resolution advisory stopped. we landed shortly after this without any further incident.cause: a tcas resolution advisory was triggered by a helicopter shortly after we received vectors to get ready for the rnav 34 approach. air traffic control did not alert us about the traffic until after the resolution advisory was resolved. there seemed to be a delay in a traffic advisory from air traffic control.suggestions: make sure that air traffic control is reviewing traffic coordination for lower altitude visual flight rules helicopter traffic in the hpn area, especially when we are at a low altitude getting set-up for the approach.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Fractional flight crew reported a GPWS pull up warning during visual approach to SDL. Crew leveled off and continued approach.
text: we were flying into sdl. winds were mostly calm but favoring runway 3 (i believe it was 320 at 3kt) and visibility was clear and unlimited. we do not have any approved approaches to this runway, so we were planning a visual approach using the garmin visual". my partner and i both noted that the papis for runway 3 are 4°. we also referenced the rnp y & z approach angles. we noted that the approach angles for those are both 3°. we are not approved for these approaches so we were simply referencing them for situational awareness and noting how they avoid the terrain to the southwest of the airport. sometime during our approach brief we decided that a 3° glide path for the garmin visual approach would suffice for terrain avoidance. we were proceeding to the airport from the west when we were cleared for the visual about 9 mi west. we cancelled instrument flight rules and proceeded to turn onto a left base for runway 3. we did this by proceeding direct to the "straight" waypoint on the visual. my partner set a lower altitude, i forget the exact amount but i believe it was the garmin calculated altitude that coincided with the "final" waypoint. my partner engaged vnav and apr mode. we began our descent on the vnav profile. as we began the turn from base to final, the glide path was captured which i believe created a pitch down moment. it was in the turn and simultaneous glide path capture that we received at gpws "terrain" and "pull up" alert. it took a moment of recognition but my partner disconnected the autopilot and we leveled off our altitude of approximately 3000' msl. immediately after level off, we stopped receiving the gpws warning. our pre briefed pattern altitude was 3000' msl so already being there and having the gpws alert stop, we did not perform a full escape maneuver. we also knew that the terrain was behind us during our level off. at this point we were still in a position to commence a stable approach, so we continued and landed without further event. looking back there are a few things that i would have done differently. i do believe that we should have programmed the vnav profile to match the papis approach angle of 4° instead of the standard 3°. that would have given us more altitude over the terrain. i also think that we should have performed an escape maneuver. even if it meant only climbing another 1000' it would have been the safe and correct thing to do. it also would have given us more time to do a lap in the pattern and re-attempt the approach with a 4° approach angle or a closer in base leg to avoid the terrain. going forward, i will be much more caution of the terrain to the south west. we train and brief so much for approaches to runway 21 into sdl, but runway 3 should also be treated with equal caution. i do believe that perhaps we need a feasibility note or foqa alert published for this runway and lack of approved published approach and the terrain. we simply don't have any guidance currently and perhaps a guided visual approach would be helpful in the future as well.suggestion: i do believe that perhaps we need a feasibility note or foqa alert published for this runway and lack of approved published approach and the terrain. we simply don't have any guidance currently and perhaps a guided visual approach would be helpful in the future as well."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Global 5500 Captain reported a Master Caution prior to 80 kts. Crew rejected the take off.
text: on takeoff from runway xxr (redacted long runway) with passengers, we aborted takeoff due to a master caution prior to 80 kts. this airplane had a current minimum equipment list for l full authority digital engine control (fadec) fault (73-xx-xx-x) and was reportedly occurring during takeoff roll for another crew. because it was already written up, we made a point to discuss the possibility that it may pop up again on our takeoff roll, but we would go unless there was a different master warning (red) or master caution (amber) prior to 80 kts. the brief goes something like this with the added discussion of that minimum equipment list:we will abort for anything prior to 80 kt. • between 80 kt & v1, we will abort for… 1.engine failure… 2.fire… 3.red master warning… 4.loss of directional control… 5.or aircraft is perceived to not fly. • after v1, we will take it airborne. you'll fly, i fix, we can request headings, run our checklists, & come back & land on runway we are taking off from. if we need a longer runway, we can go to redacted airport. • questions/comments/concerns? after adding power and about 60-70 knots (it was prior to our 80 kt callout) i recall a chime and a yellow master caution redirecting my eyes to the eicas, expecting to see an amber "l fadec fault", but it was an amber "l tr fail". i called out "abort, abort, abort". my copilot's hand was still on the thrust so we aborted. there might have been a 2-3 second reaction time from when we saw the message to the actual aborting of the takeoff.the airplane had reported to the company we were close to or at v1 when the throttles were pulled back. it's possible that this was the case in terms of processing, communication and reaction time, but was not our intent if this was the case."

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Fractional First Officer reported a terrain warning on visual approach to SDM. Crew shallowed approach and continued.
text: prior to arrival into sdm, we had briefed the elements of the charted visual for runway 26r. i was pilot monitoring and this was my first flight into sdm. the flight management system was programmed correctly and we requested the visual approach when prompted by air traffic control. we were then given a vector that lined us up straight in for 26r, south of waypoints chasr and sdmt3. we were too high to execute a straight approach from this point and the captain and the captain asked me to select direct sdmt6 to give us more room to descend. we crossed sdmt6 and were established on the vertical path to sdmt5. it was at this point that we received a terrain warning and a pull up command. the captain switched us from vnav to vertical speed and shallowed our descent rate, extinguishing the warning. our approach continued to a normal landing at sdm. in debriefing the approach, we both confirmed that we were established on the prescribed vertical path to sdmt5 and had visual contact with all terrain.suggestions: upon review we should have navigated direct to chasr rather than intercept the approach at sdmt6. while the procedure explicitly allows crew to intercept at any point on the procedure, i believe that beginning at chasr would have given us more time to configure the aircraft and slow to final approach speed prior to beginning the final descent. upon receiving the taws warning, we should have executed a go around rather than continue the approach, despite being in visual conditions and established on the approach.

synopsis: Global 6000 First Officer reported failure of a main landing gear to retract. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: upon takeoff right main gear could not retract completely resulting in us requesting priority handling and returning to redacted. once checklist were completed a normal landing was completed at redacted.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: A319 First Officer reported a CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT ECAM during climb. Crew descended and returned to departure airport.
text: i was operating from redacted as the first officer and pilot flying. the aircraft was an airbus a319. it was the first flight of the day. upon arriving to the aircraft, the plane had been powered up (assuming by maintenance), however apu was off, pre-conditioned air (pca) hose unplugged and tangled up by aircraft nose. the three temperature sensors in the plane read, ckpt 90, fwd 94, aft 98". this became a top priority to try a cool the airplane prior to boarding. with the apu bleed on, we were able to cool the aircraft and no issues noted. all things considered normal up until after engine start. we noticed pack 1 was still showing a fault, but both myself and the captain agreed it was probably a "sticky valve" and once we added a little bit of engine power, that issue would go away. prior to calling for taxi clearance, the fault went away and everything was normal. however, when taxing out to the runway, the fault came back, but would go away when engine thrust was added and would come back again when thrust was brought to idle. this process repeated itself for about 3 cycles until we decided to tell ground control we'd like to pull over and troubleshoot the fault. the ca worked with dispatch and maintenance to eventually minimum equipment list pack 1. maintenance gave us the minimum equipment list 21-redacted "packs pressurized flight (a319) x. option 2 - (limited effectivity) (speed brakes operative)". the main takeaway for this minimum equipment list is that the aircraft altitude is limited to flight level 370. the day prior, the same ca and i flew another very similar a319 with an inop apu and a minimum equipment list'ed pack 1. the minimum equipment list associated with that flight was 21-xxy ""packs pressurized flight (a319) y. option 1 - (limited effectivity) (speed brakes inoperative)", with the main takeaway from that, was it had a max altitude of flight level 310. our filed flight plan for our flight was flight level 350. we had some discussions on what the differences were and why on one flight we had y and this one we had x. we discussed the two different altitudes and noted our flight level was right in between them and would monitor the cabin altitude. but according to the minimum equipment list that maintenance gave us, fl350 was still legal and we pressed on. on the climb out the aft cabin was "ok" with temperature, but the front was high 70s/low 80s and the cockpit was 90°+, with the aircraft not cooling down on one pack. while still in the climb to fl350, i started having the discussion on different possibilities to resolve this issue. we were in the process of reaching out to dispatch via acars to send us a fuel plan with a much lower altitude so we could potentially use the apu bleed to cool the plane off. during that time, we were passing fl330 in which the ca mentioned the cabin altitude passing ~8, 000', which then prompted him to immediately request a level off, then a lower altitude. our descent started somewhere in the mid fl340s heading back down initially to fl330, never reaching our filed fl350. that's when we received the master warning and the "cab pr excess cab alt" ecam. we donned the oxygen masks, established crew communication and continued the ecam steps. i took the aircraft and the radios and requested a descent down to 10, 000' and a westbound heading to get us heading back over land (our flight path was in a northeast heading out over the water). the ca was busy with checklist, dispatch, flight attendants and passengers, so i initially elected direct redacted to have something to aim for. i'm not sure the exact altitude the cabin got to, but it was less than 14, 000' because there were no issues or indications of a pressurization issue in the back since the passenger oxygen masks did not deploy and the flight attendants had no idea any issues were going on up in the flight deck. once at 10, 000', the cabin altitude was back to normal (300' or so) and we were able to take our masks off, regroup and come to a logical solution for what would be next. dispatch requested us to head back to redacted, which we deemed was safeand appropriate. we landed back in redacted with no further issues and taxied to the gate. our debrief questions that we wanted answers for, 1. was there any correlation at the start of the morning trying to cool off an extremely hot airplane, and essentially overworking the packs? 2. we still never received an explanation for the 2 different mels and why they would have 2 different max altitudes?cause: the temperature of the aircraft was unacceptable, especially with the plane already being powered up, a working apu (that was off) and working pca which the hose was disconnected. it set the tone of the morning with, "here's something else we have to deal with." -recommendation: with summer pretty much here, and with locations that are known for hot summers, planes need to be cooled prior to crews getting there.having a fault while on taxi out is distracting, especially when running checklist and dealing with ground air traffic control. to then have a fault that affects the cooling of the aircraft, which again was already an aggravation for the entire crew (flight attendants included). the cockpit temperature was extremely distracting, and it took away some of our situational awareness away with the pack 1 minimum equipment list and the cabin altitude.having essentially the same aircraft the day prior with the same issue(s), yet a different max altitude per a different minimum equipment list has huge expectation basis. having a better understanding of what and why maintenance is giving us that minimum equipment list as well as addressing our concerns about the max altitude would be very beneficial. it's practically impossible for our specific situation where the ca is dealing with all of that while i'm monitoring air traffic control frequencies. no blame or fault to the ca, again for the reasons listed, but all of my questions came after he was done talking to maintenance and answers were left to interpretation of how we were reading the mels."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor
synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported fumes in the cabin during climb. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: upon takeoff out of redacted at approximately 13, 000 feet, me and the captain got a chime from the front fa. i was pf so my captain answered the call. she reported that she smelled fumes, felt light headed and went to go sit in first class. the captain told me to level off. after he returned, we decided to request priority handling with air traffic control and return to redacted. at this point we both smelled the fumes and it was strong, wafting into the cockpit. we got vectors back to redacted and taxied off the runway, where we met ems and fire. they scanned the plane and found no fire, so we returned to the gate and deplaned. upon talking to the crew after the flight, both fa's stated they felt light headed, and after the adrenaline wore off i reflected on the situation and remember feeling a bit light headed too. in hindsight, i definitely should've put on my o2 mask in case of carbon monoxide, but in the moment i didn't recognize the lightheadedness.cause: not sure why it happened, my best guess is either a small electrical fire/spark behind the galley, or something in the pack?

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC during visual approach to PIT. Flight continued to a safe landing.
text: we were flying direct to wyler from the haynz arrival. we were under a scattered layer of clouds and had the field in sight. the intercept angle was exceeding 90 degrees and i thought that i could aid things along by calling field in sight and commencing the turn to intercept the course. air traffic control cleared us for the visual and since i was between wyler and triny i descend to faf altitude. unfortunately i forgot about a tower in that area, which caused air traffic control to advise of a low altitude alert. we were at 2500ft, the faf altitude. in the time it took to process the alert we had intercepted the approach course and continued the approach to landing.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a runway incursion after confusing an ATC clearance to line up and wait after arriving aircraft.
text: flight number: abcd / redacted-zzzzat xa:07, redacted parking position was 1. taxi clearance was received from tower to taxi via 1 across runway xx and continue via 2-3 to runway xx. (clearance from the tower was obtained to taxi via 1 across runway xx and continue along 2-3.) the aircraft taxied out via 1-2-3 to runway xx.at xa:14, the tower cleared the preceding aircraft for takeoff.at xa:16, the tower instructed: 'aircraft x, cleared runway xx line up and wait after arrival.'at approximately xa:15 at redacted, aircraft y was on short final for runway xx.as cm2, i read back: 'line up and wait runway xx, aircraft x.' approximately one second later, i added: 'line up behind, aircraft x.' no correction or clarification was provided by air traffic control following either readback at the time.in a dynamic runway environment at redacted runway xx, the crew's actions, including runway entry during the rollout phase, were based on real-time interpretation of the received transmission and a visual scan of the runway environment.after establishing position on the runway xx centerline, the preceding aircraft had not yet cleared the runway. tower then instructed the subsequent arriving aircraft to go around and advised that our runway entry was not authorized. we were subsequently instructed to vacate runway xx via taxiway 4 at redacted. the event was subsequently classified as a runway incursion.contributing factors (human factors)contributing factors included ambiguity in the timing structure of the clearance phraseology ('line up and wait after arrival') in the context of operations on runway xx at redacted, requiring real-time interpretation in a dynamic runway environment.vhf communication characteristics and associated audio conditions may have resulted in perceived audio degradation and reduced intelligibility of the transmission. post-event review of recorded air traffic control communications was conducted using a high-fidelity audio playback system with slowed playback to enhance intelligibility. this review suggested that portions of the transmission may have been subject to audio degradation during high cockpit workload conditions, resulting in reduced transmission intelligibility.the flight crew independently perceived the transmission in real time as a line up and wait-related clearance.the absence of air traffic control correction to two separate readbacks may have reinforced the crew's understanding of the transmission.at the redacted runway xx 3 intersection, runway guard lights were available as the primary visual cue, and no runway stop bar system was present. the available lighting configuration provided limited additional visual confirmation or redundancy for runway entry verification between air traffic control and flight crews. this may have reduced an additional layer of defence that could otherwise assist in resolving ambiguity or reinforcing runway entry status during high-tempo operations.safety actions takencontinuous traffic monitoring was maintained prior to runway entry at redacted runway xx. no evasive maneuver was required during the event, and no collision or loss of separation occurred.corrective action / preventionin future operations at redacted, greater emphasis will be placed on positive confirmation of runway status prior to entering a runway under luaw clearances, particularly when sequencing is referenced in conjunction with arriving traffic.enhanced cross-checking of air traffic control instructions between crew members will be reinforced to mitigate potential interpretation divergence. additional awareness will be maintained regarding vhf communication degradation and the importance of seeking explicit clarification when any ambiguity exists in runway-related clearances.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna CE-525 pilot reported feeling a thud during initial climb; accompanied by an oil pressure anomaly; resulting in a precautionary engine shutdown of the right engine. After a successful single engine approach and landing was accomplished; it was discovered that the right engine cowl had departed the aircraft.
text: no abnormalities were noted during preflight inspection. departed redacted and were cleared to climb to 3, 000 feet. upon leveling at 3, 000 feet and accelerating, shortly after crossing the coastline, we felt a noticeable thud accompanied by a 'right engine oil pressure' audio alert and flashing master warning indication for 2 seconds. after the 2 second the annunciation was cleared and was only left with a 'master warning' light. we reduced power, requested air traffic control assistance, and requested to return to redacted. the engine precautionary shutdown checklist was completed, the right engine was shut down and secured, and we conducted a single-engine landing in visual conditions at redacted without further complication. after clearing the runway, tower advised that the right engine cowling was missing. we taxied to parking with no additional incident. following shutdown on the ramp, a walkaround inspection revealed that both the upper and lower right engine cowlings were missing. damage was also observed on the vertical stabilizer. no injuries were reported.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Tail wheel flight instructor reported loss of aircraft control during landing with a student resulting in a propeller strike.
text: student was practicing crosswind landings under my supervision while obtaining a tailwheel endorsement. during a wheel landing, after letting the tail down, the airplane began to veer towards the right side of the runway. i then took over the controls and attempted to regain directional control. i believe i engaged the brakes in an attempt to regain directional control. the airplane re-entered the runway and shortly nosed over causing a prop-strike. there were no known mechanical failures prior to the incident. no injuries noted.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor reported an incorrect control input by student during landing resulting in a tail strike and go around by instructor.
text: during an instruction flight landing in redacted the student made a wrong control input during the round out and flare that caused a tail strike. the approach to landing was normal and stable, when we entered into the round out the student made a pitch down control input after seeing that his airspeed was 2 knots slow. the student proceeded to make the pitch down control at 10 ft agl which caused the airplane to rapidly drop. as the cfi i took the controls and made the correct action to recover by performing a go-around. there was not enough distance between the ground and caused us to strike the tail of the aircraft on the runway. no one was injured nor was the plane damaged.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: General aviation flight instructor reported a low altitude alert from ATC during cruise. Flight climbed back to cleared altitude.
text: my student and i were flying on an instrument flight rules flight plan from redacted - cos - redacted. we were in full imc conditions and tracking the v389 airway from lufse to adane. we had just gotten switched to springs approach and were having some trouble hearing them (comms go in and out around that area). we were also trying to get the weather as approach and asked what approach we wanted. once we got all of that we got turned to a heading of 260, vectors to the localizer. we were at an assigned altitude of 9000. around that time the conditions started getting a little turbulent and i was trying to assist my student with loading the approach while he flew the plane (it was his first time in imc and i just wanted him to work on flying). i normally keep very close track of his altitude so i can prompt corrections but got momentarily distracted loading the approach and getting the weather and when i looked back he was over 200 ft below altitude. this is absolutely my fault as i should have kept a closer eye knowing he struggles with holding attitude at times. as soon as i checked it, he noticed it and started correcting but by that time we were probably almost 300 ft low. right then springs approach contacted us and advised to climb, check our altitude and low altitude alert. we immediately went full power and got back up quickly. this was not safe and i have learned a lot about when to step in as the instructor and how i need to be even more vigilant, especially when on an instrument flight rules flight plan as i don't want to cause traffic issues or terrain dangers. this was a r3ally big learning experience for me as an instructor and something i will absolutely learn and change because of.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air taxi pilot reported the markings and signage at Taxiway Delta and Runway 30/12 at TUS are confusing and can lead to runway and taxiway incursions.
text: i was cleared for a straight in landing on runway 22 due to approaching the airport from the east. the active runway at the time for other arrivals was runway 12. i have flown to tus a lot in the past. normally after touchdown tower will instruct me to do a 180 on the runway and back taxi to alpha and contact ground / proceed to the fbo. or sometimes i will be instructed to make a left on delta 3 and contact ground. in this case the controller was busy transmitting to another aircraft by the time i had slowed down so i made the first available exit which happened to be taxiway alpha 2. after vacating onto alpha 2 i realized i was now directly in the approach path / area of runway 12 with aircraft y on a few mile final for this very runway. i decided to hang another left and get clear of the area on taxiway delta to prevent a problem before contacting tower who then handed me off to ground. the ground controller did not mention anything about an incursion and instructed me to taxi along delta to the ramp as usual.the situation still felt weird to me after the fact however because while i taxied on delta to the ramp i crossed over a red marking on the pavement that said 30-12" that would imply i was just on an active runway without a clearance even though the taxiway turnoff that brought me here didn't say anything. after looking through other safety reports i am not the first person to get confused by the taxiway layout at this specific intersection despite having lots of experience operating here. when you are rolling out on runway 22 taxiway alpha 2 looks like a completely normal turn off. no special markings on the runway and no red signs for an intersecting runway approaching. alpha 2 is also depicted like any other taxiway on the airport diagram on initial glance. once you are on alpha 2 however you are on runway 12 and that becomes apparent when you vacate runway 22 and now see runway 12 right in front of you. when you then make either a left or right onto delta you cross over a pair of hold bars that read in red letters on the concrete "30-12" again implying you are / were on a runway even though the taxi diagram depicts it as a taxiway and there are yellow stripe markings on the ground. upon review after the situation it appears this is known as a "aligned taxiway" which the faa has since prohibited being used for new construction or reconstruction of taxiways presumably because it confuses pilots. there is currently a hot spot on the airport diagram for one side of the intersection however it does not mention the above scenario but instead only acknowledges that pilots tend to cross the hold markings when taxiing to runway 12 via delta presumably due to the uncommon layout of the intersection.i believe that something design wise visually needs to change at this intersection to prevent future issues and needless pilot deviations as in the case of some other safety reports. pilots are misinterpreting the existing markings and signage and the airport diagram doesn't add much clarity to the situation especially when the hot spot marking is only on one side of the 3 possible incursion points. in the meantime the best remedy is a reminder to be very vigilant when taxiing near runway intersections and always making sure to have the airport diagram pulled up on an efb or printed out on paper however in this case that did not help me since my immediate focus was on safely vacating the runway i had just landed on."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air traffic controller reported situation where they established communication with a NORDO VFR aircraft and issued an IFR clearance to the aircraft while the aircraft was below the MIA for the area resulting in flight towards terrain and the aircraft entering another sectors airspace without coordination.
text: redacted approach called and told my trainee, person a, that aircraft x was nordo visual flight rules and they would keep trying them. we were pretty busy and also training at the r side, and person a never got the chance to tell the r aircraft x was nordo. they're visual flight rules flight path was straight through a 15-mile-wide section at 055 and exiting the airspace, there was aircraft y that was in conflict, also visual flight rules. we finally coordinated with redacted that aircraft x was nordo, the r side called them and turned them 30 degrees left and had them check in on our frequency. the r trainee tried to climb aircraft x to 075 to avoid the traffic, but aircraft x said unable visual flight rules. by this time, we were approaching redacted's airspace. we called redacted and advised them the aircraft x was turning left, but while we were on the line, the r issued an instrument flight rules clearance to aircraft x below the mia (minimum instrument flight rules altitude) without instructing to maintain own terrain and obstruction avoidance in the climb. we flashed the flight plan on climbing to 110, but redacted didn't take the handoff in time. we did not get permission to issue the instrument flight rules flight plan. redacted called and gave us control as aircraft x entered their airspace. the climb to instrument flight rules avoided a potential collision with the visual flight rules traffic. recommendation: d side training at the same time the r was training with busy and complex traffic had us all behind. i should of stepped in the get control with redacted as soon as i realized aircraft x was up on our frequency and we were taking action to avoid the traffic in redacted's airspace.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A Center Controller reported an aircraft being vectored for an approach deviated off course and flew below the Minimum IFR Altitude.
text: working combined positions as normal this early in the morning. slightly more complex because of lower weather in redacted area but nothing too bad. aircraft x was 1 of three aircraft being sequenced with the third being a flight school who had already requested an unusual pop up instrument flight rules and had been difficult to deal with. there was icing for the departures from redacted as well which the aircraft x had experienced earlier adding a bit of complexity. again, nothing too unusual. the previous days had been bad thunderstorm days and i was working multiple extreme complexity sessions with metering to redacted and already was feeling pretty beat down and tired by the week but was powering through. aircraft x was set up on approach, read back correct. it was a 't' shaped rnav approach. i noticed almost immediately that he blew through the turn to final, but just barely and looked to be correcting which he said he was when questioned. at this point he's a few hundred feet below the minimum instrument flight rules altitude (mia) but has been established and cleared on a segment of the approach and had been following the routing and altitudes fine.shortly thereafter i realized his correction was wrong, he was well below my mia as he was following altitude guidance on approach but obviously had 'slopped'/missed the turn to final and i issued the first low altitude alert. aircraft x seemed confused and he asked 'was that for me?' to which i replied 'yes, low altitude alert, aircraft x climb and maintain 080 immediately, approach clearance cancelled' he then began his climb. i showed him about a mile and a half south of approach course that he thought he was on. i then had to re-sequence the aircraft to make aircraft x last. i was working multiple departures out of redacted while this was happening. once getting him level at 080, i asked him about being off course. he said something about the gps being weird at the turn to final, asked for the approach straight in. i told him he had to be resequenced which i started to work on. feeling completely unlucky and beat down i told the supervisor 'i need to get off position now' which could have been accomplished by breaking training that was on the adjacent scope d side that had no traffic. but they opted to let me sit there and wait for someone who was coming back from break in the next 5 minutes. so, i continued to work planes under stress and duress.overall, i had already thought that there had been a lot of unprepared and unprofessional pilots this morning with the unexpected lower weather condition in redacted area. was asked for visuals when ceiling was overcast 026. people filed to satellite airports with no approaches. aircraft asking for inactive runways, approaches that are out of service etc. pop up instrument flight rules's immediately after take off. pilots are not preparing properly. furthermore, taking action to get a controller off position imminently when they ask needs to be a priority of any means possible following an incident. sure this wasn't the worst/most imminent incident but if a controller is saying they need off to clear their head, it is a safety issue for management to not take immediate action to address that.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: TRACON Controller reported failure to observe the conflict; nor did conflict activate; between VFR aircraft resulting in a NMAC event.
text: working a routine visual flight rules during evening at redacted. after a couple of frequency changes and a request for flight following to a different aircraft, aircraft x asked on frequency if i was talking to an aircraft within a half mile of their vicinity 5 miles sw of redacted airport to which i replied that i was not. aircraft x reported that the aircraft flew through their approved block altitude (025-040) at fl027 and they 'saw them at the last minute.' no collision alert via stars sounded at any point. shortly after the exchange, aircraft y called up on frequency letting me know they were the a fore mentioned a/c and had the helicopters in sight the whole time and requested to pick up an airborne instrument flight rules. aircraft x continued the rest of their operations with no issue and aircraft y continued on their instrument flight rules flight plan with no issue.recommendation: look into the reason the ca did not sound for visual flight rules target climbing/at same altitude.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air traffic controller reported working an aircraft and observing VFR traffic climbing towards their aircraft resulting in the controller issuing a traffic alert; climb and turn to avoid a collision with the other aircraft.
text: aircraft x was direct redacted for the gps to redacted xxr. untracked 1200 code with ads-b, aircraft y, appeared to depart redacted and climbed into aircraft x. requiring a traffic alert with immediate climb and turn to avoid a midair.radar display replay shows .35nm and 0 feet with an overtake.aircraft x lost separation with aircraft z at 050 opposite direction. radar display replay shows 1.98nm and 006 feet.aircraft x stated that he had lost the 1200 in the clouds then picked them back up. i asked aircraft x, for clarification, if the other aircraft had entered the clouds and aircraft x confirmed. i did not have time, nor was it my priority, to turn aircraft z to avoid the loss with aircraft x. i have no idea of a recommendation. have fsdo suspend the license of the pilot that almost killed people.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: ZDV Controller reported an unusual traffic situation due to weather with limited radio and radar limitations that resulted in an aircraft entering a higher MVA and a CFTT event.
text: i was working sector xx which is typically responsible for final sequence of den arrivals, but due to weather, departures were being routed out of the arrival gate as well creating high complexity to due opposite direction climbing and descending operations with most aircraft also deviating. myself and other controllers expressed concern with the safety of this unusual operation, and i feel that these concerns were ignored. the weather situation was changing rapidly, and although we managed to continue for an extended period of time i feel that an unacceptable level of risk was taken. while i was working through this situation a general aviation aircraft was transitioning my airspace at 6000 through an area of poor radar/radio coverage. due to the complexity of the situation and difficulty of coordination with the operations supervisor and traffic management unit i missed that they were flying to an area with a higher minimum instrument flight rules altitude (mia) and did not issue climb until the msaw alerted me.the culture at zdv currently does not seem to support controller input, and managers seem to frequently ignore safety concerns brought forth. i feel that this situation could have been avoided had the opinions of the controllers working the sectors been considered.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a ground conflict during taxi in with another aircraft. Captain brought the aircraft to a stop then continued.
text: after crossing rw 4l at k we were cleared to taxi s a re to gate. as we were approaching b on s my first officer yelled stop. as i was processing the command i saw the aircraft coming out of taxi b to join s south bound. i had to brake aggressively to avoid a collision. the angle he was approaching from was behind and to the right making him impossible for me to see until the last minute. the sun was also setting behind the aircraft making him harder to see. we came to a full stop and questioned ground control what had happened. he stated the aircraft had made a wrong turn. this is speculation on my part but i believe he had a similar clearance to ours but instead took k then made the hard left on to b without clearance almost hitting us. no fa or customer injuries were reported from the abrupt brake application.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Other / Unknown
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the procedures for holding at the scenic pad at ORD are unclear and there are no taxi or parking markings.
text: while waiting for gate availability, we were directed to park in the scenic pad facing the north tower." no natural direction faces the north tower. there were four planes there all facing different directions. more importantly, there are no taxi or parking markings. it was up to each crew to decide if they had safe wingtip clearances. there was no control or order parking in the scenic pad."
