anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A321 flight crew reported a F/CTL FLAPS LOCKED ECAM during approach. Flight crew continued to a safe landing.
text: being vectored into redacted xxr on a right base with flaps one and slowing for next flaps. as flaps 2 were selected received a f/ctl flaps locked ecam message. asked redacted approach for delayed vectors, requested priority handling and ran ecam procedures followed by qrh. ran non-normal land app and landed xxr uneventful. stopped on runway and had emergency vehicles clear the aircraft for safe taxi to gate. end of report.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: ERJ 145 flight crew reported an APU fire indication during taxi out.
text: we experienced an apu fire indication and fire alarm bell. as we were taxiing to the runway. captain called for second engine start, i started it then went though my taxi flow. i shut down the apu and completed the taxi checklist then the before takeoff to the line checklist. we then started hearing the fire bell and the eicas indicated an apu fire. we advised air traffic control and immediately began the apu fire qrc and went into the apu fire qrh which concluded with us pushing the fire extinguish button. captain contacted the fa of the situation while i talked to ground and we then pulled into the cargo ramp. arff (airport rescue and firefighting) trucks met us and saw no indications of a fire and the apu temp was 212 degrees. the fire bell would not turn off the entire time and we taxied back to the gate and had arff follow as a precaution. we remained until all passengers exited and called company.cause: apu fire message and bell,

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Wake Vortex Encounter
synopsis: ERJ 170 First Officer reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to EWR in trail of a B787.
text: power up and push back normal. as we neared the runway, the before takeoff checklist was accomplished, during this the ca armed the at (autothrottles), when he did this we got the at fault crew awareness message. i notified air traffic control that we had a mx (maintenance) issue and could we stop where we were or did we need to move. air traffic control replied saying there was nobody behind us. the captain set the parking brake and i pulled the qrh. there was no procedure it was just crew awareness. the captain called mx and accomplished proper mx procedures while i monitored air traffic control. after 15 minutes we were ready to go. since it was the captains leg he briefed the departure with the at inop. he stated that if we get tla (throttle lever angle) not toga or if he had issues getting the toga detent he would go max thrust. i agreed to this plan. on our roll he he set the power and was unable to find toga detent and went max thrust he called this out and i agreed. to was normal besides the max thrust. on the climb out the packs turned off as expected. he pulled the throttle back to toga and at this time we got the caution 'tla not toga' by the time i identified and canceled he had restored the power to toga. rest of flight went normal besides us being extremely tight on fuel. we took off with 300 pounds over min. we monitored the fuel level and expected to land above 2660 but we did advise air traffic control that we were close to min fuel. they were very accommodating. upon our approach into ewr ils/visual 4r we were kept tight to a 787. we called it insight and we were cleared for the approach. we were switched to tower and the ca said he would get the check on with tower. he requested to slow as we were close to the 787. tower approved this. around 1500 agl we encountered what i believed to be the wake turbulence from the 787. the ca had pulled the power back to get further configured. as he did this he also looked at the rudder trim and our speed dropped 10 kts below ref. i called out speed twice and he corrected immediately. after this out speed fluctuated slightly and the landing was normal. as we got to the gate the ca and i de briefed. he said he was going to talk to the dispatcher about the fuel being so tight in the planning stage. as well as talk to air traffic control about why we're so close to the heavy 787. i stepped out of the cockpit for this to use the restroom and did not hear any of the conversation. but he said it was taken care of.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: DA42 pilot with their Flight Instructor reported an inflight shutdown of an engine. Flight crew landed safely.
text: during flight instructor (ip) controls, one engine inoperative demo, lh engine shutdown. on restart attempt, lh engine did not restart. ran qrc/qrh. lh engine still unable to restart. ip landed at redacted.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an NMAC with a UAS during descent on arrival. No evasive action was taken.
text: in the descent to redacted on the redacted noticed a large two propeller uas pass 200' laterally to the right (south side) and roughly 150' below the right side of the aircraft. noticed as the uas passed abeam the aircraft. no maneuvers needed/nor executed due to the late tally of the object.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a ground conflict with another aircraft during push back. Crew continued.
text: we pushed back from gate xx. we were push back complete, salute received, engines started with after start checklist complete and parking break set. ramp tower switched us to metering and we were monitoring ground awaiting taxi instructions when gate xy began their pushback. flight redacted off of gate xy was disconnected from the tug with less than 10 feet of separation from their tail to our nose. our parking break remained set the entire time and we informed ground we were unable to taxi due to the aircraft in front of us. the pushback crew from gate xy either did not notice the proximity of the two aircraft or felt it was safe, even though movement from either aircraft would have posed a collision risk. gate xy was eventually towed back to their gate and we exited the ramp normally.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported they were cleared to cross an active runway while aircraft was on takeoff roll. Captain delayed crossing the runway.
text: it was nighttime. we had landed on 28r and were on taxiway t, holding short of 28l with the parking brake set. tower issued the clearance, aircraft x, on t cross 28l, traffic on a 2 mile final." i began pushing the power up in order to expedite crossing. before releasing the parking brake, i looked left to visually clear the runway. as i did so i saw aircraft y that had just rotated on 28l prior to t. seeing the traffic, i delayed releasing the brakes and crossing 28l until the traffic was well clear. we continued to the gate without incident. during our debrief, the first officer and i agreed that the clearance to cross 28l in such close proximity to departing traffic seemed unnecessarily risky."

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Incursion Ramp
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported they did not set the parking brake after parking and the aircraft rolled backwards.
text: upon arrival and coming to a stop at gate xx, i'm fairly curtain i set the parking brake and called for the check list. to our surprise after the 1st item in the list was called parking brake" i looked to verify the light was on. it was not and we were slowly moving backwards. i applied the brakes and set the parking brake to see the light illuminate. we moved back about 2 feet and i called the ramp agent to make sure everyone was ok and verified chalks. i'm not sure what happened, if i just forgot all together to set the brake, if i didn't pull quite hard enough to set it, or if it just released on accident. either way it was off and i didn't verify until the check list allowing the plane to roll back. luckily no one was hurt but it was eye opening.cause: not 100% at the cause. i know if i would have just stayed on the brakes until after the checklist all would have been avoided. i don't want to point fingers because this was all my fault. i would like to say that usually the marshaller will give you the signal that the chalks are in. but the person marshalling us stepped away to put the chalks in. i don't know if i subconsciously assumed good to let off the toe brakes or what. complacency was the cause, saved by the checklist.suggestions: slow down pay attention."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: B737 MAX 8 Captain reported losing datalink communications as the aircraft was outside VHF reception coverage.
text: received a datalink lost message when the aircraft was outside of vhf reception coverage. attempted to reset the system using guidance from manuals without success. cpdlc still made the automatic position reports along our north atlantic (nat) airspace route because the reporting points were in range of vhf from various countries. redacted radio did have to send a selcal asking us to log off and then back on again to redacted. this seems to be a common occurrence on the max 8 that i'm hearing from other crews and crews from other airlines. i want to ensure we are meeting the required future air navigation system (fans) and datalink reporting requirements to operate in the north atlantic (nat) airspace.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported confusing taxiway markings at ABQ led to a runway incursion.
text: while taxiing to runway 26 via alpha at abq, we mistakenly turned onto taxiway a3 and crossed the hold short line for runway 08/26 by a few feet. captain immediately stopped the aircraft and reported to ground. ground acknowledged and subsequently cleared us to cross runway 08/26 via a3 to continue our taxi.cause: a loss of situational awareness occurred due to divided attention. i was distracted by a gate-departure logbook outage and further fixated on an unfamiliar, non-standard ramp marking near a3.suggestions: as the pm, it is my responsibility to maintain strict situational awareness and actively cross-check our taxi route to back up the pf. however, i allowed the logbook outage and the unfamiliar ramp markings to divide my attention as well, failing to provide an effective backup. additionally, having a note or description of the green oval marking on published charts would prevent crew confusion, as it remains highly distracting in its current state.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural MEL / CDL
synopsis: Airbus 321 pilot reported being dispatched with a deferred inoperative generator; requiring the APU to be used as backup electrical source. Inflight; the APU shut down; necessitating a diversion to a suitable airport; due to single generator operation.
text: flight from redacted on a a321t model. after number 1 engine start after our initial pushback from gate xx at redacted, we received elec gen 1 fault ecam message. we followed the ecam actions to reset the generator but was unsuccessful. we asked ramp if we can hold our current position and the captain called maintenance control to ask if there is another procedure to follow and how to proceed. we were advised to return to the gate for maintenance to board the aircraft. after further inspection maintenance advised us that they were going to apply minimum equipment list (24-redacted) they asked us to start the #1engine so that they could disconnect the integrated drive generator (idg) as to their procedures. apu was checked and as per the minimum equipment list, should remain on for the entire flight. additional fuel was loaded on the aircraft and we pushed back for departure.during our initial climb through approximately fl240 the apu did an auto shutdown. we accomplished our procedures and transfer of aircraft control from the captain(pf) to the first officer(pm). the captain proceeded with checklists and communications between dispatch and the cabin to come up with a solution. with concurrence from dispatch the decision was made to divert to redacted, the closest suitable airport since we were operating on just one generator. we notified air traffic control and started towards redacted airport while the captain continued with the necessary checklists. one of the checklists was for an overweight landing. captain accomplished that checklist and we decided to request priority handling so that redacted would have the fire trucks ready to meet us upon arrival to inspect the aircraft.approach and landing was without issues, landing at 180.0 lbs. speed at touchdown 145 kts and rate of decent 200fpm. brake temps never exceeded 200 degrees after touchdown with brake fans on. we cleared runway xxl and after an inspection we were cleared to the gate.cause: during the event i feel like our crm was very good, reverting to our training. we worked together and had a positive outcome in the end. my one suggestion would be, even if some item is deferrable by mel/configuration deviation list (cdl) doesn't always suggest that it is the correct action for that particular mission. in this case, we had a multiple hour flight ahead of us while needing to run the apu continuously. that in turn required us to have a bigger fuel load for apu operations and the fact that we restricted below fl330. it was a nice visual flight rules day in area x but it could have been the opposite. operating on one generator could have been a whole different animal had the weather not been as good as it was where she had the failure. also, the extra fuel caused us to be heavier than we needed to be, and luckily we were in a t-model a321, with less passenger seats. in short, deferrable doesn't always indicate a wise plan of action depending on the situation.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft
synopsis: SR-20 instructor pilot and 2 students reported hearing a thud during the takeoff roll. Upon returning to the airfield; the nose gear failed during the landing; resulting in a prop strike.
text: i was backseating the flight and therefore not on the controls. after takeoff in redacted the three of us heard a sound at approximately 600 feet agl. the student pilot on the left pilot seat assumed that the issue was with his seat. therefore the instructor pilot took over the controls in order to let the student pilot adjust his seat and ensure it's safely locked in position. therefore the crew determined that it must've been the seat and a safe continuation of the flight is guaranteed. however special awareness is needed on the next landing. the flight was continued towards redacted. when arriving in redacted airport, the student pilot performed a normal landing and flare on runway xxl. during rollout the student pilot noticed that the aircraft pitched down more than usual and therefore decided to make this landing a full stop. the instructor pilot took over the controls and contacted redacted tower while taxiing off the runway. we exited at taxiway 1 and once the crew noticed that there was a prop strike they shut down the engine in accordance with air traffic control communication. inspection after the flight revealed that the nose gear collapsed and that there was a prop strike. therefore the crew suspects that the sound after takeoff in redacted must've been the front gear and not as thought before the left pilot seat. because the nose gear was most probably already damaged before the landing, the damage to the prop was a direct result of that situation.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Aircraft maintenance technician reported while performing a final release of the Cirrus SR20 aircraft; they found play in the elevator. Upon further inspection they found loose and missing hardware from the elevator rod end to the trim cartridge.
text: upon performing final for release of aircraft x, found play in elevator, upon further inspection found elevator trim cartridge loose, found cotter pin missing on rod end from elevator to trim cartridge and elevator trim cartridge screws completely loose.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air taxi pilot reported they descended below glidepath while intercepting the final approach course and received a Low Altitude Alert from ATC.
text: final approach into redacted on the rnav xx. i received a low altitude alert from air traffic control after intercepting the final approach course on the rnav xx into redacted. i was cleared to maintain 2400 until intercepting, with a final approach fix intercept of 2500. as i was intercepting, the aircraft continued descending, down to approximately 1500 msl. after receiving the low altitude alert from air traffic control, i immediately climbed back up to 2400. i was handed off to tower, and did not have any further discussions with air traffic control over the matter. i was not given a phone number or asked to call air traffic control once on the ground.i believe i inadvertently put the autopilot into pitch mode. i think it had to do with when i adjusted the altitude alerter. i was descending to a clearance of 2400 while being vectored to final, but during my final vector i was told to maintain 2500 and cleared rnav xx, which i asked air traffic control to confirm (because i was already below 2500) and they responded back with 2400. i think moving my altitude alerter from 2400 to 2500 put me into pitch mode, which i did not catch. i was fixated on the cdi as i was watching for my course to come alive and capture while i was turning to my cleared vector heading of 210. because of my fixation on the cdi, i missed that i had not leveled out at 2400.i believe the reason i went into pitch mode is because i moved the altitude alerter from 2400 to 2500, then back to 2400. however, because the autopilot in aircraft x levels out (on the descent) 100' low, i believe i was actually slightly below 2400, as the plane was capturing, and then i moved the alerter to 2500, then back to 2400.human performance considerations: i was alert, well rested, and otherwise in excellent condition for being pilot in command. i was not distracted, but i did fixate on the horizontal situation indicator (hsi) for my course capture as the plane descended well below the authorized altitude. i noticed the error a moment before and was just beginning to react when air traffic control issued the low level alert.to avoid recurrence: i need to not fixate and continue my instrument scan, especially during a critical phase of flight, and confirm autopilot mode more diligently.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Security
synopsis: Cessna 172 flight instructor reported ground vehicle on opposite end of the runway during take off. Pilot rejected the take off.
text: at about xa:00 my student and i were doing a touch and go at redacted rwy xx for training. as we were about to rotate off the touch and go i witnessed a sedan take the runway pointed at us rolling from the xy approach end eastbound. we executed an aborted takeoff and exited 1 to taxi back to the hold short rwy xx at 2. i attempted to hail the car on the radio to no avail. the airport authority maintenance personnel announced the runway was closed and pursued the car the full length of the runway at high speed. the car was intercepted and directed to the fuel pumps via taxiway 3 which was announced closed on ctaf. we held at the runup for xx adjacent taxiway 3 until given the all clear by the airport maintenance. it is possible there was a failure in security protocol on the field that would allow an unauthorized vehicle access to the runway environment.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Single engine aircraft flight instructor reported a NMAC while in the pattern. Instructor took evasive action and continued.
text: my student and i we're on a training flight practicing landings in colorado city (azc), established in the traffic pattern (right pattern for runway 11) on the departure leg after a touch and go and aircraft y, entered the pattern on the right crosswind leg heading westbound and to enter the right downwind for runway 11. when we were climbing on the departure leg of runway 11, it was at the last second i saw aircraft y was 200 feet above and on a head on collision. i took immediate action to discontinue the climb and level off so we wouldn't fly into them. aircraft y had no regard how to enter the traffic pattern accordingly and safely. very well could have been a head on collision if i hadn't noticed them.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Conflict Airborne Conflict
synopsis: Sonex Experimental pilot reported a loss of power during takeoff. Pilot returned to the departure airport.
text: on takeoff about 300 feet i lost most of my power returned to runway. i knew there was a helicopter inbound. on my return to the runway, i requested priority handling three times i said 'loss of power' i could see him, but he didn't seem to see me. i made three more calls to helicopter. he finally made an evasive maneuver and left the runway open for me. landed with no damage.i don't know what could be done to prevent reoccurrence. everybody seemed to be following the rules, but he did not hear me.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported a RA and NMAC.
text: while conducting day visual flight rules instrument flight training, the traffic alert on foreflight indicated an aircraft off of the nose at the same altitude and closing. the aircraft was observed as a twin engine fixed wing off of the nose opposite direction within extremely close proximity to my aircraft. upon identifying the target, i took immediate evasive action and banked the aircraft hard left to avoid a collision. after the near miss, foreflight was indicating the aircraft returning to within close proximity of me at the 5 o'clock and 7' o'clock.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft
synopsis: Private pilot and instructor reported during the landing roll out the nose wheel separated for the aircraft.
text: approach to land was stable. everything until touchdown was standard. after touchdown, the plane felt as if full brakes were being used. neither my instructor or i were using the toe brakes. we were pulling back on the elevator to use aerodynamic braking. the plane started to veer to the left without any rudder or brake input from my instructor or i. i attempted to use right rudder to correct, and around that time is when the nose wheel came off, and caused us to come to a stop on the runway. no injuries to me or the instructor. there was also a prop strike.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Corporate first officer reported conflict traffic taxied onto active runway resulted in rejected take off and a critical ground conflict.
text: departing runway 28r full length at sfo we had a rejected takeoff due to aircraft y taxiing onto the runway in front of us. aircraft y had turned right on the 'e' taxiway onto the runway instead of left onto the taxiway per their taxi clearance. after we began our takeoff roll we noticed the runway safety lights illuminate red. in the few seconds between this and the time we processed the meaning of the lights air traffic control canceled our clearance and we aborted on the runway safely. estimated speed at time of about was about 70, still within the low speed regime and we were able to quickly clear the runway onto taxiway n. the incursion by aircraft y also caused closely trailing traffic that was landing to have to go around. crew discussed brake cooling and applicable procedures and due to low energy nature and very low takeoff weight determined that extended cooling times were not required. after reconfig, a short wait and brief the next takeoff was uneventful.what caused this -i can only speculate but it appeared they had been flying a long day with numerous legs so fatigue likely was a factor. how we could improve- there was a short period during the roll where the status lights had illuminated but we had not fully processed their meaning and applicable procedure. likely due in part to lack of exposure to this system as part 91 pilots mostly utilizing airports not so equipped.recommend company safety bulletin on runway status lights and possibly integrating this scenario into sim training instead of the usual red hold short light scenario that training utilizes.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: GA pilot reported loss of directional control during landing resulted in a runway excursion before pilot regained control.
text: the primary objective of the training flight was to improve and master landing techniques in the pipistrel alpha trainer aircraft. at the time of the flight, i had accumulated approximately seven (7) hours of flight experience in this aircraft make and model.during one of the landing attempts, while on final approach at approximately 200 feet above ground level (agl), i encountered gusty wind conditions that adversely affected aircraft control and approach stability. as the aircraft transitioned through the landing phase, i failed to apply sufficient aileron correction to compensate for the crosswind and gusting conditions. additionally, i did not maintain adequate power to preserve the desired approach airspeed and positive control of the aircraft.as the approach became increasingly unstable, i delayed initiating a go-around procedure. although i ultimately requested that my instructor assume flight controls, that request was made later than it should have been. during the landing rollout and recovery sequence, the aircraft momentarily departed the runway environment before control was regained and the situation was safely resolved. no injuries occurred, and the aircraft was secured without further incident.upon reflection, several contributing factors were identified:limited experience in the pipistrel alpha trainer (approximately seven hours total time in type).inadequate crosswind and gust correction inputs during the landing phase.failure to maintain proper airspeed through appropriate power management.delayed recognition of an unstable approach.delayed decision to execute a go-around.delayed transfer of flight controls to the instructor.lessons learned from this event include the importance of maintaining positive aircraft control throughout all phases of flight, recognizing and responding promptly to unstable approach conditions, and executing an immediate go-around whenever approach parameters cannot be maintained. additionally, effective crew coordination and timely communication with the instructor are critical to safe flight operations.moving forward, i will place greater emphasis on stabilized approach criteria, crosswind correction techniques, power management, and early decision-making regarding go-arounds. i will also seek additional landing practice in varying wind conditions and will not hesitate to request instructor assistance at the earliest indication that safety margins are decreasing.this event serves as a valuable learning experience and will be used as a tool to strengthen my overall airmanship, aeronautical decision-making, and aircraft handling skills.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: GA pilot reported temporary decrease in engine power in carburetor icing conditions during descent.
text: while descending into redacted we were imc at 50 deg. f. (prime carb. icing conditions) after a long descent with low power we found ourselves with low power. it caused us to descend below our assigned altitude. applying carb. heat and going to full power we were still unable to maintain assigned altitude and nearing a stall condition imc. our power was finally restored and we chose not to declare an emergency as it appeared we could maintain altitude and complete the approach. in the future i will apply full carb. heat when descending at low power in carb. icing conditions.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: PA28 pilot reported landing gear would not retract after take off. Pilot returned to departure airport.
text: had a landing gear malfunction on the upwind. would not retract. returned to airport for landing and performed a low approach for tower inspection. tower said landing gear appeared down and i had lights illuminating so i attempted landing. on landing attempt, the gear warning horn sounded while power was pulled to idle so i went around and yawed the aircraft in the downwind to ensure the gear locked. attempted second landing with no issue and taxied to park. i did not declare an emergency but air traffic control had fire standing by.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Object; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Excursion Runway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: G200 Captain reported a runway excursion during landing. Pilot was informed of damage to a taxi light.
text: on a stable approach to runway xxl at redacted, the winds were very gusty and had almost 90 degrees crosswind. upon my flare i noticed that i had to input more than normal aileron to keep the plane centerline. upon touch down, i was almost full scale deflect aileron into the wind and the jet was still being pushed to the left. when all three mains were on the ground the jet was pushed to left and i was able to get under control back to centerline. after landing were told that that the left main went off into the gravel. then after that i was told that a taxi light was broken. the ops guy came and spoke to me and told me not to worry about this and he will take care of it.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported the CJR missed approach holding pattern is too close to the Class B airspace.
text: i being given an routine instrument proficiency check (ipc) in my personal aircraft with a cfi+i in the right seat. i was flying left seat as pilot in command. we were in visual flight rules conditions and not in contact with air traffic control. i was executing the rnav (gps) runway 22 approach into culpeper regional airport (cjr). the holding pattern/procedure turn for this approach is flown at 3000 feet and underlies the class b airspace for iad which is 4500 feet msl in that area. the class b airspace steps down to 2500 feet just beyond the published procedure turn footprint as depicted on the approach chart.when flying outbound at 3000 ft msl executing the published holding pattern/procedure turn past doyat i used a standard teardrop entry east of the approach course. during the final 210 degree right turn to intercept the inbound final approach course i noted that the projected flight path on my garmin 750 gps navigation instrument indicated i was going to pass very close to if not into the adjoining class b airspace beyond where it steps down to 2500 feet. i do not know if this was due to winds loft or if i may have inadvertently exceeded the published max holding pattern length of 4 nm. i immediately executed a more aggressive right turn and a rapid decent to get below 2500 feet to avoid the class b airspace. i continued the approach uneventfully.i reviewed the ads-b track for the flight and it does not appear that i actually encroached on the class b airspace based on gps tracking information. if i did it was very limited in extent and brief. the extensive pilot training that occurs in this area and close proximity of the class b airspace to the holding pattern for the gps runway 22 approach into cjr i believe combine to increase the probability of incursions into the iad class b airspace.i suggest the faa consider modifying the approach to increase the separation between the holding pattern and the adjoining stepped down class b airspace. this could be easily done by moving doyat intersection a mile or so closer to calpe.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: A general aviation pilot reported a ground conflict with an aircraft taking off on the opposite end of the runway. Pilot rejected the take off.
text: on day 0, i had just completed a fuel stop in jms and was taxiing for departure on runway 13. the wind was out of 180 @7kts approximately. while taxiing, aircraft y made a radio transmission stating they were landing on runway 13 and would be getting off making a 180 to depart 31. once they were clear of the runway, the pilot flying with me stated ' aircraft x is holding short runway 13 and we can wait for the other traffic to depart' aircraft y never made any other radio transmissions after they said they would be landing on runway 13 and taking off 31. we held short of 13 on d for a few minutes as aircraft y stayed put holding short 31. i made a transmission stating we are ready for departure and will be taking off 13. aircraft y still had not moved or made a transmission. as i went takeoff power set and began take off roll, aircraft y moved from holding short 31 at a to entering the active runway opposite direction. as soon as aircraft y started rolling i aborted takeoff and made another radio transmission trying to get hold of the aircraft. i made the decision to try and get off the runway at d1 as fast as i could as aircraft y was taking off and had visibility began take off roll. as the aircraft approached, they rotated around 1000ft prior to my aircraft as we were exiting d1. i made another radio call trying to get that aircrafts attention and silence. the fbo got on the radio and said they could hear us loud and clear and did not hear any transmissions by the aircraft.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cessna 172 Flight Instructor reported an erratic and rough running engine while in cruise flight resulting in an immediate return to the departure airport.
text: during our cruise, we experienced a drop in rpm from 2550 down to 2200. no power adjustments or fuel adjustments were made. after a few quick remedies, i decided i was not feeling very comfortable with the conditions of this flight. i requested direct redacted so we could get back on the ground as soon as possible. no emergency was declared due to the aircraft running smoothly at a constant power setting. we were about 10-15 miles away when the aircraft started running roughly and rpm was fluctuating even more. it was at this time that priority handling and direct redacted was requested. i maintained an altitude of over 5000 feet until the runway was made and then reduced power for the descent. it was when i reduced power to below 2000 rpm that the airplane began to run even rougher. power was pulled to idle, and we floated down to the runway. a safe landing was made and we vacated runway xxr at taxiway 1 and taxied straight to the ramp. the airplane mechanic was notified immediately.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: GA Flight Instructor reported an electrical malfunction in a Cessna 172.
text: i was conducting a long cross-country flight. flew for a total of 8.2 hobbs. preflight was normal, no issues with aircraft, and set out. no issues for the entirety of flight, until nearly 30 minutes out from arrival back at redacted around 35 or so miles north. minutes away from entry into the mode c veil of redacted the transponder began turning on and off again, resetting itself. i tried turning it on and off to reset it, but it then refused to turn back on. i began skirting around the veil to troubleshoot, when shortly after the garmin radio/nav setup failed. thankfully, the aircraft is a analog six-pack so flight remained nominal. i immediately suspected alternator failure, and checked the ammeter, to still see it curiously showing charge. so at the moment, i simply suspected a garmin system failure. i still had an alternate radio/nav system through bendix/king setup, and i began getting the atis for redacted and planning the entry. midway through that atis, that system died too and reinforced that suspicion of an alternator failure. now with no comms, transponder, and navigation system, i thankfully had my foreflight pulled up and loaded with the flight plan and navigated off of that. during these events, i realized that with no radios, there was no way to enable the pilot operated lights at redacted. i began formulating a worst case scenario of calling redacted or redacted to communicate the issue through bluetooth and my bose a20's, but i saw through foreflight ads-b in, thankfully, there was someone doing touch and goes at redacted and knew the text: day 0i am a recreational flyer, but i became a part 107 certificate pilot last year to be knowledgeable about drone regulations.around xa:00 today, i launched my dji air 3s drone by the field at location x. my flight was for recreation, and my flight plan was to fly a short distance over the river to take a photograph of a landmark on the east bank through the 3x zoom lens on my drone.about a minute after taking off, i lost connection with my drone. as i waited prayerfully for my drone to reconnect and return, a law enforcement officer saw me and came up to me and informed me about a tfr that was in effect in the area. the officer was courteous and professional and explained to me that they had identified the drone and were able to use a radio signal to disable my connection as a safety precaution. after notifying me about the tfr, the officer asked his coworker to release the drone, which quickly returned to my launch point. they inspected it and gave it back to me.i had in my possession my driver's license, part 107 card, and uas registration certificate as is required per part 107/the weight of the drone. i provided all this information to the officer, showed him the sticker on my drone that had the drone's registration number, my phone number typed on it, and an indication that my drone was remote id compliant as per 14 cfr part 89. i also showed him my dji phone app to show him that i had not yet taken a picture that day.i take pride in being a responsible drone pilot, and i am reporting this incident because i think there was an error with my autopylot app (version 1.21.1) and possibly an faa database that did not allow me to see the tfr on my iphone.prior to launching my drone, i used the autopylot app to confirm i was in class g airspace, was not in an area that required laanc approval, and that i was not close to a no-fly zone.after packing up my gear, i started looking at my app to see if i had missed something. i am very familiar with what a tfr looks like in this app (red circle) because there is one regularly in place around the local stadium near where i currently live. i checked that my settings allowed me to see all map layers and they were active. i later closed and reopened the app and the tfr appeared. this is concerning because the law enforcement officer told me that the tfr was already in place when i launched my drone.i then searched the tfr.faa.gov website for more information, and to my surprise, no tfr was visible on the map on this page (note: at the time i am writing you, it is visible for other areas which suggests to me that the website is functional). additionally, no information related to a tfr is listed for today's date on the notams list for the area. in addition to this information, i want to assure the faa that i am well-informed of the responsibilities of flying a drone. i purposefully chose my launch location due to my ability to maintain vlos, fly during a time with appropriate lighting and weather conditions, and fly far away from people and boating routes. i am familiar with the area having previously lived nearby for several years, and i researched the latest regulations prior to my flight.please let me know how if i can provide additional information about this incident.

text: after a number of operational distractions on our first leg to redacted earlier that day we taxied out late on a single engine (#1) headed for redacted. while on taxiway 1, we attempted to start engine #2 using apu bleed air and received an ecam message indicating insufficient bleed air pressure. the start attempt was terminated. the ecam message cleared without secondary indications. we attempted to start engine#2 a second time with the same results. about the time the second start was terminated, an aircraft behind us reported visible sparks coming from the underside of the right (#2) engine.we stopped short of spot xx on taxiway 1 and requested a crash fire and rescue (cfr) inspection through ramp control. cfr response time appeared longer than expected, approximately five minutes. there were a number of comm challenges with cfr but we eventually received an all clear. with a cfr escort, we taxied back to the same gate on a single engine, completed our inbound checks and deplaned the aircraft.after debriefing two mechanics we completed the electronic log book (elb) write-up. i instructed the first officer to contact dispatch while i contacted the chief pilot. considering the cumulative distractions and threats of the day, i determined that the most prudent course of action was for my first officer and me not to continue the next leg to redacted.i communicated this assessment to the chief pilot, who encouraged me to characterize the situation as either fatigued" or "not fit for duty." i believe this situation is more appropriately categorized as a human factors issue and that replacing the crew was in the best interest of safety and operational decision-making. the chief pilot was resisting that assessment..risk factors included:late-night operationshunger and cumulative fatiguemultiple maintenance and operational delaysemergency response involvementreturn-to-gate following engine abnormalitieslack of immediate replacement aircraft optionselevated operational stress over an extended period.the chief pilot understandably may not have been fully aware of the cumulative operational context. in situations like this, management should rely heavily on the personnel with the greatest situational awareness: the operating flight crew.the chief pilot appeared uncertain and repeatedly referenced checking with crew scheduling and other management pilots. he later stated that he was relatively new to the position. pilot pushing is rarely overt. it is not the chief pilot "putting a gun to your head." it is more subtle than that. it occurs when pilots experiencing and managing evolving operational risks, request support for a reasonable, fact-based safety decision, only to encounter resistance or hesitation from management instead of support for captain's authority and the safety values.pilots are highly susceptible to mission completion bias. for an experienced pilot to objectively assess the totality of circumstances synopsis: PA-28 Flight Instructor with student reported loss of control on the runway during takeoff; resulting in damage to runway lights and aircraft.
text: i was just made aware of the runway excursion on day 6. in the morning of day 0, two student pilots and one instructor pilot were practicing a soft field take off on runway xxr at redacted. the student pilot lined the aircraft up on the centerline for takeoff and, when cleared by air traffic control, started the roll down the runway. there was a right crosswind during the takeoff. we started the takeoff with proper wind correction, but as we continued through the takeoff, both flight instructor (ip) and student pilot's (sp) attention was on the pitch attitude for the soft field takeoff. the student pilot had entered an excessive amount of positive pitch, and the instructor pilot stepped in to help correct the excessive pitch and to maintain flying in ground effect, as our speed was getting pretty low. while making these corrections for the soft field takeoff, the ip did not input the proper crosswind correction, causing the aircraft to be blown off to the left of the runway. after getting the aircraft to a stable airspeed and pitch attitude, the instructor pilot then realized we were left of the centerline and maneuvered back to be lined up with the runway. during this occurrence, neither the instructor pilot nor either of the student pilots saw, felt, or heard any collision between the aircraft and any runway signs or lights. the instructor pilot stated to the students how unsafe the takeoff was, but due to being unaware of any collision, the instructor pilot did not file a safety report. the crew failed to do a detailed enough post-flight inspection and missed the signs of damage from the runway sidebar light on the bottom right side of the horizontal stabilizer. although neither the instructor nor any of the students was aware of the collision with the runway light, it was made clear that there was impact and damage done to the aircraft's airframe. the instructor is completing a recurrent training to take action and learn from his mistakes.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: Reporter stated conflicting information regarding the traffic pattern direction when the MRI Tower is not operating has resulted in pilots flying opposite direction traffic patterns; causing airborne conflicts. Reporter further stated pattern procedures need to be clarified through NOTAMs or other official channels of communication.
text: the recent reduction in merrill field tower operating hours has created a significant safety concern due to conflicting information being provided regarding after-hours operations.pilots are relying on published procedures contained in the alaska supplement and merrill-specific part 93 references, while others are reportedly receiving verbal guidance from faa personnel that different procedures apply when the tower is closed. as a result, pilots operating at the same airport are following different expectations for traffic pattern direction, arrivals, departures, and traffic flow.this is not merely a regulatory interpretation issue, it has become a flight safety issue. reports from local operators indicate that aircraft are conducting opposite-direction pattern entries and conflicting maneuvers based on differing understandings of the applicable procedures. in some cases, this has resulted in head-on encounters and other situations requiring pilots to take immediate action to avoid conflicts.merrill field is a high-volume airport operating within complex anchorage-area airspace. during the alaska summer season, traffic levels remain significant after tower closure, increasing the risk associated with inconsistent pilot expectations and non-standardized operations.immediate clarification and dissemination of the expected procedures for merrill field when the tower is closed is needed. whatever the faa determines to be the correct procedure, it is essential that all operators receive the same information through official channels such as notams, faa safety team publications, alaska aviation outreach, airport safety bulletins, and updates to published guidance. standardized understanding among pilots is critical to preventing further conflicts and reducing the risk of a serious accident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported a rough running; surging engine resulting in a diversion to a nearby airfield under partial power.
text: experienced engine roughness and surging at cruise near redacted intersection, approx. 13 miles redacted. symptoms included a rough running rough, and surged between 1000 and 2300 rpm constantly, the a/c was unable to maintain 6500' altitude consistently. immediately i executed a turn to head towards redacted as i had it in sight and there was still some daylight left. to triage, i increased throttle to full, increased my mixture, turned on carburetor heat, cycled through the magnetos to check spark plug issues. i elected not to switch fuel tanks as the fuel selector was already on 'both'. i also noted lower chts on cylinders 1, 3, and 5 per the engine monitor.i drifted down to 5000' and was able to maintain partial power approximately 5-10 knots above glide speed with engine surging. i contacted redacted center and let them know i was having engine trouble and asked for vectors to the closest field (i did not elect for emergency services). because i was able to maintain altitude, i determined it was feasible to head to the closest field which was redacted. i was able to make the field and performed a power off steep spiral into a straight in approach. throughout the approach and descent i was never able to reestablish full power to the engine. i performed a ground runup with the engine continuing to sputter slightly. i believed it was either severe carb icing, or some form of vapor lock. i also inspected the engine post-flight and did not see any immediate damage to the engine or cylinders.i left the aircraft tied down and the operator's mechanic inspected the engine more closely. they discovered a wasp's nest in the fuel vent and a leak in the fuel line between primer. this likely caused excessive leaning of the mixture and a partial vapor lock. i did not experience any indication or symptoms of the oncoming failure during runup nor during the cruise portion. oil temperature and pressure continued to be stable through the entire sequence of events. and no indication of fuel contamination or vent blockage during preflight inspection.
