anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying in a TFR without authorization.
text: on day 0 and day 1, i made 5 uas flights totaling approximately 35 minutes from location x. during this time, i was not aware of a tfr that was in place. i was attempting to fly directly up and hover my uas over location x for recreational pictures and videos. i checked the map in the dji fly app used to control the uas and it appeared to show only a restricted flight zone for redacted airport, which i was just outside of. the status indicator in the top left corner of the dji control app showed green indicating good satellite connection and showed the message 'takeoff permitted', which i believed confirmed that no flight restrictions were in place. i maintained line of sight, kept the uas over private property, remained below 400 feet and believed i was following all faa uas operational rules. i was not aware of the tfr until the final flight when i was approached by law enforcement personnel.reviewing my dji app flight log shows the following:on day 0, i made one flight for approximately 2 minutes and landed without incident. on day 0, i made another flight for approximately 7 minutes and landed without incident.on day 1, i made one flight for approximately 23 minutes and landed without incident.on day 1, i made another flight for approximately 2 minutes, lost connection and the uas returned to the take off point.on day 1, i made another flight for 3 minutes. as the uas was hovering i was approached by several law enforcement personnel. they informed me i was inside a tfr and directed me to land the uas. i immediately landed the uas and complied with all instructions. they informed me i should use an faa approved mobile app to monitor for current tfrs and that the manufacturer's proprietary drone application was not sufficient. this issue was caused by inexperience, insufficient understanding of how tfrs work and the incorrect assumption that the uas manufacturer's control application showed both temporary and permanent flight restrictions, which i now do not believe it does. i have no experience operating this uas or other types of flight experience and should have waited but i was excited and wanted to try it out.in order to prevent this from occurring again i have downloaded the faa approved autopylot app to remain aware of all notams and tfr's and i have completed the faa wings safety course alc-42: airspace, special use airspace and tfrs (know before you go: navigating today's airspace).to prevent this in the future, i believe training certification should be required to purchase and operate all drones. the extremely small size, low cost and ease to purchase my dji drone gave me entirely the wrong idea about how serious the regulations are for its operation and i had no idea i could get into such trouble for its use. in conclusion, i regret flying my drone before i fully understood its possible implications. i should have had a better understanding of the faa rules and restrictions. thank you for taking the time to read this and i hope it contributes toward something useful for the future.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Embraer First Officer reported a LG WOW System Fail message during the landing rollout on a wet runway; resulting in negligible braking. The Captain took control and applied max reverse to stop the aircraft.
text: first officer pf landing wet flaps full with ice speeds and favorable winds after a stable approach. touchdown was normal and in the tdz. during rollout, difficulty actuating thrust reversers with negligible braking. ca stated get on the brakes" with no changes to braking effectiveness. eicas master caution lg wow sys fail illuminated. ca took the aircraft and attempted to use the toe brakes with no effect. i briefly and gradually engaged the emergency brake to see if there was any changes, when braking effectiveness did not improve i released the emergency brake and reapplied pressure to the toe brakes. shortly thereafter, i was able to apply max rvs and held it until stopping the aircraft and exiting runway. lg wow sys fail message cleared brakes felt normal we taxied into gate without further incident. therefore we did not alert cfr (crash fire rescue). during post-flight inspection, we noticed the flat spots on the 4 main landing gear tires and notified maintenance control."

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Incursion Ramp
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported initiating a push back thinking Tower was closed. ATC cleared flight to continue the push back.
text: morning departure out of cho. we pushed back without a push clearance thinking the tower was still closed. the generic jepp app frequency times was apparently incorrect and an hour off. i was on my last day of ca upgrade oe and the lcp (line check pilot) said it was closed after reading his jepp material. lesson learned was no matter how experienced someone is continue to trust but verify. no deviation was given at the time. air traffic control called us out after we pushed but nothing was said after.cause: incorrectly reading the jepp material and not checking the other pilot.suggestions: i always encourage using our company material such as company pages when finding times of tower open/closed. as well as recommending both verifying the times.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: General aviation instructor reported a loss of altitude awareness during a training flight while performing a ground reference maneuver; resulting in a descent below an altitude limit above the ground.
text: my student began to set up for eights on pylons, a commercial single-engine ground reference maneuver. the objective was to have her practice explaining and demonstrating the objective, tolerances, and execution of the maneuver. her pylon selection was satisfactory. however, she was going to begin the maneuver noticeably low at about 1100' msl where pivotal altitude today was closer to 1400' msl. she was reminded of this and she climbed to 1400' msl using the pivotal altitude table. she began the first turn a few minutes later which was performed well. she recovered to 1400' msl and began setting up for the second turn in the maneuver. but in doing so, a combination of turbulence and overbanking caused my student to get too low. overbanking in this maneuver causes pylons to seem to move forward, resulting in an illusion that the aircraft is higher than actual altitude. this prompts the pilot to push forward on the controls when otherwise unnecessary. my student was inadvertently overbanking the airplane (not keeping the bank fixed), resulting in a large descent to which i did not intervene in time. she was reminded to keep the bank angle fixed. in the process of instructing her to do so, we descended to 681 indicated altitude which i believe is below 500' agl, prompting this report. besides greater vigilance on behalf of instructors like myself who may find themselves too low, it is important to draw the line higher such that students do not get anywhere near the 500' agl limit. fixation on pylons and bank angle may be beneficial to the maneuver itself but can cause a loss of altitude awareness which has resulted in controlled flight into terrain in past general aviation accidents. i plan on drawing the line higher for students performing this maneuver, especially for students who are new to the maneuver from the right seat or students who have not flown the maneuver for some time.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported they crossed hold short line causing an aircraft on final approach to go-around at MTJ; a non-towered airport.
text: was preparing to takeoff from runway 35, mtj. i did not hear a landing call from aircraft y for runway 17 and crossed the hold short line at a8. i did not proceed to the runway once crew pointed out the call. i finally got control of what was happening and was preparing to do a u-turn to exit the runway when the aircraft called a missed approach. i waited until i could locate the aircraft on ads-b and proceeded to takeoff.i had issues with radio volumes and usage by the crew and should have corrected all of these before taxi, and especially after engine runup since it was still an issue. i let distractions keep me from being as diligent as i should have been.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: Vans RV9 Experimental pilot reported safely returning to departure airport after experiencing engine malfunction during initial climb.
text: departed redacted. had just fueled before this takeoff, but had checked both tanks, and also the oil was checked at 5 qts. noticed that chts were high on the ground and temps continued to climb during takeoff, as was normal. climbout at 80 mph. at 1000' and above pattern altitude elected to reduce power and slowly accelerate for engine cooling. engine failed, then restarted. switched tanks, mixture was rich, carb heat on, fuel pump was on, mags were on both . engine started and then failed again. advised other aircraft on ctaf causing a lancair to taxi clear of the runway to runup pad. was now at 1400' with the engine surges, when i elected to to pull the power to idle. did a 360 to dissipate altitude as the rv9 glides extremely well. extended full flaps and had to employ a hard slip to get it down. the engine responded to throttle inputs at 300' agl. landed on runway xx redacted and taxied, with power, to the ramp. upon shutdown, noticed oil leaking under the spinner, and shortly had a pool of oil on the ground.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: SR20 Flight Instructor with student reported the aircraft could not reach rotation speed resulting in a rejected takeoff.
text: i was conducting an instrument eoc (end of course) flight test for a student. during takeoff, the student advanced the power to full (about 3 a second advancement on the power lever). all engine indication systems were in the green ranges. i don't know exactly what the rpm was during the takeoff, but the percent power was in the green arc. the plane was picking up speed more slowly than usual. by the time we reached our abort point (the five thousand feet remaining marker), the plane still hadn't reached rotation speed. the student added a little back pressure on the controls, and the nose came up then back down onto the ground about 2 times. by that point, we decided to abort the takeoff, and the student reduced the power to zero, and i took the controls to slow the plane down and taxi off the runway at the next intersection. the student confirmed with me that he had no brake pressure inputs during takeoff. extra info: plane was an sr20. this was the first flight after it's 100hr inspection.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported GPS interference in RJJJ airspace.
text: shortly after departure, at 30, 000 we started getting terr pos eicas messages and increasing anp. shortly after accomplishing the associated checklist, we elected to run the unannunciated gps interference (cruise) checklist. while running that checklist, we received a gpws terrain pull up. we quickly assessed the necessity to execute the escape maneuver, and based on our position relative to physical terrain, deemed it not to be required, and overrode the warning. after the gps checklist was accomplished, the anp degradation was no more than 0.43 in rnp 10 airspace. an ads b-in eicas was then observed and associated checklist was accomplished without further event. once we entered airspace where gps interference procedures were no longer required, we reversed the gps checklist, but only the left gps recovered. according to the relief captain's report on the events of the second half of the the flight, the right gps never recovered and caused additional problems for the crossing.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Global 5000 Captain ferrying an aircraft reported engine failure and spoilers malfunction and diverted to a nearby airport.
text: i was the pilot in command of aircraft x operating from redacted to redacted. approximately 25 minutes into an otherwise uneventful flight, while established in cruise at fl320, we experienced a right engine failure.the event was immediately apparent to the entire crew. we heard two distinct and extremely loud bangs that were consistent with compressor stalls and were accompanied by significant airframe vibration. the severity of the noise and vibration left little doubt that we were experiencing a major engine-related event. immediately following the bangs, numerous eicas messages populated the displays. the most prominent message was a right fadec fail indication, which was followed by high itt, low oil pressure, and indications consistent with a rollback of the right engine.at the time of the event, i was serving as the non-flying pilot and immediately began running the applicable checklist associated with the right fadec fail message. as we worked through the checklist, the aircraft indications and system responses were consistent with what we were observing, reinforcing our assessment that we had experienced a significant engine malfunction.given the loud compressor stall events, severe vibration, and multiple engine-related indications, our initial assessment was that we may have suffered a catastrophic engine failure rather than a simple fadec malfunction. at that point, our primary focus became aircraft control, system management, and determining the safest and most expeditious airport for diversion.as we transitioned from redacted center to redacted center, communication difficulties introduced additional challenges during an already high-workload situation. although we had been communicating on the redacted center frequency for several minutes, when i advised air traffic control that we were operating as a priority aircraft, the initial response was a question regarding whether we were attempting to pick up an instrument flight rules flight plan. this response led us to believe that there was a significant lack of awareness regarding our situation.i immediately restated that we were requesting priority handling and required a diversion to redacted. redacted center then requested our position and destination, further indicating that they did not yet have a clear understanding of the nature or urgency of our circumstances.from a crew resource management perspective, this lack of situational awareness created additional workload at a time when both pilots were heavily engaged in checklist execution, aircraft systems monitoring, diversion planning, and threat assessment. rather than being able to focus exclusively on managing the situation, we found ourselves dedicating valuable attention to ensuring that air traffic control fully understood the seriousness of our condition.to remove any ambiguity and ensure immediate recognition of our status, i selected transponder code redacted and transmitted to air traffic control on the frequency. my intent was to clearly communicate the urgency of the situation, obtain priority handling, and expedite vectors toward redacted. following these actions, redacted center recognized the nature of the situation, coordinated appropriately, and provided the assistance necessary for us to continue the diversion and prepare for landing.as the flight progressed and we began preparing for a single-engine approach into redacted, we became aware of additional system abnormalities involving hydraulic system 2. we received a flt spoilers fault message and observed multiple yellow cautions on the flight controls synoptic page. the indications suggested that the flight spoilers were deployed and were not returning to their normal trail position.to verify the indications, both pilots visually inspected the wings from the cockpit. we observed that spoiler panels 3 and 4, as well as panels 7 and 8, appeared deployed on both wings. these observations matched the indications displayed on the aircraft systems pages and confirmed that we were dealing with an additional flight control anomaly beyond the engine failure.we completed all applicable checklists associated with the hydraulic and spoiler indications. these procedures included actions intended to restore hydraulic system 2 functionality through electric pump operation. despite completing the prescribed procedures, the spoiler panels remained deployed and the associated cautions persisted. no corrective action restored the system to a normal configuration, and the aircraft continued to experience the associated aerodynamic drag. it was then as pilot in command i took control of the flying and the sic (second in command) took control of the radios.as we approached redacted and entered the downwind for runway xxr, it became evident that we would be landing with a combination of degraded aircraft performance factors: a failed right engine and substantial additional drag from spoilers that appeared to be stuck in the deployed position. this additional time allowed us to evaluate aircraft handling characteristics, verify performance expectations, review landing considerations, and effectively 'learn how to fly' the aircraft in its current degraded state before committing to the approach.the approach and landing were ultimately completed without further incident. following a normal touchdown and rollout, we taxied clear and completed the appropriate shutdown procedures. the aircraft was subsequently towed to the fbo ramp where emergency response personnel met the aircraft. firefighters conducted a visual and thermal assessment and reported no evidence of fire, overheating, or external engine damage following landing.during the post-flight inspection, no visible external damage to the right engine was observed. however, after all hydraulic systems were powered down, the flight spoilers remained physically stuck in the deployed position, confirming that the spoiler anomaly persisted beyond aircraft shutdown. the condition of the spoilers appeared consistent with the indications we had observed in flight and likely contributed significantly to the increased drag experienced during the diversion and landing.while the crew successfully managed the event and landed safely, the combination of an apparent engine failure, subsequent hydraulic and flight spoiler anomalies, and initial communication difficulties with air traffic control created a complex and rapidly evolving situation.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Other / Unknown
synopsis: Flight attendant reported while at the gate catering opened an armed cabin door; resulting in a near inadvertent slide deployment.
text: during the demo, catering opened armed door 2l. both flight attendants agreed that we didn't need catering so b-fa told them to leave while i called captain to inform the situation and we resumed the demo once they left.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Cheetah AA5B Flight Instructor reported an NMAC and was in contact with ATC at the time.
text: i was cruising ivo (in vicinity of) redacted with redacted approach clearance. i observed a target on foreflight descending from my 5 o'clock position, 1, 000 feet above. i inquired with redacted if they were talking to him. even though they were supposed to they hadn't called redacted. as they descended they crossed my flight path as they descended through my same altitude. i evaded and crossed to the other side. they later checked in to redacted approach and when asked said they had us in sight...on their right even though we were then stable on their left. they never really saw us.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Global 500 First Officer reported engine failure; hydraulic system; and spoilers malfunction that resulted in a diversion to nearby airport.
text: i was sic (second in command) on aircraft x which was a ferry flight operating from redacted to redacted. we had been flying for approximately 30 minutes and were in the descent to redacted when we heard and felt numerous bangs which sounded like compressor stalls and had intense vibrations throughout the aircraft. we both confirmed that the right engine had failed and received many eicas messages, most prominent being r fadec (full authority digital engine control) fail. i was pilot flying throughout the engine failure, and the captain in the left seat was pm and he began running the checklist and communicating with air traffic control to start our diversion. trying to get ahold of air traffic control was more difficult than it should have been. the captain was trying to communicate with redacted center. when air traffic control got back to us they asked us repeat our callsign and say again our request. i think they were confused. when we requested that we wanted to divert to redacted, they asked if we had a flight plan on file. it was at this point that air traffic control understood who we were and that we needed priority handling. we were given direct redacted and began to descend. throughout this, i was flying the aircraft and keeping an eye on engine parameters. we had very high itt (interstage turbine temperature), low oil pressure, and rapidly reducing n1, consistent with an engine shutdown. we also had hyd pump 2b fail eicas message. we got the engine shut down, and were slowing and descending to land in redacted when we got an amber flt splrs fault message. when we checked out the window, we had some spoilers that were out, even with the handle stowed. the captain had made a call over the pa to the flight attendant earlier to let he know what the situations, but sometime around this time, the captain called her up and quickly gave her a brief of what the situation was, where we were diverting to, and told her he would communicate with her if we needed to evacuate once we were on the ground. we were aware of numerous other hydraulic issues with system 2, so we were trying to make the best plan of action to get down safely being single engine and having multiple hydraulic issues. i elected to had over controls to the captain for the landing. the captain did an excellent job on the landing and safely taxied the plane off the runway before we had the fire department look at the right engine to assess any damages. the told us there were no heat readings and no visible damages, so we completed all appropriate checklists and we got a tow into the fbo.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: B787 First Officer reported GPS jamming during cruise flight.
text: we lost one of the gpses, which subsequently presented issues later in the flight. i was on second break at the time and was not present for that specific event.however, we complied with gps spoofing/jamming checklist procedures earlier in the flight by turning the gpses off when required. once clear of the affected airspaces, the gpses were turned back on in accordance with the checklist. after completing the checklist, only one gps returned to normal operation.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Grumman AA1B pilot reported engine failure on approach. Engine restarted after advancing the throttle followed by an uneventful landing.
text: on approach to redacted, at around 1000', i pulled the throttle back and the engine quit. i advanced the throttle and around 1800rpm the engine restarted.i landed fast (110mph indicated) because i need the keep the power in. landing was uneventful. when i pulled the throttle back upon landing the engine quit again. initial diagnosis is carb ice. the a&p also noticed rust. carburetor removed for overhaul. the aa1b poh gives no clear instructions on when carb heat is needed and grumman pilots have told me they don't use carb heat, unlike in older cessnas.i believe the faa should clarify this.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: SR22 pilot reported an altitude clearance deviation due to severe turbulence.
text: during routine climb to cruise altitude, aircraft enter a building cumulus cloud and experience moderate to severe turbulence resulting in the autopilot system disengaging due to inability to maintain aircraft control within required parameters. after assuming manual control of aircraft, primary task was to maintain control of the airplane in the turbulent air and it resulted in unintentionally deviating from the assigned level off altitude. once aircraft control was assured and aircraft exited the cloud layer, immediate return to the assigned altitude and level off was resumed. flight continued uneventfully.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: Pilot reported reduced runway visibility in tailwheel aircraft resulted in runway excursion with loss of control.
text: i flew the aircraft from redacted using visual flight rules to redacted to reposition it for a project. i was unfamiliar with the airport redacted. the owner of airport gave me approval to land there to have the aircraft available for a project. before flying, i made himself aware, as best as i could, of the airport data and noted the narrow runway (4000 ft x 40) with no pavement markings. i performed a thorough preflight planning session using foreflight and obtained the notams and weather for the arrival area. wind was forecast to be light and from the se. upon arriving at the airport, i made a high recon pass in the direction of the runway xx traffic pattern and noted a building and e-w power lines just north of the north end of the runway. from the cross country trip, i had the windows and door closed. i flew the final to a displaced point on runway xx to be 100% sure that i would avoid the power lines (which i later found were actually buried underground just north of the approach end of runway xx). i configured the aircraft with full flaps and carb heat. i listened to the nearby redacted asos and, as best as i can remember, the winds were 122 @ 6, resulting in a 5 knot crosswind component. i decided to fly a wheel landing. touchdown was nice and i kept the tail up as long as i could (forward stick), and the aircraft tracking along the center of the runway. when the tail settled, i pulled the stick all the way aft. unbeknownst to me, the aircraft drifted to the left but i could not tell that, because i could no longer see over the nose, and, since the runway was narrow, i did not see any pavement in my left and right periphery. i estimate that the speed on rollout at that time was between 5 and 8 knots. suddently, i relized that my left wheel was dropping off the left edge of the concrete runway into, what turned out to be, very soft (cultivated) soil. what followed happened in the blink of an eye but takes a while to describe hereinafter. the left wheel slowed down due to the massive drag in the very soft soil, causing the aircraft to veer 90 degrees to the left. the right wheel subsequently entered the soil, and, with the 90 degree angle of the aircraft to the runway, it dug in as well. the speed at that point was probably quite slow, 3-4 kts perhaps. the aircraft tipped to the right and the right wingtip made contact with the soft soil. my right shoulder bumped into the right plexiglass window and broke it (no injury to me). the aircraft came to a stop and the right wing came back up to its normal position. i turned off the engine and all switches and got out. a walk around inspection indicated that nothing broke off the aircraft and the propeller never made contact with the ground. the right wingtip was dirty, with some dirt on top of the wing as well. the right wingtip showed some signs of contact with the ground and the wingtip light was still intact. the extent of the damage could not be ascertained at that point. the owner helped me to push the aircraft back to the runway and i taxied it back to the hangar building on the north side. while i am not at all proud about how this landing turned out, there may be some useful learning points to take from it. a lot of what i am stating below has the benefit of hindsight. first, i wish i would have used a booster cusion to get my head and line-of-sight as high up as possible. if i had seen over the nose the entire time, i would have noticed my drift to the left and stopped it. the sitting height i was at was totally adequate for landing at an airport with a runway that is wider and/or has center line and edge line markings and elevated runway lights. it is also an ok sitting height when landing in wider grass fields or grass runways where lateral position is not as critical. i am used to landing on narrrow runways with this aircraft, such as for example at redacted. however, that concrete runway transitions smoothly into a wide strip of mowed grass on each side of the runway and the outer extent of that mowed grassis marked with edge lights. all of this provides a pripheral vision cue that is completely sufficient for lateral alignment corrections. the runway at redacted is new concrete but it has no grass on either side and, in fact, there is a bit of a step down into very soft cultivated soil that, in fact, is so soft that a person could dig their hands in down to 6-10 inches without resistance. i could not ascertain that situation from the airport data during my preflight or during the recon pass i made. physiologically what happened was that when the tail settled on the ground, i lost all forward view of the runway (this is normal) but also all peripheral view (this is not normal) because the sight triangle from my eyes, across the lower window edge ended up in the uniformly colored soil to the left and right of the runwway. thus, due to the narrowness of the runwway, all i could perceive on the left and right was uniform soil from a uniformly cultivated field on both sides of the runway. this provided me with no ability to perceive lateral drift cues and it happened quickly. the small step from the concrete to the soil acted like an accelerant to pulling the left wheel off the runway, once it reached the edge during the drift to the left, with no recourse to get it back up on the concrete. unlike the mowed grass overrun that other narrow runway airports have (like redacted), this airport had very soft (cultivated) soil immediately to the left and right of the firm concrete runway. i could not ascertain that information during preflight and the recon pass. the softness of the soil provided an unforgiving environment that immediately bogged the left wheel down, while the right one was still on hard concrete. this resulted in the sudden veering turn to the left.second, and of course with the benefit of hindsight, i wish i would have opened both windows and the right folding door. this would have improved my sight triangle to the ground and i might have noticed the drift. third, i wish i could have foreseen the sudden loss of peripheral alignment cues during the tail low portion of the landing. uniformly cultivated fields abutting directly onto a runway are not suitable to provide pilots who are unfamiliar with a particular airport.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter VFR In IMC; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported inadvertently entered IMC weather resulting in a loss of aircraft control with eventual recovery and divert.
text: flight following from redacted to redacted coordinating with air traffic control following the coast and keeping clear of convective weather, as i also avoided clouds. at xa:45pm aircraft started to experience turbulence and a strong desire to climb above 11k'. once i brought us back down to 10500 and stabilized us, at about xb:05pm a heavy mist blew in from the s and overtook my visibility. we were sucked up into a climb more much more quickly and violently than before. i turned r to the n toward the coast, and tried descending us to get out of the mist/cloud and back to visual flight rules conditions. it was a very light rain, but total white out. during my descending turn to the n it felt like the aircraft was pushed by a strong gust of wind, the right wing lost lift, and we went into a spiraling dive/spin. as i worked to regain control of the aircraft, i think it was a combination of me recovering from the spin and the atmosphere rapidly changing condition (we were experiencing up and down drafts) that led to the aircraft shooting straight up in the air until stalling. my passenger and i were unsure of what was happening at that point, as all the up, down, and turns had us disoriented. all of our instruments were spinning in circles one way one second, then spinning the other direction the next second. all this in white out conditions. we experienced weightlessness, then increasing gravitational forces. air traffic control came on asking if we were ok because they had us 'losing altitude rapidly.' not having any control over the aircraft, all instruments spinning erratically, and total white out visibility... i responded: 'requesting priority handling, we are not ok. please stay with us.' my passenger pointed out the vsi got to 9 o'clock by going 'down' and i saw the airspeed indicator increasing in the yellow arc. we were in a power on vertical dive. i saw the airspeed approaching 185mph and i struggled through the g forces to pull the throttle back to idle. i then crushed the right rudder to the floor. i believe this deflection to the side of the fuselage was what slowed our straight vertical dive (maybe we were spinning in the dive too). either way, the attitude indicator then became stable and indicated a diving left bank. knowing not to pull back on the yoke hard, i gently and intermittently gave the yoke right and back pressure inputs. the g forces lessened, and the instruments all began stabilizing. we became level, but were still falling. like a parachute. in total white out still. after a few seconds of that, we gently fell below the cloud layer, like coming down an elevator. i put the power back in, and we were on our way. air traffic control came on asking if we were ok. i said something like 'i love you. thank you so much for being there for us. please get me an airport to land at as soon as possible.'i never exceeded the 214mph vne of my piper arrow ii, and i do not believe i reached the positive load factor of 3.8 g. regardless, before my next flight i called my home airport aviation mechanic and performed a visual and tactical inspection of the aircraft with him via video call. i would not have flown my aircraft again if i had any doubt about her airworthiness. regardless of not hitting the structural limitations of the aircraft... in an abundance of caution, i am having it professionally inspected by my aircraft mechanic. although i aimed to remain 20 miles away from the convective weather, i believe it was the outer edges of the cell that caused us to experience the updrafts, downdrafts, and strong wind gusts that caused us to lose control of the aircraft. i kept power in thinking i could keep control of the plane against the winds that way, but in hindsight i think i should have decreased power sooner. losing altitude and diverting n was difficult because there were other clouds to avoid beneath us, intense air traffic coming and going from all the airports in that area, and lots of different airspace, including military airspace that i was trying to remain clear of for safety. i thought my altitude and heading would keep us safe from the weather, heavy traffic in the area, and the airspaces. in hindsight, maybe i should have asked air traffic control if it was ok for me divert more n. there was a storm that had just come over the shore from the s to the n that i was trying to stay below as well though. so there was a lot going on. it also looked like small cells, but heavy precipitation over the airports i would have liked to divert to before the event happened. i kept hearing of the 12k' ceiling above me, and ceilings at different airports at 2500' and 4500'. i didn't want to get stuck in imc trying to descend to land at an airport to avoid the weather, only to end up in it so close to the ground. i wanted altitude for safety, and it was a major factor in why i was able to recover. not only am i going to make sure my aircraft is just as good as it was before the incident, but i am also intensifying my weather knowledge, and i am going to pursue spin training and aerobatics. these are 'advanced pilot techniques' that i think should be taught to every private pilot. especially since inadvertently getting caught in imc conditions is such a killer of ga pilots.what could air traffic control have done differently... i don't think their equipment showed me getting 'too close' to the danger zone that day. a lesson we can learn is how dangerous a tightly formed cell with heavy precipitation consuming its growth can create extreme wind shear around its outer perimeter. the radio was very busy that day with aircraft diverting due to rapidly changing weather conditions. i was very grateful air traffic control came on to let me know i was losing altitude rapidly. as tossed around as we were, this was helpful in the moment. i was hoping they would call out my altitude repeatedly as it changed, and hoping they would call it out as i was losing or gaining it. any information they could have given me like that could have helped. i understand they are not pilots, and probably shouldn't give the pilot in an unknown flight condition piloting advice, but the altitude and possibly heading call outs could help in a situation like that. i have no complaints. air traffic control did a great job handling the weather and workload they had that day. i have a new respect for weather, and this will make me a better pilot, and sharing my experience with others hopefully will help them stay safe. i want to be in compliance with all that is expected of me as a pilot. i want to be an incredible pilot. please let me know if anything else is expected or needed of me. thank you for the time you devote to our safety.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Bellanca Scout pilot reported a hard landing resulting in a propeller strike.
text: during landing phase 7 knot headwind (gusting 20) turned into a direct crosswind while attempting two point landing. resulting in a hard bounce and prop strike before getting the stick back and regaining full control of the aircraft.the shifting winds and the pilots limited time in tail wheel aircraft are root cause of the prop strike.further training in tail wheel landings as well as practice in go arounds will prevent future incidents.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: B747 pilot reported a possible spoofing event during cruise phase. Crew continued and landed uneventfully.
text: we were oceanic approaching position redacted. i was resting in the bunk when this event initially occurred. apparently the calculated fuel quantity remaining went blank on the fmc however the fuel tank quantity indications appeared to work correctly along with the totalizer amount. that probably has nothing to do with the subsequent issues but we lost the our predicted fuel and etas for the remaining wpts. air traffic control confirmed that our cpdlc position reports were missing the estimated times. we noticed then the fos navigation display (nd) upper right waypoint was stuck on the previously previously passed waypoint. the fos magenta line continued showing us right on course however the cross track miles number was diverging throughout the remainder of the flight and was over 16nm by the time we got to redacted. the captains nd had the correct next waypoint displayed but no eta. the captains nd magenta course showed us on the airway also. we called a engineer and he had us switch the fmc switch above the eicas screen from left to right. we also selected the captains single integrity sensor (sisp) fmc switch to right side. this ended up fixing our waypoint etas, predicted fuels, and position reports. maintenance either manually or automatically sent an acars message saying we had a possible spoofing event.when we descended into redacted there was a split in the yellow low airspeed foot between the captains and fos speed tape. the captains being a much higher airspeed foot than fos. we assumed the captains side was using the fuel weight at the time of the lost calculated fuel indicator. there was a 10 knot airspeed difference in the flap speed pointers, the captains being higher. we used the higher speed. we landed uneventfully.

text: control was expecting a phone call prior to our scheduled takeoff from redacted. no phone call was made. shortly after takeoff - upon check-in - control immediately advised me because we had deviated from our agreement to always phone ahead before departing. there was no hazard to people or property during the event, and the flight continued without incident.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: Tower Controller reported a firefighting truck and associated vehicles crossed a runway they had been instructed to hold short of at the same time a departing aircraft was taking off.
text: our facility is understaffed. we are allowed 12, 14 with training. we have 9, with 1 controller medically disqualified since the start of the busy season. day 0 is the final day of the busy season. all our controllers are burned out. everyone has been doing 6 day work weeks, lots of 10 hour days. additionally in an attempt to get more staffing, our manager has increased our required time on position and reduced break times and lunch breaks. moral of the story, we are burnt out. i had been fighting a cold or sickness of some sort and am not 100% at this time. i'm tired, i'm sick. i'm now in my 9th or 10th hour of work. the airport had an event on day 0. there were several aircraft participating. before the event, the aircraft altogether did about 100 separate ops in the traffic pattern, wearing out my supervisor and i, the only two there that morning. luckily a third, fresh controller worked the event itself when he arrived to work at xa:15.during the event, all arff (airport rescue and firefighting) units staged at location x, which is across the airfield from the fire station. after the event was over, they called to relocate back to the fire station, needing to cross both parallel runways. my supervisor was working lc, at my request, as i was just so worn out and could barely talk or think anymore, that i felt i would only be safe on ground control, if that. so arff calls me and requests to cross both runways back to the fire station. at this time, aircraft x is lining up to depart rwy xxl. i coordinate a conditional crossing reference the departing aircraft. my sup approves the conditional.'arff and company, cross runway xx right at 1. hold short runway xx left at 1.'i receive a perfect readback. i watch very carefully as the 3 arff units cross xxr. they get to the other side (taxiway 2) and come to a full stop after clearing the runway. i literally nod my head and say to myself, that's what i want to see. i turn to watch this beautiful aircraft depart xxl and to know when it has passed taxiway 1 so i can cross the arff units. looks good, roaring down the runway. i make one last check on the arff units and turn my head toward them one more time. as my eyes see arff, i observe them moving fast (25-40 mph) across taxiway 2. i key up the frequency and pretty much yell, 'arff, stop!!!' the lead fire truck slams on it's breaks. i watch as the truck tips forward in its best attempt to stop. the other trucks also stop. arf is over the hold short line. seeing that they have all come to a complete stop, i quickly glance over to the aircraft to see if there is any way to cancel take off clearance. it is just airborne between taxiways 3 and 1. at this point, it was safer to let them takeoff. i clutch my chest because i literally can't fathom the thought of what had almost just occurred.the aircraft has now passed and i give the arff units clearance to cross runway xxl. i got off position quickly thereafter and left for the day.recommendation: all of our controllers have had negative experiences with arff and how many mistakes on the airfield they have made. i love fire fighters, but these guys (and gals) need more training. the controller's have talked about having them over to the tower and giving them classes during our slow period, but it never seems to happen. given incidents like this, perhaps the faa can mandate some driver's tests or something for arff on the airfield.nothing follows.

text: i was doing a checkout flight for a member in the skylane 182. during run up no issues was found and during the flight no issues occurred. practiced power off stalls and during the recovery the prop knob stopped working it locked at 1500rpm. ran checklist and wasn't able to fix the issue. loss engine performance and landed on a dirt spot next to end of runway xx at redacted. no damage to the airplane and no injury or property damage.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported a NMAC while in the pattern at HGR.
text: i was approaching from the northwest and hgr tower cleared me for a right downwind for runway 27 and asked to look for traffic on extended final that i was to follow to land. i extended my downwind looking for my traffic but could not locate it. after a while, i asked tower if i could start my right base and they immediately replied 'negative, there is traffic right below you'. tower then gave me instructions to fly northeast and do a teardrop reentry for final 27. when i was back on final, i was able to spot the traffic well ahead of me and landed without incident. the only thing that i would have changed would be possibly set up on a wider right base to maybe be able to better spot traffic on final but i'm not sure that would have worked. maybe i should be more reliant on my ads-b linked ipad map, but i'd rather be looking outside in situations like this. i'm going to investigate a wings course to see if any other traffic pattern collision avoidance advice can be found.

anomaly: Ground Excursion Taxiway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported following taxi turnoff markers at AVO that led off the paved surface.
text: this event occurred at avon park fl, avo. i was landing at night, at this unfamiliar airport. the location of the occurrence is on the taxiway that is on the east side of 5-23. at the point of the intersecting runways, there is a grassy area that is immediately to the east of the intersecting runways. this grassy area continues east about 100 yards until it connects to the taxiway on the east side of 5-23. that is where i was.upon landing and then taxi, i was on the taxiway on the east side of 5-23. i saw the taxi turnoff markers and began following it, until i realized i had turned into the grassy area [with] rocks on the ground. i am unsure: if this is merely a grassy area, an old taxiway, or a local-use taxi cut through. at any rate, i suggest: if it is not an official aircraft area, remove the taxiway turn-off paint, and install an aircraft prohibited sign. further, whether it is allowed or not, i suggest adding a hot spot notation to alert future pilots of the confusion. thank you.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported aggressive pitch down after glide slope capture resulting in landing gear overspeed and TA. Crew landed safely after executing a go-around.
text: during the flight from redacted to redacted, while conducting the instrument landing system runway xxl approach, air traffic control issued a 10-degree heading change to the right during the final vector phase in order to provide separation from preceding traffic. we were also instructed to reduce speed to 180 knots. shortly afterward, air traffic control turned us to intercept the localizer and cleared us for the approach. at that time, the aircraft was configured with flaps 5.upon localizer capture, i made the required fma (flight mode annunciator) callout. as the aircraft intercepted the glideslope, the nose pitched down significantly more than expected. i called for the landing gear, and the first officer selected the gear down. the aircraft's pitch attitude continued to decrease, reaching approximately 10 degrees nose-down. observing the continued nose-low trend, i disconnected the autopilot and manually leveled the aircraft. airspeed increased rapidly and was approximately 230 knots, possibly higher during the recovery.at the time, i was focused on recovering from the abnormal aircraft attitude and was not aware that the landing gear operating speed had been exceeded. i later became aware of the exceedance during a follow-up discussion with safety committee representatives. looking back, my immediate reaction to the unexpected aircraft attitude was to disconnect the autopilot and level the aircraft. an upset recovery maneuver may have been appropriate given the initial aircraft attitude and energy state.after leveling at approximately 2, 800 feet msl, we were below the glideslope. airspeed remained around 230 knots and was beginning to decrease due to the landing gear extension. at that point, a tcas traffic" alert was annunciated. based on the aircraft's position below the glideslope, the traffic alert, and the unstable approach condition, i elected to execute a go-around.i pressed the toga switch and called for the go-around. my expectation was that at approximately 2, 800 feet, toga would disconnect the autopilot, provide go-around guidance, and discontinue the current instrument landing system navigation mode. however, the autothrottles immediately advanced aggressively toward maximum thrust. the aircraft responded with a significant nose-up pitch command. i disconnected the autothrottles and manually lowered the nose, but the aircraft had already climbed to approximately 3, 800 feet.i then manually flew the aircraft, returned to 3, 000 feet as assigned, and continued the published go-around procedure. we requested and conducted a second approach. all aircraft systems operated normally during the subsequent approach, and the landing was completed without further incident.after landing, the first officer and i conducted a thorough debrief of the event. an entry was made in the aircraft maintenance log regarding the landing gear overspeed exceedance, and i personally briefed the next flight crew regarding the event and the aircraft status."

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: SR20 Flight Instructor reported an NMAC while in the pattern. Flight continued to a normal touch and go.
text: i was conducting pattern work at redacted with a student pilot. following a touch-and-go, we heard another pilot announce their intention to cross midfield for runway xx at 300 feet above traffic pattern altitude. my student subsequently announced that we were turning downwind for runway xx.i began scanning for the reported traffic but was unable to acquire visual contact. a second student who was occupying the rear seat located the aircraft and pointed it out to me. upon visual acquisition, i observed that the other aircraft was at our altitude and on a converging course that presented a collision hazard.i immediately assumed control of the aircraft, initiated a descent to increase separation, and transmitted a call to the other aircraft. the pilot then reported having us in sight and began a climb. after the aircraft passed clear of our position, i returned to traffic pattern altitude.the other aircraft subsequently entered the downwind leg and announced that they were turning base for runway xx, resulting in them cutting in front of our aircraft. i advised over the radio that we would extend our downwind to maintain safe spacing behind the traffic. we extended the downwind as planned and were able to complete a normal touch-and-go landing without further conflict.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: flying mini drone at friend's house for recreational purposes. operating recreationally with trust completion certificate and an faa registered drone. used autopylot app to check restrictions as recommended by faa. did not see any restrictions in app, so proceeded to take off. also did not receive any notifications or in-flight warnings. dji app did not show restrictions. area is dead zone for cell phone service. this could have contributed to the app not properly showing restrictions. when checking back on flights, i noticed that this area is indeed a class d airspace. unsure if it was user error (such as typing the wrong address) or connectivity issues not showing the proper information. takeoff, flight and landing all succeeded without any issues, but proper laanc approval was not retrieved.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Captain reported the Garmin Guided Visual Approach function does not account for proper terrain clearance and the approaches flown seem to not contain data on topographical terrain elevation with obstacles.
text: airport: 1a5.approaches flown: rnav g runway 07 & rnav g 25.assessment: rnav g runway 07 approach via kuyes & rnav g runway 25 via jasvua test flight was flown to look at the new garmin guided visual approach functions. (note, this was a company training flight as this function was not under test with already being released to industry.) the following observations:rnav g runway 07 approach via kuyes - allowing the aircraft to enter a left arc (autopilot and autothrottles coupled), the initial arc was ok, but the multi-function flight display (mfd) vertical situation display (vsd) displayed guidance into the terrain prior to reaching the runway. the approach prior to reaching the calculated waypoint 1a504 was broken off as the terrain clarence is far too low. understanding the garmin disclaimer about this is for a visual approach in vmc and advisory guidance only. but the approach does not account for obstacles (tall trees on the approach).rnav g runway 25 via jasvu: although this approach the guidance correctly avoids much of the terrain (the arc in the approach), the terrain clearance would not be classed as acceptable from the calculated waypoint 1a501 down to the runway. (again, understanding the garmin disclaimer).these 2 approaches seemed to have been populated with no real-world use or topographical terrain elevation with obstacles such as trees.note these were flown with the database/charts valid.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a ground conflict with another aircraft during taxi. Captain brought the aircraft to an abrupt stop.
text: on taxi out from gate xx we were cleared to spot xx. we switched over to ground and were called almost immediately and given clearance to taxi to runway 17r, at the end of the clearance we were told to give way to another aircraft taxing north bound on kilo. the sun was coming up and shining directly into the cockpit impairing visibility. the fo had his window shade up with his attached visor on his window. the combination of grounds give way clearance at the end of his taxi clearance, the sunlight and visors being up made it difficult to see the north bound traffic. this resulted in an abrupt stop to avoid pulling out in front of the oncoming aircraft. after the aircraft passed we continued on our clearance and taxied out. i called back to the flight attendants and asked if everyone was ok with that abrupt stop. my purser, informed me that another fa had fell over and hit the cockpit door. i asked to talk to her and she informed me that she hit her arm but was ok. she stated she would put some ice on it but was fine to continue with the flight. i asked her again if she was sure she was ok and she repeated that she was fine. based on her inputs i continued the flight. all other flight attendants and passengers did not report any issues or injuries. during cruise i checked in with her again during our restroom break, she informed me she put ice on her arm and was feeling better. my overall impression of her upon our discussion based on her stance, body language and inflection was she appeared to be fine and performing her duties normally. the rest of the flight was uneventful. cause: a combination of factors, ground gave the clearance to taxi out and at the end of the clearance told us to give way. at this point the aircraft was coming up on us and we had forward moment as ground had cleared us to taxi, plus the direct sunlight from the morning sun was some what blinding, which led to the additional visors places on the forward windows which made it harder to see traffic approaching from the right.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Flight Instructor with student reported a NMAC in the traffic pattern. Instructor departed pattern.
text: my student and i were entering fernandinha beach municipal (fhb) for closed traffic touch and go operations. my student executed good radio calls. he reported 5 miles out with intentions, again over the field, execution of right teardrop for left downwind of runway 9, again on downwind with intention, base, and final. there was an aircraft on a base to final turn who we had in sight, and aircraft y who reported approaching from the south (he actually transitioned north to south of the field). aircraft y reported a left downwind for runway 4 and then changed his approach to final runway 9 after we had made our final call for runway 9. as we made calls to figure out where this aircraft was, we got no response. i told my student to execute a go-around because we did not have the traffic in sight. during our execution of the go-around procedure, i witnessed the aircraft y wing high, underneath us with about an average separation of 200 feet both vertically and laterally. i made radio calls to ask if they had seen us, and reported them flying directly underneath us, with no response. we exited the pattern to the north and so did aircraft y. i, again, made a radio call asking if they were monitoring frequency. when aircraft y responded. i asked if he had seen us, to which he replied, i did see you and i am sorry. he proceeded inbound and landed at fhb full stop and we continued maneuvers and then continued with pattern work before heading back to redacted. after the flight i was able to review the track and see that aircraft y has approached from the north and transitioned to a approach from the south for a final on runway 31. a runway that intersects runway 9.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC during approach to D98; a non-towered airport.
text: aircraft x near midair collision with aircraft y. aircraft x made inbound calls at 10 miles, 5 miles, entering 45 to pattern and entering left downwind for 36 at d98 airport. landing lights were on for better visibility by traffic.aircraft y did not make departing call, crosswind or downwind calls while attempting to do pattern work.both planes veered in opposite directions to avoid collision at the start of the crosswind and downwind for 36. to avoid future issues aircraft y can make calls, turn landing lights on and aircraft x can take a wider 45 entry into downwind to leave more time to scan for traffic.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft
synopsis: PA-28 pilot reported the right main landing gear collapsed on landing; and apparently did not fully extend even though there were 3 green lights.
text: on this day at xa:15 coming into land at redacted i had a gear malfunction. details are listed as follows. on the downwind at my thousand foot markers abeam [runway] xx i preformed my gumps checklist to where i lowered my gear and promptly received all three green lights. as i turned my base i verified again by a quick glance as i looked at my control instruments and one more time on short final. as i flared and proceeded to touch down there were no abnormalities. however about 3 seconds later, give or take, my auditory gear horn came on and before i could even remotely react the right wing hit the ground and dug itself into the ground. as the plane went hard right i did full left rudder and managed to keep the plane on the ground. we exited the plane and turned everything off. no other gear collapsed and functioned properly. there were no injuries and the plane received minimal damage to the wing tip. it also bruised the flaps and the ailerons on the right side. this was a great learning experience and even though it was nerve racking my training and flying had prepared me for a situation like this and am very grateful no injuries occurred.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: I90 TRACON Controller reported the direct shout line to TME Tower has been out of service for several weeks.
text: i was working lakeside satellite. aircraft x wanted an rnav 36 approach to tme. that information has to [be] passed to the tower. usually we have a direct line to the tower but for the last several weeks the shout line has been out of service. when the shout line is out of service i call flight data to call the inbound via the telephone number. usually flight data does not have a problem with that but a couple of controllers do for some reason even though that is a part of flight data job description. while i am working a radar control position i will not call on the telephone line to an outside facility. that is dangerous, a distraction and in the past at other facilities has led to fatal crashes. i called flight data and person a was working. he told me unable. he has refused to do his job dozens of times when i requested it and nothing appears to be done. i then called the controller in charge (cic) to notify them and for them to call my inbound.recommendation: first there should always be urgency when communication equipment is out of service and a rush to get it fixed as soon as possible. this is a safety issue. we need direct communication with towers that we work approach for. flight data controllers need to be trained properly and corrected when they refuse to do their job. radar control position should never be expected to call an outside facility on a phone line. that is dangerous. this has to be addressed.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a ground conflict with another air carrier aircraft during taxi in at SFO.
text: after an uneventful flight landing on 28l, we were taxing to gate xx. our clearance was taxi via b, as expected. as we were taxiing, ground told us to expedite thru q. we were travelling at around 20kts and kept the speed up. we saw aircraft y from the right vacating at q approaching at a fairly fast speed. as we were getting closer i was ready to slam the brakes, as it doesn't look like they were stopping either. shortly thereafter aircraft y came to an abrupt halt. it definitely seemed quite uncomfortable for both of us aircraft. i am not sure what tower told them, but it seems like there may have been some confusion between the tower and ground controller.

text: i stopped short of the road at gate xx because the marshallers were not in place. when marshallers arrived i was directed forward with both wing walkers showing all clear when a white sedan continued to drive on the service road in front of us while the marshaller was saying to proceed inbound. left wing walker was not paying attention. i stopped the aircraft to avoid the vehicle.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: DA40 instructor reported diverting to an alternate airport after experiencing an ECU (electronic control unit) B failure.
text: i was cruising at 6000' msl when an ecu b fail annunciation appeared. i immediately pulled the qrh and ran through the ecu (engine control unit) a or b fail in flight checklist. upon running the list i was left with diverting to the nearest suitable airport. redacted may have been a little closer, but had a 3000' runway. in general, i felt it was a bit short so i opted for redacted instead. i briefly considered redacted and redacted. while these airports were on the approved airport list and probably easier for maintenance to get to they were also both about 30nm and 25nm away respectively.leading up to the ecu b fail there were no indications that a fail was in progress. conditions were smooth at 6000' and clear. there was turbulence up to about 3, 300' msl but i had been out of it for a while at the time of the ecu annunciation. diversion due to mechanical failure.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: PA-31 Navajo pilot reported landing safely after experiencing a malfunctioning landing gear.
text: there were three pob (persons on board). left [seat] is a cpl (commercial pilot license) with ir (instrument rating) and cfii getting an ipc (instrument proficiency check) in a piper navajo. in the right seat is a cfii performing the ipc. in the back seat is the primary operator of the aircraft but does not have instructor certificate. all pilots have the cpl.the pilot flying (left) performed multiple approaches under a view limiting device in vmc. during the first approach, ilsxx into redacted noticed the right landing gear light would not illuminate. the pilot in the back seat stated they heard the gear lock and it is a known issue that the right downlink switch is not calibrated correctly and sometimes sticks. the ipc continued with a missed approach. the next approach was the ilsxy into redacted. the same issue persisted and the gear was cycled multiple times with no apparent issues other that the right main landing gear light. the light was tested (push) with no defects noted. the pilot flying executed a missed approach.the third approach was the vor-a into redacted. during the circling approach, the same landing gear issue persisted and the ipc would continue for one more approach into redacted. during the final approach, the pilot monitoring simulated a loss of power in the right engine. the pilot flying maintained control and continued the approach. the landing gear was cycled down with the right mlg light not illuminating. the pilot flying noticed the nose landing gear light was now not illuminating and the mirror check revealed the nlg was not fully extended. the gear was cycled two more times with no effect and the gear not retracting. a missed approach was executed and the pilot flying climbed to 2500' msl. the pilot in the back was notified of the defect and elected to take control. the pilot monitoring (right seat) took control of the aircraft while the pilot from the back swapped seats with the pilot in the left seat. out of an abundance of caution, the two more experienced pilots would helm for the abnormality. the current pilot flying performed the appropriate checklist items and manually extended the gear till the nose gear light illuminated. the right mlg light still would not illuminate. no emergency or priority request was made. the pilots flying now performed a min speed landing. and the landing gear did not collapse. upon shutdown, a substantial amount of hydraulic fluid was noticed by the aircrew on the left inboard trailing edge of the aircraft and the left wheel well was dripping with fluid. it appeared a flexible hydraulic line had been breached and there was substantial fluid loss.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Light aircraft pilot reported an NMAC with another light aircraft while in a practice area with no common frequency.
text: i was on an eastern heading in the practice area after maneuvering over confined space for a period of about 30 minutes. i was setting up to perform a chandelle maneuver to the left. when scanning for traffic before doing the maneuver, i spot a low wing aircraft on a northern heading about 200-300 feet below me and about a half mile to my right. i then start a climb in order to avoid a mid-air collision. the other aircraft continued on their northern heading. once i landed at laf, i had a conversation with the other aircraft's pilot to ensure that both parties noticed the threat. i believe a contributing factor to the incident was my complacency in the fact that i started to become too comfortable in the small section of airspace i was maneuvering in. even though i was clearing the area, before and while performing maneuvers, i was not looking long enough to see any traffic from further distances away. one thing that i think could help prevent this type of incident from occurring in the future would be to have a practice area radio communications frequency. i know in other parts of the country this exists and i believe that the surrounding practice areas around laf would benefit from such a tool.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance
synopsis: Cessna 172 instructor pilot reported an NMAC while in the traffic pattern; citing miscommunication with ATC as contributing.
text: around xa:30 on day 1, while conducting traffic pattern work, a student and i were cleared to take off on xxr and told to make right closed traffic. i did not catch the air traffic control instruction to 'follow traffic, ' only the takeoff clearance and right traffic instruction. in the upwind and upon reaching 700 feet, the student began a right turn. immediately upon rolling onto the crosswind, we gained sight of traffic on the downwind at the same time air traffic control called to asked if we had the downwind traffic in sight. i immediately took the flight controls and made a left turn towards the upwind to avoid traffic and reported traffic in sight. i continued in the upwind until air traffic control advised to turn right and enter the downwind, follow traffic and advise the traffic in sight. we reported the downwind traffic in sight, made a right turn into the downwind to rejoin. on the downwind, we were cleared to land on xxr. after landing, we taxied back to the ramp, shut down and debriefed. i debriefed the situation with the student and made sure to emphasize the importance of maintaining vigilance in the traffic pattern and scanning for traffic. i made it known that i wasn't upset with them and that it was a huge lesson for me and for the student as well. as an instructor, i am trusted to stay vigilant, pay full attention to every radio call and ask air traffic control for clarification if unsure. i have done a lot of reflecting on this occurrence and went back and listened to the air traffic control audio recording to figure out how all of this happened. i was pretty shaken up afterwards and still keep asking myself 'how can a 1, 000 hour pilot let something like that occur?' i believe a large contributing factor to this incident was fatigue and inadequete nutrition and hydration. i had spent the entire day before (day 0) volunteering for a non-profit as a pilot. that day had been long and involved extensive waiting on the ground for thunderstorms with insufficient food and water. i believe that had lingering effects on me that night and into the next day (the day of the occurrence). i woke up the next morning feeling a little tired, but thought i felt well enough to fly and work. feeling rushed that morning, i also did not pack a lunch that morning like i normally do. i refilled my water once that day, but i don't think i was drinking enough. knowing it was a 90 degree day and i had multiple activities scheduled, i should have taken extra care to hydrate and make sure i was getting enough food. over all this occurrence has been very eye-opening for me and has taught me huge lessons. one is the paramount importance of remaining vigilant during traffic pattern instructional flights. the other is the importance of checking myself with the imsafe checklist that we all preach. it is hugely apparent that the consequences of not doing so can potentially be deadly! i take full responsibility and realize the seriousness of the situation. i wish to use this as a learning moment for myself and my student. moving forward, i plan to take at an absolute minimum 1 day off of flying completely every week so that i can rest and ensure i am completely present for each and every flight operation and prevent anything like this from ever reoccuring.

synopsis: A319 First Officer reported the loss of a hydraulic pump during cruise. Flight continued to destination to a normal landing.
text: while in vmc cruise at fl370, ecam hyd y rsvr lo lvl and hyd y eng pump 2 lo pr annunciated. ca remained pf and took the radios while i worked the blue to do" items. we shut down the ptu (power transfer unit) and y eng 2 pump per the ecam and verified that hyd status page showed no quantity in yellow system. ca notified dispatch via acars to call on radio and requested priority handling with air traffic control. i accomplished landing distance calculations and reviewed fm (flight manual) non-normal notes and cautions. we transferred control while ca phone patched with dispatch. we determined with dispatch to continue to original destination and dispatch provided landing distance calculations which correlated to my manual calculations. we started an enroute descent with air traffic control and ca provided the fas a brief then briefed the pax (passengers) while i got landing atis. we came together again to brief the approach and landing considerations, as well as final understanding of how the loss of yellow system would affect landing. we verified that all ecam and normal checklists were complete and ca accomplished an instrument landing system approach in vmc to a normal landing. per ecam status page (appr proc blue to do) we turned the y eng 2 pump back on after extending flaps 2 and kept it on until engine shutdown. arff (airport rescue and firefighting) followed us down the runway and on taxi to the gate. we shutdown normally, closed the situation with ground control and deplaned pax through the jetbridge. fire chief came aboard and told us we had a significant leak from the center fuselage area and our tires were "shiny." we thanked him for the support, debriefed in the cockpit, and after the pax were deplaned, debriefed with the fas. ca called dispatch and chief pilot, and we spoke with company mechanics on site as they evaluated the issue."

synopsis: B737 Captain reported an inflight upset occurred when they encountered wake turbulence departing LAX in trial of an A330. Control was regained and flight continued to the destination.
text: departed lax on dotss2.cleee. prior to cleee, air traffic control informed us of possible wake turbulence from a departing a330. we had a direct tailwind at 7 knots and climbing at nearly the same rate as the a330. as we were locating the position of the aircraft, we hit the wake turbulence. we discussed a right deviation or direct pke, but air traffic control was already moving the a330 on a northerly track. the autoflight system then displayed autopilot roll authority. i disconnected the autopilot and auto throttles and verbalized the upset, which reached roughly 45 degrees of bank. the first officer acknowledged the upset. i slowly rolled the aircraft back to wings level to prevent injury to the flight attendants, who were up at the time. i also made a pa for the flight attendants to take their jump seats, in case we had another encounter. we then increased our rate of climb to stay at or above their altitude. after reporting the issue, air traffic control informed us the a330 was now on a more northerly route and eventually gave us direct to location x. no further issues were encountered and no injuries or difficulties were reported by the flight attendants.
