synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a near collision with a truck on the CLT ramp when taxiing in for parking.
text: approach and landing were normal onto runway 36r in clt. we were instructed to taxi via j" to j4 where we entered the ramp. ramp control cleared us to the gate which at this point was almost a straight ahead path into our assigned gate, redacted. as we approached the gate i remember stating that [aircraft type] is posted on the dgs system and that we were aligned with the center line for the redacted gate. as we moved down the centerline my attention was focused on the dgs screen. when we were within approximately 10 feet on the stopping point i heard the first officer say someone on the ramp outside his window is telling us to stop. i brought the aircraft to a stop and set the parking brake. he then told me that they wanting the engines shut down. as instructed both engines were shut down. i asked the first officer to please open his window to see if he could tell what was happening. he said that a truck was very close to the airplane. after completing the shutdown check list i stuck my head out the f/ o window to see for myself. at this point the truck had been moved. i asked the a ramp person what had happened. she said we did not hit the truck but came within inches of it. the dgs system did not post stop until well past the time when the engines were shutdown and the ramp. obviously we never saw the truck when pulling into the gate. i can't say how or why we missed seeing it. fixating on the dgs? confusion as to where the safety line are? fatigue?cause: i know for me moving forward i will have myself and both other pilots consciously and deliberately state individually that the gate area is clear. if there is any doubt the aircraft will not move. with the dgs system set up to receive us it may have lead to a false sense that the gate area was clear and ready. i know the final responsibility for ensuring the area is clear is my responsibility however it would have been nice if the dgs system sensed an issue and posted "stop" on the screen."

synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported a trailing edge flap asymmetry during vectors for approach.  Captain reported confusion over appropriate checklist to use and landed safely.
text: approach control began vectoring us for the visual xxl. as we started to slow down and configure, the flap handle was moved from 1 to 5. shortly after, we realized we had a problem: the flaps appeared stuck, indicating less than 1. with the handle at 5, i was the pilot monitoring, i requested to cancel the approach and received vectors for a box pattern to troubleshoot. air traffic control climbed us to 3, 000 feet to give us room to work.the first officer was the pilot flying. once we reached 3, 000 feet, i requested priority handling, stating our fuel and souls on board, and advised that we would need about 20 minutes to work through the various checklists. knowing these procedures can be lengthy, i felt comfortable because the weather in redacted was perfect and we had plenty of gas, including an alternate of indianapolis, so i was not pressed for fuel and knew we could take our time.i opened the qrh to 'trailing edge flap asymmetry.' we had no abnormal lights in the flight deck, but the flap indicator showed a slight split with the needles stuck between 0 and 1. the checklist directed us to return the flap handle to up. as we began that checklist, the flap indicator stopped showing a split. we realized we no longer had an asymmetry, and since that checklist would have required a landing at an extremely high speed which we felt wasn't appropriate for the situation we opted to look for other qrh options.we settled on 'trailing edge flap disagree.' we felt this was the correct procedure, so we extended the flaps via the alternate flap extension method. everything progressed normally with no asymmetry or abnormal lights, and we prepared for a flaps 15 landing as directed by the qrh.once stabilized, i called the flight attendant to brief her on the situation and confirmed it would be a normal landing. i then sent a message to dispatch stating we had requested priority handling, explained the issue, and confirmed we were about to land. i made a pa to the passengers to explain we had a malfunction that required us to work through checklists, and that they should not be alarmed by the presence of emergency vehicles upon arrival. i requested that air traffic control have arff (airport rescue and firefighting) standing by and that they follow us to the gate as a precaution.at this point, it was a routine flaps 15 landing. the first officer was doing a great job, given his previous experience flying this aircraft in the military, i felt comfortable letting him continue the landing while i monitored from a high level. we landed without incident and taxied to the gate, where maintenance personnel met us upon arrival.cause: we had some uncertainty about whether to use the 'trailing edge flap asymmetry' or 'trailing edge flap disagree' checklist. since the needles had a slight split but we didn't have any abnormal lights, it wasn't immediately clear which path to take. because these two choices lead to very different qrh procedures, it felt like a tricky situation to navigate. i think the main confusion was around what constituted as flap asymmetry, it was not very clear reading the qrh conditions and objectives header. could we look at putting some bullet points to consider in the qrh to help clarify.

synopsis: Pilatus PC-12 pilot reported aircraft oscillations during the initial visual approach; resulting in a late call to the Tower for landing clearance. The aircraft landed safely.
text: we were cleared for the visual approach by redacted approach controller and handed off to tower. we were told to contact tower however the airplane began to aggressively oscillate. i coached my first officer on what to do about this situation and in the interim as he got the aircraft under control in the downwind i failed to make the switch to tower. approach queried us on if we'd made the switch to tower as we started our base turn and i immediately switched over to tower once realizing my mistake. i saw one aircraft in the pattern when we were cleared for the visual approach, but had become caught up by the abnormalities in aircraft handling and had become distractingly concerned with the immediate safety of the flight pertaining to our aircraft. tower cleared us to land, asked what happened and i explained that we'd had a malfunction with the airplane that'd caused us to not make the switch. in times of disarray and confusion it is extremely pertinent to center back around our basics as pilots. i did in fact aviate, and navigate, however i failed to communicate, and while safety of the airplane was achieved, safety was equally at risk by me forgetting to make the switch over to tower in adequate time for us to be worked into the traffic pattern & not impede on any landing traffic. notify air traffic control sooner, better task delegation, and attempting to avoid become task saturated would help. possibly consider flying the instrument landing system or rnav instrument approach instead of the visual in times of known fatigue as this may have mitigated distraction issues.

synopsis: General aviation jet pilot reported severe turbulence during the climb; resulting in an altitude and heading deviation. The Captain recovered the aircraft and returned to the clearance.
text: this report is my best recollection of an altitude deviation that occurred during the oyoda two rnav departure from henderson executive airport (hnd).i was operating aircraft x single-pilot. due to high summer-like temperatures, the aircraft was operated at a moderately light weight and once airborne, exhibited strong climb performance. prior to departure, the oyoda two rnav departure was loaded into the g1000 nxi flight management system, and the initial altitude of 6, 000 feet was set.the takeoff and initial departure were normal. the aircraft was climbing at approximately 170 kias with a climb rate exceeding 2, 000 feet per minute. as the aircraft passed through approximately 5, 500 feet msl over the mountainous terrain southeast of henderson, it encountered a sudden onset of moderate-to-severe turbulence.during the turbulence encounter, my left hand was forced from the control yoke and inadvertently came down on the autopilot disconnect button, resulting in an unexpected autopilot disengagement. at the time, the aircraft was trimmed for a steep climb. i immediately took manual control and applied forward pressure on the yoke while simultaneously reducing power and commanding nose-down electric trim.despite these corrective actions, the aircraft's climb rate initially increased rather than decreased. at one point, i observed the vertical speed indication at around 3, 000 feet per minute. the turbulence required significant attention to aircraft control. it is possible that the aircraft encountered a localized area of strong rising air, although this could not be confirmed.within approximately 20 seconds, the aircraft climbed through the assigned altitude of 6, 000 feet and reached an estimated maximum altitude between 6, 600 and 6, 800 feet before i was able to arrest the climb and begin descending back toward the assigned altitude. during this period, the aircraft also deviated somewhat from the published lateral departure track as my primary focus was maintaining aircraft control and recovering from the upset.the turbulence remained significant while i worked to reengage the autopilot and reestablish both the assigned altitude and lateral course. before i could return to 6, 000 feet, the departure controller issued an altitude alert. shortly thereafter, i was instructed to continue climbing to 7, 000 feet.the entire event occurred over approximately one minute. i was surprised by the magnitude of the altitude excursion and by my inability to arrest the climb sooner despite immediate corrective action.in retrospect, i should have advised air traffic control immediately regarding the turbulence encounter. doing so would have provided important context for the deviation and would have allowed air traffic control to warn other aircraft operating in the area. my focus on regaining aircraft control, reestablishing the departure path, and complying with assigned altitudes caused me to overlook making that report.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported conducting a flight in an active TFR. The pilot landed the UAS when a law enforcement officer approached them and informed them of the TFR.
text: on day 3 at approximately xa:00, i was operating a dji mavic 3 enterprise under 14 cfr part 107, conducting a commercial construction-site progress flight at 165 ft agl. during my planning-stage airspace check three days prior, on day 0, i observed a published tfr covering the area up to 400 ft agl, scheduled to become effective day 1, but not yet in force at the time of my check. i did not log the pending restriction or set a reminder for its effective date, and by the day of the flight i had forgotten it existed.on the day of the flight, my third-party mission-planning software (dronedeploy) displayed a summary airspace status of 'no authorization required' for the planned flight area. i relied on that green status indication and launched. i did not separately verify active tfrs and notams through official faa sources before launching. a portion of my planned flight area overlapped the outer edge of the tfr boundary. the operating area is class g airspace and is normally unrestricted, which contributed to my reliance on the summary status.during my flight, a local law enforcement officer arrived on scene, informed me that an active tfr covered the area, and instructed me to land the aircraft. i landed immediately and complied with all instructions. the airspace incursion was unintentional, and i did not knowingly operate within restricted airspace. the officer issued a verbal warning.contributing factors: this was primarily a human factor (memory) failure. i learned of the pending tfr during my planning-stage check but did not log it or set a reminder for its day 1 effective date, and by the flight date i had forgotten it. on the day of the flight, i relied on the third-party application's summary status indicator, which is not an faa-approved airspace source, rather than verifying through official faa sources -- so nothing in my day-of process surfaced the restriction or prompted my recollection of it.corrective actions: going forward, i will log any pending tfr or notam observed during planning, with its effective date and a calendar reminder, at the time i first see it. i will verify active tfrs and notams directly through official faa sources (tfr.faa.gov and the b4ufly app) immediately before every flight, regardless of any third-party application's status indication. i have added a mandatory day-of official-source tfr/notam check to my preflight checklist. i will not operate at this site for the duration of the tfr period unless authorized through the faa's special governmental interest (sgi) process.

text: i was cleared into parking at gate xx by ramp and was told to reference 787 on push at gate xy. as i lined up on xx line the 787 stopped being pulled forward and actually started to be pushed back. my first officer said to go left and my wing walkers told me to go left as well so i was under the impression that contact was imminent. i was single engine and pushed the power up on the left engine but the thrust overcame my left nose wheel steering input and the nose wheel skipped and brought the nose of the aircraft to the right. i then applied brakes and decreased power to regain steering authority. i then turned the aircraft left and proceeded away from the 787 under push and set up for another parking attempt after the 787 taxied away. i made an elb (electronic log book) entry to request an inspection of the nose wheel just to make sure it was unharmed. i followed up with a call to maintenance.

synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported after pushback and starting engines preparing to taxi a ramp worked approached the aircraft to shut the communication panel.
text: ramp personnel and ca used proper commands during the pushback at night in redacted. once complete, ramp personnel gave the all clear signal and the ca gave a salute. the ramp personnel moved back toward the gate appearing to be moving into position to marshal the inbound plane behind us. because ramp did not say clear to start engines during the push, we waited to start engines once we were given the all clear from ramp. we started both engines and completed the after start flow and checklist per the ca. during this time ground was calling to see if we could move forward as there was an inbound plane waiting to park and we were blocking their gate. during this time, my attention had been inside while completing my after start tasks/checklist. after hearing ground i glanced outside my window as i was turning to look at the ca to talk about what ground was requesting. at that moment i happened to see ramp walking toward my side of the aircraft. he was walking towards the aircraft without wands and without getting our attention. i was concerned because he was walking towards the aircraft with the engines running and taxi light on and we were not in communications with him. i immediately alerted the ca of this in anticipation that he was going to ask me to clear my side of the aircraft to taxi forward. soon after the ramp individual disappeared under my window and i heard a door click. he was closing the communication door. once complete he walked back towards the gate after closing the door. ca told ground to standby and we paused everything. the ca then proceeded to call operations to have ramp call him to verbally verify the aircraft was now clear. the tug driver spoke with the ca on the radio and explained that they thought they had my attention before sending one of them out to close the comms door. i did not see anyone attempting to get my attention and they certainly did not have any signal from me that we were aware they were approaching the aircraft. this was an unsafe situation in that we had already completed the after start sequence/checklist and were preparing for the taxiing phase (taxi light on).

text: about two thirds of the way through our flight from redacted to redacted we had an equip cooling message show on the eicas. the first officer was the pilot flying, he called for the checklist and i went through it. we were just about one hour from redacted and the other first officer was just coming up from rest. the checklist is very short, we placed the equip cooling selector in ovrd expecting the eicas message to clear and it did not, it remained. the next step was to land at the nearest suitable airport. we had a quick discussion about our options and the distance to redacted. we were basically right over redacted which was our primary alternate. the decision was made that redacted was the nearest suitable airport. we were concerned that we would lose our screens or instruments so i made the priority handling call to air traffic control and told them we needed to land in redacted. we started down and requested vectors. we set up for an approach into redacted but we were just a bit over max landing weight. we needed to lose 2 or 3 thousand kilos, we told air traffic control we were going to dump fuel, went through the fuel jettison checklist, and dumped the fuel during the descent, it only took a couple of minutes. we landed in redacted and taxied to the ramp area. i called for the equip cooling checklist again since we were on the ground now and it had us place the selector to stby, the message remained. after some time we parked at our spot and shut down the engines. after some coordination was done we left the aircraft after we powered it down and closed the l1.

synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported severe turbulence during departure climb.
text: climbing out on the zzzzzx, the captain was pf, and we noticed a cell just west of redacted. another build up that was not painting appeared to be over redacted, but much shorter than the cell to the west. i called the flight attendants via the intercom and told them to remain seated. they confirmed they all were seated. i recall requesting deviations from departure, who would not give them to us at the request of center. i was handed over to redacted center and the controller was swamped. i was unable to get a response from the controller. we attempted to avoid the worst of the build up, but still penetrated a building towering cumulus cloud at around 12, 000 feet. the plane entered an updraft, banked sharply to the right, and climbed rapidly. the captain grabbed the controls but text: i was conducting practice maneuvers for an upcoming flight review. i had conducted a few stalls and steep turns. the final maneuver was an emergency descent. after descending approximately 800 feet and 360° i recovered, removed carb heat and applied full throttle, when the plane began to vibrate well in excess of what is normal.i went through a mental checklist making sure the throttle was on full, carb heat was off, fuel mixture was full, and checked engine gauges. turned on carb heat to check for ice and proper carb heat operation (conditions were not conducive for carb ice) and received expected results. after not finding anything noticeably wrong other than a loss of power (2200 rpm), i turned towards redacted and reviewed the checklist. after reviewing the checklist and making no improvements, i contacted redacted tower and pitched for best glide and made it to the runway with altitude safety margin. after shutdown on the ground, nothing was found on an initial inspection. no water in fuel, gas valve was open, plenty of fuel onboard and a preflight inspection was completed. the engine still ran rough on an attempted restart.a mechanic looked at the engine the following day and found a valve stuck completely open on one of the cylinders, which was the cause of the vibration and loss of power. the engine will be repaired on site.given the situation, i'm happy with the outcome. i chose a location to practice that was away from a population with emergency landing areas if needed, and was able to safely navigate to a runway. there were no problems communicating with tower while enroute. a (mostly) happy and uneventful landing, with a repairable problem that couldn't be corrected in the air.

synopsis: PA-11 Cub pilot reported temporary loss of control in a strong updraft resulted in a Class B airspace incursion.
text: i was acting as pilot-in-command and flight instructor on a local visual flight rules introductory/sightseeing flight in a piper pa-11. the flight departed redacted and returned to the same airport. the purpose was to provide an introductory flight experience to one passenger/student under visual meteorological conditions. no flight plan was filed, consistent with this routine local operation. i conducted preflight planning and navigation using foreflight with a current database.the route proceeded eastbound over redacted and location x, followed by a turn back to the west toward redacted. throughout the flight, the aircraft remained under the various shelves of the redacted class b airspace. i routinely fly this corridor and normally remain farther south under the higher shelves (typically those with floors at 6, 000 ft or 7, 000 ft msl) to maintain extra margin. on this particular flight, with outside air temperature at or above 100°f and reported winds from the south at 10 knots gusting to 18 knots at redacted, i observed elevated engine oil temperatures. to assist with engine cooling, i intentionally elected to remain at a lower altitude and track slightly north of my usual path under the class b shelf with a floor at 4, 500 feet msl near the redacted vor.shortly after passing the redacted vor westbound, with the engine at reduced power settings to manage the high oil temperature (and with insufficient power available for a sustained climb), the aircraft encountered a strong updraft/thermal. this thermal, likely enhanced by the high ambient temperature, caused an unintended climb that carried the aircraft from below 4, 500 feet msl to approximately 5, 000 feet msl.upon scanning the altimeter and immediately recognizing the inadvertent penetration of the class b airspace floor, i promptly reduced power and initiated a gentle descent to return below 4, 500 feet msl. the time spent above the class b floor was very brief -- estimated at approximately one minute or less. all maneuvering was gentle and smooth, the passenger/student remained unaware of the deviation or the corrective actions. no other aircraft were observed in the vicinity during this period, and there were no observed conflicts with traffic.the aircraft is an antique piper pa-11 in which i am current and have accumulated over 100 hours. as a professional pilot with approximately 30, 000 total flight hours (including extensive airline and general aviation experience), i maintain a strong focus on airspace awareness and have flown this general route many times without issue. this airspace deviation was completely unintentional. it resulted from a combination of my decision to fly a slightly more northerly track at lower altitude/power for engine temperature management, an unexpected strong thermal in that area on a warm evening. upon recognition of the deviation, immediate and effective corrective action was taken to exit the class b airspace as quickly and safely as possible.i am submitting this report to contribute to aviation safety. it illustrates how thermal activity on hot days, combined with intentional power/altitude management for engine concerns, can produce brief, inadvertent airspace penetrations even for highly experienced pilots operating in familiar territory. this underscores the importance of maintaining extra lateral margins near class b shelves and remaining vigilant to altimeter indications during thermal-prone conditions.

synopsis: C90 TRACON Controller reported an issue with the facilities STARS automation forcing yellow data blocks on aircraft that are operating IAW local procedures resulting in a distracting situation with Controller's attention being distracted by this unnecessary and unwanted automation data block change.
text: c90 stars system continues to alert controllers via forcing a yellow full or limited data block on arrival scopes any aircraft that is deemed an early decent on an ils/rnav final between selected altitudes of approximately 6200-6800 feet outside the 7000 crossing fix on all approaches into ord. since implementation this system has created more false alerts than identifying real problems for me. it continues to create distractions and unnecessary nuisance alerts to other controllers, often unrelated to the operation at hand. controllers are trained and conditioned that yellow aircraft (yellow data blocks) are special, point outs, or otherwise needing special attention. this is not useful during flow changes, configuration changes, or single/dual runway arrival situations where aircraft can legally and procedural be at those flagged altitudes. displaying aircraft unnecessarily as special aircraft via yellow highlight will soon cause controllers to get fatigue from the constant yellow alerts and start ignoring it, and become complacent. we have already seen this throughout the field with the nuisance ca (conflict alert) alerts. specifically, during a two runway arrival operation when the high runway controller can use 5-11000 to join their final/localizer, it is entirely possible an aircraft will (and should) be joining the final at 6000 or higher to allow a base turn ahead of the wider traffic at 5000 for positive separation. positive separation without nuisance alerts should be absolutely possible. it should also be noted that random miscellaneous visual flight rules aircraft also show up yellow. but only between the flagged altitudes. this could easily lead a controller to miss other vfrs not within the altitude filter or edaa box because they are expecting them to be yellow. aircraft x was being vectored for an approach to runway 10c in a two runway operation. the w controller was using their assigned altitudes in their assigned airspace but the entire arrival line received a false warning that aircraft x had descended early while at 6700 feet. this alert was a false positive. disable the edaa entirely as it is an unnecessary distraction in the operation.

descend them to 100 after redacted. the pilot read back 110, and the aircraft leveled off at 110 a few miles ahead of redacted. i took care of some other tasks. returning to aircraft x, i saw the aircraft turn at redacted as their mode-c-indicated altitude hit 105. there was no msaw alert due to proximity to the airport. i gave a low altitude alert with an instruction to climb and maintain 110. when i unkeyed, it sounded like someone else was just finishing a transmission too, so i repeated myself. with no response after a few seconds, i changed transmitters and repeated myself once approaches higher terrain.finally, after the third attempt at a low altitude alert, the pilot responded questioning that they had been cleared to 100 after redacted. i explained that they were not cleared to 100, and reiterated that i had only indicated that i'd be able to descend them to 100 after redacted, and also explained that their current heading was going into higher terrain, and that the first thing they needed to do was turn towards the airport to remain within the lower mia (minimum instrument flight rules altitude). the pilot stated that they were correcting to 110 and turning towards the airport. the aircraft was only below 110 in a 100 mia polygon for a matter of seconds after redacted (about 1-2 miles), at which point they entered the 100 polygon. had they not turned toward the airport, they would have re-entered the 110 mia polygon, which follows the redacted..redacted course almost exactly parallel, offset to the west by about 3 or 4 miles. once established on a heading direct redacted, still within a 100 mia and climbing back to 110, i called the airport position to the pilot. they stated it was in sight and i cleared them for a visual approach. it's anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the prohibition of parallel visual approaches at SFO and the resulting daily Ground Delay Program is causing chronic flight crew fatigue and unsafe; near-minimum fuel operations.
text: the ongoing prohibition of parallel visual approaches at the san francisco airport has escalated from an operational inconvenience to a critical safety hazard. the resulting daily ground delay programs (gdp) introduce two unmitigated risks into our system: chronic flight crew fatigue and unpredictable, near-minimum fuel operations.the sfo gdp frequently spans to xa:00 to xq:00, causing domestic delays ranging from 45 to over 90 minutes. this systematically pushes flight crews to the limits of their flight duty period (fdp), transforming a standard 8 to 10 hour duty day into exhausting 10 to 12 hour marathons. pilots are regularly forced to fly complex arrivals into a high-density environment after being delayed - sometimes for multiple hours - where fatigue becomes a major factor.this threat materialized on day two of our pairing. our schedule consisted of a three leg sequence: redacted - sfo, sfo - redacted, and a return to sfo. both segments into sfo were hit by gdp delays exceeding one hour. the second gdp would have pushed us past our legal 13-hour fdp limit. while the crew desk was able to proactively remove us from the final turn - at considerable financial cost and inconvenience to our customers - many other crews had not timed out. instead, they are being forced to fly into sfo fatigued, having already exhausted their mental and physical reserves waiting out ground delays.the current sfo configuration also severely compromises fuel planning predictability. because a gdp of over an hour does not guarantee a clear path upon arrival, clear weather (cavok) days now yielding traffic saturation risks usually reserved for low-visibility operations.the severity of this breakdown was demonstrated on our flight from redacted to sfo. the weather at sfo was pristine, endless blue skies with standard westerly winds. normally, a remaining fuel of 1 hour 15 minutes is sufficient fuel to conduct an approach, handle a go-around, and land with a comfortable 60-minute reserve. recognizing the sfo volatility, we planned a conservative gate fuel giving us an increased remaining fuel of 1 hour 45 minutes.the fuel preservation effort began immediately on the ground in redacted, where our wheels-up time meant a 15-minute wait at the runway end. we proactively taxied on one engine and shut down the motor during our wait to preserve our margins. however, as we approached sfo our situation deteriorated. while on the bdega arrival, zoa assigned us a published hold at bgglo due to traffic saturation on the sfo final approach.we immediately slowed the aircraft and began coordinating our fuel status with dispatch. i determined a bingo fuel of approximately 7, 500 lb. before we needed to divert to smf (1 hour remaining fuel of 5, 100 lb. plus 2, 300 lb. burn to smf). we entered the bgglo hold at 8, 900 lb. after just one circuit our fuel had dropped to 8, 300 lbs. recognizing that a third circuit would push us below our diversion threshold, i informed zoa that the second lap would have to be our final circuit, we either needed to press to sfo or immediately divert to smf.fortunately, zoa released us from the hold with 7, 700 lb. remaining. this left us with almost no buffer. to maintain a safe margin at sfo, i wanted a minimum touchdown fuel of 6, 300 lb. (1 hour remain fuel of 5, 100 lb. plus 1, 200 burn to sjc allowing for a go-around at sfo and a diversion to sjc with a 45-minute reserve). i was mentally prepared to declare minimum fuel" and even "emergency fuel" to norcal approach if given any further delay vectors, as the low-speed and low-altitude small box patterns frequently used by air traffic control during these saturation periods consume fuel at an accelerated rate. i realize 6, 300 lb. remaining fuel is higher than company policy. however i never want to box myself into a position where a go-around will result in an unsafe fuel state.norcal managed to sequence us with minimal vectoring, and we landed at sfo with 6, 500 lb. while safe, this was significantly belowour flight-planned remaining fuel of 8, 281 lb.despite departing redacted with an extra 30 minutes of fuel on a perfect clear-weather day, the compounding ground and airborne delays brought us to within minutes of an unnecessary diversion. the current sfo arrival restrictions are creating a compound hazard: crews are being kept in the air longer resulting in increasingly narrower fuel margins, all while operating at the tail end of extended and fatigue-inducing duty days. the faa must re-evaluate the prohibition on parallel visuals to restore system predictability and preserve safety margins."

synopsis: ERJ 175 First Officer reported a loss of control during climb when the autopilot was not engaged properly.  Flight crew recovered from descending banked turn after 'bank angle' warning and continued to destination.
text: i was the pilot flying. the initial climb out on the departure was non-eventful. we were given a climb to 230, and a vector to a waypoint. once established on a course towards the waypoint, and climbing through 10, 000 feet, i requested the autopilot to be selected on. i watched the captain press the button, heard the audible click", and checked that the aircraft was maintaining its climb and heading. at that point i turned my attention to the mcdu (multipurpose control display unit) to write down the top of climb numbers on my clipboard. as i was writing i was startled by the aural "bank angle" warning. i quickly glanced at the fma (flight mode annunciator) and noticed that the ap (autopilot) mode was not engaged, and we were in a right hand descent, in a steepening bank. i corrected the attitude and airspeed, and the captain engaged the autopilot. we continued the departure and the climb out without further incident.cause: my failure to ensure the ap cue was populated on the fma. there was some expectation bias in that regard, as i saw and heard the autopilot button being pressed, and the airplane was trimmed well enough to hold its climb and heading for the few seconds i concentrated on it.suggestion: the solution to this issue is constantly drilled into us during training events: to pay close attention to the fma and know for sure what the airplane is being commanded to do. an additional help would be to have the guidance panel lights activated as a secondary cue for what automation is selected on at a given time."

synopsis: Pipistrel Alpha Trainer Flight Instructor reported taking evasive action along with the conflict aircraft resulted in a NMAC.
text: a potential near midair collision occurred while operating aircraft x inbound to redacted from the northwest. the flight was returning early due to a student pilot not feeling well during the lesson.the aircraft was descending from 4, 500 feet msl to 3, 500 feet msl in preparation for passing beneath the redacted class b airspace shelf. while monitoring ads-b traffic, i observed another aircraft, aircraft y, southeast of our position and at a similar altitude. the aircraft appeared to be departing redacted. at the time, we did not have the aircraft in visual sight.in an attempt to increase separation, i initiated a descent. however, it appeared on the traffic display that the other aircraft was also descending. recognizing the potential conflict, i then initiated a climb. the other aircraft also appeared to begin climbing. during this maneuver, i acquired the aircraft visually and observed it at an estimated 300 to 500 feet of separation. the other aircraft initiated a left turn to avoid our aircraft, and i simultaneously executed a left turn to increase separation and avoid a collision.the conflict was resolved without further incident. the flight continued and terminated safely with no injuries or damage to either aircraft.at the time of the event, i was not in communication with air traffic control and was preparing to contact redacted tower. i do not know whether the other aircraft was receiving air traffic control services or operating on the local practice area frequency.this event reinforced the importance of maintaining situational awareness, utilizing available traffic information, and remaining on the appropriate practice area frequency until ready to establish communication with the destination tower. additionally, the event highlighted the importance of not assuming that another aircraft will maneuver in a predictable manner or based on perceived right-of-way considerations. early visual acquisition and conservative avoidance actions remain critical to collision avoidance.

lg wow sys fail directed us to land at the nearest suitable airport and it was at this point that we started setting up the instrument landing system approach for xy. we were concerned that the nose wheel could be stuck in a position between fully down and fully up so we requested to do a low flyby over runway xy so that the tower could take a look and see if all three wheels appeared to be down.
