had two kids in the back not feeling well and had bright red faces. a mother of an infant onboard removed all of the baby's clothing as she feared the infant was overheating. one fa in the back was dripping with sweat. another fa in the back had to sit down for a couple minutes as he began to feel faint. several customers started asking for water. i started feeling very nauseous. we got everyone on and seated and very quickly closed the overhead bins. due to this pressure to board so quickly, fa a hurt his bag rushing to assist a customer who was dropping a bag. we made him an ice pack for his back and i checked on him throughout the flight. nonetheless, we got all bins closed within about two minutes per the captain and were ready to close. then we had to wait on aft catering, then we had to wait on maintenance. i kept being told, 'a couple more minutes' which in reality was about 10-15 minutes. it was pure chaos and misery. i kept being told different things by different people. people kept telling us it would cool down. one person, even said the plane would cool when the cabin door was shut. we shut the door hoping to finally have some relief. this was the opposite of the truth. it just kept getting hotter. the pilots said we couldn't start the engine yet due to maintenance. every concern i had just kept getting completely brushed off and ignored. it was so dangerous and my crew and i genuinely felt helpless. i didn't even know what to keep telling the customers as it was not getting cooler. we finally pushed back and it was still so hot. the pilots said it was around 85° in the cabin. we did the safety video and our compliance checks. the engine was started so we were told it would cool, but then the captain said it wouldn't cool until we got into the air. it was still hot during flight, the pilots said their gauge read around 77° but would continue to go down. about one hour into the flight the temperature had gotten to 79°. the captain said the middle of the cabin has to cool before the rest of the plane cools.we kept being assured the plane would cool but several different people throughout this entire experience. the plane did not get cooler until about 3 hours into the flight. i don't understand why we were strung along. i felt so bad making pa's telling the customers the plane would cool, when in reality nothing was happening. there were so many excuses as to why the plane was so hot. no crew or customers should ever have to go through this. it creates a hazardous environment and i wish our concerns had been addressed instead of brushed off.

anomaly: Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Flight Attendant reported a severe turbulence event leading to injury to herself. Flight attendant continued duties at arrival.
text: during the flight to redacted while performing cabin compliance checks prior to landing, the aircraft experienced a severe turbulence and dropped continuously. the rapid change in g forces caused me to lose contact with the floor and become airborne for several seconds. upon descending, i landed awkwardly on my right food, resulting in an injury to my big toe and a sprain of my right ankle, i also felt mild pain in my shoulder and back.once i get up from the floor, i went to aft galley and seated on 2r inboard jumpseat since the aircraft was still experiencing turbulence and i didn't have the strength to walk to the front since i was still in shock and pain once we landed and parked to the gate, i rush down to the front to do the disarming process.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a NMAC while in the pattern. Flight crew decided to go around and returned for a landing.
text: on a right downwind, tower told us to advise when we had traffic about 1 o clock ahead of us in sight. we observed an aircraft on final, and told the tower that we had them in sight, but apparently tower was referring to another aircraft farther out in a left base. battle creek tower then told us 'number 2, clear to land runway 13 behind the traffic'. we repeated the call and then turned to follow the traffic that we observed that was coming in on final. as we turned base, we noticed there was traffic in a left base for runway 13 that we were ahead off, so we decided to go around to avoid letting our distance get too close or any potential collision. tower then informed us that they were initially referring to the traffic in the left base, and we then just continued the go-around and came in for another landing after getting re-established in the pattern.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Socata TB-20 pilot reported that the passenger door became unlatched and swung opened during climb; resulting in excessive cabin noise; and minor flight control difficulty. An immediate return to the departure airport was safely accomplished.
text: during climb at approximately 2200 msl, the passenger cabin gullwing-style door became unlatched and violently whipped opened. this caused a sudden increase in cabin noise and airflow. the aircraft remained controllable, however, handling characteristics required increased control input and attention.the situation was assessed, and out of an abundance of caution, priority handling was requested with air traffic control. the decision was made to return to the departure airport - redacted.a precautionary return and landing were completed without further incident. no injuries occurred.prior to departure, standard preflight procedures, including door closure, were accomplished. the precise cause of the door opening was not determined during flight.this report is submitted to document the event and highlight potential considerations regarding door latch security and in-flight effects of door openings on aircraft handling.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: PA46 pilot reported a flat tire during take off resulting in a runway excursion. Aircraft was towed to Maintenance.
text: we arrived at redacted from redacted, returning from a family vacation. we needed to drop one passenger off at redacted . the arrival and landing into redacted were uneventful, including a long taxi from xxr to the fbo with zero issues. after adding 20 gallons of fuel and using the bathrooms, we did a quick check of the plane and boarded our final leg to location x. we had also performed thorough preflight checks in redacted before the first flight of the day and found zero issues. we picked up our instrument flight rules clearance and taxied out behind a tbm also departing runway xy. after a quick run-up holding short, we were cleared to depart xy. entering the runway, applied take off power, verified instruments in the green, called out airspeed alive everything was normal, and right at 50kts or so, the plane almost instantly veered to the left, and we began hearing 'thuds' similar to a flat tire, so did what had to be done to keep us on the runway and was able to do so even though it was a wild ride for a moment unfortunately, we came to rest at an intersection between xy and xxr, which caused a delay in airport ops. the fbo, originally tried to come tug us to the shop within 10min of being there but with the tire blown it wasn't happening. the jack they originally brought to raise the gear got jammed and was not able to move it for a good 20min. the fire department was called out to help lift the plane off the original jack, which took some time and all of us were working to move as quickly as possible. then a local mx (maintenance) shop arrived with larger jacks, and their jack also jammed (fun times), and they broke a few smaller skid plates attempting to move the plane back to the mx shop of their own property. they finally used a forklift under the gear and towed the plane back slowly to the shop. we are grateful they were able to get it, as an airport ops manager told one of the people assisting us if it wasn't moved quickly, they 'would come drag it off with city services'. the local airport ops who were assisting us, and the fire department, the fbo, and mx shop all really did their best. we all did. it was just a series of little things getting the plane towed that took a little longer than anyone anticipated, over a simple blown tire. this is the first time i have blown a tire during takeoff at high speeds. i have found flats during preflights before, but there wasn't an indication of any issues, and the plane had flown almost 40hrs in the past 30 days without issue.it's unfortunate we stopped where we did, but with a blowout at high speeds, our first priority is keeping passengers safe and keeping the plane on the runway and intact, which i was able to do.

anomaly: Conflict Ground Conflict; Critical
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported taking the runway for departure with an aircraft on short final. Aircraft on final executed a missed approach.
text: i landed at gxy and wanted one more lap in pattern before returning to home airport. i had taxied back to the entry to runway 35 where a small jet was waiting for takeoff (to). there were two other aircraft in pattern. by the time the jet departed there was a third aircraft in pattern for 35, and aircraft y had started announcing being on the instrument landing system for 35. aircraft z waiting behind me decided the wait had been too long already and taxied for to from runway28. it had been nearly 30 minutes on the ground and i was still looking for a hole in the pattern to depart. when the last touch and go had lifted off, i heard aircraft y announce a 2 mile final and believed that would be sufficient space to execute a departure into the pattern.however, i mis-judged the distance needed to get from the taxi way onto the runway, and by the time i turned onto the runway i could see aircraft y now less than a mile from the arrival end of runway 35. as i brought the power up i heard aircraft y announce they were sides stepping to the right and going around since i was on the runway.the busy pattern and the long wait conspired together and i made a decision to try to press my into a departure there wasn't space for. this did not result in any accident, but did generate an unsafe condition that wasn't nessacary. in hindsight aircraft z behind me did the right thing, taxing to another runway for departure, that would put him clear the busy traffic pattern. if i had chosen that course of action, it would have been easier to re-enter the pattern in the air.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: RV-9 pilot reported hearing a loud bang and a loss of power from the engine during cruise resulting in a diversion to a nearby airport.
text: while in steady state cruise with the autopilot engaged at 8500' msl we heard a 'bang'. the engine started running very rough, multiple loud backfires out of the exhaust, very violent shaking from the four-cylinder o-360 engine, noticeable change in engine note, and immediate reduction in ias.i immediately disengaged the auto pilot and throttled back, with no change in the engine vibration. the aircraft continued to slow down and change in power settings had no impact.i then performed a magneto check with no change to the power setting, noise, or vibration. in addition, the ignition monitoring device showed no issues with the ignition.next was to initiate a 180-degree turn to the left, back towards redacted, which we had just passed, and requested priority handling with redacted approach. (i had been on flight following since leaving redacted.)redacted approach called out redacted and provided excellent support.due to my proximity to redacted and altitude, i did not establish vg, but rather flew quick descent towards the redacted as i was concerned with a possible fire and wanted to get on the ground as quickly as possible.as i approached the runway the runway at 4600' i circled once to get down to about 1800' to start my 'down wind' approach to the runway.the engine was still producing a little bit of power, even with the throttle pulled back to its stop (more on this). the 'high aspect' ratio wing of the rv-9, with full flaps, a full deflection slip, and a little bit of power from the engine, had me descending at around 650 fpm at 75 knots ias, which is 15 knots faster than normal. a broken valve stem from cylinder #2 migrated into the carburetor and would not allow me to close the throttle fully. the residual power from the function two cylinders produced enough thrust to significantly extend my glide.i touched down past mid-field and had enough energy to coast to a taxiway and exit the runway, where the engine stopped running without input from me.upon initial inspection, the exhaust valve stem from cylinder #2 failed and migrated through the engine. part of the valve damaged cylinder #1 and pounded close the sparkplugs, so that cylinder was not making power, but had some compression.cylinder #2 was making no compression.a part of the #2 exhaust valve cassed through the carburetor was found in the filtered airbox. the valve stem from the exhaust valve was found the throat of the carburetor and prevented the throttle to close. the throttle could only move from full open to half open, it could not be closed.this resulted in me not being able to close the throttle fully and what power the engine could make, significantly increased my glide distance.based on the data from the avionics, it was exactly eight minutes from engine failure to touchdown. during the eight-minute glide the engine continued to vibrate violently, produce loud backfires in the exhaust, and as we found out from the people on the ground, trailing black smoke.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: A Center Controller reported an aircraft departing a non-towered airport stopped climbing due to pressurization failure; flew below the Minimum IFR Altitude and returned to the departure airport.
text: aircraft x was issued a clearance on the ground at redacted climbing to 150, as filed. minutes later, aircraft x checked on over the redacted [vor] at 083, below minimum instrument flight rules altitude in that area, on course, refusing to climb. using position correlation and verifying the mode c with their report, i radar identified them. aircraft x declared that they are unable to climb due to pressurization issue so i issued them to climb and maintain 120. they were currently in a mia (minimum instrument flight rules altitude) terrain area of 119, very close to entering an area where the mia is 089. i issued a low altitude alert at this time. when aircraft x responded again with unable, they entered the area of 089 and i issued a climb to 089 or 090. at this point, i as the controller, determined that aircraft x required priority handling and was treating them as such. even though the climb was only 6-700ft above their altitude, they refused to climb. due to aircraft x continuing on course, they were about to cross into a mia of 096, so i issued a turn to a 270 heading although they were still below the terrain to prevent them from entering the higher terrain area, as i felt this was in my judgment the best thing to do for the critical situation. aircraft x never took the turn. i issued another low altitude alert and suggested the aircraft fly west to lower terrain. aircraft x declared that they wanted to return to redacted and circle over the redacted [vor] still below the terrain. i issued the notams and verified they had the weather redacted even though that was where they departed from minutes prior and aircraft x reported the airport in sight. i cleared aircraft x for the visual approach to redacted, reported multiple traffic in the vicinity, and released aircraft x to change to advisory frequency. minutes later aircraft x cancelled instrument flight rules while still in the air. i observed the target return to redacted and reach runway altitude at the airport.if aircraft x would have just climbed a few hundred more feet to get above my terrain, i would have been able to provide more services.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air traffic controller reported working an aircraft that reported their left engine was out; resulting in the controller coordinating the aircraft's status to another facility who controlled the airport at which the aircraft landed safely at.
text: aircraft x was just north of redacted airport at 7000 when they requested priority handling and left engine out. i asked for persons on board, fuel remaining and intentions. they gave me the information i requested and then they asked to go direct redacted for an approach into redacted. i offered them to land at redacted as they were much closer to our airport, we have additional services on our premises, and the aircraft was in a good spot to set up for runway xx final at redacted. they declined and asked to continue direct redacted. i told my controller in charge (cic) all this information and asked that they get a cease fire, as rxxxx was active. my cic got the cease fire for aircraft x's priority handling transition. i then called redacted [tracon] to give them a heads up of the inbound aircraft in distress. i gave aircraft x pilot discretion descent to 5000 and then i shipped them to redacted [tracon]. redacted [tracon] told us the aircraft was landing assured.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A321 Captain reported loss of hydraulic system during climb. Flight crew returned to the departure airport.
text: in the climb, at approximately 22, 000 feet, we received an ecam for hyd b elec pump lo pr and hyd b sys lo pr. after complying with the ecams, the blue hydraulic system had no pressure. we requested priority handling and requested a turn towards redacted. we consulted dispatch and decided redacted was preferable to redacted for diversion due to longer runways. we informed the flight attendants and passengers of the mecanical problem and our plan to return to redacted. emergency vehicles were requested as a precaution. an overweight landing was accomplished and the plane was inspected by emergency personnel before taxiing to the gate and deplaning normally.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: B737 First Officer reported they received a Low Altitude Alert from ATC while descending on a Visual Approach.
text: i was the pilot flying during my first trip of ioe flying from redacted-redacted. we had received several reroutes and star changes as well as looking at other, unused, stars into redacted due to thunderstorms along our initial routing. we had been planning an rnav star directly into an rnav rnp approach to xxr in redacted. after beginning the star we were given subsequent fixes to take us off the star to avoid some close in storms to the east of redacted. after these fixes we began receiving vectors for a close in visual to xxr in redacted. during these vectors we decided to load the instrument landing system as a backup to the visual in order to provide a more accurate glide slope due to the hot temperature and high altitude into redacted. as the pilot flying the captain briefed me in the approach and we then got the turn to intercept. looking out the window i noticed we were about to overshoot the localizer and had traffic to our right which we would conflict with shortly if we overshot. i disconnected the autopilot and began flying off of visual cues, this is when i realized we were not receiving the localizer or glideslope. i later realized the instrument landing system was notam'd out of service. as i was flying visually, the instrument landing system briefly came back in and showed centered on the glideslope needle, i then thought we were on slope and needed to maintain a 3 degree slope to maintain a stabilized approach. i overlooked that we had not passed the final approach fix and were at final approach fix altitude, therefore were descending too early. air traffic control issued a low altitude alert and both the captain and i immediately recognized our mistake and i began an immediate climb back to faf altitude. working with the captain we were able to begin our descent at the appropriate location and continue a stabilized approach to landing.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Bird / Animal
synopsis: B737 Captain reported an airspeed unreliable situation shortly after takeoff. Flight crew returned to the departure airport.
text: early morning takeoff, some bird activity around the runways. we were cleared for takeoff, 100 knot and v1 call uneventful, we rotated and lifted off. as the gear was coming up we received a master caution and eng (engine) indication on the six pack. we scanned the engines and they were normal. it was then that the first officer recognized his airspeed indicator was lower than the captains and he announced airspeed unreliable. he kept his 15 degree pitch attitude and at acceleration altitude we accomplished the memory items for airspeed unreliable. after setting the pitch and power for flaps extended, we compared the capt. first officer and standby airspeed indicators, capt and standby agreed and first officer was substantially lower. during this process we received intermittent stick shaker. transferred control to capt because those instruments were working. deconfigured the aircraft and set the clean pitch and power setting. contacted redacted approach and let them know we would be returning and requesting priority handling. ran the qrh and stabilized the aircraft. capt flight director and autopilot, no auto throttles. we discussed that no auto throttles would be a threat. coordinated with the fas, contacted dispatch with our situation, and informed the passengers of the return. normal check accomplished for landing at redacted. dispatch supplied landing data. requested extended final from redacted to give us time to assess the handling at approach speeds. configured as normal, landed uneventfully. taxied clear on the high speed and coordinated with the fire chief for exterior inspection. nothing noted. taxied back to our gate, xx. debriefed, dispatch, chief pilot, maintenance and local redacted operations. electronic log book report completed. exterior inspection found birdstrike had completely plugged the first officer pitot tube.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a balloon during final approach. Captain took evasive action and the flight continued without issue.
text: while on final approach to runway 28l into sfo i was pilot monitoring. we were cleared for the approach, at approximately 3000ft, approaching glideslope intercept. i was looking ahead towards landing traffic on approach to runway 28r. i noticed a small black object ahead at our altitude that was stationary in my windshield on the horizon. as i was focusing on the object i initially believed it was a drone. as we rapidly approached the object i reached up and pushed down on the control column to avoid colliding with it. the object, which was a small black ballon, cleared straight above the cockpit by about 5-10 feet. i do not believe the ballon made contact with the aircraft. the first officer continued flying the entire time and continued a stable approach. i reported the ballon's description and altitude to approach control. we continued the approach and landed without incident.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a GPWS terrain alert and escape maneuver during approach to GJT. Flight crew believed the alert to be false as another aircraft experienced a similar alert.
text: during diversion to gjt we began the rnav approach to runway 29 by entering from the north through cesba. we were instructed to cross cesba at 9000 feet and cleared the approach. after crossing cesba and beginning the descending left hand turn to hansu, we received a gpws terrain caution followed quickly by a terrain warning. the pilot flying executed the terrain escape and we terminated the approach. after recovering, we received vectors for a visual approach to runway 11 (tower changed the runway due to wind) and landed uneventfully. the event occurred around 8500 msl and while there is rising terrain to the east, the gpws warning seemed false. additionally, the flight behind us, flying the exact same approach, experienced the same gpws terrain warning. they were also in our same aircraft type.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the names of the ZSPD/PVG DUMET arrivals were different between the FMS and Jeppesen charts; and some arrivals were not selectable on the FMS.
text: i was relief pilot on this flight. while entering the route into the fmc at the gate at redacted, i was unable to select the rnav arrival in the fmc that was listed on our flight plan. i have flown to pvg many times and have never had this happen.the names of the arrivals in our fmc completely differed from those listed in our jepps for the dumet arrivals. all four of our pilot ipads were updated with the current jepp revision, yet none of the arrival names matched the box. i pointed this out to the captain and she called dispatch, but they were unfamiliar with and unaware of the issue and had no suggestions.the dumet arrivals in the fmc were as follows: dumet1, dumet2, dumet3, dumet4, dumetp and dumetq. the dumet arrivals in the jepps were: dumet 81a/82a, dumet 91a/92a, dumet 93a, dumet 83a, and dumet 01a and 11a. these were the arrivals i had always seen on previous pvg trips in the fmc, but now none of them were there and we were filed for the dumet92a.we were able to verify that the dumet2 in the flight management system exactly matched the dumet91a in our jepps, so we selected that arrival. as per normal operations for pvg, shanghai approach gave us the dumet91a after we checked in with them as we had anticipated, but we would have been unable to accept the dumet92a arrival if they had given it to us because it was not selectable in the fmc.we flew the arrival without incident, but i felt this discrepancy between the fmc and the jepp charts needs to be addressed and corrected.cause: while we were able to figure out a solution and no violations or incidences occurred, i wanted to highlight this abnormality between the fmc and our jepp charts so the problem could be examined and solved by the appropriate technical department/s.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported tailwheel shimmy during landing that caused a temporary loss of control.
text: upon a normal wheel landing, i set the tailwheel down with a crossing correction felt a shimmy followed by loss of control as the speed reduced. i brought the airplane to a stop and with difficulty made my way off the taxi way. upon post flight inspection, the tailwheel was established to be uncontrollable.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Altitude Excursion From Assigned Altitude; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A PA-32 pilot reported at FL240 they encountered severe downdrafts resulting in an uncontrolled descent.
text: i am a recently instrument-rated private pilot with approximately 450 total flight hours operating a turbocharged piper pa-32 single-engine piston aircraft not approved for flight into known icing. i departed redacted visual flight rules with flight following, returning to redacted, a non-towered airport.afternoon convective activity was present. prior to departure, i completed a weather briefing and planned a route north of the convective activity with the intent to cross in an area that appeared less active before turning south toward redacted.after departure, i proceeded northwestbound and cleared the redacted class b. based on visual observations and available weather information at the time, conditions appeared to permit a crossing while remaining clear of cloud, and i requested an instrument flight rules pop-up clearance to cross the ridge. redacted center approved the clearance. i climbed in orbits to fl240 and was subsequently cleared direct to my destination.while proceeding westbound, it became apparent that convective build-ups were developing along my route. i received air traffic control approval for multiple heading deviations, including a larger left deviation, to remain clear of weather. as i approached the ridge at fl240, the visual corridor between cloud formations narrowed and i no longer observed a clear path forward that would allow me to remain clear of clouds.at that point, i decided to request to reverse course toward area x and made two radio calls requesting a turn-back and vectors. neither transmission was acknowledged. after the unanswered calls, i became concerned that communications may not have been effective and was preparing to squawk 7600.at approximately the same time, while near the ridge at fl240, i encountered a significant downdraft and became unable to maintain assigned altitude. the aircraft began a rapid descent. i lowered the nose to maintain airspeed and made a small heading adjustment to remain clear of a nearby convective build-up.during this descent, redacted center transmitted instructions to maintain fl240 due to traffic behind and below me on a similar route of flight. i responded 'unable.' air traffic control subsequently issued traffic avoidance instructions to the trailing aircraft. based on ads-b in observations, closest proximity appeared to remain approximately 5 to 6 miles laterally with vertical separation maintained.i continued the descent through a visual opening into vmc, remained in communication with air traffic control, cancelled instrument flight rules descending through 18, 000 feet, and proceeded to an uneventful landing at redacted. no injury, aircraft damage, or loss of control occurred.contributing factors included afternoon convective activity over high terrain, acceptance of direct routing rather than continuation of my original planned route north of the weather, operation at high altitude with aircraft performance considerations, the need to remain clear of cloud due to icing concerns, and a period in which my radio transmissions requesting a turn-back were not acknowledged by air traffic control.lessons learned from this event for me include maintaining more conservative margins for mountain crossings in convective conditions, adhering to pre-planned routing around weather rather than accepting more direct options when conditions are deteriorating, and communicating changing circumstances to air traffic control earlier when weather avoidance or aircraft performance begins limiting available options. i have debriefed this flight in detail with experienced cfiis and mentors and am incorporating these lessons into future weather assessment, route selection, and mountain flying decision making.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: PA34-200 flight crew reported nose gear collapse on landing. Flight instructor also reported this has previously occurred within their fleet and the company stated this was inevitable.
text: my student and i conducted a commercial multi-engine training flight. before departure, a thorough preflight inspection was completed in accordance with the aircraft checklist and company procedures. particular attention was given to the landing gear system, including the actuators, bolts, j-hooks, springs, switches, and all visible components. no discrepancies or abnormalities were observed. following engine start, we taxied to the run-up pad of runway xxr at redacted. a normal run-up was completed per checklist, and all aircraft systems operated within normal parameters. we departed and proceeded southwest, climbing to between 4, 500 and 4, 700 feet msl. during the flight, we performed several training maneuvers, including an accelerated stall, a vmc demonstration, and an emergency descent. during the emergency descent, the landing gear was extended (below vlo) and indicated normal operation: three green gear lights were illuminated, no gear-unsafe indication was present, and the nose gear appeared down and locked when visually checked in the mirror. we recovered from the maneuver at approximately 2, 500 feet msl and continued a gradual descent to 2, 000 feet msl. i then instructed the student to don a view-limiting device for instrument training, and we conducted a simulated rnav runway xyr approach into redacted. a simulated left-engine failure was introduced, and the student completed the required procedures in accordance with the checklist standard operating procedures. we received the atis at redacted and proceeded to contact redacted tower (approximately 13 nm west of the airport) and were instructed to enter left traffic for runway xz. the approach was discontinued at approximately 1, 000 feet msl to establish proper spacing in the traffic pattern. abeam the 1, 000-foot markers on the downwind leg for runway xz, the landing gear was extended. all indications appeared normal, including three green gear lights, no red gear-unsafe indication, and visual confirmation of the nose gear position in the mirror. flaps were extended to 10° to slow the aircraft to approximately 100 mph, followed by 25° once landing was assured. at approximately 500 feet agl, the standard landing checklist and callouts were completed: fuel selectors on, mixtures full rich, propellers full forward, landing gear down (three green, no red, and one visible in the mirror), fuel pumps on, and landing lights on. final approach speed was approximately 87 mph in accordance with company operating procedures. the aircraft touched down smoothly on the runway centerline without incident and the landing gear initially supported the aircraft normally. because this was a touch-and-go landing, the student retracted the flaps and applied takeoff power. during the transition to the go portion of the maneuver, the nose landing gear suddenly collapsed. the student immediately closed both throttles, and i immediately moved both mixture controls to cutoff. i assumed control of the aircraft and elected not to apply brakes or rudder inputs to avoid aggravating the situation. the aircraft veered approximately 10-15 feet left of the runway centerline and came to rest between taxiways 1 and 2. i informed the tower that we had experienced a nose gear collapse, and the tower advised that airport rescue and firefighting personnel were responding. after the aircraft came to a complete stop, i secured the aircraft by turning off both magnetos, electric fuel pumps, lights, alternators, and the master switch. i then instructed the student to follow my lead during the evacuation, and we exited the aircraft and moved to a safe location aft of the right wing. approximately one hour later, the chief flight instructor, assistant chief flight instructor, and maintenance personnel arrived from redacted. the aircraft was lifted and towed to a parking area at redacted. after the aircraft was secured, the head of maintenance advised that the cause of the incident was not yet known and that the left main landing gear had apparently not fully locked, although it had supported the aircraft during the landing rollout. the aircraft remained supported by its landing gear and was parked at redacted. i proceeded to speak to my assistant chief flight instructor and he said something along the lines of 'they knew it was going to happen at some point' or 'it was inevitable' and that he was glad that it did not happen to him (he was the pilot that flew the aircraft before i did).for context, similar nose gear collapse events have occurred previously within our pa-34-200 fleet, including at least one involving this same aircraft. a known limitation during preflight inspection is the plastic fairing beneath the nose gear, which restricts visibility of several components of the nose gear assembly. improved inspection access either by removing the fairing during inspection or redesigning it to permit better visual access may help identify potential discrepancies before flight.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Part 135 UAS pilot reported operating test flights which they were not approved to operate.
text: i was helping at location x. i asked operations if i was able to assist and take some responsibility by handling the test flights. i was given permission and conducted 5 test flights prior to being notified that it was unauthorized due to not being at an approved control station or that the location did not have a part 107 waiver. i gave up control and a manager took over.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported aircraft continuing to roll forward after chocks-in signal was given. Brakes were applied to stop.
text: after parking and receiving the chock in signal the parking brake was released in accordance with flight manual for cooling. aircraft began to roll slightly, and settled into chocks as brakes were applied. first officer reported during the walk around the nosewheel was canted. maintenance (mx) confirmed upon inspection and determined chocks were placed too far apart and were crooked behind the nose resulting in the wheel turning. mx restored the nosewheel to proper position and flight continued without incident.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: A320 Captain reported safety concerns with the aircraft air conditioning packs during pre-flight resulting in an aircraft refusal.
text: when i got the flight plan (release 1) from dispatch i took the time to review as i typically do...including the maintenance write-ups. i noticed an inbound pilot defect report indicating the #2 pack overheated and that it was a repeat write-up. i also noticed a deferral for an inop zone hot air pressure regulating valve. zone ducts temps were over 80 and a/c zones very hot. temp was regulated by closing hot air regulating valve...and this was on deferral. additionally, there were a few previous write-ups on pack #2 overheating. there was also a previous unable-to-operate for pack 1 and 2 faults. during this review process i got input from my first officer who has lots of experience on the airbus. we talked about potential threats and what we could do to mitigate. however, those conversations were based on pack #2 actually being fixed after the initial overheat. that said, we knew of the inbound pilot defect report and the issue with pack #2 repeating. after speaking with the inbound captain about his defect report and how he handled the issue (he was told the pack was fixed but obviously the issue had not been resolved), i seriously questioned whether or not i was going to accept the aircraft. at this point i had enough data points to question the safe operation of the aircraft. so i decided to call maintenance control and discuss the pack issues. maintenance control told me they had issue with pack 1 a few times before they were to get it fixed and that they were pretty sure it was now a good pack. i didnt get the sense the fix on pack 1 was an absolute, especially with the repeat write-ups and issues with pack 2, as well as the previous unable to operate due to both packs faulting. to add to it, there was significant weather in redacted for our departure time (while at the gate we experienced light hail, heavy rain, lightning, and i was told a tornado warning). all factors considered i was leaning toward refusing the aircraft. at about that time i spoke with a redacted maintenance (mx) tech who came out to the aircraft to collect a readout from the aircraft regarding the packs and associated failures. he told me that his supervisor was considering removing the aircraft from service due to the pack issues and their history. however, mx eventually decided to defer the #2 pack under minimum equipment list redacted. this would basically put us on single pack operations, and any issues with pack one would result in an emergency descent. it was at that time i decided to refuse the aircraft. based on the history of previous issues with both packs, and #2 pack overheating multiple times after repairs, i did not feel safe operating this aircraft. to add to the confusion, while the pack deferral was pushed through and approved, the release was still red for an inop windshield wiper that could not be fixed due to the ramp being closed for lightning. i was getting pressured by redacted operations to board the aircraft, but i told them it wasn't a good idea because i was going to refuse the aircraft. so i decided to call maintenance control to see if he could help start the refusal process, which he did. i wanted the system to show the refusal so operations would be able to move forward and stop trying to board passengers. i then called dispatch to inform them and he also entered the refusal into the system. after that, things settled down and we received a new aircraft...i was coming in about an hour and half later.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B737 First Officer reported loss of hydraulic system during initial climb. Crew returned to departure airport.
text: we departed redacted, en route to redacted. i was the pilot flying (pf), and the captain was performing pilot monitoring (pm) duties.the takeoff was normal, and the aircraft became airborne without any abnormalities. shortly after gear retraction, a master caution illuminated along with a hydraulic indication. the captain advised that we had an engine no. 1 hyd pump low pressure indication.we continued the departure, accelerated as planned, selected flaps 1 and then flaps up, and completed the after takeoff checklist. i requested that the captain accomplish the applicable engine no. 1 hyd pump low pressure checklist. at that time, hydraulic system a quantity was indicating approximately 15%, with only the engine no. 1 hyd pump low pressure light illuminated. the associated checklist was completed, and no additional immediate actions were required.the captain advised air traffic control of the situation and requested to maintain 7, 000 feet while entering a holding pattern at redacted to evaluate the condition. during the hold, the applicable non-normal checklist was completed. the captain coordinated with dispatch, communicated with air traffic control, and informed the cabin crew and passengers.after all applicable non-normal checklists had been completed and all required actions had been accomplished, i transferred aircraft control to the captain to facilitate the approach briefing and arrival preparation. during the briefing, we brief the weather, landing performance, overweight landing considerations, threat assessment, and return options. we determined that returning to redacted was the safest course of action. the decision and operational plan were communicated to dispatch, air traffic control, the cabin crew, and the passengers.landing performance data was obtained and reviewed. we selected max autobrake and planned a flaps 40 landing. the approach briefing was completed, inbound course and minimums were set, and all required preparations were accomplished. i then resumed pilot flying duties and requested the descent checklist.after verifying that all required actions had been completed, we requested the approach. air traffic control cleared us direct redacted, instructed us to descend and maintain 4, 000 feet, and subsequently cleared us for the approach. i requested that the captain verify and set a re-cruise altitude of 4, 000 feet in the fmc to ensure vnav guidance remained available during the approach.the approach was flown normally. while established on final, i requested flaps 30 and subsequently flaps 40. shortly after flaps 40 extension, we observed hydraulic system a quantity decrease to zero. at that time, we were approximately 1, 000-1, 100 feet agl. the landing gear was down, flaps were fully extended, and the aircraft remained stabilized on approach. given the aircraft configuration and compliance with stabilized approach criteria, we elected to continue.prior to landing, the captain reminded me that with the loss of hydraulic system a, reverse thrust availability and braking characteristics could be affected and that accumulator performance should be monitored. i acknowledged the briefing.i disconnected the autopilot and landed the aircraft normally. only the no. 2 (right) thrust reverser was utilized. braking performance was normal, and we exited the runway at taxiway 1.after clearing the runway, i completed the after landing flow and started the apu. while reviewing the hydraulic system a loss checklist, we reached a step directing us to select nose wheel steering alternate. after selecting the alternate mode, taxi capability improved, however, we then observed hydraulic system b quantity beginning to decrease as well.recognizing the potential for further degradation of aircraft systems, the captain elected to stop the aircraft and set the parking brake. we advised air traffic control that we were unable to continue taxiing under our own power. hydraulic system b quantity continued to decrease. the apu was placed on the bus, and we continued coordinating with air traffic control, the cabin crew, passengers, and company personnel.i contacted the company and advised that a tow would be required because we could no longer safely taxi the aircraft due to the continued loss of hydraulic fluid. maintenance, dispatch, scheduling, and the chief pilot were notified.a tow vehicle arrived and towed the aircraft to gate xx without further incident. the passengers remained informed throughout the event. after arrival at the gate, passengers deplaned normally, and maintenance assumed control of the aircraft for further evaluation.no injuries occurred, and the event was managed in accordance with sops, company procedures, and non-normal checklist guidance.we were approximately 1, 400 pounds above the maximum landing weight.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation - Altitude Crossing Restriction Not Met; Deviation - Altitude Overshoot
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported possible GPS jamming/spoofing on descent into MMMZ.
text: just before the top of descent on the obrug1b, we noticed a gps-l invalid on the control display unit (cdu) scratchpad. we referred to the flight manual (fm) and since we had briefed the rnp 22 approach, we wanted to check the requirements for that approach. the nav status page showed gps (2) and we were satisfied that we could continue with the rnp approach.mazatlan control gave us a clearance to cross mures at fl230, which we programmed into the fmc. we also kept obrug at fl 230, since we were cleared to descend via the obrug1b to 5500'.at the top of descent, we descended in vnav and crossed mures at fl230, but the aircraft continued to descend (about 250 ft) below fl 230, even though we were supposed to remain at fl 230 until descending again at obrug. autopilot a was engaged. i engaged vertical speed to gradually climb the aircraft back to fl230, then re-engaged vnav (this was about 16 nm prior to obrug). the aircraft started to descend again, so i intervened again to stop the descent. at obrug, i re-engaged vnav, and the aircraft remained at or above the path throughout the remainder of the arrival and approach (rnp 22). we were monitoring it closely, of course.on short final, the first officer (pilot monitoring) observed a gps-l invalid message, followed by a gps-r invalid message on the cdu scratchpad.the conditions were vmc and i was hand flying from about 1000 feet. we landed normally and taxied to the gate, then completed two electronic log book write-ups (one about the vnav issue and one about the gps invalid messages).i contacted dispatch, who connected me with maintenance control, and we notified the local station about the write-ups. a mechanic came on board shortly, and spoke to us, as well as maintenance control. the local mechanic said that the gps issue was likely related to signal blocking. i don't know whether this is true or not, but he seemed pretty certain that this was likely the case.on a recent flight (a couple of weeks ago) going into pvr, i recall getting the gps-l invalid message, but it cleared on its own after a few minutes.there weren't any notams related to gps signal issues on our flight. this seems to be a recurring issue that probably should be put out there to the pilot group (notam or bulletin of some sort) so that crews can be aware of this potential issue and plan accordingly.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a GPWS terrain alert when descending on the initial approach course to GJT in mountainous terrain. The crew performed an escape maneuver and executed a go-around.
text: descending on the gjt rnav 29 from cesba and outside of hansu we received caution terrain ahead. as we neared hansu we had slowed to approximately 190 kias. the caution turned into a gpws warning and i executed the terrain escape. i disconnected autopilot and pushed for toga thrust. i immediately began a left hand turn away from the terrain and towards the final approach course.once the warning was gone i reconfigured the aircraft for the approach but it was evident we were going to be high and fast. we executed an early go around and eventually the captain landed on runway 11 (due to <100 hr first officer limitation of 15 kt crosswind). winds had shifted at the airport and the airport switched to runway 11 operations during the go around.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an obstacle alert was heard on short final at IAD. Crew initiated a go around and returned for a landing.
text: on the rnav y rwy 19c in iad, first officer was pf and i was pm. approach was stable and descending on the papi through 1000 ft and 500ft. at approximately 400ft a gpws alert of obstacle" was heard. a go around was initiated and the flight returned for a normal landing back on runway 19ccause: continued visual diligence on a visual approach to cross check glide path and the papi."

anomaly: Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported sinking below the glide slope during approach due to the variable winds in the area. Flight continued to a safe landing.
text: during approach instrument landing system xx redacted. inclement weather approaching the final course caused winds to vary widely in both speed and direction. upon initiation of approach through to beyond final approach course approach was stabilized despite significantly variable winds. at some point slightly beyond final approach fix aircraft began sinking below instrument landing system glideslope and glide slope aural warning was heard. corrective action taken immediately. one dot low glideslope indication noticed. runway was in sight at this time 3 red papis indicated. ground proximity switch light illuminated briefly while corrections were being applied. 'terrain terrain' aural annunciation not heard. glide path was corrected and approach continued no go around initiated.cause: variable winds caused by approaching inclement weather made for a difficult approach. pilots decision to attempt the approach despite approaching weathersuggestions: pilots should have elected to hold and wait out the weather. more assertive corrective actions would have decreased the mount of time spent in deviation from glideslope.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported there are confusing markings in green on the taxiway at ABQ.
text: after landing, taxiing to e. cleared by ground to hold short of runway 3. approaching a strange intersection of multiple taxiways, i saw green markings on the ground, and other what appeared to be non-standard markings on the taxiway, even the color green. it was not intuitive and i could not see a runway, rather it looked like just taxiways intersecting. the actual runway threshold is over 300 yards away from that point. i slowed to stop as i was confused with what i saw and intended to stop and ask ground for progressive taxi. i said on intercommunications system (ics) to the cfi in the back seat, am i supposed to stop here, " as i was coming to a stop, and he responded, "no continue to that dog leg to the left." at that point i believe my nose was on or near the hold short line and i heard from ground, aircraft x no delay cross runway 3, at which point i continued to taxi on e. i saw what looked like what used to be a hold short line closer to runway 3 and eventually saw the runway environment and overrun at the departure end of runway 3. contributing factors: confusing and non-intuitive hold short and taxiway markings that were not near the runway or like anything i had ever seen, i was stopping at the hold short line when my cfi told me to continue as it was apparently confusing to him as well."

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway; Ground Incursion Taxiway; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: The pilot of a bi-plane reported experiencing a ground loop while landing in shifting wind conditions. The aircraft departed the runway onto an adjacent taxiway and sustained no damage.
text: this was the third 20 minute ride flight of the day out of seven scheduled. the first two flights were uneventful. on the third flight while landing on runway xx at redacted, the winds were reported to be 260 degrees at 12 gust to 18 knots. during the flare for the three point landing, the wind abruptly shifted to 330 degrees at 15 gust to 23 knots, as reported by the tower after the incident. i immediately put in additional crosswind controls to prevent the airplane from being affected by the unforeseen wind shift, but it was too late. the airplane was already starting to weathervane and started to ground loop. i stayed on the surface of the runway and then began to swerve onto taxiway 'h' to the north of the runway. after stopping on the taxiway, facing opposite the landing direction, i radioed to the tower 'we're good.' i never left the prepared surface, nor did i contact the left wing with the ground. a brief conversation with the tower controller also said that he was caught by surprise with the sudden wind shift as well and he was surprised how well i had handled the situation. he also said that after the wind shift he was changing the landing runway from runway xx to runway xy. i taxied the airplane to its parking location and did a thorough post flight inspection for any possible damage to the aircraft wings and landing gear, of which there was none.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury
synopsis: Cessna 310 pilot reported a carbon monoxide warning during cruise; and experiencing physical symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning. Pilot continued to destination airport and landed safely.
text: on the date of day 0 i conducted an instrument flight rules flight from redacted to redacted. on my route i was cleared for a direct as filed at 8, 000'. at approximately 1.5 hours into my flight i received an carbon monoxide warning on my foreflight app which was detected by the carbon monoxide detector in my sentry adsb receiver. immediately following this message i equipped my nasal oxygen cannula and ensured my oxygen flow was set via my oxygen delivery system. once my cannula was mounted properly and my oxygen was flowing i contacted air traffic control and let them know of the warning and that i was on oxygen and not feeling any symptoms. due to my position and lack of apparent symptoms i decided to continue to my original destination airport redacted. in my flight bag i have a blood oxygen monitor that my company requires me to bring with me on all my flights due to the high altitude we do our single pilot aerial surveys at, but i unfortunately placed my flight bag entirely out of reach on this flight due to the fact that i knew i would be flying at a low altitude because i was ferrying the aircraft. being in and out of imc at night i decided to focus entirely on flying the plane and recognizing any symptoms that i may be encountering due to the levels of carbon monoxide detected in the cabin instead of trying to find my blood oxygen sensor. after about 15-20 more minutes into the flight and receiving clearance to descend and then to follow a 737 into redacted for a visual approach i had a much harder time finding the airport than i normally would, everything below 8, 000' was entirely clear and it being at night a larger airport like redacted should not be this hard to find. after finally finding the airport and getting clearance to land about 5-7 miles out, i ran my checklist 3 or 4 extra times to ensure myself not to miss any important pre landing checklist items. at this time i was feeling light headed but was very focused on landing my airplane and making mental notes to worry about dealing with that task before self diagnosing any symptoms i may be feeling from the situation. once i landed and had a rather smooth landing considering the circumstances i remember being told to turn right off the runway and i believe being asked where i was planning on parking. when i finally stopped moving and was clear of the active runway i remember feeling a wave of light headedness, a slight to moderate headache and a dry mouth. i remember tower reading my taxi clearance to me and was hit with what i can only describe as a wave of confusion as i was not only able to read the taxi clearance back properly but also truly couldn't put it to practice in my head. something as simple as a taxi clearance is muscle memory to me at this point in my career so i instantly knew something was definitely wrong. so i immediately opened the door and window and told tower/ground that i was experiencing carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms. i remember ground telling me i could shut off my aircraft where i was and after turning off my avionics it took me a solid 60 seconds to remember the exact process of shutting down my aircraft. after this i remember setting the parking brake and getting out of the aircraft and feeling quite light headed and my legs were weak. an airport ops manager drove up to me and offered me to sit down in his car and gave me water and i sat with him until the medics arrived. at this point i had probably been on the ground and out of the aircraft for about 12 minutes, the confusion began to fade rather quickly but the light headedness remained until the end of the evening slight fatigue and 'brain fog' persisted for the following 24ish hours following the event. the medics implemented a few tests on me and if i remember correctly they said my blood sugar/blood pressure was entirely normal range but there was another test which i think was related to co poisoning that they said was rather high but not of a hospitalization level. after this the medics cleared me to go and i and the airportops manager received clearance for him to escort me and my taxi to the ramp.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Excursion Runway
synopsis: PA-44 pilot reported a loss of aircraft control when the instructor simulated an engine failure on the takeoff roll near rotation speed; resulting in a runway excursion into the grass. The instructor took control and stopped the aircraft with no injuries or damage.
text: during a multiengine commercial pilot training flight, a simulated engine failure was introduced during the takeoff roll prior to rotation (vr). although the procedure was briefly discussed during taxi, the lack of previous practical introduction to this maneuver and single-engine muscle memory led to delayed throttle reduction, causing a loss of directional control and a runway excursion. no damage or injuries occurred.i was performing a training flight in a piper seminole (pa-44) to prepare for my upcoming commercial multiengine checkride. i had already completed some prior training sessions in the aircraft type. this specific emergency maneuver had never been practiced in my previous flights, and it was not included in our pre-flight briefing. after our third landing at redacted airport, the flight instructor requested to taxi back to active runway xx for another takeoff. during the taxi, the instructor briefed me that we would perform an engine failure during the takeoff roll. he asked me to recite the correct procedure, and i correctly stated the steps: throttles to idle, apply full braking, and maintain directional control on the runway. however, during the actual takeoff roll, prior to reaching rotation speed (vr), the instructor simulated the engine failure. despite having just discussed the procedure, my lack of practical experience with this maneuver and entrenched single-engine muscle memory caused me to freeze on the throttles. instead of immediately retarding them to idle, i attempted to maintain the centerline using rudder inputs alone. before vr, the rudder lacked the aerodynamic authority to counteract the severe asymmetric thrust of the operating engine at full takeoff power. the aircraft veered off the centerline, resulting in a low-speed runway excursion into the grass adjacent to runway xx.the instructor took control, power was reduced to idle, and the aircraft was safely stopped and secured. a thorough inspection confirmed there was no damage to the aircraft, no damage to airport property, and no injuries to either occupant. the checkride scheduled was canceled.this event highlighted a major disconnect between theoretical knowledge and practical muscle memory during high-workload multiengine emergencies. even though i knew the procedure and recited it minutes prior, the lack of previous physical repetition caused a failure in execution. moving forward, i am committing to intensive 'chair flying' and dedicated dual training to mechanize the immediate physical reaction of bringing throttles to idle during an aborted takeoff before rescheduling my checkride.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported conducting a flight in a TFR. The pilot was made aware by a law enforcement officer after landing.
text: on day 0, while acting as remote pilot in command and operator of a sub 250-gram remote id-compliant (via an equipped aftermarket remoteid module) fpv drone, i inadvertently operated within an active temporary flight restriction (tfr) airspace. the purpose of the short, 4-to-5-minute flight was to capture low-altitude video footage. prior to the flight, i conducted a pre-flight airspace check using the airhub portal roughly two hours before take-off. unfortunately, the search bar auto-populated an incorrect location, which failed to display the newly active tfr. because i had previously vetted this specific location's airspace months prior, i proceeded under the mistaken belief that the airspace remained clear. i utilized a dedicated visual observer to maintain constant line of sight while i focused on the controls. the drone was kept at a very low altitude, safely away from any full-scale aviation traffic. upon landing, a local law enforcement officer approached me regarding the tfr violation. i cooperated fully with the officer. full telemetry flight logs and onboard video recordings have been preserved. these files conclusively document the low operational altitude, the duration of the flight, and my previous airspace research logs. this oversight was entirely unintentional, caused by a mistaken localized search in my pre-flight software. i have since updated my pre-flight checklists to include checking specific coordinate verification and utilization of the b4ufly app immediately before takeoff to prevent future mapping errors.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS flight crew reported conducting two flights in a TFR; one of which was done without a LAANC authorization.
text: uas was accidentally flown within a tfr, a no uas zone, for a training mission up to 100ft altitude. incident was due to operator inexperience, not fully understanding how to read the flight advisories shared within the aloft air control application.two operators were involved in the incident, in back-to-back flights within the same geographic area. both operators were negligent in reading and understanding the tfr.training mission was being flown to check for basic understanding of drone control and safety, in order to be cleared to begin flying commercial uas flights in the near future. nerves from the 'testing' environment likely contributed to failing to properly read and process the tfr shared in the notam.this failing was further compounded by a misunderstanding by one operator on how to properly request laanc flight permission within the aloft air aware application. while one operator successfully filed their laanc auto-authorization request, the second operator did not - misunderstanding both how to file the laanc request, and misunderstanding that a laanc filed by one operator does not carry over to a second operator.the error was discovered when one operator further investigated the aloft air control application for further knowledge and better understanding after the training mission and realized the error that had been made and the gravity of the situation. the operator is self-reporting in the interest of following proper protocol, and to help cement the importance of understanding both the equipment and regulations that come into play for safe uas operation.to avoid the error in the future, additional instruction on proper usage of the aloft air control application is planned for both operators to ensure safe compliance.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in a TFR without authorization.
text: i frequently work in the area where a new tfr was put in place just days before. i utilized a third party app for laanc approval because i knew i was in class c airspace with a ceiling of 400 feet. i requested 150 feet because i'm working in close proximity to 1 building and wouldn't need to climb over it. i mistakenly assumed that my request would be denied if i couldn't fly there due to other restrictions. i didn't realize that the tfr in place (for something i haven't witnessed a tfr being used for [bridge construction]) wouldn't block my laanc approval. it wasn't until the next day, when i needed to request laanc approval again and more closely read the tfr in its entirety, that i realized my error. i immediately phoned the number on the tfr and was given directions on how to properly apply for a waiver to fly in this airspace.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: PCT TRACON Controller reported losing all methods of communication with aircraft with little to no back-up options and even after the frequency returned; the quality and coverage was less than ideal.
text: i was working the redacted position, frequency 120.45, with a string of arrivals inbound to iad on the gibbz5 arrival. it was a bit of an unusual sequence due to weather near iad. airplanes on the north leg of the arrival were being vectored off the arrival and given to the redacted / redacted sector for runway 19l and the south leg of the arrival i was vectoring to a right base leg to runway 19c. aircraft x checked in on the north leg and i instructed them to descend to 070. i then went to issue a turn to aircraft y to the base leg and got no response. i tried the turn again, no response. i reached out to two other aircraft with no response. i changed my transmitter to standby and tried again with no response. i plugged into the emergency communication system (ecs) orange box and tried that and still got no response. all of a sudden, i had lost any way of communicating with any of the aircraft i was talking to and they were all on vectors. my last chance was to plug back into the rdvs (rapid deployment voice switch) and attempt the tunable frequency which finally worked. however, due to the delay in communication, two aircraft had left my frequency (one to guard and one to a different approach sector). so now i was scrambling to keep aircraft separated and sequenced with a very limited capacity to talk to any of them, as well as coordinate with the other sectors who had gotten aircraft they weren't expecting. it made an already complicated session exponentially more difficult and affected the flow of traffic to the airport.recommendation: there needs to be more reliable equipment to start with, but certainly a wider array of backup options. for me to be working and have aircraft on headings to lose everything was a very disconcerting experience. it's almost daily that there are frequencies that are out of service or being worked on so there is no backup. and often, when they are returned to service, the quality isn't great. coverage is less than ideal. even when the actual frequency came back, i reached out to a pilot and they said they were only receiving me 3x5.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: A Center Controller reported a NORDO aircraft deviating for weather flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: aircraft x was flashing at me from the redacted artcc sector xx. the aircraft altitude was showing 030b040 and in the 4th line he was deviating left and direct redacted when able. the redacted [artcc] controller called me on the landline and apreq'd (approval request) the aircraft in the block. i advised the controller that at 030 i would most likely not be able to communicate with the a/c (aircraft) throughout my airspace. the redacted [artcc] controller told the pilot that and said that he was requesting the block for weather and suggested that he amend the block to 030b050 so he can climb higher for communications, which i approved. also the redacted [artcc] controller requested redacted approaches frequency as a backup for the aircraft, which i gave him redacted.xx.as the a/c entered my airspace, he continued to deviate for weather. as he deviated an msaw alert started on the aircraft. i then realized he was deviating into an mea of 3200 ft. and was level at 3000 ft. i immediately attempted to give the aircraft a low altitude alert warning with no response. i then attempted to contact the a/c on the guard frequency, also with no response. following that i contacted aircraft y to relay on redacted.xy (the west frequency of sector xy). aircraft y tried multiple times with no response. i also attempted contact again with my buec (backup emergency communications) transmitters with no response. with this unfortunate turn of events aircraft x traversed the 3200 mea without incident. however, there was another 3200 ft. mea coming up. i advised the supervisor of the situation and told them the steps i had been taking.i called the redacted approach controller to see if he could reach out on redacted.xx and see if aircraft x was monitoring. the redacted [tracon] controller advised that the pilot was not answering. i then called the redacted [artcc] controller to see if he could reach out to the aircraft and see if he was still on his frequency. the controller called and said he was not on frequency. i queried what frequency the redacted [artcc] controller transferred him to, and he told me that he told the a/c to monitor redacted.xz (the east frequency for sector xy). due to this new information i adjusted my attempts and contacted aircraft z and asked him to relay on redacted.xz. aircraft z was able to reach aircraft x on the first call, and i asked aircraft z to climb him immediately to 3200 ft., which aircraft x confirmed and enacted. i then asked aircraft z to amend his block altitude to 032b050 which also was accomplished. eventually i was able to reach aircraft x on redacted.xz as he got closer to the transmitter and establish communications. after i apreq'd the new block altitude and deviations to the redacted approach controller i transferred communications to the redacted approach controller. the a/c continued his flight without incident.i think this situation could have been prevented if i would have insisted on climbing the aircraft to 4000 ft. the weather was already providing an unknown to the aircrafts route of flight and the communication barrier made it so it would have been the best proactive response. however i allowed it because the a/c requested the block for weather purposes. one thing that would have also prevented this would have been if the redacted [artcc] controller would have transferred communications to the correct (west) frequency. this confusion made me take several actions that were counterproductive to fixing the situation. had i known he was on the east frequency, i believe aircraft y would have reached aircraft x the first time and avoided the mea.

synopsis: F11 TRACON Controller reported completely losing the main; standby; and emergency back-up frequencies while working numerous approaches and departures.
text: i was training person a on sector x during an extremely busy session. about 30 minutes into the session we notice that we were only getting partial readbacks and no readbacks from other aircraft. we then notified the front line manager (flm) on what was happening and then switched to standby transmitter. approximately 30 minutes after, we completely lost 125.22 on both mains and standbys.we had numerous visual flight rules departures along with arrivals, to include instrument flight rules approaches and departures. i then asked my flm to give us 2 miles in trail (mit) for visual flight rules departures off of sfb to slow the sector down. two of the departures was aircraft x off of sfb and aircraft y off of orl. we then noticed that we were not getting any readbacks. person a climbed aircraft y was issued a climb to 030 and no response. at this point both aircraft were separated by 8.64 miles. we then noticed that we completely lost the frequency and jump to the emergency backup orange jack. after multiple transmissions person a jumped up to urc-300e (tunable backup radio) with the same results of no responses. while person a was on the urc-300e, i immediately jumped on the emergency backup orange jack and transmitted multiple times with no response. we both noticed the conflict well before it happened and tried to deconflict the situation. when i realized that nothing was working, i unplugged and went back into the main jack and went on emergency guard to issue instruction to deconflict the situation and still no response. later on after the situation we found that aircraft y was trying to get us and eventually jumped to sector y. person b the sector y controller tried to deconflict the situation as well. recommendation: fix urc-300e.

synopsis: NCT TRACON Controller reported the radar scopes in the area went black resulting in the inability to provide radar services and an unsafe air traffic control environment.
text: we were told by tech ops to go to es (emergency service) mode for a system update that sometimes happens on day 0 night mids. luckily the area b controller would not agree to go to es until he had no sfo arrivals. this pushed it to xa:00. we went to es. after a few minutes, i got aircraft x instrument flight rules to redacted descending to 100. i gave instructions to proceed to the iaf for instrument landing system to redacted and descents appropriately reference mvas. when the aircraft the around 050 (guessing) but still well away from the iaf, more than half the scopes in area d went completely black, including mine and the sfo final controller who also had one airplane. the scope next to me was still up so i was able to use that for reference. in the past when a scope goes black, we usually are told to go to es, but tonight they were working the fs (full service) mode so i am unsure of going to another mode would have worked. we yelled over at tech ops and the omic (operations manager in charge) about our scopes. they acknowledged but didn't come over to offer help. tech ops seemed to be working on the issue in the middle area and for a brief time every scope went black for a few seconds before they all came back on. no issues with my aircraft, however, it raises major concerns about safety of equipment. it seems that radar equipment has lately been faulty. last week during the middle of the day, the sunol scope went completely blank. last week night mid, sfo tower scopes went black and multiple go arounds ensued with chaos at the area b mid sector. had the area b controller agreed to switch to es earlier tonight (they asked twice), it would have been terrible from a safety standpoint. why is this stuff happening now? ive been here xx years and never had a black scope. how can we have confidence in our equipment anymore?
