synopsis: Fractional Captain reported BFI Ground asked the crew during taxi to move over to the side of a taxiway to allow an opposite direction aircraft taxi past them. Reporter stated BFI Ground often clears opposite direction aircraft in this manner and it poses a safety concern.
text: cleared runway 32l at a7 to a taxiway to the ramp. after taxiing about 400 feet ground instructed us to move right as far as possible to allow an aircraft to taxi southbound on right side of taxiway a. we moved right with right wing well across non-movement line and whole aircraft to right of double hash taxi edge lines. aircraft y was taxiing south. the whole area narrows near the ramp [and] it appeared our wing tips would be closer than 5 feet. i stopped my airplane opposite traffic did also. they asked if we could move over more. we moved to where our airframe was completely into the non-movement area now. i radioed ground relaying my lack of comfort with taxiing two airplanes with a combined wingspan of nearly 150 feet in opposite directions on a taxiway that is designed and marked for single aircraft traffic.ground responded 'we do this everyday here' as if to be proud of it.suggestions: i believe this to be an unsafe practice. i believe bfi air traffic control is acting outside of safe protocols. i have never experienced this in decades of years of flying. in hindsight i should have said unable and held position. air traffic control in my opinion should have held the other plane in parking until we arrived in parking and cleared the taxiway. bfi can be busy. it was not at this time. nowhere else does this. everywhere else will tell departing from fbo traffic to hold position inbound aircraft to the ramp.if this is faa sanctioned, it is wrong, period!

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Strike - Aircraft; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: J3 Cub pilot reported a propeller ground strike during a hand prop start due to incorrect throttle setting. Aircraft was grounded.
text: i arrived at the hangar to perform routine preflight and ground servicing, which included repositioning the aircraft for a planned trip to the fuel farm and performing a ground maintenance run prior to a potential flight later in the day. the aircraft is not equipped with an electrical system or an electric starter, therefore, manual hand-propping is the standard, normal operational method for starting the engine.the aircraft was properly parked on the ramp with wheel chocks securely in place. during the starting sequence from the ground, the engine became flooded and required a clearing procedure. the cockpit throttle control was inadvertently and unintentionally left set open after the clearing procedure was completed.i pulled the propeller through, and the engine fired as expected. however, due to the incorrect throttle setting, the engine immediately produced a sudden, high-power surge of thrust. this surge pulled the aircraft forward tightly against its chocks, causing the tail to lift and the aircraft to nose-over. the propeller struck the ground, causing a prop strike, which immediately terminated engine operation.i was positioned safely on the ground outside the airframe and was never on board or inside the aircraft at any point during the sequence. the aircraft did not move from its parked tie-down location. there were no third-party injuries or third-party property damage. the aircraft sustained localized damage to the propeller, and potentially a wing strut and spar (although the wing itself never touched the ground or any objects). the strut and spar damage likely resulted from the twisting forces and sudden deceleration while the airframe was in a compromised, near-vertical attitude rather than its designed horizontal position. the aircraft was immediately grounded for maintenance inspection, a crankshaft runout check, and repair. the bow in the wing strut was subsequently observed, and the spar inspection initiated, during follow-up visual inspections over the following days.once the aircraft is repaired, future operations will utilize a secondary tail tie-down restraint system specifically configured to secure the airframe when no auxiliary ground personnel are available to assist with a hand-prop sequence. this mechanical redundancy will back up the wheel chocks and completely eliminate the possibility of a nose-over in the event of an open or malfunctioning throttle. additionally, a modified ground checklist protocol will be implemented to require a strict physical and audible verification of the throttle, mixture, and ignition controls prior to rotating the propeller. furthermore, future flooded engine clearing procedures will be performed with the throttle set strictly to the normal 'cracked' starting position, utilizing reverse engine rotations to safely clear excess fuel without exposing the operator to an unexpected high-power surge.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation Flight Instructor reported a NMAC during initial climb resulting in evasive actions being taken. Flight continued.
text: while departing runway 18 at mbt, another aircraft crossed the departure corridor during our initial climb. i spotted the aircraft on our adsb traffic page and began to look for the aircraft's tail number to ask the pilot what their intentions were. the aircraft was moving faster than i expected, so i took control from my student to level off the airplane and began visually searching for traffic. once i found the traffic, i felt it was best to pass behind or directly under the aircraft to avoid prolonging the traffic event. i informed the pilot what i was doing, and after we were clear of conflict, began our climb. i felt descending wasn't a good option given the obstacles at the departure end of 18, and climbing was an equally bad decision, so maintaining altitude seemed the best course of action. i do recall hearing calls from the other pilot, but i wasn't entirely sure what the aircraft was doing and was more focused at the time on observing my students take off and climb out. listening more intently or proactively asking other pilots what they are doing would be good practice to prevent situations like this from occurring in the future. we made a departure call and other standard calls while operating in the airport vicinity.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Cirrus SR20 flight instructor and student reported initial loss of engine power during cruise. Partial power restored during divert to a safe landing.
text: during a visual flight rules instructional training flight, my student and i departed on a planned flight to practice instrument approaches in the area. we were climbing through approximately 4, 200 feet msl while proceeding northeast and discussing approach procedures when the engine experienced a sudden and complete loss of power without warning.i immediately took control of the aircraft and established best glide speed. while maintaining aircraft control, i instructed my student to begin running the engine failure checklist. simultaneously, i assessed available landing options and determined that the most suitable airport was redacted airport.after selecting the airport, i requested priority handling with redacted tracon and advised them of our situation and intended course of action. while maneuvering toward the airport, my student continued working through the engine failure checklist. initial troubleshooting efforts were unsuccessful, and the engine remained without usable power.as part of continued troubleshooting, i moved the mixture control fully to idle cutoff and then advanced it fully forward. when the mixture control reached the idle cutoff position, the engine began producing partial power. the engine subsequently stabilized at an estimated 40 percent power output. this partial power allowed us to arrest our descent and maintain approximately a 200-foot-per-minute descent rate while continuing toward the airport.we proceeded directly to redacted airport and completed a safe landing under partial engine power. there were no injuries to either occupant, no damage to the aircraft, and no damage to persons or property on the ground.following the landing, the aircraft was secured and arrangements were made for maintenance inspection to determine the cause of the power loss.

anomaly: Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: RV-6 pilot reported inadvertent flight control contact by passenger while in the pattern causing a loss of aircraft control. Pilot regained control.
text: summary: a near stall/spin accident on the base to final turn that didn't involve poor airspeed or attitude awareness.about the plane: the rv-6a is a side by side experimental airplane. it has a stall speed of about 55 kts, approaches are flown at 70 kts and the maximum flap extension speed is about 85 kts. it has dual controls with the sticks between the legs of the pilot and passenger about 6' behind the front of the knees. there is limited room for the stick and both the pilot and passenger must bow their legs to allow full motion. the flap control can either be electric or a johnson bar manual control between the pilot and passenger seats. this plane has manual flaps. the pilot and passengers hips are in near contact and it requires reaching between the pilot and passenger legs to pull the flaps. the control is relatively short and the forces make it very difficult to apply full flaps with engine power applied or at any speed above 80 kts.about the flight: the winds were light, sky clear and daytime. i was taking a friend for his first flight in a small airplane as well as his first experience in the cockpit. it was a short flight from my local control towered airport to a nearby uncontrolled field (redacted). i did my typical brief as i go with a passenger. i made sure he knew how the seat belts worked as well as how to open the canopy. during the run-up when checking the controls for 'free and correct' i made a point to mention that he should stay clear of the stick between his legs while i was taking off or landing. as i flew to the nearby airport, my friend was enjoying the flight as well as doing some minor maneuvering with his stick.about the incident: i approached redacted by entering mid field downwind and started to slow down. i applied the 1st of 2 notches of flaps on downwind. the first notch of flaps doesn't require much effort on my part, but i do have to dig my hand between our legs to get access to the handle. at 1 notch, the end of the flap handle protrudes a little bit above the legs. as i was turning base to final i reached down to apply the 2nd notch of flaps. my friend felt me reaching near his knees decided to helpfully shift his legs away from my hand forcing the stick to the right and locking it in pitch. note, i'm 5'10' 135#, my friend is 6' and over 200#. i noticed the un-commanded roll to the right. the airspeed was slowing and the aoa alert beeped briefly. i said something to the effect of 'you've got to give me the stick' and he quickly straightened up. i finished the turn and landed safely.how this could have gone bad: if my friend hadn't quickly responded to my request, the intercom wasn't working for some reason or if i had been tongue tied or he hadn't understood the ambiguous request this could have resulted in a stall/spin. furthermore, to post crash analysis, this would have looked like poor airspeed or attitude awareness even if the logged data was examined.lessons learned for me: * the terms taking off and landing are ambiguous even to another pilot. i should have announced the phases as i went. before takeoff, 'stay clear of the stick till i let you know', start of cruise, 'ok, don't worry about bumping the stick for now', approach to land 'stay clear of the stick until i let you know', etc.* i should modify my approach to landing to apply full flaps while still at altitude and in a relatively low workload phase when flying with a non-pilot passenger. * our passenger stick is locked in with a clevis pin secured with a safety pin. if there is any concern i should always remove the stick for takeoff and landing. replacing the stick for cruise if i want to let the passenger to try out flying.suggestions: * during our build, van's sent a service bulletin to bolt the passenger stick into its socket to prevent it accidentally being pulled out by a pilot flying in the right seat during a critical flight phase. this appears to be trading one risk for another. if used for flight training, the bolt seems entirely appropriate. the stick unsecured may actually be safest if the passenger is only going to do cruise maneuvering.* a statistical analysis of accidents involving between-the-legs sticks as compared to yokes or side sticks would be interesting. an analysis of manual vs. electric flapped equipped rvs may be worthwhile for this particular accident scenario, but there are hopefully not a statistically relevant number.

anomaly: Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Ground Event / Encounter Aircraft
synopsis: Corporate jet First Officer reported aircraft rolled into another parked aircraft due to chocks removal and no brake pressure.
text: at the time of the event, the flight crew had been awake for more than 24 hours, having flown over 5 hours, and were completing the final leg of a demanding red-eye trip. extreme fatigue was a significant compounding factor. furthermore, as a low-time pilot in type (100 hours), i had not received extensive or standardized training regarding the specific nuances and verification sequence of the aircraft x parking brake system.sequence of events:the aircraft was parked on an inclined ramp with the engines shut down, parking brake disengaged, and chocks in place. the captain instructed me to set the parking brake. i pulled the parking brake handle, but did not visually verify hydraulic accumulator pressure or the corresponding brake indicator light status. the captain observed the physical handle position but did not cross-check the system pressure before exiting the aircraft to remove the chocks. no chocks were left behind the wheels to act as a secondary barrier.after re-entering the cabin to secure the cargo door and net, the aircraft began rolling backward due to the incline. because i was performing pre-flight duties for the next leg and the captain was focused on the cargo area, the initial movement went unnoticed.upon realizing the aircraft was moving, i immediately applied the toe brakes, but no braking action was achieved due to a lack of system hydraulic pressure. ground crew began alerting us to the movement. the captain hurried to the left seat and also applied the toe brakes with no effect. i attempted to assist by applying passenger-side toe brakes and verbally asked the captain if i should cycle the parking brake handle forward, i received no response due to the high-stress environment. the captain subsequently activated the standby hydraulic pump and utilized the steering tiller to steer the aircraft away from immediate hazards, but the aircraft ultimately collided with a parked airframe before coming to a complete stop.lessons learned / safety recommendations:this incident underscores the critical danger of severe crew fatigue on decision-making and cross-checking procedures. to prevent future occurrences, the exact sequential verification of the parking brake system--including verifying accumulator pressure and indicator lights--must be explicitly taught in training and verified via a mandatory checklist item before chocks are pulled. reliance on physical handle position alone creates an unsafe latent error.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Ground Event / Encounter Ground Equipment Issue
synopsis: F11 TRACON Controller reported completely losing the main; standby; and emergency back-up frequencies while working numerous approaches and departures.
text: i was training (cpc getting re-cert time) on sfb and orl departure satellite with my instructor. earlier in the session our main transmitter went out on us and we switched to standbys. the standbys are working relatively well and we have no backup frequency. i released aircraft y off runway 7 at orl who was a worms departure (north gate) while also tagging up inbounds for sfb, receiving constant visual flight rules departures off sfb and vectoring other aircraft through the airspace for approaches and over flights. aircraft y departs orl just as i finished talking to a visual flight rules inbound and he checks on and i radar him with a response for the pilot. i go to switch another aircraft to the adjacent sector and they do not respond the first time. this makes me wonder if this frequency is going to go out as well. this frequency we use (125.22) consistently fails and has multiple times over the past months and year. my trainer told the supervisor to tell sfb to put 2 miles in trail (mit) on the sfb departures and less than 30 seconds later i am trying to contact aircraft y to climb and turn away from sfb departure corridor but there is no response. i try others and a blind call and nothing. i immediately switch to the orange jack back-up and i get one transmission out to the visual flight rules that answers and then go to climb and turn aircraft y and no response. at the same time there is a steady stream of departures already airborne off sfb constantly calling and blocking the frequency so even if i could get out no one would hear me. as i am trying to contact aircraft y i also jumped up and tried to get the new urc-300e (replaced the pet-2000) turned on and usable. as all this is going on aircraft x comes off sfb on his missed approach heading southeast towards aircraft y. i am now using the orange jack and the new urc-300e thing alternating transmissions and trying to get aircraft y to turn away from aircraft x because they are wired and then if they miss aircraft x would be headed into an antenna farm in the southeast. nothing works, i mean nothing. mains, standbys, the emergency back-up, the new urc all are dead and all i can do is watch these two aircraft potentially hit each other.recommendation: the biggest problem we have is the frequencies for this position it fails more often then not and it cannot be trusted. 125.22 is the new frequency we have to replace 119.7 that constantly failed on us but it constantly fails also. this problem has constantly been bandaged and brushed under the rug but it keeps popping up and potentially killing someone. the whole system needs an overhaul now.another is when we lose either our main or standbys there should be automatic flow in place off the satellite airports. sfb is notorious for launching aircraft really close together and overloading the radar controller and radar screen. you cannot see the targets and the frequency becomes a mess. this needs to stop.after the fact was said technical operations pulled a card. they said they thought airport operations control center (aocc) gave them permissions to do so. they should check in the tracon prior to doing that. but nonetheless it would not have happened if this facility had frequencies that weren't constantly failing they wouldn't have to fix it. this facility is a dump, this isn't the first time this has happened and i am sure it won't be the last. the equipment is not trustworthy and adds extra stress in the operation. unfortunately nothing will change until two hit.

synopsis: PHL TRACON Controller reported the radar scope system failure with the radar scopes going blank resulted in an unsafe air traffic control environment.

synopsis: A300 First Officer reported aircraft began rolling after parking was completed. Aircraft was stopped.
text: once parked, i am 99% positive i observed the captain pull the parking brake, which is my personal cue to place the transponder in stby and wait for the shutdown checklist call to begin my shutdown flow. after reading through the shut down checklist, i realized the aircraft had begun rolling backwards and that the parking brake was not on. the aircraft began moving so slowly that i did not notice or feel the movement, as my attention was heads down while completing post flight responsibilities. thankfully, no one was injured and there was no damage. i'm not positive how far we rolled but my estimate is at least 50 feet. i am 99% confident that i observed the parking brake handle being pulled since it is a flow trigger i have for myself. my best guess is that the brake may not have been in the detent and either slipped out on its own or was accidentally bumped.this event is a stark reminder of how quickly an accident can occur when an action is performed but not positively verified before attention shifts to other tasks. we were not rushing however, it is easy to observe the parking brake handle being pulled and assume it has been properly set before continuing with other duties. all the captains i have flown with have setting the parking brake as pure muscle memory. i do not believe the brake wasn't actually set in the first place. again, my best guess is it was not fully in the detent. moving forward i will always verify the brake is properly set before performing other post flight duties. i am extremely grateful that no one was hurt, and this event proves to be reminder of the importance of verification during all phases operation.

synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported an NMAC with parachutists while in cruise flight. Pilot conducted evasive maneuvers and continued flight.
text: i was operating aircraft x under visual flight rules. earlier in the flight, i had been receiving visual flight rules flight following from whidbey departure before radar services were terminated and i was instructed to squawk visual flight rules. i considered requesting flight following again from seattle approach but elected not to because the frequency sounded busy and, during an earlier flight that day, i had not been successful in obtaining the service. as a result, i proceeded without radar traffic advisories while transiting the area.during this phase of the flight, i was descending from 5, 500 feet msl toward a planned altitude of 2, 500 feet msl while simultaneously maneuvering eastbound to remain clear of the 4, 000-foot shelf of the seattle class b airspace.my planned route took me approximately one nautical mile west of harvey airfield (s43). at the time of the encounter, i was level at approximately 3, 500 feet msl. i was not receiving visual flight rules flight following and was monitoring the local practice area frequency rather than the harvey airfield ctaf.as i passed west of harvey airfield (s43), i observed 2 parachutists descending in close proximity to my aircraft with little advance warning. i immediately maneuvered to avoid a potential collision. based on my observation from the cockpit, my best estimate is that each parachutist may have come within approximately 100-200 feet of my aircraft, however, i have no objective means to verify the actual separation distance. the encounter was sufficiently close that i believed immediate evasive action was necessary to avoid a collision.i did not hear any 'jumpers away' radio transmissions prior to the encounter. however, because i was monitoring the local practice area frequency, instead of the airport ctaf, it is possible that parachute activity advisories were transmitted on the ctaf and were therefore not received.no collision occurred, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.upon reflection, several factors likely contributed to the event. during this portion of the flight, i was managing a descent while navigating to remain clear of the seattle class b airspace and elected to monitor an air-to-air frequency rather than the local ctaf while transiting the vicinity of an airport with known parachute operations. although my route took me approximately one nautical mile west of the harvey airfield based on my recollection and review of foreflight track log, the encounter demonstrated that active parachutists may be encountered beyond the immediate airport environment. additionally, although visual flight rules flight following is workload permitting and not guaranteed, requesting it while operating through complex airspace and near known parachute operations may have provided additional situational awareness.this event highlighted for me the importance of proactively reassessing communications priorities when transitioning from en route flight into a congested terminal environment with both complex airspace and known parachute operations. in the future, i will monitor the appropriate ctaf when operating near airports with published parachute operations, will plan my route to provide greater lateral separation from known drop zones whenever practical, and will consider requesting visual flight rules flight following when workload and air traffic control availability permit to improve overall situational awareness.

application's default next-5-minute increment (xa:35) instead of the immediate window (xa:30). my attention shifted heavily to preflight duties, supervising an inexperienced person, and visually active authorization window. the discrepancy was caught upon post-flight log review. no manned traffic was in the area, and visual line of sight was maintained at all times. during the low-altitude standing directly underneath the aircraft, sometimes actively reaching for it.contributing factors: high cognitive workload introduced by supervising an unrated person while establishing a safe flight perimeter. additionally, my background in manned aviation accustomed me to flight plans being opened dynamically via two-way radio upon request, rather than strictly adhering to automated, fixed-time blocks used for laanc approval. i was aware that laanc worked in time authorization blocks, but i erroneously believed i was approved for the current time block. i am also accustomed to pre-flighting well in advance of the takeoff window for manned aircraft, a habit that translated poorly to a rigid digital block system.hardware design and human habits also contributed: i was utilizing a phone-display controller that lacks a native timekeeping element on its head-up display (hud). because my smartwatch was malfunctioning, i was effectively locked out of verifying the current time once the controller connected to the suas. finally, i relied on a memory-based preflight inspection rather than a structured, written checklist, which allowed the laanc time-verification step to be missed during a high-workload scenario.future corrective/mitigation actions:defer connecting the drone to the controller until the approved laanc window is actively confirmed as current, unless a reliable, independent timekeeping device is available at the control station.transition from a memory-based preflight inspection to a formalized, written checklist. this new checklist will be explicitly updated to include hard steps for checking active laanc authorization windows, ensuring adequate timekeeping equipment is available, and assessing localized environmental safety issues, specifically accounting for dynamic pedestrian traffic--such as children--who may actively seek to place themselves directly under the drone's flight path.

text: i was on cic (controller in charge) because the supervisor was on break. the departure sector had x/y/z sectors all combined. aircraft x was inbound to redacted [airport] and had requested a practice approach which was denied. aircraft x was cleared for a visual approach per the redacted [tracon] sop and the loa (letter of agreement) with redacted fct (faa contract tower). aircraft x never requested multiple approaches with redacted nor to my knowledge did the request multiple approaches with redacted [center]. entering the pattern aircraft x appeared high and fast they ended up overflying the runway and entering left traffic for xxr with redacted fct. after the second approach the aircraft departed redacted on a southwest heading well below the mva. redacted had the starts datatag in a radar handoff to x sector. redacted fct is not a tower with radar and is not authorzed to complete an automated radar handoff. as the cic i called and asked the local controller what aircraft x was doing. he responded that they are departing southwest bound. i informed the controller that the aircraft was instrument flight rules on a visual approach. the controller responded that he had no idea they were instrument flight rules the entire time aircraft x was in the pattern. at this point the local controller had already shipped aircraft x back to [sector] x before x had taken the handoff. the departure controller confimed the ifr/vfr status of aircraft x issued a climb to get them above the terrain and eventually got them turned on course. recommendation: redacted fct is understaffed and inexperienced. there is regularly only one person in the tower cab. i don't know if an extra set of eyes would have solved the problem but i cant imagine it would have hurt in this situation. an f18 into redacted is an unheard of event i'm not sure what more would draw attention to the instrument flight rules datablock.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control; Inflight Event / Encounter Unstabilized Approach
synopsis: B757 flight crew reported a momentary loss of control while conducting a visual approach.
text: we were on the redacted arrival expecting the instrument landing system to visual for xxc. got radar vector 010 descend to 4000' 190 kits abeam redacted. then turn to 100. then turn to 170 descend to 2000, still 190 knots heading us towards redacted, we were still at 190 it's, cleared for the visual, this is where the [expletive] started. it was obvious to both of us we were going to be high and fast. i spun in 2000, turned heading to 170, the fo pulled out the speed brakes. i said to the controller a heading of 120 would help us lose some altitude and speed. he gave us 120, cleared for the approach, tower frequency and said we were below glided slope passing through 3000 feet. i spun in the heading, changed altitude to 3000, noticed the fo was decreasing v/s. here is my mistake, i got the inference from the controller that we going to bust class b air space. i could see the fo was trying to shallow out to catch the g/s at 3000, i hit alt hold and did not tell the fo because i was busy reading back all the instructions to the controller. i thought the fo saw me hit alt hold. i looked down to tune in the tower frequency when i heard all the alarms go off. i looked up and we were slow. the alarm was the speed brake was out, the fo cut out the autopilot but only one click. he quickly stowed the speed brakes added power as i canceled the warning. extensive de brief followed the next 24 hours. we both were expecting a nice base to final at 4000'. the aggressive turn in and a descent immediately put us in a high and fast situation. we both recognized it and were mitigating the threat in different ways. the high work load prevented clear communication between myself and fo. it was ultimately mitigated safely but was more exciting than need be.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: B767 First Officer reported loss of hydraulic pump during initial climb. Flight continued.
text: on takeoff, we got a c hyd demand pump icas message followed by a gear disagree message as the gear was taking a long time to retract. eventually both messages went away as the gear fully retracted. during this time i missed an automatic radio change to departure and had to be prompted by tower to change frequencies. c hyd demand pump messages came back on flap retraction. we followed the checklist and turned the center demand pump from auto to on. shortly thereafter flight attendants reported a sound that resembled an alarm and they were very concerned about it. when the relief pilot went on break he went to the back to listen to the sound and report back. while on the phone with him we turned the demand pump back to auto and the sound immediately went away. we continued the flight and consulted maintenance control about the details of the problem. during approach we turned the demand pump back to on and didn't get any caution messages while configuring. after landing the flight attendants reported that there was no abnormal sound or alarm in the landing phase.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: CRJ900 First Officer reported the shattering of the Captain's windshield during cruise flight. Flight continued to destination.
text: shortly after leveling off at fl350 i heard a loud bang and noticed that the captain's windshield appeared completely shattered. the cracks were present across the entirety of the windshield. we immediately requested priority handling and began a descent to 15, 000 feet. while in the descent we ran the cracked windshield qrh procedure and contacted dispatch through acars. we monitored cabin pressurizatuon throughout the descent and found that pressurization was normal. although we considered diversion options nearby and further along the route we, along with dispatch, decided to continue to redacted. i did not notice any evidence of an impact during the post-flight inspection.cause: i am not sure of the cause. the windshield shattered suddenly and was accompanied by a loud bang. i did not see any evidence of an impact of any kind.

anomaly: Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Ground Incursion Taxiway
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that they missed the turn onto Taxiway K from Runway 15 at DCA due to insufficient taxiway signage and confusing chart depiction.
text: was told to enter runway 15 at the departure end and taxi down on the runway and exit on k into the hold bay of 19. when taxing down while referencing the airport chart/amm (airport moving map) it looked as if it was the second exit to the left. we passed s, and didn't see any signage for k on the eastern side of the runway and accidentally taxied past. ground told us to simply stop and take the next left on juliet.suggestions: there is a distinct gap and apparent separation between s and k on the eastern side exit of runway 15 on the amm chart. this is why we were confused. on the eastern side s and k join together with only signage of s visible . in either case we should have clarified with ground that they wanted us off on the first exit

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Air carrier Flight Attendant reported a cabin door handle had moved and opened during initial climb. Cabin crew closed door and continued.
text: after takeoff, while we were still climbing out of redacted and seated on our jumpseats, i was talking to person a, who was assigned to door 2r. during our conversation, i immediately noticed that the 2l door handle had moved and opened. i alerted person a right away and told her that the door had opened. she quickly reacted and, using significant force, was able to secure the handle back into place.once the door was secured, we immediately contacted the purser and informed her of what had happened. we continued to monitor the door for the remainder of the flight.we did not receive any communication from the flight deck at the time of the incident. it was only after we arrived in redacted that the captain informed the crew that they had received an alert indicating the door had been opened during flight.throughout the remainder of the flight, we felt uneasy and unsafe, as we were unsure whether the door was fully secure after the handle had opened during climb out. we continued to watch the door closely for the rest of the flight.upon arrival in redacted, maintenance personnel met the aircraft and inspected the door. after their evaluation, the aircraft was taken out of service and the next scheduled flight was canceled.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical
synopsis: Piper Seneca pilot reported landing gear extension failure during approach. Pilot followed checklist and landed normally.
text: in redacted getting into the airplane i saw that the main tire looked a little low, but did do anything at redacted. after takeoff, i became more anxious about the situation, so i resolved to get air added at redacted. along the way i checked the owner manual to find out the tire pressure for the main tires and found 55lbs. upon reaching redacted, i asked the lineman if they had a pump and would add air to the tire to make it 55lbs per the owner manual. the same lineman added air, and the tire looked more properly inflated.with passengers on board on final to runway xx @ redacted, with one notch of flaps out, and speed below 129 knots, i lowered the gear handle and heard a high pitched continuous electrical sound, but did not hear the normal mechanical movement of the gear moving down and did not get 3 illuminated gear extension indicator lights (no green lights illuminated but red gear in transition light may have illuminated). i moved the gear handle up, and the electrical sound quit. i again moved the gear handle down and got the same result, and lifted the gear handle up and the electrical noise stopped. at this point, i informed on the unicom frequency, that i had a gear extension failure. the airport fire truck moved out to the runway, and another aircraft in the pattern volunteered to look at the gear and verify their extension. i stayed at pattern altitude and moved to the upwind of runway xx and began to run the emergency gear extension checklist. step 1: slow the aircraft below 85 kts, this took a combination of flaps and power to accomplish comfortably. step 2: flip up retaining clip on gear extension release knob. step 3: lower gear handle. at this point, the gear lowered normally, all 3 gear extension lights illuminated, and i terminated the checklist. i went on crosswind for runway xx and turned downward, and the other aircraft in the pattern confirmed the gear appeared to be down. i continued to a normal landing and parked at the ramp. after some time and taking on 20 more gallons i prepared to fly back to redacted. i pulled both the gear motor circuit breakers (cb) and the gear control cb. i flew back to redacted at 3000 ft below the clouds and dodging rain storms. nearing redacted, i wanted verification that the gear were still down and locked so i pushed in the gear control cb and verified the 3 gear extension indicator lights were illuminated. after this, i made a crosswind landing to runway xy @ redacted and put the aircraft in the hangar.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported an NMAC with a UAS during initial climb. Pilot took evasive action.
text: on day 0, at approximately xa:31, i was operating aircraft x in the vicinity of 1c5, at approximately 2, 000 feet msl. i was in initial climb under the class-c airspace. while on initial climb out of 1c5 (bolingbrook claw airport) at 2, 000 going 2, 500 under the class-c airspace, my passenger stated there was a bird to my right. i observed the bird (object) at my 2 o'clock as i started my turn to remain clear of the class-c airspace. i turned right and noticed what we thought was a bird at same flight level. i immediately got a shiny reflection that became clear we were level with a drone flying same flight level and in my intended path. to avoid the object, i extended my right turn while skirting the class-c airspace to avoid the object. once i was clear of the object, i immediately corrected course 82 degrees to exit the airspace. i was not in contact with chicago approach. weather at the time was visual flight rules clear with scattered ceilings at 6, 000'. passenger also observed the drone. no aircraft damage or injuries occurred.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation - Track / Heading All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Clearance; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a CFTT event occurred during approach. Crew corrected altitude and continued approach.
text: while operating an instrument flight rules flight into redacted airport, the flight was being vectored by air traffic control for a visual approach. i was acting as pilot in command and pilot monitoring, while the second in command (sic) was pilot flying.during the arrival, air traffic control instructed the aircraft to maintain a 5-mile base for sequencing. while descending from approximately 4, 000 feet to 3, 000 feet, the crew interpreted the instruction as requiring a tight base leg in order to comply with spacing and sequencing requirements. as a result, the aircraft was maneuvered toward the base turn while in proximity to the urban area east of the airport.as the aircraft approached the turn near the high-rise area, i became concerned that the maneuver and descent profile were resulting in reduced terrain and obstacle clearance. i disconnected the autopilot, assumed control of the aircraft, and initiated an immediate climb to ensure adequate terrain and obstacle clearance.during the climb, the aircraft generated a gpws 'terrain' alert. since corrective action had already been initiated, i continued the climb, ensured positive terrain separation, and repositioned the aircraft back onto a safe and stabilized flight path for the visual approach. once established on a stable approach and aligned with the runway, control was transferred back to the sic on short final. the landing was completed without further incident.at no time during the event did air traffic control provide a warning regarding proximity to terrain or obstacles, nor was any pilot deviation issued or communication received advising unsafe separation. no damage or injuries occurred.contributing factors included air traffic control vectoring for a visual approach, interpretation of a 5-mile base instruction, compressed maneuvering space, and increased workload during descent and configuration. this event reinforced the importance of maintaining terrain awareness during visual vectoring, ensuring stabilized approach parameters, and immediately discontinuing an approach when terrain clearance or safety margins become uncertain.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: PA-23 Aztec pilot reported vibration from the nose wheel during landing. Aircraft came to a complete stop.
text: i woke up and checked the weather. weather looked good to capture photos at redacted. i then sent my emails to redacted air traffic control for coordination. i called the fbo and requested that the pull the plane out. the plane was already fueled from the previous day.i arrived at the airport and made sure my flight plan was filed, did another preflight, checked fuel and oil. i rechecked my fuel and w&b calculations.when it got close to my departure window with redacted air traffic control, i called flight services and activated my flight plan. i went engines on, spoke to ground and told them i needed to do a runup and they said i could do it when holding short of the runway.i taxied to runway xx and conducted a runup without any issues. spoke to tower and was given takeoff clearance. took off runway xx at redacted. had a slight overspeed on left engine of 2580 and took mental note to notify maintenance (mx) control.spoke with redacted departure and picked up flight following for flight into redacted.about 10 minutes into the flight i noticed the gear up indicator was out. i actuated the gear handle up and felt a slight 'clunk' of the gear fully seating in the up position and the gear up light went back on. this happened 3 more times in flight spaced 45 mins to an hour apart and i took a mental note to mention this to mx control when i speak with them about prop speed.flew up into redacted at 10, 500' to ensure fairly reliable radio reception and descended to 6, 400' to capture the photo over redacted without incident.i spoke with redacted air traffic control, notified them i was done with the redacted photo mission and that i wanted to head to redacted at 9, 500'. the request was approved.i loaded the redacted flight plan for possible capture as i flew back. when i got in contact with redacted center, the controller asked me if i was doing photo work and i told them that i would like to grab photos just north of redacted at approximately 12, 000'. they approved it and instructed me to remain visual flight rules. i asked them if they could close out my visual flight rules flight plan. they said they didn't see one active and would call redacted center and see if they had it listed there.weather was clear above redacted. i rechecked my fuel calculations and began to climb from 9, 500' to 11, 900' to capture the redacted shots. at some point during this, my fuel times went off. i turned on the boost pumps and switched tanks before turning the boost pumps off again.i captured 3 shots of the redacted photo project. experienced issues with the heater at high altitudes. i completed the capture while checking the weather at redacted.once done with the redacted photos, i turned towards redacted and began a slow descent to pattern altitude. i notified redacted center that i was descending into redacted and that i had the weather. redacted center gave me the altimeter for redacted (already had it from weather) and notified me of some traffic there.weather was clear with winds 320 at 9 kts. i loaded a rnav approach and setup my foreflight for references to runway xy at redacted. i switched my com 2 to the ctaf frequency so i could monitor traffic while i descended.i started making ctaf callouts at 20 miles since there was some traffic in front of me. at some point, i told redacted center that i wanted to cancel flight following and switch to ctaf. they cancelled radar services and told me to switch to ctaf.i continues to make radio calls on ctaf as i approached. i had com 2 on the asos for redacted so i could monitor winds. at about 8 miles from the airport, i was having issues visually spotting the field as this was my first time here. i activated the rnav approach for a reference and decided to lower the gear and begin to setup for a landing and slow down.i did my bcgumps check and lowered my landing gear. i felt the extra drag from the gear slowing the plane and added power to maintain airspeed. i entered a 3 mile left base for runway xx and made ctaf radio calls. there was no active traffic in the pattern. i then reviewed the before landing checklist quickly.at approximately a 1 mile final, i went to full flaps since i had the runway easily made with winds 320 at 9 kts landing runway xy.i reduced power to land and felt the plane touch down and then the nose gear touch down. i wanted to maintain a little speed as the ramp was quite a ways down the runway, but shortly after landing, i felt a vibration in the nose gear.the vibration felt like an issue with the shimmy damper (sp). kinda of what would happen if you were taxing too fast. i was a bit confused by this as i wasn't going very fast at all. i gently braked and ensured i was at a very low power setting to try and correct for the vibration. as i slowed, the vibrations got worse and i then turned for the closest taxiway as i expected there was something seriously wrong with the nose gear.next thing i know, the plane comes to a stop on the runway. i shut down the engines at some point and made several calls on ctaf that i was disabled on the runway. at some point, i climbed out of the plane…everything gets very confusing at that point. i was trying to call for assistance on ctaf. not sure who or what to call.after a few minutes a truck with the airport operations or airport emergency services pulled up to render assistance.working with company maintenance to determine if there was any mechanical issues.

anomaly: Conflict NMAC
synopsis: General aviation flight instructor reported a NMAC while in the pattern which required evasive action. Flight continued.
text: conducting takeoff / landing pattern work with a student. we took off of runway 23 for left closed traffic in aircraft x as we had multiple times before in the day. there were other aircraft operating in the pattern and aircraft arriving / departing at the seaplane base throughout the morning. we took off from runway 23, climbed to 700 ft msl (~550 ft agl) then turned crosswind and downwind shortly thereafter. aircraft y overflew the field at 1500 ft (tpa is 1, 000 ft) and began descending and turning into the downwind right at us. i took evasive action to descend and turn right out of the pattern and announced my actions and intention to reenter the pattern on the 45 for runway 23 (which i did). there was another aircraft following them, aircraft z who appropriately overflew the field and the downwind leg and entered the pattern on the 45 behind us. aircraft y had made a radio call previously about their intentions to overfly the field to enter the pattern, but paid no regard to the safety of aircraft already in the pattern or right of way.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported a nose gear collapse on landing and the aircraft slid to a stop. No injuries were reported.
text: coming into land extended gear confirmed three green said audibly three times gear down the passenger who is familiar with my personal flying habits confirmed 3 green two times. aircraft touchdown on the main gear relieving the pressure on the elevator that nose gradually came down and before i could react, the nose struck the runway both propellers struck the ground. we then slid for 500 to 700'. no fire occurred. confirmed engines were off turned off masters magneto, and turned fuel, selectors to off and exited the aircraft. nobody was hurt i then called to get help removing the aircraft off the active runway. i walked my passenger to the fbo walked back out to the aircraft and stayed with the aircraft until emergency services came.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Conflict NMAC; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported an NMAC with a UAS during cruise flight.
text: i was on a solo cross country training flight, returning from redacted to pae. i stopped at olm for fuel and was on my way back to pae when i encountered a drone flying in the opposite direction at extremely high speed. it appeared the aircraft was flying at least as fast as i was, approx. 95kts indicated. aircraft size was very small, probably unmanned. could not detect wings on aircraft, leading me to think it was a drone. aircraft appeared red in color. location is approximate. sighting may have occurred anywhere from pwt to winslow on a straight-line course between olm and kingston township. i was on 002 compass heading. this sighting was not expected at all, given there were no notams or tfrs for drone activity at 3000msl anywhere in the area. potential collision risk.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Conflict NMAC; Inflight Event / Encounter Object
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported multiple NMACs with other UAS and crewed aircraft at an event. The reporter also reported losing control of their own UAS; resulting in a collision with an object. The damaged UAS was recovered after the event.
text: faa part 107 certificated pilot since 2017. we have worked in every class of us faa airspace across 28 states. we operate and adhere to strict safety cases and internal policies with our authorizations. on this day detailed below, we observed what we believe to be several uas violations, unsafe operations and both uas and crewed aircraft in close proximity to location x as well as uas nearby not yielding to crewed craft. we are certain we saw uas flying over 400'+ agl, bvlos and failure to yield to approaching crewed aircraft. despite the presence of large crowds, we witnessed one personal aircraft, flying very low at location x, which we estimated to be 50-75' above structure at one point in question and climbing and diving over large crowds to more closely view the event described below.on the morning in question: i traveled from our corporate offices to location x in order to attend, photograph and video the event. we never expected the crowds that rapidly gathered. there were probably over 2500-3500 people, primarily confined in two large locations.the planning for this trip began as a personal / company photography mission but after speaking with our company contacts, we were contacted by a past client, who mentioned that companies would be interested in seeing and possibly purchasing a copy of any footage obtained. we took several drones to photograph with and we were going to decide upon arrival which to use given the observed factors on-site but we decided on the dji mavic 2 pro utilizing the dji smart controller rm500. the drone is faa registered and remote id (rid) compliant. this decision was made for a couple specific reasons, the most prominent being that the airspace was becoming notably congested with aircraft and drones approximately 15 minutes before the event start. in the pre-planning for our flights, we witnessed two aircraft that would arrive, circle and depart, estimated to be well over 1500-2500 feet agl (may have been higher) and two drones scouting the location as we did within an hour prior to the event. we began launching from east of location x due to better light but with other drones present, we decided we were too far from location x (noting some uas must likely be flying bvlos). we relocated to the west of location x where we would be within 100-200 feet of our drone and looking up at blue-sky at all times. at that time, we did seek out and met two other uas pilots before the event and discussed vlos and avoidance coordination. unfortunately, despite our coordination efforts with others, in the 30 minutes prior to the event, with our one (1) and three (3) other nearby drones up, we noted that two aircraft in particular were circling (on about each occasional third or fourth pass) too low for us to even risk to continue flying uas at this location. despite the large amount of people still arriving and large crowds, planes were flying very low (which we videoed as it seemed to be at times just 100-200 feet above the structure at location x) at one point a private aircraft seemed to be about 50' above the structure. we decided at that time not to fly. soon, the two low flying aircraft began to fly much higher and well above the structure (it seemed to us that they likely spotted the drones hovering near the top of and well-over (probably 75-125' over the surface) so the low-flying, circling manned aircraft began to climb. we also noted that drones that were launching both from the east side and west of the structure and were flying over it. this was notable to us immediately because we have noted it elsewhere as inexperience - while they were likely within 400' of their takeoff point (controller reading) they were well above the structure, which would mathematically put them well over 400' or even 500' agl despite the readings they would have had observed within 400' vertical of controller altitude. (i've always felt this is something the faa needs to teach better as many rely on the 400' alt. controller reading). with the planes now flying much higher, knowing we would be well within giving-way to them, and would stay below structure height, we took flight after discussion of our plans with two other uas pilots nearby. i had one individual helping me to maintain safe takeoff and visualize safe launch as there were people nearby including children (highly curious), which we wanted to be sure did not approach upon launch and i had a nearby visual observer as there was sun glare upon moving to the structure's westerly location. in anticipation of the event start, at approximately xa:57, i launched with a new battery (95%) and positioned to begin capturing photos and video of the event start. as i hovered in position around xb:03 the event started and we began recording and photography. immediately upon event start, i noticed not the original 2-3 aircraft but now as many as two additional (4-5 total) private aircraft suddenly circling with one flying exceedingly low again and so i called out my altitude to my vo (about 25-45 feet the structure) and immediately said i would descend to structure level or below top of the structure to give-way. i also noted not two other uas (we coordinated with) but now (at times) as many as 8-10 (estimated) drones. one zipped past traveling at a high rate from west to east. i estimate this was 15-20 feet horizontally from me and within 5-10 feet vertically, flying approximately 40 mph (possibly closer as we observed on my video afterwards). we began to discuss landing and scrapping our plans as several drones were flying sporadically, circling and changing altitude abruptly. my vo noted that several of us were in coordination but a few of these must be flying strictly through their controller screens from afar, out of vlos because they were very close to us vs. our visual (blue-sky) vo / vlos practice / technique, looking up. 13 min. 41 sec. into my flight we became more concerned. at event start, uas (data: 181' above launch, approx. 225' agl, approx. 200' from controller, est 150' horiz feet from the structure) with 35% battery remaining, two (2) drones approached us and came within several feet to my hover (unacceptable and unsafe proximity in my judgement of their speed and proximity) given the way they approached. one was behind and moving left to be between my drone and i, one near and about 50' above with another approaching. with trees below, i was worried that i had no route to home point remaining with a drone between me and mine, and i typically land with 20% battery remaining to be safe. at that time, i pushed in towards the structure, thinking if i got trapped with low battery, i could land safely on the unoccupied structure and retrieve the drone after it was clear or drop below the drones, to above tree level and turn for home point. however, knowing there were crewed aircraft potentially above (albeit well clear) other uas hovering behind, uas left and one above, i pushed in towards the structure (data: 186' above launch, approx. 230' agl, at 300' from controller, approx. 50' distance from the structure) with 30% battery remaining, i stopped to hover to assess the rth path i could take (or land). at that time, with no stick input (and confirmed none made in subsequent review of data and control inputs) i looked at my screen to confirm location and i was level with the top of the structure (or slightly above). i said to my vo, 'we have to land up there or am i clear of the others to return?' and he said i don't see you. i looked up and couldn't ascertain my drone from several others that had moved in around mine, when i looked down at the screen to regain orientation, the drone was still moving towards the structure despite no stick inputs. at this time, the screen froze. in that moment, the interpretation by myself and my vo of the situation was that despite stopping to hover at about 50-70' from the structure, i had either been struck by one of the other dronesand dropped to trees below, or without my input, the drone had continued forward and was on the structure, and/or had collided with the structure, or more unfortunately, people. i was concerned for their safety and had a concern for battery fire (having worked on wildfire drone teams, this is trained to be a primary concern upon crash) so i initiated our procedural lost-link / disconnection procedure (screen grab photo, note direction of travel, check controller link, look for possible ground fire etc) but could not retrieve uas contact or location. the last location was on the structure surface, which made me think a drone had collided with us, the drone had continued forward and collided or lost link and initiated emergency landing. it was set for rth but it never came back, which reinforced our fear of a crash. i immediately took phone photos of surroundings and the structure. i reached out first to nearby pilots (2), all of which still had full control and vlos with their uas. there was no way to contact other drones because they were flying in from afar, pilots unknown. i reached out over the next 10 minutes to law enforcement. each thanked me and confirmed they had no calls from workers or persons on-site. law enforcement then gave me permission to access the structure but only after traffic from the access road, and hundreds of cars and thousands of people cleared. they said i could be trespassing or stopped by officials but if called they noted to their agencies that i was going up on a nearby road to walk the structure and if called, they would know it was me. approximately an hour later, i found the drone on the structure. it had most likely collided with the concrete wall of the structure and was damaged. someone, i'm assuming the workers, had picked the damaged drone up and placed it upright atop one of the concrete walls (clearly positioned so that anyone coming up to search could see and find it) and it was not at a place where it could have landed given the damage encountered. the drone had no oil, paint, fabric or blood on it, so i don't believe there were injuries. the props did receive spinning damage, so i believe it went in under power, with forward flight damage (front). it did have concrete fragments and concrete dust on it, so i believe it contacted the structure. i tried to contact the company to be sure nobody was contacted, struck or injured but at this time, my calls have not been returned. i did report back to law enforcement to thank everyone for their help and support and let them know i confirmed no battery fire, retrieved the uas and they noted my calls. i have not been able to confirm that there were or were not any personal injuries.we did retrieve the drone fairly intact but damaged, with all video, photos and flight data onboard and retrieved. the drone was not recording at the time of contact. the last photo was taken at the point where i paused (released sticks to neutral / last stick inputs at approximately 50-70' off structure). there were no other stick inputs after that but we estimate over the next several seconds that based upon trajectories, gps data and onboard telemetry that the uas flew on for 0'+/- vertical and 50-60' horizontal before contact / collision and loss of data and radio contact. the last speed reading was at 15.8 mph horizontal forward with no stick manipulation. proximity and anti-collision avoidance sensors were not turned on during flight. we can't ascertain if there was any contact to or from other uas prior to contact with the structure, but all sensors were nominal with exception of the movement / forward anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported exceeding LAANC authorized altitudes during two flights.
text: i was the remote pilot in command of a 14 cfr part 107 small uas operation conducted under a laanc authorization with a maximum altitude of 100 feet agl. the operation was located approximately 3 miles northeast of redacted at approximately xa:00 on day 0. the purpose of the flight was to capture video of a private construction project nearing completion.my prior part 107 experience in controlled airspace has primarily involved dji phantom and mavic aircraft used for construction mapping and site progress photography, often on automated missions. this operation used a homebuilt first-person-view (fpv) small uas. i was operating with a visual observer who is also an experienced faa part 107 remote pilot.before the first event, my visual observer reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity of the operation. i initiated a high-rate climb. shortly after the climb began, the gps-derived altitude displayed in my fpv goggles indicated approximately 172 feet agl, or approximately 72 feet above the 100-foot laanc authorization. i immediately initiated recovery by reducing throttle, rolling the aircraft inverted, and commanding a descent back toward the operating area.during the recovery descent, the aircraft's fpv perspective indicated that it was descending, but the displayed gps altitude continued to increase and briefly indicated approximately 272 feet agl before becoming inconsistent and then decreasing. because the altitude indication was gps-derived and appeared to lag or behave unreliably during the high-rate climb and recovery, i cannot determine the aircraft's actual maximum altitude with certainty. however, i believe the aircraft exceeded the 100-foot laanc authorization, and i immediately continued the descent and landed. the altitude exceedance appeared to last approximately five seconds. after the aircraft returned to low altitude, my visual observer again reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity.i did not intend to deviate from the laanc authorization, and i took immediate corrective action as soon as i recognized the altitude exceedance. contributing factors included unreliable or delayed gps altitude indication during a high-rate climb, limited visual altitude references in the open area, and my underestimation of the climb performance of the fpv aircraft relative to the 100-foot authorized ceiling.corrective actions have already been taken. i configured audible altitude warnings and altitude callouts on my radio transmitter. before future operations i will review and set those warnings with a significant buffer below the authorized ceiling. for 100-foot laanc authorizations, i will use a substantially reduced personal maximum altitude rather than operating up to the laanc ceiling. i will also avoid high-rate vertical climbs in low-ceiling laanc airspace.a second altitude exceedance occurred later in the same operation, several battery packs later. i activated the gps return to home / gps rescue function in the same open operating area to observe its routing behavior. during the automated return, i realized the aircraft was climbing toward and then above the 100-foot laanc ceiling. i attempted to override the automation with stick inputs, which changed the aircraft attitude but did not stop the climb. i then deactivated the return function by switching back to full manual control. i observed a maximum displayed gps altitude of approximately 128 feet agl, or approximately 28 feet above the authorized altitude. i immediately descended and landed. this altitude exceedance also appeared to last approximately five seconds. my visual observer reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity.during debrief, i realized this second event likely occurred because my gps return to home / gps rescue function was configured to return at the maximum altitude recorded during the flight session. i had configured it this way to avoid an incorrectly preset return altitude. however, i misunderstood how the betaflight flight controller defined a flight session. i had kept the flight controller and gps powered during main battery changes using a usb battery pack so that gps lock would be retained. i now believe the flight controller treated the later battery pack as part of the same flight session, meaning the return altitude was based on the maximum altitude recorded earlier in the operation rather than only the current battery pack or arming cycle.although i chose the open field because it reduced collision risk with ground obstacles, i did not adequately account for the risk of testing an automated flight aid under a low laanc ceiling in controlled airspace. i will not test gps rescue, return to home, failsafe behavior, or other autonomous flight functions within laanc-controlled airspace or other altitude-sensitive airspace unless the full test profile remains safely below all applicable altitude limits. future testing of these functions will be conducted in suitable airspace with a larger altitude margin.these events highlighted gaps in my understanding of my aircraft's altitude indication, climb performance, flight controller session behavior, and automated rescue configuration. the most important lesson for me is that open terrain on the ground does not mean the airspace risk is low. i will use these lessons to improve my preflight planning, altitude margins, automation testing procedures, and overall aeronautical decision-making to better protect the airspace and the people living and working beneath it.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Speed All Types; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B767 flight crew reported a hydraulic demand pump EICAS message during initial climb after gear retraction. Flight returned to the departure airport and landed.
text: during gearing retraction we got a center demand pump eicas and a gear disagree. the gear disagree went away and while the pf/pm focused on flying i started getting the checklist ready. another aircraft went around on xx r which i guess caused a traffic conflict cause as we reached 4000ft on the climb air traffic control told us to descend to 3000feet and gave us several turns. i mention this cause it greatly increased our workload and i do think we went over 250kts at some point in the descent. however once we clearer traffic and climbed to 10, 000 feet i got into the checklist with the captain who had transferred controls to the first officer. we ran it and could not get the demand pump back. we requested priority handling, contacted dispatch/maintenance control and decided to return to redacted due to loss of our hydraulic motor generator (hmg). we dumped fuel via the checklist and coordination with atc/dispatch. we went over the overweight landing checklist (we ended up not landing overweight). after we checked landing distance we determined at our weight (316.0 at touchdown) and a 15 it additive due to gusty winds we would use auto brakes max on xx r so we looked over the hot brakes checklist and advised air traffic control we would land, exit the runway on taxiway 1 and hold position while airport rescue and firefighting (arff) and/us monitored the brakes. briefed fa's, pa'd the passengers and then started making our way back to redacted. landed, executed our plan. after 15 mins with max brake temperature monitoring system (btms) of 5 we taxied to the gate.

text: this is the second time i've had a significant wake turbulence encounter behind an a321. the first one was in phx, a few months ago. i thought maybe it was a fluke, but had another one behind an a321 that took off ahead of us. we were cleared for takeoff as the a321 was lifting off the end of the runway. both encounters remind me of being behind a 757, before wake separation distances were increased.

text: at fl350, heard a snapping sound and observed smoke. ran the smoke emergency checklist card and appropriate qrh. ultimately determined it was originating from captain's main windshield. upon completion of the checklist, smoke was removed and no additional smoke observed. requested priority handling into redacted and flight landed uneventfully.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Bird / Animal
synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported a shattered side windshield during cruise at FL350. Crew descended and continued to destination.
text: upon reaching fl350 (cruise altitude), a loud bang at the captain side windshield (felt and sounded like something hit us). the entire windshield appeared shattered. due to altitude, and unsure of extent of damage or potential for further damage, i requested priority handling, advised redacted center that we were going to descend immediately, to mitigate a threat of pressurization loss. i advised fa's to be seated, and be ready with oxygen, and that windshield had shattered, and i'd give more info soon. our descent maintained speed at which the event took place. we completed qrh in descent while advising atc and dispatch. diversion was considered while monitoring pressurization, ultimately decided to proceed to destination after monitoring cabin pressure and discussion with company. opted for direct course to redacted at fl150, 250 kts as a cautionary measure. briefed with fa's, that we would remain priority status to redacted, no expectation of brace or abnormal procedure on ground, and to remain alert of any cabin pressurization indications. i advised pax (passengers) that a layer of our windshield had shattered, but the layers protecting cabin pressure appeared intact, not to worry and that we would proceed to redacted, but to remain seated and follow fa instructions. rest of flight uneventful. post inspection didn't distinctly support an impact from outside, but inconclusive.cause: unknown. potential bird strike, other. potential defect of windshield or product fatigue

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Smoke / Fire / Fumes / Odor; Flight Deck / Cabin / Aircraft Event Illness / Injury; Ground Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence
synopsis: Embraer 145 flight crew reported a burning electrical odor upon reaching cruise. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed.
text: we operated aircraft x redacted-redacted on day 0. we departed late due to the weather in redacted and a minor maintenance issue on the ground. upon reaching our cruising altitude of 17, 000 ft both the ca and i simultaneously smelled a strong odor of something electrical that was burning (noxious and acrid). it was only a second or two before it became very strong and we immediately donned our oxygen masks, established crew communications, and followed the instructions in the qrc. we re-established that i would remain the pf and the ca would handle the radios, qrh, etc. the ca then advised air traffic control and reported a burning odor in the flight deck and requested a diversion to redacted. i agreed with that decision given the weather we had just left in redacted and the weather we were dealing with at the time, and i remembered that during our pre-departure briefing we had both pointed out that the weather near zzz1acuse (to the east) was better than in redacted or to the south.the ca worked on communicating to air traffic control and dispatch (via air traffic control), as well as to the fa and the passengers while i continued flying the aircraft. air traffic control began giving us descents and headings to bring us onto the approach to runway xx. it was difficult to establish meaningful communication with the fa because the oxygen masks are so loud, as well as the fact that the noise from heavy rain on the windshield was quite loud as well. we had trouble hearing him and he had trouble hearing us, but we were able to at least communicate that we were diverting to redacted and that there was no smoke in the passenger cabin.the ca continued working through the qrh during the descent toward the airport in heavy rain, imc, and moderate turbulence. we jointly decided not to depressurize the cabin given the fact that there was no reported smoke or fumes there.we accomplished our remaining checklists and were eventually vectored onto the approach for runway xx, whereupon we broke out of the weather, picked up the runway lights, and landed in heavy rain without incident. emergency vehicles met us on the taxiway and followed us to the gate, where firefighters entered the aircraft to inspect for smoke and we were able to deplane. ems wanted the ca and i to deplane first for treatment, but both the ca and i were uncomfortable with leaving the aircraft before the passengers so we waited until the plane was empty to leave the flight deck. ems then treated me and the ca and said we both had high blood pressure and heart rates, which is to be expected after a stressful event like this. we were both nauseated and somewhat light-headed as well, but again that was to be expected given the odor and the stress of the situation. several passengers were seen by ems as well for anxiety.in the end, i believe the ca and i handled the situation correctly and professionally, that we followed our training, and i am thankful for the safe outcome for everyone involved.root cause narrative: acrid, burning odor which smelled like something electrical was burning.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported confusing noise abatement procedure charting at BGI/TBPB.
text: during preflight prep, atis was advertising noise abatement procedures for departures. both the first officer and i checked the jepps 10-9, as well as the airport company pages departures notes for noise abatement procedures and found none. we both failed to reference the jepps 10-4 page.our air traffic control clearance was make a left turn to join aircraft y, climb to level 300, and squawk redacted".when we were cleared for takeoff, there was no mention of the noise abatement procedure. in hindsight, i feel like previous departures the controller has issued the clearance of "fly runway heading until 2, 500 ft and then left turn on course, you are cleared for takeoff". this tower controller simply gave us "cleared for takeoff" with no further instructions.we began our left turn on course after passing 400' agl. during the turn, the tower controller reminded us in the future to fly the published noise abatement procedure. this was ultimately our mistake, but i feel misled by the way the airport company pages and the jepps are constructed for bgi (tbpb). at other airports with noise abatement procedures, (aruba for example) the jepps 10-9 or 10-9a has the noise abatement procedure published on the airport diagram. it is absent from the bgi 10-9. in the airport company pages, every other airport i can find has a bold noise abatement section if procedures apply. in the bgi airport company pages there is no such designation. there is a line in red that reminds pilots to comply with departure restrictions, however there is nothing indicative of a noise abatement procedure."
