synopsis: Embraer 170 First Officer reported an engine temperature exceedance during takeoff and intermittently on the previous flight leg as well. The Captain rejected the takeoff and returned to the gate and then refused the aircraft.
text: hot summer day leaving redacted on aircraft x. we were heavy with fuel because of needing a precautionary alternate. there were long lines of thunderstorms through the northeast en route and at the destination. we had to run numbers for passengers and bags due to weight restrictions. in order to takeoff we needed to burn fuel off to make takeoff weight restrictions. we were also calculating out through landing weight restrictions. for the first leg i was pilot monitoring and the captain was pilot flying. during the takeoff roll at approximately 80 knots the engine indicating system for interstage turbine temperature (itt) engine one went red. i let about 3 seconds pass debating on calling for the reject before v1. i observed the itt go back to normal temperatures and decided not to call reject before reaching v1. on climb out after the takeoff checklist and getting the auto pilot on i informed the captain of what i had observed. on review of sops i realize i should have verbalized the indication immediately but hesitated due to there being no annunciation. throughout the flight we continued to monitor the itt temperature gauges. we noticed engine 1 itt consistently 40 degrees higher than engine 2. when the pilot selected climb one we observed itt 1 nearing overheat so we backed off the throttle to climb 2. nearing the top of climb we similarly observed itt 1 nearing limitations reaching fl280. similarly after leveling off and beginning to accelerate to 290 temperatures began spiking and nearing limitations. we slowed to cruising at 270 to avoid an exceedance. after landing in redacted the landing exceedance warning pops up and we ran the qrh. after getting to the gate in redacted we write up the excedence and maintenance (mx) come out to perform an inspection. after the inspection maintenance said the operations check was good. leaving redacted the captain and i discussed threats leaving and the plan with another potential itt 1 excedence. we speculated hot temperatures in redacted and near max weight as being causes and since we were lighter and if temperatures were lower it would be less likely. we tried to coordinate for a takeoff on xx for runway length in case of a rejected takeoff but air traffic control had difficulties coordinating it with staffing. we accepted xyl for takeoff. we also decided to do the to with no flex to increase runway remaining if needed. i was pilot flying from redacted on this flight. during the takeoff roll we observed itt 1 turn red exceeding temperature limits again at around 80 knots. the captain called the reject and took controls. we notified air traffic control and returned to the gate. maintenance came out to the aircraft and perform and another inspection. stated the exceedence were within limits and ops checked it clearing it for flight. we refused the flight since no other mx was done and they would not perform a run up of the engine.

synopsis: Beechjet 400A flight crew reported a landing gear indication malfunction on the initial approach. The pilots performed a go-around; utilized the alternate gear extension; then returned to land normally.
text: i was the pilot flying (pf), and pilot in command, and person a was the pilot monitoring (pm). we departed for redacted.while being vectored for the rnav approach into redacted, i called for the landing gear to be extended. person a selected the landing gear handle down and observed a green indication for the left main landing gear only. the nose gear and right main landing gear did not show green indications. the landing gear handle light was not illuminated red. person a made the callout that only the left main landing gear appeared to be down and locked.i initiated the missed approach and person a advised redacted approach of the landing gear indication issue and requested vectors to allow time for troubleshooting. person a retrieved the abnormal landing gear checklist and began working through the procedure.the checklist directed us to complete the emergency landing gear extension procedure. the crew discussed the available options and elected to divert to redacted due to maintenance availability at that location and better weather. we decided to leave the landing gear configuration unchanged because we could not confirm the position of the nose gear and right main gear, and we did not want to further change the aircraft configuration prior to completing the emergency gear extension procedure.during the descent into redacted, person a advised redacted approach that we would be completing the emergency gear extension checklist and requested a level-off and airspeed reduction to approximately 150 knots. air traffic control confirmed we were experiencing a landing gear issue and asked if we wanted to request priority handling. the crew agreed that priority handling was appropriate.the emergency landing gear extension checklist was completed, however, the nose gear and right main gear still did not provide green cockpit indications. we coordinated with redacted approach and redacted tower for a low approach so the tower could visually verify the landing gear position. the tower reported that the landing gear appeared to be down.person a pressed on the landing gear indication button multiple times and he was finally able to get a green light for the nose gear. this led me to believe it was more of just a light indication issue rather than an actual gear issue. after completing a circuit in the pattern, we elected to land. the landing was completed without issue. we exited the runway and were escorted back to parking by airport fire rescue.cause: landing gear indication for nose gear and right main were not indicating down.suggestions: have a way to swap or replace landing gear indicator lights in flight on the beechjet.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Ground Event / Encounter Loss Of Aircraft Control
synopsis: Cessna 172 pilot reported upon initiating turn onto taxiway after landing; both main tires went flat; and the aircraft was stuck in position.
text: skies clear, 10 statute miles of visibility. visual approach at redacted with another pilot in the right seat. i was flying the c-172 in the left downwind when air traffic control requests i make a short approach for runway xx. i accepted and landed the plane prior to the thousand foot markers. to make taxiway 1, i had to use the brakes to slow down. upon initiating the turn onto the taxiway, both main tires went flat. after both tires went flat, the aircraft became unmovable and stuck on runway xx. i immediately told redacted tower that i was unable to exit the runway and airport operations closed for approximately 30 minutes from a period of about xa:10-xa:40pm. the aircraft was moved onto the ramp and airport operations resumed at approximately xa:40. in hindsight, i believe that i made the mistake of initiating the turn onto taxiway 1 too soon. the aircraft was likely moving too fast and my judgement to utilize the breaks instead of rolling past the taxiway contributed to the event. i should have kept rolling and gotten off at the end of the runway on taxiway 2. ultimately, the aircraft never left the paved surface of the runway and taxiways. the only damage was to the tires and tubes of both main wheels, which were replaced approximately 2 hours later. there were no injuries.

synopsis: A Center Controller reported a departing Citation deviated from their clearance and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.
text: aircraft x a citation c550 departed redacted should have been on the redacted sid up to 160 they check on quickly and the beacon/target already looked possibly off but i figured that it was due to the little turn on the sid to intercept the heading to redacted, and just getting them on radar as eram attempts to provide an accurate vector line. (the occasional departure exhibits this but they have all been safely on the sid previously) i radar contact them and clear them to climb like normal. as the next radar hit is displayed i question the pilot about their route. they report flight management system issues immediately and request a vector. a low altitude alert is issued and refuse vectors for terrain, instructing an expediting climb and clearance leaving a safe altitude.better radar coverage would assist in identifying this unsafe situation more easily/quickly but i believe there is nothing more that could be done from air traffic control as this is a pilot/aircraft equipment issue.

synopsis: B767 First Officer reported an inflight upset occurred when they encountered wake turbulence at FL320 in trail of an A330. Control was regained and the flight continued to its destination.
text: at cruise altitude of 320. an a330 was climbing ahead of us and we entered wake. we turned on seat belt sign as we felt turbulence. this wake turbulence event caused an upset. aircraft rolled 30-40 degrees bank and nose down pitch of about 5 degrees. we initiated an upset recovery. called upset, disconnected autopilot and auto thrust. push, roll, thrust, stabilize calls were made as the occurrence was very quick and righted quickly. stabilized aircraft. notified air traffic control. air traffic control told us the aircraft was an a330. checked in with the flight attendants, no injuries had occurred. maintained seat belt sign for an extended time.

anomaly: Deviation - Altitude Overshoot; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter CFTT / CFIT
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a CFTT event occurred during the River Visual approach to DCA. Crew corrected altitude and continued approach.
text: on the frdmm 6 planning river visual backed up by the rnav (rnp) z rwy 19. between frdmm and stand we were given descend to 5000 and 210 or greater on the speed. i select lvl change on the mode control panel (mcp), set 210 in the speed window, call for flaps 2, and deploy speed breaks. air traffic control gives us descend to 3000. as we're slowing and descending air traffic control gives us direct daric. vertical glide path shows us 700 feet high. i direct the pm to set 2000 for suney. lnav is already engaged, but i failed to select vnav on the mcp. crossing daric i direct the pm to set touchdown zone. i configure aircraft with the 4 and 2 mile rings around suney to be fully configured. between greyz and fonzi i can see the papis for runway 15 indicating 2 red and 2 white. i've used those to monitor and cross check my path on the river visual. it isn't until approaching jubol do i realize we're low. i try to take a peak at legs page to see what altitude we should be at, but unable to see that information. i get a gpws aural obstacle". i disconnect the autopilot and pitch the nose up and add power. pm calls out to watch my airspeed. i add more power and we climb higher and accelerate. i didn't hear the radio call from tower stating "altitude alert" because i channelized getting back on airspeed and path. when i began picking up the papi for rwy 19 i could see 3 red 1 white. i corrected to 2 red 1 white."

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Inflight Event / Encounter Fuel Issue
synopsis: B767 Captain reported a HYD Demand Pump EICAS message after landing gear retraction during the initial climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and landed.
text: operating flight #abcd redacted-redacted, everything was good on preflight and blocked out on time. taxied to runway xxl and without much delay took the runway for takeoff clearance around xa:30pm. normal takeoff and on positive rate called for gear up. eicas caution c hyd demand pump came up along with press light on overhead panel. a few seconds later gear disagree eicas came on momentarily but cleared as we continued the climb. air traffic control gave us a few turn instructions for traffic conflict and then cleared up to 10, 000 and to switch to redacted departure. once with departure control, priority was requested and a level off at 10, 000ft with radar vectors was requested. flight control was transferred to the first officer while i ran the qrh along with the relief pilot. once the qrh was done, we contacted dispatch and maintenance control to confirm correct qrh was referenced. the decision was made to return to redacted. air traffic control was advised that we would dump fuel to get down below overweight landing weight and better performance for stopping on runway. dumping started at xa:52 and ended at xa:57 at 10, 0000ft. dispatch was notified of location. flight attendants were briefed and the passengers were notified of our planned return to redacted. arff (airport rescue and firefighting) was requested on arrival and notified of possible hot brakes. normal instrument landing system approach and landing on xxr with a rollout at the end. cleared the runway and stopped for hot brakes on the right gear showing 5 in the caution range and waited for the 15 minutes to see if they would continue rising. temperature decrease was noted and a taxi to the gate was commenced. upon arrival at the gate, maintenance was briefed. we then went to the chief pilot for a debriefing with the crew.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Critical; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Weight And Balance
synopsis: B737 pilots reported an engine failure during cruise at FL3. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed overweight.
text: engine failure at cruisewhile cruising at fl300 there was a sudden bang and the number two engine began to spool down. there were no warnings indication prior to this. i initially began to run the memory items for engine fire severe damage checklist but soon realized that the engine had basically shut down. there were no fire or eng (engine) vibration after the engine shut down. i moved over to the engine failure shutdown checklist and started running that after advising air traffic control and requesting lower from air traffic control. the engine out altitude was 24, 000 feet but we were given clearance to 14, 000 feet. the first officer was flying while i ran the checklist. redacted airport was approximately 40 miles due east of us while redacted was about 240 miles in front of us. i decided to proceed to redacted. i briefed the flight attendants and spoke to the passengers. while completing the checklist it was extremely busy while we were setting up for the approach but manageable. weather was clear and calm and the plane flew fine on one engine. we landed normally but with flaps 15. i calculated we were about 3100 pounds over max gross landing weight. the touchdown and rollout were all normal. we came to a gradual stop on the runway and waited for the fire trucks. the fire trucks came onto the runway and did an inspection. they told us they could see the number two engine was not running and that there was no sign of fire and all was clear. we then continued to the gate single engine without incident. air traffic control and redacted airport were all very supportive and helpful throughout the whole incident.

synopsis: Commercial aviation passenger reported seeing an unknown object pass closeby the aircraft during approach.
text: i was on a commercial flight on final approach into ewr (day 0, approx. xa:00) and saw a shiny, black object outside the right side of my aircraft. the object was irregular in shape (it was oblong and roundish almost like if bubbles were stuck together) and fairly large from my perspective on the airplane. i'd say roughly the size of a 2-person couch but cannot be certain as i only saw it very briefly before my airplane passed by. i don't know what altitude we were at at the time of my sighting, however, i remember we were passing the city of newark and i could very clearly see the ground and the buildings in city center. there were no obvious arms or propellers like a typical quad drone would have, and i have never seen an object of similar description before so it's hard to actually describe. in addition, it was fairly close (i'd estimate within a few hundred feet from my aircraft) when we passed it. i cannot be certain if it was hovering or if it was moving slowly in any direction, but it was not something that i've seen before and i definitely do not think it should've been anywhere remotely close to commercial aircraft.

synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization due to an incorrect departure time request.
text: i was serving as the remote pilot in command (rpic) for a part 107 security-related uas operation conducted on day 0, at location x. prior to the operation, i obtained a laanc authorization for the operating area. the operation was conducted approximately xa:50-xe:01 at altitudes not exceeding 300 feet agl. after the flight was completed, i reviewed the authorization details and discovered that the laanc authorization had been approved for xm:15-xq:15 rather than the morning operating period. the incorrect time period resulted from an error during the authorization request process and was not identified during the preflight review. during the operation, the flight remained within the authorized geographic area and below the approved altitude. weather and visibility conditions were suitable for flight. no conflicts with manned aircraft, air traffic control communications, injuries, property damage, equipment malfunctions, or other safety events occurred. the discrepancy was discovered during a post-flight review on the same day. upon identifying the error, i evaluated the circumstances of the operation and determined that the flight had occurred outside the authorized laanc time window. corrective action includes implementing an additional verification step during preflight planning to confirm the authorization date, start time, end time, operating area, and altitude prior to launch to ensure authorization parameters match the planned operation before flight.

synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported they were made aware by a law enforcement officer the UAS was flown out of VLOS.
text: i recently acquired a uas and was operating a dji mini 5 pro to practice my flight maneuvers at location x. prior to takeoff, i responsibly obtained a laanc authorization for the airspace and strictly maintained my altitude within the authorized 200-foot limit. during the flight, a local law enforcement officer approached me. the responding officer asked if my drone was registered, and i confirmed that it was. the officer then handed me a phone to speak directly with a supervisor.the supervisor reviewed the live telemetry data/flight logs and noted that while my flight path, registration, and altitude limits were entirely compliant, there was a specific segment of the flight where the aircraft traveled too far laterally, causing a temporary loss of direct visual line of sight (vlos). i answered all questions honestly and cooperatively, immediately terminated the flight, safely packed up my equipment, and left the area.human factors / corrective action:the primary root cause was a temporary lapse in situational awareness regarding lateral distance. because i am a new drone operator, i relied too heavily on the controller's video feed rather than maintaining strict, continuous visual line of sight with the physical aircraft.to prevent this from ever happening again, i have implemented a personal operational safety minimum that restricts my flight distance to a strict, conservative radius where the aircraft remains clearly visible to my bare eyes at all times. furthermore, i am actively reviewing part 107 visual line of sight regulations and will utilize a dedicated visual observer (vo) when flying in dense or visually complex environments to ensure absolute regulatory compliance.

synopsis: HTS TRACON Controller reported the ATC facility had multiple full radar and communication outages which led to unsafe operations and inadequate separation.
text: at around xa:30, we had a full t1 communications outage while aircraft x was enroute transitioning over our airspace. we noticed our long range radars went into the red in our radar status information area (sia). we immediately tried our external shout lines, which we found to be unresponsive. the radar controller then noticed that we lost radar contract with our other enroute transitioning aircraft, because they were too far from our local radar to pick up without fusion. the controller correctly said radar contact lost. we might have lost radar on aircraft x as well, post-situation we aren't positive. i attempted to landline call upstairs to the tower where our supervisor was, but the phone line was dead. i physically sprinted to inform them. during this moment both i and the radar controller failed to see that aircraft x was extremely near the boundary with zid. we attempted the interim voice switch replacement (ivsr) dial line with zid but it wasn't working. finally the t1 communications seemed to come back, as i pick up the landline phone and i immediately called zid supervisor who got the zid controller to take the handoff. the handoff likely occurred with less than appropriate separation from the boundary. there would be another t1 communications outage less than an hour later which caused another unsafe event to occur which will be in a different report.our equipment is not consistently reliable for the safe transition of aircraft in our airspace. we have outages constantly including these major t1 communications outages, and we seem to allow it simply because we often have low traffic, such as this instance with only two aircraft. but it only takes an unfortunate circumstance to realize that keeping our bar for safety so low is an extreme negligence to our flying public.at around xb:10 we had a full t1 radar and communication outage. we lost: our external dial lines and shout lines, flight data input/output (fdio) uplink, we lost our fusion long range radars, our landline phone line was dead (eventually we could landline dial intrafacility). at the time thankfully we had no aircraft. due to the communication outage i had to physically tell the supervisor.eventually our intrafacility landline phone worked, so i communicated with our now two supervisors in the tower, who told me we were likely going air traffic control limited or zero. due to weather we had no aircraft in our airspace, much of the airspace was instrument flight rules. at xb:20 called the supervisors again because we had two satellite instrument flight rules departure proposals both of which would immediately be entering zid airspace and thus would require coordination which we could not do, and these satellite airports were at the edges of our northern airspace where we likely couldn't provide radar service since we were on primary radar only. at xb:29 aircraft y called requesting to pick up his instrument flight rules off pmh. the fdio was down, so we had no flight plan, and we had no external communication capability to get it even though we still had the airspace. i called to the tower, a supervisor told me to just send him to zid. we switched aircraft y to zid even though he had to climb 10k feet through the heart of our airspace which we technically still controlled even without operating equipment for the last twenty minutes. it's possible that aircraft y was attempting to call us on the ground for his instrument flight rules via the landline, which was interfacility out of service, and no pilot could know that our tracon inoperative.one hour prior to this event we had an additional t1 full communication and radar outage which eventually returned but the outage caused an unsafe situation to occur.we should have a procedure to make a decision faster to close the tracon. waiting on the district and air traffic manager (atm) to tell us what to do is slow and unsafe.our equipment is not consistently reliable for the safe transition of aircraft in our airspace. we have outages constantly including these major t1 communications outages, and we seem to allow it simply because we often have low traffic, such as this instance with only one aircraft. but it only takes an unfortunate circumstance to realize that keeping our bar for safety so low is an extreme negligence to our flying public.

synopsis: B737 Captain reported losing datalink once out of VHF coverage on two separate flights on a B737 and Maintenance stated this was a common issue with the aircraft.
text: on my recent redacted redacted redacted paring, satcom datalink was lost as soon as we lost vhf radio coverage on both legs. these two legs fly in datalink mandated (dlm) airspace. on the redacted redacted leg, after losing satcom datalink, we contacted maintenance control via satcom as the phone feature still worked. they were unable to provide any guidance on how to remedy the situation. the person we spoke with also stated that he wasn't very familiar with the system. redacted control was adamant that we relog in" to cpdlc which we couldn't without the datalink. they reluctantly accepted us into the airspace via voice operations and we were able to relog into cpdlc once we were in vhf coverage. after landing in redacted. the maintenance technician reported this was a "common issue" with the b737 and reset the system for the outbound flight.on our return flight, on a different tail number, the same thing happened. i again was able to contact dispatch using the satcom as that feature still worked. i again was concerned with operating in the dlm airspace without datalink. dispatch stated we would have to exit rvsm airspace, descend to fl280, and divert to redacted only to land with very little fuel (5, 300 lb.). i then asked him to contact redacted and redacted control centers and ask if we could operate on our current route and at our current altitude without datalink. the dispatcher did so and replied that the control centers approved the request "since we lost the datalink airborne, " ultimately saving the flight from a costly divert. we also contacted maintenance control again and they said there was no way of resetting the system airborne. during the preflight, we referenced the 737 operations guide that provides a photo of the satcom page that should be checked (this information should be put in the flight manual (fm)). our page matched the picture, but once airborne, ps voice stated "unavailable." this is how i knew we would lose the datalink once out of vhf coverage. the fm provides no reference to what these prompts on the swift broadband (sbb) page of the satcom feature in the control display unit (cdu) indicate or any troubleshooting guidance. this situation created quite a distraction for the flight crew when operating in the region for both legs and is a safety concern."

synopsis: Citation Latitude Captain reported encountering severe wake turbulence departing TEB airport.
text: when departing from teb, runway 19, on the teterboro 4 departure, after turning to heading 280 while climbing through 2200 feet the airplane was struck upward by a single moment of severe to extreme turbulence. it felt as though the airplane had collided with some object. we requested priority handling and leveled off at 3000 feet. after assessing the aircraft and the situation we determined the aircraft to be safe. we were too heavy to land and the airspace was very congested so the safest course of action was to continue on our route and leave the area. we canceled the priority handling and continued on to the destination with no further issues. the company was notified when at a safe altitude.suggestions: at the time of the incident it was believed the aircraft had struck something, however after discussing the incident we believed that perhaps the airplane flew perpendicular through heavy wake turbulence. our initial thoughts were to return to land, however once we were able to assess the situation (we were too heavy to land, the airspace was very busy, the airplane seemed undamaged and operationally safe) it was determined the safest action would be to continue to our destination and if necessary land farther along our route.

text: cleared to descend via, between 11000 and 10000, experienced strong wake turbulence from aircraft coming from south and joining fewww transition. the wind at our altitude was from south at about 10 knots. i told the first officer to tell air traffic control that we experienced wake turbulence and ask for a heading. center replied cleared to offset right 1 mile." this put us on the downwind side the aircraft causing the wake. once we were slightly above the leading aircraft, i verballized and maneuvered toward returning to the arrival's final segment track after nusss. approach asked if we took someone else's heading assignment. they then gave us a heading.cause: air traffic control could anticipate wake turbulence threats on some of these arrivals, since they are probably fairly common. air traffic control should be aware that an offset downwind is not where we want to be when we are following a wake threat aircraft. a pilot monitoring whose english is a second language can slow communication with both parties."

synopsis: Embraer flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence departing CLT in trail of a B737.
text: aircraft x operated from clt to redacted without any operational irregularities other than two encounters with light wake turbulence shortly after departure.following departure from runway 36r at clt, we departed behind a b737. during the initial climb, while established on the sid and flying approximately heading 025, the aircraft encountered light wake turbulence consistent with the preceding traffic. the disturbance was minor and did not result in any significant deviation from assigned altitude or heading. aircraft control was maintained at all times. shortly thereafter, air traffic control assigned a heading of 310 degrees and instructed us to contact departure. during the turn to the assigned heading, we encountered a second brief episode of light wake turbulence, again believed to be associated with the preceding b737. this encounter was also minor in nature. the aircraft remained fully controllable, and there were no abrupt aircraft movements, exceedances, or operational concerns. no injuries were reported, and the remainder of the flight proceeded normally without incident.upon arrival at redacted, after the passengers had deplaned, the flight attendant advised me that a captain [from another airline] seated in 1a had requested to speak with the flight crew. the passenger identified himself.while still in the flight deck completing post-flight checklist items, i heard the captain attempt to return up the mobile stair ramp toward the aircraft door while the first officer was retrieving items at the door. i heard the first officer advise him that he was required to remain on the tarmac and could not come back up the ramp.i met with the captain after deplaning. he asked questions regarding the flight and inquired who had been flying the aircraft. i explained that i had been serving as pilot monitoring and that the first officer had been the pilot flying.the [other airline] captain then attempted to speak with the first officer while he was conducting the post-flight exterior inspection. the first officer advised that he would complete his assigned duties and return afterward. the captain appeared displeased with that response. during our discussion, captain stated that he had never experienced such an abrupt turn" and expressed that he was interested in seeing what the foqa data would show regarding the event, including how many gs the aircraft had experienced. i advised him that, from the flight deck's perspective, the aircraft had encountered only light wake turbulence and that the resulting movement was minimal. at no point did the wake turbulence result in a loss of control, significant deviation from assigned altitude or heading, or any indication that aircraft limitations had been approached.i was surprised by the level of concern expressed given the relatively minor nature of the wake turbulence encounter. i was further concerned when a flight attendant informed me of comments allegedly made by captain during cruise while in the presence of passengers. according to the flight attendant, the captain expressed his concerns openly and in an unprofessional manner while she was walking through the cabin. from the flight crew's perspective, the aircraft encountered two brief episodes of light wake turbulence during the departure phase. both events were managed appropriately, aircraft control was maintained at all times, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful."

text: about two thirds the way to redacted we noticed that the right flap needle was slightly past the up position. the left needle was at the up position, and the split was less than a needle width. we decided to configure early before starting the approach with flaps 1 position selected. at the flaps 1 position neither flap moved, and then we selected flaps 2. at flaps 2 there was still no movement from either flap. we pulled out the qrh and started the flaps trailing edge asymmetry checklist. at this point we requested priority handling, i flew the aircraft and took the radios while the captain ran the checklist. we also had a jumpseater that assisted during the procedure, and was a great value. once all checklists were complete and we were set up for the approach to xxr the captain took over the controls. we landed with no issues and went to the gate.

synopsis: ERJ 145 Captain reported a loss of a hydraulic system after landing. Aircraft was towed to the gate.
text: shortly after landing in redacted, i was applying breaks and thrust reversers when first officer pointed out that an eicas message presented itself.once i was slow enough and can direct my attention to the eicas, it stated a spoiler fail message was the first indication i saw after a slew of messages. i taxied out of the runway when i noticed my tiller was not as effective as it usually is. i got off the runway using rudders and i noticed the other messages of hyd 1 fail, hyd 1 low quantity. we ran the qrh, while helpful for in flight did not have much guidance for when it is on the ground. we cycled as directed and found no changes on the system. first officer and i decided to talk through our options and best decided to get towed into the gate. we coordinated with dispatch, maintenance control, as well as air traffic control, and ground staff to figure out the best method to the gate. we gave the fa a briefing for the situation at hand and that it will be a normal 'tow in' to the gate and a normal deplane. we also kept the passengers informed throughout the matter on handling the situation. the firefighters noticed hyrdraulic fluid on the left wing and did not notice any fire or heat on the aircraft.parking and shutdown was as normal in regards to the no apu minimum equipment list. contract maintenance immediately showed up at the gate and they found that the spoiler actuator was the cause of the leak and not the brakes. first officer and i also visually confirmed that that was the cause. no limitations or regulations were broken as well as zero injuries were reported.suggestions: overall crew handled the situation well, the only thing i wish was handled differently was that company ops in redacted decided to create a narrative that it was windshear resulting in a hard landing and hydraulic fluid leak as a result of it. unfortunately this has to be cleared up that it was not a result of that and company ops in redacted should have not made these comments without the full picture in hand.

synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in a TFR without authorization.
text: on day 0, at approximately xa:00, i, a part 107 certified remote pilot, flew my dji mavic air in class b airspace over location x. i had obtained laanc authorization prior to the flight and conducted preflight checks, confirming my dji aircraft firmware and flight control software (dji go 4 app) were current and up to date. i remained below the laanc-approved 150 ft agl ceiling for the entire approximately 45-minute flight, maintaining vlos throughout. no incidents, near misses, or equipment anomalies occurred. after landing and completing the flight, i discovered that a temporary flight restriction (tfr) had been in effect beginning on this day and was active during my operation. i had not checked for active tfrs during preflight planning, as my authorization efforts focused solely on obtaining laanc approval for the class b airspace. this flight was arranged on short notice, which compressed my preflight planning time and contributed to an overreliance on the laanc authorization process as a sole airspace check, rather than conducting a more thorough independent review.i was operating under the assumption that air control, the app through which i obtained my laanc authorization, would notify me of any active tfrs overlapping my planned flight area. no such alert was provided. this gap in my understanding of the app's notification capabilities contributed to the incursion. since this occurrence, i have begun manually checking for active tfrs through a separate source (such as faa dronezone, 1800wxbrief.com, or the faa's b4ufly app) prior to every flight, in addition to obtaining laanc authorization through air control.

synopsis: Government UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace without authorization.
text: on the date of the incident, while operating an unmanned aircraft system (uas) under my faa part 107 certification, i inadvertently conducted a flight within the class d airspace associated with redacted. the mission was in support of a search-and-rescue operation.prior to the flight, i completed my normal pre-flight procedures, including reviewing weather conditions and checking airspace authorization requirements through the flight ready laanc application. at the time, i believed i was operating in authorized airspace. however, i later determined that the application had not updated to my current location, resulting in an incorrect airspace display. consequently, i failed to recognize that the launch location was within the redacted class d airspace.the flight was conducted approximately three nautical miles from redacted and proceeded away from the installation, with the base located behind the direction of flight. at no point during the operation did i realize the airspace discrepancy.after completing the mission, i began reviewing and documenting my flight logs. during this process, i noted that the launch location was approximately three miles from redacted. recognizing that this distance was unusually close, i conducted a secondary review of the airspace information. upon rechecking the flight ready laanc application, i discovered that it was still displaying an incorrect location. i then manually verified the flight area and confirmed that the operation had occurred within class d airspace.this incident was the result of my failure to independently verify the accuracy of the application's location data prior to flight. the urgency and severity of the search-and-rescue call contributed to my oversight, however, responsibility for the error rests solely with me. to prevent a similar occurrence in the future, i will ensure that all airspace information is independently verified through multiple sources before flight operations begin, regardless of the urgency of the mission. this additional verification will help ensure compliance with all applicable airspace restrictions and faa regulations.

synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported confusing Taxiway Q signage exiting Runway 26 at MIA.
text: landing in mia at xa:30 local time, we rolled out 26l to exit the runway at the end. this was our briefed exit, and was instructed by air traffic control. taxiway p was closed, and indicated on the ipad moving map and by illuminated red lighting on the taxiway. we were instructed to turn left at the end of the runway and join q. i was pm for the landing, but ca, so reaching the end of the runway i initiated the change of controls and continued slowing the aircraft to taxi speed. i had developed a mental model of what i thought the taxi off would look like, and began a greater than 90 degree turn at the end of the runway. as our lights swung towards the taxiway i noticed a sign ahead of me that said q with an arrow pointing to the right. somewhat instinctively i stopped my turn and began to follow the taxiway that appeared to be indicated by the sign. this completely went against my preconceived model of the intersection, so i paused and queried my crew, 'where is q?' both first officer indicated that it should be towards the left, but agreed that the signage was confusing. i noticed the hold short lines to the approach end of runway 12 off my nose and to the right. i also noticed the white runway lights of 12/30, which is what the q-> sign was pointing towards, and where i had been heading until i stopped. at this time tower came on the radio and instructed us to exit the runway immediately with traffic landing behind us. i determined which taxiway was q by elimination, not runway 12/30 and not p by their differential lighting, white runway and red closure. i did not observe any other signage indicating taxiway q from the taxiing off perspective of 26l until we were established on the taxiway.cause: dark conditions, and a wide-open taxiway intersection with few markings caused a momentary disorientation that nearly resulted in a runway incursion.suggestions: there is already a hotspot, which is good, however it does not discuss a lack of taxiway signage. synopsis: Government UAS crew reported conducting a flight in a TFR without authorization.
text: piloting for an event for public safety and was not aware of the updated tfr. tfr was previously checked a couple days prior and operating the uas fell within the exception described in the tfr, however, it was not checked as it should have been the day of flying. i was operating for public safety purposes and we did not acquire a special government interest (sgi) waiver prior to operating. we discovered the issue a day later when it was made aware to the pilots that there was an updated tfr and we should have acquired an sgi waiver. my solution to this would be to create an sop within my agency to check for tfrs/tfr updates at least an hour prior to flying.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in a TFR without authorization.
text: i am a part 107 licensed remote pilot in command. the flight was conducted for company video work using a small unmanned aircraft system (suas) owned and registered by a coworker. prior to the flight, i conducted pre-flight research on the official faa website. i identified active tfrs at location x. i mistakenly believed these were the only active tfrs in the area. the flight location was situated in class d airspace near redacted airport. i operated under standard class d procedures, maintaining an altitude under 26 meters, which was safely below the heights of nearby buildings. during a planned 5-minute shoot, i launched the suas. the onboard dji flight application did not display any tfr restrictions or geo-fencing locks for the specific coordinate, only the expected proximity warning for the redacted class d airspace. after completing the 5-minute flight and successfully landing the aircraft, my company's security approached me regarding a potential tfr nearby.after the flight, i conducted an exhaustive search to verify security's claim. i discovered that a tfr was indeed active for that location, which had not appeared clearly in my initial generalized web search, nor was it hard-blocked by the manufacturer's software. i now recognize that manufacturer applications like dji fly are insufficient for strict airspace compliance. moving forward, i have downloaded and integrated faa-approved b4ufly applications, specifically the air aware app, into my mandatory pre-flight checklist. i will cross-reference live data across multiple laanc-supported applications prior to every takeoff to ensure all tfrs are caught.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS); Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR
synopsis: Recreational / Hobbyist UAS pilot reported they let other people fly the UAS who then flew the UAS above 400 feet and into controlled airspace.
text: on day 4, at approximately xa:00 local time, a recreational small uas flight occurred with my dji mavic 4 pro near location x. i registered the uas and completed my trust completion certificate on day 0. this occurred during my first week as a new recreational uas flyer while i was still learning the faa rules, airspace requirements, and aircraft/controller settings.during the flight, two family members manipulated the controls at different times. i was not physically manipulating the controls at the time of the altitude deviation. however, i was the registered owner and was supervising the flight, and i did not prevent or correct the altitude increase quickly enough.the dji flight record showed a maximum altitude of approximately 3, 250 feet agl relative to the takeoff/home point. this is my best estimate based on the available flight record. the flight was recreational, and the altitude deviation was not intentional. at the time, i believed the flight was being conducted from a private/open area, but i now understand that private property does not determine airspace authorization and that i must verify airspace, airport proximity, and altitude limits before every flight.i am not aware of any aircraft conflict, near-miss, collision, injury, flyaway, lost link, or evasive action.i believe the contributing factors were human factors, inexperience, insufficient monitoring of altitude, allowing untrained people to manipulate the controls, and misunderstanding of the aircraft/controller settings and altitude limitations.after this event, i reviewed the recreational uas rules more carefully and took corrective action. i contacted dji for assistance with the controller and aircraft safety settings. i learned how to set maximum altitude and distance limits and how to lock the controller so another person cannot use it without a code.to prevent recurrence, i will not allow any untrained person to manipulate the controls. before every flight, i will verify airspace, airport proximity, altitude limits, weather, and the flight location, obtain any required faa authorization, maintain visual line of sight, monitor altitude continuously, use altitude and distance limits in the controller, keep the controller locked from unauthorized use, and stop the flight if i am not fully sure it can be conducted safely and legally.i completed this report to the best of my knowledge using my recollection and the dji flight record/controller information available to me. some details, including the exact time and maximum altitude, are approximate based on the available record. my goal in filing this report is to be transparent about the safety issue and to help prevent it from happening again.

synopsis: Government UAS pilot reported briefly exceeding their LAANC authorized altitude.
text: incident occurred on day 0, at approximately xa:11. at that time, a public safety mission under rpic part 107 was being flown. the flight was conducted in a 200' grid. prior to the flight, i created a laanc, as required for class d airspace. during the creation of the laanc, i inadvertently requested an altitude of 150' instead of 200'.the entire flight lasted approximately 7min32sec. during the return flight, i accidentally breached the 150' laanc that had been requested and approved by elevating to approximately 221'. while the incident occurred within a 200' zone, the reason for this report is to document the accidental breach of the laanc and the max 200'shortly after breaching the altitude, i recognized this and immediately descended to under 150', ultimately correcting the incident.after the flight was completed, i reported the accidental breach to the suas supervisor. the rpic was then provided with reeducation and guidance to prevent the incident from recurring.during the flight, there were no aircraft in the area, no near misses, no sustained flight over people, nor vehicles.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported briefly exceeding their LAANC authorized altitude.
text: i arrived at location x at approximately xa:03 on day 0 to conduct an aerial analysis of the property. before the flight, i requested and received laanc authorization.prior to takeoff, i failed to complete a step that is normally part of my preflight process. i did not set the maximum altitude limit in the dji application used to control my dji air 2s to not exceed allowed altitude given the agl limits in the area it was set to be flown. after documenting the property from the air, i ascended alongside the building to capture imagery of the structure. between approximately xa:30 and xa:34, the aircraft reached an altitude of approximately 144 feet.after landing, it became clear that the aircraft had exceeded the authorized altitude.the event occurred because the altitude limit in the flight application had not been configured before the operation. the flight remained under control at all times and no injuries or property damage occurred.after understanding my failure to ensure that the altitude limit was correctly set, i added a specific verification to double check that the dji altitude limit is correctly set in order to reduce the likelihood of a similar occurrence again.

synopsis: TPA TRACON Controller reported having to issue a climb to an IFR aircraft that was on the approach to SPG due to conflict with a VFR aircraft. Reporter recommended airspace redesign to better protect IFR approach courses.
text: aircraft x was executing the rnav runway 07 approach to spg from the northern iaf loyil. aircraft y was visual flight rules not receiving services at 2, 000. i reached out to aircraft y to no avail. traffic was issued early to aircraft x while on the base leg. traffic was issued again as he made the turn inbound. i swapped out with the relieving controller at this point. the relieving controller was aware of the situation. i instructed the relieving controller to immediately advise aircraft x that they were converging with aircraft y at which point conflict alert activated. the relieving controller asked aircraft x if they wanted to discontinue the approach and at that point issued a climb to 2, 500.traffic was very complex at the time. with only 3 assignable altitudes, the options were limited. add a visual flight rules at 2, 000 or 3, 000 to the mix and situations can get out of control quickly.recommendation: protect approach courses. this isn't hard. let's design airspace that precludes nonparticipating visual flight rules aircraft from interfering with instrument flight rules procedures.

synopsis: Widebody aircraft Captain and First Officer reported encountering wake turbulence climbing through FL240 in trail of a B777 that resulted in a 40-degree bank. Control was re-established and the flight continued to destination.
text: departed ams (eham) behind aircraft y a 777 heading for redacted. same routing. with autopilot engaged we were climbing through 24, 000 feet to fl300. aircraft y was about 8 miles ahead of us according to tcas and was climbing to fl320. slightly hazy conditions so did not see visually. at this point we felt some light turbulence then encountered their wake. the aircraft banked approx 40 degrees to the left. our bank angle" aural alarm sounded and the autopilot remained engaged. i was the pf. i disengaged the autopilot and was able to roll wings level and proceeded initially on a heading about 30 degrees to the left and upwind from the wake. we advised air traffic control and asked for and received a 4 mile offset to the left and upwind of our route to avoid another upset event. we checked with the fas in the back and other than a forward galley cart falling sideways there was no other damage and no injuries. we continued the flight with no other events."

synopsis: B757 Captain reported encountering 'bad' wake turbulence on final approach to LAX in trail of an Airbus. Flight requested and was cleared for a slower approach speed.
text: at approximately xa:35 on the instrument landing system 25l approach following an airbus 320 or 321. air traffic control gave instructions to slow to 210 kias. at 210 and 5 miles behind traffic we encountered bad wake turbulence. the wing dipped about 45 degrees and nose pointed downward. as flying pilot i disconnected the ap (autopilot) and recovered back to path. we asked air traffic control to slow. we were given 180 kias. we encountered another bad wake turbulence encounter as the wing dipped again. we asked for slower speed. we were given 170 kias to gigii. we started to configure and slow about 2 miles prior to avoid further wake turbulence. we could still feel the burbling effects on the aircraft. we now were entering the cloud layer at 1500 feet and air traffic control asked us to speed up. we said unable due to the wake turbulence. we landed and departed runway 25l on h7 without delay and another flight landed behind.

synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in a TFR without authorization and above their LAANC authorized altitude.
text: on day 0, i operated a small uas in the vicinity of location x. prior to the flight, i conducted a pre-flight airspace check using an arcgis-based web map, which i erroneously believed displayed all active temporary flight restrictions (tfrs). because the map indicated clear airspace, i believed the operation was compliant and launched the aircraft. i subsequently learned that this specific tool did not display the active tfr in the area, resulting in an inadvertent airspace incursion.additionally, prior to this flight, my uas controller's measurement units had inadvertently been changed from imperial (feet) to metric (meters). relying on the controller's screen, i operated the aircraft believing it was below the 400-foot agl ceiling. upon later review of my flight logs, i realized the telemetry was displaying meters, resulting in an inadvertent exceedance of the maximum allowable altitude under 14 cfr § 107.51. at all times, my intent was to operate safely and in compliance with all part 107 regulations. a misunderstanding of the airspace tool's limitations and an unrecognized interface setting led to these inadvertent violations.

synopsis: Government UAS pilot reported conducting a UAS flight without authorization.
text: on day 0, at approximately xa:00, i was operating as rpic during a law enforcement community engagement event at location x. i operated a small uas under far part 107, with a visual observer present, at approximately 20 feet agl for 15 minutes. the flight was conducted visual line of sight (vlos) throughout.prior to the flight, i submitted a laanc authorization request for the class b airspace. the request was submitted within the 72-hour processing window and authorization was not granted before the event start time. i did not obtain telephone authorization from the controlling air traffic control facility as an alternative. the flight was therefore conducted without the authorization required under 14 cfr 107.41. no incidents, injuries, property damage, or equipment anomalies occurred. the uas landed normally upon mission completion.contributing factors: insufficient planning lead time between task assignment and the event date. the laanc 72-hour processing requirement was not coordinated sufficiently in advance of scheduling.proposed corrective action: establish agency policy requiring laanc requests to be submitted a minimum of 72 hours prior to any planned operation in controlled airspace, with a mandatory status check at 48 hours prior. if authorization cannot be confirmed by 24 hours prior, the operation shall be suspended pending authorization or an alternate uncontrolled airspace site identified.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported flying in controlled airspace and within an active TFR without authorization.
text: who/what/where/when/why: i am a part 107 certified remote pilot. on day 0, i conducted a brief commercial uas flight using a dji air 3 to capture roof photographs for a solar installation. the operation took place at location x, which is located in class b airspace approximately 6.5 nm from redacted airport. the flight path also briefly and inadvertently clipped the extreme outer lateral edge of an active tfr.chain of events & cause: on the day of the occurrence, i had a demanding schedule with multiple marketing shoots across different locations. i diligently performed pre-flight airspace checks for every other site throughout the day. however, due to task saturation and a momentary lapse in situational awareness at this specific location, i mistakenly assumed the airspace was clear and inadvertently omitted both the laanc authorization and the local active tfr notam checks prior to launching. i launched the drone manually, climbed to approximately 38 feet agl directly over the private property, captured the required photographs, and landed safely within 13 minutes. no manned aircraft or other hazards were present, and there was no conflict. the oversight regarding both the class b airspace and the outer edge of the tfr boundary was discovered post-flight when reviewing my flight logs and airspace charts.human factors & corrective actions: the primary root cause was human error stemming from complacency and fatigue due to a high volume of consecutive shoots on site. to prevent any future recurrence, i have updated my standard operating procedures to shift all airspace and notam/tfr analysis to the pre-trip planning phase. moving forward, i am mandating a proactive desktop airspace assessment and securing advanced laanc scheduling up to 48 hours prior to leaving for any field site. this ensures all flight boundaries and authorizations are locked into my calendar beforehand, removing the pressure of performing critical safety checks during the rush of on-site setup.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: AVP Controller reported that due to low staffing; TRACON and Tower have been combined during certain shifts and having to train and manage trainees without proper communication equipment have made operations unsafe.
text: due to low staffing numbers avp, radar positions have been combined to the tower cab outside of mid-shift hours. this has been expected of us by upper management to facilitate operating the facility with 50% staffing. during the winter months when traffic volume is low is quite a different situation than now in the summertime when traffic volume is high. we've done this for years, as it was common practice when i arrived to the facility. the current sop allows the practice but has requirements for notifications to management outside of the building if it is done outside of mid-shift hours. district management was advised this would have to become standard practice until staffing numbers increase and has elected to forego the phone call and consider a daily log entry as sufficient.on the date and time above, i was instructed to work a session on north in the tower cab. it was early afternoon and a typical busy time. traffic was moderate and complex with sequencing to the primary airport, a mix of instrument flight rules and visual flight rules overflights, plus aircraft y and aircraft z flying around the airspace sightseeing. i also had multiple flight school airplanes in the practice areas. i don't recall if i had any practice instrument approaches at that time. at least sermns (swap (severe weather avoidance plan) escape routes - metro new york area) or phlyrs (philadelphia area weather avoidance routes) weren't active. i don't think i stopped talking for the 90 minutes i was on.i was busy enough and uncomfortable enough that at one point i grabbed another cpc who was not on position at the moment and just told him to keep an eye over my shoulder. he assisted with landline coordination and making amendments for me as ground control (gc) was defaulted to covering arrival data (ad) functions, something that isn't covered by sop. the trainee in question is certified on both gc and ad but is otherwise not a cpc. i was forced to manually coordinate routing for one or two aircraft because the trainee wasn't able to complete amendments i needed correctly and in a timely manner. it took him close to 10 minutes to amend a visual flight rules's altitude so that i could hand off to the correct sector. i have no clue what the exact issue was with that, or what other traffic he had on ground at that exact time. avp was busy as a whole so there were definitely airplanes that required attention outside of the window. working arrival data is a heads-down position and completely contrary to what a ground controller should be doing. this particular day was unique in that avp was using both of our intersecting runways due to winds and traffic.to further complicate the session, while i was working with frequencies directly in my ear, many times i had trouble hearing pilots talking to me because of other speakers in the cab. there were low clouds moving in from the west forcing most of my visual flight rules traffic that was flying westbound to continue to descend lower and lower to maintain visual flight rules, which only put them in the middle of our arrival and departure corridors.upper level management almost expects us to combine to the tower in order to operate the facility and accomplish training. i understand that realistically the only way to get out of the staffing crisis is to train and certify controllers. i feel we've reached the point where doing this is inherently unsafe. the safety of day to day operations rest solely on the shoulders of the small handful of fpls (full performance level) on the shift. we're outnumbered daily by partially qualified and newly position-certified trainees. there are often times where an fpl on radar has had to correct a situation on local, or the controller in charge (cic) has had to step in, or even an fpl who is on technically on break has to step in.when combined to the tower cab, we are forced to sacrifice a lot in terms of redundancy and basic safety. there is no voice switch bypass for radar frequencies in the tower cab. this has been brought up to tech operations foryears already. there is only one interim voice switch replacement (ivsr) that radar controller can use and no spare that someone can plug in and help coordinate in a pinch. gc is defaulted to work ad functions and when training is underway on a new trainee that adds undue burden on both the trainee and the trainer as they don't even have a concept of what is happening in the airspace. the tower display workstation (tdw) is 1/3(?) of the size of a terminal controller workstation (tcw), is washed out as soon as someone bumps a window shade open.in the moments we're told to train then it feels like the trainee and i could share a chair. the small scope means i need to stand nearly in their lap to be able to even see the scope. meanwhile, the doubling of people required to train crowds the room quickly. there have been many instances where we're training on all 3 positions at the same time. sure it looks great on the cru-art (shift log), but at what cost. what is the benefit of teaching new people bad practices from the start? what is the benefit of working without a basic backup to our radios? what is the benefit of doubling the heads-down workload of a trainee who should be looking out the window? what is the benefit of forcing a trainee to complete ad functions when they haven't even received classroom training on it? what is the benefit of putting all the above-mentioned responsibility on the shoulder of the few fpls on the shift?recommendation: at this point i don't know what would be the most effective change to implement. we need more than 50% staffing. we can't continue to be pushed to exhaustion by 60-hour workweeks just to have basic staffing in the building. we can't be expected to work radar combined to the tower until further notice. we should not be forcing trainees to endure decades of bad decisions while they struggle to learn to separate airplanes.adding a full tcw has been brought up in the past but adding just installing a new screen without an addition ivsr or even so much as a bypass for the voice switch is a waste [of] time and money. splitting off ad from gc won't work because we don't have enough ivsrs or so much as enough counter space.forcing trainees to sit on position even if there's no traffic but also rushing them to check out sooner continues to rob them of the quality training.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; No Specific Anomaly Occurred Unwanted Situation
synopsis: AVL TRACON Controller reported a VFR aircraft not in communication with ATC flew through the final approach course at AVL causing the controller to cancel a visual approach for another aircraft. The reporter stated similar situations have been reported multiple times and recommended changes to AVL's Class C airspace.
text: after a moderate to heavy volume of arrivals, aircraft x was one of the last in the sequence. they were coming from the south-southwest, and had the field in sight about 18 miles out for avl. i cleared them for a visual approach to runway 35. a moment later, aircraft y, who never called approach for services (we looked up the callsign that was tied to the ads-b to find out the information on the aircraft) departed 0a7 northwest bound and then turned to the left and was climbing at a good rate. thankfully for everyone involved, i had not shipped aircraft x to the tower yet as they were descending in for the visual approach. since i've seen this exact scenario play out numerous times, i cancelled the aircraft x's visual approach clearance and had them continue on present heading followed by a right turn, and right when they crossed the 051 mva boundary, i had them maintain 050 because i had another aircraft in the right downwind for runway 35 at 060. aircraft y continued to climb, oblivious to the fact that they were flying right through our final for avl at a dangerous altitude. aircraft x was cleared for the visual approach 35 after passing behind the visual flight rules aircraft.plenty of luck was involved here that avoided any major deals or potential midairs. if i had simply shipped the aircraft x to the tower when they were 13 miles out, which is not unreasonable, the potential for a midair collision would have been significant because aircraft x would have been in frequency transition during the critical moment, and aircraft y had no need to or desire to call asheville approach for services because they were legally outside of class c airspace still. luck was involved with me not descending the aircraft on the right downwind to 051, which would have been a standard thing to do. if aircraft y had decided to depart a few minutes earlier, when my traffic volume was much greater, including many visual flight rules aircraft flying around in and around downwinds that i had to maneuver all of my arrivals around, i may not have noticed their departure as quickly as i did now.recommendation: similar reports to this have been filed multiple times over the many years that i've worked here by many different controllers. the avl class c needs to be changed to not allow 0a7 departures to fly under the runway 35 final approach course at dangerous altitudes. as it stands, it is legal for visual flight rules aircraft to cross umuxe at 040 and not violate the class charlie, which is exactly the published altitude for crossing that fix on the rnav 35 and the instrument landing system 35. the faa has been made aware that this is a highly dangerous situation on numerous occasions and the only feedback the faa has ever given the controllers at avl is that changing the class charlie would require an act of congress" aka it is too hard/too much effort for management to do. the faa spends plenty of time monitoring and figuring out how to reduce cpc breaks and other useless behaviors, there is plenty of time for them to do actual work and fix the avl class c airspace. one day, if nothing changes, all of the wrong luck will happen in this known and well reported on unsafe airspace/procedure that will cost people their lives. if that ever happens, let it be known that this safety issue was reported on numerous times and something could have been done about it."

text: on day 0, i operated a recreational uas dji neo 2 in a short (0.2) flight from my own residential property in my backyard at a low altitude of some 20 feet agl. i was checking the gesture control feature of the uas and i was in a hurry as it looked like there was rain moving into the area. there were no other people or aircraft present. the flight was completed safely without incident or conflict with any other person or aircraft. however, after landing, i realized that i had neglected to obtain a laanc (low altitude authorization and notification capability) from the faa for that flight. the class b airspace from redacted overlays my property to the surface, so the airspace in my backyard is not mine, it is the faa's. i realized immediately what happened, and then immediately applied for and received a laanc authorization for my next flight, which was to practice flight with an rc controller instead of gestures, also in my backyard at low levels. the weather had improved.i recognize that this oversight of mine, in not requesting a laanc authorization for that first flight, is inexcusable. i am well experienced in aviation. i fell into the trap of being in too much of a hurry to 'beat the weather' and skipped a critical step. i believe strongly in the attitude of compliance with all faa regulations and requirements. i will reinforce the use of checklists to avoid any recurrence.

anomaly: ATC Issue All Types; Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Landing Without Clearance; Ground Incursion Runway
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported landing without clearance at COE as the sectional charts do not indicate there is a tower and suggested this information be announced in the AWOS.
text: on day 1, i was exposed to a disturbing circumstance that i feel should be corrected for the benefit of pilots and safety. my cross-country journey began at redacted in the morning of day 0. i had a passenger, an experienced cross-country land and sea pilot as well as a photographer. we were loaded with gear for our journey to redacted. to stay within weight requirements, we were limited on fuel capacity which required us to make several short flights from airport to airport for fuel stops.we stayed overnight at redacted that night after taking a tour of the lake for photos. the next morning, we toured another lake for more photos. as we continued our journey to redacted, we took the opportunity for more photos of rivers and lakes on the way. more fuel stops were made along the path.arriving at coeur d'alene lake, we toured for more photos and noticed the sea plane base (s76) had two planes and a ferry boat docked and there was no room for another plane. we decided it would be best to fuel at coe, a non-towered airport shown on the current federal aviation administration (faa) sectional chart.after checking the awos at coe channel 135.075 for wind and other information, it favored runway 20 for landing. with no additional comments, i switched to the unicom channel 122.8 as indicated on the sectional chart and announced my intentions five to six miles out that i was approaching and planned to overfly the airport 500 feet above the pattern altitude to verify the wind to runway 20.during my approach, five miles out to the space coe, i did notice one aircraft departing to the west. otherwise, there was no other traffic in the area after checking the windsock and verifying that runway 20 was best wind for land. also noticed there was no traffic in the air or on the ground. i announced that i was maneuvering for a mid-field crossing to enter left downwind, for runway 20. after turning downwind, i made another radio call stating i was on an extended downwind for runway 20. i lowered my landing gear and flaps, then announced i left base for runway 20. i established a stabilized approach and announced final for runway 20.immediately after touching down, i heard a radio call about switching to 120 something? i exited the runway at the first taxi exit and headed for what i thought was the fuel area as there were phillips 66 signs. then i got a radio call asking my intentions. i responded that i needed some fuel. the controller told me that it was a towered airport now and i needed to switch to 120.125 frequency. i told him i had no idea as the current faa chart indicates a non-towered airport with fuel. he said it was on the notam and i made a mistake. he instructed me to taxi down to the run-up area of runway 02 for further instructions. he told me that this has been a common miscommunication with pilots for a while.after fueling up for our last leg to redacted, i called air traffic control for progressive taxi instructions to the tower for better explanation. the tower was a bit difficult to see or find as it was a makeshift setup of container boxes stacked up. after climbing to the top of containers where the controllers were, we had a nice cordial discussion regarding the lack of information available to incoming pilots. not only is it not on the currently published sectional faa charts, but it's also not on the notam. the simple solution is to have it announced in the awos recording until the charts are updated. additionally, the unicom channel should be monitored by air traffic control to give pilots the correct frequency as they enter the coe airspace and do not wait until after they have landed.furthermore, i hope that your organization can be of some help to me in this particular case. as i take aviation responsibilities very seriously and don't want this to be a blemish on my record. i am not sure what i could have done differently except going to a different airport.in conclusion, i hope for the safety of all and the fairness of other pilots, the continuation ofthis problem at coe must be corrected, regardless of their growing pains.
