synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported conducting a flight in a TFR without authorization. The pilot landed the UAS upon being informed of the TFR.
text: on day 3 i performed a drone flight to capture photography as part of my professional duties at the request of my employer. the organization i work for includes over a mile of outdoor space accessible by the general public, therefore internal drone flights and protocols are managed by the organization's robust safety and security team. the flight area included class g air space i'm familiar with and know the flight rules for. a flight plan was submitted and approved more than 3 days prior to the flight, as is our organization's protocol, and our safety and security office was again notified of the flight via phone just before launch. flight time and area were picked for a non-populated time to ensure all safety protocols were in place regarding any bystanders. the drone was launched at roughly xa:00 and in flight for roughly 8 minutes when i was approached by law enforcement officers who asked me to land the drone and informed me of a tfr in the area. i immediately cooperated and landed the drone and spoke with the officers, answering all questions. they informed me i was on the edge of and just entering a temporary flight restricted area that had earlier been established -- i had no prior knowledge of this tfr and informed them as such. furthermore, neither dji's 'before you fly' map nor the drone's geofencing advisory warning system alerted me to the tfr area. i informed the officers that i was flying as documentation for my employer and neither i nor my organization were aware of the established tfr for that date, and have been granted an faa waiver 14 cfr § 107.39 for flights over human beings (though the flight did not occur over any people) and our safety and security team has submitted information to authorities for waiver/approval to fly in the same area in which the organization is restricting external drone access for a large event occurring the next week. it is unclear whether this waiver has anything to do with not receiving a notice via dji of a restricted area, or just the apparent unreliability of the geofencing and advisory system of the application - as it was explained to me that the remote id information provided for the waiver would prevent such messages from occurring on the day of the scheduled event. the officers were understanding and took my information and proceeded on, informing me not to fly the drone again during the tfr. i informed the officers that i would contact our security office and my colleagues with drone licenses to inform them of the tfr and prevent this from happening again.when i returned to my office, i explored the situation further and was not initially finding clear information on the tfr for the area - as the faa approved service 'airspace link' showed the tfr in effect day 1 - day 4 in local time. i then searched for the tfr map via the faa and found additional information that was not present on the airspace link site including an earlier tfr on day 0. this notam report also specified the effective time window falling within my flight starting on day 1. this is especially relevant as i was approved for a flight following the same procedures earlier in the week on day 1 that began prior to the utc time listed via the airspace link site but would be another incident with the tfr according to the local time start listed on the faa notam. while the flight on day 1 also did not result in any takeoff warning via dji's 'before you fly' map nor the drone's geofencing advisory warning system, it did not result in any incident with authorities on site at that date and time.regardless of the details and circumstances around the tfr, i have greatly learned from this event as an exercise in following best practices and attention to detail, as well as cross-referencing information as important as flight zones. this experience has taught me to not be too comfortable with flight zones i am familiar with, and to rely on my own research and information prior to a flight for any special circumstances that may affect normal flight operation rather than drone alerts and the reliance of our internal security team to relay flight information. as a result of this experience, i will be certain to check both faa notams and tfr maps, in addition to the faa approved resources such as airspace link as close to launch as possible. furthermore, following this incident i have already completed and received certificates for official supplemental rules and safety courses via faasafety.gov including 'airspace, special use airspace and tfrs' and 'suas: regulations, laws, airspace ownership and faa enforcement, ' and intend to continue refreshing my airman knowledge with further supplemental coursework. i have also begun conversations with my organization's safety and security team to implement tfr check information into the pre-flight reporting procedure in order to reinforce the habit of checking for tfrs and more effectively communicate these potential risks to the rest of the organization, as there are a few other drone pilots within the organization. these discussions have already begun between our organization's drone pilots, helping to strengthen our community and awareness of flight safety and responsibility.

security team to relay flight information. as a result of this experience, i will be certain to check both faa's notams and tfr maps, in addition to the faa approved resources such as airspace link as close to launch as possible. furthermore, following this incident, i have already completed and received certificates for official supplemental rules and safety courses via faasafety.gov including 'airspace, special use airspace and tfrs' and 'suas: regulations, laws, airspace ownership and faa enforcement, ' and intend to continue refreshing my airman knowledge with further supplemental coursework. i have also begun conversations with my organization's safety and security team to implement tfr check information into the pre-flight reporting procedure in order to reinforce the habit of checking for tfrs and more effectively communicate these potential risks to the rest of the organization, as there are a few other drone pilots within the organization. these discussions have already begun between our organization's drone pilots, helping to strengthen our community and awareness of flight safety and responsibility.

anomaly: Aircraft Equipment Problem Less Severe; Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS pilot reported a UAS with cancelled FAA registration was unknowingly operated for several months before the registration issue was discovered.
text: in month 6, prior to conducting a flight operation in class e airspace, a remote pilot in command (rpic) performed a routine review of the documentation required for waivered flight operations. during this review, the rpic discovered that the aircraft registration sticker was not attached to the drone and the registration card was missing from the drone case.the rpic then verified the aircraft's registration status through the faa dronezone portal and determined that the registration had been marked as 'cancelled' effective month 0. as a result, the rpic immediately suspended the planned flight operation and did not operate the aircraft.to prevent further use, the rpic placed the drone and its remote controller into storage, labeled both the drone and its case as 'unregistered, ' and removed the aircraft from service pending further investigation.the subsequent investigation revealed that the drone had been operated despite the cancelled registration. the aircraft registration was cancelled in month 0 and was in storage until month 3. starting in month 3, three different rpics had conducted a total of 204 flights accumulating 67 flight hours using the aircraft over a period of approximately four months. the majority of these flights occurred in class g (uncontrolled) airspace, while several flights were conducted in class b (controlled) airspace after obtaining proper authorization through the low altitude authorization and notification capability (laanc) system. although all required airspace approvals and clearances had been obtained for operations in controlled airspace, the aircraft's faa registration was not in compliance during this period.the aircraft was initially operated by an experienced rpic with several years of company drone operations experience. the drone was subsequently transferred in month 4 to a new rpic for their first inspection assignment. in month 6, the drone was later handed off to another experienced rpic. that rpic performed maintenance but did not check registration documents upon receiving the aircraft. after approximately one week of operation, the final rpic recognized that the aircraft's external faa registration-number sticker was missing and initiated a review that ultimately identified a missing registration card and the cancelled registration status.the investigation determined that the registration had been cancelled in error due to a mislabeled drone case. a retired and damaged drone had been stored in a case incorrectly labeled with the identifier of an active operational drone. as a result, the faa registration associated with the operational aircraft was mistakenly cancelled.the investigation also identified weaknesses in the drone registration management process. registration documents were typically stored inside drone cases and were not readily visible during routine equipment checks, making it unlikely that a missing registration card would be immediately detected. additionally, while the faa registration sticker was missing from the aircraft, a company issued drone identifier sticker remained affixed to the drone. the presence of this identifier created the appearance that the aircraft was properly labeled, causing the absence of the faa registration number sticker to go unnoticed during pre-flight inspections and routine use.apparent cause 1 mislabeled drone case containing a damaged drone led to the cancellation of the registration of an operational active drone.apparent cause 2registration cards are often kept inside drone cases underneath equipment to keep them secure. the registration cards are not readily visible to the rpics leading uas crews to inadvertently overlook the missing registration card.corrective actions:1) conduct a safety stand-down to verify inventory and confirm all active drones have valid faa registration.2) update uncrewed aerial systems (uas) fleet management document to include recommended procedures for retired drones.3) amend the preflight checklist to require drone registration validation and part of daily pre-flight checks.4) attach a durable external registration tag to all active drone cases.5) require all uas crews to verify their assigned drone registration is present and current.6) contact faa regarding possible dronezone inventory management improvements.7) designate a single individual responsible for drone inventory management.8) require maintenance log including drone registration verification be complete before operation in the field upon transferring drones between operators.9) verify all active drones have faa registration number sticker properly displayed on external surface of the aircraft.

anomaly: Airspace Violation All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural FAR; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Unauthorized Flight Operations (UAS)
synopsis: Part 107 UAS flight crew reported they conducted flights in a TFR without authorization.
text: i secured local university permission to fly uas/uav on the university campus in advance of flights for xa:00 to xc:00/xd:00 on day 0. this is part of weekly planned flights on campus for flight practice/training hours for one student and learning in an independent study for another student. in addition to the educational outcomes, we fly to collect video and images for various business purposes on campus. on this particular day only one of the two students was present and flying as part of the planned flight, person a. while person a was manipulating the controls at the time with the mavic 2 pro, i was serving as remote pilot in command. in addition to the remote pilot in command, i also served as the visual observer. partly to assist with keeping an eye on the uas/uav, to assist with people who may be approaching nearby to the flight, and also to answer questions when individuals approach (common on a university campus). we typically meet at xa:00 and do pre-flight checks inside the office and then go out to fly. this particular morning, i was running late to meet at the office and this particular human factor led to me forgetting to do the tfr check as part of the pre-flight checklist. i also did not ask if my student had checked. come to find out, this turned out to be a very good learning experience for both of us and i doubt that either of us will ever forget to do that check again. our series of flights started at location x on campus, then we flew in the area around location y and the area around location z. our final flights to capture video and images for a campus project were to fly the east end of location z and location a. we were approached multiple times during all of our flights and we paused flight, grounded the uas/uav, and ensured the safety of all passerby's whether walking or biking on campus. flights were planned to be fairly low (below 100 feet and some at average height level of a human. the highest flight that we planned to fly was no more than 400 feet agl and that was simply to ensure that the student had the experience of what that type of height is like from an observational experience. our highest flights were along location z at 397 feet for less than 1-2 minutes. the drone at all times was above myself and the student manipulating controls, we didn't fly it beyond our line of sight and manually straight up from take off location(s) at the ends of location z. we were approached by several people during our flights that day asking questions from curiosity to technical questions. i handled most of the questions while person a collected the images/video and maintained line of site. we were never further apart than about 10-15 feet and could communicate by voice without any issue. both of us were in high visibility safety vests. while not required, we find it's best to ensure others know we are flying our uas for university business purposes as students are not allowed to fly on our campus unless part of a class or another business purpose. at roughly xc:00, just after bringing the mavic 2 pro down from the west end of location y safely (literally we hovered in the air to ensure several families and people with dogs passed by before we landed), we began walking and preparing for the next flight -- the backside of location a. we were approached by an individual. he asked if we were with the university. i turned toward him with my name tag on and stated yes and explained our learning purpose and university business purpose of shooting videos. i thought he was a typical tourist asking questions or maybe a hobbyist or other part 107 pilot. he then asked if we had checked the tfrs for the day and location and i realized i had not before we left. he then introduced himself as a law enforcement officer and flipped out his identification wallet. i immediately opened my phone and app and realized we had unknowingly been flying just inside of a tfr. the law enforcement officer acknowledged that they were aware of ourprevious flights that were just outside of the tfr and that we were brought to their attention only with our last flight that was just inside the edge of the radius of the area covered by the tfr. we immediately stopped all flights and began to put away the uas. we discussed how this will be a good learning experience for my future classes and how i am often asked the question 'who enforces tfrs?'. it truly was a mistake and we were not intending to break any tfrs when we set out for the filming and flights. we now have a printed checklist that must be checked through before leaving the office to ensure situational awareness. both person a and i will never forget to check tfrs. i also notified our campus police (the entity that approves flights on our campus) and let them know that for the rest of that week the tfr was in place and flights should be avoided in the area we were in plus several of the university areas that are more administrative/facilities related. this will be a discussion topic for our next drone committee meeting on campus, as we may want to use our uas/uav listserv to remind folks about active tfr's in the area of the university.
